raw_source.text:
Consider the following two statements related to reinforced concrete design, and identify whether they are TRUE of FALSE:

I. Curtailment of bars in the flexural tension zone in beams reduces the shear strength at the cut-off locations.
II. When a rectangular column section is subject to biaxially eccentric compression, the neutral axis will be parallel to the resultant axis of bending.
raw_source.solution:
Statement I: Curtailment of bars in the flexural tension zone in beams reduces the shear strength at the cut-off locations.
This statement is TRUE because cutting tensile reinforcement decreases dowel action and reduces shear resistance at that location.

Statement II: When a rectangular column is subjected to biaxially eccentric compression, the neutral axis will be parallel to the resultant axis of bending.
This statement is FALSE because for biaxial bending, the neutral axis is governed by the interaction:
[latex] M_x y + M_y x = 0 [/latex]
The slope of the neutral axis is:
[latex]\text{slope of N.A.} = -\frac{M_y}{M_x} [/latex]
Whereas the resultant bending axis has slope:
[latex]\text{slope of resultant moment axis} =\frac{M_y}{M_x} [/latex]
Thus, they are not parallel.
raw_source.tag2: Shear, Torsion, Bond, Anchorage and Development Length
options: Both statements I and II are TRUE
Statement I is TRUE, and statement II is FALSE
Statement I is FALSE, and statement II is TRUE
Both Statements I and II are FALSE

raw_answer.option_text: Statement I is TRUE, and statement II is FALSE

raw_source.text: A trapezoidal channel with bottom width of 3 m and side slope of IV:1.5H carries a discharge of 8.0 [latex]m^3/sec[/latex] with the flow depth of 1.5 m. The Froude number of the flow is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q&=8 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} \\ A&=\frac{1}{2}(3+7.5) \times 1.5=7.875 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ V&=\frac{Q}{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{8}{7.875}=1.015 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\\ \text{Now}\quad \frac{1}{1.5}&=\frac{1.5}{x} \\ x&=2.25\\ T&=3+2 \times 2.25=7.5 \mathrm{m} \\ D&=\frac{A}{T}=\frac{7.875}{7.5}=1.05 \\ F&=\frac{V}{\sqrt{\mathrm{g} \mathrm{D}}}=\frac{1.05}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 1.05}}=0.316 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence no any option is correct.

[latex]\tau =K(\mu u_{m})\delta[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given, } \frac{u}{u_{m}}=1.5 \eta ; \; \; &\;\eta=\frac{y}{\delta} \\ \therefore \quad u &=1.5 u_{m} \times \frac{y}{\delta} \\ \frac{d u}{d y} &=1.5 \frac{u_{m}}{\delta} \\ \text { Now, }\quad \tau&=\mu \frac{d u}{d y}=1.5 \mu \frac{u_{m}}{\delta} \\ \therefore \quad k &=1.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} k &=C_{v} m_{v} \gamma_{w} \\ T_{v} &=\frac{C_{v} t}{h^{2}} \\ \therefore \quad \text { and } \quad t_{1} &=\frac{h_{1}^{2} T_{v}}{k_{1}} m_{v} \gamma_{w} \\ \therefore \quad & t_{2}=\frac{h_{2}^{2} T_{v}}{k_{2}} m_{v} \gamma_{w} \\ & \frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\left(\frac{h_{1}}{h_{2}}\right)^{2} \times \frac{T_{v}}{T_{v}} \times \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} \times \frac{m_{v 1}}{m_{v 2}}\\ \frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}} &=\left(\frac{h_{2}}{h_{1}}\right)^{2} \times \frac{k_{1}}{k_{2}} \times \frac{m_{v 2}}{m_{v 1}} \\ &=\frac{1}{4} \times 1 \times \frac{1}{10} \times 4=\frac{1}{10} \\ t_{2} &=\frac{t_{1}}{10}=\frac{10}{10}=1 \text { year } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Given Matrix [latex][A]=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 1 &3 \\ 6&3 &4 & 7\\ 2 &1 & 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], the rank of the matrix is

Consider first [latex]3\times 3[/latex] minors, since maximum possible rank is 3
[latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 2 &1 \\ 6 & 3 & 4\\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 &3 \\ 3 & 4& 7\\ 1 & 0& 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 1 & 3\\ 6 & 4 & 7\\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0\\ \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 2 &3 \\ 6 & 3 & 7\\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since all [latex]3\times 3[/latex] minors are zero, now try [latex]2\times 2[/latex] minors.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 4 &2 \\ 6 & 3 \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}&=8-3=5\neq 0 \\ \therefore\;\; \text{rank }&=2 \end{aligned} [/latex]

If P, Q and R are three points having coordinates (3,-2,-1), (1,3,4), (2,1,-2)
in XYZ space, then the distance from point P to plane OQR (O being the origin
of the coordinate system) is given by
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex] \begin{aligned} P\left ( 3,-2,-1 \right ) &\\ Q\left ( 1,3,4 \right ) &\\ R\left ( 2,1,-2 \right ) &\\ O\left ( 0,0,0 \right )&\\ \text{Equation of plane OQR is,}&\\ \begin{vmatrix} x-x_{1} & y-y_{1} & z-z_{1}\\ x_{2}-x_{1} & y_{2}-y_{1} & z_{2}-z_{1}\\ x_{3}-x_{1} & y_{3}-y_{1} & z_{3}-z_{1} \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} x-0 & y-0 & z-0\\ 1 & 3 & 4\\ 2 & 1 & -2 \end{vmatrix}&=0\\ \text{i.e., }2x-2y+z&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now [latex]\perp[/latex] distance of [latex]\left ( x_{1},\: y_{1},\: z_{1} \right )[/latex] from [latex]ax + by + cz + d=0[/latex] is given by,
[latex]\left | \frac{ax_{1}+by_{1}+cz_{1}+d}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}} \right |[/latex]
Therefore, [latex]\perp[/latex] distance of (3, -2, 1) from plane [latex]2x-2y+z=0[/latex] is given by,
[latex]\left | \frac{2\times 3-2\times \left ( -2 \right )+\left ( -1 \right )}{\sqrt{2^{2}+\left ( -2 \right )^{2}+1^{2}}} \right |=3[/latex]

raw_source.text: If L defines the Laplace Transform of a function, [latex]L\left [ \sin \left ( at \right ) \right ][/latex] will equal to

raw_source.text:
The Fourier series expansion of a symmetric and even function, f(x) where [latex]\begin{matrix} f(x) &=1+(2x/\pi), & \; -\pi \lt x \lt 0 \\ &=1-(2x/\pi), & \; 0 \lt x \lt \pi \end{matrix}[/latex]
will be
raw_source.solution:
Since given function is symmetric and even, its Fourier series contain only cosine terms.
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{0}&=\frac{2}{c}\int_{0}^{c}f\left ( x \right )dx\\ \text{and } a_{n}&=\frac{2}{c}\int_{0}^{c}f\left ( x \right )\cos \frac{n\pi x}{c}dx\\ &\text{Using above result and using,}\\ f\left ( x \right )&=1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \text{ we get}\\ a_{0}&=\frac{2}{\pi }\int_{0}^{\pi }\left ( 1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \right )dx \\ &=\frac{2}{\pi }\left ( x-\frac{x^{2}}{\pi } \right )_{0}^{\pi }=0 \\ \text{and } a_{n}&=\frac{2}{\pi }\int_{0}^{\pi }\left ( 1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \right )\cos nx\: dx \\ &=\frac{2}{\pi }\left [ \left ( 1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \right )\frac{\sin nx}{n}-\left ( -\frac{2}{\pi } \right )\left ( -\frac{\cos nx}{n^{2}} \right ) \right ]_{0}^{\pi } \\ &=\frac{2}{\pi }\left [ -\frac{2\cos n\pi }{\pi n^{2}}+\frac{2}{\pi n^{2}} \right ] \\ &=\frac{4}{n^{2}\pi ^{2}}\left [ 1-\cos n\pi \right ]\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A box contains 10 screws, 3 of which are defective. Two screws are drawn at
random with replacement. The probability that none of the two screws is defective
will be
raw_source.solution:
Total number of screws = 10
Number of defective screws = 3
Number of non-defective screws = [latex]10 - 3 = 7[/latex]

Probability of selecting a non-defective screw in one draw:
[latex]P(\text{non-defective}) = \frac{7}{10}[/latex]

Since the screws are drawn with replacement, the two events are independent. So, the probability that both screws drawn are non-defective is:
[latex] P(\text{both non-defective}) = \left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^2 = \frac{49}{100} = 0.49 [/latex]

Hence, the required probability is 49%.

raw_source.solution:

[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \theta&=\frac{M L}{2 E I} \\ \Rightarrow \quad M&=\frac{2 E I}{L} \theta &[\because \theta=1]\\ \Rightarrow \quad M&=\frac{2 E I}{L}=K \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A granular soil possesses saturated density of 20 [latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex]. Its effective angle of internal friction is 35 degrees. If the desired factor of safety is 1.5, the safe angle of slope for this soil, when seepage occurs at and parallel to the slope surface, will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given }\phi^{\prime}&=35^{\circ}: \gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}=20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ F&=1.5 ; \beta=? ; \gamma=\gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}-\gamma_{\mathrm{w}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Factor of safety
[latex] \begin{aligned} F&=\frac{\gamma^{\prime} \tan \phi^{\prime}}{\gamma_{\text {sat }} \tan \beta} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.5&=\frac{\left(\gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}-\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}\right) \tan 35^{\circ}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{sat}} \tan \beta} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \tan \beta&=\frac{(20-10) \tan 35^{\circ}}{1.5 \times 20} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \beta&=13.14^{\circ} \simeq 13^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For a two-dimensional irrotational flow, the velocity potential defined as [latex]\phi =ln(x^{2}+y^{2})[/latex] . Which of the following is a possible stream function, [latex]\psi[/latex] for this flow ?
raw_source.solution:
We know that
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} &=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial y} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \log _{e}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}&=\frac{2 x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Integrating both sides, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \psi&=\int \frac{2 x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} d y+C\\ \Rightarrow \quad \Psi&=2 x\times \frac{1}{x} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+C \\ \Rightarrow \quad \Psi&=2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+C \end{aligned}[/latex]
However, it may be noted that 'C' is a function of x

raw_source.text:
The vertical hydraulic conductivity of the top soil at certain stage is 0.2 cm/hr. A storm of intensity 0.5 cm/hr occurs over the soil for an indefinite period.
Assuming the surfaces drainage to be adequate, the infiltration rate after the
storm has lasted for a very long time, shall be
raw_source.solution:
Permeability = Hydraulic conductivity [latex]\left ( \frac{\mu }{\rho g} \right )[/latex]
A storm of i=0.5 cm/hr occurs over the soil for an indefinite period.
What is the meaning of "indefinite period"?
In order to achieve steady state condition, continuous application of water is necessary so that the water level is maintained constant.
'Surface drainage adequate' means at steady state condition some water flows as surface runoff.
'Storm has lasted for a very long time' means the hydraulic conductivity approaches saturated hydraulic conductivity (so that Darcy's law can be obeyed) and at steady state condition infiltration rate is also constant.
The constant infiltration rate which is achieved after very long time, shall be more than 0.2 cm/hr (as hydraulic conductivity has increased) but should be less than storm intensity 0.5 cm/hr due to adequate drainage.

raw_source.text:
The Fourier series expansion of a symmetric and even function, f(x) where [latex]\begin{matrix} f(x) &=1+(2x/\pi), & \; -\pi \lt x \lt 0 \\ &=1-(2x/\pi), & \; 0 \lt x \lt \pi \end{matrix}[/latex]
will be
raw_source.solution:
Since given function is symmetric and even, its Fourier series contain only cosine terms.
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{0}&=\frac{2}{c}\int_{0}^{c}f\left ( x \right )dx\\ \text{and } a_{n}&=\frac{2}{c}\int_{0}^{c}f\left ( x \right )\cos \frac{n\pi x}{c}dx\\ &\text{Using above result and using,}\\ f\left ( x \right )&=1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \text{ we get}\\ a_{0}&=\frac{2}{\pi }\int_{0}^{\pi }\left ( 1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \right )dx \\ &=\frac{2}{\pi }\left ( x-\frac{x^{2}}{\pi } \right )_{0}^{\pi }=0 \\ \text{and } a_{n}&=\frac{2}{\pi }\int_{0}^{\pi }\left ( 1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \right )\cos nx\: dx \\ &=\frac{2}{\pi }\left [ \left ( 1-\frac{2x}{\pi } \right )\frac{\sin nx}{n}-\left ( -\frac{2}{\pi } \right )\left ( -\frac{\cos nx}{n^{2}} \right ) \right ]_{0}^{\pi } \\ &=\frac{2}{\pi }\left [ -\frac{2\cos n\pi }{\pi n^{2}}+\frac{2}{\pi n^{2}} \right ] \\ &=\frac{4}{n^{2}\pi ^{2}}\left [ 1-\cos n\pi \right ]\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A long structural column (length= L) with both ends hinged is acted upon by an axial compressive load, P. The differential equation governing the bending of column is given by :
[latex]EI\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-Py[/latex]
Where y is the structural lateral deflection and EI is the flexural rigidity. The first critical load on column responsible for its buckling is given by
raw_source.solution:
Differential equation governing the bending of column
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{E I d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}&=-P y\\ \Rightarrow \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+\frac{P}{E I} y&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solution of differential equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} y&=A\cos\left(x \sqrt{\frac{P}{E I}}\right)+B \sin \left(x \sqrt{\frac{P}{E I}}\right)\\ \text{when }x=0 . y&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0&=B \sin \left(L \sqrt{\frac{P}{E I}}\right) \\ \therefore \quad L \sqrt{\frac{P}{E I}}&=x\text{ (First value)}\\ \Rightarrow P&=\frac{\pi^{2} E I}{L^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Theory of Columns and Shear Centre

raw_source.text: In a redundant joint model, three bar members are pin connected at Q as shown in the figure. [latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \tan \theta_{1}&=\frac{M N}{N Q}=\frac{400}{500}=0.8 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta_{1}&=0.625 \\ \text{ and }\cos \theta_{1}&=0.781 \\ \text{and }\tan \theta_{2}&=\frac{N O}{N Q}=\frac{500}{500}=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta_{2}&=0.707 \\ \text{ and }\cos \theta_{2}&=0.707 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Elongation of member MQ in terms of u and v will be,

Solving (i) and (ii) we get,
[latex] u=6.64 \mathrm{mm}\text{ and }v=56.14 \mathrm{mm}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A simply supported beam of uniform rectangular cross-section of width b and depth h is subjected to linear temperature gradient 0[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] at the top and T[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] at the bottom, as shown in the figure. The coefficient of linear expansion of the beam material is [latex]\alpha[/latex]. The resulting vertical deflection at the mid-span of the beam is
raw_source.solution:
The average change in temperature [latex]=\frac{T}{2} [/latex]
The compression in the top most fibre
[latex] =\alpha \times L \times \frac{T}{2}[/latex]
Similarly, the elongation in bottom most fibre
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\alpha \times L \times \frac{T}{2}\\ \therefore\text{ Strain, }\varepsilon_{0}&=\frac{L \alpha T}{L \times 2}=\frac{\alpha T}{2} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore deflection at midpoint is downward. Now, from the equation of pure bending, we have
[latex] \frac{M}{I}=\frac{E}{R}=\frac{f}{y}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex] Curvature,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{R} &=\frac{f}{E y}=\frac{\text { Strain }}{y}\left[\because y=\frac{h}{2}\right] \\ &=\frac{2 \varepsilon_{0}}{h}=\frac{\alpha T}{h} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Also, from the property of circle, we have
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Deflection, }\delta&=\frac{L^{2}}{8 R}=\frac{L^{2}}{8} \times \frac{\alpha T}{h} \\ &=\frac{\alpha T L^{2}}{8 h} \text { downward } \end{aligned}[/latex]

Compaction of an embankment is carried out in 500 mm thick layers. The rammer used for compaction has a foot area of 0.05 [latex]m^{2}[/latex] and the energy imparted in every drop of rammer is 400 Nm. Assuming 50% more energy in each pass over the compacted area due to overlap, the number of passes required to develop compactive energy equivalent of Indian Standard light compaction for each layer would be
raw_source.solution:
As per Indian Standard light compaction test, a hammer of 2.6 kg is allowed to fall from a height of 310 mm and 3 layers are tamped 25 times in a mould of volume 1000 cc .
[latex]\therefore [/latex] Energy imparted
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =2.6 \times 25 \times 3 \times 9.81 \\ \times \frac{310}{1000}=593.01 \mathrm{N}-\mathrm{m} \end{array}[/latex]
For embankment compaction, the volume of soil covered by rammer
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=0.05 \times 10^{4} \times \frac{500}{10} \\ &=25000 \mathrm{cc} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Energy imparted in every drop of hammer
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\left(1+\frac{50}{100}\right) \times 400\\ &=600 \mathrm{N}-\mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
If 'n' number of passes are required to develop equivalent energy to Indian Standard light compaction test, then
[latex] n \times \frac{600}{25000}=\frac{593.01}{1000}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad n=24.71 \simeq 25\text{( approx.)} [/latex]
However, If the data of Standard Proctor Test are taken i.e. weight of hammer =2.495 kg; Volume of mould =944cc, then the value of 'n' will be close to 26.

raw_source.text:
A braced cut, 5 m wide and 7.5 m deep is proposed in a cohesionless soil deposit
having effective cohesion c'=0 and effective friction angle, [latex]{\phi}' =36^{\circ}[/latex]. The first row of struts is to be installed at a depth of 0.5 m below ground surface and spacing between the struts should be 1.5 m. If the horizontal spacing of struts is 3 m and unit weight of the deposit is 20 [latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex], the maximum strut load will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} K_{a} &=\frac{1-\sin \phi^{\prime}}{1+\sin \phi^{\prime}} \\ &=\frac{1-\sin 36^{\circ}}{1+\sin 36^{\circ}}=0.2596 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Uniform pressure on side of cut
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=0.65 \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}} \gamma \mathrm{H} \\ &=0.65 \times 0.2596 \times 20 \times 7.5 \\ &=25.31 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Area covered by strut
[latex] \begin{aligned} 1 &=3 \times(0.5+0.75) \\ &=3.75 \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Area covered by strut 2 and downward struts
[latex] =3 \times(0.75+0.75)=4.5 \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Maximum force will be carried by strut
2 and downward struts
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=25.31 \times 4.5=113.89 \mathrm{kN} \\ &\simeq 113.90 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the soil strata shown in figure, the water tables is lowered by drainage by 2 m and if the top 2 m thick silty sand stratum remains saturated by capillary action even after lowering of water table, the increase in effective vertical pressure in kPa at mid-height of clay layer will be
raw_source.solution:
In the capillary zone, pore pressure is negative. The total stress will not change due to lowering of water table because the stratum is still saturated. Thus, the increase in effective vertical pressure will be only due to pore pressure. Thus increase in effective stress,
[latex] =h \gamma_{w}=2 \times 10=20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]

Compressible layer thickness

Average stress at the center of layer,

Increased width of equivalent raft at depth

Pressure increase due to load on pile,

A horizontal jet strikes a frictionless vertical plate (the plan view is shown in the figure). It is then divided into two parts, as shown in the figure. If the impact loss is neglected, what is the value of [latex]\theta[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
From continuity equation, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & & Q_{0}=Q_{1}+Q_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & Q_{0}=0.25 Q_{0}+Q_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & Q_{2}=0.75 Q_{0} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since, the impact losses are neglected, the velocity will remain unchanged in the direction of [latex] Q_{1}[/latex] and [latex]Q_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \text{i.e.},\quad V_{0}=V_{1}=V_{2} [/latex]
Applying impulse momentum equation, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \rho Q_{0} V_{0} \sin \theta&=\rho Q_{2} V_{2}-\rho Q_{1} V_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{0} \sin \theta&=0.75 Q_{0}-0.25 Q_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta&=1 / 2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \theta&=30^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A hydraulic jump takes place in a triangular channel of vertex angle 90[latex]^{\circ}[/latex], as shown in figure. The discharge is 1 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] and the pre-jump depth is 0.5 m. What will be the post-jump depth ? (Take g = 981 [latex]m/s^{2}[/latex])
raw_source.solution:
Specific force will remain constant on both sides of hydraulic jump.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \frac{Q^{2}}{g A_{1}}+A_{1} \bar{Z}_{1} &=\frac{Q^{2}}{g A_{2}}+A_{2} \bar{Z}_{2} \\ A_{1} &=y_{1}^{2} ; A_{2}=y_{2}^{2} \\ \bar{Z}_{1} &=\left(\frac{y_{1}}{3}\right) ; \quad \bar{Z}_{2}=\left(\frac{y_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \text{Given}\quad Q &=1 \mathrm{m}^{3 / \mathrm{s}} ; y_{1}=0.5 \mathrm{m}\\ \therefore \frac{(1)^{2}}{9.81 \times(0.5)^{2}}&+(0.5)^{2} \times\left(\frac{0.5}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{(1)^{2}}{9.81 \times y_{2}^{2}}+\left(y_{2}\right)^{2} \times\left(\frac{y_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.4494&=\frac{0.1019}{y_{2}^{2}}+\frac{y_{2}^{3}}{3} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
By hit and trial, we get [latex]y_{2}=1.02 \mathrm{m}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two pipelines, one carrying oil (mass density 900 kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]) and the other water, are connected to a manometer as shown in figure. By what amount the pressure in the water pipe should be increased so that the mercury levels in both the limbs of the manometer become equal ? (mass density of mercury= 13550 kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex] and g = 9.81 m/[latex]s^{2}[/latex])
raw_source.solution:
Initially the pressure difference between water and oil can be given as


[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{w}+(1000 &\times 9.81 \times 1.5)+(13550 \times 9.81 \times 20 \\ \left.\times 10^{-2}\right)-(900 &\times 9.81 \times 3)=p_{0}\\ \Rightarrow \; p_{w t}+14715+26585.1-26487=p_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad p_{0}-p_{w}&=14813.1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad P_{0}-P_{w}&=14.8 \mathrm{kPa} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
To make the same level of mercury in both the limbs, the level of mercury should be decreased by 10 cm in right limb and increased by 10cm in lett limb
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{w t}+(1000 \times 9.81 &\times 1.6)-(900 \times 9.81 \times 2.9)=p_{0}\\ \Rightarrow \quad P_{0}-p_{w t}&=-9.9 \mathrm{kPa} &\ldots(ii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Subtracting (ii) from (i) we get
[latex] \begin{array}{l} P_{W}-P_{N}=14.8+99 \\ P_{\mathrm{w} t}-P_{\mathrm{w}}=24.7 \mathrm{kPa} \text { (increase) } \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A solid sphere (diameter 6 mm) is rising through oil (mass density 900 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex], dynamic viscosity 0.7 kg/ms) at a constant velocity of 1 cm/s. What is the specific weight of the material form which the sphere is made ? (Take g = 9.81 [latex]m/s^{2}[/latex])
raw_source.solution:
The solid sphere will be acted upon by three forces viz. drag force [latex]\left(\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}\right)[/latex], force of buoyancy [latex]\left(\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}\right)[/latex] and self weight of sphere (W)


[latex] \begin{array}{l} W=\rho_{s} V g \\ F_{B}=\rho_{0} V g \\ F_{D}=C_{D} A \frac{\rho_{0} V^{2}}{2} \end{array}[/latex]
Reynolds Number,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Re} &=\frac{\rho_{0} \mathrm{VD}}{\mu} \\ &=\frac{900 \times 1 \times 10^{-2} \times 6 \times 10^{-3}}{0.7} \\ &=0.07714 \lt 0.2(\mathrm{ok}) \\\; \therefore \quad \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{D}} &=\frac{24}{\mathrm{Re}}=\frac{24}{0.07714}=311.12 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, from the free body diagram, we have [latex]W+F_{D}=F_{B} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \quad W&=F_{B}-F_{D} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \rho_{s} V g&=\rho_{0} V g-C_{D} A \frac{\rho_{0} V^{2}}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad w_{\mathrm{s}} V&=\rho_{0} V g-C_{D} \frac{A \rho_{0} V^{2}}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad w_{\mathrm{s}}&=\rho_{0} g-\frac{C_{\mathrm{D}} A \rho_{0} v^{2}}{2 V} \\ \Rightarrow \quad w_{\mathrm{s}}&=900 \times 9.81 \\ & -\frac{\left[\begin{array}{l}6 \times 311.12 \times \pi \times\left(6 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2} \\ \times 900 \times\left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2}\end{array}\right]}{4 \times \pi \times\left(6 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{3}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad w_{\mathrm{s}}&=5328.9 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{3}=5.3 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
While designing a hydraulic structure, the piezometric head at bottom of the
floor is computed as 10 m. The datum is 3m below floor bottom. The assured
standing water depth above the floor is 2 m. The specific gravity of the floor 
material is 2.5. The floor thickness should be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]G=2.5[/latex]
Pressure head [latex]=10-3=7 \mathrm{m} [/latex]
At critical condition,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Uplift }&=\text { Downward pressure } \\ 7 \times \gamma_{w}&=\left(\gamma_{w} \times 2\right)+\left(\gamma_{\text {floor }} \times t\right) \\ \frac{5 \gamma_{w}}{\gamma_{\text {floor }}}&=t=\frac{5}{G}=\frac{5}{2.5}\\ \therefore \quad t&=2 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The plan area of a reservoir is 1 [latex]km^{2}[/latex]. The water level in the reservoir is observed to decline by 20 cm in certain period. During this period the reservoir receives a surface inflow of 10 hectare-meters, and 20 hectare-meters are abstracted
from the reservoir for irrigation and power. The plan evaporation and rainflow
recorded during the same period at a nearby meteorological station are 12 cm
and 3 cm respectively. The calibrated pan factor is 0.7. The seepage loss from the
reservoir during the this period in hectare-meters is
raw_source.solution:
Inflow to reservoir,
I= 10 ha-m
Outflow from reservoir,
Q=20 ha-m
Evaporation loss,
[latex]E=1\times 10^{6}\times \frac{12}{100}\times 0.7 =8.4 ha-m[/latex]
Rainfall, [latex]P=1\times 10^{6}\times \frac{3}{100} =3 ha-m[/latex]
Change in storage,
[latex]\Delta S=1\times 10^{6}\times \frac{20}{100} =-20 ha-m[/latex]
We know that,
[latex](I+P)-(E+Q+\text{Seepage})=\Delta S [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \; (10+3)-(8.4+20+\text{Seepage})=-20 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; 13-28.4-\text{Seepage} = -20 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \text{Seepage} =4.6 ha-m[/latex]

Results of a water sample analysis are as follows :

(milliequivalent weight of [latex]CaCO_3[/latex]=50 mg/meq).
Hardness of the water sample in mg/L as [latex]CaCO_3[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text{Total hardness} =\left [ Mg^{2+} \right ]\times \frac{\text{eq. wt. of}\; \; CaCO_{3}}{\text{eq. wt. of}\; \; Mg^{+}}+\left [ Ca^{2+} \right ]\times \frac{\text{eq. wt. of}\; \; CaCO_{3}}{\text{eq. wt. of}\; \; Ca^{+}} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\left ( 10\times \frac{50}{12.2} \right )+\left ( 55\times \frac{55}{20} \right ) \\ &= 178.48\simeq 179\; mg/l \end{aligned}[/latex]
In addition to [latex]Ca^{2+}[/latex] and [latex]Mg^{2+}[/latex], other divalent metallic icons like [latex]Fe^{2+}[/latex], [latex]Mn^{2+}[/latex], [latex]Sr^{2+}[/latex], etc may also cause hardness but their presence is negligible in most of the waters. [latex]Na^{2+}[/latex] and [latex]K^{+}[/latex] do not contribute in hardness.

raw_source.text: An ideal horizontal flow settling basing is 3 m deep having surface area 900 [latex]m^{2}[/latex]. Water flows at the rate of 8000 [latex]m^{3}/d[/latex], at water temperature 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C (m=[latex]10^{-3}[/latex] kg/m.s and [latex]\rho =1000 kg/m^3[/latex]). Assuming Stoke's law to be valid, the proportion (percentage) of spherical sand particles (0.01 mm in diameter with specific gravity 2.65), that will be removed, is
raw_source.solution:
Velocity of sand particles,
[latex]\begin{aligned} {V}'_{s} &=\frac{g}{18}\left ( S_{s}-1 \right )\frac{d^{2}}{\nu } \\ &=\frac{9.81}{18}\times \left ( 2.65-1 \right )\times \frac{\left ( 0.001\times 10^{-3} \right )^{2}}{\left ( 10^{-3}/1000 \right )} \\ &=\frac{9.81}{18}\times 1.65\times 10^{-4} \\ {V}'_{s} &=8.9925\times 10^{-5}\; \text{m/sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\text{settling time}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{Volume of tank}}{\text{Water flow rate}} \\ &=\frac{900\times 3}{8000}days=\frac{2700}{8000}\times 24=8.1\; hrs \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Settling velocity,}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{s} &=\frac{\text{Depth of tank}}{\text{Settling time}}=\frac{3}{8.1\times 3600} \\ &=1.0288\times 10^{-4}\; \text{m/s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \;\text{ Removal efficiency}=\frac{{V}'_{s}}{V_{s}}\times 100[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{8.9925\times 10^{-5}}{1.0288\times 10^{-4}}\times 100 \\ &=8.41\%\simeq 87.5\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

The design speed for a National Highway is 100 kmph. If the maximum permissible
superelevation is 0.10 and the coefficient of lateral friction is 0.15, the ruling
minimum radius of horizontal curve on the highway should be
raw_source.solution:
The ruling minimum radius of horizontal curve is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{\min } &=\frac{V^{2}}{127(\theta+f)} \\ &=\frac{(100)^{2}}{127(0.10+0.15)} \\ &=314.96 \mathrm{m} \simeq 315 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

speed of 50 kmph, with an average headway of 2.52 seconds . The longitudinal
distance between the two consecutive vehicles is
raw_source.solution:
The longitudinal distance [latex] =0.278 \mathrm{Vt} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=0.278 \times 50 \times 2.52 \\ &=35.03 \mathrm{m} \approx 35 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the Marshall method of mix design, the coarse aggregates, fine aggregates,
filler and bitumen, having respective specific gravities of 2.62, 2.72, 2.70 and 1.02 are
mixed in the ratio of 55, 34.6, 4.8 and 5.6 percent, respectively. The theoretical
specific gravity of the mix would be
raw_source.solution:
The theoretical specific gravity of the mix is given by,
[latex] G_{t}=\frac{100}{\frac{55}{2.62}+\frac{34.6}{2.72}+\frac{4.8}{2.70}+\frac{5.6}{1.02}}=2.44[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The plate load test conducted with a 75 cm diameter plat on soil subgrade yielded
a deflection of 2.5 mm under a stress of 800 [latex]N/cm^{2}[/latex]. The modulus of elasticity of the subgrade soil, in [latex]kN/cm^{2}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
The modulus of elasticity of the subgrade soil is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} E &=\frac{1.18 \mathrm{pa}}{\Delta} \\ &=\frac{1.18 \times 800 \times 75 \times 10}{2.5 \times 2} \\ &=141600 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}=141.6 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Group-I below gives a list of physical properties of aggregates which should be determined to judge their suitability in road construction. Group-II gives a list of laboratory tests which are conducted to determine these properties. Match Group-I with Group-II.

A beam PQRS is 18 m long and is simply supported at points Q and R, 10 m apart. Overhangs PQ and RS are 3 m and 5 m respectively. A train of two point loads of 150 kN and 100kN, 5 m apart, crosses this beam from left to right with 100 kN load leading.

The maximum sagging moment under the 150 kN load anywhere is
raw_source.solution:
Maximum sagging bending moment under 150 kN load occurs when 150 kN load and resultant of 150 kN and 100 kN are located equidistant from the centre of span. In other words, when the centre of beam lies midway between the resultant and the load under consideration, maximum sagging moment occurs under the load under consideration



[latex]\begin{aligned} (150+100)\bar{x} &=150 \times 0 +100 \times 5 \\ \bar{x}&=2m \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{ab}{L} &= \frac{4 \times 6}{10}= 2.4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Ordinate under 100 kN load [latex]= \frac{2.4}{6}\times 1= 0.4[/latex]
Therefore, sagging BM under 150 kN load
[latex]= 2.4 \times 150+ 0.4 \times 100=400 kN-m[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A reinforced concrete beam, size 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep overall is simply supported over a span of 3 m. It is subjected to two point loads P of equal magnitude placed at middle third points. The two loads are gradually increased simultaneously. Beam is reinforced with 2 HYSD bars of 16 mm diameter placed at an effective cover of 40 mm on bottom face and nominal shear reinforcement. The characteristic compressive strength and the bending tensile strength of the concrete are 20.0 N/[latex]mm^2[/latex] and 2.2 N/[latex]mm^2[/latex] respectively.

Ignoring the presence of tension reinforcement, the value of load P in kN when the first flexure crack will develop in the beam is
raw_source.solution:
Bending tensile strength, [latex]\sigma_{b t}=2.2 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} [/latex]
Characteristic compressive strength,
[latex] f_{c k}=20 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Maximum stress in concrete,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{c b c} &=0.45 f_{c k}=0.45 \times 20 \\ &=9 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]


Section modulus,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z &=\frac{b D^{2}}{6}=\frac{200 \times(300)^{2}}{6} \\ &=3 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{mm}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Maximum moment,
[latex] \begin{aligned} M_{\operatorname{rrax}} &=Z \sigma_{b t}=3 \times 10^{6} \times 2.2 \\ &=6.6 \times 10^{6}=6.6 \mathrm{kN}-\mathrm{m} \\ M_{\max } &=\frac{P L}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{P \times 3}{3} &=6.6 \\ \Rightarrow \quad P &=6.6 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A reinforced concrete beam, size 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep overall is simply supported over a span of 3 m. It is subjected to two point loads P of equal magnitude placed at middle third points. The two loads are gradually increased simultaneously. Beam is reinforced with 2 HYSD bars of 16 mm diameter placed at an effective cover of 40 mm on bottom face and nominal shear reinforcement. The characteristic compressive strength and the bending tensile strength of the concrete are 20.0 N/[latex]mm^2[/latex] and 2.2 N/[latex]mm^2[/latex] respectively.

The theoretical failure load of the beam for attainment of limit state of collapse in flexure is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A_{s t}=2 \times \frac{\pi}{4} \times(16)^{2}=402.12 \mathrm{mm}^{2} [/latex]
For limit state of collapse,
[latex] \begin{aligned} x_{u} &=\frac{0.87 f_{y} A_{s}}{0.36 f_{c k} b} \\ &=\frac{0.87 \times 415 \times 402.12}{0.36 \times 20 \times 200} \\ &=100.8 \mathrm{mm} \\ \text { But } x_{u, \lim} &=0.48 d=0.48 \times(300-40) \\ &=124.8 \mathrm{mm} \\ \text { since, } \quad x_{u} & \lt x_{u, \lim} \end{aligned}[/latex]
the section is under reinforced.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad M_{u}&=0.87 \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{y}} A_{\mathrm{st}}\left(d-0.42 x_{\mathrm{U}}\right) \\ &= 0.87 \times 415 \times 402.12 \\ & \times(260-0.42 \times 100.8) \\ &= 31.6 \mathrm{kN}-\mathrm{m}\\ \text{But } \quad M_{u}&=\frac{P L}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{P \times 3}{3}&=31.6 \\ \Rightarrow \quad P&=31.6 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A truss tie consisting of 2 ISA 75x75x8 mm carries a pull of 150 kN. At ends the two angels are connected, one each on either side of a 10 mm thick gusset plate, by 18 mm diameter rivets arranged in one row. The allowable stresses in rivet are [latex]f_s=90.0N/mm^2[/latex] and [latex]f_{br}=250N/mm^2[/latex]

Maximum tensile stress in the tie in N/[latex]mm^{2}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
(i) Assuming both thr angles as tack riveted, Gross area,
[latex] A_{g}=\left ( 75-4 \right )\times 8\times 2=1136 mm^{2}[/latex]
For angles, connected on both sides of gussets plate, Effective area,
[latex]\begin{aligned} A_{e}&=A_{1}+kA_{2} \\ A_{1}&= \text{ Net area of connected leg} \\ &=\frac{1136}{2}-\left ( 18+1.5 \right )\times 8 \\ &=412 mm^{2} \\ A_{2}&=\text{ Area of outstanding leg} \\ &=\frac{1136}{2}=568 mm^{2} \\ k&=1.0 \\ A_{e}&=412+\left ( 1.0\times 568 \right ) \\ &=980 mm^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore\;\; [/latex] Total area for both angles [latex]=2\times 980=1960\, mm^{2}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Maximum tensile stress [latex]=\frac{150\times 10^{2}}{1960}=76.5 N/mm^{2}[/latex]
(ii) Also assuming both the angle sections are not tack riveted,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\; k_{1}&=\frac{3A_{1}}{3A_{1}+A_{2}} \\ &=\frac{3\times 412}{3\times 412+568} \\ &=0.685 \\ \therefore \;\; A_{e}&=\left ( A_{1}+k_{1}A_{2} \right )\times 2 \\ &=\left ( 412+0.685\times 568 \right )\times 2 \\ &=1602.2 mm^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Maximum tensile stress [latex] =\frac{150\times 10^{3}}{1602.3}=93.6 N/mm^{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A truss tie consisting of 2 ISA 75x75x8 mm carries a pull of 150 kN. At ends the two angels are connected, one each on either side of a 10 mm thick gusset plate, by 18 mm diameter rivets arranged in one row. The allowable stresses in rivet are [latex]f_s=90.0N/mm^2[/latex] and [latex]f_{br}=250N/mm^2[/latex]

Minimum number of rivets required at each end is
raw_source.solution:
Strength of rivets in shearing,
[latex]=\frac{2\times \pi \left ( 18+1.5 \right )^{2}\times 90}{4}=53.76 kN[/latex]
Strength of rivets in bearing,
[latex]=\left ( 18+1.5 \right )\times 10\times 250 =48.75 kN [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Rivet value [latex]=48.75 kN[/latex]
Number of rivets [latex]=\frac{150}{48.75}=3.08 \approx 4[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A canal having side slopes 1:1 is proposed to be constructed in a cohesive soil to a depth of 10 m below the ground surface. The soil properties are: [latex]\phi _u=15^{\circ}[/latex], [latex]C_n[/latex]=12kPa, e=1.0, [latex]G_{s}[/latex]=2.65.

If Taylor's Stability Number, [latex]S_{n}[/latex] is 0.08 and if the canal flows full, the factor of safety with respect to cohesion against failure of the canal bank slopes will be
raw_source.solution:
When the canal flows full, the canal bank slopes will be submerged under water.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \gamma &=\left(\frac{G_{s}-1}{1+e}\right) \gamma_{w}=\left(\frac{2.65-1}{1+1}\right) \times 9.81 \\ &=8.09 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taylor's stability number,
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{n} &=\frac{C_{u}}{F_{0} \gamma_{\text {sub }} H} \\ \Rightarrow \quad F_{c} &=\frac{c_{u}}{S_{n} \times \gamma_{\text {sub }} \times H}=\frac{12}{0.08 \times 8.09 \times 10} \\ &=1.85 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A canal having side slopes 1:1 is proposed to be constructed in a cohesive soil to a depth of 10 m below the ground surface. The soil properties are: [latex]\phi _u=15^{\circ}[/latex], [latex]C_n[/latex]=12kPa, e=1.0, [latex]G_{s}[/latex]=2.65.

If there is a sudden draw down of water in the canal and if Taylor's Stability Number for the reduced value of [latex]\phi _v[/latex] is 0.126, the factor of safety with respect to cohesion against the failure of bank slopes will be
raw_source.solution:
Even if there is a sudden drawdown of water in the canal, the soil remains saturated for sometime. Hence, unit weight of the soil will be the saturated unit weight i.e.

Figure shows the geometry of a strip footing supporting the load bearing walls of a three storied building and the properties of clay layer.

If the pressure acting on the footing is 40 kPa, the consolidation settlement of the footing will be
raw_source.solution:
Initial effective stress at the centre of compressible clay layer,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{\sigma} &=18 \times 1+3 \times(20-9.81) \\ &=48.57 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
(Assuming load dispersion as 2V: 1H)
Width of strip at mid of clay layer i.e.,4m from ground surface,
[latex] B^{\prime}=1.2+2 \times 0.5 \times 3=4.2 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Increase in pressure at the centre of clay layer,
[latex] \bar{\sigma}_{0}=\frac{40 \times 1.2}{4.2}=11.43 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow[/latex] Settlement of footing,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta H &=\frac{C_{c} H_{0}}{1+e_{o}} \log _{10}\left(\frac{\bar{\sigma}+\bar{\sigma}_{0}}{\bar{\sigma}}\right) \\ &=\frac{0.08 \times 6000}{1+0.4} \log _{10}\left(\frac{48+11.43}{48}\right) \\ &=31.8 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A very wide rectangular channel carries a discharge of 8 [latex]m^3/s[/latex] per m width. The channel has a bed slope of 0.004 and Manning's roughness coefficient, n = 0.015. At a certain section of the channel, the flow depth is 1 m.

What Gradually Varied Flow profile exists at this section ?
raw_source.solution:
Critical depth,
[latex] y_{c}=\left(\frac{q^{2}}{g}\right)^{1 / 3}=\left(\frac{8^{2}}{9.81}\right)^{1 / 3}=1.868 m[/latex]
From Manning's equation, we have
[latex] \begin{aligned} q&=\frac{1}{n}\left(y_{n}\right)^{5 / 3} S^{1 / 2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 8&=\frac{1}{0.015} \times\left(y_{n}\right)^{5 / 3}(0.004)^{1 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{n}&=1.468 m \\ \text{Given that}\\ y&=1 m\\ \because \quad y_{c}&>y_{n}>y \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] The gradually varied profile will be [latex]S_{3}[/latex]

A pipeline (diameter 0.3 m, length 3 km) carries water form point P to point R (see figure). The piezometric heads at P and R are to be maintained at 100 m and 80 m, respectively. To increase the discharge, a second pipe is added in parallel to the existing pipe form Q to R. The length of the additional pipe is also 2 km. Assume the friction factor, f=0.04 for all pipes and ignore minor losses.

What is the increase in discharge if the additional pipe has same diameter (0.3 m) ?
raw_source.solution:
The difference between piezometric head between P and R is 100-80=20m. Now, if the minor losses are neglected, then the only loss is the head loss.
Let the initial discharge be [latex]Q_{1} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad h_{L}&=\frac{f L Q_{1}^{2}}{12 d^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 20&=\frac{0.04 \times 3000 \times 0_{1}^{2}}{12 \times(0.3)^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q_{1}&=0.0697 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{L}&=h_{PQ}+h_{QR}\\ \therefore \quad 20&=\frac{f L_{P Q} Q_{2}^{2}}{12 \times(0.3)^{5}}+\frac{f L_{0 R}\left(\frac{Q_{2}}{2}\right)^{2}}{12 \times(0.3)^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 20&=\frac{0.04 \times 1000 \times 0_{2}^{2}}{12 \times(0.3)^{5}}+\frac{0.04 \times 2000 \times 0_{2}^{2}}{4 \times 12 \times(0.3)^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow Q_{2}&=0.0986m^{3}/s \end{aligned}[/latex]
% increase in discharge
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\left(\frac{Q_{2}-Q_{1}}{Q_{1}}\right) \times 100 \\\\ =\left(\frac{0.0986-0.0697}{0.0697}\right) \times 100 \\ =41.4 \% \end{array}[/latex]

A water treatment plant treating 10 MLD of water requires 20 mg/L of filter Alum, [latex]AI_2(SO_4)_3.18H_2O[/latex]. The water has 6 mg/L of alkalinity as [latex]CaCO_3[/latex] (Al = 26.97, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1, Ca = 40 and C = 12).

Total alkalinity requirement ([latex]10^{6}[/latex] mg per day as [latex]CaCO_{3}[/latex]) matching filter Alum, shall be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\left ( i \right )\; \; \begin{matrix} Al_{2}\left ( SO_{4} \right )_{3}.\: 18H_{2}O+3Ca\left ( HCO_{3} \right )_{2}\\ 666\; gm\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \left ( 3\times 162 \right )gm \end{matrix}[/latex]
[latex]\rightarrow 3CaSO_{4}+2Al\left ( OH \right )_{3}\downarrow+6CO_{2}\uparrow+18H_{2}O[/latex]
[latex]\left ( ii \right )\begin{matrix} CaCO_{3}+H_{2}O+CO_{2}\rightarrow Ca\left ( HCO_{3} \right )_{2}\\ 100\: gm\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; 162\: gm \end{matrix}[/latex]
From (i) it is clear that 666 gm filter Alum can neutralize [latex]\left ( 3\times 162 \right )[/latex] gm of alkalinity as [latex]Ca\left ( HCO_{3} \right )_{2}[/latex].
Again from (ii) it is clear that this [latex]\left ( 3\times 162 \right )[/latex] gm of alkalinity as [latex]Ca\left ( HCO_{3} \right )_{2}[/latex] is equivalent to [latex]\left ( 3\times 100 \right )[/latex] gm of alkalinity as [latex]CaCO_{3}[/latex].
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Total alkalinity of filter alum as [latex]CaCO_{3}[/latex], for water requiring 20 mg/L of filter alum
[latex]=\frac{3\times 100}{666}\times 20\; mg/L=9\; mg/L[/latex]
Hence total alkalinity requirement
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=10\times 10^{6}\times 9\: mg/day \\ &=90\times 10^{6}\; mg/day \end{aligned}[/latex]

A water treatment plant treating 10 MLD of water requires 20 mg/L of filter Alum, [latex]AI_2(SO_4)_3.18H_2O[/latex]. The water has 6 mg/L of alkalinity as [latex]CaCO_3[/latex] (Al = 26.97, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1, Ca = 40 and C = 12).

raw_source.solution:
Natural alkalinity available in water =6 mg /L
Total alkalinity required to be added in the form
[latex] \text { of quick lime }=9-6=3 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{cccc} &\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} &\longrightarrow &\mathrm{CaO}+\mathrm{CO}_{2} \\ &100 \mathrm{gm} &\quad &56 \mathrm{gm} \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore 56 \mathrm{gm} [/latex] of CaO (quick lime) is required to produce
[latex] 100 \mathrm{gm} of \mathrm{CaCO}_{3} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Quantity of CaO required
[latex] =\frac{56}{100} \times 3 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}=1.68 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} &=10 \times 10^{6} \times 1.68 \times 365 \\ &=6132 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{mg} \text { per year } \end{aligned}[/latex]

Following statements are made with respect to these matrices.
I. Matrix product [latex]\left [ F \right ]^{T}[/latex] [latex]\left [ C \right ]^{T} [B] [C] [F] [/latex] is a scalar.
II. Matrix product [latex]\left [ D \right ]^{T} [F] [D][/latex] is always symmetric.

With reference to above statements, which of the following applies ?
raw_source.solution:
Statement 1 is true.
Consider statement 2
[latex]\left [ D \right ]^{T}\left [ F \right ]\left [ D \right ][/latex] is always symmetric.
Now since
[latex]\begin{aligned} \left [ {D}'FD \right ]{}'&= {\left [ FD \right ]}'{\left ( {D}' \right )}' \\ &={\left ( FD \right )}'D \\ &={D}'{F}'D \\ &={D}'FD \end{aligned}[/latex]
(Since F may or may not be symmetric)
[latex]\therefore \;\; {D}'FD[/latex] is not always symmetric is true.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] 1 is true and 2 is false.
options: Statement I is true but II is false
Statement I is false but II is true

raw_source.text: The summation of series [latex]S=2+\frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2}}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+....\infty[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
S is an arithmetico-geometric series and can be summed up as follows,
[latex] \begin{aligned} S&=2+\left ( \frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2})}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+...\infty \right ) \\ &=2+x\;\; (say)\\ \text{where } x&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{8}{2^{2}}+\frac{11}{2^{3}}+...\infty \;\; ...(i)\\ \text{Multiplying by }&\text{1/2, we get, } \\ \frac{1}{2}x&=\frac{5}{2^{2}}+\frac{8}{2^{3}}+\frac{11}{2^{4}}+...\infty \;\;...(ii) \\ \text{Substracting (ii) } & \text{from (i), we get, }\\ x-\frac{1}{2}x&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\left ( 8-5 \right )}{2^{2}} \\ &+\frac{\left ( 11-8 \right )}{2^{3}} +\frac{\left ( 13-11 \right )}{2^{4}}+...\infty \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\left ( \frac{3}{2^{2}}+\frac{3}{2^{3}}+\frac{3}{2^{4}}+...\infty \right ) \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\frac{3}{2^{2}}}{\left [ 1-\frac{1}{2} \right ]} \\ \frac{x}{2}&=\frac{5}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=4 \\ \therefore \;\; x&=8\\ \text{and } S&=2+x=10\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The value of the function [latex]f(x)=\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{x^{3}+x^{2}}{2x^{3}-7x^{2}}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]f\left ( x \right )=\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{x^{3}+x^{2}}{2x^{3}-7x^{2}} \right ][/latex]
Since this has [latex]\frac{0}{0}[/latex] form, limit can be found by repeated application of L'Hospitals rule.
[latex]\begin{aligned}f\left ( x \right )&=\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{3x^{2}+2x}{6x^{2}-14x} \right ] \\ &=\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{6x+2}{12x-14} \right ] \\ &=\left [ \frac{6\times 0+2}{12\times 0-14} \right ] \\ &=-\frac{1}{7} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The eigen values of the matrix [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 4 &-2 \\ -2& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 4-\lambda & -2\\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \left ( 4-\lambda \right )\times \left ( 1-\lambda \right )-\left [ \left ( -2 \right )\times \left ( -2 \right ) \right ]&=0 \\ \lambda ^{2}-5\lambda &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left ( \lambda -5 \right )&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence, [latex]\lambda =0,\, 5[/latex] are the eigen values.

raw_source.text: The function [latex]f (x) = 2x^{3}-3x^{2}- 36x + 2[/latex] has its maxima at
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}\text{Putting } {f}'\left ( x \right )&=6x^{2}-6x-36&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x^{2}-x-6&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x&=3 \text{ or} -2\\ \text{Now } {f}''\left ( x \right )&=12x-6 \\ \text{and } {f}''\left ( 3 \right )&=30 \gt 0\text{ (minima)} \\ \text{and } {f}''\left ( -2 \right )&=-30 \lt 0 \text{ (maxima)}\end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence maxima is at [latex]x=-2[/latex] only.

Biotransformation of an organic compound having concentration (x) can be
modeled using an ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+kx^{2}[/latex]=0, where k is the reaction rate constant, If x=a at t=0, the solution of the equation is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \frac{dx}{dt}=-kx^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=-kdt[/latex]
Integrating both sides, [latex]\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=-\int kdt[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} -\frac{1}{x}&=-kt+C \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{1}{x}&=kt+{C}'\\ \text{at }t&=0, x=a\\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{1}{a}&=k\times 0+{C}' \\ \Rightarrow \;\; {C}'&=\frac{1}{a} \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{1}{x}&=kt+\frac{1}{a}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The ratio of saturated unit weight to dry unit weight of soil is 1.25. If the specific gravity of solids ([latex]G_{s}[/latex]) is 2.65, the void ratio of the soil is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \gamma_{\text {Sat }} &=\left(\frac{G+e}{1+e}\right) \gamma_{w} &\dots(i)\\ \gamma_{d} &=\frac{G \gamma_{w}}{1+e} &\dots(ii)\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\gamma_{\text {sat }}}{\gamma_{d}} &=\frac{G+e}{G} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.25 &=\frac{2.65+e}{2.65} \\ e &=0.663 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 10 m thick clay layer is underlain by a sand layer of 20 m depth (see figure below). The water table is 5 m below the surface of clay layer. The soil above the water table is capillary saturated. The value of [latex]\gamma _{sat}[/latex] is 19 kN/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]. The unit weight of water is [latex]\gamma _{w}[/latex]. If now the water table rises to the surface, the effective stress at point P on the interface will
raw_source.solution:
In first case, when the water table is 5m below the surface and the clay over water table is capillary saturated, the effective stress is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{\sigma}_{1} &=\gamma_{\text {sat }} \times 5+\gamma \times 5 \\ &=\gamma_{\text {sat }} \times 5+\left(\gamma_{\text {sat }}-\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}\right) \times 5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \bar{\sigma}_{1} &=10 \gamma_{\text {sat }}-5 \gamma_{\mathrm{w}} \; \; \; \ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
In the second case, when water table rises to the surface, the effective stress is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} \bar{\sigma}_{2} &=\gamma \times 10=\left(\gamma_{\text {sat }}-\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}\right) \times 10 \\ &=10 \gamma_{\text {sat }}-10 \gamma_{\mathrm{w}} \\ &=\left(10 \gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}-5 \gamma_{\mathrm{w}}\right)-5 \gamma_{\mathrm{w}} \quad[\because \text { from (i) }) \\ \Rightarrow \bar{\sigma}_{2} &=\bar{\sigma}_{1}-5 \gamma_{\mathrm{w}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus in second case, the effective stress at the interface will decrease by [latex]5 \gamma_{\mathrm{w}}[/latex].

raw_source.text:
A wide channel is 1 m deep and has a velocity of flow, V, as 2.13 m/s. If a
disturbance is caused, an elementary wave can travel upstream with a velocity of
raw_source.solution:
[latex]F_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{V}{C_{0}}=\frac{\text { Flow speed }}{\text { Wave speed }}[/latex]
At low speed, [latex]F_{t} \lt 1;[/latex] a small disturbance travels u/s (with a velocity [latex]C_{0}-V[/latex] relative to a stationary observer) and affects the u/s conditions.
At high flow velocities, [latex]F_{r} \gt 1[/latex], a small disturbance travels d/s at a velocity of [latex]\mathrm{V}-\mathrm{C}_{0}[/latex] relative to a stationary observer. (As [latex]\mathrm{V} \gt \mathrm{C}_{0}[/latex] small disturbance can not travel u/s) and thus the u/s conditions can not be influenced by the d/s conditions and the flow is controlled by the u/s conditions. Therefore, we can say that the region which remains unaffected controls the flow.
[latex] F_{r}=\frac{2.13}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 1}}=0.68 \lt 1[/latex]
(Subcritical flow)
[latex] C_{0}=\sqrt{9.81 \times 1}=3.13 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
An elementary wave travels u/s with a velocity [latex] C_{0}-V[/latex] relative to a stationary observer
[latex] =3.13-2.13=1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]

In the context of flexible pavement design, the ratio of contact pressure to tyre
pressure is called the Rigidity Factor. This factor is less than unity when the tyre

The eigen values of the matrix [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 4 &-2 \\ -2& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 4-\lambda & -2\\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ \left ( 4-\lambda \right )\times \left ( 1-\lambda \right )-\left [ \left ( -2 \right )\times \left ( -2 \right ) \right ]&=0 \\ \lambda ^{2}-5\lambda &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left ( \lambda -5 \right )&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The function [latex]f (x) = 2x^{3}-3x^{2}- 36x + 2[/latex] has its maxima at
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}\text{Putting } {f}'\left ( x \right )&=6x^{2}-6x-36&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x^{2}-x-6&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x&=3 \text{ or} -2\\ \text{Now } {f}''\left ( x \right )&=12x-6 \\ \text{and } {f}''\left ( 3 \right )&=30 \gt 0\text{ (minima)} \\ \text{and } {f}''\left ( -2 \right )&=-30 \lt 0 \text{ (maxima)}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Biotransformation of an organic compound having concentration (x) can be
modeled using an ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+kx^{2}[/latex]=0, where k is the reaction rate constant, If x=a at t=0, the solution of the equation is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \frac{dx}{dt}=-kx^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=-kdt[/latex]
Integrating both sides, [latex]\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=-\int kdt[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} -\frac{1}{x}&=-kt+C \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{1}{x}&=kt+{C}'\\ \text{at }t&=0, x=a\\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{1}{a}&=k\times 0+{C}' \\ \Rightarrow \;\; {C}'&=\frac{1}{a} \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{1}{x}&=kt+\frac{1}{a}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the plane frame with an overhang as shown below, assuming negligible axial deformation, the degree of static indeterminacy, d, and the degree of kinematic indeterminacy, k, are
raw_source.solution:
Static indeterminacy, [latex]D=D_{s \theta}+D_{s i} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{where, }D_{s \theta}&=\text{ external static indeterminacy }\\ D_{s i} &=\text { internal static indeterminacy } \\ \text { alsp. } D_{s e} &=r_{\theta}-3 \\ &\quad \left[\because r_{\theta}=\right.\text { total external reactions }] \\ &=3+2+1-3=3 \\ \text { and } & D_{s i}=3 C \\ &\quad[\because C=\text { total number of closed loops }] \\ &=3 \times 2=6 \\ \therefore \quad D_{s} &=3+6=9 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively,
[latex] \begin{aligned} D_{s} &=3 m+r_{e}-3 \mathrm{j} \\ m &=\text { total members }=11 \\ r_{e} &=\text { total external reactions } \\ &=3+2+1=6 \\ j &=\text { total number of joints }=10 \\ \therefore \quad D_{s} &=(3 \times 11)+6-(3 \times 10)=9 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Kinematic indeterminacy, [latex] k=\left(3 j-r_{e}\right)-m^{\prime} [/latex]
where [latex]m^{\prime}=[/latex] total number of axially rigid members.
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad k=(3 \times 10-6)-11=13[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the linear elastic beam shown in the figure, the flexural rigidity, EI is 781250 kN[latex]m^{2}[/latex]. When w = 10 kN/m, the vertical reaction [latex]R_A[/latex] at A is 50 kN. The value of [latex]R_A[/latex] for w = 100 kN/m is
raw_source.solution:
The deflection at the free end for
[latex] \begin{aligned} w(10 k N / m) &=\frac{w L^{4}}{8 E I} \\ &=\frac{10 \times(5)^{4} \times 1000}{8 \times 781250} \\ &=1 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The gap between the beam and rigid platform is 6mm. Hence, no reaction will be developed when
[latex] w=10 kN / m [/latex]
Now, deflection at the free end for w( 100 kN /m ) will be
[latex]=10 \times 1 \mathrm{mm}=10 \mathrm{mm} [/latex]
But, this cannot be possible because margin of deflection is only 6 m.
Thus w=100 kN / m will induce a reaction [latex] \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{B}} \text{ at } \mathrm{B}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \frac{w L^{4}}{8 E !}-\frac{R_{B} L^{3}}{3 E I}&=\text{ Permissible deflection}\\ \Rightarrow \frac{100 \times(5)^{4}}{8 \times 781250}&-\frac{R_{6} \times(5)^{3}}{3 \times 781250}=\frac{6}{1000} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{10}{1000}-\frac{6}{1000}&=\frac{R_{8} \times 125}{3 \times 781250} \\ \Rightarrow \quad R_{8}&=75 \mathrm{kN} \\ \therefore \quad R_{\mathrm{A}}&=(100 \times 5-75) \\ &=425 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Uniform pressure,
[latex] p_{0}=\frac{P}{A}=\frac{320}{2 \times 2}=80 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
The critical section for shear is at a distance of d
=200 mm from the face of the column

raw_source.text:

eccentricity of 100 mm. The prestressing tensile force in the cable tendons is 1000
kN. Neglect the self weight of beam. The maximum normal compressive stress in
the beam at transfer is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P &=1000 \mathrm{kN} \\ Z &=\frac{b d^{2}}{6}=\frac{300 \times 600^{2}}{6} \\ &=18 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{mm}^{3} \\ e &=100 \mathrm{mm} \\ A &=300 \times 600=180000 \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Maximum compressive stress,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e}{Z} \\ &=\frac{1000 \times 10^{3}}{180000}+\frac{1000 \times 10^{3} \times 100}{18 \times 10^{6}} \\ &=11.11 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

An infinite soil slope with an inclination of [latex]35^{\circ}[/latex] is subjected to seepage parallel to its surface. The soil has [latex]c'=100 kN/m^{2} \; and \; {\phi}' =35^{\circ}[/latex]. Using the concept of mobilized cohesion and friction, at a factor of safety of 1.5 with respect of shear strength, the mobilized friction angle is
raw_source.solution:
The factor of safety with respect to shear strength is given by
[latex] F_{5}=\frac{\tau_{1}}{\tau}=\frac{c^{\prime}+\sigma_{n}^{\prime} \tan \phi^{\prime}}{\tau}[/latex]
The shear strength mobilised, thus may be written as
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tau &=\frac{C^{\prime}}{F_{s}}+\sigma_{n}^{\prime} \frac{\tan \phi^{\prime}}{F_{s}} \\ &=c_{m}+\sigma_{n}^{\prime} \tan \phi_{m}^{\prime}\\ \therefore \tan \phi_{m}^{\prime}&=\frac{\tan \phi^{\prime}}{F_{s}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \phi_{m}^{\prime}&=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\tan 35^{\circ}}{1.5}\right)=21.05^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 6 m thick clay layer undergoes 90% consolidation four times faster under two-way
drainage as compared to one-way drainage. In an identical clay layer of 15
m thickness, two-way drainage will be faster as compared to one-way drainage by
raw_source.solution:
The time required for any degree of consolidation, can be obtained from the Taylor's formula
[latex] T_{v}=\frac{C_{v} t}{d^{2}}[/latex]
Now, [latex]C_{v}[/latex] is constant for same type of soils, [latex]T_{v}[/latex] will also remain constant for same degree of consolidation. Thus, t \propto d^{2} where d is length of drainage path.
Hence, in the clay layer of 15m thickness, two way drainage will be four times faster in comparison to one way drainage.

[latex] =\frac{4 \times 120}{20}=24 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Actual height of cut =4m

raw_source.text:
An unsupported excavation is made to the maximum possible depth in a clay
soil having [latex]\gamma _{t}=18 kN/m^{3}[/latex], [latex]c=100 kN/m^{2}[/latex], [latex]\phi =30^{\circ}[/latex]. The active earth pressure, according to Rankine's theory, at the base level of the excavation is
raw_source.solution:
The excavation is unsupported which means the maximum possible depth upto which the clay soil can be excavated is [latex]2Z_{\mathrm{c}}[/latex]. The active earth pressure at this depth is
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{A} &=2 c \sqrt{K_{A}} \quad\left[\because K_{A}=\frac{1-\sin \phi}{1+\sin \phi}\right] \\ &=2 \times 100 \times \sqrt{\frac{1-\sin 30^{\circ}}{1+\sin 30^{\circ}}} \\ &=115.47 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively:
[latex] Z_{c}=\frac{2 c}{\gamma \sqrt{K_{A}}} \Rightarrow 2 Z_{c}=\frac{4 c}{\gamma \sqrt{K_{A}}}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex]Active pressure at a depth, [latex]2Z_{c}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\gamma_{1} \times 2 Z_{c} \times K_{A}-2 c \sqrt{K_{A}} \\ =18 \times \frac{4 \times 100 \times \sqrt{3}}{18} \times \frac{1}{3} \\ \quad-2 \times 100 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ =230.94-115.47=115.47 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A retaining wall of height 8 m retains dry sand. In the initial state, the soil is
loose and has a void ratio of 0.5, [latex]\gamma _{d}=17.8 kN/m^{3} \; and \; \phi =30^{\circ}[/latex]. Subsequently, the backfill is compacted to a state where void ratio is 0.4, [latex]\gamma _{d}=18.8 kN/m^{3} \; and \; \phi =35^{\circ}[/latex]. The ratio of initial passive thrust to the final passive thrust, according
to Rankine's earth pressure theory, is
raw_source.solution:
Passive earth pressure for loose sand is
[latex] \begin{aligned} K_{p} &=\frac{1+\sin \phi}{1-\sin \phi}=\frac{1+\sin 30^{\circ}}{1-\sin 30^{\circ}}=3 \\ \text { Now } P_{P_{1}} &=\frac{1}{2} K_{P} \gamma H^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 17.8 \times 8^{2} \\ &=1708.8 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Passive earth pressure for compacted sand is
[latex] \begin{aligned} K_{P}&=\frac{1+\sin \phi}{1-\sin \phi}=\frac{1+\sin 35^{\circ}}{1-\sin 35^{\circ}}=3.69\\ \text { Now } P_{B} &=\frac{1}{2} K_{p} \gamma H^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} \times 3.69 \times 18.8 \times 8^{2} \\ &=2219.90 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Ratio of [latex]P_{P_{1}}[/latex] and [latex]P_{P_{2}}=\frac{1708.8}{2219.90}=0.77[/latex]

raw_source.text: A velocity field is given as [latex]\vec{V}=2y\vec{i}+3x\vec{j}[/latex], where x and y are in metres. The acceleration of a fluid particle at (x,y)=(1,1) in the x direction is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given } \quad \nabla&=2 y \hat{\imath}+3 x \hat{\jmath}\\ u&=2 y and v=3 x \\ a_{x}&=\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}+u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{x}&=0+(2 y \times 0)+(3 x \times 2) \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{x}&=6 x\\ \text{Now at }(1,1)\\ a_{1}&=6 x=6 \times 1=6 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A thin flat plate [latex]0.5m\times 0.7m[/latex] in size settles in a large tank of water with a terminal velocity of 0.12 m/s. The coefficients of drag [latex]C_{D}=\frac{1.328}{\sqrt{R_{L}}}[/latex] for a laminar boundary layer and [latex]C_{D}=\frac{0.072}{(R_{L})^{1/5}}[/latex] for a turbulent boundary layer, where [latex]R_L[/latex] is the plate Reynolds number.

Assume [latex]\mu=10^{-3} N-s/m^{2}[/latex] and [latex]\rho =1000 kg/m^{3}[/latex]
The submerged weight of the plate is
raw_source.solution:
The critical Reynolds number for flat plates is [latex] 5 \times 10^{5} [/latex]
As [latex]R_{L} \lt [/latex] critical Reynolds number thus laminar boundary layer will grow through out the length
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore C_{0}&=\frac{1.328}{\sqrt{R_{L}}}=\frac{1328}{\sqrt{84 \times 10^{3}}}=4.58 \times 10^{-3}\\ \therefore &\quad \text{Drag force.}\\ F_{0} &=2 C_{D} A\left(\frac{\rho V^{2}}{2}\right) \\ &=4.58 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.5 \times 0.7 \times 1000 \times(0.12)^{2} \\ &=0.0231 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A steady flow occurs in an open channel with lateral inflow of [latex]q \; m^{3}/s[/latex] per unit width as shown in the figure. The mass conservation equation is

The mass conservation equation will be

It is a example of super critical canal intake, the reservoir water surface falls to the critical depth at the head of the canal and then towards the water surface follows the [latex]S_{2}[/latex] Curve. The critical depth occurring at the u/s end of the channel is the control for this flow.

raw_source.text:
The allowable Net Positive Sustion Head (NPSH) for a pump provided by the
manufacturer for a flow of 0.05 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s is 3.3 m. raw_source.solution:
The maximum suction lift,
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{s}&=\left(\frac{p_{a}-p_{v}}{\gamma_{w}}\right)-N P S H-h_{ts} \\ p_{a} &=100 k P a_{i} \\ \gamma_{w} &=1000 \times 9.81=9810 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \frac{p_{v}}{\gamma_{w}} &=0.44 \mathrm{m} \\ \frac{p_{a}}{\gamma_{w}} &=\frac{100 \times 10^{3}}{9810}=10.19 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad h_{s} &=10.19-0.44-3.3-0.3 \\ &=6.15 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The rainfall during three successive 2 hour periods are 0.5, 2.8 and 1.6 cm. The

Total rainfall = 0.5+2.8+1.6&=4.9 cm
Excess rainfall =4.9+3.2&=1.7 cm
Taking excess rainfall duration,
[latex] t_{e}=2\times 3=6[/latex] hrs
[latex]\phi[/latex]-index = [latex]\frac{1.7}{6}=0.28[/latex]cm/hr
This value being more than [latex]\frac{0.5}{2}=0.25[/latex] cm/hr, the excess rainfall duration will reduce by 2-hrs.
[latex]\therefore \;\; t_{e}=[/latex]4 hrs
Excess rainfall = 2.8 +1.6-3.2 =1.2 cm
[latex]\phi[/latex]-index [latex]=\frac{1.2}{4}=0.3[/latex] cm/hr

raw_source.text: The present population of a community is 28000 with an average water consumption of 4200 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/d. The existing water treatment plant has a design capacity of 6000 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/d. It is expected that the population will increase to 44000 during the next 20 years. The number of years from now when the plant will reach its design capacity, assuming an arithmetic rate of population growth, will be
raw_source.solution:
Assuming arithmetic rate of growth of population.
Increase in population per year
[latex] =\frac{44000-28000}{20}=800[/latex]
Discharge required to reach design capacity
[latex] =6000-4200=1800 m^{3} / d[/latex]
Present average water consumption per head per day
[latex] =\frac{4200}{28000}=0.15 \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
Increase in water consumption each year
[latex] =0.15 \times 800=120 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{day}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] No. of years required to reach design capacity
[latex] =\frac{1800}{120}=15 \text { years }[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An existing 300 mm diameter circular sewer is laid at a slope of 1:28 and carries a peak discharge of 1728 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/d. Use the partial flow diagram shown in the given figure and assume Manning's n = 0.015

At the peak discharge, the depth of flow and the velocity are, respectively
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=\left ( \frac{\pi }{4}D^{2} \right ).\frac{R^{\frac{2}{3}}S^{\frac{1}{2}}}{n}\; \; \; \; \; \left [ R=D/4 \right ] \\ &=\frac{\pi }{4}\times 0.3^{2}\times \left ( \frac{0.3}{4} \right )^{2/3}\times \frac{\sqrt{1/280}}{0.015} \\ &=0.05\: m^{3}/d \\ Q&=4327.3\: m^{3}/d \\ q&=1728\: m^{3}/d \\ \therefore \frac{q}{Q} &= 0.4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
From graph, [latex]\frac{d}{D}=0.4\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \therefore \; \; d=120\; mm[/latex]
From graph, [latex]\frac{v}{V}=0.4[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \; \; \; v=0.7\times \frac{1}{n}R^{2/3}\: S^{1/2}[/latex]
[latex]=0.496\: m/s\approx 0.5\: m/s[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The following data are given for a channel-type grit chamber of length 7.5 m.

1. flow-through velocity = 0.3 m/s
2. the depth of waste water at peak flow in the channel = 0.9 m
3. specific gravity of inorganic particles = 2.5
4. g = 9.80 m/[latex]s^{2}[/latex], m=[latex]1.002 \times 10^{-3} N-s/m^{2}[/latex] at 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C, [latex]\rho _{w}=1000 kg/m^{3}[/latex]

Assuming that the Stoke's law is valid, the largest diameter particles that would be removed with 100 percent efficiency is
raw_source.solution:
Flow through velocity, [latex]V=\frac{Q}{B H} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q}{B} &=V \times H \\ &=0.3 \times 0.9=0.27 \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Settling velocity,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{s}&=\frac{Q}{B L}=\frac{0.27}{7.5}=0.036 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \text{But, }\quad V_{s}&=\frac{\rho_{w} g}{18}\left(\frac{S_{s}-1}{\mu}\right) \mathrm{d}^{2}=0.036 \\ \Rightarrow \quad d^{2}&=\frac{0.036 \times \mu \times 18}{\rho_{w} \times g \times\left(S_{s}-1\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad d^{2}&=\frac{0.036 \times 1.002 \times 10^{-3} \times 18}{1000 \times 9.81 \times(2.5-1)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad d^{2}&=4.42 \times 10^{-8} \\ \therefore \quad d&=2.10 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{m}=0.21 \mathrm{mm} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The design parameter for flocculation is given by a dimensionless number Gt,
where G is the velocity gradient and t is the detention time. Values of Gt ranging
from [latex]10^{4} \; to \; 10^{5}[/latex] are commonly used, with t ranging from 10 to 30 min. The most preferred combination of G and t to produce smaller and denser flocs is
raw_source.solution:
Large G value with short times tend to produce small, dense flocs, while low G values and long times produce larger, lighter flocs. Since larger, dense flocs are more easily removed in the setting basin, it may be advantageous to vary the G values over the length of the flocculation basin.
The small dense flocs produced at high G values subsequently combine into larger flocs at the lower G values. Reduction in G values by a factor of 2 from the influent end to the effluent end of the flocculator has been shown to be effective.
options: large G values with short t
large G values with long t
smaller G values with short t
small G values with long  t

raw_answer.option_text: large G values with short t

raw_source.text:
Chlorine gas used for disinfection combines with water to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl). The HOCl ionizes to form hypochlorite [latex]\left (OCL^{-} \right )[/latex] in a reversible reaction :
[latex]HOCI \rightleftharpoons H^{+}+OCl^{-} [/latex] [latex](k=2.7\times 10^{-8} \; at\; 20^{\circ}C)[/latex],
the equilibrium of which is government by pH. The sum of HOCl and [latex]OCL^{-}[/latex] is known as free chlorine residual and HOCl is the more effective disinfectant. The 90% fraction of HOCI in the free chlorine residual is available at a pH value
raw_source.solution:
[latex]HOCI\rightleftharpoons H^{+}+OCI^{-}[/latex]
The above reaction is a reversible reaction. The formation of end products depends upon the pH value of water. raw_source.text: Which one of the following is NOT true for complex number [latex]Z_1 \; and \; Z_2[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
(A) is true since
[latex] \frac{Z_{1}}{Z_{2}}=\frac{Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}}{Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}}=\frac{Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}}{\left | Z_{2} \right |^{2}}[/latex]
(B) is true by triangle inequality of complex number.
(C) is not true since [latex]\left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |\geq \left | Z_{1} \right |-\left | Z_{2} \right |[/latex]
(D) is true since
[latex] \begin{aligned}\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}+Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}+\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}} \;\;...(i)\\ \left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}-Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=\left ( Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}-\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}-Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}-Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}\;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex]
Adding (i) and (ii) we get,
[latex]\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}+\left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}=2Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}+2Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}} =2\left | Z_{1} \right |^{2}+2\left | Z_{2} \right |^{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Transformation to linear form by substituting [latex]v =y^{1-n}[/latex] of the equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dt}+p(t)y=q(t)y^{n}; \;\; n \gt 0[/latex] will be
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )y&=q\left ( t \right )y^{n};\, n\gt 0\\ \text{putting } v&=y^{1-n} \\ \frac{dv}{dt}&=\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}\frac{dy}{dt} \\ \frac{dy}{dt}&=\frac{1}{\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}}\frac{dv}{dt}\end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in the given differential equation, we get,
[latex] \frac{1}{\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}}\frac{dy}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )y=q\left ( t \right )y^{n}[/latex]
Multiplying by [latex]\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}[/latex], we get,
[latex] \frac{dv}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )\left ( 1-n \right )y^{1-n}=q\left ( t \right )\left ( 1-n \right )[/latex]
now since [latex]y^{1-n}=v[/latex], we get
[latex] \frac{dv}{dt}+\left ( 1-n \right )pv=\left ( 1-n \right )q[/latex]
where p is p(t) and q is q(t).

raw_source.text:
A rail engine accelerates from its stationary position for 8 seconds and travels a
distance of 280 m. According to the Mean Value Theorem, the speedometer at a
certain time during acceleration must read exactly
raw_source.solution:
Since the position of rail engine S(t) is continuous and differentiable function, according to Lagranges mean value theorem
[latex]\exists t[/latex] where [latex]0\leq t\leq 8[/latex] such that
[latex]\begin{aligned}{S}'\left ( t \right )&=v\left ( t \right )=\frac{S\left ( 8 \right )-S\left ( 0 \right )}{8-0} \\ &=\frac{\left ( 280-0 \right )}{\left ( 8-0 \right )}\: m/sec \\ &=\frac{280}{8}\: m/sec \\ &=\frac{280}{8}\times \frac{3600}{1000} \;kmph\\ &=126 kmph \end{aligned}[/latex]
where [latex]v(t)[/latex] is the velocity of the rail engine.

raw_source.text: The solution of [latex]\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}+17y=0[/latex]; y(0)=1, [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}(\frac{x}{4})=0[/latex] in the range [latex]0 \lt x \lt \frac{\pi}{4}[/latex] is given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}+17y&=0 \\ y\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}\left ( \frac{\pi }{4} \right )&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
This is a linear differential equation
[latex]\begin{aligned} D^{2}+2D+17&=0 \\ D&=-1\pm 4i \\ \therefore \;\; y&=C_{1}e^{\left ( -1+4i \right )x}+C_{2}e^{\left ( -1-4i \right )x} \\ &=e^{-x}C_{1}e^{4xi}+C_{2}e^{-4xi} \\ &=e^{-x} \\ \left [ C_{1}\left ( \cos 4x+i\sin 4x \right ) \right ]& +C_{2}\left [ \cos \left ( 4x \right )+i\sin \left ( -4x \right ) \right ]\\ &=e^{-x}\left [ \left ( C_{1}+C_{2} \right )\cos 4x +\left ( C_{1}-C_{2} \right )i\sin 4x \right ] \\ \text{Let } C_{1}+C_{2}&=C_{3} \text{ and }\left ( C_{1}-C_{2} \right )i=C_{4} \\ y&=e^{-x}\left ( C_{3}\cos 4x+C_{4}\sin 4x \right )\\ \text{Since } y\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 1&=e^{-0}\left ( C_{3}\cos 0+C_{4}\sin 0 \right ) \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C_{3}&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=e^{-x}\left (-4C_{3}\sin 4x+4C_{4}\cos 4x \right ) \\ &-e^{-x}\left [ C_{3}\cos 4x+C_{4}\sin 4x \right ] \\ &=e^{-x}\left [ \left ( -4C_{3}-C_{4} \right )\sin 4x +\left ( 4C_{4}-C_{3}\cos 4x \right ) \right ] \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} \text{ at } x&=\frac{\pi }{4} \text{ is }0 \\ \therefore \; \left ( -4C_{4}-C_{3} \right )e^{-\pi /4}&=0 \\ 4C_{4}&=C_{3} \\ C_{4}&=\frac{C_{3}}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \therefore \;\; C_{3}&=1 \text{ and }C_{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ y&=e^{-x}\left ( \cos 4x+\frac{1}{4}\sin 4x \right ) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Value of the integral [latex]\oint_{c}(xydy-y^{2}dx)[/latex], where c is the square cut from the first quadrant by the line x=1 and y=1 will be (Use Green's theorem to change the line integral into double integral)
raw_source.solution:
Green's theorem is,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \oint_{c} \phi dx + \Psi dy&=\int_{E}\left ( \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}-\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x} \right )\: dxdy\\ \text{Here } I&=\oint_{c} \left ( xydy\: -\: y^{2}dx \right ) \\ &=\oint_{c} \left ( -y^{2} \right )dx\: +\: \left ( xy \right )dy \\ \therefore \;\; \phi &=-y^{2},\; \Psi = xy \\ \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}&=y,\; \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y}=-2y\end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in Green's Theorem, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I&= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\left [ y-\left ( -2y \right ) \right ]dx\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\: 3y\: dx\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\left [ 3xy \right ]_{x=0}^{1}\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}3ydy=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the likely applicability of Cauchy's Integral Theorem to evaluate the following integral counter clockwise around the unit circle c.
[latex]I=\oint_{c}\sec z dz[/latex],
z being a complex variable. The value of I will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \int \sec z\, dz=\int \frac{1}{\cos z}dz[/latex]
The poles are at
[latex] z_{0}=\left ( n+1/2 \right )p =...-3\pi /2,\: -\pi /2,\: \pi /2,\: +3\pi /2....[/latex]
None of these poles lie inside the unit circle [latex]\left | z \right |=1 [/latex]
Hence, sum of residues at poles =0
Therefore, singularities set [latex]=\phi[/latex] and
[latex]I=2\pi i[/latex] [sum of residues of [latex]f(z)[/latex] at the poles]
[latex] \;\; =2\pi i\times 0=0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Given a[latex]\gt[/latex]0, we wish to calculate its reciprocal value 1/a by using Newton Raphson method for [latex]f(x) =0[/latex]

The Newton Raphson algorithm for the function will be
raw_source.solution:
To calculate [latex]\frac{1}{a}[/latex] using N-R method, set up the equation as,
[latex] \begin{aligned} x&=\frac{1}{a}\\ \frac{1}{x}&=a \\ \frac{1}{x_k}-a&=0\\ f\left ( x \right )&=\frac{1}{x_{k}}-a=0\\ \text{Now } {f}'\left ( x \right )&=-\frac{1}{x^{2}} \\ f\left ( x_{k} \right )&=\frac{1}{x_{k}}-a \\ {f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )&=-\frac{1}{x^{2}_{k}}\\ &\text{For N-R method,}\\ x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{f\left ( x_{k} \right )}{{f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{\left ( 1/x_{k}-a \right )}{-\frac{1}{x^{2}_{k}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Simplifying which we get,
[latex] x_{k+1}=2x_{k}-ax^{2}_{k}[/latex]

For a=7 the iteration equation, becomes,

raw_source.text: Which one of the following is NOT true for complex number [latex]Z_1 \; and \; Z_2[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
(A) is true since
[latex] \frac{Z_{1}}{Z_{2}}=\frac{Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}}{Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}}=\frac{Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}}{\left | Z_{2} \right |^{2}}[/latex]
(B) is true by triangle inequality of complex number.
(C) is not true since [latex]\left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |\geq \left | Z_{1} \right |-\left | Z_{2} \right |[/latex]
(D) is true since
[latex] \begin{aligned}\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}+Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}+\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}} \;\;...(i)\\ \left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}&=\left ( Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right )\left ( \overline{Z_{1}-Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=\left ( Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right )\left ( \bar{Z_{1}}-\bar{Z_{2}} \right ) \\ &=Z_{1}\bar{Z_{1}}+Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}}-Z_{2}\bar{Z_{1}}-Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}\;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex]
Adding (i) and (ii) we get,
[latex]\left | Z_{1}+Z_{2} \right |^{2}+\left | Z_{1}-Z_{2} \right |^{2}=2Z_{1}\bar{Z_{2}}+2Z_{2}\bar{Z_{2}} =2\left | Z_{1} \right |^{2}+2\left | Z_{2} \right |^{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The components of strain tensor at a point in the plane strain case can be
obtained by measuring longitudinal strain in following directions
raw_source.solution:
In case of plane strain condition, the components
of strain tensor at a point are [latex]\epsilon_{x}, \in_{y} \text{ and }\phi_{x y} .[/latex]
Here we have three unknowns so we require 3 equations to find them and these unknowns can be find by the equations of longitudinal strain,
[latex] \epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{1}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{1}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{1} [/latex]
[latex] \epsilon_{2}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{2}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{2}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \epsilon_{3}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{3}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{3}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{3} [/latex]
Therefore to find out component of strain tensor in plain strain condition, we measure longitudinal strains [latex]\left(\epsilon_{1}, \epsilon_{2}\text{ and }\epsilon_{3}\right)[/latex] along any three arbitrary direction.
raw_source.tag2: Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain

raw_source.solution: Negative skin friction is experienced when the soil around the pile settles at a faster rate than pile.
