raw_source.text: Transformation to linear form by substituting [latex]v =y^{1-n}[/latex] of the equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dt}+p(t)y=q(t)y^{n}; \;\; n \gt 0[/latex] will be
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )y&=q\left ( t \right )y^{n};\, n\gt 0\\ \text{putting } v&=y^{1-n} \\ \frac{dv}{dt}&=\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}\frac{dy}{dt} \\ \frac{dy}{dt}&=\frac{1}{\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}}\frac{dv}{dt}\end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in the given differential equation, we get,
[latex] \frac{1}{\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}}\frac{dy}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )y=q\left ( t \right )y^{n}[/latex]
Multiplying by [latex]\left ( 1-n \right )y^{-n}[/latex], we get,
[latex] \frac{dv}{dt}+p\left ( t \right )\left ( 1-n \right )y^{1-n}=q\left ( t \right )\left ( 1-n \right )[/latex]
now since [latex]y^{1-n}=v[/latex], we get
[latex] \frac{dv}{dt}+\left ( 1-n \right )pv=\left ( 1-n \right )q[/latex]
where p is p(t) and q is q(t).

A rail engine accelerates from its stationary position for 8 seconds and travels a
distance of 280 m. According to the Mean Value Theorem, the speedometer at a
certain time during acceleration must read exactly
raw_source.solution:
Since the position of rail engine S(t) is continuous and differentiable function, according to Lagranges mean value theorem
[latex]\exists t[/latex] where [latex]0\leq t\leq 8[/latex] such that
[latex]\begin{aligned}{S}'\left ( t \right )&=v\left ( t \right )=\frac{S\left ( 8 \right )-S\left ( 0 \right )}{8-0} \\ &=\frac{\left ( 280-0 \right )}{\left ( 8-0 \right )}\: m/sec \\ &=\frac{280}{8}\: m/sec \\ &=\frac{280}{8}\times \frac{3600}{1000} \;kmph\\ &=126 kmph \end{aligned}[/latex]
where [latex]v(t)[/latex] is the velocity of the rail engine.

raw_source.text: The solution of [latex]\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}+17y=0[/latex]; y(0)=1, [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}(\frac{x}{4})=0[/latex] in the range [latex]0 \lt x \lt \frac{\pi}{4}[/latex] is given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}+17y&=0 \\ y\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}\left ( \frac{\pi }{4} \right )&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
This is a linear differential equation
[latex]\begin{aligned} D^{2}+2D+17&=0 \\ D&=-1\pm 4i \\ \therefore \;\; y&=C_{1}e^{\left ( -1+4i \right )x}+C_{2}e^{\left ( -1-4i \right )x} \\ &=e^{-x}C_{1}e^{4xi}+C_{2}e^{-4xi} \\ &=e^{-x} \\ \left [ C_{1}\left ( \cos 4x+i\sin 4x \right ) \right ]& +C_{2}\left [ \cos \left ( 4x \right )+i\sin \left ( -4x \right ) \right ]\\ &=e^{-x}\left [ \left ( C_{1}+C_{2} \right )\cos 4x +\left ( C_{1}-C_{2} \right )i\sin 4x \right ] \\ \text{Let } C_{1}+C_{2}&=C_{3} \text{ and }\left ( C_{1}-C_{2} \right )i=C_{4} \\ y&=e^{-x}\left ( C_{3}\cos 4x+C_{4}\sin 4x \right )\\ \text{Since } y\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 1&=e^{-0}\left ( C_{3}\cos 0+C_{4}\sin 0 \right ) \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C_{3}&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=e^{-x}\left (-4C_{3}\sin 4x+4C_{4}\cos 4x \right ) \\ &-e^{-x}\left [ C_{3}\cos 4x+C_{4}\sin 4x \right ] \\ &=e^{-x}\left [ \left ( -4C_{3}-C_{4} \right )\sin 4x +\left ( 4C_{4}-C_{3}\cos 4x \right ) \right ] \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} \text{ at } x&=\frac{\pi }{4} \text{ is }0 \\ \therefore \; \left ( -4C_{4}-C_{3} \right )e^{-\pi /4}&=0 \\ 4C_{4}&=C_{3} \\ C_{4}&=\frac{C_{3}}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \therefore \;\; C_{3}&=1 \text{ and }C_{4}=\frac{1}{4} \\ y&=e^{-x}\left ( \cos 4x+\frac{1}{4}\sin 4x \right ) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Value of the integral [latex]\oint_{c}(xydy-y^{2}dx)[/latex], where c is the square cut from the first quadrant by the line x=1 and y=1 will be (Use Green's theorem to change the line integral into double integral)
raw_source.solution:
Green's theorem is,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \oint_{c} \phi dx + \Psi dy&=\int_{E}\left ( \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}-\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x} \right )\: dxdy\\ \text{Here } I&=\oint_{c} \left ( xydy\: -\: y^{2}dx \right ) \\ &=\oint_{c} \left ( -y^{2} \right )dx\: +\: \left ( xy \right )dy \\ \therefore \;\; \phi &=-y^{2},\; \Psi = xy \\ \frac{\partial \Psi }{\partial x}&=y,\; \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y}=-2y\end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in Green's Theorem, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I&= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\left [ y-\left ( -2y \right ) \right ]dx\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\int_{x=0}^{1}\: 3y\: dx\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}\left [ 3xy \right ]_{x=0}^{1}\: dy \\ &= \int_{y=0}^{1}3ydy=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the likely applicability of Cauchy's Integral Theorem to evaluate the following integral counter clockwise around the unit circle c.
[latex]I=\oint_{c}\sec z dz[/latex],
z being a complex variable. The value of I will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \int \sec z\, dz=\int \frac{1}{\cos z}dz[/latex]
The poles are at
[latex] z_{0}=\left ( n+1/2 \right )p =...-3\pi /2,\: -\pi /2,\: \pi /2,\: +3\pi /2....[/latex]
None of these poles lie inside the unit circle [latex]\left | z \right |=1 [/latex]
Hence, sum of residues at poles =0
Therefore, singularities set [latex]=\phi[/latex] and
[latex]I=2\pi i[/latex] [sum of residues of [latex]f(z)[/latex] at the poles]
[latex] \;\; =2\pi i\times 0=0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a 25 cm thick cement concrete pavement, analysis of stresses gives the following values :

Wheel load stress due to corner loading : 30 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Wheel load stress due to edge loading : 32 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Warping stress at corner region during summer : 9 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Warping stress at corner region during winter : 7 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Warping stress at edge region during summer : 8 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Warping stress at edge region during summer : 6 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Frictional stress during summer : 5 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]
Frictional stress during winter : 4 kg/c[latex]m^{2}[/latex]

The most critical stress value for this pavement is
raw_source.solution:
There are four cases which should be considered:
(i) - During summer, critical combination of stresses at edges
=wheel load stress due to edge loading
+warping stress at edge region during summer
- frictional stress during summer
[latex] = 32 + 8 - 5 = 35\text{ kg/cm}^{2}[/latex]
(ii) During winter, critical combination of stresses at edges.
=wheel load stress due to edge loading
+warping stress at edge region during winter
+ frictional stress during winter
[latex] =32 + 6 + 4 = 42 \text{kg/cm}^{2}[/latex]
(iii) During summer, critical combination of stresses at corner regions
=wheel load stress at cor,ner loading
+ warping stress at corner region during
summer
[latex] =30 +9=39 \text{kg/cm}^{2}[/latex]
(iv) During winter, critical combination of stresses at corner region
=wheel load stress at corner loading
+ Warping stress at corner region during winter
[latex] =30+7=37 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} [/latex]
Hence, the critical combination is
[latex] 42 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{cm}^{2} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Match the following:

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{For }A B, \quad \theta_{B}&=\frac{M L}{4 E I} \\ \Rightarrow \text{ Stiffness at }\quad B&=\frac{4 E I}{L} \\ \text{For }B C \theta_{B}&=\frac{M L}{3 E I} \\ \Rightarrow \text{Stiffness at }\quad B&=\frac{3 E I}{L}\\ \text{For }BD, \quad \theta_{B}&=\frac{M L}{4 E I} \\ \Rightarrow \text{ Stiffness at }\quad B&=\frac{4 E I}{L} \\ \text{Total stiffness of }&\text{the joint}\\ =\frac{4 E I}{L}+\frac{3 E I}{L}+\frac{4 E I}{L}&=\frac{11 E I}{L} \\ \text{Rotation of joint }B&=\frac{M L}{11 E I} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A soil mass contains 40% gravel, 50% sand and 10% silt. This soil can be classified as

raw_source.text: A saturated soil mass has a total density 22 kN/[latex]m^{3}[/latex] and a water content of 10%. The bulk density and dry density of this soil are

raw_source.text: In a constant head permeameter with cross section area of 10 [latex]cm^{2}[/latex], when the flow was taking place under a hydraulic gradient of 0.5, the amount of water collected in 60 seconds is 600 cc. The permeability of the soil is

raw_source.text:
Assuming that a river bed level does not change and the depth of water in river
was 10 m, 15 m and 8 m during the months of February, July and December
respectively of a particular year. The average bulk density of the soil is 20 kN/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]. The density of water is 10 kN/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]. The effective stress at a depth of 10 m below the river bed during these months would be
raw_source.solution:
Since the river bed level does not change and the depth of water is changing only above the river bed, the effective stress below the river bed will not change.
Total stress at a depth of 10 m below river bed,
[latex] \sigma=20 \times 10=200 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
Pore water pressure,
[latex] u=10 \times 10=100 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Effective stress,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{\sigma} &=\sigma-u=200-100 \\ &=100 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus effective stress will be [latex]100 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} [/latex]
each in the month of February, July and December
options: 300 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in February, 350 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] July and 320 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in December
100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in February, 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] July and 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in December
200 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in February, 250 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] July and 180 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in December
300 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in February, 350 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] July and 280 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in December

raw_answer.option_text: 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in February, 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] July and 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] in December

raw_source.text:
For a tri-axial shear test conducted on a sand specimen at a confining pressure
of 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] under drained conditions, resulted in a deviator stress ([latex]\sigma_{1} - \sigma _{3}[/latex]) at failure of 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]. The angle of shearing resistance of the soil would be
raw_source.solution:
We know that
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\sigma_{1}}{\sigma_{1}}&=\frac{1+\sin \theta}{1-\sin \theta} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta&=\frac{\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2}}{\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{3}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \phi&=\frac{100}{\sigma_{1}+\sigma_{3}-\sigma_{3}+\sigma_{3}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \phi&=\frac{100}{\left(\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}\right)+2 \sigma_{3}}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta &=\frac{100}{100+2 \times 100} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \theta &=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad &=19.47^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
During the subsurface investigations for design of foundations, a standard penetration test was conducted at 4.5 m below the ground surface. The record of number of blow is given below.

Assuming the water table at ground level, soil as fine sand and correction factor for overburden as 1.0, the corrected 'N' value for the soil would be
raw_source.solution:
The number of blows required for the first 150mm of penetration is disregarded, and only the number of blows required for the last 300 mm of penetration is added together.
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Number of blows,
[latex] N^{\prime}=6+6+8+7=27[/latex]
(i) Correction for overburden pressure
Corrected value of observed
[latex] N^{\prime}=C_{N} N^{\prime}=1.0 \times 27=27[/latex]
(ii) Correction for dilatancy
It is to be applied when number of blows obtained after overburden correction exceeds 15 in saturated fine sands and silts.
[latex] \therefore N=15+0.5(27-15)[/latex]
[latex] =15+6=21[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For two infinite slopes (one in dry condition and other in submerged condition)
in a sand deposit having the angle of shearing resistance 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex], factor of safety was determined as 1.5 (for both slopes). The slope angles would have been
raw_source.solution:
For dry or submerged slopes, Factor of safety
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\tan \phi}{\tan \beta} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \tan \beta &=\frac{\tan 30^{\circ}}{1.5} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \beta=21.05^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: 21.05[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for dry slope and 21.05[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for submerged slope
19.47[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for dry slope and 18.40[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for submerged slope
18.4[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for dry slope and 21.05[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for submerged slope
22.6[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for dry slope and 19.47[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] for submerged slope

raw_source.text:
A strip footing (8 m wide) is designed for a total settlement of 40 mm. The safe
bearing capacity (shear) was 150 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] and safe allowable soil pressure was 100 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]. Due to important of the structure, now the footing is to be redesigned for total settlement of 25 mm. The new width of the footing will be
raw_source.solution:
Load per metre length of footing
[latex] P=B \times [/latex]{ Minimum of bearing capacity and allowable soil pressure}
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =8 \times \text { Minimum of }[150,100] \\ =8 \times 100=800 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m} \end{array}[/latex]
Allowable pressure for 25mm settlement
[latex] =\frac{100 \times 25}{40}=62.5 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
Load resisted = Width x Allowable pressure
[latex] \begin{array}{rr} & 800=B \times 62.5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & B=12.8 \mathrm{m}\end{array} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 3 m high retaining wall is supporting a saturated sand (saturated due to
capillary action) of bulk density 18 [latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex] and angle of shearing resistance 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. The change in magnitude of active earth pressure at the base due to rise in ground water table from the base of the footing to the ground surface shall ([latex]\gamma _{w}=10 kN/m^{3}[/latex])
raw_source.solution:
When the water tabel is at the base of footing the active earth pressure will be


[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{1} &=K_{a} \gamma R=\left(\frac{1-\sin \phi}{1+\sin \phi}\right) \times \gamma \times z \\ &=\frac{1-\sin 30^{\circ}}{1+\sin 30^{\circ}} \times 18 \times 3 \\ &=1 / 3 \times 18 \times 3=18 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When the water table rises upto the surface, the thrust due to water will also be added to the active earth pressure.

[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{2} &=K_{2} \gamma z+\gamma_{w} z \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \times(18-10) \times 3+10 \times 3 \\ &=8+30=38 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] change in active earth pressure
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =P_{2}-P_{1}=38-18 \\ =20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}(\text { increase }) \end{array}[/latex]
Note: In strict terms [latex]\gamma_{\text {sat }}[/latex] should be taker

raw_source.text:
A partially open sluice gate discharge water into a rectangular channel. The tail
water depth in the channel is 3 m and Froude number is [latex]\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[/latex]. If a free hydraulic jump is to be formed at downstream of the sluice gate after the
vena contracta of the jet coming out from the sluice gate, the sluice gate opening
should be (coefficient of contraction [latex]C_c[/latex]=0.9)
raw_source.solution:
For hydraulic jump,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{y_{1}}{y_{2}}&=\frac{1}{2}\left[-1+\sqrt{1+8 F_{2}^{2}}\right]\\ \text{Given},\quad y_{2}&=3 \mathrm{m} \\ F_{2} &=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2}} \\ \therefore \quad y_{1} &=\frac{3}{2}\left[-1+\sqrt{1+8 \times \frac{1}{4 \times 2}}\right]\\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{1}&=0.62 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Sluice gate opening
[latex] =\frac{y_{1}}{C_{c}}=\frac{0.62}{0.9}=0.69 \mathrm{m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A stream function is given by
[latex]\Psi =2x^{2}y+(x+1)y^{2}[/latex]
The flow rate across a line joining points A(3,0) and B(0,2) is
raw_source.solution:
The rate of flow is the difference in value of stream function at points A and B
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad Q &=\left|\psi_{A}-\psi_{B}\right| \\ \psi_{A} &=2 \times(3)^{2} \times 0+(3+1) \times(0)^{2}=0 \\ \psi_{B} &=2 \times(0)^{2} \times 2+(0+1) \times(2)^{2}=4 \\ \therefore & Q=|0-4|=4 \text { units } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Cross-section of an object (having same section normal to the paper) submerged into a fluid consists of a square of sides 2 m and triangle as shown in the figure. The object is hinged at point P that is one meter below the fluid free surface. If the object is to be kept in the position as shown in the figure, the value of 'x' should be
raw_source.solution:
The vertical force on the surface bounded by square and triangle would be respectively,
[latex] F_{1}=4(S-1) \gamma_{w} [/latex] for square edge and acting at 1 m from P
[latex] F_{2}=x(S-1) \gamma_{w}[/latex] for inclined edge of triangle and acting at x / 3 from P
Taking moments of both the forces about P, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} F_{ 1} \times 1 &=F_{2} \times \frac{x}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 4(\mathrm{S}-1) \gamma_{w} &=x(S-1) \gamma_{w} \times \frac{x}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad x^{2} &=12 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x &=2 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The circulation 'G' around a circle of radius 2 units for the velocity field u=2x+3y
and v=-2y is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Circulation } &=\text { Vorticity } \times \text { Area } \\ &=\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) \times \text { Area } \\ &=(0-3) \times \pi \times(2)^{2} \\ &=-12 \pi \text { units } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A tank and a deflector are placed on a frictionless trolley. The tank issues water jet (mass density of water = 1000 kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]), which strikes the deflector and turns by 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. If the velocity of jet leaving the deflector is 4 m/s and discharge is 0.1 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s, the force recorded by the spring will be
raw_source.solution:
Force in spring will be the force in horizonta direction.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad F_{H} &=\rho Q V \cos \theta \\ &=1000 \times 0.1 \times 4 \times \cos 45^{\circ} \\ &=\frac{400}{\sqrt{2}}=200 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two observation wells penetrated into a confined aquifer and located 1.5 km
apart in the direction of flow, indicate head of 45 m and 20 m. If the coefficient
of permeability of the aquifer is 30 m/day and porosity is 0.25, the time of travel
of an inert tracer from one well to another is
raw_source.solution:
The average flow velocity or discharge velocity,
[latex] v=k i=30 \times\left(\frac{45-20}{1500}\right)=0.5 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{da}[/latex]
Seepage velocity,
[latex] v_{s}=\frac{v}{n}=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{day}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Travel time [latex]=\frac{1500}{2}=750 \text{ days}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Source of Water Supply, Distribution System and Well Hydraulics

raw_source.text: A triangular irrigation lined canal carries a discharge of 25 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s at bed slope =[latex]\frac{1}{6000}[/latex]. If the side slopes of the canal are 1:1 and Manning's coefficient is 0.018, the central depth of flow is equal to
raw_source.solution:
By Manning's equation, [latex]Q=\frac{1}{n} R^{2 / 3} S^{1 / 2} A [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad 25&=\frac{1}{0.018} \times\left(\frac{y}{2 \sqrt{2}}\right)^{2 / 3} \times\left(\frac{1}{6000}\right)^{1 / 2} \times(y)^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 25&=\frac{1}{0.018} \times(y)^{8 / 3} \times \frac{1}{154.92} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=4.91 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Uplift pressure at point E and D (shown in figure ) of a straight horizonal floor of negligible thickness with a sheet pile at downstream end are 28% and 20%, respectively. If the sheet pile is at upstream end of the floor, the uplift pressures at point [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]C_{1}[/latex] are
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Uplift pressure at }\mathrm{D}_{1}, \phi_{D_{1}}&=100-\phi_{\mathrm{D}} \\ &=100-20=80 \% \\ \text{Uplift pressure at }C_{1}, \phi_{C_{1}}&=100-\phi_{E} \\ &=100-28=72 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A launching apron is to be designed at downstream of a weir for discharge intensity
of 6.5 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s/m. For the design of launching aprons the scour depth is taken two times of Lacey scour depth. The silt factor of the bed material is unity. If the tailwater
depth is 4.4 m, the length of launching apron in the launched position is
raw_source.solution:
Lacey's scour depth,
[latex] \begin{aligned} R=1.35\left(\frac{q^{2}}{f}\right)^{1 / 3}&=1.35 \times\left(\frac{6.5^{2}}{1}\right)^{1 / 3}=4.7 \mathrm{m} \\ \text{Scour depth }&=2 R=9.4 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad D&=2 R-4.4=5 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The culturable commanded area for a distributary is [latex]2\times 10^{8}m^{2}[/latex]. The intensity of irrigation for a crop is 40%. If kor water depth and kor period for the crop are 14 cm and 4 weeks, respectively, the peak demand discharge is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Area under crop } &=2 \times 10^{8} \times \frac{40}{100} \\ &=0.8 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Volume } &=\text { Area } \times \Delta \\ &=0.8 \times 10^{8} \times 14 \times 10^{-2} \\ &=1.2 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \text { Discharge, } Q &=\frac{1.12 \times 10^{7}}{4 \times 7 \times 24 \times 3600} \\ &=4.63 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If tomato juice is having a pH of 4.1, the hydrogen ion concentration will be

In a certain situation, waste water discharged into a river mixer with the river water instantaneously and completely. Following is the data available :

Waste water:
DO = 2.00 mg/L
Discharge rate = 1.10 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s

raw_source.text: A circular primary clarifier processes an average flow of 5005 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/d of municipal waste water. The overflow rate is 35 [latex]m^{3}/m^{2}[/latex]/d. The diameter of clarifier shall be
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Area of clarifier} &=\frac{\text{Average flow of waste water}}{\text{Overflow rate}} \\ &=\frac{5005}{35}=143\; m^{2} \\ \therefore \; \; \frac{\pi }{4}D^{2} &=143 \\ \Rightarrow \; \; D^{2} &=\frac{143\times 4}{\pi } \\ \Rightarrow \; \; D &=13.5\; \text{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A single lane unidirectional highway has a design speed of 65 kmph. The
perception-brake-reaction time of drivers is 2.5 seconds and the average length of
vehicles is 5 m. The coefficient of longitudinal friction of the pavement is 0.4. The
capacity of this road in term of vehicles per hour per lane is
raw_source.solution:
Space headway,
[latex] \begin{aligned} S &=0.278 \mathrm{V} t+\frac{V^{2}}{254 \mathrm{f}}+L \\ &=0.278 \times 65 \times 2.5+\frac{(65)^{2}}{254 \times 0.4}+5 \\ &=91.8 \mathrm{m}\\ \text{Capacity,}\\ C &=\frac{1000 \mathrm{V}}{S}=\frac{1000 \times 65}{91.8} \\ &=708.37 \approx 710 \end{aligned}[/latex]

A road is having a horizontal curve of 400 m radius on which a super-elevation
of 0.07 is provided. The coefficient of lateral friction mobilized on the curve when a
vehicle is travelling at 100 kmph is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\frac{V^{2}}{127(e+f)} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;e+f&=\frac{V^{2}}{127 R} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \quad f &=\frac{V^{2}}{127 R}-e \\ &=\frac{(100)^{2}}{127 \times 400}-0.07 \\ &=0.13 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Given a[latex]\gt[/latex]0, we wish to calculate its reciprocal value 1/a by using Newton Raphson method for [latex]f(x) =0[/latex]

The Newton Raphson algorithm for the function will be
raw_source.solution:
To calculate [latex]\frac{1}{a}[/latex] using N-R method, set up the equation as,
[latex] \begin{aligned} x&=\frac{1}{a}\\ \frac{1}{x}&=a \\ \frac{1}{x_k}-a&=0\\ f\left ( x \right )&=\frac{1}{x_{k}}-a=0\\ \text{Now } {f}'\left ( x \right )&=-\frac{1}{x^{2}} \\ f\left ( x_{k} \right )&=\frac{1}{x_{k}}-a \\ {f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )&=-\frac{1}{x^{2}_{k}}\\ &\text{For N-R method,}\\ x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{f\left ( x_{k} \right )}{{f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{\left ( 1/x_{k}-a \right )}{-\frac{1}{x^{2}_{k}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Simplifying which we get,
[latex] x_{k+1}=2x_{k}-ax^{2}_{k}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A class of first year B. Tech. students is composed of four batches A, B, C and
D, each consisting of 30 students. It is found that the sessional marks of students
in Enginnering Drawing in batch C havea mean of 6.6 and standard deviation of
2.3. The mean and standard deviation of the marks for the entire class are 5.5 and
4.2, respectively. It is decided by the course instructor to normalize the marks of
the students of all batches to have the same mean and standard deviation as that
of the entire class. Due to this, the marks of a student in batch C are changed from 8.5 to
raw_source.solution:
Let the mean and standard deviation of the students of batch C be [latex]\mu _{c}[/latex] and [latex]\sigma _{c}[/latex] respectively, and the mean and standard deviation of entire class of first year students be m and s respectively.
Now given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mu _{c}&=6.6 \\ \sigma _{c}&=2.3\\ \mu &=5.5 \\ \sigma &=4.2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
In order to normalise batch C to entire class, the normalised score must be equated.
since
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z&=\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma } \\ Z_{c}&=\frac{x_{c}-\mu _{c}}{\sigma _{c}}=\frac{8.5-6.6}{2.3}\\ \text{Now } Z&=\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma }=\frac{x-5.5}{4.2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equating these two and solving, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{8.5-6.6}{2.3}&=\frac{x-5.5}{4.2} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x&=8.969\simeq 9.0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] degree polynomial, f(x) has values of 1, 4 and 15 at x = 0, 1 and 2, respectively. The integral [latex]\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx[/latex] is to be estimated by applying the trapezoidal rule to this data. What is the error (defined as "true value - approximate value")
in the estimate ?
raw_source.solution:
f(x)=1, 4, 15 at x=0, 1 and 2 respectively
[latex] \int_{0}^{2}f\left ( x \right )dx =\frac{h}{2}\left ( f_{1}+2f_{2}+f_{3} \right ) [/latex](3 point Trapezoidal Rule)
Here h=1
[latex]\therefore \;\; \int_{0}^{2}f\left ( x \right )dx=\left ( 1+2\times +15 \right )=12[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] Approximate value by Trapezoidal Rule =12
Since f(x) is second degree polynomial, let,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f\left ( x \right )&=a_{0}+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2} \\ f\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}+0+0&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}&=1 \\ f\left ( 1 \right )&=4 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}&=4 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 1+a_{1}+a_{2}&=4 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{1}+a_{2}&=3 \;\;\;...(i)\\ f\left ( 2 \right )&=15 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}+2a_{1}+4a_{2}&=15 \\ \Rightarrow \;\;1+2a_{1}+4a_{2}&=15 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 2a_{1}+4a_{2}&=14 \;\;\; ...(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving (i) and (ii) [latex]a_{1}=-1[/latex] and [latex]a_{2}=4[/latex],
[latex]\therefore \;\; f\left ( x \right )=1-x+4x^{2}[/latex]
Now, exact value of
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{2}f\left ( x \right )dx \\ &=\int_{0}^{2}\left ( 1-x+4x^{2} \right ) \\ &=\left [ x-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{4x^{3}}{3} \right ]_{0}^{2}=\frac{32}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Error = Exact-Approximate value
[latex] =\frac{32}{3}-12=-\frac{4}{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Using Cauchy's integral theorem, the value of the integral (integration being
taken in counterclockwise direction) [latex]\oint_{c}\frac{z^{3}-6}{3z-i}dz[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Cauchy's integral theorem is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f\left ( a \right )&=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{c}\, \frac{f\left ( z \right )}{z-a}dz\\ \text{i.e., } \oint_{C}\, \frac{f\left ( z \right )}{z-a}dz&=2\pi i\, f\left ( a \right ) \\ \text{Now, } \oint_{C}\, \frac{z^{3}-6}{3z-i}dz&=\frac{1}{3}\oint_{c}\, \frac{z^{3-6}}{\left ( z-\frac{i}{3} \right )} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying Cauchy's integral theorem,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{3}\left ( 2\pi i\: f\left ( \frac{i}{3} \right ) \right ) \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left ( 2\pi i\left [ \left ( \frac{i}{3} \right )^{3}-6 \right ] \right ) \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left [ 2\pi i\left ( \frac{i^{3}}{27}-6 \right ) \right ] \\ &=\frac{2\pi }{81}i^{4}-4\pi i \\ &=\frac{2\pi }{81}-4\pi i \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A spherical naphthalene ball exposed to the atmosphere losses volume at a rate
proportional to its instantaneous surface area due to evaporation. If the initial
diameter of the ball is 2 cm and the diameter reduces to 1 cm after 3 months, the
ball completely evaporates in
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}&=-kA \;\;...(i) \\ \text{where } V&=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} \\ A&=4\pi r^{2} \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}&=\frac{4}{3}\pi \times 3r^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t} \\ \text{Substituting} & \text{ in (i) we get,}\\ 4\pi r^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t}&=-k\left ( 4\pi r^{2} \right ) \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t}&=-k \\ \Rightarrow \;\; dr&=-kdt\\ \text{Integrating}& \text{ we get,}\\ r&=-kt+C \\ t&=0, r&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 1&=-k\times 0+C \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C&=1 \\ \therefore \;\; r&=-kt+1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now at t=3 months r=0.5 cm
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\; 0.5&=-k\times 3+1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; k&=\frac{0.5}{3} \\ r&=-\frac{0.5}{3}t+1\end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting r=0
and solving for t gives [latex]0=-\frac{0.5}{3}t+1[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \;\;\; t=6[/latex] months

raw_source.text: The solution of the differential equation, [latex]x^{2} \frac{dy}{dx}+ 2xy - x + 1 = 0[/latex] , given that at x = 1, y = 0 is
raw_source.solution:
Giiven, [latex]x^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2xy-x+1=0 \;\; \left ( x=1, y=0 \right ) [/latex]
[latex] x^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2xy =x-1[/latex]
Dividing by [latex]x^{2}[/latex],
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+\left ( \frac{2}{x} \right )y =\left ( \frac{x-1}{x^{2}} \right )[/latex]
which is a linear first order differential equation of the form,
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+Py =Q[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Integrating factor}&=I.F=e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx} \\ &=e^{2\log x} \\ &=e^{\log_{e}x^{2}}=x^{2} \\ y\times I.F&=\int Q\left ( I.F \right )dx \\ y.x^{2}&=\int \left ( \frac{x-1}{x^{2}} \right ).x^{2}.dx \\ &=\int \left ( x-1 \right )dx \\ yx^{2}&=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-x+C \\ \text{Now at }x=1, \;y=0,\\ \text{i.e. } 0\times 1^{2}&=\frac{1^{2}}{2}-1+C \\ 0&=\frac{1}{2}-1+C \\ C&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \therefore \;\; yx^{2}&=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-x+\frac{1}{2} \\ y&=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{2x^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A class of first year B. Tech. students is composed of four batches A, B, C and
D, each consisting of 30 students. It is found that the sessional marks of students
in Enginnering Drawing in batch C havea mean of 6.6 and standard deviation of
2.3. The mean and standard deviation of the marks for the entire class are 5.5 and
4.2, respectively. It is decided by the course instructor to normalize the marks of
the students of all batches to have the same mean and standard deviation as that
of the entire class. Due to this, the marks of a student in batch C are changed from 8.5 to
raw_source.solution:
Let the mean and standard deviation of the students of batch C be [latex]\mu _{c}[/latex] and [latex]\sigma _{c}[/latex] respectively, and the mean and standard deviation of entire class of first year students be m and s respectively.
Now given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mu _{c}&=6.6 \\ \sigma _{c}&=2.3\\ \mu &=5.5 \\ \sigma &=4.2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
In order to normalise batch C to entire class, the normalised score must be equated.
since
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z&=\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma } \\ Z_{c}&=\frac{x_{c}-\mu _{c}}{\sigma _{c}}=\frac{8.5-6.6}{2.3}\\ \text{Now } Z&=\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma }=\frac{x-5.5}{4.2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equating these two and solving, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{8.5-6.6}{2.3}&=\frac{x-5.5}{4.2} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x&=8.969\simeq 9.0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] degree polynomial, f(x) has values of 1, 4 and 15 at x = 0, 1 and 2, respectively. The integral [latex]\int_{0}^{2}f(x)dx[/latex] is to be estimated by applying the trapezoidal rule to this data. What is the error (defined as "true value - approximate value")
in the estimate ?
raw_source.solution:
f(x)=1, 4, 15 at x=0, 1 and 2 respectively
[latex] \int_{0}^{2}f\left ( x \right )dx =\frac{h}{2}\left ( f_{1}+2f_{2}+f_{3} \right ) [/latex](3 point Trapezoidal Rule)
Here h=1
[latex]\therefore \;\; \int_{0}^{2}f\left ( x \right )dx=\left ( 1+2\times +15 \right )=12[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] Approximate value by Trapezoidal Rule =12
Since f(x) is second degree polynomial, let,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f\left ( x \right )&=a_{0}+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2} \\ f\left ( 0 \right )&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}+0+0&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}&=1 \\ f\left ( 1 \right )&=4 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}&=4 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 1+a_{1}+a_{2}&=4 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{1}+a_{2}&=3 \;\;\;...(i)\\ f\left ( 2 \right )&=15 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a_{0}+2a_{1}+4a_{2}&=15 \\ \Rightarrow \;\;1+2a_{1}+4a_{2}&=15 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 2a_{1}+4a_{2}&=14 \;\;\; ...(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving (i) and (ii) [latex]a_{1}=-1[/latex] and [latex]a_{2}=4[/latex],
[latex]\therefore \;\; f\left ( x \right )=1-x+4x^{2}[/latex]
Now, exact value of
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{2}f\left ( x \right )dx \\ &=\int_{0}^{2}\left ( 1-x+4x^{2} \right ) \\ &=\left [ x-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{4x^{3}}{3} \right ]_{0}^{2}=\frac{32}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Error = Exact-Approximate value
[latex] =\frac{32}{3}-12=-\frac{4}{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Using Cauchy's integral theorem, the value of the integral (integration being
taken in counterclockwise direction) [latex]\oint_{c}\frac{z^{3}-6}{3z-i}dz[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Cauchy's integral theorem is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f\left ( a \right )&=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{c}\, \frac{f\left ( z \right )}{z-a}dz\\ \text{i.e., } \oint_{C}\, \frac{f\left ( z \right )}{z-a}dz&=2\pi i\, f\left ( a \right ) \\ \text{Now, } \oint_{C}\, \frac{z^{3}-6}{3z-i}dz&=\frac{1}{3}\oint_{c}\, \frac{z^{3-6}}{\left ( z-\frac{i}{3} \right )} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying Cauchy's integral theorem,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{3}\left ( 2\pi i\: f\left ( \frac{i}{3} \right ) \right ) \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left ( 2\pi i\left [ \left ( \frac{i}{3} \right )^{3}-6 \right ] \right ) \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left [ 2\pi i\left ( \frac{i^{3}}{27}-6 \right ) \right ] \\ &=\frac{2\pi }{81}i^{4}-4\pi i \\ &=\frac{2\pi }{81}-4\pi i \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A spherical naphthalene ball exposed to the atmosphere losses volume at a rate
proportional to its instantaneous surface area due to evaporation. If the initial
diameter of the ball is 2 cm and the diameter reduces to 1 cm after 3 months, the
ball completely evaporates in
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}&=-kA \;\;...(i) \\ \text{where } V&=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} \\ A&=4\pi r^{2} \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}&=\frac{4}{3}\pi \times 3r^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t} \\ \text{Substituting} & \text{ in (i) we get,}\\ 4\pi r^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t}&=-k\left ( 4\pi r^{2} \right ) \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t}&=-k \\ \Rightarrow \;\; dr&=-kdt\\ \text{Integrating}& \text{ we get,}\\ r&=-kt+C \\ t&=0, r&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 1&=-k\times 0+C \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C&=1 \\ \therefore \;\; r&=-kt+1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now at t=3 months r=0.5 cm
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\; 0.5&=-k\times 3+1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; k&=\frac{0.5}{3} \\ r&=-\frac{0.5}{3}t+1\end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting r=0
and solving for t gives [latex]0=-\frac{0.5}{3}t+1[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \;\;\; t=6[/latex] months

raw_source.text: The solution of the differential equation, [latex]x^{2} \frac{dy}{dx}+ 2xy - x + 1 = 0[/latex] , given that at x = 1, y = 0 is
raw_source.solution:
Giiven, [latex]x^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2xy-x+1=0 \;\; \left ( x=1, y=0 \right ) [/latex]
[latex] x^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2xy =x-1[/latex]
Dividing by [latex]x^{2}[/latex],
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+\left ( \frac{2}{x} \right )y =\left ( \frac{x-1}{x^{2}} \right )[/latex]
which is a linear first order differential equation of the form,
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+Py =Q[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Integrating factor}&=I.F=e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx} \\ &=e^{2\log x} \\ &=e^{\log_{e}x^{2}}=x^{2} \\ y\times I.F&=\int Q\left ( I.F \right )dx \\ y.x^{2}&=\int \left ( \frac{x-1}{x^{2}} \right ).x^{2}.dx \\ &=\int \left ( x-1 \right )dx \\ yx^{2}&=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-x+C \\ \text{Now at }x=1, \;y=0,\\ \text{i.e. } 0\times 1^{2}&=\frac{1^{2}}{2}-1+C \\ 0&=\frac{1}{2}-1+C \\ C&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \therefore \;\; yx^{2}&=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-x+\frac{1}{2} \\ y&=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{2x^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

If a beam of rectangular cross-section is subjected to a vertical shear force V , the
shear force carried by the upper one-third of the cross-section is
raw_source.solution:
Shear stress at distance y from neutral axis,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tau&=\frac{S A \bar{y}}{1 b} =\frac{V \times\left(\frac{d}{2}-y\right) \times b \times\left(\frac{(d / 2)+y}{2}\right)}{16} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \tau&= \frac{V \times\left(\frac{d^{2}}{4}-y^{2}\right)}{21}\\ \therefore \quad d F&=\tau \times b d y=\frac{V \times\left(\frac{d^{2}}{4}-y^{2}\right)}{21} \times b d y\\ \end{aligned} [/latex]
Integrating both sides, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad F &=\frac{V b^{d / 2}}{21} \int_{d / 6}^{d}\left(\frac{d^{2}}{4}-y^{2}\right) d y \\ &=\frac{V b}{21}\left[\frac{d^{2}}{4} y-\frac{y^{3}}{3}\right]_{d / 6}^{d / 2} \\ &=\frac{V b}{21}\left[\frac{d^{3}}{8}-\frac{d^{3}}{24}-\frac{d^{3}}{24}+\frac{d^{3}}{648}\right] \\ &=\frac{V b}{21} \times \frac{d^{3}}{8} \times \frac{28}{81} \\ &=\frac{V b}{2 b d^{3}} \times \frac{d^{3}}{8} \times \frac{28}{81} \times 12=\frac{7 V}{27} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
As per IS:456-2000, consider the following statements

I. The modular ratio considered in the working stress method depends on the type of steel used.
II. There is an upper limit on the nominal shear stress in beams (even with shear reinforcement) due to the possibility of crushing of concrete in diagonal compression.
II. A rectangular slab whose length is equal to its width may not be a two-way slab for some support conditions.

The TRUE statements are
raw_source.solution:
Modular ratio, [latex]m=\frac{280}{3 \sigma_{c b c}} [/latex]
where [latex]\sigma_{c b c}[/latex] is permissible compressive stress due to bending in concrete in [latex]\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} .[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Working Stress and Limit State Method

raw_source.text:
In the design of welded tension members, consider the following statements :

I. The entire cross-sectional are of the connected leg is assumed to contribute to the effective area in case of angles.
II. Two angles back-to-back and tack-welded as per the codal requirements may be assumed to behave as a tee section.
III. A check on slenderness ratio may be necessary in some cases.

The TRUE statements are

Consider the following statements :

I. Effective length of a battened column in usually increased to account for the additional load on battens due to the lateral expansion of columns.
II. As per IS:800-1984, permissible stress in bending compression depends on both Euler buckling stress and the yield stress of steel.
III. As per IS:800-1984, the effective length of a column effectively held in position at both ends but not restrained against rotation, is taken to be greater than that in the ideal end conditions.

The TRUE statements are
raw_source.solution: The ideal condition is that column is effectively held in position at both ends but not restrained against rotation. IS 800 : 1984 prescribes the same value of effective length as taken for ideal end condition. Hence 3 is false.

raw_source.text: When the triangular section of a beam as shown below becomes a plastic hinge, the compressive force acting on the section (with [latex]\sigma _{y}[/latex] denoting the yield stress) becomes

Consider the following statements :

I. The width-to-thickness ratio limitations on the plate elements under compression in steel members are imposed by IS:800-1984 in order to avoid fabrication difficulties.
II. In a doubly reinforced concrete beam, the strain in compressive reinforcement is higher than the strain in the adjoining concrete.
III. If a cantilever I-section supports slab construction all along its length with sufficient friction between them, the permissible bending stress in compression will be the same as that in tension.
The TRUE statements are
raw_source.solution:
The width to thickness ratio limitations on the plate elements under compression in steel members are imposed by IS 800 : 1984 in order to avoid buckling at local points.
Statement (2) is wrong because strain in compression reinforcement and adjoning concrete is same to maintain compatibility.

raw_source.text: List-I below gives the possible types of failure for a finite soil slope and List-II gives the reasons for these different types of failure. Match the items in List-I with the items in List-II
raw_source.solution:
Face failure or slope failure can occur when the Slope angle [latex] \beta [/latex] is very high and the soil close to the toe is quite strong or the soil in the upper part of slope is relatively weak.
Base failure can occur when the soil below the toe is relatively weak and soft and the slope is flat.
Toe failure occurs in steep slopes when the soil mass above the base and below the base is homogeneous.

raw_source.text: For the soil profile shown in Figure below, the minimum number of precast concrete piles of 300 mm diameter required of safely carry the load for a given factor of safety of 2.5 (assuming 100% efficiency for the pile group) is equal to
raw_source.solution:
The ultimate load capacity of piles
[latex] =2.5 \times 5000=12,500 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]
The load capacity of single pile
[latex] \begin{aligned} =& c_{u} N_{c} A_{b}+\alpha \bar{c}_{u} A_{s} \\ =& 150 \times 9 \times \frac{\pi}{4} \times(0.3)^{2}+0.57 \times 100 \\ & \times 10 \times 0.3 \pi \\ =& 632.64 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] Number of piles
[latex] =\frac{12500}{632.64}=19.75 \approx 20[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a standard proctor test, 1.8 kg of moist soil was filling the mould (volume
= 94.4cc) after compaction. A soil sample weighing 23 g was taken from the
mould and ovendried for 24 hours at a temperature of 110[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Weight of the
dry sample was found to be 20 g. Specific gravity of soil solids is G = 2.7. The
theoretical maximum value of the dry unit weight of the soil at that water content
is equal to
raw_source.solution:
Bulk density of the soil
[latex] =\frac{1.8 \times 1000}{944}=1.907 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{cc}[/latex]
Water content of soil
[latex] =\left(\frac{23-20}{20}\right) \times 100=15 \%[/latex]
For, theoretical maximum dry unit weight, degree of saturation should be 100 %.
[latex] \begin{aligned} S e &=G w \\ \Rightarrow \quad e &=\frac{2.7 \times 0.15}{1} \Rightarrow e=0.405 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The theoretical maximum dry unit weight may be given as
[latex] \gamma_{d, \max }=\frac{G \gamma_{w}}{1+e}=\frac{2.7 \times 9.81}{1+0.405}=18.85 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A sample of saturated cohensionless soil tested in a drained triaxial compression
test showed an angle of internal friction of [latex]30^{\circ}[/latex]. The deviatoric stress at failure for the sample at a confining pressure of 200 kPa is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \sigma_{1} &=\sigma_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{9}{2}\right)+2 \mathrm{c} \tan \left(45+\frac{\phi}{2}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \sigma_{1} &=200 \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{30}{2}\right)+2 \times 0 \times \tan \left(45+\frac{30}{2}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \sigma_{1} &=600 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Deviatoric stress at failure
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}=600-200 \\ &=400 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The thickness of the laminar boundary layer on a flat plate at a point A is 2 cm
and at a point B, 1 m downstream of A, is 3 cm. What is the distance of A from the leading edge of the plate ?
raw_source.solution:
Laminar boundary layer thickness,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta &=5 \sqrt{\frac{x v}{V}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\delta_{A}}{\delta_{B}} &=\sqrt{\frac{x_{A}}{x_{B}}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{2}{3} &=\sqrt{\frac{x_{A}}{x_{A}+1}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{4}{9}&=\frac{x_{A}}{x_{A}+1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 5x_{A}&=4 \\ \Rightarrow x_{A}&= 0.8 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The velocity field for a flow is given by :
[latex]\vec{V}=(5x+6y+7z)\vec{i}[/latex] + [latex](6x+5y+9z)\vec{j}[/latex] + [latex](3x+2y+\lambda z)\vec{k}[/latex]
and the density varies as [latex]\rho =\rho _{0}exp(-2t)[/latex]. In order that the mass is conserved, the value of [latex]\lambda[/latex] should be
raw_source.solution:
The continuity equation is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}&+\frac{\partial(p u)}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial(\rho v)}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial(p w)}{\partial z}=0 \\ \text{Now,}\quad \rho&=\rho_{0} e^{-2 t} \\ \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} &=-2 \rho_{0} e^{-2 t}=-2 p \\ p \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=5 p, p \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}&=5 p, p \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=\lambda p \\ \therefore-2 p+5 p+5 p&+\lambda p=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 8 p+\lambda p&=0 \\ \text{or} \quad 8+\lambda&=0 \\ \text{or} \quad \lambda&=-8 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a cultivated area, the soil has porosity of 45% and field capacity of 38%. For a
particular crop, the root zone depth is 1.0m, the permanent wilting point is 10%
and the consumptive use is 15 mm/d. If the irrigation efficiency is 60%, what
should be the frequency of irrigation such that the moisture content does not fall
below 50% of the maximum available moisture ?
raw_source.solution:
Depth of maximum available moisture,
[latex] d_{w}=\frac{\gamma d}{\gamma_{w}}(F-\phi)[/latex]
Field capacity
[latex] \begin{aligned} &= \frac{\text { weight of water retained by soil }}{\text { weight of same area of soil }} \\ &=\frac{\gamma_{w} \times V_{v}}{\gamma \times V} \\ \text { But } \frac{V_{v}}{V}&=n \\ \therefore \text { Field capacity } &=\frac{\gamma_{w}}{\gamma} \times n\\ \Rightarrow \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}}{\gamma} &=\frac{n}{\text{Field capicity}} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}}{\gamma} &=\frac{0.45}{0.38} \\ \therefore \quad \quad d_{w} &=\frac{0.45}{0.38} \times 1 \times[0.38-0.1] \\ &=0.331 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
But the moisture content should not fall below 50 %
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Depth of water required
[latex] =0.5 \times 0.331=0.165 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Actual depth stored
[latex] =\frac{0.165 \times 60}{100}=0.099 \mathrm{m}=99 \mathrm{mm}[/latex]
Frequency of irrigation
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\frac{\text { Actual depth stored }}{\text { Consumptive use }}=\frac{99}{15} \\ =6.63 \mathrm{d} \simeq 6 \mathrm{d} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A hydraulic jump occurs in a rectangular, horizontal, frictonless channel. What
would be the pre-jump depth if the discharge per unit width is 2 [latex]m^{3}/s/m[/latex] and the energy loss is 1 m ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{2 q^{2}}{g} &=y_{1} y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right) \quad \ldots(i)\\ H_{L} &=\frac{\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{3}}{4 y_{1} y_{2}} \quad\ldots(ii)\\ \text{Given,}\\ H_{L} &=1 \mathrm{m} \\ \left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{3} &=4 \mathrm{y}_{1} \cdot \mathrm{y}_{2}\\ \text{Put,}\quad y_{2}&=m y_{1} \text { in equation (ii) } \\ y_{1}&=\frac{4 m}{(m-1)^{3}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly, put [latex] y_{2}=m y_{1} [/latex] in equation (i), we get
[latex] \begin{array}{l} m(m+1) y_{1}^{3}=\frac{2 \times 2^{2}}{9.81}=0.8155 \\ m(m+1)\left\{\frac{4 m}{(m-1)^{3}}\right\}^{3}=0.8155\\ \frac{m(m+1)\left(m^{3}\right)}{(m-1)^{9}}=\frac{0.8155}{4^{3}}\\ \text{By trial and error,} m=5.09 \\ y_{1}=0.3 \mathrm{m} \\ y_{2}=1.527 \mathrm{m} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
During a 3 hour storm event, it was observed that all abstractions other than
infiltration are negligible. The rainfall was idealized as 3 one hour storms of
intensity 10 mm/hr, 20 mm/hr and 10 mm/hr respectively and the infiltration
was idealized as a Horton curve, [latex]f = 6.8 + 8.7 exp(- t)[/latex] (f in mm/hr and t in hr). 
What is the effective rainfall ?
raw_source.solution:
From superposition of hyetograph and infiltration curve it is clear that first hour does not contribute to effective rainfall (i.e. rainfall excess).
For t=1 to t=3, the effective rainfall is,
[latex]\begin{aligned} r_e&=20+10-\int_{1}^{3} (6.8+8.7e^{-t})dt\\ &=30-\left [ (6.8t)_1^3+8.7 \int_{1}^{3}e^{-t} dt\right ] \\ &= 30-[6.8 \times 2 -8.7(e^{-t})_1^3]\\ &=30-13.6+8.7\left [ \frac{1}{e^3}-\frac{1}{e^1} \right ] \\ &= 16.4-2.77\\ &= 13.63mm \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A very wide rectangular channel is designed to carry a discharge of 5 [latex]m^3/s[/latex] per
meter width. The design is based on the Manning's equation with the roughness
coefficient obtained from the grain size using Strickler's equation and results in a
normal depth of 1.0 m. By mistake, however, the engineer used the grain diameter
in mm in the Strickler's equation instead of in meter. What should be the correct
normal depth?
raw_source.solution:
As per Strickler's equation, [latex]n=\frac{d^{1 / 6}}{24} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \frac{n_{\text {correct }}}{n_{\text {wrong }}}=\left(\frac{1}{1000}\right)^{1 / 6} [/latex]
Now, as per Mannings equation,
[latex] q=\frac{1}{n}(y)^{5 / 3} \sqrt{S}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Correct depth of flow,
[latex] \begin{aligned} y_{\text {contect }} &=\left(\frac{n_{\text {correct }}}{n_{\text {wrong }}}\right)^{3 / 5} \times y_{\text {wrong }} \\ &=\left[\left(\frac{1}{1000}\right)^{1 / 6}\right]^{3 / 5} \times 1 \\ &=0.50 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The flow of glycerin (kinematic viscosity [latex]v = 5 \times 10^{-4}m^{2}/s[/latex]) in an open channel
is to be modeled in a laboratory flume using water ([latex]v = 10^{-6}m^{2}/s[/latex]) as the flowing fluid. If both gravity and viscosity are important, what should be the length scale
(i.e. ratio of prototype to model dimensions) for maintaining dynamic similarity ?
raw_source.solution:
Equating Reynolds number and Froude number, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{t} L}{v_{r}} &=\frac{V_{r}}{\sqrt{L}} \\ \therefore\quad L_{r} &=\left(v_{r}\right)^{2 / 3} \\ v_{r} &=\frac{v_{m}}{v_{p}}=\frac{10^{-6}}{5 \times 10^{-4}}=2 \times 10^{-3} \\ \Rightarrow\quad L_{r} &=\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2 / 3} \\ \Rightarrow\quad L_{r} &=0.0159 \quad \text { But } \cdot L_{r}=\frac{L_{m}}{L_{p}} \\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{L_{p}}{L_{m}} &=\frac{1}{L_{r}}=\frac{1}{0.0159}=62.99 \approx 63 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The mean indoor airborne Chloroform ([latex]CHCI_3[/latex]) concentration in a room was determine to be 0.4[latex] \mu g/m^{3}[/latex]. Use the following data :
T = 293 K,
P = 1 atmosphere,
R =[latex] 82.05\times 10^{-6} atm.m^{3}[/latex]/mol-K,
Atomic weight : C=12, H=1, Cl=35.5.

This concentration expressed in parts per billion (volume basis, ppbv) is equal to
raw_source.solution:
The relation between [latex]\mu g/m^{3}[/latex] and ppm is,
[latex]1\mu g/m^{3}=\frac{1\: ppm \times \text{ molecular mass of pollutant in g/mol } }{\text{L/mol of pollutant at given temp. and pressure} \left ( V_{2} \right )} \times 10^3 \; L/m^3[/latex]
By Avogadro's law, we known that,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{1}V_{1}}{T_{1}}&= \frac{P_{2}V_{2}}{T_{2}}\\ \text{where }\; P_{1} &=1\text{atmosphere;} \\ T_{1} &=0^{\circ}C=273 \text{K} \\ V_{1} &=\text{volume at }0^{\circ}C \text{at 1 atmosphere} \\ &=22.4\: L/mol \\ \text{Given}\: P_{2} &=1\: \text{atmosphere}; \\ T_{2} &=293\text{K} \\ \therefore \; \; V_{2} &=\frac{P_{1}V_{1}T_{2}}{P_{2}T_{1}} \\ V_{2}&=\frac{22.4\times 293}{273} \\ V_{2} &=24.04\; L/mol \\ \because \; \; \; 0.4\; \mu \mu g/m^{3}\: \text{of}CHCl_{3} &=\frac{CHCl_{3}\; in\; ppm\times 119.5\times 10^{3}}{24.04} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \; \; CHCl_{3}[/latex] in ppm [latex]=8.0469\times 10^{-5}[/latex]
[latex] CHCl_{3}[/latex] in ppbv [latex]=8.0469\times 10^{-5}\times 10^{3} =0.08\; ppbv[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The composition of a certain MSW sample and specific weights of its various components are given below :

Specific weight ([latex]kg/m^3[/latex]) of the MSW sample is
raw_source.solution:
Let specific weight of MSW sample is X kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now,} \; \; \rho &= \frac{Total\; weight}{Total\; volume}\\ \frac{100}{X}&=\frac{50}{300}+\frac{30}{500}+\frac{10}{65}+\frac{10}{125} \\ \therefore \; \;\frac{100}{X} &=0.4605 \\ \therefore \;\; X &=217.15\; kg/m^{3}\approx 217\: kg/m^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A subgrade soil sample was tested using standard CBR apparatus and the observations are given below.

Assuming that the load-penetration curve is convex throughout, the CBR value(%) of the sample is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{CBR}_{2.5}&=\frac{\begin{array}{c}\text { Load sustained by }\\\text { specimend at 2.5 mm penetration} \end{array}}{\begin{array}{c}\text { Load sustained by standard }\\\text{aggregates at 2.5mm penetration} \end{array}} \times 100 \\ &=\frac{60.5}{1370} \times 100=4.4 \%\\ \text{Also} \\ \text{CBR}_{5.0}&=\frac{\begin{array}{c}\text { Load sustained by }\\\text { specimend at 5.0 mm penetration} \end{array}}{\begin{array}{c}\text { Load sustained by standard }\\\text{aggregates at 5 mm penetration} \end{array}} \times 100 \\ &=\frac{80.5}{2055} \times 100=3.9 \%\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus, the higher value of CBR which is obtained at 2.5 mm penetration is adopted i.e. 4.4%.

raw_source.text:
A vehicle moving at 60 kmph on an ascending gradient of a highway has to come
to stop position to avoid collision with a stationary object. The ratio of lag to
brake distance is 6:5. Considering total reaction time of the driver as 2.5 seconds
and the coefficient of longitudinal friction as 0.36, the value of ascending gradient(%) is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Lag distance } &=0.278 \mathrm{Vt} \\ &=0.278 \times 60 \times 2.5 \\ &=41.7 \mathrm{m} \\ \text { Brake distance }&=\frac{5}{6} \times 41.7=34.75 \mathrm{m} \\ &\left[\because \frac{\text { Lag distance }}{\text { Braking distance }}=\frac{6}{5}\right] \\ \text { Braking distance } &=\frac{V^{2}}{254(f+0.01 n)}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 34.75&=\frac{(60)^{2}}{254(0.36+0.01 n)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.01 n&=\frac{(60)^{2}}{254 \times 34.75}-0.36 \\ \Rightarrow \quad n&=4.8 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text:
For designing a 2-phase fixed type signal at an intersection having North-South and East-West road where only straight ahead traffic is permitted, the following data is available.
Total time lost per cycle is 12 seconds. The cycle lenght (second) as per webster's approach is
raw_source.solution:
For N-S road and E-W road the higher traffic volume will be taken i.e.
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{1} &=1000 \text { and } q_{2}=900 \\ S_{1} &=2500 \text { and } S_{2}=3000 \\ y_{1} &=\frac{q_{1}}{S_{1}}=\frac{1000}{2500}=0: 4\\ \text{and }\quad y_{2}&=\frac{q_{2}}{S_{2}}=\frac{900}{3000}=0.3 \\ \therefore\quad Y&=y_{1}+y_{2}=0.4+0.3=0.7 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Optimum cycle time,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{0} &=\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-Y}=\frac{1.5 \times 12+5}{1-0.7} \\ &=76.67 \approx 77 \mathrm{seconds} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
On an urban road, the free mean speed was measured as 70 kmph and the average spacing between the vehicles under jam condition as 7.0 m. The speed-flow-density equation is given by :
[latex]U=U_{sf}[1-\frac{k}{k_{j}}][/latex] and q=Uk

Where, U = space-mean speed (kmph); k= density (veh/km); [latex]U_{sf}[/latex] = free mean speed (kmph); [latex]k_j[/latex] = jam density (veh/km); q = flow (veh/hr).

The maximum flow (veh/hr) per lane for this condition is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Traffic volume }&=\text { Density } \times \text { Speed } \\ q&=U k \\ \Rightarrow \quad q&=U_{s t}\left(1-\frac{k}{k_{j}}\right) k \\ \Rightarrow \quad q&=U_{s f}\left(k-\frac{k^{2}}{k_{j}}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Jam density,
[latex] \begin{aligned} k_{j}&=\frac{1000}{\text { average spacing between vehicles }} \\ k_{j}&=\frac{1000}{7} \text { and } U_{s t}=70 \mathrm{kmph} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For maximum traffic volume,[latex] \frac{d q}{d k}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad U_{s f}\left(1-\frac{2 k}{k_{j}}\right)&=0 &\left[\because U_{sf}\neq 0 \right ]\\ \Rightarrow \quad 1-\frac{2 k}{k_{j}}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad k&=\frac{k_{j}}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] Maximum traffic volume,
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{\max }&=U_{s f}\left(\frac{k_{j}}{2}-\frac{\left(k_{j} / 2\right)^{2}}{k_{j}}\right) \\ &=U_{s t}\left(\frac{k_{j}}{2}-\frac{k_{j}}{4}\right)=U_{s t}\left(\frac{k_{j}}{4}\right) \\ &=70 \times \frac{1000}{7 \times 4}=2500 veh/hr \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
At an horizontal curve portion of a 4 lane undivided carriageway, a transition
curve is to be introduced to attain required superelevation.
The design speed is 60 kmph and radius of the curve is 245 m. Assume length of
wheel base of a longest vehicle as 6 m, superelevation rate at 5% and the rate of introduction of this superelevation as 1 in 150. The length of
the transition curve (m) required, if the pavement is rotated about inner edge is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]L_{s}=\frac{v^{3}}{C R} \dots[/latex]
according to allowable rate of centrifugal acceleration,
[latex] \begin{aligned} L_{s}&=\frac{(0.278 \times 60)^{3}}{0.59 \times 6245}=32.10 \mathrm{m}\\ C&=\frac{80}{V+75} \quad\text{(V is in kmph) }\\ \text{and}\quad L_{s}&=110.2 \mathrm{m}\\ &\dots\text{ according to superelevation}\\ L_{s}&=39.7 \mathrm{m}\\ &\dots\text{according to IRC formula }\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Maximum of above three will be the length of transition curve
[latex] L_{s}=110.2 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text:
Using IRC:37-1984 "Guidelines for the Design of Flexible Pavements" and the following data, choose the total thickness of the pavement.

NO. of commercial vehicles when construction is completed = 2723 veh/day
Annual growth rate of the traffic =5%
Design life of the pavement = 10 years
Vehicle damage factor =2.4
CBR value of the subgrade soil=5%
raw_source.solution:
Number of standard axles in msa is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{s} &=\frac{365 A\left[(1+r)^{n}-1\right]}{r \times 10^{6}}+F \\ &=\frac{365 \times 2723 \times\left[\left(1+\frac{5}{100}\right)^{10}-1\right]}{\frac{5}{100} \times 10^{6}} \times 2.4 \\ &=30 \mathrm{msa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, for 5 % CBR value, the total thickness of the pavement for 30 msa is given as 670 mm.

raw_source.text:
The observed magnetic bearing of a line OE was found to be 185[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. It was later discovered that station O had a local attraction of +1.5[latex]^{\circ}[/latex].
The true bearing of the line OE, considering a magnetic declination of 3.5[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]E shall be
raw_source.solution:
Observed magnetic bearing of [latex]\mathrm{OE}=185^{\circ} [/latex]
Local attraction at [latex]0=+1.5^{\circ} [/latex]
Corrected magnetic bearing of
[latex] O E=185^{\circ}-1.5^{\circ}=183.6^{\circ} [/latex]


[latex] \therefore [/latex] True bearing of OE = Corrected magnetic declination of OE + Magnetic declination
[latex] =103.6^{\circ}+3.5^{\circ}=187^{\circ}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A Bench Marck (BM) with Reduced Level (RL) = 155.305 m has been established
at the floor of a room. It is required to find out the RL of the underside of root
(R) of the room using Spirit Levelling. The Back Sight (BS) to the BM has been
observed as 1.500 m whereas the Fore Sight (FS) to R has been observed as 0.575
m (Shaff held inverted). The RL(m) of R will be
raw_source.solution:
Height of instrument
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\mathrm{RL} \text { of bench mark }+\mathrm{BS} \\ &=155.305+1.500 \\ &=156.805 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, the staff is held inverted and the foresight (FS) is 0.575m
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \text{ RL of R}&=\text{ Height of instrument }+ FS \\ &=156.805+0.575 \\ &=157.380 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the following figure, which is an extract from a contour map (scale =1:20,000) of an area. An alignment of a road at a ruling gradient of 4% is to be fixed from the point O and beyond. What should be the radius of the arc with O as the center to get the point of alignment on the next contour on the map ?
raw_source.solution:
The contour interval =20 m
For 4% gradient, the length needed from one contour to another

In a rapid sand filter, the time for reaching particle break through ([latex]T_B[/latex]) is defined as the time elapsed from start of filter run to the time at which the turbidity of the effluent from the filter is greater than 2.5 NTU. The time for reaching terminal head loss ([latex]T_H[/latex]) is defined as the time elapsed from the start of the filter run to the time when head loss across the filter is greater than 3 m.

The effect of increasing the filter depth (while keeping all other conditions same) on [latex]T_{B}[/latex] and [latex]T_{H}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
The effect of increase in certain rapid sand filter and influent particle characteristics on time ([latex]T_{B}[/latex]) for reaching particle breakthrough (turbidity [latex] \gt[/latex] 2.5 NTU) in the effluent, and time ([latex]T_{H}[/latex]) of reaching terminal head-loss([latex] \gt[/latex] 3 m) across filter bed are given below. Explain the results based on you understanding of filter operation and particle removal mechanisms operative in rapid sand filters. Assume that when one characteristic is changed, all other characteristic remain fixed.



Effect of increase in filter depth (L)
[latex]T_{B}[/latex] : [latex]T_{B}[/latex] will increase since particles in water will have the opportunity to potentially interact with more collectors, and hence the change for particle attachment to a collector is more.
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Since bed depth is more, water is encounter more resistance is passing through the bed. Hence [latex]T_{H}[/latex] will decrease.
Effect of increase in superdicial velocity ([latex]V_{s}[/latex])
[latex]T_{B}[/latex]: Since pore velocity is more, the shear forces experianced by collected particles will be more. Hence particle detachment will be more, leading to a decrease in [latex]T_{B}[/latex].
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Since particle loading rate on the filter and rate of particle collection in the filter will increase, the porosity of the filter bed will decrease more rapidly, leading to more rapid head-loss buildup and hence a decrease in [latex]T_{H}[/latex].
Effect of increase in influent particle concentration ([latex]C_{o}[/latex])
[latex]T_{B}[/latex]: Particle loading rate on the filter, rate of particle collection and hence porosity of the filter bed will decrease more rapidly. Thus pre velocity in the filter bed will increase more rapidly, leading to more rapid particle detachment. This will lead to decrease in [latex]T_{B}[/latex].
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Since particle loading rate on the filter and rate of particle collection in the filter will be increase, the porosity of the filter bed will decrease more rapidly, leading to more rapid head-loss buildup and hence a decrease in [latex]T_{H}[/latex].
Effect of increase in floc strength
[latex]T_{B}[/latex]: Particle detachment due to shear force will become less prominent leading to increase in [latex]T_{B}[/latex].
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Since particle retention in the filter will be more, the porosity of the filter bed will decline faster leading to faster buildup of head-loss and hence [latex]T_{H}[/latex] will decrease.
Effect of increase in collector diameter (d)
[latex]T_{B}[/latex]: Increase in collector diameter will mean the presence of a lesser number of collector in the filter media. This will result is lesser number of potential interaction between a particle and a collector. Thus [latex]T_{B}[/latex] is expected to decrease.
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Since lesser number of particle will be collected as mentioned above, the rate of head-loss buildup will be lower, leading to increase in [latex]T_{H}[/latex].
Effect of increase in porosity ([latex]\alpha [/latex])
It must be realized that the porosity of the filter media does not depend on particle size, but on grading of particles. Well-graded sand, i.e., with a broader particle size distribution will have less porosity, as compared to poorly graded sand with a narrower particle size distribution.
[latex]T_{B}[/latex] : In case poorly graded sand (with more porosity) is used as the filter media, the influent particles will potentially encounter lesser number of collectors and will not be collected efficiently.Hence [latex]T_{B}[/latex] will decrease.
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Increase in porosity of sand and poor particle collection as described above will result in lower rate of head-loss buildup and hence increase in [latex]T_{H}[/latex].
Effect of non-addition of coagulant
[latex]T_{B}[/latex]: If no coagulants are added, the particles will be stable and hence will not attach efficiently to the filter media. Hence [latex]T_{B}[/latex] will decrease.
[latex]T_{H}[/latex]: Since rate of particle clollection in the filter media will be lower as described above, the rate of head-loss buildup will also be lower, leading to an increase in [latex]T_{H}[/latex].

In the design of beams for the limit state of collapse in flexure as per IS:456-2000, let the maximum strain in concrete be limited to 0.0025 (in place of 0.0035). For this situation, consider a rectangular beam section with breadth as 250 mm, effective depth as 350 mm, area of tension steel as 1500 [latex]mm^2[/latex], and the characteristic strength of concrete and steel as 30 MPa and 250 MPa respectively.

The depth of neutral axis for the balanced failure is
raw_source.solution:
From similar triangles [latex]\Delta OAB[/latex] and [latex]\Delta OCD[/latex], we have,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{x_{u, \lim }}{0.0025}&=\frac{d-x_{u, \lim }}{\frac{f_{y}}{1.15 E_{s}}+0.002}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d-x_{u, \lim }}{x_{u, \lim }}&=\frac{\frac{f_{y}}{1.15 E_{s}}+0.002}{0.0025} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\frac{d}{x_{u, \lim }}&=1+\frac{\frac{0.87 \mathrm{f}_{y}}{E_{s}}+0.002}{0.0025} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\frac{d}{x_{u \min }}&=\frac{0.0045+\frac{0.87 f_{y}}{E_{s}}}{0.0025} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d}{x_{\text {Ulim }}}&=\frac{0.0045 E_{s}+0.87 \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{y}}}{0.0025 \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}} \\ &\qquad \left[\because E_{s}=2 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{MPa}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{x_{U, \bmod }}{d}&=\frac{500}{900+0.87 f_{y}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{u, \lim }&=\left[\frac{500}{900+0.87 \times 250}\right] \times 350 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{u, \lim}&=156.6 \mathrm{mm}=156 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

In the design of beams for the limit state of collapse in flexure as per IS:456-2000, let the maximum strain in concrete be limited to 0.0025 (in place of 0.0035). For this situation, consider a rectangular beam section with breadth as 250 mm, effective depth as 350 mm, area of tension steel as 1500 [latex]mm^2[/latex], and the characteristic strength of concrete and steel as 30 MPa and 250 MPa respectively.

At the limiting state of collapse in flexure, the force acting on the compression zone of the section is
raw_source.solution:
In strain diagram,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{O E}{O A}&=\frac{0.002}{0.0025} \\ \Rightarrow \quad O E&=\frac{4}{5} x_{u} \\ \Rightarrow \quad O E&=0.8 x_{u} \\ \therefore A E&=x_{u}-0.8 x_{u}=0.2 x_{u} \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex] \therefore \quad [/latex] Total compressive force,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &= 0.45 t_{c k} \times 0.2 x_{u} \times b+\frac{2}{3} \\ & \times 0.45 f_{c k} \times 0.8 x_{u} \times b \\ &= 0.33 f_{c k} b x_{u} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Actual NA depth,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C&=T\\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.33 f_{c k} b x_{u}&=0.87 f_{y} A_{s t} \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{u}&=\frac{0.87 \times 250 \times 1500}{0.33 \times 30 \times 250}=131.8 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Total compressive force,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=0.33 \times 30 \times 250 \times 131.8 \\ &=326 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The initial void ratio of the clay layer is

Coefficient of compression,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{c} &=\frac{e_{1}-e_{2}}{\log _{10}\left(\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{2}}{\bar{\sigma}_{1}}\right)} \\ &=\frac{0.6-0.5}{\log _{10}\left(\frac{300}{100}\right)}=0.2096\\ \text{also }\quad C_{c}&=\frac{e_{1}-e_{0}}{\log _{10}\left(\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{0}}{\bar{\sigma}_{1}}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.2096&=\frac{0.6-e_{0}}{\log _{10}\left(\frac{150}{100}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad e_{0}&=0.563 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The average effective overburden pressure on 10 m thick homogeneous saturated clay layer is 150 kPa. Consolidation test on an undisturbed soil sample taken from the clay layer showed that the void ratio decreased from 0.6 to 0.5 by increased the stress intensity from 100 kPa to 300 kPa. (G=2.65)

The total consolidation settlement of the clay layer due to the construction of a structure imposing an additional stress intensity of 200 kPa is

raw_source.text: The solution for the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{2}y[/latex] with the condition that y = 1 at x = 0 is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \frac{dy}{dx}=x^{2}y[/latex]
This is variable separable from,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dy}{y}&=x^{2}\, dx \\ \int \frac{dy}{y}&=\int x^{2}dx \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \log_{e}y&=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; y&=^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C_{1}} \\ &=e^{C_{1}}\times e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} \\ y&=C\times e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} \\ \text{Now at }& x=0, \;y=1 \\ 1&=C\times e^\frac{0}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C&=1 \\ \therefore \;\; y&=e^{\frac{x^{3}}{3}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For what values of [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] the following simultaneous equations have an infinite number of solutions ?
x + y + z = 5;
x + 3y + 3z = 9;
x + 2y + [latex]\alpha[/latex]z = [latex]\beta[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is,
[latex]\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ][/latex]
Using Gauss-elimination method we get
[latex]\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ]\xrightarrow[R_{3}-R_{1}]{\overset{R_{2}-R_{1}}{\rightarrow}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 1 & \alpha -1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -5 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R_{3}-\frac{1}{2}R_{2}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & \alpha -2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -7 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Now, for infinite solution last row must be completely zero
i.e. [latex]\alpha -2[/latex] and [latex]\beta -7=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;\; \alpha =2[/latex] and [latex]\beta =7[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A body originally at [latex]60^{\circ}C[/latex]
 cools down to 40[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C in 15 minutes when kept in air at a temperature 25[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. What will be the temperature of the body at the end of 30 minutes ?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned}\frac{d\theta }{dt}&=-K\left ( \theta -\theta _{0} \right )\\ \text{(Newtons law }&\text{of cooling)} \\ \frac{d\theta }{\theta -\theta _{0}}&=-K\, dt \\ \int \frac{d\theta }{\theta -\theta _{0}}&=\int -Kdt \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \ln \left ( \theta -\theta _{0} \right )&=-Kt+C_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \theta -\theta _{0}&=C.e^{-Kt} \\   \theta &=\theta _{0}+C.e^{-Kt}\\ \text{Given, } \theta _{0}&=25^{\circ}C \\ \text{Now at } t&=0,\, \theta =60^{\circ} \\  60&=25+ C.e^{0} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C&=35 \\ \therefore \;\;  \theta &=25+35e^{-Kt} \\ \text{at } t&=15 \text{ minutes}\\ \theta &=40^{\circ}C \\ \therefore \; 40&=25+35e^{-K\times 15} \\ \Rightarrow \;e^{-15K}&=\frac{3}{7}\\ \text{Now at }t&=30 \text{ minutes}, \\ \theta &=25+35e^{-30K} \\  &=25+35\left ( e^{-15K} \right )^{2} \\  &=25+35\times \left ( \frac{3}{7} \right )^{2} \\    &=31.428^{\circ}C\approx 31.5^{\circ}C \end{aligned}[/latex]

The following equation needs to be numerically solved using the Newton-Raphson method.

[latex]x^{3}+4x-9=0[/latex]

The iterative equation for this purpose is (k indicates the iteration level)

[latex]f\left ( x \right )=x^{3}+4x-9=0[/latex]
[latex] {f}'\left ( x \right )=3x^{2}+4[/latex]
N-R equation for iteration is,
[latex]\begin{aligned}x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{f\left ( X_{k} \right )}{{f}'\left ( X_{k} \right )} \\ f\left ( x_{k} \right )&=x_{k}^{3}+4x_{k}-9 \\ {f}'\left ( x_{k} \right )&=3x_{k}^{2}+4 \\ x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\frac{x_{k}^{3}+4x_{k}-9}{\left ( 3x_{k}^{2}+4 \right )} \\ x_{k+1}&=\frac{\left ( 3x_{k}^{3}+4x_{k} \right )-\left ( x_{k}^{3}+4x_{k}-9 \right )}{3x_{k}^{2}+4} \\ x_{k+1}&=\frac{2x_{k}^{3}+9}{3x_{k}^{2}+4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Evaluate [latex]\int_{0}^{\infty }\frac{sint}{t}dt[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Let
[latex]\begin{aligned} I\left ( \alpha \right )&=\int_{0}^{\infty }e^{-\alpha x}\frac{\sin x}{x}dx \\ \frac{dI}{d\alpha }&=\int_{0}^{\infty }\left ( -x \right )e^{-\alpha x}\left ( \frac{\sin x}{x} \right )dx \\ &=-\int_{0}^{\infty }e^{-\alpha x}\sin x\, dx \\ &=-\left [ \frac{e^{-\alpha x}}{1+\alpha ^{2}}\left ( -\alpha \sin x-1.\cos x \right ) \right ]_{0}^{\infty } \\ &=-\frac{1}{1+\alpha ^{2}} \\ \therefore\;\; \frac{dI}{d\alpha }&=-\frac{1}{1+\alpha ^{2}} \\ dI&=\frac{d\alpha }{1+\alpha ^{2}}\\ &\text{Intergrating,} \\ I&=-\tan ^{-1}\alpha +C \\ I\left ( \infty \right )&=-\frac{\pi }{2}+C\\ \text{but from (i), } & I\left ( \infty \right )=0 \\ \therefore \;\; -\frac{\pi }{2}+C&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; C&=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ \therefore \;\; I\left ( \alpha \right )&=-\tan ^{-1}\alpha +\frac{\pi }{2} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; I\left ( 0 \right )&=\frac{\pi }{2}-\tan ^{-1}0 \\ \therefore \;\; I\left ( 0 \right )&=\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}[/latex]
But from equation (i), [latex]I\left ( 0 \right )=\int_{0}^{\infty }\frac{\sin x}{x}dx [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\; \int_{0}^{\infty }\frac{\sin x}{x}dx=\frac{\pi }{2}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Given,

one root =5
Let the roots be [latex]\alpha ,\, \beta \, \text{and }\, \gamma[/latex] of equation,
[latex]\begin{aligned} ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d&=0 \\ \alpha \beta \gamma &= -\frac{d}{a}\\ \text{ and }\alpha \beta +\beta \gamma +\gamma \alpha &=+\frac{c}{a} \\ \therefore \; \alpha \beta \gamma =5\times \beta \gamma &=\frac{-\left ( -30 \right )}{1}=30 \\ \Rightarrow \;\;\beta \gamma &=6\;\;\;...(i)\\ \text{ Also } \alpha \beta +\beta \gamma +\gamma \alpha &=5\beta +\beta \gamma +5\alpha \\ &=\frac{31}{1}=31 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 5\left ( \beta +\gamma \right )+\beta \gamma &=31 \\ \text{since } \beta \gamma &=6 \text{ from (i),}\\ \therefore \;\; 5\left ( \beta +\gamma \right )+6&=31 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \beta +\gamma &=5 \\ \beta \gamma &=6\\ \text{Solving for } &\beta \text{ and }\gamma , \\ \beta \left ( 5-\beta \right )&=6 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \beta ^{2}-5\beta +6&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \beta =2 \text{ and }\gamma &=3\end{aligned}[/latex]

For what values of [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] the following simultaneous equations have an infinite number of solutions ?
x + y + z = 5;
x + 3y + 3z = 9;
x + 2y + [latex]\alpha[/latex]z = [latex]\beta[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is,
[latex]\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ][/latex]
Using Gauss-elimination method we get
[latex]\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 &1 \\ 1& 3 & 3\\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \end{matrix}\right| \begin{matrix} 5\\ 9\\ \beta \end{matrix}\right ]\xrightarrow[R_{3}-R_{1}]{\overset{R_{2}-R_{1}}{\rightarrow}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 1 & \alpha -1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -5 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R_{3}-\frac{1}{2}R_{2}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & \alpha -2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 5\\ 4\\ \beta -7 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Now, for infinite solution last row must be completely zero
i.e. [latex]\alpha -2[/latex] and [latex]\beta -7=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;\; \alpha =2[/latex] and [latex]\beta =7[/latex]

Consider the following statements :
1. The compressive strength of concrete decreases with increase in water-cement ratio of the concrete mix
2. Water is added to the concrete mix for hydration of cement and workability.

mm (depth) is prestressed by a straight tendon to an effective force of 150 kN at
an eccentricity of 20 mm (below the centroidal axis in the depth direction). The
stresses at the top and bottom fibres of the section are
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{top}} &=\frac{P}{A}-\frac{P e}{Z} \\ &=\frac{150 \times 10^{3}}{120 \times 200}-\frac{150 \times 10^{3} \times 20 \times 6}{120 \times(200)^{2}} \\ &=6.25-3.75 \\ &=2.5 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}(\text { compression }) \\ \sigma_{\text {bottom }} &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e}{Z}=6.25+3.75 \\ &=10 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \text { (compression) } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following statements :

1. Modulus of elasticity of concrete increases with increase in compressive strength of concrete.
2. Brittleness of concrete increases with decrease in compressive strength of concrete.
3. Shear strength of concrete increase with increase in compressive strength of concrete.

The TRUE statements are
raw_source.solution:
1. Modulus of elasticity of concrete increases with increase in compressive strength.
TRUE — Elastic modulus is approximately:
[latex] E_c \propto \sqrt{f_{ck}} [/latex]

2. Brittleness of concrete increases with decrease in compressive strength.
FALSE — High-strength concrete is more brittle. Lower strength → more ductile, not more brittle.

3. Shear strength of concrete increases with increase in compressive strength.
TRUE — Shear strength is roughly proportional to:
[latex] \tau_c \propto \sqrt{f_{ck}} [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Working Stress and Limit State Method

raw_source.text: A steel flat of rectangular section of size [latex]70\times 6[/latex] mm is connected to a gusset plate by three bolt each having a shear capacity of 15 kN in holes having diameter 11.5 mm. Along (2)-(2)

raw_source.text: A bracket connection is made with four bolts of 10 mm diameter and supports a load of 10 kN at an eccentricity of 100 mm. The maximum force to be resisted by any bolt will be
