[latex]\begin{aligned} F_{1}&=\frac{P}{4}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5\, kN \\ F_{2}&= \text{stress due to moment } \\ F_{2}&=\frac{\left ( Pe \right )\times r_{1}}{\sum r^{2}_{i}} \\ r_{1} &= r_{2} =r_{4} \\ &= \sqrt{30^{2}+40^{2}}=50 mm \\ F_{2}&=\frac{10\times 100\times 50}{2500\times 4}=5 kN \\ \tan \theta &=\frac{30}{40} \\ \theta &=37^{\circ} \\ &\text{Resultant force} \\ &=\sqrt{F_{1}^{2}+F^{2}_{2}+2F_{1}F_{2}\cos \theta } \\ &=\sqrt{\left ( 2.5 \right )^{2}+\left ( 5 \right )^{2}+2\times 2.5\times 5\times \cos 37^{\circ}} \\ &=7.16\, kN \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Match the following groups

The bearing capacity of a rectangular footing of plan dimensions 1.5m x 3m resting on the surface of a sand deposit was estimated as 600 kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] when the water table is far below the base of the footing. The bearing capacities in kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex] when the water level rises to depths of 3 m, 1.5 m and 0.5 m below the base of the footing are
raw_source.solution:
The bearing capacity of the sand deposit will remain same until the water table rises to a depth less than the width of the footing. Thus, when water table is 3.0 below footing, the bearing capacity is [latex]600 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex];
similarly when water table is 1.5m below footing, the bearing capacity remaining same i.e. [latex]600 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex].
But when the water table rises to a depth of 0.5m below the footing, the sand deposit will be saturated for a depth of 1.5-0.5=1m. Thus, the bearing capacity below the base of footing will decrease due to submergence of soil (1m).

raw_source.text: Flow rate of a fluid (density = 1000 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex]) in a small diameter tube is 800 [latex]mm^{3}/s[/latex]. The length and the diameter of the tube are 2 m and 0.5 mm, respectively. The pressure drop in 2 m length is equal to 2.0 MPa. The viscosity of the fluid is
raw_source.solution:
Applying Hagen-Poiseuille equation, the drop in pressure is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{1}-p_{2} &=\frac{32 \mu V L}{D^{2}} \\ \text{But}\quad Q &=A V \\ \Rightarrow\quad V &=\frac{Q}{A} \\ &=\frac{800 \times 4}{\pi \times(0.5)^{2}} \\ &=4074.37 \mathrm{mm} / \mathrm{s} \simeq 4.07 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \therefore \quad 2 \times 10^{6} &=\frac{32 \times \mu \times 4.07 \times 2}{\left(0.5 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow\quad \mu &=1.92 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Ns} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ &=0.00192 \mathrm{Ns} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The flow rate in a wide rectangular open channel is 2.0 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] per metre width. The
channel bed slope is 0.002. The Manning's roughness coefficient is 0.012. The slope of the channel is classified as
raw_source.solution:
The critical depth for a rectangular channel is given by
[latex] y_{c}=\left(\frac{q^{2}}{g}\right)^{1 / 3}=\left(\frac{(2)^{2}}{9.81}\right)^{1 / 3}=0.74 m[/latex]
Using Manning's equation, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} & q=\frac{1}{n}\left(y_{n}\right)^{5 / 3} \sqrt{S} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2&=\frac{1}{0.012} \times\left(y_{n}\right)^{5 / 3} \times \sqrt{0.002}\\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{n}&=0.69 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
For steep slopes [latex]y_{n} \lt y_{c}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two electrostatic precipitators (ESPs) are in series. The fractional efficiencies of
the upstream and downstream ESPs for size [latex]d_{p}[/latex]
 are 80% and 65%, respectively.
What is the overall efficiency of the system for the same [latex]d_{p}[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
Given data: [latex]\eta _{1}=80%;\; \; \eta _{2}=65%[/latex]
Since the efficiency of upstream ESP is 80%, only 20% of the particulate are not removed. These remaining particulates will face the downstream ESP whose efficiency is 65%.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Particulates removed by downstream,
[latex] ESP=20\times \frac{65}{100}=13\%[/latex]
The two ESPs are connected in series, therefore the overall efficiency = 80 + 13 = 93%.

raw_source.text: 50 g of [latex]CO_{2}[/latex] and 25 g of [latex]CH_{4}[/latex] are produced from the decomposition of municipal solid waste (MSW) with a formula weight of 120 g. What is the average per capita green house gas production in a city of 1 million people with a MSW production rate of 500 ton/day ?
raw_source.solution:
We know that both [latex]CO_{2}[/latex] and [latex]CH_{4}[/latex] are green house gases.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Total green house gases produced by 120 gm of MSW
= 50 g [latex]CO_{2}[/latex] +25 g of [latex]CH_{4}[/latex]=75 gm
500 ton of MSW will produce green house gases
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=500\times 10^{6}\times \frac{75}{120} \\ &= 312.5\times 10^{6}\: g/day \end{aligned}[/latex]
Per capita average production of green house gases
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{312.5\times 10^{6}}{1\times 10^{6}}\: g/day \\ &=312.5\: g/day\approx 313\: g/day \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} E_{w} &=\frac{n L^{2}}{2 R}+\frac{V}{9.5 \sqrt{R}} \\ &=\frac{2 \times(8)^{2}}{2 \times 300}+\frac{100}{9.5 \sqrt{300}}=0.82 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

While designing a hill road with a ruling gradient of 6%, if a sharp horizontal
curve of 50 m radius is encountered, the compensated gradient at the curve as per
the Indian Roads Congress specifications should be
raw_source.solution:
Grade compensation is given by,
[latex] \frac{30+R}{R}\text{ or }\frac{75}{R}[/latex] whichever is minimum
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \frac{30+50}{50}&=\frac{80}{50}=1.6 \\ \text{or }\frac{75}{50}&=1.5 \\ \therefore \quad G.C. &=1.5 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Ruling gradient =6 %
Compensated gradient =6-1.5=4.5%

raw_source.text:
The design speed on a road is 60 kmph. Assuming the driver reaction time of

stopping distance for two-way traffic on a single lane road is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} \text { Stopping Distance }=0.278 \mathrm{V} t+\frac{v^{2}}{254 \mathrm{f}} \\ =0.278 \times 60 \times 2.5+\frac{(60)^{2}}{254 \times 0.35}=82.1 \mathrm{m} \end{array}[/latex]
But the traffic is two way, therefore the stopping distance [latex]=2 \times 82.1=164.2 \mathrm{m} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The width of the expansion join is 20 mm in a cement concrete pavement. The paying temperature is [latex]20^{\circ}C[/latex] and the maximum slab temperature in summer is [latex]60^{\circ}C[/latex]. The coefficient of the thermal expansion of concrete is [latex]10\times 10^{-6} mm/mm/^{\circ}C[/latex] and the joint filler compresses up to 50% of the thickness. The spacing between expansion joints should be
raw_source.solution:
The spacing of expansion joint is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} L_{e} &=\frac{\delta^{\prime}}{100 C\left(T_{2}-T_{1}\right)} \\ \text { Given } \delta &=\frac{\text { Width of expansion joint }}{2} \\ &=\frac{20}{2}=10 \mathrm{mm} \\ L_{e} &=\frac{1}{100 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}(60-20)}=25 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A completely mixed activated sludge process is used to treat a wastewater flow of 1 million litres per day (1 MLD) having a [latex]BOD_5[/latex] of 200 mg/L. The biomass concentration in the aeration tank is 2000 mg/L and the concentration of the net biomass leaving the system is 50 mg/L. The aeration tank has a volume of 200 [latex]m^3[/latex].

What is the hydraulic retention time of the wastewater in aeration tank ?
raw_source.solution:
The hydraulic retention time is given by,
[latex] t=\frac{V}{Q} \times 24[/latex]
where V= Volume of aeration tank
Q= Quantity of waste water flow into the aeration tank excluding the quantity of recycled sludge
[latex] \therefore \quad t=\frac{200}{1 \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-3}} \times 24=4.8 \mathrm{h}[/latex]

A completely mixed activated sludge process is used to treat a wastewater flow of 1 million litres per day (1 MLD) having a [latex]BOD_5[/latex] of 200 mg/L. The biomass concentration in the aeration tank is 2000 mg/L and the concentration of the net biomass leaving the system is 50 mg/L. The aeration tank has a volume of 200 [latex]m^3[/latex].

What is the average time for which the biomass stays in the system ?
raw_source.solution:
The average time for which the biomass stays in the system is known as sludge age [latex]\left(\theta_{\mathrm{c}}\right)[/latex] and it is given by,
[latex] \theta_{c}=\frac{\text { Mass of biomass in the system }}{\text { Mass of biomass leaving the system per day }} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \theta_{c}=\frac{200 \times 10^{3} \times 2000}{50 \times 10^{6}} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \theta_{c}=8 \text{days}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A two span continuous beam having equal spans each of length L is subjected to a uniformly distributed load w per unit length. The beam has constant flexural rigidity.

The reaction at the middle support is
raw_source.solution:
Removing support C, we get deflection at C as
[latex] \delta_{c}=\frac{5}{384} \times \frac{m(2 L)^{4}}{E I}(\downarrow)[/latex]
Let reaction at support C is R, then considering only R, we get deflection at C as,
[latex] \delta_{c}^{\prime}=\frac{R(2 L)^{3}}{48 E I}(\uparrow)[/latex]
For no deflection at C,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta_{c}-\delta_{c}^{\prime}&=0\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{5}{384} \times \frac{m(2 L)^{4}}{E I}&=\frac{R \times(2 L)^{3}}{48 E I} \\ \Rightarrow R=\frac{5}{384} \times 48 w \times 2 L&=\frac{5 w L}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A two span continuous beam having equal spans each of length L is subjected to a uniformly distributed load w per unit length. The beam has constant flexural rigidity.

The bending moment at the middle support is
raw_source.solution:
Let reaction at A and B be [latex]R_{A}[/latex] and [latex]R_{B}[/latex] , then as the beam is symmetrically loaded, the reaction [latex]R_{A}[/latex] and [latex]R_{B}[/latex] will be equal.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad R_{A}=R_{B} &=\frac{w \times 2 L-\frac{5 w L}{4}}{2} \\ &=\frac{8 m-5 w}{4 \times 2}=\frac{3 w L}{8} \\ \text { Thus, } \quad B M_{C} &=\frac{3}{8} w L \times L-w \times L \times \frac{L}{2}=\frac{w L^{2}}{8} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The ground conditions at a site are as shown in the figure. The water table at the site which was initially at a depth of 5 m below the ground level got permanently lowered to a depth of 15 m below the ground level due to pumping of water over a few years. Assume the following data :

I unit weight of water= 10 [latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex]
II unit weight of sand above water table= 18 [latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex]
III unit weight of sand and clay below the water table= 20 [latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex]
IV coefficient of volume compressibility= 0.25 [latex]m^{2}[/latex]/MN

What is the change in the effective stress in [latex]kN/m^{2}[/latex] at mid-depth of the clay layer due to the lowering of the water table ?
raw_source.solution:
Initial total, pore and effective stresses at central layer are
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{c-c} &=5 \times 18+15 \times 20+2.5 \times 20 \\ &=440 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ u_{c-c} &=(15+2-5) \times 10=175 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \left(\sigma^{\prime}\right)_{1}=& 265 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
After the drawdown of GWT, changes in total and pore pressure at central layer are as follows
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{c-c}&=15 \times 18+5 \times 20+2.5 \times 20 \\ &=420 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} & \\ &\begin{aligned} u_{c-c}&=7.5 \times 10=75 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ (\sigma)_{2}&=345 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \Delta \sigma^{\prime}&=345-265 \\ \Delta \sigma^{\prime}&=80 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A rectangular open channel needs to be designed to carry a flow of 2.0 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] under uniform flow conditions. The Manning's roughness coefficient is 0.018. The channel should be such that the flow depth is equal to half the width, and the Froude number is equal to 0.5

The bed slope of the channel to be provided is
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]Q=2 m^{3} / s, n=0.018, B=2 y, F=0.5 [/latex]
We know that
[latex] F=\frac{V}{\sqrt{g D}} [/latex]
where V is velocity of flow, D is hydraulic radius
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Now }D=\frac{A}{T}&=\frac{B y}{B}=y \\ \therefore \quad F&=\frac{Q}{A \sqrt{g y}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.5&=\frac{2}{2 y^{2} \times \sqrt{g y}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.5&=\frac{1}{y^{2} \sqrt{g y}}[ \text{ Squaring both sides }] \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow 0.25&=\frac{1}{g y^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=\left(\frac{1}{0.25 \times 9.81}\right)^{1 / 5} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=0.836 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using Manning's equation, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=\frac{1}{n} A(R)^{2 / 3} \sqrt{S} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2&=\frac{1}{0.018} \times\left[2 \times(0.836)^{2}\right] \\ &\times\left(\frac{0.836}{2}\right)^{2 / 3} \sqrt{S} \\ \Rightarrow \sqrt{S}&=0.0461 \\ \Rightarrow \quad S&=0.0021 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A rectangular open channel needs to be designed to carry a flow of 2.0 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] under uniform flow conditions. The Manning's roughness coefficient is 0.018. The channel should be such that the flow depth is equal to half the width, and the Froude number is equal to 0.5

Keeping the width, flow depth and roughness the same, if the bed slope of the above channel is double, the average boundary shear stress under uniform flow conditions is
raw_source.solution:
The average shear stress, [latex]\tau_{0}=\gamma \mathrm{RS}_{0} [/latex]
Bed slope is doubled i.e.
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{0} &=2 \times 0.0021=0.0042 \\ \therefore \quad \tau &=9810 \times \frac{0.836}{2} \times 0.0042 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \tau_{0} &=17.22 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A plain sedimentation tank with a length of 20 m, width of 10 m, and a depth of 3 m is used in a water treatment plant to treat 4 million litres of water per day (4 MLD). The average temperature of water is 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. The dynamic viscosity of water is [latex]1.002 \times 10^{-3}N.s/m^2[/latex] at 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Density of water is 998.2 [latex]kg/m^3[/latex]. Average specific gravity of particles is 2.65.

What is the minimum diameter of the particle which can be removed with 100% efficiency in the above sedimentation tank ?
raw_source.solution:
Settling velocity,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{s} &=\frac{H}{t} \\ \text{But} \; \; \; \; \; \; \; t&=\frac{Volume\; of\; tank}{Rate\; of\; flow} \\ &=\frac{20\times 10\times 3\times 24\times 60\times 60}{4\times 10^{6}\times 10^{-3}} \\ &=12960\; \text {seconds} \\ \therefore \; \; \; \; \; \; \; V_{s} &=\frac{3\times 1000}{12960}=0.2315\; \text{mm/s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Let the velocity of the particle which can be removed with 100% efficiency be [latex]{V}'_{s}[/latex] then
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{{V}'_{s}}{V_{s}}\times 100 &=100 \\ \Rightarrow {V}'_{s} &=V_{s} \\ \frac{g}{18}\left ( S_{s}-1 \right )\frac{d^{2}\rho }{\mu } &=0.2315\times 10^{-3} \\ \frac{9.81}{18}\left ( 2.65-1 \right )d^{2}\times \frac{998.2}{1.002\times 10^{-3}} &=0.2315\times 10^{-3} \\ d^{2}&=2.58\times 10^{-10} \\ d &=1.6\times 10^{-5}\text{m} \\ &=16\times 10^{-3}\text{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The general solution of [latex]\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+y=0[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+y&=0 \\ D^{2}+1&=0 \\ D=\pm i &=0\pm 1i \\ &\text{General solution is,} \\ y&=e^{0x}\left [ C_{1}\cos \left ( 1\times x \right )+C_{2}\sin \left ( 1\times x \right ) \right ] \\ &=C_{1}\cos x+C_{2}\sin x \\ &=P\cos x+Q\sin x \end{aligned}[/latex]
where P and Q are some constants.

raw_source.text: The equation [latex]k_{x}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}+k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}=0[/latex] can be transformed to [latex]\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2_{t}}+\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}=0[/latex] by substituting
raw_source.solution:
Put
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{i}&=x\sqrt{\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial x}&=\sqrt{\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{\partial x}{\partial x_{t}}&=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}} \;\; ...(i)\\ &\text{Now given equation is} \\ k_{x}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} & +k_{z}\left ( \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} \right )=0 \;\; ...(ii)\\ \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}&=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{t}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\times \frac{\partial x}{\partial x_{t}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\times \sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}} \right ) \\ &\text{ [from Eqn. (i)]}\\ &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}}\times \frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \right ) \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}}\times \left ( \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\times \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \right ) \right ) \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}}\times \left ( \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}\times \sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}\times \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}&=\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}\times \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}\\ \text{Now } & \text{substitute in eq.(ii) we get,} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} k_{x}\times \frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}\times \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}\: +\: k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}+k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}+\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}&=0\\ \text{which is the desired form,}&\\ \therefore \;\; x_{t}&=x\sqrt{\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The value of [latex]\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}(6-x-y)dxdy[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Since the limit is a function of x, we first integrate w.r.t. [latex]y[/latex] and then w.r.t. [latex]x[/latex],
[latex]\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dx\: dy\\&=\int_{0}^{3}dx\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dy \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left [ 6y-xy-\frac{y^{2}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{x} \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left ( 6x-x^{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2} \right ) \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}\left ( 6x-\frac{3x^{2}}{2} \right )dx \\ &=\left [ 6\left ( \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right )-\frac{3}{2}\left ( \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right ) \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left [ 3x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=27-\frac{27}{2}=13.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Three values of x and y are to be fitted in a straight line in the form y=a+bx
 by the method of least squares. Given [latex]\sum x=6, \; \sum y=21, \; \sum x^{2}=14[/latex] and [latex]\sum xy=46[/latex], the values of a and b are respectively
raw_source.solution: [latex]   \begin{aligned} y&=a+bx\\ &\text{Given}\\    n&=3,\: \sum x=6,\\ \sum y&=21\: \sum x^{2}=14\\   \sum xy&=46 \\    b&=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^{2}-\left ( \sum x \right )^{2}} \\    a&=\bar{y}-b\bar{x} \\     &=\frac{\sum y}{n}-b\frac{\sum x}{n}\\ &\text{Substituting, we get} \\    b&=\frac{\left ( 3\times 46 \right )-\left ( 6\times 21 \right )}{\left ( 3\times 14 \right )-\left ( 6 \right )^{2}}=2 \\    a&=\frac{21}{3}-2\times \left ( \frac{6}{3} \right )=3 \\ \therefore \;\;   a&=3 \text{ and }b=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Solution of [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}[/latex] at x = 1 and y = [latex]\sqrt{3}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned}  \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=\frac{-x}{y} \\ \Rightarrow  \;\; ydy&=-xdx \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  \int ydy&=\int -xdx \\   \frac{y^2}{2}&=-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+C \\ \text{at }   x&=1,\: y=\sqrt{3} \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{\left ( \sqrt{3} \right )^{2}}{2}&=\frac{-1^{2}}{2}+C \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  C&=2 \\ \therefore \;\; \text{Solution is,} \\   \frac{y^{2}}{2}&=\frac{-x^{2}}{2}+2 \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  x^{2}+y^{2}&=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
If probability density function of random variable X is
[latex]\begin{matrix} f(x) & =x^2 &for \; -1\leq x\leq 1,and \\ & =0 & for \; any \; other \; value \; of \;x \end{matrix}[/latex]
then, the percentage probability [latex]P(-\frac{1}{3}\leq x\leq \frac{1}{3})[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex]\begin{aligned} f\left ( x \right )&=x^{2} \;\;\; -1\leq x\leq 1 \\ &=0 \;\;\; \text{elsewhere}\\ P\left ( -\frac{1}{3}\leq x\leq \frac{1}{3} \right )&=\int_{-\frac{1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{3}}f\left ( x \right )dx \\&=\int_{-\frac{1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{3}}x^{2}\: dx \\ &=\left [ \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right ]_{\frac{-1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{3}} \\ &=\frac{2}{81} \end{aligned} [/latex]
The probability expressed in percentage,
[latex]p=\frac{2}{81}\times 100=2.469\%=2.47\%[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A person on a trip has a choice between private car and public transport. The
probability of using a private car is 0.45. While using the public transport, further
choices available are bus and metro, out of which the probability of commuting
by a bus is 0.55. In such a situation, the probability (rounded up to two decimals)
of using a car, bus and metro, respectively would be
raw_source.solution:
Given, p(private car)=0.45
p(bus|public transport)=0.55
Since a person has a choice between private car and public transport,
p(public transport) = 1-p(private car)
=1-0.45=0.55
P(bus)=p(bus [latex]\cap[/latex] public transport)
=p(bus|public transport) [latex]\times[/latex] p(public transport)
=0.55 [latex]\times[/latex] 0.55
=0.3025 [latex]\simeq[/latex] 0.30
Now p(metro)=1-[p(private car)+p(bus)]
=1-(0.45+0.30)=0.25
[latex]\therefore[/latex] p(private car)=0.45
p(bus)=0.30
and p(metro)=0.25

raw_source.text:
The following simultaneous equations
x + y + z = 3
x + 2y + 3z = 4
x + 4y + kz = 6
will NOT have a unique solution for k equal to
raw_source.solution:
The augmented matrix for given system is,
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 4 & k \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 3\\ 4\\ 6 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Using Gauss elimination we reduce this to an upper triangular matrix to investigate its rank
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 4 & k \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 3\\ 4\\ 6 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[R_{3}-R_{1}]{R_{2}-R_{1}}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1\\ 0 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 3 & k-1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 3\\ 1\\ 3 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[R_{3}-3R_{2}]{}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 1 &1 & 1\\ 0 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & k-7 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 3\\ 1\\ 0 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Now if [latex] k\neq 7 \\ [/latex]
rank (A)=rank (A|B)=3
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Unique solution.
if k=7, rank (A)=rank(A|B)=2
which is less than number of variables
[latex]\therefore[/latex] when k=7
unique solution is not possible and only infinite solution is possible.

raw_source.text: The equation [latex]k_{x}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}+k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}=0[/latex] can be transformed to [latex]\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2_{t}}+\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}=0[/latex] by substituting
raw_source.solution:
Put
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{i}&=x\sqrt{\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial x}&=\sqrt{\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{\partial x}{\partial x_{t}}&=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}} \;\; ...(i)\\ &\text{Now given equation is} \\ k_{x}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} & +k_{z}\left ( \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2} \right )=0 \;\; ...(ii)\\ \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}&=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{t}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\times \frac{\partial x}{\partial x_{t}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\times \sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}} \right ) \\ &\text{ [from Eqn. (i)]}\\ &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}}\times \frac{\partial }{\partial x_{t}}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \right ) \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}}\times \left ( \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\, \left ( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\times \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \right ) \right ) \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}}\times \left ( \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}\times \sqrt{\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{k_{x}}{k_{z}}\times \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2} \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x^2}&=\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}\times \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}\\ \text{Now } & \text{substitute in eq.(ii) we get,} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} k_{x}\times \frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}\times \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}\: +\: k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}+k_{z}\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_{t}^2}+\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial z^2}&=0\\ \text{which is the desired form,}&\\ \therefore \;\; x_{t}&=x\sqrt{\frac{k_{z}}{k_{x}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The value of [latex]\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}(6-x-y)dxdy[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Since the limit is a function of x, we first integrate w.r.t. [latex]y[/latex] and then w.r.t. [latex]x[/latex],
[latex]\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dx\: dy\\&=\int_{0}^{3}dx\int_{0}^{x}\left ( 6-x-y \right )dy \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left [ 6y-xy-\frac{y^{2}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{x} \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}dx\left ( 6x-x^{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2} \right ) \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}\left ( 6x-\frac{3x^{2}}{2} \right )dx \\ &=\left [ 6\left ( \frac{x^{2}}{2} \right )-\frac{3}{2}\left ( \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right ) \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left [ 3x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{2} \right ]_{0}^{3} \\ &=27-\frac{27}{2}=13.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Three values of x and y are to be fitted in a straight line in the form y=a+bx
 by the method of least squares. Given [latex]\sum x=6, \; \sum y=21, \; \sum x^{2}=14[/latex] and [latex]\sum xy=46[/latex], the values of a and b are respectively
raw_source.solution: [latex]   \begin{aligned} y&=a+bx\\ &\text{Given}\\    n&=3,\: \sum x=6,\\ \sum y&=21\: \sum x^{2}=14\\   \sum xy&=46 \\    b&=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^{2}-\left ( \sum x \right )^{2}} \\    a&=\bar{y}-b\bar{x} \\     &=\frac{\sum y}{n}-b\frac{\sum x}{n}\\ &\text{Substituting, we get} \\    b&=\frac{\left ( 3\times 46 \right )-\left ( 6\times 21 \right )}{\left ( 3\times 14 \right )-\left ( 6 \right )^{2}}=2 \\    a&=\frac{21}{3}-2\times \left ( \frac{6}{3} \right )=3 \\ \therefore \;\;   a&=3 \text{ and }b=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Solution of [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}[/latex] at x = 1 and y = [latex]\sqrt{3}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned}  \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=\frac{-x}{y} \\ \Rightarrow  \;\; ydy&=-xdx \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  \int ydy&=\int -xdx \\   \frac{y^2}{2}&=-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+C \\ \text{at }   x&=1,\: y=\sqrt{3} \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{\left ( \sqrt{3} \right )^{2}}{2}&=\frac{-1^{2}}{2}+C \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  C&=2 \\ \therefore \;\; \text{Solution is,} \\   \frac{y^{2}}{2}&=\frac{-x^{2}}{2}+2 \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  x^{2}+y^{2}&=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Cross-section of a column consisting to two steel strips, each of thickness t and width b is shown in the figure below. The critical loads of the column with perfect bond and without bond between the strips are [latex]P[/latex] and [latex]P_0[/latex] respectively. The ratio [latex]P/P_0[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
We know that critical load for a column is proportional to moment of inertia irrespective of end conditions of the column i.e.
[latex] P_{c r} \propto 1[/latex]
When the steel strips are perfectly bonded, then
[latex] f_{p b}=\frac{b \times(2 t)^{3}}{12}=\frac{8 b t^{3}}{12}[/latex]
When the steel strips are not bonded, then
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{wb}&=2 \times \frac{b t^{3}}{12}=\frac{2 b t^{3}}{12} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{P}{P_{0}}&=\frac{8 b t^{3} / 12}{2 b t^{3} / 12}=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
The degree of static indeterminacy for a rigid hybrid frame is given by,
[latex] \begin{aligned} D_{s} &=3 m+r_{e}-r_{r}-3(j+7) \\ \text { Where, } m &=\text { total number of members }=9 \\ r_{e} &=\text { total number of external reactions } \\ &=2+1+1=4\\ r_{r}&= \text{total number of released reactions at }\\ &\text{hybrid joint}\\ &=\Sigma\left(m_{j}-1\right)=(2-1)+(2-1)=2 \\ j &=\text { total number of rigid joints }=6 \\ j &=\text { total number of hybrid joints }=2 \\ \therefore \quad D_{S} &=(3 \times 9)+4-2-3(6+2) \\ &=27+4-2-24=31-26=5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The maximum shear stress in a solid shaft of circular cross-section having diameter d subjected to a subject to a torque T is [latex]\tau[/latex]. If the torque is increased by four times and the diameter of the shaft is increased by two times, the maximum shear stress in the shaft will be
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{\tau}{R}&=\frac{T}{I_{P}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\tau_{1}}{\tau_{2}}&=\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}} \times \frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \times \frac{I_{P_{2}}}{I_{P_{1}}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\tau_{1}}{\tau_{2}}&=\frac{R_{1}}{2 R_{1}} \times \frac{T_{1}}{4 T_{1}} \times\left(\frac{2 R_{1}}{R_{1}}\right)^{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\tau_{1}}{\tau_{2}}&=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times 16 \\ \Rightarrow\quad\tau_{2}&=\frac{\tau_{1}}{2} \\ \Rightarrow\quad\tau_{2}&=\frac{\tau}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A vertical rod PQ of length L is fixed at its top end P and has a flange fixed to the bottom end Q. A weight W is dropped vertically from a height h ([latex]\lt[/latex]L) on to the flange. The axial stress in the rod can be reduced by

The kinetic energy of the weight (W) at flange level will be transformed in the form of strain energy in the rod.
We know that
[latex] \mathrm{U}=\sigma^{2} / 2 \mathrm{E} \times [/latex] Area of cross-section of rod [latex] \times [/latex] length of rod
Since, energy remains constant, hence to reduce the axial stress in the rod, the length of the rod should be increased or area of cross-section of the rod should be increased or modulus of elasticity should be decreased.

[latex] \begin{aligned} &=1.2(\mathrm{DL}+\mathrm{LL}+\mathrm{EL}) \\ &=1.2(50+80+180) \\ &=372 \mathrm{kN}-\mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A reinforced concrete column contains longitudinal steel equal to 1 percent of net

and[latex]P_{c}[/latex]

 expressed as per cent is
raw_source.solution:
If A is the net cross-sectional area of the column,
[latex]A_{s t}[/latex] is the area of steel, [latex]A_{c}[/latex] is area of concrete, m is modular ratio and [latex]f_{c}[/latex] is stress in concrete, then.
[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{s t}&=\frac{1}{100} \times A=0.01 A \\ A_{c}&=A-A_{s t}=A-0.01 A=0.99 A\\ \frac{P_{s}}{P_{c}} &=\frac{m A_{s t} f_{c}}{A_{c} \times f_{c}} \\ &=\frac{10 \times 0.01 A \times f_{c}}{0.99 A \times f_{c}} \times 100=10.10 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

Area of section in terms of concrete
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =A+(m-1) A_{s t} \\ =(200 \times 250)+(10-1) \times 500 \\ =54500 \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{array}[/latex]

[latex] =\frac{P}{A}=\frac{5 \times 10^{5}}{54500}=9.17 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A saturated clay stratum draining both at the top and bottom undergoes 50 percent consolidation in 16 year under an applied load. If an additional drainage
layer were present at the middle of the clay stratum, 50 percent consolidation would occur in
raw_source.solution:
From Taylor's formula, we have
[latex] T_{v}=\frac{C_{v} t}{d^{2}}[/latex]
Here [latex]T_{v}[/latex] and [latex]C_{v}[/latex] are constant
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad t &\propto d^{2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}&=\left(\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}\right)^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{16}{t_{2}}&=\left(\frac{H}{H / 2}\right)^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad t_{2}&=\frac{16}{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad t_{2}&=4 \text { years } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A volume of [latex]3.0 \times 10^{6} m^{3}[/latex] of groundwater was pumped form an unconfined aquifer uniformly from an area of 5 [latex]km^{2}[/latex]. The pumping lowered the water table form initial level of 102 m to 99 m. The specific yield of the aquifer is

raw_source.text: A weir on a permeable foundation with downstream sheet pile is shown in the figure below. The exit gradient as per Khosla's method is
raw_source.solution:
The exit gradient may be given as,
[latex] \begin{aligned} G_{E}&=\frac{H}{d} \times \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{\lambda}}\\ \text{where }\lambda&=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}}{2} \text{ and }\alpha=\frac{b}{d} \\ \text{Here }\quad b&=10 \mathrm{m}, d=4 \mathrm{m}, H=5 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad \alpha&=\frac{b}{d}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5 \\ \text{and }\quad \lambda&=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+(2.5)^{2}}}{2}=1.85 \\ \therefore \quad G_{E}&=\frac{5}{4} \times \frac{1}{\pi \times \sqrt{1.85}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad G_{E}&=\frac{1}{3.4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Theories of Seepage, Spillways and Miscellaneous

[latex] \begin{aligned} y_{2} &=\frac{y_{1}}{2}\left[-1+\sqrt{1+\frac{8 V_{1}^{2}}{g y_{1}}}\right] \\ &=\frac{0.3}{2} \times\left[-1+\sqrt{1+\frac{8 \times(13.72)^{2}}{9.81 \times 0.3}}\right] \\ &=3.24 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The flow of water (mass density = 100 kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex] and kinematic viscosity = [latex]10^{-6} m^{2}/s[/latex]) in a commercial pipe, having equivalent roughness [latex]k_{s}[/latex] as 0.12 mm, yields an average shear stress at the pipe boundary = 600 N/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]. The value of [latex]k_{s}/{\delta }'[/latex]
 ([latex]{\delta} '[/latex] being the thickness of laminar sub-layer) for this pipe is
raw_source.solution:
We know that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta^{\prime}&=\frac{11.6 \mathrm{v}}{V_{*}} \\ \text {But } V_{*}&=\sqrt{\frac{\tau_{0}}{\rho}} \\ \therefore \quad 8^{\prime} &=\frac{11.6 \mathrm{v}}{\sqrt{\tau_{0} / \mathrm{p}}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \delta=11.6 \times 10^{-6} \times \sqrt{\frac{1000}{600} \times 1000}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta^{\prime}&=0.015 \mathrm{mm} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{k_{s}}{\delta^{\prime}}&=\frac{0.12}{0.015}=8.0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A river reach of 2.0 km long with maximum flood discharge of 10000[latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] is to be physically modeled in the laboratory where maximum available discharge is 0.20 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex]. For a geometrically similar model based on equally of Froude number, the length of the river reach (m) in the model is
raw_source.solution:
According to Froude model law
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{V_{t}}{\sqrt{L_{r} g_{1}}}&=1 \quad\left[\because F_{r}=1\right]\\ \text{Now, we have}\\ \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=L_{1}^{2} \times V_{r}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{p}}&=L_{r}^{2} \times \sqrt{L_{r}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q_{m}}{Q_{0}}&=\left(L_{r}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{0.20}{10000}&=\left(\frac{L_{m}}{2 \times 1000}\right)^{5 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad L_{m}&=26.4 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A water treatment plant is required to process 28800 [latex]m^{3}/d[/latex] of raw water
(density=1000 kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex], kinematic viscosity= [latex]10^{-6}m^{2}/s[/latex]). The rapid mixing tank imparts a velocity gradient of [latex]900s^{-1}[/latex] to blend 35 mg/l of alum with the flow for a detention time of 2 minutes. The power input (W) required for rapid mixing is
raw_source.solution:
The power input (W) required for rapid mixing is expressed in terms of temporal mean velocity gradient, G, expressed by the equation,
[latex]G=\left [ \frac{P}{\mu V} \right ]^{1/2}\; \; \; \; \; \Rightarrow \; \; \; \; \; P=G^{2}\mu V[/latex]
where [latex]\mu[/latex]=dynamic viscosity of raw water
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\text{kinematic viscosity}\times \text{density} \\ &=10^{-6}\times 10^{3}=10^{-3}\; \text{N-s}/m^{2} \\ \text{G} &=900\; s^{-} \\ \text{t}&=2\; \text{minutes}=120\; \text{seconds} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Discharge of raw water
[latex]\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; =\frac{28800}{24\times 60\times 60}=0.33\; m^{3}/s[/latex]
Volume of water in tank,
[latex]\; \; \; \; \; \; V=0.33\times 120=40\; m^{3}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \; \; \; \; P=\left ( 900 \right )^{2}\times 10^{-3}\times 40[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; =32400\;[/latex]watts

A roundabout is provided with an average entry width of 8.4 m, width of weaving
section as 14 m, and length of the weaving section between channelizing islands
as 35 m. The crossing traffic and total on the weaving section are 1000 and 2000
PCU per hour respectively. The nearest rounded capacity of the roundabout (in
PCU per hour) is
raw_source.solution:
Width of the weaving section, W = 14 m
Average entry width, e = 8.4 m
Length of weaving section between channelizing islands, L =35 m
Proportion of weaving traffic is_given by,
[latex] p =\frac{\text{crossing traffic on the weaving section}}{\text{total traffic on the weaving section}}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad P = \frac{1000}{2000}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad p=0.5 [/latex]
The capacity of the roundabout may be given as,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q=& \frac{280 w\left(1+\frac{e}{w}\right)\left(1-\frac{p}{3}\right)}{1+\frac{w}{L}} \\ Q=& \frac{280 \times 14 \times\left(1+\frac{8.4}{14}\right) \times\left(1-\frac{0.5}{3}\right)}{1+\frac{14}{35}} \\ =& 3733.33 \approx 3700 \mathrm{PCU} \text { per hour } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The lengths and bearing of a closed traverse PQRSP are given below. The missing length and bearing, respectively of the line SP are

For a closed traverse sum of latitutes and departures should be zero respectively l.e.

A road is provided with a horizontal circular curve having deflection angle of 55[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] 
and centre line radius of 250 m. A transition curve is to be provided at each end
of the circular curve of such a length that the rate of gain of radial acceleration
is 0.3 [latex]m/s^{3}[/latex] at a speed of 50 km per hour. Length of the transition curve required at each of the ends is
raw_source.solution:
If [latex]\alpha[/latex] is the rate of change of radial acceleration,
the radial acceleration (a) attained during the time the vehicle passes over the transition curve is given by
[latex] a=\alpha t=\alpha \times \frac{L}{V}[/latex]
Radial acceleration,
[latex] \begin{aligned} a&=\frac{v^{2}}{R} \\ \therefore \quad \alpha \times \frac{L}{V}&=\frac{v^{2}}{R} \\ \Rightarrow \quad L&=\frac{V^{3}}{\alpha R} \\ \therefore \quad L&=\frac{\left(\frac{50 \times 1000}{60 \times 60}\right)^{3}}{0.3 \times 250}\\ \Rightarrow \quad L&=35.73 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A light house of 120 m height is just visible above the horizon from a ship. The
correct distance (m) between the ship and the light house considering combined
correction for curvature and refraction, is
raw_source.solution:
Correction due to curvature,
[latex] C_{c}=-0.0785 d^{2}[/latex]
Correction due to refraction,
[latex] C_{r}=+0.0112 d^{2}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Composte correction.
[latex] \begin{aligned} C &=-0.0785 d^{2}+0.0112 d^{2} \\ &=-0.0673 \phi^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
where C is in metres and d is in Klometers
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Here}\quad C&=120 \mathrm{m}, d=?\\ 120&=0.0673 \times 0^{2} \\ \Rightarrow d&=\sqrt{1783.06} \\ \Rightarrow d&=42208 \times 1000 \\ \Rightarrow d&=4206 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A rectangular channel 6.0 m wide carries a discharge of 16.0 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] under uniform flow condition with normal depth of 1.60 m. Minning's n is 0.015.

The longitudinal slope of the channel is
raw_source.solution:
The velocity as per Manning's equation is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} V &=\frac{1}{n} R^{2 / 3} S^{1 / 2} \\ \text { Here, } Q &=16 m^{3} / s, n=0.015, B=6.0 m \\ A &=6.0 \times 1.60=9.6 m^{2} \\ R &=\frac{A}{P}=\frac{9.6}{6.0+(1.6 \times 2)}=1.04 m\\ \text{But }\quad Q&=A V \\ \therefore \quad Q&=A \times \frac{1}{n} R^{2 / 3} S^{1 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 16&=9.6 \times \frac{1}{0.015} \times(1.04)^{2 / 3} \times S^{1 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad S&=0.00059 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A rectangular channel 6.0 m wide carries a discharge of 16.0 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] under uniform flow condition with normal depth of 1.60 m. Minning's n is 0.015.

A hump is to be provided on the channel bed. The maximum height of the hump without affecting the upstream flow condition is
raw_source.solution:
When a hump is introduced on the channel bed the depth of flow at this location will reduce. If [latex]\Delta Z [/latex] is the maximum height of hump so that the depth of flow remains same, then
[latex] \begin{aligned} y+\frac{Q^{2}}{2 g A^{2}}&=\Delta Z+E_{\min } \\ \Rightarrow 1.6+&\frac{(16)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times(9.6)^{2}}=\Delta Z+\frac{3}{2} y_{c} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.74&=\Delta Z+\frac{3}{2} \times\left[\frac{(16 / 6)^{2}}{9.81}\right]^{1 / 3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \Delta Z&=1.74-1.35 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \Delta Z&=0.39 \approx 0.4 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A rectangular channel 6.0 m wide carries a discharge of 16.0 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex] under uniform flow condition with normal depth of 1.60 m. Minning's n is 0.015.

The channel width is to be contracted. The minimum width to which the channel can be contracted without affecting the upstream flow condition is
raw_source.solution:
If the channel is contracted, the depth of flow at this location decreases. Thus width of the channel can be decreased till the specific energy becomes minimum. If the channel is contracted further, the depth of flow starts decreasing.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad y&+\frac{Q^{2}}{2 g A^{2}}=E_{\min } \\ \Rightarrow 1.6&+\frac{(16)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times(9.6)^{2}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{c}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.74&=\frac{3}{2} \times\left(\frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2} / \mathrm{b}^{2}}{\mathrm{g}}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1.74&=\frac{3}{2} \times\left[\frac{(16)^{2}}{9.81}\right]^{1 / 3} \times \frac{1}{(b)^{2 / 3}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad b^{2 / 3}&=2.557 \\ \Rightarrow \quad b&=4.1 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A reinforced concrete beam of rectangular cross section of breadth 230 mm and effective depth 400 mm is subjected to a maximum factored shear force of 120 kN. The grades of concrete, main steel and stirrup steel are M20, Fe415 and Fe250 respectively. For the area of main steel provided, the design shear strength [latex]\tau _c[/latex] as per IS:456-2000 is 0.48 [latex]N/mm^2[/latex]. The beam is designed for collapse limit state.

The spacing (mm) of 2-legged 8 mm stirrups to be provided is
raw_source.solution:
Ultimate design shear force,
[latex] V_{u}=120 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]
Ultimate shear capacity of concrete,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{u c} &=\tau_{c} b d \\ &=0.48 \times 230 \times 400=44.16 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Ultimate shear to be resisted by shear reinforcement,
[latex] V_{u s}=V_{u}-V_{u c}=120-44.16=75.84 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]
For vertical stirrups, spacing is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{v} &=\frac{0.87 f_{y} A_{s v} d}{V_{u s}} \\ &=\frac{0.87 \times 250 \times 2 \times \pi \times(8)^{2} \times 400}{75.84 \times 10^{3} \times 4} \\ &=115.32 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Shear, Torsion, Bond, Anchorage and Development Length

raw_source.text:
A reinforced concrete beam of rectangular cross section of breadth 230 mm and effective depth 400 mm is subjected to a maximum factored shear force of 120 kN. The grades of concrete, main steel and stirrup steel are M20, Fe415 and Fe250 respectively. For the area of main steel provided, the design shear strength [latex]\tau _c[/latex] as per IS:456-2000 is 0.48 [latex]N/mm^2[/latex]. The beam is designed for collapse limit state.

In addition, the beam is subjected to a torque whose factored value is 10.90 kNm. The stirrups have to be provided to carry a shear (kN) equal to
raw_source.solution:
Equivalent shear,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{u e} &=V_{u}+\frac{1.6 T_{u}}{b} \\ &=120+\frac{1.6 \times 10.90 \times 1000}{230} \\ &=120+75.83=195.83 \mathrm{kN} \\ v_{w} &=44.16 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] Ultimate shear to be resisted by stirrups,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{u s} &=V_{u e}-V_{u c} \\ &=195.83-44.16=151.67 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Shear, Torsion, Bond, Anchorage and Development Length

raw_source.text:
Beam GHI is supported by three pontoons as shown in the figure below. The horizontal cross-sectional area of each pontoon is [latex]8 m^{2}[/latex], the flexural rigidity of the beam is 10000 [latex]kN-m^{2}[/latex] and the unit weight of water is 10[latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex]

When the middle pontoon is removed, the deflection at H will be
raw_source.solution:
The reactions at the ends are zero as there are hinges to left of G and right of I. Hence when the middle pontoon is removed, the beam GHI acts as a simply supported beam.

The deflection at H will be due to the load at H as well as due to the downward settlement of pontoons at G and l in water. Since the loading is symmetrical, both the pontoons will be immersed to same height and produce equal reaction (24 kN). Let it be [latex]\delta_{1}. [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \delta_{1} \times [/latex] area of cross-section of pontoon [latex]\times [/latex] unit weight of water =24
[latex] \Rightarrow \delta_{1} \times 8 \times 10=24 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{1}=0.3 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Also, deflection at H due to bending in beam
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta_{2} &=\frac{P L^{3}}{48 E l} \\ &=\frac{48 \times(10)^{3}}{48 \times 10^{4}}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Final deflection at H,
[latex] \Delta=\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}=0.3+0.1=0.4 \mathrm{m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Beam GHI is supported by three pontoons as shown in the figure below. The horizontal cross-sectional area of each pontoon is [latex]8 m^{2}[/latex], the flexural rigidity of the beam is 10000 [latex]kN-m^{2}[/latex] and the unit weight of water is 10[latex]kN/m^{3}[/latex]

When the middle pontoon is brought back to its position as shown in the figure above, the reaction at H will be
raw_source.solution:
Let the elastic deflection at H be [latex]\delta_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \delta_{2}&=\frac{(P-R) L^{3}}{48 E I} \quad &\ldots(i)\end{aligned}[/latex]
The reactions at G and I will be same, as the beam is symmetrically loaded.
Let the reaction at each G and I be Q
Using principle of buoyancy, we get
[latex] \delta_{1} \times [/latex] area of cross-section of pontoon [latex]\times \gamma_{w}=Q [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{1} \times 8 \times 10&=Q \\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{1}&=\frac{Q}{80} &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]


Also, we have
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q+Q+R&=P \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 Q+R&=48 &\ldots(iii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \text{Also, }\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}\right) \times [/latex] area of cross-section of
Pontoon [latex]\times \gamma_{n}=\mathrm{R} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}\right) \times 8 \times 10&=\mathrm{R} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{1}+\delta_{2}&=\frac{R}{80} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q}{80}+\delta_{2}&=\frac{R}{80} &[\text{from (ii)}]\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{48-R}{2 \times 80}+\delta_{2}&=\frac{R}{80} \quad&[\text{from (iii)}] \\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{2}&=\frac{2 R-48+R}{160} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{2}&=\frac{3 R-48}{160} \\ \therefore \frac{(48-R) \times 10^{3}}{48 \times 10^{4}}&=\frac{3 R-48}{160} \quad&[\text{from (i)}] \\ \Rightarrow \quad R&=19.2 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The saturated unit weight of the sand (kN/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]) is

raw_source.text:
A column is supported on a footing as shown in the figure below. The water table is at a depth of 10 m below the base of the footing.

The net ultimate bearing capacity (kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]) of the footing based on Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation is
raw_source.solution:
Ultimate bearing capacity of the footing as per Terzaghi's equation for rectangular footing is given
as
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{u}=&\left(1+0.3 \frac{B}{L}\right) \mathrm{cN}_{c}+\gamma \mathrm{D}_{1} \mathrm{N}_{q} \\ &+\frac{1}{2} \gamma B\left(1-0.2 \frac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{L}}\right) \mathrm{N}_{y} \end{aligned}[/latex]
But for sand, c=0
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad q_{u}&=(18 \times 1 \times 24)+\frac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1.5\\ &\times\left(1-0.2 \times \frac{1.5}{3.0}\right) \times 20\\ \Rightarrow \quad q_{u}&=432+243 \\ \Rightarrow \quad q_{u}&=675 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
The net ultimate bearing capacity.
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{n u} &=q_{u}-\gamma D_{t} \\ &=675-18 \times 1=657 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An automobile with projected area 2.6 [latex]m^{2}[/latex] is running on a road with a speed of 120 km per hour. The mass density and the kinematic viscosity of air are 1.2 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex] and [latex]1.5 \times 10^{-5} m^{2}/s[/latex], respectively. The drag coefficient is 0.30.

The drag force on the automobile is
raw_source.solution:
The drag force on the automobile may be given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} F_{D} &=C_{D} A \times \frac{\rho V^{2}}{2} \\ \text { Here, } C_{D} &=0.30, \\ A&=2.6 \mathrm{m}^{2}, \\ \rho&=1.2 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}, \\ V&=120 \mathrm{kmph} \\\text{So, }F_{D}&=0.30 \times 2.6 \times \frac{1.2 \times(120 \times 1000)^{2}}{2 \times(60 \times 60)^{2}}\\ &=520N \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An automobile with projected area 2.6 [latex]m^{2}[/latex] is running on a road with a speed of 120 km per hour. The mass density and the kinematic viscosity of air are 1.2 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex] and [latex]1.5 \times 10^{-5} m^{2}/s[/latex], respectively. The drag coefficient is 0.30.

The metric horse power required to overcome the drag force is
raw_source.solution:
Power required to overcome the drag = Drag force [latex] \times [/latex] velocity
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=520 \times \frac{120 \times 1000}{60 \times 60}= 17333.33 \mathrm{watt} \\ &\quad (1 \mathrm{mhp}=735.5 \mathrm{watt})\\ &=\frac{17333.33}{735.5}\text{ metric horse power }\\ &=23.567 \text{ metric horse power} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A horizontal curvature curve with a centre line radius of 200 m is provided on a 2-lane, 2-way SH section. The width of the 2-lane road is 7.0 m. Design speed for this section is 80 km per hour. The brake reaction time is 2.4 s, and the coefficients of friction in longitudinal and lateral directions are 0.355 and 0.15, respectively.

The safe stopping sight distance on the section is
raw_source.solution:
Safe stopping sight distance
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=0.278 \mathrm{Vt}+\frac{v^{2}}{254 \mathrm{f}} \\ &=(0.278 \times 80 \times 2.4)+\frac{(80)^{2}}{254 \times 0.355} \\ &=124.35 \mathrm{m} \approx 125 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text:
A horizontal curvature curve with a centre line radius of 200 m is provided on a 2-lane, 2-way SH section. The width of the 2-lane road is 7.0 m. Design speed for this section is 80 km per hour. The brake reaction time is 2.4 s, and the coefficients of friction in longitudinal and lateral directions are 0.355 and 0.15, respectively.

The set-back distance from the centre line of the inner lane is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} m &=(R-d)-(R-d) \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \\ \frac{\alpha}{2} &=\frac{180 S}{2 \pi(R-d)} \\ &=\frac{180 \times 125}{2 \times \pi\left(200-\frac{7}{4}\right)}=18.063 \\ \therefore \quad m &=200-\left(200-\frac{7}{4}\right) \cos (18.063) \\ &=11.52 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus, set back distance from centre line of inner lane
[latex] =11.52-\left(\frac{7}{4}\right)=9.77 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text: For a scalar function [latex] f (x,y,z) = x^{2}+3y^{2}+2z^{2}[/latex], the gradient at the point P(1,2,-1) is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f&=x^{2}+3y^{2}+2z^{2} \\ \Delta f&=grad\: f=i\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+j\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}+k\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \\  &=i\left ( 2x \right )+j\left ( 6y \right )+k\left ( 4z \right ) \\ &\text{The gradient at P(1, 2, -1) is}\\  &=i\left ( 2\times 1 \right )+j\left ( 6\times 2 \right )+k\left ( 4\times -1 \right ) \\  &=2i+12j-4k \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex]f\left ( z \right )=\frac{z-1}{z^{2}+1}=\frac{z-1}{z^{2}-i^{2}}=\frac{z-1}{\left ( z-i \right )\left ( z+i \right )} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] The singularities arc at [latex]z=i[/latex] and [latex]-i[/latex]

raw_source.text: For a scalar function [latex]f (x,y,z) =x^{2}+3y^{2}+2z^{2}[/latex], the directional derivative at the point P(1,2,-1) in the direction of a vector [latex]\vec{i}-\vec{j}+2\vec{k}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta f&= i\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+j\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}+k\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\\ \text{Here } f&=x^{2}+3y^{2}+2z^{2} \\ \therefore  \;\; \Delta f&=i\left ( 2x \right )j\left ( 6y \right )+k\left ( 4z \right )\\ & \text{at }p\left ( 1,\, 2,\, 1 \right ) \\ \Delta f&=i\left ( 2\times 1 \right )+j\left ( 6\times 2 \right )+k\left ( 4x-1 \right ) \\  &=2i+12j-4k \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The value of the integral [latex]\int_{c}\frac{cos(2 \pi z)}{(2z-1)(z-3)}dz[/latex]  (where C is a closed curve given by |z|=1) is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{2}\oint_{c}\, \frac{\cos 2\pi z}{\left ( z-\frac{1}{2} \right )\left ( z-3 \right )}dz \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\oint_{c}\, \frac{\frac{\cos 2\pi z}{z-3}}{z-\frac{1}{2}}dz \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\pi i\left [ \frac{\cos 2\pi /2}{z-3} \right ]_{z=\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\pi i\left ( \frac{\cos \pi }{\frac{1}{2}-3} \right ) \\ &=\pi i\left ( \frac{-1}{-\frac{5}{2}} \right ) \\ &=\frac{2\pi i}{5}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Solution of the differential equation [latex]3y\frac{dy}{dx}+ 2x = 0[/latex] represents a family of
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} 3y\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2x&=0 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=\frac{-2y}{3y} \\ 3ydy&=-2xdx \\ \int 3ydy&=\int -2xdx \\ \frac{3}{2}y^{2}&=-2\times \frac{x^{2}}{2}+C \\ 3y^{2}+2x^{2}&=C \\ \frac{x^{2}}{\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )}+\frac{y^{2}}{\left ( \frac{1}{3} \right )}&=C \\ \frac{x^{2}}{\left ( \frac{1}{2}C \right )}+\frac{y^{2}}{\left ( \frac{1}{3}C \right )}&=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Which is the equation of a family of ellipses.

raw_source.text:
In the solution of the following set of linear equations by Gauss elimination using partial pivoting
5x + y + 2z = 34;
4y - 3z = 12; and
10x - 2y + z =- 4;
the pivots for elimination of x and y are
raw_source.solution:
The equations are,
[latex] \begin{aligned} 5x+y+2z&=34 \\ 0x+4y-3z&=12 \\ 10x-2y+z&=-4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The augmented matrix for gauss-elimination is,
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Since in the first column maximum element in absolute value is 10, we need to exchange row 1 with row 3.
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R\left ( 1,3 \right )}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 10 & -2 & 1\\ 0& 4 & -3\\ 5 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} -4\\ 12\\ 34 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
So the pivot for eliminating x is [latex]a_{11}=10[/latex].
Now to eliminate y, we need to compass the eliminate in second column at and below the diagonal.
Since [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] is already larger in absolute value compares to [latex]a_{32}=1 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] The pivot elementfor eliminating y is [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] itself.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] The pivots for eliminating x and y are respectively 10 and 4.

[latex]F(x_{N})=\frac{1}{1+exp(-1.7255x_{N}|x_{N}|^{0.12})}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:

This area is shown below:



The shades area in above figure is given by
[latex]F\left ( 0 \right )-F\left ( -0.44 \right )[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{1+\exp \left ( 0 \right )}-\frac{1}{1+\exp \left ( -1.7255\left ( -0.44 \right )\left ( 0.44 \right )0.12 \right )} \\ &=0.5-0.3345 \\ &=1.1655\simeq 16.55\% \end{aligned}[/latex]
closest answer is 16.7%

raw_source.text:
In the solution of the following set of linear equations by Gauss elimination using partial pivoting
5x + y + 2z = 34;
4y - 3z = 12; and
10x - 2y + z =- 4;
the pivots for elimination of x and y are
raw_source.solution:
The equations are,
[latex] \begin{aligned} 5x+y+2z&=34 \\ 0x+4y-3z&=12 \\ 10x-2y+z&=-4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The augmented matrix for gauss-elimination is,
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Since in the first column maximum element in absolute value is 10, we need to exchange row 1 with row 3.
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R\left ( 1,3 \right )}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 10 & -2 & 1\\ 0& 4 & -3\\ 5 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} -4\\ 12\\ 34 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
So the pivot for eliminating x is [latex]a_{11}=10[/latex].
Now to eliminate y, we need to compass the eliminate in second column at and below the diagonal.
Since [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] is already larger in absolute value compares to [latex]a_{32}=1 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] The pivot elementfor eliminating y is [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] itself.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] The pivots for eliminating x and y are respectively 10 and 4.

raw_source.text: The degree of static indeterminacy of rigidity jointed frame in a horizontal plane and subjected to vertical load only, as shown in figure below, is
raw_source.solution:
In general, total number of equilibrium equations for a 3-D rigidly jointed frame are 6. i.e.
[latex] \Sigma F_{x}=0, \Sigma F_{y}=0, \Sigma F_{2}=0, \Sigma M_{x}=0, \Sigma M_{y}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Sigma M_{z}=0 [/latex]
But for vertical loading, these equilibrium equations reduces to 3.
I.e. [latex]\Sigma F_{y}=0, \Sigma M_{x}=0\text{ and }\Sigma M_{z}=0 [/latex]
Also, at fixed support in a 3 -D rigidly jointed frame
total number of external reactions are 6 i.e..
[latex] R_{x^{\prime}}, R_{y^{\prime}} R_{z^{\prime}} M_{x^{\prime}} M_{y^{\prime}} M_{z}[/latex]
But for vertical loading, these external reactions reduce to 3 i.e.,
[latex] R_{y^{\prime}} M_{x^{\prime}} M_{z}[/latex]
Thus for two fixed supports total external reactions will be 6
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Degree of static indeterminacy
= Total external reactions - Total number of available equilibrium equations
[latex] =6-3=3[/latex]

A rectangular concrete beam of width 120 mm and depth 200 mm is prestressed by pretensioning to a force of 150 kN at an eccentricity of 20 mm. The crosssectional
area of the prestressing steel is 187.5[latex]mm^{2}[/latex]. Take modulus of elasticity of steel and concrete as [latex]2.1\times 10^{5}[/latex]
 MPa and [latex]3.0\times 10^{4}[/latex]
 MPa respectively. The percentage loss of stress in the prestressing steel due to elastic deformation of concrete is
raw_source.solution:
Stress in concrete at the level of tendon,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c} &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e^{2}}{I} \\ &=\frac{150 \times 10^{3}}{120 \times 200}+\frac{150 \times 20^{2} \times 12 \times 10^{3}}{120 \times 200^{3}} \\ &=7 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Loss of prestress due to elastic deformation,
[latex] \Delta f_{s}=\frac{E_{s}}{E_{c}} \times f_{c}=\frac{2.1 \times 10^{5}}{3.0 \times 10^{4}} \times 7=49 \mathrm{MPa}[/latex]
Total stress in steel,
[latex] f_{s}=\frac{P}{A_{s}}=\frac{150 \times 10^{3}}{187.5}=800 \mathrm{MPa}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Percentage loss of stress
[latex] =\frac{\Delta f_{s}}{f_{s}} \times 100=\frac{49}{800} \times 100=6.125 \%[/latex]

Percentage finer than 4.75mm = 60

Plastic limit, [latex]w_P=27 %[/latex]

Fine grained soils are those having 50% or more pass through 75[latex]\mu[/latex] sieve (0.075 mm). It is designated as sand (S) if 50% or more pass through 4.75 mm sieve otherwise designated as gravel (G).

Plasticity index corresponding to A-line, [latex]I_P=0.73(w_L-20)=10.95[/latex]
The point corresponding to [latex]w_L=35 %[/latex] and [latex]I_P=8 %[/latex] lies below A- line on the Plasticity chart. It is designated as M or O.
Therefore, the soil is classified as SM.

On a specific highway, the speed-density relationship follows the Greenbeg's model [latex][v=v_{f}ln(k_{j}/k)][/latex], where [latex]v_{f}[/latex] and [latex]k_{j}[/latex] are the free flew speed and jam density respectively. When the highway is operating at capacity, the density obtained as
per this model is
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]\quad v=v_{f} \log _{e}\left(\frac{k_{j}}{k}\right) [/latex]
But Capacity,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C &=\text { traffic density } \times \text { speed } \\ &=k \times v \\ \Rightarrow \quad C &=v_{t} k \log _{e}\left(\frac{k_{I}}{k}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For maximum capacity,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \frac{d C}{d k}=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad v_{f} \times \frac{d}{d k}\left[k \log _{\theta}\left(\frac{k_{1}}{k}\right)\right]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad k \frac{d}{d k} \log _{\theta}\left(\frac{k_{1}}{k}\right)+\log _{e}\left(\frac{k_{j}}{k}\right) \frac{d}{d k} k=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad k \times \frac{k}{k_{j}} \times k_{l} \times\left(-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\right)+\log _{e} \frac{k_{j}}{k}=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \log _{e} \frac{k_{j}}{k}=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad e=\frac{k_{j}}{k} \\ \Rightarrow \quad k=\frac{k_{j}}{e} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A parabolic cable is held between two supports at the same level. The horizontal
span between the supports is L. The sag at the mid-span is h. The equation of
the parabola is [latex]y=4h\frac{x^{2}}{L^{2}}[/latex], where x is the horizontal coordinate and y is the vertical coordinate with the origin at the center of the cable. The expression for the total length of the cable is
raw_source.solution:
Length of curve [latex]f(x)[/latex] between [latex]x=a[/latex] and [latex]x=b[/latex] is given by,
[latex] \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} \right )^{2}}dx [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} y&=4h\frac{x^{2}}{L^{2}} \;\; ...(i) \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=8h\frac{x}{L^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since, [latex]y=0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex]
and [latex]y=h[/latex] at [latex]x=\frac{L}{2}[/latex]
(As can be seen from equation (i), by substituting [latex]x=0[/latex] and [latex]x=\frac{L}{2}[/latex])
[latex]\therefore \;\; \frac{1}{2}[/latex] (Length of cable) [latex]=\int_{0}^{L/2}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{8hx}{L^{2}} \right )^{2}}dx[/latex]
Length of cable [latex]=2\int_{0}^{L/2}\sqrt{1+64\frac{h^{2}x^{2}}{L^{4}}}dx[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Given a function
[latex]f(x,y) = 4x^{2}+6y^{2}- 8x - 4y + 8. [/latex]
The optimal value of f(x,y)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f\left ( x, y \right )&=4x^{2}+6y^{2}-8x-4y+8 \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=8x-8 \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=12y-4y \\ \text{Putting, } \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=0 \\ \text{and } \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} =0 \\ 8x-8&=0 \\ \text{and }12y-4y&=0\\ \text{Given, } x&=1 \text{ and }y=\frac{1}{3} \\ \left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )& \text{ is the only stationary point.}\\ r&=\left [ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} \right ]_{\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )}=8 \\ s&=\left [ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial xdy} \right ]_{\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )}=0 \\ t&=\left [ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} \right ]_{\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )}=12 \\ \text{Since, } rt&=8\times 12=48 \\ s^{2}&=0\\ \text{Since, }rt \gt s^{2},\end{aligned}[/latex]
we have either a maxima or minima at [latex]\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )[/latex]
also since, [latex]r=\left [ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^2} \right ]_{1,\, \frac{1}{3}}=8 \gt 0[/latex], the point [latex]\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )[/latex] is a point of minima.
The minimum value is,
[latex]f\left ( 1,\frac{1}{3} \right )=4\times 1^{2}+6\times \frac{1}{3^{2}-8\times 1-4\times \frac{1}{3}+8} =\frac{10}{3}[/latex]
So the optimal value of f(x, y) is a minimum equal to [latex]\frac{10}{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The local mean time at a place located in longitude 90[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]40' E when the standard time is 6 hours and 30 minutes and the standard meridian is 82[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]30' E is
raw_source.solution:
Difference between standard meridian and the longitude of the given
[latex] \text { place }=90^{\circ} 40^{\circ} \mathrm{E}-82^{\circ} 30^{\circ} \mathrm{E}=8^{\circ} 10^{\prime}[/latex]
The longitude of the given place is more than the standard meridian. Hence the local mean time of the given place will be ahead of the standard time.
[latex] 8^{\circ}=\frac{8}{15} \text { hours }[/latex]
=0 hours and 32 minutes and 0 seconds
[latex] 10^{\prime}=\frac{10}{15} \text { minutes }[/latex]
=0 hours and 0 minutes and 40 seconds
Time for a difference of [latex] 8^{\circ} 10^{\prime}=32[/latex] minutes and 40 seconds
Local mean time = standard time +32 minutes and 40 seconds
[latex] \begin{aligned} =& 6 \text { hours and } 30 \text { minutes } \\ &+32 \text { minutes and } 40 \text { seconds } \\ =& 7 \text { hours, } 02 \text { minutes and } 40 \text{seconds} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A parabolic cable is held between two supports at the same level. The horizontal
span between the supports is L. The sag at the mid-span is h. The equation of
the parabola is [latex]y=4h\frac{x^{2}}{L^{2}}[/latex], where x is the horizontal coordinate and y is the vertical coordinate with the origin at the center of the cable. The expression for the total length of the cable is
raw_source.solution:
Length of curve [latex]f(x)[/latex] between [latex]x=a[/latex] and [latex]x=b[/latex] is given by,
[latex] \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} \right )^{2}}dx [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} y&=4h\frac{x^{2}}{L^{2}} \;\; ...(i) \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=8h\frac{x}{L^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since, [latex]y=0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex]
and [latex]y=h[/latex] at [latex]x=\frac{L}{2}[/latex]
(As can be seen from equation (i), by substituting [latex]x=0[/latex] and [latex]x=\frac{L}{2}[/latex])
[latex]\therefore \;\; \frac{1}{2}[/latex] (Length of cable) [latex]=\int_{0}^{L/2}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{8hx}{L^{2}} \right )^{2}}dx[/latex]
Length of cable [latex]=2\int_{0}^{L/2}\sqrt{1+64\frac{h^{2}x^{2}}{L^{4}}}dx[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Given a function
[latex]f(x,y) = 4x^{2}+6y^{2}- 8x - 4y + 8. [/latex]
The optimal value of f(x,y)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f\left ( x, y \right )&=4x^{2}+6y^{2}-8x-4y+8 \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=8x-8 \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=12y-4y \\ \text{Putting, } \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=0 \\ \text{and } \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} =0 \\ 8x-8&=0 \\ \text{and }12y-4y&=0\\ \text{Given, } x&=1 \text{ and }y=\frac{1}{3} \\ \left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )& \text{ is the only stationary point.}\\ r&=\left [ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} \right ]_{\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )}=8 \\ s&=\left [ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial xdy} \right ]_{\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )}=0 \\ t&=\left [ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} \right ]_{\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )}=12 \\ \text{Since, } rt&=8\times 12=48 \\ s^{2}&=0\\ \text{Since, }rt \gt s^{2},\end{aligned}[/latex]
we have either a maxima or minima at [latex]\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )[/latex]
also since, [latex]r=\left [ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^2} \right ]_{1,\, \frac{1}{3}}=8 \gt 0[/latex], the point [latex]\left ( 1,\, \frac{1}{3} \right )[/latex] is a point of minima.
The minimum value is,
[latex]f\left ( 1,\frac{1}{3} \right )=4\times 1^{2}+6\times \frac{1}{3^{2}-8\times 1-4\times \frac{1}{3}+8} =\frac{10}{3}[/latex]
So the optimal value of f(x, y) is a minimum equal to [latex]\frac{10}{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A double cover butt riveted joint is used to connect two flat of 200 mm width and 14 mm thickness as shown in the figure. There are twelve power driven rivets of 20 mm diameter at a pitch of 50 mm in both directions on either side of the plate. Two cover plates of 10 mm thickness are used. Strength of one rivet in double shear
[latex]=2\times \frac{\pi \left ( {d}' \right )^{2}}{4}\times \sigma _{s}=2\times \frac{\left ( 20+1.5 \right )^{2}\pi }{4}\times 100\times 10^{-3}=72.61 kN[/latex]
Strength of the riveted joint in double shear
[latex]=12\times 72.61=871.32 kN[/latex]
Strength of one rivet in bearing [latex] ={d}'t\times \sigma _{b} =\left ( 20+1.5 \right )\times 14\times 300\times 10^{-3}=90.3 kN[/latex]
Strength of the riveted joint in bearing
[latex]=12\times 90.3=1083.6 kN[/latex]
Thus the strength of joint will be governed by shearing and it will be equal to 871.32 kN

raw_source.text: The vertical stress at point P1 due to the point load Q on the ground surface as shown in figure is [latex]\sigma _{2}[/latex]. According to Boussinesq's equation, the vertical stress at point P2 shown in figure will be
raw_source.solution:
As per Boussinesq equation, the vertical stress [latex] \sigma_{2}[/latex] at a point located at a depth 'z' and a horizontal distance 'r' from the point of application of point load Q is
[latex] \sigma_{z}=\frac{3 Q}{2 \pi z^{2}}\left[\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{r}{z}\right)^{2}}\right]^{5 / 2}[/latex]
For a horizontal distance [latex]\frac{r}{2}[/latex] and a depth [latex]\frac{2}{2}[/latex], the stress will be
[latex] =\frac{3 Q}{2 \pi\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2}}\left[\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{r / 2}{2 / 2}\right)^{2}}\right]^{5 / 2}=4 \times \frac{3 Q}{2 \pi z^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{r}{z}\right)^{2}}\right)^{5 / 2} [/latex]
[latex] =4 \sigma_{z}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a rectangular channel seetion, Group I lists geometrical elements and Group II gives proportions for hydraulically efficient section

[latex]y_e[/latex] is the flow depth corresponding to hydraulically efficient section. The correct match of Group I with Group II is
raw_source.solution:
Let the width of rectangular channel be B and depth of flow be y.
Area of flow, A=By
Wetted perimeter,
[latex] P=B+2 y=\frac{A}{y}+2 y[/latex]
For hydraulically most efficient section, P should be minimum.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{d P}{d y}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{-A}{y^{2}}+2&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad A_{\theta}&=2 y_{e}^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad B_{e} y_{e}&=2 y_{\theta}^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad B_{\theta}&=2 y_{e} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hydraulic radius,
[latex] R=\frac{A}{P}=\frac{2 y_{e}^{2}}{2 y_{e}+2 y_{e}}=\frac{y_{e}}{2}[/latex]
Top width,
[latex] T=B=2 y_{e}[/latex]
Perimeter,
[latex] P=B+2 y_{e}=2 y_{e}+2 y_{e}=4 y_{e} [/latex]
Hydraulic depth,
[latex] D=\frac{A}{T}=\frac{2 y_{e}^{2}}{2 y_{e}}=y_{e}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The Froude number of flow in a rectangular channel is 0.8. If te depth of flow is
1.5m, the critical depth is
raw_source.solution:
Froude Number for a rectangular channel is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} F &=\frac{V}{\sqrt{g y}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad V &=0.8 \times \sqrt{9.81 \times 1.5} \\ &=3.07 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Discharge per unit width of rectangular channel is given by
[latex] q=V y=3.07 \times 1.5=4.6 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Critical depth,
[latex] y_{c}=\left(\frac{q^{2}}{g}\right)^{1 / 3}=\left(\frac{4.6^{2}}{9.81}\right)^{1 / 3}=1.29 m[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A well of diameter 20 cm fully penetrates a confined aquifer. After a long period
of pumping at rate of 2720 litres per minute, the observations of drawdown taken
at 10 m and 100 m distances from the centre of the well are found to be 3m and
0.5m respectively. The transmissivity of the aquifer is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=\frac{2 \pi T\left(s_{1}-s_{2}\right)}{\ln \left(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}\right)} \\ T &=\frac{2720 \times 10^{-3} \times 24 \times 60 \times \ln \left(\frac{100}{10}\right)}{2 \times \pi \times(3-0.5)} \\ &=574.26 \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{day} \simeq 576 \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{day} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
If the [latex]{BOD}_3[/latex] of a wastewater sample is 75mg/L and reaction rate constant k
(base e) is 0.345 per day, the amount of BOD remaining in the given sample after
10 days is
raw_source.solution:
The BOD at any instant is given by,
[latex]\begin{aligned} L_{t} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-kt} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \;75&=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.345} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L&=\frac{75}{1-0.355} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=116.32\: mg/l \end{aligned}[/latex]
BOD after 10 days,
[latex]\begin{aligned} L_{10} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.345\times 10} \right ] \\ &=116.32\times 0.968 \\ &=112.63\: mg/l \end{aligned}[/latex]
Amount of BOD remaining =[latex]L-L_{0}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=116.32-112.63 \\ &=3.69\: mg/l \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Quality and Characteristics of Waste Water

raw_source.text:
Consider the following statements in the context of geometric design of roads.
I : A simple parabolic curve is an acceptable shape for summit curves
II : Comfort to passengers is an important consideration in the design of summit curves.
The correct otption evaluating the above statements and their relationship is
raw_source.solution:
When fast moving vehicle travels along a summit curve the centrifugal force will act upwards against gravity and hence a part of the pressure on the tyres and spring of the vehicle suspensions is relieved. So there is no problem of discomfort to passengers on Summit curves. The only problem is designing summit curves is to provide adequate sight distances.
Circular summit curve is ideal curve as the sight distance available throughout the length of circular > curve is constant. The deviation angles in vertical curves of highways are very small and so between the same tangent points, a simple parabola is nearly congruent with a circular arc; also a parabola is very easy for arithmetical manipulation for computing ordinates. Thus, in actual practice a simple parabolic curve is used as a summit curve instead of the circular arc.
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning
options: I is true, II is false
I is true, II is true, and II is the correct reason for I
I is true, II is true, and II is NOT the correct reason for I
I is false, II is true

raw_answer.option_text: I is true, II is false

raw_source.text:
Ion concentrations obtained for a groundwater sample (having pH=8.1) are given below.

Total hardness (mg/L as [latex]CaCO_3[/latex]) present in the above water sample is
raw_source.solution:
Total hardness
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\left[\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\right] \times \frac{\mathrm{eq} \cdot \mathrm{wt} . \text { of } \mathrm{CaCO}_{3}}{\mathrm{eq} \cdot \mathrm{wt} \cdot \mathrm{of} \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}} \\ &\qquad +\left[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\right] \times \frac{\mathrm{eq} . \mathrm{wt} . \text { of } \mathrm{CaCO}_{3}}{\text { eq. wh. of } \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}} \\ &=6 \times \frac{50}{12}+100 \times \frac{50}{20}=275 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Ion concentrations obtained for a groundwater sample (having pH=8.1) are given below.

Carbonate hardness (mg/L as [latex]CaCO_3[/latex]) present in the above water sample is
raw_source.solution:
Total alkalinity in water consists of alkalinity caused by [latex]\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}, \mathrm{HCO}_{3}\text{ and }\mathrm{OH}^{-}.[/latex]
A little negative
alkalinity is also caused by [latex]\mathrm{H}^{+} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \text { Total Alkalinity } &=\left[\mathrm{HCO}_{3}^{-}\right] \times \frac{\mathrm{Eq} \cdot \mathrm{wt} . \text { of } \mathrm{CaCO}_{3}}{\mathrm{Eq}, \mathrm{wt} . \text { of } \mathrm{HCO}_{3}^{-}} \\ &=250 \times \frac{50}{61}=205 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Carbonate hardness is equal to the total hardness or alkalinity, whichever is less. The carbonate hardness of the sample will be [latex]205 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Non-carbonate hardness
= Total hardness - carbonate hardness
[latex] =275-205=70 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}[/latex]

A doubly reinforced rectangular concrete beam has a width of 300mm and an effective depth of 500mm. the beam is reinforced with 2200[latex]mm^2[/latex] of steel in tension and 628[latex]mm^2[/latex] of steel in compression. The effective cover for compression steel is 50mm. Assume that both tension and compression steel yield. The grades of concrete and steel used are M20 and Fe250 respectively. The stress lock parameters (rounded off to first two decimal places) for concrete shall be as per IS 456:200.

The depth of neutral axis is
raw_source.solution:
The resultant compressive force in the concrete is given by,
[latex] C_{u c}=0.36 \mathrm{f}_{c k} b x_{u}[/latex]
The resultant compressive force in the compression steel is given by,
[latex] C_{u s}=\left(f_{s c}-0.45 f_{c k}\right) A_{s c}[/latex]
The resultant tensile force in the tensile steel is given by,
[latex] T_{u}=0.87 \mathrm{f} / \mathrm{A}_{s t}[/latex]
we know that,
[latex] \begin{array}{c} C_{u c}+C_{u s}=T_{u} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.36 f_{c k} b x_{u}+\left(f_{s c}-0.45 f_{c k}\right) A_{s c} =0.87 f_{r} A_{s t} \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{u}=\frac{0.87 f_{y} A_{s t}-\left(f_{s c}-0.45 f_{c k}\right) A_{s c}}{0.36 f_{\alpha} b} \end{array}[/latex]
Assuming [latex]f_{s c}=0.87 f_{y} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad x_{u}&=\frac{-(0.87 \times 250-0.45 \times 20) \times 628}{0.36 \times 20 \times 300} \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{u}&=160.91 \mathrm{mm} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{But }x_{u, \max }&=0.53 d\text{ for }\mathrm{Fe} 250 \\ \therefore \quad x_{u, \max }&=0.53 \times 500=265 \mathrm{mm} \\ x_{u}& \lt x_{u, \max } ,\text{ hence the assumption}\\ f_{s c}&=0.87 \mathrm{f}_{y} \text{ is justified.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: [A] is a square matrix which is neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric and [latex][A]^{T}[/latex] is its transpose. The sum and difference of these matrices are defined as [latex][S] = [A]+[A]^{T}[/latex] and [latex][D] = [A]-[A]^{T}[/latex], respectively. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Since
[latex]\begin{aligned} \left ( A+{A}' \right )&=A^{t}+\left ( A^{t} \right )^{t} \\ &=A^{t}+A\\ \text{i.e. } S^{t}&=S \\ \therefore\;\; & \text{ S is symmetric}\\ \text{Since }\left ( A-A^{t} \right )^{t}&=A^{t}-\left ( A^{t} \right )^{t} \\ &=A^{t}-A \\ &=-\left ( A-A^{t} \right ) \\ \text{i.e. } D^{t}&=-D \end{aligned}[/latex]
So D is Skew-Symmetric.
