raw_source.text: For an analytic function, [latex]f(x + iy) = u(x,y)+ iv(x,y), \; u[/latex] is given by [latex]u = 3x^{2}-3y^{2}[/latex]. The expression for [latex]v[/latex], considering [latex]K[/latex] to be a constant is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] f=u+iv \text{ and } u=3x^{2}-3y^{2}[/latex]
For [latex]f[/latex] to be analysis, we have Cauchy-Riemann conditions,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \;\;\;...(i) \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \;\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{From } & \text{ (i) we have,}\\ 6x&=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\ \Rightarrow \; \int \partial v&=\int 6x\partial y \\ v&=6\frac{x^{2}}{2}+f\left ( x \right )\\ \text{i.e., } v&=3x^{2}+f\left ( x \right )\;\;...(iii)\\ \text{Now applying }&\text{equation (ii) we get,}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; -6y&=-\left [ 6x+\frac{df}{dx} \right ]\\ \Rightarrow \;\; 6x+\frac{df}{dx}&=6y \\ \frac{df}{dx}&=6y-6x \\ &\text{By integrating,}\\ f\left ( x \right )&=6yx-3x^{2}+K\\ \text{Substitute }& \text{in equation (iii),}\\ v&=3x^{2}+6yx-3x^{2}+K \\ \Rightarrow \;\; v&=6yx+K \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
if f(x) is continuous at [latex]x=\frac{\pi }{2} [/latex]
[latex]\lim_{x\rightarrow \frac{\pi }{2}}\frac{\lambda \cos x}{\frac{\pi }{2}-x}=f\left ( \frac{\pi }{2} \right )=1[/latex]
Since the limit is in form of [latex]\frac{0}{0}[/latex], we can use L'Hospitals rule on LHS of equation (i) and get
[latex]\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\rightarrow \frac{\pi }{2}}\frac{-\lambda \sin x}{-1}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \sin \frac{\pi }{2}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda &=1\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: What is the value of the definite integral, [latex]\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}}dx[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
Let
[latex]\begin{aligned} I&=\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}} dx \;\; ...(i) \\ \text{Since } \int_{0}^{a}f\left ( x \right )dx&=\int_{0}^{a}f\left ( a-x \right )dx \\ I&=\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{a-x}}{\sqrt{a-x}+\sqrt{x}}dx \;\; ...(ii)\\ (i)+(ii) \; \Rightarrow \; 2I&=\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}}dx \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 2I&=\int_{0}^{a}dx \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 2I&=a \\ \Rightarrow \;\; I&=a/2\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]\vec{a}\; and\; \vec{b}[/latex] are two arbitrary vectors with magnitudes a and b, respectively,  [latex]|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^{2}[/latex] will be equal to
The solution of the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x[/latex], with the condition that y = 1 at x = 1, is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+\frac{y}{x}=x, \; y\left ( 1 \right )=1[/latex]
This is a linear differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+Py =Q [/latex] with [latex]P=\frac{1}{x}[/latex] and [latex]Q=x[/latex]
IF = Integrating Factor
[latex] =e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{\ln x}=x[/latex]
Solution is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} y.IF&=\int Q\left ( IF \right )dx+C \\ y.x&=\int \left ( x.x \right )dx+C \\ yx&=\int x^{2}dx+C \\ yx&=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C \\ y&=\frac{x^{2}}{3}+\frac{C}{x} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, [latex]y(1)=1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \frac{1^{2}}{3}+\frac{C}{1} =1 \; \Rightarrow \; C=\frac{2}{3}[/latex]
So the solution is [latex]y=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{2}{3x}[/latex]

For an analytic function, [latex]f(x + iy) = u(x,y)+ iv(x,y), \; u[/latex] is given by [latex]u = 3x^{2}-3y^{2}[/latex]. The expression for [latex]v[/latex], considering [latex]K[/latex] to be a constant is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] f=u+iv \text{ and } u=3x^{2}-3y^{2}[/latex]
For [latex]f[/latex] to be analysis, we have Cauchy-Riemann conditions,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \;\;\;...(i) \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \;\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{From } & \text{ (i) we have,}\\ 6x&=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\ \Rightarrow \; \int \partial v&=\int 6x\partial y \\ v&=6\frac{x^{2}}{2}+f\left ( x \right )\\ \text{i.e., } v&=3x^{2}+f\left ( x \right )\;\;...(iii)\\ \text{Now applying }&\text{equation (ii) we get,}\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}&=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; -6y&=-\left [ 6x+\frac{df}{dx} \right ]\\ \Rightarrow \;\; 6x+\frac{df}{dx}&=6y \\ \frac{df}{dx}&=6y-6x \\ &\text{By integrating,}\\ f\left ( x \right )&=6yx-3x^{2}+K\\ \text{Substitute }& \text{in equation (iii),}\\ v&=3x^{2}+6yx-3x^{2}+K \\ \Rightarrow \;\; v&=6yx+K \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
What should be the value of [latex]\lambda[/latex] such that the function defined below is continuous at [latex]x = \pi /2[/latex]?
[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} \frac{\lambda \cos x}{\frac{\pi }{2}-x} &if x \neq \frac{\pi }{2} \\ 1& if x= \frac{\pi }{2} \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
if f(x) is continuous at [latex]x=\frac{\pi }{2} [/latex]
[latex]\lim_{x\rightarrow \frac{\pi }{2}}\frac{\lambda \cos x}{\frac{\pi }{2}-x}=f\left ( \frac{\pi }{2} \right )=1[/latex]
Since the limit is in form of [latex]\frac{0}{0}[/latex], we can use L'Hospitals rule on LHS of equation (i) and get
[latex]\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\rightarrow \frac{\pi }{2}}\frac{-\lambda \sin x}{-1}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \sin \frac{\pi }{2}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda &=1\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: What is the value of the definite integral, [latex]\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}}dx[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
Let
[latex]\begin{aligned} I&=\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}} dx \;\; ...(i) \\ \text{Since } \int_{0}^{a}f\left ( x \right )dx&=\int_{0}^{a}f\left ( a-x \right )dx \\ I&=\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{a-x}}{\sqrt{a-x}+\sqrt{x}}dx \;\; ...(ii)\\ (i)+(ii) \; \Rightarrow \; 2I&=\int_{0}^{a}\frac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a-x}}dx \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 2I&=\int_{0}^{a}dx \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 2I&=a \\ \Rightarrow \;\; I&=a/2\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]\vec{a}\; and\; \vec{b}[/latex] are two arbitrary vectors with magnitudes a and b, respectively,  [latex]|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^{2}[/latex] will be equal to
The solution of the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x[/latex], with the condition that y = 1 at x = 1, is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+\frac{y}{x}=x, \; y\left ( 1 \right )=1[/latex]
This is a linear differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+Py =Q [/latex] with [latex]P=\frac{1}{x}[/latex] and [latex]Q=x[/latex]
IF = Integrating Factor
[latex] =e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{\ln x}=x[/latex]
Solution is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} y.IF&=\int Q\left ( IF \right )dx+C \\ y.x&=\int \left ( x.x \right )dx+C \\ yx&=\int x^{2}dx+C \\ yx&=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C \\ y&=\frac{x^{2}}{3}+\frac{C}{x} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, [latex]y(1)=1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \frac{1^{2}}{3}+\frac{C}{1} =1 \; \Rightarrow \; C=\frac{2}{3}[/latex]
So the solution is [latex]y=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{2}{3x}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a bar of diameter 'D' embedded in a large concrete block as shown in the adjoining figure, with a pull out force P being applied. Let [latex]\sigma _b[/latex] and [latex]\sigma _{st}[/latex] be the bond strength (between the bar and concrete) and the tensile strength of the bar, respectively. If the block is held in position and it is assumed that the material of the block does not fail, which of the following options represents the maximum value of P?
raw_source.solution:
Maximum force resisted by bond strength
[latex] =\sigma_{b}(\pi D L) [/latex]
Maximum tensile force resisted by bar

[latex] \therefore [/latex] Maximum value of P= Minimum of [latex] \left\{\sigma_{b}(\pi D L)\text{or}\left(\sigma_{s t} \frac{\pi}{4} D^{2}\right)\right\}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider two RCC beams, P and Q, each having the section 400 mm x 750 mm
(effective depth, d = 750 mm) made with concrete having a [latex]\tau _{cmax}=2.1N/mm^{2}[/latex]. For the reinforcement provided and the grade of concrete used, it may be assumed that the [latex]\tau _{c}=0.75N/mm^{2}[/latex]. The design shear in beam P is 400 kN and in beam Q is 750 kN. Considering the provisions of IS 456-2000, which of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Shear strength of the concrete [latex] =\tau_{c} \times B d [/latex]
[latex] =0.75 \times 400 \times 750 \times 10^{-3}=225 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]
Maximum shear strength of concrete
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\tau_{c \max } \times B d \\ =2.1 \times 400 \times 750 \times 10^{-3}=630 \mathrm{kN} \end{array}[/latex]
Design shear in beam P is 400kN which is less than the maximum shear that the concrete can sustain. But the design shear is more than the nominal shear of 225 kN.
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Shear reinforcement is designed for
[latex] =400-225=175 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]
Design shear in beam Q is 750 kN which is more than the maximum shear that the concrete can sustain. Hence the beam Q should be redesigned.
raw_source.tag2: Shear, Torsion, Bond, Anchorage and Development Length
options:
Shere reinforcement should be designed for 175 kN for beam P and the
section for beam Q should be revised.

Nominal shear reinforcement is required for beam P and the shear
reinforcement should be designed for 120 kN for beam Q.

Shear reinforcement should be designed for 175 kN for beam P and the
shear reinforcement should be designed for 525 kN for beam Q.
The sections for both beams P and Q need to be revised.

raw_answer.option_text:
Shere reinforcement should be designed for 175 kN for beam P and the
section for beam Q should be revised.

raw_source.text: The figure shows a schematic representation of a steel plate girder to be used as a simply supported beam with a concentrated load. For stiffeners, PQ (running along the beam axis) and RS (running between the top and bottom flanges), which of the following pairs of statements will be TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
PQ is a horizontal stiffener in the given plate girder. Horizontal stiffeners are also called longitudinal stiffeners. The horizontal stiffener are provided in the compression zone of the web. The first horizontal stiffener is provided at one-fifth of the distance from the compression flange to the tension flange. If required another stiffener is provided at the neutral axis. Horizontal stiffeners are not continuous and are provided between vertical stiffeners.
RS is a vertical stiffener in the given plate girder. Vertical stiffeners are also called transverse stiffeners. It is assumed that the vertical stiffener is not subjected to any load and is selected to provide necessary lateral stiffness only and can therefore, br crimped or joggled for tight fittings. Such stiffeners increase the buckling resistance of the web caused by shear.
options:
(i) RS should be provided under the concentrated load only.
(ii) PQ should be placed in the tension side of the flange.

(i) RS helps to prevent local buckling of the web.
(ii) PQ should be placed in the compression side of the flange.

(i) RS should be provided at supports.
(ii) PQ should be placed along the neutral axis.

(i) RS should be provided away from points of action of concentrated loads.
(ii) PQ should be provided on the compression side of the flange.

raw_answer.option_text: (i) RS helps to prevent local buckling of the web. (ii) PQ should be placed in the compression side of the flange.

raw_source.text: A singly under-reamed, 8 m long, RCC pile (shown in the figure) weighing 20 kN with 350 mm shaft diameter and 750 mm under-ream diameter is installed within stiff, saturated silty clay (undrained shear strength is 50 kPa, adhesion factor is 0.3, and the applicable bearing capacity factor is 9) to counteract the impact of soil swelling on a structure constructed above. Neglecting suction and the contribution of the under-ream to the adhesive shaft capacity, what would be the estimated ultimate tensile capacity (rounded off to the nearest integer value of kN) of the pile?
raw_source.solution:
The tensile resistance of a pile is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{t} &=Q_{s}+W+Q_{b} \\ \text{Where}\quad Q_{s} &=\text { shaft resistance }=\alpha c A_{s} \\ W &=\text { weight of pile } \\ Q_{1} &=c N_{c} A_{b} \\ \therefore \quad Q_{1} &=\alpha c A_{s}+W+c N_{c} A_{b} \\ &=0.3 \times 50 \times \pi \times 0.35 \times 8+20 \\ &+\frac{50 \times 9 \times \pi\left(0.75^{2}-0.35^{2}\right)}{4} \\ &=300.796 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Identical surcharges are placed at ground surface at sites X and Y , with soil conditions shown in figure and water table at ground surface. The silty clay layers at X and Y are identical. The thin sand layer at Y is continuous and freedraining with a very large discharge capacity. If primary consolidation at X is estimated to complete in 36 months, what would be the corresponding time for completion of primary consolidation at Y ?
raw_source.solution:
The time required for any degree of consolidation can be obtained from the Taylor's formula,
[latex] T_{v}=\frac{C_{v} t}{d^{2}}[/latex]
since C_{v} is constant for same type of soil and [latex]T_{v} [/latex] is constant for same degree of consolidation,
[latex] t \propto d^{2} [/latex] where d is the length of drainage path.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}&=\left(\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}\right)^{2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{36}{t_{2}}&=\left(\frac{10}{10 / 2}\right)^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad t_{2}&=\frac{36}{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad t_{2}&=9 \;\text{months} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A field vane shear testing instrument (shown in figure) was inserted completely into a deposit of soft, saturated silty clay with the vane rod vertical such that the top of the blades were 500 mm below the ground surface. Upon application of a rapidly increasing torque about the vane rod, the soil was found to fail when the torque reached 4.6 Nm. Assuming mobilization of undrained shear strength on all failure surfaces to be uniform and the resistance mobilized on the surface of the vane rod to be neglibible, what would be the peak undrained shear strength (rounded off to the nearest integer value of kPa) of the soil?
raw_source.solution:
When the top end of the vane completely shear the soil, Then the torque at failure is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} T&=c_{u} \pi\left(\frac{d^{\prime} h}{2}+\frac{d^{3}}{6}\right)\\ \Rightarrow \frac{4.6}{1000}&=c_{u} \times \pi \times\left(\frac{(0.05)^{2} \times 0.1}{2}+\frac{(0.05)^{3}}{6}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad c_{u}&=10 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A single pipe of length 1500 m and diameter 60 cm connects two reservoirs having
a difference of 20 m in their water levels. The pipe is to be replaced by two pipes
of the same length and equal diameter d to convey 25% more discharge under the
same head loss. If the friction factor is assumed to be the same for all the pipes,
the value of d is approximately equal to which of the following options?
raw_source.solution:
For single pipe
[latex] \begin{array}{r} n=\frac{81 L Q}{\pi^{2} g D^{2}} \\ L=1500 \mathrm{m}, \mathrm{D}=0.6 \mathrm{m} \\ n_{f}=20 \mathrm{m} \\ Q_{1}=\frac{0.112}{\sqrt{1}} \end{array}[/latex]


In case of double pipe discharge is increased by 25% than that of previous case hence.
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2Q_{2}&=1.25Q_{1}\\ 20 &= \frac{8F\times 500\times(0.625Q_{1})^{2}}{9.81\times \pi^{2}\times d^{5}}\\ Q_{1}&= \frac{0.402\times d^{5/2}}{\sqrt{f}}\\ \frac{Q_{1}^{2}}{d^{5}}&=0.413\\ Q_{1}^{2}&=\frac{0.413d^{5}}{f}\\ Q_{1}&=\frac{0.642d^{5/2}}{\sqrt{f}}\ldots\\ \text{From eq }(i) &\text{and }(ii),\text{ we get}\\ d&=437 \mathrm{cm}=50 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A spillway discharges flood flow at a rate of 9 [latex]m^3[/latex]/s per metre width. If the depth
of flow on the horizontal apron at the toe of the spillway is 46 cm, the tail water
depth needed to form a hydraulic jump is approximately given by which of the
following options?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{q}&=9 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m}\\ \text{and }y_{1}&=46 \mathrm{cm}=0.46 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad V_{1}&=\frac{q}{y_{1}}=\frac{9}{0.46}=19.565 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ F_{1}&=\frac{V_{1}}{\sqrt{g y_{1}}}=\frac{19.565}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 0.46}}=9.21 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus, flow is super -critical.
Thus the sequent depth will be
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{y_{2}}{y_{1}}&=\frac{1}{2}\left[-1+\sqrt{1+8 F_{1}^{2}}\right]\\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{2}&=\frac{0.46}{2}\left[-1+\sqrt{1+8 \times(9.21)^{2}}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{2}&=0.23 \times 25.07 \\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{2}&=5.77 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In an aquifer extending over 150 hectare, the water table was 20m below ground
level. Over a period of time the water table dropped to 23m below the ground
level. If the porosity of aquifer is 0.40 and the specific retention is 0.15, what is
the change in ground water storage of the aquifer?
raw_source.solution:
We know that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} n&=S_{y}+S_{r} \\ \Rightarrow\quad S_{y}&=S_{t}-n=0.15-0.40=-0.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The negative sign signifies the decrease in storage. Change in volume of aquifer
[latex] =150 \times(23-20)=450 \mathrm{ha}-\mathrm{m}[/latex]
Specific yield is nothing but the actual volume of water that can be extracted by force of gravity from a unit volume of aquifer.
[latex]\therefore [/latex]Change in water storage
[latex] =450 \times 0.25=112.5 \mathrm{ha}-\mathrm{m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Total suspended particulate matter (TSP) concentration in ambient air is to be
measured using a high volume sampler. The filter used for this purpose had an
initial dry weight of 9.787 g. The filter was mounted in the sampler and the initial
air flow rate through the filter was set at 1.5[latex]m^3[/latex]/min. Sampling continued for
24 hours. The airflow after 24 hours was measured to be 1.4 [latex]m^3[/latex]/min. The dry
weight of the filter paper after 24 hour sampling was 10.283 g. Assuming a linear
decline in the air flow rate during sampling, what is the 24 hour average TSP
concentration in the ambient air?
raw_source.solution:
Average airflow rate
[latex]= 1.5-\left ( \frac{1.5-1.4}{24\times 60} \right )\times 12=1.45\; m^{3}/min[/latex]
Total airflow through the sampler during 24 hours
[latex] =1.45\times 24\times 60=2088\: m^{3}[/latex]
TSP concentration in the ambient air
[latex]=\left ( \frac{10.283-9.787}{2088} \right )\times 10^6=237.5\mu g/m^3[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Chlorine gas (8 mg/L as [latex]CI_2[/latex]) was added to a drinking water sample. If the free chlorine residual and pH was measured to be 2mg/L (as [latex]CI_2[/latex]) and 7.5, respectively, what is the concentration of residual [latex]OCI^{-} [/latex] ions in the water? Assume that the chlorine gas added to the water is completely converted to HOCl and [latex]OCI^{-}[/latex]. Atomic Weight of Cl: 35.5
Given: [latex]OC1^{-}+H^{+}\leftrightharpoons^k HOCI, \; \; \; K=10^{7.5}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]OCl^{-}\: +\: H^{+}\: \rightleftharpoons ^{K}\; \; HOCl;\; K=10^{7.5}[/latex]
Now,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\left [ HOCl \right ]}{\left [ OCl^{-} \right ]\left [ H^{+} \right ]} &= K\\ pH&=7.5 \\ \left [ H^{+} \right ]&=10^{7.5} \\ \left [ \frac{HOCl}{OCl^{-}} \right ]&=10^{7.5}\times 10^{-7.5}=1 \\ \therefore \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \left [ HOCl \right ] &=\left [ OCl^{-} \right ] \\ \left [ \text{Free chlorine residual} \right ]&=\left [ HOCl \right ]+\left [ OCl^{-} \right ] \\ \text{Free chlorine residual} &= 2\; \text{mg/l}\\ \left [ \text{Free chlorine residual} \right ] &=\frac{2\times 10^{-3}}{Mol.\; wt\; of\; Cl_{2}} \\ &=\frac{2\times 10^{-3}}{2\times 35.5} \\ &=2.817\times 10^{-5}\; \text{moles/l} \\ \therefore \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; 2.817\times 10^{-5} &=\left [ HOCl \right ]+\left [ OCl^{-} \right ] \\ \therefore \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \left [ OCl^{-} \right ] &=\frac{2.817\times 10^{-5}}{2} \\ \because \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \left [ OCl^{-} \right ] &=\left [ HOCl \right ] \\ &=1.4084\times 10^{-5}\; \text{moles/l} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The cumulative arrival and departure curve of one cycle of an approach lane of a signalized intersection is shown in the figure. The cycle time is 50 s and the effective red time is 30 s and the effective green time is 20 s. What is the average delay?
raw_source.solution:
Average delay
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\left(\begin{array}{c}\text { Area of triangle formed } \\ \text { by arrival curve }\end{array}\right)-\left(\begin{array}{c}\text { Area of triangle formed } \\ \text { by departure curve }\end{array}\right)}{\text { No. of vehicles }} \\ &=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 50-\frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 20}{40} \\ &=15 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A sand layer found at sea floor under 20 m water depth is characterized with relative density=40%,
maximum void ratio=1.0 ,
minimum void ratio=0.5, and
specific gravity of soil solids=2.67.
Assume the specific gravity of sea water to be 1.03 and the unit weight of fresh water to be 9.81 kN/[latex]m^3[/latex].

What would be the effective stress (rounded off to the nearest integer value of kPa) at 30 m depth into the sand layer?
raw_source.solution:
Relative density is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{D}(\%)&=\left(\frac{e_{\max }-e_{\text {nat }}}{e_{\max }-e_{\min }}\right) \times 100\\ \Rightarrow \quad 40&=\left(\frac{1-e_{n a t}}{1-0.5}\right) \times 100 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.4 \times 0.5&=1-e_{\text {nat }} \\ \Rightarrow \quad e_{\text {nat }}&=0.8 \\ \text{Also,} \quad G_{\text {sea }}&=\frac{\gamma_{\text {sea }}}{\gamma_{w}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \gamma_{\text {sea }}&=1.03 \times 9.81 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \gamma_{\mathrm{sea}}&=10.1043 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} \gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}&=\left(\frac{G \gamma_{sea}+\mathrm{Se}_{\text {nat }} \times \gamma_{\text {sea }}}{1+e_{\text {nat }}}\right)\\ &=\left(\frac{2.67 \times 10.1043 +1 \times 0.8 \times 10.1043}{1+0.8}\right) \\ &=19.48 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Total stress at the bottom of sand layer,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma &=20 \times \gamma_{\operatorname{sen}}+30 \times \gamma_{\text {sat}} \\ &=20 \times 10.1043+30 \times 19.48 \\ &=786.486 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Pore water pressure at the bottom of sand layer,
[latex] \begin{aligned} u &=(20+30) \times 10.1043 \\ &=505.215 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Effective stress at the bottom of sand layer.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{\sigma} &=\sigma-u=786.486 -505.215 \\ &=281.271 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A sand layer found at sea floor under 20 m water depth is characterized with relative density=40%,
maximum void ratio=1.0 ,
minimum void ratio=0.5, and
specific gravity of soil solids=2.67.
Assume the specific gravity of sea water to be 1.03 and the unit weight of fresh water to be 9.81 kN/[latex]m^3[/latex].

What would be the change in the effective stress (rounded off to the nearest integer value of kPa) at 30 m depth into the sand layer if the sea water level permanently rises by 2m?
raw_source.solution:
The effective stress will not alter due to change in sea water level. The total stress will increase due to increase in sea water level. The pore water pressure will also increase in the same proportion, thus nullifying the effect of each other


[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma &=22 \times 10.1043+30 \times 19.48 \\ &=806.695 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ u &=(22+30) \times 10.1043 \\ &=525.424 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \therefore\quad \bar{\sigma} &=\sigma-u=806.695-525.424 \\ &=281.271 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A storm of 6.6 cm occurs uniformly over the catchment in 3 hours. If [latex]\phi[/latex] -index is equal to 2mm/h and base flow is 5[latex]m^{3}/s[/latex], what is the peak flow due to the storm?
raw_source.solution:

The free diagram of the beam is shown below

[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{L}{\delta_{1}}=\frac{2 L}{\delta_{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{2}=2 \delta_{1} \quad &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking moments about hinge, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} P \times 2 L-k \delta_{2} \times 2 L-k \delta_{1} \times L&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 P-k\left(2 \delta_{2}+\delta_{1}\right)&=0 &[\therefore\text{ from(i)}]\\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 P-k\left(4 \delta_{1}+\delta_{1}\right)&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \delta_{1}&=\frac{2 P}{5 k} \end{aligned}[/latex]
From (i), we get
[latex] \delta_{2}=2 \times \frac{2 P}{5 k}=\frac{4 P}{5 k}[/latex]

The annual precipitation data of a city is normally distributed with mean and standard deviation as

In normal distribution

Reciprocal levelling eliminates the errors due to
(i) Error in instrument adjustment.
(ii) Combined effect of earth's curvature and the refraction of the atmosphere.
(iii) Variation in the average refraction.

raw_source.text: The error in [latex]\frac{d}{dx}f(x)|_{x=x_{0}}[/latex] for a continuous function estimated with h = 0.03 using the central difference formula [latex]\frac{d}{dx}f(x)|_{x=x_{0}}\approx \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0}-h)}{2h}, \text{ is } 2 \times 10^{-3}[/latex]. Error in central difference formula is [latex]0\left ( h^{2} \right )[/latex]

In an experiment, positive and negative values are equally likely to occur. The probability of
obtaining at most one negative value in five trials is
raw_source.solution:
Since negative and positive are equally likely, the distribution of number of negative values is binomial with n=5 and p=1/2
Let X represent number of negative values in 5 trials.
p(at most 1 negative value)
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=p\left ( x\leq 1 \right ) \\ &=p\left ( x=0 \right )+p\left ( x=1 \right ) \\ &=5C_{0}\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^{0}\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^{5}+5C_{1}\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^{1}\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^{4}\\&=\frac{6}{32} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the parallelogram OPQR shown in the sketch, [latex]\overrightarrow{OP}=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j} \; and \; \overrightarrow{OR}=c\hat{i}+d\hat{j}[/latex]. The area of the parallelogram is
raw_source.solution:
The area of parallelogram OPQR in figure shown above, is the magnitude of the vector product
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\left | \overrightarrow{OP}\times \overrightarrow{OR} \right | \\ \overrightarrow{OP}&=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j} \\ \overrightarrow{OR}&=c\hat{i}+d\hat{j} \\ \overrightarrow{OP}\times \overrightarrow{OR}&=\begin{vmatrix} i & j & k\\ a & b & 0\\ c & d & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=0\hat{i}+0\hat{j}+\left ( ad-bc \right )\hat{k} \\ \left | \overrightarrow{OP}\times \overrightarrow{OR} \right |&=\sqrt{0^{2}+0^{2}+\left ( ad-bc \right )^{2}} \\ &=ad-bc \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The solution of the ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=0[/latex] for the boundary condition, y = 5 at x = 1 is
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Given, }\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2y&=0 \text{ and } y(1)=5 \\    \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=-2y \\    \int \frac{dy}{y}&=\int -2dx \\ \Rightarrow \;\;  \ln y&=-2x+c \\ \Rightarrow   \;\; y&=e^{-2x}.e^{c}=c_{1}e^{-2x} \\    y\left ( 1 \right )&=c_{1}e^{-2}=5 \\ \Rightarrow \; c_{1}&=\frac{5}{e^{-2}} \\ \text{So, }   y&=\frac{5}{e^{-2}}e^{-2x}=5e^{2}e^{-2x} \\     &=36.95\, e^{-2x} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A layer of normally consolidated, saturated silty clay of 1 m thickness is subjected to one
dimensional consolidation under a pressure increment of 20 kPa. The properties of the soil are:
specific gravity = 2.7, natural moisture content = 45%, compression index = 0.45, and
recompression index = 0.05. The initial average effective stress within the layer is 100 kPa.

the nearest mm) is
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta \bar{\sigma} &=20 \mathrm{kPa}, \bar{\sigma}_{0}=100 \mathrm{kPa} \\ G &=2.7 \\ \mathrm{w} &=45 \% \\ \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{c}} &=0.45 \\ \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{r}} &=0.05 \\ \mathrm{H}_{0} &=1 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{H} &=\frac{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{H}_{0}}{1+\mathrm{e}_{0}} \log _{10}\left[\frac{\overline{\mathrm{\sigma}}_{0}+\Delta \overline{\mathrm{o}}}{\overline{\mathrm{\sigma}}_{0}}\right] \\ \text{Also},\quad wG&=eS \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.45 \times 2.7 &=e .1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad &=1.215 \\ \therefore \quad \Delta H &=\frac{0.45 \times 1}{1+1.215} \log _{10}\left(\frac{(100+20)}{100}\right) \\ &=\frac{0.45}{2.215} \log _{10}\left(\frac{120}{100}\right) \\ &=0.016 \mathrm{m}=16 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

width of pavement = 7.5 m.

In order to provide a stopping sight distance (SSD) of 80 m, the set back distance (in m) required from the centre line of the inner lane of the pavement is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{ccc} \text{Length of curve,} &L_{c}&=200 \mathrm{m} \\ \text{ Radius,}&R&=300 \mathrm{m}\\ \text{Width,}&w&=7.5 \mathrm{m}\\ \text{SSD, }&S&=80 \mathrm{m} \\ \because \quad L_{c} \gt S&& \end{array}[/latex]
Set back distance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} m &=(R)-(R-d) \cos \frac{\alpha}{2} \\ \frac{\alpha}{2} &=\frac{180 \cdot S}{2 \pi(R-d)}=\frac{180 \times 80}{2 \pi \times\left(300-\frac{7.5}{4}\right)} \\ &=7.687 \\ m &=300-\left(300-\frac{7.5}{4}\right) \cos (7.687) \\ &=2.67 \end{aligned}[/latex]
After this: The setback distance (in m) required from the centre line of the inner lane of the pavement is [latex]= 4.55-\frac{7.5}{4} = 2.675 m[/latex]

Capacity per lane
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1800}{2}=900 \text { Vehicle/hour } \\ k_{j} &=\frac{1000}{5}=200 \text { Veh. } / \mathrm{km} \\ q_{\max } &=\frac{V_{s t} \times k_{j}}{4} \\ 900 &=\frac{V_{s t} \times 200}{4}\\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{s t}&=18 \mathrm{kmph} \\ \therefore \quad V&=V_{s f}\left[1-\frac{k}{k_{j}}\right] \\ \therefore \quad q&=v k \\ \because \quad q&=V k \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since traffice volume =1000 vehicle/hour for two lane
So, for single lane,
[latex] \begin{aligned} q&=500 \text{ vehicle/hour } \\ q&=V_{s f}\left[1-\frac{k}{k_{l}}\right] k \\ \Rightarrow \quad 500&=18\left[1-\frac{k}{200}\right] k \\ \Rightarrow \quad 27.77&=k-\frac{k^{2}}{200} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 5554&=200 k-k^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad k^{2}-200 k&+5554=0 \\ \therefore \quad k=33.32 &\text{Veh./km (for single lane)}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, for two lane urban road,

Find the magnitude of the error (correct to two decimal places) in the estimation of following integral using Simpson's [latex]\frac{1}{3}[/latex] Rule. Take the step length as 1. __________

[latex]\int_{0}^{4}(x^{4}+10)dx[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Using Simpson's Rule,


[latex]\begin{aligned} & \int_{0}^{4}\left ( x^{4}+10 \right )dx \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left [ \left ( 10+266 \right )+2\left ( 26 \right )+4\left ( 11+91 \right ) \right ] \\ &=245.33 \\ &\text{The value of integral,} \\ \int_{0}^{4}\left ( x^{4}+10 \right )dx&=\left [ \frac{x^{5}}{5}+10x \right ]^{4}_{0} \\ &=\frac{4^{5}}{5}+10\times 4 \\ &=244.8 \\ \therefore \; &\text{ MAgnitude of error}\\ &=245.33-244.8 \\ &=0.53\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The solution for [latex]\int_{0}^{\pi /6}\cos^{4} 3\theta \sin^{3}6\theta d\theta[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi }{6}}\cos ^{4}3\theta \sin ^{3}6\theta d\theta \\    &=8\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi }{6}}\cos ^{6}3\theta \sin ^{3}3\theta \cos 3\theta \, d\theta\\ \text{Put } \sin 3\theta &=t \\ \Rightarrow \; 3\cos 3\theta \, d\theta &=dt \\ \Rightarrow \;   I&=\frac{8}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\left ( 1-t^{2} \right )^{3}\: t^{3}.\: dt \\    &=\frac{8}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\left ( t^{6}-2t^{2}+3t^{4} \right )t^{3}\: dt \\    &=\frac{8}{3}\int_{0}^{1}\left ( t^{3}-t^{9}-3t^{5}+3t^{7} \right )\: dt \\    &=\frac{8}{3}\left [ \frac{t^{4}}{4}-\frac{t^{10}}{10}-\frac{3t^{6}}{6}+\frac{3t^{8}}{8} \right ]_{0}^{1} \\    &=\frac{8}{3}\left [ \frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{10}-\frac{3}{6}+\frac{3}{8} \right ] \\    &=\frac{8}{3}\left [ \frac{30-12-60+45}{120} \right ] \\    &=\left [ \frac{1}{15} \right ] \end{aligned}[/latex]

Find the value of [latex]\lambda[/latex] such that the function f(x) is a valid probability density function. __________
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\lambda (x-1)(2-x)& for \; 1\leq x\leq 2\\ &=0& otherwise \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f\left ( x \right )dx&=1 \\ f\left ( x \right )=\left \{ \begin{matrix} \lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right ) & 1\leq x\leq 2\\ 0 & otherwise \end{matrix} \right. &\\ \therefore\;\;  \int_{1}^{2}\lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right )dx&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{x^{3}}{3}+3\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x \right ]_{1}^{2}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\left ( \frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \right )+\frac{3}{2}\left ( 4-1 \right )-2\left ( 2-1 \right ) \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{7}{3}+\frac{9}{2}-2 \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ \frac{-14+27-12}{6} \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda &=\frac{6}{1}=6 \\   \lambda &=6 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The pin-jointed 2-D truss is loaded with a horizontal force of 15 kN at joint S and another 15 kN vertical force at joint U, as shown. Find the force in member RS (in kN) and report your answer taking tension as positive and compression as negative. __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Sigma M_{T}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow R_{v} \times 8-15 \times 4+15 \times 4 & =0 \\ \therefore \quad R_{V} & =0\\ \text{Take moment about V, } M_{V}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad R_{H} \times 4&=0 \\ \therefore \quad R_{H}&=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]


We know that if two members meet at a joint which are not collinear and also there is no external forces acting on that joint then both members will carry zero forces.
[latex] \therefore F_{O V}=F_{Q R}=0[/latex]
Now, consider joint R ,
[latex] \Sigma F_{y}=0[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow F_{R U} \sin 45^{\circ}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow F_{R U}&=0\\ \text{Now},\quad \Sigma F_{x}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad F_{R S}+F_{R U} \cos 45^{\circ}&=0 \\ \therefore F_{R S}&=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

In its natural condition, a soil sample has a mass of 1.980 kg and a volume of 0.001 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]. After being completely dried in an oven, the mass of the sample is 1.800 kg. Specific gravity G is 2.7. 
Unit weight of water is 10 kN/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]. The degree of saturation of the soil is:
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \rho &=\frac{M}{V} \\ &=\frac{1.980}{0.001}=1980 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \rho_{d} &=\frac{M_{d}}{V}\\ &=\frac{1.800}{0.001}=1800 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \rho_{d} &=\frac{\rho}{1+\mathrm{w}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1800 &=\frac{1980}{1+\mathrm{w}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \mathrm{w}=0.1 \\ \because \quad & \rho_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{\mathrm{G} \cdot \rho_{\mathrm{w}}}{1+\mathrm{e}}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 1800&=\frac{2.7 \times 1000}{1+e} \\ \Rightarrow \quad e&=0.5 \\ \because wG&=e.s\\ \Rightarrow 0.1 \times 2.7&=0.5 S \\ \Rightarrow \quad S&=0.54 \end{aligned}[/latex]

It was observed that 150 vehicles crossed a particular location of a highway ina duration of 30
minutes. Assuming that vehicle arrival follows a negative exponential distribution, find out the
number of time headways greater than 5 seconds in the above observation? __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]P(x)=\frac{\lambda^{n} e^{-\lambda}}{x !}[/latex]
Where, P(x) is the probability of x events (vehicle arrivals) in some time interval (t).
[latex] \lambda [/latex] is the mean arrival rate in that interval.
[latex] \lambda=\frac{150}{30 \times 60} \times 5=\frac{5}{12}[/latex]
Now, the probability that zero vehicle arrive in an interval t, denoted as P(0), will be same as the probability that the headway (into arrival time) greater than or equal to t.
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \therefore P(x=0)=\frac{\lambda^{0} e^{-\lambda}}{0 !}=e^{-5 / 12}=0.6592 \\ \therefore P(x=0)=0.6592 \end{array}[/latex]
Number of time headway in 30 minutes
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =0.6592 \times 30 \times 60 \\ =1186.63 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f\left ( x \right )dx&=1 \\ f\left ( x \right )=\left \{ \begin{matrix} \lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right ) & 1\leq x\leq 2\\ 0 & otherwise \end{matrix} \right. &\\ \therefore\;\;  \int_{1}^{2}\lambda \left ( -x^{2}+3x-2 \right )dx&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{x^{3}}{3}+3\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x \right ]_{1}^{2}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\left ( \frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \right )+\frac{3}{2}\left ( 4-1 \right )-2\left ( 2-1 \right ) \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ -\frac{7}{3}+\frac{9}{2}-2 \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda \left [ \frac{-14+27-12}{6} \right ]&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda &=\frac{6}{1}=6 \\   \lambda &=6 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Laplace equation for water flow in soils is given below.
[latex]\frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial y^2}+\frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial z^2}=0[/latex]
Head H does not vary in y and z directions.
Boundary conditions are: at x = 0, H = 5; and [latex]\frac{dH}{dx}=-1[/latex].
What is the value of [latex]H[/latex] at [latex]x = 1.2[/latex]? __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{\partial^{2} H}{\partial x^{2}}=0[/latex]
Integrating both sides, we get
[latex] \frac{\partial H}{\partial x}=C_{1} \quad \ldots(i)[/latex]
Integrating again
[latex] \begin{aligned} H&=C_{1} x+C_{2}\\ \text{At }\quad x&=0, H=5 \\ \therefore \quad 5&=C_{2} \\ \text{At }\quad x&=0, \frac{d H}{d x}=-1 \end{aligned} [/latex]
From eq. (i)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore C_{1}&=-1 \\ \therefore \quad H&=-x+5 \\ \text { At } x &=1.2 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{H}&=5-1.2=3.8 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A uniform beam (EI=constant) PQ in the form of a quarter-circle of radius R is fixed at end P and free at the end Q, where a load W is applied as shown. The vertical downward displacement, [latex]\delta _{q}[/latex], at the loaded point Q is given by: [latex]\delta _{q}=\beta (\frac{WR^{3}}{EI})[/latex]. Find the value of [latex]\beta[/latex](correct to 4-decimal places). __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} U &=\int \frac{M^{2} d x}{2 E l}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{(W R \sin \theta)^{2} R d \theta}{2 E l} \\ &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{P^{2} R^{3}}{2 E l} \sin ^{2} \theta d \theta \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{P^{2} R^{3}}{2 E I} \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \frac{(1-\cos 2 \theta) d \theta}{2} \\ &=\frac{P^{2} R^{3}}{4 E I}\left[\theta-\frac{\sin 2 \theta}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi / 2} \\ &=\frac{P^{2} R^{3}}{4 E I}\left[\frac{\pi}{2}\right]=\frac{P^{2} R^{3} \pi}{8 E I} \\ \therefore \quad \delta_{Q}&=\frac{\partial U}{\partial W}=\frac{2 P R^{3} \pi}{8 E I}=\frac{P R^{3}}{E I} \frac{\pi}{4} \\ \therefore \quad \delta_{Q}&=\frac{\pi}{4}\left(\frac{W R^{3}}{E !}\right) \\ \therefore \quad \beta&=\frac{\pi}{4}=0.7854 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A uniform beam weighting 1800 N is supported at E and F by cable ABCD. Determine the tension (in N) in segment AB of this cable (correct to 1-decimal place). Assume the cable ABCD, BE and CF to be weightless. _____
raw_source.solution:
Taking moment about A,
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{D} \times 4 &=1800 \times 1.5 \\ \Rightarrow R_{D}&=675 \mathrm{N} \\ R_{A}= 1800-R_{D}&=1125 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At joint D,
[latex] T_{\infty}=\frac{R_{D}}{\sin 45}=675 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{N}[/latex]
Taking free body diagram as shown in figure,


[latex] \begin{aligned} \Sigma V &=0 \\ T_{A B} \sin \theta+675 \sqrt{2} \sin 45^{\circ} &=1800 \\ T_{A B} \sin \theta &=1125 &\ldots(i)\\ \Sigma H &=0 \\ T_{A B} \cos \theta &=675 \sqrt{2} \cos 45^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow \quad T_{A B} \cos \theta &=675 &\ldots(ii)\\ \text{From} e q \cdot(i) \text { and }(i i) & \\ \tan \theta &=\frac{5}{3} \\ \sin \theta &=0.8575 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting value of [latex]\sin \theta[/latex] in eq. (i)
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{A B} \times 0.8575 &=1125 \\ T_{A B} &=1311.96 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

since the tensile stress at bottom face of the beam is zero.

since the prestressing force is located at 200 mm from the bottom face of the beam.

raw_source.text: The soil profile above the rock surface for a 25[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] infinite slope is shown in the figure, where [latex]s_{u}[/latex] is the undrained shear strength and [latex]\gamma _{t}[/latex] is total unit weight. The slip will occur at a depth of

A 2 km long pipe of 0.2 m diameter connects two reservoirs. The difference between water levels
in the reservoirs is 8 m. The Darcy-Weisbachfriction factor of the pipe is 0.04. Accounting for

The normal depth in a wide rectangular channel is increased by 10%. The percentage increase in
the discharge in the channel is:
raw_source.solution:
The discharge in the channel is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=\frac{1}{n} A R^{2 / 3} S^{1 / 2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad Q&=\frac{1}{n}(B y)\left(\frac{B y}{B+2 y}\right)^{2 / 3} S^{1 / 2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For a wide rectangular channel
[latex] \begin{aligned} B &\gg y \\ \therefore\quad Q&=\frac{1}{n}(B y)(y)^{2 / 3} S^{1 / 2} \\ \therefore\quad Q &\propto y^{5 / 3} \\ \text{let} Q_{1}&=k(y)^{5 / 3} \\ \therefore\quad Q_{2}&=k(1.1 y)^{5 / 3} \\ \therefore\quad \frac{Q_{2}-Q_{1}}{Q_{1}} \times 100&=\frac{(1.1 \mathrm{y})^{5 / 3}-(\mathrm{y})^{5 / 3}}{(\mathrm{y})^{5 / 3}} \times 100 \\ &= 17.21 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A settling tank in a water treatment plant is designed for a surface overflow rate of 30 [latex]\frac{m^{3}}{day\cdot m^{2}}[/latex]. Assume specific gravity of sediment particles = 2.65, density of water ([latex]\rho= 1000 kg/m^3[/latex]), dynamic viscosity of water ([latex]\mu=0.001 N.s/m^2[/latex]), and Stokes' law is valid. The approximate minimum size of particles that would be completely removed is:
raw_source.solution:
To calculate minimum size of particles equating setteling velocity to overflow rate, we get,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{0} &=V_{s} \\ \Rightarrow\; \; V_{0} &=\frac{\left ( G_{s}-1 \right )\gamma _{W}d^{2}}{18\mu } \\ \text{Now }\; \; V_{0}&=\frac{30m^{2}}{day.m^{2}} \\ &=\frac{30}{24\times 60\times 60}\frac{m}{s} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{30}{24\times 60\times 60}&= \frac{\left ( 2.65-1 \right )\times 9.81\times 10^{3}\times d^{2}}{18\times 0.001}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving we get,
[latex]d=1.965\times 10^{-5}\; m \approx 0.02\, mm[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A student began experiment for determination of 5-day, 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C BOD on Monday. Since the [latex]5^{th}[/latex] day fell on Saturday, the final DO readings were taken on next Monday. On calculation, BOD (i.e. 7 day, 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C) was found to be 150 mg/L. What would be the 5-day, 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C BOD (in mg/L)?
Assume value of BOD rate constant (k) at standard temperature of 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C as 0.23/day (base e). __________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} BOD_{7} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ \therefore \; \; 150 &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 7} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=187.54\: mg/L \\ \therefore \; \; BOD_{5} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ &=187.539\times \left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 5} \right ] \\ &= 128.13\: mg/L \end{aligned}[/latex]

A multistory building with a basement is to be constructed. The top 4m consists of loose silt, below which dense sand layer is present up to a great depth. Ground water table is at the surface. The foundation consists of the basement slab of 6 m width which will rest on the top of dense sand as shown in the figure. For dense sand, saturated unit weight = 20kN/[latex]m^3[/latex], and bearing capacity factors [latex]N_q[/latex]=40 and [latex]N_{\gamma }[/latex]=45. For loose silt, saturated unit weight = 18kN/[latex]m^3[/latex], [latex]N_q[/latex]=15 and [latex]N_{\gamma }[/latex]=20. Effective cohesion c' is zero for both soils. Unit weight of water is 10 kN/[latex]m^3[/latex]. Neglect shape factor and depth factor.

Average elastic modulus E and Poisson's ratio [latex]\mu[/latex] of dense sand is [latex]60 \times 10^3kN/m^2[/latex] and 0.3 respectively.

Using factor of safety = 3, the net safe bearing capacity (in kN/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]) of the foundation is:
raw_source.solution:
As per GATE Official Answer Key MTA (Marks to ALL)
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q_{u}&=1.3 \mathrm{cN}_{\mathrm{c}}+\left(\gamma^{\prime}\right)_{\mathrm{silt}}\left(\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{q}}\right)_{\mathrm{silt}} \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{t}}+0.4 \mathrm{B}(\gamma)_{\mathrm{sand}} (N_{\gamma})_{\text{sand}} \\ &=8.19 \times 4 \times 15+0.4 \times 10.19 \times 6 \times 45 \\ &=1591.92 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{nu}}=\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{u}}-\gamma \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{f}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Safe bearing capacity [latex]=Q_{n s}=\frac{Q_{n u}}{F} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1591.92-8.19 \times 4}{3}=519.72 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} [/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 3 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ R_{4} & \rightarrow R_{4}-R_{2}-R_{3} \\ \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 & -2 &1 \end{vmatrix} \\ R_{4} & \rightarrow R_{4}+3R_{1} \\ \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \\ R_{3} & \rightarrow R_{3}-3R_{1} \\ \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 0 & -6 & -8\\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]
interchanging column 1 and column 2 and taking transpose,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta &=-\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & -6 & 4\\ 3 & 0 & -8 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=-1\times \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0\\ 3 & -6 & 4\\ 0 & -8 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\times \left \{ 1\left ( -60+32 \right )+2\left ( 0-30 \right ) \right \} \\ &=-\left ( -28-60 \right )=88\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A particle moves along a curve whose parametric equations are: [latex]x=t^{3}+2t[/latex], [latex]y=-3e^{-2t}[/latex]  and [latex]z=2 \sin (5t)[/latex] , where x, y and z show variations of the distance covered by the particle (in cm)with time t (in s). The magnitude of the acceleration of the particle (in [latex] cm/s^{2}[/latex]) at t = 0 is ________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x &=t^{3}+2 t \\ y &=-3 e^{-2 t} \\ z &=2 \sin (5 t) \\ \frac{d x}{d t} &=3 e^{2}+2 \\ \Rightarrow\quad a_{x} &=\frac{d^{2} x}{d t^{2}}=6 t \\ \frac{d y}{d t} &=-3 e^{-2} \times(-2)=6 e^{-2 t} \\ \Rightarrow\quad a_{y} &=\frac{d^{2} y}{d t^{3}}=-12 e^{-2 t}\\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{d z}{d t} &=2 \times 5 \cos (5 t) \\ &=10 \cos (5 t) \\ \Rightarrow\quad a_{z} &=\frac{d^{2} z}{d t^{2}}=-50 \sin 5 t \\ \vec{a} &=a_{x} \hat{i}+a_{y} \hat{j}+a_{z} \hat{k} \\ \vec{a} \text { at } t=0 &=0 \hat{i}-12 \hat{j}+0 \hat{k} \\ \vec{a} &=-12 \hat{j} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow\quad[/latex] Magnitude of acceleration at t=0
[latex] =12 \mathrm{cm} / \mathrm{s}^{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A traffic office imposes on an average 5 number of penalties daily on traffic violators. Assume that the number of penalties on different days is independent and follows a Poisson distribution. The probability that there will be less than 4 penalties in a day is ___________
raw_source.solution:
Mean [latex]\; \; \; \; \; \lambda =5[/latex]
[latex]P\left ( x \lt 4 \right )=p\left ( x=0 \right )+p\left ( x=1 \right )+p\left ( x=2 \right )+p\left ( x=3 \right )[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{e^{-5}s^{0}}{0!}+\frac{e^{-5}5^{1}}{1!}+\frac{e^{-5}5^{2}}{1!}+\frac{e^{-5}5^{3}}{3!}[/latex]
[latex]=e^{-5}\left [ 1+5+\frac{25}{2}+\frac{125}{6} \right ]=e^{-5}\left ( \frac{118}{3} \right )[/latex]
[latex]=0.265[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rectangular beam of width (b) 230 mm and effective depth (d) 450 mm is reinforced with four bars of 12 mm diameter. The grade of concrete is M20 and grade of steel is Fe500. Given that for M20 grade of concrete the ultimate shear strength, [latex]\tau _{uc} = 0.36 N/mm^{2}[/latex] for steel percentage, p = 0.25, and [latex]\tau _{uc}= 0.48 N/mm^{2}[/latex] for p = 0.50. For a factored shear force of 45 kN, the diameter (in mm) of Fe500 steel two legged stirrups to be used at spacing of 375 mm, should be

Factored [latex]S F=45 \mathrm{kN}=V_{u} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \tau_{v}&=\frac{V_{u}}{b d}=\frac{45 \times 1000}{230 \times 450}=0.4348 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}\\ \therefore \quad \%&\text{tensile steel}\\ &=\frac{4 \times \frac{\pi}{4}(12)^{2}}{230 \times 450} \times 100=0.437 \% \\ \tau_{c} &=0.36+\frac{0.12}{0.25} \times(0.437-0.25) \\ &=0.45 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since [latex]\tau_{v}-\tau_{c} \lt 0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow[/latex] Min shear reinforcement is required
[latex] \Rightarrow[/latex] Min shear reinforcement is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{A_{s v}}{b S_{v}} &=\frac{0.4}{0.87 f_{y}} \\ A_{s v} &=\frac{0.4 \times\left(S_{v}\right)(b)}{0.87 f_{y}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since we limit [latex]f_{y}[/latex] to [latex]415 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex] hence,
[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{s v}=2 \times \frac{\pi}{4}(\phi)^{2} &=\frac{0.4 \times 325 \times 230}{0.87 \times 415} \\ &= 82.814 \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ \phi &=7.26 \mathrm{mm} \\ \text { adopt } \phi&=8 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a reinforced concrete section, the stress at the extreme fibre in compression is 5.80 MPa. The depth of neutral axis in the section is 58 mm and the grade of concrete is M25. Assuming linear elastic behavior of the concrete, the effective curvature of the section (in per mm) is

raw_source.text: A venturimeter, having a diameter of 7.5 cm at the throat and 15 cm at the enlarged end, is installed in a horizontal pipeline of 15 cm diameter. The pipe carries an incompressible fluid at a steady rate of 30 litres per second. The difference of pressure head measured in terms of the moving fluid in between the enlarged and the throat of the venturimeter is observed to be 2.45 m. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 [latex]m/s^{2}[/latex], the coefficient of discharge of the venturimeter (correct up to two places of decimal) is___
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=30 \; l / \mathrm{s} \\ \left(\frac{P_{1}}{w}+Z_{1}\right)&-\left(\frac{P_{2}}{w}+Z_{2}\right) =2.45 \mathrm{m}=h \\ g&=9.81 \\ Q&=C_{d} \frac{A_{1} A_{2}}{\sqrt{A_{1}^{2}-A_{2}^{2}}} \sqrt{2 g h} \\ C_{d} &=\frac{Q_{1} A_{2}}{\sqrt{A_{1}^{2}-A_{2}^{2}} \sqrt{2 g h}}\\ &= \frac{30 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}}{\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}(0.15)^{2} \times(0.075)^{2} }{\sqrt{(0.15)^{2}-(0.075)^{2}}}\times \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 2.45}} \\ C_{\mathrm{d}}&=0.95 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rectangular channel having a bed slope of 0.0001, width 3.0 m and Manning's coefficient 'n' 0.015, carries a discharge of 1.0 [latex]m^3/s[/latex]. Given that the normal depth of flow ranges between 0.76 m and 0.8 m. The minimum width of a throat (in m) that is possible at a given section, while ensuring that the prevailing normal depth is not exceeded along the reach upstream of the contraction, is approximately equal to (assume negligible losses)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} n=0.015 \\ Q=1 m^{3} / s \end{array}[/latex]
Normal depth of flow between 0.76m to 0.8m.
If prevailing normal depth of flow is not exceeded, there must not be chocking of the section or there must be just chocking.
Thus the width of the section should be such that for the prevailing specific energy there should be critical flow at the contracted section
i.e. [latex] \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{q^{2}}{g}\right)^{1 / 3}=E_{C}=E_{\text {intia }} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \frac{3}{2}\left[\frac{\left(\frac{Q}{B_{\min }}\right)^{2}}{g}\right]^{1 / 3}=E_{\text {initie }}[/latex]
Let us now calculate [latex]E_{\text {inital }} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=\frac{1}{2} A R^{2 / 3} S_{0}^{1 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1&= \frac{1}{0.015}(3 y)\left(\frac{3 y}{3+2 y}\right)^{2 / 3}(0.0001)^{1 / 2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=0.78 m \\ \Rightarrow \quad E_{\text {initial }}&=y+\frac{q^{2}}{2 g y^{2}} \\ &=0.78+\frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times(0.78)^{2}} \\ &=0.7893 \mathrm{m} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{3}{2}\left[\frac{\left(\frac{Q}{B_{\min }}\right)^{2}}{g}\right]^{1 / 3}&=0.7893 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{3}{2} \frac{(1)^{2 / 3}}{g^{1 / 3}\left(B_{\min }\right)^{2 / 3}}&=0.7893 \\ \mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{min}}&=0.836 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

An incompressible fluid is flowing at a steady rate in a horizontal pipe. From a section, the pipe divides into two horizontal parallel pipes of diameters [latex]d_{1}[/latex]
and [latex]d_{2}[/latex] (where [latex]d_{1}=4d_{2}[/latex]) that run for a distance of L each and then again join back to a pipe of the original size. For both the parallel pipes, assume the head loss due to friction only and the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor to be the same. The velocity ratio between the bigger and the smaller branched pipes is

16 MLD of water is flowing through a 2.5 km long pipe of diameter 45 cm. The chlorine at the rate of 32 kg/d is applied at the entry of this pipe so that disinfected water is obtained at the exit. There is a proposal to increase the flow through this pipe to 22 MLD from 16 MLD. Assume the dilution coefficient, n = 1. The minimum amount of chlorine (in kg per day) to be applied to achieve the same degree of disinfection for the enhanced flow is
raw_source.solution:
In the disinfection process we have the relationship,
[latex]\begin{aligned} tC^{n} &=K \\ \text{where}\; \;t &=\text{time required to kill all organism} \\ \text{c} &=\text{concentration of disinfectant} \\ n &= \text{dilution coefficient}\\ k &=\text{constant} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; t_{1}C_{1}^{n} &=t_{2}C_{2}^{n} \\ \text{in our case}\; n &=1 \\ \Rightarrow \; \; t_{1}C_{1}&=t_{2}C_{2} \\ t_{1} &=\frac{L}{v_{1}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]L= \text{length of pipe}; [/latex]
[latex]V_{1}=\text{velocity of flow}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} t_{1} &=\frac{L}{Q_{1}/A} \\ t_{1} &=\frac{L.A}{Q_{1}} \\ C_{1} &=\frac{W_{1}}{Q_{1}}, \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{where } W_{1} &=\text{weight of disinfectant per day}; \\ Q_{1}&=\text{discharge per day} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \; \; \frac{L.A}{Q_{1}}\times \frac{W_{1}}{Q_{1}} &=\frac{L.A}{Q_{2}}\times \frac{W_{2}}{Q_{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; W_{2} &=\frac{Q_{2}^{2}}{Q_{1}^{2}}\times W_{1} \\ &=\left ( \frac{22}{16} \right )^{2}\times 32\; \text{kg/day} \\ &=60.5\; \text{kg/day} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The perception-reaction time for a vehicle travelling at 90 km/h, given the coefficient of longitudinal friction of 0.35 and the stopping sight distance of 170 m (assume g = 9.81 [latex]m/s^{2}[/latex] ), is _____________ seconds.

raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text: The speed-density (u-k) relationship on a single lane road with unidirectional flow u= 70-0.7k, where u is in km/hr and k is in veh/km. The capacity of the road (in veh/hr) is________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Capacity } &=\text { Velocity } \times \text { Density } \\ \Rightarrow \quad C &=V \times K \\ &=70 K-0.7 K^{2} \\ \text { Now, } \quad \frac{d C}{d K} &=70-1.4 K=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K &=50\\ \Rightarrow \quad \text { Capacity, } &=70 \times 50-0.7(50)^{2} \\ &=1750 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The determinant of matrix [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 &2 &3 \\ 1 &0 &3 &0 \\ 2 &3 &0 &1 \\ 3 &0 &1 &2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is__________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 3 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ R_{4} & \rightarrow R_{4}-R_{2}-R_{3} \\ \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 & -2 &1 \end{vmatrix} \\ R_{4} & \rightarrow R_{4}+3R_{1} \\ \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \\ R_{3} & \rightarrow R_{3}-3R_{1} \\ \Delta &=\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 0 & -6 & -8\\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]
interchanging column 1 and column 2 and taking transpose,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta &=-\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\\ 2 & 3 & -6 & 4\\ 3 & 0 & -8 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=-1\times \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0\\ 3 & -6 & 4\\ 0 & -8 & 10 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\times \left \{ 1\left ( -60+32 \right )+2\left ( 0-30 \right ) \right \} \\ &=-\left ( -28-60 \right )=88\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Water is flowing at a steady rate through a homogeneous and saturated horizontal soil strip of 10 m length. The strip is being subjected to a constant water head(H) of 5 m at the beginning and 1 m at the end. If the governing equation of flow in the soil strip is [latex]\frac{d^{2}H}{dx^2}=0[/latex] (where x is the distance along the soil strip), the value of H (in m) at the middle of the strip is ________.
raw_source.solution:
Given, equation of the flow of soil strip is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2} H}{d x^{2}}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{d} x}&=\mathrm{C}_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad H&=C_{1} x+C_{2} \\ \text{at }x=0, H=&5 \mathrm{m} \\ \Rightarrow \quad C_{2}&=5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad H&=C_{1} x+5 \\ \text{at }x&=10, H=1 \mathrm{m} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1&=C_{1} \times 10+5 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 10 C_{1}&=-4 \\ \Rightarrow \quad C_{1}&=-\frac{2}{5} \\ \Rightarrow \quad H&=-\frac{2}{5} x+5 \\ \text{at }x&=5 \mathrm{m} \\ H&=-\frac{2}{5} \times 5+5 \\ H&=3 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A horizontal nozzle of 30 mm diameter discharges a steady jet of water into the atmosphere at a rate of 15 liters per second. The diameter of inlet to the nozzle is 100 mm. The jet Impinges normal to a flat stationary plate held close to the nozzle end. [latex] \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{a} \mathrm{V}=15 \; litre/sec (given)[/latex]

[latex] =1000 \times \frac{15^{2}}{\pi} \times 30^{2} \mathrm{m}^{3} \times 10^{-6} \frac{\mathrm{m}^{6}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}} \times \frac{1}{10^{-6}} \mathrm{m}^{2} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A venturimeter having a throat diameter of 0.1 m is used to estimate the flow rate of a horizontal pipe having a diameter of 0.2 m. For an observed pressure difference of 2 m of water head and coefficient of discharge equal to unity, assuming that the energy losses are negligible, the flow rate (in [latex]m^3[/latex]/s) through the pipe is approximately equal to
raw_source.solution:
Diameter of throat,

Diameter of pipe,
[latex] D=0.2 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Pressure difference,
[latex] \frac{P_{1}-P_{2}}{w}=2 m=h[/latex]


Coefficient of discharge
[latex] C_{D}=1[/latex]
Discharge,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=\frac{C_{D} A_{1} A_{2} \sqrt{2 g h}}{\sqrt{A_{1}^{2}-A_{2}^{2}}}\\ A_{1} &=\frac{\pi}{4}(0.2)^{2} \\ \text { and } A_{2} &=\frac{\pi}{4}(0.1)^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad Q &=\frac{1 \times\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^{2} \times(0.2)^{2}(0.1)^{2} \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 2}}{\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \sqrt{(0.2)^{4}-(0.1)^{4}}} \\ &=0.0508=0.050 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rectangular channel of 2.5 m width is carrying a discharge of 4 [latex]m^3[/latex]/s. Considering that acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/[latex]s^2[/latex], the velocity of flow (in m/s) corresponding to the critical depth (at which the specific energy is minimum) is _______

At critical depth velocity head [latex]=\frac{y_{c}}{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{V^{2}}{2 g}&=\frac{0.639}{2}\\ \Rightarrow V&=\sqrt{0.639 \times 9} \\ &=2.504 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Irrigation water is to be provided to a crop in a field to bring the moisture content of the soil from the existing 18% to the field capacity of the soil at 28%. The effective root zone of the crop is 70 cm. If the densities of the soil and water are 1.3 g/[latex]cm^2[/latex] and 1.0 g/[latex]cm^3[/latex]respectively, the depth of irrigation water (in mm) required for irrigating the crop is ________
raw_source.solution:
Given,
Root zone depth,
[latex] d=70 \mathrm{cm}[/latex]
Field capacity,

Existing moisture content,
[latex] w=18 \%[/latex]
Density of soil,

Density of water,

Depth of irrigation water required,
[latex] \begin{aligned} d_{w} &=\frac{\gamma}{\gamma_{w}} d\left(F_{c}-w\right) \\ &=\frac{1.3}{1.0} \times(70 \times 10)(28 \%-18 \%) \\ &=1.3 \times(70 \times 10) \times \frac{10}{100} \\ &=91 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
With reference to a standard Cartesian (x,y) plane, the parabolic velocity distribution profile of fully developed laminar flow in x-direction between two parallel, stationary and identical plates that are separated by distance, h, is given by the expression
[latex]u=-\frac{h^{2}}{8\mu }\frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} x}\left [ 1-4(\frac{y}{h})^{2} \right ][/latex]
In this equation, the y=0 axis lies equidistant between the plates at a distance h/2 from the two plates, p is the pressure variable and [latex]\mu[/latex] is the dynamic viscosity term. The maximum and average velocities are, respectively
raw_source.solution:
Velocily expression for a laminar flow between two parallel plates is
[latex] U=-\frac{n^{2}}{8 u}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[1-4\left(\frac{y}{n}\right)^{2}\right][/latex]
End condition
[latex] U=U_{max}\text{ at }y=0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow U_{max} = -\frac{h^{2}}{8\mu}\left(\frac{dp}{dx} \right )[/latex]
Discharges dQ = Area x Velocily
[latex] \Rightarrow \Delta 0=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{8 \mu}\left(\frac{d \rho}{d x}\right)\left(1-4\left(\frac{y}{n}\right)^{2}\right)\right](d y \times 1)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\Rightarrow Q=-\frac{h^{2}}{8 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \int_{-h / 2}^{h / 2}\left(1-\frac{4 y^{2}}{h^{2}}\right) d y\\ &=-\frac{h^{2}}{8 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[y-\frac{4 y^{3}}{3 h^{2}}\right]_{-n / 2}^{h / 2}\\ &=-\frac{h^{2}}{8 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[\left\{\frac{h}{2}-\left(-\frac{h}{2}\right)\right\}-\left\{\frac{4}{3 h^{2}}\left(\frac{h^{3}}{8}-\left(-\frac{h^{3}}{8}\right)\right)\right\}\right]\\ &=-\frac{h^{3}}{12 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\\ &Q=A V\\ &-\frac{h^{3}}{12 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)=(h \times 1) \times U_{a v g}\\ &\Rightarrow \quad U_{a v g}=-\frac{h^{2}}{12 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A suspension of sand like particles in water with particles of diameter 0.10 mm and below is flowing into a settling tank at 0.10 [latex]m^3[/latex]/s. Assume g=9.81 m/[latex]s^{2}[/latex], specific gravity of particles=2.65, and kinematic vescosity of water=[latex]1.0105 \times 10^{-2} cm^{2}[/latex]/s. The minimum surface area (in [latex]m^{2}[/latex]) required for this settling tank to remove particles of size 0.06 mm and above with 100% efficiency is_________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{s} &=\frac{\left(G_{s}-1\right) g d^{2}}{18 v} \\ &=\frac{(2.65-1) \times 9.81 \times\left(6 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2}}{18 \times 1.0105 \times 10^{-2}} \\ &=\frac{1.65 \times 9.81 \times 36 \times 10^{-4}}{18 \times 1.0105 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{2}} \\ &=3.204 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ V_{s} &=\frac{Q}{B L} \\ \Rightarrow\quad B L &=\frac{0.1}{3.204 \times 10^{-3}}=31.214 \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Alum quantity (kg) required for 30 days

raw_source.text: An effluent at a flow rate of 2670 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/d from a sewage treatment plant is to be disinfected. The laboratory data of disinfection studies with a chlorine dosage of 15 mg/l yield the model [latex]N_{t}=N_{o}e^{-0.145t}[/latex]  where [latex]N_t[/latex]= number of micro-organisms surviving at time t (in min.) and [latex]N_o[/latex]= number of micro-organism present initially (at t=0). The volume of disinfection unit (in [latex]m^{3}[/latex]) required to achieve a 98% kill of micro-organisms is______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q&=2670 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} \\ N_{t}&=\mathrm{No} . \mathrm{e}^{-0.145 \mathrm{t}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Let x be the no. of microorganisms (M.O.) present initially.
98% kill of M.O. imlies that at time 't' 2% of M.O. are still surviving
[latex] \therefore [/latex] M.O. surviving at time 't' [latex]=\frac{2}{100} x [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{2}{100} x &=x \cdot \mathrm{e}^{-0.145 \mathrm{t}} \\ \therefore \qquad t &=26.979 \mathrm{min} \\ t &=0.018736 \text { days } \\ \therefore \qquad \text { Volume } &=Q . t \\ &=2670 \times 0.018736 \\ &=50.0244 \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A waste water stream (flow=2 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s, ultimate BOD=90 mg/l) is joining a small river (flow=12 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]/s, ultimate BOD=5 mg/l). Both water streams get mixed up instantaneously. Cross sectional area of the river is 50 [latex]m^{2}[/latex]. Assuming the de-oxygenation rate constant, k'=0.25/day the BOD (in mg/l) of the river water, 10 km downstream of the mixing point is
raw_source.solution:
Flow of waste water stream,
[latex] Q_{w}=2 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
Ultimate BOD,
[latex] Y_{w}=90 \mathrm{mg} / l=90 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
Flow of river,
[latex] Q_{R}=12 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
Ultimate BOD of river,
[latex] Y_{R}=0.5 \mathrm{mg} / l=5 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
BOD of mixture,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Y_{0} &=\frac{(2 \times 90)+(12 \times 5)}{2+12} \\ &=\frac{180+60}{14}=\frac{240}{14} \\ &=17.143 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ k_{D} &=0.434 \mathrm{K} \\ &=0.434 \times 0.25=0.1085 \\ Y_{t} &=Y_{0}\left[1-(10)^{-k_{0} t}\right] &\ldots(i)\\ \text { Area of river } &=50 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Flow of river } &=12 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \text { Stream velocity } &=\frac{14}{50}=0.28 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \text { Time taken, } & t=\frac{10 \mathrm{km}}{0.28 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}}=0.4133 \text { days } \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] From eq. (i),
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{BOD}_{\text {left }} &=Y_{0}-Y_{t} \\ &=Y_{0} \times 10^{-k t} \\ &=17.143 \times 10^{-0.1085 \times 0.4133} \\ &=15.46 \mathrm{mg} / l \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: On a section of a highway the speed-density relationship is linear and is given by [latex]v=[80-\frac{2}{3}k][/latex]; where v is in km/h and k is in veh/km. The capacity (in veh/h) of this section of the highway would be

raw_source.text: A pre-timed four phase signal has critical lane flow rate for the first three phases as 200, 187 and 210 veh/hr with saturation flow rate of 1800 veh/hr/lane for all phases. The lost time is given as 4 seconds for each phase. If the cycle length is 60 seconds, the effective green time (in seconds) of the fourth phase is _________
raw_source.solution:
Flow rates for the first three phase are given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{1}&=200 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \\ q_{2}&=187 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr}\\ \text{and}\quad q_{3}&=210 \text { veh/hr } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Saturation flow rate is 1800 veh/hr/lane
Lost time,
[latex] L=4 \times 4=16 \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
Length of the cycle,
[latex] C_{0}=60 \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Now, } \quad y_{1} &=\frac{q_{1}}{s_{1}}=\frac{200}{1800} \\ y_{2} &=\frac{q_{2}}{s_{2}}=\frac{187}{1800} \\ y_{3} &=\frac{q_{3}}{s_{3}}=\frac{210}{1800} \\ C_{0} &=\frac{1.5 L+5}{1-y} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 60 &=\frac{1.5 \times 16+5}{1-y}\\ \Rightarrow 60 &=\frac{24+5}{1-y} \\ \Rightarrow 1-y &=\frac{29}{60} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y&=\frac{1-29}{60}=\frac{60-29}{60} \\ &=0.517\\ \text{And}\quad y&=y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}+y_{4}\\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.517 &=\frac{597}{1800}+y_{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad y_{4}&=0.185 \\ G &=\frac{y_{4}}{y}\left(C_{0}-L\right)\\ &=\frac{0.185}{0.517}(60-16) \\ &=15.745 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Moving into a world of big data will require us to change our thinking about the merits of exactitude. To apply the conventional mindset of measurement to the digital, connected world of the twenty-first century is to miss a crucial point. As mentioned earlier, the obsession with exactness is an artefact of the information-deprived analog era. When data was sparse, every data point was critical, and thus great care was taken to avoid letting any bias the analysis.

From "Big DATA" Viktor Mayer-Schonberger and Kenneth Cukier

The main point of the paragraph is:
options: The twenty-first century is a digital world
Big data is obsessed with exactness
Exactitude is not critical in dealing with big data
Sparse data leads to a bias in the analysis

Consider the following probability mass function (p.m.f) of a random variable X :
[latex]p(x,q)=\begin{cases} q & \text{ if } X=0\\ 1-q& \text{ if } X=1 \\ 0 & \text otherwise \end{cases}[/latex]
If q = 0.4, the variance of X is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]\; \; \; \; q=0.4[/latex]



Required value [latex]=V\left ( X \right )=E\left ( X^{2} \right )-\left [ E\left ( X \right ) \right ]^{2}[/latex]
[latex]E\left ( X \right )=\sum_{i}^{}\, X_{i}p_{i}=0\times 0.4+1\times 0.6=0.6[/latex]
[latex]E\left ( X^{2} \right )=\sum_{i}^{}\, X_{i}^{2}p_{i}=0^{2}\times 0.4+1^{2}\times 0.6=0.6[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \; \; V\left ( X \right )=E\left ( X^{2} \right )-\left [ E\left ( X \right ) \right ]^{2}=0.6-0.36=0.24[/latex]

raw_source.text: The quadratic equation [latex]x^{2}-4x+4=0[/latex] is to be solved numerically, starting with the initial guess [latex]x_0=3[/latex]. The Newton-Raphson method is applied once to get a new estimate and then the Secant method is applied once using the initial guess and this new estimate. The estimated value of the root after the application of the Secant method is __________.
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned}  f\left ( x \right )&=x^{2}-4x+4 \\   {f}'\left ( x \right )&=2x-4 \\   x_{0}&=3 \\   f\left ( 3 \right )&=1, {f}'\left ( 3 \right )=2 \\ \text{By Newton } & \text{Rapshon method,}\\   x_{1}&=x_{0}-\frac{f\left ( x_{0} \right )}{{f}'_{x_{0}}} \\    &=3-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2} \\   f\left ( \frac{5}{2} \right )&=\frac{25}{4}-10+4=\frac{1}{4} \\ & \text{By Secant method,}\\   x_{2}&=x_{1}-\frac{\left ( x_{1}-x_{0} \right )f\left ( x_{1} \right )}{f\left ( x_{1} \right )-f\left ( x_{0} \right )} \\    &=\frac{f_{1}x_{0}-f_{0}x_{1}}{f_{1}-f_{0}} \\    &=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4}\times 3 \right )-\left ( 1\times \frac{5}{2} \right )}{\frac{1}{4}-1} \\    &=\frac{7}{3}=2.33 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following differential equation:
[latex]x(ydx+xdy)\cos \frac{y}{x}=y(xdy-ydx)\sin \frac{y}{x}[/latex]
Which of the following is the solution of the above equation (c is an arbitrary constant)?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x\left ( ydx+xdy \right )\cos \frac{y}{x}&=y\left ( xdy-ydx \right )\sin \frac{y}{x} \\ \frac{ydx+xdy}{xdy-ydx}&=\frac{y}{x}\tan \frac{y}{x}\\ \text{Let } y&=v \cdot x \\ dy&=vdx+xdv \\ \frac{vxdx+vxdx+x^{2}dv}{vxdx+x^{2}dv-vxdx}&=v\tan v \\ \frac{xdv+2vdx}{xdv}&=v\tan v \\ 1+\frac{2v}{x}\frac{dx}{dv}&=v\tan v \\ \frac{2v}{x}\frac{dx}{dv}&=v\tan v-1 \\ 2\frac{dx}{x}&=\left ( \tan v-\frac{1}{v} \right )dv \end{aligned}[/latex]
Integrating both sides.
[latex]\begin{aligned}2\log x&=\log \left | \sec v \right |-\log v+\log c \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x^{2}&=\frac{c\sec v}{v} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; x^{2}\frac{y}{x}&=c\sec \frac{y}{x} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; xy\cos \frac{y}{x}&=c \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following complex function:
[latex]f(z)=\frac{9}{(z-1)(z+2)^{2}}[/latex]
Which of the following is one of the residues of the above function?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]f(z)[/latex] has poles at [latex]z=1, -2[/latex]
Residue of [latex]f(z)[/latex] at [/latex](z=1)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\lim_{z\rightarrow 1}\left ( z-1 \right )f\left ( z \right ) \\ &=\lim_{z\rightarrow 1}\frac{9}{\left ( z+2 \right )^{2}} \\&=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Residue of [latex]f(z)[/latex] at [latex](z=-2)[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\lim_{z\rightarrow 2}\frac{d}{dz^{2-1}}\left [ \left ( z+2 \right )^{2}f\left ( z \right ) \right ] \\ &=\lim_{z\rightarrow 2}\frac{d}{dz}\left ( \frac{9}{z-1} \right ) \\ &=\lim_{z\rightarrow 2}\left ( \frac{9}{\left ( z-1 \right )^{2}} \right ) \\ &=-1\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The directional derivative of the field [latex]u(x,y,z)=x^{2}-3xy[/latex] in the direction of the vector [latex](\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k})[/latex] and point (2, -1, 4) is _________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned}u (x, y, z)&=x^{2}-3yz \\  \triangledown u&=2x\hat{i}-3z\hat{j}-3y\hat{k} \\  \triangledown ul_{at\: \left ( 2,\, -1\, 4 \right )}&=4\hat{i}+12\hat{j}-3\hat{k}\\ &\text{Directional derivative}\\   &= \left ( 4\hat{i}+12\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \right ).\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}} \\   &= \frac{4-12-6}{\sqrt{6}} =-\frac{14}{\sqrt{6}} \\   &= -\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{3}=-5.715\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In Newton-Raphson iterative method, the initial guess value ( [latex]x_{ini}[/latex]) is considered as zero while finding the roots of the euation:[latex]f(x)=-2+6x-4x^{2}+0.5x^{3}[/latex]. The correction, [latex]\Delta x[/latex], to be added to [latex]x_{ini}[/latex] in the first iteration is____________.
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned}   f\left ( x \right )&=-2+6x-4x^{2}+0.5x^{3} \\    {f}'\left ( x \right )&=6-8x+1.5x^{2} \\    x_{ini}&=0\\ \text{By Newton }&\text{Raphson Method,}\\    x_{1}&=x_{ini}-\frac{f\left ( x_{ini} \right )}{{f}'\left ( x_{ini} \right )} \\    &=  0-\frac{-2}{6} \\ \Rightarrow    \;\;x_{1}&=\frac{1}{3} \\ \therefore \;\;  \Delta x&=x_{1}-x_{ini}=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Given , [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex], the value of the definite integral, [latex]I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x+i\sin x}{\cos x-i\sin x}dx[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} I&=\int_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\cos x+i\sin x}{\cos x-i\sin x}dx \\  &=\int_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{e^{ix}}{e^{-ix}}dx=e^{2ix}dx \\  &=\frac{1}{2i}\left [ e^{2ix} \right ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2i}\left [ e^{i\pi }-1 \right ] \\ &=\frac{1}{2i}\left ( -1-1 \right ) \\  &=-\frac{1}{i}=i \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: [latex]\lim_{x\rightarrow \infty }\left ( 1+\frac{1}{x} \right )^{2x}[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex] y=\: \lim_{x\rightarrow \infty }\left ( 1+\frac{1}{x} \right )^{2x} [/latex]
[latex] \log y = \lim_{x\rightarrow \infty }2x\log \left ( 1+\frac{1}{x} \right )[/latex]
Which is in the form of [latex]\infty \times 0[/latex].
To convert this into [latex]\frac{0}{0}[/latex] form, we rewrite as,
[latex]\Rightarrow \log y= \lim_{x\rightarrow \infty }\frac{2\log \left ( 1+\frac{1}{x} \right )}{1/x}[/latex]
Now is in [latex]\frac{0}{0}[/latex] form.
Using L'Hospital's Rule,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \log y&=\lim_{x\rightarrow \infty }\frac{\frac{2\times -\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1+\frac{1}{x}}}{-\frac{1}{x^{2}}} \\ \log y&=\lim_{x\rightarrow \infty }\frac{2}{1+\frac{1}{x}}=2 \\ \therefore \;\; y&= e^{2}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For probability density function of a random variable,x is
[latex]\begin{matrix} f(x) &=\frac{x}{4}(4-x^2) &for \;\; 0\leq x\leq 2 \\ &=0 & ohterwise \end{matrix}[/latex]
The mean, [latex]\mu _{x}[/latex] of the random variable is _____.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f\left ( x \right ) &=\begin{cases} \frac{x}{4}\left ( 4-x^{2} \right ), & \text{ if } \; \; 0\leq x\leq 2\\ 0, & \text{ if } \; \; Otherwise \end{cases} \\ \mu _{x} &=\int_{0}^{2}xf\left ( x \right )dx \\ \therefore \text{Mean}\: \left ( \mu _{x} \right ) &=\int_{0}^{2}x\frac{x}{4}\left ( 4-x^{2} \right )dx \\ &=\int_{0}^{2}\left ( x^{2}-\frac{x^{4}}{4} \right )dx \\ &=\left [ \frac{x^{3}}{3}-\frac{x^{5}}{20} \right ]_{0}^{2}=\frac{8}{3}-\frac{32}{20}=\frac{16}{15} \\ &=1.066 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following second order linear differential equation:
[latex]\frac{d^2 y}{ dx^2}=-12x^{2}+24x-20[/latex]
The boundary conditions are: at x = 0, y = 5 and at x = 2, y = 21.
The value of y at x = 1 is ____________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}} y}{\mathrm{d} x^{2}}=-12x^{2}+24x-20[/latex]
Integrating both sides wrt. x,
[latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}=-4x^{3}+12x^{2}-20x+c_{1}[/latex]
Integrating both sides wrt. x, [latex]y=-x^{4}+4x^{3}-10x^{2}+c_{1}x+c_{2} \;\;...(i)[/latex]
At [latex]x=0, \; y=5 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; 5=c_{2}[/latex]
At [latex]x=2, \; y=21[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \;\; 21&=-16+32-40+2c_{1}+c_{2} \\ 2c_{1}&=21+16-2+40-5 \\ 2c_{1}&=40 \\ c_{1}&=20 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; y&=-x^{4}+4x^{3}-10x^{2}+20x+5\\ &\text{Put } x=1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; y&=-1+4-10+20+5 \\ y&=18 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The two Eigen values of the matrix [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & p \end{bmatrix}[/latex]  have a ratio of 3:1 for p = 2. What is another value of p for which the Eigen values have the same ratio of 3:1?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & p \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Let [latex]\lambda _{1}[/latex] and [latex]\lambda _{2}[/latex] be the eigen value of matrix A
[latex]\therefore \;\; \frac{\lambda _{1}}{\lambda _[2]}=\frac{3}{1}[/latex] for [latex]p=2[/latex]
Sum of eigen value
[latex] =\lambda _{1}+\lambda _{2}=2+p \;\;...(i)[/latex]
Product of eigen value
[latex] =\lambda _{1}\lambda _{2}=2p-1 \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\lambda _{1}}{\lambda _{2}}&=\frac{3}{1} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \lambda _{1}&=3\lambda _{2}\\ &\text{From eq. (i)}\\ \Rightarrow \;\; 3\lambda _{2}+\lambda _{2}&=2+p \\ 4\lambda _{2}&=2+p \\ \lambda _{2}&=\frac{p+2}{4} \\ \text{From eq. (ii)}\\ \Rightarrow \;\; 3\lambda _{2}^{2}&=2p-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; 3\left ( \frac{p+2}{4} \right )^{2}&=2p-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; p&=2,\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}[/latex]
OR
[latex] \begin{aligned} A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & p \end{bmatrix} \\ A-I\lambda &=0 \\ \begin{bmatrix} 2-\lambda & 1\\ 1 & p-\lambda \end{bmatrix}&=0 \\ \left ( 2-\lambda \right )\left ( p-\lambda \right )-1&=0 \\ \lambda ^{2}-\left ( p+2 \right )\lambda +\left ( 2p-1 \right )=0\end{aligned} [/latex]
By putting values of p from options.
By putting option (D) [latex]\frac{14}{3}[/latex] in above equations gives value 5, [latex]\frac{5}{3}[/latex].
Hence ratio of two eigen values [latex]=\frac{5}{5/3}= 3:1[/latex].

raw_source.text:
For step-size, [latex]\Delta x=0.4[/latex], the value of following integral using Simpson's 1/3 rule is _________.
[latex]\int_{0}^{0.8}(0.2+25x-200x^{2}+675x^{3}-900x^{4}+400x^{5})dx[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]a=0, b=0.8, \Delta x=0.4 [/latex]
[latex]f\left ( x \right )=0.2+25x-200x^{2}+675x^{3}-900x^{4}+400x^{5}[/latex]



By Simpson's 1/3 Rule,
[latex] \begin{aligned} y\left ( x \right )&=\int_{0}^{0.8}\left ( 0.2+25x-200x^{2}+675x^{3}-900x^{4}+400x^{5} \right )dx \\ &=\frac{4}{3}\left [ y_{0}+4y_{1}+y_{2} \right ] \\ y_{0}&=y\left ( 0 \right )=0.2 \\ y_{1}&=y\left ( 0.4 \right )=2.456 \\ y_{2}&=y\left ( 0.8 \right )=0.232 \\ y\left ( n \right )&=\frac{0.4}{3}\left ( 0.2+4\times 2.456+0.232 \right ) \\ &=1.367 \end{aligned}[/latex]
