The value of abscissa (x) and ordinate (y) of a curve are as follows:
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline 2.0 & 5.00 \\ \hline 2.5 & 7.25 \\ \hline 3.0 & 10.00 \\ \hline 3.5 & 13.25 \\ \hline 4.0 & 17.00 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
By Simpson's [latex]1 / 3^{\mathrm{rd}}[/latex] rule, the area under the curve (round off to two decimal places) is ______________
raw_source.solution:
d = 0.5 unit


[latex]\begin{aligned} A &=\frac{d}{3}\left[\left(y_{1}+y_{5}\right)+4\left(y_{2}+y_{4}\right)+2 y_{3}\right] \\ &=\frac{0.5}{3}[(5+17)+4(7.25+13.25)+2 \times 10] \\ &=20.67 \text { unit }^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Vehicular arrival at an isolated intersection follows the Poisson distribution. The mean vehicular arrival rate is 2 vehicle per minute. The probability (round off to two decimal places) that at least 2 vehicles will arrive in any given 1-minute interval is _____
raw_source.solution:
[latex]P(n,t)=\frac{(\lambda t)^n e^{-\lambda t}}{n!}[/latex]
[latex]\lambda =2 \;v/m[/latex]
[latex]t = 1 \text{ minute}[/latex]
probability of at least 2 vehicles arriving in 1 ? minute is given by,
[latex]1-(P(0,1)+P(1,1))[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &= 1-\left \{ \frac{(2 \times 1)^0 e^{-2(1)}}{0!}+\frac{(2 \times 1)^1 e^{-2(1)}}{1!} \right \}\\ &=1-\left \{ \frac{1(e^{-2})}{1}+ \frac{2(e^{-2})}{1} \right \} \\ &= 1-(e^{-2}+2e^{-2})\\ &=1-3e^{-2}=0.59 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Refer the truss as shown in the figure (not to scale).

If load, [latex]F=10 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{kN}[/latex], moment of inertia, [latex]I=8.33 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~mm}^{4}[/latex], area of cross-section, [latex]A=10^{4} \mathrm{~mm}^{2}[/latex], and length, L=2 m for all the members of the truss, the compressive stress (in [latex]\mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex],in integer) carried by the member Q-R is _________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]V_{P}=V_{S}=5 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{kN}[/latex]
Considering equilibrium of LHS of section (1 )-(1)


Taking moment about 'T'
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Sigma M_{T}(C W)&=0\\ (5 \sqrt{3} \times a)+F_{Q R}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3} a}{2}\right)&=0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad F_{O A}&=-10 \mathrm{kN} or 10 \mathrm{kN} (C) \\ \text{ Compressive} &\text{ stress in member QR} \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{C}}\right)\\ \sigma_{\mathrm{C}}&=\frac{F_{Q A}}{2 A} \\ &=\frac{10 \mathrm{kN}}{2 \times\left(10^{4} \times 10^{-6}\right) \mathrm{m}^{2}} \\ &=500 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A prismatic cantilever prestressed concrete beam of span length, L=1.5 m has one straight tendon placed in the cross-section as shown in the following figure (not to scale). The total prestressing force of 50 kN in the tendon is applied at [latex]d_{c}=50 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex] from the top in the cross-section of width, b=200 mm and depth, d=300 mm.

If the concentrated load, P=5 kN, the resultant stress (in Mpa,in integer) experienced at point 'Q' will be _________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{e} &=\frac{D}{2}-50=\frac{300}{2}-50=100 \mathrm{~mm} \\ \mathrm{DL} &=0.2 \times 0.3 \times 1.0 \times 25=1.50 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m} \\ P &=50 \mathrm{kN}=50000 \mathrm{~N} \\ W &=5 \mathrm{kN} \\ \text { Maximum BM } &=\frac{w^{2}}{2}+\mathrm{W} \\ &=\frac{1.5 \times 1.5^{2}}{2}+5 \times 1.50=9.1875 \mathrm{kNm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P}{A}&=\frac{50000}{200 \times 300}=0.833 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ \frac{P e}{Z}&=\frac{50000 \times 100}{200 \times \frac{300^{2}}{6}}=1.67 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ \frac{M}{Z}&=\frac{9.1875 \times 10^{6}}{200 \times \frac{300^{2}}{6}}=3.0625 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}\\ \text{Stress at Q,}\qquad \qquad\\ \text { Stress at } Q &=\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e}{Z}-\frac{M}{Z} \\ &=0.833+1.67-3.0625 \\ &=-0.56 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \text { (Tensile) } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A column is subjected to a total load (P) of 60 kN supported through a bracket connection, as shown in the figure (not to scale).

The resultant force in bolt R (in kN,round off to one decimal place) is ________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} F_{1}&=\frac{P}{n}=\frac{60}{6}=10 \mathrm{kN}\\ F_{2}&=\frac{P \cdot e}{\sum r_{i}^{2}} \times r_{R}=\frac{60 \times 100\mathrm{~mm}}{4 \times 50^{2}+2 \times 40^{2}} \times 40\\ F_{2}&=\frac{60 \times 100 \times 40}{10000+3200}=\frac{60 \times 100 \times 40}{13200}=\frac{200}{11} \mathrm{kN}\\ F_{R}&=F_{1}+F_{2}\\ &=10+\frac{200}{11}=\frac{310}{11}=28.2 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Employ stiffness matrix approach for the simply supported beam as shown in the figure to calculate unknown displacements/rotations. Take length, L=8 m; modulus of elasticity, [latex]E=3 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex]; moment of inertia, [latex]I=225 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{mm}^{4}[/latex].

The mid-span deflection of the beam (in mm,round off to integer) under P=100 kN in downward direction will be ___________
raw_source.solution:
By stiffness matrix method
Step-1 : Generation of stiffness matrix
Column-1

[latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{k}_{11}&=\frac{3 E(2 I)}{(L / 2)^{3}}+\frac{3 E(I)}{(L / 2)^{3}}=\frac{72 \mathrm{E} I}{L^{3}}\\ k_{21}&=-\frac{3 E(2 I)}{(L / 2)^{2}}+\frac{3 E(I)}{(L / 2)^{2}}=-\frac{12 E I}{L^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Column-2

[latex]\begin{aligned} k_{22}&=\frac{3 E(2 I)}{(L / 2)}+\frac{3 E(I)}{(L / 2)}=18 \frac{E I}{L} \\ \text { Stiffness matrix }[k]&=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 72 \frac{E I}{L^{3}} & -\frac{12 E I}{L^{2}} \\ -\frac{12 E I}{L^{2}} & \frac{E I}{L} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Step-2: Calculation of unknown Nodal displacements [latex]\left(\Delta_{\mathrm{B}}, \theta_{\mathrm{B}}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Using} \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad [P]&=[k][\Delta]\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad & \quad\left[\begin{array}{l} P \\ O \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc} \frac{72 E I}{L^{2}} & -\frac{12 E I}{L^{2}} \\ -\frac{12 E I}{L^{2}} & \frac{8 E I}{L} \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} \Delta_{B} \\ \theta_{B} \end{array}\right]\\ \text{On solving} \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad\\\Delta_{\mathrm{B}}&=\frac{P L^{3}}{64 E I}(\downarrow) \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \theta_{\mathrm{B}}&=\frac{P L^{2}}{96 E I}(\mathrm{CW}) \\ \Delta_{\mathrm{B}}&=\frac{\left(100 \times 10^{3}\right) \times(8000)^{3}}{64 \times 3 \times 10^{4} \times 225 \times 10^{6}}\\ &=118.519 \mathrm{~mm} \simeq 119 \mathrm{~mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A square plate O-P-Q-R of a linear elastic material with sides 1.0 m is loaded in a state of plane stress. Under a given stress condition, the plate deforms to a new configuration O-P'-Q'-R' as shown in the figure (not to scale). Under the given deformation, the edges of the plate remain straight.

The horizontal displacement of the point (0.5 m, 0.5 m) in the plate O-P-Q-R (in mm,round off to one decimal place) is ________

So horizontal displacement of the point (0.5 m, 0.5 m)

raw_source.text:
A small project has 12 activities - N, P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, and Z. The relationship among these activities and the duration of these activities are given in the Table.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text { Activity } & \begin{array}{c} \text { Duration } \\ \text { (in weeks) } \end{array} & \begin{array}{c} \text { Depends } \\ \text { upon } \end{array} \\ \hline N & 2 & - \\ \hline \mathrm{P} & 5 & \mathrm{~N} \\ \hline \mathrm{Q} & 3 & \mathrm{~N} \\ \hline \mathrm{R} & 4 & \mathrm{P} \\ \hline \mathrm{S} & 5 & \mathrm{Q} \\ \hline \mathrm{T} & 8 & \mathrm{R} \\ \hline \mathrm{U} & 7 & \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S} \\ \hline \mathrm{V} & 2 & \mathrm{U} \\ \hline \mathrm{W} & 3 & \mathrm{U} \\ \hline \mathrm{X} & 5 & \mathrm{~T}, \mathrm{~V} \\ \hline \mathrm{Y} & 1 & \mathrm{~W} \\ \hline \mathrm{Z} & 3 & \mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
The total float of the activity 'V' (in weeks, in integer) is _________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} F_{T_{V}} &=T_{L_{j}}-T_{E_{i}}-t_{i_{j}} \\ &=20-18-2 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The soil profile at a construction site is shown in the figure (not to scale). Ground water table (GWT) is at 5 m below the ground level at present. An old well data shows that the ground water table was as low as 10 m below the ground level in the past. Take unit weight of water, [latex]\gamma_{W}=9.81 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex].

The overconsolidation ratio (OCR)(round off to two decimal places) at the mid-point of the clay layer is _______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{OCR} &=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{c}}{\bar{\sigma}_{0}} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{c} &=\text { Preconsolidation stress } \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=\text { Present effective stress } \\ \bar{\sigma}_{c} &=17.5 \times 10+(18.5-9.81) \times 5+(17-9.81) \times 4 \\ &=247.21 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=17.5 \times 5+(18.5-9.81) \times 10+(17-9.81) \times 4 \\ &=203.16 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \mathrm{OCR} &=\frac{247.21}{203.16}=1.22 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A retaining wall of height 10 m with clay backfill is shown in the figure (not to scale). Weight of the retaining wall is 5000 kN per m acting at 3.3 m from the toe of the retaining wall. The interface friction angle between base of the retaining wall and the base soil is [latex]20^{\circ}[/latex]. The depth of clay in front of the retaining wall is 2.0 m. The properties of the clay backfill and the clay placed in front of the retaining wall are the same. Assume that the tension crack is filled with water. Use Rankine's earth pressure theory. Take unit weight of water, [latex]\gamma_{w}=9.81 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex].

The factor of safety (round off to two decimal places) against sliding failure of the retaining wall after ignoring the passive earth pressure will be ________________
raw_source.solution:
Depth of tension crack,
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{C}&=\frac{2 C}{\gamma } \text { If } \phi=0 \\ &=\frac{2 \times 30}{17.2 }=3.488 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Tension crack develops only in the back fill (clay)
The tension crack will not develop in the clay which is infront of the wall.
The total active thrust on the wall, due to the backfill, and the water in the tension crack
[latex]F_a=k_a\cdot \frac{\gamma H^2}{2}-2C\sqrt{k_a}\cdot H+\frac{2C^2}{\gamma }+\frac{\gamma _wz_c^2}{2}[/latex]
[latex]k_a=1 \text{ since }\phi =0[/latex]
[latex]F_a=1 \times \frac{17.2 \times 10^2}{2}-2 \times 30\sqrt{1} \times 10+\frac{2 \times 30^2}{17.2 }+\frac{9.81 \times 3.488^2}{2}=424.326 \; kN[/latex]
Factor of safety against sliding neglecting passive earth pressure on front side, [latex]F_s[/latex]

[latex]F_s=\frac{\mu \cdot W}{F_a}[/latex]
[latex]\mu =[/latex] coefficient of friction at base [latex]= \tan \delta[/latex]
[latex]F_s=\frac{\tan \delta \cdot W}{F_a}=\frac{\tan 20^{\circ} \times 5000}{424.326}=4.2888\approx 4.29[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A combined trapezoidal footing of length L supports two identical square columns ([latex]P_{1}[/latex] and [latex]P_{2}[/latex]) of size 0.5m x 0.5m, as shown in the figure. The columns [latex]P_{1}[/latex] and [latex]P_{2}[/latex] carry loads of 2000 kN and 1500 kN, respectively.

If the stress beneath the footing is uniform, the length of the combined footing L (in m,round off to two decimal places) is _____
raw_source.solution:
C.G. of load from [latex]P_{1}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{R} \bar{x} &=P_{1} \times 0+P_{2} \times 5 \\ \bar{x} &=\frac{1500 \times 5}{3500}=2.143 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Distance of C.G. of footing from face of [latex]P_{1}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{y}=\bar{x}+0.25=2.393 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]

C.G of footing [latex]\begin{aligned} \bar{y} &=\left(\frac{B_{1}+2 B_{2}}{B_{1}+B_{2}}\right) \times \frac{L}{3} \\ 2.393 &=\left(\frac{5+2 \times 1.5}{5+1.5}\right) \times \frac{L}{3} \\ L &=5.833 \mathrm{~m} \text { say } 5.83 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An unsupported slope of height 15 m is shown in the figure (not to scale), in which the slope face makes an angle [latex]50^{\circ} [/latex] with the horizontal. The slope material comprises purely cohesive soil having undrained cohesion 75 kPa. A trial slip circle KLM, with a radius 25 m, passes through the crest and toe of the slope and it subtends an angle [latex]60^{\circ} [/latex] at its center O. The weight of the active soil mass (W, bounded by KLMN) is 2500 kN/m, which is acting at a horizontal distance of 10 m from the toe of the slope. Consider the water table to be present at a very large depth from the ground surface.

Considering the trail slip circle KLM, the factor of the safety against the failure of slope under undrained condition (round off to two decimal places) is ___________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} \mathrm{FOS} &=\frac{\text { Resisting moment }}{\text { Actuating moment }} \\ \mathrm{FOS} &=\frac{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{u}} l R}{w \bar{x}} \\ l &=\text { Length of ac } \mathrm{KLM} \\ \bar{x} &=\text { Distance of ' } \mathrm{w}^{\prime} \text { from toe } \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \quad \mathrm{FOS} &=\frac{75 \times 2 \pi \times 25 \times \frac{60}{36} \times 25}{2500 \times 10} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \quad \mathrm{FOS} &=1.96 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An unlined canal under regime conditions along with a silt factor of 1 has a width of flow 71.25m. Assuming the unlined canal as a wide channel, the corresponding average depth of flow (in m, round off to two decimal places) in the canal will be ______________
raw_source.solution:
R = D (for wide rectangular channel)
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} A f^{2} &=140\left(\frac{2}{5} f R\right)^{5 / 2} \\ (B D) f^{2} &=140\left(\frac{2}{5} f \times D\right)^{5 / 2} \\ (71.25 \times D) \times 1 &=140\left(\frac{2}{5} \times 1 \times D\right)^{5 / 2} \\ D \times 0.5089 &=\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{5 / 2} \times(D)^{5 / 2} \\ D^{3 / 2} &=5.029 \\ \text { or } \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad D &=2.94 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylinder (2.0 m diameter, 3.0 m long and 25 kN weight) is acted upon by water on one side and oil (specific gravity=0.8) on other side as shown in the figure.

The absolute ratio of the net magnitude of vertical forces to the net magnitude of horizontal forces (round off to two decimal places) is _____________
raw_source.solution:
Net horizontal force [latex]\left(F_{H}\right)[/latex] due to liquids
[latex]\begin{aligned} F_{H} &=F_{H 1}-F_{H 2} \\ &=\rho_{w} g \bar{h}_{1} A_{v_{1}}-\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} g \bar{h}_{2} A_{v_{2}} \\ &=\left(10^{3}\right)(9.81)\left(1+\frac{2}{2}\right)(2 \times 3)-(800)(9.81)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(1 \times 3) \\ F_{H} &=105.948 \mathrm{kN}(\rightarrow) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net vertical force [latex]\left(F_{v}\right)[/latex] due to liquids
[latex]\begin{aligned} F_{v} &=F_{1}+F_{2} \\ &=\rho_{w} g \forall_{1}+\rho_{o i l} g \forall_{2} \\ &=\left(10^{3}\right)(9.81)\left(\frac{\pi(1)^{2} \times 3}{2}\right)+(800)(9.81)\left(\frac{\pi}{4}(1)^{2} \times 3\right) \\ &=64.7199 \mathrm{kN}(\uparrow) \\ \frac{F_{V}}{F_{H}} &=\frac{64.7199}{105.948}=0.61 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A tube-well of 20 cm diameter fully penetrates a horizontal, homogeneous and isotropic confined aquifer of infinite horizontal extent. The aquifer is of 30 m uniform thickness. A steady pumping at the rate of 40 litres/s from the well for a long time results in a steady drawdown of 4 m at the well face. The subsurface flow to the well due to pumping is steady, horizontal and Darcian and the radius of influence of the well is 245 m. The hydraulic conductivity of the aquifer (in m/day,round off to integer) is ______________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} 40 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} &=\frac{2 \pi k \times 30 \mathrm{~m} \times 4 \mathrm{~m}}{\ln \left(\frac{245}{0.1}\right)} \\ k &=4.14 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \text{or, } \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad k &=35.77 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{d} \\ &\approx 36 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{d} (\text{ round off to nearest integer}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Precipitation and General Aspects of Hydrology

raw_source.text: A baghouse filter has to treat [latex]12 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}[/latex] of waste gas continuously. The baghouse is to be divided into 5 sections of equal cloth area such that one section can be shut down for cleaning and/or repairing, while the other 4 sections continue to operate. An air-to-cloth ratio of [latex]6.0 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{min}-\mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex] cloth will provide sufficient treatment to the gas. The individual bags are of 32 cm in diameter and 5 m in length. The total number of bags (in integer) required in the baghouse is ________________
raw_source.solution:
Given, discharge to be passed = [latex]12 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
Out of 5 sections, 4 will operate at a time.
Each bag is

Thus, surface area of each bag [latex]=\pi \times 0.32 \times 5 \mathrm{~m}^{2}=5.0265 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex]
Total surface area required wr.t. given discharge
[latex]=\frac{12 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}}{6 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{min}-\mathrm{m}^{2}}=\frac{12 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}}{\frac{6}{60} \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}-\mathrm{m}^{2}}=120 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Working bag filters required [latex]=\frac{120 m^{2}}{5.0265 m^{2}}=[/latex] 23.87 or 24 bag filters
But, since it is asked total (which includes a standby set also), then,Total no. of bag filters [latex]=24 \times \frac{5}{4}=30[/latex]

raw_source.text: A secondary clarifier handles a total flow of [latex]9600 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{d}[/latex] from the aeration tank of a conventional activated-sludge treatment system. The concentration of solids in the flow from the aeration tank is 3000 mg/L. The clarifier is required to thicken the solids to 12000 mg/L, and hence it is to be designed for a solid flux of [latex]3.2 \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^{2} \cdot \mathrm{h}}[/latex]. The surface area of the designed clarifier for thickening (in [latex]\mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex], in integer) is _________________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=9600 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} \\ X &=3000 \mathrm{mg} / l \\ X_{u} &=12000 \mathrm{mg} / l \\ \text {Solid flux }& =3.2 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{2}-\mathrm{h}\\ \text{Surface area,}  \qquad \mathrm{A}&=\frac{\text { Total quantity of solids entering }}{\text { Solid flux }}\\ A &=\frac{9600 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} \times 3000 \mathrm{mg} / l}{3.2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{m}^{2}-\mathrm{h}} \\ &=\frac{9600 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{lld} \times 3000 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{l}}{3.2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{m}^{2}-\mathrm{h} \times 24 \mathrm{~h} / \mathrm{d}} \\ &=375 \mathrm{~m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Spot speeds of vehicles observed at a point on a highway are 40, 55, 60, 65 and 80 km/h. The space-mean speed (in km/h, round off to two decimal places) of the observed vehicles is ______________

The longitudinal section of a runway provides the following data:
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text { End-to-end runway (m) } & \text { Gradient (\%) } \\ \hline 0 \text { to 300 } & +1.2 \\ \hline 300 \text { to } 600 & -0.7 \\ \hline 600 \text { to } 1100 & +0.6 \\ \hline 1100 \text { to } 1400 & -0.8 \\ \hline 1400 \text { to } 1700 & -1.0 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
The effective gradient of the runway (in %, round off to two decimal places) is _____________
raw_source.solution:
Assuming RL of start of runway as datum i.e., RL = 0 m)

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Effective gradient } &=\left[\frac{\text { Maximum difference in reduced level }}{\text { Total runway length }}\right] \\ &=\left[\frac{4.5-(-0.9)}{1700} \times 100\right] \% \\ &=0.3176 \% \simeq 0.32 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\oplus[/latex] and [latex]\odot[/latex] are two operators on numbers p and q such that [latex]p \oplus q=\frac{p^{2}+q^{2}}{p q}[/latex] and [latex]p \odot q=\frac{p^{2}}{q}[/latex];
If [latex]x \oplus y=2 \odot 2[/latex], then x =
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} x \oplus y &=2 \odot 2 \\ \frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{x y} &=\frac{2^{2}}{2} \\ x^{2}+y^{2} &=2 x y \\ (x-y)^{2} &=0 \\ x &=y \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A function, [latex]\lambda[/latex], is defined by
[latex]\lambda(p, q)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} (p-q)^{2}, & \text { if } p \geq q \\ p+q, & \text { if } p \lt q \end{array}\right.[/latex]
The value of the expression [latex]\frac{\lambda(-(-3+2),(-2+3))}{(-(-2+1))}[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{\lambda(-(-3+2),(-2+3))}{(-(2+1))}=\lambda \frac{(1,1)}{1}=\lambda(1,1)[/latex]
So, 1st definition will be applicable as p = q.
[latex]\text { Hence, } \qquad \lambda(1,1)=(1-1)^{2}=0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Humans have the ability to construct worlds entirely in their minds, which don't exist in the physical world. So far as we know, no other species possesses this ability. This skill is so important that we have different words to refer to its different flavors, such as imagination, invention and innovation.
Based on the above passage, which one of the following is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Option (B) and (D) are weekend by the word 'UNRELATED SKILLS'. Option (A) is weekend by the expression, no species posses the ability.
Hence answer is option (C) which reflects the information given in the passage.
options: No species possess the ability to construct worlds in their minds
The terms imagination, invention and innovation refer to unrelated skills
We do not know of any species other than humans who possess the ability to construct mental worlds
Imagination, invention and innovation are unrelated to the ability to construct mental worlds

raw_answer.option_text: We do not know of any species other than humans who possess the ability to construct mental worlds

raw_source.text: The value of [latex]\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{x \ln (x)}{1+x^{2}}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{x \ln x}{x^{2}+1}\right) \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \left(\frac{\infty}{\infty} \text { form }\right)\\ &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{x\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+\ln x}{2 x}\right) \qquad \qquad \qquad \left(\frac{\infty}{\infty} \text { form }\right)\\ \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{0+\frac{1}{x}}{2}\right)&=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{1}{2 x}\right)=\frac{1}{2 \times \infty}=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The unit normal vector to the surface [latex]X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}-48=0[/latex] at the point (4,4,4) is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \phi &=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-48, P(4,4,4) \\ \operatorname{grad} \phi &=\vec{\nabla} \phi=\hat{i} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}+\hat{j} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}+\hat{k} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} \\ &=(2 x) \hat{i}+(2 y) \hat{j}+(2 z) \hat{k} \\ \vec{n} &=(\operatorname{grad} \phi)_{P}=8 \hat{i}+8 \hat{j}+8 \hat{k} \\ \hat{n} &=\frac{\vec{n}}{|\vec{n}|}=\frac{8 \hat{i}+8 \hat{j}+8 \hat{k}}{\sqrt{64+64+64}}=\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ & \simeq\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Strain hardening of structural steel means
raw_source.solution:
Strain hardening is experiencing higher stress than yield stress with increased deformation
In the figure AB = Strain hardening zone
OA = Linear elastic zone
Stress corresponding to point 'A' is yield stress.

strengthening steel member externally for reducing strain experienced
strain occurring before plastic flow of steel material
decrease in the stress experienced with increasing strain

raw_source.text:
A single story building model is shown in the figure. The rigid bar of mass 'm' is supported by three massless elastic columns whose ends are fixed against rotation. For each of the columns, the applied lateral force (P) and corresponding moment (M) are also shown in the figure. The lateral deflection [latex](\delta)[/latex] of the bar is given by [latex]\delta=\frac{P L^{3}}{12 E I}[/latex], where L is the effective length of the column, E is the Young's modulus of elasticity and I is the area moment of inertia of the column cross-section with respect to its neutral axis.

For the lateral deflection profile of the columns as shown in the figure, the natural frequency of the system for horizontal oscillation is

raw_source.text:
A frame EFG is shown in the figure. All members are prismatic and have equal flexural rigidity. The member FG carries a uniformly distributed load w per unit length. Axial deformation of any member is neglected.

Considering the joint F being rigid, the support reaction at G is
raw_source.solution:
Compatibility condition

[latex]\begin{array}{l} \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \frac{\partial U}{\partial R}=0 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial R}\left[\int \frac{M^{2}}{2 E \mid} d x\right]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial R}\left[\int_{0}^{L} \frac{\left(R x-\frac{w x^{2}}{2}\right)^{2}}{2 E I} d x+\int_{0}^{2 L} \frac{\left(R L-\frac{w L^{2}}{2}\right)^{2}}{2 E I} d x\right]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \int_{0}^{L} \frac{2\left(R x-\frac{w x^{2}}{2}\right)}{2 E I}(x) d x+\int_{0}^{2 L} \frac{\left(R L-\frac{w L^{2}}{2}\right)}{E I}(L) d x=0 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{R L^{3}}{3}-\frac{W}{2} \times \frac{L^{4}}{4}+R L^{2}(2 L)-\frac{W^{3}}{2}(2 L)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{R L^{3}}{3}-\frac{w^{4}}{8}+2 R L^{3}-w L^{4}=0 \\ \Rightarrow 2 R L^{3}+\frac{R L^{3}}{3}=\frac{w^{4}}{8}+w^{4}=\frac{9}{8} w^{4} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{7 R L^{3}}{3}=\frac{9}{8} w L^{4} \\ \Rightarrow R=\frac{27}{56} w L=0.482 w L \end{array}[/latex]
Alternative
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{w L^{4}}{8 E I}+\frac{w L^{2}(2 L)}{2 E I} \times L &=\frac{R L^{3}}{3 E I}+\frac{R L \times 2 L \times L}{E I} \\ \frac{w^{4}}{8 E I}+\frac{w^{4}}{E I} &=\frac{R L^{3}}{3 E I}+\frac{2 R L^{3}}{E I} \\ \frac{9 W^{4}}{8 E I} &=\frac{7 R L^{3}}{3 E I} \\ R &=\frac{27 w L}{56}=0.482 \mathrm{wL} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A clay layer of thickness H has a preconsolidation pressure [latex]p_{c}[/latex]
 and an initial void ratio [latex]e_{0}[/latex].The initial effective overburden stress at the mid-height of the layer is [latex]p_{0}[/latex]. At the same location, the increment in effective stress due to applied external load is [latex]\Delta p[/latex]. The compression and swelling indices of the clay are [latex]C_{c}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
As the soil is initially in over consolidate state [latex](p_o \lt p_c)[/latex], due to the external applied load [latex](\Delta p)[/latex] the soil initially undergoes re-compression upto [latex](p_c)[/latex] and then changes to virgin compression from [latex](p_c)[/latex] to [latex](p_f)[/latex]

The re-compression index [latex](C_r)[/latex] is also called Swelling index, [latex](C_S)[/latex].

[latex]s_{c}=\frac{H}{I+e_{0}} \left[C_{s} \log \frac{p_{c}}{p_{0}}+C_{c} \log \frac{p_{0}+\Delta p}{p_{c}}\right][/latex]

raw_source.text: A function is defined in Cartesian coordinate system as [latex]f(x, y)=x e^{y}[/latex]. The value of the directional derivative of the function (in integer) at the point (2,0) along the direction of the straight line segment from point (2,0) to point [latex]\left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right)[/latex] is _______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x, y)&=x e^{y}\\ \mathrm{P}(2,0) \text{ and } Q\left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right)\\ \operatorname{grad} f &=\hat{i}\left(e^{y}\right)+\hat{j}\left(x e^{y}\right)+\hat{k}(0) \\ \Rightarrow  \qquad \qquad \qquad (\operatorname{grad} f)_{p} &=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j} ]\\ \overline{P Q}&=\left(\frac{1}{2}-2\right) \hat{i}+(2-0) \hat{j}=-\frac{3}{2} \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}\\ \text{Required directional derivative} &=(\text { grad } f)_{P} \widehat{P Q}\\ &=(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}) \times \frac{\left(-\frac{3}{2} \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}\right)}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+4}}=\frac{\frac{-3}{2}+4}{\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}}} \\ &=\frac{\frac{-3+8}{2}}{\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)}=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The difference between the book values (in Rs, in integer) obtained at the end of 4th year using straight line method and sum of years digit method of depreciation is _____

A rectangular footing of size 2.8m x 3.5m is embedded in a clay layer and a vertical load is placed with an eccentricity of 0.8 m as shown in the figure (not to scale). Take Bearing capacity factors: [latex]N_{c}=5.14[/latex],[latex]N_{q}=1.0[/latex], and [latex]N_{\gamma}=0.0[/latex]; Shape factors: [latex]s_{c}=1.16[/latex],[latex]s_{q}=1.0[/latex] and [latex]s_{\gamma}=1.0[/latex]; Depth factors: [latex]d_{c}=1.1[/latex],[latex]d_{q}=1.0[/latex] and [latex]d_{\gamma}=1.0[/latex]; and Inclination factors: [latex]i_{c}=1.0[/latex] and [latex]i_{q}=1.0[/latex] and [latex]i_{\gamma}=1.0[/latex].

Using Meyerhoff's method, the load (in kN, round off to two decimal places) that can be applied on the footing with a factor of safety of 2.5 is _________________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}& \text { Given data: } 2.8 \times 3.56, e=0.8, D_{f}=1.5 \mathrm{~m} \\ N_{c}&=5.14, \qquad N_{q}=1, \qquad N_{r}=0 \\ S_{c}&=1.16, \qquad S_{q}=1, \qquad S_{r}=1.0 \\ d_{c}&=1.1, \qquad d_{q}=1, \qquad d_{f}=1.0 \\ i_{c}&=1, \qquad \quad i_{q}=1, \qquad i_{r}=1.0 \\ \gamma&=18.2, \qquad c=40 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ B^{\prime}&=B-2 e_{x}=2.8-2(0.8)=1.2 \mathrm{~m} \\ L^{\prime}&=L=3.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Ultimate bearing capacity
[latex]\begin{aligned} q_{u} &=C N_{c} S_{c} d_{c} i_{c}+\gamma D_{p} N_{q} S_{q} d_{q} i_{q}+0.5 B^{\prime} \gamma N_{r} S_{r} d_{r} \\ q_{u} &=40 \times 5.14 \times 1.16 \times 1.1+18.2 \times 1.5 \times 1+0 \\ q_{n u} &=q_{u}-\gamma D_{f}=262.346 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ q_{n s} &=\frac{q_{n u}}{F}=104.938 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Net safe load } &=q_{n s} \times A=\frac{q_{n u}}{F} \times\left(B^{\prime} \times L\right) \\ &=104.938 \times 1.2 \times 3.5 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Load applied on the footing = 440.740 kN

The soil profile at a road construction site is as shown in figure (not to scale). A large embankment is to be constructed at the site. The ground water table (GWT) is located at the surface of the clay layer, and the capillary rise in the sandy soil is negligible. The effective stress at the middle of the clay layer after the application of the embankment loading is [latex]180 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]. Take unit weight of water, [latex]\gamma_{w}=9.81 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex].

The primary consolidation settlement (in m, round off to two decimal places) of the clay layer resulting from this loading will be ______
raw_source.solution:
Primary consolidation settlement
[latex]\Delta H=\frac{C_{c} H}{1+e_{0}} \log _{10}\left(\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{0}+\Delta \bar{\sigma}}{\bar{\sigma}_{0}}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\bar{\sigma}_{0}+\Delta \bar{\sigma}=[/latex]Effective stress at the center of clay layer after embankment loading
[latex]=180 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{\sigma}_{0}=[/latex] Effective stress at the centre of clay layer before embankment loading
[latex]\begin{aligned} \gamma_{\text {sub }} \text { of clay layer } &=\frac{G-1}{1+e} \gamma_{w}=\frac{(2.65-1)}{1+\frac{w G}{1}} \times 9.81 \\ &=\frac{1.65 \times 9.81}{1+0.45 \times 2.65}=7.383 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=(18.5 \times 2)+(7.383) \times 3=59.149 \mathrm{kNm} /{ } \\ e_{0} &=\frac{w G}{1}=0.45 \times 2.65=1.1925 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad & \Delta \mathrm{H}=\frac{0.25 \times 6}{1+1.1925} \log _{10}\left(\frac{180}{59.149}\right)=0.33 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Numerically integrate, [latex]f(x)=10 x-20 x^{2}[/latex] from lower limit a=0 to upper limit b=0.5. Use Trapezoidal rule with five equal subdivisions. The value (in units,round off to two decimal places) obtained is ____________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y&=10 x-20 x^{2} \\ a&=0, b=0.5, n=5 \\ \text { So, } \qquad \qquad \qquad h&=\frac{b-a}{n}=0.1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
And

[latex]\begin{aligned} I &=\int_{0}^{0.5} f(x) d x=\frac{h}{2}\left[y_{0}+y_{5}+2\left(y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}+y_{4}\right)\right] \\ &=\frac{0.1}{2}[0+0+2(0.8+1.2+1.2+0.8)] \\ &=0.40 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The void ratio of a clay soil sample M decreased from 0.575 to 0.510 when the applied pressure is increased from 120 kPa to 180 kPa. For the same increment in pressure, the void ratio of another clay soil sample N decreases from 0.600 to 0.550. If the ratio of hydraulic conductivity of sample M to sample N  is 0.125, then the ratio of coefficient of consolidation of sample M to sample N (round off to three decimal places) is ______________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} m_{v}&=\frac{a_{V}}{1+e_{0}}=\frac{\Delta e}{\left(1+e_{0}\right) \times(\Delta \bar{\sigma})} & (\Delta \bar{\sigma} \text { is same for both } M \text { and } N)\\ m_{v 1}&=\frac{0.575-0.510}{(1+0.575) \times \Delta \bar{\sigma}}\\ m_{v 2}&=\frac{0.600-0.550}{(1+0.600) \times \Delta \bar{\sigma}}\\ \frac{C_{v_{1}}}{C_{V_{2}}} &=\frac{\frac{k_{1}}{m_{v_{1}} \gamma_{w}}}{\frac{k_{2}}{m_{v_{2}} \gamma_{w}}}=\frac{k_{1}}{k_{2}} \times \frac{m_{v_{2}}}{m_{v_{1}}} \\ &=0.125\left(\frac{1.575}{1.6}\right) \times\left(\frac{0.60-0.55}{0.575-0.510}\right) \\ &=0.0947 \simeq 0.095 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The hyetograph in the figure corresponds to a rainfall event of 3 cm.

If the rainfall event has produced a direct runoff of 1.6 cm, the [latex]\phi[/latex]-index of the event (in mm/hour,round off to one decimal place) would be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Total rainfall } &=3 \mathrm{~cm} \\ \text { Total runoff } &=1.6 \mathrm{~cm} \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad \qquad\text { Total infiltration } &=3-1.6=1.4 \mathrm{~cm}\\ \therefore \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad\qquad\text { W-index }&=\frac{\text { Total infiltration }}{\text { Total duration of storm }}\\ &=\frac{1.4}{(210 / 60)} \mathrm{cm} / \mathrm{hr} \\ &=0.4 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{hr}=4 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{hr}\\ \text { As } \phi \text { -index }>\text { W-index }\qquad \qquad \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence storm of intensities 4 mm/hr and 3 mm/hr will not produce rainfall exam.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \phi \text { -index } &=\frac{\text { Total infiltration in which rainfall excess occur }}{\text { Time period in which rainfall excess occur }} \\ &=\frac{\text { Total infiltration }-\text { Infiltration in which no rainfall excess occur }}{T_{\text {excess }}} \\ &=\frac{14 \mathrm{~mm}-\left(4 \times \frac{30}{60}+3 \times \frac{30}{60}\right) \mathrm{mm}}{\left(\frac{150}{60}\right) \mathrm{hr}} \\ &=4.2 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{hr} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A venturimeter as shown in the figure (not to scale) is connected to measure the flow of water in a vertical pipe of 20 cm diameter.

Assume [latex]g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}[/latex]. When the deflection in the mercury manometer is 15 cm, the flow rate (in lps, round off to two decimal places) considering no loss in the venturimeter is ___________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Discharge }(Q) &=C_{d} \frac{A_{1} A_{2}}{\sqrt{A_{1}^{2}-A_{2}^{2}}} \sqrt{2 g h} \\ h &=X\left(\frac{\rho_{m}}{\rho}-1\right)=0.15\left(\frac{13.6 \times 10^{3}}{10^{3}}-1\right) \\ &=1.89 \mathrm{~m}\\ Q &=\frac{A_{1} A_{2}}{A_{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}\right)^{2}-1}} \times \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 1.89} \\&= \frac{\frac{\pi}{4}(0.2)^{2}}{\sqrt{(2)^{4}-1}} \times \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 1.89} \\&= 49.395 \mathrm{l} / \mathrm{s} \simeq 49.40 \mathrm{l} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A reservoir with a live storage of 300 million cubic metre irrigates 40000 hectares ( 1 hectare= [latex]10^{4} \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex]) of a crop with two fillings of the reservoir. If the base period of the crop is 120 days, the duty for this crop (in hectares per cumec, round off to integer) will then be ________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Live storage } &=300 \mathrm{Mm}^{3} \\ \text { Area } &=40000 \text { hectare }\\ \text {Since 2 filling,} & \text{ so volume of water needed,} \\ &=600 \mathrm{Mm}^{3}\\ B&=120 days \\\text { Duty } &=\frac{8.64 B}{\Delta} \\ \Delta &=\frac{600 \times 10^{6}}{40000 \times 10^{4}}=1.5 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { Duty } &=\frac{8.64 \times 120}{1.5}=691.2 \text { ha/cumec } \end{aligned}[/latex]

An activated sludge process (ASP) is designed for secondary treatment of [latex]7500 m^{3} / day[/latex] of municipal wastewater. After primary clarifier, the ultimate BOD of the influent, which enters into ASP reactor is 200 mg/L. Treated effluent after secondary clarifier is required to have an ultimate BOD of 20 mg/L. Mix liquor volatile suspended solids (MLVSS) concentration in the reactor and the underflow is maintained as 3000 mg/L and 12000 mg/L, respectively. The hydraulic retention time and mean cell residence time are 0.2 day and 10 days, respectively. A representative flow diagram of the ASP is shown below.

The underflow volume (in [latex]m^{3} / day[/latex], round off to one decimal place) of sludge wastage is _________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given,} \qquad X &=3000 \mathrm{mg} / l, \quad X_{\mathrm{u}}=12000 \mathrm{mg} / l \\ \text{Since} \qquad \mathrm{HRT} &=\frac{V}{Q_{0}}\\ \Rightarrow &\text{Volume of reactor,}\\ V &=Q_{0} \times H R T \\ &=7500 \times 0.2 \mathrm{~m}^{3} \\ &=1500 \mathrm{~m}^{3} \\ &\text{Sludge age,} \\ \theta_{\mathrm{C}} &=\frac{V X}{\left(Q_{0}-Q_{w}\right) X_{e}+Q_{w} X_{u}} \qquad \left(X_{e} \simeq 0\right)\\ 10&=\frac{1500 \times 3000}{Q_{W} \times 12000}\\ Q_{w}&=37.5 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / day \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A grit chamber of rectangular cross-section is to be designed to remove particles with diameter of 0.25 mm and specific gravity of 2.70. The terminal settling velocity of the particles is estimated as 2.5 cm/s. The chamber is having a width of 0.50 m and has to carry a peak wastewater flow of [latex]9720 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{d}[/latex] giving the depth of flow as 0.75 m. If a flow-through velocity of 0.3 m/s has to be maintained using a proportional weir at the outlet end of the chamber, the minimum length of the chamber (in m,in integer) to remove 0.25 mm particles completely is _________
raw_source.solution:
Minimum length of chamber
[latex]\begin{aligned} L_{\min } &=V_{\text {flow }} \times t_{d} \\ V_{\text {fow }} &=0.30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ t_{d} &=\frac{H}{V_{\text {settling }}}=\frac{0.75}{2.5 \times 10^{-2}}=30 \mathrm{sec} \\ L_{\text {min }} &=0.3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec} \times 30 \mathrm{sec} \\ &=9 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The stopping sight distance (SSD) for a level highway is 140 m for the design speed of 90 km/h. The acceleration due to gravity and deceleration rate are [latex]9.81 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s^2}[/latex] and [latex]3.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s^2}[/latex], respectively. The perception/reaction time (in s,round off to two decimal places) used in the SSD calculation is ______________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SSD} &=140 \mathrm{~m} \\ V &=90 \mathrm{kmph} \\ a &=3.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \\ \mathrm{SSD} &=V t_{R}+\frac{V^{2}}{2 g f} \\ a &=g f \\ 140 &=\left(\frac{5}{18} \times 90 \times t_{R}\right)+\frac{\left(\frac{5}{18} \times 90\right)^{2}}{2 \times 3.5} \\ t_{R} &=2.028 \mathrm{~seconds} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text: For a [latex]2^{\circ} [/latex] curve on a high speed Broad Gauge (BG) rail section, the maximum sanctioned speed is 100 km/h and the equilibrium speed is 80 km/h. Consider dynamic gauge of BG rail as 1750 mm. The degree of curve is defined as the angle subtended at its center by a 30.5 m arc. The cant deficiency for the curve (in mm,round off to integer) is ________________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Length of curve }&=\text { Radius } \times \text { Degree of curve }\\ \frac{30.5 \times 180}{2^{\circ} \times \pi}&=R\\ R &=873.76 \mathrm{~m} \\ C_{d} &=C_{t h}-C_{a c t} \\ C_{\mathrm{act}} &=\frac{G V^{2}}{127 R}=\frac{1750 \times 100^{2}}{127 \times 873.76}=157.70 \mathrm{~mm} \\ C_{\mathrm{ev}} &=\frac{G V^{2}}{127 R}=\frac{1750 \times 80^{2}}{127 \times 873.76}=100.930 \mathrm{~mm} \\ C_{\mathrm{def}} &=C_{\mathrm{act}}-C_{t h}=157.70-100.930=56.77 \mathrm{~mm} \\ &=57 \mathrm{~mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following expression:
[latex]z=\sin(y+it)+\cos(y-it)[/latex]
where [latex]z, y,[/latex] and [latex]t[/latex] are variables, and [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex] is a complex number. The partial differential equation derived from the above expression is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
z&=\sin(y+it)+ \cos (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}&=\cos (y+it)-\sin (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 y^2}&=-\sin(y+it)- \cos (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 y^2}&=-z \;\;...(i)\\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}&=i \cos (y+it)+i\sin (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 t^2}&=+\sin(y+it)+ \cos (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 t^2}&=z\;\;...(ii)\\
&\text{Adding (i) and (ii)}\\
&\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 y^2}+\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 t^2}=0
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_answer.option_text: an ordinary differential equation of order 3 and degree 2.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following recursive iteration scheme for different values of variable P with the initial guess [latex]x_1=1[/latex]:
[latex]x_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left ( x_n+\frac{P}{x_n} \right ),\;\;\;n=1,2,3,4,5[/latex]
For [latex]P=2,x_5[/latex] is obtained to be 1.414, rounded-off to three decimal places. For [latex]P=3,x_5[/latex] is obtained to be 1.732, rounded-off to three decimal places.
If [latex]P=10[/latex], the numerical value of [latex]x_5[/latex] is _________ . (round off to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]x_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left ( x_n+\frac{P}{x_n} \right )[/latex]
Converges when [latex]x_{n+1}=x_{n}=\alpha[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \alpha &=\frac{1}{2}\left ( \alpha+\frac{P}{\alpha} \right )\\ \frac{\alpha}{2}&=\frac{P}{2\alpha}\\ \alpha&=\sqrt{P} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When [latex]P=2, x_5=\sqrt{2}=1.4124[/latex]
When [latex]P=3, x_5=\sqrt{3}=1.732[/latex]
When [latex]P=10, x_5=\sqrt{10}=3.162[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The Fourier cosine series of a function is given by:
[latex]f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }f_n\cos nx[/latex]
For [latex]f(x)=\cos ^4x[/latex], the numerical value of [latex]f_4+f_5[/latex] is ______ . (round off to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]
\begin{aligned}
\cos ^4 x&=\cos ^2 x\cos ^2 x\\
&=\left ( \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2} \right )\left ( \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2} \right )\\
&=\frac{1}{4}(1+2 \cos 2x+ \cos ^2 2x)\\
&=\frac{1}{4}(1+2 \cos 2x+ \frac{(1+\cos 4x)}{2})\\
&=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\cos 2x}{2}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\cos 4x}{8}\\
&=\frac{3}{8}+\frac{\cos 2x}{2}+\frac{\cos 4x}{8}\\
f_4&=\frac{1}{8}=0.125\\
f_5&=0\\
\rightarrow f_4+f_5&=0.125
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following expression:
[latex]z=\sin(y+it)+\cos(y-it)[/latex]
where [latex]z, y,[/latex] and [latex]t[/latex] are variables, and [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex] is a complex number. The partial differential equation derived from the above expression is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
z&=\sin(y+it)+ \cos (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}&=\cos (y+it)-\sin (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 y^2}&=-\sin(y+it)- \cos (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 y^2}&=-z \;\;...(i)\\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial t}&=i \cos (y+it)+i\sin (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 t^2}&=+\sin(y+it)+ \cos (y-it)\\
\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 t^2}&=z\;\;...(ii)\\
&\text{Adding (i) and (ii)}\\
&\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 y^2}+\frac{\partial ^2 z}{\partial ^2 t^2}=0
\end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider the following recursive iteration scheme for different values of variable P with the initial guess [latex]x_1=1[/latex]:
[latex]x_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left ( x_n+\frac{P}{x_n} \right ),\;\;\;n=1,2,3,4,5[/latex]
For [latex]P=2,x_5[/latex] is obtained to be 1.414, rounded-off to three decimal places. For [latex]P=3,x_5[/latex] is obtained to be 1.732, rounded-off to three decimal places.

raw_source.solution:

Converges when [latex]x_{n+1}=x_{n}=\alpha[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \alpha &=\frac{1}{2}\left ( \alpha+\frac{P}{\alpha} \right )\\ \frac{\alpha}{2}&=\frac{P}{2\alpha}\\ \alpha&=\sqrt{P} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When [latex]P=2, x_5=\sqrt{2}=1.4124[/latex]

The Fourier cosine series of a function is given by:
[latex]f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }f_n\cos nx[/latex]
For [latex]f(x)=\cos ^4x[/latex], the numerical value of [latex]f_4+f_5[/latex] is ______ . (round off to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]
\begin{aligned}
\cos ^4 x&=\cos ^2 x\cos ^2 x\\
&=\left ( \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2} \right )\left ( \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2} \right )\\
&=\frac{1}{4}(1+2 \cos 2x+ \cos ^2 2x)\\
&=\frac{1}{4}(1+2 \cos 2x+ \frac{(1+\cos 4x)}{2})\\
&=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\cos 2x}{2}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\cos 4x}{8}\\
&=\frac{3}{8}+\frac{\cos 2x}{2}+\frac{\cos 4x}{8}\\
f_4&=\frac{1}{8}=0.125\\
f_5&=0\\
\rightarrow f_4+f_5&=0.125
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A weld is used for joining an angle section ISA 100 mm x 100 mm x 10 mm to a gusset plate of thickness 15 mm to transmit a tensile load. The permissible stress in the angle is 150 MPa and the permissible shear stress on the section through the throat of the fillet weld is 108 MPa. The location of the centroid of the angle is represented by [latex]C_{yy}[/latex] in the figure, where [latex]C_{yy}=28.4mm[/latex]. The area of cross-section of the angle is 1903 [latex]mm^2[/latex]. Assuming the effective throat thickness of the weld to be 0.7 times the given weld size, the lengths [latex]L_1[/latex] and [latex]L_2[/latex] (rounded- off to the nearest integer) of the weld required to transmit a load equal to the full strength of the tension member are, respectively
raw_source.solution:
As per IS:800-2007 Clause no. 11.2.1
Full strength of tension member,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P&=\sigma _{at} \times A_g\\ P&=150 \times 1903\\ P&=285450N \end{aligned}[/latex]
Weld strength of [latex]L_1[/latex],
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_1&=L_1\times (0.7 \times s) \times 108\\ P_1&=L_1\times (0.7 \times 5) \times 108\\ P_1&=378L_1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Weld strength of [latex]L_2[/latex],
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_2&=L_2\times (0.7 \times s) \times 108\\ P_2&=L_2\times (0.7 \times 5) \times 108\\ P_2&=378L_2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying moment CG equal to zero,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_1 \times 28.4 &=P_2 \times (100-28.4)\\ \frac{P_1}{P_2}&=\frac{71.6}{28.4}\\ \frac{L_1 \times 378}{L_2 \times 378}&=\frac{71.6}{28.4}=2.521\\ L_1&=2.521L_2\\ \text{Total weld strength}&=\text{Tensile strength}\\ (L_1+L_2) \times 3.5 \times 108&=285450\\ L_1+L_2&=755.158\\ 2.521L_2+L_2&=755.152\\ L_2&=214.472mm\\ L_1&=540.685mm\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider the differential equation
[latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=4(x+2)-y[/latex]
For the initial condition [latex]y = 3[/latex] at [latex]x = 1[/latex], the value of [latex]y[/latex] at [latex]x = 1.4[/latex] obtained using Euler's method with a step-size of 0.2 is _________. (round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_0&=1\rightarrow y_0=3\\ x_1&=1.2\rightarrow y_1=?\\ x_2&=1.4\rightarrow y_2=?\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using Euler's forward methods
[latex]\begin{aligned} y_n&=y_n+hf(x_n,y_n)\\ y_1&=y_0+hf(x_0,y_0)\\ &=3+0.2 \times (4(1+2)-3)\\ &=4.8\\ y_2&=y_1+hf(x_1,y_1)\\ &=4.8+0.2 \times (4(1.2+2)-4.8)\\ &=6.4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Depth of water flowing in a 3 m wide rectangular channel is 2 m. The channel carries a discharge of 12 [latex]m^3/s [/latex]. Take g = 9.8 [latex]m/s ^2[/latex].
The bed width (in m) at contraction, which just causes the critical flow, is _________ without changing the upstream water level. (round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]B = 3m, y = 2m, Q = 12 m^3 /sec[/latex]
[latex] Velocity(v)=\frac{Q}{A} =\frac{12}{2 \times 3}=2m/sec [/latex]

Specific energy at section (1-1)
[latex]E=y+\frac{v^2}{2g}=2+\frac{2^2}{2 \times 9.8}=\frac{108}{49}m[/latex]
When channel section is contracted to minimum width and for constant discharge Q, the flow over contracted section will be critical flow and under the assumption that no energy loss has taken place.
[latex]E=E_c=\frac{108}{49}[/latex]
We have that, [latex]E_c=\frac{3}{2}y_c[/latex] (for rectangular crosssection)
[latex]y_c=\frac{2}{3}E_c=\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{108}{49}=\frac{72}{49}[/latex]
For critical flow condition,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{Q^2T}{gA^3}&=1\\ \frac{Q^2B_{min}}{g(B_{min} \times y_c)^3}&=1\\ (B_{min})^2&=\frac{Q^2}{gy_c^3}\\ B_{min}&=\left ( \frac{(12)^2}{9.8 \times \left ( \frac{72}{49} \right )^3} \right )^{1/2}\\ &=2.152m \end{aligned} [/latex]

A water treatment plant has a sedimentation basin of depth 3 m, width 5 m, and length 40 m. The water inflow rate is 500 [latex]m^3/h [/latex]. The removal fraction of particles having a settling velocity of 1.0 m/h is_______. (round off to one decimal place)
(Consider the particle density as 2650 [latex]kg/m^3 [/latex] and liquid density as 991 [latex]kg/m^3 [/latex])
[latex]P[/latex] and [latex]Q[/latex] are two square matrices of the same order. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
If P and Q are invertible then [latex](PQ)^{-1} = Q^{-1}P^{-1}[/latex] is correct. Let,
[latex] \begin{aligned} PQ&=C \\ P^{-1}PQ&=P^{-1}C \\ Q&=P^{-1} C\\ Q^{-1}Q&=Q^{-1}P^{-1}C \\ I&=Q^{-1}P^{-1}C \\ IC^{-1}&=Q^{-1}P^{-1}CC^{-1} \\ C^{-1}&= Q^{-1}P^{-1}\\ (PQ)^{-1}&= Q^{-1}P^{-1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence, proved. Similarly, we can prove if P, Q are invertible then [latex](QP)^{-1}= P^{-1}Q^{-1} [/latex]
options: If P and Q are invertible, then [latex][PQ]^{-1}=Q^{-1}P^{-1}[/latex]
If P and Q are invertible, then [latex][QP]^{-1}=P^{-1}Q^{-1}[/latex]
If P and Q are invertible, then [latex][PQ]^{-1}=Q^{-1}P^{-1}[/latex]
If P and Q are not invertible, then [latex][PQ]^{-1}=P^{-1}Q^{-1}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
At a traffic intersection, cars and buses arrive randomly according to independent
Poisson processes at an average rate of 4 vehicles per hour and 2 vehicles per
hour, respectively. The probability of observing at least 2 vehicles in 30 minutes
is ______. (round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
\lambda _C&=4 \; vehical/hr=2 \; vehical /30 \;min\\
\lambda _C&=2 \; vehical/hr=1 \; vehical /30 \;min\\
\lambda _{Vehical}&=3 \; vehical/30 \;min\\
P(x \lt  2)&=1-P(x\leq 1)\\
&=1-[P(x=0)+P(x=1)]\\
&=1-\left [ \frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^0}{0!} +\frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^1}{1!}\right ]\\
&=1-e^{-3}(1+3)\\
&=1-\frac{4}{e^3}\\
&=0.8
\end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Read the following statements relating to flexure of reinforced concrete beams:

I. In over-reinforced sections, the failure strain in concrete reaches earlier than the yield strain in steel.
II. In under-reinforced sections, steel reaches yielding at a load lower than the load at which the concrete reaches failure strain.
III. Over-reinforced beams are recommended in practice as compared to the under-reinforced beams.
IV. In balanced sections, the concrete reaches failure strain earlier than the yield strain in tensile steel.

Each of the above statements is either True or False.
Which one of the following combinations is correct?
raw_source.solution:
The question is based on LSM design principle as it is describing different conditions related to strain
Depending on amount of reinforcement in a cross- section, here ca be three types of sections viz. balanced, under reinforced and over reinforced.
Balanced section is a section that is expected to result in a balanced failure. It means at the ultimate limit state in flexure, the concrete will attain a limiting compressive strain of 0.0035 and steel will attain minimum specified tensile strain of [latex]0.002+\frac{0.87f_y}{E_s}[/latex]
Under reinforced section is a section in which steel yield before collapse. Over reinforced section is a section in which crushing of concrete in compression i.e. attainment of compressive strain of 0.0035 occurs prior to yielding of steel.
In case of over reinforced section the deflection, crack width remain relatively low and failure occurs without any sign of warning and hence over reinforced flexural members are not recommended by IS code.
Based on the above information:
Statement I is true.
Statement II is true.
Statement III is false.
Statement IV is false.

To design an optimum municipal solid waste collection route, which of the

following is/are NOT desired:
raw_source.solution:
Some heuristic guidelines that should be taken into consideration when laying out routes are as follows :
1. Existing policies and regulations related to such items as the point of collection and frequency of collection must be identified.
2. Existing system characteristics such as crew size and vehicle types must be coordinated.
3. Wherever possible, routes should be laid out so that they begin and end near arterial streets, using topographical and physical barriers as route boundaries.
4. In hilly area, routes should start at the top of the grade and proceed downhill as the vehicle becomes loaded.
5. Routes should be laid out so that the last container to be collected on the route is located nearest to the disposal site.
6. Waste generated at traffic-congested locations should be collected as early in the day as possible.
7. Sources at which extremely large quantities of waste are generated should be serviced during the first part of the days.
8. Scattered pickup points (where small quantities of solid waste are generated) that receive the same collection frequency should, if possible, be serviced during one trip or on the same day.
options: Collection vehicle should not travel twice down the same street in a day.
Waste collection on congested roads should not occur during rush hours in morning or evening.
Collection should occur in the uphill direction.
The last collection point on a route should be as close as possible to the waste disposal facility.

option_texts: Collection should occur in the uphill direction.

Let us assume k'=2k and m'=m/2, here k' and m' represent the stiffness and mass of the modified system respectively.
[latex] \omega '=\sqrt{\frac{k'}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2k}{\left ( \frac{m}{2} \right )}}=\sqrt{\frac{4k}{m}}=2\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=2\omega \;\;\; \left ( \because \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\right )[/latex]
[latex] T'=\frac{2\pi}{\omega '}=\frac{2 \pi}{2\omega }=\frac{1}{2}\left ( \frac{2 \pi}{\omega } \right )=\frac{T}{2} \;\;\left ( T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega } \right )[/latex]
[latex] \omega '[/latex] and [latex]T' [/latex] are natural frequency and natural period of the modified system.
hence, the natural frequency of the modified system is doubled and natural period is halved compared to the original given system. Hence option (A) is correct.

tendons and the modular ratio to be 6. The average loss of prestress, due to
elastic deformation of concrete, considering all three tendons is
raw_source.solution:
This is a question of calculation of elastic shortening loss in post tensioned member.
Given data,
length = 15 m
b x D = 450 mm x 450 mm
Numberof tendons = 3
Cross-section area of each tendon [latex] (A_s)=200 mm^2[/latex].
Prestress = 1500 MPa
Modular ratio (m) = 6

From the given data, eccentricity (e) = 450/2-125 = 100 mm
Force in each cable [latex](P) = 1500 \times 200 \times 10^{-3} = 300 kN[/latex]
The tendons are tensioned one after another, and hence when tendon (1) is pulled no loss in tenson (1)
When tendon (2) is pulled, loss in tendon (1) but no loss in tendon (2).
When tendon (3) is pulled, loss in tendon (1) and (2), but no loss in tendon (3).
Hence, there will be 2 times losses in tendon (1), time loss in tendon (1) and no loss in tendon (3).
While calculating elastic shortening loss, self weight of the structure is neglected to be on the conservative side.
Consider tensioning of tendon-1
No loss in tendon (1)
Consider tensioning of tendon-2

Stress in concrete at the level of prestressing tendon
[latex]\begin{aligned} f_c&= \frac{P}{A}+\frac{Pe}{I}\\ e&=\frac{300 \times 10^3}{450 \times 450}+\frac{300 \times 10^3 \times 100 \times 100}{\frac{450 \times 450^3}{12}} \\ &= 2.36MPa \end{aligned} [/latex]

I = moment of inertial of the section about the centroidal axis.
As the tendons are horizontal and at the same level [latex]f_{c,avg} = f_c[/latex].
Loss due to elastic deformation [latex]= mfc = 6 \times 2.36 = 14.16 MPa.[/latex]
Considering tensioning of tendon 3
Loss due to elastic deformation in (1) [latex]= mfc = 6 \times 2.36 = 14.16 MPa.[/latex]
Loss due to elastic deformation in (2) [latex]= mfc = 6 \times 2.36 = 14.16 MPa.[/latex]
Total loss in tendon (1) = 2 x 14.16 = 28.32 MPa
Total loss in tendon (1) = 2 x 14.16 = 28.32 MPa
In tendon (2) = 14.16 MPa
In tendon (3) = 0
Average loss of pre-stress, considering all three tendons is [latex] =\frac{28.32+14.16+0}{3}=14.16MPa[/latex]

Let vector

A group of total 16 piles are arranged in a square grid format. The center-to- center spacing (s) between adjacent piles is 3 m. The diameter (d) and length of embedment of each pile are 1 m and 20 m, respectively. The design capacity of each pile is 1000 kN in the vertical downward direction. The pile group efficiency ( [latex]\eta _g[/latex]) is given by
[latex]\eta _g=1-\frac{\theta }{90}\left [ \frac{(n-1)m+(m-1)n}{mn} \right ][/latex]
where m and n are number of rows and columns in the plan grid of pile arrangement, and [latex]\theta =\tan ^{-1}\left ( \frac{d}{s} \right )[/latex].
The design value of the pile group capacity (in kN) in the vertical downward direction is __________________. (round off to the nearest integer)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
\eta _g&=1-\frac{\theta }{90}\left \{ \frac{m(n-1)+n(m-1)}{mn} \right \} \\
\theta &=\tan ^{-1}\left ( \frac{d}{s} \right )=\tan ^{-1}\left ( \frac{1}{3} \right )=18.43^{\circ}\\
\eta _g&=\frac{Q_{ug}}{nQ_{up}}\\
Q_{ug}&=\left [ 1-\frac{18.43}{90}\left \{ \frac{4(4-1)+4(4-1)}{4 \times 4} \right \} \right ](16 \times 1000)\\
&=11085kN
\end{aligned} [/latex]

Construction of a building caused an additional total vertical stress of 100 kPa at P. When the vertical effective stress at P is 175 kPa, the percentage of consolidation in the clay layer at P is _____________. (in integer)
raw_source.solution:

[latex]\sigma _{P_1}'=150-25=125kPa [/latex]
After construction,

Percentage of consolidation when vertical effective stress is at P is 175 kPa.
[latex]=\frac{175-125}{225-125} \times 100=\frac{50}{100} \times 100=50 [/latex]

A hydraulic jump takes place in a 6 m wide rectangular channel at a point where
the upstream depth is 0.5 m (just before the jump). If the discharge in the
channel is 30 [latex]m^3/s[/latex] and the energy loss in the jump is 1.6 m, then the Froude
number computed at the end of the jump is ___________. (round off to two
decimal places)
(Consider the acceleration due to gravity as 10 [latex]m/s^2[/latex].)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]Q=30m^3/sec [/latex]
[latex]B=6m [/latex]
[latex]y_1=0.5m [/latex]
[latex]E_L=1.6m [/latex]
[latex]q= \frac{Q}{B} =\frac{30}{6}=5m^3/sec/m [/latex]
We know that,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_L=\frac{(y_2-y_1)^3}{4y_1y_2}&=1.6m\\ \frac{(y_2-0.5)^3}{4 \times 0.5 \times y_2}&=1.6\\ y_2^3-1.5y_2^2+0.75y_2-0.125&=3.2y_2\\ y_2=2.5m,-0.0527m,&-0.0947m \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, [latex] y_2=2.5m[/latex]
Post jump Froude's No.
[latex](F_2)=\frac{V_2}{\sqrt{\sqrt{gy_2}}}=\frac{\left ( \frac{30}{6 \times 2.5} \right )}{\sqrt{10 \times 2.5}}=0.4 [/latex]
[latex] [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A pump with an efficiency of 80% is used to draw groundwater from a well for irrigating a flat field of area 108 hectares. The base period and delta for paddy crop on this field are 120 days and 144 cm, respectively. Water application efficiency in the field is 80%. The lowest level of water in the well is 10 m below the ground. The minimum required horse power (h.p.) of the pump is ________. (round off to two decimal places)
(Consider 1 h.p. = 746 W; unit weight of water = 9810 [latex]N/m^3[/latex])
raw_source.solution:
Base period (B) = 120 days
[latex]\begin{aligned} Delta (\Delta )&=144 cm=1.44m\\ Duty(D)&=\frac{8.64B}{\Delta }=\frac{8.64 \times 120}{1.44}\\ D&=720\frac{hec}{cumec}\\ Q&=\frac{Area}{D}=\frac{108}{720}=\frac{3}{20}m^3/s\\ Q_{applied}&=\frac{Q}{\eta _a}=\frac{3}{20 \times 0.8}=\frac{3}{16}\\ \text{Power required}&=\frac{mgh}{t}\\ &=\rho _w \times \left ( \frac{volume}{t} \right )g \times h\\ &=\rho _w Qgh=\gamma Qh\\ &=9810 \times \frac{3}{16} \times 10\\ &=\frac{73575}{4}watt \end{aligned} [/latex]
Horse power of pump [latex]= \frac{\text{Power required}}{746 \times \text{efficiency}}=\frac{73575}{4 \times 746 \times 0.8}=30.82hp [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two discrete spherical particles (P and Q) of equal mass density are independently released in water. Particle P and particle Q have diameters of 0.5 mm and 1.0 mm, respectively. Assume Stokes' law is valid.
The drag force on particle Q will be________ times the drag force on particle P. (round off to the nearest integer)
raw_source.solution:
In case of discrete particle settling and Stoke's law valid, at terminal velocity, since there is no change in velocity, the net force on the body is zero. Hence,


[latex]F_D=\left ( \frac{\pi}{6}D^3\rho _sg-\frac{\pi}{6}D^3\rho _sg \right )=\frac{\pi}{6}gD^3(\rho _s-\rho _f) [/latex]
For density of medium [latex](\rho _f) [/latex] and mass density of sphere [latex](\rho _s) [/latex] constant,
Drag force [latex](F_D)\propto D^3 [/latex]
For particle P, diameter [latex](D_P)=0.5 mm [/latex]
For particle Q, diameter [latex](D_Q)=1 mm [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{(F_D)_Q}{(F_D)_P}=\frac{(D_Q)^3}{(D_P)^3}=\left ( \frac{1}{0.5} \right )^3=8 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow (F_D)_Q=8 \times (F_D)P[/latex]

Consider the polynomial [latex]f(x)=x^3-6x^2+11x-6[/latex] on the domain S given by [latex]1 \leq x \leq 3[/latex]. The first and second derivatives are [latex]f'(x)[/latex] and [latex]f''(x)[/latex].

II. There exists one local maxima of [latex]f(x)[/latex] within the domain S.
III. The second derivative [latex]f''(x) \gt 0[/latex] throughout the domain S.

raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^3-6x^2+11x-6 \\ f(1)&=1-6+11-6=0 \\ f(3)&=3^3-6 \times 3^2+11 \times 3-6=0 \\ &\text{Statement (I) is correct.} \\ f'(x)&=3x^2-12x+11 \\ f'(x)&=0\Rightarrow x=2\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] f(x)[/latex] has local maxima at [latex] x=2-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=6x-12\\ f''(x) &\gt 0\\ 6x-12 &\gt 0\\ x & \gt 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Statement (III) is incorrect statement (IV) is also correct.
[latex]\because x=2+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} [/latex] is point of minima.

[latex] \begin{aligned} M M X & =\lambda M X \\ M^{2} X & =\lambda(\lambda X) \\ M^{2} X & =\lambda^{2} X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[\lambda^{2}\right.[/latex] (non negative) is eigen value of [latex]\left.\mathrm{M}^{2}\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M X & =\lambda X \\ M^{\top} X & =\lambda X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[M, M^{\top}\right.[/latex] have same eigen values]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & M M^{\top} X=\lambda M X \\ & M M^{\top} X=\lambda(\lambda X) \\ & M M^{\top} X=\lambda^{2} X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[\lambda^{2}\right.[/latex] (none negative) is eigen value of [latex]\left.M M^{\top}\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M X & =\lambda X \\ M^{\top} X & =\lambda X \\ M^{\top} M X & =\lambda M X \\ M^{\top} M X & =\lambda(\lambda X) \\ M^{\top} M X & =\lambda^{2} X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[\lambda^{2}\right.[/latex] (non negative) is eigen value of [latex]\left.M^{\top} M\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M X & =\lambda X \\ M M X & =\lambda M X \\ M^{2} X & =\lambda(\lambda X) (M^T)^2 X&= \lambda ^2 X \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\left[\because M, M^{\top}\right.[/latex] have same eigen value]
[latex] \left(M^{\top}\right)^{2} X=\lambda^{2} X [/latex]
[ [latex]\lambda^{2}[/latex] is eigen value of [latex]\left(M^{\top}\right)^{2}[/latex] which non negative] Hence, option A, B, C, D are correct.

raw_source.text:
The following function is defined over the interval [latex][-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{L}][/latex] :

[latex] f(x)=p x^{4}+q x^{5} [/latex]

If it is expressed as a Fourier series,

[latex] f(x)=a_{0}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left\{a_{n} \sin \left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)+b_{n} \cos \left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)\right\} \text {, } [/latex]

which options amongst the following are true?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x) & =p x^{4}+q x^{5} \\ b_{n} & =\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} f(x) \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x\\ & =\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell}\left(p x^{4}+q x^{5}\right) \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x \\ & =\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} \mathrm{p}\left(\mathrm{x}^{4}\right) \cos \frac{\mathrm{n} \pi \mathrm{x}}{\ell} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \left(\because q x^{5} \frac{\cos n \pi x}{\ell} \text { is odd function }\right) \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, [latex]b_{n}[/latex] depends on [latex]p[/latex].
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{n}= & \frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} f(x) \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x \\ a_{n}= & \frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell}\left(p x^{4}+q x^{5}\right) \sin \frac{n \pi x}{\ell} d x \\ a_{n}= & 0+\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} q x^{5} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x \\ & \left(\because p x^{4} \frac{\sin n \pi x}{\ell}\right. \text { is odd function) } \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, [latex]a_{n}[/latex] depends on [latex]p[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for
the Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF) in the context of
Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) management?
raw_source.solution:
(A) is false. The Higher Heating Value (HHV) of Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF) processed from Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) is typically higher than the HHV of unprocessed MSW. This is because RDF processing removes non-combustible materials from MSW and concentrates the combustible fraction.

(B) is true. RDF can be produced in various forms including pellets, fluff, and powdered form. The form of RDF depends on the specific process and intended end use.

(C) is partially true. RDF processing typically removes a significant portion of the inorganic fraction of MSW, but not all of it. The remaining inorganic fraction is typically mixed with the RDF product.

(D) is false. RDF can be used as a fuel in a variety of combustion systems, including those that burn oil. In fact, RDF is often used as a supplemental fuel in cement kilns and other industrial processes that also use oil as a fuel.
options:
Higher Heating Value (HHV) of the unprocessed
MSW is higher than the HHV of RDF processed
from the same MSW.
RDF can be made in the powdered form

Inorganic fraction of MSW is mostly converted
to RDF.
RDF cannot be used in conjunction with oil.

raw_source.text: The probabilities of occurrences of two independent events [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are [latex]0.5[/latex] and [latex]0.8[/latex], respectively. What is the probability of occurrence of at least [latex]A[/latex] or [latex]B[/latex] (rounded off to one decimal place)?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} & P(A)=0.5 \\ & P(B)=0.8 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Probability of occurence of atleast [latex]A[/latex] or [latex]B=[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} P(A \cap B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B) \\ & =0.5+0.8-P(A) \times P(B) \\ & =0.5+0.8-0.5 \times 0.8 \\ & =1.3-0.4 \\ & =0.9 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: In the differential equation [latex]\frac{d y}{d x}+a x y=0[/latex], [latex]a[/latex] is positive constant. If [latex]y=1.0[/latex] at [latex]x=0.0[/latex], and [latex]y=0.8[/latex] at [latex]x=1.0[/latex], the value of [latex]a[/latex] is ___ (rounded off to three decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x}+\alpha x y & =0 \\ \frac{d y}{d x} & =-\alpha x y \\ \frac{d y}{y} & =-\alpha x d x \\ \frac{d y}{y} & =-\alpha \int x d x+C \\ \text { In } y & =-\frac{\alpha x^{2}}{2}+C \\ \text { Put } y&=1 \text { at } =0 \\ \ln 1 & =0+C \\ C & =0 \\ \ln y & =-\frac{\alpha x^{2}}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Put [latex]y=0.8[/latex] at [latex]x=1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \ln (0.8) & =-\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ \alpha & =-2 \ln (0.8) \\ \alpha & =0.4462 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A canal supplies water to an area growing wheat over 100 hectares. [latex]{Area}(A)=100[/latex] ha
Total duration of irrigation [latex]=120[/latex] days
Total depth of water required [latex]=35 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]

Intense irrigation [latex](A)[/latex]
Time [latex]\left(B_{A}\right)=30[/latex] days
Depth of water [latex]\left(\Delta_{A}\right)=12 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]{Duty}\left(D_{A}\right)=\frac{8.64 B_{A}}{\Delta_{A}} [/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{8.64 \times 30}{0.12} [/latex]
[latex]D_{A}=2160 \mathrm{ha} / \text { cumec } [/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} & Q_{A}=\frac{A}{D_{A}} \\ & Q_{A}=\frac{100}{2160}=0.0463 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Depth of water [latex]\left(\Delta_{\mathrm{B}}\right)=23 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}=0.0296 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a doubly reinforced RCC beam with the option of using either Fe250 plain bars or Fe500 deformed bars in the compression zone. The modulus of elasticity of steel is [latex]2 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex]. As per IS456-2000, in which type(s) of the bars, the stress in the compression steel [latex]\left(f_{s c}\right)[/latex] can reach the design strength [latex]\left(0.87 f_{y}\right)[/latex] at the limit state of collapse?
raw_source.solution:
In a doubly reinforced beam, at the limit state of collapse. The strain in the extreme corression fibre will be [latex]0.0035[/latex]. As the compression reinforcement will be below this, the strain in if will be always less than [latex]0.0035[/latex].
For Fe250, the yield strain
[latex]=\frac{0.87 \times 250}{2 \times 10^{5}}=0.0010875 [/latex]

For Fe500, the yield strain
[latex]\begin{aligned} & =0.002+\frac{0.87 \mathrm{f}_{y}}{E_{s}} \\ & =0.002+\frac{0.87 \times 500}{2 \times 10^{5}} \\ & =0.004175>0.0035 \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, it is possible that [latex]\mathrm{Fe} 250[/latex] can reach upto its yield strain and hence can reach the design strength [latex]0.87 \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{y}}[/latex].
options:
Both Fe250 plain bars and Fe500 deformed
bars

Neither Fe250 plain bars nor Fe500 deformed
bars

raw_source.text: Consider the pin-jointed truss shown in the figure (not to scale). All members have the same axial rigidity, [latex]\mathrm{AE}[/latex]. Members [latex]\mathrm{QR}, \mathrm{RS}[/latex], and [latex]\mathrm{ST}[/latex] have the same length L. Angles OBT, RCT, SDT are all [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex]. Angles BQT, CRT, DST are all [latex]30^{\circ}[/latex]. The joint [latex]T[/latex] carries a vertical load [latex]P[/latex]. The vertical deflection of joint [latex]T[/latex] is [latex]k \frac{P L}{A E}[/latex]. What is the value of [latex]k[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
Considering joint [latex]T[/latex],

[latex]\sum F_{y}=0, \quad F_{Q T} \sin 60^{\circ}=P[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{QT}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\sqrt{3}}[/latex]
[latex]\sum \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{X}}=0, \mathrm{~F}_{\mathrm{BT}}=-\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{QT}} \cos 60^{\circ}=-\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Strain energy [latex](U)=\left(\frac{P^{2} L}{2 A E}\right)_{Q T}+\left(\frac{P^{2} L}{2 A E}\right)_{B T}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2}(3 \mathrm{~L})}{2 \mathrm{AE}}+\frac{\left(-\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{2}\right)}{2 \mathrm{AE}} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{2 P^{2} \times L}{A E}+\frac{P^{2} \times L}{4 A E} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{8 P^{2} L+P^{2} L}{4 A E}=\frac{9 P^{2} L}{4 A E}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Vertical deflection of joint [latex]T[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{\partial \mathrm{U}}{\partial \mathrm{P}}=\frac{18 \mathrm{PL}}{4 \mathrm{AE}}=4.5 \frac{\mathrm{PL}}{\mathrm{AE}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{K}=4.5[/latex]

Consider that a force [latex]P[/latex] is acting on the surface of a half-space (Boussingesq's problem). The expression for the vertical stress [latex]\left(\sigma_{z}\right)[/latex] at any point [latex](r, z)[/latex] with the half-space is given as,

where, [latex]r[/latex] is the radial distance, and [latex]z[/latex] is the depth with downward direction taken as positive. At any given [latex]r[/latex], there is a variation of [latex]\sigma_{z}[/latex] along [latex]z[/latex], and at a specific [latex]z[/latex], the value of [latex]\sigma_{z}[/latex] will be maximum. Considering that the groundwater table is located at the base of the footing, the unit weights of soil above and below the groundwater table are [latex]18 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] and [latex]20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex], respectively, and the bearing capacity factor [latex]N_{q}[/latex] is 58 , the net ultimate baring capacity of the soil is estimated as [latex]1706 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] (unit weight of water [latex]10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] ).
Earlier, a plate load test was carried out with a circular place of [latex]30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] diameter in the same foundation pit during a dry season, when the water table was located beyond the plate influence zone. Using Terzaghi's bearing capacity formulation, what is the ultimate bearing capacity (in [latex]\mathrm{kPa}_{-}[/latex]of the plate ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{nu}}=1706 \mathrm{kPa}, \quad \gamma_{\mathrm{w}}=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Plate load test data:
dia. (d) [latex]=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] with no water able effect.
[latex]\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{u} \text { plate }}=\text { ? } [/latex]

For footing :
[latex]\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{nu}}=1706 \mathrm{kPa} \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{nu}}=0+\mathrm{q}\left(\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{q}}-1\right)+0.4 \mathrm{~B} \gamma \mathrm{N}_{\gamma} \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{nu}}=18 \times 1 \times(58-1 \times)+0.4 \times 2.5 \times(20-10 \times) \times \mathrm{N}_{\gamma} \\ & \mathrm{N}_{\gamma}=\frac{(1706-18 \times 57)}{(0.4 \times 2.5 \times 10)} \Rightarrow \mathrm{N}_{\gamma}=68 \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\text {yplage }}=0.3 \times \mathrm{d} \times \gamma_{\mathrm{t}} \times \mathrm{N}_{\gamma} \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\text {uplate }}=0.3 \times 0.3 \times 18 \times 68 \\ &=110.16 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A very wide rectangular channel carries a discharge (Q) of [latex]70 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}[/latex] per meter width. Its bed slope changes from [latex]0.0001[/latex] to [latex]0.0009[/latex] at a point [latex]P[/latex], as shown in the figure (not to scale). The Manning's roughness coefficient of the channel is [latex]0.01[/latex]. What water surface profile(s) exist(s) near the point [latex]P[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\eta=0.01[/latex]
Critical depth, [latex]y_{C}=\left(\frac{q^{3}}{g}\right)^{1 / 3}=\left(\frac{70^{2}}{9.81}\right)^{1 / 3}=7.934 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
For normal depth of flow for wide rectangular channel.
For bed slope [latex](0.001)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q & =\left(\frac{1}{\eta} R^{2 / 3} \sqrt{S}\right) \times A \\ R & =\frac{A}{P}=\frac{\beta y}{B+2 y}=y \\ Q & =\frac{1}{n}(y)^{2 / 3} \sqrt{S} \times B y \\ q & =\frac{1}{n} y^{5 / 3} \sqrt{S} \\ y_{1} & =\left(\frac{q n}{\sqrt{S}}\right)^{3 / 5}\left(\frac{70 \times 0.01}{\sqrt{0.0001}}\right)^{3 / 5} \\ & =12.796 \mathrm{~m} \gt y_{c} \text { (Mild slope) } \\ y_{2} & =6.619 \mathrm{~m} \lt y_{c} \text { (Steep slope) } \end{aligned} [/latex]
The profile would be [latex]\mathrm{M}_{2}[/latex] and [latex]S_{2}[/latex].

raw_source.text: A jet of water having a velocity of [latex]20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex] strikes a series of plats fixed radially on a wheel revolving in the same direction a the jet at [latex]15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]. What is the percentage efficiency of the plates ? (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given water jet velocity [latex]\left(V_{1}\right)=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
Wheel velocity [latex](u)=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]

[latex]F_{x}=\rho A V_{1}\left(V_{1}-u\right)[/latex]
[latex]\%[/latex] efficiency of the plates
[latex]\begin{aligned} & =\frac{F_{x} u \times 100}{\frac{1}{2} \rho Q V_{1}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{P \times Q\left(V_{1}-u\right) u \times 100}{\frac{1}{2} \rho Q V_{1}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{2\left(V_{1}-u\right) u \times 100}{V_{1}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{2(20-15) \times 15}{20^{2}} \times 100 \\ & =37.5 \% \end{aligned} [/latex]
