Which of the following options match the test reporting conventions with the given material tests in the table?
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Test reporting convention} & \text{Material test} \\ \hline \text{(P) Reported as ratio} & \text{(I) Solubility of bitumen} \\ \hline \text{(Q) Reported as percentage} & \text{(II) Softening point of bitumen }\\ \hline \text{(R) Reported in temperature} & \text{(III) Los Angeles abrasion test} \\ \hline \text{(S) Reported in length} & \text{(IV) Flash point of bitumen} \\ \hline & \text{(V) Ductility of bitumen} \\ \hline & \text{(VI) Specific gravity of bitumen} \\ \hline & \text{(VII) Thin film oven test} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
(I) Solubility of bitumen: It is defined as weight of bitumen soluble in [latex]100 \mathrm{ml}[/latex] of carbon disulphide.
(II) Softening point of bitumen: It is the temperature at which bitumen attains a particular degree of softneess.
(III) Los angles abrasion test: It is reported as percentage of material finer than [latex]1.7 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex] with respect to total weight.
(IV) Flash point of bitumen: It is the lowest temperature at which bitumen catch five momentarily.
(V) Ductility of bitumen: Ductility is measured by stretching a standard briquette of bitumen. The distance in [latex]\mathrm{cm}[/latex] that the briquette can be stretched before breaking is the ductility.
(VI) Specific gravity of bitumen: It is the ratio of unit weight of bitumen to unit weight of water.
(VII) Thin film oven test: It measure mass charge a sample as a percent of initial mass.

raw_source.text:
The differential equation,

[latex]\frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dt}}+2 \mathrm{tu}^{2}=1 [/latex]

is solved by employing a backward differnce scheme within the finite difference framework. The value of [latex]u[/latex] at the [latex](n-1)^{\text {th }}[/latex] time-step, for some [latex]n[/latex], is 1.75. The corresponding time [latex](\mathrm{t})[/latex] is [latex]3.14 \mathrm{~s}[/latex]. Each time step is [latex]0.01 \mathrm{~s}[/latex] long. Then, the value of [latex](u_{n}-u_{n-1})[/latex] is ____ (round off to three decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d u}{d t} & =1-2 t u^{2} \\ \frac{d u}{d t} & =f(t, u) \\ \Rightarrow \quad f(t, u) & =1-2 \mathrm{tu}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Eulers backward difference scheme
[latex]\begin{aligned} u_{n}-u_{n-1} & =h f\left(t_{n}, u_{n}\right)=h\left(1-2 t_{n} u n^{2}\right) \\ & =0.01\left(1-2 \times 3.14 \times 1.75^{2}\right) \\ & =-0.1822 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The infinitesimal element shown in the figure (not to scale) represents the state of stress at a point in a body. What is the magnitude of the maximum principal stress (in [latex]\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex], in integer) at the point?
raw_source.solution:
On plane [latex]x^{\prime} \rightarrow \quad \sigma_{x^{\prime}}=5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex]
[latex]\tau_{x^{\prime} y^{\prime}}=4 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex]

Using transformation equations:
[latex]\begin{aligned} & \sigma_{x^{\prime}}=\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-\sigma_{y}}{2}\right) \cos 2 \theta+\tau_{x y} \sin 2 \theta \\ & 5=\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}+6}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-6}{2}\right) \cos \left(2 \times 45^{\circ}\right)+3 \sin \left(2 \times 45^{\circ}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \sigma_{x}=-2 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ & \sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-\sigma_{y}}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{x y}^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=\frac{-2+6}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{-2-6}{2}\right)^{2}+3^{2}}[/latex]
[latex]\sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=2 \pm 5[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \sigma_{\text {major }}=7 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}, \sigma_{\text {minor }}=-3 \mathrm{MPa}[/latex]
Hence, magnitude of maximum principal stress is [latex]7 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}[/latex].

raw_source.text: The cross-section of a girder is shown in the figure (not to scale). The section is symmetric about a vertical axis [latex](Y-Y)[/latex]. The moment of inertia of the section about the horizontal axis [latex](X-X)[/latex] passing through the centroid is _____ [latex]\mathrm{cm}^{4}[/latex] (round off to nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
As section is symmetric about given [latex]y-y [/latex]axis, hence centroid will lie on this axis.
To calculate location of C.G. from reference axis (bottom horizontal line); [latex]\bar{y}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{y}=\frac{A_{1} \bar{y}_{1}+A_{2} \bar{y}_{2}}{A_{1}+A_{2}}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{y}=\frac{(40 \times 10) \times 55+(20 \times 50) \times(25)}{40 \times 10+20 \times 50}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{y}=33.5714 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] (from bottom)
MOI of section about [latex]x x[/latex] (centroidal horizontal axis)
[latex]I=I_{I, x x}+I_{I I, x x}[/latex]
[latex]I_{1, x x}=\frac{b_{1} d_{1}^{3}}{12}+\left(b_{1} d_{1}\right) \times d^{2}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_{1, x x}=\frac{40 \times 10^{3}}{12}+(40 \times 10)(55-33.57)^{2} \\ & \mathrm{I}_{1, x x}=187031.29 \mathrm{~cm}^{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{d}^{\prime}=\overline{\mathrm{y}}-25[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{d}^{\prime}=8.5714 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{II}, x x}=\frac{\mathrm{b}_{2} \mathrm{~d}_{2}^{3}}{12}+\left(\mathrm{b}_{2} \times \mathrm{d}_{2}\right) \times \mathrm{d}^{\prime 2}[/latex]
[latex]I_{I I, x x}=\frac{20 \times 50^{3}}{12}+(20 \times 50) \times(8.57)^{2}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{II}, \mathrm{xx}}=281778.23 \mathrm{~cm}^{4}[/latex]

Hence, MOI of whole section
[latex]\mathrm{I}_{x \mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{I}, x \mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Il}, \mathrm{xx}}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{I}_{x x}=468809.52 \mathrm{~cm}^{4}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A soil having the average properties, bulk unit weight [latex]=19 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]; angle of internal friction [latex]=25^{\circ}[/latex] and cohesion [latex]=15 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex], is being formed on a rock slope existing at an inclination of [latex]35^{\circ}[/latex] with the horizontal. The critical height (in [latex]\mathrm{m}[/latex] ) of the soil formation up to which it would be stable without any failure is _____ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\quad \gamma_{\mathrm{t}}=19 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
[latex]\phi=25^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex]C= 15 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
[latex]\beta=35^{\circ}[/latex]
For [latex]\mathrm{C}-\phi[/latex] soil
[latex]\mathrm{FOS}=\frac{\mathrm{C}+\gamma_{\mathrm{t}} z \cos ^{2} \beta \tan \phi}{\gamma_{\mathrm{t}} z \cos \beta \sin \beta}[/latex]

For critical height FOS=1
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { FOS } & =\frac{\mathrm{C}+\gamma_{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{z} \cos ^{2} \beta \tan \phi}{\gamma_{\mathrm{t}} \mathrm{zcos} \beta \sin \beta}=1 \\ & =19 \times \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}} \times \cos 35^{\circ} \sin 35^{\circ} \\ & =15+19 \times \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}} \times \cos ^{2} 35 \tan 25 \\ \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}} & =5.03 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A smooth vertical retaining wall supporting layered soils is shown in figure. According to Rankine's earth pressure theory, the lateral active earth pressure acting at the base of the wall is ____ [latex]\mathrm{kPa}[/latex] (round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a} 2}=\frac{1-\sin 25^{\circ}}{1+\sin 25^{\circ}}[/latex]
Active earth pressure at the base of the wall.
[latex]\begin{aligned} &(\mathrm{Pa})_{\text {Base }}=\mathrm{Ka}_{2}\left(\mathrm{q}+\gamma_{1} \mathrm{z}_{1}+\gamma_{2} \mathrm{z}_{2}\right)-2 \mathrm{C} \sqrt{\mathrm{Ka}_{2}} \\ &=0.405+8(20+18 \times 3+19 \times 4)-2 \times 20 \times \sqrt{0.4058} \\ &= 35.39 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A vertical trench is excavated in a clayey soil deposit having a surcharge load of [latex]30 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]. A fluid of unit weight [latex]12 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] is poured in the trench to prevent collapse as the excavation proceeds. Assume that the fluid is not seeping through the soil deposit. If the undrained cohesion of the clay deposit is [latex]20 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] and saturated unit weight is [latex]18 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex], what is the maximum depth of unsupported excavation (in [latex]\mathrm{m}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) ? ____
raw_source.solution:
We know, [latex]\alpha=45+\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{2}[/latex] here [latex]\mathrm{Q}=0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Failure plane is at [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex]
It is said that there is no seepage hence no flow of fluid. But considering the fluid is there in the pores.
Also, considering given [latex]\gamma_{\text {sat }}[/latex] is the value for given fluid.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \gamma_{\text {sub }} & =\gamma_{\text {sat }}-\gamma_{\text {fluid }} \\ & =18-12 \\ & =6 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, equating the forces on the considered failure plane. As it is clay [latex]\mathrm{Q}=0, \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{a}}=1[/latex].
[latex]\therefore \quad \frac{1}{2} \times x \times x \times 1 \times \gamma_{\text {sub }} \times \sin 45^{\circ}+30 \times x \sin 45^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex]=C \times x \sqrt{2}[/latex]
[latex]3 x=10[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad x=3.33 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]


Solving with lateral earth pressure approach.
[latex]\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}}=1 [/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} & P=\sigma_{v} K_{a}-2 C \sqrt{K_{a}} \\ & P=\left(30+\gamma_{\text {sub }} z\right) \times 1-2 C \times \sqrt{1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When [latex]\mathrm{P}=0[/latex],
[latex]30+6 z-2 \times 20=0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad 6 z=10[/latex]
[latex] z=\frac{10}{6}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Unsupported excavation [latex]=2 \times \frac{10}{6}=3.33 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 12-hour storm occurs over a catchment and results in a direct runoff depth of [latex]100 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]. The time-distribution of the rainfall intensity is shown in the figure (not to scale). The [latex]\phi[/latex]-index of the storm is (in [latex]\mathrm{mm}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places)_____
raw_source.solution:
[latex]D=12[/latex] hrs.
Direct runoff [latex](R)=100 \mathrm{~mm}=10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{P}=[/latex] total rainfall
[latex]P=[/latex] Area under above diagram
[latex]P=\frac{1}{2} \times(12+2) \times 20[/latex]
[latex]=14 \times 10=140 \mathrm{~mm}=14 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
Total Infiltration [latex]=[/latex] Total rainfall [latex]-[/latex] runoff
[latex]=140-100=40 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
Assuming infiltration rate as [latex]x\; \mathrm{ mm} / \mathrm{hr}[/latex].

[latex]\frac{x}{y_{1}}=\frac{20}{4}[/latex]
[latex]y_{1}=\frac{x}{5}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} & y_{2}=\frac{x}{y_{2}}=\frac{20}{6} \\ & y_{2}=\frac{3 x}{10} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Total Infiltration
= Area under rainfall intensity duration curve Area of same curve below [latex]\phi[/latex]-index line.
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{x}{5} \times x+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3 x}{10} \times x+\left(12-\frac{5 x}{10}\right) \times x=40[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{10}+\frac{3 x^{2}}{20}+12 x-\frac{5 x^{2}}{10}=40[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow-\frac{5 x^{2}}{20}+12 x=40[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{x}^{2}-48 \mathrm{x}+160=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{x}=3.6[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{x}=44.39[/latex] [Discarded]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \phi=3.6 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{hr}[/latex].

raw_source.text: A hydraulic jump occurs in a [latex]1.0 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] wide horizontal, frictionless, rectangular channel, with a pre-jump depth of [latex]0.2 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] and a post-jump depth of [latex]1.0 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]. The value of [latex]g[/latex] may be taken as [latex]10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}[/latex]. The values of the specific force at the pre-jump and post-jump sections are same and are equal to (in [latex]\mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) ____
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned} & B=1.0 \mathrm{~m} \\ & y_{1}=0.2 \mathrm{~m} \\ & y_{2}=1.0 \mathrm{~m} \\ & g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The value of specific force
[latex]\begin{aligned} & =\frac{\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{M}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}}=\text { constant } \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{P}_{1}+\mathrm{M}_{1}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{2}+\mathrm{M}_{2}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{w}}} \\ & =A \overline{\mathrm{y}}_{1}+\frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2}}{\mathrm{Ag}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

For horizontal, frictionless rectangular channel
[latex]\therefore \quad \frac{2 q^{2}}{g}=y_{1} y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right) [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q & =\sqrt{\frac{1 \times 0.2 \times(1.2) \times 10}{2}} \quad(B=1 \mathrm{~m}) \\ & =1.095 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m} \\ Q & =1.095 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, specific force [latex]=0.2 \times 1 \times \frac{0.2}{2}+\frac{1.095^{2}}{1 \times 0.2 \times 10} =(0.62) \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In Horton's equation fitted to the infiltration data for a soil, the initial infiltration capacity is [latex]10 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{h}[/latex]; final infiltration capacity is [latex]5 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{h}[/latex]; and the exponential decay constant is [latex]0.5 \mathrm{~h}[/latex]. Assuming that the infiltration takes place at capacity rates, the total infiltration depth (in [latex]\mathrm{mm}[/latex] ) from a uniform storm of duration [latex]12 \mathrm{~h}[/latex] is ____. (round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f_{0} & =10 \text { meter } \\ f_{C} & =5 \text { meter } \\ K & =0.5 h r^{-1} \\ f & =f_{c}+\left(f_{0}-f_{c}\right) e^{-k t} \\ f & =5+5 e^{-0.5 \times t} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At capacity rates i.e. [latex]t \rightarrow \infty[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} f & =5+5 e^{-0.5 \times \infty} \\ & =5 \text { meters } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Infiltration in [latex]12 \mathrm{hr} .=5 \times 12=60 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
If above is not the case :
then
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Infiltration } & =\int \mathrm{fdt} \\ & =\int_{0}^{12} 5+5 \mathrm{e}^{-0.5 \mathrm{t}} \mathrm{dt} \\ & =5 \times(\mathrm{t})_{0}^{12}+\left.\frac{5}{-0.5} \mathrm{e}^{-0.5 \mathrm{t}}\right|_{0} ^{2} \\ & =60+10\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5 \times 12}\right) \\ & =69.975 \mathrm{~mm}=70 \mathrm{~mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The composition and energy content of a representative solid waste sample are given in the table. If the moisture content of the waste is [latex]26 \%[/latex], the energy content of the solid waste on dry-weight basis is _____ [latex]\mathrm{MJ} / \mathrm{kg}[/latex] (round off to one decimal place).
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline Component & \text{Percent} & \text{Energy} \\ & \text{by mass} & \text{content} \\ & & \text{as-discarded} \\ & &\text{basis} \\& & (\mathbf{M J} / \mathbf{k g}) \\ \hline Food \; waste & 20 & 4.5 \\ \hline Paper & 45 & 16.0 \\ \hline Cardboard & 5 & 14.0 \\ \hline Plastics & 10 & 32.0 \\ \hline Others & 20 & 8.0 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

A flocculator tank has a volume of [latex]2800 \mathrm{~m}^{3}[/latex]. The temperature of water in the tank is [latex]15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex], and the average velocity gradient maintained in the tank is [latex]100 / \mathrm{s}[/latex]. The temperature of water is reduced to [latex]5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex], but all other operating conditions including the power input are maintained as the same. The decrease in the average velocity gradient (in %) due to the reduction in water temperature is ____ (round off to nearest integer).
[Consider dynamic viscosity of water at [latex]15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and [latex]5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] as [latex]1.139 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex] and [latex]1.518 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex], respectively]
raw_source.solution:
Given,
Volume of flocculation tank [latex](V)=2800 \mathrm{~m}^{3}[/latex]
At [latex]\mathrm{T}=15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{G}_{15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}=100 / \mathrm{s}, \\ & \eta_{15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}=1.139 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At [latex]\mathrm{T}=5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{G}_{5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}=? \\ & \mu_{5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}=1.518 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\because[/latex] Temporal mean velocity gradient,
[latex] G=\sqrt{\frac{P}{\mu V}}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{P}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{V}[/latex] are constant.
So, [latex]\quad G^{2} \mu=[/latex] constant
[latex]100^{2} \times 1.139 \times 10^{-3}=G_{5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}^{2} \times 1.518 \times 10^{-3}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{G}_{5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}=86.62 \mathrm{sec}^{-1}[/latex]
The decrease in velocity gradient
[latex]\begin{aligned} & =\frac{G_{15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}-\mathrm{G}_{5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}}{\mathrm{G}_{15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}} \times 100 \\ & =13.38 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A vertical sheet pile wall is installed in an anisotropic soil having coefficient of horizontal permeability, [latex]k_{H}[/latex] and coefficient of vertical permeability, [latex]k_{V}[/latex]. In order to draw the flow net for the isotropic condition, the embedment depth of the wall should be scaled by a factor of _____, without changing the horizontal scale.
raw_source.solution:
We know that, for 2D flow.
[latex] \mathrm{K}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}} \frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{dx}}+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}} \frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{dz}}=0 [/latex]
When [latex]\mathrm{K}_{1}=\mathrm{K}_{\text {horizontal }}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{K}_{2}=\mathrm{K}_{\text {vertical }}[/latex] as shown in figure.
[latex] \frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{~h}}{\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}}} \partial \mathrm{x}^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{~h}}{\partial \mathrm{z}^{2}}=0 [/latex]
From the above equation we can note that, when soil is anisotropic with respect to permeability i.e. [latex]k_{x}=k_{z}[/latex], the flow and equipotential line are not necessarily to be orthogonal as because [latex]\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}}}=1[/latex], and we cannot get the actual form of Laplace equation which is [latex]\frac{\partial^{2} h}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} h}{\partial z^{2}}=0[/latex].
But if we replace
[latex] x_{t}=x \sqrt{\frac{K_{z}}{\mathrm{~K}_{x}}} [/latex]
Then, [latex]\quad \partial x_{t}^{2}=\partial x^{2} \frac{K_{z}}{\mathrm{~K}_{x}}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial^{2} h}{\partial x_{t}^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} h}{\partial z^{2}}=0 [/latex]
Thus, new flow line and equipotential lines are drawn on transformed section with [latex]\mathrm{x}[/latex]-distance changed to [latex]x \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}}}}[/latex] while keeping the vertical dimension constant.
If we scale up the depth by keeping the horizontal distance same the depth will be scaled by factor [latex]\sqrt{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}} / \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}}}[/latex].

[latex]\lambda=0,1,3[/latex]

raw_source.text: With regard to the shear design of RCC beams, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Option A is true, because when the area of shear reinforcement is large i.e. in case of excessive shear reinforcement, concrete becomes stronger is diagonal tension on failure compared to diagonal compression failure and compression failure may occur before the shear reinforcement has yielded.
Option '[latex]B[/latex]' is true because for beams without shear reinforcement, once the flexural crack crosses the longitudinal reinforcement, the propagation of crack will be sudden and there can be brittle failure.
Option '[latex]C[/latex]' is not true, as main reinforcement increases the shear resitance by providing dowel action, limiting crack width and by increasing the depth of concrete. Design shear strength of concrete is a function of grade of concree and percentage tensile reinforcement.
Option 'D' is true, as for beams with varying depth, nominal shear stress,
[latex]\tau_{v}=\frac{V_{u} \pm \frac{M_{u} \tan \beta}{d}}{b d}([/latex] clause 40.1.1, IS456: 2000)
it is dependent on both the design shear force and design bending moment.
Hence, options (A), (B) and (D) are true.
options: Excessive shear reinforcement can lead to compression failure in concrete
Beams without shear reinforcement, even if adequately designed for flexure, can have brittle failure
The main (longitudinal) reinforcement plays no role in the shear resistance of beam
As per IS456:2000, the nominal shear stress in the beams of varying depth depends on both the design shear force as well as the design bending moment

raw_source.text: As per the Indian Roads Congress guidelines (IRC 86: 2018), extra widening depends on which of the following parameters?
raw_source.solution:
As per IRC [latex]86: 2018[/latex] Clause 8.6 Widening of Carriageway on Curves:
At sharp horizontal curves, it is necessary to widen the carriageway to provide for safe passage of vehicles. The widening required has two components: (i) mechanical widening to components for the extra width occupied by a vehicle on the curve due to tracking of the rare wheels, and (ii) psychological widening to permit easy crossing of vehicles since vehicles in a lane tend to wander more on a curve than on a straight reach.
On two-lane or wider roads, it is necessary that both the above components should be fully catered for so that the lateral clearance between vehicles of curves is maintained equal to the clearance available on straight. Position of single-lane roads however is somewhat different.
Since during crossing maneuvers outer wheels of vehicles have in any case to use the shoulder whether on the straight or on the curve. It is, therefore sufficient on single lane roads if only the mechanical component of widening is taken into account.
Based on the above considerations, the extra width of carriageway to be provided at horizontal curves on single and two-lane roads is given in Table For multi-lane roads, the pavement widening may be calculated by adding half the widening for two-lane roads to each lane.
Table : Extra width of Pavement at Horizontal Curves

raw_source.text: The steady-state temperature distribution in a square plate [latex]A B C D[/latex] is governed by the 2-dimensional Laplace equation. The side [latex]A B[/latex] is kept at a temperature of [latex]100{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and the other three sides are kept at a temperature of [latex]0{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Ignoring the effect of discontinuities in the boundary conditions at the corners, the steady-state temperature at the center of the plate is obtained as  [latex]T_0 ^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Due to symmetry, the steady-state temperature at the center will be same [latex]\left(\mathrm{T_0}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)[/latex], when any one side of the square is kept at a temperature of [latex]100{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and the remaining three sides are kept at a temperature of [latex]0{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Using the principle of superposition, the value of [latex]T_0[/latex] is ___ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
We know, Laplace equation in two dimensional on a unit square with Dirichlet boundary condition :
[latex] \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial y^{2}}=0, \quad 0 \lt (x, y) \lt 1 [/latex]
This Laplace equation is called harmonic function. Solution of Laplace equation,
[latex]u(x, y)=\left(C_{1} \cos \beta x+C_{2} \sin \beta x\right)\left(C_{3} e^{\text {By }}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right)[/latex]
Let square [latex]A B C D[/latex] is unit square.
Now, given
[latex] \begin{aligned} & u(x, 0)=0 \\ & u(0, y)=0 \\ & u(1, y)=0 \\ & u(x, 1)=100 \end{aligned} [/latex]

For [latex]u(x, 0)=0[/latex]
[latex]\quad 0=\left(C_{1} \cos \beta x+0\right)(C_3+C_4)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{C}_{3}=-\mathrm{C}_{4}[/latex]

For [latex]u(0, y)=0[/latex];
[latex]0=\left(C_{1}+0\right)\left(C_{3} e^{\beta y}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{C}_{1}=0[/latex]

Now,
[latex] \begin{aligned} u(x, y) & =0+C_{2} \sin \beta x\left(C_{3} e^{\beta y}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right) \\ & =a_{x} \sin \beta x\left(e^{\beta y}-e^{-\beta y}\right) \quad ...(1) \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\left[\because \mathrm{C}_{3}=-\mathrm{C}_{4}\right.[/latex] and Let [latex]\left.\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{3}=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{x}}\right][/latex]

For [latex]u(1, y)=0[/latex]
[latex] 0=a_{x} \sin \beta x\left(e^{\beta y}-e^{\beta y}\right) [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \beta=\mathrm{n} \pi[/latex]

For [latex]u(x, 1)=100[/latex]
[latex]a_{x} \sin n\pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)=100[/latex]
[latex] a_{x}=\frac{100}{\sin n\pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)} [/latex]

From eqn. (1), we get
[latex] \begin{gathered} u(x, y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\sin n \pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n\pi}\right)} \times \sin n\pi x\left(e^{n \pi y}-e^{- n\pi y}\right) \\ =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)}\left[e^{n\pi y}-e^{-n\pi y}\right] \end{gathered} [/latex]
Now, at mid point [latex](x, y)=\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)[/latex]
[latex] u\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)=T_{0} \text { [given] } [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_0&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{n\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi}\right)}\left[\mathrm{e}^{n\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi / 2}\right] \\ &=100\left [ \left ( \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi / 2}}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}} \right ) +\left ( \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}}{\mathrm{e}^{2\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi}} \right )+...\right ]\\ &=100\left [ \frac{1}{(\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi / 2})}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{3\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-3\pi / 2}} +...(neglect) \right ]\\ &=100[0.199+0.043+0.008]\\ &\approx 25^{\circ}C \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: An unconfined compression strength test was conducted on a cohesive soil. The test specimen failed at an axial stress of [latex]76 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]. The undrained cohesion (in [latex]\mathrm{kPa}[/latex], in integer) of the soil is ___
raw_source.solution:
UCS Test :
[latex]\sigma_{3}=0[/latex] [Cell pressure]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Axial stress [latex]=[/latex] Deviatoric stress [latex]=\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{1}[/latex]
Given, [latex]\sigma_{1}=76 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
We know,
[latex]\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45^{\circ}+\frac{\phi}{2}\right)+2 C \tan \left(45^{\circ}+\frac{\phi}{2}\right)[/latex]
[latex][\mathrm{C}=[/latex] Undrained cohesion, [latex]\phi=0[/latex] (Cohesive soil)]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \sigma_{1}=2 \mathrm{C}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad 76=2 \mathrm{C}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad C=38 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]

The absolute pressure at [latex]X[/latex] is [latex]\mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex] (round off to one decimal place).

raw_source.text:
The solution of the differential equation.

[latex] \frac{d^{3} y}{d x^{3}}-5.5 \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+9.5 \frac{d y}{d x}-5 y=0 [/latex]

is expressed as [latex]y=C_{1} e^{2.5 x}+C_{2} e^{\alpha . x}+C_{3} e^{\beta x}[/latex], where [latex]\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \mathrm{C}_{3}[/latex] and [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] are constants, with [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] being distinct and not equal to 2.5. which of the following options is correct for the values of [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
The differential eqn. can be written as :
[latex] D^{3}-5.5 D^{2}+9.5 D-5=0 [/latex]
Solving we get,
[latex] D=1,2,2.5 [/latex]
Hence, the solution is given as
[latex] y=C_{1} e^{2.5 x}+C_{2} e^{1 x}+C_{3} e^{2 x} [/latex]
Comparing we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \alpha=1 \\ & \beta=2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, option (A) is correct.

raw_source.text: Two vectors [latex]\left[\begin{array}{llll}2 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right]^{\top}[/latex] and [latex]\left[\begin{array}{llll}1 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right]^{\top}[/latex] belong to the null space of a [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] matrix of rank 2 . Which one of the following vectors also belongs to the null space?

Given matrix is [latex]4 \times 4 [/latex] and rank of matrix is 2 .
Therefore, rank of matrix [latex]\neq[/latex] No. of variables Thus, there two linearly dependent vectors \& two linearly independent vectors are present.
[latex] \begin{aligned} & X_{1}=\left[\begin{array}{llll} 2 & 1 & 0 & 3 \end{array}\right]^{\top} \\ & X_{2}=\left[\begin{array}{llll} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array}\right]^{\top} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad X=\mathrm{K}_{1}\left[\begin{array}{l}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{array}\right]+\mathrm{K}_{2}\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{array}\right][/latex]
For [latex]\mathrm{K}_{1}=1 \text{ and } \mathrm{~K}_{2}=-1[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Cholesky decomposition is carried out on the following square matrix [latex][\mathrm{A}][/latex].

[latex] [A]=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 8 & -5 \\ -5 & a_{22} \end{array}\right] [/latex]

Let [latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{ij}}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{ij}}[/latex] be the [latex](i, j)^{\text {th }}[/latex] elements of matrices [latex][L][/latex] and [latex][A][/latex], respectively. If the element [latex]I_{22}[/latex] of the decomposed lower triangular matrix [latex][\mathrm{L}][/latex] is 1.968 , what is the value (rounded off to the nearest integer) of the element [latex]a_{22}[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
We know, cholesky decomposition,
[latex]A=LL^{T}[/latex]
Where, [latex]L=[/latex] lower tringular matrix
[latex]\left[\begin{array}{ll}a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}L_{11} & 0 \\ L_{21} & L_{22}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{L}_{11} & L_{21} \\ 0 & L_{22}\end{array}\right][/latex]

[latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}8 & -5 \\ -5 & \mathrm{a}_{22}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{L}_{11}^{2} & \mathrm{~L}_{11} \mathrm{~L}_{21} \\ \mathrm{~L}_{11} \mathrm{~L}_{21} & \mathrm{~L}_{21}^{2}+\mathrm{L}_{22}^{2}\end{array}\right][/latex]
On comparison on both sides,
[latex]\mathrm{L}_{11}=\sqrt{8}=2 \sqrt{2}[/latex]
[latex]and,\;\; L_{11} L_{21}=-5[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{L}_{21}=\frac{-5}{2 \sqrt{2}}[/latex]
[latex]and,\;\; a_{22}=L_{21}^{2}+L_{22}^{2}[/latex]
[latex]=\left(\frac{-5}{2 \sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+1.968^{2}[/latex]
[latex]=6.998 \approx 7[/latex]

The critical flow condition in a channel is given by ____
[Note: [latex]\alpha -[/latex] kinetic energy correction factor; [latex]Q -[/latex] discharge; [latex]A_{C} -[/latex] cross-sectional area of flow at critical flow condition; [latex]T_{C}-[/latex] top width of flow at critical flow condition; [latex]g-[/latex] acceleration due to gravity]
raw_source.solution:
Specific Energy [latex](E)=y+\frac{v^{2}}{2 g}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad E=y+\alpha \cdot \frac{Q^{2}}{2 g A^{2}}\left[\right.[/latex] as [latex]\left.\frac{Q}{A}=v\right][/latex]

For critical flow condition,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d y} & =0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d E}{d y} & =1+\frac{\alpha Q^{2}}{2 g} \frac{d}{d y}\left(A^{-2}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d E}{d y} & =1+\frac{\alpha Q^{2}}{2 g}\left(-\frac{2}{A^{3}}\right) \frac{d A}{d y} \end{aligned} [/latex]
'dA' can be written as 'Tdy' [latex]\Rightarrow \frac{d A}{d y}=T[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{dE}}{\mathrm{dy}}=1-\frac{\alpha \mathrm{Q}^{2} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{gA} \mathrm{A}^{3}}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow 1-\frac{\alpha Q^{2} \mathrm{~T}}{g A^{3}}=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\alpha Q^{2}}{g}=\frac{\mathrm{A}^{3}}{\mathrm{~T}}[/latex]

At critical flow, [latex]A=A_{C}[/latex];
[latex]\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{C}}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\alpha Q^{2}}{g}=\frac{A_{C}^{3}}{T_{C}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Match the following air pollutants with the most appropriate adverse health effects:
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \textbf{Air pollutant} & \textbf{Health effect to human and/or test animal} \\ \hline \text{(P) Aromatic hydrocarbons} & \text{(I) Reduce the capability of the blood to carry oxygen} \\ \hline \text{(Q) Carbon monoxide} & \text{(II) Bronchitis and pulmonary emphysema}\\ \hline \text{(R) Sulfur oxides}& \text{(III) Damage of chromosomes} \\ \hline \text{(S) Ozone} & \text{(IV) Carcinogenic effect} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Aromatic hydrocarbons such as 3, 4benzpyrene, other polycyclic organic compounds which are originated due to incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons are considered to be carcinogenic agents. These are responsible for cancer.
Sulphur dioxide [latex]\left(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\right)[/latex] : It is an irritant gas which effects mucous membrane when inhaled. It leads to bronchial spasms. Asthma patients are badly affected.
Carbon Monoxide (CO) : Carbon monoxide has a strong affinity for combining with the haemoglobin of the blood to form carboxyhemoglobin, [latex]\mathrm{COHb}[/latex]. This reduces the ability of the haemoglobin to carry oxygen to the body tissues. CO has about two hundred time the affinity of oxygen for attaching itself to the haemoglobin, so that low levels of CO can still result in high levels of [latex]\mathrm{COHb}[/latex]. Carbon monoxide also affects the central nervous system.
Ozone [latex]\left(\mathrm{O}_{3}\right)[/latex] can damage the tissue of the respiratory tract, causing inflammation and irritation, and result in symptoms such as coughing, chest tightness and worsening of asthma symptoms. In addition, ozone causes substantial damage to crops, forests and native plants.

raw_source.text: In the context of water and wastewater treatments, the correct statements are:
raw_source.solution:
Total dissolved solids comprise of inorganic salts, principally calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium bicarbonates, chlorides, sulfates and some small amount of organic matter that are dissolved in water.
Hardness is due to presence of multivalent cations. In most cases, it is due to the presence of soluble bicarbonates, chlorides and sulfates of calcium and magnesium.
Too much phosphorous can cause increased growth of algae and large aquatic plants. It can result in decreased levels of dissolved oxygen and the process is called 'Eutrophication'.
Ammonia creates a large chlorine demand, as the ammonia is converted to nitrogen gas and the chlorine becomes chloride during disinfection of water by chlorination.
Presence of particulate matter decreases the effectiveness of UV disinfection or chlorine disinfection by shielding the targeted microorganisms.
options: particulate matter may shield microorganisms during disinfection
phosphorous stimulates algal and aquatic growth
calcium and magnesium increase hardness and total dissolved solids

option_texts: particulate matter may shield microorganisms during disinfection
phosphorous stimulates algal and aquatic growth
calcium and magnesium increase hardness and total dissolved solids

raw_source.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for the aerobic composting of sewage sludge?
raw_source.solution:
A bulking agent (wood ships shredded leaves or types) is intended to support the structure of sludge by increasing its porosity to encourage effective aeration.

In-vessel composting systems can be divided into plug flow and agitated bed modes. In plug flow mode, the relationship between particles in the composting mass stays the same through the process and the system operates on first-in, first-out principle. In an agitated bed system, composting material is mixed mechanically during the processing.

The heat produced in aquatic composting cause any surplus moisture to be extracted as water vapour and hence no leachate is produced.

Actinomycetes are aerobic, spore forming positive bacteria. These are thermophilic species and their development depends on aerobic conditions, temperature and water content. The heat produced in aerobic composting helps support the growth of these species.

Leachate can generated from vegetable wastes.
options: Bulking agent is added during the composting process to reduce the porosity of the solid mixture
Leachate can be generated during composting
Actinomycetes are involved in the process
In-vessel composting systems cannot be operated in the plug-flow mode

option_texts: Leachate can be generated during composting
Actinomycetes are involved in the process

raw_source.text:
[latex]A 5 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] long metal rod [latex]A B[/latex] with initially at a uniform temperature of [latex]T_{0}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Thereafter, temperature at both the ends are maintained at [latex]0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Neglecting the heat transfer from the lateral surface of the rod, the heat transfer in the rod is governed by the one-dimensional diffusion equation [latex]\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=D \frac{\partial^{2} T}{\partial x^{2}}[/latex], where [latex]D[/latex] is the thermal diffusively of the metal, given as [latex]1.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} / \mathrm{s}[/latex].
The temperature distribution in the rod is obtained as
[latex]T(x, t)=\sum_{n=13,5 \ldots .}^{\infty} C_{n} \sin \frac{n \pi x}{5} e^{-\beta n^{2} t}[/latex] where [latex]x[/latex] is in [latex]\mathrm{cm}[/latex] measured from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex] with [latex]x=0[/latex] at [latex]A, t[/latex] is [latex]s, C_{n}[/latex] are constants in [latex]{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{T}[/latex] is in [latex]{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] is in [latex]\mathrm{s}^{-1}[/latex].

The value of [latex]\beta[/latex] (in [latex]\mathrm{s}^{-1}[/latex], rounded off to three decimal places) is ___
raw_source.solution:
Given: Diffusion equation:
[latex] \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=\mathrm{D} \frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{~T}}{\partial \mathrm{x}^{2}} [/latex]
And also,
[latex]D=1[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{T}(0, \mathrm{t})=0[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{T}(5,5)=0[/latex]
[latex]T(x, 0)=T_{0}[/latex]
We know, solution of equation is given by,
[latex]T(x, t)=\left(C_{1} \cos \alpha x+C_{2} \sin \alpha x\right) C_{3} e^{-\alpha^{2} t} \;\;\; ...(1)[/latex]

For [latex]\mathrm{T}(0, t)=0[/latex]
[latex]\left(C_{1}+0\right) C_{3} e^{-\alpha^{2} t}=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{1}=0[/latex]

For [latex]\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{t})=0[/latex]
[latex]\left(C_{2} \sin \alpha 5\right) C_{3} \mathrm{e}^{-25 t}=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sin 5 \alpha=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{5}[/latex]

Now, from equation (1)
[latex]T(x, t)=C_{2} C_{3} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\frac{n^{2} \pi^{2}}{25} t}[/latex]
[latex]=b_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\frac{n^{2} \pi^{2} t}{25}}[/latex]

Generalize solution
[latex]T(x, t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\frac{n^{2} \pi^{2} t}{25}}[/latex]
For [latex]\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{x}, 0)=\mathrm{T}_{0}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow T_{0}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right)[/latex]

From fourier series,
[latex]b_{n}=0[/latex] for even value of [latex]n[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \mathrm{T}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{t})=\sum_{\mathrm{n}=13,5 \ldots .}^{\infty} \mathrm{b}_{\mathrm{n}} \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi \mathrm{x}}{5}\right) \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{n}^{2} \pi^{2} \mathrm{t}}{25}}[/latex]

Given: [latex]T(x, t)=\sum_{n=13,5 \ldots .}^{\infty} C_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\beta n^{2} t}[/latex]
On comparison;
[latex]\beta=\frac{\pi^{2}}{25}=0.395 \mathrm{sec}^{-1}[/latex]

Depth of neutral axis, [latex]x_{u}=\frac{0.87 f_{y} A_{s}}{0.36 f_{c k} b}=\frac{0.87 \times 415 \times 1847.26}{0.36 \times 25 \times 300} =247.02 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A [latex]\quad  2 \mathrm{D}[/latex] thin plate with modulus of elasticity, [latex]E=1.0[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex], and Poisson's ratio, [latex]\mu=0.5[/latex], is in plane stress condition. The displacement field in the plate is given by [latex]\mu=C^{2} y[/latex] and [latex]v=0[/latex], where us and [latex]v[/latex] are displacements (in [latex]m[/latex] ) along the [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] directions, respectively, and [latex]C[/latex] is constant (in [latex]\mathrm{m}^{-2}[/latex] ). The distance [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] along [latex]X[/latex] an [latex]Y[/latex], respectively, are in [latex]\mathrm{m}[/latex]. The stress in the [latex]X[/latex] direction is [latex]\sigma_{x x}=40 x y \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex], and the shear stress is [latex]\tau_{x y}=a x^{2} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]. What is the value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] (in [latex]\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{4}[/latex], in integer) ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]
\begin{aligned}
& \epsilon_{x}=\frac{\sigma_{x}}{E}-\frac{\mu \sigma_{y}}{E} \\
& \epsilon_{y}=\frac{\sigma_{y}}{E}-\frac{\mu \sigma_{x}}{E} \\
& \tau_{x y}=\frac{\gamma_{x y}}{G_{1}} \\
& G=\frac{E}{2(1+\mu)} \\
& \epsilon_{x}+\mu \epsilon_{y}=\frac{\sigma_{x}}{E}-\frac{\mu \sigma_{y}}{E}+\frac{\mu \sigma_{y}}{E}-\frac{\mu^{2} \sigma_{x}}{E} \\
& \epsilon_{x}+\mu \epsilon_{y}=\frac{\sigma_{x}}{E}\left(1-\mu^{2}\right) \\
& \sigma_{x}=\frac{E}{1-\mu^{2}}\left[\epsilon_{x}+\mu \epsilon_{y}\right] \\
& \sigma_{x}=\frac{E}{1-\mu^{2}}\left[\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\mu \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right] \\
& \sigma_{x}=\frac{E}{1-\mu^{2}}[2(x y+0)] \\
& \sigma_{x}=\frac{2 \mathrm{ECxy}}{1-\mu^{2}} \\
& \sigma_{x}=40 x y \text { (Given) } \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{2 \mathrm{ECxy}}{1-\mu^{2}}=40 x y \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \mathrm{EC}}{1-\mu^{2}}=40 \\
& Y_{x y}=\frac{\tau_{x}}{G} \\
& G \gamma_{x y}=\tau_{x y} \\
& \frac{E}{2(1+\mu)}\left[\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\right]=\tau_{x y} \\
& \frac{E}{2(1+\mu)}\left[C^{2}+0\right]=\alpha x^{2} \\
& \alpha=\frac{C E}{2(1+\mu)} \\
& \alpha=\frac{40\left(1-\mu^{2}\right)}{2 E} \frac{E}{2(1+\mu)} \\
& \alpha=10(1-\mu)=10(1-0.5)=5
\end{aligned}
[/latex]

depth factor [latex]d_{c}, d_{v}, d_{r}=1[/latex]

[latex]i_{c} i_{q} i_{r}=1[/latex]
For [latex]\phi=0^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{c}}=5.14 \\ & N_{\mathrm{q}}=1 \\ & N_{r}=0 \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{u}}=25 \times 5.14 \times 1 \times 1 \times 1+19 \times 1 \times \\ & 1 \times 1 \times 1 \\ & =147.5 \mathrm{kPa} \\ & \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{nu}}=\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{u}}-\mathrm{rD}_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & =147.5-19 \times 1 \\ & =128.5 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]q_{n s}=\frac{q_{n u}}{F O S}=\frac{128.5}{3}=42.83 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
Hence, [latex]\frac{500}{B^{2}} \leq 42.83[/latex]
or [latex]B \geq 3.416 m[/latex]
Hence [latex]B=3.4 m[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A circular pile of diameter [latex]0.6 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] and length [latex]8 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] was constructed in a cohesive soil stratum having the following properties: bulk unit weight [latex]=[/latex] [latex]19 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]; angle of internal friction [latex]=0^{\circ}[/latex] and cohesion [latex]=25 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex].
The allowable load the pile can carry with a factor of safety of 3 is ____ [latex]\mathrm{kN}[/latex] (round off to one decimal place).
[Adopt: Adhesion factor, [latex]\alpha=1.0[/latex] and Bearing capacity factor, [latex]\left.\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{C}}=9.0\right][/latex]
raw_source.solution:
End bearing capacity
[latex] \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{pu}}=\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{u}} \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{b}} [/latex]
where, [latex]\quad C_{u}=25 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
[latex]N_{c}=9[/latex]
[latex]A_{b}=\frac{\pi}{4} \times 0.6^{2}=0.283 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{Pu}}=25 \times 9 \times 0.283[/latex] [latex]=63.62 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]

Skin friction capacity
[latex] \mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{s}}=\alpha \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{u}} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{s}} [/latex]
Where,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \alpha & =1.0 \\ \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{u}} & =25 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{s}} & =\pi \mathrm{DL}=\pi \times 0.6 \times 8 \\ & =15.08 \mathrm{~m}^{2} \\ \therefore \quad Q_{\mathrm{s}} & =1 \times 25 \times 15.08=377 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Ultimate pile capacity [latex]=63.62+377[/latex] [latex] =440.62 \mathrm{kN} [/latex]
Allowable load [latex]=\frac{440.62}{3}=146.87 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the flow setup shown in the figure (not to scale), the hydraulic conductivities of the two soil samples, Soil 1 and Soil 2, are [latex]10 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{s}[/latex] and [latex]1 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{s}[/latex], respectively. Assume the unit weight of water as [latex]10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] and ignore the velocity head. At steady state, what is the total head (in [latex]m[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) at any point located at the junction of the two samples? ____
raw_source.solution:
External pressure of [latex]10 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] can be converted to equivalent hydrostatic, head [latex]=\frac{10 \mathrm{kPa}}{10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}}=1 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
Total head at [latex]A[/latex],
[latex]\mathrm{TH}_{\mathrm{A}}=[/latex] Datum head + Pressure head
[latex]\mathrm{TH}_{\mathrm{A}}=3 \mathrm{~m}+(1 \mathrm{~m}+1 \mathrm{~m})[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{TH}_{\mathrm{A}}=5 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
Total head loss due to seepage through soil
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{L}}=5 \mathrm{~m} \\ & Q=K_{e q} \mathrm{i} A\\ & =\left(\frac{L_1+L_2}{\frac{L_1}{K_1}+\frac{L_2}{K_2}}\right) \times \frac{h_L}{L} \times \mathrm{A} \\ & =\left(\frac{1+1}{\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{1}}\right) \times \frac{5}{2} \times \mathrm{A} \\ & =4.545 \mathrm{~A} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Head loss through soil - 1 only
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{h}_{L_{1}} & =\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{K}_{1} \mathrm{~A}} \times \mathrm{L}_{1} \\ & =\frac{4.545 \mathrm{~A}}{10 \times \mathrm{A}} \times 1 \\ & =0.4545 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Total head at junction [latex]=\mathrm{TH}_{\mathrm{A}}-\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{L} 1}[/latex] [latex] =5-0.4545=4.545 \mathrm{~m} \approx 4.54 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A consolidated drained (CD) triaxial test was carried out on a sand sample with the known effective shear strength parameters, [latex]C^{\prime}=0[/latex] and [latex]\phi^{\prime}=30^{\circ}[/latex]. In the test, prior to the failure, when the sample was undergoing axial compression under constant cell pressure, the drainage valve was accidentally closed. At the failure, [latex]360 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] deviatoric stress was recorded along with [latex]70 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] pore water pressure. If the test is repeated without such error, and no back pressure is applied in either of the tests, what is the deviatoric stress (in [latex]\mathrm{kPa}[/latex], in integer) at the failure? _____
raw_source.solution:
We know that,
[latex]\bar{\sigma}_{1 F}=\bar{\sigma}_{3 \mathrm{~F}} \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right)+20 \tan \left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right)[/latex]
Assuming [latex]c^{\prime}=0[/latex] under both the conditions when drainage line in suddenly dosed.
[latex] \left(\sigma_{\mathrm{cf}}+360-70\right)=\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{cy}}-70\right) \tan ^{2} 60+0\;\;\;...(i) [/latex]
When drainage is open and assuming the confining stress [latex]\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{cf}}\right)[/latex].
[latex] \left[\left(\sigma_{\mathrm{cf}}+\sigma_{2}\right)-0\right]=\left[\sigma_{\mathrm{cf}}-0\right] \tan ^{2} 60^{\circ}+0 \;\;\;...(ii) [/latex]
From (i) and (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 290-\sigma_{2} & =-70 \times \tan ^{2} 60^{\circ} \\ 290-\sigma_{d} & =-210 \\ \sigma_{d} &=500 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

G2, G3, G4, G5

raw_source.text:
The theoretical aerobic oxidation of biomass [latex](\mathrm{C} 5 \mathrm{H} 7 \mathrm{O} 2 \mathrm{~N}[/latex] ) is given below:

[latex] \mathrm{C}_{5} \mathrm{H}_{7} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{~N}+5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 5 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{NH}_{3}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} [/latex]

The biochemical oxidation of biomass is assumed as a first-order reaction with a rate constant of [latex]0.23 / \mathrm{d}[/latex] at [latex]20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] (logarithm to base e). Neglecting the second-stage oxygen demand from its biochemical oxidation, the ratio of [latex]\mathrm{BOD} 5[/latex] at [latex]20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] to total organic carbon (TOC) of biomass is (round off to two decimal places).
[Consider the atomic weights of [latex]\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{O}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{N}[/latex] as [latex]12 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}, 1 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}, 16 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}[/latex] and [latex]14 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}[/latex], respectively]
raw_source.solution:
Calculation of [latex]B O D_{s}[/latex] :
[latex] \mathrm{C}_{5} \mathrm{H}_{7} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{~N}+5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 5 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{NH}_{3}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} [/latex]
Considering 1 mole of biomass
[latex]\mathrm{BOD}_{4}=160 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{mol}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{BOD}_{5}=\mathrm{BOD}_{4}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{k}_{0} \mathrm{t}}\right)[/latex]
[latex]=160\left(1-e^{-0.23 \times 5}\right)[/latex]
[latex]=160 \times 0.6833[/latex]
[latex]=109.34 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{mol}[/latex]

Calculation of TOC:
[latex]\mathrm{TOC}=\frac{12 \times 5}{113} \times 113=60 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{mol}[/latex]
( [latex]\because 1[/latex] mole biomass is considered)
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Required Ratio [latex]=\frac{109.34}{60}=1.82[/latex]

raw_source.text: A system of seven river segments is shown in the schematic diagram. The [latex]\mathrm{R}_{1}{ }^{\prime} \mathrm{s}, \mathrm{Q}_{1}{ }^{\prime} \mathrm{s}[/latex], and [latex]\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{i}}[/latex] 's ( [latex]\mathrm{i}=1[/latex] to 7 ) are the river segments, their corresponding flow rates, and concentrations of a conservative pollutant, respectively. Assume complete mixing at the intersections, no additional water loss or gain in the system and steady state condition. Given : [latex]\mathrm{Q}_{1}=5 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} ; \mathrm{Q}_{2}=15 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} ; \mathrm{Q}_{4}=3 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} ; \mathrm{Q}_{6}=8 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} ; C_{1}=8 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} ; C_{2}=12 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} ; C_{6}=10 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]. What is the steady state concentration in [latex]\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal place) of the pollutant in the river segment 7 ? ____
raw_source.solution:
At 1-1, for [latex]\mathrm{R}_{3}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Q}_{3} & =\mathrm{Q}_{1}+\mathrm{Q}_{2} \\ & =5+15=20 \mathrm{~m}^{2} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \mathrm{C}_{3} & =\frac{\mathrm{Q}_{1} \mathrm{C}_{1}+\mathrm{Q}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{2}}{\mathrm{Q}_{1}+\mathrm{Q}_{2}} \\ &=\frac{5 \times 8+15 \times 12}{5+15} \\ & =11 \mathrm{Kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At 2-2, For [latex]\mathrm{R}_{5}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{Q}_{5}=\mathrm{Q}_{3} \mathrm{Q}_{4}=10-3=17 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{C}_{5}=\mathrm{C}_{3}=11 \mathrm{Kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]

At 3-3 for [latex]\mathrm{R}_{7}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Q}_{7} & =\mathrm{Q}_{6}+\mathrm{Q}_{5}=17+8=25 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \mathrm{C}_{7} & =\frac{\mathrm{Q}_{6} \mathrm{C}_{6}+\mathrm{Q}_{6} \mathrm{C}_{5}}{\mathrm{Q}_{6}+\mathrm{Q}_{5}} \\ & =\frac{8 \times 10+17 \times 11}{8+17}=10.68 \mathrm{Kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Answer : [latex]10.6 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex].

raw_source.text:
For the integral

[latex] \mathrm{I}=\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{\mathrm{x}^{2}} \mathrm{dx} [/latex]

which of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]
\begin{aligned}
I & =\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^{2}} d x \\
& =2 \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x^{2}} d x \quad(\because \quad f(-x)=f(x)) \\
& =2 \lim _{t \rightarrow 0^{+}} \int_{t}^{1} \frac{d x}{x^{2}} \\
& =2 \lim _{t \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right)_{t}^{1} \\
& =-2 \lim _{t \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(1-\frac{1}{t}\right) \\
& =2 \lim _{t \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(\frac{1}{t}-1\right) \\
& =2 \lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}}\left(\frac{1}{0+h}-1\right)\\
& =2(\infty-1) \\
& =\infty \;\;\; (Divergent)
\end{aligned}
[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]M[/latex] is an arbitrary real [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix, then which of the following matrices will have non-negative eigenvalues?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] M X=\lambda X [/latex]
[latex][\lambda[/latex] is eigen value of [latex](M)][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M M X & =\lambda M X \\ M^{2} X & =\lambda(\lambda X) \\ M^{2} X & =\lambda^{2} X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[\lambda^{2}\right.[/latex] (non negative) is eigen value of [latex]\left.\mathrm{M}^{2}\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M X & =\lambda X \\ M^{\top} X & =\lambda X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[M, M^{\top}\right.[/latex] have same eigen values]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & M M^{\top} X=\lambda M X \\ & M M^{\top} X=\lambda(\lambda X) \\ & M M^{\top} X=\lambda^{2} X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[\lambda^{2}\right.[/latex] (none negative) is eigen value of [latex]\left.M M^{\top}\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M X & =\lambda X \\ M^{\top} X & =\lambda X \\ M^{\top} M X & =\lambda M X \\ M^{\top} M X & =\lambda(\lambda X) \\ M^{\top} M X & =\lambda^{2} X \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\left[\lambda^{2}\right.[/latex] (non negative) is eigen value of [latex]\left.M^{\top} M\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M X & =\lambda X \\ M M X & =\lambda M X \\ M^{2} X & =\lambda(\lambda X) (M^T)^2 X&= \lambda ^2 X \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\left[\because M, M^{\top}\right.[/latex] have same eigen value]
[latex] \left(M^{\top}\right)^{2} X=\lambda^{2} X [/latex]
[ [latex]\lambda^{2}[/latex] is eigen value of [latex]\left(M^{\top}\right)^{2}[/latex] which non negative] Hence, option A, B, C, D are correct.

raw_source.text:
The following function is defined over the interval [latex][-\mathrm{L}, \mathrm{L}][/latex] :

[latex] f(x)=p x^{4}+q x^{5} [/latex]

If it is expressed as a Fourier series,

[latex] f(x)=a_{0}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left\{a_{n} \sin \left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)+b_{n} \cos \left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)\right\} \text {, } [/latex]

which options amongst the following are true?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x) & =p x^{4}+q x^{5} \\ b_{n} & =\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} f(x) \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x\\ & =\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell}\left(p x^{4}+q x^{5}\right) \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x \\ & =\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} \mathrm{p}\left(\mathrm{x}^{4}\right) \cos \frac{\mathrm{n} \pi \mathrm{x}}{\ell} \mathrm{dx} \\ & \left(\because q x^{5} \frac{\cos n \pi x}{\ell} \text { is odd function }\right) \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, [latex]b_{n}[/latex] depends on [latex]p[/latex].
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{n}= & \frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} f(x) \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x \\ a_{n}= & \frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell}\left(p x^{4}+q x^{5}\right) \sin \frac{n \pi x}{\ell} d x \\ a_{n}= & 0+\frac{1}{\ell} \int_{-\ell}^{\ell} q x^{5} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{\ell}\right) d x \\ & \left(\because p x^{4} \frac{\sin n \pi x}{\ell}\right. \text { is odd function) } \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, [latex]a_{n}[/latex] depends on [latex]p[/latex].

raw_source.text: The probabilities of occurrences of two independent events [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are [latex]0.5[/latex] and [latex]0.8[/latex], respectively. What is the probability of occurrence of at least [latex]A[/latex] or [latex]B[/latex] (rounded off to one decimal place)?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} & P(A)=0.5 \\ & P(B)=0.8 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Probability of occurence of atleast [latex]A[/latex] or [latex]B=[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} P(A \cap B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B) \\ & =0.5+0.8-P(A) \times P(B) \\ & =0.5+0.8-0.5 \times 0.8 \\ & =1.3-0.4 \\ & =0.9 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: In the differential equation [latex]\frac{d y}{d x}+a x y=0[/latex], [latex]a[/latex] is positive constant. If [latex]y=1.0[/latex] at [latex]x=0.0[/latex], and [latex]y=0.8[/latex] at [latex]x=1.0[/latex], the value of [latex]a[/latex] is ___ (rounded off to three decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x}+\alpha x y & =0 \\ \frac{d y}{d x} & =-\alpha x y \\ \frac{d y}{y} & =-\alpha x d x \\ \frac{d y}{y} & =-\alpha \int x d x+C \\ \text { In } y & =-\frac{\alpha x^{2}}{2}+C \\ \text { Put } y&=1 \text { at } =0 \\ \ln 1 & =0+C \\ C & =0 \\ \ln y & =-\frac{\alpha x^{2}}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Put [latex]y=0.8[/latex] at [latex]x=1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \ln (0.8) & =-\frac{\alpha}{2} \\ \alpha & =-2 \ln (0.8) \\ \alpha & =0.4462 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The differential equation,

[latex]\frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dt}}+2 \mathrm{tu}^{2}=1 [/latex]

is solved by employing a backward differnce scheme within the finite difference framework. The value of [latex]u[/latex] at the [latex](n-1)^{\text {th }}[/latex] time-step, for some [latex]n[/latex], is 1.75. The corresponding time [latex](\mathrm{t})[/latex] is [latex]3.14 \mathrm{~s}[/latex]. Each time step is [latex]0.01 \mathrm{~s}[/latex] long. Then, the value of [latex](u_{n}-u_{n-1})[/latex] is ____ (round off to three decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d u}{d t} & =1-2 t u^{2} \\ \frac{d u}{d t} & =f(t, u) \\ \Rightarrow \quad f(t, u) & =1-2 \mathrm{tu}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Eulers backward difference scheme
[latex]\begin{aligned} u_{n}-u_{n-1} & =h f\left(t_{n}, u_{n}\right)=h\left(1-2 t_{n} u n^{2}\right) \\ & =0.01\left(1-2 \times 3.14 \times 1.75^{2}\right) \\ & =-0.1822 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The steady-state temperature distribution in a square plate [latex]A B C D[/latex] is governed by the 2-dimensional Laplace equation. The side [latex]A B[/latex] is kept at a temperature of [latex]100{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and the other three sides are kept at a temperature of [latex]0{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Ignoring the effect of discontinuities in the boundary conditions at the corners, the steady-state temperature at the center of the plate is obtained as  [latex]T_0 ^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Due to symmetry, the steady-state temperature at the center will be same [latex]\left(\mathrm{T_0}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)[/latex], when any one side of the square is kept at a temperature of [latex]100{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and the remaining three sides are kept at a temperature of [latex]0{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Using the principle of superposition, the value of [latex]T_0[/latex] is ___ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
We know, Laplace equation in two dimensional on a unit square with Dirichlet boundary condition :
[latex] \frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial y^{2}}=0, \quad 0 \lt (x, y) \lt 1 [/latex]
This Laplace equation is called harmonic function. Solution of Laplace equation,
[latex]u(x, y)=\left(C_{1} \cos \beta x+C_{2} \sin \beta x\right)\left(C_{3} e^{\text {By }}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right)[/latex]
Let square [latex]A B C D[/latex] is unit square.
Now, given
[latex] \begin{aligned} & u(x, 0)=0 \\ & u(0, y)=0 \\ & u(1, y)=0 \\ & u(x, 1)=100 \end{aligned} [/latex]

For [latex]u(x, 0)=0[/latex]
[latex]\quad 0=\left(C_{1} \cos \beta x+0\right)(C_3+C_4)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{C}_{3}=-\mathrm{C}_{4}[/latex]

For [latex]u(0, y)=0[/latex];
[latex]0=\left(C_{1}+0\right)\left(C_{3} e^{\beta y}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{C}_{1}=0[/latex]

Now,
[latex] \begin{aligned} u(x, y) & =0+C_{2} \sin \beta x\left(C_{3} e^{\beta y}+C_{4} e^{-\beta y}\right) \\ & =a_{x} \sin \beta x\left(e^{\beta y}-e^{-\beta y}\right) \quad ...(1) \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\left[\because \mathrm{C}_{3}=-\mathrm{C}_{4}\right.[/latex] and Let [latex]\left.\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{3}=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{x}}\right][/latex]

For [latex]u(1, y)=0[/latex]
[latex] 0=a_{x} \sin \beta x\left(e^{\beta y}-e^{\beta y}\right) [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \beta=\mathrm{n} \pi[/latex]

For [latex]u(x, 1)=100[/latex]
[latex]a_{x} \sin n\pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)=100[/latex]
[latex] a_{x}=\frac{100}{\sin n\pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)} [/latex]

From eqn. (1), we get
[latex] \begin{gathered} u(x, y)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\sin n \pi x\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n\pi}\right)} \times \sin n\pi x\left(e^{n \pi y}-e^{- n\pi y}\right) \\ =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\left(e^{n\pi}-e^{-n \pi}\right)}\left[e^{n\pi y}-e^{-n\pi y}\right] \end{gathered} [/latex]
Now, at mid point [latex](x, y)=\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)[/latex]
[latex] u\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)=T_{0} \text { [given] } [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_0&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{100}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{n\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi}\right)}\left[\mathrm{e}^{n\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi / 2}\right] \\ &=100\left [ \left ( \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi / 2}}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}} \right ) +\left ( \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}}{\mathrm{e}^{2\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi}} \right )+...\right ]\\ &=100\left [ \frac{1}{(\mathrm{e}^{\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi / 2})}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\pi}-\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{3\pi / 2}-\mathrm{e}^{-3\pi / 2}} +...(neglect) \right ]\\ &=100[0.199+0.043+0.008]\\ &\approx 25^{\circ}C \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The solution of the differential equation.

[latex] \frac{d^{3} y}{d x^{3}}-5.5 \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+9.5 \frac{d y}{d x}-5 y=0 [/latex]

is expressed as [latex]y=C_{1} e^{2.5 x}+C_{2} e^{\alpha . x}+C_{3} e^{\beta x}[/latex], where [latex]\mathrm{C}_{1}, \mathrm{C}_{2}, \mathrm{C}_{3}[/latex] and [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] are constants, with [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] being distinct and not equal to 2.5. which of the following options is correct for the values of [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
The differential eqn. can be written as :
[latex] D^{3}-5.5 D^{2}+9.5 D-5=0 [/latex]
Solving we get,
[latex] D=1,2,2.5 [/latex]
Hence, the solution is given as
[latex] y=C_{1} e^{2.5 x}+C_{2} e^{1 x}+C_{3} e^{2 x} [/latex]
Comparing we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \alpha=1 \\ & \beta=2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, option (A) is correct.

raw_source.text: Two vectors [latex]\left[\begin{array}{llll}2 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right]^{\top}[/latex] and [latex]\left[\begin{array}{llll}1 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right]^{\top}[/latex] belong to the null space of a [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] matrix of rank 2 . Which one of the following vectors also belongs to the null space?

Given matrix is [latex]4 \times 4 [/latex] and rank of matrix is 2 .

For [latex]\mathrm{K}_{1}=1 \text{ and } \mathrm{~K}_{2}=-1[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Cholesky decomposition is carried out on the following square matrix [latex][\mathrm{A}][/latex].

[latex] [A]=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 8 & -5 \\ -5 & a_{22} \end{array}\right] [/latex]

Let [latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{ij}}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{ij}}[/latex] be the [latex](i, j)^{\text {th }}[/latex] elements of matrices [latex][L][/latex] and [latex][A][/latex], respectively. If the element [latex]I_{22}[/latex] of the decomposed lower triangular matrix [latex][\mathrm{L}][/latex] is 1.968 , what is the value (rounded off to the nearest integer) of the element [latex]a_{22}[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
We know, cholesky decomposition,
[latex]A=LL^{T}[/latex]
Where, [latex]L=[/latex] lower tringular matrix
[latex]\left[\begin{array}{ll}a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}L_{11} & 0 \\ L_{21} & L_{22}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{L}_{11} & L_{21} \\ 0 & L_{22}\end{array}\right][/latex]

[latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}8 & -5 \\ -5 & \mathrm{a}_{22}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\mathrm{L}_{11}^{2} & \mathrm{~L}_{11} \mathrm{~L}_{21} \\ \mathrm{~L}_{11} \mathrm{~L}_{21} & \mathrm{~L}_{21}^{2}+\mathrm{L}_{22}^{2}\end{array}\right][/latex]
On comparison on both sides,
[latex]\mathrm{L}_{11}=\sqrt{8}=2 \sqrt{2}[/latex]
[latex]and,\;\; L_{11} L_{21}=-5[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{L}_{21}=\frac{-5}{2 \sqrt{2}}[/latex]
[latex]and,\;\; a_{22}=L_{21}^{2}+L_{22}^{2}[/latex]
[latex]=\left(\frac{-5}{2 \sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}+1.968^{2}[/latex]
[latex]=6.998 \approx 7[/latex]

raw_source.text:
[latex]A 5 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] long metal rod [latex]A B[/latex] with initially at a uniform temperature of [latex]T_{0}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Thereafter, temperature at both the ends are maintained at [latex]0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]. Neglecting the heat transfer from the lateral surface of the rod, the heat transfer in the rod is governed by the one-dimensional diffusion equation [latex]\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=D \frac{\partial^{2} T}{\partial x^{2}}[/latex], where [latex]D[/latex] is the thermal diffusively of the metal, given as [latex]1.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} / \mathrm{s}[/latex].
The temperature distribution in the rod is obtained as
[latex]T(x, t)=\sum_{n=13,5 \ldots .}^{\infty} C_{n} \sin \frac{n \pi x}{5} e^{-\beta n^{2} t}[/latex] where [latex]x[/latex] is in [latex]\mathrm{cm}[/latex] measured from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex] with [latex]x=0[/latex] at [latex]A, t[/latex] is [latex]s, C_{n}[/latex] are constants in [latex]{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{T}[/latex] is in [latex]{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] is in [latex]\mathrm{s}^{-1}[/latex].

The value of [latex]\beta[/latex] (in [latex]\mathrm{s}^{-1}[/latex], rounded off to three decimal places) is ___
raw_source.solution:
Given: Diffusion equation:
[latex] \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=\mathrm{D} \frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{~T}}{\partial \mathrm{x}^{2}} [/latex]
And also,
[latex]D=1[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{T}(0, \mathrm{t})=0[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{T}(5,5)=0[/latex]
[latex]T(x, 0)=T_{0}[/latex]
We know, solution of equation is given by,
[latex]T(x, t)=\left(C_{1} \cos \alpha x+C_{2} \sin \alpha x\right) C_{3} e^{-\alpha^{2} t} \;\;\; ...(1)[/latex]

For [latex]\mathrm{T}(0, t)=0[/latex]
[latex]\left(C_{1}+0\right) C_{3} e^{-\alpha^{2} t}=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{1}=0[/latex]

For [latex]\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{t})=0[/latex]
[latex]\left(C_{2} \sin \alpha 5\right) C_{3} \mathrm{e}^{-25 t}=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sin 5 \alpha=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{5}[/latex]

Now, from equation (1)
[latex]T(x, t)=C_{2} C_{3} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\frac{n^{2} \pi^{2}}{25} t}[/latex]
[latex]=b_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\frac{n^{2} \pi^{2} t}{25}}[/latex]

Generalize solution
[latex]T(x, t)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\frac{n^{2} \pi^{2} t}{25}}[/latex]
For [latex]\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{x}, 0)=\mathrm{T}_{0}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow T_{0}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right)[/latex]

From fourier series,
[latex]b_{n}=0[/latex] for even value of [latex]n[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \mathrm{T}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{t})=\sum_{\mathrm{n}=13,5 \ldots .}^{\infty} \mathrm{b}_{\mathrm{n}} \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi \mathrm{x}}{5}\right) \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\mathrm{n}^{2} \pi^{2} \mathrm{t}}{25}}[/latex]

Given: [latex]T(x, t)=\sum_{n=13,5 \ldots .}^{\infty} C_{n} \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\beta n^{2} t}[/latex]
On comparison;
[latex]\beta=\frac{\pi^{2}}{25}=0.395 \mathrm{sec}^{-1}[/latex]

The three-dimensional state of stress at a point is given by
[latex]\sigma=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 40 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right) \mathrm{MPa}[/latex].

A vector field [latex]\vec{p}[/latex] and a scalar field [latex] r[/latex] are given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{p} & = \left(2 x^{2}-3 x y+z^{2}\right) \hat{i}+\left(2 y^{2}-3 y z+x^{2}\right) \hat{j}+\left(2 z^{2}-3 x z+x^{2}\right) \hat{k} \\ r & =6 x^{2}+4 y^{2}-z^{2}-9 x y z-2 x y+3 x z-y z \end{aligned}[/latex]
Consider the statement [latex] P[/latex] and [latex] Q[/latex] :

[latex] P[/latex] : Curl of the gradient of the scalar field [latex] r[/latex] is a null vector.
[latex] Q[/latex] : Divergence of curl of the vector field [latex]\vec{p}[/latex] is zero.

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} r & =6 x^{2}+4 y^{2}-z^{2}-9 x y z-2 x y+3 x z-y z \\ \text { grad } r & =\hat{i} \frac{\partial r}{\partial x}+\hat{j} \frac{\partial r}{\partial y}+\hat{k} \frac{\partial r}{\partial z} \\ & =\hat{i}(12 x-9 y z-2 y+3 z)+\hat{j}(8 y-9 x z-2 x-z)+\hat{k}(-2 z-9 x y+3 x-y) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad} \vec{r})&=\vec{\nabla} \times \operatorname{grad} \vec{r} \\ & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ (12 x-9 y z-2 y+3 z) & (8 y-9 x z-2 x-z) & (-2 z-9 x y+3 x-y) \end{array}\right| \\ & =\hat{i}(-9 x-1+9 x+1)-\hat{j}(-9 y+3+9 y-3)+\hat{k}(-9 z-2+9 z+2) \\ P & =\overrightarrow{0} \text { i.e. } P=\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad} \vec{r})=\overrightarrow{0} \\ Q & =\operatorname{div}(\text { curl } \vec{P})=0 \text { (By vector identity) } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence both are true. Hence option (D).
options: Both P  and Q  are FALSE
P  is TRUE and Q  FALSE.
P  is FALSE and Q  is TRUE.
Both P  and Q  are TRUE.

raw_answer.option_text: Both P  and Q  are TRUE.

raw_source.text: For assessing the compliance with the emissions standards of incineration plants, correction needs to be applied to the measured concentrations of air pollutants. The emission standard (based on [latex] 11 \%[/latex]  Oxygen) for [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] is [latex] 50 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}[/latex] and the measured concentrations of [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] and Oxygen in flue gas are [latex] 42 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}[/latex] and [latex] 13 \%[/latex] , respectively. Assuming [latex] 21 \%[/latex]  Oxygen in air, the CORRECT statement is:
raw_source.solution:
As per [latex]\mathrm{CPCB}[/latex], oxygen correction factor is calculated as shown below-
[latex] E_{s}=\frac{\left(21-0_{s}\right) E_{m}}{21-0_{m}}[/latex]
Where
[latex] E_{s}=[/latex] Calculated emission concentration in [latex]\%[/latex] at the standard percentage oxygen concentration in %
[latex] E_{m}=[/latex] Measured emission concentration in %
[latex]\mathrm{O}_{s}=[/latex] Standard oxygen concentration in %
[latex]\mathrm{O}_{m}=[/latex] Measured oxygen concentration in %
Note: This correction is done only when measured % oxygen concentration is higher than standard % oxygen (i.e. [latex] 11 \%[/latex] )
So, [latex] E_{s}=\frac{21-11}{21-13} \times 42=52.5 \mathrm{Mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}[/latex]
Hence, no compliance, the corrected [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] emission is greater than emission standard i.e. [latex] 50 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}[/latex].
options: No compliance, as the corrected [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] emission is greater than the emission standard.
Compliance is there, as the corrected [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] emission is lesser than the emission standard
Compliance is there, as there is no need to apply the correction since Oxygen is greater than [latex] 11 \%[/latex]  and [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] emission is lesser than the emission standard.
No compliance, as the Oxygen is greater than [latex] 11 \%[/latex]  in the flue gas.

raw_answer.option_text: No compliance, as the corrected [latex]\mathrm{HCl}[/latex] emission is greater than the emission standard.

raw_source.text: The free mean speed is [latex]60 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{hr} [/latex] on a given road. The average space headway at jam density on the road is [latex]8 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]. For a linear speed density relationship the maximum flow (in veh/hr/lane) expected on the road is
raw_source.solution:
Given, Free mean speed, [latex]V_{f}=60 \mathrm{kmph} [/latex]
Speed headway, [latex]s=8 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]
At jam density, [latex]k=k_{j}=\frac{1000}{s}=\frac{1000}{8}=125 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{km} [/latex]
For linear speed density relationship,
Maximum flow, [latex] \begin{aligned} q_{\max } & =\frac{V_{f} k_{j}}{4} \\ & =\frac{60 \times 125}{4}=1875 \mathrm{veh} / \mathrm{hr} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A map is prepared with a scale of 1: 1000 and a contour interval of [latex]1 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]. If the distance between two adjacent contours on the map is [latex]10 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex], the slope of the ground between the adjacent contours is

[latex]\Rightarrow \quad [/latex] Gradient [latex]=\frac{\text { Contour Interval }}{\text { Distance between contour }} [/latex] [latex]=\frac{1000 \mathrm{~mm}}{10,000 \mathrm{~mm}} [/latex] [latex]=\frac{1}{10}=\frac{1}{10} \times 100=10 \% [/latex]

raw_source.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Shrinkage limit is defined as the maximum water content at which further reduction in water content of soil does not lead to reduction in the volume of soil as water is being just replaced by air.
Higher is the shrinkage limit lower is the compressibility (volume change).
Dilatancy correction is applied to the already corrected N-values for overburden pressure.
At large value of shearing strain, both the initially loose and initially dense sands approach a constant value of void ratio called critical void ratio.

Both loose and dense sands with different initial void ratios can attain similar void ratio at large strain during shearing.
Among the several corrections to be applied to the SPT-N value, the dilatancy correction is applied before all other corrections.
In electrical resistivity tomography, the depth of current penetration is half of the spacing between the electrodes.

raw_source.text: The return period of a large earthquake for a given region is 200 years. Assuming that earthquake occurrence follows Poisson's distribution, the probability that it will be exceeded at least once in 50 years is ______[latex]\% [/latex]. (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad \text { Risk } & =1-\left[\frac{\lambda^{r} \cdot e^{-\lambda}}{r !}\right] \\
& =1-\left[\frac{\lambda^{0} \cdot e^{-\lambda}}{0 !}\right] \\
\lambda & =n p=50 \times \frac{1}{200}=0.25 \\
\text { Now, } \quad \text { Risk } & =1-\left[e^{-0.25}\right] \\
& =0.2211 \text { or } 22.11 \%
\end{aligned}
 [/latex]
