raw_source.text:
A [latex] 2 \mathrm{~m} \times 2 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] tank of [latex] 3 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] height has inflow, outflow and stirring mechanisms. Initially, the tank was half filled with fresh water. At [latex] t=0 [/latex], an inflow of salt a solution of concentration [latex] 5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] at the rate of 2 litre/s and an outflow of the well stirred mixture at the rate of 1 litre/s are initiated. This process can be modeled using the following differential equation.
[latex]\frac{d m}{d t}+\frac{m}{6000+t}=0.01 [/latex]
where [latex] m[/latex] is the mass (grams) of salt at time [latex] t[/latex] (seconds). The mass of the salt (in grams) in the tank at [latex] 75 \%[/latex] of its capacity is ______(rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Total capacity of tank [latex] =2 \times 2 \times 3=12 \mathrm{~m}^{3}[/latex]

At [latex] 50 \%[/latex] capacity,
[latex]\text { Volume }\left(V_{50}\right)=0.5 \times 12=6 \mathrm{~m}^{3}[/latex]

At [latex] 75 \%[/latex] capacity,
[latex]\text { Volume }\left(V_{75}\right)=0.75 \times 12 \mathrm{~m}^{3}=9 \mathrm{~m}^{3}[/latex]

Now, increase in volume [latex]\Delta V=V_{75}-V_{50}=(9-6) \mathrm{m}^{3}=3 \mathrm{~m}^{3}[/latex]
Also,
[latex]\text { Inflow }(I)=2 \mathrm{l} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
Outflow [latex] (Q)=1 \mathrm{l} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]

Rate of change storage,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\Delta S}{\Delta t} & =I-Q=2-1=1 \mathrm{l} / \mathrm{s} \\ & =\frac{3000 l}{1 \mathrm{l} / \mathrm{s}}=3000 \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Now,
[latex]\frac{d m}{d t}+\frac{m}{6000+t}=0.01 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d m}{d t}+\frac{m}{6000+3000}=0.01[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d m}{d t}+\frac{m}{9000}=0.01[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d m}{0.01-\frac{m}{9000}}=d t[/latex]

Integrating both sides
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \int_{m_{0}=0}^{m} \frac{d m}{0.01-\frac{m}{9000}}=\int_{t=0}^{t=3000} d t[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\left[\ln \left(0.01-\frac{m}{9000}\right)\right]_{0}^{m}}{-\frac{1}{9000}}=(3000-0)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \ln \left(0.01-\frac{m}{9000}\right)-\ln 0.01=-\frac{1}{9000} \times 3000 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{array}{rlrl} \Rightarrow & & \ln \left(0.01-\frac{m}{9000}\right) & =-4.938 \\ \Rightarrow & 0.01-\frac{m}{9000} & =7.165 \times 10^{-3} \\ \Rightarrow & m & =25.5 \mathrm{gm} \end{array}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Precipitation and General Aspects of Hydrology

raw_source.text:
The plane truss shown in the figure has 13 joints and 22 members. The truss is made of a homogeneous, prismatic, linearly elastic material. All members have identical axial rigidity. [latex]\mathrm{A} [/latex] to [latex]\mathrm{M} [/latex] indicate the joints of the truss. The truss has pin supports at joints [latex]\mathrm{A} [/latex] and [latex]L [/latex] and roller support at joint [latex]K [/latex]. The truss is subjected to a [latex]10 \mathrm{kN} [/latex] vertically downward force at joint [latex]\mathrm{H} [/latex] and a [latex]10 \mathrm{kN} [/latex] horizontal force in the rightward direction at joint [latex]\mathrm{B} [/latex] as shown

The magnitude of the reaction (in [latex]\mathrm{kN} [/latex] ) at the pin support [latex]\mathrm{L} [/latex] is ____ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Considering left portion of section 1-1
[latex] \begin{array}{rlrl} \Sigma M_{D} & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & V_{A} \times 2-H_{A} \times 2 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & V_{A} & =H_{A} \end{array} [/latex]

Considering right portion of section 2 - 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Sigma M_{I}=0 \Rightarrow & H_{L} \times 2=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & H_{L} \times 2=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Considering left portion of section 2 - 2
[latex]\Sigma M_{I}=0 \Rightarrow V_{A} \times 6-H_{A} \times-10 \times 1=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad 6 V_{A}-2 H_{A}=10 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad V_{A}=2.5 \mathrm{kN} \quad\left[\because H_{A}=V_{A}\right] [/latex]
Now, [latex]\quad \Sigma F_{y}=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad V_{A}+V_{L}-10=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad V_{L}=7.5 \mathrm{kN} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
An inverted T-shaped concrete beam (B1) in the figure, with centroidal axis [latex]X-X [/latex] is subjected to an effective prestressing force of [latex]1000 \mathrm{kN} [/latex] acting at the bottom kern point of the beam cross-section. Also consider an identical concrete beam (B2) with the same grade of concrete but without any prestressing force.

The additional cracking moment (in [latex]\mathrm{KNm} [/latex] ) that can be carried by beam [latex]\mathrm{B} 1 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] comparison to beam B2 is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
At bottom fibre,
[latex] \frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e y_{b}}{I}-\frac{M_{c r}}{I} y_{b}=0 \;\;\;...(i) [/latex]
where
[latex] \begin{aligned} P & =\text { Prestressing force } \\ e & =\text { Eccentricity of P-force } \\ M_{c r} & =\text { cracking moment for beam B1 } \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]y_{t} [/latex] and [latex]y_{b} [/latex] are distance of top and bottom fibre from neutral axis respectively, At top fibre
[latex] \frac{P}{A}-\frac{P e y_{t}}{I}=0 [/latex]

[P-force is at kern point]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \frac{I}{A}=e y_{t} \;\;\;...(ii) [/latex]
Putting (ii) in (i)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{M_{c r}}{I} y_{b} & =\frac{P}{A}+\frac{P e y_{t}}{I} \\ \Rightarrow \quad M_{c r} & =\frac{P I}{A y_{b}}+P e \\ & =\frac{P e y_{t}}{y_{b}}+P e \\ & =\frac{P e(2 H / 3)}{(H / 3)}+P e \\ & =3 P e=3 \times 1000 \times \frac{100}{1000}=300 \mathrm{kNm} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The initial cost of an equipment is Rs. 1,00,000. Its salvage value at the end of accounting life of 5 years is Rs. 10,000. The difference in depreciation (in Rs.) computed using 'double-declining balance method' and 'straight line method' of depreciation in Year-2 is ____ (in positive integer)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Initial cost, [latex] C_{i} =\text { Rs. } 1,00,000 [/latex]
Salvage value, [latex]C_{s} =\text { Rs. } 10,000 [/latex]
Useful life, [latex] n =5 \text { years } [/latex]
Straight line method,
Depreciation, [latex] \begin{aligned} D & =\frac{C_{i}-C_{s}}{n} \\ & =\frac{10^{5}-10^{4}}{5} \\ & =\text { Rs. } 18,000 \end{aligned} [/latex]

As per double declining method,
Fixed factor, [latex]\quad [/latex] FDDB [latex]=\frac{2}{n}=\frac{2}{5}=0.4 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \text { Book value, } D_{1} & =\text { FDDB } \times C_{i}=0.4 \times 1,00,000=40,000 \text { Rs } \\ B_{1} & =\text { Rs. } 1,00,000-\text { Rs. } 40,000=\text { Rs. } 60,000 \\ D_{2} & =\text { FDDB } \times B_{1}=0.4 \times 60,000 \\ & =\text { Rs. } 24,000 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad [/latex] Difference in depreciation [latex]= \text { Rs. } 24,000- \text { Rs. } 18,000 =\text { Rs. } 6000 [/latex]

raw_source.text: A slab panel with an effective depth of [latex]250 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex] is reinforced with [latex]0.2 \% [/latex] main reinforcement using [latex]8 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex] diameter steel bars. The uniform center-to-center spacing (in [latex]\mathrm{mm} [/latex] ) at which the [latex]8 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex] diameter bars are placed in the slab panel is _____ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Effective depth, [latex]d=250 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex]
Reinforcement, [latex]A_{s t}=0.2 \% [/latex]
Diameter of bar, [latex]\phi=8 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex]
[latex]S= [/latex] ?
[latex] \begin{aligned} & A_{s t}(\text { in } \%)=\frac{A_{s t}}{B \cdot d} \times 100 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 0.2=\frac{\left(n \times \frac{\pi}{4} \phi^{2}\right) \times 100}{\text { B.d }} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{0.2}{100}=\frac{\left(\frac{B}{S}\right) \times \frac{\pi}{4} \times 8^{2}}{B \times 250} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad S=\frac{\frac{\pi}{4} \times 8^{2} \times 100}{0.2 \times 250} \\ & S=100.53 \mathrm{~mm} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Provide spacing [latex]100 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex].

raw_source.text: The total primary consolidation settlement [latex]\left(S_{C}\right)[/latex] of a building constructed on a [latex] 10 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] thick saturated clay layer is estimated to be [latex] 50 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]. After 300 days of the construction of the building. primary consolidation settlement was reported as [latex] 10 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]. The additional time (in days) required to achieve [latex] 50 \%[/latex]  of [latex] S_{c}[/latex] will be ____ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
As we know, [latex]\quad\left(T_{v}\right)_{50}=\frac{C_{v} t}{d^{2}} \quad[/latex] where, [latex] C_{v}[/latex] is coefficient of consolidation
[latex]\frac{\pi}{4}(0.5)^{2}=\frac{C_{v}}{d^{2}} \times t_{2}[/latex]

For [latex] 10 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex] settlement, [latex]\% U=\frac{\Delta h}{\Delta H} \times 100=\frac{10}{50} \times 100 \%=20 \%[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \left(T_{v}\right)_{20} & =\frac{C_{v}}{d^{2}} \times t \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\pi}{4}(0.2)^{2} & =\frac{C_{v}}{d^{2}} \times 300 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\frac{\pi}{4}(0.5)^{2}}{\frac{\pi}{4}(0.2)^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{C_{v}}{d^{2}} \times t_{2}}{\frac{C_{v}}{d^{2}} \times 300} \\ \Rightarrow \quad t_{2} & =\left(\frac{0.5}{0.2}\right)^{2} \times 300=1875 \text { days } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Additional number of days [latex] =(1875-300)[/latex] days [latex] =1575[/latex] days

raw_source.text:
An infinite slope is made up of cohesionless soil with seepage parallel to and upto the sloping surface. The angle of slope is [latex] 30^{\circ}[/latex] with respect to horizontal ground surface. The unit weight of the saturated soil and water are [latex] 20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] and [latex] 10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] respectively.
The minimum angle of shearing resistance of soil (in degrees) for the critically stable condition of the slope is _____ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { FOS }&=\frac{\gamma_{\text {sub }}}{\gamma_{\text {sat }}} \times \frac{\tan \phi}{\tan \beta}\\ \text{Here, } \beta & =30^{\circ} \\ \gamma_{\text {sat }} & =20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \gamma_{w} & =10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \gamma_{\text {sub }} & =\gamma_{\text {sat }}-\gamma_{w} \\ & =20-10=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \gamma_{\text {sub }}=\gamma_{\text {sat }}-\gamma_{w}[/latex]
For critically stable condition, [latex]\mathrm{FOS}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{array}{ll}\because & 1=\frac{20-10}{20} \times \frac{\tan \phi}{\tan 30^{\circ}} \\ \Rightarrow & \phi=49.10^{\circ}\end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A soil sample was consolidated at a cell pressure of [latex] 20 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] and a back pressure of [latex] 10 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] for 24 hours during a consolidated undrained (CU) triaxial test. The cell pressure was increased to [latex] 30 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] on the next day and it resulted in the development of pore water pressure of [latex] 1 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]. The soil sample failed when the axial stress was gradually increased to [latex] 50 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]. The pore water pressure at failure was recorded as [latex] 21 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]. The value of skempton's pore pressure parameter [latex] B[/latex]  for the soil sample is ______ (round off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{3} & =20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Back pressure } & =10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \Delta u_{c} & =1 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \sigma_{3}^{\prime} & =30 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \Delta \sigma_{3} & =(30-20) \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ B & =\frac{\Delta u_{c}}{\Delta \sigma_{3}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The ordinates of a 1-hour unit hydrograph [latex](\mathrm{UH}) [/latex] are given below.

These ordinates are used to derive a 3-hour UH. The peak discharge (in [latex]\mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} [/latex] ) for the derived 3-hour UH is ______(rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Maximum ordinate of [latex]3 \mathrm{H} \mathrm{UH} [/latex] is [latex]86.67 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]
Maximum ordinate is [latex]87 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} [/latex] (to nearest integer)

raw_source.text:
A standard round bottom triangular canal section as shown in the figure has a bed slope of 1 in 200. Consider the Chezy's coefficient as 150 1/2/s.

The normal depth of flow, [latex] y[latex] (in meters) for carrying a discharge of [latex] 20 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}[/latex] is ____ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Discharge, [latex] Q=A \times V[/latex]
Now, Cross-section area, [latex] A=y^{2}\left(\theta_{\text {radian }}+\cot \theta\right)=y^{2}(0.588+1.5) =2.088 y^{2}[/latex]
Perimeter, [latex] P=2 y\left(\theta_{\text {radian }}+\cot \theta\right)[/latex]
Hydraulic radius, [latex] R=\frac{A}{P}=\frac{y^{2}\left(\theta_{\text {radian }}+\cot \theta\right)}{2 y\left(\theta_{\text {radian }}+\cot \theta\right)}=\frac{y}{2}[/latex]
Now, Velocity, [latex] V=C \sqrt{R . S}=150 \sqrt{\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) \times \frac{1}{200}}=\frac{150}{20} y^{1 / 2}[/latex]
Now, [latex] Q=A \times V[/latex]
[latex] 20=2.088 y^{2} \times \frac{150}{20} \cdot y^{1 / 2}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad y=1.10 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A spillway has unit discharge of [latex]7.5 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m} [/latex]. The flow depth at the downstream horizontal apron is [latex]0.5 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]. The tail water depth (in meters) required to form a hydraulic jump is _____ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Unit discharge [latex](q)=7.5 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{q^{2}}{g} & =\frac{y_{1} y_{2}\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right)}{2} \\ \frac{7.5^{2}}{9.81} & =0.5 y_{2}\left(\frac{0.5+y_{2}}{2}\right) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Tail water depth, [latex]y_{2}=4.54 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A [latex] 5 \mathrm{~m} \times 5 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] closed tank of [latex] 10 \mathrm{~m}[/latex] height contains water and oil, is connected to an overhead water reservoir as shown in the figure.
Use [latex]\gamma_{w}=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] and specific gravity of oil [latex] =0.8[/latex] .

The total force (in [latex]\mathrm{kN}[/latex] ) due to pressure on the side [latex]\mathrm{PQR}[/latex] of the tank is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{P}+(800)(10)(4)&=\left(10^{3}\right)(10)(10), \quad \text { where } P_{p} \text { is pressure at } P\\ P_{P}+\left(32 \times 10^{3}\right)&=\left(100 \times 10^{3}\right)\\ P_{P}&=68 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~Pa}\\ P_{P}&=68 \mathrm{kPa}\end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, force on PQR, [latex] F=\left[\frac{1}{2}(68+100) 4+\frac{1}{2}(100+160) 6\right] 5=(336+780) 5 =5580 \mathrm{kN}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Activated carbon is used to remove a pollution from wastewater in a mixed batch reactor, which follows first-order reaction kinetics.
At a reaction rate of 0.38 /day, the time (in days) required to remove the pollutant by [latex]95 \% [/latex] is ______ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
For first order kinetics,
[latex] N_{t}=N_{0} e^{-k t} [/latex]
For efficiency of [latex]95 \% [/latex],
[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{t} & =\left(1-\frac{95}{100}\right)^{L_{0}} \\ & =0.05 N_{0} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad 0.05=e^{-0.38 t} [/latex]
Taking In on both sides,
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} & \ln 0.05 =-0.38 t \times \operatorname{lne} \\ \Rightarrow &t =7.9 \text { days } \end{array} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A water treatment plant treats [latex] 25 \mathrm{MLD}[/latex] water with a natural alkalinity of [latex] 4.0 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{l}[/latex] (as [latex]\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}[/latex] ). It is estimated that during coagulation of this water, [latex] 450 \mathrm{~kg} [/latex] day of calcium bicarbonates [latex]\left(\mathrm{Ca}\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}\right)_{2}\right)[/latex] is required based on alum dosage.
Consider the atomic weight as: [latex]\mathrm{Ca}-40, \mathrm{H}-1, \mathrm{C}-12, \mathrm{O}-16[/latex] .
The quantity of pure quick lime [latex]\mathrm{CaO}[/latex] (in [latex]\mathrm{kg}[/latex] ) required for this process per day is ______ (round off to 2 decimal places)

Consider two ordinary differential equations (ODEs):

[latex] P: \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x^{4}+3 x^{2} y^{2}+2 y^{4}}{x^{3} y} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{Q}: \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\frac{-\mathrm{y}^{2}}{\mathrm{x}^{2}} [/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex] P: \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x^{4}+3 x^{2} y^{2}+2 y^{4}}{x^{3} y} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d y}{d x}=\left(\frac{x^{4}}{x^{3} y}\right)+\left(\frac{3 x^{2} y^{2}}{x^{3} y}\right)+\left(\frac{2 y^{4}}{x^{3} y}\right) [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d y}{d x}=\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+3\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+2\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^{3} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d y}{d x}=\left(\frac{1}{y / x}\right)+3\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+2\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^{3} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d y}{d x}=f\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) [/latex]
So [latex] P [/latex] is a homogenous ODE

[latex] \mathrm{Q}: \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\frac{-\mathrm{y}^{2}}{\mathrm{x}^{2}} [/latex]
[latex] x^{2} d y=-y^{2} d x [/latex]
[latex] y^{2} d x+x^{2} d y=0 [/latex]
[latex] M=y^{2} \quad \frac{d M}{\partial y}=2 y [/latex]
[latex] N=x^{2} \quad \frac{\partial N}{\partial \mathrm{x}}=2 \mathrm{x} [/latex]
So [latex] \mathrm{Q} [/latex] is non exact [latex] \mathrm{ODE} [/latex]
options: P is a homogeneous ODE and Q is an exact ODE.
P is a homogeneous ODE and Q is not an exact ODE.
P is a nonhomogeneous ODE and Q is an exact ODE.
P is a nonhomogeneous ODE and Q is not an exact ODE.

raw_answer.option_text: P is a homogeneous ODE and Q is not an exact ODE.

The following figure shows a plot between shear stress and velocity gradient for materials/fluids P, Q, R, S, and T.

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Various types of newtonian \& non-newtonian fluids are shown in the figure.
Fluids which obeys Newton's law of viscosity [latex] \left(\tau=\mu \frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dy}}\right) [/latex] are called Newtonian Fluids and those fluids which do not obey this rule are called Non-Newtonian Fluids.
General relationship between shear stress and velocity gradient is given by
[latex] \tau=\mathrm{A}\left(\frac{\mathrm{du}}{\mathrm{dy}}\right)^{\mathrm{n}}+\mathrm{B} [/latex]
In the figures shown above, slope of the curve is called apparent viscosity.
Fluid for which apparent viscosity increases with du/dy are called Dilatant.
Dilatant fluids are also called shear thickening fluids. Examples of dilatant fluids are solution with suspended starch or sand, sugar in water.
Fluids for which apparent viscosity decreases with du/dy are called Pseudo Plastic.
Pseudo plastic fluid are also called shear thinning fluid. Examples are paints, polymer solutions, blood, paper pulp, syrup, molasses, milk, gelatine.
Bingham Plastic (ideal plastic) fluids require a certain minimum shear stress [latex] t_{y} [/latex] (yield stress) before they start flowing. Examples: tooth paste, sewage sludge, drilling mud have time dependent Newtonian Behaviour.

Filters

(e) Electrostatic precipitators
(f) Scrubbers or wet collectors

(II) Following treatment techniques are used to remove/control gaseous contaminants
Combustion techniques
This method is used when gases are of organic nature.
Equipments used in combustion are:
(i) vapour incinerators
(ii) after burners
(iii) Flares (process is called as flaring)
Note: Flaring (i.e. combustion method) is suitable for the removal of carbon monoxide because during combustion, carbon reacts with carbon monoxide to form [latex] \mathrm{CO}_{2} [/latex].

Absorption
In this method, effluent gases are passed through absorbers (or scrubbers) which contain liquid absorbents that remove various gaseous pollutants.
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Gaseous pollutant} & \text{Common absorbent used as solid form} \\ \hline \mathrm{SO}_{2} & \text{Dimethylaniline, ammonium sulphite, sodium sulphite etc. } \\ \hline \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S} & \text{Mixture of NaOH and phenol,soda Ash etc. } \\ \hline \mathrm{NO}_{\mathrm{x}} & \text{Water, aqueous nitric acid} \\ \hline \mathrm{HF} & Water, \mathrm{NaOH} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Adsorption technique
In this method, the effluent gases are passed through adsorbers which contain solids of porous structure.
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Gaseous pollutant} & \text{Common absorbent used as solid form} \\ \hline \mathrm{SO}_{2} & \text{Pulverised limestone or Dolomite } \\ \hline \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S} &\text{ Iron oxide} \\ \hline \mathrm{NO}_{\mathrm{x}} & \text{Silica gel} \\ \hline \mathrm{HF} & \text{Lump limestone} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Let the settling velocity of anthracite pacticle at top, silica pacticle at middle \& ilmenite pacticle at bottom, after back washing be [latex] \left(V_{S}\right)_{T},\left(V_{S}\right),\left(V_{S}\right)_{B} [/latex] respectively.
For Middle silica sand
[latex] \begin{aligned} & v_{S}=\frac{\left(G_{s_{1}}-1\right) \gamma_{w} D_{1}^{2}}{18 \mu} \\ & v_{S}=K(2.6-1)(0.2)^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] V_{S}=K(1.6)(0.2)^{2} \text { where, } K=\frac{\gamma_{w}}{18 \mu} [/latex]
For Top Anthracite
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}}\right)_{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{K}\left(\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{S}_{2}}-1\right)\left(\mathrm{D}_{2}\right)^{2} \\ & \left(\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{S}}\right)_{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{K}(0.5)\left(\mathrm{D}_{2}\right)^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
As anthracite lies above silica layer
So, anthracite particles should have settling velocity less than silica particles
[latex] \left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}}\right)_{\mathrm{T}} \lt \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}} [/latex]
So, [latex] K(0.5)\left(D_{2}\right)^{2} \lt K(1.6)(0.2)^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{D}_{2} [/latex] or [latex] \mathrm{D}_{\text {Top }} \lt \sqrt{\frac{1.6 \times(0.2)^{2}}{0.5}} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{D}_{2} [/latex] or [latex] \mathrm{D}_{\text {Top }} \lt 0.357 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex]

[latex] \left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}}\right)_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{K}(4.2-1)\left(\mathrm{D}_{3}^{2}\right) [/latex]
As, ilimite layer lies below silica lyers
So, ilimite particles should have settling velocity greater than silica
i.e., [latex] \left(V_{S}\right)_{B} \gt V_{S} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{K}(3.2)\left(\mathrm{D}_{3}^{2}\right) \gt \mathrm{K}(1.6)(0.2)^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{D}_{3} [/latex] or [latex] \mathrm{D}_{\text {bottom }} \gt \sqrt{\frac{1.6 \times(0.2)^{2}}{3.2}} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{D}_{3} [/latex] or [latex] \mathrm{D}_{\text {bottom }} \gt 0.141 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex]
Hence, diameter of anthracite particle is slightly greater than [latex] 0.35 \mathrm{~mm} \& [/latex] diameter of ilmenite particle is slightly greater than [latex] 0.141 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Three vectors [latex] \vec{p}, \vec{q} [/latex] and [latex] \vec{r} [/latex] are given as

[latex] \vec{p}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} [/latex]
[latex] \overrightarrow{\mathrm{q}}=\hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{k}} [/latex]
[latex] \vec{r}=2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k} [/latex]

Which of the following is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
(A) [latex] \vec{p} \times(\vec{q} \times \vec{r})=(\vec{p} \cdot \vec{r}) \vec{q}-(\vec{p} \cdot \vec{q}) \vec{r} [/latex]
(This is always true for any three given vectors)

(B) We know that [latex] \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} [/latex] is always true but [latex] \vec{a} \times \vec{b} \neq \vec{b} \times \vec{a} [/latex] because [latex] \vec{a} \times \vec{b}=-\vec{b} \times \vec{a} [/latex]
This can be true only when [latex] \vec{a} \times \vec{b}=0 [/latex]
So, [latex] \quad \vec{r} \cdot(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})=\vec{r} .(\vec{q} \times \vec{p}) [/latex]
[latex] \vec{r} \cdot(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})=-\vec{r} \cdot(\vec{p} \times \vec{q}) [/latex]
This can be true if
[latex] \begin{aligned} \vec{r} \cdot(\vec{p} \times q) & =0 \\ \vec{p} \times \vec{q} & =\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+j \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] (\vec{r} \cdot \vec{p} \times \vec{q})=0 [/latex] this is true in this case

(C) [latex] \vec{p} \times(\vec{q} \times \vec{r}) [/latex] can't be equal to [latex] (\vec{p} \times \vec{q}) \times \vec{r} [/latex] because
[latex] \vec{p} \times(\vec{q} \times \vec{r}) \perp \vec{p} [/latex] and [latex] (\vec{p} \times \vec{q}) \times \vec{r}) \perp \vec{r} [/latex]
So, [latex] (\vec{p} \times(\vec{q} \times \vec{r}) \neq(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})) \times \vec{r} [/latex]

(D) [latex] \vec{p} \times(\vec{q} \times \vec{r})+\vec{q} \times(\vec{r} \times \vec{p})+\vec{r} \times(\vec{p} \times \vec{q})=\overrightarrow{0} [/latex]
[latex] (\vec{p} . \vec{r}) \vec{q}-(\vec{p} . \vec{q}) \vec{r}+(\vec{q} . \vec{p}) \vec{p}-(\vec{q} \cdot \vec{r}) \vec{p}+(\vec{r} . \vec{q}) \vec{p}-(\vec{r} . \vec{q})) \vec{q} [/latex]
[latex] 0=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \vec{p} \cdot \vec{r}=\vec{r} \cdot \vec{p} \\ & \vec{p} \cdot \vec{q}=\vec{q} \cdot \vec{p} \\ & \vec{q} \cdot \vec{r}=\vec{r} \cdot \vec{q} \end{aligned} [/latex]
(Hence proved)

raw_source.text: A homogeneous earth dam has a maximum water head difference of [latex] 15 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] between the upstream and downstream sides. A flownet was drawn with the number of potential drops as 10 and the average length of the element as [latex] 3 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]. Specific gravity of the soil is 2.65 . For a factor of safety of 2.0 against piping failure, void ratio of the soil is ____(rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex] (\Delta \mathrm{H}) [/latex] total head loss [latex] =15 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]
[latex] \left(n_{d}\right) [/latex] number of equipotential drops [latex] =10 [/latex]
(I) length of flow field [latex] =3 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]
(G) specific gravity [latex] =2.65 [/latex]
(FOS) factor of safety [latex] =2 [/latex]
(e) void ratio [latex] = [/latex] ?

[latex] (\Delta h) [/latex] equipotential drop of head
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\frac{\text { Total head loss }}{\text { no. of equipotential drop }} \\ \Delta \mathrm{h} & =\frac{\Delta \mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}}}=\frac{15}{10}=1.5 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
FOS against quick sand condition [latex] =\frac{i_{c r}}{i} [/latex]
(i) hydraulic gradient [latex] =\frac{\Delta \mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{l}}=\frac{1.5}{3}=0.5 [/latex]
[latex] 2=\frac{i_{c r}}{0.5},\left(i_{c r}\right) [/latex] ciritical hydraulic gradient [latex] =1 [/latex]
Critical hydraulic gradient [latex] \left(\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{cr}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{G}-1}{1+\mathrm{e}}=1=\frac{2.65-1}{1+\mathrm{e}} [/latex]
(e)void ratio [latex] =0.65 [/latex]

The maximum and minimum densities of sand determined from the laboratory tests are [latex] 1.8 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} [/latex] and [latex] 1.3 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} [/latex], respectively. Assume the specific gravity of sand as 2.7 .
The relative density index of the in-situ sand is ______ (rounded off to 2 decimal places)

maximum density [latex] \left(\gamma_{\mathrm{d}}\right)_{\max }=1.8 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} [/latex]
minimum density [latex] \left(\gamma_{\mathrm{d}}\right)_{\min }=1.3 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} [/latex]
specific gravity [latex] (G)=2.7 [/latex]
[latex] \left(I_{D}\right) [/latex] relative density [latex] =\frac{\gamma_{d \max }\left(\gamma_{d}-\gamma_{d \min }\right)}{\gamma_{d}\left(\gamma_{d \max }-\gamma_{d \min }\right)} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad(n) [/latex] percentage of voids

[latex] =\frac{\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{v}}\right) \text { volume of voids } \times 100}{\left(\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{T}}\right) \text { Total volume }}=50 \% [/latex]
Porosity( [latex] n [/latex] ) [latex] =0.5 [/latex]
void ratio (e) [latex] =\frac{\mathrm{n}}{1-\mathrm{n}}=\frac{0.5}{1-0.5}=1 [/latex]
[latex] \left(\gamma_{\mathrm{d}}\right)_{\text {insitu }}=\frac{\mathrm{G} \cdot \gamma_{\mathrm{w}}}{1+\mathrm{e}}=\frac{2.7 \times 1}{1+1}=1.35 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3} [/latex]
[latex] \left(I_{D}\right)=\frac{1.8(1.35-1.3)}{1.35(1.8-1.3)}=0.13 [/latex]
Relative density [latex] \left(I_{D}\right)=0.13 [/latex]

raw_source.text: A [latex] 500 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] long water distribution pipeline [latex] P [/latex] with diameter [latex] 1.0 \mathrm{~m} [/latex], is used to convey [latex] 0.1 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} [/latex] of flow. A new pipeline [latex] Q [/latex], with the same length and flow rate, is to replace [latex] P [/latex]. The friction factors for [latex] P [/latex] and [latex] \mathrm{Q} [/latex] are 0.04 and 0.01 , respectively. The diameter of the pipeline [latex] \mathrm{Q} [/latex] (in meters) is _____(rounded off to 2 decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Initially, we have,

To replace the pipe, head loss has to be same
[latex] \begin{aligned} & h_{f p}=h_{f Q} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \frac{f_{f p} L Q^{2}}{12.1 D_{P}^{5}}=\frac{f_{f Q} L Q^{2}}{12.1 D_{Q}^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \frac{0.04 \times 500 \times Q^{2}}{12.1 \times 1^{5}}=\frac{0.01 \times 500 \times Q^{2}}{12.1 \times D_{Q}^{5}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & D_{Q}^{5}=\frac{0.01}{0.04} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & D_{Q}=\left(\frac{0.01}{0.04}\right)^{1 / 5}=0.7579 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \simeq 0.76 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A [latex] 2 \mathrm{~m} \times 1.5 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] tank of [latex] 6 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] height is provided with a [latex] 100 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex] diameter orifice at the center of its base. The orifice is plugged and the tank is filled up to [latex] 5 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] height. Consider the average value of discharge coefficient as 0.6 and acceleration due to gravity (g) as [latex] 10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} [/latex]. After unplugging the orifice, the time (in seconds) taken for the water level to drop from [latex] 5 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] to [latex] 3.5 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] under free discharge condition is _____ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Let at any instant depth of liquid in tank is ' [latex] h [/latex] ' [latex] m [/latex] and in time (dt), the depth falls by (-dh)


[latex] \Rightarrow\left(C_{d} \cdot\left(\frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}\right) \sqrt{2 g h}\right) d t=A_{0}(-d h) [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{t}=\int \mathrm{dt}=\frac{\mathrm{A}_{0}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{d}} \cdot \frac{\pi \mathrm{d}^{2}}{4} \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g}}} \int_{\mathrm{H}_{1}}^{\mathrm{H}_{2}}\left(\frac{-\mathrm{dH}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{h}}}\right) [/latex]
[latex] t=\frac{A_{0}}{C_{d} \cdot \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4} \sqrt{2 g}}\left[2\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{H}_{1}}-\sqrt{\mathrm{H}_{2}}\right)\right] [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{t}=\left[\frac{2 \times 1.5 \mathrm{~m}^{2}}{0.6 \times \frac{\pi}{4}(0.1)^{2} \mathrm{~m}^{2} \sqrt{2 \times 10 \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^{2}}}} \times 2(\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{3.5}) \mathrm{m}^{1 / 2}\right] \mathrm{sec} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{t}=103.985 \mathrm{sec} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A rectangular channel is [latex] 4.0 \mathrm{~m} [/latex] wide and carries a discharge of [latex] 2.0 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} [/latex] with a depth of [latex] 0.4 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]. The channel transitions to a maximum width contraction at a downstream location, without influencing the upstream flow condtions. The width (in meters) at the maximum contraction is _____ (rounded off to 2 decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
width of channel [latex] (B)=4 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]
discharge [latex] (Q)=2 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]
depth of [latex] \operatorname{flow}(\mathrm{y})=0.4 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]

Specific energy at section (1) - (1) (E)
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{y}_{1}+\frac{\mathrm{V}_{1}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{~g}} \\ & =0.4+\frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2}}{\mathrm{~B}_{1}^{2} \times 2 \mathrm{~g} \times \mathrm{y}_{1}^{2}} \\ & =0.4+\frac{2^{2}}{4^{2} \times 2 \times 9.81 \times 0.4^{2}} \\ & =0.4796 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
When channel section is contracted to minimum width and for constant discharge Q. The flow over contracted section will be critical flow.
[latex] \begin{aligned} E & =E_{c}=\frac{3}{2} \cdot y_{c} \\ \therefore \quad 0.4796 & =\frac{3}{2} \times y_{c} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \quad \quad y_{c} & =0.4796 \times \frac{2}{3}=0.3197 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
For critical flow condition, [latex] \frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{gA}^{3}}=1 [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2} \mathrm{~B}_{\min }}{\mathrm{gB}_{\min \mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{c}}^{3}}^{3}}=1 [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{B}_{\min }^{2} & =\frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2}}{9 \mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{c}}^{3}}=1 \\ \mathrm{~B}_{\min } & =\left(\frac{\mathrm{Q}^{2}}{\mathrm{gy_{c } ^ { 3 }}}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ & =\left(\frac{2^{2}}{9.81 \times 0.3197^{3}}\right)^{1 / 2} \\ & =3.5325 \mathrm{~m} \simeq 3.53 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A circular settling tank is to be designed for primary treatment of sewage of a flow rate of 10 million liters/day. Assume a detention period of 2.0 hours and surface loading rate of 40000 liters [latex] / \mathrm{m}^{2} / [/latex] day. The height (in meters) of the water column in the tank is _____ (rounded off to 2 decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given,
Discharge, [latex] \mathrm{Q}=10 \mathrm{MLD} [/latex]
Detention period, [latex] \mathrm{t}_{\mathrm{d}}=2 \mathrm{hr} [/latex]
Over flow rate, [latex] \mathrm{V}_{0}=40,000 [/latex] litres [latex] / \mathrm{m}^{2} / [/latex] day
[latex] \mathrm{H}= [/latex] ?

As, Surface area of tank [latex] =\frac{\text { Discharge }}{\text { Over flow rate }}=\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{V}_{0}} [/latex]
So,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \text { S.A. }=\frac{10 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~L} / \text { day }}{40,000 \mathrm{~L} / \mathrm{m}^{2} / \text { day }} \\ & \text { S.A }=250 \mathrm{~m}^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Volume of tank [latex] (V)=Q \times t_{d} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\frac{10 \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-3}}{24} \times 2 \mathrm{~m}^{3} \\ & \mathrm{~V}=833.33 \mathrm{~m}^{3} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence,
Height of water in tank or Height of setting zone
[latex] \begin{aligned} H & =\frac{833.33 \mathrm{~m}^{3}}{250 \mathrm{~m}^{2}} \\ H & =3.33 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Note: In reality, height of water in tank OR height of settling zone is estimated by above approach but if the bottom of sedimentation tank is assumed to be sloping or hoppered (i.e sludge zone is also considered) then height of water in tank is determined as follows:
Using,
Volume of tank [latex] (V)=D^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4} H+0.011 D\right) [/latex]
As,

[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { S.A. } & =\frac{\pi}{4} D^{2}=250 \mathrm{~m}^{2} \\ D & =17.835 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

So, [latex] 833.33=(17.835)^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4} H+0.011(17.835)\right) [/latex]
So, [latex] \mathrm{H}=3.085 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]

An organic waste is represented as

(Atomic weights: S-32, H-1, C-12, O-16, N-14)
Assume complete conversion of [latex] \mathrm{S} [/latex] to [latex] \mathrm{SO}_{2} [/latex] while burning.
[latex] \mathrm{SO}_{2} [/latex] generated (in grams) per [latex] \mathrm{kg} [/latex] of this waste is _____ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Organic waste [latex] =\mathrm{C}_{240} \mathrm{O}_{200} \mathrm{H}_{180} \mathrm{~N}_{5} \mathrm{~S} [/latex]
Weight of organic waste [latex] =1 \mathrm{~kg} [/latex]
Burning of organic waste converts
sulphur into sulphur dioxide as follows:
[latex] \mathrm{C}_{240} \mathrm{O}_{200} \mathrm{H}_{180} \mathrm{~N}_{5} \mathrm{~S}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{xCO}_{2}+\mathrm{yH}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{zH}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{SO}_{2} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A vertical summit curve on a freight corridor is formed at the intersection of two gradients, [latex] +3.0 \% [/latex] and [latex] -5.0 \% [/latex].

Assume the following:
Only large-sized trucks are allowed on this corridor.
Design speed [latex] =80 \mathrm{kmph} [/latex]
Eye height of truck drivers above the road surface [latex] =2.30 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]
Height of object above the road surface for which trucks need to stop [latex] =0.35 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]
Total reaction time of the truck drivers [latex] =2.0 \mathrm{~s} [/latex]
Coefficient of longitudinal friction of the road [latex] =0.36 [/latex]
Stopping sight distance gets compesnated on the gradient.

The design length of the summit curve (in meters) to accommodate the stopping sight distance is _____ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Algebraic difference of gradients
[latex] A = |+3 - (-5)| = 8% = 0.08 [/latex]

Step 2: Conversion of speed
[latex] V = \frac{80 \times 1000}{3600} = 22.22 , \text{m/s} [/latex]

Step 3: Reaction distance
[latex] S_r = V \times t = 22.22 \times 2 = 44.44 , \text{m} [/latex]

Step 4: Braking distance
[latex] S_b = \frac{V^2}{2 g f} = \frac{(22.22)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.36} = 69.94 , \text{m} [/latex]

Step 5: Stopping Sight Distance (SSD)
[latex] S = S_r + S_b = 44.44 + 69.94 = 114.38 , \text{m} [/latex]

Step 6: Length of summit curve (SSD criterion)
For summit curve, when
[latex] L \ge S [/latex]

[latex] L = \frac{A S^2}{2(\sqrt{h_1} + \sqrt{h_2})^2} [/latex]

[latex] \sqrt{h_1} = \sqrt{2.30} = 1.517, \quad \sqrt{h_2} = \sqrt{0.35} = 0.592 [/latex]

[latex] (\sqrt{h_1} + \sqrt{h_2})^2 = (2.109)^2 = 4.448 [/latex]

[latex] L = \frac{0.08 \times (114.38)^2}{2 \times 4.448} = \frac{1046.6}{8.896} = 117.70 , \text{m} [/latex]

Check condition:
[latex] L = 117.70 , \text{m} \ge S = 114.38 , \text{m} [/latex]
Hence, the condition is satisfied.

raw_source.text: Suppose [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of matrix A and [latex]x[/latex] is the corresponding eigenvector. Let [latex]x[/latex] also be an eigenvector of the matrix [latex]B=A-2 I[/latex], where [latex]I[/latex] is the identity matrix. Then, the eigenvalue of [latex]B[/latex] corresponding to the eigenvector [latex]x[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
Solution:
We are given:
[latex] A x = \lambda x [/latex]
So, [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of matrix [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]x[/latex] is its corresponding eigenvector

We are also told that:
[latex] B = A - 2I [/latex], where [latex]I[/latex] is the identity matrix

Now we need to find the eigenvalue of [latex]B[/latex] corresponding to the same eigenvector [latex]x[/latex]

Step 1: Apply [latex]B[/latex] on [latex]x[/latex]:
[latex] Bx = (A - 2I)x = Ax - 2Ix [/latex]
[latex] Bx = \lambda x - 2x = (\lambda - 2)x [/latex]

Step 2: Since [latex]Bx = (\lambda - 2)x[/latex], this shows that [latex]x[/latex] is also an eigenvector of [latex]B[/latex], with eigenvalue:
[latex] \lambda_B = \lambda - 2 [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex]\lambda - 2[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3\end{array}\right][/latex] and [latex]b=\left[\begin{array}{l}b_{1} \\ b_{2} \\ b_{3}\end{array}\right][/latex]. For [latex]A x=b[/latex] to be solvable, which one of the following options is the correct condition on [latex]b_{1}, b_{2}[/latex] and [latex]b_{3}[/latex] :
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Let [latex] x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
Then [latex] Ax = b [/latex] means:
[latex] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \ b_2 \ b_3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

This leads to the system:
[latex] x_1 + x_2 = b_1 \quad \text{(1)} [/latex]
[latex] x_1 + 3x_2 = b_2 \quad \text{(2)} [/latex]
[latex] -2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 \quad \text{(3)} [/latex]

Step 2: From equation (1), solve for [latex] x_1 = b_1 - x_2 [/latex]
Substitute into equation (2):
[latex] (b_1 - x_2) + 3x_2 = b_2 \Rightarrow b_1 + 2x_2 = b_2 [/latex]
So,
[latex] x_2 = \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} [/latex] and then [latex] x_1 = \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} [/latex]

Step 3: Plug into equation (3) to ensure consistency:
[latex] -2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 [/latex]
Substitute values:
[latex] -2\left( \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} \right) - 3\left( \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} \right) = b_3 [/latex]

Simplify:
[latex] - (3b_1 - b_2) - \frac{3(b_2 - b_1)}{2} = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] -3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2 - 3b_1}{2} = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] -3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2} + \frac{3b_1}{2} = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] (-3b_1 + \frac{3b_1}{2}) + (b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2}) = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] -\frac{3b_1}{2} - \frac{b_2}{2} = b_3 [/latex]

Multiply both sides by 2:
[latex] -3b_1 - b_2 = 2b_3 [/latex]

Rearranged:
[latex] 3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 [/latex]

Final Answer: (B) [latex] 3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Which one of the following options is the correct Fourier series of the periodic function [latex]f(x)[/latex] described below:

[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}0 & \text { if } &-2 < x < -1 \\ 2 k &\text { if } &-1 < x < 1 ; \; \; \text { period }=4 \\ 0 &\text { if }& -1 < x < 2\end{array}\right.[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_0 &= \frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^{L} f(x) \, dx \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \int_{-2}^{2} f(x) \, dx \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \int_{0}^{2} f(x) \, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} 2k \, dx = 2k \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & f(x)=\text { even function } \\ & b_{n}=0 \\ & \text { Period }=4 \text { i.e. i.n (-2, 2) } \\ & L=2 \\ & a_{n}=\frac{1}{L} \int_{-L}^{L} \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{2}\right) f(x) d x \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \int_{-2}^{2} \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{2}\right) f(x) d x \\ & =2 \times \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{2}\right) 2 k \cdot d x \\ & =2 k \int_{0}^{1} \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{2}\right) d x \\ & =2 k\left[\frac{\sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{n \pi}{2}\right)}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac{4 k}{n \pi}\left[\sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{2}\right)\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & a_{n}=\frac{4 k}{n \pi} \sin \frac{n \pi}{2} \\ & f(x)=\frac{a_{0}}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) \\ & =\frac{2 k}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n} \cos \left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) \\ & =k+\frac{4 k}{\pi} \cos \frac{\pi x}{2}+\frac{4 k}{2 \pi} \times 0+\frac{4 k}{3 \pi}(-1) \cos \left(\frac{3 \pi x}{2}\right)+0+\frac{4 k}{5 \pi} \times \cos \frac{5 \pi x}{2}+\ldots \\ & =k+\frac{4 k}{\pi}\left[\cos \left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)-\frac{1}{3} \cos \frac{3 \pi x}{2}+\frac{1}{5} \cos \frac{5 \pi x}{2}-. .\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
[latex] X[/latex] is the random variable that can take any one of the values, [latex]0,1,7,11[/latex] and 12 . The probability mass function for [latex]X[/latex] is

[latex]\mathrm{P}(X=0)=0.4 ; \mathrm{P}(X=1)=0.3 ; \mathrm{P}(X=7)=0.1[/latex];
[latex]\mathrm{P}(X=11)=0.1 ; \mathrm{P}(X=12)=0.1[/latex]

Then, the variance of [latex]X[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Compute the expected value [latex]E(X)[/latex]
[latex] E(X) = \sum X_i \cdot P(X_i) [/latex]
[latex] = 0 \cdot 0.4 + 1 \cdot 0.3 + 7 \cdot 0.1 + 11 \cdot 0.1 + 12 \cdot 0.1 [/latex]
[latex] = 0 + 0.3 + 0.7 + 1.1 + 1.2 = 3.3 [/latex]

Step 2: Compute [latex]E(X^2)[/latex]
[latex] E(X^2) = \sum X_i^2 \cdot P(X_i) [/latex]
[latex] = 0^2 \cdot 0.4 + 1^2 \cdot 0.3 + 7^2 \cdot 0.1 + 11^2 \cdot 0.1 + 12^2 \cdot 0.1 [/latex]
[latex] = 0 + 1 \cdot 0.3 + 49 \cdot 0.1 + 121 \cdot 0.1 + 144 \cdot 0.1 [/latex]
[latex] = 0.3 + 4.9 + 12.1 + 14.4 = 31.7 [/latex]

Step 3: Compute Variance
[latex] \text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - (E(X))^2 [/latex]
[latex] = 31.7 - (3.3)^2 = 31.7 - 10.89 = 20.81 [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \text{Var}(X) = 20.81 [/latex]

raw_source.text: As per IS 456:2000 provisions for two-way slabs with continuous edges, the longitudinal steel reinforcement to be provided in the edge strip is based on
raw_source.solution:
As per IS 456:2000, in the design of two-way slabs with continuous edges, the slab is divided into middle strips and edge strips. The bending moment is primarily resisted by the middle strip, while the edge strip is provided mainly for distribution and minimum reinforcement.

According to Clause 27.4.3 of IS 456:2000:
Reinforcement in the edge strip is not based on calculated moments or reinforcement in the middle strip. Instead, it is based on the prescribed minimum requirement for slabs.

Therefore,
Reinforcement in edge strip = Prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

Final Answer:
The prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the longer span
the prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

raw_source.text: Identify the FALSE statement from the following options:
raw_source.solution:
Let's examine each option to find the FALSE statement.
Option A: The compressive strength of a concrete specimen can vary depending on its shape and size.
This is true. The shape (cube vs. cylinder) and size of a specimen affect the test results due to variations in stress distribution and failure patterns.

Option B: Air-dried and saturated test specimens show the same compressive strength for concrete.
This is false. Air-dried specimens typically show higher compressive strength compared to saturated ones because excess moisture can weaken the internal structure during loading.

Option C: Curing conditions, such as temperature and relative humidity, can influence the compressive strength of concrete.
This is true. Proper curing ensures complete hydration and strength development, while poor curing can reduce final strength.

Option D: Compressive strength depends on the water-to-binder ratio used in the concrete mixture.
This is true. Lower water-to-binder ratios generally result in higher strength due to denser microstructure and improved bonding.

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\text{B}}[/latex] [latex]\text{Air-dried and saturated test specimens show the same compressive strength for concrete}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:

[latex]\text{Final FC concentration (after treatment)} = 23 \ \text{cfu/100 ml}[/latex]

[latex]\text{Log Kill} = \log_{10} \left( \frac{\text{Initial concentration}}{\text{Final concentration}} \right)[/latex]
[latex]\quad = \log_{10} \left( \frac{10780}{23} \right)[/latex]
[latex]\quad = \log_{10} (468.7)[/latex]
[latex]\quad \approx 2.67[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A hydrocarbon [latex]\left(\mathrm{C}_{n} \mathrm{H}_{m}\right)[/latex] is burnt in air [latex]\left(\mathrm{O}_{2}+3.78 \mathrm{~N}_{2}\right)[/latex]. The stoichiometric fuel to air mass ratio for this process is
Note: Atomic Weight: C(12), H(1)
Effective Molecular Weight: Air(28.8)
Ignore any conversion of [latex]N_2[/latex] in air to the oxides of nitrogen [latex]\left(\mathrm{NO}_{x}\right)[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text{Given hydrocarbon: } \text{C}_n\text{H}_m[/latex]
[latex]\text{Air composition: O}_2 + 3.78 \text{N}_2[/latex]
[latex]\text{Molecular weight of air} = 28.8[/latex]

[latex]\text{Balanced reaction:}[/latex]
[latex]\text{C}_n\text{H}_m + \left(n + \frac{m}{4}\right)\text{O}_2 + 3.78\left(n + \frac{m}{4}\right)\text{N}_2 \rightarrow \cdots[/latex]

**Mass of fuel per mole:**
[latex]= 12n + m[/latex]
**Mass of air required per mole of fuel:**
[latex]= \left(n + \frac{m}{4}\right) \times 4.78 \times 28.8 = (4n + m) \times 0.0291^{-1}[/latex]

**Fuel-to-air mass ratio:**
[latex]= \frac{12n + m}{(4n + m) \times \frac{1}{0.0291}} = 0.0291 \cdot \frac{12n + m}{4n + m}[/latex]

[latex]\boxed{\text{Stoichiometric fuel-to-air mass ratio} = 0.0291 \cdot \frac{12n + m}{4n + m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: All the vehicles that come during a particular peak hour come during a 10-minute period within this hour. The 15-minute peak hour factor for this peak hour is
raw_source.solution:
Given:
All vehicles during the peak hour arrive within a 10-minute period.

To find:
15-minute Peak Hour Factor (PHF)

Formula:
[latex]\text{PHF} = \frac{\text{Hourly Volume}}{4 \times \text{Peak 15-minute Volume}}[/latex]

Since all vehicles arrive within a 10-minute period, they are included within the peak 15-minute period.

Therefore,
[latex]\text{PHF} = \frac{V}{4 \times V} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25[/latex]

Final Answer: [latex]0.25[/latex]

raw_source.text: Which of the following equations belong/belongs to the class of second-order, linear, homogeneous partial differential equations:
raw_source.solution:
Equation 1:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \left( \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} \right) + xy [/latex]
- Second-order: Yes
- Linear: Yes
- Homogeneous: No (due to the term [latex] +xy [/latex])

Equation 2:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} = 0 [/latex]
- Second-order: Yes
- Linear: Yes
- Homogeneous: Yes

Equation 3:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = c \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} [/latex]
- Second-order: No

Equation 4:
[latex] \left( \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} \right)^2 = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} [/latex]
- Second-order: Yes
- Linear: No (square of a second derivative makes it nonlinear)

Final Answer: Only Equation 2 belongs to the class of second-order, linear, homogeneous partial differential equations.
options: [latex]\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial t^{2}}=c^{2}\left(\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial y^{2}}\right)+x y[/latex]
[latex]\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial y^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial z^{2}}=0[/latex]

raw_answer.option_text: [latex]\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial y^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial z^{2}}=0[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the frame shown in the figure under the loading of [latex]100 \mathrm{kN} . \mathrm{m}[/latex] couples at the joints [latex]B[/latex] and [latex]G[/latex]. Considering only the effects of flexural deformations, which of the following statements is/are true:
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Analyze the structure
- It's a symmetric frame with members: AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, and FG.
- Moments of [latex]100 \, \text{kN} \cdot \text{m}[/latex] are applied at joints B and G (clockwise and counterclockwise respectively).
- All vertical columns (AB, DE, FG) have different stiffnesses as per EI values.
- Assume fixed supports at A, D, and F.

Step 2: Moment Distribution - focus on joints B, C, and D

Let's denote member stiffness factors:
- Stiffness of member BC from joint B is:
[latex] K_{BC} = \frac{4EI}{L} = \frac{4EI}{6} = \frac{2EI}{3} [/latex]
- Stiffness of member AB from joint B:
[latex] K_{BA} = \frac{2EI}{6} = \frac{EI}{3} [/latex]
Distribution Factor (DF) at Joint B:
[latex] DF_{BC} = \frac{K_{BC}}{K_{BA} + K_{BC}} = \frac{\frac{2EI}{3}}{\frac{EI}{3} + \frac{2EI}{3}} = \frac{2}{3} [/latex]
[latex] DF_{BA} = \frac{1}{3} [/latex]

Similarly at Joint C (connecting BC, CD, and CE):
All members have same length and stiffness [latex]2EI[/latex], so:
[latex] K_{CB} = \frac{4EI}{6} = \frac{2EI}{3} [/latex]
[latex] K_{CD} = \frac{2EI}{8} = \frac{EI}{4} [/latex]
[latex] DF_{CB} = \frac{\frac{2EI}{3}}{\frac{2EI}{3} + \frac{EI}{4}} = \frac{8}{11} [/latex]
[latex] DF_{CD} = \frac{3}{11} [/latex]

Step 3: Apply the moment at B and perform moment distribution
- Moment at B = [latex]100 \, \text{kN} \cdot \text{m}[/latex] (clockwise), so fixed-end moment to BC is [latex]+100[/latex]
- Apply moment distribution considering carry-over and distribution factors.

After a few iterations (or by symmetry), we get:
[latex] M_{BC} = 50 \, \text{kN} \cdot \text{m} [/latex]
[latex] M_{CB} = 50 \, \text{kN} \cdot \text{m} [/latex]
Because of symmetric load and structure, the moment gets equally distributed between BC and CD.

Conclusion:
- Moment at joint C is exactly [latex]50 \, \text{kN} \cdot \text{m}[/latex], not more.
- Thus, option D ("more than 50") is False.
- Joint C has no rotation due to symmetry - option C is True.
- CD has zero axial force and zero shear since there?s no direct force acting - options A and B are True.
options: Axial force is zero in the member CD
Shear force is zero in the member CD
There is no rotation in the joint C
The magnitude of bending moment developed in the member BC at the end C is more than [latex]50 \mathrm{kN} . \mathrm{m}[/latex]

option_texts: Shear force is zero in the member CD
There is no rotation in the joint C

raw_source.text: For the Bernoulli's equation to be applicable in a fluid flow situation, which of the following conditions is/are to be satisfied:
raw_source.solution:
Bernoulli's equation is applicable under the following assumptions:

(A) Fluid should be frictionless - no energy loss due to viscosity.
(B) Fluid should be incompressible - [latex]\rho = \text{constant}[/latex]
(C) Flow should be steady - [latex]\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = 0[/latex]
(D) Flow should be rotational - Incorrect, because Bernoulli's equation assumes irrotational flow.

Hence, the correct conditions are:
(A), (B), and (C)

raw_source.text: The Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) in a rectangular sedimentation tank is [latex]45 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{d}[/latex]. Minimum diameters of spherical inorganic and organic particles expected to be completely removed in this tank are calculated. Assume that Stoke's law is applicable. Which of the following options is/are correct:
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) = [latex] 45 \, \text{m}^3/\text{m}^2/\text{day} = \frac{45}{86400} \, \text{m/s} \approx 5.208 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{m/s} [/latex]
Specific gravity of inorganic particles [latex] (G_{in}) = 2.65 [/latex]
Specific gravity of organic particles [latex] (G_{org}) = 1.20 [/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity [latex] g = 9.81 \, \text{m/s}^2 [/latex]
Kinematic viscosity [latex] \nu = 1 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{m}^2/\text{s} [/latex]

Using Stoke?s Law for settling velocity:
[latex] V_s = \frac{g (G - 1) d^2}{18 \nu} [/latex]
Setting [latex] V_s = \text{SOR} = 5.208 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{m/s} [/latex]
Solving for [latex] d [/latex]:
[latex] d = \sqrt{ \frac{18 \nu V_s}{g (G - 1)} } [/latex]

For inorganic particles (G = 2.65):
[latex] d = \sqrt{ \frac{18 \times 1 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.208 \times 10^{-4}}{9.81 \times (2.65 - 1)} } [/latex]
[latex] d \approx \sqrt{ \frac{9.3744 \times 10^{-9}}{16.0665} } \approx \sqrt{5.83 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 2.414 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{m} = 24.14 \, \mu\text{m} [/latex]

For organic particles (G = 1.20):
[latex] d = \sqrt{ \frac{18 \times 1 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.208 \times 10^{-4}}{9.81 \times (1.20 - 1)} } [/latex]
[latex] d \approx \sqrt{ \frac{9.3744 \times 10^{-9}}{1.962} } \approx \sqrt{4.78 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 6.91 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{m} = 69.1 \, \mu\text{m} [/latex]

Correct options:
(A) Minimum diameter of inorganic particles is 24 ?m
(B) Minimum diameter of organic particles is 69 ?m
options: Minimum diameter of inorganic particles is [latex]24 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
Minimum diameter of organic particles is [latex]69 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
Minimum diameter of inorganic particles is [latex]15 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
Minimum diameter of organic particles is [latex]55 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex]

option_texts: Minimum diameter of inorganic particles is [latex]24 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
Minimum diameter of organic particles is [latex]69 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Aeration is employed as a treatment option for the removal of several pollutants from contaminated water.
Identify the pollutant(s), where aeration is employed as a part of their removal:
raw_source.solution:
Aeration is a process where air is introduced into water to allow oxidation reactions to occur.
It is commonly used to oxidize soluble iron and manganese into insoluble forms, which can then be removed by filtration.

Let?s analyze the options:
(A) Iron - Aeration oxidizes [latex] \text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+} [/latex], which precipitates as [latex] \text{Fe(OH)}_3 [/latex].
(B) Cadmium - Not removed by aeration; it requires chemical precipitation or adsorption.
(C) Manganese - Aeration helps oxidize [latex] \text{Mn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{MnO}_2 [/latex] under suitable pH conditions.

raw_source.text: If the weights retained on the [latex]2.36 \mathrm{~mm}, 1.18 \mathrm{~mm}, 600 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex], and [latex]300 \mu \mathrm{~m}[/latex] sieves are [latex]30 \%[/latex], [latex]35 \%, 15 \%[/latex], and [latex]20 \%[/latex], respectively, of the total weight of an aggregate sample, then the fineness modulus of the sample is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
To calculate the Fineness Modulus (FM), we take the cumulative percentage retained on each standard sieve and divide the sum by 100.

Given weights retained:
On 2.36 mm sieve = 30%
On 1.18 mm sieve = 35%
On 600 [latex]\mu m[/latex] sieve = 15%
On 300 [latex]\mu m[/latex] sieve = 20%

Step 1: Compute cumulative percentages retained:
- 2.36 mm sieve: [latex] 30\% [/latex]
- 1.18 mm sieve: [latex] 30 + 35 = 65\% [/latex]
- 600 [latex]\mu m[/latex] sieve: [latex] 65 + 15 = 80\% [/latex]
- 300 [latex]\mu m[/latex] sieve: [latex] 80 + 20 = 100\% [/latex]

Step 2: Sum of cumulative percentages retained:
[latex] 30 + 65 + 80 + 100 = 275 [/latex]

Step 3: Fineness Modulus:
[latex] \text{FM} = \frac{275}{100} = 2.75 [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{2.75} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A water resources project with an expected life of 25 years has to be designed for an acceptable risk of [latex]5 \%[/latex] against a design flood. The return period for the design flood (in years) is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
To find the return period (T) for a given acceptable risk (R) over the project life (n), we use the formula:

[latex] R = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right)^n [/latex]

Given:
[latex] R = 0.05 [/latex] (5% acceptable risk)
[latex] n = 25 [/latex] years

Rearranging the formula to solve for T:
[latex] 0.05 = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right)^{25} [/latex]
[latex] \left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right)^{25} = 0.95 [/latex]
Taking natural log on both sides:
[latex] 25 \cdot \ln\left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right) = \ln(0.95) [/latex]
[latex] \ln\left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right) = \frac{\ln(0.95)}{25} [/latex]
[latex] 1 - \frac{1}{T} = e^{\frac{\ln(0.95)}{25}} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{T} = 1 - e^{\frac{\ln(0.95)}{25}} [/latex]
Now calculate:
[latex] \frac{1}{T} = 1 - e^{-0.002051} \approx 1 - 0.99795 = 0.00205 [/latex]
[latex] T = \frac{1}{0.00205} \approx 487.8 [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{488} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Road [latex]A[/latex] and Road [latex]B[/latex] are joined by a circular horizontal curve of radius 200 m as shown in the figure. Road [latex]A[/latex] and Road [latex]B[/latex] are tangential to the curve at the points [latex]C[/latex] and [latex]D[/latex], respectively. Had the curve not been there, straight roads [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] would have met at the point [latex]E[/latex]. The distance from [latex]C[/latex] to [latex]E[/latex] is 92 m . The value of angle [latex]\theta[/latex] (in degrees) is ________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).

Note: The value of angle is to be calculated only from the consideration of Euclidean geometry and the data given in the problem.
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] R = 200 , \text{m} [/latex] (radius of curve)
[latex] CE = 92 , \text{m} [/latex] (distance from C to E)

From geometry:
[latex] CE = R \cdot \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) [/latex]

Substitute values:
[latex] \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{92}{200} = 0.46 [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\theta}{2} = \tan^{-1}(0.46) \approx 24.8^\circ [/latex]
[latex] \theta = 2 \times 24.8^\circ = \boxed{49.6^\circ} [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \theta = 49.6^\circ [/latex]
