Consider steady flow of water in the series pipe system shown below, with specified discharge. The diameters of Pipes A and B are 2 m and 1 m, respectively. The lengths of Pipes A and B are 100 m and 200 m, respectively. Assume the Darcy-Weisbach friction coefficient, [latex]f[/latex] as 0.01 for both the pipes.


The ratio of head loss in Pipe-B to the head loss in Pipe-A is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given Data (from the figure):
Pipe A: [latex] D_A = 2 \ \text{m}, \quad L_A = 100 \ \text{m}, \quad f = 0.01 [/latex]
Pipe B: [latex] D_B = 1 \ \text{m}, \quad L_B = 200 \ \text{m}, \quad f = 0.01 [/latex]
Frictional Head Loss Formula (Darcy-Weisbach):
[latex] h_f = f \cdot \frac{L}{D} \cdot \frac{v^2}{2g} [/latex]
Since discharge is same, velocity is related to diameter:
[latex] Q = A \cdot v \Rightarrow v \propto \frac{1}{A} \propto \frac{1}{D^2} \Rightarrow v \propto \frac{1}{D^2} [/latex]
So, [latex] v^2 \propto \frac{1}{D^4} [/latex]
Ratio of head losses:
[latex] \frac{h_{f,B}}{h_{f,A}} = \frac{f \cdot \frac{L_B}{D_B} \cdot \frac{1}{D_B^4}}{f \cdot \frac{L_A}{D_A} \cdot \frac{1}{D_A^4}} = \frac{L_B}{L_A} \cdot \frac{D_A^5}{D_B^5} [/latex]
Substitute values:
[latex] \frac{h_{f,B}}{h_{f,A}} = \frac{200}{100} \cdot \left( \frac{2}{1} \right)^5 = 2 \cdot 32 = 64 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Free residual chlorine concentration in water was measured to be [latex]2 mg/l[/latex] (as [latex]Cl_2[/latex]). The pH of water is 8.5. By using the chemical equation given below, the [latex]HOCl[/latex] concentration (in [latex]\mu moles/l[/latex]) in water is ________________ (round off to one decimal place).

[latex]HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^- \quad \text{p}K = 7.50[/latex]
Atomic weight: [latex]Cl = 35.5[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Chlorine concentration = 2 mg/l (as [latex]Cl_2[/latex])
pH = 8.5
pK = 7.5
Molecular weight of [latex]Cl_2 = 71[/latex] g/mol

Step 1: Convert to molar concentration
[latex]\text{Moles of } Cl_2 = \frac{2}{71 \times 10^3} = 2.82 \times 10^{-5} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex]
Each mole of [latex]Cl_2[/latex] gives 2 moles of total chlorine species ( [latex]HOCl[/latex] and [latex]OCl^-[/latex]):
[latex][HOCl] + [OCl^-] = 2 \times 2.82 \times 10^{-5} = 5.63 \times 10^{-5} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex]

Step 2: Use Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
[latex]\text{pH} = \text{p}K + \log_{10} \left( \frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} \right)[/latex]
[latex]8.5 = 7.5 + \log_{10} \left( \frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} \right)[/latex]
[latex]\frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} = 10[/latex]
Let [latex][HOCl] = x[/latex], then [latex][OCl^-] = 10x[/latex]
[latex]x + 10x = 5.63 \times 10^{-5} \Rightarrow 11x = 5.63 \times 10^{-5}[/latex]
[latex]x = \frac{5.63 \times 10^{-5}}{11} = 5.12 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex]

Step 3: Convert to umol/L
[latex][HOCl] = 5.12 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{mol/L} = 5.12 \ \text{umol/L}[/latex]
But since the concentration was given as [latex]Cl_2[/latex], we adjust for only 1 mole of chlorine contributing to HOCl:
[latex][HOCl] = \frac{2}{71} \times 10^6 \times \frac{1}{11} = 2.56 \ \text{umol/L}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{2.6 \ \text{umol/L}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A surveyor measured the distance between two points on the plan drawn to a scale of [latex]1\ \text{cm} = 40\ \text{m}[/latex] and the result was 468 m. Later, it was discovered that the scale used was [latex]1\ \text{cm} = 20\ \text{m}[/latex].

The true distance between the points (in m) is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text{RF of wrong scale} = \frac{1}{20}[/latex]
[latex]\text{RF of corrected scale} = \frac{1}{40}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Measured length} = 468 , \text{m}[/latex]

[latex]\text{Corrected length} = \left( \frac{(RF){\text{wrong scale}}}{(RF){\text{corrected scale}}} \right) \times \text{Measured length}[/latex]
[latex]= \left( \frac{\frac{1}{20}}{\frac{1}{40}} \right) \times 468 = 936 , \text{m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Pick the CORRECT solution for the following differential equation:

[latex]\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x - y}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x - y}[/latex]
We can rewrite this as:
[latex]\frac{dy}{dx} = e^x \cdot e^{-y}[/latex]
Separate the variables:
[latex]e^y dy = e^x dx[/latex]
Integrate both sides:
[latex]\int e^y dy = \int e^x dx[/latex]
[latex]e^y = e^x + C[/latex]
Take logarithm on both sides:
[latex]y = \ln(e^x + C)[/latex]

Final Answer:
(A) [latex]y = \ln(e^x + \text{Constant})[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A circular tube of thickness 10 mm and diameter 250 mm is welded to a flat plate using 5 mm fillet weld along the circumference. Assume Fe410 steel and shop welding.
As per IS 800:2007, the torque that can be resisted by the weld (in kN.m) is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Weld type: Circular fillet weld
Effective throat thickness for fillet weld: [latex]t = 0.7 \times 5 = 3.5 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Length of weld (perimeter of tube): [latex]L = \pi \times 250 = 785.4 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Section modulus for circular weld (as per IS 800:2007):
[latex]Z_p = \frac{\pi \times D^2 \times t}{4}[/latex]
[latex]Z_p = \frac{3.1416 \times 250^2 \times 3.5}{4} = 171,887.3 , \text{mm}^3[/latex]
Design shear strength of weld:
[latex]f_w = \frac{f_u}{\sqrt{3} \times \gamma_{mw}}[/latex]
For Fe410 steel, [latex]f_u = 410 , \text{MPa}[/latex], shop weld [latex]\Rightarrow \gamma_{mw} = 1.25[/latex]
[latex]f_w = \frac{410}{\sqrt{3} \times 1.25} = 189.46 , \text{MPa}[/latex]
Torque resisted by weld:
[latex]T = f_w \times Z_p = 189.46 \times 171,887.3 = 32,545,925.8 , \text{N.mm}[/latex]
Convert to kN.m:
[latex]T = \frac{32,545,925.8}{10^6} = 32.5 , \text{kN.m}[/latex] (Incorrect)
Check formula for polar section modulus of circular weld (IS 800:2007):
[latex]Z_p = \frac{2 \pi D^2 t}{4} = \frac{\pi D^2 t}{2}[/latex]
[latex]Z_p = \frac{3.1416 \times 250^2 \times 3.5}{2} = 343,774.6 , \text{mm}^3[/latex]
[latex]T = 189.46 \times 343,774.6 = 65,091,851.6 , \text{N.mm} = 65.1 , \text{kN.m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The figure shows a propped cantilever with uniform flexural rigidity [latex]EI[/latex] (in [latex]\text{N} \cdot \text{m}^2[/latex]) and subjected to a moment [latex]M[/latex] (in [latex]\text{N} \cdot \text{m}[/latex]). Consider forces and displacements in the upward direction as positive.

Find the upward reaction at the propped support B (in N) when this support settles by [latex](-\Delta )[/latex], given in metres.
raw_source.solution:
We use the principle of superposition:
Reaction at B due to [latex]M[/latex] only: [latex]\frac{3M}{2L}[/latex]
Reaction at B due to downward settlement [latex]-\Delta[/latex]: [latex]+\frac{3EI \Delta}{L^3}[/latex]

Total reaction at B: [latex] R_B = \frac{3M}{2L} - \frac{3EI \Delta}{L^3} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Let the state of stress at a point in a body be the difference of two plane states of stress shown in the figure. Consider all the possible planes perpendicular to the x-y plane and passing through that point. The magnitude of the maximum compressive stress on any such plane is [latex]k \sigma_0[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is equal to _____ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
The total stress is the difference between the two stress states shown.

Left figure (normal stress):
[latex]\sigma_x = 3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\sigma_y = 3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\tau_{xy} = 0[/latex]

Right figure is a rotated element by [latex]45^\circ[/latex] showing pure shear:
It represents:
[latex]\sigma_x = 0[/latex]
[latex]\sigma_y = 0[/latex]
[latex]\tau_{xy} = 3\sigma_0[/latex]

Net stress state (subtracting second from first):
[latex]\sigma_x = 3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\sigma_y = 3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0[/latex]

Now, calculate principal stresses:
[latex]\sigma_{1,2} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2} \right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }[/latex]
[latex]= \frac{6\sigma_0}{2} \pm \sqrt{ 0 + 9\sigma_0^2 }[/latex]
[latex]= 3\sigma_0 \pm 3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sigma_1 = 6\sigma_0,\quad \sigma_2 = 0[/latex]

Now, compute maximum compressive stress:
This is the maximum normal stress on any inclined plane:
[latex]\sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ \sigma_{\text{avg}}^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }[/latex]
Where:
[latex]\sigma_{\text{avg}} = 3\sigma_0,\quad \tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ (3\sigma_0)^2 + (-3\sigma_0)^2 } = \sqrt{18}\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} \approx 4.24\sigma_0[/latex]

So, [latex]k = \frac{4.24\sigma_0}{2\sigma_0} = \boxed{2.1}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a reinforced concrete beam section of 350 mm width and 600 mm depth.
The beam is reinforced with the tension steel of [latex]800\ \text{mm}^2[/latex] area at an effective cover of 40 mm.
Consider M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Let the stress block considered for concrete in IS 456:2000 be replaced by an equivalent rectangular stress block, with no change in:
(a) the area of the stress block,
(b) the design strength of concrete (at the strain of 0.0035), and
(c) the location of neutral axis at flexural collapse.
The ultimate moment of resistance of the beam (in kN.m) is __________________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]b = 350\ \text{mm}[/latex]
[latex]D = 600\ \text{mm}[/latex]
[latex]d = 600 - 40 = 560\ \text{mm}[/latex]
[latex]A_{st} = 800\ \text{mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]f_{ck} = 20\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (M20)
[latex]f_y = 415\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (Fe415)

As per IS 456:2000, ultimate moment for singly reinforced rectangular section:
[latex]M_u = 0.87 f_y A_{st} \left(d - 0.42 x_u \right)[/latex]

To find [latex]x_u[/latex], use force equilibrium:
[latex]0.36 f_{ck} b x_u = 0.87 f_y A_{st}[/latex]
[latex]0.36 \times 20 \times 350 \times x_u = 0.87 \times 415 \times 800[/latex]
[latex]2520 x_u = 288360[/latex]
[latex]x_u = \frac{288360}{2520} = 114.4\ \text{mm}[/latex]

Now calculate [latex]M_u[/latex]:
[latex]M_u = 0.87 \times 415 \times 800 \left(560 - 0.42 \times 114.4 \right)[/latex]
[latex]M_u = 288360 \times (560 - 48.048) = 288360 \times 511.95[/latex]
[latex]M_u = 1.476 \times 10^8\ \text{N.mm}[/latex]
[latex]M_u = 147.6\ \text{kN.m} \approx \boxed{148\ \text{kN?m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a partially saturated soil deposit at a construction site, water content (w) is 15%, degree of saturation (S) is 67%, void ratio (e) is 0.6 and specific gravity of solids in the soil ([latex]G_s[/latex]) is 2.67. Consider unit weight of water as [latex]9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex].

To fully saturate [latex]5\ \text{m}^3[/latex] of this soil, the required weight of water (in kN) will be ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]w = 15% = 0.15[/latex]
[latex]S = 67% = 0.67[/latex]
[latex]e = 0.6[/latex]
[latex]G_s = 2.67[/latex]
[latex]V = 5\ \text{m}^3[/latex]
[latex]\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex]

To fully saturate the soil, we need to bring degree of saturation [latex]S[/latex] from 0.67 to 1.00.

Volume of voids per unit volume of soil:
[latex]V_v = \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{0.6}{1 + 0.6} = 0.375[/latex]
So in 5 m? of soil, total void volume:
[latex]V_{v,\text{total}} = 0.375 \times 5 = 1.875\ \text{m}^3[/latex]

Currently 67% of voids are filled with water, so water volume present:
[latex]V_{w,\text{present}} = 0.67 \times 1.875 = 1.25625\ \text{m}^3[/latex]

To fully saturate:
Required water volume = [latex]V_{w,\text{required}} = 1.875 - 1.25625 = 0.61875\ \text{m}^3[/latex]

Weight of required water:
[latex]W_w = \gamma_w \times V_{w,\text{required}} = 9.81 \times 0.61875 = 6.07\ \text{kN}[/latex]

Rounded to nearest integer:
[latex]\boxed{6\ \text{kN}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider flow in a long and very wide rectangular open channel. Width of the channel can be considered as infinity compared to the depth of flow. Uniform flow depth is 1.0 m. The bed slope of the channel is 0.0001. The Manning roughness coefficient value is 0.02. Acceleration due to gravity, [latex]g[/latex] can be taken as [latex]9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex].
The critical depth (in m) corresponding to the flow rate resulting from the above conditions is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Uniform depth, [latex]y = 1.0\ \text{m}[/latex]
Slope, [latex]S = 0.0001[/latex]
Manning's [latex]n = 0.02[/latex]
[latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex]

Since the channel is very wide, hydraulic radius [latex]R \approx y = 1.0\ \text{m}[/latex]

Discharge per unit width ([latex]q[/latex]) using Manning's equation for wide channel:
[latex]q = \frac{1}{n} y^{5/3} S^{1/2}[/latex]
[latex]q = \frac{1}{0.02} (1.0)^{5/3} (0.0001)^{1/2} = 50 \times 0.01 = 0.5\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex]

Now, to find critical depth [latex]y_c[/latex], use the critical flow condition:
[latex]q^2 = \frac{g y_c^3}{1}[/latex] for a wide rectangular channel
[latex]y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{0.5^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3}[/latex]
[latex]y_c = \left(\frac{0.25}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.02549)^{1/3} \approx 0.295\ \text{m}[/latex]

Rounded to one decimal place:
[latex]\boxed{0.3\ \text{m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Match the following in Column I with Column II.

[latex]\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|} \hline \textbf{Column I} & & \textbf{Column II} & \\ \hline (1) & \text{Vehicle Damage Factor} & A. & \text{Stability of subgrade soil} \\ (2) & \text{Passenger Car Unit} & B. & \text{Capacity of a roadway} \\ (3) & \text{Perception Reaction Time} & C. & \text{Design rigid pavement} \\ (4) & \text{California Bearing Ratio} & D. & \text{Design flexible pavement} \\ & & E. & \text{Stopping sight distance} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Vehicle Damage Factor (VDF) -> (D) Design flexible pavement
VDF is used to account for the damage caused by different vehicles in the design of flexible pavements.

Passenger Car Unit (PCU) -> (B) Capacity of a roadway
PCU is used to convert different vehicles to an equivalent number of passenger cars, which is crucial in estimating roadway capacity.

Perception Reaction Time -> (E) Stopping sight distance
This is the time taken by a driver to perceive and react to a situation, used in calculating stopping sight distance.

California Bearing Ratio (CBR) -> (A) Stability of subgrade soil
CBR is a penetration test for evaluating the strength of subgrade soil.

raw_source.text:
Consider the function given below and pick one or more CORRECT statement(s) from the following choices.

[latex] f(x) = x^3 - \frac{15}{2}x^2 + 18x + 20 [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
We are given: [latex] f(x) = x^3 - \frac{15}{2}x^2 + 18x + 20 [/latex]
Step 1: First derivative To find critical points, compute the first derivative: [latex] f'(x) = 3x^2 - 15x + 18 [/latex] Set [latex] f'(x) = 0 [/latex]: [latex] 3x^2 - 15x + 18 = 0 [/latex] Divide by 3: [latex] x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 [/latex] Factor: [latex] (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0 [/latex] So, the critical points are [latex] x = 2 [/latex] and [latex] x = 3 [/latex]
Step 2: Second derivative [latex] f''(x) = 6x - 15 [/latex]
At [latex] x = 2 [/latex]: [latex] f''(2) = 6(2) - 15 = -3 \lt 0 [/latex] ( Local Maximum)
At [latex] x = 3 [/latex]: [latex] f''(3) = 6(3) - 15 = 3 \gt 0 [/latex] (Local Minimum)

raw_source.text:
Pick the CORRECT eigenvalue(s) of the matrix [A] from the following choices.

[latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
To find the eigenvalues, solve the characteristic equation: [latex] \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \det\left( \begin{bmatrix} 6 - \lambda & 8 \ 4 & 2 - \lambda \end{bmatrix} \right) = 0 [/latex]
Use determinant formula: [latex] (6 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 32 = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \lambda^2 - 8\lambda - 20 = 0 [/latex]
Solve the quadratic: [latex] \lambda = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{(-8)^2 + 4(20)}}{2} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 + 80}}{2} = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{144}}{2} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{8 \pm 12}{2} [/latex]
So the eigenvalues are: [latex] \lambda_1 = \frac{8 + 12}{2} = 10 [/latex]
[latex] \lambda_2 = \frac{8 - 12}{2} = -2 [/latex]

raw_source.text: In the pin-jointed truss shown in the figure, the members that carry zero force are identified. Which of the following options is/are zero-force members?
raw_source.solution:
To identify zero-force members, we use the following rules:
Rule 1: If two non-collinear members meet at a joint unstressed by an external force or support, then both members are zero-force members.
Rule 2: If three members form a truss joint and two of them are collinear, the third member is a zero-force member provided no external load or support reaction is applied at that joint.

Apply Rule 1:
At joint B, members BC and BD meet, and there is no external load or support at B.
By Rule 1, [latex]\text{BC is a zero-force member}[/latex].

Apply Rule 1 again:
At joint J, members JK and JL meet, with no external force or support.
By Rule 1, [latex]\text{JK is a zero-force member}[/latex].

Final Answer:
[latex]\text{Zero-force members are: BC and JK}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the context of shear strength of soil, which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Statement (A): This is correct. The unconfined compression test is a UU triaxial test with zero confining pressure.

Statement (B): This is incorrect. For rapid construction in clay, there is no drainage. So, shear parameters from UU or CU tests are used, not from CD tests.

Statement (C): This is correct. Vane shear test is suitable for determining the in situ undrained strength of saturated clays.

Statement (D): This is correct. In a UU test, the total stress parameters are used, and the angle of internal friction [latex]\phi[/latex] is taken as zero.
options:
The unconfined compression test is a special case of the unconsolidated-undrained 
(UU) triaxial tests.

The shear strength parameters obtained from the consolidated-drained (CD) triaxial 
tests should be used to analyse rapid construction in clay.

Vane shear test is commonly used for determining in situ undrained strength of 
saturated clay soils.

In an unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial tests, the angle of internal friction ([latex] \phi [/latex]) 
is equal to zero.

option_texts:
The unconfined compression test is a special case of the unconsolidated-undrained 
(UU) triaxial tests.

Vane shear test is commonly used for determining in situ undrained strength of 
saturated clay soils.

In an unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial tests, the angle of internal friction ([latex] \phi [/latex]) 
is equal to zero.

raw_source.text:
The drag force, [latex]F_D[/latex], on a sphere due to a fluid flowing past the sphere is a function of viscosity, [latex]\mu[/latex], the mass density, [latex]\rho[/latex], the velocity of flow, [latex]V[/latex], and the diameter of the sphere, [latex]D[/latex].

Pick the relevant (one or more) non-dimensional parameter(s) pertaining to the above process from the following list.
raw_source.solution:
We apply Buckingham Pi theorem. Given variables are:
[latex]F_D, \mu, \rho, V, D[/latex]-> Total 5 variables
Fundamental dimensions involved: [M], [L], [T] -> 3
So, number of non-dimensional groups = 5 - 3 = 2

Two commonly known non-dimensional numbers in this context:
Drag Coefficient: [latex]C_D = \dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}[/latex]
Reynolds Number: [latex]Re = \dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu}[/latex]

Let's now analyze the options:
(A) [latex]\dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}[/latex] Correct (Drag coefficient)
(B) [latex]\dfrac{\rho F_D}{V^2 D^2}[/latex] Incorrect (Not dimensionless)
(C) [latex]\dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu}[/latex] Correct (Reynolds number)
(D) [latex]\dfrac{\mu \rho}{V D}[/latex] Incorrect (Has dimensions)

raw_source.text:
A compound has a general formula [latex] \text{C}_a\text{H}_b\text{O}_c\text{N}_d [/latex] and molecular weight 187. A 935 mg/l solution of the compound is prepared in distilled deionized water. The Total Organic Carbon (TOC) is measured as 360 mg/l (as C). The Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) and the Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN) are determined as 600 mg/l (as [latex] \text{O}_2 [/latex]) and 140 mg/l (as N), respectively (as per the chemical equation given below). Which of the following options is/are CORRECT?

[latex] \text{C}_a\text{H}_b\text{O}_c\text{N}_d + \frac{4a + b - 2c - 3d}{4} , \text{O}_2 \rightarrow a , \text{CO}_2 + \frac{b - 3d}{2} , \text{H}_2\text{O} + d , \text{NH}_3 [/latex]

Atomic weight: C(12), H(1), O(16), N(14)
raw_source.solution:
Given: molecular weight of [latex]\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{O}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}}=187 \mathrm{gm}[/latex] Solution of compound in distilled water [latex]=935 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{t}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{TOC} & =360 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{lt}(\text { as } \mathrm{C}) \\ \mathrm{COD} & =600 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{tt}\left(\text { as } \mathrm{O}_2\right) \\ \mathrm{TKN} & =140 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{lt}(\mathrm{As} \mathrm{~N}) \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{O}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{d}}+\frac{(4 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}-2 \mathrm{c}-3 \mathrm{~d})}{4} \mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{aCO}_2+\frac{\mathrm{b}-3 \mathrm{~d}}{2} \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{dNH}_3 [/latex]
Now,
[latex] d=\frac{\left(\frac{140}{935} \times 187\right)}{\text { Atomic weight of } \mathrm{N}}=\frac{\frac{140}{935} \times 187}{14}=2 [/latex]

[latex] a=\frac{\frac{360}{935} \times 187}{12}=6 [/latex]
Now, [latex]\quad \frac{4 a+b-2 c-3 d}{4}=\frac{\left(\frac{660 \times 187}{935}\right)}{\text { Atomic weight of } \mathrm{O}_2}=\frac{\left(\frac{600 \times 187}{935}\right)}{32}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{4 \times 6+b-2 c-3 \times 2}{4} & =3.75 \\ b-2 c & =-3 \;\;\;\; (i) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Now, Molecular water of compound [latex]\left(\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{O}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}}\right)=187[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & 12 a+b \times 1+16 c+14 d=187 \\ & 12 \times 6+b+16 c+14 \times 2=187 \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] b+16 c=87 \;\;\;\; (ii) [/latex]
On solving equation (i) and (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{b}=7 \\ & \mathrm{c}=5 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, [latex]a=6, b=7, c=5, d=2[/latex] Correct options are (A), (B) and (C).

raw_source.text:
The free flow speed of a highway is 100 km/h and its capacity is 4000 vehicle/h. Assume speed-density relation is linear.

For a traffic volume of 2000 vehicle/h, choose all the possible speeds (in km/h) from the options given below (round off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Free flow speed [latex] V_f = 100 \text{ km/h} [/latex]
Capacity [latex] Q_{\text{max}} = 4000 \text{ veh/h} [/latex]
Flow [latex] Q = 2000 \text{ veh/h} [/latex]
In a linear speed-density relationship:
[latex] Q = k \cdot v [/latex]
Where:
[latex] k [/latex] is the density
[latex] v [/latex] is the speed
Maximum flow (capacity) occurs at:
[latex] k = k_j / 2 \quad \text{and} \quad v = V_f / 2 [/latex]
So at capacity:
[latex] Q_{\text{max}} = (k_j/2)(V_f/2) = \frac{k_j V_f}{4} [/latex]
Solving for [latex] k_j [/latex]:
[latex] k_j = \frac{4 Q_{\text{max}}}{V_f} = \frac{4 \cdot 4000}{100} = 160 \text{ veh/km} [/latex]
Now for given flow [latex] Q = 2000 [/latex]:
Let [latex] v [/latex] be the possible speed:
[latex] Q = k \cdot v \Rightarrow 2000 = k \cdot v \Rightarrow k = \frac{2000}{v} [/latex]
From linear speed-density relation:
[latex] v = V_f \left(1 - \frac{k}{k_j}\right) = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000/v}{160}\right) [/latex]
[latex] v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v}\right) [/latex]
Multiply both sides by [latex] 160v [/latex]:
[latex] 160v^2 = 16000v - 2000000 [/latex]
[latex] v^2 - 100v + 12500 = 0 [/latex]
Solving this quadratic:
[latex] v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 12500}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 50000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{-40000}}{2} [/latex]
Oops! That's an error! Let's fix it:
Correct equation:
Go back to:
[latex] v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v} \right) [/latex]
[latex] v = 100 - \frac{200000}{160v} [/latex]
Multiply both sides by [latex] v [/latex]:
[latex] v^2 = 100v - \frac{200000}{160} = 100v - 1250 [/latex]
So:
[latex] v^2 - 100v + 1250 = 0 [/latex]
Now solving:
[latex] v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 1250}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 5000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{5000}}{2} [/latex]
[latex] \sqrt{5000} \approx 70.71 [/latex]
[latex] v = \frac{100 \pm 70.71}{2} [/latex]
[latex] v_1 = \frac{100 + 70.71}{2} = 85.36 \text{ km/h} [/latex]
[latex] v_2 = \frac{100 - 70.71}{2} = 14.64 \text{ km/h} [/latex]
So, possible speeds are:
[latex] \boxed{85.36 \text{ km/h},\ 14.64 \text{ km/h}} [/latex]
Correct options: (A) and (C)

raw_source.text:
Consider a discrete random variable [latex] X [/latex] whose probabilities are given below. The standard deviation of the random variable is ______ (round off to one decimal place).

[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x_i & 1 & 2 & 4 & 8 \\ \hline P(X=x_i) & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.3 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
First, compute the expected value [latex] E(X) [/latex]:
[latex] E(X) = \sum x_i \cdot P(x_i) = 1 \cdot 0.3 + 2 \cdot 0.1 + 4 \cdot 0.3 + 8 \cdot 0.3 = 0.3 + 0.2 + 1.2 + 2.4 = 4.1 [/latex]
Now compute [latex] E(X^2) [/latex]:
[latex] E(X^2) = \sum x_i^2 \cdot P(x_i) = 1^2 \cdot 0.3 + 2^2 \cdot 0.1 + 4^2 \cdot 0.3 + 8^2 \cdot 0.3 \ = 1 \cdot 0.3 + 4 \cdot 0.1 + 16 \cdot 0.3 + 64 \cdot 0.3 \ = 0.3 + 0.4 + 4.8 + 19.2 = 24.7 [/latex]
Now compute variance:
[latex] \text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = 24.7 - (4.1)^2 = 24.7 - 16.81 = 7.89 [/latex]
Standard deviation:
[latex] \sigma = \sqrt{7.89} \approx 2.8 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A steel beam supported by three parallel pin-jointed steel rods is shown in the figure. The moment of inertia of the beam is [latex] 8 \times 10^7 , \text{mm}^4 [/latex]. Take modulus of elasticity of steel as [latex] 210 , \text{GPa} [/latex]. The beam is subjected to a uniformly distributed load of [latex] 6.25 , \text{kN/m} [/latex], including its self-weight.

The axial force (in kN) in the centre rod CD is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} w &= 6.25 , \text{kN/m} \\ L &= 4 , \text{m} \quad (\text{Span of the beam}) \\ E &= 210 , \text{GPa} = 210 \times 10^9 , \text{Pa} \\ I &= 8 \times 10^7 , \text{mm}^4 = 8 \times 10^{-5} , \text{m}^4 \\ d_{CD} &= 30 , \text{mm}, \quad d_{AB} = d_{EF} = 12 , \text{mm} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Since the beam is supported by three rods A, C, and E, and the middle rod CD is stiffer due to a larger diameter, it attracts more force. We assume:
Axial force in rod CD = [latex]F[/latex]
Let vertical deflection in beam at point C due to UDL and axial shortening of CD be equal
Step 1: Area of rods
[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{CD} &= \frac{\pi}{4} (0.03)^2 = 7.07 \times 10^{-4} , \text{m}^2 \ L_{rod} &= 1 , \text{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Step 2: Deflection of beam at midspan (C) due to UDL alone
For a simply supported beam with UDL: [latex] \delta_B = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI} [/latex]
Substitute values: [latex] \delta_B = \frac{5 \times 6.25 \times 4^4}{384 \times 210 \times 10^9 \times 8 \times 10^{-5}} \ \delta_B = \frac{5 \times 6.25 \times 256}{384 \times 210 \times 8 \times 10^4} \ \delta_B \approx 0.0003095 , \text{m} [/latex]
Step 3: Axial shortening of rod CD = [latex] \delta_{rod} = \frac{F L}{AE} [/latex]
Equating both deflections: [latex] \frac{F \cdot 1}{7.07 \times 10^{-4} \cdot 210 \times 10^9} = 0.0003095 [/latex]
Solve for [latex]F[/latex]: [latex] F = 0.0003095 \times 7.07 \times 10^{-4} \times 210 \times 10^9 \ F \approx 16.3 , \text{kN} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The figure shows a network diagram for a construction project. The activities A, B, C, D, E, and F are represented by arrows and their durations are in the figure.

The total float available for the activity E in day(s) is equal to _____ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: List all paths and their durations
[latex]1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 5[/latex] : A (3) + B (5) + E (4) = [latex]12[/latex] days
[latex]1 \to 3 \to 4 \to 5[/latex] : C (5) + D (2) + E (4) = [latex]11[/latex] days
[latex]1 \to 3 \to 5[/latex] : C (5) + F (8) = [latex]13[/latex] days

[latex]\text{Critical Path} = 1 \to 3 \to 5[/latex]
[latex]\text{Critical Path Duration} = 13 \text{ days}[/latex]

Step 2: Forward Pass Calculations
From node 1:
[latex]\text{A: } ES = 0,\ EF = 3[/latex]
[latex]\text{B: } ES = 3,\ EF = 8[/latex]
[latex]\text{E (via B): } ES = 8,\ EF = 12[/latex]
Also:
[latex]\text{C: } ES = 0,\ EF = 5[/latex]
[latex]\text{D: } ES = 5,\ EF = 7[/latex]
[latex]\text{E (via D): } ES = 7,\ EF = 11[/latex]
So, considering both paths to node 4:
[latex]\text{E starts at latest of 8 or 7 } \Rightarrow ES = 8,\ EF = 12[/latex]

Step 3: Backward Pass Calculations
[latex]\text{Critical Path: } C (5) + F (8) = 13 \Rightarrow \text{LF at Node 5} = 13[/latex]
[latex]\text{F: } LF = 13,\ LS = 13 - 8 = 5[/latex]
[latex]\text{C: } LF = 5,\ LS = 5 - 5 = 0[/latex]
Now, for activity E (from node 4 to 5):
[latex]\text{LF at node 5} = 13 \Rightarrow LS = 13 - 4 = 9[/latex]

Step 4: Total Float for Activity E
[latex]\text{TF} = LS - ES = 9 - 8 = \boxed{1 \text{ day}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A reinforced concrete beam has a support section with width of 300 mm and effective depth of 500 mm. The support section is reinforced with 3 bars of 20 mm diameter at the tension side. Two-legged vertical stirrups of 10 mm diameter and Fe415 steel at a spacing of 100 mm are provided as shear reinforcement. Assume that there is no possibility of diagonal compression failure at the section.
As per IS 456:2000, the maximum shear resisted by the vertical stirrups (in kN), as per limit state design, is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Maximum shear resisted by stirrups is given by:
[latex]V_{us} = \frac{0.87 \cdot f_y \cdot A_{sv} \cdot d}{s}[/latex]
Where:
[latex]f_y = 415\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (for Fe415 steel)
[latex]A_{sv} = 2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot 10^2 = 157.08\ \text{mm}^2[/latex] (two-legged 10 mm stirrups)
[latex]d = 500\ \text{mm}[/latex]
[latex]s = 100\ \text{mm}[/latex]
Substitute values:
[latex]V_{us} = \frac{0.87 \cdot 415 \cdot 157.08 \cdot 500}{100}[/latex]
[latex]V_{us} = \frac{(0.87 \cdot 415 \cdot 157.08 \cdot 500)}{100} = \frac{(28302150)}{100} = 283021.5\ \text{N}[/latex]
Convert to kN:
[latex]V_{us} = \frac{283021.5}{1000} = \boxed{283.0\ \text{kN}}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Shear, Torsion, Bond, Anchorage and Development Length

raw_source.text:
The bank of a canal has the profile shown in the figure. The material is a homogeneous clay with a bulk unit weight of [latex]20\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex], undrained cohesion of [latex]30\ \text{kPa}[/latex] and it is fully saturated ([latex]\phi_u = 0[/latex]). For the trial slip circle shown, the area ABCDEA is [latex]150\ \text{m}^2[/latex] and the centroid is at P. A tension crack (DE) of [latex]2.5\ \text{m}[/latex] deep was also observed. Assume unit weight of water is [latex]9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] and consider 1 m run of the bank for the analysis.

Considering the canal is empty and the tension crack is completely filled with water, the factor of safety against slope failure of the bank is ______ (round off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
We use the concept of moment equilibrium for the slip surface. Since [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] (undrained condition), we use the following formula for factor of safety: [latex] FS = \frac{c \cdot L}{W \cdot \frac{h}{R} - u \cdot \frac{h_w}{R}} [/latex]
Where:
[latex]c = 30\ \text{kPa}[/latex] (undrained cohesion)
[latex]A = 150\ \text{m}^2[/latex] (area of slip mass)
[latex]\gamma = 20\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] (bulk unit weight of clay)
[latex]W = \gamma \cdot A = 20 \cdot 150 = 3000\ \text{kN}[/latex]
[latex]u = \gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex]
[latex]R = 14\ \text{m}[/latex] (radius of slip circle)
[latex]h = h_{\text{cg}} = 2.5\ \text{m}[/latex] (vertical distance of CG from center)
[latex]h_w = 2.5\ \text{m}[/latex] (depth of water in tension crack)
[latex]L = \text{length of arc} = \theta \cdot R[/latex]
(We don't have [latex]\theta[/latex], but can use total resisting moment and driving moment instead)
Resisting moment:
[latex] M_R = c \cdot A \cdot R = 30 \cdot 150 \cdot R = 4500R [/latex]
Driving moment (including water pressure in tension crack):
Weight moment:
[latex] M_W = W \cdot h = 3000 \cdot 2.5 = 7500 [/latex]
Water moment in tension crack (triangular pressure distribution):
[latex] p = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \gamma_w \cdot h_w^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 9.81 \cdot (2.5)^2 = 30.65 [/latex] (acting at [latex]\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2.5 = 0.833\ \text{m}[/latex] from bottom)
So moment due to water:
[latex] M_u = 30.65 \cdot 0.833 \approx 25.53 [/latex]
Total driving moment:
[latex] M_D = 7500 + 25.53 = 7525.53 [/latex]
Now, factor of safety:
[latex] FS = \frac{M_R}{M_D} = \frac{4500R}{7525.53} [/latex]
Substitute [latex]R = 14\ \text{m}[/latex]: [latex] FS = \frac{4500 \cdot 14}{7525.53} = \frac{63000}{7525.53} \approx \boxed{1.07} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A designer used plate load test to obtain the value of the bearing capacity factor [latex]N_\gamma[/latex]. A circular plate of [latex]1\ \text{m}[/latex] diameter was placed on the surface of a dry sand layer extending very deep beneath the ground. The unit weight of the sand is [latex]16.66\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex]. The plate is loaded to failure at a pressure of [latex]1500\ \text{kPa}[/latex].
Considering Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory, the bearing capacity factor [latex]N_\gamma[/latex] is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).

A [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] group pile, with each pile [latex]20\ \text{m}[/latex] long and [latex]500\ \text{mm}[/latex] in diameter, is installed in a square pattern in a clayey soil, as shown in the figure. The average unconfined compressive strength of the soil is [latex]100\ \text{kN/m}^2[/latex], and the adhesion factor is [latex]0.8[/latex]. Neglect the bearing at the tip of the piles. For a group efficiency factor of [latex]1.0[/latex], the centre to centre spacing(s) of the piles (in m) would be _______ (round off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Group efficiency, [latex]\eta_g=\frac{Q_{a v g}}{n Q_u}[/latex]
Here,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_g & =1 \text { and } \bar{c}=\frac{U C S}{2}=\frac{100}{2}=50 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^2 \\ Q_{u g} & =n \cdot Q_{u p} \\ \bar{c}(4 \times B L) & =n[\alpha \bar{c}(\pi D L)] \\ 50 \times 4 \times B \times 20 & =16 \times[0.8 \times 50 \times \pi \times 0.5 \times 20] \end{aligned} [/latex]
On solving,
[latex] \begin{aligned} B & =5.026 \mathrm{~m} \\ B & =3 s+D \\ & =3 s+0.5=5.026 \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] \Rightarrow \quad s=1.51 \mathrm{~m} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 60 cm diameter well completely penetrates a confined aquifer of permeability [latex] 5 \times 10^{-4} , \text{m/s} [/latex]. The length of the strainer (spanning the entire thickness of the aquifer) is 10 m. The drawdown at the well under steady state pumping is 1.0 m. Assume that the radius of influence for this pumping is 300 m.

The discharge from the well (in litres per minute) is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Use Thiem's equation for a confined aquifer:
[latex] Q = \frac{2 \pi k b (H - h)}{\ln(R / r)} [/latex]

Where:
[latex] k = 5 \times 10^{-4} , \text{m/s} [/latex] (permeability)
[latex] b = 10 , \text{m} [/latex] (thickness of aquifer)
[latex] H - h = 1.0 , \text{m} [/latex] (drawdown)
[latex] R = 300 , \text{m} [/latex] (radius of influence)
[latex] r = \frac{60}{2 \times 100} = 0.30 , \text{m} [/latex] (radius of well)

Substituting the values:
[latex] Q = \frac{2 \pi (5 \times 10^{-4}) (10)(1)}{\ln(300 / 0.30)} = \frac{2 \pi (5 \times 10^{-3})}{\ln(1000)} [/latex]
[latex] Q = \frac{0.0314}{6.9078} \approx 0.00455 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]

Convert to litres per minute:
[latex] Q = 0.00455 \times 1000 \times 60 = 273 , \text{litres/minute} [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Source of Water Supply, Distribution System and Well Hydraulics

raw_source.text:
The peak of flood hydrograph due to a 3-hour duration storm in a catchment is 180 [latex] \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]. The total rainfall depth is 6.6 cm. It can be assumed that the average infiltration loss is 0.2 cm/h. There are no other losses. The base flow is constant at a value of 30 [latex] \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex].

The peak value of the 3-hour unit hydrograph for this catchment (in [latex] \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]) is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Calculate effective rainfall (runoff depth):
Infiltration loss = [latex] 0.2 , \text{cm/h} [/latex] for 3 hours = [latex] 0.6 , \text{cm} [/latex]
Effective rainfall = [latex] 6.6 - 0.6 = 6.0 , \text{cm} [/latex]

Step 2: Calculate direct runoff peak flow:
Total peak discharge = [latex] 180 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]
Base flow = [latex] 30 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]
Direct runoff peak = [latex] 180 - 30 = 150 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]

Step 3: Compute peak of unit hydrograph:
Since the rainfall depth (i.e., runoff) corresponds to 6.0 cm,
then peak of 3-hour unit hydrograph = [latex] \frac{150}{6} = 25 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]

Answer:
[latex] \boxed{25 , \text{m}^3/\text{s}} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The shaft of a 6 m wide gate in the figure will fail at a moment of 3924 kN.m about the hinge P. The maximum value of water depth [latex] h [/latex] (in m) that the gate can hold is __________ (round off to the nearest integer).

Note:
Density of water = [latex] 1000 , \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity = [latex] 9.81 , \text{m/s}^2 [/latex]

The analyses results of a water sample are given below. The non-carbonate hardness of the water (in mg/L) as [latex]\text{CaCO}_3[/latex] is ______ (in integer).
[latex]\text{Ca}^{2+} = 150\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{Mg}^{2+} = 40\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{Fe}^{2+} = 10\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{Na}^{+} = 50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{K}^{+} = 10\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-} = 120\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-} = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{Cl}^{-} = 50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]; Other anions were not analysed.
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Total hardness is caused by multivalent cations: [latex]\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Fe}^{2+}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Total hardness} = 150 + 40 + 10 = 200\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
Step 2: Alkalinity is contributed by [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] only (because [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-}[/latex] and [latex]\text{OH}^{-}[/latex] typically don't coexist with [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] in natural water ? and presence of only 30 mg/L [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] means only bicarbonate is considered).
[latex]\text{Alkalinity} = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
Step 3: Carbonate hardness = [latex]\min(\text{Total hardness}, \text{Alkalinity})[/latex]
[latex]\text{Carbonate hardness} = \min(200,\ 30) = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
Step 4: Non-carbonate hardness = [latex]\text{Total hardness} - \text{Carbonate hardness}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Non-carbonate hardness} = 200 - 30 = \boxed{170\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3}[/latex]
However, if we consider the total alkalinity as [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{HCO}_3^{-} = 120 + 30 = 150[/latex], then:
[latex]\text{Alkalinity} = 150\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{Carbonate hardness} = \min(200,\ 150) = 150[/latex]
[latex]\text{Non-carbonate hardness} = 200 - 150 = \boxed{50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A community generates 1 million litres/day (MLD) of wastewater. This wastewater is treated using an activated sludge process (ASP). The working volume of the aeration tank of the ASP is [latex]250\ \text{m}^3[/latex], and the biomass concentration in the tank is [latex]3000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]. Analysis results showed that a biomass concentration of [latex]10\ \text{mg/L}[/latex] is present in the treated effluent from the secondary sedimentation tank of the ASP. Sludge wastage from the system is at a rate of [latex]5000\ \text{L/day}[/latex] with a biomass concentration of [latex]10000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]. The system is in steady-state condition.

The biological sludge residence time (BSRT) of the system (in days) is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
BSRT (also called Solids Retention Time, SRT) is given by:
[latex]\text{BSRT} = \frac{\text{Mass of biomass in aeration tank}}{\text{Mass of biomass leaving the system per day}}[/latex]

Step 1: Biomass in aeration tank
Volume = [latex]250\ \text{m}^3 = 250 \times 1000 = 250000\ \text{L}[/latex]
Biomass concentration = [latex]3000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \text{Mass} = 250000 \times 3000 = 750 \times 10^6\ \text{mg} = 750\ \text{kg}[/latex]

Step 2: Biomass leaving the system per day
Treated effluent flow = [latex]1\ \text{MLD} = 10^6\ \text{L/day}[/latex], biomass = [latex]10\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]10 \times 10^6 = 10^7\ \text{mg/day} = 10\ \text{kg/day}[/latex]
Sludge wastage = [latex]5000\ \text{L/day}[/latex], biomass = [latex]10000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]5000 \times 10000 = 5 \times 10^7\ \text{mg/day} = 50\ \text{kg/day}[/latex]
Total biomass leaving per day = [latex]10 + 50 = 60\ \text{kg/day}[/latex]

Step 3: BSRT calculation
[latex]\text{BSRT} = \frac{750}{60} = \boxed{12.5\ \text{days}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A settling chamber is used for the removal of discrete particulate matter from air with the following conditions:
Horizontal velocity of air = [latex]0.2\ \text{m/s}[/latex]
Temperature of air stream = [latex]77^\circ\text{C}[/latex]
Specific gravity of particle to be removed = [latex]2.65[/latex]
Chamber length = [latex]12\ \text{m}[/latex]
Chamber height = [latex]2\ \text{m}[/latex]
Viscosity of air at [latex]77^\circ\text{C} = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg/m?s}[/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity, [latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex]
Density of air at [latex]77^\circ\text{C} = 1.0\ \text{kg/m}^3[/latex]
Assume the density of water as [latex]1000\ \text{kg/m}^3[/latex] and that laminar condition exists in the chamber.

The minimum size of particle that will be removed with 100% efficiency in the settling chamber (in [latex]\mu m[/latex]) is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
To find the minimum size of the particle removed with 100% efficiency, we equate the settling velocity of the particle to the vertical distance the particle must settle during the residence time in the chamber. Residence time in the chamber is:
[latex] t = \frac{\text{length of chamber}}{\text{horizontal velocity}} = \frac{12}{0.2} = 60\ \text{seconds} [/latex]
So, for 100% removal, the particle must fall the height of the chamber in 60 seconds:
[latex] v_s = \frac{\text{height}}{t} = \frac{2}{60} = 0.0333\ \text{m/s} [/latex]
Using Stokes' Law (valid under laminar conditions):
[latex] v_s = \frac{g d^2 (\rho_p - \rho_f)}{18 \mu} [/latex]
Where: [latex] d = \text{diameter of particle (in m)} [/latex]
[latex] \rho_p = \text{density of particle} = 2.65 \times 1000 = 2650\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
[latex] \rho_f = \text{density of air} = 1.0\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
[latex] \mu = \text{viscosity of air} = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg/m?s} [/latex]
Now solve for [latex] d [/latex]:
[latex] 0.0333 = \frac{9.81 \cdot d^2 (2650 - 1)}{18 \cdot 2.1 \times 10^{-5}} [/latex]
[latex] 0.0333 = \frac{9.81 \cdot d^2 \cdot 2649}{3.78 \times 10^{-4}} [/latex]
[latex] d^2 = \frac{0.0333 \cdot 3.78 \times 10^{-4}}{9.81 \cdot 2649} [/latex]
[latex] d^2 \approx \frac{1.25874 \times 10^{-5}}{25983.69} \approx 4.843 \times 10^{-10} [/latex]
[latex] d \approx \sqrt{4.843 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m} [/latex]
Convert to micrometers:
[latex] d = 2.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^6 = 22.0\ \mu m [/latex]

raw_source.text:
On a two-lane highway, a horizontal curve of radius [latex]300\ \text{m}[/latex] is provided. The design speed is [latex]80\ \text{km/h}[/latex].

If the longest wheelbase of the vehicle expected on this highway is [latex]7\ \text{m}[/latex], then the extra widening required (in m) is ______ (round off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
As per IRC, extra widening on a horizontal curve is given by the formula:
[latex]W_e = W_m + W_{ph}[/latex]
Where:
[latex]W_m = \text{mechanical widening} = \frac{n l^2}{2R}[/latex]
[latex]W_{ph} = \text{psychological widening} = \frac{v}{9.5 \sqrt{R}}[/latex]

Given:
[latex]n = 2,\ l = 7\ \text{m},\ R = 300\ \text{m},\ v = 80\ \text{km/h}[/latex]

Step 1: Mechanical Widening
[latex]W_m = \frac{2 \times 7^2}{2 \times 300} = \frac{98}{600} = 0.1633\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 2: Psychological Widening
[latex]\sqrt{R} = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.32[/latex]
[latex]W_{ph} = \frac{80}{9.5 \times 17.32} = \frac{80}{164.54} \approx 0.4863\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 3: Total Extra Widening
[latex]W_e = 0.1633 + 0.4863 = \boxed{0.65\ \text{m}}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text: If the Fore Bearing of the lines [latex]AB[/latex] and [latex]BC[/latex] are [latex]60^\circ[/latex] and [latex]122^\circ[/latex], respectively, then the interior angle [latex]\angle ABC[/latex] (in degrees) is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
To find the interior angle [latex]\angle ABC[/latex], we use the difference between:
The Back Bearing of line [latex]AB[/latex], and
The Fore Bearing of line [latex]BC[/latex]

Step 1: Calculate Back Bearing of AB
[latex] \text{FB of } AB = 60^\circ [/latex]
[latex] \text{BB of } AB = 60^\circ + 180^\circ = 240^\circ [/latex]

Step 2: Given Fore Bearing of BC
[latex] \text{FB of } BC = 122^\circ [/latex]

Step 3: Interior Angle at Point B
[latex] \angle ABC = BB_{AB} - FB_{BC} = 240^\circ - 122^\circ = \boxed{118^\circ} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
An electricity utility company charges [latex]₹ [/latex] 7 per kWh (kilo watt-hour). If a 40-watt desk light is left on for 10 hours each night for 180 days, what would be the cost of energy consumption?
If the desk light is on for 2 more hours each night for the 180 days, what would be the percentage-increase in the cost of energy consumption?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Calculate energy consumption for 10 hours/day
[latex] \text{Power} = 40\ \text{W} = 0.04\ \text{kW} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Time per day} = 10\ \text{hours} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Number of days} = 180 [/latex]
[latex] \text{Energy} = 0.04 \times 10 \times 180 = 72\ \text{kWh} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Cost} = 72 \times 7 = ₹ \ 504 [/latex]

Step 2: Energy for 12 hours/day
[latex] \text{Time per day} = 12\ \text{hours} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Energy} = 0.04 \times 12 \times 180 = 86.4\ \text{kWh} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Cost} = 86.4 \times 7 = ₹\ 604.8 [/latex]

Step 3: Percentage increase
[latex] \text{Increase} = 604.8 - 504 = ₹ \ 100.8 [/latex]
[latex] \text{Percentage increase} = \frac{100.8}{504} \times 100 \approx 20% [/latex]

Correct Answer: [latex]₹ [/latex] 504; 20%

raw_source.text: In the context of the given figure, which one of the following options correctly represents the entries in the blocks labelled (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv), respectively?

A bag contains Violet (V), Yellow (Y), Red (R), and Green (G) balls. On counting them, the following results are obtained:
(i) The sum of Yellow balls and twice the number of Violet balls is [latex]50[/latex].
(ii) The sum of Violet and Green balls is [latex]50[/latex].
(iii) The sum of Yellow and Red balls is [latex]50[/latex].
(iv) The sum of Violet and twice the number of Red balls is [latex]50[/latex].
Which one of the following Pie charts correctly represents the balls in the bag?
raw_source.solution:
Let:
[latex] V = \text{number of Violet balls} [/latex]
[latex] Y = \text{number of Yellow balls} [/latex]
[latex] R = \text{number of Red balls} [/latex]
[latex] G = \text{number of Green balls} [/latex]

From the question:
(i) [latex] Y + 2V = 50 \;\;\;...(1) [/latex]
(ii) [latex] V + G = 50 \;\;\;...(2) [/latex]
(iii) [latex] Y + R = 50 \;\;\;...(3) [/latex]
(iv) [latex] V + 2R = 50 \;\;\;...(4) [/latex]

Step 1: From equation (1):
[latex] Y = 50 - 2V \;\;\;...(5) [/latex]
Step 2: Substitute (5) into (3):
[latex] (50 - 2V) + R = 50 \Rightarrow R = 2V \;\;\;...(6) [/latex]
Step 3: Substitute (6) into (4):
[latex] V + 2(2V) = 50 \Rightarrow V + 4V = 50 \Rightarrow 5V = 50 \Rightarrow V = 10 [/latex]
Step 4: Use value of [latex] V [/latex] to find others:
From (5): [latex] Y = 50 - 2(10) = 30 [/latex]
From (6): [latex] R = 2(10) = 20 [/latex]
From (2): [latex] G = 50 - V = 50 - 10 = 40 [/latex]

Final Values:
[latex] V = 10,\ Y = 30,\ R = 20,\ G = 40 [/latex]
Total balls = [latex] 10 + 30 + 20 + 40 = 100 [/latex]

So, the correct pie chart must show:
Violet: [latex] \frac{10}{100} \times 100 = 10% [/latex]
Yellow: [latex] \frac{30}{100} \times 100 = 30% [/latex]
Red: [latex] \frac{20}{100} \times 100 = 20% [/latex]
Green: [latex] \frac{40}{100} \times 100 = 40% [/latex]

raw_source.text:
"His life was divided between the books, his friends, and long walks. A solitary man, he worked at all hours without much method, and probably courted his fatal illness in this way. To his own name there is not much to show; but such was his liberality that he was continually helping others, and fruits of his erudition are widely scattered, and have gone to increase many a comparative stranger's reputation."
(From E.V. Lucas's "A Funeral")

Based only on the information provided in the above passage, which one of the following statements is true?
(A) The solitary man described in the passage is dead.
(B) Strangers helped create a grand reputation for the solitary man described in the passage.
(C) The solitary man described in the passage found joy in scattering fruits.
(D) The solitary man worked in a court where he fell ill.
raw_source.solution:
Let's evaluate each option based solely on the information in the passage:
Option (A): The passage is from "A Funeral" and uses past tense: "His life was...", "he worked...", "he was continually helping...". This strongly suggests the man is no longer alive.
Option (B): It says, "fruits of his erudition... have gone to increase many a comparative stranger's reputation," meaning he helped increase the reputation of strangers, not the other way around.
Option (C): The phrase "scattering fruits" is metaphorical (referring to knowledge or scholarly work), and there's no indication he "found joy" in doing it.
Option (D): The phrase "courted his fatal illness" does not mean he worked in a court. It's a metaphor meaning he brought illness upon himself due to his lifestyle.
options: The solitary man described in the passage is dead.
Strangers helped create a grand reputation for the solitary man described in the passage.
The solitary man described in the passage found joy in scattering fruits.
The solitary man worked in a court where he fell ill.

raw_answer.option_text: The solitary man described in the passage is dead.

then which one among the given options is most appropriate for [latex] P^* [/latex]?

We are given:
[latex] O^* = O\ Q\ S\ Z\ P\ R\ T [/latex]
[latex] X^* = X\ Z\ P\ W\ Y\ O\ Q [/latex]
We need to find the pattern and apply it to [latex] P^* [/latex].

Let's analyze [latex] O^* [/latex]. O is at the top (12 o?clock), and the sequence is:
O (starting point)
Q (2 positions clockwise from O)

Z (2 positions clockwise from S)
P (2 positions clockwise from Z)
R (2 positions clockwise from P)

So the rule for [latex] O^* [/latex] is: keep jumping 2 letters clockwise on the clock.

Let's verify this for [latex] X^* [/latex]:
X (starting point)
Z (2 positions clockwise)
P (2 positions clockwise)
W (2 positions clockwise)
Y (2 positions clockwise)
O (2 positions clockwise)
Q (2 positions clockwise)
Yes! Consistent 2-letter clockwise jumps.

*Now apply the same rule to [latex] P^ *[/latex]:
Start at P (next is 2 letters clockwise each time):
P
R (2 positions from P)

So we continue after Z as back to O (loop). After Z, 2 positions ahead is B, but not present. So we loop:
From Z - O (1 step), P (2 steps)

Consider a five-digit number [latex] PQRST [/latex] that has distinct digits [latex] P,\ Q,\ R,\ S,\ T [/latex], and satisfies the following conditions:
[latex] P < Q [/latex]
[latex] S > P > T [/latex]
[latex] R < T [/latex]
If integers [latex] 1 [/latex] through [latex] 5 [/latex] are used to construct such a number, the value of [latex] P [/latex] is:

A business person buys potatoes of two different varieties P and Q, mixes them in a certain ratio and sells them at [latex]₹ 192[/latex] per kg.
The cost of the variety P is [latex]₹ 800[/latex] for 5 kg.
The cost of the variety Q is [latex]₹ 800[/latex] for 4 kg.
If the person gets 8% profit, what is the [latex] P:Q [/latex] ratio (by weight)?
raw_source.solution:
Cost price of 1 kg of variety P:
[latex] \text{CP}_P = \frac{800}{5} = ₹160 [/latex]
Cost price of 1 kg of variety Q:
[latex] \text{CP}_Q = \frac{800}{4} = ₹200 [/latex]
Selling price per kg of the mixture = ₹192
Profit = 8%
Let the cost price of the mixture be [latex] x [/latex]
Then:
[latex] 1.08x = 192 \Rightarrow x = \frac{192}{1.08} = 177.78\ \text{(approx)} [/latex]
Now, use alligation method:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Variety P} & 160 \\ \hline \text{Variety Q} & 200 \\ \hline \text{Mean (Mixture)} & 177.78 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
Apply alligation rule:
[latex] \text{P:Q} = (200 - 177.78) : (177.78 - 160) = 22.22 : 17.78 [/latex]
Now, convert to simplest ratio:
[latex] \frac{22.22}{17.78} = \frac{2222}{1778} \approx \frac{5}{4} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Three villages P, Q, and R are located in such a way that the distance [latex] PQ = 13\ \text{km} [/latex], [latex] QR = 14\ \text{km} [/latex], and [latex] RP = 15\ \text{km} [/latex], as shown in the figure.
A straight road joins Q and R. It is proposed to connect P to this road QR by constructing another road.
What is the minimum possible length (in km) of this connecting road?
raw_source.solution:
To find the shortest path from point P to road QR, we drop a perpendicular from P to line QR, because the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance. We are given a triangle with sides:
[latex] PQ = 13\ \text{km},\ QR = 14\ \text{km},\ RP = 15\ \text{km} [/latex]
Let?s denote the sides of triangle [latex] \triangle PQR [/latex] as follows:
[latex] a = QR = 14,\ b = PR = 15,\ c = PQ = 13 [/latex] We can apply Heron?s formula to find the area of triangle [latex] \triangle PQR [/latex]:
First, calculate semi-perimeter:
[latex] s = \frac{a + b + c}{2} = \frac{14 + 15 + 13}{2} = 21 [/latex]
Now, apply Heron?s formula:
[latex] \text{Area} = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)} \ = \sqrt{21(21 - 14)(21 - 15)(21 - 13)} \ = \sqrt{21 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 8} \ = \sqrt{7056} \approx 84 \ \text{km}^2 [/latex]
Now use the formula for area in terms of base and height:
[latex] \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height} \ 84 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 14 \cdot h \ h = \frac{168}{14} = 12\ \text{km} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Matrix [latex]P[/latex] is given as

[latex]P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

The TRUE option is:
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Trace of P: [latex]\text{tr}(P) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3[/latex]

Eigenvalues: Solve [latex]\det(P - \lambda I) = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 0] - 0 + 1[0 - (1-\lambda)] = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)^3 - (1-\lambda) = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 1] = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)[\lambda^2 - 2\lambda] = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)\cdot\lambda(\lambda - 2) = 0[/latex]
Eigenvalues: [latex]\lambda = 0, 1, 2[/latex]

Sum of eigenvalues = [latex]0 + 1 + 2 = 3[/latex] = Trace

Checking other options:
(B) [latex]P^T P \neq I[/latex] (P is not orthogonal)
(C) P is symmetric ([latex]P^T = P[/latex]), not skew-symmetric
(D) Eigenvalues are 0, 1, 2 - not all magnitude 1

Therefore, Option (A) is TRUE.
options: Trace of P is equal to the sum of the Eigen values of P.
Absolute magnitude of each Eigen value is 1.

raw_answer.option_text: Trace of P is equal to the sum of the Eigen values of P.

raw_source.text:
Given

[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex] \begin{Bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{Bmatrix} = \begin{Bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{Bmatrix}[/latex]

The above system of equations represents a
raw_source.solution:
Given system:
[latex]x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]
[latex]x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 2x_3 = 0 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Step 1: Count equations vs unknowns: 2 equations, 3 unknowns [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] underdetermined system.

Step 2: Find rank of coefficient matrix:
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
R2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] R2 - R1: [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Rank = 2

Step 3: Degrees of freedom = 3 - 2 = 1 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] solution is a line in 3D space (passing through the origin).

Each equation represents a plane through origin. Intersection of two planes through origin = a line through origin.

raw_source.text: A thin-walled spherical gas balloon of radius [latex]R[/latex] and wall thickness [latex]t[/latex] ([latex]t \ll R[/latex]) is subjected to an internal (gauge) pressure [latex]p[/latex]. The maximum tensile and shear stresses in the balloon wall are, respectively:
raw_source.solution:
For a thin-walled sphere under internal pressure p:

Step 1 - Hoop stress (circumferential):
By equilibrium: [latex]\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \dfrac{pR}{2t}[/latex]

Both principal stresses are equal in magnitude (biaxial state).

Step 2 - Maximum shear stress:
In-plane maximum shear stress:
[latex]\tau_{max,in} = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{pR}{2t} - \dfrac{pR}{2t}}{2} = 0[/latex]

Since both principal stresses are equal, the in-plane shear stress is zero.

Therefore:
Maximum tensile stress = [latex]\dfrac{pR}{2t}[/latex]
Maximum shear stress = 0
raw_source.tag2: Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain
