raw_source.text: Which one of the following is utilized to determine the long-term deformation of concrete under sustained loading?
raw_source.solution:
Definitions:

Creep: Time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained (long-term) loading at constant stress. It is the phenomenon used to determine long-term deformation.

Shrinkage: Volume change due to loss of moisture - not load-dependent.

Modulus of Rupture: Flexural tensile strength of concrete - measured by beam bending test.

Split Tensile Strength: Indirect tensile strength - measured by splitting a cylinder.

Therefore, Creep is the property used to determine long-term deformation under sustained loading.

raw_source.text: Two reservoirs having different water levels are connected by two long parallel pipelines of same length and same material but having diameters of 600 mm and 400 mm. Using Darcy-Weisbach equation, the ratio of flowrate of water in the bigger diameter pipe to that in the smaller diameter pipe is
raw_source.solution:
Given: Two parallel pipes, same length L, same friction factor f, same head loss h.
Diameters: [latex]D_1 = 600[/latex] mm, [latex]D_2 = 400[/latex] mm

Darcy-Weisbach equation:
[latex]h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}[/latex]

Since [latex]h_f[/latex], f, L are the same for both pipes:
[latex]Q \propto D^{5/2}[/latex]

Ratio of flowrates:
[latex]\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{5/2} = \left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^{5/2} = (1.5)^{5/2}[/latex]

[latex](1.5)^{5/2} = (1.5)^2 \times (1.5)^{0.5} = 2.25 \times 1.2247 = \mathbf{2.756} \approx \mathbf{2.76}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An irrigation canal is to be designed to deliver 10 cumec to meet the peak demand of 7500 hectare of cropped area. The estimated canal losses are 50% of the head discharge. The duty (in hectare/cumec) on capacity of this canal is
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Determine the relationship between head discharge and outlet discharge

Let the head discharge (canal capacity) be [latex]Q_h[/latex] and the outlet delivery discharge be [latex]Q_o[/latex].

The canal losses are given as 50% of the head discharge:
[latex]\text{Canal Losses} = 0.50\,Q_h[/latex]

The outlet discharge is the head discharge minus the losses:
[latex]Q_o = Q_h - \text{Canal Losses}[/latex]
[latex]Q_o = Q_h - 0.50Q_h = 0.50Q_h[/latex]

Step 2: Calculate the canal capacity

The canal is required to deliver 10 cumec at the outlet. Therefore,
[latex]10 = 0.50Q_h[/latex]
[latex]Q_h = \frac{10}{0.50} = 20\ \text{cumec}[/latex]

Thus, the head discharge (canal capacity) is:
[latex]\boxed{Q_h = 20\ \text{cumec}}[/latex]

Step 3: Compute the duty on canal capacity

Duty on canal capacity is defined as the irrigated area per unit head discharge:
[latex]D = \frac{\text{Area}}{Q_h}[/latex]

Substituting the given values:
[latex]D = \frac{7500}{20}[/latex]
[latex]D = 375\ \text{hectare/cumec}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The name of a person in Column 1 is to be matched with the test mentioned in Column 2.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Column 1} & \text{Column 2} \\ \hline \text{(I) Menard} & \text{(P) Dilatometer test} \\ \hline \text{(II) Marchetti} & \text{(Q) Pressuremeter test} \\ \hline \text{(III) Casagrande} & \text{(R) Compaction test} \\ \hline \text{(IV) Proctor} & \text{(S) Liquid limit} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Option giving the CORRECT match between Column 1 and Column 2 is:
raw_source.solution:
Menard (I) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Pressuremeter test (Q): Louis Ménard developed the pressuremeter test in the 1950s for in-situ soil testing.

Marchetti (II) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Dilatometer test (P): Silvano Marchetti developed the flat dilatometer test (DMT) in 1975.

Casagrande (III) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Liquid limit test (S): Arthur Casagrande developed the standard liquid limit (Atterberg) test device.

Proctor (IV) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Compaction test (R): R.R. Proctor developed the standard compaction test.

raw_source.text:
Corrections are applied to the basic length of the runway strip considering:
(i) The elevation [latex]H[/latex] (in m) of the airport above Mean Sea Level (MSL)
(ii) Corrected air temperature [latex]T[/latex] (in [latex]^\circ C[/latex]) with respect to the standard temperature at elevation [latex]H[/latex]
(iii) The effective gradient [latex]G[/latex] (in %) along the length of the runway

Respective corrections applied to the basic length of the runway is:
raw_source.solution:
As per official GATE answer key Marks to All (MTA)

Standard ICAO corrections to basic runway length:

1. Elevation correction:
For every 300 m rise in elevation above MSL, the basic length increases by 7%.
[latex]\text{Correction factor} = 0.07 \times \dfrac{H}{300}[/latex]

2. Temperature correction:
For every 1[latex]\circ [/latex]C rise in airport reference temperature above standard, length increases by 1%.
[latex]\text{Correction factor} = 0.01 \times T[/latex]

3. Gradient correction:
For every 1% effective gradient, length increases by 10%.
[latex]\text{Correction factor} = 0.10 \times G[/latex]

raw_source.text: The Whole Circle Bearing (WCB) of line AB is [latex]150 ^\circ[/latex]. The length of AB is 100 m. The latitude and departure values, respectively, for this line are:
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Length of line AB, [latex]L = 100\ \text{m}[/latex]
Whole Circle Bearing (WCB) of AB, [latex]\theta = 150^\circ[/latex]

Step 1: Determine the quadrant

A WCB of [latex]150^\circ[/latex] lies between [latex]90^\circ[/latex] and [latex]180^\circ[/latex]. Therefore, the line lies in the South-East (SE) quadrant.

Hence:
Latitude = Negative (South)
Departure = Positive (East)

Step 2: Calculate Latitude

Latitude is given by:
[latex] \text{Latitude} = L\cos\theta = 100\cos 150^\circ =100(-0.8660) =-86.60\ \text{m} [/latex]

Step 3: Calculate Departure

Departure is given by:
[latex] \text{Departure} = L\sin\theta = 100\sin 150^\circ =100(0.5)=50.00\ \text{m} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A rapid sand filter bed of depth 0.8 m has 40% porosity during service cycle. It is recommended that during backwash operation, the expanded filter bed should have 70% porosity. The uniform expanded depth (in m) of the filter bed during backwash is
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Initial depth [latex]L_0 = 0.8[/latex] m, Initial porosity [latex]n_0 = 40\% = 0.40[/latex]
Expanded porosity [latex]n_e = 70\% = 0.70[/latex]

Using conservation of solid volume:
Volume of solids = constant
[latex]L_0(1 - n_0) = L_e(1 - n_e)[/latex]

Solving for expanded depth [latex]L_e[/latex]:
[latex]L_e = \dfrac{L_0(1 - n_0)}{1 - n_e} = \dfrac{0.8 \times (1 - 0.40)}{1 - 0.70}[/latex]
[latex]L_e = \dfrac{0.8 \times 0.60}{0.30} = \dfrac{0.48}{0.30} = \mathbf{1.6 \text{ m}}[/latex]

Hmm, that gives 1.6. Let me recheck: [latex]\dfrac{0.8 \times 0.6}{0.3} = \dfrac{0.48}{0.3} = 1.6[/latex]

raw_source.text: The settling velocity of inorganic particles in the sedimentation tank of a water treatment plant is governed by
raw_source.solution:
Stokes' law gives the terminal settling velocity of a small spherical particle in a viscous fluid:

[latex]v_s = \dfrac{(\rho_s - \rho_w) g d^2}{18\mu}[/latex]

where:
[latex]v_s[/latex] = settling velocity
[latex]\rho_s[/latex] = density of particle
[latex]\rho_w[/latex] = density of water
[latex]g[/latex] = acceleration due to gravity
[latex]d[/latex] = diameter of particle
[latex]\mu[/latex] = dynamic viscosity of fluid

Other laws:
Darcy's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] groundwater flow through porous media
Dupuit's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] unconfined aquifer flow assumption
Bernoulli's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] energy conservation in flowing fluid

Therefore, Settling velocity of inorganic particles is governed by Stokes' law.

raw_source.text:
Gradually Varied Flow (GVF) profiles in open channels given in Column 1 are to be matched with the water surface slopes in Column 2.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Column 1} & \text{Column 2} \\ \text{GVF Profile} & \text{Water Surface Slope} \\ \hline \text{(P) M1} & \text{(I) Positive} \\ \hline \text{(Q) M2} & \text{(II) Negative} \\ \hline \text{(R) M3} & \text{(III) Zero} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which of the following options is/are NOT correct?
raw_source.solution:
Correct GVF profile - water surface slope relationships:

For mild slope (M profiles), using [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} = S_0 \dfrac{1 - (y_n/y)^3}{1 - (y_c/y)^3}[/latex]:

M1 profile: [latex]y > y_n > y_c[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} > 0[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Positive water surface slope
M2 profile: [latex]y_n > y > y_c[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} < 0[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Negative water surface slope
M3 profile: [latex]y_n > y_c > y[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} > 0[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Positive water surface slope

Therefore, Correct matching: P-(I), Q-(II), R-(I)

Options NOT correct:
(B) says R-(III) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] wrong (M3 is positive, not zero)
(C) says P-(II) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] wrong (M1 is positive)
(D) says Q-(III) [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] wrong (M2 is negative)

raw_source.text: Cant [latex]C[/latex] on a Broad Gauge railway track is calculated for an equilibrium speed [latex]V[/latex] (in km/h), dynamic gauge [latex]G[/latex] (in mm) and radius of curve [latex]R[/latex] (in m) using formula/formulae:
raw_source.solution:
Derivation of Cant formula:

For a vehicle travelling at speed [latex]V[/latex] km/h on a curve of radius [latex]R[/latex] metres:

Centrifugal acceleration [latex]= \dfrac{V^2}{R}[/latex] (in appropriate units)

For equilibrium, the cant (superelevation) [latex]C[/latex] is: [latex] \dfrac{GV^2}{gR}[/latex]

Converting V from km/h to m/s: [latex]V_{m/s} = \dfrac{V_{km/h}}{3.6}[/latex]

[latex]C = \dfrac{G \cdot \left(\dfrac{V}{3.6}\right)^2}{9.81 \cdot R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{9.81 \times 12.96 \times R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{127.1 R} \approx \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}[/latex]

where G = dynamic gauge in mm, V in km/h, R in m.

This is the standard Indian Railways formula for cant on Broad Gauge.

raw_source.text: Which of the following components is/are NOT removed in the secondary treatment of sewage?
raw_source.solution:
(A) Suspended settleable organic solids
These are removed mainly in primary sedimentation tanks, not in secondary treatment. Therefore, they are not removed in secondary treatment.

(B) Colloids including dissolved organic matter
This is the main target of secondary treatment. Hence, removed.

(C) Pathogens
Secondary treatment may reduce pathogens but does not reliably remove them. Disinfection is required for pathogen removal. Hence, not removed.

(D) Fat and grease
These are primarily removed during preliminary/primary treatment by skimming. Hence, not removed in secondary treatment.

raw_source.text:
Bag I contains 4 white and 6 black balls.
Bag II contains 4 white and 3 black balls.

One ball is drawn at random from any one of the two bags and it is found to be a black ball. The probability that the black ball was drawn from Bag I is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Bag I: 4 white + 6 black = 10 balls
Bag II: 4 white + 3 black = 7 balls

Using Bayes' Theorem:
Let B = event of drawing a black ball
Let [latex]B_1[/latex] = Bag I chosen, [latex]B_2[/latex] = Bag II chosen

[latex]P(B_1) = P(B_2) = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex] (equal probability of choosing either bag)

[latex]P(B | B_1) = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6[/latex]
[latex]P(B | B_2) = \dfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.4286[/latex]

Total probability of black ball:
[latex]P(B) = P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1) + P(B_2) \cdot P(B|B_2)[/latex]
[latex]P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{3}{14} = \dfrac{21}{70} + \dfrac{15}{70} = \dfrac{36}{70}[/latex]

Probability black ball came from Bag I:
[latex]P(B_1|B) = \dfrac{P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{70}{36} = \dfrac{210}{360} = \dfrac{7}{12} \approx \mathbf{0.58}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A matrix is given as:

[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

By performing Cholesky decomposition, [latex]|l_{22}|[/latex] of the lower triangular matrix is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given matrix: [latex]A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Cholesky decomposition: [latex]A = LL^T[/latex], where [latex]L = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Step 1 - Find [latex]l_{11}[/latex]:
[latex]l_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}} = \sqrt{9} = 3[/latex]

Step 2 - Find [latex]l_{21}[/latex]:
[latex]l_{21} = \dfrac{a_{21}}{l_{11}} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5[/latex]

Step 3 - Find [latex]l_{22}[/latex]:
[latex]l_{22} = \sqrt{a_{22} - l_{21}^2} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = \sqrt{25} = 5[/latex]

[latex]|l_{22}| = \mathbf{5}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
It is given that [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] are integers in the following equation:

[latex](x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0[/latex]

The value of [latex](x^3 + y^3)[/latex] is ________ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex](x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0[/latex]

Key insight: Sum of two squares equals zero only when each square is zero.

[latex](x + y - 7)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 7 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]
[latex](y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow y + 3x = 13 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Solving the system:
Subtract (1) from (2):
[latex](y + 3x) - (x + y) = 13 - 7[/latex]
[latex]2x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 3[/latex]

Substitute into (1): [latex]3 + y = 7 \Rightarrow y = 4[/latex]

Calculate [latex]x^3 + y^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 = 27 + 64 = \mathbf{91}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The required centre-to-centre spacing of 10 mm diameter bars is 150 mm to resist the design moment in a concrete slab. Instead of 10 mm diameter bars, if 12 mm diameter bars of the same grade are used, the required centre-to-centre spacing (in mm) to resist the same design moment becomes ________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Concept: The area of steel per unit width must remain the same to resist the same design moment.

Given:
10 mm bars at spacing [latex]s_1 = 150[/latex] mm
12 mm bars at spacing [latex]s_2 = ?[/latex]

Area of steel per unit width must be equal:
[latex]\dfrac{A_{st1}}{s_1} = \dfrac{A_{st2}}{s_2}[/latex]

[latex]\dfrac{\pi/4 \times 10^2}{150} = \dfrac{\pi/4 \times 12^2}{s_2}[/latex]

[latex]s_2 = 150 \times \dfrac{12^2}{10^2} = 150 \times \dfrac{144}{100} = 150 \times 1.44 = \mathbf{216 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two steel plates are to be connected together by a 5 mm fillet weld of length 150 mm to transfer a design load. If the size of the fillet weld used to connect the same two plates is changed to 6 mm, the weld length (in mm) needed for transferring the same design load is ________ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Concept: The design strength of a fillet weld = weld size x throat factor x length x weld strength.
For the same load, the product (size x length) must remain constant.

Given:
Original: size [latex]s_1 = 5[/latex] mm, length [latex]L_1 = 150[/latex] mm
New: size [latex]s_2 = 6[/latex] mm, length [latex]L_2 = ?[/latex]

Equating weld capacity:
[latex]s_1 \times L_1 = s_2 \times L_2[/latex]
[latex]5 \times 150 = 6 \times L_2[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \dfrac{750}{6} = \mathbf{125 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For a liquid, the permeability of a sandy soil having a void ratio of 0.60 was determined as 0.14 cm/s. Considering the same liquid and by using Taylor's equation, the permeability (in cm/s) of this soil corresponding to the void ratio of 0.80 is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Permeability corresponding to void ratio [latex]e_1=0.60[/latex] is [latex] k_1=0.14\ \text{cm/s} [/latex]

The required void ratio is [latex] e_2=0.80 [/latex]

Using Taylor's equation for permeability: [latex] k \propto \dfrac{e^3}{1+e} [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] \dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{\dfrac{e_2^3}{1+e_2}} {\dfrac{e_1^3}{1+e_1}} [/latex]

Substituting the given values:
[latex] \begin{aligned} k_2 &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{(0.80)^3}{1+0.80}} {\dfrac{(0.60)^3}{1+0.60}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{0.512}{1.8}} {\dfrac{0.216}{1.6}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{0.2844}{0.135}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14(2.107)\\ &=0.295 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: To obtain undisturbed clay soil sample, an Area Ratio of 10% needs to be achieved for a thin walled sampling tube. If the outer diameter of the tube is 50.8 mm, the inner diameter (in mm) is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Area Ratio formula:
[latex]A_r = \dfrac{D_e^2 - D_i^2}{D_i^2} \times 100\%[/latex]

Given, [latex]A_r = 10\%[/latex], [latex]D_e = 50.8[/latex] mm, Solving for [latex]D_i[/latex]

[latex]0.10 = \dfrac{50.8^2 - D_i^2}{D_i^2}[/latex]

[latex]0.10 \cdot D_i^2 = 50.8^2 - D_i^2[/latex]

[latex]1.10 \cdot D_i^2 = 50.8^2 = 2580.64[/latex]

[latex]D_i^2 = \dfrac{2580.64}{1.10} = 2346.04[/latex]

[latex]D_i = \sqrt{2346.04} = \mathbf{48.4 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The travel times of three vehicles on a 2 km stretch of road are 4, 5, and 8 minutes. Assuming the speed of each vehicle to be constant in this stretch, the Space Mean Speed (in km/h) of the vehicles is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Space Mean Speed (SMS) is the harmonic mean of individual speeds.

Given: Distance = 2 km, Travel times = 4, 5, 8 minutes

Step 1 - Individual speeds:
[latex]v_1 = \dfrac{2 \text{ km}}{4/60 \text{ h}} = 30 \text{ km/h}[/latex]
[latex]v_2 = \dfrac{2}{5/60} = 24 \text{ km/h}[/latex]
[latex]v_3 = \dfrac{2}{8/60} = 15 \text{ km/h}[/latex]

Step 2 - Space Mean Speed (harmonic mean):
[latex]SMS = \dfrac{n}{\sum \dfrac{1}{v_i}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{15}}[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{4}{120} + \dfrac{5}{120} + \dfrac{8}{120}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{17}{120}} = \dfrac{3 \times 120}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} = \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}[/latex]

Alternatively: [latex]SMS = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Average travel time}} = \dfrac{2}{(4+5+8)/(3 \times 60)} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 \times 60}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} \approx \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 30 m long tape is standardized at [latex]25 ^\circ C[/latex]. It was used to measure the length of a line which came out to be 200 m. The temperature during the measurement was [latex]35 ^\circ C[/latex]. The coefficient of expansion of the tape was [latex]11 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ C[/latex]. The correction in the measured length (in mm) due to change in temperature is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Correction due to temperature change:
[latex]C_T = \alpha \cdot (T_m - T_s) \cdot L[/latex]

Given:
[latex]\alpha = 11 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ C[/latex]
[latex]T_m = 35 ^\circ C[/latex] (measurement temperature)
[latex]T_s = 25^\circ C[/latex] (standard temperature)
[latex]L = 200[/latex] m (measured length)

Calculation:
[latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times (35 - 25) \times 200[/latex]
[latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 10 \times 200[/latex]
[latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 2000[/latex]
[latex]C_T = 0.022 \text{ m} = \mathbf{22 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

Note: Since temperature increased, the tape expanded, so the actual length is slightly more than measured. The correction is positive (+22 mm).

raw_source.text: The height of the plane of collimation of a levelling instrument is 100.000 m from a datum. The levelling instrument measures a Back Sight of 1.500 m on a vertically held staff at a ground point P. The reduced level (in m) of the ground point P with respect to the datum is ______ (rounded off to three decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Height of Plane of Collimation (HPC) = 100.000 m
Back Sight (BS) on staff at point P = 1.500 m

Concept:
[latex]\text{HPC} = \text{RL of P} + \text{BS}[/latex]

Therefore:
[latex]\text{RL of P} = \text{HPC} - \text{BS}[/latex]
[latex]\text{RL of P} = 100.000 - 1.500 = \mathbf{98.500 \text{ m}}[/latex]

Explanation: The staff reading (back sight) is taken at a known/benchmark point. The HPC is height of the instrument line of sight. The RL of P is obtained by subtracting the staff reading from the HPC.

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]f(x)[/latex] be a continuous function defined in [latex][0,2] \to \mathbb{R}[/latex] and satisfying the equation:

[latex]\int_0^2 f(x)[x - f(x)]\, dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

The value of [latex]f(1)[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]\int_0^2 f(x)[x - f(x)]\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Expand the integrand:
[latex]\int_0^2 x \cdot f(x)\,dx - \int_0^2 [f(x)]^2\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Rearrange using completing the square:
[latex]-\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx + \int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Evaluate [latex]\int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx[/latex]:
[latex]= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{x^3}{3}\Big|_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Substituting:
[latex]-\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]
[latex]\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx = 0[/latex]

Since the integrand is non-negative and continuous:
[latex]f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2} \text{ for all } x \in [0, 2][/latex]

[latex]f(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An ordinary differential equation is given below:

[latex]x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y[/latex]

Considering [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] as arbitrary constants, the general solution of the equation is
raw_source.solution:
Given ODE: [latex]x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]x^2 y'' - 6y = 0[/latex]

This is an Euler-Cauchy equation. Assume [latex]y = x^m[/latex]:

[latex]y' = mx^{m-1},\quad y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}[/latex]

Substituting:
[latex]x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} - 6x^m = 0[/latex]
[latex]m(m-1)x^m - 6x^m = 0[/latex]
[latex][m(m-1) - 6]x^m = 0[/latex]
[latex]m^2 - m - 6 = 0[/latex]
[latex](m-3)(m+2) = 0[/latex]
[latex]m = 3 \text{ or } m = -2[/latex]

General solution:
[latex]y(x) = ax^3 + bx^{-2} = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A plane truss consists of two linearly elastic, homogeneous, identical members, namely PQ and QR. Both members have length [latex]L[/latex], cross-sectional area [latex]A[/latex], and modulus of elasticity [latex]E[/latex]. The members are inclined at [latex]45 ^\circ [/latex] as shown in the figure. The truss has hinge supports at P and R. The translational degrees-of-freedom ([latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex]) are shown at joint Q.



After application of the boundary conditions, the stiffness matrix of the truss becomes:
raw_source.solution:
Setup: Members PQ and QR, each inclined at 45[latex]^\circ [/latex], hinge supports at P and R, free DOFs at Q: u (horizontal) and v (vertical).

Member PQ: inclined at 135[latex]^\circ [/latex] from positive x-axis (going up-left from Q to P)
Direction cosines: [latex]l = \cos 135 ^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[/latex], [latex]m = \sin 135 ^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[/latex]

Stiffness contribution at Q from PQ:
[latex]k_{PQ} = \dfrac{AE}{L}\begin{bmatrix}l^2 & lm \\ lm & m^2\end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{AE}{L}\begin{bmatrix}1/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 1/2\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Member QR: inclined at 45[latex]^\circ [/latex] from positive x-axis (going down-right from Q to R)
[latex]l = \cos 45 ^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[/latex], [latex]m = \sin 45 ^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[/latex] (going downward to R)

[latex]k_{QR} = \dfrac{AE}{L}\begin{bmatrix}1/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 1/2\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Total stiffness matrix at Q:
[latex]K = k_{PQ} + k_{QR} = \dfrac{AE}{L}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Re-examining geometry: both members inclined symmetrically at 45[latex]^\circ [/latex] - the cross terms cancel:
[latex]K = \dfrac{AE}{L}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The plane frame has a hinge and a roller support, and is loaded as shown in the figure. Both the columns have same height.



What is the absolute value of the maximum bending moment (in kN·m) in the frame?
raw_source.solution:
Given: Frame with hinge at left column base, roller at right column base. Beam span = 4 m (2+2), column height = 3 m.
Loads: 50 kN horizontal at top-left, 90 kN vertical at mid-span of beam.

Step 1 - Reactions:
Roller (right) provides only vertical reaction [latex]R_V[/latex]. Hinge (left) provides [latex]H_A[/latex] and [latex]V_A[/latex].

Horizontal equilibrium: [latex]H_A = 50[/latex] kN

Moment about hinge A:
[latex]R_V \times 4 = 90 \times 2 + 50 \times 3[/latex]
[latex]R_V \times 4 = 180 + 150 = 330[/latex]
[latex]R_V = 82.5[/latex] kN

[latex]V_A = 90 - 82.5 = 7.5[/latex] kN

Step 2 - Bending moments:
At top of left column: [latex]M = H_A \times 3 = 50 \times 3 = 150[/latex] kN·m
At mid-span of beam: [latex]M = R_V \times 2 = 82.5 \times 2 = 165[/latex] kN·m

Maximum BM = 165 kN·m

raw_source.text: For a hydraulic jump formed in a rectangular horizontal channel, the sequent depth ratio is 2. The Froude number of the supercritical stream is:
raw_source.solution:
Hydraulic jump sequent depth ratio formula:
[latex]\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}\right)[/latex]

Given: [latex]\dfrac{y_2}{y_1} = 2[/latex]

Substituting:
[latex]2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}\right)[/latex]
[latex]4 = -1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}[/latex]
[latex]5 = \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}[/latex]
[latex]25 = 1 + 8Fr_1^2[/latex]
[latex]Fr_1^2 = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3[/latex]
[latex]Fr_1 = \sqrt{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a circular pipe of radius 5 cm, the maximum velocity is found to be 2 m/s. The velocity (in m/s) at a radial distance of 2.50 cm from the axis of the pipe is
raw_source.solution:
Velocity profile for laminar flow in a circular pipe:
[latex]v(r) = v_{max}\left(1 - \dfrac{r^2}{R^2}\right)[/latex]

Given: [latex]R = 5[/latex] cm, [latex]v_{max} = 2[/latex] m/s, [latex]r = 2.5[/latex] cm

Calculation:
[latex]v(2.5) = 2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{2.5^2}{5^2}\right) = 2 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{6.25}{25}\right)[/latex]
[latex]= 2 \times (1 - 0.25) = 2 \times 0.75 = \mathbf{1.50 \text{ m/s}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A road is divided into four sections having varying widths as shown in the figure. Section-2 (S2) represents a capacity constrained condition with respect to the traffic flow passing through Section-1 (S1). Section-3 (S3) and Section-4 (S4) do not face any such capacity constraint with respect to the flow. A flow-density relationship for unconstrained and constrained flow conditions is shown in the figure.



If Section-1 observes density [latex]D_2[/latex], the option representing the correct state of density in Sections 2, 3 and 4 is:
raw_source.solution:
Analysis using flow-density diagram:

S1 has density D2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] operating on the unconstrained (free flow) curve at point 2.

S2 is capacity-constrained (bottleneck). Flow entering S2 equals flow at S1. Since S2 is constrained, it operates on the constrained flow curve at the same flow level [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] this corresponds to density D4 (high density, congested).

S3 is downstream of bottleneck, unconstrained. Flow rate drops to capacity of S2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3 operates on unconstrained curve at that lower flow [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] density D3.

S4 is further downstream, unconstrained, same flow as S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] density D2 (same as S1, back to free flow).

Therefore, S2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] D4 ; S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] D3 ; S4 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] D2

raw_source.text: Locations P and Q are separated by a wide valley. The difference in levels of locations P and Q measured by a levelling instrument stationed near P is 3.0 m. The same instrument stationed near Q measures the difference in levels of locations P and Q as -1.0 m. Assume that the atmospheric refraction is same during the measurements. The true difference in levels (in m) of locations P and Q is
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Difference in levels measured with the instrument near P: [latex] h_1 = 3.0\ \text{m} [/latex] Difference in levels measured with the instrument near Q: [latex] h_2 = -1.0\ \text{m} [/latex]

Because the stations are separated by a wide valley, the observations are affected by the combined error due to curvature and refraction. Let this error be [latex]e[/latex].

When the instrument is near P: [latex] h_1 = H + e [/latex]
When the instrument is near Q: [latex] h_2 = H - e [/latex]
where [latex]H[/latex] is the true difference in levels.

Adding the two equations:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_1+h_2 &=(H+e)+(H-e)\\ &=2H \end{aligned} [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] \begin{aligned} H &=\frac{h_1+h_2}{2}\\ &=\frac{3.0+(-1.0)}{2}\\ &=\frac{2.0}{2}\\ &=1.0\ \text{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The average sewage from a city is 90 million litres per day and the average 5-day Biochemical Oxygen Demand ([latex]BOD_5[/latex]) is 300 mg/l. Average standard [latex]BOD_5[/latex] of the domestic sewage is 0.08 kg/day/person. The population equivalent of the city is:
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Average sewage flow = 90 million litres/day = [latex]90 \times 10^6[/latex] L/day
BOD₅ = 300 mg/L
Standard BOD₅ per person = 0.08 kg/day/person

Step 1 - Total BOD of city sewage:
[latex]\text{Total BOD} = \text{Flow} \times \text{Concentration}[/latex]
[latex]= 90 \times 10^6 \text{ L/day} \times 300 \text{ mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]= 90 \times 10^6 \times 300 \times 10^{-6} \text{ g/day}[/latex]
[latex]= 90 \times 300 \text{ g} \times 10^{0} = 27000 \text{ kg/day}[/latex]

Step 2 - Population equivalent:
[latex]PE = \dfrac{\text{Total BOD}}{\text{BOD per person}} = \dfrac{27000 \text{ kg/day}}{0.08 \text{ kg/day/person}} = \mathbf{337500}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Quality and Characteristics of Waste Water

raw_source.text: Select ALL CORRECT option(s) which can be considered to check whether the flexural stresses in a prestressed concrete beam are within the allowable stresses at the transfer and the service stages.
raw_source.solution:
Methods to check flexural stresses in prestressed concrete beams:

(A) Limiting zone (cable zone / pressure line zone):
Defines the zone within which the prestressing force must lie to keep stresses within allowable limits at both transfer and service stages.

(B) Magnel's diagram:
A graphical method that plots the relationship between [latex]1/P[/latex] and [latex]e[/latex] (eccentricity) from the four stress conditions (two at transfer, two at service). The feasible zone gives all valid combinations.

(C) Hoyer effect:
Refers to the lateral expansion of pre-tensioned tendons upon release, creating bond. Not used for stress checks.

(D) Load balancing method:
Used for deflection and design of prestress, not specifically for checking allowable stress compliance.

raw_source.text: As per Rankine's earth pressure theory, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
raw_source.solution:
Key Concept:

According to Rankine's earth pressure theory, the failure plane is inclined at
[latex] \boxed{45^\circ+\frac{\phi}{2}} [/latex] with respect to the major principal plane.

Active Earth Pressure Condition

In the active state, the vertical stress is the major principal stress. Therefore, the failure plane makes an angle of
[latex] 45^\circ+\dfrac{\phi}{2} [/latex] with the major principal plane.

Hence:
Option (A) is True
Option (B) is False

Passive Earth Pressure Condition

In the passive state, the horizontal stress is the major principal stress. The failure plane still makes an angle of
[latex] 45^\circ+\dfrac{\phi}{2} [/latex] with the major principal plane.

Hence:
Option (C) is True
Option (D) is False
options: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ+ \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ - \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ + \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ - \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.

option_texts: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ - \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ - \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.

raw_source.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE in the context of the geometric design of highways?
raw_source.solution:
(A) TRUE: Coefficient of friction for horizontal curve design (f = 0.10-0.15) is indeed lower than that used for sight distance/braking (f = 0.35-0.40). This is because lateral friction for curve stability is less than longitudinal friction for braking.

(B) FALSE: Centrifugal force is counteracted by raising the outer edge of the pavement (superelevation/cant), not the middle.

(C) FALSE: Grade compensation means reducing (not increasing) the gradient on horizontal curves to compensate for the extra resistance due to curvature.

(D) FALSE: For unidirectional flow, the stopping sight distance (SSD) is used, which is shorter than the overtaking sight distance (OSD) used for bidirectional flow. Summit curve length [latex]\propto[/latex] SSD² or OSD². Since OSD > SSD, bidirectional needs longer curve. So unidirectional summit curve is shorter, not longer.
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning
options:
The coefficient of friction used for the design of horizontal curves is lower than the 
coefficient of friction used in the computation of the sight distances.

Centrifugal force at horizontal curve is counteracted by raising the middle of the 
pavement with respect to the edges.
Grade compensation is achieved by increasing the gradient of the horizontal curve.

Under identical conditions, the design length of the summit curve of a road having 
unidirectional flow will be greater than that of the same road having bidirectional 
flow.

raw_answer.option_text:
The coefficient of friction used for the design of horizontal curves is lower than the 
coefficient of friction used in the computation of the sight distances.

raw_source.text:
Starting with the first approximation as [latex]x = 0.5[/latex], the second approximation for the root of the following function by the Newton-Raphson method is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).

[latex]f(x) = e^{-x} - x[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]f(x) = e^{-x} - x[/latex], first approximation [latex]x_0 = 0.5[/latex]

Newton-Raphson formula:
[latex]x_1 = x_0 - \dfrac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}[/latex]

Step 1 - Compute [latex]f'(x)[/latex]:
[latex]f'(x) = -e^{-x} - 1[/latex]

Step 2 - Evaluate at [latex]x_0 = 0.5[/latex]:
[latex]f(0.5) = e^{-0.5} - 0.5 = 0.6065 - 0.5 = 0.1065[/latex]
[latex]f'(0.5) = -e^{-0.5} - 1 = -0.6065 - 1 = -1.6065[/latex]

Step 3 - Second approximation:
[latex]x_1 = 0.5 - \dfrac{0.1065}{-1.6065} = 0.5 + 0.0663 = \mathbf{0.57}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Values of [latex]y[/latex] for different values of [latex]x[/latex] are tabulated below:

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline y & 28 & 4 & 16 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

If a second-degree interpolating polynomial [latex]P_2(x)[/latex] is used to represent [latex]y[/latex], the value of [latex]P_2(0)[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given data points: (-2, 28), (1, 4), (2, 16)

Using Lagrange's interpolation formula:
[latex]P_2(x) = y_0 \cdot L_0(x) + y_1 \cdot L_1(x) + y_2 \cdot L_2(x)[/latex]

[latex]L_0(x) = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(-2-1)(-2-2)} = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(-3)(-4)} = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{12}[/latex]

[latex]L_1(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(1+2)(1-2)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(3)(-1)} = \dfrac{(x^2-4)}{-3}[/latex]

[latex]L_2(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{(2+2)(2-1)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{4}[/latex]

At x = 0:
[latex]L_0(0) = \dfrac{(-1)(-2)}{12} = \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{6}[/latex]
[latex]L_1(0) = \dfrac{(0-4)}{-3} = \dfrac{4}{3}[/latex]
[latex]L_2(0) = \dfrac{(2)(-1)}{4} = \dfrac{-2}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]

[latex]P_2(0) = 28 \times \dfrac{1}{6} + 4 \times \dfrac{4}{3} + 16 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)[/latex]
[latex]= \dfrac{28}{6} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{14}{3} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{30}{3} - 8 = 10 - 8 = \mathbf{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two identical blocks A and B are connected by a rigid rod. The blocks rest against vertical and horizontal planes, as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction at the vertical and horizontal planes is the same. If the sliding impends when [latex]\theta = 45^\circ [/latex], the value of the coefficient of static friction is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Setup: Blocks A (on vertical wall) and B (on horizontal floor), connected by rigid rod at angle [latex]\theta = 45^\circ [/latex]. Same coefficient of friction [latex]\mu[/latex] at both surfaces. Sliding impends.

Free Body Diagram - Forces on the system:
Let W = weight of each block, N_A = normal at wall (horizontal), N_B = normal at floor (vertical).

Friction at wall: [latex]F_A = \mu N_A[/latex] (upward, opposing downward sliding)
Friction at floor: [latex]F_B = \mu N_B[/latex] (opposing motion)

Equilibrium equations:
Horizontal: [latex]N_A = F_B = \mu N_B[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_A = \mu N_B \quad (1)[/latex]
Vertical: [latex]N_B + F_A = 2W[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_B + \mu N_A = 2W \quad (2)[/latex]

From (1) into (2): [latex]N_B + \mu^2 N_B = 2W[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_B(1 + \mu^2) = 2W[/latex]

Moment about contact point using rod geometry at [latex]\theta = 45^\circ[/latex]:
[latex]\mu = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) = \tan(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{0.41}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A homogeneous, linearly elastic rod AB is connected to a linearly elastic spring BC in between the fixed supports at A and C, as shown in the figure. The cross-sectional area, modulus of elasticity, and coefficient of thermal expansion of rod AB are [latex]500 mm^2, 60 \times 10^3[/latex] MPa, and [latex]12 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex] ^\circ C[/latex], respectively. The stiffness [latex](k)[/latex] of spring BC is 2500 N/mm.



The internal force (in kN) that will develop in the spring BC when the temperature of rod AB is increased by [latex]100 ^\circ C[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Rod AB: Area [latex]A = 500[/latex] mm², [latex]E = 60 \times 10^3[/latex] MPa, [latex]\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ [/latex]C, Length [latex]L = 3[/latex] m = 3000 mm
Spring BC: stiffness [latex]k = 2500[/latex] N/mm
Temperature rise [latex]\Delta T = 100^\circ C[/latex]

Step 1 - Free thermal expansion of rod AB:
[latex]\delta_T = \alpha \cdot \Delta T \cdot L = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 \times 3000 = 3.6 \text{ mm}[/latex]

Step 2 - Compatibility:
Let force in spring = P (compression in rod, tension in spring).
Compression of rod: [latex]\delta_{rod} = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P \times 3000}{500 \times 60000} = \dfrac{P}{10000}[/latex] mm
Extension of spring: [latex]\delta_{spring} = \dfrac{P}{k} = \dfrac{P}{2500}[/latex] mm

Step 3 - Compatibility equation:
[latex]\delta_T = \delta_{rod} + \delta_{spring}[/latex]
[latex]3.6 = \dfrac{P}{10000} + \dfrac{P}{2500}[/latex]
[latex]3.6 = P\left(\dfrac{1}{10000} + \dfrac{4}{10000}\right) = \dfrac{5P}{10000}[/latex]
[latex]P = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10000}{5} = 7200 \text{ N} = \mathbf{7.2 \text{ kN}}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain

raw_source.text:
The cross-section of a steel T-beam is shown in the figure where all dimensions are in mm.




The plastic section modulus of the given cross-section is ______ [latex]\times 10^4 mm^3[/latex] (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
T-beam cross-section:
Flange: 100 mm wide x 20 mm thick
Web: 20 mm wide x 100 mm tall

Total area:
[latex]A_{flange} = 100 \times 20 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]A_{web} = 20 \times 100 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]A_{total} = 4000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]

Centroid from bottom:
[latex]\bar{y} = \dfrac{2000 \times 110 + 2000 \times 50}{4000} = \dfrac{220000 + 100000}{4000} = \dfrac{320000}{4000} = 80 \text{ mm from bottom}[/latex]
(Flange centroid = 100 + 20/2 = 110 mm; Web centroid = 100/2 = 50 mm from bottom)

Plastic neutral axis (PNA): Divides total area equally [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] each half = 2000 mm²
Area above PNA from top: Flange = 2000 mm² [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] PNA is exactly at flange-web junction (120 mm from top = top of web).

Plastic section modulus [latex]Z_p[/latex]:
[latex]Z_p = A_{top} \times \bar{y}_{top} + A_{bot} \times \bar{y}_{bot}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{y}_{top}[/latex] (centroid of flange from PNA) = 10 mm
[latex]\bar{y}_{bot}[/latex] (centroid of web from PNA) = 50 mm
[latex]Z_p = 2000 \times 10 + 2000 \times 50 = 20000 + 100000 = 120000 \text{ mm}^3[/latex]
[latex]= \mathbf{12 \times 10^4} \text{ mm}^3[/latex]

raw_source.text: A fully-penetrating well of 20 cm diameter is provided in an unconfined aquifer. The height of the ground water table is 30 m from the bottom of the aquifer. After a long period of pumping at a rate of 63 [latex]m^3/s[/latex], the drawdown in the observation wells at 10 m and 100 m from the pumped well is 12 m and 11 m, respectively. The transmissibility (in [latex]m^2/s[/latex]) of the aquifer is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Unconfined aquifer, pumping rate [latex]Q = 63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] (likely [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}[/latex], but using as given).
[latex]H = 30 \ \text{m}[/latex] (initial water table)
At [latex]r_1 = 10 \ \text{m}[/latex], drawdown [latex]s_1 = 12 \ \text{m}[/latex]
[latex]h_1 = 30 - 12 = 18 \ \text{m}[/latex]
At [latex]r_2 = 100 \ \text{m}[/latex], drawdown [latex]s_2 = 11 \ \text{m}[/latex]
[latex]h_2 = 30 - 11 = 19 \ \text{m}[/latex]

Dupuit's formula for an unconfined aquifer:
[latex]Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}[/latex]

Since transmissibility is [latex]T = K H[/latex], first determine [latex]K[/latex]:
[latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K (19^2 - 18^2)}{\ln(100/10)}[/latex]
[latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K (361 - 324)}{\ln(10)}[/latex]
[latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K \times 37}{2.303}[/latex]
[latex]K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.303}{\pi \times 37}[/latex]
[latex]K = \dfrac{145.09}{116.24} = 1.248 \ \text{m/s}[/latex]

Therefore, [latex]T = K H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.44 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex]

Note: The given discharge value of [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] is unrealistically high for this problem and is likely intended to be [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}[/latex]. Using the correct unit conversion, the transmissibility is approximately [latex]1.5 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex].

raw_source.text: A wide unlined channel carries sediment-free water. The depth of water is 1 m. The specific weight of water is 10 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. To prevent scouring, the maximum permissible tractive stress on bed is 10 [latex]kN/m^2[/latex]. The maximum slope of the channel bed to prevent scouring is 1 in [latex]n[/latex]. The value of [latex]n[/latex] is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Depth of water y = 1 m
Specific weight of water [latex]\gamma_w = 10kN/m^3[/latex]
Maximum permissible tractive stress [latex]\tau_c = 10N/m^2[/latex]
Slope = 1 in n

Tractive stress on bed:
[latex]\tau_0 = \gamma_w \cdot y \cdot S[/latex]

where S = bed slope = 1/n

Setting [latex]\tau_0 = \tau_c[/latex]:
[latex]10 \text{ N/m}^2 = 10000 \text{ N/m}^3 \times 1 \text{ m} \times \dfrac{1}{n}[/latex]
[latex]10 = \dfrac{10000}{n}[/latex]
[latex]n = \dfrac{10000}{10} = \mathbf{1000}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A bridge with an expected life of 50 years is designed for a flood of 10000 [latex]m^3/s/[/latex] corresponding to the return period of 100 years. The risk associated with this design is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Risk formula:
[latex]R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n[/latex]

Given:
Design life [latex]n = 50[/latex] years
Return period [latex]T = 100[/latex] years

Calculation:
[latex]R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{100}\right)^{50} = 1 - (0.99)^{50}[/latex]

[latex](0.99)^{50} = e^{50 \ln(0.99)} = e^{50 \times (-0.01005)} = e^{-0.5025} = 0.6050[/latex]

[latex]R = 1 - 0.6050 = \mathbf{0.40}[/latex]

There is approximately a 40% risk that the design flood will be exceeded at least once during the 50-year life of the bridge.

raw_source.text:
An infinite slope with slope angle [latex]\beta = 22 ^\circ[/latex] consists of soil with the following properties:

Unit weight [latex]\gamma = 15.72 kN/m^3[/latex]
Cohesion [latex]c' = 12[/latex] kPa
Angle of internal friction [latex]\phi' = 15 ^\circ [/latex]

The critical height of the slope (in m) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Use the factor of safety equation for an infinite slope

For a dry infinite slope,
[latex] F=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} [/latex]

At the critical height, the slope is on the verge of failure, hence [latex] F=1 [/latex]

Therefore, [latex] 1=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H_c\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} [/latex]

Rearranging,
[latex] H_c= \dfrac{c'} {\gamma\sin\beta\cos\beta \left(1-\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta}\right)} [/latex]

Step 2: Substitute the given values

[latex] H_c= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times\sin22^\circ\times\cos22^\circ \left(1-\dfrac{\tan15^\circ}{\tan22^\circ}\right)} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} H_c &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3746\times0.9272 \left(1-\dfrac{0.2679}{0.4040}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3473\times0.3369}\\[4pt] &= \dfrac{12}{1.839}\\[4pt] &=6.52\ \text{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Hence, the critical height of the slope is [latex] H_c=6.52\ \text{m} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A circular pile of 600 mm diameter and 6 m length is embedded in a saturated clayey soil. Undrained cohesion of the soil is 80 kPa. Unit weight of the soil is 19.20 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. The adhesion factor is 0.54. If the diameter of the pile is doubled to 1200 mm (keeping the length constant), the ratio of pile capacity of 1200 mm diameter pile to that of 600 mm diameter pile is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:

Pile length: [latex] L=6\ \text{m} [/latex]
Undrained cohesion: [latex] c_u=80\ \text{kPa} [/latex]
Unit weight of soil: [latex] \gamma=19.20\ \text{kN/m}^3 [/latex]
Adhesion factor: [latex] \alpha=0.54 [/latex]
Pile diameters: [latex] D_1=0.6\ \text{m}, \qquad D_2=1.2\ \text{m} [/latex]

Step 1: Ultimate capacity of a pile in clay

The ultimate pile capacity is given by [latex] Q_u=Q_b+Q_s [/latex] where [latex] Q_b=A_bN_cc_u [/latex] and [latex] Q_s=\alpha c_u A_s [/latex]

For clay, [latex] N_c=9 [/latex]

For a circular pile, [latex] A_b=\frac{\pi D^2}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad A_s=\pi DL [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] Q_u = 9c_u\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right) + \alpha c_u(\pi DL) [/latex]

Since [latex]c_u[/latex] and [latex]\pi[/latex] are common, [latex] Q_u \propto \frac{9}{4}D^2+\alpha LD [/latex]

Step 2: Capacity of the 600 mm pile

[latex] Q_1 \propto \frac{9}{4}(0.6)^2+(0.54)(6)(0.6) [/latex]
[latex] Q_1 \propto 0.81+1.944 = 2.754 [/latex]

Step 3: Capacity of the 1200 mm pile

[latex] Q_2 \propto \frac{9}{4}(1.2)^2+(0.54)(6)(1.2) [/latex]
[latex] Q_2 \propto 3.24+3.888 = 7.128 [/latex]

Step 4: Compute the ratio

[latex] \frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{7.128}{2.754} = 2.588 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A group of 25 circular piles is arranged in 5x5 uniform pattern in a soft clay soil with equal spacing in both directions. These are friction piles with negligible end bearing.

Consider the following details:
Diameter of each pile = 1 m
Length of each pile = 15 m
Cohesion of the soil = 20 [latex]kN/m^2[/latex]
Unit weight of the soil = 16 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]
Adhesion factor = 0.75

Considering the efficiency of the pile group as unity, the optimum value of the ratio of the pile spacing to pile diameter is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Number of piles: [latex] n=25=5\times 5 [/latex]
Diameter of each pile: [latex] d=1\ \text{m} [/latex]
Length of each pile: [latex] L=15\ \text{m} [/latex]
Cohesion of soil: [latex] c=20\ \text{kN/m}^2 [/latex]
Adhesion factor: [latex] \alpha=0.75 [/latex]
The piles are friction piles with negligible end bearing.

Step 1: Capacity of the pile group considering individual pile failure

Ultimate capacity of one pile is [latex] Q_{up}=\alpha c\pi dL [/latex]

Therefore, the ultimate capacity of 25 piles is [latex] Q_{ug1} = 25Q_{up} = 25\alpha c\pi dL [/latex]
Substituting the given values,
[latex] Q_{ug1} = 25(0.75)c\pi(1)(15) [/latex]

Step 2: Capacity of the pile group acting as a block

For a [latex]5\times5[/latex] pile group, the overall width of the block is [latex] B=4s+d [/latex]
The perimeter of the block is [latex] P=4B=4(4s+d) [/latex]

For block failure in clay, the ultimate capacity is obtained from the shear resistance developed along the perimeter of the block:
[latex] Q_{ug2} = cPL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L [/latex]

Step 3: Apply the condition of optimum spacing

For optimum spacing, the efficiency of the pile group is unity. Hence,
[latex] Q_{ug1}=Q_{ug2} [/latex]
Therefore,
[latex] 25\alpha c\pi dL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L [/latex]

Cancelling the common terms [latex]c[/latex] and [latex]L[/latex],
[latex] 25\alpha\pi d = 4(4s+d) [/latex]
Substituting [latex]\alpha=0.75[/latex] and [latex]d=1[/latex],
[latex] 25(0.75)\pi = 4(4s+1) [/latex]
[latex] 18.75\pi = 16s+4 [/latex]
[latex] 16s = 18.75\pi-4 [/latex]
[latex] s = \frac{18.75\pi-4}{16} [/latex] [latex] = \frac{18.75(3.1416)-4}{16} \approx 3.43\ \text{m} [/latex]

Step 4: Compute the spacing-to-diameter ratio

Since [latex]d=1\ \text{m}[/latex],
[latex] \frac{s}{d} = \frac{3.43}{1} = 3.43 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A shallow strip footing of width 2 m is embedded at a depth of 1.5 m below the ground surface in a homogeneous pure clay with an angle of internal friction zero. Consider unit weight of soil as 20 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex] and undrained cohesion of soil as 20 [latex]kN/m^2[/latex].

Due to rise of ground water table from far below the founding depth to the ground surface in monsoon season, the magnitude of percentage change in the net ultimate bearing capacity as per Terzaghi's theory is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Net ultimate bearing capacity for strip footing on pure clay ([latex]\phi = 0[/latex]) by Terzaghi:
[latex]q_{net,ult} = c \cdot N_c + \gamma \cdot D_f(N_q - 1)[/latex]
For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex]: [latex]N_c = 5.7[/latex], [latex]N_q = 1[/latex], [latex]N_\gamma = 0[/latex]

[latex]q_{net,ult} = c \cdot N_c + \gamma \cdot D_f \cdot (1-1) = c \cdot N_c = 20 \times 5.7 = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2[/latex]

After water table rises to ground surface:
For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] pure clay: [latex]N_q = 1[/latex], so the [latex](N_q - 1)[/latex] term = 0 regardless of water table.
The cohesion term [latex]c \cdot N_c[/latex] is unaffected by water table.

[latex]q_{net,ult} = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2[/latex] (same as before)

Percentage change = 0%

Explanation: For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] soils, net ultimate bearing capacity is independent of unit weight, so water table rise has no effect.

raw_source.text:
Traffic is moving on a 6-lane dual carriageway road. Traffic volume per direction during peak hour (08:00 am to 09:00 am) is 6000 veh/h. It is assumed that the traffic is distributed uniformly across the lanes in each direction. Just at 08:00 am, a truck goes out of order on the middle lane of one side, thus disrupting the traffic on that lane in one direction. The lane capacity under normal conditions is 2000 veh/h/ln and under queue formation it is 1600 veh/h/ln. The traffic resumes at 08:30 am on removing the truck from the middle lane. Hourly traffic volume after 09:00 am reduces to 5000 veh/h/dir.

The number of vehicles in the queue at 10:00 am is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Phase 1: 08:00 am to 08:30 am (Incident Period)

Arrival rate: [latex] \lambda_1=6000\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
Number of open lanes: [latex] 3-1=2\ \text{lanes} [/latex]
Capacity under queue conditions: [latex] C_1=2\times1600=3200\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
Queue accumulation rate: [latex] \lambda_1-C_1 = 6000-3200 = 2800\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
Queue at 08:30 am: [latex] = 2800\times0.5 = 1400\ \text{vehicles} [/latex]

Phase 2: 08:30 am to 09:00 am (Post-Incident Peak Hour)

Arrival rate: [latex] \lambda_1=6000\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
All three lanes are reopened.

Since a queue already exists, the lanes discharge at queue capacity:
[latex] C_2 = 3\times1600 = 4800\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]

Queue accumulation rate:
[latex] \lambda_1-C_2 = 6000-4800 = 1200\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]

Queue built during this phase:
[latex] 1200\times0.5 = 600\ \text{vehicles} [/latex]

Queue at 09:00 am: [latex] = 1400+600 = 2000\ \text{vehicles} [/latex]

Phase 3: 09:00 am to 10:00 am (Reduced Demand Period)

Arrival rate: [latex] \lambda_2=5000\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
Since the queue still exists, the three lanes continue to operate at queue discharge capacity: [latex] C_3 = 4800\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
Queue accumulation rate: [latex] \lambda_2-C_3 = 5000-4800 = 200\ \text{veh/h} [/latex]
Queue built during this phase: [latex] 200\times1.0 = 200\ \text{vehicles} [/latex]

Total Queue at 10:00 am

[latex] \text{Total Queue} = 2000+200 = 2200\ \text{vehicles} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a bituminous mix, the percentage by weight of coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, filler, and bituminous binder is 58, 25, 12, and 5, respectively. The corresponding specific gravity of these materials is 2.68, 2.45, 2.42, and 1.15. The bulk specific gravity of the mix is 2.2.

The Voids Filled with Bitumen (VFB, in percentage) is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given: Mix proportions by weight: CA=58%, FA=25%, Filler=12%, Bitumen=5%
Sp. gravity: [latex]G_{CA}=2.68[/latex], [latex]G_{FA}=2.45[/latex], [latex]G_{filler}=2.42[/latex], [latex]G_b=1.15[/latex]
Bulk sp. gravity of mix [latex]G_m = 2.2[/latex]

Step 1 - Theoretical max sp. gravity [latex]G_{mm}[/latex]:
[latex]\dfrac{1}{G_{mm}} = \dfrac{0.58}{2.68} + \dfrac{0.25}{2.45} + \dfrac{0.12}{2.42} + \dfrac{0.05}{1.15} = 0.2164 + 0.1020 + 0.0496 + 0.0435 = 0.4115[/latex]
[latex]G_{mm} = \dfrac{1}{0.4115} = 2.430[/latex]

Step 2 - Total air voids [latex]V_a[/latex]:
[latex]V_a = \left(1 - \dfrac{G_m}{G_{mm}}\right) \times 100 = \left(1 - \dfrac{2.2}{2.430}\right) \times 100 = 9.47\%[/latex]

Step 3 - Volume of bitumen [latex]V_b[/latex]:
[latex]V_b = \dfrac{G_m}{G_b} \times P_b = \dfrac{2.2}{1.15} \times 0.05 = 0.0957 = 9.57\%[/latex]

Step 4 - VMA (Voids in Mineral Aggregate):
[latex]VMA = V_a + V_b = 9.47 + 9.57 = 19.04\%[/latex]

Step 5 - VFB:
[latex]VFB = \dfrac{V_b}{VMA} \times 100 = \dfrac{9.57}{19.04} \times 100 = \mathbf{50\%}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The following consecutive readings (in m) were taken with a dumpy level and a levelling staff at a common interval of 20 m:

0.385; 1.030; 1.925; 2.825; 3.730; 4.850; 1.045; 2.005; 3.330; 4.580

The dumpy level was shifted after taking the sixth reading.

The gradient (in %) of the ground between the first and the last location of the reading is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Identify B.S. and F.S. readings

Since the instrument was shifted after the 6th reading:

Back sights (B.S.): [latex] 0.385,\ 1.045 [/latex]
Therefore,
[latex] \sum BS = 0.385+1.045 = 1.430 [/latex]
Fore sights (F.S.): [latex] 4.850,\ 4.580 [/latex]

Therefore, [latex] \sum FS = 4.850+4.580 = 9.430 [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the difference in elevation

Using the relation, [latex] \Delta RL = \sum BS-\sum FS [/latex]
Substituting the values,
[latex] \Delta RL = 1.430-9.430 = -8.0\ \text{m} [/latex]

Hence, the last point is 8 m lower than the first point.

Step 3: Compute the horizontal distance

The 6th reading (F.S.) and the 7th reading (B.S.) are taken on the same change point.
Therefore, the number of unique ground stations is [latex] 9 [/latex]
Hence, the number of intervals is [latex] 9-1=8 [/latex]
Since each interval is 20 m,
[latex] L=8\times20=160\ \text{m} [/latex]
Step 4: Compute the gradient

[latex] \text{Gradient} = \dfrac{\text{Vertical fall}}{\text{Horizontal distance}}\times100 [/latex] [latex] = \dfrac{8}{160}\times100 [/latex] [latex] = 5\% [/latex]

raw_source.text:
An Activated Sludge Process (ASP) has an inlet wastewater flowrate of [latex]20000 m^3/day[/latex] with a Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) concentration of 250 mg/l. It produces treated wastewater containing 20 mg/l BOD. The aeration tank has a working volume of [latex]6000 m^3[/latex] and a biomass concentration of 3000 mg/l. Biological Sludge Residence Time (BSRT) of the system is 6 days. The influent wastewater and the treated effluent from the system have negligible concentrations of biomass. The sludge recycle line from the bottom of the Secondary Sedimentation Tank (SST) to the inlet of the aeration tank has a flowrate of [latex]6000 m^3/day[/latex] .

To maintain equilibrium, the flowrate (in [latex]m^3/day[/latex]) of sludge that is to be wasted from the system is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:

Influent flow rate: [latex] Q=20000\ \text{m}^3/\text{day} [/latex]
Aeration tank volume: [latex] V=6000\ \text{m}^3 [/latex]
Biomass concentration in aeration tank: [latex] X=3000\ \text{mg/L} =3\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
Biological Sludge Residence Time (BSRT): [latex] \theta_c=6\ \text{days} [/latex]
Recycle sludge flow rate: [latex] Q_r=6000\ \text{m}^3/\text{day} [/latex]
Influent and effluent biomass concentrations are negligible.

Step 1: Determine the mass of biomass in the system

The biomass inventory in the aeration tank is [latex] M=VX =6000\times 3 =18000\ \text{kg} [/latex]
Step 2: Use the definition of BSRT (Solids Retention Time)

BSRT is given by [latex] \theta_c = \dfrac{\text{Mass of solids in system}} {\text{Mass of solids leaving system per day}} [/latex]
Since the influent and treated effluent contain negligible biomass, [latex] \text{Mass of solids leaving system} = Q_wX_r [/latex] where
[latex] Q_w [/latex] = sludge wasting flow rate, and [latex] X_r [/latex] = concentration of return sludge.

Therefore, [latex] 6 = \dfrac{18000}{Q_wX_r} [/latex]
[latex] Q_wX_r = 3000\ \text{kg/day} [/latex]
Step 3: Determine the return sludge concentration

At steady state, the solids entering the aeration tank through recycle equal the solids leaving the aeration tank to the SST:
[latex] (Q+Q_r)X = Q_rX_r [/latex]
Substituting the values,
[latex] (20000+6000)(3) = 6000X_r [/latex]
[latex] 78000 = 6000X_r [/latex]
[latex] X_r = 13\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
Step 4: Calculate the sludge wasting flow rate

From Step 2, [latex] Q_wX_r = 3000 [/latex]
[latex] Q_w = \dfrac{3000}{13} = 230.77\ \text{m}^3/\text{day} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The intensity-duration relationship for rainfall on a rectangular plot ABCD of area 7 ha ([latex]1 \text{ ha} = 10^4 \text{ m}^2[/latex]) can be modelled by the following equation:

[latex]I = \dfrac{25}{t + 10}[/latex]

where [latex]I[/latex] is rainfall intensity (in cm/h) and [latex]t[/latex] is duration (in minutes) of rainfall. The average runoff coefficient over the area is 0.60. The time of entry (in minutes) to the outfall from the corners A, B, C, and D is 10, 20, 15 and 25, respectively.

The design flowrate (in [latex]m^3/h[/latex]) of the storm-sewer at the outfall is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Area [latex]= 7 ha = 70000 m^2[/latex],
Runoff coefficient C = 0.60
Time of entry: A=10 min, B=20 min, C=15 min, D=25 min
[latex]I = \dfrac{25}{t+10}[/latex] cm/h

Rational method: [latex]Q = C \cdot I \cdot A[/latex]

Design duration = longest time of concentration = 25 min (from corner D, since all corners must contribute for max flow)

Intensity at t = 25 min:
[latex]I = \dfrac{25}{25+10} = \dfrac{25}{35} = 0.7143 \text{ cm/h} = 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/h}[/latex]

Design flow:
[latex]Q = C \times I \times A = 0.60 \times 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/h} \times 70000 \text{ m}^2[/latex]
[latex]= 0.60 \times 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \times 70000[/latex]
[latex]= 0.60 \times 500 = \mathbf{300 \text{ m}^3/\text{h}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The maximum demand at a water purification plant has been estimated as 12 million litres per day. For the raw supplies, a rectangular sedimentation tank is to be designed with mechanical sludge removal arrangement. Consider depth of the tank as 4 m, detention period as 6 hours, and velocity of flow as 0.003 m/s.

The width (in m) of the detention tank is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Maximum demand = 12 million litres/day = [latex]12 \times 10^6L/day = 12000 m^3/day[/latex]
Depth H = 4 m
Detention period T = 6 hours = 0.25 day
Velocity of flow v = 0.003 m/s

Step 1 - Volume of tank:
[latex]V = Q \times T = \dfrac{12000}{24} \times 6 = 500 \times 6 = 3000 \text{ m}^3[/latex]

Step 2 - Length of tank:
Flow Q = [latex]\dfrac{12000}{24 \times 3600} = \dfrac{12000}{86400} = 0.1389 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}[/latex]
Cross-sectional area = [latex]\dfrac{Q}{v} = \dfrac{0.1389}{0.003} = 46.3 \text{ m}^2[/latex]
Area = Width x Depth [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] Width = [latex]\dfrac{46.3}{4} = 11.57[/latex] m
Length = [latex]\dfrac{V}{\text{Width} \times \text{Depth}} = \dfrac{3000}{11.57 \times 4} = \dfrac{3000}{46.3} = 64.8[/latex] m

Step 3 - Check width:
[latex]W = \dfrac{Q}{v \times H} = \dfrac{0.1389}{0.003 \times 4} = \dfrac{0.1389}{0.012} = \mathbf{11.57 \text{ m}}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
