raw_source.text: A shallow footing is subjected to a vertical load. Within the elastic limit of the underlying soil, the TRUE statement(s) is/are:
raw_source.solution:
Behavior of rigid vs flexible footings:

(A) TRUE - Rigid footing, uniform settlement:
A rigid footing does not deform, so all points beneath it settle by the same amount (uniform vertical displacement), regardless of soil type (clay or sand).

(B) FALSE - Rigid footing, contact pressure:
Contact pressure under a rigid footing is NOT uniform:
In clay: parabolic (higher at edges)
In sand: higher at centre, lower at edges
The contact pressure distribution varies with soil type.

(C) FALSE - Flexible footing, uniform settlement:
A flexible footing conforms to the soil surface, so settlement is non-uniform - higher at centre, lower at edges (in most soils).

(D) TRUE - Flexible footing, uniform contact pressure:
A perfectly flexible footing applies a uniform contact pressure equal to the applied load per unit area (like a uniformly loaded mattress).
options: Vertical displacement below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
Vertical contact pressure below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
Vertical displacement below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
Vertical contact pressure below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

option_texts: Vertical displacement below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
Vertical contact pressure below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

raw_source.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the type of stresses to be considered for the design of rigid pavements?
raw_source.solution:
Option A:
Warping stresses develop in a rigid pavement due to the temperature difference between the top and bottom surfaces of the slab during a day.
The temperature gradient causes the slab to curl upward or downward, producing warping stresses.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option A is TRUE}} [/latex]
Option B:
Seasonal changes in temperature cause the entire slab to expand or contract. Since the slab movement is restrained by subgrade friction, frictional stresses are developed.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option B is TRUE}} [/latex]
Option C:

In rigid pavement design, the critical tensile stress is not obtained by taking the maximum of wheel load stress, warping stress, and frictional stress individually.
The design stress is generally obtained by combining the wheel load stress and temperature-related stresses at the critical location.
Hence, taking only the maximum of the individual stresses is incorrect.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option C is FALSE}} [/latex]
Option D:

Wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner do not occur simultaneously at the same location.
The critical condition is obtained by considering the most critical loading position, not by summing all three stresses.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option D is FALSE}} [/latex]
options: Warping stress due to temperature differential between top and bottom of the pavement slab as a result of daily variation in temperature
Frictional stress due to overall increase or decrease in temperature of the pavement slab as a result of seasonal variation in temperature
Critical stress obtained as the maximum of the wheel load stress, the warping stress, and the frictional stress
Critical stress obtained as the sum of wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner of the pavement slab

option_texts: Warping stress due to temperature differential between top and bottom of the pavement slab as a result of daily variation in temperature
Frictional stress due to overall increase or decrease in temperature of the pavement slab as a result of seasonal variation in temperature

raw_source.text:
Consider differential equation [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex] with the condition [latex]y = 0[/latex] at [latex]x = 0[/latex].

The value of [latex]y[/latex] at [latex]x = 1.0[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given ODE: [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex], [latex]y(0) = 0[/latex]

Step 1 - This is a linear first-order ODE. Rewrite:
[latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex]

Step 2 - Integrating factor (IF):
[latex]IF = e^{\int x\,dx} = e^{x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 3 - Multiply both sides by IF:
[latex]\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y \cdot e^{x^2/2}\right) = x \cdot e^{x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 4 - Integrate both sides:
[latex]y \cdot e^{x^2/2} = \int x \cdot e^{x^2/2}\,dx[/latex]
Let [latex]t = x^2/2[/latex], [latex]dt = x\,dx[/latex]:
[latex]= \int e^t\,dt = e^t + C = e^{x^2/2} + C[/latex]

Step 5 - General solution:
[latex]y = 1 + Ce^{-x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 6 - Apply initial condition y(0) = 0:
[latex]0 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -1[/latex]
[latex]y = 1 - e^{-x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 7 - Find y at x = 1:
[latex]y(1) = 1 - e^{-1/2} = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 1 - 0.6065 = \mathbf{0.39}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The age (in years) of a population is normally distributed with a mean of 36 and standard deviation of 12. The height (in cm) of the same population is also normally distributed with a mean of 160 and standard deviation of 10.

If the probability of age greater than 50 years is equal to the probability of height greater than [latex]h[/latex], the value of [latex]h[/latex] (in cm) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Age distribution: Mean [latex]\mu_a = 36[/latex], SD [latex]\sigma_a = 12[/latex]
Height distribution: Mean [latex]\mu_h = 160[/latex], SD [latex]\sigma_h = 10[/latex]

Step 1 - Find z-score for age > 50:
[latex]z = \dfrac{50 - 36}{12} = \dfrac{14}{12} = 1.1\overline{6} \approx 1.167[/latex]

Step 2 - The probability P(age > 50) = P(Z > 1.167)
This equals the same probability for height:
[latex]P(\text{height} > h) = P(Z > 1.167)[/latex]

Step 3 - Find h using the same z-score:
[latex]\dfrac{h - 160}{10} = 1.167[/latex]
[latex]h = 160 + 1.167 \times 10 = 160 + 11.67 = \mathbf{171.67 \text{ cm}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep rectangular concrete beam is prestressed by means of 4 high-tensile tendons, each of 14 mm diameter. The centre of the tendons is 200 mm from the soffit of the beam. The effective stress in each tendon is 700 N/mm².

The maximum bending moment (in kN·m), that can be applied to the section without causing tension at the soffit of the beam due to prestressing only, is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).

Use [latex]\pi = 3.14[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given: Beam: 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep. 4 tendons of 14 mm diameter, centred 200 mm from soffit. Effective stress [latex]= 700 N/mm^2. \; \pi = 3.14[/latex]

Step 1 - Area of each tendon:
[latex]A_t = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 14^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 196}{4} = \dfrac{615.44}{4} = 153.86 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]

Step 2 - Total prestress force P:
[latex]P = 4 \times A_t \times f_{pe} = 4 \times 153.86 \times 700 = 430808 \text{ N} \approx 430.8 \text{ kN}[/latex]

Step 3 - Eccentricity e (from centroid to tendon):
Centroid of beam from soffit = 600/2 = 300 mm
[latex]e = 300 - 200 = 100 \text{ mm}[/latex]

Step 4 - Section modulus (bottom fibre):
[latex]Z_b = \dfrac{bD^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 600^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 360000}{6} = 15 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3[/latex]

Step 5 - Maximum BM without tension at soffit:
Stress at soffit = [latex]\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b} - \dfrac{M}{Z_b} \geq 0[/latex]
[latex]M \leq \left(\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b}\right) \times Z_b = P \cdot \dfrac{Z_b}{A} + P \cdot e[/latex]
[latex]A = 250 \times 600 = 150000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]M \leq 430.8 \times \dfrac{15 \times 10^6}{150000} + 430.8 \times 100[/latex]
[latex]M \leq 430.8 \times 100 + 430.8 \times 100 = 43080 + 43080 = 86160 \text{ kN mm} = 86.2 \text{ kN m}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A rigid-jointed portal frame, shown in the figure, consists of beam and columns of equal length [latex]L[/latex]. The frame has a fixed support at one end and a roller support at the other end. The frame is subjected to a uniformly distributed load [latex]w[/latex] and a lateral load [latex]P[/latex] as shown in the figure. The plastic moment capacity of the beam and column sections is [latex]M_p[/latex]. Consider a combined beam-column mechanism for plastic collapse. By applying the virtual work equation corresponding to the combined plastic collapse mechanism, [latex]M_p[/latex] is expressed as

[latex]M_p = C_1 PL + C_2 wL^2[/latex]

where [latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex] are constants.


The value of [latex](C_1/C_2)[/latex] is ______ (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Identify the collapse mechanism
For the combined beam-column mechanism, plastic hinges form at:
- Left column base (fixed support)
- Left beam-column joint
- Right beam-column joint
- One plastic hinge at the mid-span of the beam
Thus, total plastic hinges formed: [latex] 4 [/latex]
Since the frame has degree of indeterminacy 3, four plastic hinges are required to form a mechanism.

Step 2: External work done by lateral load
Let the sway displacement at the beam level be [latex] \Delta. [/latex] Let the rotation of the columns be [latex] \theta. [/latex] Since column height is [latex] L, [/latex] [latex] \Delta=L\theta. [/latex] External work done by the lateral load: [latex] W_P=P\Delta [/latex] [latex] =P(L\theta). [/latex]
Step 3: External work done by UDL

Due to the beam mechanism, a plastic hinge forms at mid-span. The vertical displacement at the beam center is [latex] \delta=\dfrac{L}{2}\theta. [/latex] For a uniformly distributed load, [latex] W_w = wL\left(\dfrac{\delta}{2}\right) [/latex]
since the average displacement of the load is [latex] \dfrac{\delta}{2}. [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] W_w = wL\left(\dfrac{L\theta}{4}\right) = \dfrac{wL^2\theta}{4}. [/latex]
Step 4: Internal work
Plastic hinge rotations are:
Left base hinge: [latex] \theta [/latex]
Left beam-column joint: [latex] \theta [/latex]
Right beam-column joint: [latex] \theta [/latex]
Mid-span beam hinge: [latex] 2\theta [/latex]
Hence, [latex] W_i = M_p(\theta+\theta+\theta+2\theta) [/latex] [latex] = 5M_p\theta. [/latex]
Step 5: Apply virtual work equation
[latex] W_P+W_w=W_i [/latex]
[latex] PL\theta+\dfrac{wL^2\theta}{4} = 5M_p\theta. [/latex]
Cancelling [latex] \theta, [/latex]
[latex] 5M_p = PL+\dfrac{wL^2}{4}. [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] M_p = \dfrac{1}{5}PL+\frac{1}{20}wL^2. [/latex]
Comparing with [latex] M_p=C_1PL+C_2wL^2, [/latex]
we get [latex] C_1=\dfrac{1}{5}, \qquad C_2=\dfrac{1}{20}. [/latex]
Hence, [latex] \dfrac{C_1}{C_2} = \dfrac{1/5}{1/20} = 4. [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Linearly elastic, homogeneous, uniform bars BCD and FG shown in the figure have fixed supports at B and G, respectively. For both the bars, axial rigidity is 20000 kN. A gap of 2 mm exists between D and F prior to application of any load (i.e. P = 0). Small deformation and infinitesimal strain assumptions are valid for the given bars.



The magnitude of the horizontal reaction (in kN) at B after application of the axial force P of 20 kN at C is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Axial rigidity of both bars: [latex] AE=20000\ \text{kN} [/latex]
Applied load: [latex] P=20\ \text{kN} [/latex]
Gap between D and F: [latex] g=2\ \text{mm}=0.002\ \text{m} [/latex]
Lengths: [latex] BD=10\ \text{m} \qquad FG=5\ \text{m} [/latex]
Step 1: Check whether the gap closes

If only the left bar acts, the displacement of point D due to the 20 kN load is
[latex] \delta_D = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{20\times10}{20000} = 0.01\ \text{m} = 10\ \text{mm} [/latex]
Since [latex] 10\ \text{mm}>2\ \text{mm}, [/latex] the gap closes and the right bar also starts carrying load.

Step 2: Let the final reactions be
[latex] R_B = \text{reaction at B} [/latex]
[latex] R_G = \text{reaction at G} [/latex]
From equilibrium, [latex] R_B+R_G=20 \;\; ...(1) [/latex]
Step 3: Apply compatibility condition
After contact, the displacement of D must be equal to:
Gap closed [latex] (2\ \text{mm}) [/latex] plus
Compression of the right bar FG.
Compression of left bar: [latex] \delta_L = \dfrac{R_B(10)}{20000} [/latex]
Compression of right bar: [latex] \delta_R = \dfrac{R_G(5)}{20000} [/latex]
Hence, [latex] \delta_L = 0.002+\delta_R [/latex]
Substituting, [latex] \dfrac{10R_B}{20000} = 0.002+\dfrac{5R_G}{20000} [/latex]
Multiplying by 20000, [latex] 10R_B = 40+5R_G \; \; ...(2) [/latex]
Using Equation (1), [latex] R_G=20-R_B [/latex]
Substituting into Equation (2),
[latex] 10R_B = 40+5(20-R_B) [/latex]
[latex] 10R_B = 140-5R_B [/latex]
[latex] 15R_B=140 [/latex]
[latex] R_B=15.33\ \text{kN} [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] R_B\approx16\ \text{kN} [/latex] to the nearest integer.
raw_source.tag2: Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain

raw_source.text:
A simply-supported rectangular reinforced concrete beam has a width 250 mm and an overall depth 600 mm. The effective span of the beam is 6.23 m. The beam carries a live load of 5 kN/m and super imposed dead load of 5 kN/m, in addition to its own weight. The unit weight of reinforced concrete is 25 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. Consider the load factor of 1.5 for all stated loads.

The design bending moment (in kN·m) for the limit state of collapse is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given: b = 250 mm, overall depth D = 600 mm, span L = 6.23 m
Live load = 5 kN/m, SIDL = 5 kN/m, Unit weight of RC = 25 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex], Load factor = 1.5

Step 1 - Self weight of beam:
[latex]w_{SW} = b \times D \times \gamma = 0.25 \times 0.60 \times 25 = 3.75 \text{ kN/m}[/latex]

Step 2 - Total factored load:
[latex]w_u = 1.5 \times (w_{LL} + w_{SIDL} + w_{SW}) = 1.5 \times (5 + 5 + 3.75) = 1.5 \times 13.75 = 20.625 \text{ kN/m}[/latex]

Step 3 - Design bending moment (simply supported):
[latex]M_u = \dfrac{w_u L^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times (6.23)^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times 38.81}{8} = \dfrac{800.5}{8} = \mathbf{100.06 \text{ kN.m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Width (in m) of a rectangular channel required to carry a discharge of [latex]96 m^3/s[/latex] at a critical depth of 9.8 m is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).

Use acceleration due to gravity [latex]g = 9.8 m/s^2[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
At critical depth in a rectangular channel:
[latex]Q = A\sqrt{g \cdot y_c}[/latex] where [latex]A = B \times y_c[/latex] for rectangular channel

Given: [latex]Q = 96 m^3/s, y_c = 9.8 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2[/latex]

Formula:
[latex]Q = B \cdot y_c \cdot \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}[/latex]

Solving for B:
[latex]B = \dfrac{Q}{y_c \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times \sqrt{9.8 \times 9.8}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{96}{96.04} \approx \mathbf{1.00 \text{ m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The cross section of a 0.5 m wide vertical gate holding water and oil is shown in the figure. The unit weights of water and oil are [latex]10 kN/m^3[/latex] and [latex]7.5 kN/m^3[/latex], respectively.



The horizontal hydrostatic force (in kN) acting on the vertical gate is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given: Gate width = 0.5 m; Oil depth = 0.5 m (top); Water depth = 1.0 m (bottom)
[latex]γ_{oil} = 7.5 kN/m^3, γ_{water} = 10 kN/m^3[/latex]

Horizontal hydrostatic force = pressure at centroid x area

Force due to oil layer (0 to 0.5 m depth):
Centroid of oil at depth 0.25 m from oil surface.
Pressure at centroid = [latex]\gamma_{oil} \times 0.25 = 7.5 \times 0.25 = 1.875 kN/m^2[/latex]
Area = [latex]0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 m^2[/latex]
[latex]F_{oil} = 1.875 \times 0.25 = 0.469[/latex] kN

Force due to water layer (0.5 m to 1.5 m depth from oil surface):
Pressure at top of water = [latex]\gamma_{oil} \times 0.5 = 7.5 \times 0.5 = 3.75 kN/m^2[/latex]
Pressure at bottom = [latex]3.75 + \gamma_w \times 1.0 = 3.75 + 10 = 13.75 kN/m^2[/latex]
Average pressure = [latex](3.75 + 13.75)/2 = 8.75 kN/m^2[/latex]
Area = [latex]1.0 \times 0.5 = 0.5 m^2[/latex]
[latex]F_{water} = 8.75 \times 0.5 = 4.375[/latex] kN

Total force:
[latex]F = F_{oil} + F_{water} = 0.469 + 4.375 = \mathbf{4.84 \text{ kN}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A centrifugal pump is delivering water from an underground tank to an overhead reservoir against a static head of 35 m through a 2 km long, 250 mm diameter pipe. The head-discharge characteristic of the pump is given by

[latex]H = 140 - 9000Q^2[/latex]

where [latex]H[/latex] is the head (in m) generated by the pump and [latex]Q[/latex] is the discharge (in [latex]m^3/s[/latex]) of the pump.

Neglecting all minor losses, the head (in m) generated by the pump is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).

Use: Darcy-Weisbach friction factor [latex]f = 0.04[/latex], Acceleration due to gravity[latex] = 9.81 m/s^2[/latex], [latex]\pi = 3.14[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given: Static head [latex]= 35 m, L = 2000 m, D = 250 mm = 0.25 m, f = 0.04, g = 9.81 m/s^2, \pi= 3.14[/latex]
Pump curve: [latex]H = 140 - 9000Q^2[/latex]

Step 1 - Friction head loss (Darcy-Weisbach):
[latex]h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{fL}{2gD} \times \dfrac{16Q^2}{\pi^2 D^4}[/latex]...

Using: [latex]h_f = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}[/latex]
[latex]h_f = \dfrac{8 \times 0.04 \times 2000 \times Q^2}{(3.14)^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.25)^5}[/latex][latex]= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{9.8596 \times 9.81 \times 0.000977}[/latex][latex]= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{0.09444}[/latex][latex]= 6778 Q^2[/latex]

Step 2 - System curve:
[latex]H_{sys} = 35 + 6778 Q^2[/latex]

Step 3 - Operating point (pump curve = system curve):
[latex]140 - 9000Q^2 = 35 + 6778Q^2[/latex]
[latex]105 = 15778 Q^2[/latex]
[latex]Q^2 = \dfrac{105}{15778} = 0.006655[/latex]
[latex]Q = 0.08158 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}[/latex]

Step 4 - Head generated:
[latex]H = 140 - 9000 \times 0.006655 = 140 - 59.9 = \mathbf{80 \text{ m}} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The flow depth for a discharge of 10 [latex]m^3/s[/latex] in a wide rectangular channel is 2.0 m. Assume that the flow is uniform.

If the discharge is doubled, the flow depth (in m) in this channel is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Manning's equation for a wide rectangular channel:
[latex]Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times A \times R^{2/3} \times S^{1/2}[/latex]
For wide channel: [latex]R \approx y[/latex] (hydraulic radius ≈ depth)
[latex]Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times B \times y \times y^{2/3} \times S^{1/2} = \dfrac{B S^{1/2}}{n} \times y^{5/3}[/latex]

So for a wide channel: [latex]Q \propto y^{5/3}[/latex] (when B, n, S are constant)

Given: [latex]Q_1 = 10m^3/s[/latex] at [latex]y_1 = 2.0[/latex] m
[latex]Q_2 = 20[/latex] m³/s (doubled)

Ratio:
[latex]\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{5/3}[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{20}{10} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3}[/latex]
[latex]2 = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2}\right)^{5/3}[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{y_2}{2} = 2^{3/5} = 2^{0.6} = 1.5157[/latex]
[latex]y_2 = 2 \times 1.5157 = \mathbf{3.03 \text{ m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a clayey soil stratum, the time required for degree of consolidation from 25% to 50% is 30 days.

The total time (in days) required for 90% degree of consolidation of the same soil stratum is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Consolidation theory - Time factor [latex]T_v[/latex]:
[latex]T_v = \dfrac{C_v \cdot t}{H^2}[/latex]

For a given soil layer, [latex]C_v/H^2[/latex] is constant [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]t \propto T_v[/latex]

Time factors for different degrees of consolidation (U):
For U = 25%: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{25}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.0625 = 0.04909[/latex]
For U = 50%: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{50}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.25 = 0.1963[/latex]
For U = 90%: [latex]T_v = 0.848[/latex] (standard value)

Ratio [latex]t_{90}/t_{25\to50}[/latex]:
Time from 25% to 50% = 30 days corresponds to [latex]\Delta T_v = 0.1963 - 0.04909 = 0.1472[/latex]

[latex]\dfrac{C_v}{H^2} = \dfrac{0.1472}{30} = 0.004907 \text{ day}^{-1}[/latex]

Time for U = 90%:
[latex]t_{90} = \dfrac{0.848}{0.004907} = \mathbf{172.8 \approx 173 \text{ days}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The ultimate bearing capacity of a 1 m wide strip footing is 532.80 kPa, when embedded at 1 m depth in dry cohesionless soil. The soil has a unit weight of 18 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. The ultimate bearing capacity is 864 kPa when the depth of embedment becomes 2 m.

Neglecting the effect of the depth factor, the bearing capacity factor [latex]N_q[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Terzaghi's bearing capacity for strip footing (cohesionless soil, c = 0):
[latex]q_u = q N_q + \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma B N_\gamma[/latex]
where [latex]q = \gamma D_f[/latex] (surcharge from overburden)

Given:
[latex]B = 1 m, y = 18 kN/m^3[/latex]

Case 1: [latex]D_f = 1[/latex] m [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]q_1 = 18 \times 1 = 18 kN/m^2[/latex]
[latex]532.80 = 18 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]

Case 2: [latex]D_f = 2[/latex] m [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]q_2 = 18 \times 2 = 36 kN/m^2[/latex]
[latex]864 = 36 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Subtracting (1) from (2):
[latex]864 - 532.80 = (36 - 18)N_q[/latex]
[latex]331.20 = 18 N_q[/latex]
[latex]N_q = \dfrac{331.20}{18} = \mathbf{18.4}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A building is proposed in an area having thick deposit of silty clay. The water table is at the ground surface. The saturated unit weight of soil is 18 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex] and unit weight of water is 10 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. The maximum vertical load ([latex]P[/latex]) on a column of the proposed building is 2000 kN.

Consider [latex]\sigma_z \leq 0.1\,\sigma'_v[/latex] for computation of minimum depth of soil exploration.

[latex]\sigma'_v[/latex] is the effective vertical overburden stress. [latex]\sigma_z [/latex] is the increase in the vertical stress at depth [latex]z[/latex] below load [latex]P[/latex] as per the Boussinesq's stress theory.

Based on above, the minimum depth (in m) of soil exploration required for the foundation design is ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Water table at ground surface, [latex]\gamma_{sat} = 18kN/m^3, \gamma_w = 10 kN/m^3[/latex]
Column load P = 2000 kN
Condition: [latex]\sigma_z \leq 0.1 \sigma'_v[/latex] at depth z

Step 1 - Effective vertical stress at depth z (water table at surface):
[latex]\sigma'_v = (\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w) \times z = (18 - 10) \times z = 8zkN/m^2[/latex]

Step 2 - Stress increase below column (Boussinesq, for circular/point load):
For a point load P: [latex]\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2}[/latex] (at depth z directly below load)

Step 3 - Apply condition:
[latex]\dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.1 \times 8z[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{3 \times 2000}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.8z[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{6000}{2\pi z^2} = 0.8z[/latex]
[latex]z^3 = \dfrac{6000}{2\pi \times 0.8} = \dfrac{6000}{5.027} = 1193.7[/latex]
[latex]z = (1193.7)^{1/3} = \mathbf{10.61 \text{ m}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A soil sample has the following properties:

Natural water content = 30%
Plasticity index = 40%
Liquidity index = 50%

The estimated plastic limit (in %) of the soil is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Natural water content [latex]w = 30\%[/latex]
Plasticity Index [latex]PI = 40\%[/latex]
Liquidity Index [latex]LI = 50\% = 0.5[/latex]

Liquidity Index formula:
[latex]LI = \dfrac{w - PL}{PI}[/latex]

Solving for Plastic Limit (PL):
[latex]0.5 = \dfrac{30 - PL}{40}[/latex]
[latex]30 - PL = 0.5 \times 40 = 20[/latex]
[latex]PL = 30 - 20 = \mathbf{10\%}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a given traffic stream, the speed-density relationship is given as:

[latex]v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)[/latex]

where [latex]v[/latex] is the mean speed (in km/h) and [latex]k[/latex] is the density (in veh/km).

Considering [latex]v_o = 45[/latex] km/h and [latex]k_j = 200[/latex] veh/km, the maximum flow (in veh/h) for the given stream is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given speed-density model: [latex]v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)[/latex]

where [latex]v_o = 45[/latex] km/h, [latex]k_j = 200[/latex] veh/km

Step 1 - Flow = speed x density:
[latex]q = v \cdot k = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) \cdot k[/latex]

Step 2 - Maximize flow [latex]\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0[/latex]:
[latex]\dfrac{dq}{dk} = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) + k \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)\right] = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) - 1\right] = 0[/latex]
[latex]\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{k_j}{k} = e \Rightarrow k^* = \dfrac{k_j}{e} = \dfrac{200}{e} = \dfrac{200}{2.718} = 73.57[/latex] veh/km

Step 3 - Speed at maximum flow:
[latex]v^* = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k^*}\right) = 45 \times \ln(e) = 45 \times 1 = 45[/latex] km/h

Step 4 - Maximum flow:
[latex]q_{max} = v^* \times k^* = 45 \times 73.57 = \mathbf{3311 \text{ veh/h}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A vertical curve is formed by a descending gradient of 1 in 40 meeting an ascending gradient of 1 in 50. Consider the following:

Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) = 90 m
Height of headlight of a vehicle above the road surface = 0.75 m
Headlight beam angle with respect to the longitudinal axis of the vehicle = 1.2[latex]^\circ [/latex]

Based on the sight distance criteria, the design length (in m) of the vertical curve is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Descending gradient: [latex] g_1=-\frac{1}{40}=-0.025=-2.5\% [/latex]
Ascending gradient: [latex] g_2=\frac{1}{50}=0.02=2.0\% [/latex]
Algebraic difference of grades: [latex] N=|g_1-g_2| =|-2.5-2.0| =4.5 [/latex] (percent)
Stopping Sight Distance: [latex] S=90\ \text{m} [/latex]
Headlight height: [latex] h=0.75\ \text{m} [/latex]
Headlight beam angle: [latex] \phi=1.2^\circ [/latex]
Step 1: Identify the type of vertical curve
A descending gradient meeting an ascending gradient forms a sag vertical curve.
For a sag curve, when sight distance is governed by headlights and [latex] L > S, [/latex]
IRC recommends [latex] L=\dfrac{N S^2}{200\left(h+S\tan\phi\right)} [/latex]
Step 2: Calculate the denominator
[latex] \tan(1.2^\circ)\approx 0.02095 [/latex]
[latex] h+S\tan\phi = 0.75+90(0.02095) [/latex] [latex] = 0.75+1.8855 = 2.6355 [/latex]
Thus, [latex] 200(h+S\tan\phi) = 200(2.6355) = 527.1 [/latex]
Step 3: Calculate the curve length
[latex] L = \frac{4.5\times90^2}{527.1} [/latex] [latex] = \frac{4.5\times8100}{527.1} [/latex] [latex] = \frac{36450}{527.1} [/latex] [latex] \approx69.15\ \text{m} [/latex]
Since [latex] L < S [/latex], the assumption is not valid.

Therefore, use the IRC equation for [latex] L < S: [/latex]
[latex] L = 2S-\dfrac{200(h+S\tan\phi)}{N} [/latex]
Substituting values,
[latex] L = 2(90)-\dfrac{200(2.6355)}{4.5} [/latex] [latex] = 180-117.13 [/latex] [latex] = 62.87\ \text{m} [/latex]
Rounded to the nearest integer, [latex] \boxed{63\ \text{m}} [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning

raw_source.text:
Interior angles measured at the locations of a closed traverse ABCDA are given below:

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Location} & \textbf{Interior\ Angle} \\ \hline A & 71^\circ\ 1'\ 40'' \\ \hline B & 104^\circ\ 54'\ 23'' \\ \hline C & 107^\circ\ 54'\ 10'' \\ \hline D & 76^\circ\ 20'\ 42'' \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

The total error in the measured angles (in degrees) is ______ (rounded off to three decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Sum of interior angles of a closed traverse
For a closed traverse with [latex] n=4 [/latex] sides, the theoretical sum of interior angles is [latex] ( n-2 )\times 180^\circ [/latex] [latex] =(4-2)\times 180^\circ [/latex] [latex] =360^\circ [/latex]
Step 2: Sum the measured angles
[latex] A=71^\circ 1' 40'' [/latex]
[latex] B=104^\circ 54' 23'' [/latex]
[latex] C=107^\circ 54' 10'' [/latex]
[latex] D=76^\circ 20' 42'' [/latex]

Adding seconds: [latex] 40''+23''+10''+42''=115''=1'55'' [/latex]

Adding minutes: [latex] 1'+54'+54'+20'+1'=130'=2^\circ10' [/latex]

Adding degrees: [latex] 71^\circ+104^\circ+107^\circ+76^\circ+2^\circ=360^\circ [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] \sum \theta = 360^\circ 10' 55'' [/latex]
Step 3: Determine angular error
[latex] \text{Angular Error} = 360^\circ 10' 55'' - 360^\circ [/latex] [latex] = 10'55'' [/latex]

Convert to degrees:
[latex] 10'55'' = \dfrac{10}{60} + \dfrac{55}{3600} [/latex] [latex] = 0.166667+0.015278 [/latex] [latex] = 0.181944^\circ [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] \boxed{0.182^\circ} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The analysis of major cations and anions in a water sample collected from a city's water supply is given below. Ions present in minor concentrations are not given.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Anions} & Cl^- & SO_4^{2-} & HCO_3^- & CO_3^{2-} \\ \hline \textbf{Concentration (mM)} & 1.5 & 0.5 & 1.0 & 0.01 \\ \hline \textbf{Cations} & Na^+ & Ca^{2+} & Mg^{2+} & K^+ \\ \hline \textbf{Concentration (mM)} & 2.0 & 0.5 & 0.25 & 0.02 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{HCl} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{Cl}^-, & pK &= -3 \\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4} &\rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}, & pK &= -3 \\ \mathrm{H_2CO_3} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{HCO_3^-}, & pK &= 6.3 \\ \mathrm{HCO_3^-} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}, & pK &= 10.3 \\ \mathrm{HOCl} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{OCl^-}, & pK &= 7.5 \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]HOCl[/latex] (in %) present in the total free chlorine in the water is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Determine the pH of the water
Using the carbonate system:
[latex] \mathrm{HCO_3^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + CO_3^{2-}} [/latex] with [latex] pK_2=10.3 [/latex]
Applying the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation,
[latex] pH=pK_2+\log\left(\dfrac{[CO_3^{2-}]}{[HCO_3^-]}\right) [/latex]

Substituting the given concentrations,
[latex] pH=10.3+\log\left(\dfrac{0.01}{1.0}\right) [/latex] [latex] =10.3+\log(10^{-2}) [/latex] [latex] =10.3-2 [/latex] [latex] =8.3 [/latex]
Step 2: Determine the fraction of HOCl

The chlorine equilibrium is [latex] \mathrm{HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^-} [/latex] with [latex] pK=7.5 [/latex]
Again using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation,
[latex] pH=pK+\log\left(\dfrac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]}\right) [/latex]
[latex] 8.3=7.5+\log\left(\dfrac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]}\right) [/latex]
[latex] \log\left(\dfrac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]}\right)=0.8 [/latex]
[latex] \dfrac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} = 10^{0.8} \approx 6.31 [/latex]
Thus, [latex] [OCl^-]=6.31[HOCl] [/latex]

Total free chlorine is
[latex] [HOCl]+[OCl^-] = [HOCl](1+6.31) [/latex] [latex] = 7.31[HOCl] [/latex]

Therefore, [latex] \%HOCl = \dfrac{[HOCl]} {[HOCl]+[OCl^-]} \times100 [/latex] [latex] = \dfrac{1}{7.31}\times100 [/latex] [latex] =13.68\% [/latex]
Rounded to the nearest integer, [latex] \boxed{14\%} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Anaerobic bacteria are being utilized for the destruction of biodegradable organic content of wastewater measured in terms of Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD). The yield coefficient (Y) is 0.06 gram Volatile Suspended Solids (VSS) per gram of COD. Bacterial biomass forms the sludge during the process. The proximate chemical formula of anaerobic bacteria is [latex]C_6H_7NO_2[/latex].

The COD (in %) converted into bacterial biomass is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Calculate the molecular weight of biomass

[latex] MW=(6\times12)+(7\times1)+(1\times14)+(2\times16) [/latex] [latex] =72+7+14+32 [/latex] [latex] =125 \ \text{g/mol} [/latex]
Step 2: Determine oxygen required for complete oxidation

The oxidation reaction is
[latex] C_6H_7NO_2+6.25\,O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2+2H_2O+NH_3 [/latex]
Thus, 1 mole of biomass requires [latex] 6.25 \ \text{moles of }O_2 [/latex] for complete oxidation.

COD equivalent of 1 mole biomass:
[latex] COD = 6.25\times32 [/latex] [latex] =200 \ \text{g O}_2 [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] 1\ \text{g biomass} = \dfrac{200}{125} = 1.6 \ \text{g COD} [/latex]
Step 3: COD stored in biomass

Given, [latex] 0.06\ \text{g biomass} [/latex] is produced per [latex] 1\ \text{g COD removed} [/latex]
COD contained in the produced biomass:
[latex] 0.06\times1.6 = 0.096 \ \text{g COD} [/latex] per gram of COD removed.

Therefore, fraction of COD converted to biomass is [latex] 0.096 [/latex] or [latex] 0.096\times100 = 9.6\% [/latex]
Rounded to the nearest integer, [latex] \boxed{10\%} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In an industry, a cyclone collector with 80% efficiency is installed for air purification, followed by an electrostatic precipitator with 50% efficiency. The concentration of particles entering the cyclone collector is 10 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex].

The concentration (in [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]) of particles exiting the precipitator is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Inlet concentration = 10 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Cyclone efficiency = 80%
ESP efficiency = 50%

Step 1 - After cyclone collector:
Particles removed = 80% of 10 = 8 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Particles exiting cyclone = 10 − 8 = 2 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]

Step 2 - After electrostatic precipitator (ESP):
Particles entering ESP = 2 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Particles removed by ESP = 50% of 2 = 1 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Particles exiting ESP = 2 − 1 = 1.00 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]

Final concentration exiting the precipitator = 1.00 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]

raw_source.text:
'The team ______ more than 300 runs in 20 overs __________ rains.
However, some players needed to improve their batting skills.'

Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
raw_source.solution:
Analysis of the sentence:
'The team ______ more than 300 runs in 20 overs __________ rains.'

Blank 1 - verb tense:
The sentence is in the past tense (indicated by 'However, some players needed to improve'). The correct past tense form of 'score' is 'scored'. Options using 'scoring' or 'score' are incorrect for a finite verb in past tense.

Blank 2 - conjunction/preposition:
The team scored runs in spite of the rains - showing contrast/adversity. Both 'despite' and 'in spite of' express this. However, 'despite' is followed directly by a noun ('rains'), while 'in spite of' is also followed by a noun - both are grammatically valid here.

'Despite rains' is more concise and natural. Option (C) gives scored; despite.

Option (D) gives 'scoring; in spite of' - 'scoring' is not a finite verb and fails the tense requirement. Therefore, (C) is correct.

raw_source.text:
If a positive real [latex]x[/latex] satisfies the following equation

[latex]\log_2 x + \log_{\sqrt{2}} x = 48[/latex]

then the value of [latex]x[/latex] is ________________.
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]\log_2 x + \log_{\sqrt{2}} x = 48[/latex]

Step 1 - Convert [latex]\log_{\sqrt{2}} x[/latex] to base 2:
[latex]\log_{\sqrt{2}} x = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 \sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{1/2} = 2\log_2 x[/latex]

Step 2 - Substitute:
[latex]\log_2 x + 2\log_2 x = 48[/latex]
[latex]3\log_2 x = 48[/latex]
[latex]\log_2 x = 16[/latex]

Step 3 - Solve for x:
[latex]x = 2^{16}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The next figure (indicated by '?') in the sequence is:

'All the mangoes in the basket are good.'

If the above statement is false, then which one of the following statements is necessarily true?
raw_source.solution:
Logic analysis using negation of universal quantifier:

The original statement is: 'All mangoes are good' [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] In logic: [latex]\forall x: G(x)[/latex]

The negation of a universal statement [latex]\forall x: P(x)[/latex] is the existential statement [latex]\exists x: \neg P(x)[/latex].

So if 'All mangoes are good' is FALSE, then:
[latex]\exists x: \neg G(x)[/latex] = 'There exists at least one mango that is NOT good'

Why other options are wrong:
(A) 'All mangoes are not good' = None are good - too strong, not necessarily true
(B) 'No mango is good' - same as (A), too extreme
(C) 'Some good and some not good' - possible but not necessarily true (could be all bad)

Only (D) is the logical negation that is necessarily true.
options: All the mangoes in the basket are not good.
No mango in the basket is good.
In the basket some of the mangoes are good and some are not good.
There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.

raw_answer.option_text: There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following statements about four numbers:

(S1) The average of the four numbers is 25
(S2) Each number is at most 40
(S3) Each number is at least 20

Choose the option that is necessarily correct.
raw_source.solution:
Testing each option:

Option (A): S1 + S2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3?
S1: average = 25, S2: each ≤ 40. Can a number be < 20? Yes - e.g., {5, 30, 30, 35}: avg = 25, all ≤ 40, but 5 < 20. So S3 is NOT guaranteed.

Option (B): S2 + S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S1?
S2: each ≤ 40, S3: each ≥ 20. Average could be anything between 20 and 40. Not necessarily 25.

Option (C): S1 + S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S2?
S1: average = 25, so sum = 100. S3: each ≥ 20.
If one number > 40, say [latex]a > 40[/latex], then [latex]a + b + c + d = 100[/latex] with [latex]b, c, d \geq 20[/latex].
So [latex]b + c + d \geq 60[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]a \leq 40[/latex]. Contradiction! Therefore no number can exceed 40.

Option (D): S1 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3?
Average = 25 doesn't mean each ≥ 20 (e.g., {5, 25, 35, 35}).

Therefore, (C) is necessarily correct.

raw_source.text:
'People are crowding around ___ pit into which ___ elephant has fallen. I have never seen an elephant looking more bewildered ___ miserable. Here it is in a most undignified position, thrust into a pit and made to look up ___ a vast, curiosity-stricken crowd.'

Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
raw_source.solution:
Filling the blanks one by one:

Blank 1: '___ pit' - 'pit' begins with a consonant sound [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] use 'a' (not 'an')

Blank 2: '___ elephant' - 'elephant' begins with a vowel sound /e/ [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] use 'an'

Blank 3: 'bewildered ___ miserable' - connecting two adjectives in a comparison [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] use 'and' (coordinating conjunction)

Blank 4: 'made to look up ___ a vast crowd' - 'look up at' is a phrasal expression meaning to gaze upward toward [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] use 'at'

Therefore, Sequence: a; an; and; at

raw_source.text:
The table lists the unit selling price of five products P, Q, R, S, and T. On a particular day, 250 items were sold with the average selling price of Rs. 60.

The following observations were made:

(i) The quantity of S sold was twice that of T.
(ii) The quantity of R sold was thrice that of T.
(iii) The quantity of Q sold was four times that of T.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Product} & P & Q & R & S & T \\ \hline \text{Unit selling price (Rs.)} & 100 & 50 & 40 & 60 & 60 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

What is the quantity of product P sold on that day?
raw_source.solution:
Let quantity of T = t
Then: S = 2t, R = 3t, Q = 4t

Step 1 - Total quantity equation:
[latex]P + Q + R + S + T = 250[/latex]
[latex]P + 4t + 3t + 2t + t = 250[/latex]
[latex]P + 10t = 250 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]

Step 2 - Total revenue equation:
Average price = Rs. 60, Total items = 250
Total revenue = [latex]250 \times 60 = 15000[/latex] Rs.

[latex]100P + 50(4t) + 40(3t) + 60(2t) + 60t = 15000[/latex]
[latex]100P + 200t + 120t + 120t + 60t = 15000[/latex]
[latex]100P + 500t = 15000[/latex]
[latex]P + 5t = 150 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Step 3 - Subtract (2) from (1):
[latex](P + 10t) - (P + 5t) = 250 - 150[/latex]
[latex]5t = 100 \Rightarrow t = 20[/latex]

Step 4 - Find P:
[latex]P = 250 - 10(20) = 250 - 200 = \mathbf{50}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a string P of length [latex]l[/latex] that is laid out as a straight-line segment. Another string K is laid out as a semicircular arc with string P as its diameter as represented in Figure (i). When both strings are shortened by a length [latex]x[/latex], they can be re-arranged such that the shortened string K forms a full circle with the shortened string P as its diameter, as represented in Figure (ii).

The value of [latex]\dfrac{x}{l}[/latex] is __________.
raw_source.solution:
Setup:
String P (diameter) has original length [latex]l[/latex].
String K (semicircle) has original length [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex] (semicircle of diameter [latex]l[/latex]).

After shortening by x:
New P length = [latex]l - x[/latex] (this is now the diameter of the full circle)
New K length = [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x[/latex] (this now forms a full circle)

Condition - K forms a full circle with P as diameter:
Circumference of full circle = [latex]\pi \times \text{diameter} = \pi(l - x)[/latex]

Setting equal to new K length:
[latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x = \pi(l - x)[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x = \pi l - \pi x[/latex]
[latex]\pi x - x = \pi l - \dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex]
[latex]x(\pi - 1) = \dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{x}{l} = \dfrac{\pi}{2(\pi - 1)}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The Roman senator Meritorius, his brother, his son, and his daughter have varying oratory skill levels. They are seated in rows and columns as shown in the figure with exactly one person sitting in each box. It is known that:

(i) Meritorius' daughter and his brother are seated in the same column.
(ii) His son is seated diagonally across the sibling of the worst orator.
(iii) The best and worst orators are seated in the same row.

Who is the best orator?
raw_source.solution:
Setup: 2x2 grid - Row 1 (C1, C2), Row 2 (C1, C2). Four people: Meritorius (M), Brother (Br), Son (S), Daughter (D).

Clue (i): Daughter and Brother are in the same column.
So {D, Br} are in Column 1 or Column 2 together (one in Row 1, one in Row 2).

Clue (ii): Son is seated diagonally across from the sibling of the worst orator.
The siblings in this group are: Br is sibling of M; D is sibling of S... wait - Br and M are siblings (brothers). D and S are children of M (so siblings to each other).
Worst orator's sibling: if worst = D, sibling = S; if worst = Br, sibling = M.

Clue (iii): Best and worst orators are in the same row.

Working through:
From clue (i): Let D = Row1-C1, Br = Row2-C1 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] M and S fill Row1-C2 and Row2-C2.
From clue (ii): Son is diagonal from worst's sibling. If Son = Row2-C2, diagonal = Row1-C1 = D. D is sibling of Son [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] worst orator = Son? But Son can't be diagonal from his own sibling to himself. Try Son = Row1-C2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] diagonal = Row2-C1 = Br. Br is sibling of M [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] worst orator = M.
From clue (iii): Best and worst (M) in same row. M = Row2-C2. So best is also in Row 2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] best = Br or M. Since M = worst, best = Meritorius' brother

A computer uses 46-bit virtual address, 32-bit physical address, and a three-level paged page table organization. The page table base register stores the base address of the first-level table (T1) ,which occupies exactly one page. Each entry of T1 stores the base address of a page of the second-level table (T2 ) Each entry of T2 stores the base address of a page of the third-level table (T3 ) Each entry of T3 stores a page table entry (PTE). The PTE is 32 bits in size. The processor used in the computer has a 1 MB 16 way set associative virtually indexed physically tagged cache. The cache block size is 64 bytes.

What is the size of a page in KB in this computer?

Let page size = [latex]2^p[/latex] bytes. Each table page holds [latex]2^p/4=2^{p-2}[/latex] entries, and T1 fits in one page.

[latex]46=p+3(p-2)\Rightarrow4p=52\Rightarrow p=13[/latex]

Page size = [latex]2^{13}[/latex] = 8 KB

Answer: 8

Consider the operations

Post's theorem: a function alone is complete if it is not 0-preserving, not 1-preserving, not self-dual, not monotone and not linear.

g: g(0,0,0) = 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0-preserving, so {g} cannot produce 1 from 0s [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not complete.

A Young tableau is a 2D array of integers increasing from left to right and from top to bottom. Any unfilled entries are marked with [latex]\infty[/latex], and hence there cannot be any entry to the right of, or below a [latex]\infty[/latex]. The following Young tableau consists of unique entries.

When an element is removed from a Young tableau, other elements should be moved into its place so that the resulting table is still a Young tableau (unfilled entries may be filled in with a [latex]\infty[/latex]). The minimum number of entries (other than 1) to be shifted, to remove 1 from the given Young tableau is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Removing 1 leaves a hole. Repeatedly fill it with the smaller of its right and lower neighbour:

- hole (1,1): min(2, 3) = 2 moves left
- hole (1,2): min(5, 4) = 4 moves up
- hole (2,2): min(6, 12) = 6 moves left
- hole (2,3): min(23, 18) = 18 moves up
- hole (3,3): min(25, [latex]\infty[/latex]) = 25 moves left
- hole (3,4) gets [latex]\infty[/latex]

Shifted: 2, 4, 6, 18, 25 = 5 entries

Answer: 5

raw_source.text:
Consider the sequence of machine instructions given below:
MUL R5, R0, R1
DIV R6, R2, R3
ADD R7, R5, R6
SUB R8, R7, R4
In the above sequence, R0 to R8 are general purpose registers. In the instructions shown, the first register stores the result of the operation performed on the second and the third registers. This sequence of instructions is to be executed in a pipelined instruction processor with the following 4 stages: (1) Instruction Fetch and Decode (IF), (2) Operand Fetch (OF), (3) Perform Operation (PO) and (4) Write back the result (WB). The IF, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for any instruction. The PO stage takes 1 clock cycle for ADD or SUB instruction, 3 clock cycles for MUL instruction and 5 clock cycles for DIV instruction. The pipelined processor uses operand forwarding from the PO stage to the OF stage.

The number of clock cycles taken for the execution of the above sequence of instructions is ___________.
raw_source.solution:
Cycle-by-cycle (PO stage can hold one instruction at a time; results forwarded from PO):

- MUL: IF 1, OF 2, PO 3-5, WB 6
- DIV: IF 2, OF 3, PO 6-10, WB 11
- ADD: IF 3, OF 4, waits for R6, PO 11, WB 12
- SUB: IF 4, OF 5, waits for R7, PO 12, WB 13

Answer: 13

Let [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be a directed, weighed graph with weight function [latex]w:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex]. For some function [latex]f:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex], for each edge [latex](u,v) \in E[/latex], define [latex]w'(u,v)[/latex] as [latex]w(u,v)+f(u)-f(v)[/latex].

Which one of the options completes the following sentence so that it is TRUE?

"The shortest paths in G under [latex]w[/latex] are shortest paths under [latex]w'[/latex] too,_________".
raw_source.solution:
For any path [latex]s=v_0\rightarrow v_1\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow v_k=t[/latex], the f-terms cancel in pairs:
[latex]w'(\text{path})=w(\text{path})+f(s)-f(t)[/latex]

Every s-to-t path changes by the same constant [latex]f(s)-f(t)[/latex], so the shortest one stays shortest, for any f. (This is the reweighting trick in Johnson's algorithm.)

Answer: for every [latex]f:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a non-pipelined processor operating at 2.5 GHz. It takes 5 clock cycles to complete an instruction. You are going to make a 5-stage pipeline out of this processor. raw_source.text: A processor has 64 registers and uses 16-bit instruction format. It has two types of instructions: I-type and R-type. R-type opcodes = 16 [latex]-[/latex] 2 = 14

Accesses = 3 (tree) + 1 (record block) = 4

Let [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be an undirected unweighted connected graph. The diameter of [latex]G[/latex] is defined as:
[latex]diam(G)=\displaystyle \max_{u,v \in V} \{ \text{the length of shortest path between }u \text{ and }v \}[/latex]

Let [latex]M[/latex] be the adjacency matrix of [latex]G[/latex].
Define graph [latex]G_2[/latex] on the same set of vertices with adjacency matrix [latex]N[/latex], where

[latex]N_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array} {lcl} 1 &\text{if}\; M_{ij}>0 \text{ or } P_{ij}>0, \text{ where }P=M^2\\0 &\text{otherwise} \end{array}\right.[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex]P=M^2[/latex] has [latex]P_{ij} \gt 0[/latex] exactly when there is a path of length 2. So in [latex]G_2[/latex], u and v are adjacent whenever their distance in G is 1 or 2.

A shortest path of length d in G can be covered with [latex]\lceil d/2\rceil[/latex] such jumps, so [latex]diam(G_2)=\lceil diam(G)/2\rceil[/latex].

Answer: [latex]diam(G_2)\le\lceil diam(G)/2\rceil[/latex]

Consider a dynamic hashing approach for 4-bit integer keys:

6. To resolve more collisions, each node of the binary tree is further sub-divided into left and right subtrees based on the 4th least significant bit.

raw_source.text:
Consider a computer system with multiple shared resource types, with one instance per resource type. Each instance can be owned by only one process at a time. Owning and freeing of resources are done by holding a global lock (L). The following scheme is used to own a resource instance:
 function OWNRESOURCE(Resource R) 
    Acquire lock L // a global lock 
    if R is available then 
        Acquire R        
        Release lock L 
    else
        if R is owned by another process P then        
        Terminate P, after releasing all resources owned by P        
        Acquire R        
        Restart P        
        Release lock L        
        end if
    end if    
end function
Which of the following choice(s) about the above scheme is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each statement:
- A process never waits while holding resources (the owner is terminated instead), so there is no circular wait [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no deadlock.
- Two processes can keep terminating and restarting each other without progress [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] livelock possible.
- A process may be terminated again and again and never finish [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] starvation possible.
- Each resource still has only one owner at a time [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] mutual exclusion is kept.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

The scheme may lead to live-lock
The scheme may lead to starvation
The scheme violates the mutual exclusion property

The scheme may lead to starvation

Consider a pipelined processor with 5 stages, Instruction Fetch(IF), Instruction Decode(ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Write Back (WB). Each stage of the pipeline, except the EX stage, takes one cycle. Assume that the ID stage merely decodes the instruction and the register read is performed in the EX stage. The EX stage takes one cycle for ADD instruction and the register read is performed in the EX stage, The EX stage takes one cycle for ADD instruction and two cycles for MUL instruction. Ignore pipeline register latencies.
Consider the following sequence of 8 instructions:

ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL

Assume that every MUL instruction is data-dependent on the ADD instruction just before it and every ADD instruction (except the first ADD) is data-dependent on the MUL instruction just before it. The speedup defined as follows.

[latex]\textit{Speedup} = \dfrac{\text{Execution time without operand forwarding}}{\text{Execution time with operand forearding}}[/latex]

The Speedup achieved in executing the given instruction sequence on the pipelined processor (rounded to 2 decimal places) is _____________
raw_source.solution:
Each instruction depends on the one before it. ADD uses EX for 1 cycle, MUL for 2.

With forwarding: the EX stages run back to back: 4 [latex]\times[/latex] (1 + 2) = 12 EX cycles from cycle 3 to 14, then MEM and WB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 16 cycles.

Without forwarding: each instruction's EX (register read) waits until the previous one's WB. Each ADD/MUL pair then takes 1 + 2 EX cycles plus 2 waiting cycles (MEM, WB) each [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] the last WB is at cycle 30.

Speedup = 30 / 16 = 1.875 [latex]\approx[/latex] 1.87

Answer: 1.87

raw_source.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
raw_source.solution:

- A TLB hit means the page is in main memory, so on a cache miss the word is surely in main memory [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Inverted page table: the frame is found by searching (or hashing and following a chain), so the time depends on the address [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- In a hashed page table, colliding addresses sit on the same chain at different positions, so their access times differ [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Option 3 is FALSE

If the virtual address of a word given by CPU has a TLB hit, but the subsequent search for the word results in a cache miss, then the word will always be present in the main memory.
The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all incoming virtual addresses.
In a system that uses hashed page tables, if two distinct virtual addresses V1 and V2 map to the same value while hashing, then the memory access time of these addresses will not be the same.

raw_answer.option_text: The memory access time using a given inverted page table is always same for all incoming virtual addresses.

raw_source.text: Consider four processes P, Q, R, and S scheduled on a CPU as per round robin algorithm with a time quantum of 4 units. raw_source.text: Consider a simple undirected weighted graph G, all of whose edge weights are distinct. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees of G is/are TRUE?

raw_source.text: Consider a system with 2 KB direct mapped data cache with a block size of 64 bytes. The system has a physical address space of 64 KB and a word length of 16 bits. - Q and R share line 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every R access evicts Q True
- At the end, P's block (with S) and R are in the cache, not "only R and S" False

Edge [latex]i\rightarrow j[/latex] exists only when [latex]j\le i[/latex], so edges go from larger to smaller vertices (self-loops are useless in a tree).

In a tree rooted at 5, each other vertex k needs exactly one parent, which must be a vertex larger than k:
- vertex 4: parent 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 choice
- vertex 3: 4 or 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices
- vertex 2: 3 choices
- vertex 1: 4 choices

Parents are always larger, so no cycle can form. Total [latex]=1\times2\times3\times4=24[/latex]

Consider the pushdown automaton (PDA) [latex]P[/latex] below, which runs on the input alphabet [latex]\{a,b\}[/latex], has stack alphabet [latex] \{ \perp ,A\}[/latex], and has three states [latex] \{s,p,q\}[/latex], with [latex]s[/latex] being the start state. A transition from state [latex]u[/latex] to state [latex]v[/latex] , labelled [latex]c/X/\gamma [/latex] , where [latex]c[/latex] is an input symbol or , [latex]X[/latex] is a stack symbol, and [latex]\gamma [/latex] is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state [latex]u[/latex], the PDA can read [latex]c[/latex] from the input, with [latex]X[/latex] on the top of its stack, pop [latex]X[/latex] from the stack, push in the string [latex]\gamma [/latex] on the stack, and go to state [latex]v[/latex]. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol [latex]\perp [/latex] in it. The PDA accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by [latex]P[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Read the PDA transitions:
- In s, every a pushes an A (so m a's give m A's).
- The first b moves to p and pops an A; each further b pops another A.
- To empty the stack we must go to q, and both moves into q need an A on top. In q, the remaining A's and [latex]\perp[/latex] are popped.

So at least one A must be left after reading the b's: [latex]n \lt m[/latex], and [latex]m\ge1[/latex] (with no a's there is no A to move to q).

Answer: [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid 1\le m,\ n \lt m\}[/latex]

- Onto and one-to-one [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] bijective.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

Suppose you are asked to design a new reliable byte-stream transport protocol like TCP. This protocol, named myTCP, runs over a 100 Mbps network with Round Trip Time of 150 milliseconds and the maximum segment lifetime of 2 minutes.
Which of the following is/are valid lengths of the Sequence Number field in the myTCP header?
raw_source.solution:
The sequence numbers must not wrap around within one MSL. Bytes sent in 2 minutes:
[latex]\frac{100\times10^6}{8}\times120=1.5\times10^9[/latex] bytes

[latex]2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex] (too small), [latex]2^{31}\approx2.15\times10^9[/latex] (enough). So the field needs at least 31 bits.

32, 34 and 36 bits are valid; 30 bits is not.

Answer: 32 bits, 34 bits, 36 bits

Let [latex]X[/latex] be a set and [latex]2^X[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]X[/latex].
Define a binary operation [latex] \Delta [/latex] on [latex]2^X[/latex] as follows:
[latex]A \Delta B=(A-B) \cup (B-A)[/latex]
Let [latex] H=(2^X,\Delta ) [/latex]. Which of the following statements about [latex]H[/latex] is/are correct?

- Associative: yes (it behaves like XOR on membership)
- Identity: [latex]\phi[/latex], since [latex]A\Delta\phi=A[/latex]
- Inverse: [latex]A\Delta A=\phi[/latex], so every A is its own inverse (not its complement: [latex]A\Delta A^c=X[/latex])

Answer: H is a group; the inverse of A is A

Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host) over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached anywhere across all DNS servers.
Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers in the DNS hierarchy. The round trip time between the local host and the web server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML file associated with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on the same web server.
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?
raw_source.solution:
DNS (iterative, 3 tiers: root, TLD, authoritative) = 3 RTT.

Non-persistent, 5 parallel connections: base HTML = TCP setup + request = 2 RTT. The 10 objects go in 2 batches of 5, each batch 2 RTT (new connection each) = 4 RTT.
Total = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 RTT.

Persistent with pipelining: TCP setup 1 RTT + HTML 1 RTT + all 10 objects pipelined in 1 RTT.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 RTT.

Answer: 9 RTTs (non-persistent, 5 parallel) and 6 RTTs (persistent with pipelining)

Consider a random experiment where two fair coins are tossed. Let A be the event
that denotes HEAD on both the throws, B be the event that denotes HEAD on
the first throw, and C be the event that denotes HEAD on the second throw.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]P(A)=\frac14,\ P(B)=P(C)=\frac12[/latex].

- A and B: [latex]P(A\cap B)=P(A)=\frac14\ne P(A)P(B)=\frac18[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not independent (same for A and C).
- B and C: [latex]P(B\cap C)=\frac14=\frac12\cdot\frac12[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.
- So [latex]P(B|C)=P(B)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: B and C are independent; Prob(B|C) = Prob(B)

Consider functions Function 1 and Function 2 expressed in pseudocode as follows:

Let [latex]f_1(n)[/latex] and [latex]f_2(n)[/latex] denote the number of times the statement [latex]"x = x + 1"[/latex] is executed in Function 1 and Function 2, respectively.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Count how many times x = x + 1 runs in each function:
- Function 1: the inner loop runs n, then n/2, n/4, [latex]\ldots[/latex] times: [latex]f_1(n)\approx n+\frac n2+\frac n4+\cdots\lt2n[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- Function 2: [latex]f_2(n)=100n[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Both are linear: [latex]f_1\in\Theta(f_2)[/latex] and [latex]f_1\in O(n)[/latex]. They are not strictly smaller or larger than each other, so o and [latex]\omega[/latex] fail.

Let [latex]G[/latex] be a simple, finite, undirected graph with vertex set [latex] \{v_1,...,v_n\}[/latex]. Let [latex] \Delta (G)[/latex] denote the maximum degree of [latex]G[/latex] and let [latex] N=\{1,2,...\} [/latex] denote the set of all possible colors. Color the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] using the following greedy strategy: for [latex]i = 1,...,n[/latex]
[latex]color(v_i)\leftarrow min\{ j \in N: \text{ no neighbour of } v_i \text{ is colored } j\}[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Each vertex gets the smallest colour not used by any neighbour, so no edge joins equal colours [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] proper colouring [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A vertex has at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex] neighbours, so among colours [latex]1\ldots\Delta+1[/latex] one is always free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] at most [latex]\Delta(G)+1[/latex] colours [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]K_n[/latex] needs n = [latex]\Delta+1[/latex] colours, so "at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex]" is FALSE.
- A bad vertex order can use more colours than the chromatic number (e.g. on some bipartite graphs) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

Let [latex]U = \{1, 2, 3\}[/latex]. Let [latex]2^U[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]U[/latex]. Consider an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] whose vertex set is [latex]2^U[/latex]. For any [latex]A,B \in 2^U, (A,B)[/latex] is an edge in [latex]G[/latex] if and only if (i) [latex]A \neq B[/latex], and (ii) either [latex]A \subseteq B[/latex] or [latex]B \subseteq A[/latex]. For any vertex [latex]A[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], the set of all possible orderings in which the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] can be visited in a Breadth First Search (BFS) starting from [latex]A[/latex] is denoted by [latex]B(A)[/latex].
If [latex]\phi [/latex] denotes the empty set, then the cardinality of [latex]B(\phi ) [/latex] is ____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\phi[/latex] is a subset of every set, so [latex]\phi[/latex] is adjacent to all the other [latex]2^3-1=7[/latex] vertices.

BFS from [latex]\phi[/latex] visits all 7 neighbours at level 1, and these 7 can be visited in any order: [latex]7!=5040[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Consider the following two-dimensional array D in the C programming language, which is stored in row-major order:

int D[128][128];

Demand paging is used for allocating memory and each physical page frame holds 512 elements of the array D. The Least Recently Used (LRU) page-replacement policy is used by the operating system. A total of 30 physical page frames are allocated to a process which executes the following code snippet:

for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++)
       for (int j = 0; j < 128; j++) 
                   D[j][i] *= 10;

The number of page faults generated during the execution of this code snippet is _____.
raw_source.solution:
One page = 512 ints = 4 rows of D (each row has 128 ints). D has 128 rows [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 32 pages.

The loop accesses D[j][i] column-wise: for each i, j goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 127, touching all 32 pages in order (one page per 4 rows).

With 30 frames and LRU, cycling through 32 pages means each page is evicted before it is needed again. So every new page in each pass faults: 32 faults per value of i.

Total [latex]=128\times32=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

raw_source.text:
Consider a computer system with 57-bit virtual addressing using multi-level tree-structured page tables with L levels for virtual to physical address translation. The page size is 4 KB (1 KB = 1024 B) and a page table entry at any of the levels occupies 8 bytes.
The value of L is ______.
raw_source.solution:
Page size 4 KB [latex]=2^{12}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 12 offset bits. VPN bits [latex]=57-12=45[/latex].

One page-table page holds [latex]\frac{4096}{8}=512=2^9[/latex] entries [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] each level resolves 9 bits.

Levels [latex]L=\frac{45}{9}=5[/latex]

Answer: 5

raw_source.text:
Consider a sequence [latex]a[/latex] of elements [latex]a_0 = 1, a_1 = 5, a_2 = 7, a_3 = 8, a_4 = 9, \; and \; a_5 = 2[/latex]. The following operations are performed on a stack [latex]S[/latex] and a queue [latex]Q[/latex], both of which are initially empty.

I: push the elements of a from [latex]a_0[/latex] to [latex]a_5[/latex] in that order into [latex]S[/latex].
II: enqueue the elements of a from [latex]a_0[/latex] to [latex]a_5[/latex] in that order into [latex]Q[/latex].
III: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
IV: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex].
V: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
VI: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex].
VII: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex] and push the same element into [latex]S[/latex].
VIII: Repeat operation VII three times.
IX: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
X: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].

The top element of [latex]S[/latex] after executing the above operations is ___.
raw_source.solution:
After I and II: S = [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2] (top = 2), Q = [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2] (front = 1).
- III: pop S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 2
- IV: dequeue Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 1
- V: pop S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S = [1, 5, 7, 8]
- VI: dequeue Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q = [7, 8, 9, 2]
- VII + VIII (4 times): move 7, 8, 9, 2 from Q to S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S = [1, 5, 7, 8, 7, 8, 9, 2]
- IX, X: pop 2 and 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] top = 8

Answer: 8

raw_source.text:
Consider the syntax directed translation given by the following grammar and semantic rules. Here [latex]N, I, F \; and \; B[/latex] are non-terminals. [latex]N[/latex] is the starting non-terminal, and [latex]\#,0 \; and \; 1[/latex] are lexical tokens corresponding to input letters [latex]"\#","0" \; and \; "1"[/latex], respectively. [latex]X.val[/latex] denotes the synthesized attribute (a numeric value) associated with a non-terminal [latex]X[/latex]. [latex]I_1[/latex] and [latex]F_1[/latex] denote occurrences of [latex]I[/latex] and [latex]F[/latex] on the right hand side of a production, respectively. For the tokens [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex], [latex]0.val=0[/latex] and [latex]1.val=1[/latex].

The value computed by the translation scheme for the input string
[latex]\begin{aligned} N & \rightarrow I \# F & N.val=I.val+F.val \\ I &\rightarrow I_1B & I.val = (2 I1.val) + B.val\\ I &\rightarrow B&I.val = B.val\\ F &\rightarrow BF_1& F.val = \frac{1}{2}(B.val + F1.val)\\ F &\rightarrow B& F.val = \frac{1}{2} B.val\\ B&\rightarrow 0& B.val = 0.val\\ B &\rightarrow 1&B.val = 1.val \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]10\# 011[/latex]

is ____ (Rounded off to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Integer part "10" (binary):
I for "1" = 1; I for "10" = [latex]2\times1+0=2[/latex].

Fraction part "011" (evaluated right to left):
- F("1") = [latex]\frac12\times1=0.5[/latex]
- F("11") = [latex]\frac12(1+0.5)=0.75[/latex]
- F("011") = [latex]\frac12(0+0.75)=0.375[/latex]

N.val = 2 + 0.375 = 2.375 (i.e. binary 10.011).

Answer: 2.375

Consider a database of fixed-length records, stored as an ordered file. The database has 25,000 records, with each record being 100 bytes, of which the primary key occupies 15 bytes. The data file is block-aligned in that each data record is fully contained within a block. The database is indexed by a primary index file, which is also stored as a block-aligned ordered file. The figure below depicts this indexing scheme.

Suppose the block size of the file system is 1024 bytes, and a pointer to a block occupies 5 bytes. The system uses binary search on the index file to search for a record with a given key. You may assume that a binary search on an index file of [latex]b[/latex] blocks takes [latex]\left \lceil \log_2 b \right \rceil [/latex] block accesses in the worst case.
Given a key, the number of block accesses required to identify the block in the data file that may contain a record with the key, in the worst case, is _____
raw_source.solution:
Compute the index size step by step:
- Records per data block = [latex]\lfloor1024/100\rfloor=10[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] data blocks = 25000 / 10 = 2500.
- Primary (sparse) index has one entry per data block: 2500 entries of [latex]15+5=20[/latex] bytes.
- Entries per index block = [latex]\lfloor1024/20\rfloor=51[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index blocks = [latex]\lceil2500/51\rceil=50[/latex].

Binary search on the index: [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] block accesses identify the data block.

Answer: 6

raw_source.text:
Consider the language L over the alphabet {0, 1}, given below:

[latex]L = \{w \in \{0, 1\}^* | w \text{ does not contain three or more consecutive 1's} \}.[/latex]
The minimum number of states in a Deterministic Finite-State Automaton (DFA) for L is _____.
raw_source.solution:
The DFA only needs to remember how many 1s have just been seen in a row:
- q0: last symbol 0 (or start)
- q1: one 1
- q2: two 1s
- q3: three 1s seen [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] dead (non-final) state

q0, q1, q2 are final. A 0 returns q0/q1/q2 to q0. All 4 states are distinguishable.

Answer: 4

raw_source.text: Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} [/latex] be a function such that [latex]f(x)=\max \left\{x, x^3\right\}, x \in \mathbb{R} [/latex], where [latex]\mathbb{R} [/latex] is the set of all real numbers. The set of all points where [latex]f(x) [/latex] is NOT differentiable is
raw_source.solution:
Compare [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]x^3[/latex]: they are equal at [latex]x=-1,0,1[/latex]. So [latex]f(x)=x[/latex] for [latex]x\le -1[/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] on [latex][-1,0][/latex], [latex]x[/latex] on [latex][0,1][/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] for [latex]x\ge1[/latex].

At every switching point the two pieces have different slopes ([latex]\frac{d}{dx}x=1[/latex], [latex]\frac{d}{dx}x^3=3x^2[/latex]):
- [latex]x=-1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=0[/latex]: slopes [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner

Everywhere else [latex]f[/latex] is a polynomial, hence differentiable.

Answer: [latex]\{-1,0,1\}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of [latex]\{1,2,3, \cdots, n\} [/latex] for some [latex]n \geq 4 [/latex]. Let [latex]X [/latex] be the event that 1 occurs before 2 in the permutation, and [latex]Y [/latex] the event that 3 occurs before 4 . Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
By symmetry, 1 is before 2 in half of all permutations, so [latex]P(X)=\frac12[/latex]; similarly [latex]P(Y)=\frac12[/latex].

The relative order of {1,2} and the relative order of {3,4} involve different elements, and all 4 combinations (12/21 with 34/43) are equally likely, so [latex]P(X\cap Y)=\frac14=P(X)P(Y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.

- Not mutually exclusive: 1 2 3 4 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies both.
- Neither must occur: 2 1 4 3 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies none.
- Equally likely, so X is not more likely than Y.

Answer: X and Y are independent

Bijection [latex]A\times A\to A\cup B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n^2=|A\cup B|[/latex].

But [latex]n\le|A\cup B|\le 2n[/latex], so [latex]n\le n^2\le 2n[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n\le2[/latex].

- [latex]n=1[/latex]: [latex]A=B[/latex], [latex]|A\cup B|=1=1^2[/latex] True
- [latex]n=2[/latex]: take A and B disjoint, [latex]|A\cup B|=4=2^2[/latex] True

So [latex]|A|\in\{1,2\}[/latex].

Answer: 2

Consider the operator precedence and associativity rules for the integer arithmetic operators given in the table below.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|l|l|} \hline Operator & Precedence & Associativity \\ \hline+ & Highest & Left \\ \hline- & High & Right \\ \hline* & Medium & Right \\ \hline / & Low & Right \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
The value of the expression [latex]3+1+5 * 2 / 7+2-4-7-6 / 2 [/latex] as per the above rules is _____
raw_source.solution:
Precedence: + (highest) [latex]\gt[/latex] [latex]-[/latex] [latex]\gt[/latex] * [latex]\gt[/latex] / (lowest). The lowest-precedence operator is applied last, so / splits the expression:
[latex](3+1+5*2)\;/\;(7+2-4-7-6)\;/\;2[/latex]

First part: + binds before *, so [latex](3+1+5)*2=9*2=18[/latex].
Second part: + first: [latex]7+2=9[/latex]. Then [latex]-[/latex] is right associative: [latex]9-(4-(7-6))=9-(4-1)=6[/latex].

/ is right associative: [latex]18/(6/2)=18/3=6[/latex].

Answer: 6

Consider a network path [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] between nodes [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] via router [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Node [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] sends a file of size [latex]10^6 [/latex] bytes to [latex]R [/latex] via this path by splitting the file into chunks of [latex]10^3 [/latex] bytes each. Node [latex]P [/latex] sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.
Each of the links [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] has a bandwidth of [latex]10^6 \mathrm{bits} / \mathrm{sec} [/latex], and negligible propagation latency. Router [latex]Q [/latex] immediately transmits every packet it receives from [latex]P [/latex] to [latex]R [/latex], with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router [latex]Q [/latex] can simultaneously receive on link [latex]P-Q [/latex] and transmit on [latex]\operatorname{link} Q-R [/latex].
Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time [latex]t=0 [/latex]. Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] receives all the chunks of the file?
raw_source.solution:
Number of chunks [latex]=10^6/10^3=1000[/latex]. Each chunk [latex]=8000[/latex] bits, so transmission time on a link [latex]=\frac{8000}{10^6}=8[/latex] ms.

P sends the chunks back to back: the last chunk is fully sent by P at [latex]1000\times8\text{ ms}=8[/latex] s.
Q forwards each chunk while receiving the next, so only the last chunk adds one more transmission of 8 ms on Q-R.

Total [latex]=8+0.008=8.008[/latex] s.

Answer: 8.008

Consider the following grammar [latex]G [/latex], with [latex]S [/latex] as the start symbol. The grammar [latex]G [/latex] has three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3).

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow d a T \mid \quad(1) \\ & T \rightarrow a S|b T|(2) \\ & R \rightarrow \text { (3) } \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The set of terminals is [latex]\{a, b, c, d, f\} [/latex]. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows.

[latex] \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{FIRST}(S)=\{c, d, f\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(T)=\{a, b, \epsilon\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(R)=\{c, \epsilon\} \\ & \operatorname{FOLLOW}(S)=\operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)=\{c, f, \$\}, \operatorname{FOLLOW}(R)=\{f\} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?

Use the given FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(S)=\{c,d,f\}[/latex] but [latex]daT[/latex] gives only d, so (1) must give c and f. [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex] gives [latex](FIRST(R)-\epsilon)\cup\{f\}=\{c,f\}[/latex] True ([latex]S\rightarrow fR[/latex] gives only f).
- [latex]\epsilon\in FIRST(T)[/latex], so (2) is [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(R)=\{c,\epsilon\}[/latex], so (3) starts with c.

Check FOLLOW with [latex]R\rightarrow cTR[/latex]: [latex]FOLLOW(T)\supseteq FIRST(R)-\epsilon=\{c\}[/latex] and [latex]FOLLOW(R)=\{f\}[/latex] (from [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex]); together with $ this gives [latex]FOLLOW(S)=FOLLOW(T)=\{c,f,\$\}[/latex] True. With [latex]R\rightarrow cR[/latex], c could never follow T.

Answer: (1) [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex] (2) [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] (3) [latex]R\rightarrow cTR[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:
[latex] T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n})+n \text { for } n \geq 1, \\ 1 \quad \text { for } n=1 . \end{array}\right. [/latex]
Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Divide both sides by [latex]n[/latex]: [latex]\frac{T(n)}{n}=\frac{T(\sqrt n)}{\sqrt n}+1[/latex].

Let [latex]S(n)=\frac{T(n)}{n}[/latex]. Then [latex]S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1[/latex].

Taking square roots repeatedly, [latex]n\to n^{1/2}\to n^{1/4}\to\cdots[/latex] reaches a constant after [latex]\log\log n[/latex] steps, adding 1 each step. So [latex]S(n)=\Theta(\log\log n)[/latex].

[latex]T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

In a min-heap every parent is smaller than its children, so the maximum element cannot have a child [latex]\text{---}[/latex] it must be a leaf. Any leaf can hold it.

In an array heap of [latex]n[/latex] elements, leaves are at indices [latex]\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex].

[latex]n=105[/latex]: leaves are 53 to 105 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]105-52=53[/latex] positions.

Answer: 53

raw_source.text: Let [latex] G [/latex] be a directed graph and [latex] T [/latex] a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in [latex] G [/latex] that is rooted at a vertex [latex] v [/latex]. Suppose [latex] T [/latex] is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in [latex] G [/latex], rooted at [latex] v [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex] G [/latex] and tree [latex] T [/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
In a BFS tree, every edge [latex]u\rightarrow w[/latex] of G satisfies [latex]level(w)\le level(u)+1[/latex].

A forward edge goes from [latex]u[/latex] to a non-child descendant [latex]w[/latex], so [latex]level(w)\ge level(u)+2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

The others can fail:
- Back edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v}. Tree {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v is a back edge.
- Cross edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b, b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a}. DFS visits a then b; b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree.
- So G can also have edges outside T.

Answer: There are no forward-edges in G with respect to T
