raw_source.text: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. Let [latex] G [/latex] be any graph with [latex] n [/latex] vertices and chromatic number [latex] k [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Complete subgraph of size k: FALSE. The 5-cycle [latex]C_5[/latex] has [latex]\chi=3[/latex] but no triangle.
- Independent set of size [latex]\ge n/k[/latex]: TRUE. The k colour classes are independent sets covering n vertices, so the largest has at least [latex]n/k[/latex] vertices.
- At least [latex]k(k-1)/2[/latex] edges: TRUE. In a minimum colouring, every pair of colour classes must have an edge between them (otherwise merge the two classes and use [latex]k-1[/latex] colours). That gives [latex]\binom{k}{2}[/latex] edges.
- Vertex of degree [latex]\ge k[/latex]: FALSE. [latex]K_k[/latex] has [latex]\chi=k[/latex] but every degree is [latex]k-1[/latex].

Answer: Options 2 and 3

raw_source.text: Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the DFA given below?
raw_source.solution:
The start state loops on 0 and goes to the final state on 1; the final state loops on 0 and returns on 1. So the DFA accepts strings with an odd number of 1s.

[latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]: [latex]0^*[/latex] stays at start, [latex]1[/latex] reaches the final state, then [latex]0[/latex] (self-loop) or [latex]10^*1[/latex] (go back and return) keeps it final. This is exactly "odd number of 1s".

Others fail on "1" (odd, accepted): [latex]0^*(10^*11)^*0^*[/latex], [latex]0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*[/latex] cannot give "111", and [latex]0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*[/latex] must start with 0.

Node X has a TCP connection open to node Y. The packets from X to Y go through an intermediate IP router R. Ethernet switch S is the first switch on the network path between X and R. Consider a packet sent from X to Y over this connection.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination IP and MAC addresses on this packet at the time it leaves X?
raw_source.solution:
Recall how addresses change along the path:
- IP addresses are end-to-end: the destination IP stays the IP of Y on the whole path.
- MAC addresses are hop-by-hop: the destination MAC is that of the next IP hop, which is router R. A switch only forwards frames; it is never the destination MAC.

So the only true statement is: destination IP = IP of Y.

Answer: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y

raw_source.text: Which of the following file organizations is/are I/O efficient for the scan operation in DBMS?
raw_source.solution:
A scan reads every record of the file.

- Heap and sorted files store records packed in consecutive pages, so each page is read once [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I/O efficient.
- Unclustered tree / hash index: following the index, records are scattered in random pages; the same page may be read many times (about one I/O per record) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not efficient for a scan.

Answer: Sorted, Heap

Consider the following context-free grammar where the start symbol is [latex] S [/latex] and the set of terminals is [latex] \{a, b, c, d\} [/latex].

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow A a A b \mid B b B a \\ & A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\ & B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & a & b & c & d & \$ \\ \hline S & S \rightarrow A a A b & S \rightarrow B b B a & (1) & (2) & \\ \hline A & A \rightarrow \epsilon & (3) & A \rightarrow c S & & \\ \hline B & (4) & B \rightarrow \epsilon & & B \rightarrow d S & \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Note: In the options, "blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty.

Fill the LL(1) table using FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(AaAb)=\{c,a\}[/latex] (A is c[latex]\ldots[/latex] or [latex]\epsilon[/latex]) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (1) [S, c] = [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(BbBa)=\{d,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (2) [S, d] = [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex].
- [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] goes under FOLLOW(A). A appears before a and before b, so [latex]FOLLOW(A)\supseteq\{a,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (3) [A, b] = [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].
- Similarly [latex]FOLLOW(B)\supseteq\{b,a\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (4) [B, a] = [latex]B\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].

Answer: (1) [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex] (2) [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex] (3) [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] (4) [latex]B\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex]

Let M be the 5-state NFA with [latex]\epsilon[/latex]-transitions shown in the diagram below:

Which one of the following regular expressions represents the language accepted by M ?
raw_source.solution:
From state 1 we move by [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to 2 (final) or 4.

- Via 2: 2 and 3 swap on 0. Ending at 2 gives [latex](00)^*[/latex]. From 3 (after [latex]0(00)^*[/latex]), [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to 5, then [latex](11)^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]0(00)^*(11)^*[/latex].
- Via 4: 1 to reach 5, then [latex](11)^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]1(11)^*[/latex].

[latex]L=(00)^*+0(00)^*(11)^*+1(11)^*[/latex]. Since [latex](00)^*+0(00)^*=0^*[/latex]:
[latex]L=0^*+(1+0(00)^*)(11)^*[/latex]

(The other options miss "0" or [latex]\epsilon[/latex], or wrongly accept "11".)

Answer: [latex]0^*+(1+0(00)^*)(11)^*[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex] x [/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval [latex] [0,1] [/latex]. Let [latex] z=x y [/latex] and let the mean values of [latex] x, y, z [/latex] be [latex] \bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z} [/latex], respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Since [latex]0\le y\le1[/latex], we always have [latex]z=xy\le x[/latex]. Taking means: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always TRUE.

Others depend on how x and y are related:
- [latex]y=x[/latex] uniform on [0, 1]: [latex]\bar z=E[x^2]=\frac13 \gt \frac14=\bar x\bar y[/latex] (so = and [latex]\le[/latex] fail).
- [latex]y=1-x[/latex]: [latex]\bar z=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16 \lt \frac14[/latex] (so [latex]\ge[/latex] fails).

Answer: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The relation schema, Person(pid,city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least 3 persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is
raw_source.solution:
Without aggregation, "at least 3 persons in a city" means finding 3 different pids with the same city. That needs 3 copies of Person in one tuple:

[latex]\pi_{P1.city}\big(\sigma_{cond}(P1\times P2\times P3)\big)[/latex]
cond: P1.city = P2.city = P3.city and P1.pid, P2.pid, P3.pid all different.

Joining 3 copies needs 2 cross products; with only one cross product we can compare just 2 tuples.

Answer: 2

Let S1 and S2 be two stacks. S1 has capacity of 4 elements. S2 has capacity of 2 elements. S1 already has 4 elements: 100, 200, 300, and 400, whereas S2 is empty, as shown below.

PushToS1: Pop the top element from S2 and push it on S1.

Consider 4-variable functions [latex] f 1, f 2, f 3, f 4 [/latex] expressed in sum-of-minterms form as given below.
[latex] \begin{aligned} & f 1=\sum(0,2,3,5,7,8,11,13) \\ & f 2=\sum(1,3,5,7,11,13,15) \\ & f 3=\sum(0,1,4,11) \\ & f 4=\sum(0,2,6,13) \end{aligned} [/latex]


With respect to the circuit given above, which of the following options is/are CORRECT?

Compute the AND, OR and XOR outputs as minterm sets:

- OR: [latex]f_3+f_4=\{0,1,4,11\}\cup\{0,2,6,13\}=\{0,1,2,4,6,11,13\}[/latex]
- XOR keeps minterms present in exactly one of them: [latex]\{3,5,7\}\cup\{0,1,2,4,6\}[/latex]; 11 and 13 are in both, so they drop.

[latex]Y=\Sigma(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7)=\Pi(8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15)[/latex] (i.e. [latex]Y=\bar A[/latex]).

raw_source.text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected connected graph in which every edge has a positive integer weight.  Suppose  that  every  spanning  tree  in  [latex]G[/latex]  has  even  weight.  Which  of  the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex]G[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
Take any cycle C and two edges [latex]e,f[/latex] on it. Extend the path [latex]C-f[/latex] to a spanning tree T (it contains [latex]e[/latex], not [latex]f[/latex]). Then [latex]T'=T-e+f[/latex] is also a spanning tree.

[latex]w(T')-w(T)=w(f)-w(e)[/latex]. Both trees are even, so [latex]w(f)-w(e)[/latex] is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]e[/latex] and [latex]f[/latex] have the same parity. So in every cycle all edges are even or all are odd [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Counter-examples for the rest:
- Triangle with all weights 1: every spanning tree has weight 2 (even), yet edges are odd [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- Path with weights 1, 1, 2: only spanning tree has weight 4, but edges are mixed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 2 FALSE.

Answer: In each cycle, either all edges have even weight OR all edges have odd weight

raw_source.text:
Consider a context-free grammar [latex] G [/latex] with the following 3 rules.
[latex] S \rightarrow a S, S \rightarrow a S b S, S \rightarrow c [/latex]
Let [latex] w \in L(G) [/latex]. Let [latex] n_a(w), n_b(w), n_c(w) [/latex] denote the number of times [latex] a, b, c [/latex] occur in [latex] w [/latex], respectively. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Count symbols contributed by each rule:
- Every S finally becomes one c. [latex]S\rightarrow aSbS[/latex] adds one b and one extra S; [latex]S\rightarrow aS[/latex] adds no S. Starting with one S: [latex]n_c=n_b+1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (so [latex]n_c=2n_b[/latex] is FALSE, e.g. w = c).
- Each b comes with an a, so [latex]n_a\ge n_b=n_c-1 \gt n_c-2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]n_a \gt n_b[/latex] fails for w = acbc ([latex]n_a=n_b=1[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: [latex]n_a(w) \gt n_c(w)-2[/latex] and [latex]n_c(w)=n_b(w)+1[/latex]

average seek time of 5 milliseconds, 500 sectors/track, 512-byte sectors.
A file has content stored in 3000 sectors located randomly on the disk. Assuming

Transfer time of one sector [latex]=10/500=0.02[/latex] ms.

[latex]5+5+0.02=10.02[/latex] ms

A functional dependency [latex]F:X \rightarrow Y[/latex] is termed as a useful functional dependency if and only if it satisfies all the following three conditions:

[latex]X[/latex] is not the empty set. [latex]Y[/latex] is not the empty set. Intersection of [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] is the empty set.

instruction format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register

raw_source.text: The number of distinct minimum-weight spanning trees of the following graph is _______
raw_source.solution:
Use Kruskal's idea.

- All four weight-1 edges (a-b, a-f, c-d, d-e) form no cycle, so every MST contains them. Components: {a, b, f}, {c, d, e}, {g}.
- Now g must be joined to both components using weight-2 edges:
[latex]\quad[/latex]g to {a, b, f}: g-a, g-b, g-f [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 choices
[latex]\quad[/latex]g to {c, d, e}: g-c, g-d, g-e [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 choices
- Weight-3 edges are never needed.

Number of MSTs [latex]=3\times3=9[/latex] (each of weight 8).

Answer: 9

raw_source.text: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. The chromatic number of the following graph is _______
raw_source.solution:
Number the 8 vertices 1 to 8 around the octagon.

- The 8 outer sides join consecutive vertices (odd-even).
- Every inner line (the 2 vertical, 2 horizontal and 4 slanted lines) joins two vertices 3 steps apart around the octagon, which is again one odd and one even vertex.

So colour odd vertices with colour 1 and even vertices with colour 2: no edge has both ends the same colour. The graph is bipartite, and it has edges, so it needs at least 2 colours.

Answer: 2

A processor uses a 32-bit instruction format and supports byte-addressable memory access. The ISA of the processor has 150 distinct instructions. The instructions are equally divided into two types, namely R-type and I-type, whose formats are shown below.

- I-type: [latex]8+2\times6+Z=32\Rightarrow[/latex] Z = 12.

[latex]X+2Y+Z=6+16+12=34[/latex]

Consider a 32-bit system with [latex]4 \mathrm{~KB} [/latex] page size and page table entries of size 4 bytes each. Assume [latex] 1 \mathrm{~KB}=2^{10} [/latex] bytes. The OS uses a 2-level page table for memory management, with the page table containing an outer page directory and an inner page table. The OS allocates a page for the outer page directory upon process creation. The OS uses demand paging when allocating memory for the inner page table, i.e., a page of the inner page table is allocated only if it contains at least one valid page table entry.

The value of [latex] X+Y [/latex] is _____

raw_source.text:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

(i) The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
raw_source.solution:
On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control:

1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction.
2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off.
3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR.

Answer: (iii), (i), (ii)

raw_source.text: Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each statement about the symbol table:

- It tracks variable scope — true, this is one of its core jobs.
- It can be implemented using a BST — true, BSTs (or hash tables) are standard implementations.
- It is created during lexical analysis — true, entries are typically first added as identifiers are tokenized.
- "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" — FALSE. The symbol table is essential well beyond parsing: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, and code optimization (e.g. register allocation) all continue to rely on it.

Answer: "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" is FALSE.

raw_source.text: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
raw_source.solution:
Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment.

Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does.

Answer: Register assignment to variables

The page table needs one entry per possible page number, so the maximum number of entries [latex]=2^{21}[/latex].

The transaction [latex]T_1[/latex] aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

raw_source.text:
[latex]g(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex], [latex]f(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]B[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex], and their composition defined as [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] is a mapping from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex].
If [latex]f(. )[/latex] and [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function [latex]g(. )[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
We're told [latex]f[/latex] is onto (B→C) and the composite [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is onto (A→C), and asked what this forces about [latex]g[/latex] (A→B).

Intuitively: since [latex]f[/latex] alone is already onto [latex]C[/latex], every element of [latex]C[/latex] has some preimage in [latex]B[/latex] regardless of [latex]g[/latex]. The fact that [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is also onto just says [latex]g[/latex]'s image happens to hit enough of [latex]B[/latex] to cover all of [latex]f[/latex]'s "useful" preimages — but [latex]g[/latex] itself doesn't need to be onto all of [latex]B[/latex] (there could be elements of [latex]B[/latex] entirely outside [latex]g[/latex]'s range, as long as [latex]f[/latex] still reaches every element of [latex]C[/latex] through the range [latex]g[/latex] does cover), nor does [latex]g[/latex] need to be one-to-one (multiple elements of [latex]A[/latex] could map to the same element of [latex]B[/latex]).

A simple counterexample confirms it: let [latex]B=\{1,2\}[/latex], [latex]C=\{1\}[/latex], [latex]f[/latex] onto, and [latex]g[/latex] mapping every element of [latex]A[/latex] to just [latex]1\in B[/latex] — [latex]g[/latex] is neither onto nor one-to-one, yet [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is trivially onto.

Answer: g(.) is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

[latex]g(. )[/latex] is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

raw_source.text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and [latex]T[/latex] be a minimum spanning tree of [latex]G[/latex]. For any two vertices, [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex], let [latex]d_1(u, v)[/latex] and [latex]d_2(u, v)[/latex] be the shortest distances between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex], respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible [latex]G[/latex], [latex]T[/latex], [latex]u[/latex], and [latex]v[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]T[/latex] is a subgraph of [latex]G[/latex] using only a subset of [latex]G[/latex]'s edges, so any path that exists inside [latex]T[/latex] between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] is also a valid path in [latex]G[/latex] (with the exact same total weight). This means the shortest path in [latex]G[/latex] can never be longer than the shortest path in [latex]T[/latex] — [latex]G[/latex] has strictly more routing options available (all of [latex]T[/latex]'s edges, plus possibly more), so it can only match or beat [latex]T[/latex]'s best distance.

So [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex] always holds (equality is common but not guaranteed — a shortcut through a non-tree edge in [latex]G[/latex] can make [latex]d_1[/latex] strictly smaller).

Answer: [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex], where [latex]S[/latex], [latex]A[/latex], and [latex]B[/latex] are the variables (non-terminals), [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are the terminal symbols, [latex]S[/latex] is the start variable, and the rules of [latex]G[/latex] are described as:

[latex]S \to aaB \mid Abb[/latex]
[latex]A \to a \mid aA[/latex]
[latex]B \to b \mid bB[/latex]

Which ONE of the languages [latex]L(G)[/latex] is accepted by [latex]G[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A\to a\mid aA[/latex] generates exactly the strings [latex]a^n[/latex] for [latex]n\ge1[/latex] (one or more [latex]a[/latex]'s), and similarly [latex]B\to b\mid bB[/latex] generates [latex]b^n[/latex] for [latex]n\ge1[/latex].

So:
- [latex]S\to aaB[/latex] generates [latex]aa[/latex] followed by [latex]b^n[/latex] ([latex]n\ge1[/latex]), i.e. the set [latex]\{a^2b^n\mid n\ge1\}[/latex].
- [latex]S\to Abb[/latex] generates [latex]a^n[/latex] ([latex]n\ge1[/latex]) followed by [latex]bb[/latex], i.e. the set [latex]\{a^nb^2\mid n\ge1\}[/latex].

[latex]L(G)[/latex] is the union of these two alternatives.

Answer: [latex]L(G)=\{a^2b^n\mid n\ge1\}\cup\{a^nb^2\mid n\ge1\}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

[latex]T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n2^n \quad \text{for} \quad n > 0, \quad T(0) = 1[/latex]

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]T(n)=2T(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]. Substitute [latex]T(n)=2^nS(n)[/latex]:
[latex]2^nS(n)=2\cdot2^{n-1}S(n-1)+n2^n=2^nS(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]
Dividing through by [latex]2^n[/latex]: [latex]S(n)=S(n-1)+n[/latex].

Unrolling this simple recurrence: [latex]S(n)=S(0)+\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=1+\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

So [latex]T(n)=2^n\cdot\Theta(n^2)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the following [latex]B^+[/latex] tree with 5 nodes, in which a node can store at most 3 key values. The value 23 is now inserted in the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Inserting a new key into a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree always follows the same pattern: search down to the correct leaf, insert the key there in sorted order, and if that leaf now holds more than the maximum allowed keys (here, more than [latex]3[/latex]), it must split into two leaves, pushing/copying up a separator key into the parent.

Since the target leaf here is already at its maximum capacity of [latex]3[/latex] keys before inserting [latex]23[/latex], it overflows and must split; this new separator key then gets inserted into the parent node, which can itself overflow and split further, potentially propagating all the way up to a new root. Whenever a split reaches (or creates a new) root, the height of the tree increases by one level. Splitting always increases the total node count (a leaf becomes two, or an internal node splits into two) — it never leaves the count unchanged, and "no node splits" is only possible if the target leaf had spare capacity, which it did not here.

Answer: At least one node will split and redistribute; and the height of the tree will increase.

Click here for detail solution
options: None of the nodes will split.
At least one node will split and redistribute.
The total number of nodes will remain same.
The height of the tree will increase.

option_texts: At least one node will split and redistribute.
The height of the tree will increase.

raw_source.text: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
raw_source.solution:
TCP's 3-way handshake, packet by packet:

- P1 (client → server): the client initiates with SYN=1 (and ACK=0, since there's nothing to acknowledge yet).
- P2 (server → client): the server both acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN, so SYN=1, ACK=1 simultaneously (this combined SYN-ACK packet is the hallmark of TCP's handshake).
- P3 (client → server): the client only needs to acknowledge the server's SYN, so SYN=0, ACK=1 (not SYN=1,ACK=1 as one distractor suggests).

So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1.

Answer: P2 (SYN=1, ACK=1), and P1 (SYN=1)

raw_source.text:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

[latex]x + k y = 1[/latex]
[latex]k x + y = -1[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}[/latex], with determinant [latex]\Delta=1-k^2[/latex].

No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines):
- [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution.
- [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution."

So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.

There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

raw_source.text: Let [latex]X[/latex] be a 3-variable Boolean function that produces output as '1' when at least two of the input variables are '1'. Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT, where [latex]a, b, c, d, e[/latex] are Boolean variables?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]X[/latex] is the 3-input majority function: [latex]X(p,q,r)=1[/latex] iff at least [latex]2[/latex] of [latex]p,q,r[/latex] are [latex]1[/latex]. A useful fact: whenever two of the three inputs to [latex]X[/latex] are the same variable [latex]v[/latex], the output is forced to equal [latex]v[/latex] regardless of the third input (e.g. [latex]X(v,v,\text{anything})=v[/latex]).

Checking [latex]X(a,b,X(a,b,c))=X(a,b,c)[/latex]: let [latex]m=X(a,b,c)[/latex]. If [latex]a=b[/latex], then [latex]m=a[/latex] too, and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,a,a)=a=m[/latex]. If [latex]a\ne b[/latex], then (since one of [latex]a,b[/latex] is [latex]0[/latex] and the other [latex]1[/latex]) [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,b,c)=m[/latex]. Either way it checks out. True.

Checking [latex]X(a,b,c)=X(a,X(a,b,c),X(a,c,c))[/latex]: note [latex]X(a,c,c)=c[/latex] (two matching inputs). Let [latex]m=X(a,b,c)[/latex]. If [latex]a=b[/latex]: [latex]m=a[/latex], and [latex]X(a,m,c)=X(a,a,c)=a=m[/latex]. If [latex]a\ne b[/latex]: [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,m,c)=X(a,c,c)=c=m[/latex]. Checks out both ways. True.

The other two options can be shown false with a direct counterexample assignment of [latex]a,b,c,d[/latex] (the two sides disagree for some input combination) — they do not hold as general identities.

Answer: X(a,b,X(a,b,c)) = X(a,b,c); and X(a,b,c) = X(a, X(a,b,c), X(a,c,c))

raw_source.text: The number [latex]-6[/latex] can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2's complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2's complement representation(s) of [latex]-6[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Correctly extending a two's-complement number to more bits requires sign-extension: replicate the sign bit (here, the leading [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]-6[/latex] is negative) into all the new higher-order bit positions — you cannot just prepend arbitrary/zero bits.

[latex]-6[/latex] in 4-bit: [latex]1010[/latex].
Correct 8-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1010[/latex] (four [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,1010[/latex] incorrectly prepends [latex]1000[/latex] instead of replicating the sign bit — wrong.
Correct 16-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1111\,1111\,1010[/latex] (twelve [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,0000\,0000\,1010[/latex] is similarly wrong.

Answer: 1111 1010 (8-bit) and 1111 1111 1111 1010 (16-bit)

raw_source.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each BST claim for [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers:

- Maximum path length from root to any node is [latex]n-1[/latex]: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all [latex]n[/latex] nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only [latex]n[/latex] nodes total.
- Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree [latex]<[/latex] node [latex]<[/latex] right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape.
- Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2n)[/latex] time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left [latex]<[/latex] parent [latex]<[/latex] right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order.

Answer: Max path length is n-1; and inorder traversal always gives sorted order.

Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

raw_source.text: A partial data path of a processor is given in the figure, where [latex]RA[/latex], [latex]RB[/latex], and [latex]RZ[/latex] are 32-bit registers. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT related to arithmetic operations using the data path as shown?
raw_source.solution:
The given data path consists of:

- Two 32-bit registers: RA and RB.
- Two multiplexers (Mux_A and Mux_B).
- Each multiplexer can select either: - the corresponding register value, or - a 32-bit immediate value.
- The selected inputs are fed to the ALU, whose output is stored in register RZ.

Thus, the ALU can receive the following combinations of operands:

Mux_A Mux_B Operands
RA RB Two registers
RA Immediate One register + one immediate
Immediate RB One immediate + one register
Immediate Immediate Two immediate values

Now, evaluate each statement.

Option A: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.

Since Mux_A can select RA and Mux_B can select RB, the ALU can perform operations such as [latex] RZ \leftarrow RA + RB [/latex]

Hence, Option A is Correct.

Option B: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
Examples:
[latex] RZ \leftarrow RA + 10 [/latex] or [latex] RZ \leftarrow 20 + RB [/latex]
Therefore, Option B is Correct.

Option C: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values. Both multiplexers can independently select their immediate inputs. Therefore, the ALU can perform operations like [latex] RZ \leftarrow 15 + 25 [/latex]
Hence, Option C is Correct.

Option D: The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value. This is false because the data path also supports:
- Register + Register
- Immediate + Immediate
- Register + Immediate

Therefore, Option D is Incorrect.

raw_source.text: A regular language [latex]L[/latex] is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]n[/latex] states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?
raw_source.solution:
For a regular language [latex]L[/latex] accepted by some [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist.

- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": could well be true (this [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement.
- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false).
- "There exists a DFA with [latex]\le 2^n[/latex] states accepting [latex]L[/latex]": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false.
- "Every DFA that accepts L has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states": this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE.

Answer: "Every DFA that accepts L has more than [latex]2^n[/latex] states" is the FALSE statement.

raw_source.text: Let [latex]S[/latex] be the set of all ternary strings defined over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex]. Consider all strings in [latex]S[/latex] that contain at least one occurrence of two consecutive symbols, that is, "aa", "bb" or "cc". The number of such strings of length 5 that are possible is _______. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Total ternary strings of length [latex]5[/latex] over [latex]\{a,b,c\}[/latex]: [latex]3^5=243[/latex].

It's easier to count the complement: strings with no two consecutive equal symbols anywhere. The first symbol has [latex]3[/latex] choices; each subsequent symbol just needs to differ from its immediate predecessor, giving [latex]2[/latex] choices each time: [latex]3\times2^4=3\times16=48[/latex] such "no-repeat" strings.

So strings containing at least one consecutive repeat [latex]=243-48=195[/latex].

Answer: 195

raw_source.text:
Consider the given function [latex]f(x)[/latex].

[latex]f(x) = \begin{cases} ax + b & \text{for } x < 1 \\ x^3 + x^2 + 1 & \text{for } x \geq 1 \end{cases}[/latex]

If the function is differentiable everywhere, the value of [latex]b[/latex] must be ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
For [latex]f[/latex] to be differentiable at [latex]x=1[/latex], it must first be continuous there, and then have matching one-sided derivatives.

Continuity: left-hand value [latex]=a(1)+b=a+b[/latex]; right-hand value [latex]=1^3+1^2+1=3[/latex]. So [latex]a+b=3[/latex].

Matching derivatives: left derivative [latex]=\dfrac{d}{dx}(ax+b)=a[/latex]. Right derivative [latex]=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+x^2+1)=3x^2+2x[/latex], evaluated at [latex]x=1[/latex]: [latex]3+2=5[/latex]. So [latex]a=5[/latex].

Substituting back: [latex]b=3-a=3-5=-2[/latex].

Answer: -2.0

raw_source.text: A box contains 5 coins: 4 regular coins and 1 fake coin. When a regular coin is tossed, the probability [latex]P(\text{head}) = 0.5[/latex] and for a fake coin, [latex]P(\text{head}) = 1[/latex]. You pick a coin at random and toss it twice, and get two heads. The probability that the coin you have chosen is the fake coin is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
By Bayes' theorem, [latex]P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{P(HH\mid\text{fake})P(\text{fake})}{P(HH)}[/latex].

[latex]P(HH\mid\text{fake})=1\times1=1[/latex] (fake coin always shows heads). [latex]P(HH\mid\text{regular})=0.5\times0.5=0.25[/latex].
[latex]P(\text{fake})=\dfrac15[/latex], [latex]P(\text{regular})=\dfrac45[/latex].

[latex]P(HH)=1\times\dfrac15+0.25\times\dfrac45=0.2+0.2=0.4[/latex].

[latex]P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.4}=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.50

raw_source.text:
The pseudocode of a function fun() is given below: 

fun(int A[0,...,n-1])
{
    for i=0 to n-2
	for j=0 to n-i-2
	    if (A[j] > A[j+1])
		then swap A[j] and A[j+1]
}
Let [latex]A[0, \dots, 29][/latex] be an array storing 30 distinct integers in descending order. The number of swap operations that will be performed, if the function fun() is called with [latex]A[0, \dots, 29][/latex] as argument, is __________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
This is exactly the standard bubble-sort pseudocode. On a fully descending-order array, every single adjacent-pair comparison across the entire double loop finds the pair out of order, so a swap happens on every comparison — there are no comparisons at all that skip the swap.

Total comparisons (and hence swaps) [latex]=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i)=\binom{n}{2}[/latex] for an [latex]n[/latex]-element array. With [latex]n=30[/latex]: [latex]\binom{30}{2}=\dfrac{30\times29}{2}=435[/latex].

Answer: 435

#include <stdio.h>
void foo(int *p, int x) {
    *p = x;
}

int main() {
    int *z;
    int a = 20, b = 25;
    z = &a;
    foo(z, b);
    printf("%d", a);
    return 0;
}
The output of the given C program is __________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text{z}=\&\text{a}[/latex] makes [latex]z[/latex] point to [latex]a[/latex] (currently [latex]20[/latex]).

[latex]\text{foo(z, b)}[/latex] passes [latex]z[/latex] (the address of [latex]a[/latex]) and [latex]b[/latex]'s value ([latex]25[/latex]) into [latex]\text{foo(int *p, int x)}[/latex], so inside [latex]\text{foo}[/latex], [latex]p[/latex] points to [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]x=25[/latex].

[latex]{*}\text{p}=\text{x}[/latex] writes [latex]25[/latex] into whatever [latex]p[/latex] points to — i.e. directly into [latex]a[/latex] itself (since pointers give real access to the caller's variable). So [latex]a[/latex] becomes [latex]25[/latex].

[latex]\text{printf}[/latex] then prints the now-updated [latex]a[/latex].

Answer: 25

raw_source.text: The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node. Suppose a Min-Heap [latex]T[/latex] stores 32 keys. The height of [latex]T[/latex] is _____________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
A min-heap with [latex]N[/latex] keys is stored as a nearly-complete binary tree, and its height (max edges from root to a leaf) is [latex]\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor[/latex].

Level [latex]0[/latex] holds [latex]1[/latex] node, level [latex]1[/latex] holds [latex]2[/latex], level [latex]2[/latex] holds [latex]4[/latex], level [latex]3[/latex] holds [latex]8[/latex], level [latex]4[/latex] holds [latex]16[/latex] — cumulatively [latex]1+2+4+8+16=31[/latex] nodes fill levels [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]4[/latex] completely. The [latex]32[/latex]nd key must then start a new level, level 5.

Answer: 5

raw_source.text: Consider a memory system with 1M bytes of main memory and 16K bytes of cache memory. Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache block size is 16 bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be required to store all the tag values? [Assume memory is byte addressable, 1K = [latex]2^{10}[/latex], 1M = [latex]2^{20}[/latex].]
raw_source.solution:
Cache [latex]=16\text{K}=2^{14}[/latex] bytes, block size [latex]=16=2^4[/latex] bytes, so number of cache lines [latex]=\dfrac{2^{14}}{2^4}=2^{10}[/latex] — index field [latex]=10[/latex] bits, offset field [latex]=4[/latex] bits.

Main memory [latex]=1\text{M}=2^{20}[/latex] bytes, byte-addressable, so the address is [latex]20[/latex] bits wide. Tag field [latex]=20-10-4=6[/latex] bits per line.

Total bits needed to store all tag values [latex]=6\text{ bits}\times2^{10}\text{ lines}=6\times2^{10}[/latex].

Answer: 6×2^10

raw_source.text:
A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?

ADD R1, #25 // R1 = R1 + 25
raw_source.solution:
With [latex]64=2^6[/latex] registers, each register-number field needs [latex]6[/latex] bits. With [latex]50[/latex] distinct instruction types, the opcode field needs [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits (since [latex]2^5=32<50\le64=2^6[/latex]).

The instruction [latex]\text{ADD R1, \#25}[/latex] (meaning [latex]\text{R1}=\text{R1}+25[/latex]) only needs to name one register (used as both source and destination), plus an immediate value. So the [latex]32[/latex]-bit instruction splits as: opcode ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] one register field ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] immediate field (the rest).

Immediate field width [latex]=32-6-6=20[/latex] bits.

Answer: 20

raw_source.text:
A computer has two processors, [latex]M_1[/latex] and [latex]M_2[/latex]. Four processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4[/latex] with CPU bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

[latex]M_1[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_1 > P_3 > P_2 > P_4[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
[latex]M_2[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_2 > P_3 > P_4 > P_1[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_2[/latex] and [latex]P_1[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process [latex]P_i[/latex] is scheduled to a processor [latex]M_k[/latex], if the processor is free and no other process [latex]P_j[/latex] is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?
raw_source.solution:
All four processes arrive together at [latex]t=0[/latex] with two free processors, so two of them start immediately. Since [latex]P_1[/latex] is [latex]M_1[/latex]'s top priority and [latex]P_2[/latex] is [latex]M_2[/latex]'s top priority (and conveniently each is the other machine's lowest priority, so there's no conflict), the natural non-conflicting start is [latex]P_1\to M_1[/latex] and [latex]P_2\to M_2[/latex], both beginning at [latex]t=0[/latex].

[latex]P_2[/latex] (burst [latex]16[/latex]) finishes first, at [latex]t=16[/latex], freeing [latex]M_2[/latex]. Among the still-waiting [latex]P_3,P_4[/latex], [latex]M_2[/latex]'s priority order ([latex]P_2{>}P_3{>}P_4{>}P_1[/latex]) favors [latex]P_3[/latex], so [latex]P_3[/latex] starts on [latex]M_2[/latex] at [latex]t=16[/latex], running until [latex]16+25=41[/latex].

[latex]P_1[/latex] (burst [latex]20[/latex]) finishes next, at [latex]t=20[/latex], freeing [latex]M_1[/latex]. Only [latex]P_4[/latex] remains waiting, so it starts on [latex]M_1[/latex] at [latex]t=20[/latex], running until [latex]20+10=30[/latex].

Waiting times: [latex]P_1{:}\,0[/latex], [latex]P_2{:}\,0[/latex], [latex]P_3{:}\,16-0=16[/latex], [latex]P_4{:}\,20-0=20[/latex].

Average [latex]=\dfrac{0+0+16+20}{4}=\dfrac{36}{4}=9[/latex].

Answer: 9

raw_source.text:
Consider two relations describing teams and players in a sports league:

[latex]teams(tid, tname):tid, tname [/latex] are team-id and team-name, respectively
[latex]players(pid, pname, tid):pid,pname,tid[/latex] denote player-id, player-name and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having name as 'MI'?
raw_source.solution:
We want, for each player [latex]p[/latex] in [latex]\text{players}[/latex], their name, restricted to only those players whose [latex]tid[/latex] matches some team [latex]t[/latex] in [latex]\text{teams}[/latex] with [latex]t.tname=\text{'MI'}[/latex].

This is exactly:
[latex]\{p.pname\mid p\in players\ \wedge\ \exists t(t\in teams\ \wedge\ p.tid=t.tid\ \wedge\ t.tname=\text{'MI'})\}[/latex]

The key correctness checks: the outer variable [latex]p[/latex] must range over [latex]players[/latex] (not [latex]teams[/latex], since we want player names), and the join condition [latex]p.tid=t.tid[/latex] must actually be present inside the existential (options that drop this join condition would incorrectly return every player's name whenever team 'MI' exists at all, regardless of which team the player is actually on).

Answer: {p.pname | p∈players ∧ ∃t(t∈teams ∧ p.tid=t.tid ∧ t.tname='MI')}

A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Subnet Address} & \textbf{Subnet Mask (in CIDR notation)} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 145.36.0.0 & /16 & E1 \\ \hline 145.36.128.0 & /17 & E2 \\ \hline 145.36.64.0 & /18 & E3 \\ \hline 145.36.255.0 & /24 & E4 \\ \hline \text{Default} & -- & E5 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Routers use longest-prefix matching: find every subnet entry that contains the destination address, and among those, forward via the one with the most specific (longest) prefix.

Let [latex]A[/latex] be a 2x2 matrix as given:
[latex]A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right][/latex]
What are the eigenvalues of the matrix [latex]A^{13}[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Find the eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] from its characteristic equation:
[latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-1\times1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2-1-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2=2\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=\pm\sqrt2[/latex]

If [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of [latex]A[/latex], then [latex]\lambda^{13}[/latex] is the corresponding eigenvalue of [latex]A^{13}[/latex] (eigenvalues of a matrix power are just the original eigenvalues raised to that power):
[latex](\sqrt2)^{13}=2^{13/2}=2^{6}\cdot2^{1/2}=64\sqrt2[/latex], and similarly [latex](-\sqrt2)^{13}=-64\sqrt2[/latex].

Answer: 64√2, -64√2

Consider the following four-variable Boolean function in sum-of-product form

[latex]F(b_3, b_2, b_1, b_0) = \sum(0, 2, 4, 8, 10, 11, 12)[/latex].

Where the value of the function is computed by considering [latex]b_3b_2b_1b_0[/latex] as a 4-bit binary number, where [latex]b_3[/latex] denotes the most significant bit and [latex]b_0[/latex] denotes the least significant bit. Note that there are no don't care terms. Which ONE of the following options is the CORRECT minimized Boolean expression for [latex]F[/latex]?

raw_source.text: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be an undirected and unweighted graph with 100 vertices. Let [latex]d(u, v)[/latex] denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]V[/latex]. Let the maximum value of [latex]d(u, v)[/latex], [latex]u, v \in V[/latex] such that [latex]u \neq v[/latex], be 30. Let [latex]T[/latex] be any breadth-first-search tree of [latex]G[/latex]. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph [latex]G[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Let the diameter of the graph be the maximum shortest distance between any two vertices.
It is given that [latex] \max_{u,v\in V,\;u\ne v} d(u,v)=30. [/latex]
Thus, the diameter of the graph is 30.

Relation between BFS Tree Height and Graph Diameter

A Breadth-First Search (BFS) tree rooted at a vertex (r) has the following property:

- The level of every vertex equals its shortest distance from the root.
- Therefore, the height of the BFS tree is the maximum shortest distance from the root to any vertex, which is called the eccentricity of the root.

Let the height of the BFS tree be (h). Then, [latex] h=\max_{v\in V} d(r,v). [/latex]

Using the Diameter

Let the diameter of the graph be (D=30). A well-known property of graphs is [latex] \text{Radius} \ge \left\lceil\frac{D}{2}\right\rceil. [/latex]

Since [latex] D=30, [/latex] we get [latex] \left\lceil\frac{30}{2}\right\rceil=15. [/latex]

Every vertex has eccentricity at least the radius. Hence, regardless of the chosen BFS root, [latex] h\ge 15. [/latex]

The height need not be exactly 15 or exactly 30. It can be any value between 15 and 30 depending on the chosen root.

For example:

- If the BFS starts from a central vertex, the height can be 15.
- If it starts from an end vertex of a diameter, the height can be 30.

Correct Answer: (C) The height of (T) is at least 15.

The height of [latex]T[/latex] is at least 30.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b\}[/latex]:

[latex]L_1 = \{ \alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a, b\}^+ \text{ and } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \{ \alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a\}^+ \text{ and } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}[/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]L_1=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}[/latex] (α completely unrestricted): checking membership genuinely requires comparing an arbitrary-length prefix against an arbitrary-length suffix for exact equality. For instance, "[latex]abbaab[/latex]" is in [latex]L_1[/latex] (via [latex]\alpha=ab,\beta=ba[/latex]) even though its very first and very last characters differ — so no bounded "look at a few characters" trick works; a finite automaton cannot carry the unbounded memory needed to remember an arbitrarily long prefix for later comparison. This is the same style of argument used to show languages like [latex]\{ww\}[/latex] are non-regular. [latex]L_1[/latex] is not regular.

[latex]L_2=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha\in\{a\}^+,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}[/latex] (α restricted to all-a's): here, since [latex]\alpha[/latex] consists only of [latex]a[/latex]'s, we can always just use the shortest valid split ([latex]|\alpha|=1[/latex]): any string of length [latex]\ge3[/latex] that starts with [latex]a[/latex] and ends with [latex]a[/latex] can always be decomposed as (first character [latex]a[/latex]) + (everything in between, as [latex]\beta[/latex]) + (last character [latex]a[/latex]). So [latex]L_2[/latex] is exactly "strings of length [latex]\ge3[/latex] starting and ending with [latex]a[/latex]," which is simply matched by the regular expression [latex]a(a|b)^+a[/latex]. [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular.

Answer: L1 is not regular but L2 is regular.

Click here for detail solution
options: [latex]L_1[/latex] is a regular language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is not a regular language.
[latex]L_1[/latex] is not a regular language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is a regular language.
Neither [latex]L_1[/latex] nor [latex]L_2[/latex] is a regular language.

raw_answer.option_text: [latex]L_1[/latex] is not a regular language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is a regular language.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex], where [latex]m[/latex] and [latex]n[/latex] are natural numbers:

[latex]L_1 = \{ a^m b^m c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \{ a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]L_1=\{a^mb^mc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: this requires two separate comparisons tied to the same value [latex]m[/latex] — matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s exactly (using up a stack), and independently comparing the [latex]c[/latex]-count against that same [latex]m[/latex] again. A single-stack PDA can only "remember and compare" one running count at a time; once the stack is used up matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s, the value of [latex]m[/latex] is no longer available to compare against the [latex]c[/latex]'s. This mirrors the classic non-context-free pattern [latex]a^nb^nc^n[/latex]. [latex]L_1[/latex] is not context-free.

[latex]L_2=\{a^mb^nc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: here the [latex]c[/latex]-count only needs to match the combined total of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s (not two separate comparisons). A single stack handles this easily: push one symbol for every [latex]a[/latex] and every [latex]b[/latex] (treating them the same way), then pop one symbol per [latex]c[/latex], accepting if the stack empties exactly when the input ends. [latex]L_2[/latex] is context-free.

Answer: L1 is not context-free but L2 is context-free.

[latex]L_1[/latex] is not a context-free language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is a context-free language.

raw_source.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE while computing [latex]First[/latex] and [latex]Follow[/latex] during top-down parsing by a compiler?
raw_source.solution:
Standard rules for computing [latex]\text{First}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets:

- "For [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex], add [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to First(A)": TRUE — this is exactly the base rule for handling nullable productions in First-set computation.
- "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to First(S)": FALSE — the end marker [latex]\$[/latex] belongs in [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets (marking "nothing more can follow"), never in a [latex]\text{First}[/latex] set.
- "For [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex], add [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to Follow(A)": FALSE — [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is never placed into any [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] set; [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets only ever contain actual terminals (and possibly [latex]\$[/latex]).
- "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to Follow(S)": TRUE — this is the standard initialization rule, since nothing legitimately follows the start symbol except the end of input.

Answer: "ε is added to First(A) for A→ε" and "the end marker is added to Follow(S)" are both TRUE.

Consider a relational schema [latex] team(name, city, owner) [/latex], with functional dependencies [latex]\{ name \to city [/latex], [latex] name \to owner \} [/latex] .

The relation [latex] team [/latex] is decomposed into two relations, [latex] t_1(name, city) [/latex] and [latex] t_2(name, owner) [/latex]. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]team(name,city,owner)[/latex] with [latex]name\to city,\ name\to owner[/latex]. Since [latex]name[/latex] alone functionally determines every other attribute, [latex]name[/latex] is already a candidate key of [latex]team[/latex] — and since every FD's left-hand side ([latex]name[/latex]) is already a superkey, [latex]team[/latex] is already in BCNF (and hence also in 3NF) even before decomposing. So both "team is NOT in BCNF" and "team is NOT in 3NF" are false.

Decomposing into [latex]t_1(name,city)[/latex] and [latex]t_2(name,owner)[/latex]: in each projection, [latex]name[/latex] remains a key (it determines the sole remaining attribute), so both [latex]t_1[/latex] and [latex]t_2[/latex] are trivially in BCNF. True.

For losslessness, the common attribute of the decomposition is [latex]name[/latex], and [latex]name\to city[/latex] (i.e. [latex]name[/latex] alone determines all of [latex]t_1[/latex]) — satisfying the standard lossless-join test ([latex]R_1\cap R_2[/latex] is a superkey of at least one of the two pieces). True.

Answer: t1 and t2 are in BCNF; and the decomposition is lossless.

raw_source.text:
Which of the following predicate logic formulae/formula is/are CORRECT representation(s) of the statement: "Everyone has exactly one mother"?

The meanings of the predicates used are:
[latex]mother(y,x): y[/latex] is the mother of [latex] x [/latex]
[latex]noteq(x,y): x[/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] are not equal
raw_source.solution:
We want: for every person [latex]x[/latex], there is exactly one [latex]y[/latex] who is [latex]x[/latex]'s mother — meaning both existence (someone is the mother) and uniqueness (nobody else also qualifies as a distinct mother).

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))][/latex]: says "[latex]y[/latex] is a mother of [latex]x[/latex], and every [latex]z[/latex] different from [latex]y[/latex] is not a mother of [latex]x[/latex]" — this correctly captures existence plus uniqueness. Correct.

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))][/latex]: by De Morgan's law, [latex]\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))[/latex] is logically identical to [latex]\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))[/latex] — so this is just a different (but equivalent) way of writing the same correct statement above. Correct.

The other two options fail to properly express uniqueness: one only asserts some non-mother exists (too weak, says nothing about all other candidates), and the other is a vacuous implication that never actually forces a mother to exist at all.

Answer: Both the ∀x∃y[...∀z(noteq→¬mother)] form and its De Morgan-equivalent ∀x∃y[...¬∃z(noteq∧mother)] form are correct.

[latex] \forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \forall z (noteq(z, y) \to \neg mother(z, x))] [/latex]
[latex] \forall x \forall y [mother(y, x) \to \exists z (mother(z, x) \land \neg noteq(z, y))] [/latex]

raw_source.text:
[latex] A = \{ 0,1,2,3,\dots \} [/latex] is the set of non-negative integers. Let [latex] {F} [/latex] be the set of functions from [latex] A [/latex] to itself. For any two functions, [latex] f_1, f_2 \in {F} [/latex], we define

[latex] (f_1 \odot f_2)(n) = f_1(n) + f_2(n)[/latex]

for every number [latex] n [/latex] in [latex] A [/latex]. Which of the following is/are CORRECT about the mathematical structure [latex] ({F}, \odot ) [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
[latex](f_1\odot f_2)(n)=f_1(n)+f_2(n)[/latex] — pointwise addition of functions into the non-negative integers.

- Closure: the sum of two non-negative-integer values is still a non-negative integer, so [latex]F[/latex] is closed under [latex]\odot[/latex].
- Associativity: inherited directly from ordinary integer addition being associative.
- Identity: the constant-zero function [latex]z(n)=0[/latex] satisfies [latex]f\odot z=f[/latex] for every [latex]f[/latex] — an identity element exists.
- Commutativity: [latex]f_1(n)+f_2(n)=f_2(n)+f_1(n)[/latex] pointwise, so [latex]\odot[/latex] is commutative.
- Inverses: for a general [latex]f[/latex] (e.g. [latex]f(n)=n[/latex]), we'd need some [latex]g[/latex] with [latex]f(n)+g(n)=0[/latex], forcing [latex]g(n)=-f(n)[/latex] — but negative values aren't allowed in the codomain [latex]A[/latex]. So inverses generally don't exist.

Since it's closed, associative, has an identity, and is commutative, but lacks inverses, [latex](F,\odot)[/latex] is exactly an Abelian monoid (not a group).

Answer: (F, ⊙) is an Abelian monoid.

raw_source.text: Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA) defined over the alphabet, [latex] \Sigma = \{ a, b \} [/latex]. Identify which of the following language(s) is/are accepted by the given DFA.
raw_source.solution:
This DFA, on inspection of its states and transitions, is built to track only the most recently seen [latex]3[/latex] input symbols, entering its unique accepting state precisely when those last three symbols read are exactly "[latex]bab[/latex]" — i.e. it's a standard "suffix detector" construction (a small sliding window of recent symbols, accepting whenever that window matches the target pattern at the very end of the input read so far).

This is a different (and stricter) condition than merely "contains bab somewhere" (that DFA would need to stay accepting once the pattern is seen, regardless of what comes after, rather than resetting/tracking only the tail) or "even number of b's" or "excludes aba" (which are entirely different acceptance conditions with different structural transitions).

Answer: The set of all strings ending with the pattern bab.

raw_source.text: A disk of size [latex] 512M [/latex] bytes is divided into blocks of [latex] 64K [/latex] bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. Each data block reserves 4 bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of [latex] 1M [/latex] bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, [latex] 1K=2^{10}, 1M=2^{20} [/latex]. The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Disk block size [latex]=64K=2^{16}[/latex] bytes. In linked allocation, every block (including the last) reserves [latex]4[/latex] bytes for its "next" pointer field, leaving usable data capacity per block [latex]=65536-4=65532[/latex] bytes.

File size [latex]=1M=2^{20}=1{,}048{,}576[/latex] bytes. Number of blocks needed [latex]=\lceil1{,}048{,}576/65532\rceil[/latex]: since [latex]65532\times16=1{,}048{,}512[/latex] (short of the file size by [latex]64[/latex] bytes), a [latex]17[/latex]th block is required, giving [latex]17[/latex] blocks total.

Total disk space allocated [latex]=17\times65536=1{,}114{,}112[/latex] bytes. Space genuinely "useful" (actual file data plus the [latex]4[/latex]-byte pointer overhead in each of the [latex]17[/latex] blocks) [latex]=1{,}048{,}576+17\times4=1{,}048{,}576+68=1{,}048{,}644[/latex] bytes.

Internal fragmentation (wasted space) [latex]=1{,}114{,}112-1{,}048{,}644=65{,}468[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 65468

Refer to the given 3-address code sequence. This code sequence is split into basic blocks. The number of basic blocks is _________. (Answer in integer)

1001: i = 1
1002: j = 1
1003: t1 = 10*i
1004: t2 = t1+j
1005: t3 = 8*t2
1006: t4 = t3-88
1007: a[t4] = 0.0

1009: if j <= 10 goto 1003
1010: i = i+1
1011: if i <= 10 goto 1002
1012: i = 1
1013: t5 = i-1
1014: t6 = 88*t5
1015: a[t6] = 1.0
1016: i = i+1
1017: if i <= 10 goto 1013
raw_source.solution:
A new basic block begins at every leader statement: the very first statement, any statement that is the target of a jump/goto, and any statement immediately following a conditional or unconditional jump.

Scanning the code for leaders: [latex]1001[/latex] (first statement); [latex]1003[/latex] (target of the [latex]\text{goto }1003[/latex] at [latex]1009[/latex]); [latex]1010[/latex] (follows the conditional jump at [latex]1009[/latex]); [latex]1002[/latex] (target of [latex]\text{goto }1002[/latex] at [latex]1011[/latex]); [latex]1012[/latex] (follows the conditional jump at [latex]1011[/latex]); [latex]1013[/latex] (target of [latex]\text{goto }1013[/latex] at [latex]1017[/latex]).

That's [latex]6[/latex] leaders, giving [latex]6[/latex] basic blocks: [latex]\{1001\},\{1002\},\{1003\text{-}1009\},\{1010\text{-}1011\},\{1012\},\{1013\text{-}1017\}[/latex].

raw_source.text: A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into L1 cache. If the data is not found in L1 cache, it goes to L2 cache. If it fails to get the data from L2 cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is _________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
This system uses hierarchical (serial) cache access: to reach L2, the processor must have already tried and missed in L1; to reach main memory, it must have already tried and missed in both L1 and L2. This means the given access-time figures for L2 and main memory already include the time already spent checking the earlier levels: L1 access time [latex]T_1=10[/latex] ns, L2 access time (which already includes the L1 miss penalty) [latex]T_2=20[/latex] ns, and main memory access time (already including both L1 and L2 miss penalties) [latex]T_3=200[/latex] ns. Hit rates: [latex]H_1=0.95[/latex] (L1), [latex]H_2=0.85[/latex] (L2).

The average memory access time is a weighted sum over the three possible outcomes — hit in L1, miss-L1-then-hit-L2, or miss-both-then-go-to-memory:
[latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)H_2T_2+(1-H_1)(1-H_2)T_3[/latex]
[latex]=0.95(10)+0.05(0.85)(20)+0.05(0.15)(200)[/latex]
[latex]=9.5+0.85+1.5=11.85[/latex] ns.

Answer: 11.85

raw_source.text:
In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page replacement algorithm is as follows:
The OS correctly predicts only up to next 4 page references (including the current page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.
A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:

1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4.

If the system has three memory frames that are initially empty, the number of page faults that will occur during execution of the process is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
With the OS able to correctly predict only the next [latex]4[/latex] references (including the current one) at the moment a frame is allocated, simulate the reference string [latex]1,3,2,4,2,3,1,2,4,3,1,4[/latex] with [latex]3[/latex] initially-empty frames:

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Ref}&\text{Frames after}&\text{Fault?}\\\hline1&\{1\}&\text{Fault}\\3&\{1,3\}&\text{Fault}\\2&\{1,3,2\}&\text{Fault}\\4&\{4,3,2\}\ (\text{evict }1\text{, unused within next window }2,3,1)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\1&\{4,2,1\}\ (\text{evict }3\text{, farthest-future within window }2,4,3)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,1,3\}\ (\text{evict }2\text{, no longer used in remaining string})&\text{Fault}\\1&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\end{array}[/latex]

Total page faults [latex]=6[/latex] (at references [latex]1,3,2,4,1,3[/latex] in the sequence, marked "Fault" above).

Answer: 6

raw_source.text: Suppose a 5-bit message is transmitted from a source to a destination through a noisy channel. The probability that a bit of the message gets flipped during transmission is 0.01. Flipping of each bit is independent of one another. The probability that the message is delivered error-free to the destination is _________. (rounded off to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Each of the [latex]5[/latex] bits is flipped independently with probability [latex]0.01[/latex], so each bit survives correctly with probability [latex]0.99[/latex]. The whole message arrives error-free only if every bit survives:

[latex]P(\text{error-free})=(0.99)^5\approx0.951[/latex]

Answer: 0.951

raw_source.text: Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header. The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Assume the standard [latex]20[/latex]-byte IPv4 header (no options), so the original datagram is [latex]15000+20=15020[/latex] bytes.

At Router-1 (MTU [latex]5000[/latex]): max data per fragment [latex]=5000-20=4980[/latex] bytes, but fragment data must be a multiple of [latex]8[/latex] bytes, so usable data per (non-last) fragment [latex]=\lfloor4980/8\rfloor\times8=4976[/latex] bytes.
[latex]15000[/latex] bytes of data [latex]\div4976\approx3.01[/latex]: so [latex]3[/latex] full fragments of [latex]4976[/latex] bytes ([latex]14928[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]15000-14928=72[/latex] bytes. Total after Router-1: 4 fragments.

At Router-2 (MTU [latex]3000[/latex]): each fragment bigger than [latex]3000[/latex] bytes must be split again; the small [latex]72[/latex]-byte-data fragment (total size [latex]92[/latex] bytes) passes straight through unchanged.
Max data per new sub-fragment [latex]=3000-20=2980[/latex], rounded down to a multiple of [latex]8[/latex]: [latex]\lfloor2980/8\rfloor\times8=2976[/latex] bytes.
Each of the [latex]3[/latex] big fragments (data [latex]=4976[/latex] bytes) splits into: one sub-fragment of [latex]2976[/latex] bytes, plus a final sub-fragment of [latex]4976-2976=2000[/latex] bytes — [latex]2[/latex] sub-fragments each, so [latex]3\times2=6[/latex] sub-fragments total.

Total fragments reaching the destination [latex]=6[/latex] (from the split large fragments) [latex]+1[/latex] (the small fragment that passed through) [latex]=7[/latex].

Answer: 7

Consider a probability distribution given by the density function [latex] P(x) [/latex].

[latex] P(x) = \begin{cases} Cx^2, &\text{for } 1 \leq x \leq 4 \\ 0, & \text{for }x < 1 \text{ or } x > 4 \end{cases}[/latex]

The probability that [latex] x [/latex] lies between 2 and 3, i.e., [latex] P(2 \leq x \leq 3) [/latex] is _________. (rounded off to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
First find [latex]C[/latex] using the normalization condition [latex]\int_1^4Cx^2\,dx=1[/latex]:
[latex]C\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4=C\cdot\dfrac{64-1}{3}=21C=1\ \Rightarrow\ C=\dfrac1{21}[/latex]

[latex]P(2\le x\le3)=\displaystyle\int_2^3\dfrac{x^2}{21}\,dx=\dfrac1{21}\left[\dfrac{x^3}3\right]_2^3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{27-8}3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{19}3=\dfrac{19}{63}\approx0.302[/latex]

Answer: 0.302

raw_source.text: Consider a finite state machine (FSM) with one input [latex] X [/latex] and one output [latex] f [/latex], represented by the given state transition table. The minimum number of states required to realize this FSM is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Group states by their immediate output behavior first: states with outputs [latex](f_0,f_1)=(0,0)[/latex] are [latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex]; [latex](1,0)[/latex] are [latex]\{D,H\}[/latex]; [latex](1,1)[/latex] is [latex]\{F\}[/latex]; [latex](0,1)[/latex] is [latex]\{G\}[/latex] — four initial groups.

Refine [latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex] by checking which group each state's next-states fall into: [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]C[/latex] both go to (group-of-[latex]F[/latex], group-of-[latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex]) on [latex](X{=}0,X{=}1)[/latex], while [latex]B[/latex] and [latex]E[/latex] both go to (group-of-[latex]\{D,H\}[/latex], group-of-[latex]\{A,B,C,E\}[/latex]). So this group splits into [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex] and [latex]\{B,E\}[/latex].

Checking again with the new, finer partition [latex]\{A,C\},\{B,E\},\{D,H\},\{F\},\{G\}[/latex]: every state's next-state signature now matches consistently within its own group (e.g. both [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]C[/latex] go to [latex]F[/latex] on [latex]0[/latex] and into [latex]\{B,E\}[/latex] on [latex]1[/latex]; both [latex]D[/latex] and [latex]H[/latex] go to [latex]G[/latex] on [latex]0[/latex] and into [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex] on [latex]1[/latex]) — so the partition is stable and no further splitting occurs.

Final equivalence classes: [latex]\{A,C\},\{B,E\},\{D,H\},\{F\},\{G\}[/latex] — [latex]5[/latex] classes.

Answer: 5

raw_source.text: Consider the given sequential circuit designed using D-Flip-flops. The circuit is initialized with some value (initial state). The number of distinct states the circuit will go through before returning back to the initial state is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
This circuit is a [latex]4[/latex]-bit twisted-ring (Johnson) counter: the flip-flops are connected in a shift-register chain ([latex]Q_0\to D_1,\ Q_1\to D_2,\ Q_2\to D_3[/latex]), with the feedback from the last stage back into [latex]D_0[/latex] being inverted.

A Johnson counter built from [latex]n[/latex] flip-flops with inverted feedback is well known to cycle through [latex]2n[/latex] distinct states before returning to its starting state (e.g. starting from [latex]0000[/latex]: [latex]0000\to1000\to1100\to1110\to1111\to0111\to0011\to0001\to0000[/latex]). For [latex]n=4[/latex] flip-flops, that's [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] states in the full cycle — i.e. [latex]7[/latex] other distinct states are visited before the circuit returns to repeat its initial state (with the full period being [latex]8[/latex] steps, depending on whether the initial state itself is counted in the tally).

Answer: 8 (equivalently 7, depending on whether the initial state is counted)

#include <stdio.h>  
int foo(int S[],int size){  
    if(size == 0) return 0;  
    if(size == 1) return 1;  
    if(S[0] != S[1]) return 1+foo(S+1,size-1);  
    return foo(S+1,size-1);  
}  
int main(){  
    int A[]={0,1,2,2,2,0,0,1,1};  
    printf("%d",foo(A,9));  
    return 0;  
}
The value printed by the given C program is _________. (Answer in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Trace the recursion on [latex]A=[0,1,2,2,2,0,0,1,1][/latex] (comparing each element to its immediate neighbor, adding [latex]1[/latex] whenever they differ):

[latex] egin{array}{l}foo([0,1,\ldots])=1+foo([1,2,\ldots])\quad(0 e1)\foo([1,2,\ldots])=1+foo([2,2,\ldots])\quad(1 e2)\foo([2,2,2,0,\ldots])=foo([2,2,0,\ldots])\quad(2=2)\foo([2,2,0,\ldots])=foo([2,0,0,\ldots])\quad(2=2)\foo([2,0,0,1,1])=1+foo([0,0,1,1])\quad(2 e0)\foo([0,0,1,1])=foo([0,1,1])\quad(0=0)\foo([0,1,1])=1+foo([1,1])\quad(0 e1)\foo([1,1])=foo([1])\quad(1=1)\foo([1])=1\quad( ext{base case, size}=1)\end{array}[/latex]

Unwinding: [latex]foo([1,1])=1[/latex], [latex]foo([0,1,1])=1+1=2[/latex], [latex]foo([0,0,1,1])=2[/latex], [latex]foo([2,0,0,1,1])=1+2=3[/latex], [latex]foo([2,2,0,\ldots])=3[/latex], [latex]foo([2,2,2,\ldots])=3[/latex], [latex]foo([1,2,\ldots])=1+3=4[/latex], [latex]foo([0,1,\ldots])=1+4=5[/latex].

Answer: 5

raw_source.text: The maximum value of [latex] x [/latex] such that the edge between the nodes B and C is included in every minimum spanning tree of the given graph is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
From the given graph (vertices A, B, C, D with edges [latex]AB{=}7,\ AD{=}6,\ CD{=}8,\ AC{=}1,\ BD{=}3[/latex], and [latex]BC{=}x[/latex]), we want the largest [latex]x[/latex] for which edge [latex]BC[/latex] is forced into every MST.

Checking systematically for increasing [latex]x[/latex] (e.g. by comparing the total weight of all spanning trees that include [latex]BC[/latex] versus all spanning trees that exclude it): for [latex]x\le5[/latex], every minimum spanning tree happens to include edge [latex]BC[/latex] (any spanning tree avoiding it ends up strictly heavier, since the cheapest way to connect [latex]B[/latex] and [latex]C[/latex]'s side of the graph without directly using [latex]BC[/latex] costs strictly more than [latex]5[/latex] extra). But once [latex]x=6[/latex], an alternative spanning tree that avoids edge [latex]BC[/latex] entirely becomes just as cheap (tied for minimum), so [latex]BC[/latex] is no longer forced into every MST.

So the maximum value of [latex]x[/latex] that still guarantees [latex]BC[/latex] is in every MST is the last value before this tie appears.

Answer: 5

In a double hashing scheme, [latex] h_1(k) = k \mod 11 [/latex] and [latex] h_2(k) = 1 + (k \mod 7) [/latex] are the auxiliary hash functions. The size [latex] m [/latex] of the hash table is 11. The hash function for the [latex] i [/latex]-th probe in the open address table is [latex] [h_1(k) + i h_2(k)] \mod m [/latex] The following keys are inserted in the given order: 63, 50, 25, 79, 67, 24.

The slot at which key 24 gets stored is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Double hashing: [latex]h_1(k)=k\bmod11[/latex], [latex]h_2(k)=1+(k\bmod7)[/latex], probe [latex]i[/latex]: [latex][h_1(k)+ih_2(k)]\bmod11[/latex], table size [latex]11[/latex].

Insert in order, computing initial slot (and probing forward on collision):
[latex]63[/latex]: [latex]h_1=8[/latex] → slot [latex]8[/latex] (empty).
[latex]50[/latex]: [latex]h_1=6[/latex] → slot [latex]6[/latex] (empty).
[latex]25[/latex]: [latex]h_1=3[/latex] → slot [latex]3[/latex] (empty).
[latex]79[/latex]: [latex]h_1=2[/latex] → slot [latex]2[/latex] (empty).
[latex]67[/latex]: [latex]h_1=1[/latex] → slot [latex]1[/latex] (empty).
[latex]24[/latex]: [latex]h_1=2[/latex] (taken by [latex]79[/latex]), [latex]h_2=1+(24\bmod7)=1+3=4[/latex]. Probe [latex]i=1[/latex]: [latex](2+4)\bmod11=6[/latex] (taken by [latex]50[/latex]). Probe [latex]i=2[/latex]: [latex](2+8)\bmod11=10[/latex] (empty) → placed at slot [latex]10[/latex].

Answer: 10

Ravi had _____________ younger brother who taught at _____________ university. He was widely regarded as _____________ honorable man.
Select the option with the correct sequence of articles to fill in the blanks.
raw_source.solution:
"Younger brother" and "honorable man" are both non-specific, first-mention nouns (indefinite), so they take the indefinite article "a"/"an" (chosen by the following sound: "a" before a consonant sound in "younger," "an" before the vowel sound in "honorable," since the "h" is silent). "University," despite starting with a vowel letter, starts with a consonant sound ("yoo-niversity"), so it takes "a," not "an."

So the sequence is: a (younger brother), a (university), an (honorable man).

Answer: a; a; an

"I put the brown paper in my pocket along with the chalks, and possibly other things. I suppose everyone must have reflected how primeval and how poetical are the things that one carries in one's pocket: the pocket-knife, for instance the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword. Once I planned to write a book of poems entirely about the things in my pocket. But I found it would be too long: and the age of the great epics is past."

Checking each option strictly against what the passage actually says: the author never mentions a mirror at all; he doesn't decide to write "a poem on epics" (he considers a book of poems about the things in his pocket, not about epics, and abandons the idea because it would be too long, not because epics are "inconvenient to write").

Answer: The pocket-knife is described as the infant of the sword.

raw_source.text:
In the diagram, the lines QR and ST are parallel to each other. The shortest distance between these two lines is half the shortest distance between the point P and line QR. What is the ratio of the area of the triangle PST to the area of the trapezium SQRT?
Note: The figure shown is representative.
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]h[/latex] be the perpendicular distance from [latex]P[/latex] to line [latex]QR[/latex] (the full height of triangle [latex]PQR[/latex]). We're told the distance between the parallel lines [latex]ST[/latex] and [latex]QR[/latex] is [latex]h/2[/latex], which means [latex]ST[/latex] sits exactly halfway between [latex]P[/latex] and [latex]QR[/latex] (height from [latex]P[/latex] down to [latex]ST[/latex] is also [latex]h/2[/latex], since [latex]h/2+h/2=h[/latex]).

Since [latex]ST\parallel QR[/latex] and [latex]ST[/latex] is at exactly half the height from [latex]P[/latex], triangle [latex]PST[/latex] is similar to triangle [latex]PQR[/latex] with linear scale factor [latex]\tfrac12[/latex], so its area is [latex]\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=\tfrac14[/latex] of triangle [latex]PQR[/latex]'s area.

Area of trapezium [latex]SQRT[/latex] [latex]=[/latex] Area([latex]PQR[/latex]) [latex]-[/latex] Area([latex]PST[/latex]) [latex]=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34[/latex] of Area([latex]PQR[/latex]).

Ratio [latex]=\dfrac{\text{Area}(PST)}{\text{Area}(SQRT)}=\dfrac{1/4}{3/4}=\dfrac13[/latex]

Answer: 1/3

raw_source.text: A fair six-faced dice, with the faces labelled '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', and '6', is rolled thrice. What is the probability of rolling '6' exactly once?
raw_source.solution:
Rolling exactly one [latex]6[/latex] in [latex]3[/latex] independent rolls follows a Binomial([latex]n{=}3,p{=}1/6[/latex]) pattern:

[latex]P(\text{exactly one }6)=\binom31\left(\dfrac16\right)^1\left(\dfrac56\right)^2=3\times\dfrac16\times\dfrac{25}{36}=\dfrac{75}{216}[/latex]

Answer: 75/216
