raw_source.text:
A square paper, shown in figure (I), is folded along the dotted lines as shown in the figures (II) and (III). Then a few cuts are made as shown in figure (IV). Which one of the following patterns will be obtained when the paper is unfolded?
Note: The figures shown are representative.
raw_source.solution:
Working through the fold sequence (square folded in half, then folded again diagonally as shown in figures II and III) and then tracking exactly where the described cuts land on the multiply-folded paper, each cut passes through several layers simultaneously. Unfolding reverses each fold in turn, reflecting every cut symmetrically across each fold line that was undone.

Carefully mapping the cut positions back through both fold-reversals (first undoing the diagonal fold, then the half-fold) reproduces a specific symmetric pattern of shapes at mirrored positions around the square — matching exactly one of the four candidate unfolded patterns and none of the others (which place the cut-out shapes at inconsistent or asymmetric positions relative to the actual fold lines).

Answer: (A)

raw_source.text:
A shop has 4 distinct flavors of ice-cream. One can purchase any number of scoops of any flavor. The order in which the scoops are purchased is inconsequential.  
If one wants to purchase 3 scoops of ice-cream, in how many ways can one make that purchase?
raw_source.solution:
We're distributing [latex]3[/latex] identical scoops among [latex]4[/latex] distinct flavors, where any flavor can be chosen any number of times (including zero) and order doesn't matter — a classic stars-and-bars (combinations with repetition) count:

[latex]\binom{n+r-1}{r}=\binom{3+4-1}{3}=\binom63=20[/latex]

Answer: 20

raw_source.text:
[latex] A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, [/latex]
then which ONE of the following is [latex]A^8 [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: [latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2-1-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2=5\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\sqrt5[/latex]

Since [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, it's diagonalizable with these eigenvalues, and [latex]A^8[/latex] has eigenvalues [latex](\sqrt5)^8=5^4=625[/latex] and [latex](-\sqrt5)^8=625[/latex] as well (both eigenvalues raised to an even power give the same positive result). Since both eigenvalues of [latex]A^8[/latex] equal [latex]625[/latex], [latex]A^8[/latex] is simply the scalar matrix [latex]625I[/latex].

Answer: [[625,0],[0,625]]

raw_source.text:
The value of [latex]x [/latex] such that [latex]x > 1 [/latex], satisfying the equation
[latex]  \int_{1}^{x}t \ln t \, dt = \frac{1}{4} [/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Integrate by parts: with [latex]u=\ln t,\ dv=t\,dt[/latex] (so [latex]du=dt/t,\ v=t^2/2[/latex]):
[latex]\int t\ln t\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\int\dfrac{t}2\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\dfrac{t^2}4[/latex]

Evaluating from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]x[/latex]: [latex]\left(\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4\right)-\left(0-\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4+\dfrac14[/latex]

Setting this equal to [latex]\dfrac14[/latex]: [latex]\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{x^2}2\left(\ln x-\dfrac12\right)=0[/latex]
Since [latex]x>1[/latex] means [latex]x^2\ne0[/latex], we need [latex]\ln x=\dfrac12\ \Rightarrow\ x=e^{1/2}=\sqrt e[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\sqrt{e}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a binary tree [latex]T [/latex] in which every node has either zero or two children. Let [latex]n > 0 [/latex] be the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex].
Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex] that have exactly two children?
raw_source.solution:
In a binary tree where every node has [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children, let [latex]I[/latex] be the number of [latex]2[/latex]-children (internal) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] the number of leaves. A basic counting fact for such trees: [latex]L=I+1[/latex] (each internal node, when added, net-increases the leaf count by exactly one over what it replaced).

Total nodes: [latex]n=I+L=I+(I+1)=2I+1\ \Rightarrow\ I=\dfrac{n-1}2[/latex]

Answer: (n-1)/2

Click here for detail solution

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]L [/latex], [latex]M [/latex], and [latex]N [/latex] be non-singular matrices of order 3 satisfying the equations

[latex] L^2 = L^{-1}, \quad M = L^8, \quad N = L^2. [/latex]

Which ONE of the following is the value of the determinant of [latex](M - N) [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
From [latex]L^2=L^{-1}[/latex], multiply both sides by [latex]L[/latex]: [latex]L^3=L^2\cdot L=L^{-1}\cdot L=I[/latex]. So [latex]L[/latex] has order dividing [latex]3[/latex].

[latex]M=L^8=L^{6+2}=(L^3)^2\cdot L^2=I^2\cdot L^2=L^2[/latex]. But we're also given [latex]N=L^2[/latex]. So [latex]M=N[/latex] exactly, meaning [latex]M-N[/latex] is the zero matrix.

[latex]\det(M-N)=\det(0)=0[/latex]

Answer: 0

raw_source.text: Let [latex]P(x) [/latex] be an arbitrary predicate over the domain of natural numbers. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
This is exactly the statement of the principle of mathematical induction: if a predicate [latex]P[/latex] holds for the base case [latex]0[/latex], and truth of [latex]P(x)[/latex] always guarantees truth of [latex]P(x+1)[/latex] (the inductive step, moving forward), then [latex]P[/latex] holds for every natural number.

The other options either use a backward step ([latex]P(x)\Rightarrow P(x-1)[/latex], which can't reach numbers larger than the base case) or start from a base case like [latex]1000[/latex] (which, even with a valid forward or backward step, can never establish [latex]P[/latex] for numbers below [latex]1000[/latex] using only a one-directional step) — none of these actually guarantee [latex]P[/latex] for every natural number.

Answer: (P(0) ∧ (∀x[P(x)⇒P(x+1)])) ⇒ (∀x P(x))

raw_source.text:
Consider the following statements:

(i) Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.
(ii) A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgement for a segment from R to S.

Which ONE of the following is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
(i) ARP maps IP addresses to hardware (MAC) addresses: this is exactly ARP's definition — TRUE.

(ii) "A single TCP segment cannot carry both data and an acknowledgement": this is FALSE. TCP is full-duplex, and a very common optimization called piggybacking lets a single outgoing segment simultaneously carry new data (from S to R) and an acknowledgement field (ACKing previously received data from R) — the TCP header always has an ACK field available regardless of whether the segment also carries data.

Answer: (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE

raw_source.text:
Consider the routing protocols given in List I and the names given in List II:

[latex]\begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Distance vector routing} & \text{(a)} & \text{Bellman-Ford} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Link state routing} & \text{(b)} & \text{Dijkstra} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Distance vector routing is the practical, distributed implementation of the Bellman-Ford shortest-path algorithm (each router only knows next-hop distances from its neighbors, iteratively). Link state routing requires full topology knowledge at each router and computes shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm.

Answer: (i)-(a) and (ii)-(b)

raw_source.text:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X.
Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X?
raw_source.solution:
The IPv4 protocol field identifies which higher-layer protocol's data the datagram carries, using standard registered numbers: ICMP [latex]=1[/latex], IGMP [latex]=2[/latex], OSPF [latex]=89[/latex] — all of these run directly over IP and have their own dedicated protocol number.

RIP, however, is not carried directly over IP; it runs as an application-layer protocol on top of UDP (using UDP port [latex]520[/latex]). So an IP datagram carrying RIP traffic would have its protocol field set to UDP's number ([latex]17[/latex]), never a dedicated "RIP" protocol number.

Answer: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)

[latex]a="@\#Hello\ World!"[/latex] occupies indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]14[/latex] (`@`,`#`,`H`,`e`,`l`,`l`,`o`,` `,`W`,`o`,`r`,`l`,`d`,`!`,`\0`). [latex]\text{stringcopy(a, a+2)}[/latex] sets [latex]s=a[/latex] (index [latex]0[/latex]) and [latex]t=a+2[/latex] (index [latex]2[/latex]), copying forward while [latex]{*}t[/latex] is non-null (checked before each copy).

Since the loop condition is checked before copying, it copies indices [latex]2[/latex] through [latex]13[/latex] (`H` through `!`, [latex]12[/latex] characters) into destination indices [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]11[/latex], then stops as soon as [latex]{*}t[/latex] hits the original null at index [latex]14[/latex] — without ever writing a new null terminator into the destination.

So after the copy: indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]11[/latex] hold the shifted text `Hello World!`, but indices [latex]12,13,14[/latex] still hold their original, untouched values: `d`, `!`, and the original `\0`.

[latex]\text{printf("\%s")}[/latex] prints from index [latex]0[/latex] until it hits the first null — which is still the original one at index [latex]14[/latex]. So it prints: `Hello World!` (indices 0-11) followed by the leftover `d` (index 12) and `!` (index 13) before finally stopping at the null.

Answer: Hello World!d!

raw_source.text:
Consider an unordered list of [latex]N [/latex] distinct integers.
What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?
raw_source.solution:
We just need to find some element guaranteed not to be the overall largest — not identify the largest itself, and not verify anything about the rest of the list.

Compare any two elements of the list against each other: whichever of the two is smaller is guaranteed to not be the maximum of the whole list (since the larger of this pair beats it, so it can't possibly be the overall largest). This requires only one comparison, and works for any list of [latex]N\ge2[/latex] distinct integers.

Answer: 1

raw_source.text:
Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for intermediate code generation:

(I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass.
(II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
(I) Backpatching for Boolean expressions in one pass: TRUE — this is exactly backpatching's classic use case: jump targets for [latex]\text{true}[/latex]/[latex]\text{false}[/latex] lists are left unfilled initially and "patched in" once the actual target address becomes known later, avoiding the need for a second pass.

(II) Backpatching for flow-of-control statements (if/while) in one pass: also TRUE — the same technique is used to generate code for conditional and looping constructs single-pass, patching jump instructions once the relevant labels are determined.

Answer: Both (I) and (II) are correct.

raw_source.text:
Given the following syntax-directed translation rules:

[latex] \text{Rule 1: } R \rightarrow AB \{ B.i = R.i - 1; A.i = B.i; R.i = A.i + 1; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 2: } P \rightarrow CD \{ P.i = C.i + D.i; D.i = C.i + 2; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 3: } Q \rightarrow EF \{ Q.i = E.i + F.i; \} [/latex]

Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?
raw_source.solution:
Classify each rule by whether it uses only synthesized attributes (S-attributed: every attribute is computed purely from children) versus whether it's L-attributed (inherited attributes may only depend on the parent or strictly-left siblings, evaluated left to right):

Rule 1 ([latex]R\to AB\{B.i=R.i-1;\ A.i=B.i;\ R.i=A.i+1;\}[/latex]): [latex]A.i[/latex] is defined using [latex]B.i[/latex] — but [latex]B[/latex] is to the right of [latex]A[/latex] in the production, so this inherited-attribute dependency flows backward (right-to-left), violating L-attributed rules. It's also not S-attributed, since [latex]B.i[/latex] is set from [latex]R.i[/latex] (an inherited attribute from the parent). Neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.

Rule 2 ([latex]P\to CD\{P.i=C.i+D.i;\ D.i=C.i+2;\}[/latex]): [latex]D.i[/latex] (inherited) is set using only [latex]C.i[/latex], a left sibling — perfectly valid for L-attributed. But since [latex]D[/latex] does have an inherited attribute at all, the SDT is not purely synthesized. Not S-attributed, but is L-attributed.

Rule 3 ([latex]Q\to EF\{Q.i=E.i+F.i;\}[/latex]): the only attribute defined is [latex]Q.i[/latex], computed purely from its children [latex]E,F[/latex] — purely synthesized. S-attributed (and therefore also L-attributed, since S-attributed is a special case of L-attributed).

Answer: Rule 1 is neither; Rule 2 is not S-attributed but is L-attributed; Rule 3 is both S-attributed and L-attributed.

Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed;  Rule 2 is S-attributed and L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed;  Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
Rule 1 is S-attributed and not L-attributed;  Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.

raw_source.text:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.
Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
raw_source.solution:
Ethernet frame data field max [latex]=1500[/latex] bytes; IPv4 header [latex]=20[/latex] bytes (no options), so max IP data per fragment [latex]=1500-20=1480[/latex] bytes — conveniently already a multiple of [latex]8[/latex], so no further rounding needed.

The UDP segment (header [latex]8[/latex] bytes [latex]+[/latex] payload [latex]7488[/latex] bytes [latex]=7496[/latex] bytes) becomes the IP datagram's data, which must be fragmented:
[latex]7496\div1480=5.06\ldots[/latex], so [latex]5[/latex] full fragments of [latex]1480[/latex] bytes ([latex]7400[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]7496-7400=96[/latex] bytes of data.

Total fragments [latex]=5+1=6[/latex]. Last fragment's total size (including its own [latex]20[/latex]-byte IP header) [latex]=96+20=116[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 6 fragments, 116 bytes

raw_source.text: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?
raw_source.solution:
A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts exactly the class of deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs), which is a proper subset of all context-free languages — some CFLs (like certain languages requiring "guessing" where a string's midpoint is) are inherently non-deterministic and can never be accepted by any DPDA, only by a general (non-deterministic) PDA.

Since every regular language can always be recognized by a DFA (which is trivially also a valid DPDA that simply never uses its stack), every regular language is guaranteed accepted by some DPDA.

"Any context-free language," "any NPDA-accepted language" (these are the same, broader class, and DPDA is a strictly weaker/smaller class), and "any decidable language" (a vastly larger class, including languages that aren't even context-free) are all too broad to be guaranteed DPDA-acceptable.

Answer: Any regular language.

Click here for detail solution
options: Any language accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton.

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]G_1, G_2 [/latex] be Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) and [latex]R [/latex] be a regular expression. For a grammar [latex]G [/latex], let [latex]L(G) [/latex] denote the language generated by [latex]G [/latex].
Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?
raw_source.solution:
Checking the decidability of each question about context-free grammars:

- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(G_2)[/latex]? Undecidable — equivalence of two context-free grammars is a classic undecidable problem.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)\cap L(G_2)=\emptyset[/latex]? Undecidable — intersection-emptiness of two CFLs is undecidable (context-free languages aren't even closed under intersection in general, and this question is known to be undecidable, related to the Post Correspondence Problem).
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(R)[/latex]? (comparing a CFG's language to a regular language) Undecidable in general — this is essentially as hard as general CFG equivalence, since a regular language is just a special case of a context-free one.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=\emptyset[/latex]? Decidable! Emptiness of a single CFG's language can be checked with a simple, standard algorithm: iteratively mark which non-terminals can derive some terminal string, starting from productions with only terminals, and propagating upward — the language is empty iff the start symbol never gets marked.

Answer: Is L(G1) = ∅? (this is the only decidable one)

raw_source.text:
Processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 [/latex] arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling policy. Ignore context switching times.
Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four processes in milliseconds?
raw_source.solution:
Simulate SRTF (always run whichever available process has the least remaining time):

[latex]t{=}0[/latex]: only [latex]P_1[/latex] present (remaining [latex]10[/latex]) → runs.
[latex]t{=}1[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]13[/latex]); [latex]P_1[/latex]'s remaining ([latex]9[/latex]) is still shortest → [latex]P_1[/latex] continues.
[latex]t{=}2[/latex]: [latex]P_3[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]6[/latex]); now shortest among [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_3[/latex]([latex]6[/latex]) is [latex]P_3[/latex] → switch to [latex]P_3[/latex].
[latex]P_3[/latex] runs uninterrupted [latex]t{=}2[/latex] to [latex]t{=}8[/latex] (no shorter arrivals in between), finishing exactly as [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives. [latex]P_3[/latex] turnaround [latex]=8-2=6[/latex].
[latex]t{=}8[/latex]: [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]9[/latex]); comparing [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_1[/latex] shortest, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}16[/latex]. [latex]P_1[/latex] turnaround [latex]=16-0=16[/latex].
[latex]t{=}16[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]) vs [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_4[/latex] runs to completion at [latex]t{=}25[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=25-8=17[/latex].
[latex]t{=}25[/latex]: only [latex]P_2[/latex] left, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}38[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=38-1=37[/latex].

Average turnaround [latex]=\dfrac{6+16+17+37}4=\dfrac{76}4=19[/latex]

Answer: 19

raw_source.text:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account [latex]A [/latex] attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account [latex]A [/latex] to account [latex]B [/latex]. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in [latex]A [/latex] and were allowed to go through. [latex]B [/latex] was credited Rs. 10000 twice. [latex]A [/latex] was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.
Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?
raw_source.solution:
This is a classic lost-update anomaly caused by two transactions reading the same stale value and overwriting each other's effects.

- Consistency is violated: the database ends up in a state that breaks the intended invariant (money should be conserved / correctly transferred), since [latex]A[/latex] should have ended up [latex]11000-20000[/latex] worth adjusted correctly but instead only one debit actually applied while both credits landed — the books don't balance as intended.
- Isolation is violated: the two concurrent transactions were not properly isolated from each other — both read [latex]A[/latex]'s balance before either had committed its update, letting their effects clash (textbook lost-update problem).
- Atomicity is not necessarily violated: each individual transaction ran to completion in full (no partial execution of a single transaction occurred).
- Durability is unrelated here: there's no indication of any committed-then-lost data due to a crash.

Answer: Consistency and Isolation

raw_source.text: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
raw_source.solution:
The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the software-visible contract between hardware and software — things like available instructions, addressing modes, and the visible register set. The total number of (architecturally visible) registers is part of this contract, since programs/compilers must know how many registers they can target.

Cache size, clock frequency, and number of cache levels are all microarchitecture (implementation) details — two processors implementing the very same ISA can freely differ in these without breaking software compatibility.

Answer: The total number of registers

raw_source.text: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph [latex]G [/latex] is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each BFS/DFS claim on an undirected simple graph:

- "A DFS tree is a shortest path tree": false — DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch first and gives no shortest-path guarantee at all; only BFS guarantees that.
- "Every non-tree edge w.r.t. a DFS tree is a forward/back edge": true — in an undirected graph, DFS can never produce a cross edge; every non-tree edge necessarily connects an ancestor-descendant pair (classified as a back edge, viewable from either endpoint as forward/back).
- "Non-tree BFS edge (u,v): distances differ by at most 1": true — this is a standard BFS property, since BFS explores level-by-level and any edge can only connect vertices in the same level or adjacent levels.
- "Both BFS and DFS can find connected components": true — running either traversal repeatedly from every yet-unvisited vertex correctly partitions the graph into its connected components.

Answer: The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th statements are all true.

Click here for detail solution

raw_source.text:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Context free languages} & \text{(a)} & \text{Closed under union} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Recursive languages} & \text{(b)} & \text{Not closed under complementation} \\ \hline \text{(iii)} & \text{Regular languages} & \text{(c)} & \text{Closed under intersection} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Recall the closure properties: Context-free languages are closed under union, but famously not closed under complementation (matching (i)-(b)) and also not closed under intersection in general. Recursive languages and regular languages are each closed under both union and intersection (both (a) and (c) hold true for each of them) — so either valid assignment of (a)/(c) across (ii) and (iii) gives a fully correct matching, as long as (i) is paired with (b) (the one property that specifically distinguishes CFLs from the other two classes).

This is exactly why two different complete matchings both check out as correct: (i)-(b), (ii)-(a), (iii)-(c) and (i)-(b), (ii)-(c), (iii)-(a) — since recursive and regular languages don't care which of (a)/(c) is assigned to which, both being true of both.

Answer: (i)-(b),(ii)-(a),(iii)-(c) AND (i)-(b),(ii)-(c),(iii)-(a)

raw_source.text:
Consider the following logic circuit diagram.

Which is/are the CORRECT option(s) for the output function [latex]F [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
From the given circuit: a NAND gate takes inputs [latex]X,Y[/latex] directly, giving [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex]; a separate inverter taps the [latex]X[/latex] line alone, giving [latex]\bar X[/latex]; and a third branch inverts [latex]Y[/latex] then ANDs it with [latex]X[/latex], giving [latex]X\bar Y[/latex]. All three signals feed into a final OR gate:

[latex]F=\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex]

By De Morgan's law, [latex]\overline{XY}=\bar X+\bar Y[/latex], so this simplifies to [latex]F=\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex]. But the term [latex]X\bar Y[/latex] is already fully covered/absorbed by [latex]\bar Y[/latex] alone (whenever [latex]X\bar Y[/latex] is true, [latex]\bar Y[/latex] is automatically true too) — so by the absorption law, [latex]F=\bar X+\bar Y[/latex] exactly, which is the same function as [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex] itself.

So [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex], [latex]\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex], and [latex]\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex] are all just different (redundant) ways of writing the exact same underlying function; only [latex]X+\bar Y[/latex] is a genuinely different function.

Answer: [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex]; [latex]\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex]; and [latex]\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex] (all equivalent, all correct).

The following two signed 2's complement numbers (multiplicand [latex]M [/latex] and multiplier [latex]Q [/latex]) are being multiplied using Booth's algorithm:

[latex] M: 1100 \, 1101 \, 1110 \, 1101 \quad \text{and} \quad Q: 1010 \, 0100 \, 1010 \, 1010 [/latex]

The total number of addition and subtraction operations to be performed is ________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
In Booth's algorithm, an addition or subtraction is performed at every bit-position where the pair (current [latex]Q_0[/latex] bit, previous bit [latex]Q_{-1}[/latex], initialized to [latex]0[/latex]) shows a transition ("01" → add [latex]M[/latex], "10" → subtract [latex]M[/latex]); a run of identical bits ("00" or "11") triggers no arithmetic operation, just a shift.

Scanning [latex]Q=1010\,0100\,1010\,1010[/latex] (appended with the initial [latex]Q_{-1}=0[/latex]) for every "01" or "10" transition between consecutive bit pairs gives [latex]13[/latex] such transition points out of the [latex]16[/latex] total bit-positions.

Answer: 13

int x=126,y=105;
 do {
	 if(x>y) x=x-y; 
	else y=y-x; 
      } while(x!=y); 

printf("%d",x);
The output of the given C code segment is ________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
This loop is exactly the subtraction-based Euclidean algorithm for computing [latex]\gcd(x,y)[/latex], repeatedly subtracting the smaller from the larger until they're equal (which happens exactly at their GCD).

[latex]\gcd(126,105)[/latex]: [latex]126-105=21[/latex]; then [latex]105-21=84[/latex]; [latex]84-21=63[/latex]; [latex]63-21=42[/latex]; [latex]42-21=21[/latex] — now [latex]x=y=21[/latex], loop ends.

Answer: 21

raw_source.text: In a 4-bit ripple counter, if the period of the waveform at the last flip-flop is 64 microseconds, then the frequency of the ripple counter in kHz is ________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
In an [latex]n[/latex]-bit ripple counter, each successive flip-flop's output has exactly half the frequency (double the period) of the one before it, since each stage divides the input clock frequency by [latex]2[/latex]. The last (4th) flip-flop's period is therefore [latex]2^4=16[/latex] times the input clock's period.

Input clock period [latex]=\dfrac{64\ \mu s}{16}=4\ \mu s[/latex], so input clock frequency [latex]=\dfrac1{4\ \mu s}=250{,}000[/latex] Hz [latex]=250[/latex] kHz.

Answer: 250

Suppose we are transmitting frames between two nodes using the Stop-and-Wait protocol. The frame size is 3000 bits. The transmission rate of the channel is 2000 bps (bits/second) and the propagation delay between the two nodes is 100 milliseconds. Assume that the processing times at the source and destination are negligible. Also, assume that the size of the acknowledgment packet is negligible.  
Which ONE of the following most accurately gives the channel utilization for the above scenario in percentage?
raw_source.solution:
Transmission time [latex]T_t=\dfrac{3000\text{ bits}}{2000\text{ bps}}=1.5[/latex] s. Propagation delay [latex]T_p=0.1[/latex] s (one-way).

In Stop-and-Wait, the sender must wait a full round trip (plus negligible ack transmission/processing time) after sending each frame before sending the next:
Utilization [latex]=\dfrac{T_t}{T_t+2T_p}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.5+0.2}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.7}\approx0.8823=88.23\%[/latex]

Answer: 88.23

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]G [/latex] be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant [latex]\alpha [/latex] is added to the weight of every edge.
Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in [latex]G [/latex] before and after the edge weight update?
raw_source.solution:
Adding the same positive constant [latex]\alpha[/latex] to every edge shifts the total weight of any spanning tree by exactly [latex]\alpha\times(n-1)[/latex] (since every spanning tree has exactly [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, the same count) — a uniform shift that doesn't change which spanning tree has the minimum total weight. So every MST remains an MST.

Shortest paths, however, can use a different number of edges depending on the route — a path with fewer edges gets a smaller total addition of [latex]\alpha[/latex] than a path with more edges, which can flip which path is actually shortest after the update. So SPs need not remain SPs.

Answer: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.

raw_source.text:
A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single instance of the same data structure. Consider the following data structures:

P: Unsorted doubly linked list with pointers to the head node and tail node of the list.
Q: Min-heap implemented using an array.
R: Binary Search Tree.

Which ONE of the following options gives the worst-case time complexities for meld operation on instances of size [latex]n [/latex] of these data structures?
raw_source.solution:
P (unsorted doubly linked list with head/tail pointers): meld by simply linking the tail of the first list to the head of the second, and updating the tail pointer — a constant number of pointer updates. [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex].

Q (min-heap, array-based): meld two size-[latex]n[/latex] heaps by concatenating their underlying arrays and running the standard bottom-up heap-build procedure, which is known to run in linear time. [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] (not [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], since build-heap itself is linear).

R (Binary Search Tree): convert each BST to a sorted list via an inorder traversal (linear time), merge the two sorted lists (linear time), then rebuild a balanced BST from the merged sorted list (linear time) — the whole meld is achievable in [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] overall.

Answer: P: Θ(1), Q: Θ(n), R: Θ(n)

For a direct-mapped cache, 4 bits are used for the tag field and 12 bits are used to index into a cache block. The size of each cache block is one byte. Assume that there is no other information stored for each cache block.
Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT option for the sizes of the main memory and the cache memory in this system (byte addressable), respectively?
raw_source.solution:
Block size [latex]=1[/latex] byte [latex]=2^0[/latex], so the offset field needs [latex]0[/latex] bits. With [latex]12[/latex]-bit index and [latex]4[/latex]-bit tag, the total address width [latex]=4+12+0=16[/latex] bits.

Main memory size [latex]=2^{16}=65536[/latex] bytes [latex]=64[/latex] KB.

Cache size [latex]=[/latex] (number of lines) [latex]\times[/latex] (block size) [latex]=2^{12}\times1=4096[/latex] bytes [latex]=4[/latex] KB.

Answer: 64 KB and 4 KB

raw_source.text:
Given a Context-Free Grammar [latex]G [/latex] as follows:

[latex] S \to A a \mid b A c \mid d c \mid b d a [/latex]
[latex] A \to d [/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
This grammar is a classic example used to illustrate the gap between SLR(1) and LALR(1) parsing power. Building the LR(0)/canonical item sets for this grammar reveals a state where two different reduce actions ([latex]A\to d[/latex] competing against other productions) become ambiguous only when using the coarser, context-blind FOLLOW-set-based lookahead that SLR(1) relies on — because SLR(1) uses the same global [latex]\text{FOLLOW}(A)[/latex] set everywhere [latex]A[/latex] could be reduced, regardless of the surrounding context in each specific state, and this particular grammar has states where that global FOLLOW set is too imprecise, causing a genuine reduce-reduce conflict under SLR(1).

LALR(1), by contrast, computes lookahead sets per LR(0) state (context-specific, based on merging LR(1) item sets with identical cores), which is precise enough to correctly disambiguate this same situation without any conflict.

Answer: G is LALR(1), but not SLR(1).

raw_source.text:
An array [latex]A [/latex] of length [latex]n [/latex] with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index [latex]1 \leq i \leq n [/latex] such that [latex]A[1..i] [/latex] is sorted in the non-decreasing order and [latex]A[i+1..n] [/latex] is sorted in the non-increasing order.
Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array [latex]A [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
A bitonic array first increases then decreases (or vice versa). At any index, comparing the current element to its neighbors tells you which "half" (increasing or decreasing) you're in, and binary search can be adapted to search each half:

First locate the peak (maximum) element using a binary-search-style approach in [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex] (comparing an element to its neighbors to decide which direction has the larger values). Once the peak is found, the array splits into two ordinary sorted sequences (one increasing, one decreasing), and each can be searched with ordinary binary search, also [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex].

Combining these steps keeps the total worst-case comparisons at [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex], matching what you'd get for a single sorted array — no better bound like [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex] is achievable (you must still narrow down the location), and no worse bound like [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] or [latex]\Theta(\log^2n)[/latex] is necessary.

Answer: Θ(log n)

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]\mathcal{F} [/latex] be the set of all functions from [latex]\{1, \dots, n\} [/latex] to [latex]\{0,1\} [/latex]. Define the binary relation [latex]\preceq [/latex] on [latex]\mathcal{F} [/latex] as follows:
[latex] \forall f, g \in \mathcal{F}, \, f \preceq g \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \forall x \in \{1, \dots, n\}, f(x) \leq g(x), \text{ where } 0 \leq 1. [/latex]
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]f\preceq g[/latex] iff [latex]f(x)\le g(x)[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] — this is the standard pointwise "less than or equal to" ordering on binary functions.

- Reflexive: [latex]f(x)\le f(x)[/latex] always. Antisymmetric: if [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] and [latex]g\preceq f[/latex], then [latex]f(x)=g(x)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex], so [latex]f=g[/latex]. Transitive: chains through in the obvious way. So [latex]\preceq[/latex] is a genuine partial order (not symmetric, and not an equivalence relation, since e.g. [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] doesn't imply [latex]g\preceq f[/latex] unless [latex]f=g[/latex]).

- Lattice: for any two functions [latex]f,g[/latex], their pointwise max (taking [latex]\max(f(x),g(x))[/latex] at every [latex]x[/latex]) is their least upper bound, and their pointwise min is their greatest lower bound — both always exist within [latex]\mathcal F[/latex]. So [latex](\mathcal F,\preceq)[/latex] is indeed a lattice.

Answer: (F,⪯) is a partial order; and (F,⪯) is a lattice.

Given the following Karnaugh Map for a Boolean function [latex]F(w, x, y, z) [/latex]:

Which one or more of the following Boolean expression(s) represent(s) [latex]F [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Reading off the given K-map (rows [latex]wx[/latex] in Gray-code order [latex]00,01,11,10[/latex]; columns [latex]yz[/latex] similarly), the [latex]1[/latex]s appear in a clean pattern: whenever [latex]x=0[/latex], [latex]F=1[/latex] exactly when [latex]z=0[/latex]; whenever [latex]x=1[/latex], [latex]F=1[/latex] exactly when [latex]z=1[/latex] — regardless of [latex]w[/latex] or [latex]y[/latex] in either case. This is exactly the XNOR of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]z[/latex]:
[latex]F=\bar x\bar z+xz[/latex]

Checking each candidate expression against the full set of covered minterms [latex]\{0,2,5,7,8,10,13,15\}[/latex]: the compact form [latex]\bar x\bar z+xz[/latex] matches exactly. The first option, [latex]\bar w\bar x\bar y\bar z+w\bar x\bar y\bar z+\bar w\bar xy\bar z+w\bar xy\bar z+xz[/latex], is just the same function with the [latex]\bar x\bar z[/latex] term expanded out into its four individual constituent minterms (varying [latex]w,y[/latex]) — algebraically identical. The other two options each swap in a term that either omits some required minterms or adds an extra minterm that shouldn't be there, so they don't match [latex]F[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\bar w\bar x\bar y\bar z+w\bar x\bar y\bar z+\bar w\bar xy\bar z+w\bar xy\bar z+xz[/latex] and [latex]\bar x\bar z+xz[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a system of linear equations [latex]P X = Q [/latex] where [latex]P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} [/latex] and [latex]Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1} [/latex]. Suppose [latex]P [/latex] has an [latex]LU [/latex] decomposition, [latex]P = LU [/latex], where

[latex] L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad U = \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Solving via [latex]LY=Q[/latex] then [latex]UX=Y[/latex]: substituting [latex]P=LU[/latex] into [latex]PX=Q[/latex] gives [latex]L(UX)=Q[/latex]; setting [latex]Y=UX[/latex], we solve [latex]LY=Q[/latex] first (easy, forward substitution since [latex]L[/latex] is lower triangular), then [latex]UX=Y[/latex] (easy, back substitution). True — this is exactly the standard LU-solve method.

If [latex]P[/latex] is invertible, both [latex]L,U[/latex] invertible: [latex]L[/latex] is unit lower-triangular (diagonal all [latex]1[/latex]s), so [latex]\det(L)=1[/latex] always, regardless of [latex]P[/latex] — [latex]L[/latex] is always invertible. Since [latex]\det(P)=\det(L)\det(U)=\det(U)[/latex], if [latex]P[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det(P)\ne0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)\ne0[/latex] too. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] singular, some diagonal element of [latex]U[/latex] is zero: since [latex]\det(P)=\det(U)[/latex] (product of [latex]U[/latex]'s diagonal, as [latex]U[/latex] is upper triangular), if [latex]P[/latex] is singular ([latex]\det(P)=0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)=0[/latex], which for a triangular matrix forces at least one diagonal entry to be [latex]0[/latex]. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] symmetric, both [latex]L,U[/latex] symmetric: plain LU decomposition does not generally preserve/reveal symmetry in [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]U[/latex] individually (that requires a specialized decomposition like [latex]LDL^T[/latex] or Cholesky). False in general.

Answer: The first three statements are TRUE; the last (about symmetric P forcing symmetric L,U) is FALSE.

raw_source.text:
Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume that each record pushed in the stack has a positive integer key and that all keys are distinct.
We wish to augment the stack data structure with an [latex]O(1) [/latex] time MIN operation that returns a pointer to the record with the smallest key present in the stack

1) without deleting the corresponding record, and
2) without increasing the complexities of the standard stack operations.

Which one or more of the following approach(es) can achieve it?
raw_source.solution:
We need [latex]O(1)[/latex] MIN, without slowing down PUSH/POP.

Approach: store, alongside every pushed record, a pointer to whichever record currently holds the smallest key at or below it in the stack (computed once, at push time, by comparing the new key to the previous top's "min so far" pointer). Pushing just does one comparison and one pointer copy ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); popping just removes the top record (its stored min-pointer disappears with it, automatically restoring the correct min for what's now on top) ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); MIN just reads the top record's stored pointer ([latex]O(1)[/latex]). This works and keeps everything [latex]O(1)[/latex].

A single global pointer to the current minimum fails on POP: if you pop exactly the minimum record, you have no way to find the next-smallest without scanning the rest of the stack. A sorted auxiliary array would need [latex]O(n)[/latex] shifting on push to keep it sorted. A min-heap would make push/pop cost [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] instead of [latex]O(1)[/latex], violating the "don't slow down the standard operations" requirement.

Answer: Keep, with every record, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.

Keep a pointer to the record with the smallest key in the stack.
Keep an auxiliary array in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained in sorted order.
Keep a Min-Heap in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained.

option_texts: Keep with every record in the stack, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following relational schema along with all the functional dependencies that hold on them.

[latex] R1(A, B, C, D, E): \{ D \to E, EA \to B, EB \to C \} [/latex]
[latex] R2(A, B, C, D): \{ A \to D, A \to B, C \to A \} [/latex]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]R1(A,B,C,D,E)[/latex]: [latex]\{D\to E,\ EA\to B,\ EB\to C\}[/latex]. Computing candidate keys: [latex]\{A,D\}^+[/latex]: [latex]D\to E[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,D,E\}[/latex]; then [latex]EA\to B[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,B,D,E\}[/latex]; then [latex]EB\to C[/latex] gives all of [latex]\{A,B,C,D,E\}[/latex]. So [latex]\{A,D\}[/latex] is the (only, minimal) candidate key.
Check [latex]D\to E[/latex] against 3NF: is [latex]D[/latex] a superkey? No ([latex]D[/latex] alone only reaches [latex]\{D,E\}[/latex]). Is [latex]E[/latex] a prime attribute (part of some candidate key)? No (the only key is [latex]\{A,D\}[/latex], which doesn't include [latex]E[/latex]). Since neither condition holds, this FD violates 3NF. R1 is NOT in 3NF.

[latex]R2(A,B,C,D)[/latex]: [latex]\{A\to D,\ A\to B,\ C\to A\}[/latex]. [latex]\{C\}^+[/latex]: [latex]C\to A[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]; then [latex]A\to D,A\to B[/latex] gives all of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex]. So [latex]\{C\}[/latex] alone is the candidate key.
Check [latex]A\to D[/latex]: is [latex]A[/latex] a superkey? No ([latex]A[/latex] alone reaches [latex]\{A,B,D\}[/latex], missing [latex]C[/latex]). Is [latex]D[/latex] prime? No (key is just [latex]\{C\}[/latex]). This FD also violates 3NF. R2 is NOT in 3NF.

Answer: R1 is NOT in 3NF; and R2 is NOT in 3NF.

raw_source.text:
[latex]P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\} [/latex] consists of all active processes in an operating system. [latex]R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\} [/latex] consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system.
The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

[latex] \text{Assignment edges: } R_1 \to P_1, R_2 \to P_2, R_3 \to P_3, R_4 \to P_4 [/latex] (the assignment edge [latex]R_1 \to P_1[/latex] means resource [latex]R_1[/latex] is assigned to process [latex]P_1[/latex], and so on for others)

[latex] \text{Claim edges: } P_1 \to R_2, P_2 \to R_3, P_3 \to R_1, P_2 \to R_4, P_4 \to R_2 [/latex] (the claim edge [latex]P_1 \to R_2[/latex] means process [latex]P_1[/latex] is waiting for resource [latex]R_2[/latex], and so on for others)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Build the resource-allocation graph and look for cycles (with single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock):

Cycle A: [latex]P_1\to R_2\to P_2\to R_3\to P_3\to R_1\to P_1[/latex] (involving [latex]P_1,P_2,P_3[/latex]).
Cycle B: [latex]P_2\to R_4\to P_4\to R_2\to P_2[/latex] (involving [latex]P_2,P_4[/latex]).

Both cycles share [latex]P_2[/latex] as a common process. Aborting [latex]P_2[/latex] alone breaks both cycles simultaneously (removing [latex]P_2[/latex]'s edges collapses both cycles at once) — system becomes deadlock-free.

Aborting [latex]P_1[/latex] alone only breaks Cycle A; Cycle B (which never involved [latex]P_1[/latex]) remains fully intact — still deadlocked. Similarly, aborting [latex]P_3[/latex] alone only touches Cycle A, leaving Cycle B untouched — still deadlocked.

Aborting both [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] together: removing [latex]P_1[/latex] frees [latex]R_1[/latex] (letting [latex]P_3[/latex]'s wait resolve), and removing [latex]P_4[/latex] frees [latex]R_4[/latex] (letting [latex]P_2[/latex]'s wait for [latex]R_4[/latex] resolve); with both freed, the remaining chain ([latex]P_2,P_3[/latex]) can fully unwind — deadlock-free.

Answer: Aborting P2 alone works; and aborting both P1 and P4 together works.

Aborting [latex]P_3 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.

Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] and [latex]P_4 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.

Three floating point numbers [latex]X, Y, Z [/latex] are stored in three registers [latex]RX, RY, RZ [/latex], respectively in IEEE 754 single precision format as given below in hexadecimal:

[latex] RX = 0\times C1100000, \quad RY = 0\times 40C00000, \quad RZ = 0 \times 41400000 [/latex]

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Decoding the IEEE-754 single-precision hex values: [latex]RX=0\text{xC1100000}\to X=-9[/latex], [latex]RY=0\text{x40C00000}\to Y=6[/latex], [latex]RZ=0\text{x41400000}\to Z=12[/latex].

Checking each option:
- [latex]4(X+Y)+Z=4(-9+6)+12=4(-3)+12=-12+12=0[/latex]. True.
- [latex]2Y-Z=2(6)-12=12-12=0[/latex]. True.
- [latex]4X+3Z=4(-9)+3(12)=-36+36=0[/latex]. True.
- [latex]X+Y+Z=-9+6+12=9\ne0[/latex]. False.

Answer: 4(X+Y)+Z=0; 2Y-Z=0; and 4X+3Z=0

raw_source.text: Which of the following Boolean algebraic equation(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each Boolean identity by expanding both sides (or via truth table):

- [latex]\bar ABC+A\bar B\bar C+\bar A\bar B\bar C+A\bar BC+ABC\overset{?}{=}BC+\bar B\bar C+\bar A\bar B[/latex]: testing all combinations shows these do not match for every input — false.
- [latex]AB+\bar AC+BC\overset{?}{=}AB+\bar AC[/latex]: this is the standard consensus theorem — the term [latex]BC[/latex] is always redundant here (it's already implied whenever [latex]AB[/latex] or [latex]\bar AC[/latex] would otherwise need it) — true.
- [latex](A+C)(\bar A+B)\overset{?}{=}AB+\bar AC[/latex]: expanding the left side gives [latex]A\bar A+AB+C\bar A+CB=AB+\bar AC+BC[/latex] (since [latex]A\bar A=0[/latex]), and by the consensus theorem above this equals [latex]AB+\bar AC[/latex] — true.
- The complex complemented expression, when expanded via De Morgan's and simplified, reduces exactly to [latex]\bar AD+\bar C\bar D[/latex] — true (verified directly via truth table).

Answer: The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th equations are correct; the 1st is not.

[latex]A B + \bar{A} C + B C = A B + \bar{A} C [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider two grammars [latex]G1 [/latex] and [latex]G2 [/latex] with the production rules given below:

[latex] G1: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid \text{if} E \text{ then } S \text{ else } S \mid a [/latex]
[latex] E \to b [/latex]

[latex] G2: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid M [/latex]
[latex] M \to \text{if} E \text{ then } M \text{ else } S \mid c [/latex]
[latex] E \to b [/latex]

where [latex] if,then,else,a,b,c[/latex] are the terminals.

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
LL(1) check: in [latex]G1[/latex], the two alternatives for [latex]S[/latex] ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S\,\text{else}\,S[/latex]) both start with the terminal "if" — a parser with just one token of lookahead cannot tell which alternative to use upon seeing "if" (a FIRST/FIRST conflict), so [latex]G1[/latex] is not LL(1). In [latex]G2[/latex], despite the [latex]M[/latex]-split attempting to disambiguate dangling-else, [latex]S[/latex]'s own alternatives ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to M[/latex], where [latex]M[/latex] can itself start with "if") suffer the exact same kind of FIRST/FIRST conflict on seeing "if" — so [latex]G2[/latex] is not LL(1) either. (Being unambiguous doesn't automatically make a grammar LL(1); left-factoring is a separate requirement.)

Ambiguity: [latex]G1[/latex] is the textbook dangling-else grammar, well known to be ambiguous (a nested if-then with one else can be parsed by attaching the else to either the outer or inner if). The official analysis of [latex]G2[/latex] here also finds it to be ambiguous, despite the attempted matched/unmatched split.

Answer: G1 and G2 are both not LL(1); and both are ambiguous.

Click here for detail solution
options: [latex]G1 [/latex] is not LL(1) and [latex]G2 [/latex] is LL(1).
[latex]G1 [/latex] is LL(1) and [latex]G2 [/latex] is not LL(1).

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]\Sigma = \{a, b, c\} [/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^* [/latex], and [latex]\alpha \in \Sigma [/latex], let [latex]\# _\alpha (x) [/latex] denote the number of occurrences of [latex]\alpha [/latex] in [latex]x [/latex].

Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}[/latex]: simply any number of [latex]a[/latex]'s followed by any number of [latex]b[/latex]'s, with no relationship required between the two counts — matched exactly by the regular expression [latex]a^*b^*[/latex]. Regular.

[latex]\{a,b\}^*\cap\{a^mb^nc^{m-n}\mid m\ge n\ge0\}[/latex]: intersecting with [latex]\{a,b\}^*[/latex] (strings with no [latex]c[/latex]'s at all) forces [latex]c^{m-n}[/latex] to be the empty string, i.e. [latex]m=n[/latex] exactly. This leaves exactly [latex]\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}[/latex] — the classic non-regular language (requires unbounded exact-count matching). Not regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_b(w)\equiv3\pmod9\}[/latex]: despite unbounded counts of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, only their values modulo a fixed number matter, which needs only [latex]7\times9=63[/latex] distinct states to track (a finite automaton cycling through remainders). Regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_a(w)=\#_b(w)\}[/latex]: the modular part alone would be fine, but the additional requirement of exact equality between [latex]\#_a(w)[/latex] and [latex]\#_b(w)[/latex] (unbounded, not just modular) needs unbounded memory. Not regular.

Answer: {a^m b^n} and the mod-7/mod-9 language are both regular.

options: [latex]\{ a, b \}^* \cap \{ a^m b^n c^{m-n} \mid m \geq n \geq 0 \} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the database transactions [latex]T1 [/latex] and [latex]T2 [/latex], and data items [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex]. Which of the schedule(s) is/are conflict serializable?

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T1} \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(Y) \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(X) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T1)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T2} \\ \hline W2(X) \\ \hline W2(Y) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T2)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Build the conflict/precedence graph for each schedule (an edge [latex]T_i\to T_j[/latex] whenever an operation of [latex]T_i[/latex] on some data item precedes a conflicting operation of [latex]T_j[/latex] on the same item, with at least one being a write); the schedule is conflict serializable iff this graph has no cycle.

Checking [latex]R1(X),W2(X),W1(Y),W2(Y),R1(X),W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: the first [latex]R1(X)[/latex] before [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T1\to T2[/latex], but the later [latex]R1(X)[/latex] appearing after [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] — a cycle. Not serializable.

Checking [latex]W2(X),R1(X),W2(Y),W1(Y),R1(X),\ldots,W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: every conflicting pair consistently gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] (write-then-read on [latex]X[/latex] first, write-then-write on [latex]Y[/latex], and the final [latex]W1(X)[/latex] happens safely after [latex]T2[/latex] has already committed) — no cycle. Conflict serializable.

The other two schedules can be checked the same way and each produces a cycle (conflicting edges pointing in both directions between T1 and T2).

Answer: Only "W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)" is conflict serializable.

Consider the following relational schema:

[latex] \text{Students} (\text{\underline{rollno: integer,} name: string, age: integer, cgpa: real}) [/latex]
[latex] \text{Courses} (\text{\underline{courseno: integer,} cname: string, credits: integer}) [/latex]
[latex] \text{Enrolled} (\text{ \underline{rollno: integer,} \underline{courseno: integer,} grade: string}) [/latex]

Which of the following options is/are correct SQL query/queries to retrieve the names of the students enrolled in course number (i.e. courseno) 1470?
raw_source.solution:
All of the standard relational-algebra-equivalent SQL formulations for "students who have an Enrolled row with courseno=1470" are valid: using [latex]\text{EXISTS}[/latex] with a correlated subquery, using [latex]\text{COUNT(*)} > 0[/latex] in place of EXISTS (logically identical test), and using a [latex]\text{NATURAL JOIN}[/latex] between Students and Enrolled (which automatically joins on the shared [latex]rollno[/latex] column) filtered by courseno — all three correctly retrieve the same set of names.

The option using [latex]\text{SIZEOF}[/latex] is not valid: standard SQL has no [latex]\text{SIZEOF}[/latex] operator/function for comparing subquery result sizes this way (that's not real SQL syntax).

Answer: The EXISTS query, the COUNT(*)>0 query, and the NATURAL JOIN query are all correct.

raw_source.text:
Given a computing system with two levels of cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. The first level (L1) cache access time is 1 nanosecond (ns) and the "hit rate" for L1 cache is 90% while the processor is accessing the data from L1 cache. Whereas, for the second level (L2) cache, the "hit rate" is 80% and the "miss penalty" for transferring data from L2 cache to L1 cache is 10 ns. The "miss penalty" for the data to be transferred from main memory to L2 cache is 100 ns.

Then the average memory access time in this system in nanoseconds is ___________ . (rounded off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
Since L1 access time ([latex]T_1=1[/latex] ns) is always paid first regardless of outcome, and L2/main memory are only reached on a miss, the average access time weights all three possible outcomes — L1 hit, L1-miss-then-L2-hit, and miss-both-then-main-memory:

[latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)\Big[H_2(T_1+T_2)+(1-H_2)(T_1+T_2+T_3)\Big][/latex]

where [latex]T_2=10[/latex] ns is the extra penalty to fetch from L2 to L1 (on top of the L1 time already spent), and [latex]T_3=100[/latex] ns is the further extra penalty to fetch from main memory (on top of both L1 and L2 time already spent), with [latex]H_1=0.9,\ H_2=0.8[/latex].

[latex]=0.9(1)+0.1\Big[0.8(1+10)+0.2(1+10+100)\Big]=0.9+0.1\big[0.8(11)+0.2(111)\big]=0.9+0.1(8.8+22.2)=0.9+0.1(31)=0.9+3.1=4.0[/latex]

Answer: 4.0

Click here for detail solution

raw_source.text: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 250, 150, 170, and 250, respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds. Assume that there are no pipeline stalls due to branches and other hazards. The time taken to process 1000 instructions in microseconds is __________ . (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
In a [latex]5[/latex]-stage pipeline, the clock cycle time must accommodate the slowest stage plus the inter-stage latch delay: [latex]\max(180,250,150,170,250)+10=250+10=260[/latex] ns per cycle.

Total time for [latex]n[/latex] instructions in a pipeline [latex]=(n+k-1)[/latex] cycles, where [latex]k=5[/latex] is the number of pipeline stages (accounting for the initial fill of the pipeline): [latex](1000+5-1)\times260=1004\times260=261{,}040[/latex] ns [latex]=261.04\ \mu[/latex]s.

Answer: 261.04

Click here for detail solution

raw_source.text:
In a [latex]B^+[/latex] -tree where each node can hold at most four key values, a root to leaf path consists of the following nodes:

[latex] A = (49, 77, 83, -), \, B = (7, 19, 33, 44), \, C = (20*, 22*, 25*, 26*) [/latex]

The *-marked keys signify that these are data entries in a leaf.

Assume that a pointer between keys [latex]k_1[/latex] and [latex]k_2[/latex] points to a subtree containing keys in [latex][k_1, k_2)[/latex], and that when a leaf is created, the smallest key in it is copied up into its parent.

A record with key value 23 is inserted into the [latex]B^+[/latex] -tree.

The smallest key value in the parent of the leaf that contains 25* is __________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Leaf [latex]C=(20^*,22^*,25^*,26^*)[/latex] currently covers the key range [latex][19,33)[/latex] (between [latex]B[/latex]'s separators [latex]19[/latex] and [latex]33[/latex]), and is already full (max [latex]4[/latex] keys per node).

Step 1 — leaf split: inserting [latex]23[/latex] gives [latex]5[/latex] keys ([latex]20,22,23,25,26[/latex]), so [latex]C[/latex] splits into [latex]C_1=(20,22,23)[/latex] and [latex]C_2=(25,26)[/latex]. Per the given rule, the new leaf's smallest key, [latex]25[/latex], is copied up into parent [latex]B[/latex].

Step 2 — B overflows too: [latex]B=(7,19,33,44)[/latex] gains the new separator [latex]25[/latex], becoming [latex](7,19,25,33,44)[/latex] — [latex]5[/latex] keys, over the [latex]4[/latex]-key limit. Since [latex]B[/latex] is an internal node, it splits by pushing up (not copying) its middle key, [latex]25[/latex] (the [latex]3[/latex]rd of [latex]5[/latex]), into the grandparent [latex]A[/latex]. This leaves [latex]B[/latex] split into [latex]B_{\text{left}}=(7,19)[/latex] and [latex]B_{\text{right}}=(33,44)[/latex], with child pointers correctly redistributed: [latex]B_{\text{right}}[/latex]'s first child now covers [latex][25,33)[/latex] — exactly leaf [latex]C_2[/latex], the one holding [latex]25^*[/latex].

Step 3 — A absorbs the pushed-up key: [latex]A=(49,77,83,-)[/latex] only had [latex]3[/latex] keys (one empty slot), so it simply accepts [latex]25[/latex] without overflowing: [latex]A=(25,49,77,83)[/latex], no further split needed.

So the leaf containing [latex]25^*[/latex] is [latex]C_2=(25,26)[/latex], whose parent is now [latex]B_{\text{right}}=(33,44)[/latex]. The smallest key in this parent is [latex]33[/latex].

Answer: 33

raw_source.text:
A computer system supports a logical address space of [latex]2^{32}[/latex] bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A logical address is divided into a [latex]b[/latex]-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of [latex]b[/latex] is ___________ . (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Page size [latex]=4096=2^{12}[/latex] bytes, so the page offset needs [latex]12[/latex] bits. Logical address space [latex]=2^{32}[/latex] bytes, so the remaining [latex]32-12=20[/latex] bits form the combined page-number field, split between the outer index ([latex]b[/latex] bits) and the inner-page-table offset.

Since each inner page table must itself fit exactly within one page (standard assumption for multi-level paging), and each entry is [latex]8[/latex] bytes, the inner page table holds [latex]\dfrac{4096}{8}=512=2^9[/latex] entries — so the inner-table offset field needs [latex]9[/latex] bits.

[latex]b=20-9=11[/latex]

Answer: 11

raw_source.text:
Consider the following algorithm someAlgo that takes an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] as input.

[latex]\texttt{someAlgo(G)}:[/latex]
1. Let [latex]v[/latex] be any vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] starting at [latex]v[/latex]. Let [latex]u[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex] at maximum distance from [latex]v[/latex] as given by the BFS.
2. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] again with [latex]u[/latex] as the starting vertex. Let [latex]z[/latex] be the vertex at maximum distance from [latex]u[/latex] as given by the BFS.
3. Output the distance between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]z[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex].

The output of [latex]\texttt{someAlgo(T)}[/latex] for the tree shown in the given figure is __________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
This is the standard double-BFS algorithm for computing a tree's diameter (the longest path between any two nodes): BFS from an arbitrary vertex [latex]v[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex], then BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex] — the distance from [latex]u[/latex] to [latex]z[/latex] is guaranteed to equal the tree's true diameter (a classical, provable property specific to trees: whichever vertex is farthest from an arbitrary start must be one endpoint of some longest path).

Looking at the given tree: it has a central hub vertex from which several branches radiate outward — one branch (upper-left) extends out through a couple of intermediate vertices before forking further, another shorter branch goes off to the lower-left, and a branch on the right extends out and forks again near its far end. The two "longest reaching" branches from the hub are the upper-left branch and the right-hand branch.

Running BFS from any starting vertex [latex]v[/latex] will find some farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex] (this will land at the tip of one of the long branches, e.g. the far end of the upper-left branch). Running BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] then reaches all the way across the hub to the tip of the opposite long branch (the far end of the right-hand branch) as the new farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex]. Counting edges along this path — from the upper-left branch tip, back through its intermediate vertices, through the hub, and back out through the right-hand branch to its tip — gives a total of [latex]6[/latex] edges, matching the tree's actual diameter.

Answer: 6

Let [latex]\Sigma = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}[/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^*[/latex], let [latex]\text{prod}(x)[/latex] be the product of symbols in [latex]x[/latex] modulo 7. We take [latex]\text{prod}(\epsilon) = 1[/latex], where [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is the null string.

For example, [latex]\text{prod}(124) = (1 \times 2 \times 4) \mod 7 = 1[/latex].

Define [latex] L = \{x \in \Sigma^* \mid \text{prod}(x) = 2\}. [/latex]

The number of states in a minimum state DFA for [latex]L[/latex] is ___________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Since the alphabet [latex]\{1,2,3,4\}[/latex] contains no multiple of [latex]7[/latex] and no [latex]0[/latex], the running product modulo [latex]7[/latex] can never become [latex]0[/latex] — it always stays within the [latex]6[/latex] nonzero residues [latex]\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}[/latex].

A minimal DFA for this language just needs one state per possible running-product value (tracking "current product mod 7 so far," starting at the state for [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]\text{prod}(\epsilon)=1[/latex]), with the state representing residue [latex]2[/latex] being the unique accepting state. Since multiplying by [latex]1,2,3,4[/latex] can move between any pair of these [latex]6[/latex] nonzero residues in different ways, all [latex]6[/latex] states are reachable and pairwise distinguishable (no two can be merged without changing the language).

Answer: 6

An application executes [latex]6.4 \times 10^8[/latex] number of instructions in 6.3 seconds. There are four types of instructions, the details of which are given in the table. The duration of a clock cycle in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Instruction type} & \text{Clock cycles required per instruction (CPI)} & \text{Number of instructions executed} \\
\hline
\text{Branch} & 2 & 2.25 \times 10^8 \\
\text{Load} & 5 & 1.20 \times 10^8 \\
\text{Store} & 4 & 1.65 \times 10^8 \\
\text{Arithmetic} & 3 & 1.30 \times 10^8 \\
\hline
\end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Total clock cycles [latex]=\sum(\text{CPI}\times\text{count})[/latex]:
[latex]=2(2.25\times10^8)+5(1.20\times10^8)+4(1.65\times10^8)+3(1.30\times10^8)[/latex]
[latex]=4.5\times10^8+6.0\times10^8+6.6\times10^8+3.9\times10^8=21.0\times10^8=2.1\times10^9[/latex] cycles.

Clock cycle duration [latex]=\dfrac{\text{total time}}{\text{total cycles}}=\dfrac{6.3\text{ s}}{2.1\times10^9}=3\times10^{-9}\text{ s}=3[/latex] ns.

Answer: 3

raw_source.text:
A quadratic polynomial [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta)[/latex] over complex numbers is said to be square invariant if [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = (x - \alpha^2)(x - \beta^2)[/latex]. Suppose from the set of all square invariant quadratic polynomials we choose one at random.

The probability that the roots of the chosen polynomial are equal is ______. (rounded off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
[latex](x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=(x-\alpha^2)(x-\beta^2)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex] means the root sets [latex]\{\alpha,\beta\}[/latex] and [latex]\{\alpha^2,\beta^2\}[/latex] must be identical (as unordered pairs). Two cases:

Case 1 (each root is individually fixed by squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\alpha,\ \beta^2=\beta[/latex], forcing each of [latex]\alpha,\beta[/latex] independently into [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] (the only solutions of [latex]z^2=z[/latex]). This gives root-pairs [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\}[/latex] ([latex]3[/latex] distinct polynomials, of which [latex]2[/latex]—[latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]—have a repeated root).

Case 2 (roots swap under squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\beta,\ \beta^2=\alpha[/latex], giving [latex]\alpha^4=\alpha\Rightarrow\alpha(\alpha^3-1)=0[/latex]. Besides the [latex]\alpha=0,1[/latex] solutions already counted, this adds the genuinely new pair of primitive cube roots of unity [latex]\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex] (distinct, non-repeated roots).

So there are [latex]4[/latex] distinct square-invariant polynomials total: [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\},\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex], of which exactly [latex]2[/latex] ([latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]) have equal (repeated) roots.

Probability [latex]=\dfrac24=0.5[/latex]

Answer: 0.5

raw_source.text:
The unit interval [latex](0, 1)[/latex] is divided at a point chosen uniformly distributed over [latex](0,1)[/latex] in [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex] into two disjoint subintervals.

The expected length of the subinterval that contains 0.4 is ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]U\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)[/latex] be the split point. If [latex]U>0.4[/latex], the sub-interval containing [latex]0.4[/latex] is [latex](0,U)[/latex], with length [latex]U[/latex]. If [latex]U<0.4[/latex], the sub-interval containing [latex]0.4[/latex] is [latex](U,1)[/latex], with length [latex]1-U[/latex].

[latex]E[\text{length}]=\displaystyle\int_0^{0.4}(1-u)\,du+\int_{0.4}^1u\,du[/latex]
[latex]=\Big[u-\tfrac{u^2}2\Big]_0^{0.4}+\Big[\tfrac{u^2}2\Big]_{0.4}^1=(0.4-0.08)+(0.5-0.08)=0.32+0.42=0.74[/latex]

Answer: 0.74

raw_source.text: If [latex]Pe^{x} = Q e^{-x} [/latex] for all real values of [latex]x [/latex], which one of the following statements is true?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]Pe^x=Qe^{-x}[/latex] for every real [latex]x[/latex]. Multiply both sides by [latex]e^x[/latex]: [latex]Pe^{2x}=Q[/latex]. Since [latex]e^{2x}[/latex] genuinely varies with [latex]x[/latex] (it's not constant), the only way the left side can stay equal to the constant [latex]Q[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] is if the coefficient [latex]P[/latex] itself is [latex]0[/latex]. With [latex]P=0[/latex], the equation becomes [latex]0=Q[/latex], so [latex]Q=0[/latex] too.

Checking directly at [latex]x=0[/latex]: [latex]P=Q[/latex]. Combined with the "must hold for all [latex]x[/latex]" requirement, [latex]P=Q=0[/latex] is the only consistent solution.

Answer: P = Q = 0

So on the folded cube: front = [latex]\triangle[/latex], top = [latex]\bullet[/latex], right = [latex]\blacktriangle[/latex], bottom = [latex]\circ[/latex], left = blank.

Checking the candidate cubes (each drawn showing the front face with [latex]\triangle[/latex] and one other visible face): the cube where the dot appears on the top face alongside the triangle on the front — exactly matching the derived front/top relationship — is option A. The other options place a different symbol (or the same symbol in the wrong position/face) adjacent to the front triangle, which contradicts the adjacency established directly from the net.

raw_source.text: Let [latex]p_1 [/latex] and [latex]p_2 [/latex] denote two arbitrary prime numbers. Which one of the following statements is correct for all values of [latex]p_1 [/latex] and [latex]p_2 [/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Test each claim against simple examples with actual primes:

- "[latex]p_1+p_2[/latex] is not prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=2,p_2=3\Rightarrow5[/latex] (prime!). False in general.
- "[latex]p_1p_2[/latex] is not prime": since both [latex]p_1[/latex] and [latex]p_2[/latex] are themselves prime (each [latex]\ge2[/latex]), their product always has at least two prime factors when counted with multiplicity — even if [latex]p_1=p_2[/latex], the product [latex]p_1^2[/latex] is still composite (divisible by [latex]p_1[/latex], which is neither [latex]1[/latex] nor the product itself). So the product can never be prime. Always true.
- "[latex]p_1+p_2+1[/latex] is prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=2,p_2=3\Rightarrow6[/latex] (not prime). False in general.
- "[latex]p_1p_2+1[/latex] is prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=3,p_2=5\Rightarrow16[/latex] (not prime). False in general.

Answer: p1p2 is not a prime number.

In the given figure, PQRS is a square of side 2 cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of the rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square.

What is the area (in [latex]cm^{2} [/latex]) of the rectangle PLMN?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
raw_source.solution:
Set up coordinates matching the figure: [latex]P=(0,2),\ Q=(0,0),\ R=(2,0),\ S=(2,2)[/latex] (square side [latex]2[/latex]). Let [latex]L=(\ell,0)[/latex] be the point on [latex]QR[/latex] where the rectangle's corner lands.

Side [latex]PL[/latex] has direction vector [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex] and length [latex]\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. Since [latex]PLMN[/latex] is a rectangle, side [latex]LM[/latex] is perpendicular to [latex]PL[/latex], along direction [latex](2,\ell)/\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. If the rectangle's width (side [latex]LM[/latex]) is [latex]h[/latex], then:
[latex]N=P+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}},\qquad M=L+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex]

Since side [latex]MN[/latex] must pass through [latex]S=(2,2)[/latex], substituting [latex]S[/latex] into the line through [latex]M,N[/latex] (which runs parallel to [latex]PL[/latex], direction [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex]) and solving the resulting two equations simultaneously gives:
[latex]h=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex]

So the rectangle's area is:
[latex]\text{Area}=PL\times LM=\sqrt{\ell^2+4}\times\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}=4[/latex]

Remarkably, this is independent of [latex]\ell[/latex] — the area comes out to exactly [latex]4[/latex] regardless of where [latex]L[/latex] sits on [latex]QR[/latex], as long as [latex]MN[/latex] passes through [latex]S[/latex].

Answer: 4

raw_source.text: An urn contains one red ball and one blue ball. At each step, a ball is picked uniformly at random from the urn, and this ball together with another ball of the same color is put back in the urn. The probability that there are equal number of red and blue balls after two steps is
raw_source.solution:
Let the urn start with [latex]1[/latex] red and [latex]1[/latex] blue ball.

Step 1: A ball is picked uniformly (prob [latex]1/2[/latex] each). If red is picked, the urn becomes [latex](2R,1B)[/latex]; if blue is picked, the urn becomes [latex](1R,2B)[/latex]. Each case has probability [latex]1/2[/latex].

Step 2: We want the urn to end up with equal red and blue balls, i.e. [latex](2R,2B)[/latex] (since after 2 steps there are always [latex]4[/latex] balls total).
- From [latex](2R,1B)[/latex]: we need to pick the blue ball, probability [latex]=1/3[/latex].
- From [latex](1R,2B)[/latex]: we need to pick the red ball, probability [latex]=1/3[/latex].

So required probability [latex]=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{3}[/latex].

Answer: 1/3

raw_source.text: Consider [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] matrices with their elements from [latex]\{\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\}[/latex]. The number of such matrices with even number of [latex]\mathbf{1}[/latex] s in every row and every column is

Freely choose the top-left [latex]3\times3[/latex] sub-block: this can be filled in any of [latex]2^{9}=512[/latex] ways.

Once this [latex]3\times3[/latex] block is fixed, the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th column (for the first [latex]3[/latex] rows) are forced so that each of those rows has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s, and similarly the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th row (for the first [latex]3[/latex] columns) are forced by the column parity condition. The single remaining corner entry (row [latex]4[/latex], column [latex]4[/latex]) is then also forced, and it is easy to check the row-[latex]4[/latex] parity and column-[latex]4[/latex] parity conditions become consistent automatically.

So the count of valid matrices [latex]=2^{(4-1)^2}=2^9=512[/latex].

Answer: 512

raw_source.text:
Consider a processor [latex]\text{P}[/latex] whose instruction set architecture is the load-store architecture. The instruction format is such that the first operand of any instruction is the destination operand.

Which one of the following sequences of instructions corresponds to the high-level language statement [latex]{Z}={X}+{Y}[/latex] ?
Note: X, Y, and Z are memory operands. R[latex]0[/latex], R[latex]1[/latex], and R[latex]2[/latex] are registers.
raw_source.solution:
In a load-store (register-register) architecture, arithmetic instructions can only operate on registers, never directly on memory. So to compute [latex]Z=X+Y[/latex] where [latex]X,Y,Z[/latex] are memory locations, we must:

1. LOAD both memory operands into registers: [latex]\text{LOAD } R0, X[/latex] and [latex]\text{LOAD } R1, Y[/latex].
2. Perform the addition on registers: [latex]\text{ADD } R2, R0, R1[/latex] (destination is first operand, per the given convention).
3. STORE the result back to memory: [latex]\text{STORE } Z, R2[/latex].

Any option that uses a memory operand directly inside an ADD instruction (e.g. [latex]\text{ADD } Z, X, Y[/latex] or [latex]\text{ADD } Z, R0, Y[/latex]) is invalid for a load-store machine, since ADD can only take register operands.

Answer: LOAD R0,X; LOAD R1,Y; ADD R2,R0,R1; STORE Z,R2

raw_source.text: Which one of the following dependencies among the register operands of different instructions can cause a data hazard in a pipelined processor?
raw_source.solution:
A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on the result of a nearby instruction that has not yet completed in the pipeline.

- Read-after-Write (RAW): a later instruction tries to read a register before an earlier instruction has written its new value — this is a true/flow dependency, and causes a genuine data hazard in a pipeline.
- Write-after-Read (WAR) and Write-after-Write (WAW) are anti-/output-dependencies; they cause hazards only in pipelines that allow out-of-order completion, not in a simple in-order pipeline.
- Read-after-Read is not a dependency at all — reads never conflict with each other.

Answer: Read-after-write

raw_source.text:
Consider the following recurrence relations:
For all [latex]n>1[/latex],

[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}(n)=4 T_{1}\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+T_{2}(n) \\ T_{2}(n)=5 T_{2}\left(\frac{n}{4}\right)+\Theta\left(\log _{2} n\right) \end{array} [/latex]

Assume that for all [latex]n \leq 1, T_{1}(n)=1[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}(n)=1[/latex].
Which one of the following options is correct?
raw_source.solution:
First solve [latex]T_2(n)=5T_2(n/4)+\Theta(\log_2 n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=5,\,b=4[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_4 5}[/latex]. Since [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^{\log_4 5}[/latex] (as [latex]\log_4 5\approx1.16>0[/latex]), by the Master theorem (Case 1):
[latex]T_2(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_4 5}\right)[/latex].

Now solve [latex]T_1(n)=4T_1(n/2)+T_2(n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=4,\,b=2[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 4}=n^2[/latex]. The extra term [latex]f(n)=T_2(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_4 5})=\Theta(n^{1.16\ldots})[/latex], which is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^2[/latex] (since [latex]n^2/n^{1.16}=n^{0.84}\to\infty[/latex]).
By Master theorem Case 1: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

raw_source.text: With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which one of the following statements is true?
raw_source.solution:
Checking each statement about a TCP connection:

- TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), not a two-way handshake — false.
- Either side (client or server) is free to initiate connection termination first; the server is not required to wait for the client — false.
- TCP is a full-duplex protocol — data can flow in both directions simultaneously — so "half-duplex" is false.
- TCP supports simultaneous close: both client and server can send a FIN at (roughly) the same time, and each independently acknowledges the other's FIN. This is a valid connection-termination scenario in TCP's state machine.

Answer: The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time
