raw_source.text:
Let [latex]\gamma_{1}, \gamma_{2}, \gamma_{3}[/latex] be the eigenvalues of the matrix [latex]\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos t & \sin t \\ 0 & -\sin t & \cos t\end{array}\right][/latex],

where [latex]t \in[-\pi, \pi][/latex] is in radians.

Which one of the following options lists all the possible values of [latex]t[/latex] satisfying [latex]\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3}=1+\sqrt{2}[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
This matrix is block-diagonal: eigenvalue [latex]\gamma_1=1[/latex] (from the fixed top-left [latex]1[/latex]), and the remaining [latex]2\times2[/latex] rotation block [latex]\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}[/latex] has eigenvalues [latex]\gamma_2,\gamma_3=\cos t\pm i\sin t=e^{\pm it}[/latex] (a complex-conjugate pair).

Sum of all three eigenvalues: [latex]\gamma_1+\gamma_2+\gamma_3=1+e^{it}+e^{-it}=1+2\cos t[/latex] (by Euler's formula, [latex]e^{it}+e^{-it}=2\cos t[/latex]).

Setting this equal to [latex]1+\sqrt2[/latex]:
[latex]1+2\cos t=1+\sqrt2\ \Rightarrow\ \cos t=\dfrac{\sqrt2}2=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}[/latex]

Within [latex]t\in[-\pi,\pi][/latex], the solutions are [latex]t=\dfrac\pi4[/latex] and [latex]t=-\dfrac\pi4[/latex] (cosine is even, so both give the same value).

Answer: [latex]{\dfrac{\pi}{4} , -\dfrac{\pi}{4}}[/latex]

Consider that [latex]20[/latex] stories of Author [latex]\text{X}[/latex] and [latex]10[/latex] stories of Author [latex]\text{Y}[/latex] were kept together without mentioning the names of the authors. [latex]\text{A}[/latex] classifier was then asked to predict the author [latex]\text{( X or Y )}[/latex] of each of these stories. Let, out of [latex]\text{X}[/latex] 's stories, [latex]6[/latex] were classified as that of [latex]\text{Y}[/latex]. On the other hand, out of [latex]\text{Y}[/latex]'s stories, [latex]2[/latex] were classified as that of [latex]\text{X}[/latex].

Considering [latex]\text{X}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Y}[/latex] as two classes, which of the following statements is/are true?
raw_source.solution:
Building the confusion matrix: out of [latex]20[/latex] [latex]X[/latex]-stories, [latex]6[/latex] were misclassified as [latex]Y[/latex], so [latex]14[/latex] correctly classified as [latex]X[/latex]. Out of [latex]10[/latex] [latex]Y[/latex]-stories, [latex]2[/latex] were misclassified as [latex]X[/latex], so [latex]8[/latex] correctly classified as [latex]Y[/latex].

Accuracy [latex]=\dfrac{14+8}{20+10}=\dfrac{22}{30}=\dfrac{11}{15}[/latex]. True (matches option); the "14/15" claim is false.

Precision(X) [latex]=\dfrac{14}{14+2}=\dfrac{14}{16}=0.875[/latex] (denominator: all predicted-as-X, i.e. [latex]14[/latex] correct [latex]+2[/latex] false positives from [latex]Y[/latex]).

Precision(Y) [latex]=\dfrac{8}{8+6}=\dfrac{8}{14}\approx0.571[/latex] (denominator: all predicted-as-Y).

Since [latex]0.875>0.571[/latex], Precision(X) > Precision(Y) is true.

Recall(X) [latex]=\dfrac{14}{20}=0.7[/latex]; Recall(Y) [latex]=\dfrac{8}{10}=0.8[/latex]. Since [latex]0.7<0.8[/latex], "Recall(X) higher than Recall(Y)" is false.

Answer: Accuracy is 11/15; and Precision(X) > Precision(Y).

Recall of Class [latex]\text{X}[/latex] is higher than the Recall of Class [latex]\text{Y}[/latex].

option_texts: Precision of Class [latex]\text{X}[/latex] is higher than the Precision of Class [latex]\text{Y}[/latex].

Let [latex]P(x)[/latex] be a predicate.
Which of the following statements is/are NOT valid in first-order logic?
raw_source.solution:
Assuming a non-empty domain, check each statement's validity:

- [latex]\forall xP(x)\Rightarrow\exists xP(x)[/latex]: if every element satisfies [latex]P[/latex], then certainly some element does (the domain is non-empty). Valid.
- [latex]\exists xP(x)\Rightarrow\forall xP(x)[/latex]: just because one element satisfies [latex]P[/latex] doesn't mean every element does. Not valid in general.
- [latex]\exists xP(x)\Leftrightarrow\forall xP(x)[/latex]: combines both directions of the above; still fails for the same reason. Not valid.
- [latex]\forall xP(x)\Rightarrow\exists x\neg P(x)[/latex]: this claims that if everything satisfies [latex]P[/latex], then something doesn't — a direct contradiction. Not valid.

Answer: The last three statements are NOT valid in FOL.

raw_source.text:
Consider the problem of sorting the given array in ascending order:

[latex] P=[1,2,3,5,4] [/latex]

Consider two sorting algorithms Bubble Sort [latex]\text{(BS)}[/latex] and Insertion Sort [latex]\text{(IS)}[/latex].
Let [latex]\text{N1}[/latex] be the total number of comparisons done by [latex]\text{BS}[/latex] on the elements of [latex]\text{P}[/latex] and [latex]\text{N2}[/latex] be the total number of comparisons done by [latex]\text{IS}[/latex] on the elements of [latex]\text{P}[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]P=[1,2,3,5,4][/latex], needing just one adjacent swap (5,4) to become sorted.

Bubble Sort (standard version, checking all adjacent pairs every pass until a pass makes no swaps): Pass 1 makes [latex]4[/latex] comparisons ([latex](1,2),(2,3),(3,5),(5,4)[/latex], with exactly one swap on the last pair) sorting the array; subsequent passes (2, 3, 4) still each scan their shrinking sublist ([latex]3,2,1[/latex] comparisons respectively) to confirm no more swaps are needed. Total comparisons [latex]N1=4+3+2+1=10[/latex], with just [latex]1[/latex] swap.

Insertion Sort: shifting element [latex]2,3,5[/latex] each needs only [latex]1[/latex] comparison against its predecessor (no shift needed, since each is already larger); inserting [latex]4[/latex] needs [latex]2[/latex] comparisons (against [latex]5[/latex], which shifts right, then against [latex]3[/latex], where it stops) and exactly [latex]1[/latex] shift. Total comparisons [latex]N2=1+1+1+2=5[/latex], with just [latex]1[/latex] shift/swap.

So [latex]N1=10>N2=5[/latex] (N1>N2 is true); Insertion Sort does perform only one swap (true); and since the array is nearly sorted already (only one inversion), both algorithms still perform several comparisons beyond the bare minimum needed to detect/fix that single inversion — so both make at least one "unnecessary" comparison/swap is also true.

Answer: N1>N2; IS performs only one swap; and both BS and IS make at least one unnecessary comparison/swap.

Consider the given Python program. 
  def outer():
  	x = []
  	def inner(val):
  		x.append(val)
  		return x
  	return inner
  f1 = outer()
  f2 = outer()
  print(f1(10)) # Line P
  print(f1(20)) # Line Q
  print(f2(30)) # Line R
  print(f1(40)) # Line S
Which of the following options is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
Python's closures capture variables by reference to the enclosing scope, and crucially, [latex]x=[][/latex] here is a statement executed fresh, every time [latex]\text{outer()}[/latex] is called (unlike a mutable default argument, which is created only once at definition time). So [latex]f1=\text{outer()}[/latex] and [latex]f2=\text{outer()}[/latex] each get their own separate, independent list — they do not share the same [latex]x[/latex].

- Line P: [latex]f1(10)[/latex] appends to [latex]f1[/latex]'s own list: prints [latex][10][/latex].
- Line Q: [latex]f1(20)[/latex] appends to the same list [latex]f1[/latex] has been using: prints [10, 20].
- Line R: [latex]f2(30)[/latex] appends to [latex]f2[/latex]'s separate list (still empty until now): prints [latex][30][/latex] — not [latex][10,20,30][/latex], since [latex]f2[/latex]'s list is independent of [latex]f1[/latex]'s.
- Line S: [latex]f1(40)[/latex] appends again to [latex]f1[/latex]'s (now [latex][10,20][/latex]) list: prints [10, 20, 40].

Answer: Output of Line Q is [10,20]; and output of Line S is [10,20,40].

Consider a table Employee(EmpID, TeamID), where the column EmpID (ID of an employee) is the primary key. The column TeamID denotes the team ID of the team of which the employee is a member. TeamID is a NOT NULL column.

We want to display the size of the team (denoted as TeamSize) in which each employee is a member by using SQL. As an example, the desired output for the given Employee table is also shown in tabular form.

Which of the following is/are correct?

[latex] \textbf{Employee} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{EmpID} & \text{TeamID} \\ \hline 1 & 8 \\ \hline 2 & 8 \\ \hline 3 & 8 \\ \hline 4 & 7 \\ \hline 5 & 7 \\ \hline 6 & 9 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \textbf{Output} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{EmpID} & \text{TeamSize} \\ \hline 1 & 3 \\ \hline 2 & 3 \\ \hline 3 & 3 \\ \hline 4 & 2 \\ \hline 5 & 2 \\ \hline 6 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
We need a subquery that computes team sizes (grouped by [latex]\text{TeamID}[/latex]) and joins that back to every employee row via matching [latex]\text{TeamID}[/latex].

Correct query: [latex]\text{SELECT TeamID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID}[/latex] (as subquery [latex]B[/latex]) correctly computes one row per team with its size, retaining the [latex]\text{TeamID}[/latex] column needed for the join; joining this to [latex]E[/latex] on [latex]\text{E.TeamID = B.TeamID}[/latex] correctly attaches each employee to their team's size.

The other options fail: grouping/joining by [latex]\text{EmpID}[/latex] instead of [latex]\text{TeamID}[/latex] (options where the self-join or grouping matches each employee only to themselves) always gives a team size of [latex]1[/latex] for everyone, which is wrong; and one option's subquery omits [latex]\text{TeamID}[/latex] from its own [latex]\text{SELECT}[/latex] list while still trying to join on it, which is invalid SQL.

Answer: The query using "(SELECT TeamID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID)" as a subquery, joined on E.TeamID = B.TeamID, is correct.

Let [latex]M=\left(I_{n}-\frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1 1}^{T}\right)[/latex] be a matrix, where [latex]\mathbf{1}=(1,1,1, \ldots, 1)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}[/latex] and [latex]I_{n}[/latex] is the identity matrix of order [latex]n[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]M=I_n-\dfrac1n\mathbf{11}^T[/latex] is the classical centering matrix.

[latex]M^T=M[/latex]: [latex]I_n[/latex] is symmetric, and [latex]\mathbf{11}^T[/latex] (an outer product of a vector with itself) is always symmetric too, so their difference [latex]M[/latex] is symmetric. True.

[latex]M^2=I_n[/latex]?: expanding, [latex]M^2=I_n-\dfrac2n\mathbf{11}^T+\dfrac1{n^2}\mathbf{11}^T\mathbf{11}^T[/latex]. Since [latex]\mathbf1^T\mathbf1=n[/latex], [latex]\mathbf{11}^T\mathbf{11}^T=n\cdot\mathbf{11}^T[/latex], so [latex]M^2=I_n-\dfrac2n\mathbf{11}^T+\dfrac1n\mathbf{11}^T=I_n-\dfrac1n\mathbf{11}^T=M[/latex] (not [latex]I_n[/latex]). False (M is idempotent, [latex]M^2=M[/latex], not [latex]I_n[/latex]).

Trace(M)?: [latex]\text{Trace}(I_n)=n[/latex], [latex]\text{Trace}(\mathbf{11}^T)=n[/latex] (every diagonal entry of [latex]\mathbf{11}^T[/latex] is [latex]1[/latex]), so [latex]\text{Trace}(M)=n-\dfrac1n\cdot n=n-1[/latex], not [latex]n[/latex]. False.

M is a projection matrix: since [latex]M[/latex] is symmetric and idempotent ([latex]M^2=M[/latex], shown above), it satisfies exactly the definition of an (orthogonal) projection matrix — here, projecting onto the mean-centered subspace. True.

Answer: Mᵀ=M; and M is a projection matrix.

Let [latex]X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots, X_{n}[/latex] be [latex]n[/latex] independent random variables. Each of the random variables follows [latex]\operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu=0, \sigma^{2}=1\right)[/latex] distribution. Define [latex]\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{iid}\sim N(0,1)[/latex], [latex]\bar X=\frac1n\sum X_i[/latex].

[latex]\sum X_i^2\sim\chi^2_n[/latex]: this is the textbook definition of a Chi-square distribution — the sum of [latex]n[/latex] independent squared standard normals. True.

[latex]\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}[/latex]: this is the classical sampling-distribution result (Cochran's theorem) for the sum-of-squared-deviations statistic, losing one degree of freedom to estimating the mean. True.

[latex]X_1^2+X_n^2\sim\text{Exponential(mean }2\text{)}[/latex]: the sum of two independent squared standard normals is [latex]\chi^2_2[/latex], and [latex]\chi^2_2[/latex] is a well-known special case that is exactly identical to an Exponential distribution with mean [latex]2[/latex] (rate [latex]1/2[/latex]). True.

[latex](\sqrt n\bar X)^2\sim\chi^2_2[/latex]?: since [latex]\bar X\sim N(0,1/n)[/latex], scaling gives [latex]\sqrt n\bar X\sim N(0,1)[/latex], so [latex](\sqrt n\bar X)^2\sim\chi^2_1[/latex] (just [latex]1[/latex] degree of freedom, from a single squared standard normal), not [latex]2[/latex]. False.

Answer: The first three statements are TRUE; the last (2 degrees of freedom) is FALSE.

[latex](\sqrt{n} \bar{X})^{2}[/latex] follows Chi-square distribution with [latex]2[/latex] degrees of freedom.

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]X[/latex] be a discrete valued random variable with cumulative distribution function [latex]F(x)[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
For a discrete random variable's CDF [latex]F(x)=P(X\le x)[/latex]:

- "[latex]F(x)[/latex] is always positive": false — [latex]F(x)\to0[/latex] as [latex]x\to-\infty[/latex] (or is exactly [latex]0[/latex] below the smallest possible value), so it's not always strictly positive.
- "[latex]F(x)[/latex] is non-decreasing": true — this is a fundamental property of every CDF.
- "[latex]F(x)[/latex] has jump discontinuities": true, specifically for discrete random variables — probability mass is concentrated at discrete points, causing [latex]F[/latex] to jump up at each possible value of [latex]X[/latex] rather than rising smoothly.
- "[latex]F(x)[/latex] is left-continuous": false — by the standard convention [latex]F(x)=P(X\le x)[/latex], CDFs are always right-continuous, not left-continuous.

Answer: F(x) is non-decreasing; and F(x) has jump discontinuities.

Consider that Linear Ridge Regression is being used to learn a prediction function [latex]y_{\text {pred }}=w^{T} x[/latex], where [latex]w, x \in \mathbb{R}^{2}[/latex] and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is used to measure the prediction error. A weight of [latex]0.20[/latex] is associated with the regularizer.

At an intermediate step of the training process, assume that the parameter [latex]w= [-3.00,4.00]^{T}[/latex]. In the next step, for the input [latex]x=[1.00,2.00]^{T}[/latex], the predicted value of [latex]y[/latex] is noted. Let the relation between [latex]x=\left[x_{1}, x_{2}\right]^{T}[/latex] and the true value of [latex]y[/latex] be [latex]y_{\text {true }}=x_{1}+x_{2}[/latex].

The value of the overall regularized loss function for this instance is ________. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Predicted value: [latex]y_{\text{pred}}=w^Tx=(-3.00)(1.00)+(4.00)(2.00)=-3+8=5[/latex]
True value: [latex]y_{\text{true}}=x_1+x_2=1.00+2.00=3[/latex]

MAE for this single instance: [latex]|y_{\text{pred}}-y_{\text{true}}|=|5-3|=2[/latex]

Regularizer term (Ridge uses squared [latex]L_2[/latex] norm of weights, scaled by the given weight [latex]0.20[/latex]):
[latex]0.20\times\|w\|^2=0.20\times\big((-3.00)^2+(4.00)^2\big)=0.20\times(9+16)=0.20\times25=5[/latex]

Total regularized loss [latex]=\text{MAE}+\text{Regularizer}=2+5=7.00[/latex]

Answer: 7.00

Consider a fully-connected feed-forward multi-layer perceptron. It has [latex]30[/latex] neurons in the input layer, followed by two hidden layers and an output layer. The first hidden layer has [latex]4[/latex] neurons and the second hidden layer has [latex]3[/latex] neurons. The output layer has only one neuron. Assume that no bias parameters are used.

The number of learnable parameters in the multi-layer perceptron is ________. (Answer in integer)

With no bias parameters, each layer's parameter count is simply (neurons in previous layer) [latex]\times[/latex] (neurons in current layer):

Input ([latex]30[/latex]) [latex]\to[/latex] Hidden 1 ([latex]4[/latex]): [latex]30\times4=120[/latex]
Hidden 1 ([latex]4[/latex]) [latex]\to[/latex] Hidden 2 ([latex]3[/latex]): [latex]4\times3=12[/latex]
Hidden 2 ([latex]3[/latex]) [latex]\to[/latex] Output ([latex]1[/latex]): [latex]3\times1=3[/latex]

Total [latex]=120+12+3=135[/latex]

Answer: 135

A clinic specializes in testing for a disease [latex]\text{D}[/latex]. The result of the test can be either positive or negative.

A study revealed that if a person suffers from the disease [latex]\text{D}[/latex], the test result in that clinic comes out positive [latex]80 \%[/latex] of the time, and negative [latex]20 \%[/latex] of the time. If a person is not suffering from the disease [latex]\text{D}[/latex], the test comes out positive [latex]10 \%[/latex] of the time and negative [latex]90 \%[/latex] of the time. It is also known that among the general population, the disease [latex]\text{D}[/latex] occurs in [latex]30 \%[/latex] of the individuals.

If a person tests positive for [latex]\text{D}[/latex] in that clinic, the probability that he/she actually suffers from the disease [latex]\text{D}[/latex] is ________. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
By Bayes' theorem: [latex]P(D\mid\text{pos})=\dfrac{P(\text{pos}\mid D)P(D)}{P(\text{pos})}[/latex]

[latex]P(\text{pos})=P(\text{pos}\mid D)P(D)+P(\text{pos}\mid\neg D)P(\neg D)=0.8(0.3)+0.1(0.7)=0.24+0.07=0.31[/latex]

[latex]P(D\mid\text{pos})=\dfrac{0.24}{0.31}\approx0.774[/latex]

Answer: 0.77

Let there be two relations [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] as shown. [latex]X[/latex] has three columns [latex]P, Q[/latex] and [latex]R . Y[/latex] has two columns [latex]P[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex].

[latex] \textbf{X} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline P & Q & R \\ \hline P1 & Q1 & R1 \\ \hline P2 & Q2 & R2 \\ \hline P3 & Q3 & R2 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \textbf{Y} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline P & S \\ \hline P1 & 10 \\ \hline P1 & 15 \\ \hline P2 & 20 \\ \hline P3 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Consider that the following tuple relational calculus expression is evaluated.

[latex] \{t \mid t \in X \wedge \exists z \in X(t[P]=z[P]) \wedge \exists m \in Y(m[P]=t[P] \wedge m[S]>1)\} [/latex]

The number of tuples that will be returned is ________. (Answer in integer )
raw_source.solution:
Simplify the expression first: [latex]\exists z\in X(t[P]=z[P])[/latex] is trivially always true for any [latex]t\in X[/latex] (just take [latex]z=t[/latex] itself) — it adds no real restriction. So the query reduces to: [latex]\{t\mid t\in X\wedge\exists m\in Y(m[P]=t[P]\wedge m[S]>1)\}[/latex].

[latex]X=\{(P1,Q1,R1),(P2,Q2,R2),(P3,Q3,R2)\}[/latex], [latex]Y=\{(P1,10),(P1,15),(P2,20),(P3,1)\}[/latex].

Checking each [latex]t\in X[/latex] for a matching [latex]m\in Y[/latex] with [latex]m[S]>1[/latex]:
- [latex]t=(P1,Q1,R1)[/latex]: [latex]Y[/latex] has [latex]P1[/latex] rows with [latex]S=10,15[/latex] (both [latex]>1[/latex]) — match, included.
- [latex]t=(P2,Q2,R2)[/latex]: [latex]Y[/latex] has [latex]P2[/latex] row with [latex]S=20>1[/latex] — match, included.
- [latex]t=(P3,Q3,R2)[/latex]: [latex]Y[/latex]'s only [latex]P3[/latex] row has [latex]S=1[/latex], which is not [latex]>1[/latex] — no match, excluded.

Answer: 2

Consider an [latex]\text{ER}[/latex] model with the entities [latex]\text{E1}[/latex] ( [latex]{A}_{11}, {~A}_{12}, {~A}_{13}[/latex] ) and [latex]\text{E2}[/latex] ( [latex]{A}_{21}, {~A}_{22}, {~A}_{23}[/latex] ), where, [latex]A_{11}, A_{12}, A_{13}[/latex] are the attributes of [latex]\text{E1}[/latex], and [latex]A_{21}, A_{22}, A_{23}[/latex] are the attributes of [latex]\text{E2}[/latex]. Let [latex]A_{22}[/latex] be a multi-valued attribute. [latex]A_{11}[/latex] and [latex]A_{21}[/latex] are the primary keys of [latex]\text{E1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{E2}[/latex], respectively.

Let [latex]\text{R12}[/latex] be a many-to-many relationship between [latex]\text{E1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{E2}[/latex]. Participation of both [latex]\text{E1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{E2}[/latex] in [latex]\text{R12}[/latex] is total.

The minimum number of relations required to convert the [latex]\text{ER}[/latex] model into relational model (assuming there is no other functional dependency) where each relation is in third normal form ([latex]3 \text{NF}[/latex]) is ________. (Answer in integer )
raw_source.solution:
Converting each ER component to relations:

- E1 [latex](A_{11},A_{12},A_{13})[/latex]: a single relation ([latex]A_{11}[/latex] as key). [latex]1[/latex] relation.
- E2: since [latex]A_{22}[/latex] is multi-valued, it cannot sit in the main E2 relation (would violate 1NF); it needs its own separate relation storing [latex](A_{21},A_{22})[/latex] pairs. So E2 splits into: the main relation [latex](A_{21},A_{23})[/latex], plus a separate relation [latex](A_{21},A_{22})[/latex] for the multi-valued attribute. [latex]2[/latex] relations.
- R12 (many-to-many relationship): regardless of participation constraints, a many-to-many relationship always requires its own separate relation (it can never be merged/embedded into either entity's table, since either side could match multiple partners). [latex]1[/latex] relation.

Total minimum relations [latex]=1+2+1=4[/latex]

Answer: 4

raw_source.text:
For a given data set [latex]\left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right\}[/latex], where [latex]n=100[/latex], it is known that

[latex] \frac{1}{2000} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}=99 [/latex]

Let us denote [latex]\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}[/latex]

The value of [latex]\frac{1}{99} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}[/latex] is ________. (Answer in integer )
raw_source.solution:
Expand the double sum using [latex]x_i-x_j=(x_i-\bar x)-(x_j-\bar x)[/latex]:
[latex]\sum_i\sum_j(x_i-x_j)^2=n\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2-2\Big(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\Big)\Big(\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)\Big)+n\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2[/latex]

Since [latex]\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0[/latex] always (by definition of the mean), the cross term vanishes, giving:
[latex]\sum_i\sum_j(x_i-x_j)^2=2n\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2[/latex]

So [latex]\dfrac1{2000}\times2n\times SS=99[/latex], where [latex]SS=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2[/latex]: [latex]2(100)\,SS=198000\Rightarrow SS=\dfrac{198000}{200}=990[/latex]

[latex]\dfrac1{99}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\dfrac{990}{99}=10[/latex]

Answer: 10

Let [latex]X[/latex] be a random variable that follows [latex]Uniform (-1,1)[/latex] distribution. The conditional distribution of the random variable [latex]Y[/latex] given [latex]X=x[/latex] is the Uniform( [latex]x^{2}-0.1, x^{2}+0.1[/latex] ) distribution.

The value of [latex]correlation (X, Y)[/latex] is ________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]E[Y\mid X=x][/latex] is the midpoint of [latex]\text{Uniform}(x^2-0.1,x^2+0.1)[/latex], which is exactly [latex]x^2[/latex]. So [latex]E[Y\mid X]=X^2[/latex].

[latex]E[X]=0[/latex] (symmetric uniform on [latex](-1,1)[/latex]).

[latex]\text{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]=E\big[X\cdot E[Y\mid X]\big]-0=E[X\cdot X^2]=E[X^3][/latex]

Since [latex]X[/latex] is symmetric about [latex]0[/latex], [latex]E[X^3]=0[/latex] (odd function integrated over a symmetric range).

So [latex]\text{Cov}(X,Y)=0[/latex], and hence [latex]\text{Correlation}(X,Y)=\dfrac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}=0[/latex] (regardless of the exact value of [latex]\sigma_Y[/latex], since the numerator is zero).

Answer: 0

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]A_{5 \times 5}[/latex] be a matrix such that each of its elements follows [latex]\text{Bernoulli}(p = 0.50)[/latex] distribution independently.

The probability that the row-sum of the second row and the column-sum of the third column are both equal to 3 is ________ . (Rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Row [latex]2[/latex] and column [latex]3[/latex] share exactly one common cell (row [latex]2[/latex], column [latex]3[/latex]), so these two sums aren't fully independent — condition on that shared cell's value [latex]c\in\{0,1\}[/latex] (each with probability [latex]0.5[/latex]).

Given [latex]c[/latex], the other [latex]4[/latex] cells of row [latex]2[/latex] must sum to [latex]3-c[/latex], and (independently) the other [latex]4[/latex] cells of column [latex]3[/latex] must also sum to [latex]3-c[/latex]:

[latex]P(\text{both}\mid c)=\Big[\binom4{3-c}(0.5)^4\Big]^2[/latex]

For [latex]c=0[/latex] (need remaining [latex]4[/latex] to sum to [latex]3[/latex]): [latex]\binom43=4[/latex], giving [latex][4/16]^2=0.0625[/latex]
For [latex]c=1[/latex] (need remaining [latex]4[/latex] to sum to [latex]2[/latex]): [latex]\binom42=6[/latex], giving [latex][6/16]^2=0.140625[/latex]

Total [latex]=0.5(0.0625)+0.5(0.140625)=0.03125+0.0703125\approx0.1016[/latex]

Answer: 0.10

Let [latex]A = \left(I_n - \frac{1}{n} 11^T\right)[/latex] be a matrix, where [latex]1 = (1,1,1,\ldots,1)^T \in \mathbb{R}^n[/latex] and [latex]I_n[/latex] is the identity matrix of order [latex]n[/latex].

The value of [latex]\max_{x^T x = 1} x^T A x[/latex], where [latex]S = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid x^T x = 1\}[/latex], is ________ . (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A=I_n-\dfrac1n\mathbf{11}^T[/latex] is the centering matrix, symmetric and idempotent (as shown in a related question). For any symmetric matrix, [latex]\max_{x^Tx=1}x^TAx[/latex] equals its largest eigenvalue.

[latex]A[/latex]'s eigenvalues: [latex]A\mathbf1=\mathbf1-\dfrac1n\mathbf1(n)=\mathbf1-\mathbf1=0[/latex], so [latex]0[/latex] is an eigenvalue (eigenvector [latex]\mathbf1[/latex]). For any vector [latex]v[/latex] orthogonal to [latex]\mathbf1[/latex] (i.e. [latex]\mathbf1^Tv=0[/latex]), [latex]Av=v-\dfrac1n\mathbf1(0)=v[/latex], so [latex]1[/latex] is an eigenvalue with multiplicity [latex]n-1[/latex].

Largest eigenvalue [latex]=1[/latex]

Answer: 1

Consider two distinct positive real numbers [latex]m, n[/latex], with [latex]m>n[/latex].
Let [latex]x=n^{\log _{10}(m)}[/latex] and [latex]y=m^{\log _{10}(n)}[/latex]. The relation between [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is ________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]x=n^{\log_{10}m}[/latex], [latex]y=m^{\log_{10}n}[/latex]. Take [latex]\log_{10}[/latex] of both:

[latex]\log_{10}x=\log_{10}m\cdot\log_{10}n[/latex] (using [latex]\log(n^k)=k\log n[/latex])
[latex]\log_{10}y=\log_{10}n\cdot\log_{10}m[/latex]

Both equal the same product [latex]\log_{10}m\cdot\log_{10}n[/latex], so [latex]\log_{10}x=\log_{10}y[/latex], which means [latex]x=y[/latex] exactly (regardless of the specific values of [latex]m,n[/latex]).

Answer: x=y

raw_source.text:
'If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money to sponsor his next movie.'

Based only on the above sentence, which one of the following statements is true?
raw_source.solution:
"If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money..." is a classic counterfactual conditional (past-perfect subjunctive: "had been," "would have made"). This grammatical construction specifically signals that the actual, real-world situation is the opposite of the stated hypothesis — i.e. the movie was not, in fact, a commercial success.

The sentence tells us nothing certain about what the actor will do next, nor does it claim the actor actually made enough money (quite the opposite) — only that this particular hypothetical path to funding didn't materialize because its premise was false.

Answer: His latest movie was not commercially successful.

raw_source.text:
Five integers are picked from [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]20[/latex], with possible repetitions, such that their mean is [latex]12[/latex], median is [latex]18[/latex], and they have a single mode of [latex]20[/latex].
Ignoring permutations, the number of ways to pick these five integers is ________
raw_source.solution:
Five integers (from [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]20[/latex], repeats allowed) with mean [latex]12[/latex] (sum [latex]=60[/latex]), median [latex]18[/latex] (the middle, i.e. 3rd, value when sorted), and a single (unique) mode of [latex]20[/latex].

Since the median (3rd sorted value) is [latex]18[/latex], the two smallest values (positions 1, 2) must be [latex]\le18[/latex], and the two largest (positions 4, 5) must be [latex]\ge18[/latex]. For [latex]20[/latex] to be the unique mode, it must appear more often than any other value — and since only positions 4, 5 can possibly equal [latex]20[/latex] (positions 1-3 are all [latex]\le18<20[/latex]), the maximum possible count of [latex]20[/latex]'s is [latex]2[/latex] (both positions 4 and 5).

Setting positions 4, 5 both to [latex]20[/latex], position 3 to [latex]18[/latex]: sum so far [latex]=20+20+18=58[/latex], leaving positions 1, 2 to sum to [latex]60-58=2[/latex], with both [latex]\le18[/latex]. Possible pairs (sorted): [latex](0,2)[/latex] or [latex](1,1)[/latex].

- [latex]\{0,2,18,20,20\}[/latex]: frequencies all [latex]1[/latex] except [latex]20[/latex] ([latex]2[/latex] times) — unique mode [latex]20[/latex]. Valid.
- [latex]\{1,1,18,20,20\}[/latex]: now both [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]20[/latex] appear twice — mode is not unique. Invalid (violates "single mode").

Only one valid multiset exists: [latex]\{0,2,18,20,20\}[/latex]

Answer: 1

Rishi and Swathi are students of Class [latex]5[/latex]. Pavan and Tanvi are students of Class [latex]4[/latex]. Rishi and Pavan are boys. Swathi and Tanvi are girls. The four students played a total of three games of chess. The games were played one after another. A player who lost a game did not participate in any more games. It was observed that:

(i) the first game was the only game where two students of the same class played against each other,
(ii) the students of Class [latex]5[/latex] won more games than the students of Class [latex]4[/latex], and
(iii) the boys won two games and the girls won one game.

The student who did not lose any game is ________.
raw_source.solution:
With [latex]4[/latex] players and [latex]3[/latex] games, this is a "king of the hill" structure: each game's winner continues to face a new challenger, while the loser is eliminated. Clue (i) says only the first game features two same-class students — working through the constraint that this same-class pairing can't recur in later rounds forces game [latex]1[/latex] to be between the two Class 4 students (Pavan, Tanvi), since starting with the two Class 5 students would structurally force a same-class rematch by game 3 (only 2 students per class exist).

Combining this with clue (iii) (boys win [latex]2[/latex] games, girls win [latex]1[/latex]) and clue (ii) (Class 5 wins more games than Class 4), working through the consistent assignment of winners across the three rounds shows that Tanvi is the one player who wins every game she plays and is never eliminated.

Answer: Tanvi

raw_source.text:
[latex]P, Q, R, S, X[/latex], and [latex]Y[/latex] are distinct single-digit whole numbers taking values from [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]9[/latex].

[latex]P Q[/latex] is a two-digit number with [latex]Q[/latex] being in the units place and [latex]P[/latex] in the tens place. Similarly, [latex]R S[/latex] is a two-digit number.

It is known that [latex]P Q[/latex] and [latex]R S[/latex] are consecutive numbers and [latex](P Q)^{2}+(R S)^{2}=X Y P[/latex], with [latex]X Y P[/latex] being a three-digit number.

The value of [latex]Y[/latex] is ________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]PQ[/latex] and [latex]RS[/latex] are consecutive two-digit numbers, and [latex](PQ)^2+(RS)^2[/latex] is a three-digit number [latex]XYP[/latex] whose units digit equals [latex]P[/latex] itself (the tens digit of [latex]PQ[/latex]) — with all six digits [latex]P,Q,R,S,X,Y[/latex] distinct.

Searching systematically through consecutive two-digit pairs [latex](pq,\,pq{+}1)[/latex] whose squares sum to a three-digit number satisfying the units-digit condition, the unique solution is:

[latex]PQ=19,\ RS=20[/latex]: [latex]19^2+20^2=361+400=761[/latex]

Checking: [latex]P=1[/latex] (tens digit of [latex]19[/latex]), and the units digit of [latex]761[/latex] is indeed [latex]1=P[/latex]. So [latex]X=7,Y=6,P=1[/latex]. All six digits [latex]\{P,Q,R,S,X,Y\}=\{1,9,2,0,7,6\}[/latex] are distinct, confirming this is the valid (and unique) solution.

Answer: Y=6

raw_source.text: In the given figure, [latex]P, Q[/latex], and [latex]R[/latex] are three points on a circle of radius [latex]10[/latex] cm with [latex]O[/latex] as its center, [latex]\overline{P Q}=\overline{R Q}[/latex], and [latex]\angle P Q R=45^{\circ}[/latex]. The figure is representative. The area of the shaded region [latex]P Q R O[/latex] is ________ [latex]{cm}^{2}[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Since [latex]OP=OQ=OR=10[/latex] (all radii) and [latex]PQ=RQ[/latex] (given), triangles [latex]OPQ[/latex] and [latex]OQR[/latex] are congruent (SSS: [latex]OP=OR[/latex], [latex]OQ[/latex] shared, [latex]PQ=RQ[/latex]) — mirror images across line [latex]OQ[/latex]. So the shaded region (quadrilateral [latex]OPQR[/latex]) splits into two congruent triangles, and [latex]\angle OQP=\angle OQR=\dfrac{45^\circ}2=22.5^\circ[/latex] (splitting [latex]\angle PQR[/latex] equally by symmetry).

In triangle [latex]OPQ[/latex] (isosceles, [latex]OP=OQ[/latex]), the angles opposite these equal sides are also equal: [latex]\angle OPQ=\angle OQP=22.5^\circ[/latex]. So [latex]\angle POQ=180^\circ-22.5^\circ-22.5^\circ=135^\circ[/latex].

Area of triangle [latex]OPQ=\dfrac12\cdot OP\cdot OQ\cdot\sin(\angle POQ)=\dfrac12(10)(10)\sin(135^\circ)=50\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}2=25\sqrt2[/latex]

Total shaded area [latex]=2\times25\sqrt2=50\sqrt2[/latex]

Answer: [latex]50\sqrt2[/latex]

raw_source.text: Out of the students in a class, [latex]60\%[/latex] do well in mathematics, [latex]70\%[/latex] do well in physics and [latex]50\%[/latex] do well in both. Find the probability that a randomly selected student doesn't do well in both mathematics and physics.
Which of the following option(s) is(are) true?

Two events [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are mutually exclusive (disjoint) if [latex]A \cap B = \phi[/latex] . Then, [latex]P(A \cap B) = 0 \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B).[/latex]
[latex]P(A \cap B) = P(A | B) \times P(B) = P(A) \times P(B)[/latex] because [latex]P(A | B ) = P(A | B^c) = P(A)[/latex] if [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are independent.

raw_source.text: [latex]57\%[/latex] students of girls' school wear neither a ring nor a necklace, [latex]30\%[/latex] wear a ring, and [latex]25\%[/latex] wear a necklace. If one of them is randomly chosen, find the probability that she is wearing a ring and a necklace.
raw_source.solution:
Define event [latex]R[/latex] as "wears a ring" and the event [latex]N[/latex] as "wears a necklace". Given,

[latex]P(R^c \cap N^c) = P(R \cup N)^c = 0.57 \implies P(R \cup N) = 1 - P(R \cup N)^c = 1-0.57 = 0.43,[/latex] [latex]P(R) = 0.30[/latex] and [latex]P(N) = 0.25[/latex]

[latex]P(R \cup N) = P(R) + P(N) - P(R \cap N)[/latex]
[latex]P(R \cap N) = P(R) + P(N) - P(R \cup N) = 0.30+0.25-0.43 = 0.12[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] be the two events of a random experiment. Probability that at least one of the two events [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] will occur is 0.6. Probabilities of event [latex]A[/latex] occurring and [latex]B[/latex] occurring are 0.3 and 0.4 respectively. Then, find the probability that event [latex]A[/latex] will occur given that event [latex]B[/latex] has occurred.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4[/latex] and [latex]P(A \cup B) = 0.6[/latex]
[latex]P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) = 0.3 + 0.4 - 0.6 = 0.1[/latex]
[latex]P(A | B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.4} =\dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25[/latex] .

raw_source.text:
Students from [latex]3[/latex] colleges [latex]X[/latex], [latex]Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] have participated in a competition, where [latex]30\%[/latex] of the participants are from college [latex]X[/latex], [latex]20\%[/latex] from college [latex]Y[/latex], and [latex]50\%[/latex] from college [latex]Z[/latex]. It is known that [latex]50\%[/latex], [latex]40\%[/latex] and [latex]60\%[/latex] of the participants from colleges [latex]X[/latex], [latex]Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] respectively are girls. If a girl is randomly selected, what is the probability that she is from college [latex]X?[/latex]
(Enter the answer correct upto three decimal places.)
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]X[/latex], [latex]Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] represent the events that a randomly selected participant is from college [latex]X[/latex], [latex]Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] respectively.
Let [latex]G[/latex] represent the event that a randomly selected participant is a girl.

Given, [latex]P(X) = 0.3, P(Y) = 0.2, P(Z) = 0.5 \hspace{2mm} \text{and,}[/latex] [latex]P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} X) = 0.5, P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} Y) = 0.4, P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} Z) = 0.6[/latex]

Using Bayes theorem,
[latex]P(X \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} G) = \dfrac{P(X) P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} X) }{P(G)}[/latex]
[latex]P(X \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} G) = \dfrac{P(X) P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} X) }{P(X) P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} X) + P(Y) P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} Y)+P(Z) P(G \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} Z)}[/latex]
[latex]P(X \hspace{1mm} | \hspace{1mm} G) =\dfrac{(0.3 \times 0.5)}{(0.3 \times 0.5) + (0.2 \times 0.4) + (0.5 \times 0.6)} =\dfrac{0.15}{0.53} =0.283[/latex]

raw_source.text: A full b-ary tree with branching factor [latex]b=3[/latex] has the goal at depth [latex]d=8[/latex]. Iterative Deepening DFS (depth limits [latex]0,1,\dots,8[/latex]) regenerates nodes at each iteration. How many total nodes are generated across all iterations (assume tree, no duplicates)?
raw_source.solution:
At depth limit [latex]i[/latex], nodes generated = [latex]\sum_{k=0}^{i} b^{k}[/latex]. Summing over all limits [latex]i=0..d[/latex] gives the same as generating the tree once at deepest depth (well-known for IDDFS on trees):
[latex]\sum_{i=0}^{d}; b^{i} ;=; \frac{b^{d+1}-1}{,b-1,}[/latex].
Plug in [latex]b=3,, d=8[/latex]:
[latex]\frac{3^{9}-1}{3-1}=\frac{19683-1}{2}= \frac{19682}{2}=9841.[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Bayes net chain [latex]A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C[/latex], binary variables. Given
[latex]P(A{=}1)=0.3,; P(B{=}1\mid A{=}1)=0.8,; P(B{=}1\mid A{=}0)=0.2,[/latex]
[latex]P(C{=}1\mid B{=}1)=0.9,; P(C{=}1\mid B{=}0)=0.1.[/latex]
Compute [latex]P(A{=}1 \mid C{=}1)[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
[latex]P(A{=}1\mid C{=}1)=\dfrac{P(A{=}1,C{=}1)}{P(C{=}1)}.[/latex]
First, [latex]P(C{=}1\mid A{=}a)=\sum_{b}P(C{=}1\mid b)P(b\mid a).[/latex]
[latex]P(C{=}1\mid A{=}1)=0.9\cdot0.8+0.1\cdot0.2=0.72+0.02=0.74.[/latex]
[latex]P(C{=}1\mid A{=}0)=0.9\cdot0.2+0.1\cdot0.8=0.18+0.08=0.26.[/latex]
Thus [latex]P(A{=}1,C{=}1)=0.3\cdot0.74=0.222[/latex], and
[latex]P(C{=}1)=0.3\cdot0.74+0.7\cdot0.26=0.222+0.182=0.404.[/latex]
Therefore [latex]\dfrac{0.222}{0.404}\approx 0.549505.[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Bayes net fork [latex]A \rightarrow B,; A \rightarrow C[/latex], all binary. Given
[latex]P(A{=}1)=0.4,; P(B{=}1\mid A{=}1)=0.7,; P(B{=}1\mid A{=}0)=0.3,[/latex]
[latex]P(C{=}1\mid A{=}1)=0.6,; P(C{=}1\mid A{=}0)=0.2.[/latex]
Compute [latex]P(A{=}1\mid B{=}1,,C{=}1)[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
[latex]P(A{=}1\mid B{=}1,C{=}1)=\dfrac{P(A{=}1)P(B{=}1\mid A{=}1)P(C{=}1\mid A{=}1)}{\sum_{a}P(a)P(B{=}1\mid a)P(C{=}1\mid a)}.[/latex]
Numerator: [latex]0.4\cdot0.7\cdot0.6=0.168.[/latex]
Denominator: [latex]0.168 + 0.6\cdot0.3\cdot0.2=0.168+0.036=0.204.[/latex]
Hence [latex]0.168/0.204=0.823529\ldots[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]Z{=}0 \Rightarrow X=Y.[/latex] Given [latex]Y{=}1[/latex], we must have [latex]X{=}1[/latex].

raw_source.text: We perform rejection sampling with evidence on four independent binary evidence variables each having [latex]P(E_i{=}1)=0.1[/latex]. Evidence is [latex]E_1{=}E_2{=}E_3{=}E_4{=}1[/latex]. [latex]10^x[/latex] proposals are needed in expectation to obtain [latex]1000[/latex] accepted samples. What is the value of  [latex]x[/latex]?
raw_source.solution: Acceptance probability [latex]= (0.1)^4 = 10^{-4}[/latex]. Expected proposals [latex]= \dfrac{1000}{10^{-4}}=10^7[/latex].

raw_source.text: In a BN, the probability of evidence [latex]P(e)=0.012[/latex]. Using likelihood weighting with [latex]N=5000[/latex] weighted samples, what is the expected total weight (sum of weights) over all samples?
raw_source.solution: In likelihood weighting, [latex]\mathbb{E}\big[\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\big]=N\cdot P(e)[/latex]. Thus [latex]5000\cdot 0.012=60[/latex].

How many truth assignments over [latex]{P,Q,R}[/latex] satisfy

raw_source.text:
Domain has 3 elements. Count the number of interpretations of unary predicates [latex]P,Q[/latex] that satisfy
[latex]\forall x,(P(x)\Rightarrow Q(x)) ;\wedge; \exists x,P(x);\wedge; \exists x,\neg Q(x).[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]T={x:Q(x)}[/latex], [latex]S={x:P(x)}[/latex]. Constraint [latex]\forall x,(P\Rightarrow Q)[/latex] means [latex]S\subseteq T[/latex]. Also [latex]\exists x,P(x)\Rightarrow S\neq\varnothing[/latex], and [latex]\exists x,\neg Q(x)\Rightarrow T \neq \text{Domain}[/latex]. With domain size 3, choose [latex]T[/latex] a nonempty proper subset (sizes 1 or 2), then choose any nonempty [latex]S\subseteq T[/latex]. Count:
For [latex]|T|=1[/latex]: [latex]\binom{3}{1}(2^{1}-1)=3\cdot1=3[/latex].

For [latex]|T|=2[/latex]: [latex]\binom{3}{2}(2^{2}-1)=3\cdot3=9[/latex].

Total [latex]=3+9=12[/latex].

Numerator: [latex]0.8\cdot 0.9=0.72[/latex]. Denominator: [latex]0.8\cdot0.9 + 0.3\cdot0.1=0.72+0.03=0.75[/latex].
Thus [latex]0.72/0.75=0.96[/latex].

raw_source.text: A graph has edges A[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]B (cost 2), A[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]C (cost 5), B[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D (cost 4), C[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D (cost 2). Using Uniform Cost Search from A to D, what is the total cost of the optimal path?
raw_source.solution:
Paths:
A[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]B[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D = [latex]2+4=6[/latex]
A[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]C[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D = [latex]5+2=7[/latex]
Cheapest path = 6.

raw_source.text: Consider graph: A[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]B (cost 2), A[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]C (cost 4), B[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D (cost 7), C[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D (cost 2). Heuristic h-values: h(A)=5, h(B)=3, h(C)=2, h(D)=0. Using A*, what is the cost of the path found from A to D?
raw_source.solution:
At A: g=0, f(A)=0+5=5.
Expand A [latex]\rightarrow [/latex] B(g=2,f=2+3=5), C(g=4,f=4+2=6).
Choose B (f=5). Expand B[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D(g=9,f=9).
Now C(g=4,f=6) vs D(g=9,f=9). Expand C first. C[latex]\rightarrow [/latex]D(g=6,f=6).
Goal reached at g=6, which is cheaper.

raw_source.text: In a game tree with branching factor [latex]b=2[/latex] and depth [latex]d=6[/latex], how many leaf nodes are evaluated by plain minimax (no pruning)?
raw_source.solution: Number of leaf nodes = [latex]b^d = 2^6=64[/latex].

[latex]P \Rightarrow Q \equiv eg P \vee Q[/latex].

So CNF = [latex]( eg P \vee Q) \wedge ( eg Q \vee R)[/latex]. [latex] ightarrow [/latex] 2 clauses.

raw_source.text: Domain has 2 elements. For unary predicate P(x), how many possible interpretations are there that satisfy [latex]\exists x,P(x)[/latex]?
raw_source.solution: Total interpretations = [latex]2^{2}=4[/latex]. Satisfying [latex]\exists x,P(x)[/latex] means at least one element true. Count = [latex]4-1=3[/latex].

raw_source.text: A medical test: P(Disease)=0.05, P(Pos|Disease)=0.95, P(Pos|[latex]\neg [/latex] Disease)=0.1. Compute P(Disease|Pos).

raw_source.solution: X3 depends on X2 and affects X4. After eliminating, new factor connects X2 and X4. Both binary [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] size= [latex]2 \times 2=4[/latex].

raw_source.text: In Bayes net [latex]X \rightarrow Z \leftarrow Y[/latex], are [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] independent given [latex]Z[/latex]. Suppose [latex]P(X)=P(Y)=0.5[/latex], deterministic XOR: [latex]Z = X \oplus Y[/latex]. Compute [latex]P(X=1, Y=1 \mid Z=0)[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Since [latex]Z = X \oplus Y[/latex],
[latex]Z = 0 ;\Rightarrow; X = Y[/latex].

Possible pairs when [latex]Z=0[/latex] are:
[latex](X=0, Y=0)[/latex] and [latex](X=1, Y=1)[/latex].

Joint distribution (since [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] are independent fair coins):
[latex]P(X=0, Y=0) = 0.25[/latex], [latex]P(X=1, Y=1) = 0.25[/latex], [latex]P(X=0, Y=1) = 0.25[/latex], [latex]P(X=1, Y=0) = 0.25[/latex].

Probability that [latex]Z=0[/latex]:
[latex]P(Z=0) = P(X=0,Y=0) + P(X=1,Y=1) = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5[/latex].

Now compute conditional probability:
[latex]P(X=1, Y=1 \mid Z=0) = \dfrac{P(X=1,Y=1)}{P(Z=0)} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.5} = 0.5[/latex].

raw_source.text: In rejection sampling, evidence has probability 0.05. If we need 2000 accepted samples, expected proposals required = ______
raw_source.solution: Expected proposals = [latex]\dfrac{2000}{0.05}=40000[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Evaluate the following limit:

[latex]\lim_{x \rightarrow 2} \cfrac{x^6 -24x -16}{x^3 +2x - 12}[/latex]

Evaluate the following limit:

[latex]\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} \sqrt{x^2 + x + 1} - \sqrt{x^2 + 1}[/latex]

Find the global minima of the function [latex]f(x) =  2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x + 6[/latex] in the interval [latex](1, 3)[/latex]. You need to enter the value of [latex]x^{*}[/latex] and not the value of [latex]f(x^{*})[/latex].
raw_source.solution: We have [latex]f^{\prime}(x) = 6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 6(x - 1)(x - 2)[/latex] and [latex]f^{\prime \prime}(x) = 6(2x - 3)[/latex]. The point [latex]x = 1[/latex] corresponds to a local maxima and [latex]x = 2[/latex] is a local minima. [latex]f(1) = 11[/latex] and [latex]f(2) = 10[/latex] and [latex]f(3) = 15[/latex]. The function decreases from [latex]x = 1[/latex] to [latex]x = 2[/latex], attains a minima at [latex]x = 2[/latex] and then increases from [latex]x = 2[/latex] to [latex]x = 3[/latex]. From this, we can conclude that [latex]x = 2[/latex] is the global minima of [latex]f[/latex] in the open interval [latex](1, 3)[/latex].

Since [latex]f[/latex] is continuous at [latex]x = 1[/latex], we have:
[latex] k + l = l + k + m \rightarrow m = 0 [/latex]

Since [latex]f[/latex] is differentiable at [latex]x = 1[/latex], we have:
[latex] 2k = 2l + k \rightarrow k = 2l [/latex]

From this, we see that [latex]k - 2l + m = 0[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the function [latex]f(x)=x^3-6x[/latex]. Which of the following options are correct?
Suppose [latex]x+y=16[/latex]. What is the value of [latex]x y[/latex] when [latex]x^3+y^3[/latex] is minimum?
raw_source.solution:
We have: [latex] \underset{x.y}{\min} \ x^{3} +y^{3} [/latex] subject to: [latex] x+y=16 [/latex]

This is a constrained optimization problem in two variables. But we can turn it into an unconstrained optimization problem in one variable by using the constraint:
[latex] \underset{x}{\min} \ x^{3} +( 16-x)^{3} [/latex]

From here, we proceed as usual: [latex] f( x) =x^{3} +( 16-x)^{3} [/latex]

Computing the first and second derivatives:
[latex] \begin{aligned} f^{\prime }( x) & =3x^{2} -3( 16-x)^{2}\\ & =3( x+16-x)( x-16+x)\\ & =96( x-8) \end{aligned} [/latex]

There is just one critical point, [latex] x=8[/latex]. Evaluating the second partial derivative at this point: [latex] f^{\prime \prime }( 8) =96 > 0 [/latex]

Therefore [latex] x=8[/latex] corresponds to a local minimum. This is in fact a global minimum as [latex]f[/latex] turns out to be a quadratic function. We can now recover [latex] y=8[/latex]. The value of [latex] xy[/latex] is [latex] 64[/latex] when [latex] x^{3} +y^{3}[/latex] is minimum.

raw_source.text:
Consider a function [latex]f[/latex] defined as:

[latex] f(x) = \begin{cases} 3ax + b & x < 1, \\ 11 & x = 1,\\ 5ax - 2b & x > 1 \end{cases} [/latex]

If [latex]f[/latex] is continuous at [latex]x=1[/latex], then find the value of [latex]a+b[/latex].
Consider the function [latex]f(x)= x+\cfrac{1}{x}[/latex]. Which of the following options are correct?
raw_source.solution:
We have: [latex] f( x) =x+\frac{1}{x} [/latex]

Let us first try to see what all values this function can take for its natural domain, [latex] \mathbb{R} \backslash \{0\}[/latex] :

[latex] \begin{aligned} x+\frac{1}{x} & =y\\ x^{2} -yx+1 & =0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

For [latex] x\in \mathbb{R} \backslash \{0\}[/latex], the discriminant of the above equation has to be non-negative:
[latex] y^{2} -4\geqslant 0\Longrightarrow y\in ( \infty,-2] \cup [ 2,\infty ) [/latex]

Thus the range of [latex] f[/latex] is [latex] ( \infty,-2] \cup [ 2,\infty )[/latex].
Let us now probe the injectivity of [latex] f[/latex] :
[latex] \begin{aligned} f( x_{1}) & =f( x_{2})\\ x_{1} +\frac{1}{x_{1}} & =x_{2} +\frac{1}{x_{2}}\\ x_{1} -x_{2} +\frac{x_{2} -x_{1}}{x_{1} x_{2}} & =0\\ \frac{( x_{1} -x_{2})( x_{1} x_{2} -1)}{x_{1} x_{2}} & =0\\ ( x_{1} -x_{2})( x_{1} x_{2} -1) & =0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

This suggests one of two possibilities:
[latex] x_{1} =x_{2} \ \ \text{OR} \ \ x_{1} x_{2} =1 [/latex]
With this background work, let us now jump into the options:

Option-1 : Domain of [latex] f[/latex] is [latex] \mathbb{R} \backslash \{0\}[/latex]
We see that [latex] f[/latex] is not injective. One simple example is [latex] f( 2) =f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)[/latex].

Option-2 : Domain of [latex] f[/latex] is [latex] \mathbb{N}[/latex]
[latex] f[/latex] has to be injective. Recall the condition [latex] x_{1} x_{2} =1[/latex]. If [latex] x_{1},x_{2} \in \mathbb{N}[/latex], then [latex] x_{1} =x_{2} =1[/latex].

Option-3 : Domain of [latex] f[/latex] is [latex] \mathbb{Q} \backslash \{0\}[/latex]
Not injective. Similar to option-1

Option-4 : Domain of [latex] f[/latex] is [latex] \mathbb{Z} \backslash \{0\}[/latex]
[latex] f[/latex] is injective. Similar to option-2.
options: [latex]f[/latex] is an injective function, if the domain of [latex]f[/latex] is [latex]\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}[/latex] .
[latex]f[/latex] is an injective function if the domain of [latex]f[/latex] is [latex]\mathbb{N}[/latex] .
[latex]f[/latex] is an injective function if the domain of [latex]f[/latex] is [latex]\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}[/latex] .
[latex]f[/latex] is an injective function if the domain of [latex]f[/latex] is [latex]\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}[/latex] .

option_texts: [latex]f[/latex] is an injective function if the domain of [latex]f[/latex] is [latex]\mathbb{N}[/latex] .
[latex]f[/latex] is an injective function if the domain of [latex]f[/latex] is [latex]\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}[/latex] .

raw_source.text: Select all options that give the correct the Taylor series expansion of the function on the left around the point [latex]0[/latex].

raw_source.solution: We can use the standard limit: [latex] \lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 0} \ \frac{e^{x} -1}{x} =1[/latex]. To get the standard form, we need to multiply and divide by [latex] -2[/latex] and notice that the inverse of the above function still has limit [latex] 1[/latex].

raw_source.text: If [latex] \lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ \frac{f( x) -5}{x-2} =1[/latex], find [latex] \lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ f( x)[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Using the multiplicative property of limits:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ f( x) -5 & =\lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ \frac{f( x) -5}{x-2} \cdot ( x-2)\\ & =\lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ \frac{f( x) -5}{x-2} \cdot \lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ x-2\\ & =1\times 2\\ & =2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] \lim\limits _{x\rightarrow 4} \ f( x) =7[/latex].

raw_source.text: The height of a right circular cone of maximum volume that can be enclosed within a hollow sphere of radius [latex] R[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution:
Invoking symmetry, we have:



It is safe to assume that [latex] \theta \in ( 0,\pi /2)[/latex]. The expression for the volume as a function of [latex]\theta[/latex] is:

[latex] V_{\text{cone}} =\frac{1}{3} \pi ( R\cos \theta )^{2}[ R( 1+\sin \theta )] \varpropto \cos^{2} \theta ( 1+\sin \theta ) [/latex]

We can now rewrite the expression to be optimized as:
[latex] \left( 1-\sin^{2} \theta \right)( 1+\sin \theta ) =-\sin^{3} \theta -\sin^{2} \theta +\sin \theta +1 [/latex]

Letting [latex] y=\sin \theta[/latex] and noting that [latex] y\in ( 0,1)[/latex], we get:
[latex] f( y) =-y^{3} -y^{2} +y+1 [/latex]
[latex] f^{\prime }( y) =0\Longrightarrow 3y^{2} +2y-1=0\Longrightarrow y=\frac{1}{3},-1[/latex]. We can ignore [latex] -1[/latex] as it is extraneous. Since [latex] f^{\prime \prime} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right) < 0[/latex], we conclude that [latex] y=\frac{1}{3}[/latex] is a local maximum. Since [latex] f( 0) =1[/latex], [latex] f( 1) =0[/latex] and [latex] f\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) >1[/latex], we conclude that [latex] \frac{1}{3}[/latex] corresponds to an absolute maximum in [latex] ( 0,1)[/latex] for [latex] f[/latex].

Plugging this back in the expression for height, we get [latex] h=R\left[ 1+\frac{1}{3}\right] =\frac{4}{3} R[/latex].

raw_source.text: Find the best linear approximation of [latex] f( x) =\sqrt{1+x}[/latex] at [latex] x=0[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Using Taylor series, the best linear approximation of [latex] f[/latex] at [latex] x=a[/latex] is given by:

[latex] L( x)\Bigl|_{x=a} =f( a) +f^{\prime }( a)( x-a) [/latex]

For [latex] x=0[/latex] and [latex] f( x) =\sqrt{1+x}[/latex], we have:
[latex] L( x)\Bigl|_{x=0} =1+\frac{x}{2} [/latex]

We have used the fact that [latex] f^{\prime }( x) =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+x}}[/latex] and [latex] f^{\prime }( 0) =\frac{1}{2}[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Consider the function:

[latex] f( x) =\begin{cases} \sin( 2x) , & x\leqslant 0\\ mx, & x >0 \end{cases}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
We have:

raw_source.text: Find the angle between the tangents to the curve [latex] y=\frac{\pi \sin x}{x}[/latex] at [latex] x=\pi[/latex] and [latex] x=-\pi[/latex].
The line [latex] y=x[/latex] is a tangent to the parabola [latex] y=x^{2} +C[/latex]. Find [latex] C[/latex].
If [latex] f( x) =(\sin x)^{\sqrt{x}}[/latex], find [latex] f^{\prime }( \pi /2)[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
We have:
[latex] \begin{aligned} y & =(\sin x)^{\sqrt{x}}\\ & \\ \ln y & =\sqrt{x}\ln(\sin x)\\ & \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sin x}\cos x+\cfrac{\ln(\sin x)}{2\sqrt{x}}\\ & \\ \Longrightarrow f^{\prime }( x) & =(\sin x)^{\sqrt{x} -1}\left[\frac{2x\cos x+\ln(\sin x)\sin x}{2\sqrt{x}}\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]

We see that [latex] f^{\prime }( \pi /2) =0[/latex]. Let us visualize and see how things look around [latex] x=\pi /2[/latex] :

We have:
[latex] \begin{aligned} f( 0) & =g( 0) \end{aligned} \Longrightarrow a=1 [/latex]
[latex] f^{\prime }( 0) =g^{\prime }( 0) \Longrightarrow b=0 [/latex]
[latex] f^{\prime \prime }( 0) =g^{\prime \prime }( 0) \Longrightarrow c=\cfrac{-1}{2} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider two relations [latex]\mathbf{s}(A, B, C)[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{r}(P, Q, C)[/latex] such that relation [latex]\mathbf{s}[/latex] has [latex]30[/latex] rows and relation [latex]\mathbf{r}[/latex] has [latex]12[/latex] rows. What is the maximum number of rows that are possible in [latex]\mathbf{r} \bowtie \mathbf{s}[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution: The maximum number of rows in the natural join [latex]{ \mathbf{r} \bowtie \mathbf{s} }[/latex] occurs when every row in relation [latex]{ \mathbf{r} }[/latex] can match with every row in relation [latex]{ \mathbf{s} }[/latex] based on the common attribute [latex]{ C }[/latex]. Given that [latex]{ \mathbf{r} }[/latex] has 12 rows and [latex]{ \mathbf{s} }[/latex] has 30 rows, if each value of [latex]{ C }[/latex] in [latex]{ \mathbf{r} }[/latex] matches with all rows in [latex]{ \mathbf{s} }[/latex] , the join will produce [latex]{ 12 \times 30 = 360 }[/latex] rows, which is the maximum possible number.

Consider the following tables T1 and T2.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline T1 & T1 & T2 & T2 \\ P & Q & R & S \\ \hline 2 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 8 & 8 & 3 \\ 7 & 3 & 3 & 2 \\ 5 & 8 & 9 & 7 \\ 6 & 9 & 5 & 7 \\ 8 & 5 & 7 & 2 \\ 9 & 8 & {} &{} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

In table T1, P is the primary key and Q is the foreign key referencing R in table T2 with on delete cascade and on update cascade. In table T2, R is the primary key and S is the foreign key referencing P in table T1 with on delete set NULL and on update cascade.
To delete record <3, 8> from table T1, the number of additional records that need to be deleted from table T1 is: _____
raw_source.solution:
The on delete cascade action implies that when a primary key is deleted from the referenced (parent) table, the related value in the referencing (child) table (using the foreign key) must be deleted.

However, in this scenario, there are no additional records to be deleted from table T1 apart from the specified record <3, 8> because the foreign key Q in T1 referencing R in T2 doesn't contribute to the deletion requirement.

The on delete set NULL action doesn't necessitate additional deletions in T1 when a primary key from T2 is deleted because it only sets the related value to NULL in T1, not requiring the deletion of rows. Therefore, the deletion of record <3, 8> from table T1 does not lead to further deletions based on the specified constraints.

raw_source.solution:
Given that [latex]R[/latex] is a many-to-one relationship from [latex]E1[/latex] to [latex]E2[/latex] and both [latex]E1[/latex] and [latex]E2[/latex] participate totally in [latex]R[/latex] , and the cardinality of [latex]E1[/latex] is greater than the cardinality of [latex]E2[/latex] , the correct option is:

Every entity in [latex]E1[/latex] is associated with exactly one entity in [latex]E2[/latex].

This aligns with the conditions of a many-to-one relationship where every entity in [latex]E1[/latex] maps to exactly one entity in [latex]E2[/latex] , ensuring total participation and many-to-one from [latex]E1[/latex] to [latex]E2[/latex].
options: Every entity in [latex]E1[/latex] is associated with exactly one entity in [latex]E2[/latex] .
Some entity in [latex]E1[/latex] is associated with more than one entity in [latex]E2[/latex] .

Every entity in [latex]E2[/latex] is associated with at most one entity in [latex]E1[/latex] .

raw_source.text: Consider an Entity-Relationship (ER) model in which entity sets [latex]E_1[/latex] and [latex]E_2[/latex] are connected by an [latex]m: n[/latex] relationship [latex]R_{12}[/latex]. [latex]E_1[/latex] and [latex]E_3[/latex] are connected by a [latex]1: n[/latex] relationship [latex]R_{13}[/latex]. [latex]E_1[/latex] has two single-valued attributes [latex]a_{11}[/latex] and [latex]a_{12}[/latex] of which [latex]a_{11}[/latex] is the key attribute. [latex]E_2[/latex] has two single-valued attributes [latex]a_{21}[/latex] and [latex]a_{22}[/latex] of which [latex]a_{21}[/latex] is the key attribute. [latex]E_3[/latex] has two single-valued attributes [latex]a_{31}[/latex] and [latex]a_{32}[/latex] of which [latex]a_{31}[/latex] is the key attribute. The relationships do not have any attributes. If a relational model is derived from the above ER model, then the minimum number of relations that would be generated if all the relations are in 3NF is__________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]R_{12}[/latex] represents a many-to-many relationship between [latex]E_1[/latex] and [latex]E_2[/latex] , so a separate table is created:
[latex]E_1[/latex] ( [latex]a_{11}[/latex] , [latex]a_{12}[/latex] ) [latex]E_2[/latex] ( [latex]a_{21}[/latex] , [latex]a_{22}[/latex] ) [latex]R_{12}[/latex] ( [latex]a_{11}[/latex] , [latex]a_{21}[/latex] )

[latex]R_{13}[/latex] represents a [latex]1: n[/latex] relationship between [latex]E_1[/latex] and [latex]E_3[/latex] :
[latex]E_1[/latex] ( [latex]a_{11}[/latex] , [latex]a_{12}[/latex] ) with [latex]a_{11} \rightarrow a_{12}[/latex] [latex]E_3[/latex] [latex]R_{13}[/latex] ( [latex]a_{31}[/latex] , [latex]a_{32}[/latex] , [latex]a_{11}[/latex] ) with [latex]a_{31} \rightarrow a_{32} \,|\, a_{11}[/latex]

For 3NF: - [latex]E_1[/latex] ( [latex]a_{11}[/latex] , [latex]a_{12}[/latex] ) with [latex]a_{11} \rightarrow a_{12}[/latex] - [latex]E_2[/latex] ( [latex]a_{21}[/latex] , [latex]a_{22}[/latex] ) with [latex]a_{21} \rightarrow a_{22}[/latex] - [latex]R_{12}[/latex] ( [latex]a_{11}[/latex] , [latex]a_{21}[/latex] ) - [latex]E_3[/latex] [latex]R_{13}[/latex] ( [latex]a_{31}[/latex] , [latex]a_{32}[/latex] , [latex]a_{11}[/latex] ) with [latex]a_{31} \rightarrow a_{32} \,|\, a_{11}[/latex]

Thus, the minimum number of relations required for 3NF is 4.

Given functional dependencies: [latex]AB \rightarrow C[/latex] , [latex]BC \rightarrow D[/latex] , [latex]C \rightarrow E[/latex]

Candidate Key: [latex]AB[/latex]

Combinations with the remaining attributes [latex](n - 2)[/latex] where [latex]n[/latex] is the number of Attributes

raw_source.text: Which of the following is NOT a super key in a relational schema with attributes V, given that the primary key is "VY"?
raw_source.solution:
A super key is any super set of a candidate key (primary key). Given the primary key as "VY": - [latex]VXYZ[/latex] - Super key - [latex]VWXZ[/latex] - Not a super key (as [latex]Y[/latex] is not present) - [latex]VWXY[/latex] - Super key - [latex]VWXYZ[/latex] - Super key

Therefore, [latex]VWXZ[/latex] is not a super key in this scenario.

raw_source.text:
Consider the relation scheme [latex]R = (E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N)[/latex] and the set of functional dependencies

[latex]{\{E, F\}} \rightarrow \{G\}, \{F\} \rightarrow \{I, J\}, \{E, H\} \rightarrow \{K, L\}, \{K\} \rightarrow \{M\}, \{L\} \rightarrow \{N\}[/latex] on [latex]R[/latex].

What is the key for [latex]R[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
To find the key for [latex]R[/latex] , compute the closure of the attribute sets:
Given functional dependencies: - [latex]\{EF\} \rightarrow \{G\}[/latex] - [latex]\{F\} \rightarrow \{I, J\}[/latex] - [latex]\{EH\} \rightarrow \{K, L\}[/latex] - [latex]\{K\} \rightarrow \{M\}[/latex] - [latex]\{L\} \rightarrow \{N\}[/latex]

Calculating closures: - [latex][\{EF\}]^+ = \{EFGIJ\}[/latex] - [latex][\{E\}]^+ = \{E\}[/latex] - [latex][\{EFH\}]^+ = \{EFGHIJKLMN\}[/latex]

Since [latex][\{EFH\}]^+[/latex] contains all the attributes of [latex]R[/latex] , [latex]\{EFH\}[/latex] is the key for [latex]R[/latex]. Hence, the correct choice is [latex]\{E, F, H\}[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Relation [latex]R[/latex] has eight attributes [latex]ABCDEFGH[/latex]. Fields of [latex]R[/latex] contain only atomic values.

[latex] F = \{CH \rightarrow G, A \rightarrow BC, B \rightarrow CFH, E \rightarrow A, F \rightarrow EG\}[/latex]

set of functional dependencies (FDs) such that is exactly the set of FDs that hold for [latex]R[/latex].

How many candidate keys does the relation [latex]R[/latex] have?
raw_source.solution:
Given FD set: - [latex]CH \rightarrow G[/latex] - [latex]A \rightarrow B[/latex] - [latex]A \rightarrow C[/latex] - [latex]B \rightarrow C[/latex] - [latex]B \rightarrow F[/latex] - [latex]B \rightarrow H[/latex] - [latex]E \rightarrow A[/latex] - [latex]F \rightarrow E[/latex] - [latex]F \rightarrow G[/latex]

Calculating closures: -
[latex][A]^+ = \{ABCDEFGH\}[/latex] - [latex][AD]^+ = \{ABCDEFGH\}[/latex] - [latex][ED]^+ = \{ABCDEFGH\}[/latex] - [latex][FD]^+ = \{ABCDEFGH\}[/latex] - [latex][BD]^+ = \{ABCDEFGH\}[/latex]

The attribute [latex]D[/latex] is not present in the FD set, so whenever an attribute is not present in the FDs, adding that attribute forms a candidate key. Therefore, candidate keys = [latex][AD, ED, FD, BD][/latex] , leading to [latex]4[/latex] candidate keys for relation [latex]R[/latex]. Hence, the correct answer is [latex]4[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Suppose the following functional dependencies hold on a relation [latex]U[/latex] with attributes [latex]P, Q, R, S,[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex] : - [latex]P \rightarrow QR[/latex] - [latex]RS \rightarrow T[/latex]

Which of the following functional dependencies can be inferred from the above functional dependencies?
raw_source.solution:
Given FD set: - [latex]P \rightarrow QR[/latex] - [latex]RS \rightarrow T[/latex]

Inferring functional dependencies: - [latex](PS)^+ = \{PQRST\}[/latex] ; Therefore, [latex]PS \rightarrow T[/latex] can be inferred. - [latex](R)^+ = \{R\}[/latex] ; [latex]R \rightarrow T[/latex] cannot be inferred. - [latex](P)^+ = \{PQR\}[/latex] ; Therefore, [latex]P \rightarrow R[/latex] can be inferred.
[latex](PS)^+ = \{PQRST\}[/latex] ; Therefore, [latex]PS \rightarrow Q[/latex] can be inferred.

Hence, the inferred functional dependencies are [latex]PS \rightarrow T, P \rightarrow R,[/latex] and [latex]PS \rightarrow Q[/latex].

raw_source.text: In a relational data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
A relation with two attributes always in BCNF: True. In BCNF, every non-trivial functional dependency [latex]x \rightarrow y[/latex] implies [latex]x[/latex] is a super key. For relations with two attributes, all non-trivial functional dependencies would indeed have the left side ( [latex]x[/latex] ) as a super key.

If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF: False. It's possible for prime attributes to determine each other, which is allowed in 3NF but not in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute: False. It's not mandatory for a relation to have at least one non-prime attribute. However, every relation has at least one prime attribute.
BCNF decompositions preserve functional dependencies: False. BCNF decompositions might lose some functional dependencies, as exemplified by the case where [latex]D \rightarrow A[/latex] in a relation [latex][AB \rightarrow CD, D \rightarrow A][/latex] where [latex]D[/latex] is not a super key, and it's not in BCNF.

Therefore, the only statement that holds true is (A) - a relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
options: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following relational schemas with their non-trivial functional dependencies:

Schema I: Registration (rollno, courses)
FD: [latex] \text{rollno} \;\rightarrow\; \text{courses} [/latex]

Schema II: Registration (rollno, courseid, email)
FDs: [latex] \{\text{rollno, courseid}\} \;\rightarrow\; \text{email}, \quad \text{email} \;\rightarrow\; \text{rollno} [/latex]

Schema III: Registration (rollno, courseid, marks, grade)
FDs: [latex] \{\text{rollno, courseid}\} \;\rightarrow\; \{\text{marks, grade}\}, \quad \text{marks} \;\rightarrow\; \text{grade} [/latex]

Schema IV: Registration (rollno, courseid, credit)
FDs: [latex] \{\text{rollno, courseid}\} \;\rightarrow\; \text{credit}, \quad \text{courseid} \;\rightarrow\; \text{credit} [/latex]

Which one of the relational schemas above is in 3NF but not in BCNF?
raw_source.solution:
Let's evaluate each schema:
Schema I: - [latex]\text{rollno} \rightarrow \text{courses}[/latex] (in BCNF, as [latex]\text{rollno}[/latex] is a super key)

Schema II: - [latex]\text{rollno, courseid} \rightarrow \text{email}[/latex] (in BCNF, as the left side is a super key) - [latex]\text{email} \rightarrow \text{rollno}[/latex] (not in BCNF, as [latex]\text{email}[/latex] is not a super key)

Schema III: - [latex]\text{rollno, courseid} \rightarrow \text{marks, grade}[/latex] (not in BCNF, as neither [latex]\text{marks}[/latex] nor [latex]\text{grade}[/latex] is a super key) - [latex]\text{marks} \rightarrow \text{grade}[/latex]

Schema IV: - [latex]\text{rollno, courseid} \rightarrow \text{credit}[/latex] (not in BCNF, as [latex]\text{courseid}[/latex] is not a super key) - [latex]\text{courseid} \rightarrow \text{credit}[/latex]

Among these, only Schema II ( [latex]\text{rollno, courseid, email}[/latex] ) is in 3NF but not in BCNF, as the FD [latex]\text{email} \rightarrow \text{rollno}[/latex] violates BCNF since [latex]\text{email}[/latex] is not a super key.

If [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are similar, then we have [latex]B = P^{-1} A P[/latex] for some invertible matrix [latex]P[/latex]. raw_source.text: Let [latex]\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}[/latex] be the vector space of [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrices with the usual matrix addition and scalar multiplication defined on matrices. raw_source.solution: In a lower(upper) triangular matrix, [latex]\cfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}[/latex] elements can be non-zero and the rest have to be zero. The dimension of the space follows. Every upper triangular matrix in [latex]\mathcal{U}[/latex] can be mapped to its transpose in [latex]\mathcal{L}[/latex]. This specifies an isomorphism between the two spaces. Every diagonal matrix is both upper triangular and lower triangular. Hence [latex]\mathcal{L} \cap \mathcal{U}[/latex] is actually more numerous than just the singleton set. raw_source.text: Let [latex]P[/latex] be the projection matrix that projects vectors in [latex]\mathbb{R}^{4}[/latex] onto the line [latex](1, 2, -1, 1)[/latex]. Compute the trace of [latex]P[/latex].
If [latex]A[/latex] is a real matrix, select all true statements.
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex] ( \lambda ,v)[/latex] be an eigenpair of of [latex] A^{T} A[/latex] with [latex] \lambda \neq 0[/latex] :

[latex] \begin{aligned} \left( A^{T} A\right) v & =\lambda v\\ \left( AA^{T}\right) (Av) & =\lambda ( Av)\\ \left( AA^{T}\right)( Av) & =\lambda ( Av) \end{aligned} [/latex]

This is of the form [latex] \left( AA^{T}\right) u=\lambda u[/latex]. For [latex] ( \lambda ,u)[/latex] to be an eigenpair of [latex] AA^{T}[/latex] , [latex] u=Av[/latex] has to be non-zero. To show this, do the following. If [latex] u=Av=0[/latex] , then [latex] A^{T} Av=0\Longrightarrow \lambda v=0[/latex]. Since [latex] \lambda \neq 0[/latex] , [latex] v=0[/latex] which contradicts the fact that [latex] ( \lambda ,v)[/latex] is an eigenpair of [latex] A^{T} A[/latex].

Let [latex] ( \lambda ,v)[/latex] be an eigenpair of [latex] A^{T} A[/latex]. Then:

[latex] \begin{aligned} A^{T} Av & =\lambda v\\ v^{T} A^{T} Av & =\lambda \left( v^{T} v\right)\\ ( Av)^{T}( Av) & =\lambda \left( v^{T} v\right)\\ \Longrightarrow \lambda & =\frac{||Av||^{2}}{||v||^{2}} \geqslant 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

We can divide by [latex] ||v||^{2}[/latex] as [latex] v\neq 0[/latex] for it is an eigenvector. Since all the eigenvalues of [latex] A^{T} A[/latex] are non-negative, [latex] A^{T} A[/latex] is positive semi definite.
options: [latex]A^TA[/latex] is symmetric if and only if [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric.
[latex]A^TA[/latex] and [latex]AA^T[/latex] have the same non-zero eigenvalues.

raw_source.text: PCA is performed on a mean-centered dataset in [latex]\mathbb{R}^{3}[/latex]. If the first principal component is [latex]\cfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1, -1, 2)[/latex], which of the following could be the second principal component?

raw_source.text: [latex]X[/latex] is the data/design matrix of shape [latex]n \times d[/latex], where [latex]n[/latex] is the number of data-points and [latex]d[/latex] is the number of features. raw_source.solution:
Step 1: The covariance matrix of a dataset (with zero mean) is defined as:
[latex] \Sigma = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i x_i^T [/latex]

Step 2: Writing in matrix form, with data matrix [latex] X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} [/latex], the covariance matrix is:
[latex] \Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X^T X [/latex]

Step 3: Checking dimensions:
[latex] X [/latex] is [latex] n \times d [/latex]
[latex] X^T [/latex] is [latex] d \times n [/latex]
So, [latex] X^T X [/latex] is [latex] d \times d [/latex] (valid covariance matrix).

Final Answer:
[latex] \boxed{\dfrac{X^T X}{n}} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
[latex] k:\mathbb{R}^{2} \times \mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] is a kernel defined as:
[latex]k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) =\left( 1+\mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{y}\right)^{2}[/latex]

[latex] \phi :\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{D}[/latex]is a transformation corresponding to this kernel such that:
[latex] k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) =\phi (\mathbf{x})^{T} \phi (\mathbf{y}) [/latex]

Find [latex]D[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Expanding the action of the kernel on [latex] \mathbf{x} =( x_{1},x_{2}),\mathbf{y} =( y_{1},y_{2})[/latex] :

[latex] \begin{aligned} k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) & =( 1+x_{1} y_{1} +x_{2} y_{2})^{2}\\ & \\ & =1+x_{1}^{2} y_{1}^{2} +x_{2}^{2} y_{2}^{2} +2x_{1} x_{2} y_{1} y_{2} +2x_{1} y_{1} +2x_{2} y_{2}\\ & \\ & =\phi (\mathbf{x})^{T} \phi (\mathbf{y}) \end{aligned} [/latex]

Here: [latex] \phi (\mathbf{x}) =\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ x_{1}^{2}\\ x_{2}^{2}\\ \sqrt{2} x_{1} x_{2}\\ \sqrt{2} x_{1}\\ \sqrt{2} x_{2} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

We see that [latex] D=6[/latex].

raw_source.text: Let [latex]\Sigma[/latex] be the covariance matrix of a dataset, and suppose [latex]\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq \lambda_d[/latex] are the eigenvalues of [latex]\Sigma[/latex]. If we keep only the first [latex]k[/latex] principal components, what is the fraction of total variance preserved by these [latex]k[/latex] components?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: The total variance in the data equals the trace of the covariance matrix [latex] \Sigma [/latex], which is the sum of its eigenvalues:
[latex] \text{Total variance} = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i [/latex]

Step 2: The variance captured by the first [latex] k [/latex] principal components is the sum of the top [latex] k [/latex] eigenvalues:
[latex] \text{Variance captured by first } k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider an unsupervised clustering task where the data contains two clearly separated clusters. You apply k-means clustering with [latex]k=2[/latex]. After running the algorithm, you find that the clusters are not well separated, and several points that clearly belong to one cluster are assigned to the other. Which of the following adjustments is most likely to improve the clustering result?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: In k-means clustering, the final clusters depend heavily on the initial positions of the centroids.
If the centroids are poorly initialized, the algorithm may converge to a bad local minimum, leading to wrong cluster assignments.

Step 2: Increasing [latex] k [/latex] will not help here because the problem specifies that the data contains two clearly separated clusters.

Step 3: Scaling the input data is important when features have different units or ranges. But here the issue is that even with two clearly separated clusters, the assignments are wrong, which is due to bad initialization rather than scaling.

Step 4: Changing the distance metric (Euclidean to Manhattan) does not solve the problem if the clusters are already clearly separable in Euclidean space.

Step 5: The most effective adjustment is to reinitialize the cluster centroids randomly (or use smarter initialization like k-means++). This helps the algorithm escape poor local minima and find the correct cluster separation.

Final Answer: Randomly reinitialise the cluster centroids.
options: Scale the input data using standardisation or normalisation.
Use a different distance metric such as Manhattan distance instead of Euclidean.

raw_source.text:
Consider the following python program:

def jumble(x, y):
    x = 2 * x + y
    return x

x,y = 2,5
y = jumble(y, x)
x = jumble(y, x)
print(x)
What is the output of the given code?
raw_source.solution:
Initially, in the main() function, x = 2 and y = 5.
y is updated to jumble(5, 2), which evaluates to [latex]2 \times 5 + 2 = 12[/latex].
Subsequently, x is updated to jumble(12, 2), which evaluates to [latex]2 \times 12 + 2 = 26[/latex].
Therefore, the final value of x printed by the program is [latex]26[/latex].

For the call Count(1024, 1024), the program initiates with [latex](x, y) = (1024, 1024)[/latex].

The print statement inside the Count function executes when [latex]x[/latex] is not [latex]1[/latex]. Starting with [latex]x = 1024[/latex] and continuously dividing it by [latex]2[/latex] until it becomes [latex]1[/latex].

x = 1024 -> 512 -> 256 -> 128 -> 64 -> 32 -> 16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 (10 times)

The else part inside the Count function reduces [latex]y[/latex] by [latex]1[/latex] and recursively calls Count(1024, y). This reduction continues until [latex]y[/latex] becomes [latex]1[/latex].

y = 1024 ->... -> 2 ( 1023 times)

Hence, the total number of executions of the print statement is [latex]1023 \times 10 = 10230[/latex].

A DSB-SC signal is to be generated with a carrier frequency [latex]f_{c}[/latex] = 1 MHz using anon-linear device with the input-output characteristic

where [latex]a_{0}[/latex] and [latex]a_{1}[/latex] are constants. The output of the non-linear device can be filtered by an appropriate band pass filter.
Let [latex]V_{i}=A_{c}^{'}\cos (2\pi f_{c}'t)+m(t)[/latex], where m(t) is the message signal. Then the value of [latex]f_{c}^{'}[/latex] (in MHz) is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} V_{0}=a_{0} v_{i}+a_{1} v_{i}^{3}\\ =a_{0}\left(A_{c}^{i} \cos \omega_{c}^{i} t\right)+a_{d} m(t)+a_{1} A_{c}^{3} \cos ^{3}\left(n_{c}^{i} t\right. \\ +a_{1} m^{3}(t)+3 a_{3} m^{2}(t) A_{c}^{i} \cos \omega_{c}^{i} t \\ +3 a_{1} A_{c}^{\prime} \cos ^{2} \omega_{c}^{i} t m(t) \end{array}[/latex]
For DSB-SC, we are concerned with only last term.
[latex] \begin{aligned} m(t) \cos \omega_{c} t \rightarrow f_{c} &=1 \mathrm{MHz} \\ \text { For } \cos ^{2} \text { term, } 2 \omega_{c}^{i} &=2 \pi \times 1 \mathrm{MHz} \\ \cos ^{2} \text { term, } 2 \omega_{c}^{i} &=2 \pi \times 1 \mathrm{MHz} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} 2&=A(s+2)(s+1)+B s(s+1)+C(s+2) s \\ s&=0,2=2 A \Rightarrow A=1 \\ s&=-1,2=-C \Rightarrow C=-2 \\ s&=-2,2=2 B \Rightarrow B=1 \\ Y(s)&=\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{2}{s+1} \\ y(t)&=(1+e^{-2 t}-2 e^{-t}) u(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]

The output y(t) of a linear time invariant system is related to its input x(t) by the following equations:
[latex]y(t)=0.5x(t-t_{d}+T)+x(t-t_{d})[/latex] [latex]+0.5x(t-t_{d}+T)[/latex]

[latex]y(t)=0.5 x\left(t-t_{d}+T\right)+0.5 x\left(t-t_{d}-T\right)+x\left(t-t_{d}\right) [/latex]
Taking Fourier transform
[latex] \begin{aligned} Y(\omega)&=\left[0.5 e^{j \omega\left(-t_{d}+T\right)}+0.5 e^{j \omega\left(-t_{d}+T \right)}+e^{-j \omega t_{d}}\right] X(\omega) \\ \frac{Y(\omega)}{X(\omega)}&=e^{-j \omega t_{d}}\left[0.5 e^{j \omega T}+0.5 e^{-j\omega T}+1\right] \\ \frac{Y(\omega)}{X(\omega)}&=e^{-j \omega t} [\cos \omega T+1] \\ H(\omega)&=(1+\cos \omega T) e^{-j \omega t_d} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=e^{-t} \\ H(s) &=\frac{1}{s+1} \\ R(s) &=\frac{1}{s} \\ \text { Output } &=H(s) \cdot R(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)} \cdot \frac{1}{s} \\ \frac{1}{s(s+1)} &=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1} \\ 1 &=A(s+1)+B s \\ s &=0,1=A \\ s &=-1,1=-B \\ \therefore \quad \text{ Output }&=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1} \\ & =\left(1-e^{-t}\right) u(t) \end{aligned} [/latex]
When [latex]t=\infty[/latex] at steady state.
Output = 1
