raw_source.solution:
Maximum phase shift
[latex] \begin{aligned} \phi_{m} &=\angle G_{\theta}(s) \\ \phi &=\tan ^{-1} 3 \omega T-\tan ^{-1} \omega T \end{aligned}[/latex]
For maximum phase shift
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d \phi}{d \omega} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{3 T}{1+(3 T \omega)^{2}} &=\frac{T}{1+(T \omega)^{2}} \\ 3\left[1+(T \omega)^{2}\right] &=1+(3 T \omega)^{2} \\ 3+3 T^{2} \omega^{2} &=1+9 T^{2} \omega^{2} \\ 2 &=6(\omega T)^{2} \\ (\omega T)^{2} &=\frac{1}{3} \\ \omega T=& \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\\phi_{\max } &=\tan ^{-1} 3 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A control system with PD controller is shown in the figure. If the velocity error constant [latex]K_{V}[/latex]=1000 and the damping ratio [latex]\varsigma[/latex]=0.5, then the value of [latex]K_{P}[/latex] and [latex]K_{D}[/latex] are
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} K_{v} &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s G(s) H(s) \\ 1000 &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \times \frac{\left(K_{P}+K_{D} s\right) 100}{s(s+10)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{P} &=100 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now characteristics eq. [latex](1+G(s) H(s))=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 1+\frac{\left(K_{P}+K_{D}\right) 100}{s(s+10)}&=0 \\ \text { Putting } \quad K_{P}&=100 \\ s^{2}+10 s+10^{4}+100 K_{0} s&=0 \\ s^{2}+\left(10+100 K_{0}\right) s+10^{4}&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing with standard second order eq.
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \text{i.e.}\quad s^{2}+2 \xi \omega_{n} s+\omega_{n}^{2}=0\\ \text{So,} \quad \omega_{n}=100 ; 2 \xi \omega_{n}=10+100 K_{0} \\ \text{Given,}\quad \xi=0.5 \\ 2 \times 0.5 \times 100=10+100 K_{0} \\ K_{D}=0.9 \end{array}[/latex]

The state space representation of a separately excited DC servo motor dynamics is given as
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \frac{d\omega }{dt}\\ \frac{di_{a}}{dt} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1\\ -1&-10 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \omega \\ i_{a} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 10 \end{bmatrix}u[/latex]
where [latex]\omega[/latex] is the speed of the motor, [latex]i_{a}[/latex] is the armature current and u is the armature voltage. The transfer function [latex]\frac{\omega (s)}{U(s)}[/latex] of the motor is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{d \omega}{d t} \\\frac{d i_{a}}{d t}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{cc} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -10 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} \omega \\ i_{a} \end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 10 \end{array}\right] u\\ \Rightarrow \frac{d \omega}{d t}&=-\omega+i_{\mathrm{a}} &\ldots(i)\\ \Rightarrow \frac{d i_{\mathrm{a}}}{d t}&=-\omega-10 i_{\mathrm{a}}+10 u &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking Laplace transform (i) \& (ii)
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow s \omega(s)=-\omega(s)+I_{a}(s) \\ \Rightarrow(s+1) \omega(s)=I_{a}(s) \quad\ldots(iii)\\ \Rightarrow s I_{e}(s)=-\omega(s)-10 I_{a}(s)+10 U(s) \\ \Rightarrow \omega(s)=(-10-s) I_{a}(s)+10 U(s) \\ =(-10-s)(s+1) \omega(s)+10 U(s) \\ =-\left[s^{2}+11 s+10\right] \omega(s)+10 U(s) \\ \Rightarrow\left[s^{2}+11 s+11\right] \omega(s)=10 U(s) \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\omega(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{10}{\left(s^{2}+11 s+11\right)} \end{array}[/latex]

An input to a 6-level quantizer has the probability density function f(x) as shown in the figure. Decision boundaries of the quantizer are chosen so as t maximize the entropy of the quantizer output. It is given that 3 consecutive decision boundaries are '-1', '0' and '1' .

The values of a and b are
raw_source.solution:
To maximize the entropy, all the decision
boundaries should be equiprobable
[latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{1}^{5} \rho_{x}(x) d x&=\frac{1}{3}\\ \int_{1}^{5} b d x&=\frac{1}{3} \\ b|x|_{1}^{5}&=\frac{1}{3} \\ b[5-1]&=\frac{1}{3} \\ 4 b&=\frac{1}{3} \\ b&=\frac{1}{12} \\ \int_{-1}^{1} p_{x}(x) d x&=\frac{1}{3}\\ \int_{-1}^{1} a d x &=\frac{1}{3} \\ a[x]_{-1}^{1} &=\frac{1}{3} \\ a[1-(-1)] &=\frac{1}{3} \\ 2 a &=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{6} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An input to a 6-level quantizer has the probability density function f(x) as shown in the figure. Decision boundaries of the quantizer are chosen so as t maximize the entropy of the quantizer output. It is given that 3 consecutive decision boundaries are '-1', '0' and '1' .

Assuming that the reconstruction levels of the quantizer are the mid-points of the decision boundaries, the ratio of signal power to quantization noise power is
raw_source.solution:
Signal power,
[latex] \begin{aligned} S &=E\left[X^{2}\right]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} f_{X}(x) d x \\ &=2\left[\int_{0}^{1} a x^{2} d x+\int_{1}^{5} b x^{2} d x\right]=2\left[a\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)^{1}+b\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)^{5}\right]_{1} \\ &=2\left[\frac{a}{3}+\frac{124 b}{3}\right]=2\left[\frac{1}{6 \times 3}+\frac{124}{12 \times 3}\right]=7 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Quantization noise power,
[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{Q}&=\sum_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\Delta_{i}^{2}}{12} P\left(\Delta_{i}\right) \\ \Delta_{1}&=1 \vee ; \\ for 1 \lt x \lt 1 \\ \Delta_{2}&=2 V ; \\ for 1 \lt |x| \lt 5 \\ P\left(\Delta_{1}\right)&=P\{-1 \lt x \lt 1\}=2 a=\frac{1}{3} \\ P\left(\Delta_{2}\right)&=1-P\left(\Delta_{1}\right)=\frac{2}{3} \\ So, N_{Q}&=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1^{2}}{12}\right)+\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{2^{2}}{12}\right)=\frac{1}{4} \\ \text{Hence, SQNR}&=\frac{S}{N_{Q}}=28 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The recursion relation to solve [latex]x=e^{-x}[/latex] using Newton - Raphson method is
raw_source.solution:
The given equation to be solved is
[latex] x=e^{-x}[/latex]
Which can be rewritten as
[latex] \begin{array}{l} f(x)=x-e^{x}=0 \\ f^{\prime}(x)=1+e^{-x} \end{array}[/latex]
The Newton-raphson iterative formula is
[latex] \begin{aligned} x_{n+1}&=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)}\\ f\left(x_{n}\right)&=x_{n}-e^{-x_{n}} \\ f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right) &=1+e^{-x_{n}} \\ \therefore \quad x_{n+1} &=x_{n}-\frac{x_{n}-e^{-x_{n}}}{1+e^{-x_{n}}} \\ &=\frac{e^{-x_{n}} x_{n}+e^{-x_{n}}}{1+e^{-x_{n}}} \\ &=\left(1+x_{n}\right) \frac{e^{-x_{n}}}{1+e^{-x_{n}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The residue of the function [latex]f(z)=\frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}(z-2)^{2}}[/latex] at z=2 is
raw_source.solution:
since, [latex]\lim _{z \rightarrow 2}\left[(z-2)^{2} f(z)\right] [/latex] is finite and non-zero.
f(z) has a pole of order two at, z=2
The residue at z=a is given for a pole of order n as
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \text{Res} f(a)=\frac{1}{(n-1) !} \frac{d^{n-1}}{d z^{n-1}}\left[(z-a)^{n} f(z)\right]_{z=a} \\ \text{Here, }n=2 \text{ (pole of order 2 ) } \& a=2 \\ \therefore \text{Res} f(2)=\frac{1}{1 !} \frac{d}{d z}\left[(z-2)^{2} f(z)\right]_{z=2} \\ =\frac{d}{d z}\left[(z-2)^{2} \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}(z-2)^{2}}\right]_{z=2} \\ =\frac{d}{d z}\left[\frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}}\right]_{z=2} \\ =\left[-2(z+2)^{-3}\right]_{z=2} \\ =\frac{-2}{(2+2)^{3}}=-\frac{1}{32} \end{array}[/latex]

Now about [latex]x=\pi [/latex]
[latex] f(x)=f(\pi)+(x-\pi) f^{\prime}(\pi)+\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{2 !} f^{\prime \prime}(\pi)+\ldots [/latex]
The coefficient of [latex](x-\pi)^{2} is \frac{f^{\prime \prime}(\pi)}{2 !} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Here } f(x) &=e^{x}+\sin x \\ f^{\prime}(x)&=e^{x}+\cos x \\ f^{\prime \prime}(x)&=e^{x}-\sin x \\ \rho^{\prime}(\pi)&=e^{\pi}-\sin \pi=e^{\pi}-0=e^{\pi} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The coefficient of [latex] (x-n)^{2}[/latex] is therefore
[latex] \frac{e^{\pi}}{2 !}=0.5 \exp (\pi)[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
The given equation to be solved is

Which can be rewritten as
[latex] \begin{array}{l} f(x)=x-e^{x}=0 \\ f^{\prime}(x)=1+e^{-x} \end{array}[/latex]
The Newton-raphson iterative formula is
[latex] \begin{aligned} x_{n+1}&=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)}\\ f\left(x_{n}\right)&=x_{n}-e^{-x_{n}} \\ f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right) &=1+e^{-x_{n}} \\ \therefore \quad x_{n+1} &=x_{n}-\frac{x_{n}-e^{-x_{n}}}{1+e^{-x_{n}}} \\ &=\frac{e^{-x_{n}} x_{n}+e^{-x_{n}}}{1+e^{-x_{n}}} \\ &=\left(1+x_{n}\right) \frac{e^{-x_{n}}}{1+e^{-x_{n}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:

The residue at z=a is given for a pole of order n as
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \text{Res} f(a)=\frac{1}{(n-1) !} \frac{d^{n-1}}{d z^{n-1}}\left[(z-a)^{n} f(z)\right]_{z=a} \\ \text{Here, }n=2 \text{ (pole of order 2 ) } \& a=2 \\ \therefore \text{Res} f(2)=\frac{1}{1 !} \frac{d}{d z}\left[(z-2)^{2} f(z)\right]_{z=2} \\ =\frac{d}{d z}\left[(z-2)^{2} \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}(z-2)^{2}}\right]_{z=2} \\ =\frac{d}{d z}\left[\frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}}\right]_{z=2} \\ =\left[-2(z+2)^{-3}\right]_{z=2} \\ =\frac{-2}{(2+2)^{3}}=-\frac{1}{32} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Transfer functions can be written as,
[latex] \begin{aligned} H(s)&=\frac{K(s+1)}{(s+2)(s+4)} \\ \text{Input,}\quad R(s)&=\frac{1}{s}\\ C(s)&=R(s) H(s) \\ \text{Given:} \quad \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s C(s)&=1 \\ \text{or,} \quad\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{s \cdot K(s+1)}{s(s+2)(s+4)}&=1 \\ \text{Or }\quad \frac{K}{8}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K &=8 \\ H(s) &=\frac{8(s+1)}{(s+2)(s+4)} \\ &=-\frac{4}{s+2}+\frac{12}{s+4} \\ h(t) &=\left(-4 e^{-2 t}+12 e^{-4 t}\right) u(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The cross section of a JFET is shown in the following figure. Let [latex]V_{G}[/latex] be -2V and let [latex]V_{P}[/latex] be the initial pinch -off voltage. [latex]\begin{aligned} g_{m} &=g_{m 0}\left[1-\left(\frac{-V_{G}}{V_{P}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right] \\ \text { where, } g_{m o} &=\frac{2 a z}{\rho L} \end{aligned}[/latex]
a [latex]\rightarrow [/latex] Half channel height
L [latex]\rightarrow [/latex] Length of channel
z [latex]\rightarrow [/latex] Depth of channel
[latex]\rho \rightarrow [/latex] Resistivity of channel
since all the parameters are same except width 'W'. So.
[latex] \begin{aligned} W &\propto a\\ \therefore \quad g_{m 0}&=\frac{2 W z}{\rho L} \\ g_{m}&=g_{m o}\left[1-\left(-\frac{V_{G}}{V_{p}}\right)^{1 / 2}\right] \\ g_{\text {initial }}&=W\left[1-\left(-\frac{V_{G_{1}}}{V_{P_{1}}}\right)^{1 / 2}\right] &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, the width is doubled. So,
[latex] \begin{aligned} g_{\text {mmodifed}}&=2 W\left[1-\left(-\frac{V_{G_{1}}}{4 V_{P_{1}}}\right)^{1 / 2}\right] &\ldots(ii)\\ &\qquad \left[\because V_{p}=\frac{q N_{0} a^{2}}{2 \epsilon}\right] \\ \frac{g_{\text {mmodifes }}}{g_{\text {minitial }}}&=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1-\sqrt{\frac{2}{V_{p}}}}{1-\sqrt{\frac{1}{2 V_{p}}}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A speech signal, band limited to 4kHz and peak voltage varying between +5V and -5V, is sampled at the Nyquist rate. Each sample is quantized and represented by 8 bits.

The number of quantization levels required to reduce the quantization noise by a factor of 4 would be
raw_source.solution:
Quantization noise, [latex]N_{q}=\frac{S^{2}}{12} [/latex]
where S= Step size of quantization level
[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{q}^{\prime}&=\frac{N_{q}}{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{S^{2}}{12}&=\frac{S^{2}}{12 \times 4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad s&=\frac{S}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad S&=\frac{V_{P p}}{2^{n}} \\ \text{where,} V_{p}&= \text{ peak-to-peak value}\\ n&= \text{no. of bits/sample} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{v_{\mathrm{rP}}}{2^{n}}&=\frac{V_{p 0}}{2.2^{n}}=\frac{V_{p p}}{2.2^{8}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2^{\pi}&=2^{9}=512 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, number of quantization levels required to reduce the quantization noise by a factor 4 would be 512 .

raw_source.text:
The impulse response h(t) of a linear time invariant continuous time system is given by
h(t)=exp(-2t)u(t), where u(t) denotes the unit step function

The frequency response H([latex]\omega[/latex]) of this system in terms of angular frequency [latex]\omega[/latex], is given by H([latex]\omega[/latex])=
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=\exp (-2 t) u(t) \\ H(\omega) &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t) e^{-j \omega t} d t \\ &=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2 t} e^{-j \omega t} d t=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(2+j \omega) t} d t \\ &=-\left.\frac{1}{2+j \omega} \cdot e^{-(2+j \omega) t}\right|_{0} \\ &=\frac{1}{2+j \omega} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The impulse response h(t) of a linear time invariant continuous time system is given by

Frequency response
[latex] \begin{aligned} X(\omega)&=2 \pi[\delta(\omega-2)+\delta(\omega+2)]\\ H(\omega)&=\frac{1}{2+j \omega} \\ \text{output}\quad Y(\omega)&=H(\omega) X(\omega) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\frac{1}{2+j \omega} \cdot 2 \pi[\delta(\omega-2)+\delta(\omega+2)] \\ =\frac{2 \pi}{2+j 2} \delta(\omega-2)+\frac{2 \pi}{2-j 2} \delta(\omega+2) \\ =\frac{2 \pi}{8}[(2-j 2) \delta(\omega-2)+(2+j 2) \delta(\omega+2)] \\ \left.=\frac{\pi}{4}[2\{\delta(\omega-2)+\delta(\omega+2)\}+j 2\{\delta(\omega)+2)-\delta(\omega-2)\}\right] \\ =\frac{\pi}{2}[\delta(\omega-2)+\delta(\omega+2)]-j \frac{\pi}{2}[\delta(\omega-2)-\delta(\omega+2)] \\ \therefore \quad y(t)=\frac{\cos 2 t}{2}+\frac{\sin 2 t}{2} \\ =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos 2 t+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin 2 t\right] \\ =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos (2 t-0.25 \pi) \\ =2^{-0.5} \cos (2 t-0.25 \pi) \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider two independent random variables X and Y with identical distributions. The variables X and Y take values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities [latex]\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}\;  and \; \frac{1}{4}[/latex] respectively. What is the conditional probability P(X+Y=2|X-Y=0)?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{c} P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0) \\ =\frac{P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)}{P(X-Y=0)} \\ P(X-Y=0)=P(X=0, Y=0)\\ +P(X=1, Y=1)+P(X=2, Y=2) \\ =P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0)+P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ +P(X=2) \cdot P(Y=2) \\ =\frac{3}{8} \\ P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)=P(X=1, Y=1) \\ =P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ =\frac{1}{16} \\ \therefore \quad P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0)=-\frac{1}{16} \times \frac{8}{3}=\frac{1}{6} \end{array}[/latex]

Signal power,

raw_source.text: A function [latex]n(x)[/latex]  satisfied the differential equation [latex]\frac{ d^{2}n(x)}{dx^{2}}-\frac{n(x)}{L^{2}}=0[/latex] where L is a constant. The boundary conditions are : [latex]n(0) = K[/latex] and [latex]n(\infty )[/latex] = 0. The solution to this equation is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \left(D^{2}-\frac{1}{L^{2}}\right) n(x) &=0 \\ D^{2}-\frac{1}{L^{2}} &=0 \\ D &=\pm \frac{1}{L} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, the solution is
[latex] \begin{aligned} n(x) &=C_{1} e^{x / L}+C_{2} e^{-x / L} \\ n(0) &=K \Rightarrow C_{1}+C_{2}=K \\ n(\infty) &=0 \Rightarrow C_{1}=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad C_{2} &=K \\ \text { Therefore, } n(x) &=K \exp (-x / L) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]e^{y}=x^{1/x}[/latex], then y has a
raw_source.solution:
[latex]e^{y}=x^{1 / x}[/latex]
Taking natural log on both sides.
[latex] y=\frac{1}{x} \ln x[/latex]
Differentiating on both sides,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}-\frac{\ln x}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}(1-\ln x) \\ \Rightarrow & d x \\ \Rightarrow 1-\ln x &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \ln x &=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x &=\mathrm{e} \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-2}{x^{3}}[1-\ln x]+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[2-\ln x+1] \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[3-\ln x]\\ \text{Putting, }x&=e_{1} \\ \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\right|_{x=e}&=\frac{-1}{e^{3}}[3-1]=\frac{-2}{e^{3}} \lt 0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, second derivative is negative, therefore,
y has maxima at x= e.

since fair coin is tossed independently four times,

relative permittivity of the medium is 4, the magnitude of the time-average
power density vector (in W/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]) is
raw_source.solution:
Magnitude of the time-average power density
vector
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{a v} &=\frac{E^{2}}{2 \eta} \\ \text { where, } \quad\eta &=\sqrt{\mu / \epsilon} \\ \eta &=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{4 \epsilon_{0}}}=\frac{\eta_{0}}{2}=\frac{120 \pi}{2} \\ P_{a v} &=\frac{1^{2}}{2\left(\frac{120 \pi}{2}\right)}=\frac{1}{120 \pi} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]e^{y}=x^{1/x}[/latex], then y has a
raw_source.solution:
[latex]e^{y}=x^{1 / x}[/latex]
Taking natural log on both sides.
[latex] y=\frac{1}{x} \ln x[/latex]
Differentiating on both sides,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}-\frac{\ln x}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}(1-\ln x) \\ \Rightarrow & d x \\ \Rightarrow 1-\ln x &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \ln x &=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x &=\mathrm{e} \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-2}{x^{3}}[1-\ln x]+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[2-\ln x+1] \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[3-\ln x]\\ \text{Putting, }x&=e_{1} \\ \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\right|_{x=e}&=\frac{-1}{e^{3}}[3-1]=\frac{-2}{e^{3}} \lt 0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, second derivative is negative, therefore,
y has maxima at x= e.

raw_source.text:
A fair coin is tossed independently four times. The probability of the event "the
number of time heads shown up is more than the number of times tail shown up"
raw_source.solution:
The only 5 events when the number of times of
heads show up is more than the number of times
tails show up are given below:
[latex] \begin{array}{cccc} H&H&H&H\\ H&H&H&T\\ H&H&T&H\\ H&T&H&H\\ T&H&H&H \end{array}[/latex]
since fair coin is tossed independently four times,
the probability of each above events is
[latex] \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{16} [/latex]
All above events are mutually exclusive, so, total
probability
[latex] =\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}=\frac{5}{16}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the circuit shown, the switch S is open for a long time and is closed at [latex]t=0[/latex]. The current [latex]i(t)[/latex] for [latex]t\geq 0^{+}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Method 1:
At [latex]t = 0^{-}[/latex]. the circuit is shown below:


Current will divide equally in both [latex]10\Omega[/latex] resistors as shown in diagram.
At [latex]t\geq 0^{+}[/latex], the circuit ins-domain is shown below:


[latex] [L = 15 mH, i(O+) = i(O^{-}) = 0.75 A][/latex]
The above circuit can be rearranged as given below:


Applying nodal analysis,
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\frac{V(s)-\frac{1.5}{s}}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)+15 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s}=0 \\ &\frac{\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s}}{10 s}-\frac{15 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}} \\ &=\frac{15}{10}\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s+5}{5\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right]\\ & \text { V(s) }\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}+5}{5\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right] \\ =& 15\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}-10 \mathrm{s} \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right] \\ & \text { (1 }\left.+10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right) V(s)=\frac{\left(10+7.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}{2 s}\left[\frac{s+1000}{1000}\right] \\ &V(s) =\frac{10000+7.5 \mathrm{s}}{2000 \mathrm{s}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{array}{l} V(s)=\frac{10000+7.5 s}{2 s(s+1000)} \\ =\frac{10000}{2 \times 1000 s}+\frac{\{10000+7.5(-1000)\}}{2(-1000)(s+1000)} \\ =\frac{5}{s}-\frac{1.25}{s+1000} \end{array}[/latex]
Taking inverse Laplace transform,
[latex] \begin{aligned} v(t)&=5-1.25 e^{-1000 t} \mathrm{V}\\ i(t) &=\frac{v(t)}{10} \\ &=0.5-0.125 e^{-1000 t} \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A continuous time LTI system is described by [latex]\frac{d^{2}y(t)}{dt^{2}}+4\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+3y(t)=2\frac{dx(t)}{dt}+4x(t)[/latex]
Assuming zero initial conditions, the response y(t) of the above system for the input [latex]x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)[/latex] is given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{d^{2} y(t)}{d t^{2}}+\frac{4 d y(t)}{d t}+3 y(t)=\frac{2 d x(t)}{d t}+4 x(t) [/latex]
Taking Laplace transform on both sides (assuming
zero initial conditions).
[latex] \begin{aligned} s^{2} Y(s)+4 s Y(s)+3 Y(s)&=2 s X(s)+4 X(s) \\ \text{or }\quad \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}&=\frac{2 s+4}{s^{2}+4 s+3} \\ &=\frac{2(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that
[latex] \begin{aligned} x(t) &=e^{2 t} u(t) \\ x(s) &=\frac{1}{s+2} \\ Y(s) &=\frac{2(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+2)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking inverse Laplace transform on both sides.
[latex] y(t)=(e^{-t}-e^{-3t})u(t)[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The transfer function of a discrete time LTI system is given by
[latex]H(z)=\frac{2-\frac{3}{4}z^{-1}}{1-\frac{3}{4}z^{-1}+\frac{1}{8}z^{-2}}[/latex]
Consider the following statements:
S1: The system is stable and causal for ROC: |z| [latex]\gt[/latex] 1/2
S2: The system is stable but not causal for ROC:| z| [latex]\lt[/latex] 1/4
S3: The system is neither stable nor causal for ROC: 1/4 [latex]\lt[/latex] |z| [latex]\lt[/latex] 1/2
Which one of the following statements is valid ?
raw_source.solution:
A discrete-time LTI system is causal if and only if the ROC of its system function is the exterior of a circle, including infinity.
A discrete-time LTI system is stable if and only if the ROC of its system function includes the unit circle, [latex]|z|=1 [/latex]
[latex] H(z)=\begin{array}{l}\left(1-\frac{1}{4} z^{-1}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{2} z^{-1}\right) \\ \left(1-\frac{1}{4} z^{-1}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{2} z^{-1}\right)\end{array} [/latex]
or [latex]H(z)=\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{4} z^{-1}}+\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2} z^{-1}} [/latex]
For [latex]\mathrm{ROC}:|z| \gt \frac{1}{2},[/latex]
the system is stable and causal.
For [latex]\mathrm{ROC}:|z| \lt \frac{1}{4}, [/latex]
ROC does not include unit circle. So, system is not stable.
For [latex]ROC: \frac{1}{4} \lt |z| \lt \frac{1}{2},[/latex]
ROC does not include unit circle. So, system is not stable. Also ROC is not the exterior of [latex]|z|=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] .So, it is not causal.
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Both S2 and S3 are true
Both S1 and S3 are true
S1, S2 and S3 are all

raw_answer.option_text: Both S1 and S3 are true

feed forward path. For a unit set input, the transfer function of the controller that

raw_source.solution:
Steady state error,
[latex] \begin{aligned} e_{s s} &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{s R(s)}{1+G(s) G_{c}(s)} \\ r(t) &=u(t) \\ R(s) &=\frac{1}{s} \\ e_{ss} &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{s \cdot \frac{1}{s}}{1+G(s) G_{c}(s)} \\ e_{ss}&=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{1+G(s) G_{c}(s)} \\ \text { Taking, } \quad G_{c}(s) &=\frac{s+1}{s+2}, e_{s s}=\frac{2}{3} \\ \text { Taking, } \quad G_{c}(s) &=\frac{s+2}{s+1}, e_{s s}=\frac{1}{3} \\ \text { Taking, } \quad G_{c}(s) &=\frac{(s+1)(s+4)}{(s+2)(s+3)}, e_{s s}=\frac{3}{5} \\ \text { Taking, } \quad & G_{c}(s)=1+\frac{2}{s}+3 s, e_{s s}=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

the probability of bit error

For phase cross-over frequency, [latex]\phi=-180^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad-180 &=-90^{\circ}-2 \tan ^{-1}(\omega / 10) \\ \Rightarrow & \omega=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ s &=j \omega \\ \text { Put, } \quad G(j \omega) H(j \omega) &=\frac{100}{j \omega(j \omega+100)^{2}} \\ |G(j \omega) H(j \omega)|_{\omega=10} &=\frac{100}{\omega\left(\omega^{2}+100\right)} \\ &=\frac{100}{10(200)}=\frac{1}{20} \\ \text { G.M. } &=\frac{1}{\mid G(j \omega) H(j \omega)}=20 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.solution:
For M-ary
[latex] d=2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{M}\right) \sqrt{E_{s}}[/latex]
Distance of any point from origin is [latex]\sqrt{E}_{s} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{For, 4-ary}, r_{1}&=\sqrt{E_{s_{1}}} \\ 8-\text { ary, } \quad r_{2}&=\sqrt{E_{s_{2}}}\\ \text { For, } 4-\text { ary } M=4, d_{1}&=2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) r_{1} \\ 8-\text { ary } M=8 ; d_{2}&=2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right) r_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \text { if } d_{1}=d_{2}=d \text { then } \\ 2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) r_{1}=d \Rightarrow r_{1}=\frac{d}{\sqrt{2}}=0,707 d \\ 2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right) r_{2}=d \\ \Rightarrow r_{2}=\frac{d}{2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)}=1.307 d \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:

Which is a linear differential equation
[latex] \frac{d x}{d t}+P x=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P t t=e^{1 \frac{1}{t} d t}} [/latex]
[latex] =e^{\log _{e} t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex] \begin{aligned} x \cdot(I F)&=\int Q \cdot(I F) d t+C \\ x \cdot t&=\int 1 \cdot t \cdot d t+C \\ x t&=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C \\ x&=\frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t} \\ \text{Put},x(1)=\frac{1}{2}&\\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow\quad C&=0 \\ \text{So, }\left[x=\frac{t}{2}\right]& \text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Given [latex]f(z)=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3}[/latex]. If C is a counterclockwise path in the z-plane such that |z+1|=1, the value of [latex]\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint_{C}f(z)dz[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(z) &=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3} \\ &=\frac{(z+3)-2(z+1)}{(z+1)(z+3)} \\ &=\frac{-z+1}{(z+1)(z+3)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Poles are at -1 and -3 i.e. (-1,0) and (-3,0)
From figure below of |z+1|=1
we see that (-1,0) is inside the circle and (-3,0) is outside the circle.


Residue theorem says,
[latex] \frac{1}{2 \pi j} \oint_{C} f(z) d z= [/latex] Residue of those poles which are inside C .
So, the required integral [latex]\frac{1}{2 \pi j} \oint_{C} f(z) d z [/latex] is given by the residue of function at pole (-1,0) (which is inside the circle).
This residue is [latex]=\frac{-(-1)+1}{(-1+3)}=\frac{2}{2}=1[/latex]

raw_source.text: The direction of vector A is radially outward from the origin, with [latex]|A|=kr^{n}[/latex]  where [latex]r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}[/latex] and [latex]k[/latex] is a constant. The value of [latex]n[/latex] for which [latex]\bigtriangledown \cdot A=0[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]|A|=k r^{n} [/latex]
[latex] \vec{A}=k r^{n} \hat{a}_{r}[/latex] (since it is radially outward)
[latex] abla \cdot \vec{A}[/latex] in spherical coordinate is
[latex] egin{aligned} abla \cdot \vec{A} &= rac{1}{r^{2}} 2 rac{\partial}{\partial A}\left(r^{2} A_{r} ight)+ rac{1}{r \sin heta} rac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(A_{0} \sin heta ight)+ rac{1}{r \sin heta} rac{\partial}{\partial \phi} A_{0} \ & abla \cdot \vec{A}= rac{1}{r^{2}} rac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{2} k r^{n} ight)+0+0 \ & abla \cdot \vec{A}= rac{k}{r^{2}} rac{\partial}{\partial r_{2}}\left(r^{n+2} ight) \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, [latex] abla \cdot \vec{A}[/latex] will be zero if [latex] rac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{n+2} ight)[/latex] will be zero.
and [latex] rac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{n+2} ight)[/latex] will be zero if [latex]r^{n+2}[/latex] will be constant

raw_source.text: The maximum value of [latex]f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5[/latex] in the interval [1, 6] is
raw_source.solution:
We need absolute maximum of
[latex] f(x)=x^{3}-9 x^{2}+24 x+5 [/latex] in the interval [1,6]
First find local maximum if any by putting [latex]f^{\prime}(x)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{i.e.}\quad f^{\prime}(x)&=3 x^{2}-18 x+24=0\\ \text{i.e.}\quad x^{2}-6 x+8&=0 \\ x &=2,4 \\ \text { Now } \quad f^{\prime \prime}(x) &=6 x-18 \\ f^{\prime \prime}(2) &=12-18=-6 \lt 0\\ &\text{(So x=2 is a point of local maximum)}\\ \text{ and }f^{\prime \prime}(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ &\text{(So x=4 is a point of local minimum)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now tabulate the values of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below:
[latex] \begin{array}{l|l} x & f(x) \\ 1 & 21 \\ 2 & 25 \\ 6 & 41 \end{array}[/latex]
Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.

raw_source.solution:

[latex] \frac{d x}{d t}+P x=Q[/latex]

Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P t t=e^{1 \frac{1}{t} d t}} [/latex]
[latex] =e^{\log _{e} t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex] \begin{aligned} x \cdot(I F)&=\int Q \cdot(I F) d t+C \\ x \cdot t&=\int 1 \cdot t \cdot d t+C \\ x t&=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C \\ x&=\frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t} \\ \text{Put},x(1)=\frac{1}{2}&\\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow\quad C&=0 \\ \text{So, }\left[x=\frac{t}{2}\right]& \text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex]F(\theta)=\cos ^{4} \theta, 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi / 2[/latex]
we know that directivity D is
[latex] D=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\pi_{\mathrm{rad}}} \qquad\ldots(1)[/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{F}(\theta) [/latex] is nothing but radiation intensity [latex] u(\theta, \phi)[/latex] and
[latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}} [/latex] is radiated power.
[latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \phi\qquad\ldots(2)[/latex]
above equation is written from the formula
[latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\iint_{\theta \phi} u(\theta, \phi) d \Omega[/latex]
where [latex]\alpha \Omega[/latex] is solid angle and [latex]d \Omega=\sin \theta d \theta d \phi [/latex]
So from (2)
[latex] \begin{aligned} W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin d \theta d \phi \\ W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=2 \pi \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \theta \\W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=-2 \pi\left[\frac{\cos ^{5} \theta}{5}\right]_{0}^{\pi / 2}\\ W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=\frac{2 \pi}{5}&\ldots(3)\\ \text { So, } \quad D&=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{5}\right)}=10 u_{\max }=10\\ &\text { In } \mathrm{dB} \text { directivity }=10 \mathrm{log}_{10} \mathrm{D}=10 \mathrm{dB}\end{aligned}[/latex]

A system with transfer function
[latex]G(s)=\frac{(s^{2}+9)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)}[/latex]
is excited by sin([latex]\omega[/latex] t). The steady-state output of the system is zero at
raw_source.solution:
Transfer function is
[latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \\ \text{Input }\quad X(s)&=L \cdot T[\sin \omega t]\\ X(s)&=\frac{\omega}{s^{2}+\omega^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So output
[latex] Y(s)=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}[/latex]
Now
[latex] \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} y(t)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} S Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}[/latex]
this will be zero if [latex] s^{2}+\omega^{2}[/latex] will cancel [latex]\left(s^{2}+9\right)[/latex] term as only then final value theorem will be applicable.
So at [latex]\omega^{2}=9 \Rightarrow \omega=3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec},[/latex] steady state output will be zero.

raw_source.text: T he input [latex]x(t)[/latex] and output [latex]y(t)[/latex] of a system are related as [latex]y(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x(\tau )cos(3\tau )d\tau[/latex]. The system is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y&=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau) \cos (3 \tau) d \tau \\ y\left(t-t_{0}\right)&=\int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} x(\tau) \cos (3 \tau) d \tau \\ y^{\prime}(t) \text { for input } &x\left(t-t_{0}\right) \text { , is }\\ y^{\prime}(t)&=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x\left(\tau-t_{0}\right) \cos 3 \tau d \tau \\ y^{\prime}(t)&=\int_{-\infty}^{\left(t-t_{0}\right)} x(\tau) \cos 3\left(\tau+t_{0}\right) d \tau \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] y^{\prime}(t) \neq y\left(t-t_{0}\right)[/latex]
so system is not time invariant for input [latex]x(\tau)=\cos (3 \tau)[/latex] (bounded input)
[latex] y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t} \cos ^{2}(3 \tau) d \tau \rightarrow \infty \text { as } t \rightarrow \infty[/latex]
So, for bounded i/p, o/p is not bounded therefore system is not stable.

First find local maximum if any by putting [latex]f^{\prime}(x)=0 [/latex]

Now tabulate the values of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below:

raw_source.solution:
Case (i):
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=10 \mathrm{V}, R_{L}=1 \Omega, I=3 \mathrm{A} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=I\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+R_{L}\right)=3\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+1\right)\\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=3 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+3 &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Case (ii):
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{L}&=2.5 \Omega, I=2 \mathrm{A}, V_{\mathrm{DC}}=10 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+2.5\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+5 &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From equations (i) and (ii)
[latex] V_{\mathrm{Th}}=9 \mathrm{V} and R_{\mathrm{TH}}=2 \Omega \quad\ldots(iii)[/latex]
Now, [latex]V_{Th}[/latex] depends on independent voltage source and varies with applied voltage. [latex]R_{Th}[/latex] does not depend on voltage source and is same for any applied voltage source, since voltage_ source is short circuited while calculating [latex]R_{Th}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{For }V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=6 \mathrm{V}, R_{\mathrm{L}}=1 \Omega, I=7 / 3 \\ V_{T h}&=I\left(R_{T h}+R_{L}\right) \\ V_{T h}&=\frac{7}{3}(2+1)=7 V &\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \because [/latex]The network is linear and non reciprocal, it may
contain dependent voltage source
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad V_{T h}&=a V+b \\ \Rightarrow \quad 9&=a 10+b \quad \text{from equation (iii)} \\ \text{and }\quad 7&=a 6+b \quad\text{from equation (iv)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving, we get a=1/2 and b=4
[latex] \therefore \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}=\frac{V}{2}+4=\frac{8}{2}+4=8 \mathrm{V}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]U[/latex] and [latex]V[/latex] be two independent zero mean Gaussian random variables of variances [latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex] and [latex]\frac{1}{9}[/latex] respectively. The probability [latex]P\left ( 3V\geq 2U \right )[/latex] is

U and V are independent random variables and can be expressed in terms of mean and variance as shown below:
[latex] \begin{aligned} U &=N\left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) \\ V &=N\left(0, \frac{1}{9}\right) \\ \because \quad W &=3 v-2 U \\ \therefore W &=N\left(0,9 \times \frac{1}{9}+4 \times \frac{1}{4}\right)=N(0,2) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence W is Gaussian variable with mean 0 and variance 2.

raw_source.text: A system described by a linear, constant coefficient, ordinary, first order differential equation has an exact solution given by y(t) for t > 0, when the forcing function is x(t) and the initial condition is y(0). raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{d y(t)}{d t}+k y(t)=x(t) [/latex]
Taking Laplace transform of both sides, we have
[latex] s Y(s)-y(0)+k Y(s)=X(s) [/latex]
[latex] Y(s)[s+k]=X(s)+y(0) [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow Y(s)=\frac{X(s)}{s+k}+\frac{y(0)}{s+k} [/latex]
Taking inverse Laplace transform, we have
[latex] y(t)=e^{-k t} x(t)+y(0) e^{-k t} [/latex]
So if we want -2y(t) as a solution both x(t) and y(0) has to be multiplied by -2; hence change x(t) by -2x(t) and y(0) by -2y(0).

raw_source.text:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly till both head and tail appear at least once. The
average number of tosses required is____.
raw_source.solution:
To get both head and Tail atleast once. We have to toss minimum two times. The random variable x represents first toss starting with Head.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(x) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ E(x) &=\Sigma x \cdot P(x) & \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Y represents first toss starting with Tail.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline y & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(y) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] The average number of tosses required
[latex] =E(x)+E(y)=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=3[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A continuous, linear time-invariant filter has an impulse response h(t) described by
[latex]h(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} 3 &for \; 0\leq t\leq 3 \\ 0&otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
When a constant input of values 5 is applied to this filter, the steady state output is_____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}3, & \text { for } 0 \leq t \leq 3 \\0, & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right.\\ h(t) &=3[u(t)-u(t-3)] \\ H(s) &=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \\ \therefore \quad x(t) &=5 \\ \text { Then } x(s) &=\frac{5}{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that
[latex] Y(s)=H(s) X(s)=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \cdot \frac{5}{s} [/latex]
Steady state output
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot \frac{15}{s} \frac{\left(1-e^{-3 s}\right)}{s} \\ =15 \cdot \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} 3 e^{-3 s} \quad[\because \quad \text { L-Hospital's rule }] \\ \quad=45 \end{array}[/latex]

Given that, [latex]\quad G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)} [/latex]
Using root locus method, the break point can be obtain as


[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad 1+G(s)&=0 \\ 1+\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)} &=0 \\ \text{or }\quad K&=-(s+2)(s-1)\\ \frac{d K}{d s} &=-2 s-1=0 \\ \text{or }\quad s &=-0.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]
To have, both the poles at the same directions
[latex] \begin{aligned} |G(s)|_{s=0.5} &=1 \\ K &=2.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A BJT is biased in forward active mode. Assume [latex]V_{BE}[/latex] = 0.7 V, kT/q = 25mV and reverse saturation current [latex]I_{S}=10^{-13} A[/latex]. The transconductance of the BJT (in mA/V) is _____.
raw_source.solution:
We know that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} g_{m} &=\frac{I_{c}}{V_{T}} \\ \text{where}\quad I_{c} &=I_{s} e^{\frac{V_{B E}}{V_{T}}}\\ \text { So, } I_{c}&=10^{-13} \times e^{\frac{0.7}{0.025}} \\ I_{c}&=0.144 \mathrm{mA}\\ \text { Hence, }\quad g_{m}&=\frac{0.144}{0.025}=5.76 \mathrm{mAN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The doping concentrations on the p-side and n-side of a silicon diode are [latex]1\times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex]1 \times 10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex], respectively. A forward bias of 0.3 V is applied to the diode. At T=300K, the
intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon [latex]n_{i}=1.5 \times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex] and [latex]\frac{KT}{q}=26mV[/latex]. The electron concentration at the edge of
the depletion region on the p-side is
raw_source.solution:
The electron concentration at the edge of the depletion region on the p-side is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} n_{p} &=n_{p_{0}} \exp \left[\frac{q V_{t}}{k T}\right] \\ \text { where, } n_{p_{0}} &=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{N_{A}} \\ n_{p_{0}} &=\frac{\left(1.5 \times 10^{10}\right)^{2}}{10^{16}}=2.25 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
We then have
[latex] \begin{array}{l} n_{p}=2.25 \times 10^{4} \exp \left[\frac{0.3}{0.026}\right]\\ n_{p}=2.25 \times 10^{4} \times 1.025 \times 10^{5} \\ n_{0}=2.306 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{cm}^{-3} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The output F in the digital logic circuit shown in the figure is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} A &=X \oplus Y \\ B &=A \odot Z=A \cdot Z+\bar{A} \bar{Z} \\ &=Z(X \oplus Y)+(X \odot Y) \bar{Z} \\ F &=A B \\ &=(X \oplus Y)[Z(X \oplus Y)+\bar{Z}(\overline{X \oplus Y})] \\ &=Z[(X \oplus Y)(X \oplus Y)+\bar{A}(\overline{X \oplus Y})(X \oplus Y)] \\ &\begin{aligned} \text { as we know } A \cdot A &=A \\ A \cdot \bar{A} &=0 \\ &=Z[(X \oplus Y)+0] \\ &=\bar{X} Y Z+X \bar{Y} Z \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The digital logic shown in the figure satisfies the given state diagram when [latex]Q_{1}[/latex] is connected to input A of the XOR gate.

Suppose the XOR gate is replaced by an XNOR gate. Which one of the following options preserves the state diagram ?
raw_source.solution:
Initially when X-OR gate is connected to the input of flip flop 2 i.e. input of [latex]D_{2}[/latex] , i.e.
[latex] D_{2}=A \oplus S=Q_{1} \oplus S[/latex]
Now, X-OR is replaced by X-NOR, keeping state diagram to be unchanged it means the input to [latex] D_{2}[/latex] should not get changed.
When replaced by X-NOR gate
Now [latex]D_{2}=A \odot S [/latex]
Also, we know that
[latex] \overline{A \oplus B}= \overline{A} \oplus B=A \odot B [/latex]
We require output to be as [latex]D_{2}=A \oplus S [/latex]
So, to keep this output, A should be connected to
[latex] \bar{Q}_{1}[/latex] as

options: Input A is connected to [latex]\bar{Q}_{1}[/latex] and S is complemented

raw_source.text: Let [latex]x[n]=(-\frac{1}{9})^{n} u(n)-(-\frac{1}{3})^{n} u(-n-1)[/latex]. The Region of Convergence (ROC) of the z -transform of x[n].
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(n) &=\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)^{n} u(n)-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n} u(-n-1)}{x_{1}(n)} \frac{1}{x_{2}(n)} \\ x_{1}(n) &=\left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)^{n} u(n) \rightarrow \text { Right sided signal } \\ x_{1}(z) &=\frac{1}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{9}\right) z^{-1}} \\ \operatorname{ROC}|z| & \geq\left|\frac{1}{9}\right| \text { or }|z|>\frac{1}{9} \\ x_{2}(n) &=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n} u(-n-1) \rightarrow \text { Left sided signal } \\ x_{2}(z) &=\frac{1}{1-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) z^{-1}} ; \quad|z| \leq \frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, when both the transforms are added using linearity property.
ROC must be between
[latex] \frac{1}{3}>|z|>\frac{1}{9}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a discrete time periodic signal [latex]x[n]=sin(\frac{\pi n}{5})[/latex]. Let [latex]a_{k}[/latex] be the complex Fourier series coefficients of x[n]. The coefficients [latex]\{a_{k}\}[/latex] are non-zero when
k = Bm[latex]{\pm }[/latex]1, where m is any integer. The value of B is ____.
raw_source.solution:
From discrete Fourier series definition
[latex] \begin{array}{l} x[n]=\sum_{K=0}^{N-1} a_{K} e^{j K\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}\right) n}\\ =a_{-1} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}+a_{0}+a_{1} e^{i \frac{2 \pi}{N} n} \quad \ldots(i)\\ x[n]=\frac{-1}{2 j} e^{-i \frac{\pi}{5} n}+\frac{1}{2 j} e^{i \frac{\pi}{5} n} \end{array}[/latex]
Also given
[latex] x[n]=\sin \left(\frac{\pi n}{5}\right) [/latex]
where [latex] N=10\left[\frac{2 \pi}{N}=\frac{\pi}{5} \Rightarrow N=10\right] [/latex]
By comparison [latex]a_{1}=\frac{1}{2 j} and a_{9}=a_{-1}=\frac{-1}{2 j} [/latex]
As the TFS coefficient [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is also periodic with period N=10.
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{1} &=a_{11}=a_{21} \cdots \\ a_{-1} &=a_{9}=a_{19} \cdots \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is non-zero for [latex]K=B m \pm 1 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{cc} B m \pm 1=1& \quad 9 \cdots\\ -1 &\quad11\ldots\\ \text{For }m=0 \quad for& \quad m=1 \\ \end{array}[/latex]
To satisfy this condition B must be '10' where 'm' is any integer.

raw_source.text:
A system is described by the following differential equation, where u(t) is the input to the system and y(t) is the output of the system.
[latex]\dot{y}(t)+5y(t)=u(t)[/latex]
when y(0) = 1 and u(t) is a unit step function, y(t) is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\dot{y}(t)+5 y(t)=u(t) [/latex]
Taking the Laplace transform of the above equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} s Y(s)-y(0)+5 & r(s)=\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+5) r(s)-1 & =\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+5) r(s) & =\frac{s+1}{s} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{(s+1)}{s(s+5)} \\ \frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+5)} & =\frac{(s+1)}{s(s+5)} \\ A&=0.2 \\ B&=\frac{-4}{-5}=0.8 \\ r(s) &=\frac{0.2}{s}+\frac{0.8}{(s+5)}\\ y(t)&=0.2+0.8 e^{-5 t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the state space model of a system, as given below [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_{1}\\ \dot{x}_{2}\\ \dot{x}_{3} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 1&0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\\ 0&0 & -2 \end{vmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 4\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}u;y\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 &1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix}[/latex] The system is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \left[\begin{array}{c}\dot{x}_{1} \\ \dot{x}_{2} \\ \dot{x}_{3}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{array}\right] u \\ y&=[1 \;1 \;1 ]\left[\begin{array}{r}x_{3} \\ x_{3} \\ x_{3}\end{array}\right] \\ A&=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ 0\end{array}\right], C=\left[1\;1\;1\right] \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Check for controllability:
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{C} &=\left[B: A B: A^{2} B\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 0 & 4 & -8 \\ 4 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
For controllable.
[latex] \left|Q_{c}\right| \neq 0[/latex]
Here , [latex]\quad\left|Q_{c}\right|=4(0)=0 \quad \therefore[/latex] Uncontrollable
Check for observability:
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{0} &=\left[C^{T}: A^{T} C^{T}: A^{2 T} C^{T}\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
For observable,
[latex] \left|Q_{0}\right| \neq 0[/latex]
Here, [latex]\left|Q_{o}\right|=1 \quad \therefore [/latex] Observable

raw_source.text:
The phase margin in degrees of [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+0.1)(s+1)(s+10)}[/latex]
 calculated using the asymptotic Bode plot is _____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} \frac{10}{0.7 \times 10\left(\frac{s}{0.1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{10}+1\right)} \\ =\frac{10}{\left(\frac{s}{0.1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{10}+1\right)} \\ \text { Amount of shitt }=2010 \mathrm{g} \mathrm{K}=20 \mathrm{log} 10=20 \mathrm{dB} \end{array}[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} -20dB&=\frac{20-0}{\log0.1-\log\omega_{gc}}\\ \text{or},\omega_{gc}&=1\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{sec}&\ldots(i)\\ \mathrm{PM}&=180^{\circ}+\angle GH(j\omega|_{at\omega=\omega_{wc}}&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From the given transfer function,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \angle G(j \omega)&=-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{g c}}{0.1}\right)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{g c}}{1}\right) \\ &-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{g c}}{10}\right) \\ \alpha \angle G(j(1)) &=-84.289^{\circ}-45^{\circ}-5.711^{\circ} \\ &=-135^{\circ} &\ldots(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] From equation(ii) and (iii) we get,

raw_source.text: For the following feedback system [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex]. The 2% settling time of the step response is required to be less than 2 seconds. Which one of the following compensators C(s) achieves this ?
raw_source.solution:
Given open loop transfer function is
[latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} \\ \therefore T(s)&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)+1} \\ T(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+3 s+3} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing equation (i) with standard transfer function
[latex] \xi \omega_{n}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] 2% settling time
[latex] \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{1.5}=2.67>2 \mathrm{sec} [/latex]
Thus, in order to make settling time [latex]\left(\tau_{s}\right)[/latex] less than 2 sec, PD controller should be used. Hence, option (C) is the correct choice.
Where, [latex]C(s)=2(s+4) [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] New transfer function [latex]=T^{\prime}(G)[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{C(s) G(s)}{1+C(s) G(s)}=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+3 s+2+2 s+8} [/latex]
or [latex]T^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+5 s+10}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{5 / 2}=\frac{4}{2.5}=1.6[/latex]

Let X be a real-valued random variable with E[X] and [latex]E[X^{2}][/latex]
 denoting the mean values of X and [latex]X^{2}[/latex]
, respectively. The relation which always holds true is
raw_source.solution:
Variance [latex]\sigma_{X}^{2}=E[X^{2}]-[E(X)]^{2} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a random process [latex]X(t)=\sqrt{2}sin(2\pi t+\varphi )[/latex], where the random phase [latex]\varphi[/latex] is uniformly distributed in the interval [latex][0, 2\pi ][/latex] . The auto-correlation [latex]E[X(t_{1})X(t_{2})][/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \left.E\left[X\left(t_{1}\right) X\left(t_{1}\right)\right]=E\left[A \sin \left(2 \pi t_{1}+\phi\right)\right] \times A \sin \left(2 \pi t_{2}+\phi\right)\right] \\ =\frac{A^{2}}{2} E\left[\cos \left[2 \pi\left(t_{1}-t_{2}\right)\right]-\cos \left[2 \pi\left(t_{1}+t_{2}+2 \phi\right)\right]\right. \\ =\frac{A^{2}}{2} \cos \left[2 \pi\left(t_{1}-t_{2}\right)\right. \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]Q(\sqrt{\gamma })[/latex] be the BER of a BPSK system over an AWGN channel with twosided noise power spectral density [latex]N_{0}/2[/latex]. The parameter [latex]\gamma [/latex] is a function of bit energy and noise power spectral density.
A system with two independent and identical AWGN channels with noise power spectral density [latex]N_{0}/2[/latex] is shown in the figure. The BPSK demodulator receives the sum of outputs of both the channels.

If the BER of this system is [latex]Q(b\sqrt{\gamma })[/latex] , then the value of [latex]b[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
since the same signal is passed through two parallel channels and added at the receiver input, the effective distance between the adjacent message points will be [latex]d_{\min }=4 \sqrt{E_{b}}[/latex] and the effective noise PSD(one-sided) will be [latex] N_{\alpha \text { ett }}=2 N_{o} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So},\quad B E R &=Q(\sqrt{\frac{d_{\min }^{2}}{2 N_{o(\mathrm{etl})}}})=Q(\sqrt{\frac{16 E_{D}}{4 N_{o}}}) \\ &=Q(\sqrt{4 \frac{E_{b}}{N_{0}}})=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{0}}}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For single channel case.
[latex] \mathrm{BER}=\alpha(\sqrt{\gamma})=Q(\sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{o}}})[/latex]
So, for the given problem,
[latex] \begin{aligned} B E R=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{0}}})&=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\gamma})=Q(b \sqrt{\gamma}) \\ \text{So, }\quad b=\sqrt{2}&=1.414 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until a 'Head' appears for the first time. Let
L be the number of tosses to get this first ' Head' . The entropy H (L) in bits is
_____.
raw_source.solution:
If P=1, i.e. if 1 toss is required to gets first head.
Then probability to get the first head
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad P_{1}=\frac{1}{2} [/latex]
If P=2; i.e. if 2 tosses are required to get first head.
Then probability to get the first head
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad P_{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]
If P=3; i.e. if 3 tosses are required to get first head.
Then probability to get the first head
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \quad P_{3}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8} \\ \text { Entropy } H=\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i} \log _{2} \frac{1}{P_{i}} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 2}+\frac{1}{4} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 4}+\log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 8}+\frac{1}{16} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 16} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \times 1+\frac{1}{4} \times 2+\frac{1}{8} \times 3+\frac{1}{16} \times 4+\cdots \\ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{(2)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(2)^{3}}+\frac{4}{(2)^{4}}+\cdots \\ H \simeq 2 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In spherical coordinates, let [latex]\hat{a}_{\theta },\hat{a}_{\phi }[/latex] denote unit vectors along the [latex]\theta, \phi[/latex] directions.
[latex]E=\frac{100}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\theta V/m[/latex]
and
[latex]E=\frac{0.265}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\phi A/m[/latex]
represent the electric and magnetic field components of the EM wave at large distances [latex]r[/latex] from a dipole antenna, in free space. The average power (W) crossing the hemispherical shell located at r = 1 km, [latex]0\leq \theta \leq \pi /2[/latex] is ____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E} &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{100}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\theta} V / m \\ &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{0.265}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta \beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\phi} V / m \end{aligned}[/latex]
Poynting vector,
[latex] \vec{P}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{Re}\left[\vec{E} \times \vec{H}^{*}\right]=\frac{26.5}{2 r^{2}} \sin ^{2} \theta \hat{a}_{r} W / m^{2}[/latex]
The average power crossing the given
hemispherical shell is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Power } &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \vec{P} \cdot r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \hat{a}_{r} \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^{3} \theta d \theta \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \frac{2}{3}=55.5 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a parallel plate transmission line, let v be the speed of propagation and Z

raw_source.text: The input impedance of a [latex]\frac{\lambda }{8}[/latex] section of a lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] is found to be real when the other end is terminated by a load [latex]Z_{L}=(R+jX)\Omega[/latex]. [latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{o} \tan \beta l}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right)\\ \text{at }\;l&=\frac{\lambda}{8} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \beta l&=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ \therefore \quad\tan \frac{\pi}{4}&=1 \\ Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{o}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j 50}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given},\quad Z_{L}&=R+j X=R+j 30 \text{ and }Z_{0}=50 \Omega \\ 30 R &=80(50+R) \\ Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{R+j 30+j 50}{50+j(R+j 30)}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{(50-30)+j R}\right]=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{20+j R}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{(R+j 80)(20-j R)}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, only real part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}[/latex] exists, so imaginary
part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{20 R+1600 j-j R^{2}+50 R}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \\ \text { Zimaginary } &=0=\frac{1600-R^{2}}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\\ \therefore \quad R^{2} &=1600 \\ R &=40 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} X(\omega) &=\sum_{K=-\infty}^{\infty} 2 \pi a_{k} \delta\left(0-K \omega\right) \\ a_{K} &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2} x(t) e^{-j K \omega_{0} t} d t \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]7^{\text {th }}[/latex] harmonic power [latex]=\left(2 \pi a_{7}\right)^{2} [/latex]

The capacity of a band-limited additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel is given by [latex]C=Wlog_{2}(1+\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}W})[/latex] bits per second (bps), where W is the channel bandwidth, P is the average power received and [latex]{\sigma^{2}}[/latex] is the one sided power spectral density of the AWGN.

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} C&=W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right) \\ C&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \times \frac{\sigma^{2}}{P} W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{when }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty \\ C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \lim _{w \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{as }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty, \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}\text{ also }\rightarrow \infty \\ \therefore C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \frac{\lim _{\alpha} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}}\right)}{P} \\ &\quad \left[\because \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} x \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)=\log\right]\\ C_{\infty} &=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \log _{2} e\\ C_{\infty} &=1.44\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Input-output relation is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} y[n]&=\alpha_{\mathcal{Y}}(n-1)+\beta x[n] \\ \text{Taking Z-transform, }\\ r(z)&=\alpha z^{-1} \quad Y (z)+\beta X(z) \\ Y(z)&\left[1-\alpha z^{-1}\right]=\beta X(z) \\ \frac{\gamma(z)}{X(z)}&=H(z)=\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha z^{-1}} \\ h[n]&=\beta \cdot \alpha^{n} u[n] \\ \text{Also }&\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h[n]=2 \Rightarrow \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \beta \cdot \alpha^{n} u[n]=2 \\ \frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}&=2 \Rightarrow \beta=2-2 \alpha \\ \Rightarrow 2 a &=2-\beta \\ \alpha &=1-\frac{\beta}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a rectangular waveguide of internal dimensions [latex]a \times b(a \gt b)[/latex], the cur-off

raw_source.solution:
Cut-off frequency of a rectangular waveguide is
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m \pi}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n\pi}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{10}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{20}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text { for } \quad T E_{11} &=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^{2}}+\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ \text { Given, } f_{C T_{11}} &=\frac{f_{C_{I E 10}}+f_{C I E_{20}}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{\frac{c}{2 a}+\frac{c}{a}}{2} \\ \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{1}{2 a}+\frac{1}{a}=\frac{3}{2 a} \\ \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}&=\frac{9}{4 a^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2} &=\frac{5}{4 a^{2}} \\ b &=\frac{2 a}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2 \times \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\ &=2 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A series RC circuit is connected to a DC voltage source at time t = 0. The relation between the source voltage [latex]V_{S}[/latex], the resistance R, the capacitance C, and the current [latex]i(t)[/latex] is given below :

Given that:
[latex] V_{s}=R i(t)+\frac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{t} i(t) d t\qquad\ldots(i)[/latex]
Using Laplace transform,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { WS) }&=R I(s)+\frac{1}{C s} I(s) &\ldots(ii)\\ \text { or } I(s)&=\frac{V(s)}{\left(R+\frac{1}{C S}\right)} &\ldots(iii)\\ \text { For, } V(s)&=\frac{1}{s}&\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From equation (iii) and (iv),
[latex] I(s)=\frac{C}{(R C s+1)}=\frac{1}{R\left(s+\frac{1}{R C}\right)}\qquad\ldots(v)[/latex]
Using inverse Laplace transform in equation (v), we get,
[latex] i(t)=\frac{1}{R} e^{-t / R C}[/latex]
Thus, option (A) is correct.

raw_source.text:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly till both head and tail appear at least once. The
average number of tosses required is____.
raw_source.solution:
To get both head and Tail atleast once. We have to toss minimum two times. The random variable x represents first toss starting with Head.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(x) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ E(x) &=\Sigma x \cdot P(x) & \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Y represents first toss starting with Tail.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline y & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(y) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] The average number of tosses required
[latex] =E(x)+E(y)=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=3[/latex]

We get,,

Also,

raw_source.text: In the circuit shown in the figure, the angular frequency [latex]\omega[/latex] (in rad/s), at which the Norton equivalent impedance as seen from terminals [latex]b-b'[/latex] is purely resistive, is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Finding [latex]Z_{N}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{1 \times j 0.5 \omega}{1+j 0.5 \omega}+\frac{1}{j \omega}=\frac{j \omega}{2+j \omega}+\frac{1}{j \omega} \\ \text { or } Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{2-\omega^{2}+j \omega}{2 j \omega-\omega^{2}}&\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Rationalizing equation (i), we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{\left(2-\omega^{2}\right)+j \omega}{2 j \omega-\omega^{2}} \times \frac{-\omega^{2}-j 2 \omega}{-\omega^{2}-j 2 \omega} \\ &=-\frac{2 \omega^{2}+\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}+j \frac{\left(\omega^{3}-4 \omega\right)}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
In order to have a purely resistive impedance [latex]Z_{\text {bb }}^{\prime} [/latex], the imaginary part of equation (ii) will be equaled to zero.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\therefore \frac{-4 \omega+\omega^{3}}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}=0\\ &\text{or}\quad \omega^{3}=4 \omega \\ &\text{or}\quad \omega=\sqrt{4}=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Let [latex]H_{1}(z)=(1-pz^{-1})^{-1}[/latex], [latex]H_{2}(z)=(1-qz^{-1})^{-1}[/latex], [latex]H(z)=H_{1}(z)+rH_{2}(z)[/latex]. The

raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Here } H_1(z)&=\frac{1}{1-pz^{-1}} \\ H_2(z)&= \frac{1}{1-qz^{-1}}\\ \text{also } p&=\frac{1}{2},\; q=-\frac{1}{4} \\ \therefore \; H(z)&=H_1(z)+rH_2(z) \\ &= \frac{1}{1-pz^{-1}}+\frac{r}{1-qz^{-1}}\\ &= \frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}+\frac{r}{1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1}}\\ H(z)&=\frac{\left ( 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1} \right )+r\left ( 1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1} \right )}{\left ( 1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1} \right )}\;\;...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
zero of [latex]H(z) \Rightarrow [/latex]
[latex] (1+r)-(q+p r) z^{-1}=0 \; \; ...(ii)[/latex]
or [latex]\quad z=\frac{q+p r}{1+r} [/latex]
Since, the zero of H(z) lies on the unit circle
therefore [latex]|z|=1[/latex] or [latex] z=\pm 1 [/latex]
Taking z=1, we get
[latex] z=\frac{q+p r}{1+r}=1 \; \; ...(iii)[/latex]
By solving above expression with [latex]p=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] and [latex] q=-\frac{1}{4},[/latex] we get
[latex] r=-2.5[/latex]
But [latex]|r| \lt 1 \quad [/latex] or [latex]\quad-1 \lt r \lt 1 [/latex]
Taking z=-1 in equation (iii), we get
[latex] r=-0.5[/latex]

The state equation of a second-order linear system is given by

raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]\dot{x}(t)=A x(t), \quad x(0)=x_{0} [/latex]
Taking the Laplace transform
[latex] \begin{aligned} s X(s)-x(0) &=A X(s) \\ [s I-A] X(s) &=x(0) \\ X(s) &=[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) \\ x(t) &=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Condition given are
[latex] \begin{aligned} For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{c}e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t}\end{array}\right] \\ For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{l}e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t}\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using the linearity property in equation (i)
[latex] K_{1} x_{1}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{1}(0) K_{1} [/latex]
[latex] K_{2} x_{2}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{2}(0) K_{2} [/latex]
Using the linearity property as
[latex] \begin{aligned} K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t)&=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} \\ \left[K_{1} x_{1}(0)+K_{2} x_{2}(0)\right] & \quad \ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad X_{3}(s)&=[s I-A]^{-1} x_{3}(0) \\ \text{So, } \quad K_{1}\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]+&K_{2}\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \left[\begin{array}{l}K_{1}+O K_{2} \\ -K_{1}+K_{2}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{1}&=3 \\ K_{2}&=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, from equation (ii), we get x(t)
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t) \\ &=3\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t} \end{array}\right]+8\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{c} 11 e^{-t}-8 e^{-2 t} \\ -1 t e^{-t}+16 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let X be a zero mean unit variance Gaussian random variable. E[|X|] is equal to ______.
raw_source.solution:
For a Gaussian random variable,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{x}(x)&=\frac{1}{\sigma_{x} \sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\left(\frac{\mu-x}{2 \sigma^{2}}\right)^{2}} \\ \text{For mean} (\mu)&=0 \text{ and Variance }\left(\sigma_{x}^{2}\right)=1 \\ f_{X}(x) &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}} \\ E[|x|] &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x| f_{X}(x) d x \\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x| \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x \\ =& \int_{-\infty}^{0}-x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-x^{2}} d x+\int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x\\ &=2 \int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x \\ &\text{Let }\quad -\frac{x^{2}}{2}=t \\ &\therefore \quad-\frac{2 x d x}{2}=d t \\ &\text{Hence }\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty}-e^{-t} d t=0.8 \\ &\therefore \quad E[|x|]=0.8 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

A Fourier transform pair is given by
[latex](\frac{2}{3})^{n} \; u[n+3]\overset{FT}{\leftrightarrow}\frac{Ae^{-j6\pi f}}{1-(\frac{2}{3})e^{-j2 \pi f}}[/latex]
where u [n] denotes the unit step sequence. The values of A is _____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} u(n+3) \stackrel{F.T.}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{Ae^{j6\pi f}}{1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) e^{-i 2 \pi f}}[/latex]
Let, [latex] x[n]=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} u(n+3) [/latex]
Discrete Fourier transform is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} X\left(e^{j \omega}\right)&=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{-j \omega n} \\ &=\sum_{n=-3}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} e^{-j \omega n} \\ \text { Put, } n+3 &=m \\ \text { So, } x\left(e^{i \omega}\right) &=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m-3} e^{-j \omega(m-3)} \\ &=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-3} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m} e^{-j \omega m \cdot e^{j \omega 3}} \\ &=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{3} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3} e^{-j \omega}\right)^{m} \cdot e^{j \omega 3} \\ &=\frac{3.375 \cdot e^{i 2 \pi / 3}}{1-\frac{2}{3} e^{-i 2 \pi t}} \\ &=\frac{3.375 e^{j \pi \pi f}}{1-\frac{2}{3} e^{-i 2 \pi t}} \\ \text{So,}\quad A&=3.375 \end{aligned}[/latex]

A real-valued signal x(t) limited to the frequency band [latex]|f|\leq \frac{W}{2}[/latex] is passed through a linear time invariant system whose frequency response is

The output of the system is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given:} \quad H(f)&=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}e^{-j 4 \pi t}, & |f| \leq \frac{\omega}{2} \\ 0, & |f|>\frac{\omega}{2}\end{array}\right. \\ \text{So, } \quad|H(t)|&=1 \\ H(f)&=e^{-j 2.2 \pi t} \\ H(\omega)&=e^{j 2 \omega} &|f| \leq \frac{\omega}{2} \\ h(t)&=\delta(t-2)\\ \text{As we know that}\\ y(t)&=x(t) * h(t)\\ \text{or}\quad y(t)&=X(\omega) \cdot H(\omega) \\ y(t)&=x(t) * \delta(t-2) \\ y(t)&=x(t-2) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The sequence [latex]x[n]=0.5^{n}u[n][/latex], where u[n] is the unit step sequence, is convolved with itself to obtain y[n]. Then [latex]\sum_{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }y[n][/latex] is _____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given } x[n] &=0.5^{n} u[n] \\ y[n] &=x[n] * x[n] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(k) h(n-k)\\ &=\sum_{K=-\infty}^{\infty}(0.5)^{k} u(k)(0.5)^{n-k} u(n-k) \\ &=(0.5)^{n}\left[\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} u(k) u(n-k)\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Also we know that [latex] u[n] * u[n]=(n+1) u[n] [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Using the above formula, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} y[n]&=(0.5)^{n}(n+1) u[n] \\ \text{Let }p&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(0.5)^{n}(n+1) \\ \text{Also let }a&=0.5 \\ \therefore \quad p&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^{n}(n+1) \\ \rho&=a^{0}(1)+a^{1}(1+1)+a^{2}(2+1)+a^{3}(3+1)+\ldots \\ a p&=a(1)+a^{2}(2)+a^{3}(3)+\cdots \\ p-a p&=a^{0} \cdot 1+a^{1}+a^{2}+\cdots \\ p(1-a)&=\frac{1}{1-a} \\ p&=\frac{1}{(1-a)^{2}} \\ a&=0.5 \text{ or } \frac{1}{2} \\ p&=\frac{1}{\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]

voltages (in mV) of the two BJTs (i.e.,[latex]V_{BE1}-V_{BE2}[/latex]) is _____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]I_{C}[/latex] is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{C} &=I_{S} \exp \left[\frac{V_{B E}}{\eta V_{T}}\right] \\ I_{G} &=I_{S_{1}} \exp \left[\frac{V_{B E_{1}}}{\eta V_{T}}\right] &\ldots(i)\\ I_{C_{2}} &=I_{S_{2}} \exp \left[\frac{V_{B E_{2}}}{\eta V_{T}}\right]&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
According to given condition,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{G}&= I_{C_{2}} \\ I_{S_{1}} \exp \left[\frac{V_{B E_{1}}}{\eta V_{T}}\right]&=I_{S_{2}} \exp \left[\frac{V_{B E_{2}}}{\eta V_{T}}\right] \\ V_{B E_{1}}-V_{B E_{2}} &=\eta V_{T} \ln \left[\frac{I_{S_{2}}}{I_{S_{1}}}\right] \\ V_{B E_{1}}-V_{B E_{2}} &=26 \ln \left[\frac{300 \times 300}{0.2 \times 0.2}\right]\\ \because \quad\eta&=2 for Si BJT\\ V_{B E_{1}}-V_{B E_{2}}&=380 .28 \mathrm{mV} \end{aligned}[/latex]

If [latex]E_{C}[/latex] is the lowest energy level of the conduction band, [latex]E_{V}[/latex] is the highest energy level of the valance band and [latex]E_{F}[/latex] is the Fermi level, which one of the following represents the energy band diagram for the biased N -type semiconductor ?

Consider the common-collector amplifier in the figure (bias circuitry ensures that the transistor operates in forward active region, but has been omitted forsimplicity). Let [latex]I_{C}[/latex] be the collector current, [latex]V_{BE}[/latex] be the base-emitter voltage and [latex]V_{T}[/latex] be the thermal voltage. Also, [latex]g_{m}[/latex] and [latex]r_{0}[/latex] are the small-signal transconductance and output resistance of the transistor, respectively. Which one of the following conditions ensures a nearly constant small signal voltage gain for a wide range of values of [latex]R_{E}[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
AC equivalent circuit for given common collector amplifier is


[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\text {in }}&=\beta r_{e} i_{b}+(1+\beta) i_{b} R_{E} \quad\cdots(i)\\ V_{o}&=(1+\beta) R_{E} i_{b}\quad\cdots(ii)\\ \text{Then}\\ \frac{V_{0}}{V_{\text {in }}}&=\frac{(1+\beta) R_{E}}{\beta r_{e}+(1+\beta) R_{E}}\\ \frac{V_{o}}{V_{\text {in }}}&=\frac{\beta R_{E}}{\beta r_{e}+\beta R_{E}}=\frac{R_{E}}{r_{e}+R_{E}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The condition for small signal voltage gain to be nearly constant is
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{E} & \gt \gt r_{e} \\ R_{E} & \gt \gt \frac{V_{T}}{I_{C}} \\ I_{C} R_{E} &\gt \gt V_{T} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 16-bit ripple carry adder is realized using 16 identical full adders (FA) as shown in the figure. The carry-propagation delay of each FA is 12 ns and the sumpropagation delay of each FA is 15 ns. The worst case delay (in ns) of this 16-bit adder will be ______.

Full adder is a combinational circuit that performs the sum of three bits i.e. add two bits and a carry from previous addition and produces output as sum and carry.
Given carry propagation delay of each [latex] FA= 12\mathrm{nsec}.[/latex]
Sum-propagation delay of each [latex]FA= 15\mathrm{nsec}.[/latex]


As can be seen from above diagram, full adder is not received from previous full adder.
So, in 16-bit ripple carry adder, worst case delay of this 16-bit adder will be
[latex] \begin{aligned} &= (15 \times 12) \mathrm{nsec}. + 15 \mathrm{nsec}.\\ &= 195 \mathrm{nsec}. \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The state transition matrix [latex]\phi (t)[/latex] of a system [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_{1}\\ \dot{x}_{2} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0&0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given } &\left[\begin{array}{l} \dot{x}_{1} \\ \dot{x}_{2} \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{array}\right] \\ A &=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right] \\ [s I-A] &=\left[\begin{array}{ll} s & 0 \\ 0 & s \end{array}\right]-\left[\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll} s & -1 \\ 0 & s \end{array}\right] \\ [s I-A]=s^{2} & \\ \phi(t) &=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{s^{2}}\left[\begin{array}{ll} s & 1 \\ 0 & s \end{array}\right] \\ &=L^{-1}\left[\begin{array}{cc} \frac{1}{s} & \frac{1}{s^{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{s} \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a transfer function [latex]G_{p}(s)=\frac{ps^{2}+3ps-2}{s^{2}+(3+p)s+(2-p)}[/latex] with [latex]p[/latex] a positive real parameter. The maximum value of [latex]p[/latex] until which [latex]G_{p}[/latex] remains stable is ____.
raw_source.solution:
Given transfer function
[latex] G_{p}(s)=\frac{p s^{2}+3 p s-2}{s^{2}+(3+p) s+(2-p)} \qquad\ldots(i)[/latex]
The characteristic equation is
[latex] =s^{2}+(3+p) s+(2-p)\qquad\ldots(ii)[/latex]
Using Routh Hurtwiz criterion,
[latex] \begin{array}{l|ll} s^{2} & 1 & (2-P) \\ s^{1} & (3+p) & 0 \\ s^{0} & (2-p) & 0 \end{array}[/latex]
For system to be remain stable
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2-p & \geq 0 \\ p_{\max } &=1.99 \end{aligned}[/latex]

From (i) and (iv) we get [latex]s=-0.25+j 4.33 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a communication scheme where the binary valued signal X satisfies P{X =+1} = 0.75 and P{X =-1} = 0.25. The received signal Y = X + Z , where Z is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean and variance [latex]\sigma ^{2}[/latex]. The received signal Y is fed to the threshold detector. The output of the threshold detector [latex]\hat{X}[/latex] is:
[latex]\hat{X}=\left\{\begin{matrix} +1 & Y>\tau \\ -1&Y \leq \tau \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
To achieve a minimum probability of error [latex]P\lbrace \hat{X}\neq X \rbrace[/latex] the threshold [latex]\tau[/latex] should be
raw_source.solution:
The optimum threshold value is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \lambda_{0} &=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}\left[\ln \frac{P\left(x_{2}\right)}{P\left(x_{1}\right)}+\frac{x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}\right] \\ x_{1} &=1, \quad x_{2}=-1 \\ P\left(X_{1}\right) &=0.75, P\left(X_{2}\right)=0.25 \\ \lambda_{0} &=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\left[\ln \frac{0.25}{0.75}\right]=-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, [latex]\lambda_{o}[/latex] should be strictly negative.
options:
strictly positive, zero, or strictly negative depending on the nonzero value
of  [latex]\sigma ^{2}[/latex]
