raw_source.text: Consider an n-channel MOSFET having width W, length L, electron mobility in the channel [latex]\mu_{n}[/latex] and oxide capacitance per unit area [latex]C_{ox}[/latex]. If gate-to-source voltage [latex]V_{GS}[/latex]=0.7V, drain-tosource voltage [latex]V_{DS}=0.1V,(\mu_{n}C_{ox})=100\mu A/V^{2}[/latex],threshold voltage [latex]V_{TH}=0.3 V [/latex] and (W/L)=50,then the transconductance [latex]g_{m}[/latex](in mA/V) is ___________.
raw_source.solution:
Given that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{G S} &=0.7 \mathrm{V}, V_{T H}=0.3 \mathrm{V}, V_{D S}=0.1 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{G S}-V_{T H} &=0.4>V_{D S} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow[/latex] MOSFET is in linear region
In linear region,
[latex] I_{D}=K_{n}\left[2\left(V_{G S}-V_{T H}\right) V_{O S}-V_{D S}^{2}\right][/latex]
Transconductance
[latex] \begin{aligned} g_{m}&=\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{G S}}=2 K_{n} V_{D S} \\ K_{n}&=\frac{K_{n}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)=\frac{\mu_{n} C_{O x}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\\ \text{So,}\quad g_{m} &=2 K_{n} V_{D S}=\mu_{n} C_{O x}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right) V_{D S} \\ &=100 \times 50 \times 0.1 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V} \\ &=0.5 \mathrm{mA} N \end{aligned}[/latex]

Required value [latex]= |5| =5[/latex]

raw_source.text: The general solution of the differential equation [latex]\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+2\frac{dy}{dx}-5y=0[/latex] in terms of arbitrary constants [latex]K_{1} \; and \; K_{2}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
The general solution of the differential equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+2 \frac{d y}{d x}-5 y&=0 \\ \left(D^{2}+2 D-5\right) y&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Auxillary equation is
[latex] \begin{aligned} m^{2}+2 m-5 &=0 \\ m &=\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4+20}}{2}=\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{24}}{2} \\ &=\frac{-2 \pm 2 \sqrt{6}}{2}=-1 \pm \sqrt{6} \\ \text { Solution is } \quad y &=K_{1} e^{(-1+\sqrt{6}) x}+K_{2} e^{(-1-\sqrt{6}) x} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If the vector function [latex]\bar{F}=\hat{a_{x}}(3y-k_{1}z)+\hat{a_{y}}(k_{2}x-2z)-\hat{a_{z}}(k_{3}x+z)[/latex] is irrotational, then the values of the constants [latex]k_{1}, k_{2}[/latex] and [latex]k_{3} [/latex] respectively, are

raw_source.text:
An electron ([latex]q_1[/latex]) is moving in free space with velocity [latex]10^{5}[/latex] m/s towards a stationary electron ([latex]q_2[/latex]) far away. The closest distance that this moving electron gets to the stationary electron before the repulsive force diverts its path is ___________ [latex]\times 10^{-8}[/latex]m.
[Given, mass of electron [latex]m=9.11 \times 10^{-31}[/latex] kg, charge of electron [latex]e=-1.6 \times 10^{-19}[/latex]C, and permittivity [latex] \varepsilon_{0}=(1/36\pi)\times 10^{-9}F/m][/latex]
raw_source.solution:
r is the distance at which kinetic energy of [latex]q_{1}[/latex] becomes zero [(because kinetic energy (KE) is converted into potential energy (PE)].
When [latex]q_{1}[/latex] reaches 'r', it starts diverting.
Kinetic energy, [latex]K E=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}[/latex] and work done in moving [latex]q_{1}[/latex] charge to distance 'r' is
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{1} v_{2}&=q_{1} \frac{q_{2}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} r} \\ &\qquad\left(q_{1}=q_{2}=-1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right)\\ Now, \quad \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}&=\frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} r} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow r=\frac{\left(2 \times-1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) \times\left(-1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)}{4 \pi \times \frac{10^{-9}}{36 \pi} \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times\left(10^{5}\right)^{2}}[/latex]
[latex] \simeq 5.06 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{m}[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \text { Integral } I_{1}=\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \frac{x-y}{(x+y)^{3}} d y d x\\ \left.=\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \int\left(\frac{2 x}{(x+y)^{3}}-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}\right) d y\right] d x \\ =\int_{0}^{1}\left(2 x\left(\frac{-1}{2(x+y)^{2}}\right)_{0}^{1}+\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right)_{0}^{1}\right] d x \\ =\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} d x=-\left[\frac{1}{x+1}\right]_{0}^{1}=0.5\\ \text { and Integral } \quad I_{2}=\int_{0}^{1}\left(\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x-y}{(x+y)^{3}} d x\right) d y \\ \left.=\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}-\frac{2 y}{(x+y)^{3}} d x\right] d y \\ =\int_{0}^{1}\left[\frac{-1}{(x+y)}+\frac{2 y}{2(x+y)}\right]_{0}^{1} d y \\ =\int_{0}^{1} \frac{-1}{(1+y)^{2}} d y=-\left.\left[\frac{-1}{y+1}\right]\right|_{0} ^{1}=-0.5 \end{array}[/latex]

Propatiility of failure [latex]=\frac{6}{10} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &E[X]=\sum x_{i} P\left(x_{i}\right) \\ E[X]&=1 \times \frac{4}{10}+2 \times \frac{4}{10} \times \frac{6}{10}\\ &+3 \times \frac{4}{10}\left(\frac{6}{10}\right)^{2}+\ldots \; \; \; \ldots(i) \\ \frac{6}{10} E[X]&=1 \times \frac{4}{10} \times \frac{6}{10}\\ &+2 \times \frac{4}{10} \times\left(\frac{6}{10}\right)^{2} \ldots \; \; \; \ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
subtracting (ii) from (i), we get

raw_source.text:
A unity feedback control system is characterized by the open-loop transfer function
[latex]G(s)=\frac{10K(s+2)}{s^{3}+3s^{2}+10}[/latex]
The Nyquist path and the corresponding Nyquist plot of G(s) are shown in the figures below.

If [latex]0 \lt K \lt 1[/latex], then the number of poles of the closed-loop transfer function that lie in the right half of the s-plane is
raw_source.solution:
Given that, the open loop transfer function of a unity feedback system is,
[latex] G(s) =\frac{10 k(s+2)}{s^{3}+3 s^{2}+10} [/latex]
From the given Nyquist plot, for [latex]0 \lt k \lt 1[/latex] the encirclements about the point (-1+j 0) is,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} N=0 \\ N=P-Z \end{array}[/latex]
P= number of open loop poles in the right half of s-plane
Z= number of closed loop poles in the right half of s-plane
To determine the value of P :
Applying R-H criteria to G(s)
[latex] G(s)=\frac{10 k(s+2)}{s^{3}+3 s^{2}+10}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{c|cc} s^{3} & 1 & 0 \\ s^{2} & 3 & 10 \\ s^{1} & -10 / 3 & 0 \\ s^{0} & 10 & 0 \end{array}[/latex]
Two sign changes are there in the first column of the RH table. So, two open loop poles are there in right half of s-plane.
So,
[latex] P=2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} N=P-Z \\ 0=2-Z \\ Z=2 \end{array}[/latex]
Z=2 indicates, there are two closed loop poles in right half of s-plane.

raw_source.solution:
Poles are [latex]z^{2}+1=0 [/latex]
[latex] z=\pm i[/latex]
z=i lies inside |z|=3
z=-i lies inside |z|=3
Residue at z=i is
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\lim _{z \rightarrow i}(z-i) \frac{z^{2}-1}{(z-i)(z+i)} e^{z} \\ &=\frac{-1-1}{2 i} e^{i}=i e^{i} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Residue at z=-i is
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\lim _{z \rightarrow-i}(z+i) \frac{z^{2}-1}{(z-i)(z+i)} e^{z}\\ &=\frac{-1-1}{-2 i} e^{-i}=\frac{1}{i} e^{-i}=-i e^{-i} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By Residues theorem
[latex] \begin{aligned} I &=2 \pi i\left(i e^{i}-i e^{-i}\right) \\ &=-2 \pi\left(e^{i}-e^{-i}\right) \\ &=-2 \pi(\cos 1+i \sin 1-\cos 1+i \sin 1) \\ &=-2 \pi(2 i \sin 1)=-4 \pi i \sin (1) \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} Let \quad[P(X)]&=[\alpha(1-\alpha)] \\ \text{Then } H(x)&=\\ -\alpha \log _{2} \alpha-(1-\alpha) &\log _{2}(1-\alpha)\text{ bits/symbol}\\ [P(Y)]&=[P(X)]\left[P\left(\frac{Y}{X}\right)\right]=[0.25\; \; 0.75] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]f(x,y)=\frac{ax^{2}+by^{2}}{xy}[/latex] ,where a and b are constants. If [latex]\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}[/latex]  at x=1 and y=2 , then the relation between  a and b is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x, y) &=\frac{a x^{2}+b y^{2}}{x y}=a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+b\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \\\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(1,2)} &=\left.\left[\frac{a}{y}-\frac{b y}{x^{2}}\right]\right|_{(12)}-\frac{a}{2}-2 b \\\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(1,2)} &=\left.\left[-\frac{a x}{y^{2}}+\frac{b}{x}\right]\right|_{(1,2)}=-\frac{a}{4}+b \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \\ \text{So,}\quad \frac{a}{2}-2 b &=-\frac{a}{4}+b \\ \frac{3 a}{4}&=3 b \\ a&=4 b \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A curve passes through the point (x =1, y = 0) and satisfies the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2y} + \frac{y}{x}[/latex]. The equation that describes the curve is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{x^{2}}{2 y}+\frac{y}{2}+\frac{y}{x} \\ \text { Put. } \frac{y}{x}=t \\ \frac{d y}{d x}&=t+x \frac{d t}{d x} \\ t+x \frac{d t}{d x} &=\frac{x}{2 t}+\frac{t x}{2}+t \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1}{2 t}+\frac{t}{2}\right) \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1+t^{2}}{2 t}\right) \\ \frac{2 t}{1+t^{2}} d t &=\int d x+C \\ \ln \left(1+t^{2}\right) &=x+c \\ t &=\frac{y}{x}\\ \text{So, }\ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x+C \\ \text{At }x=1, y=0 \\ \ln \left(1+\frac{0}{1}\right) &=\ln (1)=0=1+C \\ C &=-1 \\ \text{So,} \ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x-1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The position of a particle y(t) is described by the differential equation:

[latex]\frac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}=-\frac{dy}{dt}-\frac{5y}{4}[/latex]

The initial conditions are y(0) = 1 and [latex]\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{dy}{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{t=0}=0[/latex] . The position (accurate to two decimal places) of the particle at [latex]t = \pi[/latex] is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2}}{d t^{2}}+\frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{5Y}{4}&=0\\ y(0)&=1 \\ y^{\prime}(0)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
By applying Laplace transform,
[latex] \begin{aligned} s^{2} Y(s)-s(1)+s Y(s)-1+\frac{5}{4} Y(s)=0 & \\ Y(s)=\frac{s+1}{s^{2}+s+\frac{5}{4}}=\frac{s+1}{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+1} \\ =\frac{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+1}+\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By taking inverse Laplace transform.
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(t)&=e^{-t / 2}\left[\cos (t)+\frac{1}{2} \sin (t)\right] ; t>0\\ \text{At }t=\pi &\\ y(t=\pi) &=e^{-\pi / 2}[(-1)+(0)] \\ &=-e^{-\pi / 2}=-0.2078 \simeq-0.21 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The contour C given below is on the complex plane z=x+jy , where [latex] j=\sqrt{-1} [/latex].

The value of the integral [latex]\frac{1}{\pi j}\oint_{C}^{}\frac{dz}{z^{2}-1}[/latex] is _______.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \frac{1}{\pi \dot{i}} \oint \frac{d z}{z^{2}-1}=2\left[\frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{C_{1}} \frac{d z}{(z+1)(z-1)}+\frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{C_{2}} \frac{d z}{(z+1)(z-1)}\right] \\ =2\left[-\left.\left(\frac{1}{z-1}\right)\right|_{z=-1}+\left.\left(\frac{1}{z+1}\right)\right|_{z=1}\right] \\ =2\left[-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right]=2 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]r=x^{2}+y-z[/latex] and [latex]z^{3}-xy+yz+y^{3}=1[/latex]. Assume that x and y are independent
variables. At [latex](x, y, z) = (2, -1,1)[/latex], the value (correct to two decimal places) of [latex]\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}[/latex] is _________ .
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} r &=x^{2}+y-z &\ldots(i)\\ z^{3}-x y+y z+y^{3} &=1 &\ldots(ii)\\ \frac{\partial r}{\partial x} &=2 x-\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} &\ldots(iii)\\ 3 z^{2} \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}-y+y \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} &=0 \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} &=\frac{y}{3 z^{2}+y} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By substituting [latex]\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}[/latex] in equation (iii), we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=2 x-\frac{y}{3 z^{2}+y} \\ \operatorname{At}(2 .-1.1),& \\ \frac{\partial r}{\partial x}&=2(2)-\frac{(-1)}{3(1)^{2}+(-1)} \\ &=4+\frac{1}{2}=4.50 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x, y) &=\frac{a x^{2}+b y^{2}}{x y}=a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+b\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \\\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(1,2)} &=\left.\left[\frac{a}{y}-\frac{b y}{x^{2}}\right]\right|_{(12)}-\frac{a}{2}-2 b \\\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(1,2)} &=\left.\left[-\frac{a x}{y^{2}}+\frac{b}{x}\right]\right|_{(1,2)}=-\frac{a}{4}+b \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \\ \text{So,}\quad \frac{a}{2}-2 b &=-\frac{a}{4}+b \\ \frac{3 a}{4}&=3 b \\ a&=4 b \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A discrete-time all-pass system has two of its poles at 0.25[latex]\angle 0^{\circ}[/latex]  and 2[latex]\angle 30^{\circ}[/latex]. Which one of the following statements about the system is TRUE?
raw_source.solution: The AOC should include unit circle to make the system stable. From the given pole pattern it is clear that, to make the system stable, the ROC should be finite circular strip or finite annular strip and hence the impulse response of the system should be also two-sided.
options: It has two more poles at 0.5[latex]\angle 0^{\circ}[/latex]  and 4[latex]\angle 0^{\circ}[/latex]  .
It is stable only when the impulse response is two-sided.
It has constant phase response over all frequencies.
It has constant phase response over the entire z-plane.

raw_answer.option_text: It is stable only when the impulse response is two-sided.

raw_source.text:
Let x(t) be a periodic function with period T = 10. The Fourier series coefficients for this series are denoted by [latex] a_{k} [/latex], that is

[latex]x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }a_{k}e^{jk\frac{2\pi }{T}t}[/latex]

The same function x(t) can also be considered function with period [latex]{T=40}'[/latex]. Let [latex]b_{k}[/latex] be the fourier series cofficients when period is taken as [latex]{T}'[/latex]. If [latex]\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}|a_{k}|=16[/latex] ,then [latex]\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}|a_{k}| [/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
Change in only time period or frequency does not change in the value of Fourier series coefficients
So,
[latex] \begin{aligned} b_{k} &=a_{k} \\ \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\left|b_{k}\right| &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\left|a_{k}\right|=16 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the following amplitude modulated signal: [latex]s(t)=cos(2000\pi t)+4cos(2400\pi t)+cos(2800\pi t).[/latex] The ratio (accurate to three decimal places) of the power of the message signal to the power of the carrier signal is __________.
raw_source.solution:
The power of the carrier signal is,
[latex] P_{c}=\frac{(4)^{2}}{2}=8 \mathrm{W}[/latex]
The power of message signal can be taken as the power carried by the sidebands.
So, the power of the message signal is,
[latex] P_{m}=2\left[\frac{(1)^{2}}{2}\right]=1 \mathrm{W}[/latex]
Required ratio,
[latex] \frac{P_{m}}{P_{c}}=\frac{1}{8}=0.125[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a binary channel code in which each codeword has a fixed length of 5 bits. The
Hamming distance between any pair of distinct codewords in this code is at least 2. The
maximum number of codewords such a code can contain is _________.
raw_source.solution:
According to the Plotkin bound.
[latex] \begin{aligned} d_{\min } &\leq \frac{n 2^{k-1}}{2^{k}-1}\\ n&= \text{ Length of each code word }\\ k&= \text{ Length of each message word} \\ \text{Given that.}\\ d_{\min }&=2 \text { and } n=5\\ \text{So, } \frac{2^{k}}{2\left(2^{k}-1\right)} &\geq \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2^{k}}{2^{k}-1} &\geq \frac{4}{5} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For any value of k, the above bound will be satisfied. But as [latex]n > k[/latex] and n is fixed at 5. The maximum value of k that can be selected is 4.
So, the maximum number of codewords possible is [latex]2_{4} = 16[/latex].

raw_source.text:
A binary source generates symbols [latex] X \in \{-1,1\} [/latex]which are transmitted over a noisy channel. The probability of transmitting X= 1 is 0.5. Input to the threshold detector is R= X + N. The probability density function [latex]f_{N}(n)[/latex] of the noise N is shown below.
If the detection threshold is zero, then the probability of error (correct to two decimal places) is __________.
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]s_{0}[/latex] and [latex]s_{1}[/latex] be the transmitted symbols representing the transmitted value {-1 , 1} respectively and let [latex]r_{0}[/latex] and [latex]r_{1}[/latex] be the received symbols.

Probability of error,
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{e} &=P\left(s_{1}\right) P\left(r_{0} \mid s_{1}\right)+P\left(s_{0}\right) P\left(r_{1} \mid s_{0}\right) \\ P\left(r_{0} \mid s_{1}\right) &=P\left(r_{1} \mid s_{0}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}\\ \text{Given that,}\\ P\left(s_{0}\right)&=P\left(s_{1}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\\ \text{So}\quad P_{e}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}\right)=\frac{1}{8}=0.125 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A p-n step junction diode with a contact potential of 0.65V has a depletion width of 1[latex]\mu[/latex]m
at equilibrium. The forward voltage (in volts, correct to two decimal places) at which this
width reduces to 0.6 [latex]\mu[/latex]m is _______.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} W_{\mathrm{dep}} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 \varepsilon}{q}\left(\frac{1}{N_{A}}+\frac{1}{N_{D}}\right)\left(V_{b i}-V_{A K}\right)} \\ \frac{\sqrt{\left(0.65-V_{A K}\right)}}{\sqrt{0.65}} &=\frac{0.6 \mu \mathrm{m}}{1 \mu \mathrm{m}}=0.6 \\ 1-\frac{V_{A K}}{0.65} &=0.36 \\ V_{A K} &=0.65(1-0.36) \\ &=0.65 \times 0.64=0.416 \mathrm{V} \simeq 0.42 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A traffic signal cycles from GREEN to YELLOW, YELLOW to RED and RED to GREEN.
In each cycle, GREEN is turned on for 70 seconds, YELLOW is turned on for
5 seconds and the RED is turned on for 75 seconds. This traffic light has to be implemented
using a finite state machine (FSM). The only input to this FSM is a clock of 5 second period.
The minimum number of flip-flops required to implement this FSM is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{GREEN }&\rightarrow 70 \text{seconds}\\ \text { YELLOW } & \rightarrow 5 \text { seconds } \\ \text { RED } &\rightarrow 75 \text { seconds }\\ \text{Clock period }&\rightarrow 5 \text{seconds }\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Total number of unique states required
[latex] =\frac{70+5+75}{5}=30[/latex]
Minimum number of flip-flops required is,
[latex] n=\left\lceil\log _{2}(30)\right\rceil=\lceil 4.91\rceil=5[/latex]

raw_source.text:
There are two photolithography systems: one with light source of wavelength [latex]\lambda _{1}[/latex] = 156 nm
(System 1) and another with light source of wavelength [latex]\lambda _{2}[/latex] = 325 nm (System 2). Both
photolithography systems are otherwise identical. If the minimum feature sizes that can be
realized using System1 and System2 are [latex] L_{min1} \; and \; L_{min2} [/latex] respectively, the ratio [latex] L_{min1}/L_{min2} [/latex](correct to two decimal places) is__________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} L_{min}&\propto \lambda \\ \frac{L_{min1}}{L_{min2}}&=\frac{\lambda _1}{\lambda _2} \\ &= \frac{156nm}{325nm}=0.48 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A lossy transmission line has resistance per unit length R = 0.05 [latex]\Omega [/latex] /m. The line is
distortionless and has characteristic impedance of 50 [latex]\Omega [/latex]. The attenuation constant (in Np/m, correct to three decimal places) of the line is _______.
raw_source.solution:
For a distortionless transmission line,
[latex] \frac{L}{R}=\frac{C}{G}[/latex]
Propagation constant,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \gamma &=\alpha+j \beta=\sqrt{(R+j \omega L)(G+j \omega C)} \\ &=\sqrt{R G}\left(1+j \omega \frac{L}{R}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Attenuation constant,
[latex] \alpha=\sqrt{R G}[/latex]
Characteristic impedance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{0} &=\sqrt{\frac{(R+j \omega L)}{(G+j \omega C)}}=\sqrt{\frac{R}{G}} \\ \sqrt{G} &=\frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}} \\ \text{So,}\quad\alpha &=\sqrt{R} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}}=\frac{R}{Z_{0}} \\ &=\frac{0.05}{50}=\frac{0.01}{10}=0.001 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider matrix [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} k & 2k\\ k^{2}-k & k^{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]  and vector [latex]x=\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]. The number of distinct real values of k for which the equation  Ax=0 has infinitely many solutions is _______.
raw_source.solution:
A X=0 has infinitely many solutions
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So, }\quad|A|=0 ;&\left|\begin{array}{cc}k & 2 k \\ k^{2}-k k^{2}\end{array}\right|=0 \\ k^{3}-2 k^{3}+2 k^{2} &=0 ; \quad k^{2}(2-k)=0 \\ k &=0,2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex] "two" distinct values of k

raw_source.text: Let [latex] X_{1} , X_{2} , X_{3} \; and \;  X_{4} [/latex] be independent normal random variables with zero mean and unit variance. The probability that [latex] X_{4} [/latex]  is the smallest among the four is _______.

raw_source.text:
Taylor series expansion of [latex]f(x)=\int_{0}^{x} e^{-({\frac{t^{2}}{2}})}dt[/latex] at around x=0 has the form

[latex]f(x)=a_{0}+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2}+... [/latex].

The coefficient [latex]a_{2}[/latex] (correct to two decimal places) is equal to _______.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x) &=\int_{0}^{x} e^{-t^{2} / 2} d t \\ f^{\prime}(x) &=e^{-x^{2} / 2} \text { and } f^{\prime \prime}(x)=e^{-x^{2} / 2}(-x) \\ f^{\prime \prime}(0) &=0 \\ a_{2} &=\frac{f^{\prime \prime}(0)}{2 !}=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The ABCD matrix for a two-port network is defined by:

[latex]\begin{bmatrix} V_{1}\\ I_{1} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} A & B\\ C & D \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} V_{2}\\ - l_{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]


The parameter B for the given two-port network (in ohms, correct to two decimal places) is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]B=-\left.\frac{V_{1}}{I_{2}}\right|_{V_{2}=0}[/latex]
When [latex]V_{2}=0[/latex] (i.e., when port-2 is short circuited)


[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{1}&=\frac{V_{1}}{2 \Omega+(5 \Omega \| 2 \Omega)}=\frac{7 V_{1}}{24 \Omega}\\ I_{2}&=-I_{1} \times \frac{5 \Omega}{5 \Omega+2 \Omega}=\frac{-5 V_{1}}{24 \Omega}\\ \text { So, } \quad B&=-\frac{V_{1}}{I_{2}}=\frac{24}{5} \Omega=4.80 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The circuit shown in the figure is used to provide regulated voltage (5 V) across the 1k[latex]\Omega[/latex] resistor. Assume that the Zener diode has a constant reverse breakdown voltage for a current range, starting from a minimum required Zener current, [latex] I_{Z_{min}} = 2 mA [/latex] to its maximum allowable current. The input voltage [latex] V_{I} [/latex] may vary by 5% from its nominal value of 6 V. The resistance of the diode in the breakdown region is negligible.

The value of R and the minimum required power dissipation rating of the diode, respectively, are
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{I} &=6 \mathrm{V} \pm 5 \%=6 \mathrm{V} \pm 0.3 \mathrm{V} \\ &=5.7 \mathrm{V} \text { to } 6.3 \mathrm{V}\\ I_{L} &=\frac{5 \mathrm{V}}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=5 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{A} \\ I_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{min})} &=I_{L}+I_{Z_{\mathrm{Tmin}}}=5 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{A}+2 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{A} \\ &=7 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{A} \\ I_{s} &=\frac{V_{I}-V_{z}}{R} \\ I_{\mathrm{s}(\min )} &=\frac{V_{I(\min )}-V_{z}}{R}=7 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{A} \\ \text{So,}\quad R &=\frac{5.7-5}{7} \mathrm{k} \Omega=\frac{700}{7} \Omega=100 \Omega\\ \text{When},\quad R=100 \Omega \\ I_{s(\max )} &=\frac{6.3-5}{100} \mathrm{A}=13 \mathrm{mA} \\ I_{z(\max )} &=I_{s(\max )}-I_{L}=13 \mathrm{mA}-5 \mathrm{mA} \\ &=8 \mathrm{mA} \\ P_{z(\min )} &=V_{z} I_{z(\max )}=(5 \times 8) \mathrm{mW}=40 \mathrm{mW} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex] c(t)=A_{c} cos(2\pi f_{c}t) \; and  \; m(t)=cos(2\pi f_{m}t) [/latex]. It is given that [latex] f_{c}>>5f_{m} [/latex]. The signal [latex] c(t) +m(t) [/latex]  is applied to the input of a non-linear device, whose output [latex] v_{o}(t) [/latex] is related to the input [latex] v_{i}(t)+bv_{i}(t) [/latex],where a and b  are positive constants. The output of the non-linear device is passed through an ideal band-pass filter with center frequency [latex] f_{c} [/latex] and bandwidth [latex] 3f_{m}[/latex] ,to produce an amplitude modulated (AM) wave. If it is desired to have the sideband power of the AM wave to be half of the carrier power, then [latex]a/b[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} v_{f t}^{(t)} &=A_{c} \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right)+\cos \left(2 \pi t_{m} t\right) \\ v_{d}(t) &=a v_{i}(t)+b v_{i}^{2}(t) \\ =&\left[a A_{c} \cos \left(2 \pi t_{c} t\right)+a \cos \left(2 \pi f_{m} t\right)\right] \\ \quad &+b\left[\begin{array}{c}A_{c}^{2} \cos ^{2}\left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right)+\cos ^{2}\left(2 \pi f_{m} t\right) \\ +2 A_{c} \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right) \cos \left(2 \pi t_{m} t\right)\end{array}\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]
After passing through the given BPF,
[latex] y(t)=a A_{c} \cos 2 \pi f_{c} t+2 b A_{c} \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right) \cos \left(2 \pi f_{m} t\right) [/latex]
[latex] =a A_{c}\left[1+\frac{2 b}{a} \cos \left(2 \pi f_{m} t\right)\right] \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right) [/latex]
Modulation index,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mu &=\begin{array}{l}2 b \\ a\end{array} \\ P_{S B} &=\frac{\mu^{2}}{2} P_{C}=\frac{1}{2} P_{C} \\ \mu^{2} &=1 \Rightarrow \mu=1 \\ \frac{2 b}{a} &=1 \\ \frac{a}{b} &=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a white Gaussian noise process N(t) with two-sided power spectral density [latex] S_{N}(f)=0.5 W/Hz [/latex] as input to a filter with impulse response [latex]0.5e^{\frac{-t^{2}}{2}}[/latex] (where t is in seconds) resulting in output Y(t). The power in Y(t) in watts is
raw_source.solution:
PSD of noise input.
[latex] S_{(t)}^{S}(f)=0.50 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{Hz} [/latex]
Power of y(t)
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{y} &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S_{N}(f)|H(f)|^{2} d f \\ &=0.50 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(f)|^{2} d f \\ &=0.50 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|^{2} d t\\ \text{Given that,}\\ h(t)&=\frac{1}{2} e^{-t^{2} / 2}\\ \text{So}\quad P_{y} &=\frac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{2} e^{-t^{2} / 2}\right)^{2} d t \\ &=\frac{1}{8} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-t^{2}} d t \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{8}=0.2215 \mathrm{W} \simeq 0.22 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The state equation and the output equation of a control system are given below:

[latex]\dot{x}=\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -1.5\\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 0\end{bmatrix}u,[/latex]
[latex]y=\begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 0.625 \end{bmatrix}x.[/latex]

The transfer function representation of the system is
raw_source.solution:
Transfer function
[latex]\begin{aligned} T(s) &=\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\mathrm{C}(s I-A]^{-1} \mathrm{B} \\ A &=\left[\begin{array}{cc} -4 & -1.5 \\ 4 & 0 \end{array}\right] \\ B &=\left[\begin{array}{c} 2 \\ 0 \end{array}\right] \\ C&=[1.5\quad0.625]\\ {[s I-A]} & =\left[\begin{array}{cc}s+4 & 1.5 \\-4 & s\end{array}\right] \\ {[s I-A]^{-1}} & =\frac{1}{\left(s^{2}+4 s+6\right)}\left[\begin{array}{cc}s & -1.5 \\4 & s+4 \end{array}\right] \\ {[s I-A]^{-1} B} & =\frac{1}{s^{2}+4 s+6}\left[\begin{array}{c}2 s \\8 \end{array}\right] & \\ C[s I-A]^{-1} B & =\frac{1}{s^{2}+4 s+6}[1.5 \quad 0.625]\left[\begin{array}{c}2 s \\ 8\end{array}\right] \\ T(s) & =\frac{3 s+5}{s^{2}+4 s+6} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Red (R), Green (G) and Blue (B) Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) were fabricated using p-n
junctions of three different inorganic semiconductors having different band-gaps. The builtin
voltages of red, green and blue diodes are [latex] V_{R}, V_{G} \; and \; V_{B} [/latex], respectively. Assume donor and acceptor doping to be the same [latex] (N_{A} \; and \; N_{D} [/latex], respectively) in the p and n sides of all the three diodes. Which one of the following relationships about the built-in voltages is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\lambda_{R} \gt \lambda_{G} \gt \lambda_{B}[/latex]
Energy gap, [latex] E_{g} \propto \frac{1}{\lambda} [/latex]
So, [latex]E_{g R} \lt E_{g G} \lt E_{g B}[/latex]
Materials with high energy gap will have high built-in voltages, when doping concentrations are same.
So, [latex]V_{R} \lt V_{G} \lt V_{B}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The distance (in meters) a wave has to propagate in a medium having a skin depth of 0.1 m
so that the amplitude of the wave attenuates by 20 dB, is
raw_source.solution:
Attenuation constant,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \alpha &=\frac{1}{\text { skin depth }}=10 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \\ \text { 20log }_{10}\left(\frac{E_{0}}{E_{x}}\right) &=20 \mathrm{dB} \\ \frac{E_{o}}{E_{x}} &=10 \Rightarrow E_{x}=\frac{E_{0}}{10} \\ E_{x} &=E_{0} e^{-\alpha x}=E_{0} e^{-10 x}=\frac{E_{0}}{10} \\ e^{-10 x} &=\frac{1}{10} \\ x &=\frac{1}{10} \ln (10)=0.23 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A curve passes through the point (x =1, y = 0) and satisfies the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2y} + \frac{y}{x}[/latex]. The equation that describes the curve is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{x^{2}}{2 y}+\frac{y}{2}+\frac{y}{x} \\ \text { Put. } \frac{y}{x}=t \\ \frac{d y}{d x}&=t+x \frac{d t}{d x} \\ t+x \frac{d t}{d x} &=\frac{x}{2 t}+\frac{t x}{2}+t \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1}{2 t}+\frac{t}{2}\right) \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1+t^{2}}{2 t}\right) \\ \frac{2 t}{1+t^{2}} d t &=\int d x+C \\ \ln \left(1+t^{2}\right) &=x+c \\ t &=\frac{y}{x}\\ \text{So, }\ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x+C \\ \text{At }x=1, y=0 \\ \ln \left(1+\frac{0}{1}\right) &=\ln (1)=0=1+C \\ C &=-1 \\ \text{So,} \ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x-1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the circuit given in the figure, the magnitude of the loop current (in amperes, correct to three decimal places) 0.5 second after closing the switch is _______.

raw_source.text:
A DC current of 26[latex]\mu A[/latex] flows through the circuit shown. The diode in the circuit is forward biased and it has an ideality factor of one. At the quiescent point, the diode has a junction capacitance of 0.5 nF . Its neutral region resistances can be neglected. Assume that the room temperature thermal equivalent voltage is 26 mV.

For [latex] \omega =2 \times 10^{6} \; rad/s [/latex], the amplitude of the small-signal component of diode current (in [latex]\mu A[/latex], correct to one decimal place) is _______.
raw_source.solution:
The small-signal equivalent model of the given circuit can be drawn as shown below.


[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Given that, }\omega&=2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ C_{j} &=0.5 \mathrm{nF} \\ I_{\mathrm{DC}} &=26 \mu \mathrm{A} \\ V_{T} &=26 \mathrm{mV} \\ \eta &=1\\ \mathrm{So} \quad r_{d} &=\frac{\eta V_{T}}{I_{\mathrm{DC}}}=\frac{26 \mathrm{mV}}{26 \mu \mathrm{A}}=1 \mathrm{k} \Omega \\ \frac{1}{\omega C_{j}} &=\frac{1}{2 \times 10^{6} \times 0.5 \times 10^{-9}} \Omega=1 \mathrm{k} \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, total impedance of the circuit will be,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z &=\left(r_{d} \| \frac{1}{j \omega C_{j}}\right)+100 \Omega \\\left(r_{d} \| \frac{1}{j \omega C_{j}}\right) &=\frac{(1000)(-j 1000)}{1000-j 1000} \Omega \\ &=\frac{-j(1+j)}{2} \mathrm{k} \Omega \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(1-j) \mathrm{k} \Omega=(500-j 500) \Omega \\ \therefore \quad Z &=600-j 500 \Omega \\|Z| &=100 \sqrt{36+25}=100 \sqrt{61} \Omega \\ I_{m} &=\frac{V_{m}}{|Z|} \\ &=\frac{5 \mathrm{mV}}{100 \sqrt{61} \Omega}=\frac{50}{\sqrt{61}} \mu \mathrm{A}=6.40 \mu \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An op-amp based circuit is implemented as shown below.

In the above circuit, assume the op-amp to be ideal. The voltage (in volts, correct to one decimal place) at node A, connected to the negative input of the op-amp as indicated in the figure is _________.
raw_source.solution:
Applying the concept of virtual ground, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{o}&=-\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}} \cdot V_{i n}\\ [\therefore & \text{ non-inverting amplifiel}]\\ \therefore \quad V_{o}&=-\frac{31 \mathrm{k} \Omega}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega} \times 1 \mathrm{V}\\ V_{0}&=-31 \mathrm{V} \lt -15 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]
which is not possible
Hence, the output voltage of the op-amp is equal to [latex] -15 \mathrm{V}[/latex]


Now applying KCL of node 'A', we get.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{A}-(-15)}{31 \mathrm{k} \Omega}+\frac{V_{A}-1}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega} &=0 \\ \frac{V_{A}}{31 \mathrm{k} \Omega}+\frac{V_{A}}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega} &=\frac{-15}{31 \mathrm{k} \Omega}+\frac{1}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega} \\ V_{A}\left[\frac{1}{31}+\frac{1}{1}\right] &=-\frac{15}{31}+1 \\ V_{A} &=0.5 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The input 4sinc(2t) is fed to a Hilbert transformer to obtain y(t), as shown in the figure below:

Here [latex]sinc(x)=\frac{sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}[/latex]. The value (accurate to two decimal places) of [latex]\int_{-\infty }^{\infty } |y(t)|^{2}dt[/latex] is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Hilbert transform does not alter the amplitude spectrum of the signal.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So, }\quad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|y(t)|^{2} d t&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^{2} d t=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|X(f)|^{2} d f \\ x(t)&=4 \sin \mathrm{c}(2 t) \\ \text{sinc}(t) &\stackrel{CTFT}{\longleftrightarrow} \text{rect}(f) \\ 4 \text{sinc}(2 t) &\stackrel{CTFT}{\longleftrightarrow}+\frac{4}{2} \text{rect}\left(\frac{f}{2}\right)=2 \text{rect}\left(\frac{f}{2}\right) \end{aligned}\\ \begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|X(f)|^{2} d f &=2 \times(2)^{2}=8 \\ \text { So. } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|y(t)|^{2} d t &=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A random variable X takes values -0.5 and 0.5 with probabilities 1/4 and 3/4, respectively. The noisy observation of X is Y = X + Z, where Z has uniform probability density over the interval (-1, 1). X and Z are independent. If the MAP rule based detector outputs [latex]\hat{X}[/latex] as

[latex]\hat{X}=\left\{\begin{matrix} -0.5 \; \; \; Y \lt \alpha \\ 0.5 \; \; \; Y \geq \alpha \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

then the value of [latex]\alpha [/latex] (accurate to two decimal places) is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{c} P\left(x_{0}\right)=\frac{1}{4} ; P\left(x_{1}\right)=\frac{3}{4} \\ \text { MAP criteria, } f_{Y}\left(y \mid x_{0}\right) P\left(x_{0}\right) \overset{x_{2}}{\underset{x_{1}}{\gtrless}}\left(y \mid x_{1}\right) P\left(x_{1}\right) \end{array}[/latex]


[latex]\text{So}\quad \alpha=-0.5[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a unity feedback control system with the forward path transfer function

[latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)}[/latex]

The peak resonant magnitude [latex]M_{r}[/latex], of the closed-loop frequency response is 2. The corresponding value of the gain K (correct to two decimal places) is _________.
raw_source.solution:
Maximum resonant peak,
[latex]\begin{aligned} M_{r} &=\frac{1}{2 \xi \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}}}=2 \\ 2 \xi \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}} &=\frac{1}{2} \\ \xi^{2}\left(1-\xi^{2}\right) &=\frac{1}{16} \\ \xi^{4}-\xi^{2}+\frac{1}{16} &=0 \\ \xi^{2}&=\frac{1}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{1-\frac{1}{4}}{4}}=\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \\ \text { As } M_{r}=2 \gt 1, \xi& \lt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text { and } \xi^{2} \lt \frac{1}{2} \\ \text { So. } \quad\xi^{2}&=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\\ Given, \quad G(s)&=\frac{K}{s(s+2)}=\frac{\omega_{n}^{2}}{s\left(s+2 \xi \omega_{n}\right)} \\ \text{So} \quad\omega_{n} &=\sqrt{K} \\ 2 \xi \sqrt{K} &=2\\ \sqrt{K} &=\frac{1}{\xi} \\ K &=\frac{1}{\xi^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)} \\ &=\frac{4}{2-\sqrt{3}}=14.928 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The figure below shows the Bode magnitude and phase plots of a stable transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{n_{o}}{s^{2}+d_{2}s^{2}+d_{1}+d_{0}}[/latex]
Consider the negative unity feedback configuration with gain k in the feedforward path. The closed loop is stable for [latex] k \lt k_{o} [/latex]. The maximum value of [latex]k_{o} [/latex] is ______.
raw_source.solution:
For G(s)
[latex] M_{\mathrm{dB}}\left(\omega_{p c}\right)=20 \mathrm{dB} [/latex]
When cascaded with k ,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{dB}} &=-20 \mathrm{dB}-20 \log _{10}(k) \gt 0 \mathrm{dB} \\ 20+20 \log _{10}(k) & \lt 0 \\ 20 \log _{10}(k) & \lt -20 \\ k & \lt 10^{-1}=0.10\\ \text{So,}\quad k_{0}&=0.10 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the circuit shown below, the (W/L) value for [latex] M_{2} [/latex] is twice that for [latex] M_{1} [/latex]. The two nMOS transistors are otherwise identical. The threshold voltage [latex]V_{T}[/latex] for both transistors is 1.0V. Note that [latex] V_{GS} \; for M_{2} [/latex] must be [latex]\gt[/latex] 1.0 V.
The voltage (in volts, accurate to two decimal places) at [latex] V_{x} [/latex] is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Let},\quad K_{n}&=\frac{\mu_{n} C_{o x}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\\ \text{Given that,}\\ \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{2} &=2\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1} \\ \text{So,}\quad K_{n 2} &=2 K_{n 1}\\ \text{For }M_{1}, \quad V_{G S 1}-V_{T}&=2-1=1 V \\ \text{For }M_{2}, \quad V_{G S 2}-V_{T}&=2-V_{x}-1=1 \mathrm{V}-V_{x}<1 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{D S 2}&=\left(3.3-V_{x}\right)>\left(V_{G S 2}-V_{T}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, [latex]M_{1}[/latex] will be in linear region and [latex]M_{2}[/latex] will be in saturation region.
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{D_{1}}&=I_{D_{2}} \\ K_{n 1}\left[2\left(V_{G S 1}-V_{T}\right) V_{D S 1}-V_{D S 1}^{2}\right]&=K_{n 2}\left(V_{G S 2}-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ K_{n 1}\left[2(2-1) V_{x}-V_{x}^{2}\right]&=2 K_{n 1}\left(2-V_{x}-1\right)^{2} \\ 2 V_{x}-V_{x}^{2} &=2\left(1+V_{x}^{2}-2 V_{x}\right) \\ &=2 V_{x}^{2}-4 V_{x}+2\\ 3V_{x}^{2}-6 V_{x}+2 &=0 \\ V_{x}^{2}-2 V_{x}+\frac{2}{3} &=0 \\ V_{x} &=1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{4-\frac{8}{3}}{4}}=1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} V \\ V_{GS2}&=\left(2-V_{x}\right) \geq V_{T}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \left(1-V_{x}\right) &\geq0\\ \text{So, valid value,} \quad V_{x}&=1-\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}=0.4226 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A solar cell of area  1.0 [latex]cm^{2}[/latex] , operating at 1.0 sun intensity, has a short circuit current of
20 mA, and an open circuit voltage of 0.65 V. Assuming room temperature operation and
thermal equivalent voltage of 26mV, the open circuit voltage (in volts, correct to two
decimal places) at 0.2 sun intensity is _______.
raw_source.solution:
For solar cell,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{OC}} &=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{I_{S C}}{I_{O}}\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2}-V_{\mathrm{OC} 1} &=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{I_{S C 2}}{I_{S C}}\right)=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{0.20}{1.0}\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2} &=V_{\mathrm{OC} 1}-0.026 \mathrm{ln}(5) \\ &=0.65-0.041845=0.608 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A junction is made between [latex] p^{-} Si [/latex] with doping density [latex] N_{A1} = 10^{15} cm^{-3}[/latex] and pSi with doping density[latex] N_{A2} = 10^{17} cm^{-3} [/latex].
Given: Boltzmann constant [latex]k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} JK^{-1} [/latex], electronic charge [latex] q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} C [/latex]. Assume 100% acceptor ionization.
At room temperature (T = 300K), the magnitude of the built-in potential (in volts, correct to two decimal places) across this junction will be _________________.
raw_source.solution:
Built-in potential,

The XOR gate outputs 3.3 volts for logic HIGH and 0 volts for logic LOW levels. The data bit and clock periods are equal and the value of[latex] \Delta T/T_{CK} = 0.15 [/latex], where the parameters [latex]\Delta T [/latex] and [latex] T_{CK} [/latex] are shown in the figure. raw_source.text:
The cutoff frequency of [latex] TE_{01} [/latex] mode of an air filled rectangular waveguide having inner
dimensions [latex]a cm \times b cm ( a \gt b)[/latex] is twice that of the dominant [latex] TE_{10}[/latex] mode. When the
waveguide is operated at a frequency which is 25% higher than the cutoff frequency of the
dominant mode, the guide wavelength is found to be 4 cm. The value of b (in cm, correct to
two decimal places) is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} f_{c(01)}=2 f_{c(10)}=\frac{2 c}{2 a}=\frac{c}{a} \\ \frac{c}{2 b}=\frac{c}{a} \Rightarrow a=2 b \Rightarrow b=\frac{a}{2} \end{array}[/latex]
Operating frequency,
[latex] f=1.25 f_{c(10)}[/latex]
[latex] f_{c(10)}\lt 1.25 f_{c(10)} \lt \left[f_{c(01)}=2 f_{c(10)}\right][/latex]
So, for the given frequency, the waveguide will work in [latex]\mathrm{TE}_{10}[/latex] mode.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { So, } \lambda_{g} &=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{f_{c(10)}}{f}\right)^{2}}} \\ &=\frac{c / f}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{1.25}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{c / f}{0.6} \\ \frac{c}{(1.25) f_{c(10)}(0.6)} &=\lambda_{g}=4 \mathrm{cm} \\ \frac{c}{f_{c(10)}} &=3 \times 10^{-2}=2 a \\ a &=1.5 \mathrm{cm} \\ b &=\frac{a}{2}=0.75 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A uniform plane wave traveling in free space and having the electric field
[latex]\vec{E}=(\sqrt{2}\hat{a}_{x}-\hat{a}_{z})cos[6\sqrt{3}\pi \times 10^{8}t-2\pi (x+\sqrt{2}z)]V/m[/latex]
is incident on a dielectric medium (relative permittivity [latex]\gt[/latex]1, relative permeability = 1) as shown in the figure and there is no reflected wave.

The relative permittivity (correct to two decimal places) of the dielectric medium is___________.
raw_source.solution:
The wave has [latex]E_{i}[/latex] direction and propagation direction both in same plane (ZX).
The wave is plane of incidence (P) polarized.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \beta_{x} &=1, \quad \beta_{2}=\sqrt{2} \\ \tan \theta_{i} &=\frac{\beta_{z}}{\beta_{x}}=\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
No reflection in P polarized wave under Brewster's angle of incidence.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \theta_{i} &=\theta_{B} \\ \tan \theta_{B} &=\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}} \\ \epsilon_{r} &=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The position of a particle y(t) is described by the differential equation:

[latex]\frac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}=-\frac{dy}{dt}-\frac{5y}{4}[/latex]

The initial conditions are y(0) = 1 and [latex]\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{dy}{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{t=0}=0[/latex] . The position (accurate to two decimal places) of the particle at [latex]t = \pi[/latex] is _______.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2}}{d t^{2}}+\frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{5Y}{4}&=0\\ y(0)&=1 \\ y^{\prime}(0)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
By applying Laplace transform,
[latex] \begin{aligned} s^{2} Y(s)-s(1)+s Y(s)-1+\frac{5}{4} Y(s)=0 & \\ Y(s)=\frac{s+1}{s^{2}+s+\frac{5}{4}}=\frac{s+1}{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+1} \\ =\frac{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+1}+\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\left(s+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By taking inverse Laplace transform.
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(t)&=e^{-t / 2}\left[\cos (t)+\frac{1}{2} \sin (t)\right] ; t>0\\ \text{At }t=\pi &\\ y(t=\pi) &=e^{-\pi / 2}[(-1)+(0)] \\ &=-e^{-\pi / 2}=-0.2078 \simeq-0.21 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The contour C given below is on the complex plane z=x+jy , where [latex] j=\sqrt{-1} [/latex].

The value of the integral [latex]\frac{1}{\pi j}\oint_{C}^{}\frac{dz}{z^{2}-1}[/latex] is _______.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \frac{1}{\pi \dot{i}} \oint \frac{d z}{z^{2}-1}=2\left[\frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{C_{1}} \frac{d z}{(z+1)(z-1)}+\frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{C_{2}} \frac{d z}{(z+1)(z-1)}\right] \\ =2\left[-\left.\left(\frac{1}{z-1}\right)\right|_{z=-1}+\left.\left(\frac{1}{z+1}\right)\right|_{z=1}\right] \\ =2\left[-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right]=2 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]r=x^{2}+y-z[/latex] and [latex]z^{3}-xy+yz+y^{3}=1[/latex]. Assume that x and y are independent
variables. At [latex](x, y, z) = (2, -1,1)[/latex], the value (correct to two decimal places) of [latex]\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}[/latex] is _________ .
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} r &=x^{2}+y-z &\ldots(i)\\ z^{3}-x y+y z+y^{3} &=1 &\ldots(ii)\\ \frac{\partial r}{\partial x} &=2 x-\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} &\ldots(iii)\\ 3 z^{2} \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}-y+y \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} &=0 \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} &=\frac{y}{3 z^{2}+y} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By substituting [latex]\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}[/latex] in equation (iii), we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=2 x-\frac{y}{3 z^{2}+y} \\ \operatorname{At}(2 .-1.1),& \\ \frac{\partial r}{\partial x}&=2(2)-\frac{(-1)}{3(1)^{2}+(-1)} \\ &=4+\frac{1}{2}=4.50 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The magnitude of the current (in amperes, accurate to two decimal places) through the source is _______.
raw_source.solution:

[latex]V_{A}= V_{B} and V_{C}= V_{D}[/latex]

Total resistance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{T} &=2\left(R_{1} \| R_{1}\right)+\left(R_{1}\left\|R_{1}\right\| R_{3} \| R_{3}\right) \\ &=R_{1}+\left(\frac{R_{1}}{2} \| \frac{R_{3}}{2}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that, [latex]R_{1}=1 \Omega[/latex] and [latex]R_{3}=3 \Omega [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So,}\qquad R_{T} &=1+\left(\frac{1}{2} \| \frac{3}{2}\right) \Omega=1+\frac{3 / 2}{4}=\frac{11}{8} \Omega \\ I &=\frac{11 \mathrm{V}}{R_{T}}=\frac{11}{(11 / 8)}=8 \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The families of curves represented by the solution of the equation

[latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=-\left (\frac{x}{y} \right )^n[/latex]

for [latex]n = -1[/latex] and [latex]n = +1[/latex], respectively, are
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=-\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{n} \\ n=-1\quad\quad \frac{d y}{d x} &=-\frac{y^{\prime}}{x} \\ \frac{d y}{y} &=-\frac{d x}{x} \\ \int \frac{1}{y} d y &=-\int \frac{1}{x} d x \\ \ln y &=-\ln x+\ln c \\ \ln (y x) &=\ln c \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] x y=c \quad [/latex] (Represents rectangular hyporbola)
[latex] \begin{aligned} n=1, \quad \frac{d y}{d x}&=-\frac{x}{y} \\ y d y &=-x d x \\ y d y &=-\int x d x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} &=-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+c \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] x^{2}+y^{2}=2 c \quad [/latex] (Represents family of circles)

z=0 lies inside the circle,

[latex]\begin{aligned} x(n) &=c_{1} e^{-j \frac{\pi}{2} n}+c_{2} e^{j \frac{\pi}{2} n} \\ \omega_{0} &=\frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ H\left(e^{i \omega}\right) &=1+a e^{-j \omega}+b e^{-j 2 \omega}\\ \text{To get }y(n)=0& \\ H\left(e^{j \omega_{o}}\right)&=\left.H\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|_{\omega=\frac{\pi}{2}}=0\\ 1+a e^{-i \frac{\pi}{2}}+b e^{-i 2 \frac{\pi}{2}}&=0 \\ 1-j a-b&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a causal second-order system with the transfer function

[latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{1+2s+s^2}[/latex]

with a unit-step [latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s}[/latex] as an input. Let C(s) be the corresponding output. The time taken by the system output c(t) to reach 94% of its steady-state value [latex]\lim_{t \to \infty }c(t)[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places, is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+2 s+1}=\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ R(s)&=\frac{1}{s} \\ \alpha (s)&=G(s) R(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using partial fraction expansion, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C(s) & =\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+1)}+\frac{C}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ A\left(s^{2}+2 s+1\right)&+B\left(s^{2}+s\right)+C s=1 \\ A&=1 \\ A+B & =0 \Rightarrow B=-1 \\ 2 A+B+C & =0 \Rightarrow C=-1 \\ \therefore \quad C(s) & =\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{(s+1)}-\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ \text{and}\quad c(t) & =\left(1-e^{-t}-t e^{-t}\right) u(t) \\ \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} c(t) & =1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
In order to reach 94 % of its steady-state value,
[latex] \left(1-e^{-t}-t e^{-t}\right)=0.94[/latex]
By trial and error, we get,
[latex] t \approx 4.50 \mathrm{sec}[/latex]

Let the state-space representation of an LTI system be [latex]\dot{x}(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)[/latex], [latex]\dot{y}(t)=Cx(t)+du(t)[/latex] where A, B, C are matrices, d is a scalar, u(t) is the input to the system, and y(t) is its output. Let [latex]B=[0\;0\;1]^T[/latex] and d=0. Which one of the following options for A and C will ensure that the transfer function of this LTI system is
[latex]H(s)=\frac{1}{s^3+3s^2+2s+1}[/latex]?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} X(t) &=A x(t)+B u(t) \\ y(t) &=C x(t) \\ B &=\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] \\ \frac{\gamma(s)}{U(s)} &=\\ \frac{\gamma(s)}{X_{1}(s)} \times \frac{X_{1}(s)}{U(s)}=& 1 \times \frac{1}{s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+1} \\ x_{1}(s)\left(s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+1\right]&=U(s) \\ x_{2} &=\dot{x}_{1}(t) \\ x_{2}(s) &=s x_{1}(s) \\ x_{3} &=\dot{x}_{2}(t) \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{3}(s) &=s x_{2}(s)=s^{2} X_{1}(s) \\ \text { So, } \quad s x_{3}(s) &=-x_{1}(s)-2 x_{2}(s)-3 x_{3}(s)+u(s) \\ \dot{x}_{3}(t) &=-x_{1}(t)-2 r_{2}(t)-3 x_{3}(t)+u(t) \\ y(t) &=x_{1}(t) \\ \dot{x}(t) &=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 & -3\end{array}\right] x(t)+\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] u(t) \\ y(t) &=[1 \quad 0 \quad 0] x(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]

Binary signaling, with [latex]0\rightarrow p(t)[/latex] and [latex]1\rightarrow q(t)[/latex], is used for the transmission, along with an optimal receiver that minimizes the bit-error probability.

Let [latex]\varphi _1(t),\varphi _2(t)[/latex] form an orthonormal signal set.
If we choose [latex]p(t)=\varphi _1(t)\; and \; q(t)=-\varphi _2(t)[/latex], we would obtain a certain bit-error probability [latex]P_b[/latex].
If we keep [latex]p(t)=\varphi _1(t)[/latex], but take [latex]q(t)=\sqrt{E}\varphi _2(t)[/latex], for what value of E would we obtain the same bit-error probability [latex]P_b[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text { When } p(t)=\phi_{1}(t) \text { and } q(t)=-\phi_{1}(t) [/latex]


[latex] d_{\min }=2[/latex]
[latex] \text { When } p(t)=\phi_{1}(t) \text { and } q(t)=-\sqrt{E}\phi_{2}(t)[/latex]
[latex] d_{\min }=\sqrt{(\sqrt{E})^{2}+1}=\sqrt{E+1}[/latex]


To obtain same bit-error probability, [latex]\sigma_{\text {min }} [/latex] should be same.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { So, } \quad \sqrt{E+1} &=2 \\ E &=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The quantum efficiency ([latex]\eta[/latex]) and responsivity (R) at a wavelength [latex]\lambda (in \; \mu m)[/latex] in a p-i-n photodetector are related by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \eta&=\frac{I_{\text {out }}}{q} \times \frac{h f}{P_{\text {in }}} \\ R&=\frac{I_{\text {out }}}{P_{\text {in }}}\\ \text{So, }\quad R&=\eta \times \frac{q}{h f}=\eta \times \frac{q \lambda}{h c} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
If [latex]\lambda[/latex] is given in [latex]\mu \mathrm{m},[/latex] then
[latex] \begin{aligned} R &=\eta \lambda \times \frac{q \times 10^{-6}}{h c} \\ \frac{h c}{q \times 10^{-6}} & \simeq 1.24\\ \text{So, }\quad R&=\frac{\eta \lambda}{1.24} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two identical copper wires W1 and W2, placed in parallel as shown in the figure, carry currents I and 2I, respectively, in opposite directions. If the two wires are separated by a distance of 4r, then the magnitude of the magnetic field [latex]\vec{B}[/latex] between the wires at a distance r from W1 is
raw_source.solution:
Magnetic flux density [latex](\vec{B})[/latex] at r distance due to infinite line carrying current I is [latex]|\vec{B}|=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi \rho} .[/latex]
[latex] \vec{B} [/latex] at r distance due to [latex]W_{1}[/latex] wire
[latex] =\left|\vec{B}_{1}\right|=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r}\qquad \ldots(i)[/latex]
[latex] \vec{B} [/latex] at 3r distance due to [latex]W_{2}[/latex] wire
[latex] =\left|\vec{B}_{2}\right|=\frac{\mu_{0}(2 I)}{2 \pi(3 r)}\qquad \ldots(ii)[/latex]
From right hand thumb rule, [latex]\vec{B} [/latex] due to both lines add in between conductors.
[latex] \begin{aligned} {So,}\qquad |\vec{B}|&=\left|\vec{B}_{1}\right|+\left|\vec{B}_{2}\right|\\ \therefore \qquad |\vec{B}|&=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r}+\frac{2 \mu_{0} I}{6 \pi r}=\frac{5 \mu_{0} I}{6 \pi r} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The dispersion equation of a waveguide,which relates the wavenumber kto the frequency [latex]\omega[/latex], is

[latex]k(\omega) =(1/c)\sqrt{\omega ^2 -{\omega _0}^2}[/latex]

where the speed of light [latex]c=3 \times 10^8[/latex] m/s, and [latex]\omega_0[/latex] is a constant. If the group velocity is [latex]2 \times 10^8[/latex] m/s, then the phase velocity is
raw_source.solution:
By definition [latex]v_{p}=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{\omega}{k} [/latex]
where, [latex]k(\omega)=\left(\frac{1}{c}\right) \sqrt{\omega^{2}-\omega_{0}^{2}} \quad [/latex](given)
[latex] \therefore v_{p}=\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}}[/latex]
by definition,
[latex] \begin{aligned} v_{g} &=\frac{d \omega}{d \beta}=\frac{d \omega}{d k} \\ &=\frac{d k}{d \omega}=\frac{1}{c} \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\omega^{2}-\omega_{0}^{2}}} \times 2 \omega \\ \text{or}\quad v_{g} &=c \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}\\ \because \quad v_{p} \cdot v_{g} &=c^{2} \\ \therefore \quad v_{p} &=\frac{c^{2}}{v_{g}}=\frac{\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right)^{2}}{2 \times 10^{8}} \\ &=4.5 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the circuit shown, the breakdown voltage and the maximum current of the Zener diode are 20 V and 60 mA, respectively. The values of [latex]R_1 \; and \; R_L[/latex] are [latex]200\Omega \; and \; 1k\Omega[/latex], respectively. What is the range of [latex]V_i[/latex] that will maintain the Zener diode in the 'on' state?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{z} &=20 \mathrm{V} \\ I_{z \max } &=60 \mathrm{mA} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Set zener diode be OFF
[latex] V_{o}=\frac{V_{i} \times 1}{0.2+1}=\frac{V_{i}}{1.2}[/latex]
Zener diode can become ON i.e. it goes into
breakdown, when
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{i}}{1.2} & \gt 20 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{i} & \gt 24 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When Zener diode is in breakdown region,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} I_{1}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2} \mathrm{mA}\\ I_{L}=\frac{V_{0}}{R_{L}}=\frac{20}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=20 \mathrm{mA} \\ I_{z}=I_{1}-I_{L}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2}-20 \end{array}[/latex]
For safe operation, [latex]I_{z} \leq I_{z \max } [/latex]
[latex] \frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2}-20 \leq 60[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow V_{i} \leq 36 \mathrm{V}[/latex]
Hence, [latex]24 \lt V_{i} \lt 36 V[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the homogeneous ordinary differential equation

[latex]x^2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-3x\frac{dy}{dx}+3y=0, \; x \gt 0[/latex]

with y(x) as a generalsolution. Given that
y(1)=1 and y(2)=14
the value of y(1.5), rounded off to two decimal places, is ______.

Let h[n] be a length-7 discrete-time finite impulse response filter, given by

h[0]=4, h[1]=3, h[2]=2, h[3]=1,
h[-1]=-3, h[-2]=-2, h[-3]=-1,

and h[n] is zero for [latex]|n|\geq 4[/latex]. A length-3 finite impulse response approximation g[n] of g[n] has to be obtained such that

[latex]E(h,g)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H(e^{j\omega })-G(e^{j\omega })|^2d\omega[/latex]

is minimized, where [latex]H(e^{j\omega })[/latex] and [latex]G(e^{j\omega })[/latex] are the discrete-time Fourier transforms of h[n] and g[n], respectively. For the filter that minimizes E(h,g), the value of 10g[-1]+g[1], rounded off to 2 decimal places, is ________
raw_source.solution:
From Parseval's theorem,
[latex] \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|x[n]|^{2}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|X\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|^{2} d \omega[/latex]
So,
[latex] \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|H\left(e^{j \omega}\right)-G\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|^{2} d \omega=2 \pi \sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2} [/latex]
The solution of g(n) that minimizes E(h, g) also
minimizes [latex]\sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2}[/latex]
[latex] =|4-g(0)|^{2}+|3-g(1)|^{2}+|-3-g(-1)|^{2}+10 [/latex]
The solution of g(n) that minimizes the above
equation is
[latex] g(n)=(-3,4,3\}[/latex]
[latex] So, 10 g(-1)+g(1)=10(-3)+3=-27[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let a random process Y(t) be described as Y(t)=h(t)*X(t)+Z(t), where X(t) is a white noise process with power spectral density [latex]S_X(f)=5[/latex] W/Hz. The filter h(t) has a magnitude response given by |H(f)|=0.5 for [latex]-5\leq f\leq 5[/latex], and zero elsewhere. Z(t) is a stationary random process, uncorrelated with X(t), with power spectral density as shown in the figure. The power in Y(t), in watts, is equal to ________ W (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Let, } \quad X_{1}(t) &=h(t) * X(t) \\ S_{X 1}(f) &=|H(f)|^{2} S_{X}(f) \end{aligned}[/latex]


Given that, Z(t) and X(t) are uncorrelated
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\quad S_{y}(f)=S_{X 1}(f)+S_{z}(f)\\ & \text{Power in }\mathrm{y}(t) \\ P_{Y}&=\left[\text { Area under } S_{X 1}(f)\right]+\left[\text { Area under } S_{z}(f)\right] \\ &=(10 \times 1.25)+(5 \times 1)=17.5 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A voice signal m(t) is in the frequency range 5 kHz to 15 kHz. The signal is amplitude-modulated to generate an AM signal [latex]f(t)=A(1+m(t))cos 2\pi f_c t[/latex], where [latex]f_c[/latex]=600kHz. The AM signal f(t) is to be digitized and archived. This is done by first sampling f(t) at 1.2 times the Nyquist frequency, and then quantizing each sample using a 256-level quantizer. Finally, each quantized sample is binary coded using K bits, where K is the minimum number of bits required for the encoding. The rate, in Megabits per second (rounded off to 2 decimal places), of the resulting stream of coded bits is _______ Mbps.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Nyquist rate } &=2 \times 615 \mathrm{kHz} \\ &=1230 \mathrm{kHz}=1.23 \mathrm{MHz} \\ f_{s} &=1.2 \times 1.23=1.476 \mathrm{MHz} \\ \text { Bits/sample }, n &=\log _{2}(256)=8 \\ \text { So, } \quad A_{D} &=n f_{s}=8 \times 1.476 \\ &=11.808 \simeq 11.81 \mathrm{Mbps} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A Germanium sample of dimensions 1cmx1cm is illuminated with a 20 mW, 600 nm laser light source as shown in the figure. The illuminated sample surface has a 100 nm of loss-less Silicon dioxide layer that reflects one-fourth of the incident light. From the remaining light, one-third of the power is reflected from the Silicon dioxide-Germanium interface, one-third is absorbed in the Germanium layer, and one-third is transmitted through the other side of the sample. If the absorption coefficient of Germanium at 600 nm is [latex]3 \times 10^4 cm^{-1}[/latex] and the bandgap is 0.66 eV, the thickness of the Germanium layer, rounded off to 3 decimal places, is ______ [latex]\mu m[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{\text {absorbed }} &=P_{\text {incident }}\left(1-e^{-\alpha T}\right) \\ \frac{1}{3} &=\frac{2}{3}\left(1-e^{-\alpha T}\right) \\ \frac{2}{3} e^{-\alpha T} &=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
where [latex]\alpha=3 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{cm}^{-1}[/latex], absorption coefficient of Ge sample.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad T &=\frac{1}{\alpha} \ln (2)=\frac{1}{3 \times 10^{4}} \ln (2) \mathrm{cm} \\ &=0.231 \mu \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

In an ideal pn junction with an ideality factor of 1 at T=300 K, the magnitude of the reverse-bias voltage required to reach 75% of its reverse saturation current, rounded off to 2 decimal places, is ____mV.
[[latex]k=1.38 \times 10^{-23}JK^{-1}[/latex], [latex]h=6.625 \times 10^{-34}J-s[/latex], [latex]q=1.602 \times 10^{-19}C[/latex]]
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{T} &=\frac{k T}{q}=\frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \mathrm{V} \\ &=25.843 \mathrm{mV} \\ I &=I_{0}\left(e^{V / V_{T}}-1\right)=-\frac{3}{4} I_{0} \\ \Rightarrow\quad V &=V_{T} \ln 0.25=-35.83 \mathrm{mV} \\ V_{R} &=|V|=35.83 \mathrm{mV} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The drain saturation current ([latex]I_{Dsat}[/latex]) for a gate voltage of 5 V is _____mA(rounded off to two decimal places).

raw_source.text: A rectangular waveguide of width w and height h has cut-off frequencies for [latex]TE_{10} \; and \;TE_{11}[/latex] modes in the ratio 1:2. The aspect ratio w/h, rounded off to two decimal places, is ___________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]f_{c m n}=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^{2}}[/latex]
For TE mode
[latex] f_{c10}=\frac{c}{2 w} \quad\ldots(i)[/latex]
and For [latex]TE_{11}[/latex] mode.
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c11} &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\frac{1}{w}^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{h}\right)^{2}} &\ldots(i)\\ &=\frac{c}{2 w} \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}} &\ldots(ii)\\ \text{given}\quad\frac{f_{c10}}{f_{11}} &=\frac{1}{2} &\ldots(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
put (i). (in) in (ii)
[latex] \Rightarrow \frac{\frac{c}{2 w}}{\frac{c}{2 w} \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}}=2[/latex]
On solving above equation, we get,
[latex] \frac{w}{h}=\sqrt{3}=1.732[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the circuit shown, [latex]V_s[/latex] is a 10 V square wave of period, T=4 ms with R= 500[latex]\Omega[/latex] and C = 10 [latex]\mu F[/latex]. The capacitor is initially uncharged at t=0, and the diode is assumed to be ideal. The voltage across the capacitor ([latex]V_c[/latex]) at 3 ms is equal to ____ volts (rounded off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \tau &=R C=500 \times 10 \times 10-6=5 \mathrm{m}_{8} \\ 0 \lt t \lt \frac{t}{2} \; :\; \; v_{\mathrm{cap}} &=v_{f}+\left(v_{i}-v_{f}\right) e^{-t / \tau} \\ &=10+(0-10) e^{-t / \mathrm{Rc}}\\ \text{At }t&=2 \mathrm{msec,} \\ v_{\mathrm{cap}}&=10-10 e^{\frac{-2 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-3}}}\\ &=3.296 \mathrm{V} \simeq 3.3 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For [latex]2 \mathrm{ms} \lt t \lt 4 \mathrm{ms},[/latex] diode is OFF and Capacitor
has no path to discharge. Hence, at t=3 ms [latex] V_{\text {cap }}=3.3 \mathrm{V}[/latex]

A CMOS inverter, designed to have a mid-point voltage [latex]V_I[/latex] equal to half of [latex]V_{dd}[/latex], as shown in the figure, has the following parameters:

[latex]I_{D n}=I_{D p} [/latex] and both will be in saturation
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{If }\quad V_{\mathrm{IN}}&=\frac{V_{D D}}{2}=1.5 \mathrm{V}=V_{\mathrm{GSN}}=V_{S G P} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}&\left(\mu_{n} C_{O x}\right)\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{n}\left[V_{\mathrm{GSN}}-V_{T N}\right]^{2} \\ =& \frac{1}{2}\left(\mu_{p} C_{Q x}\right)\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{p}\left[V_{G S P}+V_{T P}\right]^{2} \\ 100 \times 10^{-6}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{n} &[1.5-0.7]^{2} \\ &=40 \times 10^{-6}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{p}[1.5-0.9]^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{n}}{\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{p}}&=\frac{40}{100} \times \frac{(0.6)^{2}}{(0.8)^{2}}=0.225 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the circuit shown, the threshold voltages of the pMOS (|[latex]V_{tp}[/latex]|) and nMOS ([latex]V_{tn}[/latex]) transistors are both equal to 1 V. All the transistors have the same output resistance [latex]r_{ds}[/latex] of 6 M[latex]\Omega[/latex]. The other parameters are listed below:

[latex]\mu_n C_{ox}=60\mu A/V^2[/latex]; [latex]\left ( \frac{W}{L} \right )_{nMOS}=5[/latex]
[latex]\mu_p C_{ox}=30\mu A/V^2[/latex]; [latex]\left ( \frac{W}{L} \right )_{pMOS}=10[/latex]

[latex]\mu_n \; and \; \mu_p[/latex] are the carrier mobilities, and [latex]C_{ox}[/latex] is the oxide capacitance per unit area. Ignoring the effect of channel length modulation and body bias, the gain of the circuit is____ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]M_{3}[/latex] and [latex]M_{4}[/latex] are identical PMOS transistor and they have equal current.
Hence their [latex]V_{SG}[/latex] should be equal.


[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{S G 3} &=V_{S G 4}=\frac{V_{D D}}{2}=2 V \\ I_{S D} &=\frac{\mu_{p} C_{o x}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{p}\left(V_{S G}-\left|V_{T}\right|\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{30}{2} \times 10(2-1)^{2}=150 \mu \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]
now, by using current mirror property all transistor should have equal current.
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{\mathrm{DSN}}&=I_{\mathrm{SDP}}=150 \mu \mathrm{A} \\ \text { For } M_{1} \quad g_{m 1}&=\sqrt{2 \mu_{n} C_{o x} \frac{W}{L} \times I_{D S}} \\ &=\sqrt{2 \mu_{n} C_{0 x}} \frac{W}{L} \times I_{D S}\\ & =\sqrt{2 \times 60 \times 5 \times 150}=300 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] M_{2}, M_{3} [/latex] and [latex] M_{4}[/latex] from active load for [latex]M_{1}[/latex]. This active load in equivalent to resistance [latex]r_{d s 2} i.e. 6 \mathrm{M} \Omega [/latex]


[latex] M_{1}[/latex] is common source amplifier.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{V_{\text {out }}}{V_{\text {in }}} &=A_{v}=-g_{m 1} \times\left(r_{\text {ds2 }} \| r_{\text {ds1 }}\right) \\ &=-300 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{C} \times 3 \mathrm{M} \Omega=-900 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the circuit shown, [latex]V_1=0 \; and \; V_2=V_{dd}[/latex]. The other relevant parameters are mentioned in the figure. Ignoring the effect of channel length modulation and the body effect, the value of [latex]I_{out}[/latex] is _____mA(rounded off to 1 decimal place).

[latex] M_{4}[/latex] is ON because [latex]V_{2}=V_{D D} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{5} &=I_{4}=I_{2}=1.5 \mathrm{mA} \\ \frac{I_{6}}{I_{5}} &=\frac{(W / L)_{6}}{(W / L)_{5}}=\frac{40}{10}=4 \\ I_{6} &=4 I_{5}=4 \times 1.5=6 \mathrm{mA} \\ \therefore \quad I_{\text {out }} &=I_{6}=6 \mathrm{mA} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]v_1, v_2,..., v_6[/latex] are six vectors in [latex]\mathbb{R}^4[/latex], which one of the following statements is False?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]v_1, v_2,..., v_6[/latex] are six vectors in [latex]\mathbb{R}^4[/latex].
For a 4-dimensional vector space,
(i) any four linearly independent vectors form a basis (or)
(ii) Any set of four vectors in [latex]\mathbb{R}^4[/latex] spans [latex]\mathbb{R}^4[/latex], then it forms a basis.
Therefore, clearly options (A), (B), (D) are true.
Option (C) is FALSE
options: It is not necessary that these vectors span [latex]\mathbb{R}^4[/latex].

The random variable

where [latex]\phi (t) =\left\{\begin{matrix} 1; & 5\leq t\leq 7\\ 0; & otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

and W(t) is a real white Gaussian noise process with two-sided power spectral density [latex]S_W(f) = 3[/latex] W/Hz, for all f. The variance of Y is _________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Given: }\phi (t) &=\left\{\begin{matrix} 1 & 5\leq t\leq 7\\ 0 & otherwise \end{matrix}\right. \\ s_{\omega }(f)& =3 \text{ Watts/Hz} \\ R_{\omega }(\tau )&=3\delta (\tau )=3\delta (t_{1}-t_{2}) \\ Var[y]&=E[y^{2}]-{E[y]}^{2} \\ {E[W(t)]}^{2}&=\text{DC power} \\ &=\text{Area under PSD at }f=0 \\ {E[W(t)]}^{2}&=0 \\ E[W(t)]&=0 \\ y&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }W(t)\phi (t)dt \\ E[y]&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }E[W(t)]\phi (t)dt \\ y&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }W(t)\phi (t)dt\rightarrow E[y^{2}]\\ &=S_{\omega }(f)\cdot Energy[\phi (t)]\\ & =3 \times 2=6\\ \text{Var}[y]&=6-0=6\end{aligned}[/latex]

Detailed Explanations for:
[latex]\begin{aligned}y&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }W(t)\phi (t)dt \\ E(y^{2})&=E[y \cdot y] \\ &=E[\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }W(t_{1})\phi (t_{1})dt_{1}\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }W(t_{2})\phi (t_{2})dt_{2}] \\ &=E[\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }W(t_{1})W(t_{2})\phi (t_{1})\phi (t_{2})dt_{1}\cdot dt_{2}] \\ &=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }E[W(t_{1})W(t_{2}) \cdot \phi (t_{1})\phi (t_{2})dt_{1} dt_{2}] \\ &=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }R_{W}(t_{1}-t_{2})\phi (t_{1})\phi (t_{2})dt_{1}dt_{2} \\ &=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }3\delta (t_{1}-t_{2})\phi (t_{1})\phi (t_{2})dt_{1}dt_{2}\end{aligned}[/latex]

Above Integration Exists Provided
[latex]\begin{aligned}t_{1}&=t_{2}=t\\ &=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }3\delta (0)\phi (t)\phi (t)dt \, dt\\ &=3 \int_{-\infty }^{\infty } \delta (0) dt + \int_{-\infty }^{\infty } \phi ^2 (t) dt\\&=2 \times 1 \times \text{Energy}[\phi (t)] \\E[y^{2}]&=6\end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]x[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{7}x[n]e^{-j\frac{\pi kn}{4}}[/latex], k=0,1,...,7.

Which one of the following statement is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\cos 200\pi t\\ t&=\frac{n}{400}\\ x(n)&=\cos \left ( 200\pi \frac{n}{400} \right )\\&=\cos \left ( \frac{\pi }{2} n\right ); \; \; n=0,1,...,7\\ &=\left \{ \cos 0,\cos \frac{\pi }{2},\cos \pi ,\cos \frac{3\pi }{2} ,\cos 2\pi ,\cos \frac{5\pi }{2},\cos 3\pi ,\cos \frac{7\pi }{2}\right \} \\ &={1,0,-1,0,1,0,-1,0}\xLeftrightarrow{\text{DFT}} X(K) \\ \text{suppose, } y(n)&={1,-1,1,-1}\xLeftrightarrow{\text{DFT}} Y(k)\end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex][Y(K)]=\left.\begin{matrix} [W_{N}] \end{matrix}\right|_{N=4}[y(n)]=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &1 &1 &1 \\ 1 &-j &-1 &j \\ 1&-1 &1 &-1 \\ 1&j& -1 &-j \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -1\\ 1\\ -1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &0 &4 &0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Now,as we know,
If for [latex]\, \left \{ a,b,c,d \right \}\xLeftrightarrow{\text{DFT}} \left \{ A,B,C,D \right \} [/latex]
Then for, [latex]\left \{ a,0,b,0,c,0,d,0 \right \}\xLeftrightarrow{\text{DFT}}\left \{A,B,C,D,A,B,C,D \right \}[/latex]
Similarly for [latex] y(n)={1,-1,1,-1}\xLeftrightarrow{\text{DFT}}Y(k)=\left \{ 0,0,4,0\right \}[/latex]
Here, for [latex]x(n)=\left \{ 1,0,-1,0,1,0,-1,0 \right \} [/latex]
[latex]X(k)=\left \{ \underset{0}{\uparrow},0,4,0,0,0,4,0 \right \}[/latex]
options: Only X[2] and X [6] are non-zero
Only X[3] and X [5] are non-zero

raw_answer.option_text: Only X[2] and X [6] are non-zero

raw_source.text: A one-sided abrupt [latex]pn[/latex] junction diode has a depletion capacitance CD of 50 pF at a reverse bias of 0.2 V. The plot of [latex]1/C_D^2[/latex] versus the applied voltage V for this diode is a straight line as shown in the figure below. The slope of the plot is ____[latex]\times 10^{20} F^{-2} V^{-1}[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
As per GATE official answer key MTA (Marks to ALL)

Depletion or transition capacitance is,
[latex]C_{D}=\frac{A_{\epsilon }}{W}[/latex]
For one-sided PN junction [latex]\left (EX:P^{+}N Junction \right )[/latex]
[latex]W=\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon V_{B}}{eN_{D}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon \left ( V_{bi}-V \right )}{eN_{D}}}[/latex]
where V is anode to cathode applied potential.
[latex]\Rightarrow \, \, \, \, C_{D}=\frac{A\epsilon }{\sqrt{\frac{2\, \epsilon \left ( V_{bi}-V \right )}{eN_{D}}}} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \, \, \, \, \frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}=\frac{2}{A^{2}\epsilon eN_{D}}\left ( V_{bi}-V \right )[/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}\, becomes \, zero \, at V=V_{bi}[/latex]
From above graph,[latex]y=\frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}=0\, at\, x_{1}=V_{bi}[/latex]
[latex] And \, \, \, y_{2}=\frac{1}{C_{D}^{2}}=4\times 10^{20}\, at\, x_{2}=-0.2V [/latex]
[latex]Slope=\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-X_{1}}=\frac{4\times 10^{20}-0}{-0.2-V_{bi}}[/latex]
[latex] V_{bi}[/latex] is not provided,slope cannot be found.

raw_source.text: For the modulated signal [latex]x(t)= m(t) \cos(2 \pi f_c t)[/latex], the message signal [latex]m(t) = 4 \cos (1000 \pi t)[/latex] and the carrier frequency [latex]f_c[/latex] is 1 MHz. raw_source.solution:
Output of multiplier
[latex]=x(t)\cos 2\pi (f_{c}+40)t=m(t)\cos 2\pi f_{c}t\cdot \cos2\pi (f_{c}+40)t[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{m(t)}{2}[\cos 2\pi (2f_{c}+40)t+\cos 2\pi (40)t][/latex]
Given, [latex]m(t)=4\cos 1000\pi t[/latex]
So, output of multiplier
[latex]=2\cos 2\pi (500)t[\cos 2\pi (2f_{c}+40)t+\cos 2\pi (40)t][/latex]

Output of Low pass filter
[latex]=\cos [2\pi (460)]t[/latex]
[latex] =\cos 920\pi t[/latex]

raw_source.text: For an infinitesimally small dipole in free space, the electric field [latex]E_\theta[/latex] in the far field is proportional to [latex](e^{-jkr}/r) \sin \theta[/latex], where [latex]k = 2 \pi /\lambda[/latex]. A vertical infinitesimally small electric dipole ([latex]\delta l \lt \lt \lambda[/latex]) is placed at a distance [latex]h(h \gt 0)[/latex] above an infinite ideal conducting plane, as shown in the figure. The minimum value of h, for which one of the maxima in the far field radiation pattern occurs at [latex]\theta =60^{\circ}[/latex], is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned}\left | \text{Total E }\right |&=\left | (E_{\text{single element}}) \right | \left | (A.F.) \right | \\ \left | (A.F.) \right |&=\frac{\sin\left ( N\frac{\psi }{2} \right )}{\sin (\frac{\psi }{2})}=\frac{\sin \left ( 2\frac{\psi }{2} \right )}{\sin \left ( \frac{\psi }{2} \right )} \\ & =\frac{2\sin \left ( \frac{\psi }{2} \right )\cos (\frac{\psi }{2})}{\sin \frac{\psi }{2}} \\ & =2\cos (\frac{\psi }{2})\\ \left | A.F_{N} \right | &=\frac{A.F}{A.F_{max}}=\frac{2\cos (\frac{\psi }{2})}{2} \\ &=\left | \cos \left ( \frac{\psi }{2} \right ) \right | \\ \text{where, }\psi &=\beta d\cos \theta =\frac{2\pi }{\lambda }(2h)\cos \theta \\ \left.\begin{matrix} \left | A.F_{N} \right |_{\theta =60^{\circ}} \end{matrix}\right|& =\left | \cos (\frac{2\pi }{\lambda }h\cos 60^{\circ}) \right |\\ &=\left | \cos \left ( \frac{\pi h}{\lambda } \right ) \right |\\ \cos \theta \text{ is maximum ,where } \theta &=n\pi \;\; n=0,1,2..\\ \frac{\pi h}{\lambda }&=n\pi \Rightarrow h=n\lambda \\ \Rightarrow \; \text{For } n=1, \;\; h_{min}&=\lambda \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The magnetic field of a uniform plane wave in vacuum is given by

[latex]\vec{H}(x,y,z,t)=(\hat{a}_x+2\hat{a}_y+b\hat{a}_z) \cos (\omega t+3x-y-z)[/latex]

The value of b is _____
raw_source.solution:
For uniform plane wave
[latex]\hat{a}_{H}\cdot \hat{a}_{\rho }=0[/latex]
[latex]\hat{a}_{H}[/latex]is unit vector in magnetic field direction [latex]\hat{a}_{\rho }[/latex] is unit vector in power flow direction
[latex]\hat{a}_{H }=\frac{1\hat{a}_{x}+2\hat{a}_{y}+b\hat{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+b^{2}}} [/latex]
[latex]\hat{a}_{\rho }=\frac{-3\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}+\hat{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}}}[/latex]
[latex] \hat{a}_{H}\cdot \hat{a}_{\rho }=0 (\hat{a}_{x}+2\hat{a}_{y}+b\hat{a}_{z})\cdot (-3\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}+\hat{a}_{z})=0[/latex]
[latex] -3+2+b=0[/latex]
[latex] b=1[/latex]

raw_source.text:
[latex]S_{PM}(t)\; and \; S_{FM}(t)[/latex] as defined below, are the phase modulated and the frequency modulated waveforms, respectively, corresponding to the message signal m(t) shown in the figure.

[latex]S_{PM}(t)= \cos (1000 \pi t+K_p m(t))[/latex]
and [latex]S_{FM}(t)= \cos (1000 \pi t+K_f \int_{-\infty }^{t} m(\tau )d\tau )[/latex]

where [latex]K_p[/latex] is the phase deviation constant in radians/volt and [latex]K_f[/latex] is the frequency deviation constant in radians/second/volt. If the highest instantaneous frequencies of [latex]S_{PM}(t)\; and \; S_{FM}(t)[/latex] are same, then the value of the ratio [latex]\frac{K_p}{K_f}[/latex] is ______ seconds.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}S(t)_{pm}&=A_c \cos [2\pi f_{c}t+k_pm(t)]\\ S(t)_{Fm}&=A_c \cos [2\pi f_{c}t+k_{f}\int_{0}^{\infty }m(t)dt]\end{aligned}[/latex]
Instantaneous frequency are equal
[latex]\begin{aligned}f_{i}&=\frac{1}{2\pi }\frac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} t}\theta (t)\\f_{iPM}&=f_{c}+\frac{K_p}{2\pi }\frac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} t} m(t)\\ f_{iFM}&=f_{c}+\frac{K_f}{2\pi }m(t)\\ \text{Given that, } (f_{iPM})_{max}&=(f_{iFM})_{max} \\ f_{c}+\frac{k_P}{2\pi}[\frac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} t}m(t)]_{max}&=f_{c}+\frac{K_{f}}{2\pi }[m(t)]_{max}\\ \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{k_P}{2\pi}\frac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} t}m(t) \end{matrix}\right|_{max} &= \left. \begin{matrix} \frac{K_{f}}{2\pi }[m(t)] \end{matrix}\right|_{max}\\ \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} t}m(t) \end{matrix}\right|_{max} &=5, \left.\begin{matrix} m(t) \end{matrix}\right|_{max}=10 \\ 5k_{p}&=10k_{f} \\ \frac{k_{p}}{k_{f}}&=2\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system with transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+a)}, a \gt 0[/latex] is subjected an input [latex]5\cos 3t[/latex].
The steady state output of the system is [latex]\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \cos (3t-1.892)[/latex]. The value of [latex]a[/latex] is ____.
raw_source.solution:
Given that,
[latex]\begin{aligned}G(j\omega )&=\frac{1}{(1+j\omega )(\alpha +j\omega )} \\ \left |G(j\omega ) \right |&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(\omega ^{2}+1)(\omega ^{2}+\alpha ^{2})}} \\ \text{According to }& \text{question,}\\ \left | G(j\omega ) \right |_{\omega =3}&=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{10}}\\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{(\omega ^{2}+1)(\omega ^{2}+\alpha ^{2})}}&=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{10}} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{10(a^{2}+9)}}&=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{10}} \alpha ^{2}+9=25 \\ \alpha ^{2}&=16 \\ \alpha &=4\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: [latex]X(\omega )[/latex] is the Fourier transform of [latex]x(t)[/latex] shown below. The value of [latex]\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }|X(\omega )|^2 d\omega[/latex] (rounded off to two decimal places) is ______.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\left | X(\omega ) \right |^{2}d\omega &=2\pi \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\left | x(t) \right |^{2}dt \\ &=2\pi \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\left | y(t) \right |^{2}\\      &=2\times 2\pi \int_{-2}^{0}\left | y(t) \right |^{2}dt\\      &=2\times 2\pi\left [ \int_{-2}^{-1}(t+2)^{2}dt+\int_{-1}^{0}(2t+3)^{2}dt \right ]\\&=4\pi \left [\left \{ \frac{(t+2)^{3}}{3} \right \} _{-1}^{-2}+\left \{ \frac{(2t+3)^3}{3\times 2} \right \}_{0}^{-1} \right ]\\&=4\pi \left [ \frac{1-0}{3}+\frac{3^{3}-1}{6} \right ]\\&=4\pi \left [ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{26}{6} \right ]\\&=     4\pi \times \left [ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{26}{6} \right ] \\ &=4\pi \times \left [ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{13}{3} \right ]\\&=4\pi \times \frac{14}{3} \\&=\frac{56\pi }{3}=58.61\end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: X is a random variable with uniform probability density function in the interval [-2,10]. For Y = 2X-6, the conditional probability [latex]P(Y \leq 7|X \geq 5)[/latex] (rounded off to three decimal places) is _____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]x[/latex] follows uniform distribution over [-2, 10]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \; f(x)&=\frac{1}{b-a}=\frac{1}{10-(-2)}=\frac{1}{12}\\ \text{Given: } y &= 2x - 6\\ \Rightarrow \; x&=\frac{y+6}{2}\\ \text{For } y = 7 \\ x&=\frac{7+6}{2}=\frac{13}{2}=6.5\\ P\left [ \frac{y\lt7}{x\gt 5} \right ]&=P\left [ \frac{x\lt6.5}{x\gt 5} \right ] \\ &=\frac{P\left [ x\gt 5\, and\, x\lt6.5 \right ]}{P\left [ x\gt 5 \right ]} \\ &=\frac{P\left [ 5\lt x \lt 6.5 \right ]}{P[x\gt 5]} \\ &=\frac{\int_{5}^{6.5}f(x)dx}{\int_{5}^{10}F(x)dx} \\ &=\frac{\int_{5}^{6.5}\frac{1}{12}dx}{\int_{5}^{10}\frac{1}{12}dx} \\ &=\frac{(x)_{6.5}^{5}}{(x)_{5}^{10}}=\frac{1.5}{5}=0.3\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following closed loop control system

where [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)}[/latex] and [latex]C(s)=K\frac{s+1}{s+3}[/latex]. If the steady state error for a unit ramp input is 0.1, then the value of K is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Open loop transfer function for the system [latex]=C(s)\times G(s)=\frac{K(s+1)}{ (s+3)}\times \frac{1}{s(s+1)}[/latex]
Since the system is type-1, so far a given unit ramp input steady state

Consider the differential equation given below.
[latex]\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}y=x\sqrt{y}[/latex]
The integrating factor of the differential equation is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}} y&=x \sqrt{y}, \quad \text { IF }=?\\ \text{Divided by }\sqrt{y}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}} \sqrt{y}&=x \\ 2 \frac{d u}{d x}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}} u&=x\\ \text{Let }\qquad x \sqrt{y}&=u\\ \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{v}} \frac{d y}{d x}&=\frac{d u}{d x}\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \frac{d u}{d x}+\frac{x}{2\left(1-x^{2}\right)} u&=\frac{x}{2} \rightarrow \text{ lines diff. equ.} \\ \text { I. } F&=e^{\int \frac{x}{2\left(1-x^{2}\right)} d x}=e^{-\frac{1}{4} \log \left(1-x^{2}\right)}&=e^{\log \left(1-x^{2}\right) \frac{-1}{4}} \\ \text { I.F }&=\frac{1}{\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Two continuous random variables X and Y are related as

Let [latex]\sigma ^{2}_{X}[/latex] and [latex]\sigma ^{2}_{Y}[/latex] denote the variances of X and Y, respectively. The variances are related as
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Y &=2 X+3 \\ \operatorname{Var}[Y] &=E\left[(Y-\bar{Y})^{2}\right] \\ E[Y] &=\bar{Y}=2 \bar{X}+3 \\ \operatorname{Var}[Y] &=E\left[(2 X+3-2 \bar{X}-3)^{2}\right] \\ &=E\left[4(X-\bar{X})^{2}\right] \\ &=4 \cdot E\left[(X-\bar{X})^{2}\right] \\ \sigma_{Y}^{2} &=4 \cdot \sigma_{X}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Poles are given by [latex]x^{2}=0[/latex] and [latex]x^{2}+4=0[/latex]
