raw_source.text:
Box contains the following three coins.

i. A fair coin with head on one face and tail on the other face.
ii. A coin with heads on both the faces.
iii. A coin with tails on both the faces.

A coin is picked randomly from the box and tossed. Out of the two remaining coins in the box, one coin is then picked randomly and tossed. If the first toss results in a head, the probability of getting a head in the second toss is
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]\quad P\left(H_{2}\right)=[/latex] Probability of getting head in second toss
[latex] P\left(H_{1}\right)=[/latex] Probability of getting head in first toss
[latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(\frac{H_{2}}{H_{1}}\right) &=\frac{P\left(H_{2} \cap H_{1}\right)}{P\left(H_{1}\right)} \\ P\left(H_{1}\right) &=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3} \times 1+\frac{1}{3} \times 0=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
To get head in second toss when head came in first toss, following cases can be made
1. Fair coin :
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Both head coin }=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 1=\frac{1}{12} \\ \text { Both tail coin }=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 0=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2. Both head coin :
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Fair coin }&=\frac{1}{3} \times 1 \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{12}\\ \text{Both tail coin }&=0\\ \therefore \qquad P\left(H_{2} \cap H_{1}\right)&=\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \therefore \qquad P\left(H_{2} / H_{1}\right)&=\frac{1 / 6}{1 / 2}=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A real [latex]2\times2[/latex] non-singular matrix A with repeated eigenvalue is given as
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} x & -3.0\\ 3.0 & 4.0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
where x is a real positive number. The value of x (rounded off to one decimal place) is ________________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc} x & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right][/latex]
Characteristic equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} |A-\lambda I| &=\left|\begin{array}{cc} x-\lambda & -3 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{array}\right|=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}-(4+x) \lambda+(4 x+9)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Roots are repeating
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad b^{2}-4 a c&=0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \left(4+x^{2}\right)-4(4 x+9) &=0 \\ 16+x^{2}+8 x-16 x-20 &=0 \\ x &=10 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad x^{2}-8 x+20 &=0\\ x&=\frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64+80}}{2} \\ &=\frac{8 \pm 12}{2}=-2,10 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, x is positive
[latex] \therefore x=10[/latex]

raw_source.text: A bar of silicon is doped with boron concentration of [latex]10^{16} \text{cm}^{-3}[/latex]  and assumed to be fully ionized. It is exposed to light such that electron-hole pairs are generated throughout the volume of the bar at the rate of [latex]10^{20} \text{cm}^{-3} s^{-1}[/latex]. If the recombination lifetime is [latex]100 \;\mu s[/latex], intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon is [latex]10^{10} \text{cm}^{-3}[/latex] and assuming [latex]100\%[/latex] ionization of boron, then the approximate product of steady-state electron and hole concentrations due to this light exposure is
raw_source.solution:
Boron [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Acceptor type doping


[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{A} &=10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \\ g_{0 p} &=1020 \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \\ \tau &=100 \mu \mathrm{s} \\ n_{i} &=10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Product of steady state electron-hole concentration =?
At thermal equilibrium (before shining light)
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} \text { Hole concentration, } & p_{o} \simeq N_{A}=10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \\ \text { Electron concentration, } & n_{0}=\frac{n_{i}^{2}}{p_{0}}=\frac{10^{20}}{10^{16}}=10^{4} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{array}[/latex]
After, illumination of light,
Hole concentration, [latex]p=p_{o}+\delta p[/latex]
Electron concentration, [latex]\quad n=n_{o}+\delta n[/latex]
Due to shining light, excess carrier concentration,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta p &=\delta n=g_{o p} \cdot \tau=10^{20} \times 100 \times 10^{-6}=10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \\ \therefore \qquad p &=10^{16}+10^{16}=2 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}\\ n&=10^{4}+10^{16} \simeq 10^{16} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, product of steady state electron-hole concentration
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=n p=10^{16} \times 2 \times 10^{16} \\ &=2 \times 10^{32} \mathrm{~cm}^{-6} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Box contains the following three coins.

i. A fair coin with head on one face and tail on the other face.
ii. A coin with heads on both the faces.
iii. A coin with tails on both the faces.

A coin is picked randomly from the box and tossed. Out of the two remaining coins in the box, one coin is then picked randomly and tossed. If the first toss results in a head, the probability of getting a head in the second toss is
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]\quad P\left(H_{2}\right)=[/latex] Probability of getting head in second toss
[latex] P\left(H_{1}\right)=[/latex] Probability of getting head in first toss
[latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(\frac{H_{2}}{H_{1}}\right) &=\frac{P\left(H_{2} \cap H_{1}\right)}{P\left(H_{1}\right)} \\ P\left(H_{1}\right) &=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3} \times 1+\frac{1}{3} \times 0=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
To get head in second toss when head came in first toss, following cases can be made
1. Fair coin :
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Both head coin }=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 1=\frac{1}{12} \\ \text { Both tail coin }=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 0=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2. Both head coin :
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Fair coin }&=\frac{1}{3} \times 1 \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{12}\\ \text{Both tail coin }&=0\\ \therefore \qquad P\left(H_{2} \cap H_{1}\right)&=\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \therefore \qquad P\left(H_{2} / H_{1}\right)&=\frac{1 / 6}{1 / 2}=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Assume that, [latex]\left | V_{BS} \right | \gg 2\Phi _{B}[/latex], where [latex]q\Phi _{B}[/latex] is the separation between the Fermi energy level [latex]E_{F}[/latex] and the intrinsic level [latex]E_{i}[/latex] in the bulk. Parameters given are
Electron charge [latex](q) = 1.6 \times 101^{-19}\:C[/latex]
Vacuum permittivity [latex](\varepsilon _{0}) = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\: F/m[/latex]
Relative permittivity of silicon [latex](\varepsilon _{Si}) = 12[/latex]
Relative permittivity of oxide [latex](\varepsilon _{ox}) = 4[/latex]
The doping concentration of the substrate is
raw_source.solution:
Given, N -channel MOSFET
[latex] \begin{aligned} t_{o x}&=10 \mathrm{~nm}=10 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~cm} & \\ \frac{\partial V_{T}}{\partial\left|V_{B S}\right|}&=50 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{V}, & \left|V_{B S}\right|=2 \mathrm{~V} \\ \qquad q&=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C} & \left|V_{B S}\right|>>2 \phi_{B} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \epsilon_{o} &=8.85 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~F} / \mathrm{cm} \\ \epsilon_{r_{\mathrm{Si}}} &=12 \\ \epsilon_{r_{O x}} &=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Threshold voltage, including body effect,
[latex] V_{T}=\phi_{m s}+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}\left(2 \phi_{B}-V_{B S}\right)}}{C_{o x}}+2 \phi_{B}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{In question, we need, } \left|V_{B S}\right|&=\left|V_{S B}\right| \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad V_{T}&=\phi_{m s}+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}\left(2 \phi_{B}+V_{S B}\right)}}{C_{o x}}+2 \phi_{B}\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad V_{T}&=\phi_{m s}+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}\left(2 \phi_{B}+\left|V_{S B}\right|\right)}}{C_{O x}}+2 \phi_{B}\\ \therefore \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial V_{T}}{\partial\left|V_{B S}\right|}&=0+\frac{\sqrt{2 \epsilon_{s i} q N_{A}}}{C_{O x}} \cdot \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2 \phi_{B}+\left|V_{S B}\right|}}+0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad 50 \times 10^{-3}&=\frac{\sqrt{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14} \times 12 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~N}_{A}}}{\epsilon_{\alpha x} / t_{0 x}} \cdot \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\left|V_{S B}\right|}}\\ \left(\frac{50 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14}}{10 \times 10^{-7}}\right)^{2}&=\frac{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14} \times 12 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{4 \times 2}\\ &\left[\because\left|V_{S B}\right| \gt \gt 2 \phi_{B}\right]\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad N_{A}&=7.375 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Given codewords:[latex] \left.\begin{array}{l} C_{1}=0101100 \\ C_{2}=0011110 \\ C_{3}=1000110 \end{array}\right\}[/latex]
in given above codewords, first n - k = 3 bits are parity bits and last K = 4 bits are message bits.
Given is (7, 4) systematic linear hamming code. For a linear code, sum of two codewords belong to the code is also a codeword belonging to the code.
[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{1} \oplus C_{2}&=0110010=C_{4} \\ C_{2} \oplus C_{3}&=1011000=C_{5} \\ C_{1} \oplus C_{3}&=1101010=C_{6} \\ C_{3} \oplus C_{4}&=1110100=C_{7} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Based on codewords [latex]C_{6}[/latex] and [latex]C_{7}[/latex] options (a) and (d) will incorrect.

[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { From observation } \Rightarrow & P_{1}=d_{1} \oplus d_{2} \oplus d_{4} \\ & P_{2}=d_{2} \oplus d_{3} \oplus d_{4} \\ & P_{3}=d_{1} \oplus d_{2} \oplus d_{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
From given options, option (C) only satisfying above relations.
So, that option (C) will be correct.

A real [latex]2\times2[/latex] non-singular matrix A with repeated eigenvalue is given as
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} x & -3.0\\ 3.0 & 4.0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
where x is a real positive number. The value of x (rounded off to one decimal place) is ________________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc} x & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right][/latex]
Characteristic equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} |A-\lambda I| &=\left|\begin{array}{cc} x-\lambda & -3 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{array}\right|=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}-(4+x) \lambda+(4 x+9)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Roots are repeating
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad b^{2}-4 a c&=0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \left(4+x^{2}\right)-4(4 x+9) &=0 \\ 16+x^{2}+8 x-16 x-20 &=0 \\ x &=10 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad x^{2}-8 x+20 &=0\\ x&=\frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64+80}}{2} \\ &=\frac{8 \pm 12}{2}=-2,10 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, x is positive
[latex] \therefore x=10[/latex]

The exponential Fourier series representation of a continuous-time periodic signal x(t) is defined as

where [latex]\omega _0[/latex] is the fundamental angular frequency of x(t) and the coefficients of the series are [latex]a_{k}[/latex]. The following information is given about [latex]x(t)[/latex] and [latex]a_{k}[/latex].

[latex]1. x(t)[/latex] is real and even so [latex]a_{k}[/latex] is also real and even [latex]a_{k}=a_{-k}[/latex]
2. Average of x(t) is 2 i.e., [latex]a_{0}=2.[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{llll} 3. \;x(t) \rightarrow a_{k}=k &1 \leq k \leq 3 \quad& a_{1}=1 \quad& a_{-1}=1 \\ \quad \quad \quad \quad \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;0 & k>3 & a_{2}=2 & a_{-2}=2 \\ && a_{3}=3 & a_{-3}=3 \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] 4. \quad T_{0}=6[/latex]
Parsval's Power Theorem
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T}\left|x(t)^{2}\right| d t &=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty}\left|a_{k}\right|^{2} \\ P(t) &=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty}\left|a_{k}\right|^{2}=\left|a_{-3}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{-2}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{-1}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{0}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{1}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{2}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{3}\right|^{2} \\ &=2\left|a_{1}\right|^{2}+2\left|a_{2}\right|^{2}+2\left|a_{3}\right|^{2}+\left|a_{0}\right|^{2} \\ &=2 \times 1^{2}+2 \times(2)^{2}+2(3)^{2}+(2)^{2} \\ &=2+8+18+4 \\ P_{x(t)} &=32 \end{aligned}[/latex]

For a unit step input u[n], a discrete-time [latex]\text{LTI}[/latex]
 system produces an output signal [latex]\left ( 2\delta \left [ n+1 \right ] +\delta \left [ n \right ]+\delta \left [ n-1 \right ]\right )[/latex]. Let [latex]y[n][/latex]
 be the output of the system for an input [latex]\left ( \left ( \dfrac{1}{2} \right )^n u\left [ n \right ]\right )[/latex]. The value of [latex]y[0][/latex]
 is ______
raw_source.solution:
The impulse response [latex]h(n)=s(n)-s(n-1) [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} h(n)=2 \delta(n+1)+\delta(n)&+ \delta(n-1)-2 \delta(n)-\delta(n-1)-\delta(n-1-1) \\ &=2 \delta(n+1)+\delta(n)+\delta(n-1)-2 \delta(n)-\delta(n-1)-\delta(n-2) \\ h(n) &=2 \delta(n+1)-\delta(n)-\delta(n-2) \\ \text{For input }\qquad x_{1}(n)&=(1 / 2)^{n} u(n) \text{ then output } y_{1}(n)=x_{1}(n) * h(n)\\ y_{1}(n)&=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} u(n) *[2 \delta(n+1)-\delta(n)-\delta(n-2)]\\ y_{1}(n)&=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} u(n) * 2 \delta(n+1)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} u(n) * \delta(n)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} u(n) * \delta(n-2) \\ y_{1}(n)&=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n+1} u(n+1)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} u(n)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2} u(n-2) \\ \left.y_{1}(n)\right|_{n=0} &=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1} u(1)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{0} u(0)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2} u(-2) \\ &=1-1 \\ y_{1}(0) &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider the signals [latex]x\left [ n \right ]=2^{n-1}u\left [ -n+2 \right ][/latex] and [latex]y\left [ n \right ]=2^{-n+2}u\left [ n+1 \right ][/latex], where [latex]u[n][/latex] is the unit step sequence. Let [latex]X(e^{jw})[/latex] and [latex]Y(e^{jw})[/latex] be the discrete-time Fourier transform of [latex]x[n][/latex] and [latex]y[n][/latex], respectively. The value of the integral
[latex]\frac{1}{2\pi } \int_{0}^{2\pi }X\left ( e^{j\omega } \right )Y\left ( e^{-j\omega } \right )d\omega[/latex]
(rounded off to one decimal place) is ______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x[n] &=2^{n-1} u[-n+2] \\ y[n] &=2^{-n+2} u[n+1] \\ y[-n] &=2^{n+2} u[-n+1] \\ V &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} X\left(e^{j \omega}\right) Y\left(e^{-j \omega}\right) d \omega &\ldots(i)\\ z[n] &=x[n] * y[-n] \\ z[n] & \rightarrow Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) \\ z[n] &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) e^{j \omega n} d \omega \\ \text { Put } n=0, \qquad z[0] &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) d \omega &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Compare equations (i) and (ii)
[latex] \begin{aligned} z[0] &=V \\ Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) &=X\left(e^{j \omega}\right) Y\left(e^{-j \omega}\right) \\ \text{Apply IDTFT},\qquad Z[n] &=x[n] * y[-n]=x[n] * p[n]\\ \because \qquad p[n]&=y[-n]=2^{n+2} u[-n+1]\\ z[n] &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} 2^{k-1} u[-k+2] 2^{n-k+2} u[-n+k+1] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{k-1} 1 \cdot 2^{n-k+2} u[k+1-n] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{k-1+n-k+2} u[k+1-n] \\ z[n] &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{n+1} u[k-n+1] \\ \text { Put } n=0,\qquad \qquad V &=z[0]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{1} \cdot u[k+1]=2 \sum_{k=-1}^{2} 1=2[1+1+1+1] \\ V &=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Built-in voltage [latex]\left ( \Phi _{\text{bi}} \right ) = 0.8\:V[/latex]
Electron charge [latex](q) = 1.6\times10^{-19} C\:[/latex]
Vacuum permittivity [latex]\left ( \varepsilon _{0} \right ) = 8.85\times10^{-12}\:F/m[/latex]

he magnitude of reverse bias voltage that would completely deplete one of the two regions (P or N) prior to the other (rounded off to one decimal place) is _________V.

Vacuum permittivity, [latex]\epsilon_{o}=8.85 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~F} / \mathrm{m}=8.85 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~F} / \mathrm{cm}[/latex]

So, depletion region width on N -side [latex]=x_{n}=0.2 \mu \mathrm{m}[/latex]

where, [latex]V_{R} \rightarrow [/latex] Magnitude of reverse bias potential
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad 0.2 \times 10^{-4}&=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 12 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-14}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \cdot \frac{5 \times 10^{16}}{10 \times 10^{16}} \cdot \frac{1}{\left(15 \times 10^{16}\right)}\left(\phi_{b i}+V_{R}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad \phi_{b j}+V_{R}&=9.039\\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad V_{R}&=9.039-0.8\\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad V_{R}&=8.239 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

For the transistor [latex]M_{1}[/latex] in the circuit shown in the figure, [latex]\mu_{n} C_{\text{ox}} = 100\:\mu A/V^{2}[/latex] and [latex](W/L)=10[/latex], where [latex]\mu_{n}[/latex] is the mobility of electron, [latex]C_{\text{ox}}[/latex] is the oxide capacitance per unit area , W is the width and L is the length.

The channel length modulation coefficient is ignored. If the gate-to-source voltage [latex]V_{\text{GS}}\text{ is } 1\:V[/latex] to keep the transistor at the edge of saturation, then the threshold voltage of the transistor (rounded off to one decimal place) is _______ V.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{D S}&=\frac{\mu_{n} C_{O x}}{2} \times \frac{W}{L}\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ \text{Given}\qquad V_{G S}&=1 \mathrm{~V} \\ I_{D S}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{D S}=3-20 \times I_{D S} \\ V_{D S}=3-\frac{20}{2}\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ V_{D S}=3-10\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
MOSFET operates in saturation if
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{D S} &\geq V_{G S}-V_{T}\\ \text{So, we take},\qquad \quad V_{D S}&=V_{G S}-V_{T} \\ V_{G S}-V_{T}&=3-10\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ 1-V_{T}&=3-10\left(1-V_{T}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let,}\qquad 1-V_{T} &=x \\ 3-10 x^{2} &=x \\ 10 x^{2}+x-3 x &=0 \\ \text{We get,}\qquad x &=-\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+120}}{20}\\ x &=-\frac{1 \pm 11}{20}\\ \therefore \qquad \quad x&=0.5 \text { and }-0.6\\ x&=0.5\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \quad 1-V_{T} & =0.5 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \quad V_{T} & =0.5 \mathrm{~V} \\ x & =-0.6 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \quad 1-V_{T} & =-0.6 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \quad V_{T} & =1.6 \mathrm{~V} \\ \text { But }\qquad \quad V_{G S} & \gt V_{T} \\ \text { or }\qquad \quad V_{T} & \lt V_{G S} \\ \text { i.e., }\qquad \quad V_{T} & \lt 1 \\ \therefore\qquad \quad V_{T} & =0.5 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The circuit in the figure contains a current source driving a load having an inductor and a resistor in series, with a shunt capacitor across the load. The ammeter is assumed to have zero resistance. The switch is closed at time t = 0.

Initially, when the switch is open, the capacitor is discharged and the ammeter reads zero ampere. After the switch is closed, the ammeter reading keeps fluctuating for some time till it settles to a final steady value. The maximum ammeter reading that one will observe after the switch is closed (rounded off to two decimal places) is _______________ A.
raw_source.solution:
Apply Laplace transform,

[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{s} &=\frac{V(s)}{1 / C s}+\frac{V(s)}{R+L s} \\ \frac{1}{s} &=V(s)\left[C s+\frac{1}{R+L s}\right] \\ V(s) &=\frac{(1 / s)}{C s+\frac{1}{R+L s}} \\ V(s) &=\frac{(1 / s)(R+L S)}{L C s^{2}+R C s+1} \\ I(s) &=\frac{(1 / s)(R+L s)}{L C s^{2}+R C s+1} \cdot \frac{1}{(R+L s)} \\ I(s) &=\frac{1 / L C}{s\left(s^{2}+\frac{R}{L} s+\frac{1}{L C}\right)} \\ L &=10 \mathrm{mH} ; C=100 \mathrm{pF} ; R=5 \times 10^{3} \Omega\\ \xi &=\frac{R}{2} \sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}=\frac{5 \times 10^{3}}{2} \sqrt{\frac{100 \times 10^{-12}}{10 \times 10^{-3}}}=0.25 \\ \text{Max}. \text { over shoot } &=e^{-\pi \xi / \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}}}=0.44 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Maximum value = Steady state + Max. overshoot
[latex] =1+0.44[/latex]
[latex] =1.44 \mathrm{~A}[/latex]

A unity feedback system that uses proportional-integral ([latex]\text{PI}[/latex] ) control is shown in the figure.

The stability of the overall system is controlled by tuning the [latex]\text{PI}[/latex] control parameters [latex]K_{P}[/latex] and [latex]K_{I}[/latex]. The maximum value of [latex]K_{I}[/latex] that can be chosen so as to keep the overall system stable or, in the worst case, marginally stable (rounded off to three decimal places) is ______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} G H &=\left(\frac{s K_{p}+K_{I}}{s}\right)\left(\frac{2}{s^{3}+4 s^{2}+5 s+2}\right) \\ q(s) &=s^{4}+4 s^{3}+5 s^{2}+s\left(2+2 k_{p}\right)+2 k_{I} \\ \text{Necessary}:\qquad K_{p} & \gt -1 ; K_{I} \gt 0\\ &\begin{array}{l|ccc} s^{4} & 1 & 5 & 2 K_{I} \\ s^{3} & 4 & 2+2 K_{p} & \\ s^{2} & \frac{18-2 K_{p}}{4} & 2 K_{I} & \\ s^{1} & \left(9-K_{p}\right)\left(1+K_{p}\right)-8 K_{I} & & \\ s^{0} & 2 K_{I} & & \end{array}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Sufficient:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{18-2 K_{p}}{4}& \gt 0\\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{p}& \lt 9\\ \therefore \quad-1& \lt K_{p} \lt 9\\ \left(18-2 K_{p}\right)\left(2+2 K_{p}\right)-32 K_{I}& \gt 0\\ 32 K_{I}& \lt 36+32 K_{p}-4 K_{p}^{2}\\ \therefore \qquad \qquad 0& \lt K_{I} \lt \frac{36+32 K_{p}-4 K_{p}^{2}}{32} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{If }K_{p}&=-1 \Rightarrow k_{I}=0\\ \text{If }K_{p}&=9 \Rightarrow k_{I}=0\\ \end{aligned}[/latex],
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \qquad \qquad \frac{d K_{I}}{d K_{p}}&=0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad 32-8 K_{p}&=0=0 \Rightarrow K_{p}=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] For [latex]K_{p}=4, K_{I}[/latex] is maximum, which is
[latex] K_{I}=\frac{36+32 \times 4-64}{32}=3.125[/latex]
For [latex]K_{p}=4, K_{I} \lt 3.125[/latex] for stability
[latex] \therefore K_{I \max }=3.125[/latex]

A sinusoidal message signal having root mean square value of [latex]4\:V[/latex]
 and frequency of [latex]\text{1 kHz}[/latex]
 is fed to a phase modulator with phase deviation constant 2 rad/ volt. If the carrier signal is [latex]c\left ( t \right )=2\cos\left ( 2\pi 10^{6} t\right )[/latex], the maximum instantaneous frequency of the phase modulated signal (rounded off to one decimal place) is ______ [latex]\text{Hz}[/latex]
.
raw_source.solution:
Given sinusoidal message signal [latex]\rightarrow V_{\mathrm{rms}}=4 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{m} &=1 \mathrm{kHz} \\ V_{\text {peak }} &=\sqrt{2} \times V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{2} \times 4 \mathrm{~V} \\ m(t) &=4 \sqrt{2} \sin 2 \pi \times 10^{3} t\\ K_{p}&=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{volt}\\ c(t) &=2 \cos 2 \pi \times 10^{6} \mathrm{t} \\ \left(f_{i}\right)_{\max } &=f_{c}+\frac{K_{p}}{2 \pi}\left[\frac{d}{d t} m(t)\right]_{\max } \\ \frac{d}{d t} m(t) &=4 \sqrt{2} \times\left(2 \pi \times 10^{3}\right) \cos 2 \pi \times 10^{3} t \\ \left[\frac{d}{d t} m(t)\right]_{\max } &=4 \sqrt{2} \times 2 \pi \times 10^{3} \\ \left(f_{i}\right)_{\max } &=10^{6}+\frac{2}{2 \pi}\left(4 \sqrt{2} \times 2 \pi \times 10^{3}\right)=1011313.7 \mathrm{~Hz} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a high school having equal number of boy students and girl students, [latex]75\%[/latex]
 of the students study Science and the remaining [latex]25\%[/latex]
 students study Commerce. Commerce students are two times more likely to be a boy than are Science students. The amount of information gained in knowing that a randomly selected girl student studies Commerce (rounded off to three decimal places) is ______ bits.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\qquad P(G)&=\frac{1}{2} \text { and } P(B)=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(C)&=\frac{1}{4} \text { and } P(S)=\frac{3}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Let probability of selected science student is a boy is [latex]P(B/S) = x[/latex]
Given that Commerce students are two time more likely to be a boy than are Science students.
Then, probability of selected Commerce student is a boy
[latex] P\left(\frac{B}{C}\right)=2 x[/latex]
We have to find probability of randomly selected girl studies Commerce i.e.
[latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(\frac{C}{G}\right)&=\frac{P(C \cap G)}{P(G)}=\frac{P(C) P(G / C)}{P(G)} \\ P\left(\frac{C}{G}\right)&=\frac{\frac{1}{4} \times P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
To find [latex]P(G / C)[/latex], first we have to find [latex]P(B/C).[/latex]
The probability of selected student is a boy
[latex]\begin{aligned} P(B) &=P(S) P(B / S)+P(C) \times P(B / C) \\ \frac{1}{2} &=\frac{3}{4} \times x+\frac{1}{4} \times 2 x \\ \Rightarrow\qquad\qquad x &=\frac{2}{5}\\ \text{Then},\qquad \qquad P(B / C)&=2 x=\frac{4}{5}\\ \text{We know that},\qquad \\ P\left(\frac{B}{C}\right)+P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right)&=1 \\ P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right) =1- \frac{4}{5}&=\frac{1}{5} \\ \text{From equation (i),} \\ P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right) = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{\frac{5}{1/2}} &= \frac{1}{10} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The amount of information gained in knowing that a randomly selected girl student studies Commerce
[latex]I\left ( \frac{C}{G} \right )=\log _2 \frac{1}{P\left ( \frac{C}{G} \right )}= \log _2 10=3.32[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A message signal having peak-to-peak value of [latex]2\:V[/latex], root mean square value of [latex]0.1\:V[/latex]
 and bandwidth of [latex]\text{5 kHz}[/latex]
 is sampled and fed to a pulse code modulation [latex](\text{PCM})[/latex]
 system that uses a uniform quantizer. The [latex]\text{PCM}[/latex]
 output is transmitted over a channel that can support a maximum transmission rate of [latex]\text{50 kbps}[/latex]. Assuming that the quantization error is uniformly distributed, the maximum signal to quantization noise ratio that can be obtained by the [latex]\text{PCM}[/latex] system (rounded off to two decimal places) is  ______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} v_{p-p} &=2 \mathrm{~V} \\ \text { Root MSQ }[m(t)] &=0.1 \mathrm{~V} ; \quad f_{m}=5 \mathrm{kHz} \\ \text { Channel capacity, } \quad C &=50 \mathrm{kbps} \\ \text{Max} \frac{S}{N_{Q}}=?\\ & \text{Signal power},\\ S&=\text{MSQ}[m(t)]=(0.1)^{2}=0.01\\ C &\geq R_{b} \Rightarrow 50 \mathrm{kbps} \geq n f_{s}\\ \because \qquad f_{s}&=N R=2 f_{m}=10 \mathrm{kHz}\\ n &\leq 5 \Rightarrow n_{\max }=5\\ N_{Q} &=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{12} \\ \therefore\qquad \Delta &=\frac{V_{p-p}}{2^{n}} \\ \Delta_{\min } &=\frac{V_{p-p}}{2^{7} \max }=\frac{2 V}{2^{5}}=\frac{1}{16} \\ \left(N_{Q}\right)_{\min } &=\frac{\Delta_{\min }^{2}}{12}=3.25 \times 10^{-4} \\ \left(\frac{S}{N Q}\right)_{\max } &=\frac{S}{\left(N_{Q}\right)_{\min }}=\frac{0.01}{3.25 \times 10^{-4}}=30.72 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a polar non-return to zero [latex](\text{NRZ})[/latex]
 waveform, using [latex]+2\:V[/latex]
 and [latex]-2\:V[/latex]
 for representing binary '1' and '0' respectively, is transmitted in the presence of additive zero-mean white Gaussian noise with variance [latex]0.4\:V^{2}[/latex]. If the a priori probability of transmission of a binary '1' is 0.4, the optimum threshold voltage for a maximum a posteriori [latex](\text{MAP})[/latex]
 receiver (rounded off to two decimal places) is ______ V.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} H_{1}: X &=+2 \mathrm{~V} \\ H_{0}: X &=-2 \mathrm{~V} \\ \text{Var}[N] &=\sigma_{n}^{2}=0.4 \mathrm{~V}^{2} \\ \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{N}] &=0 \\ P(1) &=0.4 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad P(0) &=0.6 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Opt [latex]V_{\text {Th }}[/latex] by using MAP theorem
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{T h}\left[a_{1}-a_{2}\right]}{\sigma^{2}}-\frac{a_{1}^{2}-a_{2}^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}} &=\ln \frac{P(0)}{P(1)} \\ H_{1}: a_{1} &=E[2+N]=E[2]+E[N]=2 \\ H_{0}: a_{2} &=-2 V=E[-2+N]=E[-2]+E[N]=-2 \\ \sigma^{2} &=\text{Var}[Y]=\text{Var}[X+N] \\ &=\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[N]=0+0.4=0.4 \\ \frac{V_{T h}[2+2]}{0.4}-\frac{4-4}{2 \times 0.4} &=\ln \frac{0.6}{0.4} \\ V_{T h} &=\frac{0.4}{4} \ln \frac{0.6}{0.4}=0.0405 \\ \text { Opt } V_{\text {Th }} &=0.0405 \text { Volts } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following partial differential equation (PDE)
[latex]a\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2} +b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex]
, where [latex]a[/latex]and [latex]b[/latex] are distinct positive real numbers. Select the combination(s) of values of the real parameters [latex]\xi [/latex] and [latex]\eta [/latex] such that [latex]f(x,y)=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)} [/latex] is a solution of the given PDE.
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x,y)&=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x}&=\xi \cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}&=\xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly,
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=\eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex]
Now, as given
[latex]a \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}+b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex]
or
[latex]a \times \xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}+b \times \eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}= e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex]
[latex] a\cdot \xi ^2+b\cdot \eta ^2=1[/latex]
Thus, [latex]\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}}[/latex]
[latex](\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}, \eta = 0)[/latex] and [latex](\xi =0, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{b}})[/latex] satisfy the above result.

Differentiating both side,

f(x) is maximum for x = 2

Let [latex] \alpha ,\beta [/latex] be two non-zero real numbers and [latex]v_1,v_2[/latex] be two non-zero real vectors of size 3 x 1. Suppose that [latex]v_1[/latex] and [latex]v_2[/latex] satisfy [latex]v_1^Tv_2=0,v_1^Tv_1=1[/latex], and [latex]v_2^Tv_2=1[/latex]. Let [latex]A[/latex] be the 3x3 matrix given by:
[latex] A=\alpha v_1v_1^T+ \beta v_2v_2^T[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
After multiply by [latex] v_1[/latex] on both sides,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Av_1&=\alpha v_1v_1^Tv_1+ \beta v_2v_2^Tv_1 Av_1&=\alpha v_1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \alpha [/latex] is an eigen value of A.

After multiply by [latex] v_2[/latex] on both sides,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Av_2&=\alpha v_1v_1^Tv_2+ \beta v_2v_2^Tv_2 Av_2&=\beta v_2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \beta [/latex] is an eigen value of A.
[latex] v_1v_1^T [/latex] and [latex] v_2v_2^T [/latex] both are singular matrieces.
Therefore, A is also a singular matrix.
[latex] |A|=0\Rightarrow \lambda _A=0[/latex]
Hence [latex] \lambda _A= 0,\alpha ,\beta [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following series:
[latex]\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n^d}{c^n} [/latex]
For which of the following combinations of [latex]c,d[/latex] values does this series converge?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Sigma u_n&=\Sigma \frac{n}{2^n}\\ &\text{Ratio test; }\\ \lim_{n \to \infty }\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}&=\lim_{n \to \infty }\frac{n+1}{2^{n+1}} \times \frac{2^n}{n}=\frac{1}{2}\\ \frac{1}{2}& \lt 2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] By ratio test, [latex] \Sigma u_n [/latex] is convergent.
(A) c=1, d=-1
[latex]\Sigma u_n=\Sigma \frac{1}{n} [/latex] is divergent by P-test
(B) c=0.5, d=-10
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Sigma u_n&=\Sigma \frac{n^{-10}}{(0.5)^n}\\ &\text{Ratio test; }\\ \lim_{n \to \infty }\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}&=\lim_{n \to \infty }\frac{(n+1)^{-10}}{(0.5)^{n+1}} \times \frac{(0.5)^n}{n^{10}}\\ &=\frac{1}{0.5}=2\\ 2& \gt 1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] By ratio test, [latex] \Sigma u_n [/latex] is divergent.
(D) c=1,d=-2 [latex]\Sigma u_n=\Sigma \frac{n^{-2}}{(1)^n}=\Sigma \frac{1}{n^2} [/latex]
[latex] \Sigma u_n [/latex] is convergent by P-test.

raw_source.text:
Consider a long rectangular bar of direct bandgap p-type semiconductor. The
equilibrium hole density is [latex]10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex] and the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. Electron and hole diffusion lengths are [latex]2\mu m[/latex]and [latex]1\mu m[/latex], respectively.
The left side of the bar ([latex]x=0[/latex]) is uniformly illuminated with a laser having photon
energy greater than the bandgap of the semiconductor. Excess electron-hole pairs
are generated ONLY at [latex]x=0[/latex] because of the laser. The steady state electron density
at [latex]x=0[/latex] is [latex]10^{14}cm^{-3}[/latex]
 due to laser illumination. Under these conditions and ignoring
electric field, the closest approximation (among the given options) of the steady state
electron density at [latex]x=2 \mu m[/latex], is _____
raw_source.solution:
From continuity equation of electrons
[latex]\frac{dn}{dt}=n\mu _n\frac{dE}{dx}+\mu _nE\frac{dn}{dx}+G_n-R_n+x_n\frac{d^2x}{dx^2} \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[Because [latex]\vec{E}[/latex] is not mentioned hence
[latex]\frac{dE}{dx}=0[/latex]
For [latex] x \gt 0, G_n[/latex] is also zero
[latex]n=\frac{n_i^2}{N_A}=\frac{10^{20}}{10^{17}}=10^3[/latex]
[latex]n=n_0+\delta n=10^3+10^{14}=10^{14}[/latex]
at steady state, [latex]\frac{db}{dt}=0[/latex]
Hence equation (i) becomes:
[latex]O=D_n\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}-\frac{\delta n}{\tau _n}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}=\frac{\delta n}{L_n^2} \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
From solving equation (ii)
[latex]\delta _n(x)=\delta _n(0)e^{-x/L_n}[/latex]
at [latex]x=2\mu m[/latex]
[latex]\delta _n(2\mu m)=10^{14}e^{-2/2}=10^{14}e^{-1}=0.37 \times 10^{14}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a non-degenerate bulk semiconductor with electron density [latex]n=10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex], the
value of [latex]E_C-E_{Fn}=200meV[/latex], where [latex]E_C[/latex] and [latex]E_{Fn}[/latex] denote the bottom of the
conduction band energy and electron Fermi level energy, respectively. Assume
thermal voltage as 26 meV and the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. For [latex]n=0.5 \times 10^{16}cm^{-3}[/latex], the closest approximation of the value of ([latex]E_C-E_{Fn}[/latex]), among
the given options, is ______.
raw_source.solution:
Here we have to find the value of [latex]E_c-E_{fn}[/latex]
As we know,
[latex]E_C-E_F=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n} \right ) \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex]E_C-E_{F1}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_1} \right ) \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
[latex]E_C-E_{F2}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_2} \right ) \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
Equation (ii) - Equation (iii)
[latex](E_C-E_{F1})-(E_C-E_{F2})=kT \ln \left ( \frac{\frac{N_c}{n_1}}{\frac{N_c}{n_2}} \right )=kT \ln \frac{n_2}{n_1}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=26meV \times \ln \left ( \frac{0.5 \times 10^{16}}{1 \times 10^{16}} \right )[/latex]
[latex] 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=+26meV \ln (0.5)=-18[/latex]
[latex](E_C-E_{F2})=200+8=218meV[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the following partial differential equation (PDE)
[latex]a\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2} +b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex]
, where [latex]a[/latex]and [latex]b[/latex] are distinct positive real numbers. Select the combination(s) of values of the real parameters [latex]\xi [/latex] and [latex]\eta [/latex] such that [latex]f(x,y)=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)} [/latex] is a solution of the given PDE.
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x,y)&=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x}&=\xi \cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}&=\xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly,
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=\eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex]
Now, as given
[latex]a \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}+b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex]
or
[latex]a \times \xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}+b \times \eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}= e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex]
[latex] a\cdot \xi ^2+b\cdot \eta ^2=1[/latex]
Thus, [latex]\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}}[/latex]
[latex](\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}, \eta = 0)[/latex] and [latex](\xi =0, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{b}})[/latex] satisfy the above result.

Consider the following series:

For which of the following combinations of [latex]c,d[/latex] values does this series converge?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Sigma u_n&=\Sigma \frac{n}{2^n}\\ &\text{Ratio test; }\\ \lim_{n \to \infty }\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}&=\lim_{n \to \infty }\frac{n+1}{2^{n+1}} \times \frac{2^n}{n}=\frac{1}{2}\\ \frac{1}{2}& \lt 2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] By ratio test, [latex] \Sigma u_n [/latex] is convergent.
(A) c=1, d=-1
[latex]\Sigma u_n=\Sigma \frac{1}{n} [/latex] is divergent by P-test
(B) c=0.5, d=-10

[latex]\therefore [/latex] By ratio test, [latex] \Sigma u_n [/latex] is divergent.

[latex] \Sigma u_n [/latex] is convergent by P-test.

raw_source.text: A p-type semiconductor with zero electric field is under illumination (low level injection) in steady state condition. Excess minority carrier density is zero at [latex] x=\pm 2l_n[/latex], where [latex] l_n=10^{-4} cm[/latex] is the diffusion length of electrons. Assume electronic charge, [latex] q=-1.6 \times 10^{-19}C[/latex]. The profiles of photo-generation rate of carriers and the recombination rate of excess minority carriers (R) are shown. Under these conditions, the magnitude of the current density due to the photo-generated electrons at [latex] x=+2l_n[/latex] is _________ [latex] mA/cm^2[/latex] (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta _n(x)&=R\tau _n=10^{20}e^{-|x|/l_n}\cdot \tau _n\\ \delta (l_n)&=10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n \;\;\;...(i)\\ for \;\; l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n \end{aligned}[/latex]
Continuity equation is given by
[latex] D_n\frac{\partial^2 \delta _n}{\partial x^2}+G-R \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
G and R both are zero - for [latex] [l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n][/latex]
Hence Equation (i) reduced to [latex] D_n \frac{\partial^n \delta _n }{\partial x^2}=0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \delta _n(x)=Ax+B[/latex]
For calculating A and B we use Boundary condition
[latex] \delta _n(2l_n)=0\; \Rightarrow A=\frac{-B}{2l_n}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \delta _n(x)=\frac{-B}{2l_n}x+B=B\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
At [latex]x=l_n [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n&=B\left [ 1-\frac{l_n}{2l_n} \right ] \\ B&= 2 \times 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n\\ \therefore \; \delta _n(x) &=2 \times 10^{20} e^{-1}\tau _n\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \end{aligned} [/latex]
for [latex]l_n \leq x \leq 2l_n [/latex]
Electron diffusion current density is given by [latex] |J_n|_{diff}=qD_n\frac{d\eta }{dx}=qD_n \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} \times \tau _n\left [ 0-\frac{1}{2l_n} \right ][/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n ^2 \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1}}{2l_n}[/latex]
[latex]=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} [/latex]
[latex] =1.6 \times 10 \times 1 \times 10^{-4} \times e^{-1}[/latex]
[latex] =0.59mA/cm^2[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The transition diagram of a discrete memoryless channel with three input symbols and three output symbols is shown in the figure. The transition probabilities are as marked.
The parameter [latex] \alpha [/latex] lies in the interval [0.25, 1]. The value of [latex] \alpha [/latex] for which the capacity of this channel is maximized, is ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Channel capacity,
[latex]C_s=Max[I(X:Y)] [/latex]
[latex]I[(X:Y)]=H(Y)-H\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right ) [/latex]
Where,
[latex] H\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right )=-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\sum_{i=1}^{3}P(x_i,y_i) \log_2P\left ( \frac{y_i}{x_i} \right )[/latex]
[latex] P\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right )=\begin{matrix} &y_1 & y_2 & y_3\\ x_1 &1-\alpha & \alpha & 0\\ x_2 &0 &1-\alpha &\alpha \\ x_3 & \alpha & 0 & 1-\alpha \end{matrix}[/latex]
For simplication convenience, let [latex][P(X)]=[1\;\;0\;\;0] [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} [P(X,Y)]&=[P(X)]_d\cdot \left [ P\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right ) \right ]\\ [P(X,Y)]&=\begin{bmatrix} 1-\alpha & \alpha &0 \\ 0& 0&0 \\ 0 & 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}\\ H\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right )&=-((1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+\alpha \log _2 \alpha )\\ I(X:Y)&=H(Y)+(1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+ \log _2 \alpha \\ C_s&=MAX\left \{ (X:Y) \right \}\\ &=MAX\left \{ H(Y)+(1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+ \log _2 \alpha \right \}\\ &=log_2 3+(1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+\alpha \log _2 \alpha \end{aligned} [/latex]
Plot of [latex] (1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+\alpha \log _2 \alpha[/latex]

[latex] C_s[/latex] will be maximum at [latex]\alpha =0 [/latex] and 1.
Given [latex] \alpha \in [0.25,1][/latex]
Hence, [latex]\alpha =1 [/latex] is correct answer.

raw_source.text:
Consider a channel over which either symbol [latex] x_A [/latex] or symbol [latex] x_B [/latex] is transmitted. Let the output of the channel Y be the input to a maximum likelihood (ML) detector at the receiver. The conditional probability density functions for Y given [latex] x_A [/latex]and [latex] x_B [/latex] are:

[latex] f_{Y|x_A}(y)=e^{-(y+1)}u(y+1), [/latex]
[latex] f_{Y|x_B}(y)=e^{(y-1)}(1-u(y-1)), [/latex]

where [latex] u(\cdot ) [/latex] is the standard unit step function. The probability of symbol error for this system is _________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
ML decoding [latex] \rightarrow \; f_{Y/X_A}(y)\underset{\overset{ \lt }{X_B}}{\overset{X_A}{ \gt }} f_{Y/X_B}(y)[/latex]
[latex]i.e. \;\; f_{Y/X_A}(y) \gt f_{Y/X_B}(y) \rightarrow \text{ Decision favor of }X_A[/latex]
[latex]i.e. \;\; f_{Y/X_A}(y) \lt f_{Y/X_B}(y) \rightarrow \text{ Decision favor of }X_B[/latex]
For [latex]-1 \lt y \lt 0 [/latex] and [latex] 1 \lt y \lt \infty \rightarrow f_{Y/X_A}(y) \gt f_{Y/X_B}(y)[/latex]
For above internal decision in favor of [latex]X_A [/latex]
For [latex]-\infty \lt y \lt -1 [/latex] and [latex] 0\lt y \lt 1 \rightarrow f_{Y/X_B}(y) \gt f_{Y/X_A}(y)[/latex]
For above internal decision in favor of [latex]X_B [/latex]
[latex]P_e=P(X_A)\cdot P_{eX_A}+P(X_B)\cdot P_{eX_A} [/latex]
[latex] P_{eX_A}\rightarrow[/latex] Probability of error [latex] X_A[/latex] transmitted
[latex] P_{eX_B}\rightarrow[/latex] Probability of error [latex] X_B[/latex] transmitted
[latex]P_{eX_A}=\int_{0}^{1} f_{Y/X_A}(y)dy=\int_{0}^{1}e^{-(y+1)}u(y+1)dy= \int_{0}^{1}e^{-(y+1)} dy=e^{-1}-e^{-2}=0.23[/latex]
[latex]P_{eX_B}=\int_{0}^{1} f_{Y/X_B}(y)dy=\int_{0}^{1}e^{(y-1)} [1-u(y-1)]dy= \int_{0}^{1}e^{(y-1)} dy=e^{-1}-e^{-2}=0.23[/latex]
[latex] P_e=P(X_A) \times 0.23+P(X_B) \times 0.23 =0.23[P(X_A)+P(X_B)]=0.23 [/latex]

If [latex] \alpha ^* [/latex]and [latex] \beta ^* [/latex] are the respective choices for [latex] \alpha [/latex] and [latex] \beta [/latex] that minimize the mean square quantization error, then [latex] (\alpha ^*- \beta ^*)= [/latex] _________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{1}{2} \times K \times 2+1 \times K=1\Rightarrow K=0.5[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_X(x)&=mx+C \\ &=0.25+C \;\;;\;(-2\leq x\leq 0) \\ when \; x &=-2 \Rightarrow f_X(x)=0\\ 0&=0.25x-2+C \\ C&=0.5 \\ f_X(x)&= \frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{2}=-2\leq x\leq 0\\ f_X(x)&=0.5;\;\;0\leq x\leq 1 \\ x_q&=\alpha ;\;\; for\; 0\leq x\leq 1 \\; x_q&= \beta ;\;\; for\; -2\leq x\leq 0 \\; \end{aligned}[/latex]
Again, [latex]MSQ[Q_e]=E\left [ (X-X_q)^2 \right ][/latex]
Quantization noise power [latex]=N_o[/latex]
[latex]=MSQ[Q_e]=\int (X-X_a)^2 f_X(x)dx[/latex]
for [latex]-2 \leq x\leq 0\Rightarrow N_Q=\int_{-2}^{0}(x-\beta )^2 \times \left ( \frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{2} \right )dx[/latex]
[latex]=\int_{-2}^{0}[x^2+\beta ^2-2x\beta ] \left [ \frac{x}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \right ]dx[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow N_Q=\frac{\beta ^2}{2}+\frac{2}{3}\beta -\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
[latex]N_Q[/latex] to be minimum:
[latex]\frac{dN_Q}{d\beta }=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 2\beta +\frac{2}{3}=0[/latex]
[latex]\beta =-\frac{2}{3}[/latex]
for [latex]0\leq x\leq 1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow N_Q=\int_{0}^{1}(x-\alpha )^2 \times \frac{1}{2}dx =\frac{1}{6} [(1-\alpha )^3+\alpha ^3][/latex]
Similarly for [latex]'\alpha '[/latex]
[latex]\frac{dN_Q}{d\alpha }=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\frac{1}{6} [3(1-\alpha )^2(-1)+3\alpha ^2]=0 [/latex]
[latex]\alpha =1/2[/latex]
For [latex]N_q[/latex] to be minimum
[latex]\alpha -\beta =\frac{1}{2}-\left ( -\frac{2}{3} \right )=\frac{7}{6}=1.167[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex]\vec{D}(x,y,z)=(x^3\vec{i}+y^3\vec{j}+xy^2\vec{k})c/m^2[/latex]
[latex]Q_{enc.}=\int _v \rho _v\cdot dV=\int (\triangledown \cdot \vec{D})dV[/latex]
[latex]\triangledown \cdot \vec{D}=3x^2+3y^2[/latex]
[latex]dV=dxdydz[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; Q_{enc.}=\int _v 3(x^2+y^2)dxdydz =3\left [ \int_{-0.5}^{0.5} x^2 dx \int_{-0.5}^{0.5}dy \int_{-0.5}^{0.5} dz+\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}dx\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}y^2dy\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}dz \right ][/latex]

raw_source.text: The open loop transfer function of a unity negative feedback system is [latex]G(s)=\frac{k}{s\left(1+s T_{1}\right)\left(1+s T_{2}\right)}[/latex], where [latex]k, T_{1}[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}[/latex] are positive constants. The phase crossover frequency, in rad/s, is

[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad G(s) & =\frac{K}{s\left(1+s T_{1}\right)\left(1+s T_{2}\right)} \\ G(j \omega) & =\frac{K}{(j \omega)\left(1+j \omega T_{1}\right)\left(1+j \omega T_{2}\right)} \\ \text{Phase of }G(j \omega) & =\phi =-90-\tan ^{-1}\left(\omega T_{1}\right) - \tan ^{-1}\left(\omega T_{2}\right) \\ \therefore \quad \text { At } \omega &=\omega_{p c}, \phi =-180 \\ -180 & =-90-\tan ^{-1}\left(\omega_{p c} T_{1}\right)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\omega_{p c} T_{2}\right) \\ 9 \quad 90 & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\omega_{p c} T_{1}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\omega_{p c} T_{2}\right) \\ \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{p c} T_{1}+\omega_{p c} T_{2}}{1-\omega_{p c}^{2} T_{1} T_{2}}\right) & =90 \\ 1-\omega_{p c}^{2} T_{1} T_{2} & =0 \\ \omega_{p c} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{T_{1} T_{2}}} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Now,
[latex]\begin{aligned} Energy \left(E^{\prime}\right)&=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|Y(\omega)|^{2} \cdot d \omega\\ &=\frac{1}{2 \pi}\left[\int_{-11 B}^{-9 B}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \cdot d \omega+\int_{9 B}^{11 B}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \cdot d \omega\right]\\ & =\frac{1}{2 \pi}\left[\frac{1}{4} \times 2 B+\frac{1}{4} \times 2 B\right] \\ E^{\prime} & =\frac{B}{2 \pi}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{B}{\pi}\right)=\frac{E}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a discrete-time periodic signal with period [latex]N=5[/latex]. Let the discrete-time Fourier series (DTFS) representation be [latex]x[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{4} a_{k} e^{\frac{j k 2 \pi n}{5}}[/latex], where [latex]a_{0}=1, a_{1}=3 j, a_{2}=2 j[/latex], [latex]a_{3}=-2 j[/latex] and [latex]a_{4}=-3 j[/latex]. The value of the sum [latex]\sum_{n=0}^{4} x[n] \sin \frac{4 \pi n}{5}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Let, [latex]I=\sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \sin \frac{4 \pi n}{5}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2 j} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot\left[e^{j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}-e^{-j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2 j}\left[\sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) e^{j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}-\sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}\right] \quad (i) \end{aligned} [/latex]
As we know, [latex]\quad a_{k}=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j k \cdot \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}[/latex] [latex] =\frac{1}{5} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} k n} [/latex]

Put [latex]K=2 ; \quad a_{2}=\frac{1}{5} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}[/latex]

Put [latex]K=-2 ; \quad a_{-2}=\frac{1}{5} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}[/latex]

From equation (i),

[latex] \begin{aligned} I&=\frac{1}{2 j}\left[5 a_{-2}-5 a_{2}\right] & =\frac{5}{2 j}\left[a_{3}-a_{2}\right] \\ I & =\frac{5}{2 j}[-2 j-2 j]=-10 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{rl} a_{-2} & =a_{-2+N} \\ \because \quad & =a_{-2+5} \\ & =a_{3} \end{array} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let an input [latex]x[n][/latex] having discrete time Fourier transform.
[latex]X\left(e^{j \Omega}\right)=1-e^{-j \Omega}+2 e^{-3 j \Omega}[/latex] be passed through an LTI system. The frequency response of the LTI system is [latex]H\left(e^{j \Omega}\right)=1-\frac{1}{2} e^{-j 2 \Omega}[/latex]. The output [latex]y[n][/latex] of the system is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} y[n] & =x[n] * h[n] \\ Y\left(e^{j \Omega}\right) & =X\left(e^{j \Omega}\right) H\left(e^{j \Omega}\right) \\ & =\left[1-e^{-j \Omega}+2 e^{-3 j \Omega}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{2} e^{-2 j \Omega}\right] \\ & =1-e^{-j \Omega}+2.5 e^{-3 j \Omega}-0.5 e^{-j 2 \Omega}-e^{-j 5 \Omega} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Taking IDTFT;
[latex] y[n]=\delta[n]-\delta[n-1]-0.5 \delta[n-2]+2.5 \delta[n-3]-\delta[n-5] [/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]x(t)=10 \cos (10.5 \mathrm{Wt})[/latex] be passed through an LTI system having impulse response [latex]h(t)=\pi\left(\frac{\sin W t}{\pi t}\right)^{2} \cos 10 W t[/latex]. The output of the system is
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]h(t)[/latex] is Real and Even. When sinusoidal input applied to LTI system having even impulse response, then output will also be sinusoidal.

here, [latex] y(t)=\left.H(W)\right|_{W=10.5 W} \cdot 10 \cos (10.5 W t) [/latex]
let, [latex] h(t)=f(t) \cos 10 W t [/latex]
where, [latex] f(t)=\pi\left(\frac{\sin W t}{\pi t}\right)^{2} [/latex]

Now; [latex] H(W)=\frac{1}{2}[F(W+10 W)+F(W-10 W)] [/latex]

[latex]\left.\therefore \quad H(W)\right|_{W=10.5 W}=\frac{3}{8} W[/latex]
Hence, [latex] \begin{aligned} y(t) & =\left(\frac{3}{8} W\right)(10 \cos 10.5 W t) \\ & =\frac{15}{4} W \cos 10.5 W t \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The S-parameters of a two port network is given as

[latex] [S]=\left[\begin{array}{ll} S_{11} & S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{array}\right] [/latex]

with reference to [latex]Z_{0}[/latex]. Two lossless transmission line sections of electrical lengths [latex]\theta_{1}=\beta l_{1}[/latex] and [latex]\theta_{2}=\beta l 2[/latex] are added to the input and output ports for measurement purposes, respectively. The S-parameters [latex]\left[S^{\prime}\right][/latex] of the resultant two port network is
raw_source.solution:
Let us evaluate [latex]S_{11}[/latex] and [latex]S_{21}[/latex] first at [latex]V_{2}^{+}=0[/latex]

(A) [latex]S11:[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{1}&=V_{1}^{+}+V_{1}^{-}=\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}}+\left(V_{1}^{-}\right) e^{+j \beta l_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad V_{1}^{+}&=\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}} \\ V_{1}^{-}&=\left(V_{1}^{-}\right) e^{+j \beta l_{1}} \\ S_{11}&=\frac{V_{1}^{-}}{V_{1}^{+}}=\frac{\left(V_{1}^{-}\right) e^{+j \beta l_{1}}}{\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}}}=S_{11}^{\prime} e^{+j 2 \beta l_{1}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad S_{11}^{\prime}&=S_{11} e^{-j 2 \beta l_{1}}=S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad S_{11}^{\prime}&=S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} \end{aligned} [/latex]

(B) [latex]S_{21}[/latex] :
[latex] V_{2}=V_{2}^{+} e^{+j \beta l_{2}}+V_{2}^{-} e^{-j \beta l_{2}}=\left(V_{2}^{+}\right)^{\prime}+\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime} [/latex]
Here, [latex]V_{2}^{+}=0[/latex]
Hence,
[latex] V_{2}=\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime}=V_{2}^{-} e^{-j \beta l_{2}} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad V_{2}^{-}=\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime} e^{+j \beta l_{2}} [/latex]

From previous discussion in [latex]S_{11}[/latex],
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{1}^{+}&=\left(V_{1}^{+}\right) e^{-j l_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad S_{21}&=\frac{V_{2}^{-}}{V_{1}^{+}}=\frac{\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime} e^{+j \beta l_{2}}}{\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}}}=S_{21}^{\prime} e^{+j\left(\beta l_{2}+\beta l_{1}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow S_{21}^{\prime}&=S_{21} e^{-j\left(\beta l_{2}+\beta l_{1}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad S_{21}^{\prime}&=S_{21} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \end{aligned} [/latex]
options: [latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} & S_{12} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\ S_{21} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} & S_{22} e^{-j 2 \theta_{2}}\end{array}\right][/latex]

[latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}S_{11} e^{j 2 \theta_{1}} & S_{12} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\ S_{21} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} & S_{22} e^{j 2 \theta_{2}}\end{array}\right][/latex]

[latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}S_{1} e^{j 2 \theta_{1}} & S_{12} e^{e j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\ S_{21} e^{j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} & S_{22} e^{j 2 \theta_{2}}\end{array}\right][/latex]

[latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} & S_{12} e^{e j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\ S_{21} e^{j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} & S_{22} e^{-j 2 \theta_{2}}\end{array}\right][/latex]

raw_answer.option_text: [latex]\left[\begin{array}{cc}S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} & S_{12} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \\ S_{21} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} & S_{22} e^{-j 2 \theta_{2}}\end{array}\right][/latex]

raw_source.text: The standing wave ratio on a [latex]50 \Omega[/latex] lossless transmission line terminated in an unknown load impedance is found to be 2.0. The distance between successive voltage minima is [latex]30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] and the first minimum is located at [latex]10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] from the load. [latex]Z_{L}[/latex] can be replaced by an equivalent length [latex]l_{m}[/latex] and terminating resistance [latex]R_{m}[/latex] of the same line. The value of [latex]R_{m}[/latex] and [latex]l_{m}[/latex], respectively, are
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]S=2, Z_{\min }=10 \mathrm{~cm}, Z_{0}=50 \Omega[/latex]
As we know that, [latex]\quad|\Gamma|=\frac{S-1}{S+1}=\frac{2-1}{2+1}=\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
Now, distance between successive voltage minima [latex]=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda}{2}=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=60 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]

Also, for minima,
[latex] 2 \beta Z_{\min }=(2 n+1) \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]

At [latex]n=0,1 \mathrm{st}[/latex] minima, [latex]Z_{\text {min }}=10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{4 \pi}{\lambda} Z_{\min }=\pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4 \pi}{60} * 10=\pi+\theta_{\Gamma}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \pi}{3}-\pi=\theta_{\Gamma}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \theta_{\Gamma}=\frac{-\pi}{3} \quad \therefore \Gamma=\frac{1}{3} \angle-60^{\circ}[/latex]

Now, [latex] \Gamma=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}} [/latex]


[latex]\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow \quad & Z_{L}=Z_{0}\left[\frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma}\right] \\ \Rightarrow & Z_{L}=50\left[\frac{1+0.33 e^{-j \frac{\pi}{3}}}{1-0.33 e^{-j \frac{\pi}{3}}}\right]\end{array}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad Z_{L}=67.97 \angle-32.67^{\circ}[/latex]
Now [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{0}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{0} \tan \beta l}{Z_{0}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right][/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad Z_{\text {in }}=50\left[\frac{R_{m}+j 50 \tan \beta l_{m}}{50+j R_{m} \tan \beta l_{m}}\right][/latex]
Here, [latex]\quad Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{L}=67.97 \angle-32.67^{\circ}[/latex]
Going through options,
[latex]\left.\begin{array}{l}R_{m}=100 \Omega \text { and } L_{m}=5 \mathrm{~cm} \\ R_{m}=25 \Omega \text { and } L_{m}=20 \mathrm{~cm}\end{array}\right\}[/latex] satisfy this identity, hence option (B) and (C) are correct.

raw_source.text:
The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave is

[latex]E=a_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+a_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta) \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m}[/latex]

Which of the following combination(s) will give rise to a left handed elliptically polarized (LHEP) wave?
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+\hat{a}_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta)[/latex]
at [latex]z=0[/latex]
[latex] \vec{E}=C_{1 x} \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t+\theta) \hat{a}_{y} [/latex]
Going by options,

Option (A) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+\pi / 4) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.



Option (B) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=2 \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+\pi / 2) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=-1 \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.



Option (C) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+2 \cos (\omega t+3 \pi / 2) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \quad \quad \omega t=0, \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is RHEP.



Option (D) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=2 \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+3 \pi / 4) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{x}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.


[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option (A), (B) and (D) are correct.

raw_source.text: The following circuit(s) representing a lumped element equivalent of an infinitesimal section of a transmission line is/are

The value of the integral [latex]\iint_{R} x y d x d y[/latex] over the region [latex]R[/latex], given in the figure, is ___
(rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} I & =\iint_{R} x y d x d y \\ & =\int_{y=0}^{1} \int_{x=-y}^{y} x y d x d y+\int_{y=1}^{2} \int_{x=y-2}^{2-y} x y d x d y \\ & =\int_{0}^{1} y\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)_{-y}^{y} d y+\int_{1}^{2} y\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)_{y-2}^{2-y} d y \\ & =0+0=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In an extrinsic semiconductor, the hole concentration is given to be [latex]1.5 n_{i}[/latex] where [latex]n_{i}[/latex] is the intrinsic carrier concentration of [latex]1 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. The ratio of electron to hole mobility for equal hole and electron drift current is given as ___
(rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given, intrinsic carrier concentration [latex]n_{i}=1 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]
Hole concentration,
[latex]\quad p=1.5 \times n_{i}[/latex]
[latex] p=1.5 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} [/latex]

Given, electron and hole current are equal
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{p \text { dritt }} & =I_{n \text { dritt }} \\ p q \mu_{p} E A & =n q \mu_{n} E A \\ 1.5 \times 10^{10} \mu_{p} & =n \mu_{n} \quad ...(i) \end{aligned} [/latex]

But according to mass action law,
[latex] \begin{aligned} n p & =n_{i}^{2} \\ n & =\frac{n_{i}}{1.5}=\frac{10^{10}}{1.5} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Put in equation (i)
[latex]\therefore \quad 1.5 \times 10^{10} \mu_{p}=\frac{10^{10}}{1.5} \times \mu_{n}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{\mu_{n}}{\mu_{p}}=2.25 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The asymptotic magnitude Bode plot of a minimum phase system is shown in the figure. The transfer function of the system is [latex](s)=\frac{k(s+z)^{a}}{s^{b}(s+p)^{c}}[/latex], where [latex]k, z, p, a, b[/latex] and [latex]c[/latex] are positive constants. The value of [latex](a+b+c)[/latex] is ___
(rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
From the Bode magnitude plot, it is clear that there is one pole at origin,
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]b=1[/latex]
and at frequency [latex] \omega_{1} [/latex], system has a zero
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]a=1[/latex]

and at frequency [latex] \omega_{2} [/latex], system has a two poles
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad c&=2 \\ \therefore \quad a+b+c&=1+1+2 \\ a+b+c&=4 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]x_{1}(t)=u(t+1.5)-u(t-1.5)[/latex] and [latex]x_{2}(t)[/latex] is shown in the figure below. For [latex]y(t)=x_{1}(t) * x_{2}(t)[/latex], the [latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y(t) d t[/latex] is ___. (rounded off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
[latex] x_{1}(t)=u(t+1.5)-u(t-1.5) [/latex]

[latex] ]\Rightarrow x_1(t)=rect\left ( \frac{t}{3} \right )[/latex]
[latex] ] x_1(t)=rect\left ( \frac{t}{3} \right ) \overset{FT}{\leftrightarrow} 3Sa(1.5\omega )[/latex]
Now, [latex] x_{2}(t)=\delta(t+3)+\operatorname{rect}\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)+2 \delta(t-2) [/latex]

Taking Fourier transform
[latex] \begin{aligned} X_{2}(\omega) & =e^{3 j \omega}+2 S a(\omega)+2 e^{-2 j \omega} \\ y(t) & =x_{1}(t) * x_{2}(t) \\ Y(\omega) & =X_{1}(\omega) \cdot X_{2}(\omega) \\ Y(\omega) & =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y(t) \cdot e^{-j \omega t} \cdot d t \end{aligned} [/latex]

We know
[latex]\therefore \quad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y(t)=Y(0)[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad Y(0)=X_{1}(0) \cdot X_{2}(0)[/latex] [latex]=3[1+2+2]=15[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]X(t)[/latex] be a white Gaussian noise with power spectral density [latex]\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{Hz}[/latex]. If [latex]X(t)[/latex] is input to an LTI system with impulse response [latex]e^{-t} u(t)[/latex]. The average power of the system output is ___ [latex]\mathrm{W}[/latex]. (Rounded off to two decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]h(t)=e^{-t} u(t)[/latex]
Given: Input PSD
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad S_{x}(f)=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{Hz}[/latex]

We know output PSD,
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{Y}(f) & =S_{X}(f)|H(f)|^{2} \\ S_{Y}(f) & =\frac{1}{2}|H(f)|^{2} \\ \text { Power }[y(t)] & =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S_{Y}(f) d f=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2}|H(f)|^{2} d f \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h^{2}(t) d t=\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2 t} d t \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}=0.25 \mathrm{~W} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A transparent dielectric coating is applied to glass [latex]\left(\epsilon_{r}=4, \mu_{r}=1\right)[/latex] to eliminate the reflection of red light [latex]\left(\lambda_{0}=0.75 \mu \mathrm{m}\right)[/latex]. The minimum thickness of the dielectric coating, in [latex]\mu \mathrm{m}[/latex], that can be used is ____ (rounded off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
For no reflection, impedance must be matched.
Hence, [latex]\eta_{2}[/latex] acts like a quarter wave impedance transformer.

So,
[latex] (i) \quad \eta_{2}=\sqrt{\eta_{1} \cdot \eta_{3}} \Rightarrow \epsilon_{r_{2}}=\sqrt{\epsilon_{r_{1}} \cdot \epsilon_{r_{3}}} \Rightarrow \epsilon_{r_{2}}=2 [/latex]

(ii) For impedance matching,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & d=(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{4} ; n=0,1,2 \ldots \\ & \lambda=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}}}=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r_{2}}}} \\ Here \;\;& \lambda=\frac{0.75 \times 10^{-6}}{\sqrt{2}}=0.53 \times 10^{-6} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, for minimum distance, [latex]n=0[/latex]
So, [latex] d=\frac{\lambda}{4}=\frac{0.53 \times 10^{-6}}{4}=0.133 \mu \mathrm{m} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a semiconductor device, the Fermi-energy level is [latex]0.35 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] above the valence band energy. The effective density of states in the valence band at [latex]T=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is [latex]1 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. The thermal equilibrium hole concentration in silicon at [latex]400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is ___ [latex]\_\times 10^{13} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. (rounded off to two decimal places).
Given [latex]\mathrm{kT}[/latex] at [latex]300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is [latex]0.026 \mathrm{eV}[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] E_{F}-E_{V}=0.35 \mathrm{eV} \quad \text { [Considering it is given at } 400 \mathrm{~K} \text { ] } [/latex]
Also, [latex]V_{T_{1}}=K T_{1}=0.026 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] at [latex]T_{1}=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]\frac{V_{T_{1}}}{V_{T_{2}}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \Rightarrow V_{T_{2}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} \times V_{T_{1}}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]V_{T_{2}}=\frac{400}{300} \times 0.026[/latex]
[latex]V_{T_{2}}=0.03466 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] at [latex]T_{2}=400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A sample and hold circuit is implemented using a resistive switch and a capacitor with a time constant of [latex]1 \mu \mathrm{s}[/latex]. The time for sampling switch to stay closed to charge a capacitor adequately to a full scale voltage of [latex]1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex] with 12-bit accuracy is ____ [latex]\mu \mathrm{s}[/latex]. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given: Time constant [latex](\tau)[/latex] of [latex]1 \mu \mathrm{sec}[/latex].
Full scale voltage [latex]=1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]

The voltage across capacitor is given as
[latex]\quad \quad V_{c}(t)=V_{\text {in }}\left(1-e^{-t / \tau}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad V_{c}(t)=\left(1-e^{-t / 1 \mu \mathrm{sec}}\right) \quad ...(i)[/latex]
To calculate the voltage to stay closed to charge capacitor adequately to a full scale voltage with 12-bit accuracy is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{c}(t) & =V_{\text {ref }}\left[1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right] \\ n & =\text { Number of bit }=12 \\ V_{c}(t) & =\left[1-\frac{1}{4096}\right] \quad ...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Comparing equations (i) and (ii), we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} e^{-t / 1 \mu \mathrm{sec}} & =\frac{1}{4096} \\ -\frac{t}{1 \mu \mathrm{sec}} & =\ln \left\{\frac{1}{4096}\right\} \\ t & =8.3177 \mu \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] be the unit vectors along [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] axes, respectively and let [latex]A[/latex] be a positive constant. raw_source.solution:
For an electrostatic field, [latex]\nabla \times \bar{F}=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \bar{F}_{1}=A[y \hat{i}+x \hat{j}] \\ & \Rightarrow \\ & \Delta \times \bar{F}_{1}=A\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial / \partial x & \partial / \partial y & \partial / \partial z \\ y & x & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ & =A[0 \hat{i}-0 \hat{j}+(1-1) \hat{k}] \\ & =0 \\ & \bar{F}_{2}=A[y \hat{i}-x \hat{j}] \\ & \Rightarrow \\ & \Delta \times \bar{F}_{2}=A\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial / \partial x & \partial / \partial y & \partial / \partial z \\ y & -x & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ & =A[0 \hat{i}-0 \hat{j}+(-1-1) \hat{k}] \\ & =-2 A \hat{k} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, [latex]\bar{F}_{1}[/latex] is electrostatic, [latex]\bar{F}_{2}[/latex] is not electrostatic.
options: Neither [latex]\vec{F}_{1}[/latex] nor [latex]\vec{F}_{2}[/latex] is an electrostatic field.

raw_source.text: A White Gaussian noise [latex]w(t)[/latex] with zero mean and power spectral density [latex]\frac{N_{0}}{2}[/latex], when applied to a first-order [latex]R C[/latex] low pass filter produces an output [latex]n(t)[/latex]. At a particular time [latex]t=t_{k}[/latex], the variance of the random variable [latex]n\left(t_{k}\right)[/latex] is _____

[latex] \begin{aligned} E[n(t)] & =E[W(t)] \cdot H(0) \\ E[n(t)] & =0 \\ E\left[n^{2}(t)\right] & =\left\{E(n(t)\}^{2}+\operatorname{var}[n(t)]\right. \\ \operatorname{var}[n(t)] & =E\left[n^{2}(t)\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]
at [latex]t=t_{k}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\operatorname{var}[n(t)]\right|_{t=t_{k}} & =E\left[n^{2}\left(t_{k}\right)\right]=E\left[n\left(t_{k}\right) \cdot n\left(t_{k}\right)\right]=R_{n}(0) \\ S_{n}(f) & =S_{W}(f) \cdot|H(f)|^{2} \\ & =\frac{N_{0}}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1+(\omega R C)^{2}} \\ R_{n}(\tau) & =\operatorname{IFT}\left[S_{n}(f)\right]=\frac{N_{0}}{4 R C} \cdot e^{\frac{-|\tau|}{R C}} \\ R_{n}(0) & =\frac{N_{0}}{4 R C} \end{aligned} [/latex]

For a causal discrete-time LTI system with transfer function

raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]H(z)=\frac{2 z^{2}+3}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}[/latex]
System is non-minimum phase system. Since zero are lying outside the unit circle.
Final value:
[latex] h(\infty)=\lim _{z \rightarrow 1}(z-1) \frac{2 z^{2}+3}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}=0 [/latex]
Initial value:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h(0) & =\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left(2 z^{2}+3\right)}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}=\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{z^{2}\left[2+\frac{3}{z^{2}}\right]}{z^{2}\left[1+\frac{1}{3 z}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{3 z}\right]} \\ & =\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left[2+\frac{3}{z^{2}}\right]}{\left[1+\frac{1}{3 z}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{3 z}\right]}=\frac{2}{1 \times 1}=2 \\ |z| & =\frac{1}{3}=0.33 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]z=-\frac{1}{3}, z=\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
System is stable. Since [latex]\mid[/latex] pole [latex]\mid \lt 1[/latex] i.e. pole are lying inside the unit circle.

The final value of the impulse response is 0.

[latex] n=6 \text {-bits } [/latex]
Each register field requires 5 -bits.
Instruction format would be


[latex]\therefore[/latex] Immediate value bits [latex]=32-(6+5+5+5)=32-21=11[/latex]-bits

raw_source.text: As shown in the circuit, the initial voltage across the capacitor is [latex]10 \mathrm{~V}[/latex], with the switch being open. The switch is then closed at [latex]t=0[/latex]. raw_source.text: Consider the Earth to be a perfect sphere of radius [latex]R[/latex]. Then the surface area of the region, enclosed by the [latex]60^{\circ} \mathrm{N}[/latex] latitude circle, that contains the north pole in its interior is _______

Earth's North pole [latex]=90^{\circ}[/latex]
Earth's equator [latex]=0^{\circ}[/latex]

Earth's North pole, [latex]\theta=0^{\circ}[/latex]
Earth's equator, [latex]\theta=90^{\circ}[/latex]
The area of the shaded portion,
[latex] \overline{d S}=d S \hat{a}_{r} [/latex]
Hence, in spherical coordinate system
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex]

[latex] \overline{d S}=r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \hat{a}_{r} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad S=\int d & =\int r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \\ & =r^{2} \int_{\theta=0^{\circ}}^{30^{\circ}} \sin \theta d \theta \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} d \phi \text { at } r=R \\ & =R^{2}-\left.\left[-\left.\cos \theta\right|_{0} ^{30^{\circ}}\right] \cdot \phi\right|_{0} ^{2 \pi} \\ & =R^{2}\left\{-\left[\cos 30^{\circ}-\cos 0^{\circ}\right]\right\} \cdot 2 \pi \\ & =R^{2}\left\{-\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right]\right\} \cdot 2 \pi=R^{2} \cdot \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot 2 \pi \\ & =(2-\sqrt{3}) \pi R^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a unity negative feedback control system with forward path gain [latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}[/latex] as shown. The impulse response of the closed-loop system decays faster than [latex]e^{-t}[/latex] if ______
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] G(s)=\frac{K}{(S+1)(S+2)(S+3)} [/latex]
Impulse response of system is
[latex] Y(S)=\frac{K}{(S+1)(S+2)(S+3)+K} [/latex]
Given: At impulse response of closed loop system decay faster than [latex]e^{-t}[/latex] Hence, put [latex]s=s-1[/latex],
[latex]\therefore[/latex] The new characteristic equation is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & (s-1+1)(s-1+2)(s-1+3)+K=0 \\ & s(s+1)(s+2)+K=0 \\ & s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+K=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
By [latex]\mathrm{RH}[/latex] criterion,
[latex] \begin{array}{c|cc} s^{3} & 1 & 2 \\ s^{2} & 3 & K \\ s^{1} & \frac{6-K}{3} & \\ s^{0} & K & \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \therefore K \gt 0 ; \quad \frac{6-K}{3} \gt 0 \Rightarrow K \lt 6 [/latex]

[latex] \therefore \quad 0 \lt K \lt 6 [/latex]
Hence, option satisfies above range of [latex]K[/latex].

raw_source.text:
A satellite attitude control system, as shown below, has a plant with transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{s^{2}}[/latex] cascaded with a compensator [latex]C(s)=\frac{K(s+\alpha)}{s+4}[/latex], where [latex]K[/latex] and [latex]\alpha[/latex] are positive real constants.

In order for the closed-loop system to have poles at [latex]-1 \pm j \sqrt{3}[/latex], the value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] must be ____
raw_source.solution:
[latex] G(S) C(s)=\frac{1}{S^{2}} \frac{k(S+\alpha)}{(S+4)} [/latex]
Characteristic equation is
[latex] S^{3}+4 S^{2}+k S+\alpha=0 [/latex]
Poles of the system present at [latex]=-1 \pm j \sqrt{3}[/latex]
Characteristic equation is
[latex] \begin{aligned} &(S+a)\left[(S+1)^{2}+3\right]=0 \\ &(S+a)\left(S^{2}+2 S+4\right)=0 \\ & S^{3}+(2+a) S^{2}+(4+2 a) S+4 a=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Compare equation (I) and (II)
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2+a & =4 \\ a & =2 \\ 4+2 a & =k \\ k & =8 \\ k \alpha & =4 a \\ \alpha & =\frac{8}{8}=1 \\ \alpha & =1 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A uniform plane wave with electric field [latex]\vec{E}(x)=A_{y} \hat{a}_{y} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi x}{3}} \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}[/latex] is travelling in the air (relative permittivity, [latex]\epsilon_{r}=1[/latex] and relative permeability, [latex]\mu_{r}=1[/latex] ) in the [latex]+x[/latex] direction [latex]\left(A_{y}\right.[/latex] is a positive constant, [latex]\hat{a}_{y}[/latex] is the unit vector along the [latex]y[/latex] axis). It is incident normally on an ideal electric conductor (conductivity, [latex]\sigma=\infty[/latex] ) at [latex]x=0[/latex]. The position of the first null of the total magnetic field in the air (measured from [latex]x=0[/latex], in metres) is ________
raw_source.solution:
At perfect conductor,
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} & \Gamma=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \Gamma=1 \mid \pi \end{array} [/latex]
As we know that [latex]H_{\min }[/latex] occurs at [latex]E_{\max }[/latex]. Hence,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & E_{\max }=E_{0}[1+|\Gamma|] \\ & H_{\min }=\frac{E_{0}}{\eta}[1-|\Gamma|] \text { at } 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} \end{aligned} [/latex]
So,
[latex] 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4 \pi}{\lambda} x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\pi[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad x_{\max }=(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{4} ; n=0,1,2,3 \ldots [/latex]
So, for [latex]1^{\text {st }}[/latex] value of [latex]x[/latex] for [latex]\mathrm{H}[/latex]-field to be zero is
[latex] x_{\max }=\frac{\lambda}{4} \quad[\text { at } n=0] [/latex]
Now, from the equation given,
[latex] \begin{array}{rlrl} \beta & =\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} & =\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \lambda & =3 \end{array} [/latex]
Hence,
[latex] x_{\max }=\frac{3}{4} [/latex]
If the reference is not at interference then [latex]x=-\frac{3}{4}[/latex].

raw_source.text: The sequence of states [latex]\left(Q_{1} Q_{0}\right)[/latex] of the given synchronous sequential circuit is ______

[latex]R_{1}=[/latex] Residue of [latex]f(z)=[/latex] at [latex](z=2)[/latex]

raw_source.text: A source transmits a symbol [latex]s[/latex], taken from [latex](-4,0,4)[/latex] with equal probability, over an additive white Gaussian noise channel. The received noisy symbol [latex]r[/latex] is given by [latex]r=s+w[/latex], where the noise [latex]w[/latex] is zero mean with variance 4 and is independent of [latex]s[/latex]. Using [latex]Q(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{x}^{\infty} e^{\frac{-t^{2}}{2}} d t[/latex], the optimum symbol error probability is ______
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} r & =s+\omega \\ f_{\omega}(\omega) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-\omega^{2}}{2 \times 4}}=N(0,4) \end{aligned} [/latex]
transmission of [latex]-4 \rightarrow r=-4+\omega[/latex]
[latex] f(r /-4)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-(r+4)^{2}}{2 \times 4}} [/latex]
transmission of [latex]0 \rightarrow r=\omega[/latex]
[latex] f(r / 0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{2 \times 4}} [/latex]
transmission of [latex]4 \rightarrow r=4+n[/latex]
[latex] f(r / 4)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-(r-4)^{2}}{2 \times 4}} [/latex]

[latex] P_{e}=P(-4) P_{e-4}+P(0) P_{e 0}+P(4) P_{e 4} [/latex]
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} & P(-4)=P(0)=P(4)=\frac{1}{3} \\ & P_{e-4}=P(r \gt -2) \\ & =1-\left(1-F_{r}(2)\right) \\ & =1-\left(1-Q\left(\frac{-2+4}{2}\right)\right) \\ & =Q(1) \\ & P_{e 0}=P(r \lt -2)+P(r \gt 2) \\ & =F_{r}(-2)+\left\{1-F_{r}(2)\right\} \\ & =\left(1-Q\left(\frac{-2-0}{2}\right)\right)+Q\left(\frac{2-0}{2}\right) \\ & =[1-Q(-1)]+Q(1)=2 Q(1) \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{e 4} & =P(r \lt 2) \\ & =F_{r}(2) \\ & =1-Q\left(\frac{2-4}{2}\right) \\ & =1-Q(-1) \\ & =Q(1) \\ P_{e} & =\frac{1}{3} Q(1)+\frac{2}{3} Q(1)+\frac{1}{3} Q(1) \\ & =\frac{4}{3} Q(1) \end{aligned} [/latex]
where, [latex]r=N(4,4)[/latex]

Let [latex]p(t)=\frac{\sin 2 \pi t}{\pi t}[/latex]


After sampling: [latex]\quad X_{s}(\omega)=f_{s} \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} X\left(\omega-n \omega_{s}\right)[/latex]
Frequency components present in sampler output [latex]n \omega_{s} \pm \omega_{0}[/latex]
[latex]\omega_{o}, \omega_{s}+ \pm \omega_{o}, 2 \omega_{s} \pm \omega_{o}, \ldots[/latex]
[latex]8 \pi, 30 \pi \pm 8 \pi, 60 \pi \pm 8 \pi[/latex], ..
[latex]8 \pi, 22 \pi, 38 \pi, 52 \mathrm{p}, 68 \pi, \ldots(\mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec})[/latex]
System will pass '[latex]38 \pi[/latex]' component of input.

raw_source.text: Let [latex]F_{1}, F_{2}[/latex], and [latex]F_{3}[/latex] be functions of [latex](x, y, z)[/latex]. Suppose that for every given pair of points [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] in space, the line integral [latex]\int_{C}\left(F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z\right)[/latex] evaluates to the same value along any path [latex]C[/latex] that starts at [latex]A[/latex] and ends at [latex]B[/latex]. Then which of the following is/are true?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\because[/latex] Given integral is independent of contour ' [latex]C[/latex] ' [latex]\int_{C}\left(F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z\right)=\int_{C} \bar{F} \cdot \overline{d r}[/latex] is independent of ' [latex]C[/latex] '
Then [latex]\bar{F}[/latex] is conservative field
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \bar{F}=\overline{\nabla \phi} \\ \Rightarrow & F_{1}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}, F_{2}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}, F_{3}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} \end{array} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is true.
[latex]\because \bar{F}[/latex] is conservative
Then,
[latex] \nabla \times \bar{F}=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}i & j & K \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ F_{1} & F_{2} & F_{3}\end{array}\right|=\overrightarrow{0}[/latex]
[latex]=i\left(\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial z}\right)-j\left(\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial z}\right)+K\left(\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}\right)=0 \hat{i}+0 \hat{j}+0 \hat{k}[/latex]
Equate on both sides,
We get,
[latex] \frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial z}, \quad \frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial z}, \quad \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is true.
If [latex]\bar{F}[/latex] is irrotational then,
[latex] \oint_{C} F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z=0 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is also true. But,
[latex] \bar{\nabla} \cdot \bar{F}=\bar{\nabla} \cdot(\bar{\nabla} \phi) \neq 0 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is false.
options: There exists a differentiable scalar function [latex]f(x, y, z)[/latex] such that [latex]F_{1}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, F_{2}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, F_{3}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}[/latex].
For every closed path [latex]\Gamma[/latex], we have [latex]\oint_{\Gamma}\left(F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z\right)=0[/latex]
[latex]\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial z}=0[/latex].

[latex]\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}[/latex]

option_texts: There exists a differentiable scalar function [latex]f(x, y, z)[/latex] such that [latex]F_{1}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, F_{2}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, F_{3}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}[/latex].
For every closed path [latex]\Gamma[/latex], we have [latex]\oint_{\Gamma}\left(F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z\right)=0[/latex]

[latex]\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}[/latex]

The relationship between any [latex]\mathrm{N}[/latex]-length sequence [latex]x[n][/latex] and its corresponding [latex]\mathrm{N}[/latex]-point discrete Fourier transform [latex]X[k][/latex] is defined as

Another sequence [latex]y[n][/latex] is formed as below

For the sequence [latex]x[n]=\{1,2,1,3\}[/latex], the value of [latex]Y[0][/latex] is _______
