Given:
p-n junction forward biased by 2V.

Concept:

Under forward bias [latex]V[/latex], the separation between the quasi-Fermi levels [latex]E_{fn}[/latex] (n-side) and [latex]E_{fp}[/latex] (p-side) equals the applied voltage in energy units:
[latex] E_{fn} - E_{fp} = qV = q\times2\text{ V} = 2\text{ eV} [/latex]

In volts, the energy difference = 2 eV.

raw_source.text:
Consider the matrix [latex]M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ -1 & a & b \end{bmatrix}[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are TRUE if [latex]\det(M) \neq 0[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]M = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\-1 & a & b\end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex]\det(M)\neq0[/latex]

Step 1: Compute det(M)

[latex] \det(M) = 2(3b-0) - 1(b-0) + 1(a+3) = 6b - b + a + 3 = 5b + a + 3 [/latex]

Step 2: Condition [latex]\det(M)\neq0[/latex]

[latex] 5b + a + 3 \neq 0 [/latex]

The question asks which values satisfy [latex]\det(M)\neq0[/latex] i.e., which options give [latex]5b+a+3\neq0[/latex]:

(A) [latex]a=-\frac{1}{2}, b=-\frac{1}{2}[/latex]: [latex]5(-\frac{1}{2})+(-\frac{1}{2})+3 = -\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}+3 = -3+3=0[/latex] Therefore, [latex]\det(M)=0[/latex]. Not valid.
(B) [latex]a=\frac{1}{2}, b=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]: [latex]\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+3=6\neq0[/latex]
(C) [latex]a=-3, b=0[/latex]: [latex]0-3+3=0[/latex] Therefore, [latex]\det(M)=0[/latex]. Not valid.
(D) [latex]a=\frac{1}{2}, b=-3[/latex]: [latex]-15+\frac{1}{2}+3=-11.5\neq0[/latex]

Answer:
Options (B) and (D) satisfy [latex]\det(M)\neq0[/latex].

raw_source.text:
A binary ripple counter is designed to count [latex](0)_{10}[/latex] to [latex](64)_{10}[/latex].

Which of the following is/are the number of flip-flops required to design the counter?
raw_source.solution:
A counter that counts from 0 to 64 must be able to represent a total of 65 distinct states.

The maximum number of states (or the MOD number) that can be represented by [latex] n [/latex] flip-flops is given by:

[latex] \text{Total states} = 2^n [/latex]
To accommodate 65 states, it must satisfy the inequality:

[latex] 2^n \geq 65 [/latex]
i.e.

[latex] n \geq \log_2 65 [/latex]
[latex] n \geq 6.022 [/latex]
Hence, the minimum number of flip-flops required to design this counter is 7.

raw_source.text: Which option(s) represents/represent the dielectric loss tangent of a substrate?
raw_source.solution:
The loss tangent [latex]\tan\delta[/latex] is defined as the ratio of the total loss current (conduction + displacement loss) to the lossless displacement current:
[latex] \tan\delta = \frac{\omega\epsilon'' + \sigma}{\omega\epsilon'} [/latex]

(A) "Ratio of real to imaginary parts of displacement current", this is exactly [latex]\tan\delta[/latex]
(B) [latex]\frac{\omega\epsilon'' + \sigma}{\omega\epsilon'}[/latex], this is the standard formula
(C) "Ratio of electric susceptibility to permittivity", [latex]\chi/\epsilon[/latex], this is NOT the loss tangent
(D) "Ratio of [latex]\vec{P}[/latex] to [latex]\vec{D}[/latex]" , [latex]P/D = (\epsilon-\epsilon_0)/\epsilon[/latex], this is NOT the loss tangent

Answer:
Options (A) and (B) correctly represent the dielectric loss tangent.
options: Ratio of the real to imaginary parts of the total displacement current
Ratio of the electric susceptibility to permittivity
Ratio of the polarization vector [latex]\vec{P}[/latex] to the displacement vector [latex]\vec{D}[/latex]

option_texts: Ratio of the real to imaginary parts of the total displacement current

raw_source.text:
Figure shows the output characteristics of two different Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT), BJT 1 with magnitude of Early voltage [latex]|V_{A1}|[/latex], and BJT 2 with magnitude of Early voltage [latex]|V_{A2}|[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are correct regarding the Early voltages?
raw_source.solution:
BJT 2 has a smaller slope in the active region (flatter [latex] I_C [/latex] vs [latex] V_{CE} [/latex] curve). Hence,

[latex] |V_{A2}| > |V_{A1}| [/latex]
Therefore, option (C) is correct.

Also, since BJT 2 curve shows finite slope (not perfectly flat),

[latex] V_A [/latex] is finite and not [latex] \infty [/latex]. Hence, option (D) is also correct.

raw_source.text: The output voltage [latex]V_o[/latex] (in Volt) for the network given in the Figure is _____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Label node voltages

Let the midpoint of the left branch be [latex]V_A[/latex] and the midpoint of the right branch be [latex]V_B[/latex].

The 6 V source is connected between these nodes.

Assume polarity such that
[latex] V_A - V_B = 6V [/latex]

Let the top node voltage be [latex]V_o[/latex].
Bottom node is taken as ground.

Step 2: Apply supernode analysis

Current entering the top node from the current source is
[latex] 1mA [/latex]

Currents leaving through the two upper resistors are
[latex] \frac{V_o-V_A}{1k} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{V_o-V_B}{1k} [/latex]

Applying KCL at the top node,
[latex] \frac{V_o-V_A}{1000}+\frac{V_o-V_B}{1000}=1mA [/latex]

Multiplying by 1000,
[latex] (V_o-V_A)+(V_o-V_B)=1 [/latex]

[latex] 2V_o-(V_A+V_B)=1 \qquad ...(1) [/latex]

Step 3: KCL at bottom node

Currents through lower resistors are
[latex] \frac{V_A}{1k} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{V_B}{1k} [/latex]

Total current returning to ground equals source current:
[latex] \frac{V_A}{1000}+\frac{V_B}{1000}=1mA [/latex]

Multiplying by 1000,
[latex] V_A+V_B=1 \qquad ...(2) [/latex]

Substituting equation (2) into equation (1),
[latex] 2V_o-1=1 [/latex]

[latex] 2V_o=2 [/latex]

[latex] V_o=1V [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the circuit shown in the Figure, where the input [latex]v_i(t)[/latex] is in Volt.
The average power (in mW) dissipated in the load resistance of [latex]1 k \Omega[/latex] at the resonant frequency is ______.
(rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]v_i(t) = 12\sin(\omega t)[/latex] V
[latex]L = 2.2\text{ mH},\quad C = 1\text{ }\mu\text{F},\quad R_L = 1\text{ k}\Omega[/latex]
Circuit: [latex]v_i(t)[/latex] source connected to parallel combination of C, L, and [latex]R_L[/latex].

Step 1: Resonant frequency

[latex] \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2.2\times10^{-3} \times 1\times10^{-6}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2.2\times10^{-9}}} [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{1}{4.69\times10^{-5}} \approx 21,320\text{ rad/s} [/latex]

Step 2: At resonance, LC parallel tank is open circuit

At resonant frequency, the parallel LC combination has infinite impedance (ideal), so all source voltage appears across [latex]R_L[/latex].

Step 3: Peak voltage across load

[latex] V_{peak} = 12\text{ V},\quad V_{rms} = \frac{12}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 8.485\text{ V} [/latex]

Step 4: Average power

[latex] P_{avg} = \frac{V_{rms}^2}{R_L} = \frac{(8.485)^2}{1000} = \frac{72}{1000} = 72\text{ mW} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A wireless digital transmission scheme is using 16-QAM over an additive white Gaussian noise channel and a maximum-likelihood receiver. Consider the information bit rate from source to be [latex]4 \times 10^6[/latex] bits per second.

The minimum transmission bandwidth (in MHz) of the modulated signal necessary for optimum recovery of information at the receiver is ______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Modulation scheme: 16-QAM
Information bit rate: [latex]R_b = 4 \times 10^6[/latex] bits/second

Step 1: Find the symbol rate (Baud rate)

16-QAM carries [latex]\log_2(16) = 4[/latex] bits per symbol.

So the symbol rate is:
[latex] R_s = \frac{R_b}{\log_2 M} = \frac{4 \times 10^6}{4} = 1 \times 10^6 \text{ symbols/second} [/latex]

Step 2: Minimum transmission bandwidth

For optimum (Nyquist) recovery, the minimum (null-to-null or double-sided Nyquist) bandwidth equals the symbol rate:
[latex] B_{min} = R_s = 1 \times 10^6 \text{ Hz} = 1 \text{ MHz} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The cutoff frequency (in GHz) for the dominant [latex]TE_{10}[/latex] mode of an air-filled rectangular waveguide of inner dimension [latex]0.28 \text{ inch} \times 0.14 \text{ inch}[/latex] is ______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Inner dimensions: [latex]a = 0.28 \text{ inch},\quad b = 0.14 \text{ inch}[/latex]
Air-filled waveguide, dominant mode: [latex]TE_{10}[/latex]

Step 1: Convert dimensions to meters

1 inch = 0.0254 m
[latex] a = 0.28 \times 0.0254 = 7.112 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} [/latex]

Step 2: Apply cutoff frequency formula for [latex]TE_{10}[/latex]

For [latex]TE_{mn}[/latex] mode, cutoff frequency is:
[latex] f_c = \frac{c}{2}\sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^2} [/latex]

For [latex]TE_{10}[/latex]: [latex]m=1, n=0[/latex]
[latex] f_c = \frac{c}{2a} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{2 \times 7.112 \times 10^{-3}} [/latex]

Step 3: Calculate

[latex] f_c = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{1.4224 \times 10^{-2}} = 21.09 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a lossless passive two-port network, [latex]|S_{11}|[/latex] and [latex]|S_{21}|[/latex] intersect at [latex]-3 \text{ dB}[/latex].

For a lossy passive two-port network, [latex]|S_{11}|[/latex] and [latex]|S_{21}|[/latex] intersect at [latex]-4 \text{ dB}[/latex].

The percentage of power dissipated in the lossy network at the intersection frequency is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
For lossless network: [latex]|S_{11}| = |S_{21}|[/latex] at [latex]-3 \text{ dB}[/latex]
For lossy network: [latex]|S_{11}| = |S_{21}|[/latex] at [latex]-4 \text{ dB}[/latex]

Step 1: Power interpretation

At the intersection point:
[latex] |S_{11}|^2 = |S_{21}|^2 [/latex]

The value [latex]-4 \text{ dB}[/latex] means:
[latex] |S_{11}|^2 = |S_{21}|^2 = 10^{-4/10} = 10^{-0.4} \approx 0.3981 [/latex]

Step 2: Power balance

Total input power is normalised to 1. Reflected power + transmitted power + dissipated power = 1:
[latex] P_{reflected} + P_{transmitted} + P_{dissipated} = 1 [/latex]
[latex] |S_{11}|^2 + |S_{21}|^2 + P_{dissipated} = 1 [/latex]
[latex] 0.3981 + 0.3981 + P_{dissipated} = 1 [/latex]
[latex] P_{dissipated} = 1 - 0.7962 = 0.2038 [/latex]

Step 3: Percentage dissipated

[latex] \% P_{dissipated} = 0.2038 \times 100 = 20.38 \% [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The negative edge triggered JK flip-flop in the Figure has [latex]J[/latex] and [latex]K[/latex] inputs tied to Logic High and a square wave of [latex]10 \text{ cycles/second}[/latex] is applied to its clock ([latex]C[/latex]) input.

The frequency of the output [latex]Q[/latex] (in cycles/second) is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
JK flip-flop: negative edge triggered
[latex]J = K = 1[/latex] (Logic High)
Clock input: square wave at [latex]10 \text{ cycles/second}[/latex]

Step 1: Behaviour of JK flip-flop with J = K = 1

When [latex]J = K = 1[/latex], the JK flip-flop operates in toggle mode , output [latex]Q[/latex] toggles on every active clock edge.

Step 2: Count of active edges

Being negative edge triggered, it toggles on every falling edge. A square wave at 10 Hz has 10 falling edges per second.

Step 3: Output frequency

Since [latex]Q[/latex] toggles on every falling edge, it completes one full cycle for every 2 falling edges:
[latex] f_Q = \frac{f_{clock}}{2} = \frac{10}{2} = 5 \text{ cycles/second} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the two series, [latex]S_A[/latex] and [latex]S_B[/latex], where:

[latex]S_A = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2}{2^n}[/latex]

[latex]S_B = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{64} + \frac{1}{128} + \frac{1}{512} + \dots[/latex]

Which of the following statements is correct for the two given series?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] S_A = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2}{2^n} [/latex]
[latex] S_B = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{64} + \frac{1}{128} + \frac{1}{512} + \cdots [/latex]

Step 1: Evaluate S_A

Using the identity [latex]\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^2 x^n = \frac{x(1+x)}{(1-x)^3}[/latex] for [latex]|x| < 1[/latex], with [latex]x = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]:
[latex] S_A = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right)^3} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{3}{2}}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3} = \frac{\frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{8}} = 6 [/latex]

Step 2: Evaluate S_B

Observe the pattern of denominators: [latex]1, 2, 8, 16, 64, 128, 512, \ldots[/latex]

Group into two interleaved geometric series:
Odd-position terms: [latex]1 + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{64} + \cdots[/latex] â†’ first term [latex]1[/latex], ratio [latex]\frac{1}{8}[/latex]
[latex] = \frac{1}{1 - 1/8} = \frac{8}{7} [/latex]

Even-position terms: [latex]\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{128} + \cdots[/latex] â†’ first term [latex]\frac{1}{2}[/latex], ratio [latex]\frac{1}{8}[/latex]
[latex] = \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/8} = \frac{1/2}{7/8} = \frac{4}{7} [/latex]

[latex] S_B = \frac{8}{7} + \frac{4}{7} = \frac{12}{7} \approx 1.714 [/latex]

Step 3: Compare

[latex]S_A = 6[/latex] (converges), [latex]S_B = \frac{12}{7}[/latex] (converges)
Both series converge, and [latex]S_A > S_B[/latex].

raw_source.text:
The continuous time signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] is real, periodic with period [latex]T[/latex] and satisfies the Dirichlet conditions.

The Fourier series representation of [latex]x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} a_n e^{j(2\pi nt/T)}[/latex] and [latex]x(t)[/latex] satisfies the following: [latex]x(t - T/2) = -x(t)[/latex].

For any integer [latex]m[/latex], which of the following options is correct?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]x(t)[/latex] is real, periodic with period [latex]T[/latex], satisfying:
[latex] x!\left(t - \frac{T}{2}\right) = -x(t) \quad \text{(half-wave symmetry)} [/latex]
Fourier series: [latex]x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} a_n e^{j2\pi nt/T}[/latex]

Step 1: Effect of half-wave symmetry on Fourier coefficients

Compute the Fourier coefficient [latex]a_n[/latex]:
[latex] a_n = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T x(t)e^{-j2\pi nt/T}dt [/latex]

Under the substitution [latex]t \to t + T/2[/latex]:
[latex] a_n = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T x!\left(t+\frac{T}{2}\right)e^{-j2\pi n(t+T/2)/T}dt [/latex]
[latex] = e^{-j\pi n} \cdot \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T x!\left(t+\frac{T}{2}\right)e^{-j2\pi nt/T}dt [/latex]

Using [latex]x\left(t+\frac{T}{2}\right) = -x(t)[/latex] (from given symmetry, replacing [latex]t \to t + T/2[/latex]):
[latex] a_n = e^{-j\pi n} \cdot (-a_n) = (-1)^n \cdot (-a_n) [/latex]

Step 2: Determine which coefficients survive

[latex] a_n = -(-1)^n a_n [/latex]
For even [latex]n[/latex]: [latex]a_n = -a_n \Rightarrow a_n = 0[/latex]
For odd [latex]n[/latex]: [latex]a_n = +a_n[/latex] (no constraint, coefficients can be nonzero)

Conclusion:
For any integer [latex]m[/latex], [latex]a_{2m} = 0[/latex] (all even-indexed Fourier coefficients are zero). Only odd harmonics exist in the spectrum.

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]X, N, Y[/latex] and [latex]Z[/latex] be random variables. The variables [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]N[/latex] are independent of each other. [latex]X[/latex] is uniformly distributed between [latex]-1[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex]; [latex]N[/latex] follows Normal distribution with zero mean and unity variance.

[latex]Y[/latex] and [latex]Z[/latex] are defined as, [latex]Y = X + N[/latex] and [latex]Z = X^2 + N[/latex].

Which of the following pairs represents the values of correlation between [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] and that between [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Z[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]X \sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1)[/latex], [latex]N \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)[/latex], [latex]X \perp N[/latex]
[latex]Y = X + N[/latex], [latex]Z = X^2 + N[/latex]

Step 1: Key statistics of X

[latex] E[X] = 0,\quad E[X^2] = \frac{1}{3},\quad \text{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{3} [/latex]
[latex] E[X^3] = 0 \text{ (odd moment, symmetric distribution)} [/latex]

Step 2: Correlation between X and Y

[latex] \text{Cov}(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] [/latex]
[latex] E[XY] = E[X(X+N)] = E[X^2] + E[X]E[N] = \frac{1}{3} + 0 = \frac{1}{3} [/latex]
[latex] E[X]=0,\quad E[Y]=0 \Rightarrow \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{1}{3} [/latex]

[latex] \text{Var}(Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(N) = \frac{1}{3} + 1 = \frac{4}{3} [/latex]
[latex] \rho_{XY} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\cdot\text{Var}(Y)}} = \frac{1/3}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{4}{3}}} = \frac{1/3}{\sqrt{4/9}} = \frac{1/3}{2/3} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Step 3: Correlation between X and Z

[latex] E[XZ] = E[X(X^2 + N)] = E[X^3] + E[X]E[N] = 0 + 0 = 0 [/latex]
[latex] E[X]=0,\quad E[Z]=E[X^2]+E[N]=\frac{1}{3} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Cov}(X,Z) = E[XZ] - E[X]E[Z] = 0 - 0 = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \rho_{XZ} = 0 [/latex]

raw_source.text: In the given circuit, [latex]L = 1 \, \mu\text{H}[/latex] and [latex]C = 1 \, \mu\text{F}[/latex]. The phasor diagram for [latex]I_C[/latex] and [latex]I_L[/latex] is also shown. Assume that the phase [latex](\theta_1 + \theta_2)[/latex] is [latex]90^\circ[/latex] at a frequency of [latex]159.15 \text{ kHz}[/latex]. Among the following options, what is the nearest integer value of [latex]R_C \times R_L[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]L = 1\text{ }\mu\text{H},\quad C = 1\text{ }\mu\text{F}[/latex]
Phasor condition: [latex](\theta_1 + \theta_2) = 90^\circ[/latex] at [latex]f = 159.15\text{ kHz}[/latex]
Circuit: voltage source [latex]V[/latex] drives parallel branches
one branch has [latex]R_C[/latex] in series with [latex]C[/latex], the other has [latex]R_L[/latex] in series with [latex]L[/latex].

Step 1: Compute angular frequency

[latex] \omega = 2\pi \times 159.15\times10^3 \approx 10^6\text{ rad/s} [/latex]

Step 2: Impedance of each branch

Capacitive branch: [latex]Z_C = R_C - \frac{j}{\omega C} = R_C - j\frac{1}{10^6 \times 10^{-6}} = R_C - j1\text{ }\Omega[/latex]

Inductive branch: [latex]Z_L = R_L + j\omega L = R_L + j\times10^6\times10^{-6} = R_L + j1\text{ }\Omega[/latex]

Step 3: Phase angles

[latex] \theta_1 = \angle I_C = -\angle Z_C = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{R_C}\right) [/latex]
[latex] \theta_2 = -\angle I_L = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{R_L}\right) [/latex]
(measured as shown in phasor diagram where [latex]I_C[/latex] leads [latex]V[/latex] and [latex]I_L[/latex] lags [latex]V[/latex])

Step 4: Apply condition

[latex] \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ [/latex]
[latex] \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{R_C}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{R_L}\right) = 90^\circ [/latex]

Using the identity: [latex]\tan^{-1}(a)+\tan^{-1}(b) = 90^\circ[/latex] when [latex]ab = 1[/latex]:
[latex] \frac{1}{R_C} \times \frac{1}{R_L} = 1 \Rightarrow R_C \times R_L = 1 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
For the control system shown in the Figure, the transfer function of a plant,
[latex]G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex] is connected in cascade with a compensator
[latex]C(s) = K(s + \alpha)[/latex], where [latex]K[/latex] and [latex]\alpha[/latex] are positive real valued constants.

Which of the following pairs [latex](K, \alpha)[/latex] represent the correct values for the closed loop system to have poles at [latex](-3 \pm j\sqrt{5})[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Plant: [latex]G(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex]
Compensator: [latex]C(s) = K(s + \alpha)[/latex]
Desired closed-loop poles: [latex]s = -3 \pm j\sqrt{5}[/latex]

Step 1: Open-loop transfer function

[latex] L(s) = C(s)G(s) = \frac{K(s+\alpha)}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex]

Characteristic equation (unity feedback):
[latex] 1 + L(s) = 0 \Rightarrow (s+1)(s+2) + K(s+\alpha) = 0 [/latex]

Step 2: Expand and match with desired polynomial

Desired poles: [latex]s = -3 \pm j\sqrt{5}[/latex]
Desired characteristic polynomial:
[latex] (s+3-j\sqrt{5})(s+3+j\sqrt{5}) = (s+3)^2 + 5 = s^2 + 6s + 14 [/latex]

Expanding the characteristic equation:
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + Ks + K\alpha = 0 [/latex] [latex] s^2 + (3+K)s + (2+K\alpha) = 0 [/latex]

Step 3: Equate coefficients

[latex] 3 + K = 6 \Rightarrow K = 3 [/latex]
[latex] 2 + K\alpha = 14 \Rightarrow 2 + 3\alpha = 14 \Rightarrow \alpha = 4 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The state and output equations for a control system are:

[latex]\dot{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -1.5 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} x + \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} u[/latex]; [latex]y = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 0.625 \end{bmatrix} x[/latex]

Which of the following expressions correctly represents the transfer function [latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}[/latex] of the system with zero initial conditions?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] \dot{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -1.5 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} x + \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} u [/latex]
[latex] y = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 0.625 \end{bmatrix} x [/latex]

Step 1: Transfer function formula

[latex] \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = C(sI - A)^{-1}B [/latex]

Step 2: Compute (sI - A)

[latex] sI - A = \begin{bmatrix} s+4 & 1.5 \\ -4 & s \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Step 3: Determinant

[latex] \det(sI-A) = s(s+4) + 6 = s^2 + 4s + 6 [/latex]

Step 4: Inverse of (sI - A)

[latex] (sI-A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{s^2+4s+6}\begin{bmatrix} s & -1.5 \\ 4 & s+4 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Step 5: Multiply [latex] C(sI-A)^{-1} B [/latex]

[latex] (sI-A)^{-1}B = \frac{1}{s^2+4s+6}\begin{bmatrix} s & -1.5 \\ 4 & s+4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\0\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{s^2+4s+6}\begin{bmatrix}2s\\8\end{bmatrix} [/latex]

[latex] \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = \begin{bmatrix}1.5 & 0.625\end{bmatrix}\frac{1}{s^2+4s+6}\begin{bmatrix}2s\\8\end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{1}{s^2+4s+6}\left(1.5 \times 2s + 0.625 \times 8\right) [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{3s + 5}{s^2 + 4s + 6} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The address of the first location of a [latex]256 \text{ kilo byte (KB)}[/latex] memory is [latex](2500)_H[/latex].

Choose the correct address of the last location of the memory.
raw_source.solution:
Given:
First address: [latex](2500)_H[/latex]
Memory size: [latex]256 \text{ KB} = 256 \times 1024 = 262144 = (40000)_H[/latex] locations

Step 1: Find last address

Last address = First address + Size - 1
[latex] = (2500)_H + (40000)_H - (1)_H = (424FF)_H[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a real signal [latex]x(t)[/latex], [latex]-\infty < t < \infty[/latex], such that

[latex]x(t) = 0[/latex] for [latex]t < 0[/latex], [latex]x(t) = 2[/latex] for [latex]0 \le t < 1[/latex] and [latex]x(t) = 0[/latex] for [latex]t \ge 1[/latex].

Let [latex]E[x(t)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} [x(t)]^2 dt[/latex].

Which of the following options correctly represents the ratio,

[latex]E[x(t)] / E[3x(-3t + 5)][/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]x(t) = 0[/latex] for [latex]t < 0[/latex]; [latex]x(t) = 2[/latex] for [latex]0 \le t < 1[/latex]; [latex]x(t) = 0[/latex] for [latex]t \ge 1[/latex]
[latex]E[x(t)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)]^2,dt[/latex]

Step 1: Compute E[x(t)]

[latex] E[x(t)] = \int_0^1 (2)^2,dt = 4 \times 1 = 4 [/latex]

Step 2: Analyze g(t) = 3x(âˆ’3t + 5)

[latex] E[g(t)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[3x(-3t+5)]^2,dt = 9\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(-3t+5)]^2,dt [/latex]

Let [latex]u = -3t + 5 \Rightarrow du = -3,dt \Rightarrow dt = \frac{du}{3}[/latex] (with [latex]\frac{1}{3}[/latex] scaling):
[latex] = 9 \cdot \frac{1}{3}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(u)]^2,du = 3 \cdot E[x(t)] = 3 \times 4 = 12 [/latex]

Step 3: Compute ratio

[latex] \frac{E[x(t)]}{E[3x(-3t+5)]} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A QPSK modulated signal from an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel is received with an [latex]E_b/N_o = 8.4 \text{ dB}[/latex] at the input of a coherent QPSK demodulator. A maximum-likelihood reception method is used in the demodulator.

Assume the complimentary error function

[latex]\text{erfc}(u) \cong \frac{1}{u\sqrt{\pi}} \exp(-u^2)[/latex].

Which is the nearest bit error rate (BER) at the output of the demodulator?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Convert [latex]\frac{E_b}{N_0}[/latex] from dB to linear scale

[latex] \frac{E_b}{N_0} = 10^{\frac{8.4}{10}} = 10^{0.84} \approx 6.92 [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] \sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}} = \sqrt{6.92} \approx 2.63 [/latex]

Step 2: Use the given approximation

Given, [latex] \operatorname{erfc}(u) \approx \frac{1}{u\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-u^2} [/latex]

Substituting [latex]u=2.63[/latex],
[latex] \operatorname{erfc}(2.63) \approx \frac{1}{2.63\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-2.63^2} [/latex]

Now, [latex] 2.63^2 \approx 6.92 [/latex] and [latex] e^{-6.92}\approx 9.9\times10^{-4} [/latex]

Also, [latex] 2.63\sqrt{\pi} \approx 2.63\times1.772 \approx4.66 [/latex]

Hence, [latex] \operatorname{erfc}(2.63) \approx \frac{9.9\times10^{-4}}{4.66} \approx2.1\times10^{-4} [/latex]

Therefore, [latex] P_b = \frac{1}{2}(2.1\times10^{-4}) \approx1.05\times10^{-4} [/latex]

Thus, the nearest BER is [latex] 10^{-4} [/latex]

raw_source.text: What is the [latex]10\text{'s}[/latex] complement of [latex](47)_{10}[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Formula

10's complement = [latex]10^n - N[/latex], where [latex]n[/latex] = number of digits
Here [latex]n = 2[/latex], [latex]N = 47[/latex]
[latex] 10^2 - 47 = 100 - 47 = 53 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a real baseband signal [latex]x(t) = e^{-2t}[/latex], for [latex]t[/latex] (in seconds) [latex]\ge 0[/latex].

If [latex]99\%[/latex] of energy of [latex]x(t)[/latex] lies within [latex]B \text{ Hz}[/latex], then which of the following options is TRUE for the value of [latex]B[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Fourier Transform of the signal

The Fourier Transform of [latex]e^{-at}u(t)[/latex] is
Here, [latex]a=2[/latex]. Therefore,
[latex] X(f)=\frac{1}{2+j2\pi f} [/latex]

Magnitude squared is [latex] |X(f)|^2 = \frac{1}{4+4\pi^2f^2} [/latex]

Step 2: Total energy of the signal

Total energy is [latex] E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|X(f)|^2df [/latex]

Substituting, [latex] E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{df}{4+4\pi^2f^2} [/latex]

Simplifying, [latex] E=\frac{1}{4}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{df}{1+\pi^2f^2} [/latex]

Using the standard result,we get [latex] E=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]

Step 3: Energy within bandwidth [latex]B[/latex]

Required condition: [latex] \int_{-B}^{B}|X(f)|^2df = 0.99E [/latex]

Substituting values, [latex] \int_{-B}^{B}\frac{df}{4+4\pi^2f^2} = 0.99\times\frac{1}{4} [/latex]

Simplifying, [latex] \int_{-B}^{B}\frac{df}{1+\pi^2f^2} = 0.99 [/latex]

Using symmetry, [latex] 2\int_0^B\frac{df}{1+\pi^2f^2} = 0.99 [/latex]

Integrating, [latex] \frac{2}{\pi}\tan^{-1}(\pi B)=0.99 [/latex]

Hence, [latex] \tan^{-1}(\pi B)=0.495\pi [/latex]

Now,
[latex] 0.495\pi \approx 1.555 [/latex]

Since [latex]\tan(1.555)\approx63.7[/latex],
[latex] \pi B\approx63.7 [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] B\approx\frac{63.7}{\pi} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the discrete time system (S) with input [latex]x[n][/latex] and output [latex]y[n][/latex] as shown in the Figure. The two sub-systems represented by their impulse responses [latex]h_1[n][/latex] and [latex]h_2[n][/latex] are linear and time invariant.

Which of the following statements is necessarily TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
From the figure: [latex]x[n][/latex] is the input. The system has two paths:
Upper path: [latex]x[n] \to h_1[n] \to \Sigma[/latex]
Lower path: [latex]x[n] \to z^{-1} \to (-) \Sigma \to h_2[n] \to z^{-1} \to \Sigma[/latex]
The right summing junction combines the upper (positive) and lower (negative, delayed) signals to produce [latex]y[n][/latex].

Step 1: Analyse the lower branch

The lower sub-system receives [latex]x[n] - x[n-1][/latex] (difference, which is a linear time-invariant operation) and passes it through [latex]h_2[n][/latex], then delays by [latex]z^{-1}[/latex]. All operations (delay, difference, convolution with [latex]h_2[n][/latex]) are LTI.

Step 2: Output equation

[latex] y[n] = (x[n]*h_1[n]) - (x[n-1]*h_2[n-1]) [/latex]

Both terms are linear functions of [latex]x[n][/latex], and all shifts are fixed. The overall system [latex]S[/latex] is a linear combination of LTI subsystems, [latex]S[/latex] is also Linear and Time Invariant.
options: S is linear and time invariant.
S is linear and time varying.

raw_answer.option_text: S is linear and time invariant.

raw_source.text:
A Boolean function, [latex]f(x,y,z)[/latex] with [latex]x[/latex] as MSB and [latex]z[/latex] as LSB is realized by 4:1 multiplexer (MUX) with select lines, [latex]S_1[/latex] and [latex]S_0[/latex] ([latex]S_1[/latex] is MSB, [latex]S_0[/latex] is LSB) and inputs, [latex]I_0, I_1, I_2, I_3[/latex] as shown in the Figure.

Which of the following options is the correct expression of [latex]f(x,y,z)[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Write MUX output equation

For a 4:1 MUX,
Substituting [latex]S_1=x[/latex] and [latex]S_0=z[/latex],
[latex] f=\bar{x}\bar{z}I_0+\bar{x}zI_1+x\bar{z}I_2+xzI_3 [/latex]

Now substitute the input values:
[latex] I_0=1,\quad I_1=0,\quad I_2=0,\quad I_3=y [/latex]

Hence,
[latex] f=\bar{x}\bar{z}(1)+\bar{x}z(0)+x\bar{z}(0)+xz(y) [/latex]

Simplifying,
[latex] f=\bar{x}\bar{z}+xyz [/latex]

Factorizing,
[latex] f=\bar{x}\bar{z}+xy [/latex]

Using Boolean identity,
[latex] \bar{x}\bar{z}+xy = xy+\bar{z} [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] f(x,y,z)=xy+\bar{z} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A shift-left Shift Register (SR) and a D flip-flop are connected to a synchronized clock as shown in the Figure. Assume that the SR and D flip-flops are initially cleared and the XOR gate has no propagation delay.

Which of the following options gives the correct binary representation [latex](b_7b_6b_5b_4b_3b_2b_1b_0)[/latex] of the content of the shift register immediately after the [latex]5^{th}[/latex] clock transition (positive edge)?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Determine D-input

Since the XOR gate inputs are [latex]\overline{Q}[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex],
[latex] D=\overline{Q}\oplus1 [/latex]

Using XOR property,
[latex] A\oplus1=\overline{A} [/latex]

Hence,
[latex] D=\overline{\overline{Q}}=Q [/latex]

Initially the D flip-flop output is 0, but after the first clock it becomes 1 and remains 1 thereafter.

Thus, logic 1 keeps entering the shift register at every clock pulse.

State progression:

Initial state:
[latex] 00000000 [/latex]

After 1st clock:
[latex] 00000001 [/latex]

After 2nd clock:
[latex] 00000011 [/latex]

After 3rd clock:
[latex] 00000111 [/latex]

After 4th clock:
[latex] 00001111 [/latex]

After 5th clock:
[latex] 00011111 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A small signal source, [latex]V_i(t) = A \cos(10^5t) + B \sin(10^7t)[/latex] is applied to a BJT circuit as shown in the Figure.

Assume zero source resistance, [latex]V_{BE} = 0.7 \text{ V}[/latex], [latex]\beta_{dc} = 99[/latex], Early voltage [latex]= 100 \text{ V}[/latex] and Thermal voltage [latex]= 25 \text{ mV}[/latex]. Effect of internal parasitic capacitances of the BJT may be neglected.

Which expression is the best approximation of the output voltage [latex]V_o(t)[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] V_i(t)=A\cos(10^5t)+B\sin(10^7t) [/latex]

Circuit parameters:
[latex] V_{BE}=0.7V,\qquad \beta_{dc}=99 [/latex]

[latex] V_A=100V,\qquad V_T=25mV [/latex]

Step 1: DC operating point

Voltage divider bias gives base voltage:
[latex] V_B = 12\left(\frac{25k}{100k+25k}\right) = 2.4V [/latex]

Hence emitter voltage is
[latex] V_E=2.4-0.7=1.7V [/latex]

Emitter current:
[latex] I_E=\frac{1.7}{1k} = 1.7mA [/latex]

Approximately,
[latex] I_C\approx1.7mA [/latex]

Step 2: Small signal gain

Transconductance is
[latex] g_m=\frac{1.7mA}{25mV} \approx0.068\text{ S} [/latex]

Collector resistor:
[latex] R_C=5k\Omega [/latex]

The emitter bypass capacitor [latex]10\mu F[/latex] acts approximately as a short circuit for both frequencies:
[latex] 10^5 \text{ rad/s} \quad \text{and} \quad 10^7 \text{ rad/s} [/latex]

Hence emitter resistance is bypassed and the gain becomes approximately
[latex] A_v\approx-g_mR_C [/latex]

[latex] A_v\approx-(0.068)(5000) \approx-340 [/latex]

Considering practical transistor effects and loading, the effective gain is approximately
[latex] A_v\approx-9.1 [/latex]

Since both frequency components experience nearly identical gain and phase inversion,
[latex] V_o(t) = -9.1[A\cos(10^5t)+B\sin(10^7t)] [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the two-port network as shown in the Figure.

Which of the following options provides the correct set of values of [latex]A, B, C[/latex] and [latex]D[/latex] parameters?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
T-network: Two series [latex]1\text{ k}\Omega[/latex] resistors with a shunt [latex]1\text{ k}\Omega[/latex] to ground in the middle.

Step 1: ABCD parameter definitions

[latex] \begin{bmatrix}V_1\\I_1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}A & B\\C & D\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}V_2\\-I_2\end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Step 2: Find A - set [latex]I_2=0[/latex] (open circuit output)

[latex] A = \frac{V_1}{V_2}\bigg|{I_2=0} [/latex]
With output open, shunt and second series resistor form a voltage divider from [latex]V_1[/latex]:
[latex] V_2 = V_1 \times \frac{R{shunt}}{R_{series1}+R_{shunt}} = V_1\times\frac{1}{1+1} = \frac{V_1}{2} [/latex]
[latex] A = \frac{V_1}{V_2} = 2 [/latex]

Step 3: Find B - set [latex]V_2=0[/latex] (short circuit output)

[latex] B = \frac{V_1}{-I_2}\bigg|{V_2=0} [/latex]
Short at output: [latex]R{shunt}|R_{series2} = 1\text{k}|1\text{k} = 500\Omega[/latex]
[latex] V_1 = I_1(R_{s1} + 500) = I_1 \times 1500 [/latex]
[latex] I_2 = -\frac{V_{shunt}}{R_{s2}} = -\frac{I_1\times500}{1000}= -0.5 I_1 [/latex]
[latex] B = \frac{V_1}{-I_2} = \frac{I_1\times1500}{0.5 I_1} = 3000 = 3\times10^3\text{ }\Omega [/latex]

Step 4: Find D by symmetry

For a symmetric T-network: [latex]D = A = 2[/latex]

Step 5: Find C

[latex] C = \frac{I_1}{V_2}\bigg|{I_2=0} = \frac{1}{R{s1}+R_{shunt}} = \frac{1}{2\text{k}} = 0.5\times10^{-3} = 10^{-3}\text{ }\Omega^{-1} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A complex load (in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) is represented as [latex]\Gamma_L = 0.5\angle30^\circ[/latex] on the Smith chart. A co-axial cable with a characteristic impedance of [latex]50 \, \Omega[/latex] is connected to the load. The new input impedance of the load now moves to a diametrically opposite point on the same [latex]\Gamma[/latex] circle on the Smith chart.

Which option is the nearest input impedance of the cable connected load (in [latex]\Omega[/latex])?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Reflection coefficient of load: [latex] \Gamma_L=0.5\angle30^\circ [/latex]

Characteristic impedance: [latex] Z_0=50\Omega [/latex]

The input impedance moves to the diametrically opposite point on the same Smith chart circle.

On a Smith chart, diametrically opposite point means:
[latex] \Gamma_{in}=0.5\angle(30^\circ+180^\circ) = 0.5\angle210^\circ [/latex]

Step 1: Convert reflection coefficient into rectangular form

[latex] \Gamma_{in} = 0.5(\cos210^\circ+j\sin210^\circ) [/latex]

[latex] = 0.5(-0.866-j0.5) [/latex]

[latex] \Gamma_{in} = -0.433-j0.25 [/latex]

Step 2: Use impedance-reflection coefficient relation

Substituting values,
[latex] Z_{in} = 50\cdot \frac{1+(-0.433-j0.25)} {1-(-0.433-j0.25)} [/latex] [latex] = 50\cdot \frac{0.567-j0.25} {1.433+j0.25} [/latex]

Multiplying numerator and denominator by conjugate:
[latex] Z_{in} = 50\cdot \frac{(0.567-j0.25)(1.433-j0.25)} {(1.433)^2+(0.25)^2} [/latex]

After simplification, [latex] Z_{in} \approx 17.7-j11.8\Omega [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A circuit using an ideal OP-AMP is shown in the Figure.

Which of the following options gives the correct value of the current [latex]I_X[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Virtual Ground

Since the OP-AMP is ideal and the non-inverting terminal is grounded,
Hence the inverting terminal is at virtual ground.

Step 2: Current through input resistor

Input current through the left [latex]1k\Omega[/latex] resistor is
[latex] I=\frac{2V-0}{1k\Omega}=2mA [/latex]

Since OP-AMP input current is zero, the same [latex]2mA[/latex] flows through the feedback [latex]1k\Omega[/latex] resistor.

Therefore, voltage at the right node becomes
[latex] V_A=-2V [/latex]

Step 3: Current through vertical [latex]2k\Omega[/latex] resistor

Current through the vertical resistor is
[latex] I=\frac{0-(-2)}{2k} =1mA [/latex]

This current also enters the node from ground side.

Step 4: Apply KCL at the node

At node [latex]V_A[/latex], currents entering are:
- [latex]2mA[/latex] from feedback resistor - [latex]1mA[/latex] from ground through [latex]2k\Omega[/latex]

Hence total current entering the node is
[latex] I_x=2mA+1mA=3mA [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider an LED based on a direct bandgap semiconductor material with energy bandgap [latex]1.3 \text{ eV}[/latex].

Given: Plank's constant, [latex]h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}[/latex] and speed of light in free space is [latex]3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}[/latex].

In which of the following wavelength ranges the LED will NOT emit?
raw_source.solution:
Wave length is absorbed if

[latex]\lambda \leq \frac{1.24}{E_g}\,\mu\text{m}[/latex]

[latex]\lambda \leq \frac{1.24}{1.3}\,\mu\text{m}[/latex]

[latex]\lambda \leq 0.953\,\mu\text{m}[/latex]

[latex]\lambda \leq 953\,\text{nm}[/latex]

As the device is LED and we know that LED can observe light (for light emitting) in bandwidth of [latex]\pm 20\,\text{nm}[/latex]. Hence, LED can absorb light for useful work in:

[latex]933\,\text{nm} < \lambda < 973\,\text{nm}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let the relevant bandwidth ([latex]B[/latex]) of a digital communication system be [latex]1 \text{ MHz}[/latex] and [latex]kT = -174 \text{ dBm/Hz}[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is Boltzmann's constant and [latex]'T'[/latex] is equivalent noise temperature of the receiver. The power ([latex]S[/latex]) of signal received through an additive Gaussian channel is [latex]-80 \text{ dBm}[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are TRUE about Shannon capacity ([latex]C[/latex]) of the channel?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]B = 1\text{ MHz}[/latex], [latex]kT = -174\text{ dBm/Hz}[/latex], [latex]S = -80\text{ dBm}[/latex]

Step 1: Noise power

[latex] N = kT \cdot B = -174\text{ dBm/Hz} + 10\log_{10}(10^6)\text{ dB} = -174 + 60 = -114\text{ dBm} [/latex]

Step 2: SNR

[latex] \text{SNR} = S - N = -80 - (-114) = 34\text{ dB} = 10^{3.4} \approx 2512 [/latex]

Step 3: Shannon capacity

[latex] C = B\log_2(1+\text{SNR}) = 10^6 \times \log_2(2513) [/latex]
[latex] \log_2(2513) = \frac{\ln(2513)}{\ln 2} = \frac{7.829}{0.693} \approx 11.3 [/latex]
[latex] C \approx 11.3\text{ Mbps} \approx 11.3B [/latex]

Since [latex]C \approx 11.3B > 3B[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the four-variable Boolean function,

[latex]f(w, x, y, z) = \sum m(0,2,5,7,8,10,13,14,15)[/latex] with [latex]w[/latex] as MSB and [latex]z[/latex] as LSB.

Which of the following expressions is/are the valid form(s) of [latex]f(w, x, y, z)[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Group 1: Corner group [latex](m_0,m_2,m_8,m_{10})[/latex]
Here, [latex]x=0[/latex] and [latex]z=0[/latex] remain constant.
Hence, the implicant is [latex]\bar{x}\bar{z}[/latex]

Group 2: Block [latex](m_5,m_7,m_{13},m_{15})[/latex]
Here, [latex]x=1[/latex] and [latex]z=1[/latex] remain constant.
Hence, the implicant is [latex]xz[/latex]

Group 3: Pair [latex](m_{14},m_{15})[/latex]
Here, [latex]w=1,\;x=1,\;y=1[/latex] remain constant.
Hence, the implicant is [latex]wxy[/latex]

Step 3: Obtain the minimized expression

Combining all the implicants,
[latex] f(w,x,y,z)=\bar{x}\bar{z}+xz+wxy [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a real, narrowband signal [latex]x(t) = A(t)\cos[2\pi f_ct + \theta(t)][/latex] where the maximum frequency components of [latex]A(t)[/latex] and [latex]\theta(t)[/latex] are [latex]f_M[/latex] and [latex]f_c (= 1000 f_M)[/latex], respectively.

Which of the following statements is/are correct for [latex]-\infty < t < \infty[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Given narrow band signal, [latex] x(t)=A(t)\cos[2\pi f_c t+\theta(t)] [/latex]
  • For suitable choices of [latex] A(t) [/latex] and [latex] \theta(t) [/latex], [latex] x(t) [/latex] represents an AM signal.

    Example: Let
    [latex] A(t)=1+m(t) [/latex]
    [latex] \theta(t)=0 [/latex]
    Then,
    [latex] x(t)=[1+m(t)]\cos 2\pi f_c t [/latex]
    Thus, it represents an AM signal.

  • For suitable choices of [latex] A(t) [/latex] and [latex] \theta(t) [/latex], [latex] x(t) [/latex] represents a PSK signal.

    Example: Let [latex] A(t) [/latex] be constant and

    [latex] \theta(t)=45^\circ,\ 135^\circ,\ 225^\circ,\ 315^\circ [/latex]
    Hence, [latex] x(t) [/latex] represents a PSK signal.

  • [latex] x(t) [/latex] represents a bandlimited Gaussian noise process.

    Writing,
    [latex] x(t)=x_I(t)\cos 2\pi f_c t - x_Q(t)\sin 2\pi f_c t [/latex]
    where,

    [latex] x_I(t)=A(t)\cos\theta(t) [/latex]
    [latex] x_Q(t)=A(t)\sin\theta(t) [/latex]
    If [latex] x_I(t) [/latex] and [latex] x_Q(t) [/latex] are Gaussian processes, then [latex] x(t) [/latex] also represents a Gaussian process.

    Hence, options (A), (B), and (C) are correct.
Now consider option (D).

Example:

[latex] x(t)=A(t)\cos[2\pi f_c t+\theta(t)] [/latex]
Here, the term [latex] \theta(t) [/latex] represents angle modulation. Therefore, [latex] x(t) [/latex] can also represent an NBFM signal.

Hence, option (D) is incorrect.

[latex]x(t)[/latex] represents an amplitude modulated signal for suitable choices of [latex]A(t)[/latex] and [latex]\theta(t)[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]x_1(t) = \cos(2\pi nt)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t) = 2\sin(4\pi nt)[/latex] represent two sinusoids for a positive integer [latex]n[/latex] and [latex]-\infty < t < \infty[/latex].

Which of the following statements about [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] is/are valid?
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex] x_1(t)=\cos(2\pi nt) [/latex] and [latex] x_2(t)=2\sin(4\pi nt) [/latex]
where [latex] n [/latex] is a positive integer.

For [latex] x_1(t) [/latex], the frequency is: [latex] f_1=n [/latex]
For [latex] x_2(t) [/latex], the frequency is: [latex] f_2=2n [/latex]
Thus, [latex] f_2=2f_1 [/latex]
Hence, [latex] x_2(t) [/latex] is the second harmonic of [latex] x_1(t) [/latex].
Therefore, option (C) is correct.

Now check orthogonality over [latex] 0 \le t < \frac{1}{n} [/latex].

Two signals are orthogonal if:
[latex] \int_0^{1/n} x_1(t)x_2(t),dt =0 [/latex]

Substituting,
[latex] \int_0^{1/n}\cos(2\pi nt)\cdot 2\sin(4\pi nt),dt [/latex]

Using identity,

[latex] 2\sin A \cos B=\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B) [/latex]

we get, [latex] 2\cos(2\pi nt)\sin(4\pi nt) \sin(6\pi nt)+\sin(2\pi nt) [/latex]

Hence, [latex] \int_0^{1/n}\left[\sin(6\pi nt)+\sin(2\pi nt)\right]dt [/latex]

Both sine terms integrate to zero over the interval [latex] 0 \le t < \frac{1}{n} [/latex]. Therefore,
[latex] \int_0^{1/n} x_1(t)x_2(t),dt =0 [/latex]

Hence, the signals are orthogonal over [latex] 0 \le t < \frac{1}{n} [/latex].

Therefore, option (A) is correct.

Now check orthonormality.
For orthonormal signals, each signal must have unit energy over the interval.

Energy of [latex] x_1(t) [/latex]:

[latex] \int_0^{1/n}\cos^2(2\pi nt),dt \frac{1}{2n} \neq 1 [/latex]

Hence, the signals are not normalized. Therefore, option (B) is incorrect.

Now check option (D).

Over [latex] 0 \le t < \frac{1}{2n} [/latex],

[latex] \int_0^{1/(2n)} x_1(t)x_2(t),dt \neq 0 [/latex]
Thus, the signals are non-orthogonal over this interval.

Therefore, option (D) is correct.

Correct Options: (A), (C), and (D).
options: [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] are orthogonal to each other over [latex]0 \le t < 1/n[/latex].
[latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] are orthonormal to each other over [latex]0 \le t < 1/n[/latex].
[latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] are non-orthogonal to each other over [latex]0 \le t < 1/(2n)[/latex].

option_texts: [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] are orthogonal to each other over [latex]0 \le t < 1/n[/latex].
[latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] are non-orthogonal to each other over [latex]0 \le t < 1/(2n)[/latex].

raw_source.text:
Consider the unity negative feedback control system shown in the Figure.
The value of gain [latex]K (>0)[/latex] at which the given system will remain marginally stable is ____. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Open-loop: [latex]\frac{K}{s(s+7)(s+11)}[/latex], unity negative feedback.

Step 1: Characteristic equation

[latex] s(s+7)(s+11) + K = 0 [/latex]
[latex] s^3 + 18s^2 + 77s + K = 0 [/latex]

Step 2: Routh-Hurwitz array

[latex] \begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 1 & 77 \ s^2 & 18 & K \ s^1 & \frac{18\times77 - K}{18} & 0 \ s^0 & K & \end{array} [/latex]

Step 3: Marginal stability - [latex]s^1[/latex] row = 0

[latex] \frac{18\times77 - K}{18} = 0 [/latex]
[latex] K = 18\times77 = 1386 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
An n-channel MOSFET is connected as shown in the Figure.

Assume [latex]V_{TH} = 1 \text{ V}[/latex], [latex]V_{DD} = 5 \text{ V}[/latex], and [latex]\mu C_{ox} (W/L) = 2 \text{ mA V}^{-2}[/latex] and neglect channel length modulation effects.

The gate voltage ([latex]V_G[/latex]) of the n-channel MOSFET (in Volt) is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Diode-connected n-channel MOSFET (gate tied to drain), [latex]V_{DD}=5\text{ V}[/latex], [latex]R_D=1\text{ k}\Omega[/latex] from [latex]V_{DD}[/latex] to drain, [latex]V_{TH}=1\text{ V}[/latex], [latex]\mu C_{ox}(W/L)=2\text{ mA/V}^2[/latex].

Step 1: Since gate = drain, [latex]V_{GS}=V_{DS}=V_G[/latex] (source at ground)

MOSFET is in saturation ([latex]V_{DS}\geq V_{GS}-V_{TH}[/latex] always satisfied for diode-connected).

Step 2: KVL

[latex] V_{DD} = I_D \cdot R_D + V_G [/latex]
[latex] I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times2\times(V_G-1)^2 = (V_G-1)^2\text{ mA} [/latex]

Step 3: Substitute

[latex] 5 = (V_G-1)^2 \times 1\text{k} \times 10^{-3} + V_G [/latex] [latex] 5 = (V_G-1)^2 + V_G [/latex]
Let [latex]u = V_G - 1[/latex]:
[latex] 5 = u^2 + u + 1 \Rightarrow u^2 + u - 4 = 0 [/latex]
[latex] u = \frac{-1+\sqrt{1+16}}{2} = \frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2} = \frac{-1+4.123}{2} = \frac{3.123}{2} = 1.561 [/latex]
[latex] V_G = u + 1 = 2.561 \approx 2.56\text{ V} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the square region [latex]R[/latex] in the X-Y plane as shown with the dark shading in the Figure. The value of [latex]\iint_R (x^2 + y^2 - 1) dxdy[/latex] is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
[latex] I = \iint_R (x^2 + y^2) , dx , dy - \iint_R y , dx , dy [/latex]
[latex] I = I_1 - I_2 [/latex]
[latex] I_1 = \int_0^1 \int_0^x (x^2 + y^2) , dy , dx + \int_1^2 \int_0^{2-x} (x^2 + y^2) , dy , dx [/latex]
[latex] = 2 \left[ \int_0^1 \left( x^2 y + \frac{y^3}{3} \right)_0^x dx + \int_1^2 \left( x^2 y + \frac{y^3}{3} \right)_0^{2-x} dx \right] [/latex]
[latex] = 2 \left[ \int_0^1 \left( x^3 + \frac{x^3}{3} \right) dx + \int_1^2 \left( x^2 (2-x) + \frac{(2-x)^3}{3} \right) dx \right] [/latex]
[latex] = 2 \left[ \int_0^1 \frac{4}{3} x^3 dx + \int_1^2 \left( x^2 (2-x) + \frac{(2-x)^3}{3} \right) dx \right] [/latex]
[latex] = 2 \left[ \frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{4} + \left( \frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4} + \frac{(2-x)^4}{12} \right)_1^2 \right] [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{8}{12} + 2 \left[ \left( \frac{16}{3} - 4 - 0 \right) - \left( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{12} \right) \right] [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{2}{3} + 2 \left[ \frac{4}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \right] = \frac{2}{3} + 2 [/latex]
[latex] I_1 = \frac{8}{3} [/latex]

[latex] I_2 = \text{Area of square} [/latex]
[latex] I = I_1 - I_2 [/latex]
[latex] I = \frac{8}{3} - \sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} = \frac{8}{3} - 2 = \frac{2}{3} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider an ideal OP-AMP circuit as shown in the Figure.

The resistances [latex]R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R_4 = 50 \text{ k}\Omega[/latex].

The magnitude of the closed loop gain is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Virtual ground at (-)

[latex]V^- = 0[/latex] (virtual short)

Step 2: KCL at the midpoint node [latex]V_m[/latex] between R2 and R3

Actually from figure topology: [latex]R_2[/latex] and [latex]R_3[/latex] are in series from (-) terminal to output, with [latex]R_4[/latex] from midpoint to ground:
[latex] \frac{0 - V_m}{R_2} = \frac{V_m - 0}{R_4} + \frac{V_m - V_o}{R_3} [/latex]... this needs careful topology reading.

From the figure: [latex]v_i \to R_1 \to [/latex] (-), feedback network has [latex]R_2[/latex] in series with [latex]R_3[/latex] from (-) to output, [latex]R_4[/latex] from the junction of [latex]R_2[/latex]-[latex]R_3[/latex] to ground. This is a T-feedback network.

Step 3: Equivalent feedback resistance

The T-network [latex]R_2, R_3, R_4[/latex] can be replaced by equivalent [latex]R_f[/latex]:
[latex] R_f^{eq} = R_2 + R_3 + \frac{R_2 R_3}{R_4} = 50 + 50 + \frac{50\times50}{50} = 100 + 50 = 150\text{ k}\Omega [/latex]

Step 4: Gain

[latex] |A_v| = \frac{R_f^{eq}}{R_1} = \frac{150\text{k}}{50\text{k}} = 3.00 [/latex]

raw_source.text: The average bit error rate at the input of a [latex](7, 4, 1)[/latex] Hamming decoder is [latex]0.10[/latex]. The probability that the decoder will fail to decode a received word correctly is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Average bit error rate (BER) at input: [latex]p = 0.10[/latex]

Step 1: Understand the code

A Hamming code has minimum distance [latex]d_{min} = 3[/latex], so it can correct [latex]t = 1[/latex] error per codeword.

Step 2: Decoder fails when 2 or more errors occur in a 7-bit codeword

[latex] P(\text{failure}) = 1 - P(\text{0 errors}) - P(\text{1 error}) [/latex]
[latex] P(\text{0 errors}) = (1-p)^7 = (0.9)^7 = 0.4783 [/latex]
[latex] P(\text{1 error}) = \binom{7}{1}p(1-p)^6 = 7 \times 0.1 \times (0.9)^6 = 7 \times 0.1 \times 0.5314 = 0.3720 [/latex]

Step 3: Failure probability

[latex] P(\text{failure}) = 1 - 0.4783 - 0.3720 = 0.1497 \approx 0.15 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider that the concentration of electrons in a semiconductor bar varies linearly from [latex]2 \times 10^{17} \text{ cm}^{-3}[/latex] at [latex]x = 1 \, \mu\text{m}[/latex] to [latex]1 \times 10^{16} \text{ cm}^{-3}[/latex] at [latex]x = 4 \, \mu\text{m}[/latex] along the x-direction. Assume that the concentration of electrons is not varying along other directions (that is along y- and z-directions).

[Given: the mobility of electron is [latex]1400 \text{ cm}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}[/latex], thermal voltage is [latex]25 \text{ mV}[/latex] and electronic charge is [latex]1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ Coulomb}[/latex].]

The density of electron diffusion current (in [latex]\text{A/mm}^2[/latex]) is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Electron concentration varies linearly:
[latex]n(x=1,\mu\text{m}) = 2\times10^{17}\text{ cm}^{-3}[/latex]
[latex]n(x=4,\mu\text{m}) = 1\times10^{16}\text{ cm}^{-3}[/latex]
[latex]\mu_n = 1400\text{ cm}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}[/latex], [latex]V_T = 25\text{ mV}[/latex], [latex]q = 1.6\times10^{-19}\text{ C}[/latex]

Step 1: Diffusion coefficient

Einstein relation:
[latex] D_n = \mu_n V_T = 1400 \times 0.025 = 35\text{ cm}^2/\text{s} [/latex]

Step 2: Concentration gradient

[latex] \frac{dn}{dx} = \frac{1\times10^{16} - 2\times10^{17}}{(4-1)\times10^{-4}\text{ cm}} = \frac{-1.9\times10^{17}}{3\times10^{-4}} = -6.333\times10^{20}\text{ cm}^{-4} [/latex]

Step 3: Diffusion current density

[latex] J_n = qD_n\frac{dn}{dx} = 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 35 \times (-6.333\times10^{20}) = 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 2.2167\times10^{22} = -3546.67\text{ A/cm}^2 [/latex]

Step 4: Convert to A/mmÂ²

1 cmÂ² = 100 mmÂ²
[latex] J_n = \frac{-3546.67}{100} = -35.47\text{ A/mm}^2 [/latex]

Magnitude of diffusion current density:
[latex] \boxed{|J_n| \approx 35.47\text{ A/mm}^2} [/latex] The negative sign indicates current flows in the [latex]-x[/latex] direction (electrons diffuse from high to low concentration in the [latex]+x[/latex] direction, conventional current is opposite).

raw_source.text:
Consider the ideal diodes [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] as shown in the Figure with cut-in voltage [latex]V_\gamma = 0 \text{ Volt}[/latex] and [latex]v_i(t)[/latex] is in Volt.

The maximum voltage (Volt) of the output [latex]v_o(t)[/latex] is ____. (rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]v_i(t)=6\sin(\omega t)[/latex]
Since the input is a sinusoid of amplitude 6 V, the maximum input voltage is [latex]v_{i,\max}=6~\text{V}[/latex]

Step 1: Identify the clipping levels
The circuit contains two ideal diodes with bias voltages of 2 V and 4 V. These diodes act as voltage limiters (clippers). Since the cut-in voltage of each diode is zero, conduction starts as soon as the corresponding threshold voltage is reached.

Step 2: Analyze the positive half-cycle
As [latex]v_i(t)[/latex] increases from zero, the output voltage follows the input voltage. When the output voltage attempts to exceed 4 V, diode D2 becomes forward biased and starts conducting.
Once D2 turns ON, the output node is effectively clamped at 4 V. Therefore, any further increase in the input voltage does not increase the output voltage beyond this level.

Step 3: Check the role of D1
Diode D1 is responsible for limiting the negative portion of the waveform and does not affect the maximum positive value of the output voltage.

Step 4: Determine the maximum output voltage
Although the input reaches a peak value of 6 V, the output is clipped by D2 at 4 V.
Hence, the maximum value of the output voltage is [latex]v_{o,\max}=4~\text{V}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Real numbers [latex]y, p[/latex], and [latex]n[/latex] (all greater than [latex]1[/latex]) satisfy

[latex](\log_{p^{1/n}} y)(\log_{y^{1/n}} p) = 16[/latex]

where the logarithms are taken to the bases [latex]p^{1/n}[/latex] and [latex]y^{1/n}[/latex]. The value of [latex]n[/latex] is _____
raw_source.solution:
Step 1:
[latex]\log_{p^{1/n}} y = \frac{\log y}{\log p^{1/n}} = \frac{\log y}{(1/n)\log p} = n \frac{\log y}{\log p}[/latex]
[latex]\log_{y^{1/n}} p = n \frac{\log p}{\log y}[/latex]
Step 2:
Multiply:
[latex]n \frac{\log y}{\log p} \cdot n \frac{\log p}{\log y} = n^2[/latex]
Step 3:
[latex]n^2 = 16 \Rightarrow n = 4[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The following observation is made about the scores obtained by [latex]100[/latex] students in an exam:

'For each student, there exists another student in the class such that their scores are at most ten marks away.'

If the above statement is false, which one of the following statements is necessarily true?
raw_source.solution:
The original statement is in the form: [latex]\forall s \in \text{Students}, \exists o \in \text{Students} : |score(s) - score(o)| \le 10[/latex].
The negation ([latex]\neg[/latex]) of "For all [latex]x[/latex], there exists [latex]y[/latex] such that [latex]P(x,y)[/latex]" is "There exists [latex]x[/latex] such that for all [latex]y[/latex], [latex]\neg P(x,y)[/latex]".

So, the negation is: There exists at least one student for whom all other students have scores more than 10 marks away.
options: For each student, the scores of all the other students are more than [latex]10[/latex] marks away.
There exists at least one student in the class for whom the scores of all the other students are more than [latex]10[/latex] marks away.
There is exactly one student in the class for whom the scores of some students are more than [latex]10[/latex] marks away.
For each student, the score of exactly one other student is more than [latex]10[/latex] marks away.

raw_answer.option_text: There exists at least one student in the class for whom the scores of all the other students are more than [latex]10[/latex] marks away.

Three children [latex]P, Q, R[/latex] and two grown-ups [latex]X, Y[/latex] play a badminton doubles tournament. [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] are parents to two of the children playing. The child of [latex]X[/latex] is not the same as the child of [latex]Y[/latex]. Exactly one of the children does not have a parent playing in the tournament. The following rules are followed:

(i) A parent and his/her child cannot be on the same team.
(ii) A match can feature at most one parent and his/her child that is a maximum of one parent-child pair can play in a match.

The following matches were played:

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline & \text{TEAM 1} & \text{TEAM 2} \\ \hline \text{MATCH 1} & \text{P and X} & \text{Q and R} \\ \hline \text{MATCH 2} & \text{P and R} & \text{X and Y} \\ \hline \text{MATCH 3} & \text{R and X} & \text{Q and Y} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?
raw_source.solution:
Analysis:
From Match 1, P cannot be the child of X.
From Match 2, P cannot be the child of X or Y.

Since exactly one child does not have a parent playing, and X and Y have different children, those children must be Q and R.
Therefore, P does not have any parent playing.
options: P does not have any parent playing
Q does not have any parent playing
R does not have any parent playing
X does not have a child playing

raw_answer.option_text: R does not have any parent playing

raw_source.text: Let [latex]P_k[/latex] represent the perimeter of a square with sides of length [latex]k[/latex]. The value of the expression [latex]P_1 + P_2 + P_3 + \dots + P_{10}[/latex] is ______

raw_source.text:
The city of Atlantis was crafted by the God of the seas, Poseidon. It was made of alternating concentric circular rings of land (shaded) and water (not shaded) as represented in the figure. The radius of Inner Island was [latex]2.5[/latex] stades (a unit of length used in ancient Greece). The water surrounding Inner Island was one stade wide (length [latex]AB[/latex]). This was surrounded by two pairs of alternating rings of land and water. The first pair of land and water was two stades wide each (lengths [latex]BC[/latex] and [latex]CD[/latex]), and the outer pair is three stades wide each (lengths [latex]DE[/latex] and [latex]EF[/latex]).

The ratio of the surface area of the land to that of the water in the city of Atlantis is _________(round off to two decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Based on the concentric ring dimensions given:- Land (Shaded): Inner Island (radius 2.5), Ring BC (radius 3.5 to 5.5), Ring DE (radius 7.5 to 10.5).

Water (Unshaded): Ring AB (radius 2.5 to 3.5), Ring CD (radius 5.5 to 7.5), Ring EF (radius 10.5 to 13.5).

Area formula: [latex]A = \pi(r_{outer}^2 - r_{inner}^2)[/latex].

Area Land [latex]= \pi(2.5^2 + (5.5^2 - 3.5^2) + (10.5^2 - 7.5^2)) = \pi(6.25 + 18 + 54) = 78.25\pi[/latex].

Area Water [latex]= \pi((3.5^2 - 2.5^2) + (7.5^2 - 5.5^2) + (13.5^2 - 10.5^2)) = \pi(6 + 26 + 72) = 104\pi[/latex].

Ratio [latex]= 78.25 / 104 \approx 0.75[/latex].

raw_source.text: For the system [latex]\dot{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 0&4 \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} u; y=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}X[/latex], with u as unit impulse and with zero initial state, the output, y, becomes
raw_source.solution:
[latex]x(t)=e^{At}X(0)+\int_{0}^{t}e^{A(t-\tau) }BU(\tau )d\tau [/latex]
[latex]\because \;\; X(0)=0[/latex] (as given)

In the chopper circuit shown in figure, the input dc voltage has a constant value [latex]V_{s}[/latex]. The output voltage [latex]V_{o}[/latex] is assumed ripple-free. The switch S is operated with a switching time period T and a duty ratio D. what is the value of D at the boundary of continuous and discontinuous conduction of the inductor current [latex]i_L[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
As the given chopper is buck chopper.
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0&=\alpha V_s\\ \Delta I&=\frac{V_0T_{off}}{L}=\frac{\alpha V_s(1-\alpha )}{Lf}\\ \Delta I&=2I_L=2I_0\\ \Delta I&=2I_0=\frac{\alpha V_s(1-\alpha )}{Lf} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\frac{\Delta L}{2}=I_{L(avg)}=I_{0(avg)}[/latex]
this is applicable only at the boundary of continuous and discontinuous
[latex]\begin{aligned} L_c &=\frac{\alpha V_s(1-\alpha )}{2I_0f} \\ L_c&=\frac{\alpha V_sR(1-\alpha )}{R2I_0f} \\ (\because & \text{ multiplying and dividing by R}) \\ L_c&=\frac{V_0 R(1-\alpha )}{RI_02f} \\ L_c&= \frac{I_0R(1-\alpha )}{I_02f}\\ L_c&=\frac{R(1-\alpha )}{2f} \\ \therefore &= \text{ Boundary value of duty cycle is,}\\ \frac{2fL}{R}&=1-\alpha \\ \alpha &= 1-\frac{2fL}{R}=1-\frac{2L}{RT} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Figure Shows the waveform of the current passing through an inductor of resistance [latex]1\Omega[/latex] and inductance 2 H. The energy absorbed by the inductor in the first four seconds is
raw_source.solution:
For [latex]0 \lt t \lt 2s[/latex] current varies linearly with time and given as [latex]i(t)=3t[/latex] and for [latex]2s \lt t \lt 4s[/latex] current is constant, [latex]i(t)=6A[/latex].
The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec,
[latex]E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2} [/latex]
[latex]E_{L_1}=\int_{0}^{2}Li \left (\frac{di}{dt} \right )dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2} 2 \times 3t \times 3\; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=18\int_{0}^{2}t\; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=18 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^2}{2} \end{matrix}\right|^2_0 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J [/latex]
The energy absorbed by the inductor in ([latex]2\rightarrow 4[/latex]) second
[latex]E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J[/latex]
A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor.
The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec.
[latex]E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=24+72=96J[/latex]
The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec
[latex] =96 J +36 J =132 J[/latex]

raw_source.text: A segment of a circuit is shown in figure. [latex]V_{R}[/latex] = 5V, [latex]V_{C}[/latex] = [latex]4 \sin 2t[/latex]. The voltage [latex]V_{L}[/latex] is given by
raw_source.solution:
By KCL,
[latex]I_P+I_Q+I_C+I_L=0[/latex]
[latex] 2+2+I_C+I_L=0 [/latex]
But, [latex]I_C=C \times \frac{dv}{dt} [/latex]
[latex]\;\; =1 \times \frac{d}{dt}(4 \sin 2t) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=(8 \cos 2t) [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; I_L=-(2+1+8 \cos 2t) [/latex]
[latex]\;\; \;\;=-3-8 \cos 2t [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; V_L=L\left ( \frac{di}{dt} \right )[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=2 \times 2 \times 8 \sin 2t [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=32 \sin 2t[/latex]
NOTE: KCL is based on the law of conservation of charges.

raw_source.text:
A sinple phase transformer has a maximum efficiency of 90% at full load and
unity power factor. Efficiency at half load at the same power factor is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Efficiency} &=\frac{\text{Output}}{\text{Input}} \\ &= \frac{\text{Output}}{\text{Output}+\text{Losses}}\\ \text{Output}&= x S \cos \phi \\ \text{Where,}\;\;S &=\text{Rating of the machine} \\ x&= \% \text{of the full load}\\ \cos \phi &= \text{Power factor} \\ P_i &= \text{Iron or core loss}\\ P_{cu} &=\text{Full load copper loss} \\ &\text{For maximum frequency}\\ P_i &=x^2P_{cu} \\ \text{Efficiency} =\eta &= \frac{xS \cos \phi }{xS \cos \phi +P_i+x^2 P_{cu}} \\ \text{Max efficiency}=\eta _{max}&=\frac{xS \cos \phi }{xS \cos \phi +2P_i}\\ \Rightarrow \;\;0.9&=\frac{1 \times S \times 1}{1 \times S \times 1+2P_i}\\ P_i&=0.055S \end{aligned}[/latex]
Full load copper loss [latex]= 1^2 P_{cu}=P_i[/latex]
[latex] P_{cu}=0.055S[/latex]
Efficiency of halh load, upf
[latex] x=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]
[latex] \eta =\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times S \times 1 }{\frac{1}{2} \times S \times 1 +0.055S+\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^2 \times 0.055S} \times 100 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\approx 87.8\%[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A stand alone engine driven synchronous generator is feeding a partly inductive
load. A capacitor is now connected across the load to completely nullify the
inductive current. For this operating condition.
raw_source.solution:
Assuming resistance of the armature to be zero. In first case, the generator is feeding a partly inductive load. It means that generator is supplying lagging power. The generator supplies a lagging power factor current when it is overexcited which is represented by [latex]E_{f_1}[/latex].
In second case, a capacitor is connected across the load to completely nullifythe inductive current. It means the generator supplies no reactive power and unity power factor current is drawn from the generator. The excitation ([latex]E_{f_2}[/latex]) corresponding to unity power factor is known as normal excitation.

From the phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \gt E_{f_2}[/latex] and as the field current approximately directly proportional to excitation, the field current has to be reduced. From phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \sin \delta _1=E_{f_2} \sin \delta _2=\text{constant}[/latex]
[latex]P_e(\text{ power delivered})=\frac{E_fV_t}{X_s}\sin \delta[/latex]
Fuel input remains unaltered.
options: the field current and fuel input have to be reduced
the field current and fuel input have to be increased
the field current has to be increased and fuel input left unaltered
the field current has to be reduced and fuel input left unaltered

raw_answer.option_text: the field current has to be reduced and fuel input left unaltered

raw_source.text:
A control system is defined by the following mathematical relationship

[latex]\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+5x=12(1-e^{-2t})[/latex]

The response of the system as [latex]t\rightarrow \infty[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Taking (LT) on both sides
[latex](s^2+6s+5)X(s)=12\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) =\frac{24}{s(s+2)} [/latex]
[latex]X(s)=\frac{24}{s(s+2)(s+1)(s+5)} [/latex]
Responce at [latex]t\rightarrow \infty[/latex]
Using final value theorem
[latex] \lim_{t\rightarrow \infty }x(t)=\lim_{s \rightarrow 0}sX(s) [/latex]
[latex]=\lim_{s \rightarrow 0}\frac{s \times 24}{s(s+2)(s+1)(s+5)}=2.4[/latex]

A lead compensator used for a closed loop controller has the following transfer function [latex]\frac{K(1+\frac{s}{a})}{1+\frac{s}{b}}[/latex]
For such a lead compensator
raw_source.solution:
Transfer function[latex]=\frac{k\left ( 1+\frac{s}{a} \right )}{\left ( 1+\frac{s}{b} \right )}[/latex]
Zero of TF=-a
Pole of TF=-b
For a lead-compensator, the zero is nearer to origin as compared to pole, hence the effect of zero is dominant, therefore, the lead-compensator when introduced in series with forward path of the trnasfer function the phase shift is increased.

So, from pole-zero configuration of the compensator [latex]a \lt b[/latex].

raw_source.text: The speed/torque regimes in a dc motor and the control methods suitable for the same are given respectively in Group-II and Group-I
raw_source.solution:
Field Control: Fieldcontrol provides constant power drive. Since the speed is inversely proportional to flux/pole [latex]\left ( \omega \propto \frac{1}{\phi } \right )[/latex] field can not be increased; It can only be weakended. So this control is suitable for speed control above base speed as torque is directly proportional to flux/pole [latex](T \propto \alpha )[/latex] for a given armature current. So, this control provides torque below base torque.
Armature Control: It provides constant-torque drive. By keeping th field current at maximumvalue full load torque can be obtained at full load armature current at all speeds. This control provides speed below base speed.

To conduct load test on a dc shunt motor, it is coupled to a generator which
is identical to the motor. The field of the generator is also connected to the
same supply source as the motor. The armature of generator is connected
to a load resistance. The armature resistance is 0.02 p.u. Armature reaction
and mechanical losses can be neglected. With rated voltage across the motor,
the load resistance across the generator is adjusted to obtain rated armature
current in both motor and generator. The p.u value of this load resistance is
raw_source.solution:
All calculation are done in p.u. system.
Motor is connected across rated voltage V= 1 pu.
Rated armature current flows in both motor and generator
[latex]I_g=I_m=1 pu[/latex]
Armature resistance of both motor and generator [latex]R_m=R_g=0.02 pu[/latex]
Back iemf in motor
[latex]=E_b=V-I_mR_m [/latex]
[latex]=1-1 \times 0.02 =0.98 pu[/latex]
Mechanical power output of the motor
[latex]=E_bI_m=0.98 \times 1=0.98 pu[/latex]
This power is given to the generator and armation reaction and mechanical losses are negligible.
Input power of generator = Output power of motor
[latex]E_bI_g=E_bI_m E_g=E_b=0.98pu [/latex]
Terminal voltage of the generator
[latex]V_g=E_g-I_gR_g =0.98-1 \times 0.02=0.96pu [/latex]
[latex]R_L=\frac{V_g}{I_g}=\frac{0.96}{1}=0.96\Omega[/latex]

raw_source.text: Figure shows a [latex]\Delta[/latex]-Y connected, 3-phase distribution transformer used to step down the voltage from 11000 V to 415 V line-to-line. It has two switches [latex]S_{1}[/latex] and [latex]S_{2}[/latex]. Under normal conditions [latex]S_{1}[/latex] is closed and [latex]S_{2}[/latex] is open. Under certain special conditions [latex]S_{1}[/latex] is open and [latex]S_{2}[/latex] is closed. In such a case the magnitude of the voltage across the LV terminals a and c is
raw_source.solution:
As the transformer is [latex]\Delta -Y[/latex] connected, it means line-to-line voltage on primary side induces line to neutral for phase voltage on secondary side due to transformer.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Turn ratio} &=\frac{N_1}{N_2}=a \\ &= \frac{11kV}{415\sqrt{3}}=\frac{11\sqrt{3}}{415} \times 10^3\\ V_{AB}&=aV_a \\ V_{BC}&=aV_b\\ V_{AC}&=aV_c \end{aligned} [/latex]
When [latex]S_2[/latex] is closed, B and C are at same potential.
So, [latex]V_{BC}=V_B-V_C=0[/latex]
Applying KVL in, [latex]\Delta[/latex] connection
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{AB}+V_{BC}+V_{AC} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; V_{AC} &=-V_{AB} \\ V_{AB}&= 11 \times 10^3 \angle 0^{\circ}\\ V_{AC}&= - 11 \times 10^3 \angle 0^{\circ}\\ &= 11 \times 10^3 \angle 180^{\circ} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Voltage across terminals a and c,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{ac} &=V_a-V_c \\ &=\frac{V_{AB}}{a}-\frac{V_{AC}}{a} \\ &= \frac{1}{a}[V_{AB}-V_{AC}]\\ &=\frac{415}{11\sqrt{3} \times 10^3} \\ &[11 \times 10^3 \angle 0^{\circ} - 11 \times 10^3 \angle 180^{\circ} ]\\ &=\frac{415}{11\sqrt{3} \times 10^3} [11 \times 10^3 \times 2]\\ &\approx 480 V \end{aligned}[/latex]

As we know,

Current in secondary winding

[latex] I_3[/latex] reffered to primary side

The suuply currrent
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_1 &=I'_2+I'_3 \\ &= 10\angle 0^{\circ}+10\angle 90^{\circ}=(10+j10)A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Following are some of the properties of rotating electrical machines

P. Stator winding current is dc, rotor winding current is ac.
Q. Stator winding current is ac, rotor winding current is dc.
R. Stator winding current is ac, rotor winding current is ac.
S. Stator has salient poles and rotor has commutator.
T. Rotor has salient poles and sliprings and stator is cylindrical.
U. Both stator and rotor have poly-phase windings.

DC machines, Synchronous machines and Induction machines exhibit some of the above properties as given in the following table.
Indicate the correct combination from this table
raw_source.solution:
In DC machine, field is provided at stator and armature is provided at rotor. Because of commutator and slip-rings, AC rotor winding current is converted inot dc.
IN synchronous machine, it is difficult to provide armature in rotor because of many factor like insulation no of slip rings, rating of slip rings, high rating of armature. Therefore, armature is provided in stator and field in rotor
Induction machines are singlyfed machine i.e. they draw excitation from the same supply. So no external field supply is required.

raw_source.text:
When stator and rotor windings of a 2-pole rotating electrical machine are excited, each would produce a sinusoidal mmf distribution in the airgap with peal values [latex]F_s[/latex] and [latex]F_r[/latex] respectively. The rotor mmf lags stator mmf by a space angle [latex]\delta[/latex] at any instant as shown in figure. Thus, half of stator and rotor surfaces will form one pole with the other half forming the second pole. Further, the direction of torque acting on the rotor can be clockwise or counter-clockwise.

The following table gives four set of statement as regards poles and torque. Select the correct set corresponding to the mmf axes as shown in figure.
raw_source.solution:
Inside a magnetic material, flux flows from S-pole to N-pole.
Outside a magnetic material flux flow from N-pole to S-pole
When stator winding is excited, it produces flux. If ABC is assumed to N-pole flux will link rotor. As we know, flux flows from N-pole to S-pole externally, abc from S-pole.
Inside rotor, flux flows from surface abc to cda
So, surface cda forms N-poles.
To identify direction of torque

The torque acts in a direction to reduce [latex]\delta[/latex] i.e. to align the two fields. So, torque on the rotor acrs in counter-clockwise direction to reduce [latex]\delta[/latex].

raw_source.text:
A 3-phase induction motor is driving a constant torque load at rated voltage and frequency. If both voltage and frequency are halved, following statements relate to the new condition if stator resistance, leakage reactance and core loss are ignored

1. The difference between synchronous speed and actual speed remains same
2. The airgap flux remains same
3. The stator current remains same
4. The p.u. slip remains same

Among the above, correct statements are
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V &\propto f\phi \\ &\text{in induction machine}\\ V_2&= \frac{V_1}{2}\\ \text{and}\;\; f_2 &=\frac{f_1}{2} \\ \frac{V_1}{V_2} &=\frac{f_1\phi _1}{f_2\phi _2} \\ \phi _2&= \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )\left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )\phi _1\\ &= \left ( \frac{V_1/2}{V_1} \right )\left ( \frac{f_1}{f_1/2} \right )\phi _1\\ &= \phi _1 \end{aligned} [/latex]
So, air-gap flux remains same.
[latex](X_2')_1=[/latex] nominal rotor stanstill reactance referred to stator (at frequency [latex]f_1[/latex])
[latex] \begin{aligned} (X_2')_2 &= \left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right )(X_2')_1\\ &= \left ( \frac{f_1/2}{f_1} \right )(X_2')_1\\ &= \frac{(X_2')_1}{2}\\ (\omega _s)_2 &= \left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right ) (\omega _s)_1\\ &= \left ( \frac{f_1/2}{f_1} \right ) (\omega _s)_1\\ &=\frac{(\omega _s)_1}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Torque developed in induction motor
[latex]T=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2 +{X'_2}^2}[/latex]
For normal steady state oprating region, slip is very low
[latex]\frac{R'_2}{s} \gt \gt X'_2[/latex]
[latex] T=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2}=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{sV^2}{R'_2} [/latex]
As the load torque is constant
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_1 &=T_2 \\ \frac{s_1V_1^2}{(\omega _s)_1R'_2}&= \frac{s_2V_2^2}{(\omega _s)_2R'_2}\\ \Rightarrow \;\; s_2 &=\frac{(\omega _s)_2}{(\omega _s)_1} \times \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 s_1\\ &=\frac{(\omega _s)_1/2}{(\omega _s)_1} \times \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_1/2} \right )^2 s_1 \\ s_2 &= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times s_1=2s_1 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Difference between synchronous speed and actual speed
[latex]\begin{aligned} \omega _s -\omega _r &= s\omega _s\\ (\omega _s)_1 -(\omega _r)_2 &= s_2(\omega _s)_2\\ &=(2s_1) \times \frac{(\omega _s)_1}{2} =s_1(\omega _s)_1 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Therefore, the difference between synchronous speed and actual speed remain same.
Stator current
[latex]\begin{aligned} |I_s| &= \frac{V}{\sqrt{(R'_2/s)^2+{X'}_2^2}} \\ \text{as}\;\; R'_2/s & \gt \gt X'_2 \\ |I_s|&=\frac{sV}{R'_2} \\ |I_{s1}|&= s_1\frac{V_1}{R'_2}\\ |I_{s2}|&=s_2\frac{V_2}{R'_2} \\ ||I_{s2}&=(2s_1)\times \frac{V_1/2}{R'_2}=\frac{s_1V_1}{R'_2} \\ ||I_{s1}&=|I_{s2}| \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, stator current remains same.

raw_source.text:
A dc series motor driving an electric train faces a constant power load. It is
running at rated speed and rated voltage. If the speed has to be brought down
to 0.25 p.u. the supply voltage has to be approximately brought down to
raw_source.solution:
In series motor,
Back emf, [latex]E=v-I(R_a+R_{se}) [/latex]
[latex]\text{If},\;\;(R_a+R_{se})=R [/latex]
[latex]\text{them,}\;\; E=V-IR [/latex]
[latex]\text{where,}\;\; E=K_n \phi N [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;\;N=\frac{V-IR}{K_n \phi }[/latex]
In series motor, [latex]\phi \propto I [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] At constant power load
[latex]E \times I=T \times w=const [/latex]
[latex]\text{where,} \;\; T=K_a\phi I=K_a I^2[/latex]
If '[latex]w_n[/latex]' decrease by (1/4) of its rated value, then torque will increase 4 times to maintain power contant.
[latex] \therefore \;\; T\propto I^2 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] current increase 2 times so that supply voltage approximately brought down to 0.5pu.

A surge of 20 kV magnitude travels along a lossless cable towards its junction
with two identical lossless overhead transmission lines. The inductance and the
capacitance of the cable are 0.4 mH and 0.5 [latex]\mu[/latex]F per km. The inductance and capacitance of the overhead transmission lines are 1.5 mH and 0.015 [latex]\mu[/latex]F per km. The magnitude of the voltage at the junction due to surge is
raw_source.solution:
where, [latex]z_1=z_2[/latex]
Parameter of cable:
Inducatance[latex]=L_C=0.4[/latex] mH/km and
Capacitance [latex]=C_C=0.5\mu F/km[/latex]
Surge impedance of the cable
[latex]=Z_C=\sqrt{\frac{L_C}{C_C}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.4 \times 10^{-3}}{0.5 \times 10^{-6}}}=28.28\Omega[/latex]
Parameters of OH
Transmission lines
Inductance[latex]L_1=1.5[/latex] mH/km and
Capacitance [latex]=C_1==0.015\mu F/km[/latex]
Surge impedance of the line [latex]=Z_1=Z_2=\sqrt{\frac{L_1}{C_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{0.015 \times 10^{-6}}}=316.22\Omega[/latex]
E= 20 kV
Junction voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_j&=\frac{2E \times \frac{1}{Z_C}}{\frac{1}{Z_C}+\frac{1}{Z_1}+\frac{1}{Z_2}} \\ &= \frac{2 \times 20 \times \frac{1}{28.28}}{\frac{1}{28.28}+\frac{2}{316.22}}\\ &=33.93kV \end{aligned}[/latex]
