raw_source.text:
A 3-phase 11 kV generator feeds power to a constant power unity power factor
load of 100 MW through a 3-phase transmission line. The line-to line voltage
at the terminals of the machine is maintained constant at 11 kV. The per unit
positive sequence impedance of the line based on 100 MVA and 11 kV is j0.2.
The line to line voltage at the load terminals is measured to be less than 11 kV. The total reactive power to be injected at the terminals of the load to increase
the line-to-line voltage at the load terminals to 11 kV is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]|V_s|=|V_R|=11kV[/latex]
p.u. impedance of the line = j0.2 p.u.
Impedance of the line = p.u. impedance x Base impedance
[latex]x= j0.2 \times \frac{11^2}{100}=j0.242\Omega[/latex]
Active power at receiving end [latex]=P_R=100 MW[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_R&=\frac{|V_s||V_R|}{x}\sin \delta \\ 100 &= \frac{11 \times 11}{0.242} \sin \delta \\ \delta &=11.54^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Reactive power at receiving end
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q_R&=\frac{|V_s||V_R|}{x}\cos \delta -\frac{|V_R|^2}{x} \\ &= \frac{11 \times 11}{0.242} \cos 11.54 -\frac{11^2}{0.242} \\ &=-10.1 \text{ MVAR} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since poer factor =1
Load reactive power should be zero
Therefore, reactive power to be injected at terminals [latex]=-Q_R=-(-10.1)=10.1 \text{ MVAR}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The bus impedance matrix of a 4-bus power system is given by
[latex]Z_{bus}=\begin{bmatrix} j0.3435 & j0.2860 & j0.2723 & j0.2277\\ j0.2860& j0.3408 & j0.2586& j0.2414\\ j0.2723 & j0.2586 & j0.2791& j0.2209\\ j0.2277 &j0.2414 & j0.2209 & j0.2791 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
A branch having an impedance of [latex]j0.2 \Omega[/latex] is connected between bus 2 and the reference. Then the values of [latex]Z_{22,new}[/latex] and [latex]Z_{23,new}[/latex] of the bus impedance matrix of the modified network are respectively
raw_source.solution:
[latex]Z_{B}(new)=Z_{B}(old)-\frac{1}{Z_{jj}+Z_{b}}\begin{bmatrix} Z_{1j}\\ \vdots \\ Z_{nj} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} Z_{j1} & \cdots & Z_{jn} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
New elements ([latex]Z_B[/latex]) is connected between [latex]j^{th}[/latex] and reference bus.
Here, j=2, b=4
[latex]\therefore \;\;\frac{1}{Z_{jj}+Z_{b}}\begin{bmatrix} Z_{12}\\ Z_{22} \\ Z_{32}\\Z_{42} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} Z_{21} & Z_{22} & Z_{23}& Z_{24} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\frac{1}{j0.3408+j0.2}\begin{bmatrix} j0.2860\\ j0.3408\\ j0.2586\\j0.2414 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} j0.2860 & j0.3408 & j0.2586& j0.2414 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
We are required only changes in [latex]Z_{22}Z_{23}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} - & - & - & -\\ -& j0.2147 &j0.16296 & -\\ - & - &- &- \\ - &- & - & - \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{22}(new)&=Z_{22}(old)-j0.2147=j0.1260 \\ Z_{23}(new)&=Z_{23}(old)-j0.16296 \\ &= j0.2586-j0.16296=j0.0956\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 20-MVA, 6.6-kV, 3-phase alternator is connected to a 3-phase transmission
line. The per unit positive sequence, negative sequence and zero sequence
impedances of the alternator are j0.1, j0.1 and j0.04 respectively. The neutral
of the alternator is connected to ground through an inductive reactor of
j0.05 p.u. The per unit positive, negative and zero sequence impedances of
transmission line are
j0.1, j0.1 and j0.3, respectively. All per unit values are based on the machine
ratings. A solid ground fault occurs at one phase of the far end of the
transmission line. The voltage of the alternator neutral with respect to ground
during the fault is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{For alternator} \\ Z_{1g}&=j0.1p.u. \\ Z_{2g}&=j0.1p.u.\\ Z_{3g}&=j0.04p.u. \\ &\text{For line} \\ Z_{1l}&=j0.1p.u. \\ Z_{2l}&=j0.1p.u. \\ Z_{0l}&=j0.3p.u. \\ Z_{n}&=j0.05p.u. \\ \text{Equivalent}& \text{sequence impedance:} \\ Z_{1eq}&=Z_{1g}+Z_{1l} \\ &= j0.1+j0.1=j0.2p.u.\\ Z_{2eq}&=Z_{2g}+Z_{2l} \\ &= j0.1+j0.1=j0.2p.u.\\ Z_{0eq}&=Z_{0g}+Z_{0l}+3Z_n \\ &= j0.04+j0.3+3 \times j0.05\\ &=j0.49p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]
For single line to ground fault

[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a1}&=I_{a2}=I_{a0}\\ &=\frac{1\angle 0}{Z_{1eq}+Z_{2eq}+Z_{0eq}}\\ &=\frac{1\angle 0}{j(0.2+0.2+0.49)}\\ &=-j1.1236 p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]
Fault current [latex]=I_f=3I_{a1}=-j3.3708p.u.[/latex]
Voltage of neutral w.r.t. ground
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_n&=I_f \times Z_n \\ &= -j3.3708 \times j0.05\\ &= 0.16854p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]
Per phase base voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_p&=\frac{6.6}{\sqrt{3}}kV=\frac{6.6}{\sqrt{3}}\times 10^3V \\ V_n&=\frac{6.6}{\sqrt{3}} \times 0.16854 \times 10^3 \\ &= 642.2V \end{aligned}[/latex]

Minimum and maximum loads on each unit are 50 MW and 300 MW respectively. If the plant is operating on economic load dispatch to supply the total power demand of 700 MW, the power generated by each unit is
raw_source.solution:

When [latex]P_2[/latex] is minimum i.e. [latex]P_2=50MW[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A generator delivers power of 1.0 p.u. to an infinite bus through a purely
reactive network. The maximum power that could be delivered by the generator
is 2.0 p.u. A three-phase fault occurs at the terminals of the generator which
reduces the generator output to zero. The fault is cleared after [latex]t_{c}[/latex] second. The
original network is then restored. The maximum swing of the rotor angle is
found to be [latex]\delta _{max}[/latex] = 110 electrical degree. Then the rotor angle in electrical degrees at [latex]t =t_{c}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Power generated by the generator
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_e &=P_{max} \sin \delta \\ \text{At }\delta _0& \\ P_e&=1 pu \\ P_{max}&=2pu \\ \delta _{cr}&=\text{roto angle at }t =t_c\\ P_e&= P_{max} \sin \delta \\ 1&=2 \sin \delta _0 \\ \delta _0 &=30^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
During fault, [latex]P_e[/latex] become zero and the fault is cleared at [latex]\delta _{cr}[/latex], Mechanical input to the generator remains constant, [latex]P_m=1pu[/latex]
Applying equal areal criterion,
[latex]\begin{aligned} A_1&= A_2\\ A_1&= \int_{\delta _0}^{\delta _{cr}} (P_m-0)d\delta \\ &= P_m(\delta _{cr} -\delta _0)\;\;...(i)\\ A_2&=\int_{\delta _{cr}}^{\delta _{max}}(P_{max} \sin \delta -P_m)d\delta \\ &= P_{max}(\cos \delta _{cr} - \cos \delta _{max})\\ &-P_m(\delta _{max}-\delta _{cr})\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{Equating eq. (i) and (ii),} \\ P_m(\delta _{cr}-\delta _0)&=P_{max}( \cos \delta _{cr} - \cos \delta _{max}) \\ &-P_m(\delta _{max} -\delta _{cr}) \\ \cos \delta _{cr} &= \frac{P_m}{P_{max}} (\delta _{max} - \delta _{0}) +\cos \delta _{max}\\ \cos \delta _{cr}&= \frac{1}{2} \times (110-30) \times \frac{\pi}{180}+\cos 110\\ \delta _{cr}&=69.14^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: three-phase alternator generating unbalanced voltages is connected to an unbalanced load through a 3-phase transmission line as shown in figure. The neutral of the alternator and the star point of the load are solidly grounded. The phase voltages of the alternator are [latex]E_{a}=10\angle 0^{\circ}V[/latex], [latex]E_b=10\angle -90^{\circ}V[/latex], [latex]E_{c}=10\angle 120^{\circ}V[/latex]. The positive sequence component of the load current is
raw_source.solution:
Since both sides are grounded, we can take it as 3 independent circuit.
Hence,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_a&=\frac{E_a}{Z_a}=\frac{10\angle 0^{\circ}}{2j}=-5jA\\ I_b&=\frac{E_b}{Z_b}=\frac{10\angle -90^{\circ}}{3j}=3.33\angle -180\\ I_c&=\frac{E_c}{Z_c}=\frac{10\angle 120^{\circ}}{4j}=2.5\angle 30\\ I_{a1}&=1/3(I_a+\alpha I_b+\alpha ^2I_c)\\ &=1/3[5\angle -90+3.33\angle (-180+120) +2.5\angle (240+30)]\\ &=1/3(5\angle 90+3.33\angle -60+2.5\angle 270)\\ &=3.510 \angle -81^{\circ}A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the n-channel enhancement MOSFET shown in figure, the threshold voltage [latex]V_{th}[/latex] = 2 V. The drain current [latex]I_{D}[/latex] of the MOSFET is 4 mA when the drain resistance [latex]R_{D}[/latex] is 1 k[latex]\Omega[/latex]. If the value of [latex]R_{D}[/latex] is increased to 4 k[latex]\Omega[/latex], drain current [latex]I_{D}[/latex] will become
raw_source.solution:
[latex]I_D=K(V_{GS}-V_{th})^2 [/latex]
[latex]4=K(6-2)^2 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; K=\frac{1}{4}mA/V^2 [/latex]
[latex]V_{GS}=10-4\times 1=6V[/latex]
when [latex]R_D[/latex] is increased to [latex]4k\Omega[/latex]
[latex]V_{GS}=10-4I_D [/latex]
[latex]I_D=\frac{1}{4}(10-4I_D-2)^2[/latex]
[latex] 4I_D=16I^2_D+64-64I_D [/latex]
[latex]16I^2_D-68I_D+64=0 [/latex]
[latex]I_D=2.84 \; mA,1.4 \; mA[/latex]
For MOSFET to be on, [latex]V_{GS}[/latex] must be greater than [latex]V_{th}[/latex] and this is possible only if
[latex]\;\;\; I_D=1.4\; mA [/latex]
[latex]If \; I_D=2.84\; mA[/latex]
then [latex]V_{GS}[/latex] become -ve and less than [latex]V_{th}[/latex] so transistor will be off for this value which is not possible since [latex]V_{DG}=0\geq -V_{th}[/latex].

The following program is written for an 8085 microprocessor to add two bytes located at memory addresses 1FFE and 1FFF

LXI H, 1FFE
MOV B, M
INR L
MOV A, M
ADD B
INR L
MOV M, A
XOR A

On completion of the execution of the program, the result of addition is found
raw_source.solution:
LXI H, 1FFE [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Load 1FFE in H-L memory
MOV B, M [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] move the content of 1FFE memory location to register B
INR L [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Increment the content of 'HL' by 1 (1FFE[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1FFF)
MOV A, M [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] move content of 1FFF memory location to accumulator

raw_source.text:
A control system with certain excitation is governed by the following mathematical equation
[latex]\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{1}{18}x=10+5e^{-4t}+2e^{-5t}[/latex]
The natural time constant of the response of the system are
raw_source.solution:
Natural time constant of the response depends only on poles of the system.
[latex]T(s)=\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{1}{s^2+s/2+1/18} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{18}{18s^2+9s+1} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{(6s+1)(3s+1)} [/latex]
This is in the form [latex]\frac{1}{(1+sT_1)(1+sT_2)} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; T_1,T_2=6sec, 3 sec[/latex]

raw_source.text: The block diagram shown in figure gives a unity feedback closed loop control system. The steady state error in the response of the above system to unit step input is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]G(s)=\left ( \frac{3}{s+15} \right )\times \left ( \frac{15}{s+1} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{45}{(s+1)(s+15)} [/latex] and [latex] H(s)=1 [/latex]
Open loop transfer function
[latex]\;\;=G(s)H(s)=\frac{45}{(s+1)(s+15)} [/latex]
The system is type-0.
Steady state error to unit-step input
[latex]e_{ss}=\frac{1}{1+k_p}[/latex]
where,
[latex]k_p=[/latex]Position error constant [latex]=\lim_{s \to 0}G(s)H(s) [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; k_p=\lim_{s \to 0}\frac{45}{(s+1)(s+15)}=3 [/latex]
[latex]\;\; e_{ss}=\frac{1}{1+k_p}=\frac{1}{1+3}=0.25[/latex] or [latex]25[/latex]%

raw_source.text: The roots of the closed loop characteristic equation of the system shown in figure are
raw_source.solution:
1+ GH= 0 (characteristic equation),
[latex]\; \; \; 1\, +\, \frac{45}{\left ( s+15 \right )\left ( s+1 \right )}\, =\, 0[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; \; s^{2}+16s+60\, =\, 0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \; \; \left ( s+10 \right )\left ( s+6 \right )\, =\, 0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] Roots are [latex]\left ( -6,\, -10 \right ).[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The following equation defines a separately excited dc motor in the form of a differential equation
[latex]\frac{d^{2}\omega }{dt}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{K^{2}}{LJ}\omega =\frac{K}{LJ}V_{a}[/latex]
The above equation may be organized in the state-space form as follows
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \frac{d^2\omega}{dt^2}\\ \frac{d\omega}{dt} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{d\omega}{dt}\\ \omega \end{bmatrix}+QV_a[/latex]
where the P matrix is given by
raw_source.solution:
Let, [latex]x_1=\frac{d\omega }{dt}[/latex] and [latex]x_2=\omega [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; \dot{x_2}=x_1 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega =\frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}=-\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}-\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega + \frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \dot{x_1}=-\frac{B}{J}x_1-\frac{k^2}{LJ}x_2+\frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\dot{x_2}=x_1 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_1}\\ \dot{x_2} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+QV_a [/latex]
where,
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -\frac{B}{J} & -\frac{k^2}{LJ}\\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex]Q=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{k}{LJ}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The loop gain GH of a closed loop system is given by the following expression
[latex]\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s+4)}[/latex]
The value of K for which the system just becomes unstable is
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation = 1 + GH = 0
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \; \; 1+\frac{K}{s\left ( s+2 \right )\left ( s+4 \right )}\, =\, 0[/latex]
Characteristic equation,
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \; \; s^{2}\, +\, 6s^{2}\, +\, 8s\, +\, K\, =\, 0[/latex]
The Routh-array is formed as follows:



According to Routh-Hurwitz criterion, for a stable system there should be no charge of sign in the first column of routh array.
So, [latex]\; \; \; \frac{48-K}{6} \gt 0[/latex] and [latex]K\gt 0[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; \; 0 \lt K \lt 48[/latex]
Hence for K=48, the system just becomes unstable.

raw_source.text: The asymptotic Bode plot of the transfer function [latex]\frac{K}{1 + \frac{s}{a}}[/latex] is given in figure. The error in phase angle and dB gain at a frequency of [latex]\omega = 0.5[/latex] are respectively
raw_source.solution:
Transfer function[latex]=G(s)=\frac{k}{1+\frac{s}{a}} [/latex]
Put [latex] s=j\omega [/latex]
[latex]G(j\omega )=\frac{k}{1+j\frac{\omega }{a}} [/latex]
Magnitude of [latex]G(j\omega )=|G(j\omega )|=\frac{k}{\sqrt{1+\frac{\omega ^2}{a^2}}}[/latex]
Phase of [latex]G(j\omega )\angle G(j\omega )=-tan^{-1\left ( \frac{\omega }{a}\right )} \; at\; \omega =0.5a[/latex]
[latex] |G(j\omega )|_{\omega =0.5a}=\frac{k}{\sqrt{1+\frac{(0.5a)^2}{a^2}}}=\frac{k}{\sqrt{1.25}}[/latex] in dB
[latex]=20\log k-20 \log (1.25)^{1/2} [/latex]
[latex]=20 \log k-0.97 dB [/latex]
From the plot
magnitude[latex]=20 \log k[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] error in dB gain = 0.97 dB
[latex] \angle G(j\omega )|_{\omega =0.5a}[/latex]
[latex]=-tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{0.5a}{a} \right )[/latex]
[latex]=26.56^{\circ}[/latex]
Since it is [latex]-45^{\circ}/dec [/latex] (-ve slope) at [latex]\omega =0.5a[/latex] phase [latex]=-22.5^{\circ}[/latex]
Error in phase of [latex]\angle G(j\omega )|_{\omega =0.5a} [/latex]
[latex]=-22.5-(-26.56) [/latex]
[latex]=+4.06^{\circ}\approx +4.9^{\circ}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The block diagram of a control system is shown in figure. The transfer function G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) of the system is
raw_source.solution:
Integrator are represented as 1/s in s-domain



As per the block diagram, the corresponding signal flow graph is drawn



One forward path [latex]P_{1}\, =\, 2/s^{2}[/latex]
The individual loops are,
[latex]\; \; \; L_{1}\, =\, -\frac{3}{s},\: L_{2}\, =\, -\frac{12}{s} and L_{3}\, =\, -\frac{18}{s^{2}}[/latex]
[latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] are non-touching loops
[latex]\; \; \; L_{1}L_{2}\, =\, \frac{36}{s^{2}}[/latex]
The loops touches the forward path [latex]\Delta _{1}=1[/latex]
The graph determinant is
[latex]\; \; \; \Delta \, =\, 1-\left ( L_{1}+L_{2}+L_{3} \right )+L_{1}L_{2}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}[/latex]
Applying mason's gain formula,
[latex]\; \; \; G\left ( s \right )=\frac{Y\left ( s \right )}{U\left ( s \right )}=\frac{P_{1}\Delta _{1}}{\Delta }[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{2/s^{2}}{1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{2}{s^{2}+15s+54}=\frac{2}{\left ( s+9 \right )\left ( s+6 \right )}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{1}{27\left ( 1+\frac{s}{9} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{6} \right )}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A wattmeter reads 400 W when its current coil is connected in the R-phase
and its pressure coil is connected between this phase and the neutral of a
symmetrical 3-phase system supplying a balanced star connected 0.8 p.f.
inductive load. This phase sequence is RYB. What will be the reading of this
wattmeter if its pressure coil alone is reconnected between the B and Y phases,
all other connections remaining as before ?
raw_source.solution:
Taking [latex]V_R[/latex] as the reference and assuming phase to neutral voltage [latex]=V[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_R &=V\angle 0^{\circ} \\ V_Y &= V\angle -120^{\circ}\\ and \;\; V_B &=V\angle -240^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_RI_R \cos \phi &=400 W \\ VI_R \times 0.8&= 400W\\ VI_R&=400\;\;...(i) \\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[p.f. =0.8 lag, inductive load]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{YB} &=V_{YB}-V_B \\ &= V\angle -120^{\circ}- V \angle -240^{\circ}\\ &=\sqrt{3}V\angle -90^{\circ} V\\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ}A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Angle between [latex]V_{YB}[/latex] and [latex]I_{R}[/latex]
[latex]\theta =-90^{\circ}-(-36.87^{\circ})=53.13^{\circ}[/latex]
As pressure coil connected between Y and B phase.
Reading of wattmeter[latex]=V_{YB}I_R\cos \theta[/latex]
From equation (i)
[latex]=\sqrt{3}V \times I_R \times \cos (-53.13) =\sqrt{3}\times 500 \times 0.6=519.6W[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The inductance of a certain moving-iron ammeter is expressed as
L = [latex]10+30 -\frac{\theta ^{2}}{4} \; \mu H[/latex], where  [latex]\theta[/latex] is the deflection in radians from the zero position. The control spring torque is [latex]25 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] Nm/radian. The deflection of the pointer in radian when the meter carries a current of 5 A, is
raw_source.solution:
Deflection torque in moving-iron ammeter,
[latex]T_d=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta }[/latex]
Inductance, [latex]L=\left ( 10+3\theta -\frac{\theta ^2}{4} \right )\mu H [/latex]
Rate of change of inductance with deflection
[latex]\frac{dL}{d\theta }=\frac{d}{d\theta }\left ( 10+3\theta -\frac{\theta ^2}{4} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\left ( 3- \frac{\theta }{2}\right )\mu H/rad [/latex]
Current , [latex]I=5A [/latex]
Deflecting torque,
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_d &=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta } \\ T_d &= \frac{1}{2} \times 5^2 \times \left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right ) \times 10^{-6}\\ &= \frac{25}{2}\left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right )\times 10^{-6} Nm \end{aligned} [/latex]
Controlling torque
[latex]T_c=k\theta =25 \times 10^{-6}\theta [/latex]
At equilibrium,
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_c &= T_d\\ 25 \times 10^{-6}\theta &= \frac{25}{2}\left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right )\times 10^{-6} \\ \frac{5\theta }{2} &= 3\\ \theta &= 1.2 \text{rad} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 500A/5A, 50 Hz transformer has a bar primary. The secondary burden is
a pure resistance of 1 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and it draws a current of 5 A. If the magnetic core
requires 250 AT for magnetization, the percentage ratio error is
raw_source.solution:
Nominal ratio [latex]=\frac{500}{5}=100[/latex]
Number of turn in primary N=1 (primary bar)
Magnetizing current,
[latex]I_m=\frac{\text{mmf}}{\text{No. of turns}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{250}{1}=250A [/latex]
Secondary current,
[latex]I_s=5A n=\frac{500}{5}=100 [/latex]
Primary current,
[latex] I_P=\sqrt{(nI_s)^2+I_m^2}[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=\sqrt{(100\times 5)^2 +(250)^2} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; I_P=559.017A [/latex]
Actual ratio
[latex] \;\;=\frac{I_P}{5}=\frac{559.017}{5}=111.803 [/latex]
Ratio error
[latex]\;\;=\frac{\text{Nominal Ratio} - \text{Actual Ratio}}{\text{Actual Ratio}} \times 100 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{100-111.803}{111.803}\times 100=-10.56\%[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The voltage-flux adjustment of a certain 1-phase 220 V induction watt-hour
meter is altered so that the phase angle between the applied voltage and the
flux due to it is 85[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] (instead of 90[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]). The errors introduced in the reading of this meter when the current is 5 A at power factor of unity and 0.5 lagging are respectively
raw_source.solution:
Measured value [latex]=VI \sin (\Delta -\phi )[/latex]
where,
[latex]\Delta =[/latex] Phase angle between voltage and flux
[latex]\cos \phi[/latex] = Poer factor
True value=[latex]VI \cos \phi[/latex]
Error=Measured value - True value
CASE-I:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 80^{\circ}\\ pf&= \cos \phi =1\\ \phi &= 0^{\circ}\\ V&= 220V\\ I&= 5A \\ \text{Error}&=VI \sin (\Delta -\phi )-VI \cos \phi \\ &=220 \times 5 \sin(85-0^{\circ})-220 \times 1 \times 1\\ &\approx -4.2W \end{aligned}[/latex]
CASE-II:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 85^{\circ}\\ pf&= \cos \phi =0.5\\ \phi &= 60^{\circ}\\ V&= 220V\\ I&= 5A \\ \text{Error}&=VI \sin (\Delta -\phi )-VI \cos \phi \\ &=220 \times 5 \sin(85-60^{\circ})-220 \times 5 \times 0.5\\ &= -85.1W \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Group-II represents the figures obtained on a CRO screen when the voltage signals [latex]V_x = V_{xm} \sin \omega t[/latex] and [latex]V_{y}=V_{ym}\sin \left ( \omega t+\Phi \right )[/latex] are given to its X and Y plates respectively and [latex]\Phi[/latex] is changed. Choose the correct value of [latex]\Phi[/latex] from Group-I to match with the corresponding figure of Group-II
raw_source.solution:
when two voltages are in phase i.e. [latex][\phi =0^{\circ}\; \text{or} \;180^{\circ}][/latex], the trace is straight line. But for [latex]\phi =0^{\circ}[/latex], the trace has positive slope and [latex]\phi =180^{\circ}[/latex], the trace has negative slope.
When the two voltage has phase displacement of [latex]\phi =90^{\circ}[/latex], the trace is a circle. If the direction of the trace is in the clockwise direction then the phase difference is [latex]\phi =90^{\circ}[/latex].
If the direction of the trace is anti-clockwise direction the phase difference is
[latex](2 \pi-\phi )=\left ( 2\pi-\frac{\pi}{2} \right )=3\frac{\pi}{2}[/latex]
When the difference is not equal to [latex]0^{\circ}[/latex] or [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex], the trace is an ellipse. For [latex]\pi \leq \phi \leq \frac{3\pi}{2}[/latex], the trace is an ellipse in anti-clockwise direction.

raw_source.text: A parallel plate capacitor is shown in figure. It is made two square metal plates of 400 mm side. [latex]\begin{aligned} V_a&=V_m \sin \omega t \\ V_b&=V_m \sin (\omega t-120^{\circ}) \\ V_c &=V_m \sin (\omega t+120^{\circ}) \\ I_a&=\frac{V_a}{Z_L}=\frac{V_m \sin \omega t}{|Z|\angle \theta _L} \\ &= I_M \sin (\omega t-\theta _L)\\ \text{where, } I_m&=\frac{V_m}{|Z|}\\ \text{Similarly,}&\\ I_b&=I_m \sin (\omega t-120-\theta _L)\\ I_c&=I_m \sin (\omega t+120-\theta _L)\\ & \text{Instantaneous power}\\ &=P=V_aI_a+V_bI_b+V_cI_c\\ P&=V_mI_m[\sin \omega t\cdot \sin (\omega t-\theta _L)\\ &+\sin (\omega t-120^{\circ}) \cdot \sin (\omega t-120-\theta _L)\\ &+\sin (\omega t+120^{\circ})\cdot \sin (\omega t+120-\theta _L)]\\ &=\frac{V_mI_m}{2}[(\cos \theta _L -\cos(2\omega t-\theta _L) ) \\ &+(\cos \theta _L -\cos(2\omega t-240-\theta _L) )\\ &+(\cos \theta _L -\cos(2\omega t+240-\theta _L) )]\\ P&=\frac{3V_mI_m}{2}\cos \phi = \text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The armature resistance of a permanent magnet dc motor is 0.8 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. At no load,
the motor draws 1.5 A from a supply voltage of 25 V and runs at 1500 rpm.
The efficiency of the motor while it is operating on load at 1500 rpm drawing a
current of 3.5 A from the same source will be
raw_source.solution:
At no load,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a0} &= 1.5A\\ \text{supply voltage} &= V_t=250V\\ &\text{Back emf at no load,}\\ E_{b0}&=V_t-I_{a0}R_a \\ &= 25-1.5 \times 0.8\\ &= 23.8V\\ &\text{Power developed by the motor} \\ P_0=E_{b0}I_{a0} &=23.8 \times 1.5 \\ &= 35.7 W \end{aligned}[/latex]
As the motor is working at no load, power [latex]P_0[/latex] supplies no load losses.
When the motor is on load,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a1} &= 3.5A\\ E_{a1}&=V_t-I_{a1}R_a \\ &= 25-3.5 \times 0.8\\ &= 22.2V\\ &\text{Power developed by the motor} \\ P_1=E_{a1}I_{a1} &=22.2 \times 3.5 \\ &= 77.7 W\\ &\text{Power available at shaft}\\ P_s&=P_1-\text{no load losses}\\ &=77.7-35.7=42W\\ \text{Efficiency}&=\frac{\text{Output power}}{input power} \times 100\\ &=\frac{P_0}{V_tT_{a_1}} \times 100\\ &=\frac{42}{25 \times 3.5} \times 100=48\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

The resistance and reactance of a 100 kVA, 11000/400 V, [latex]\triangle[/latex]-Y distribution

raw_source.solution:
Rated kVA = 100kVA

Rated primary line to line coltage
[latex] V_{l-l}=11000V[/latex]
Rated primary phase voltage
[latex]V_p=V_{l-l}=11000V[/latex]
Rated primary side line current
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_1 &=\frac{\text{Rated kVA} \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3}V_{l-l}} \\ &= \frac{100 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3}\times 11000}A \end{aligned} [/latex]
Rated primary phase current,

raw_source.text:
A single-phase, 230 V, 50 Hz, 4-pole, capacitor-start induction motor had the following stand-still impedances.

Main winding [latex]Z_{m} = 6.0 + j4.0 \Omega[/latex]
Auxiliary winding [latex]Z_{a} = 8.0 + j6.0 \Omega[/latex]

The value of the starting capacitor required to produce [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex] phase difference between the currents in the main and auxiliary windings will be
raw_source.solution:
Supply voltage V is taken as reference.
Current in main winding
[latex]I_m=\frac{V}{Z_m} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; I_m=\frac{230\angle 0^{\circ}}{6+j4}=31.89\angle -33.7^{\circ}[/latex]
Staring capacitor (C) wil be connected in series with the auxilary winding, so modified auxiliary winding impedance.
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z_m &= 8+j6-\frac{j}{\omega C}\\ &= 8+j\left ( 6-\frac{1}{\omega C} \right )\\ &= 8-j\left ( \frac{1}{\omega C}-6 \right ) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Current in auxiliary winding,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_a &=\frac{V}{Z_a} \\ &= \frac{230\angle 0^{\circ}}{8-j\left ( \frac{1}{\omega C}-6 \right )}\\ &=|I_a|\angle \tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{\frac{1}{\omega C}-6 }{8} \right ) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Capacitor is provided to make angle between [latex]I_a[/latex] and [latex]I_m90^{\circ}.[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So,}\;\; \angle I_m+\angle I_a&=90^{\circ} \\ \angle I_a&= 90^{\circ}-33.7^{\circ}=56.3^{\circ}\\ \tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{\frac{1}{\omega C}-6 }{8} \right )&= 56.3^{\circ}\\ \frac{1}{\omega C} &= 18\\ \omega &= 2 \pi f=2 \pi \times 50 \text{rad/sec} \\ C&=176.84\mu F \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Single Phase Induction Motors, Special Purpose Machines and Electromechanical Energy Conversion System

raw_source.text:
Two 3-phase, Y-connected alternators are to be paralleled to a set of common
bus bars. The armature has a per phase synchronous reactance of 1.7[latex]\Omega[/latex] and
negligible armature resistance. The line voltage of the first machine is adjusted
to 3300 V and that of the second machine is adjusted to 3200 V. The machine
voltages are in phase at the instant they are paralleled. Under this condition,
the synchronizing current per phase will be
raw_source.solution:
Per phase synchronizing current [latex]=\frac{|E_1-E_2|}{Z_{s_1}-Z_{s_2}} [/latex]
We have [latex]Z_{s_1}=Z_{s_2}[/latex]
[latex] E_1 [/latex] and [latex] E_2[/latex] must be phase quantities
[latex]\therefore \;\;I_{sy}=\frac{\left [ \frac{3300}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{3200}{\sqrt{3}} \right ]}{2 \times 1.7}=16.98A[/latex]

A 8-pole, DC generator has a simplex wave-wound armature containing 32 coils

raw_source.solution:

raw_source.text:
A 400 V, 50 kVA, 0.8 p.f. leading [latex]\triangle[/latex]-connected, 50 Hz synchronous machine has
a synchronous reactance of 2 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and negligible armature resistance. The friction
and windage losses are 2 kW and the core loss is 0.8 kW. The shaft is supplying
9 kW load at a power factor of 0.8 leading. The line current drawn is
raw_source.solution:
Power available at shaft [latex]=P_{shaft}=9kW[/latex]
Losses = Core loss + Friction and windage loss + Copper loss
Core loss = 0.8 kW
Friction and windage loss = 2kW
Armature resistance is negligibl, so copper loss is neglected.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \; \text{Losses} &= 0.8+2=2.8 kW \\ \text{Input power(P)}&=P_{shaft}+Losses \\ &=9+2.8=11.8kW \\ &\text{Line current drawn}\\ &= \frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_L \cos \phi }\\ &= \frac{11.8 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \times 400 \times 0.8}\\ &= 21.29A \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]3-\phi[/latex] power [latex]=\sqrt{3}V_LI_L \cos \phi[/latex]

Rated line voltage [latex]=V_L=21.5kV[/latex]
Rated line current [latex]=I_L=\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_L \cos \phi }[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; I_L=\frac{500 \times 10^6}{\sqrt{3} \times 21.5 \times 10^3 \times 0.85}[/latex]
= 15.79 kA

raw_source.text:
A 800 kV transmission line is having per phase line inductance of 1.1 mH/km

raw_source.solution:
Parameter of the line

raw_source.text:
A 110 kV, single core coaxial, XLPE insulated power cable delivering power at

[latex]2 \times 10^{-4}[/latex], then dielectric power loss in this cable in W/km is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{V(Phase voltage)} &=\frac{110}{\sqrt{3}}kV \\ C&=125 nF/km \\ \tan \delta &= 2 \times 10^{-4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Dielectric power loss in cable
[latex]\begin{aligned} P&=V62 \omega C \tan \delta \\ P&=\left ( \frac{110 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2 \times 2 \\ & \times \pi \times 50 \times 125 \times 10^{-9} \times 2 \times 10^{-4}\\ &\approx 31.7 W/km \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 50 Hz, 4-pole, 500 MVA, 22 kV turbo-generator is delivering rated megavoltamperes
at 0.8 power factor. Suddenly a fault occurs reducing in electric power
output by 40%. Neglect losses and assume constant power input to the shaft.
The accelerating torque in the generator in MNm at the time of fault will be
raw_source.solution:
Before fault, mechanical input [latex](P_m)=[/latex] Electrical output [latex](P_e)[/latex]
[latex]= 500 \times 0.8=400MW[/latex]
After fault, mechanical input remains same [latex]=P_m=400MW[/latex]
While electrical output reduces by 40 %.
So, electrical output at the time of fault
[latex]=(P_e)_f= 0.6 \times 400 =240MW[/latex]
Accelerating power [latex]=P_a=P_m-(P_e)_f[/latex]
[latex]=400-240=160MW[/latex]
Synchronous speed (in rpm)
[latex]N_s=\frac{120 \times f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500\; rpm[/latex]
Synchronous speed (in rad/sec)
[latex]\omega _s=\frac{2 \pi N_s}{60}=\frac{2 \pi \times 1500}{60}=157 \text{ rad/sec}[/latex]
[latex]P_a=T_a\omega[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;T_a\omega[/latex] (accelerating Torque)
[latex]=\frac{P_a}{\omega _s}=\frac{160}{157}MN-m=1.018MN-m[/latex]

[latex]sI-A=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} s &-2 \\ -2& s \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
Characteristic equation [latex]\Rightarrow |sI-A|=0 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} s &-2 \\ -2& s \end{bmatrix}=0 [/latex]

Roots of the characteristic equation are -2 and +2.

raw_source.text: The block diagram of a closed loop control system is given by figure. The values of K and P such that the system has a damping ratio of 0.7 and an undamped natural frequency [latex]\omega _n[/latex] of 5 rad/sec, are respectively equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]G(s)=\frac{k}{s(s+2)} [/latex] and [latex] H(s)=1+sP[/latex]
Closed-loop transfer function,
[latex]T(s)=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{\frac{k}{s(s+2)}}{1+\frac{k}{s(s+2)}\cdot (1+sP)} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{k}{s(s+2)+k(1+sP)} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; T(s)=\frac{k}{s^2+(2+kP)s+k} [/latex]
So, characteristic equation [latex]= s^2+(2+kP)s+k[/latex]
Comparing with standard equation [latex]=s^2+2\xi \omega _n s+\omega _n^2[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; k=\omega _n^2=5^2=25 [/latex]
(where [latex]\omega _n = [/latex] undamped natueal frequency)
[latex]\;\; 2\xi \omega _n=2+kP[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 0.7 \times 5=2+25P [/latex]
(where [latex]\xi =[/latex] damping ratio)
[latex]P=0.2[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The unit impulse response of a second order under-damped system starting from rest is given by
[latex]c(t) = 12.5e^{-6t}sin8t,\; t\geq 0[/latex]
The steady-state value of the unit step response of the system is equal to
raw_source.solution:
Transfer function of a system is the unit impulse response of the system.
Transfer function=[latex]\frac{C\left ( s \right )}{R\left ( s \right )}=\left [ 12.5e^{-6t}\sin 8t \right ][/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =12.5\times \frac{8}{\left ( s+6 \right )^{2}+8^{2}}=\frac{100}{\left ( s+6 \right )^{2}+8^{2}}[/latex]
when input is unit step, R(s)=[latex]\frac{1}{s}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; C\left ( s \right )=\frac{1}{s}.\frac{100}{\left ( s+6 \right )^{2}+8^{2}}[/latex]Steady-state value of response, using final value theorem
[latex]C_{steady-state}=\lim_{s\rightarrow \infty }C\left ( t \right )=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}s\left ( s \right )[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}s\left [ \frac{1}{s}.\frac{100}{\left ( s+6 \right )^{2}+8^{2}} \right ]=1[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The open loop transfer function of a unity feedback control system is given as
[latex]G\left ( s \right )=\frac{as+1}{s^{2}}[/latex]
The value of 'a' to give a phase margin of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]G(s)=\frac{as+1}{s^2} [/latex]
[latex]\omega _g[/latex] = gain crossover frequency at which open gain is loop
Phase margin[latex]=180+\angle G(j\omega ) [/latex]
[latex]45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle G(j\omega_g ) [/latex]
[latex]\angle G(j\omega_g =-130^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]\angle G(j\omega_g )=\frac{ja \omega _g +1}{(j\omega _g)^2} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=-2 \times 90^{\circ}+tan^{-1}a\omega _g [/latex]
[latex]\angle G(j\omega_g )=-180^{\circ}+tan^{-1}a\omega _g=-135^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]tan^{-1}a\omega _g=45^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]a\omega _g=1 [/latex]
[latex]\omega _g=\frac{1}{a} [/latex]
[latex]Gain=|G(j\omega_g )|=1 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{\sqrt{1+a^2\omega ^2_g}}{\omega ^2_g}=1[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \frac{\sqrt{1+a^2 \times \frac{1}{a^2}}}{1/a^2}=1 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{1}{a^2}=\sqrt{2}[/latex]
[latex] a=\frac{1}{2^{1/4}}=0.841[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A moving coil of a meter has 100 turns, and a length and depth of 10 mm and
20 mm respectively. It is positioned in a uniform radial flux density of 200 mT.
The coil carries a current of 50 mA. The torque on the coil is
raw_source.solution:
T=Torque on the coil=NBAI
where,
[latex]\begin{aligned} N &= \text{Number of turns}=100 \\ B&= \text{Flux density}\\ &= 200mT =200 \times 10^{-3}T\\ A &= \text{Area of the coil} \\ &= \text{length} \times \text{depth}\\ &= (10 \times 10^{-3}) \times (20 \times 10^{-3})\\ &= 200 \times 10^{-6} m^2\\ I&= \text{Current through the coil}\\ &= 50mA=50 \times 10^{-3}\\ T&= NBAI \\ &=100 \times (200 \times10^{-3}) \times (200 \times 10^{-6}) \\ &= \times (50 \times 10^{-3})\\ &=2 \times 10^{-4} N-m=200\mu N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A moving iron ammeter produces a full scale torque of 240 [latex]\mu[/latex]Nm with a deflection of [latex]120^{\circ}[/latex] at a current of 10 A . The rate of change of self induction ([latex]\mu[/latex]H/radian) of the instrument at full scale is
raw_source.solution:
Torque produced,
[latex]\begin{aligned} T&= \frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta }\\ Where\;\; I &= 10A\\ T &= 240 \mu N-m\\ T&= \frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta } \\ 240 \times 10^{-6}&= \frac{1}{2} \times 10^2 \times \frac{dL}{d\theta } \\ \frac{dL}{d\theta } &= 4.8 \times 10^{-6} \text{H/radian} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Rate of change of self-inductance
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{dL}{d\theta } = 4.8 \times 10^{-6} \text{H/radian}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single-phase load is connected between R and Y terminals of a 415 V, symmetrical, 3-phase, 4-wire system with phase sequence RYB. A wattmeter is connected in the system as shown in figure. The power factor of the load is 0.8 lagging. The wattmeter will read
raw_source.solution:
Line of line voltage [latex]=450V[/latex]
Phase to neutral voltage [latex]=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}V[/latex]
Taking [latex]V_R[/latex] as the reference
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{RN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle 0^{\circ}V\\ V_{yN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -120^{\circ}V\\ \text{and } V_{BN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -240^{\circ}\\ V_{Ry} &=V_{RN}-V_{yN} \\ &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle 0^{\circ}- \frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -120^{\circ} \\ &=415 \angle 30^{\circ}V \\ & \text{Load current,}\\ I_L&= \frac{V_{Ry}}{Z}=\frac{415 \angle 30^{\circ}}{100 \angle 36.87^{\circ}}\\ &= 4.15 \angle -6.87^{\circ} A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Current through current coil,
[latex]I_{cc}=I_L=4.15\angle -6.87^{\circ}A [/latex]
Voltage across pressure coil
[latex]V_{BN}=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}\angle -240^{\circ}V [/latex]
Phase angle between [latex]V_{BN} \text{and} I_{cc}[/latex]
[latex] \phi =-240^{\circ}-(-6.87^{\circ})=233.13^{\circ} [/latex]
Wattmeter reading [latex]=|V_{BN}||I_L| \cos \phi[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; =\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \times 4.15 \times \cos 233.13[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; \approx -597W[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 50 Hz, bar primary CT has a secondary with 500 turns. The secondary supplies 5 A current into a purely resistive burden of 1[latex]\Omega[/latex]. The magnetizing ampere-turns is 200. The phase angle between the primary and second current is [latex]175.4^{\circ}[/latex]. The core flux in the CT under the given operating conditions is

raw_source.text: A MOSFET rated for 15 A, carries a periodic current as shown in figure. The ON state resistance of the MOSFET is 0.15 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. The average ON state loss in the MOSFET is
raw_source.solution:
Rated current during on state [latex]I=10[/latex]
ON state resistance [latex]R_{ON}=0.15\Omega [/latex]
MOSFET is ON
[latex]\begin{aligned} 0\lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ 0 \lt t \lt \pi/ \omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
MOSFET is OFF
[latex]\begin{aligned} \pi \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ \pi/ \omega \lt t \lt 2\pi/ \omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
Average ON state Loss,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{avg}&=\frac{1}{2 \pi/\omega }\int_{0}^{\pi/\omega }I^2R_{ON}dt\\ &=\frac{\omega }{2 \pi}\times I^2 R_{ON}\times \frac{\pi}{\omega }\\ &=\frac{I^2R_{ON}}{2}=\frac{10^2 \times 0.15}{2}=7.5W \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Figure shows a chopper operating from a 100 V dc input. The duty ratio of the main switch S is 0.8. The load is sufficiently inductive so that the load current is ripple free. The average current through the diode D under steady state is
raw_source.solution:
During the period [latex]T_{ON}[/latex] chopper on and load voltage is equal to source voltage ([latex]V_{s}=100V[/latex]). During the interval [latex]T_{OFF}[/latex], chopper is off, load current ([latex]I_{0}[/latex]) flows through the diode as result load voltage is zero during [latex]T_{OFF}[/latex].
Average load voltage,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0 &=\frac{T_{ON}}{T_{ON}+T_{OFF}}V_s=\alpha V_s \\ &=\frac{0.8}{100}=80V \end{aligned}[/latex]
Average load current,
[latex]I_0=\frac{V_0}{R}=\frac{80}{10}=8A[/latex]
As load current is ripple free, so average diode current,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_D&=\frac{1}{T}\int_{T_{ON}}^{T}I_0dt \\ &= \frac{(T-T_{ON})}{T}I_0\\ &=(1-\alpha )I_0\\ &=(1-0.8)\times 8=1.6A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Figure shows a chopper. The device [latex]S_1[/latex] is the main switching device. [latex]S_2[/latex] is the auxiliary commutation device. [latex]S_1[/latex] is rated for 400 V, 60 A. [latex]S_2[/latex] is rated for 400 V, 30 A. The load current is 20 A. The main device operates with a duty ratio of 0.5. The peak current through [latex]S_1[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Initially main thyristor [latex](S_1)[/latex] and auxiliary thyristor [latex](S_2)[/latex] are off and capacitor is assumed chargeed to voltage [latex]V_s[/latex] with upper plate positive. When [latex]S_1[/latex] is turned on, source voltage [latex]V_s[/latex] is applied across load and load current [latex]I_0[/latex] begins to flow which is assumed to remain constant. With [latex]S_1[/latex] ON another oscillatory circuit consisting of C, [latex]S_1[/latex] and L is formed where the capacitor current is given by
[latex]i_c=V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
So current through [latex]S_1[/latex],
[latex]I_{s1}=I_0+i_c=I_0+V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
Pek value of
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{s1}&=I_0+V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \\ &= 20+200\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{200 \times 10^{-6}}}=40A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A single-phase half-controlled rectifier is driving a separately excited dc motor.
The dc motor has a back emf constant of 0.5 V/rpm. The armature current is 5A without any ripple. The armature resistance is 2[latex]\Omega[/latex]. The converter is working
from a 230V, single-phase ac source with a firing angle of [latex]30^{\circ}[/latex]. Under this
operating condition, the speed of the motor will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Back emf }&=E_a=k\phi N\\ E_a&=k_bN \end{aligned}[/latex]
where,
[latex]k_b=[/latex] Back-emf constant =0.25 V/rpm
Average output voltage of [latex]1-\phi[/latex] half controlled rectifier =V
[latex]\begin{aligned} V &=\frac{V_m}{\pi} (1+ \cos \alpha ) \\ &= \frac{230\sqrt{2}}{2 \pi} (1+ \cos 30^{\circ})\\ \Rightarrow \; V &=96.6V \\ E_a&=V-I_aR_a \\ &= 96.6-5 \times 2=86.6V\\ \text{Speed}&=N=\frac{E_a}{k_b}=\frac{86.6}{0.25}=346.4V \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A variable speed drive rated for 1500 rpm, 40 Nm is reversing under no load. Figure shows the reversing torque and the speed during the transient. The moment of inertia of the drive is
raw_source.solution:

So angular acceleration,

raw_source.text: If P and Q are two random events, then the following is TRUE
raw_source.solution:
(A) is false since of P and Q are independent
[latex]Pr(P\cap Q)=Pr(P) \times Pr(Q)[/latex]
which need not be zero.
(B) is false since
[latex]Pr(P\cup Q)=Pr(P) + Pr(Q)-Pr(P\cap Q)[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; Pr(P\cup Q)\leq Pr(P) + Pr(Q)[/latex]
(C) is false since independence and mutually exclusion are unrelated properties.
(D) is true
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{since } P\cap Q&\subseteq P \\ \Rightarrow \;\; n(P\cap Q) &\leq n(P) \\ \Rightarrow \;\; Pr(P\cap Q) &\leq Pr(P) \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: Independence of P and Q implies that probability (P[latex]\cap[/latex]Q)=0
If P and Q are mutually exclusive, then they must be independent

raw_source.text: The solution of the first order differential equation [latex]\dot{x} (t) =- 3x(t), x(0) = x_0[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given, } \dot{x}(t)&=-3x(t) \\ i.e.\;\;\; \frac{dx}{dt}&= -3x\\ \frac{dx}{x}&=-3 dt \\ \int \frac{dx}{x}&=\int -3 dt \\ \ln x&= -3t+C\\ x&=e^{-3t+C}=e^C \times e^{-3t} \\ \text{Putting }e^C&=C_1 \\ x&=C_1 \times e^{-3t} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now putting initial condition [latex]x(0)=x_0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_0 &=C_1e^{0}=C_1 \\ C_1&=x_0 \\ \therefore \;\;\text{Solution is } x&=x_0e^{-3t} \\ i.e. \;\; x(t)&=x_0e^{-3t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For the matrix
[latex]p=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2&2 \\ 0& -2 & 1\\ 0 &0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
one of the eigen values is equal to -2. Which of the following is an eigen vector ?
raw_source.solution:
Since matrix is triangular, the eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves namely [latex]\lambda =3, -2[/latex] and 1.
Corresponding to eigen value [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] let us find the eigen vector
[latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & -2 & 2\\ 0 & -2-\lambda & 1\\ 0& 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] in above equation we get,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0& 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\\ 3x_3&=0 \;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since equation (ii) and (iii) are same we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex] Putting [latex]x_2=k[/latex], we get
[latex]x_3=0, x_2=k[/latex] and [latex]5x_1-2k+2 \times 0=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;x_1=2/5 \;k[/latex]
Eigen vectors are of the form
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2/5 k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1:x_2:x_3&=2/5k:k:0\\ &=2/5:1:0\\ &=2:5:0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 5\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is an eigen vector of matrix p.

raw_source.text: If [latex]R=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0&-1 \\ 2& 1 & -1\\ 2&3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], then top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2& 3& 2 \end{bmatrix} \\ R^{-1} &=\frac{adj(R)}{|R|}=\frac{[\text{cofator }(R)]^T}{|R|} \\ |R|&=\begin{vmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2 & 3& 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=1(2+3)-0(4+2)-1(6-2) \\ &= 5-4=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since we need only the top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex], we need to find only first column of (R) which after transpose will become first row of Adj(A).
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{co-factor of (1,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 1 &-1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=2+3=5 \\ \text{co-factor of (2,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=-3 \\ \text{co-factor of (3,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=+1\\ \therefore \;\text{ co-factor of (A)} &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &- &- \\ -3 & - &- \\ 1& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ Adj(A)&= [cof.(A)]^T\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &-3 &1 \\ - & - &- \\ -& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ \text{Dividing by |R|} &= 1 \text{ gives}\\ R^{-1}&= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &-3 &1 \\ - & - &- \\ -& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ \therefore \;\; \text{top row of }R^{-1}&=[5\;-3\;1] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A fair coin is tossed three times in succession. If the first toss produces a head,
then the probability of getting exactly two heads in three tosses is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ \therefore \; &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses }| \text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{P(\text{3 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})}{P(\text{ first toss is head})}\\ &=P(\text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\\ &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})\\ &=P(HHT)+P(HTH)\\ &=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} =\frac{1}{4}\\ \therefore \;&\text{ Required probability}=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the function [latex]f (x) = x^{2}e^{x}[/latex], the maximum occurs when [latex]x[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^2e^{-x}\\ f'(x)&=x^2(-e^{-x})+e^{-x} \times 2x\\ &=e^{-x}(2x-x^2)\\ \text{Putting, } f'(x)&=0\\ e^{-x}(2x-x^2)&=0\\ e^{-x}x(2-x)&=0\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] x =0 [/latex] or [latex] x=2[/latex] are the stationary points.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, } f''(x) &= e^{-x}(2-2x)+(2x-x^2)(-e^{-x})\\ &= e^{-x}(2-2x-(2x-x^2))\\ &= e^{-x}(x^2-4x+2)\\ At\;x=0& \\ f''(0)&= e^{-0}(0-0+2)=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since [latex]f''(x)=2[/latex] is [latex]\gt 0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] we have a minima.
Now at [latex]x=2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} f''(2)&=e^{-2}(2^2-4\times 2 +2) \\ &=-2e^{-2} \lt 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; At \;\; x=2[/latex] we have a maxima.

[latex]\begin{aligned} x_0 &=C_1e^{0}=C_1 \\ C_1&=x_0 \\ \therefore \;\;\text{Solution is } x&=x_0e^{-3t} \\ i.e. \;\; x(t)&=x_0e^{-3t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The RL circuit of the figure is fed from a constant magnitude, variable frequency sinusoidal voltage source [latex]V_{IN}[/latex]. At 100 Hz, the R and L elements each have a voltage drop [latex]\mu _{RMS}[/latex]. If the frequency of the source is changed to 50 Hz, then new voltage drop across R is
raw_source.solution:
At f = 100Hz
[latex]|V_R|=|V_L| [/latex]
as R and L are series connected, current through R and L is same, so
[latex]\begin{aligned}IR&=IX_L=I\omega L \\ \Rightarrow \; R&=X_L=\omega L \\ I&=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}} \\ &=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+R^2}}=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{2}R} \\ V_R&=u_{rms}=IR \\ V_R&=\left ( \frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{2}R} \right ) \times R=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{2}} \\ V_{in}&=\sqrt{2}u_{rms}\;\;...(i) \\ f&=50 Hz \\ X_l & \propto f \\ \text{So, } X'_L&=X_L \times \frac{50}{100} \\ &=\frac{X_L}{2}=\frac{R}{2} \\ I'&=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+(X'_L)^2}} \\ &=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+\left ( \frac{R}{2} \right )^2}} \\ &=\frac{2V_{in}}{\sqrt{5}R} \\ V'_R&=I'R \\ &=\left ( \frac{2V_{in}}{\sqrt{5}R} \right )R \\ &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}V_{in} \\ &\text{From equation (i), }\\ V'_R&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \times (\sqrt{2}u_{rms}) \\ &=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{5}}u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{5}}u_{rms}\end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]P_{1}=\left ( -1 \right )\times \frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{-2}{s+2}[/latex] and
[latex]P_2=\frac{3}{s}\frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{6}{s(s+2)} [/latex]
Individual loop,
[latex]L_1=-1 \times \frac{3}{s}\times \frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{-6}{s(s+2)}[/latex]
Loop touches forward paths, therefore,
[latex]\Delta _1=1 \text{ and } \Delta _2=1 [/latex]
[latex]D=1-L_1 =1+\frac{6}{s(s+2)}=\frac{s(s+2)+6}{s(s+2)} [/latex]
Using Mason's gain formula,
[latex] \frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta } =\frac{-\frac{2}{s+2}\times 1+\frac{6}{s(s+2)}\times 1}{\frac{s(s+2)+6}{s(s+2)}} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} [/latex]
For unit step input, [latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Y(s)&=R(s)\cdot \left ( \frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ) \\ Error&=E(s)=R(s)-Y(s) \\&=R(s)-R(s)\left (\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ) \\ &=R(s)\left [ 1-\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ]\\ E(s)&=\frac{1}{s}\left [ \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Steady state value of error, using final value theoram,
[latex]\begin{aligned}e_{ss}&=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}sE(s) \\ &=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}s\left [ \frac{1}{s}\cdot \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ] \\ &=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ]=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For the matrix
[latex]p=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2&2 \\ 0& -2 & 1\\ 0 &0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
one of the eigen values is equal to -2. Which of the following is an eigen vector ?
raw_source.solution:
Since matrix is triangular, the eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves namely [latex]\lambda =3, -2[/latex] and 1.
Corresponding to eigen value [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] let us find the eigen vector
[latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & -2 & 2\\ 0 & -2-\lambda & 1\\ 0& 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] in above equation we get,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0& 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\\ 3x_3&=0 \;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since equation (ii) and (iii) are same we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex] Putting [latex]x_2=k[/latex], we get
[latex]x_3=0, x_2=k[/latex] and [latex]5x_1-2k+2 \times 0=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;x_1=2/5 \;k[/latex]
Eigen vectors are of the form
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2/5 k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1:x_2:x_3&=2/5k:k:0\\ &=2/5:1:0\\ &=2:5:0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 5\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is an eigen vector of matrix p.

raw_source.text: If [latex]R=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0&-1 \\ 2& 1 & -1\\ 2&3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], then top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2& 3& 2 \end{bmatrix} \\ R^{-1} &=\frac{adj(R)}{|R|}=\frac{[\text{cofator }(R)]^T}{|R|} \\ |R|&=\begin{vmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2 & 3& 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=1(2+3)-0(4+2)-1(6-2) \\ &= 5-4=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since we need only the top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex], we need to find only first column of (R) which after transpose will become first row of Adj(A).
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{co-factor of (1,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 1 &-1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=2+3=5 \\ \text{co-factor of (2,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=-3 \\ \text{co-factor of (3,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=+1\\ \therefore \;\text{ co-factor of (A)} &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &- &- \\ -3 & - &- \\ 1& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ Adj(A)&= [cof.(A)]^T\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &-3 &1 \\ - & - &- \\ -& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ \text{Dividing by |R|} &= 1 \text{ gives}\\ R^{-1}&= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &-3 &1 \\ - & - &- \\ -& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ \therefore \;\; \text{top row of }R^{-1}&=[5\;-3\;1] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A fair coin is tossed three times in succession. If the first toss produces a head,
then the probability of getting exactly two heads in three tosses is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ \therefore \; &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses }| \text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{P(\text{3 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})}{P(\text{ first toss is head})}\\ &=P(\text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\\ &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})\\ &=P(HHT)+P(HTH)\\ &=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} =\frac{1}{4}\\ \therefore \;&\text{ Required probability}=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the function [latex]f (x) = x^{2}e^{x}[/latex], the maximum occurs when [latex]x[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^2e^{-x}\\ f'(x)&=x^2(-e^{-x})+e^{-x} \times 2x\\ &=e^{-x}(2x-x^2)\\ \text{Putting, } f'(x)&=0\\ e^{-x}(2x-x^2)&=0\\ e^{-x}x(2-x)&=0\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] x =0 [/latex] or [latex] x=2[/latex] are the stationary points.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, } f''(x) &= e^{-x}(2-2x)+(2x-x^2)(-e^{-x})\\ &= e^{-x}(2-2x-(2x-x^2))\\ &= e^{-x}(x^2-4x+2)\\ At\;x=0& \\ f''(0)&= e^{-0}(0-0+2)=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since [latex]f''(x)=2[/latex] is [latex]\gt 0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] we have a minima.
Now at [latex]x=2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} f''(2)&=e^{-2}(2^2-4\times 2 +2) \\ &=-2e^{-2} \lt 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; At \;\; x=2[/latex] we have a maxima.

A 50 kW dc shunt is loaded to draw rated armature current at any given speed.
When driven
(i) at half the rated speed by armature voltage control and
(ii) at 1.5 times the rated speed by field control, the respective output powers
delivered by the motor are approximately.
raw_source.solution:
Armature control provides constant torque drive.In the shunt motor case by keeping the filed current at maximum value full load torque can be obtaineda at full load armaturecurrent at all speeds
[latex]\begin{aligned} T &= \text{constant}\\ T\omega &= \text{output power}(P_o)\\ \Rightarrow \;\frac{P_o}{\omega }&= constant\\ (P_0)_1 &= 50kW\\ \omega _2&= \frac{\omega _1}{2}\\ \frac{(P_o)_1}{\omega _1} &= \frac{(P_o)_2}{\omega _2}\\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{50}{\omega _1} &=\frac{(P_o)_2}{\omega _1/2} \\ (P_o)_2 &= 25kW \end{aligned}[/latex]
(output power delivered at half the rated speed by armature control).
Filed control provides constant-power drive. Since the speed is inversely proportional to the flux/pole [latex]\left ( \omega \propto \frac{1}{\phi } \right )[/latex] while the torque is direclty proportional to flux/pole [latex](T\propto \phi )[/latex] for a given armature current.
Output power [latex]=T\omega =\left ( \frac{k_1}{\phi } \right )(k_2\phi ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=k_1k_2=constant[/latex]
Output power delivered by the motor remains constant i.e. 50kW

at the rated voltage. If the starting current drawn is 6 times the full load
current, and the full load slip is 4%, then ratio of the starting developed torque
to the full load torque is approximately equal to
raw_source.solution:
Torque in induction motor is given by,
[latex]\begin{aligned} T &=\frac{3}{\omega _s}(I'_2)\frac{R'_2}{s} \\ & \text{Full load torque}\\ T_{fl} &= \frac{2}{\omega _s}(I'_{2fl})^2 \frac{R'_2}{S_{fl}}\\ & \text{At starting,}\\ s &= 1\\ & \text{Starting torque}\\ T_{st}&= \frac{3}{\omega _s}(I'_{2st})^2 R'_2\\ \frac{T_{st}}{T_{fl}}&=\left ( \frac{I'_{2st}}{I'_{2fl}} \right )^2 S_{fl} \\ &= 6^2 \times 0.04=1.44 \end{aligned}[/latex]

In a single phase induction motor driving a fan load, the reason for having a
high resistance rotor is to achieve
raw_source.solution:

[latex]T_{total}=T_f-T_b [/latex]
where,
[latex]T_f=[/latex] Torque developed due ot forward field.
[latex]T_b=[/latex] Torque developed due to backward field

raw_source.text:
Determine the correctness or otherwise of the following assertion[A] and the reason[R].

Assertion [A] : Under V/f control of induction motor, the maximum value of the developed torque remains constant over a wide range of speed in the subsynchronous region.

Reason [R] : The magnetic flux is maintained almost constant at the rated value by keeping the ration V/f constant over the considered speed range.
raw_source.solution:
The resultant air-gap flux per pole is given by
[latex]\phi _r=\frac{1}{4.44k_{\omega _1}N_{pn_1}}\left ( \frac{V}{f} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\phi _r\propto \left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )[/latex]
Therefore, in order to avoid saturation in stator and rotor cores which would cause sharp increase in magnetization current, the flux [latex]f_p[/latex] must be kept constant. To achieve this, [latex]\frac{V}{f}[/latex] ratio must be kept constant.
Let, [latex]V_0=[/latex] Nominal voltage
[latex]f_0=[/latex] Nominal frequency
[latex]X'_{20}=[/latex] Nominal rotor standstill reactance reffered to stator then at any frequency f.
Then at any frequency f,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right ) V_0\\ X'_2 &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right ) X'_{20} \\ \omega _s &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )\omega _{20} \\ T_{max}&= \frac{3}{\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )\omega _{s_0}}\left [ \frac{0.5 \left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )^2 V_0^2}{\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )X'_{20}} \right ]\\ &= \frac{3}{\omega _{s_0}}\frac{0.5V_0^2}{X'_{20}}\\ &=\text{constant, independent of f} \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: Both [A] and [R] are true and [R] is the correct reason for [A]
Both [A] and [R] are true and but [R] is not the correct reason for [A]

raw_answer.option_text: Both [A] and [R] are true and [R] is the correct reason for [A]

[latex]F_2=a+bP_2+2cP_2^2 \; \text{Rs/hour}[/latex]
The slope of the fuel-cost curve i.e. [latex]\frac{dF_i}{dP_i}[/latex] is called the incremental fuel-cost (IC) and is expressed in Rs/MWh.
[latex]\begin{aligned} IC_1&=\frac{dF_1}{dP_1}=b+2cP_1 \\ IC_2&=\frac{dF_2}{dP_2}=b42cP_2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
For economic generation
[latex]\begin{aligned} IC_1&=IC_2\\ b+2cP_1&=b+4cP_2\\ P_1&=2P_2\;\;...(i) \\ &\text{To meet 300 MW of load}\\ P_1+P_2&=300\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{Solving eq. (i) and (ii)}\\ P_1&=200MW\\ P_2&=100MW \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A generator with constant 1.0 p.u. terminal voltage supplies power through a step-up transformer of 0.12 p.u. reactance and a double-circuit line to an infinite bus bar as shown in the figure. When double-circuit line is connected

Steady state stability power limit

raw_source.text: The figure shows the voltage across a power semiconductor device and the current through the device during a switching transitions. Is the transition a turn ON transition or a turn OFF transition ? What is the energy lost during the transition ?
raw_source.solution:
During interval [latex]t_2[/latex], voltage starts decreasing and becomes zero and current starts increasing and becomes constant (I), so transition is turn on.

During [latex]t_1[/latex] interval:
Power loss [latex]=vi[/latex]
[latex]E_1=\text{Energy loss}=\int vi\; dt=V\int i\; dt[/latex]
V is constant during this period v=V
[latex]\int i\; dt[/latex] represents area under i-t curve
[latex]\int i\; dt=\frac{1}{2} \times I \times t_1[/latex]
[latex]E_1=V\int i\; dt=\frac{1}{2} V I t_1\;\;...(i)[/latex]
During [latex]t_2[/latex] interval:
Power loss = vi
[latex]E_2=\text{Energy loss}=\int vi\; dt=I\int v\; dt[/latex]
i is constant during this period i=I
[latex]\int v\; dt[/latex] represents area under v-t curve
[latex]\int v\; dt=\frac{1}{2} VIt_2[/latex]
[latex]E_2=I\int v\; dt=\frac{1}{2} V I t_2\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Total energy lost during the transition
[latex]E=E_1+E_2[/latex]
[latex]E=\frac{1}{2}VIt_1+\frac{1}{2}VIt_2[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Power Semiconductor Devices and Commutation Techniques

raw_source.text:
A state variable system
[latex]\dot{X}\left ( t \right )=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}X\left ( t \right )+ \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}u\left ( t \right )[/latex],
with the initial condition [latex]X\left ( 0 \right )=\begin{bmatrix} -1, &3 \end{bmatrix}^{T}[/latex] and the unit step input [latex]u\left ( t \right )[/latex] has

The state transition matrix
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\dot{x}(t)=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}V(t) \;\;...(i) [/latex]
[latex]\dot{x}(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t) \;\;...(ii) [/latex]
Comparing equation (i) and (ii), we get
[latex]A= \text{System matrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned}[sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s &0 \\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-3 \end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s &-1 \\ s &s+3 \end{bmatrix} \\ [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+3 &1 \\ 0 &s \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+3)-0x(-1)} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s} & \frac{1}{s(s+3)}\\ 0 &\frac{1}{s+3} \end{bmatrix} \\ [sI-A]^{-1}&=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s} & \frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+3} \right )\\ 0 &\frac{1}{s+3} \end{bmatrix} \\ &\text{State transition matrix } \\ &=L^{-1}[(sI-A)^{-1}]\\ \phi (t)&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &\frac{1}{3}(1-e^{-3t}) \\ 0& e^{-3t} \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A state variable system
[latex]\dot{X}\left ( t \right )=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}X\left ( t \right )+ \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}u\left ( t \right )[/latex],
with the initial condition [latex]X\left ( 0 \right )=\begin{bmatrix} -1, &3 \end{bmatrix}^{T}[/latex] and the unit step input [latex]u\left ( t \right )[/latex] has

the state transition equation
raw_source.solution:
ZIR (zero Input Response) [latex]=\phi (t) \times X(0)[/latex]
[latex] =\begin{bmatrix} 1 &\frac{}{3}(1-e^{-3t}) \\ 0& e^{-3t} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -1\\ 3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} -1+1-e^{-3t} \\ 3 e^{-3t} \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} -e^{-3t} \\ 3 e^{-3t} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
ZSR (Zero State Response)
[latex]=L^{-1}[(sI-A)^{-1}BU(s)] [/latex]
[latex]=L^{-1}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s} & \frac{1}{s(s+3)}\\ 0& \frac{1}{s+3} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{1}{s}\right \} [/latex]
[latex]=l^{-1}\begin{bmatrix} 1/s^2\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} t\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] State transition equation
[latex]\;\;\; =ZIR+ZSR=\begin{bmatrix} -e^{-3t} \\ 3 e^{-3t} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} t\\0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} t-e^{-3t}\\ 3 e^{-3t} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

A 1000 kVA , 6.6 kV, 3-phase star connected cylindrical pole synchronous generator has a synchronous reactance of 20[latex]\Omega[/latex]. Neglect the armature resistance and consider operation at full load and unity power factor.

raw_source.solution:
Rated output power [latex]=S = 1000kVA[/latex]
Rated line to line voltage [latex]=V_{l-l} = 6.6kV[/latex]
Rated current,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_a &=\frac{S}{\sqrt{3}V_{l-l}} \\ &= \frac{1000}{\sqrt{3} \times 6.6}\\ &=87.477A \end{aligned}[/latex]
As generator is star connected.
Phase to neutral voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_t &=\frac{V_{l-l}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \frac{6.6}{\sqrt{3} }\\ &=3.81kV \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex]V_t[/latex] as the reference
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_t &=3.81 \angle 0^{\circ}kV\\ I_a&= 87.477\angle 0^{\circ}A\\ E_f &=V_t+I_a X_s \\ &= 3.81 \angle 0^{\circ}+ 87.477 \angle 0^{\circ} \\ &\times (j20) \times 10^{-3} \\ &= 4.19\angle 24.6^{\circ}kV \end{aligned}[/latex]
Induced emf(line to line)
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\sqrt{3}E_f \\ &= \sqrt{3} \times 4.19\\ &=7.2 kV \end{aligned}[/latex]

Pre-fault line voltage [latex]=V_{prefault}=220kV[/latex]

Let positive sequence driving point reactance =[latex]=X_1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} X_1&=\frac{V_{present}/\sqrt{3}}{I_f}\\ X_1&=\frac{220/\sqrt{3}}{10.5}=12.1\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

At a 220 kV substation of a power system, it is given that the three-phase fault level is 4000 MVA and single-line to ground fault level is 5000 MVA Neglecting the resistance and the shunt suspectances of the system.

Let negative sequence reactance [latex]=X_2[/latex]
Assuming, [latex]X_2=X_1[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The speed of a 4-pole induction motor is controlled by varying the supply
frequency while maintaining the ratio of supply voltage to supply frequency (V/f) constant. At rated frequency of 50 Hz and rated voltage of 400 V its speed is
1440 rpm. Find the speed at 30 Hz, if the load torque is constant
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_{s_1} &=\frac{120f_1}{P} \\ &= \frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500\; \text{rpm}\\ s_1 &=\frac{N_{s_1}-N_{R_1}}{N_{s_1}} \\ &= \frac{1500-1440}{1500}=0.04\\ \text{as}\;\;\frac{V}{f} &=\text{Constant} \\ \frac{V_1}{f_1}&=\frac{V_2}{f_2} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; V_2&=V_1\left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right ) \\ &= 400 \times \frac{30}{50}=240V \end{aligned}[/latex]

Torque developed in induction motor
[latex]T=\frac{3}{\omega _s}\frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2 +{X'_2}^2} [/latex]
In stable region, slip is very low, so [latex]\frac{R'_2}{s} \gt \gt X'_2[/latex]
So, T can be approximated as
[latex]\begin{aligned} T &=\frac{3}{\omega _s}\frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2} \\ &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{8V^2}{R'_2} \\ T&\propto \frac{sV^2}{f} \\ \frac{T_1}{T_2}&= \frac{s_1}{s_2}\left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 \times \frac{f_2}{f_1} \end{aligned} [/latex]
as load torque is constant, [latex]T_1=T_2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} s_2 &=s_1 \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 \times \frac{f_2}{f_1}\\ &= 0.04 \times \left ( \frac{400}{240} \right )^2 \times \left ( \frac{30}{50} \right )\\ &= 0.067\\ N_{s2} &=\frac{120f_2}{P} \\ &= \frac{120 \times 30}{4}=900 \; \text{rpm}\\ &\text {Rotor speed,}\\ N_{r2}&=N_{s2(1-s_2)} \\ &= 900(1-0.067)\\ &\approx 840 \; \text{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} N_s &=\frac{120f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4} \\ &=1500 \;\text{rpm} \\ \omega _s &=\frac{2 \pi N_s}{60}=\frac{2 \pi \times 1500}{50} \\ &= 157.08 \; \text{rad/sec} \\ s&= 1\, \; \text{at starting}\ \\ &\text{Starting torque} \\ T_s&= \frac{3}{\omega _s}\frac{V_P^2r'_2}{(r_1+r'_2)^2+(x_1+x'_2)^2}\\ T_s &= \frac{3}{157.08} \times \frac{(400\sqrt{3})^2 \times 0.5}{(1+0.5)^2+(1.2+1.2)^2}\\ &\approx 63.6 \; N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]

A 3-phase, 10 kW, 400 V, 4-pole, 50Hz, star connected induction motor draws 20 A on full load. Its no load and blocked rotor test data are given below.

Neglecting copper loss in no load test and core loss in blocked rotor test, estimate motor's full load efficiency
raw_source.solution:
No-load losses, [latex]P_1=1002W=1.002kW[/latex] (does not depends on load)
Copper loss at 15A
[latex]P_{cu}=762W[/latex]
Full load current =20A
So, copper loss on full load
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{cu,fl} &= (P_{cu}) \left ( \frac{20}{15} \right )^2\\ P_{cu,fl} &= 762 \times \left ( \frac{20}{15} \right )^2=1.354 kW \\ & \text{Total losses,}\\ P-1 +P_{cu,fl} &=1.002+1.354 \\ &= 2.356kW \end{aligned} [/latex]
Power available at shaft or output power on full load
[latex]P_0=10kW [/latex]
Input power=Output power +losses
[latex]=10+2.356=12.356kW[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \% \text{efficiency} &=\frac{\text{Output power}}{Input Power}\times 100 \\ &= \frac{10}{12.356}\times 100\approx 81\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 3-phase, 400 V, 5 kW, star connected synchronous motor having an internal
reactance of 10 [latex]\Omega[/latex] is operating at 50% load, unity p.f. Now, the excitation is increased by 1%. What will be the new load in percent, if the power factor is to be kept same? Neglect all losses and consider linear magnetic circuit.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]I_{fl}=\frac{5 \times 10^{3}}{\sqrt{3} \times 400 \times 1}=7.21A[/latex]
For synchronous motor,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E^2 &=(V \cos \theta -I_aR_a)^2 +(V\sin \theta -I_aX_s)^2 \\ E&= \sqrt{(400/\sqrt{3})^2+(10 \times 3.6)^2}\\ &= 233.729V \end{aligned} [/latex]
If there is 1% increase in [latex]E_2[/latex], then [latex]E_2[/latex] becomes,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_2 &=233.729 \times 1.01=236V \\ \therefore \;\; I_aX &=\sqrt{E_2^2-V^2} \\ &= \sqrt{(236)^2-(400/\sqrt{3})^2}\\ &= 48.93\\ \therefore \;\; I_a&=4.893A \\ \therefore \;\;\% \;\text{load} &= \frac{4.893}{7.21}=67.86\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

The Bode magnitude plot of
[latex]H(j\omega )=\frac{10^{4}(1+j\omega )}{(10+j\omega )(100+j\omega )^{2}}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]H(j\omega )=\frac{10^4(1+j\omega )}{(10+j\omega)(100+j\omega)^2} [/latex]
[latex]H(j\omega )=\frac{(1+j\omega)}{10\times \left ( 1+\frac{j\omega}{10} \right )\times \left ( 1+\frac{j\omega}{100} \right )^2} [/latex]
[latex]H(j\omega )=\frac{k(1+j\omega)}{ \left ( 1+\frac{j\omega}{10} \right ) \left ( 1+\frac{j\omega}{100} \right )^2} [/latex]
[latex]where \;\; k=\frac{1}{10}=0.1[/latex]
Corner frequencys
[latex]\omega _1= 1[/latex] rad/sec; [latex]\omega _2= 10[/latex] rad/sec and [latex]\omega _3=100[/latex] rad/sec
For frequency less than [latex]\omega _1 \; i.e. \; \omega \lt \omega _1[/latex]
Gain of the system is constant aas there is no pole at origin.
Gain[latex]=20 log k=20 log 0.1=-20 dB[/latex]
At [latex]\omega =\omega _1= 1[/latex] rad/sec or [latex]\omega _1= log 1 =0[/latex]
There is zero, so system gain increases with slope +20dB/decades and system gain become 0 dB at [latex]\omega = 10[/latex] rad/sec or [latex]log\omega |_{\omega =10}=log 10=1[/latex]

At [latex]\omega _2 =10[/latex] or [latex]log \omega |_{\omega _2=10}=log 10=1[/latex]
there is pole, so slope is -20 dB/decade.
Overall slope [latex]\omega _2 \lt \omega \lt \omega _3[/latex]
= 20 dB/decade - 20 dB/decade
= 0 dB/decade
So, gain remain constant between
[latex]\omega _2 \lt \omega \lt\omega _3[/latex]
or [latex]1 \lt log \omega \lt 2[/latex]

At [latex]\omega =\omega _3 =100[/latex] rad/sec or
[latex]log\omega |_{\omega _3=100}=log 100=2[/latex]
the double pole are present.
So, system gain decrease with -40 dB/decade.

raw_source.text: A closed-loop system has the characteristic function [latex](s^{2}- 4) (s + 1) + K(s - 1) = 0[/latex]. Its root locus plot against K is
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic function
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;(s^2-4)(s+1)+k(s-1) [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;1+\frac{k(s-1)}{(s^2-4)(s+1)}\equiv 1+G(s)H(s) [/latex]
Open loop transfer function[latex] =G(s)H(s) [/latex]
[latex]=\frac{k(s-1)}{(s^2-4)(s+1)} [/latex]
Zero of OLTF s=1; z=1
Poles of OLTS s=-1,-2,+2,P=3

The root locus starts from open-loop poles and terminates either on open-loop zero or infinity.
Root locus exist on section of real axis it the sum of the open-loop poles and zeros to the right of the section is odd.
Number of branches teminating on infinity.
=P-Z=3-1=2
Angle of asymptotes
[latex]=\frac{(2k+1)\times 180^{\circ}}{P-Z}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{(2k+1)\times 180^{\circ}}{2} [/latex]
[latex]=90^{\circ} \; and \; 270^{\circ}[/latex]
Intersection of asymptotes on real axis (centroid)
[latex]=\frac{\Sigma poles-\Sigma zeros}{P-Z}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{(-1-2+2)-(1)}{2}=-1 [/latex]
Option (B) is correct on the basic of above analysis.

raw_source.text:
A variable w is related to three other variables x, y, z as w=xy/z. The variables
are measured with meters of accuracy [latex]\pm[/latex]0.5% reading, [latex]\pm[/latex]1% of full scale value and [latex]\pm[/latex]1.5% reading. The actual readings of the three meters are 80, 20 and 50 with 100 being the full scale value for all three. The maximum uncertainty in the measurement of w will be
raw_source.solution:
Full scale reading of all three =100
Reading of x =80
Reading of y =20
Reading of z =50
[latex]\delta x=\pm 0.5[/latex]% of reading [latex]=\pm \frac{0.5 \times 80}{100}=\pm 0.4[/latex]
[latex]\delta y=\pm 1[/latex]% of reading [latex]=\pm \frac{1 \times 100}{100}=\pm 1 [/latex]
[latex]\delta z=\pm 1.5[/latex]% of reading [latex]=\pm \frac{1.5 \times 50}{100}=\pm 0.75 [/latex]
Given [latex] \omega =\frac{xy}{z} [/latex]
taking log, we get,
[latex]\log \omega = \log x +\log y - \log z [/latex]
differenting w.r.t. [latex]\omega[/latex] we get
[latex]\frac{\delta \omega }{\omega }=\frac{\delta x}{x}+\frac{\delta y}{y}-\frac{\delta z}{z} [/latex]
For maximum limiting error,
[latex]\frac{\delta \omega }{\omega }=\pm \left ( \frac{0.4}{80}+\frac{0.1}{20}+\frac{0.75}{100} \right ) \times 100=\pm 7%[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 200/1 Current transformer (CT) is wound with 200 turns on the secondary
on a toroidal core. When it carries a current of 160 A on the primary, the ratio
and phase errors of the CT are found to be -0.5% and 30 minutes respectively.
If the number of secondary turns is reduced by 1 new ratio-error(%) and phaseerror(
min) will be respectively
raw_source.solution:
Nominal ratio [latex]=k_n=\frac{200}{1}=200 [/latex]
Primary current [latex]=I_P=160A [/latex]
Actual ratio [latex]= R_1=n_1\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex] \% \text{Ratio error} [/latex] [latex]=\frac{k_n - R_1}{R_1}\times 100[/latex]
[latex] -0.5=\frac{200-R_1}{R_1} \times 100 [/latex]
Actual ratio [latex]=R_1=201 [/latex]
[latex]n_1=\text{turn ratio}=200 [/latex]
[latex]R_1=200\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
when number of secondary is reduced by 1
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_s &= 199\\ n_2&=199 \\ R_2&=n_2\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right ) \\ &= 199\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(iii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Dividing equation (ii) and (iii),
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{R_1}{R_2} &=\frac{200}{199} \\ \Rightarrow \;R_2 &= R_1 \times \left ( \frac{200}{199} \right )\\ &=201 \times \frac{200}{199}\approx 200 \\ \% \text{Ratio error} &=\frac{k_n-R_2}{R_2} \times 100\\ &= \frac{200-200}{200}\times 100=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Phase angle error [latex]=\theta =\frac{180}{\pi}\left ( \frac{I_m}{I_P} \right ) [/latex]
Reduction of one or two turns of the secondary winding, no doubt, reduces the ration error, but it has no effect on the phase angle error.

raw_source.text: A student has made a 3-bit binary down counter and connected to the R-2R ladder type DAC [Gain=(-1K[latex]\Omega[/latex]/2R)] as shown in figure to generate a staircase waveform. The output achieved is different as shown in figure. What could be the possible cause of this error ?

Initial stage of the counter [latex]=(111)_2=(7)_10[/latex]

Next state of counter [latex]=(110)_2=(6)_10[/latex]

Input to DAC [latex]=(101)_2=(5)_10[/latex]
So, output = 5V
When counter goes to [latex](100)_2[/latex] then input to DAC [latex]=(001)_2=(1)_10[/latex]
So output = 1 V
So connections are not proper.

A software delay subroutine is written as given below :
DELAY : MVI H, 255D
MVI L, 255D
LOOP : DCR L
JNZ LOOP
DCR H
JNZ LOOP
How many times DCR L instruction will be executed ?
raw_source.solution:
First of all DCR L will be executed for 255 times till content of L becomes 0.
After that for every decrement of H it will be executed 256 times ( first when L is decremented by 1 and becomes [latex]FF_H[/latex] and then [latex]FF_H=255_D[/latex] times ) and this will be happen till content of H become 1 i.e. 254 times.
So, overall it will be executed
=255 + 254 x 256 =65279
