raw_source.text:
A 3-phase fully controlled bridge converter with free wheeling diode is fed from
400 V, 50 Hz AC source and is operating at a firing angle of 60[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. The load current
is assumed constant at 10 A due to high load inductance. The input displacement
factor (IDF) and the input power factor (IPF) of the converter will be
raw_source.solution:
Load current is constant
[latex]I_0=10A[/latex]
In [latex]3-\phi[/latex] full converter with free wheeling diode, input displacement factor (IDF) [latex]= \cos \alpha = \cos 60^{\circ}=0.5[/latex]
RMS value of source current
[latex]I_s=\sqrt{I_0^2 \times \frac{2 \pi}{3} \times \frac{1}{\pi}}=I_0\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}[/latex]
RMS value of [latex]n^{th}[/latex] harmonic
[latex]I_{sh}=\frac{4I_0}{\sqrt{2}n \pi}\sin \frac{n \pi}{3}[/latex]
RMS value of fundamental current
[latex]I_{s1}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi}I_0 \sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\pi}I_0[/latex]
Current distortion factor (CDF)
[latex]=\frac{I_{s1}}{I_s}=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\pi}I_0 \times \left ( \frac{1}{I_0}\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \right )[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{3}{\pi}=0.955[/latex]
Input power factor [latex](IPF) =CDF \times IDF = 0.955 \times 0.5\approx 0.478[/latex]

raw_source.text: A voltage commutation circuit is shown in figure. If the turn-off time of the SCR is 50 [latex]\mu[/latex]sec and a safety margin of 2 is considered, then what will be the approximate minimum value of capacitor required for proper commutation ?
raw_source.solution:
In this type of commutation, athyristor carrying load current is commutated by transferring its load current to another incoming thyristor.
Firing of SCR [latex]Th_1[/latex] commutates [latex]Th_2[/latex] and subsequently, firing of SCR [latex]Th_2[/latex] would turn-off [latex]Th_1[/latex].
Circuit turn-off time [latex]t_{c1}[/latex] for [latex]Th_1[/latex]
[latex]t_{c1}=R_1C \ln 2[/latex]
and circuit turn-off time [latex]t_{c2}[/latex] for [latex]Th_2[/latex]
[latex]t_{c2}=R_2C \ln 2[/latex]
as [latex]R_1=R_2=50 \Omega[/latex]
[latex]t_{c2}=t_{c1}=R_1 C \ln 2[/latex]
Safety margin =2
So, [latex]R_1C \ln 2=2 t_{c1}[/latex]
[latex]C=\frac{2 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}}{50 \times \ln 2}=2.88 \mu F[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Power Semiconductor Devices and Commutation Techniques

raw_source.text:
A solar cell of 350 V is feeding power to an ac supply of 440 V, 50 Hz through a
3-phase fully controlled bridge converter. A large inductance is connected in the
dc circuit to maintain the dc current at 20 A. If the solar cell resistance is 0.5 [latex]\Omega[/latex], then each thyristor will be reverse biased for a period of
raw_source.solution:
Solar cell emf = 350V
DC current [latex]I_{dc}=20A[/latex]
Solar cell resistance
[latex]\begin{aligned} R_{cell}&=0.5\Omega \\ V_0&=\text{Voltage across inverter} \\ &=-(E-I_{dc}R_{cell}) \\ &=-(350-20 \times 0.5)=-340V \end{aligned}[/latex]
The bridge acts as inverter,
Output voltage of [latex]3-\phi[/latex] fully controlled bridge
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0&=\frac{3V_{ml} \cos \alpha }{\pi}\\ -340&=\frac{3V_{ml} \cos \alpha }{\pi}\\ -340&=\frac{3 \times 440\sqrt{2} \cos \alpha }{\pi}\\ \Rightarrow \; \alpha &=125^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, each thyristor will be reverse biased for a period of [latex]55^{\circ}[/latex].

raw_source.text: A single-phase bridge converter is used to charge a battery of 200 V having an internal resistance of 0.2 [latex]\Omega[/latex] as shown in figure. The SCRs are triggered by a constant dc signal. If [latex]SCR_2[/latex] gets open circuited, what will be the average charging current ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]T_1[/latex] and [latex]T_4[/latex] gets forward biased, when
[latex]V_m \sin \theta _1 \leq E[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{avg}&= \text{(average current)} \\ &=\frac{1}{2 \pi R}\int_{\theta _1}^{\pi-\theta _1}(V_m \sin \omega t-E)d\theta \\ \therefore \; I_0 (avg) &=\frac{1}{2 \pi R}[2V_m \cos \theta -E(\pi -2\theta _1)] \\ &=\frac{1}{2 \pi \times 2}[2 \times (230 \times \sqrt{2}) \cos \theta _1\\ &-200(\pi-2\theta _1)] \\ \text{where, } \theta _1&=\sin ^{-1} \left ( \frac{E}{V_m} \right )\\ &= \sin ^{-1}\left ( \frac{200}{230 \times \sqrt{2}} \right )\\ &= 38^{\circ}=0.66\; rad\\ \therefore I_0 (avg) &= \frac{1}{2 \pi \times 2}[2\sqrt{2} \times 230 \cos 38^{\circ}\\ &-200( \pi-2 \times 0.66)]\\ &=11.9A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An SCR having a turn ON times of 5 [latex]\mu[/latex]sec, latching current of 50 mA and holding current of 40 mA is triggered by a short duration pulse and is used in the circuit shown in figure. The minimum pulse width required to turn the SCR ON will be

To turn on [latex]i_a \geq[/latex] latching current

raw_source.text:
A 4 pole, 50 Hz, synchronous generator has 48 slots in which a double layer winding is housed. Each coil has 10 turns and is short pitched by an angle to 36[latex]^\circ[/latex] electrical. The fundamental flux per pole is 0.025 Wb.

The line-to-line induced emf(in volts), for a three phase star connection is approximately
raw_source.solution:
In double layer winding
No. of coil = No. of slots =48
Each coil has 10 turns
Total no. of turns [latex]=48 \times 10=480[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{ph} &=\text{No. of turns/phase} \\ &= \frac{480}{3}=160 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Slots/pole/phase [latex]=m=\frac{48}{4 \times 3}=4 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \gamma &= \text{slot angle}\\ &=\frac{180 \times \text{poles}}{\text{slots}} \\ &= \frac{180 \times 4}{48}=15^{\circ}\\ &\text{Distribution factor,}\\ k_d&=\frac{\sin \frac{m\gamma }{2}}{m \sin \frac{\gamma }{2}} \\ &= \frac{\sin \left ( \frac{4 \times 15}{2} \right )}{2 \sin \left ( \frac{15}{2} \right )}\\ &= 0.957\\ & \text{Short-pitching angle,}\\ \alpha &=36^{\circ} \end{aligned} [/latex]
For the [latex]n^{th}[/latex] harmonic, pitch factor,
[latex]k_p=\cos \frac{n\alpha }{2}[/latex]
pitch factor due to fundamental component
[latex]\begin{aligned} k_p&=\cos \frac{\alpha }{2}=\cos 18^{\circ}=0.951 \\ &\text{Winding factor,} \\ k_w&=k_dk_p \\ &=0.957 \times 0.951=0.910 \\ &\text{Induced emf per phase,} \\ E_{ph}&= 4.44 k_w f T_{ph}\phi \\ &=4.44 \times 0.91 \times 50 \times 160 \times 0.025 \\ &\approx 808\\ \Rightarrow \;\; E_{line} &=\sqrt{3} E_{ph}=1400V \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A generator feeds power to an infinite bus through a double circuit transmission line. A 3-phase fault occurs at the middle point of one of the lines. The infinite bus voltage of the generator is 1.1 pu and the equivalent transfer admittance during fault is 0.8 pu. The 100 MVA generator has an inertia constant of 5 MJ/MVA and it was delivering 1.0 pu power prior of the fault with rotor power angle of 30[latex]^\circ[/latex]. The system frequency is 50 Hz.

The initial accelerating power (in pu) will be
raw_source.solution:
Before fault:
Electrical power delivered by the generator [latex]=P_e=1.0p.u.[/latex]
Mechanical input to the generator [latex]=P_m[/latex]
At steady state,
[latex]P_m=P_e=1.0p.u.[/latex]
During Fault:
Initial rotorr angle [latex]=\delta =30^{\circ}[/latex]
Internal voltage of the generator [latex]=|E_g|=1.1p.u.[/latex]
Voltage of the bus [latex]=|V|=1p.u.[/latex]
Equivalent transfer admittance =0.8
Transfer reactance [latex]=x=\frac{1}{0.8}=1.25[/latex]
[latex](P_e)_f = [/latex] Electrical power delivered by the generator
[latex]\text{During fault}=\frac{|E_g||V_t|}{x}\sin \delta[/latex]
[latex](P_e)_f=\frac{1.1 \times 1}{1.25}\sin 30^{\circ}=0.44p.u.[/latex]
Mechanical input do not change during fault
So, [latex](P_m)_f=1p.u.[/latex]
Accelerating power
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_a&= (P_m)_f-(P_e)_f\\ P_a&=1-0.44 \\ &= 0.56p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A generator feeds power to an infinite bus through a double circuit transmission line. A 3-phase fault occurs at the middle point of one of the lines. The infinite bus voltage of the generator is 1.1 pu and the equivalent transfer admittance during fault is 0.8 pu. The 100 MVA generator has an inertia constant of 5 MJ/MVA and it was delivering 1.0 pu power prior of the fault with rotor power angle of 30[latex]^\circ[/latex]. The system frequency is 50 Hz.

raw_source.solution:
Inertia constant (in MJ-s/elec deg)
[latex]M=\frac{GH}{180f}[/latex]
where,
G = Machine rating = 100MVA
H = Ineria constant in MJ/MVA = 5 MJ/MVA
[latex]\begin{aligned} M&=\frac{GH}{180f}=\frac{5 \times 100}{180 \times 50} \\ &=0.056\; \text{MJ-s/elec deg }\\ M_{in \; pu}&= \frac{H}{180f}=\frac{5}{180 \times 50}\\ \alpha &= \text{Acceleration in elect deg/sec}\\ M\alpha &=P_a \\ P_a&= \text{Accelerating power}=X \\ \alpha &= \frac{P_a}{M}=\frac{X}{(5/180 \times 50)}\\ &= 1800 \; \text{X elec deg/sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Initially, main thyristor (m) and auxiliary thyristor (A) are off and capacitor is assumed charged to voltage V with upper plate positive. When 'm' is turned on at t=0, source voltage V is applied across load and load current [latex]I_0[/latex] begins to flow which is assumed to remain constant.
With 'm' ON at t=0, anotheroscillatory circuit consisting of C, m, L and D is formed where the capacitor current is given by

When, [latex]\omega _0 t=\pi, i_c=0[/latex]
Between [latex]0 \\lt t \\lt \frac{\pi}{\omega _0}, i_{T1}=I_0+I_P \sin \omega _0 t[/latex] capacitor voltage charges from [latex]+V_s \; to \; -V_s[/latex] sinusoidally and the lower plate becomes positive.
At [latex]\omega _0 t=\pi, i_c=0, i_{T1}=I_0 \text{ and }V_c=-V_s[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{min}&=\frac{\pi}{\omega _0}=\pi\sqrt{LC} \\ &= \pi\sqrt{2 \times 10^{-3} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}}=140\mu s \end{aligned}[/latex]

Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2\\ -2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

[latex]A[/latex] satisfies the relation
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} A&= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2\\ -1& 0 \end{bmatrix}\\ |A-\lambda I|&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} -3-\lambda & 2\\ -1 & 0-\lambda \end{vmatrix}&= 0\ (-3-\lambda )(-\lambda )+2&=0 \\ \lambda ^2+3\lambda +2 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
A will satisfy this equation according to cayley hamition theorem
i.e. [latex]A^2+3A+2I=0[/latex]
multiplying by [latex]A^{-1}[/latex] on both sides we get
[latex]A^{-1}A^2+3A^{-1}A+2A^{-1}I=0[/latex]
[latex]A+3I+2A^{-1}=0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2\\ -2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

[latex]A^9[/latex] equals
raw_source.solution:
To calculate [latex]A^9[/latex]
start from [latex]A^2+3A+2I=0[/latex] which has been derived above
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \; A^2 &=-3A-2I \\ AA^4&=A^2 \times A^2 \\ &= (-3A-2I)(-3A-2I)\\ &=9A^2+12A+4I \\ &= 9(-3A-2I)+12A+4I\\ &= -15A-14I\\ A^8&=A^4 \times A^4 \\ &= (-15A-14I)(-15A-14I)\\ &=225A^2+420A+156I \\ &=225(-3A-2I)+420A+196I \\ &=-225A-254I \\ A^9&=A \times A^8 \\ &=A(-255A-254I) \\ &=-255A^2-254A \\ &=-255(-3A-2I)-254A \\ &= 511A+510I \end{aligned}[/latex]

A single phase full-wave half-controlled bridge converter feeds an inductive load.
The two SCRs in the converter are connected to a common DC bus. The converter
has to have a freewheeling diode.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]1-\phi[/latex] full wave half controlled bridge converter without free wheeling diode is shown in the figure.

At [latex]\omega t=\alpha , T_1[/latex] is fired and [latex] T_1[/latex] starts conducting load current flows through [latex]T_1D_1[/latex] for [latex]\alpha \lt \omega t \lt \pi[/latex].
At [latex]\omega t=\pi, V_s[/latex] becomes negative and At [latex]D_1[/latex] gets reverse biased and [latex]D_2[/latex] is forward biased. So during [latex]\pi \lt \omega t \lt \pi+\alpha[/latex], free wheeling action takes place through [latex]T_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] and output voltage becomes zeros.
At [latex]\omega t=\pi+\alpha[/latex], Load [latex]T_2[/latex] is triggered and load current is transferred from [latex]T_1[/latex] to [latex]T_2[/latex]. So, during [latex]\pi +\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi[/latex], [latex]T_2D_2[/latex] conducts.
At [latex]\omega t=\pi+\alpha[/latex], It may be possible that load current is not transferred completely from [latex]T_1[/latex] to [latex]T_2[/latex], and [latex]T_1[/latex] and [latex]T_2[/latex] may be conducting simultaneously which results in short circuit of the supply for short direction.
options: because the converter inherently does not provide for free-wheeling
because the converter does not provide for free-wheeling for high values of triggering angles

or else the free-wheeling action of the converter will cause shorting of the
AC supply

or else if a gate pulse to one of the SCRs is missed, it will subsequently
cause a high load current in the other SCR.

or else the free-wheeling action of the converter will cause shorting of the
AC supply

A three phase balanced star connected voltage source with frequency [latex]\omega[/latex] rad/s is connected to a star connected balanced load which is purely inductive. The instantaneous line currents and phase to neutral voltages are denoted by ([latex]i_{a},i_{b},i_{c}[/latex]) and ([latex]v_{an},v_{bn},v_{cn}[/latex]) respectively, and their rms values are denoted by V and I.

If [latex]R=[v_{an}\; v_{bn}\; v_{cn}]\begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}& 0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], then the magnitude of R is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]R=\begin{bmatrix} V_{an} &V_{bn} &V_{cn} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}& -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} i_a\\ i_b\\ i_c \end{bmatrix}\;...(i)[/latex]
Assuming phase sequence abc, taking [latex]V_{an}[/latex] as the reference,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{an}&=V\angle 0^{\circ}; \\ V_{bn}&=V\angle -120^{\circ}; \\ V_{cn}&=V\angle 120^{\circ};\;\;...(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
V is the rms value of [latex]V_{an}, V_{bn}[/latex] and [latex]V_{cn}[/latex]
I is the rms value of [latex]i_{a}, i_{b}[/latex] and [latex]i_{c}[/latex]
From equation (ii), we can say
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{an}&=\sqrt{2}V \sin \omega t;\\ V_{bn}&=\sqrt{2}V \sin (\omega t-120^{\circ}); \\ V_{cn}&=\sqrt{2}V \sin (\omega t+120^{\circ});\;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
and similarly due to lagging load
[latex]\begin{aligned} i_{a}&=\sqrt{2}I \sin (\omega t-90^{\circ});\\ i_{b}&=\sqrt{2}I \sin (\omega t-90-120^{\circ}); \\ i_{c}&=\sqrt{2}I \sin (\omega t-90+120^{\circ}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From equation (iii) by considering line values of voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{ab}&=\sqrt{6}V \sin (\omega t+30^{\circ});\\ V_{bc}&=\sqrt{6}V \sin (\omega t-90^{\circ}); \\ V_{ac}&=\sqrt{6}V \sin (\omega t+150^{\circ}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From equation (i), we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=-\left [ \frac{V_{bn}-V_{cn}}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{V_{cn}-V_{cn}}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{V_{an}-V_{bn}}{\sqrt{3}} \right ]\begin{bmatrix} i_a\\ i_b\\ i_c \end{bmatrix}\\ &=-[(\sqrt{2}V \sin (\omega t-90^{\circ}))(\sqrt{2}I \sin (\omega t-90^{\circ}))\\ &+(\sqrt{2}V \sin (\omega t+150^{\circ}))(\sqrt{2}I \sin (\omega t+150^{\circ}))\\ &+(\sqrt{2}V \sin (\omega t+30^{\circ}))(\sqrt{2}I \sin (\omega t+30^{\circ}))]\\ \because \; &\left ( \sin A \sin B= \frac{\cos (A-B)-\cos (A+B)}{2}\right )\\ &=-[VI-VI \cos (2\omega t+180^{\circ})+VI\\ & -VI \cos (2\omega t+300^{\circ})+VI-VI \cos (2\omega t+60^{\circ})+]\\ &=-[3VI-VI \cos (2\omega t-180^{\circ})\\ &+ \cos (2\omega t+300^{\circ})+ \cos (2\omega t+60^{\circ})]\\ &=R=-3VI\\ &=|R|=3VI \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The system [latex]\frac{900}{s(s+1)(s+9)}[/latex] is to be compensated such that its gain-crossover frequency
becomes same as its uncompensated phase crossover frequency and provides a 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] phase margin. To achieve this, one may use
raw_source.solution:
Let uncompensated syatem,
[latex]T(s)=\frac{900}{s(s+1)(s+9)} [/latex]
Phase crossover frequency of uncompensated system [latex]=(\omega _{pc})[/latex], at this frequency phase of [latex]T(j \omega )[/latex] is [latex]-180^{\circ}[/latex]
Put [latex] s=j\omega \text{ in } T(s) [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} T(j\omega )&=\frac{900}{j\omega (j\omega +1)(j\omega +9)} \\ \angle T(j\omega )&=-90^{\circ}-tan ^{-1}\omega -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right ) \\ \text{At, } & (\omega _{pc})_1,\angle T(j\omega )=-180^{\circ}\\ -180^{\circ}&=-90^{\circ}-tan^{-1}(\omega _{pc})_1 -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9} \right )\\ -90^{\circ}&=tan^{-1}\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1+\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9}}{1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}} \\ \Rightarrow 1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow (\omega _{pc})_1&= 3 \text{ rad/sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Gain cross frequency of compensated system, [latex](\omega _{gc})_2[/latex]= phase cross frequency of uncompensated system, [latex](\omega _{pc})_1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;(\omega _{gc})_2=(\omega _{gc})_1=\; 3[/latex] rad/sec
Phase-margin [latex]=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{gc})_2} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \; \; 45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{pc})_2} [/latex]
At [latex] (\omega _{gc})_2=3[/latex] rad/sec,
phase angle of [latex]\angle T(j\omega )[/latex] is [latex] -135^{\circ}[/latex] and phase of uncompensated systen is [latex]-180^{\circ}[/latex] at 3 rad/sec.
Therefore, the compensator provides phase lead of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] at the frequency of 3 rad/sec.
Let X dB is the gain provided by the compensator, so at gain cross frequency, [latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}[/latex]=1 or 0 dB. Gain of uncompensated system [latex]=|T(j\omega )|_{un-com} =\frac{100}{\omega \sqrt{1+\omega ^2}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}} [/latex]
[latex]|T(j\omega )|_{un-com}[/latex] in dB
[latex]\;=40-20 \log \omega -20 \log \sqrt{1+\omega ^2} -20 \log \sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}[/latex]
Gain of compensated system,

raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]g(1)=g(2)=1[/latex]
i.e. [latex]g[n]=\delta [n-1]+\delta [n-2][/latex]
Therefore,
[latex]G(z)=z^{-1}+z^{-2}[/latex]
Therefore overall transfer function of closed loop system,
[latex]\begin{aligned} T(z)&=\frac{G(z)}{1-kG(z)} \\ &=\frac{z^{-1}+z^{-2}}{1-k(z^{-1}+z^{-2})} \\ &= \frac{z+1}{z^2-k(z+1)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So the system will be stable if it's outer most pole will lie inside the unit circle.
Location of poles,
[latex]\begin{aligned} z=\frac{+k\pm \sqrt{k^2+4k}}{2}\\ \frac{k+ \sqrt{k^2+4k}}{2} \lt 1\\ k+ \sqrt{k^2+4k} \lt 2\\ \sqrt{k^2+4k} \lt (2-k)\\ k^2+4k \lt (2-k)^2\\ k^2+4k \lt 4+k^2-4k\\ 8k \lt 4\\ k \lt \frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A 230 V (Phase), 50 Hz, three-phase, 4-wire, system has a phase sequence ABC.
A unity power-factor load of 4 kW is connected between phase A and neutral N.
It is desired to achieve zero neutral current through the use of a pure inductor
and a pure capacitor in the other two phases. The value of inductor and capacitor
is
raw_source.solution:
Taking [latex]V_{AN}[/latex] as the reference
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{AN}&=230\angle 0^{\circ} V\\ V_{BN}&=230\angle -120^{\circ}V \\ V_{CN}&=230\angle 120^{\circ}V \\ I_A&= \frac{P}{V_{AN} \cos \phi }\\ &= \frac{4 \times 10^3}{230 \times 1}\\ &=17.4\angle 0^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
If an pure inductor is present in phase B, then [latex]I_B[/latex] lags [latex]V_{BN}[/latex] by [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex].
If a pure capacitor is present in phase C, then [latex]I_C[/latex] leads [latex]V_{CN}[/latex] by [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex].
If current through neutral is to be zero.
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_B \sin 30^{\circ} &=I_C \sin 30^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow \; I_B &=I_C=I \\ I_A&=I_B \cos 30^{\circ} +I_C \cos 30^{\circ} \\ &=2I \cos 30^{\circ}=\sqrt{3}I \\ |I_B|&=|I_C|=|I|=\frac{|I_A|}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \frac{17.04}{\sqrt{3}}=10.05\\ |I_B|&=\frac{|V_{BN}|}{\omega L} \\ 10.05 &=\frac{230}{2 \pi \times 50 \times L} \\ L&=72.847 mH \\ |I_C| &=|V_{CN}| \cdot \omega C\\ 10.05&=230 \times 2 \times \pi \times 50 \times C \\ C&=139.087 \mu F \end{aligned}[/latex]

42.12 mH in Phase B and 240.79 [latex]\mu[/latex]F in Phase C

raw_source.text: The circuit in the figure is a current commutated dc-dc chopper where, [latex]Th_M[/latex] is the main SCR and [latex]Th_{AUX}[/latex] is the auxiliary SCR. The load current is constant at 10 A. [latex]Th_M[/latex] is ON. [latex]Th_{AUX}[/latex] is trigged at t = 0. [latex]Th_M[/latex] is turned OFF between.
raw_source.solution:
At [latex]t=0^-,v_c=V_s, i_c=0\; and \; i_{T1}=I_0[/latex]
At t=0, [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex] is triggered, a resonant current [latex]i_c[/latex] designs to flow from C through [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex], L and back to C.
This resonant current is given by
[latex]i_c=-V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
[latex]i_c=-I_P \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
after half a cycle of [latex]i_c\left \{ t_1=\frac{\pi}{\omega _0} \right \}[/latex]; [latex]i_c=0, v_c=-V_s \; and \; i_{T1}=I_0[/latex]. As [latex]i_c[/latex] tends to reverse, [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex] is turned off.
When [latex]v_c=-V_s[/latex] right hand plate has positive polarity, resonant current [latex]i_c[/latex] now builds up through C, L, D and [latex]Th_m[/latex]. As this current [latex]i_c[/latex] grows opposite to forward thyristor current of [latex]Th_m[/latex], net forward current [latex]i_m=I_0-i_c[/latex] begins to decrease. Finalyy when [latex]i_c[/latex] in the reversed direction attains the value [latex]I_0, i_m[/latex] is reduced to zero and [latex]Th_m[/latex] is turned off.
[latex]i_m=I_0-i_c=I_0-I_p \sin \omega _0\Delta t=0[/latex]
[latex]\Delta t=\frac{1}{\omega _0}\sin ^{-1}\left ( \frac{I_0}{I_p} \right )[/latex]
So, [latex]Th_m[/latex]is turned off between
[latex]t_1 \lt t \lt t_1+\Delta t[/latex]
[latex]t_1 =\frac{\pi}{\omega _0}= \pi \sqrt{LC}=\pi \times \sqrt{10 \times 25.28}=50\mu sec[/latex]
Since commutation of [latex]Th_m[/latex] starts from [latex]t_1=50\mu sec[/latex].

A 3 V DC supply with an internal resistance of 2 [latex]\Omega[/latex] supplies a passive non-linear

raw_source.text: Consider the feedback system shown below which is subjected to a unit step input. The system is stable and has following parameters [latex]k_{p}=4,k_{i}=10,\omega =500 \; and \; \xi =0.7[/latex]. The steady state value of z is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]Step-input \; \Rightarrow R\; (s)=1/s[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned}G(s)&=\left ( k_p+\frac{k_i}{s} \right )\left ( \frac{\omega ^2}{s^2 +2\xi \omega s+\omega ^2} \right ) \\ \text{and } H(s)&=1\\ \frac{C(s)}{R(s)}&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)}\\ &=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)} \\ E(s)&=R(s)-C(s) \\&=R(s)\left [ 1-\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} \right ] \\&=R(s)\left [ 1-\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)} \right ]\\ &=\frac{R(s)}{1+G(s)} \\ Z(s)&=\frac{k_i}{s}E(s)=\frac{\frac{k_i}{s}\cdot R(s)}{1+G(s)} \\ \text{Steady} &\text{ state value of Z,} \\Z_{ss}&=\lim_{s \to 0}sZ(s) \\ &=\lim_{s \to 0}\frac{s\cdot \frac{k_i}{s}\cdot \frac{1}{s}}{1+\left ( k_p+\frac{k_i}{s} \right )\left ( \frac{\omega ^2}{s^2 +2\xi \omega s+\omega ^2} \right )} \\ &=\frac{k_i}{k_i\frac{\omega ^2}{\omega ^2}}=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A three-phase squirrel cage induction motor has a starting torque of 150% and a maximum torque of 300% with respect to rated torque at rated voltage and rated
frequency. Neglect the stator resistance and rotational losses. The value of slip
for maximum torque is
raw_source.solution:
Assuming rated torque [latex]=T_{rated}[/latex]
Starting torque
[latex]T_s=150\% \; \text{of} \; T_{rated}=1.5T_{rated}[/latex]
Maximum torque,
[latex]T_m=300\% \; \text{of} \; T_{rated}=3.0T_{rated}[/latex]
as we know,
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_s &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2}{{R'_2}^2+{X'_2}^2}\\ T_m &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{0.5V^2}{X'_2} \\ \frac{T_m}{T_s}&= \frac{0.5}{X'_2} \frac{{R'_2}^2 \times {X'_2}^2}{R'_2}\\ &= 0.5\left [ \frac{(R_2/X'_2)^2 +1}{(R'_2/X'_2)} \right ] \end{aligned} [/latex]
as we know, maximum torque occurs at
[latex]\begin{aligned} s_m &=\frac{R'_2}{X'_2} \\ \frac{T_m}{T_s} &= 0.5\left ( \frac{{s_m}^2 +1}{s_m} \right )\\ \frac{3T_{rated}}{1.5T_{rated}}&=0.5 \left ( \frac{{s_m}^2 +1}{s_m} \right ) \\ {s_m}^2 -4s_m +1&=0 \\ s_m&= 3.73 \; \text{or} \; 0.2679 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]s_m=3.73[/latex] is rejected, as for this value of slip motor works in braking mode. Therefore, for motoring mode [latex]s_m=0.2679[/latex] or [latex]26.79\%[/latex]

raw_source.text: A bridge circuit is shown in the figure below. Which one of the sequence given below is most suitable for balancing the bridge ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]x_1=\omega L_1 [/latex] and [latex] x_4=\frac{1}{\omega C_4} [/latex]
[latex]z_1=R_1+jx_1=R_1+j\omega L_1 [/latex]
[latex]z_2=R_2 [/latex]
[latex]z_3=R_3 [/latex]
[latex]z_4=R_4-jx_4=R_4-\frac{j}{\omega C_4} [/latex]
Under balanced condition
[latex]z_1z_4=z_2z_3[/latex]
[latex] (R_1+j\omega L_1)(R_4-jx_4)=R_2R_3 [/latex]
[latex]\left ( R_1R_4+\frac{L_1}{C_4} \right )+j\left ( \omega L_1R_4-\frac{R_1}{\omega C_4} \right )=R_2R_3[/latex]
Equating real and imaginary terms, we obtain
[latex]R_1R_4+\frac{L_1}{C_4} =R_2R_3 [/latex]
[latex]\omega L_1R_4-\frac{R_1}{\omega C_4}=0[/latex]
Solving above equations, we get
[latex]L_1=\frac{R_2R_3C_4}{1+\omega ^2C_4^2R_4^2} [/latex]
and [latex]R_2=\frac{\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2}{1+\omega ^2C_4^2R_4^2} [/latex]
Q-factor of the coil [latex]Q=\frac{\omega L_1}{R_1}=\frac{1}{\omega C_4R_4} [/latex]
Therefore, [latex]L_1=\frac{R_2R_3C_4}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{Q} \right )^2}\;\;...(i) [/latex]
[latex]R_1=\frac{\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{Q} \right )^2}\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
For a value of a greater than 10, the term [latex](1/Q)^2[/latex] will be smaller than 1/1000 and can be neglected. Therefore equation (i) and (ii) reduces to
[latex]L_1=R_2R_3C_4 \;\;...(iii) [/latex]
[latex]R_1=\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2\;\;...(iv)[/latex]
[latex] R_4[/latex] appears only in equation (iv) and [latex]R_2[/latex] appears in both equation (iii) and (iv).
So first [latex]R_2[/latex] is adjusted and then [latex]R_4[/latex] is adjusted.

raw_source.text: Consider function  [latex]f (x) =(x^{2}-4)^{2}[/latex] where x is a real number. Then the function has
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x) &=(x^2-4)^2 \\ f'(x)&=2(x^2-4) \times 2x \\ &= 4x(x^2-4)=0\\ & x=0, \; x=2 \; \text{and} \; x=-2 \\ & \text{are the stationary points}\\ f''(x)&=4[x(2x)+(x^2-4) \times 1] \\ &= 4[2x^2+x^2-4]\\ &= 12x^2-16\\ f''(0)&=-16 \lt 0\; \text{ maxima at } x=0 \\ f'(2)&=(12)2^2-16 \\ &= 32 \gt 0\text{ minima at } x=2\\ f'(-2)&=12(-2)^2-16 \\ &= 32 \gt 0\text{ minima at } x=-2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Equation [latex]e^{x} - 1 = 0[/latex] is required to be solved using Newton's method with an initial guess [latex]x_0=-1[/latex]. Then, after one step of Newton's method, estimate [latex]x_1[/latex] of the solution will be given by
raw_source.solution:
Here, [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=e^x-1\\ f(x)&=e^x \end{aligned}[/latex]
The newton raphson iterative equation is
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{i+1}&=x_i-\frac{f(x_i)}{f'(x_i)}\\ f(x_i)&=e^{xi}-1\\ f'(x_i)&=e^{xi}\\ \therefore \;\; x_{i+1}&=x_i-\frac{e^{x_i}-1}{e^{x_i}}\\ i.e.\;\;x_{i+1}&=\frac{x_ie^{x_i}-(e^{x_i}-1)}{e^{x_i}}\\ &=\frac{e^{x_i}(x_i-1)+1}{e^{x_i}}\\ \text{Now put }i&=0\\ x_1&=\frac{e^{x_0}(x_0-1)+1}{e^{x_0}}\\ \text{put, }x_0&=-1 \text{ as given,}\\ x_1&=[e^{-1}(-2)+1]/e^{-1}\\ &=0.71828 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system with x(t) and output y(t) is defined by the input-output relation :

[latex]y(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau)d\tau[/latex]

The system will be
raw_source.solution:
First of all we will check for causality,
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau ) d\tau \\ \text{So for }t&=2 \\ y(-2)&=\int_{-\infty }^{4}x(\tau ) d\tau \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, output depends on future values of input along with past and present values of input, so system is non-casual.
Let us find output for shifted input [latex]x(t-t_0)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau -t_0) d\tau \\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{2(t-t_0)}x(\tau ) d\tau\;\;...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, shift the output by [latex]t_0[/latex]
then,
[latex]y(t-t_0)=\int_{-\infty }^{2(t-t_0)}x(\tau ) d\tau \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
so from eq. (i) and (ii),
[latex] y'(t) \neq y(t-t_0)[/latex]
Therefore system is time varient.
Non-causal and time variant is present only in option (D).

[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=h(t)*x(t)\\ Y(j\omega )&=X(j\omega )H(j\omega ) \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\frac{1}{\beta }Sa( \pi \alpha t)\;\;\; if \; \alpha \lt \beta \\ y(t)&=\frac{1}{\beta } \sin c(\alpha t)\;\;\; if \; \alpha \lt \beta \\ y(t)&=\frac{1}{\alpha }\sin c( \beta t)\;\;\; if \; \alpha \gt \beta \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, output is of the form [latex]k \sin c (\gamma t)[/latex]

Let x(t) be a periodic signal with time period T, Let [latex]y(t)=x(t-t_0)+x(t+t_0)[/latex]
for some [latex]t_0[/latex]. The Fourier Series coefficients of y(t) are denoted by [latex]b_k[/latex]. If [latex]b_k=0[/latex] for
all odd k , then [latex]t_0[/latex] can be equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]y(t)=x(t-t_0)+x(t+x_0)[/latex]
Since, [latex]x(t)[/latex] is periodic with period T.
Therefore, [latex]x(t-t_0)[/latex] and [latex]x(t+t_0)[/latex] will also be periodic with period T.
[latex]\therefore \; b_k=a_ke^{-jk\omega _0t_0}+a_ke^{jk\omega _0t_0}[/latex]
[latex]a_k [/latex] is Fourier series coefficient of signal [latex]x(t)[/latex]
therefore,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \; b_k&=a_k(e^{-jk\omega _0t_0}+e^{jk\omega _0t_0}) \\ b_k&=2a_k \cos k\omega _0t_0 \\ \text{since, }b_k &=0 \text{ for odd k} \\ \text{i.e. } k\omega _0t_0&=k\frac{\pi}{2}\\ \text{ where } k&=\pm 1,\pm 3,\pm 5... \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \omega _0t_0 &=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ t_0&=\frac{\pi}{2} \times \frac{T}{2 \pi}=\frac{T}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: H(z) is a transfer function of a real system. When a signal [latex]x[n] =(1+j)^{n}[/latex] is the input to such a system, the output is zero. Further, the Region of convergence (ROC) of [latex](1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1})[/latex]H(z) is the entire Z-plane (except z = 0). It can then be inferred that H(z) can have a minimum of
Given [latex]X(z)=\frac{z}{(z-a)^2}[/latex] with [latex]|z| \gt a[/latex], the residue of [latex]X(z)z^{n-1}[/latex] at z=a for [latex]n\geq 0[/latex] will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(z)&=\frac{z}{(z-a)^2}\\ \therefore \; z^{n-1}X(z)&=\frac{z^n}{(z-a)^2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, z-a is a pole of second order, therefore residue at z=a
[latex]=\frac{d}{dz}\left [ (z-a)^2 \frac{z^n}{(z-a)^2}\right ]_{at\; z=a}=[nz^n-1]_{z=a}=na^{n-1}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider function  [latex]f (x) =(x^{2}-4)^{2}[/latex] where x is a real number. Then the function has
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x) &=(x^2-4)^2 \\ f'(x)&=2(x^2-4) \times 2x \\ &= 4x(x^2-4)=0\\ & x=0, \; x=2 \; \text{and} \; x=-2 \\ & \text{are the stationary points}\\ f''(x)&=4[x(2x)+(x^2-4) \times 1] \\ &= 4[2x^2+x^2-4]\\ &= 12x^2-16\\ f''(0)&=-16 \lt 0\; \text{ maxima at } x=0 \\ f'(2)&=(12)2^2-16 \\ &= 32 \gt 0\text{ minima at } x=2\\ f'(-2)&=12(-2)^2-16 \\ &= 32 \gt 0\text{ minima at } x=-2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, there is only one maxima and only two minima for this function.

raw_source.text: Equation [latex]e^{x} - 1 = 0[/latex] is required to be solved using Newton's method with an initial guess [latex]x_0=-1[/latex]. Then, after one step of Newton's method, estimate [latex]x_1[/latex] of the solution will be given by
raw_source.solution:
Here, [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=e^x-1\\ f(x)&=e^x \end{aligned}[/latex]
The newton raphson iterative equation is
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{i+1}&=x_i-\frac{f(x_i)}{f'(x_i)}\\ f(x_i)&=e^{xi}-1\\ f'(x_i)&=e^{xi}\\ \therefore \;\; x_{i+1}&=x_i-\frac{e^{x_i}-1}{e^{x_i}}\\ i.e.\;\;x_{i+1}&=\frac{x_ie^{x_i}-(e^{x_i}-1)}{e^{x_i}}\\ &=\frac{e^{x_i}(x_i-1)+1}{e^{x_i}}\\ \text{Now put }i&=0\\ x_1&=\frac{e^{x_0}(x_0-1)+1}{e^{x_0}}\\ \text{put, }x_0&=-1 \text{ as given,}\\ x_1&=[e^{-1}(-2)+1]/e^{-1}\\ &=0.71828 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A is [latex]m \times n[/latex] full rank matrix with [latex]m \gt n[/latex] and I is identity matrix. Let matrix
[latex]A^{+} = (A^{T}A)^{-1}A^{T}[/latex]. Then, which one of the following statement is FALSE ?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Choice (A) } AA^+A&=A \text{ is corect} \\ \text{Since, } AA^+A&=A[(A^TA)^{-1}A^T]A \\ &=A[(A^TA)^{-1}A^TA] \\ \text{Put, }A^TA&=P \\ &= A[P^{-1} P]\\ &= AI=A\\ \text{Choice (C) } A^+A&=I \text{ is also correct since} \\ A^+A&=(A^TA)^{-1}A^TA \\ &= P^{-1}P=I \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A differential equation [latex]\frac{dx}{dt} = e^{-2t}[/latex]u(t), has to be solved using trapezoidal rule of integration with a step size h=0.01s. Function u(t) indicates a unit step function. If x(0-)=0, then value of x at t=0.01s will be given by

raw_source.text: Let P be a 2x2 real orthogonal matrix and [latex]\vec{x}[/latex] is a real vector [latex][x_{1},x_{2}]^{T}[/latex] with length [latex]|\vec{x}|=(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})^{1/2}[/latex]. Then, which one of the following statements is correct?
raw_source.solution:
Let on orthogonal matrix
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Properly of orthogonal matrix A
[latex]\begin{aligned} AA^T &=I \\ \text{So }\vec{P_x} &=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \cos \theta -x_2 \sin \theta \\ x_1 \sin \theta +x_2 \cos \theta \end{bmatrix} \\ ||\vec{P_x}|| &=\sqrt{(x_1 \cos \theta -x_2 \sin \theta)^2+\sqrt{(x_1 \sin \theta +x_2 \cos \theta )^2}} \\ ||\vec{P_x}|| &=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2} \\ ||\vec{P_x}|| &= ||\bar{x}|| \text{ for any vector }\bar{x} \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: [latex]|P{\vec{x}}|\leq |\vec{x}|[/latex] where at least one vector satisfies [latex]|P{\vec{x}}|\lt|\vec{x}|[/latex]
[latex]|P{\vec{x}}|\geq |\vec{x}|[/latex] where at least one vector satisfies [latex]|P{\vec{x}}|\gt |\vec{x}|[/latex]
No relationship can be established between [latex]|{\vec{x}}| \; and \; |P\vec{x}|[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]x(t)= rect(t-\frac{1}{2}[/latex]) (where [latex]rect(x) = 1[/latex] for [latex]-\frac{1}{2}\leq x\leq \frac{1}{2}[/latex] and zero otherwise. Then if [latex]sinc(x)=\frac{sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}[/latex], the Fourier Transform of [latex]x(t) + x(-t)[/latex] will be given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
x(t)&= \text{rect}[t-1/2]\\
x(t)&=1 \;\;\;0\leq t\leq 1\\
    &=0 \;\;\; \text{otherwise}\\
F[x(t)]&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt\\
&=\int_{0}^{1}1e^{-j\omega t}dt=\frac{1}{j\omega }(1-e^{-j\omega })\\
&=\frac{2}{\omega }\left [ \frac{e^{j\omega t} -e^{-j\omega /2}}{2j} \right ]xe^{-j\omega /2}\\
&=\frac{\sin \omega /2}{\omega /2}\cdot e^{-j\omega /2}\\

&=2 \sin c\left ( \frac{\omega }{2 \pi} \right ) \cos \left ( \frac{\omega }{2} \right ) 
\end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]C_{2}(P_{G1})=3 P_{G2}+0.03 \times P^{2}_{G2}[/latex]

Solving equation (i) and (ii),
we get, [latex]P_{G1}=100MW[/latex] and [latex]P_{G2}=150MW[/latex]

A single-phase half controlled converter shown in the figure feeding power to highly inductive load. The converter is operating at a firing angle of 60[latex]^{\circ}[/latex].

If the firing pulses are suddenly removed, the steady state voltage ([latex]v_0[/latex]) waveform of the converter will become
raw_source.solution:
Single phase half controlled converter.
As load is highly inductive, it means laod current is continuous and almost constant.

[latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{During,}\\ &0 \lt \omega t \lt \alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_2D_1, V_0=0\\ &\alpha \lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ &T_1D_1 \text{ conducts }V_0=V_s\\ &\pi \lt \omega t \lt \pi+\alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_1D_2, V_0=0\\ &\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ &T_2D_2 \text{ conducts }V_0=-V_s\\ &T_1 \text{ is again triggered at }2 \pi+\alpha \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, during [latex]2\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 3\pi , T_1D_1[/latex] conducts.
Now, if firing pulses are removed after [latex]T_1[/latex] is triggered at [latex]2 \pi+\alpha[/latex].
At [latex]\omega t=3 \pi+\alpha[/latex], no firing pulse will be available to trigger [latex]T_2[/latex]. So, load current will flow through [latex]T_1D_2[/latex] as load current is continuos. So during [latex]3 \pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 4 \pi,\;\; T_1D_2[/latex] will continue to conduct and [latex]V_0=0[/latex].
At [latex]\omega t=4 \pi,\; D_1[/latex] will become forward biassed and [latex]D_2[/latex] will become reverse biased. So, [latex]D_1[/latex] will conduct and [latex]T_1[/latex] is already conducting.
So, load current will flow through [latex]T_1D_1[/latex] and [latex]V_0=V_s[/latex].

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Fault current}&=I_f=\frac{V_s}{Z_1}=\frac{1\angle 0^{\circ}}{0.002+j0.02}\\ &=49.75\angle -84.29 \; p.u.\\ |I_f|p.u.&=49.75\\ \text{Base current}&=\frac{\text{Base MVA}}{\sqrt{3} \times \text{Voltage Base}}kA\\ I_B&=\frac{100}{\sqrt{3} \times 400}kA\\ |I_f|&=|I_f|_{p.u.} \times I_B\\ &=49.75 \times \frac{100}{\sqrt{3} \times 400}\\ &=7.18 kA\\ I_x^f&=\frac{|I_f|}{2}=\frac{7.18}{2}kA=3.59kA \end{aligned}[/latex]

A 3-phase, 440 V, 50 Hz, 4-pole slip ring induction motor is feed from the rotor side through an auto-transformer and the stator is connected to a variable resistance as shown in the figure.

The motor is coupled to a 220 V, separately excited d.c generator feeding power to fixed resistance of 10 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. Two-wattmeter method is used to measure the input power to induction motor. The variable resistance is adjusted such the motor runs at 1410 rpm and the following readings were recorded

[latex]W_1=1800 W , W_2=-200 W[/latex].

The speed of rotation of stator magnetic field with respect to rotor structure will be
raw_source.solution:
If the three phase supply is given to the rotor winding through an autotransformer, the three phase rotor current will generate a rotating field in the air-gap, rotating at the synchronous speed woth respect to rotor. If the rotor is kept stationary, this rotating field will also rotate in the gap at the synchronous speed voltage and current will be induced in the stator winding and a torque will be developed. If rotor is allowed to move, it will rotate as per the Lenz's law, opposing the rotation of the rotating field decreasing the induced voltage in the stator winding. Thus at a particular speed, the frequency of the stator circuit will correspond to the slip speed.
Synchronous speed,
[latex]N_s=\frac{120f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500 \; \text{rpm} [/latex]
Rotor speed,
[latex]N_r=1410 \; \text{rpm} [/latex]
[latex]\text{Slip}=\frac{N_s-N_r}{N_s}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1500-1410}{1500}=0.06 [/latex]
Slip frequency induced in stator
[latex]sf=0.06 \times 50=3 Hz[/latex]
Slip speed [latex]= \frac{120 \times 3}{4}=90\; \text{rpm}[/latex]
As stator magnetic field rotates 90 rpm in the opposite direction of the rotation of rotor, therefore, speed of the stator field with respect to rotor [latex]=1410+90=1500 rpm[/latex]
options: 90 rpm in the direction of rotation
90 rpm in the opposite direction of rotation
1500 rpm in the direction of rotation
1500 rpm in the opposite direction of rotation

raw_answer.option_text: 1500 rpm in the opposite direction of rotation

The state space equation of a system is described by

[latex]\dot{x}=Ax+Bu[/latex],
[latex]y=Cx[/latex]

where [latex]x[/latex] is state vector, u is input, y is output and [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex]C=[1 \; \; 0][/latex]

The transfer function G(s) of this system will be
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{x}&=Ax+Bu \\ \text{and   }y&=Cx \\ \text{where, }  A&=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix} \\ B&=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\ C&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\ \text{ and  } D&=0 \\ [sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix}\\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s &-1 \\ 0 &s+2 \end{bmatrix} \\  [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{1}{s(s+2)}\begin{bmatrix} s+2 & 1\\ 0& s \end{bmatrix} \\ & \text{Transfer function} \\ &=C[sI-A]^{-1}B+D  \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 & 1\\ 0& s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+2)} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ s \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+2)} \\ &=\frac{1}{s(s+2)} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A unity feedback is provided to the above system G(s) to make it a closed loop system as shown in figure.

Steady state error, using final value theorem

[latex]\;\;\lim{s\rightarrow 0}\frac{s(s+2)}{s(s+2)+1}=0[/latex]

If [latex]R_1=R_2=R_A[/latex] and [latex]R_3=R_4=R_B[/latex], the circuit acts as a
raw_source.solution:
[latex]V_A=\frac{R_4}{R_4+R_3} \times V_i, [/latex]

raw_source.text: The single phase, 50 Hz iron core transformer in the circuit has both the vertical arms of cross sectional area 20 [latex]cm^2[/latex] and both the horizontal arms of cross sectional area 10 [latex]cm^2[/latex]. If the two windings shown were wound instead on opposite horizontal arms, the mutual inductance will
raw_source.solution:
Mutual inductance is where the flux of two or more coils are linked so that voltage is induced in one coil proportional to the rate of change of current in another.
The mutual inductance that exist between the coils can be greatly increased by positioning them on a common soft iron core or by increasing the number of turns of either coil.
Consider:
The changing flux on coil 1 is proportional to changing current in coil 2.
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_1 \frac{d\phi _{12}}{dt}&=M_{12}\frac{dI_2}{dt} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;M_{12} &=N_1 \frac{\phi _{12}}{I_2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly time rate of change of magnetic flux [latex]\phi _{21}[/latex] in coil 2 is proportional to time rate of change of current in coil 1
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_2 \frac{d\phi _{21}}{dt}&=M_{21}\frac{dI_1}{dt} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;M_{21} &=N_2 \frac{\phi _{21}}{I_1}\\ \text{Also} \;\; M_{12}&=M_{21}=M \end{aligned} [/latex]
We can observe that none of the parameters changes due to placing of coils on horizontal arms. Hence, mutual inductance will remain unchanged.

raw_source.text: A 3-phase squirrel cage induction motor supplied from a balanced 3-phase source drives a mechanical load. raw_source.solution:
Let torque developed by the motor [latex]=T_m[/latex]
Load torque [latex]=T_L[/latex]
Accelerating torque,[latex]T_a=T_m-T_L[/latex]
At point A,
[latex]T_m=T_L[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;T_a=T_m-T_L=0[/latex]
So, no accelerating , hence the motor rums at speed [latex]N_A[/latex].
When a smal disturbance decreases speed to [latex]N_c[/latex]
At point C,
[latex]T_m \gt T_L[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;T_a \gt 0[/latex]
So, motor will accelerate and comes to point A. When the disturbance increases speed to [latex]N_D[/latex].
At point D,
[latex]T_m \lt T_L[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;T_a \lt 0[/latex]
Motor will decelerate and comes at point A
So, motor is stable at point A.
When the motor is operating at point B.,
[latex]T_m = T_L[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;T_a= 0[/latex]
If a small disturbance decreases speed to [latex]N_E[/latex].
[latex]T_m \lt T_L[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;T_a \lt 0[/latex]
Motor will decelerate and motor speed will keep on decreasing.
If the disturbance increases speed to [latex]N_F[/latex].
At point F,
[latex]T_m \gt T_L[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;T_a \gt 0[/latex]
Motor will accelerate and motor speed will keep on increasing.
So, motor is unstable at point B.
options: A is stable, B is unstable
A is unstable, B is stable

[latex]G(s)=\frac{k\left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )}{s^2\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )}[/latex]
At [latex] \omega =0.1(\omega \leq 2 \;rad/sec)[/latex]
[latex] Gain(dB)=20 \log k-40 \log \omega [/latex]
[latex]80=20 \log k-40 \log 0.1 [/latex]

[latex]k=100 [/latex]
[latex]G(s)=\frac{100 \left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )}{s^2\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )} =\frac{1000(s+5)}{s^2(s+2)(s+25)}[/latex]

A cascade of three Linear Time Invariant systems is causal and unstable. From
this, we conclude that
raw_source.solution:
Since in cascade overall impulse response
[latex]h(t)=h_1(t)*h_2(t)*h_3(t)[/latex]
[latex]h_1(t),h_2(t),h_3(t)[/latex] are impulse response of individual systems.
Since, initial point where h(t) is nonzero is [latex]t \geq 0[/latex] and since in convolution initial point
[latex]=t_1+t_2+t_3[/latex]
where, [latex]t_1,t_2,t_3[/latex] are initial point of [latex]h_1(t), h_2(t),h_3(t)[/latex] respectively.
So for it to be greater than or equal to zero at least one of them [latex]t_1, t_2\; or \; t_3[/latex] must be +ve i.e. greater than zero so atleast one of them must be causal. Similarly if one (atleast) of the system become unstable then overall system will become unstable.
options: each system in the cascade is individually causal and unstable
at least on system is unstable and at least one system is causal
at least one system is causal and all systems are unstable
the majority are unstable and the majority are causal

raw_answer.option_text: at least on system is unstable and at least one system is causal

raw_source.text: The Fourier Series coefficients of a periodic signal x(t), expressed as [latex]x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }a_{k}e^{j2 \pi kt/T}[/latex] are given by [latex]a_{-2}=2-j1[/latex], [latex]a_{-1}=0.5+j0.2[/latex], [latex]a_{0}=j2[/latex], [latex]a_{1}=0.5-j0.2[/latex], [latex]a_{2}=2+j1[/latex] and [latex]a_{k}=0[/latex] for [latex]|k| \gt 2[/latex] Which of the following is true ?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} x(t)&=a_{-2}e^{-j2\omega _0t}+a_{-1}e^{-j\omega _0t}\\ &+a_{1}e^{j\omega _0t} +a_{2}e^{j2\omega _0t}\\ &=(2-j)e^{-j2\omega _0t}+(2+j)e^{j2\omega _0t}\\ &+(0.5+j0.2)e^{-j\omega _0t}+(0.5-j0.2)e^{j\omega _0t}+2j\\ &=2(e^{-j2\omega _0t}+e^{j2\omega _0t})+j(e^{j2\omega _0t}-e^{-j2\omega _0t})\\ &+0.5(e^{j\omega _0t}+e^{-j\omega _0t})-j0.2(e^{j\omega _0t}-e^{-j\omega _0t})+2j\\ &=4 \cos 2\omega _0t-2 \sin 2\omega _0t+ \cos \omega _0t \\ &+0.4 \sin \omega _0t+2j\\ &=\text{Real}[x(t)]+j\text{Img}[x(t)]\\ &\text{where,}\\ \text{Real}[x(t)]&=4 \cos 2\omega _0t-2 \sin 2\omega _0t+ \cos \omega _0t \\ &+0.4 \sin \omega _0t\\ &= \text{neither even nor odd signal}\\ \text{Img}[x(t)]&=2=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: x(t) has finite energy because only finitely many coefficients are non-zero
x(t) has zero average value because it is periodic
The imaginary part of x(t) is constant
The real part of x(t) is even

raw_answer.option_text: The imaginary part of x(t) is constant

equation of starting line [latex]\frac{y-y_1}{x-x_1}=\frac{y_1-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\Rightarrow \;y=2-x\;\;\;dy=-dx[/latex]
[latex]\bar{F}\cdot \bar{dl}=(x^2+xy)dx+(y^2+xy)dy[/latex]
Putting [latex]y=2-x[/latex] and [latex]dy=-dx[/latex]
[latex]\int \bar{F}\cdot \bar{dl}=\int_{0}^{2}2xdx-\int_{0}^{2}(4-2x)dx=0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system is described by the following state and output equations
[latex]\frac{dx_1(t)}{dt}=-3x_1(t)+x_2(t)+2u(t)[/latex]
[latex]\frac{dx_2(t)}{dt}=-2x_2(t)+u(t)[/latex]
[latex]y(t)=x_1(t)[/latex]
when u(t) is the input and y(t) is the output

The system transfer function is
raw_source.solution:
Selecting [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] as state variable,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{x}_1(t)&=\frac{dx_1(t)}{dt} \\&=-3x_1(t)+x_2(t)+2u(t) \\ \dot{x}_2(t)&=\frac{dx_2(t)}{dt} =-2x_2(t)+u(t) \\ \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1(t)\\ \dot{x}_2(t) \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u(t) \\ \dot{x}&=AX+BU \\ \text{So, } A&=\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix}, \; B=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\ y(t)&=x_1(t) \\ y(t)&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix} \\ y&=CX+DU \\ \text{So, } C&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix} \text{ and } D=0 \\ [sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s+3 &-1\\ 0& s+2 \end{bmatrix} \\ [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 &1\\ 0& s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)} \\ &\text{Transfer function} \\ &=C[sI-A]^{-1}B+D \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 &1\\ 0& s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)}\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}+0 \\ &=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2(s+2)+1\\ s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{2s+5}{(s+2)(s+3)}=\frac{2s+5}{s^2+5s+6}\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An eigenvector of [latex]P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1&0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0&0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 &0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0& 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
P is triangular. So eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves. Eigen values are therefore, [latex]\lambda _1=1,\lambda _2=2,\lambda _3=3.[/latex]
Now, the eigen value problem is [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda &1 &0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 2\\ 0& 0 &3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda _1=1[/latex], we get the eigen vector corresponding to this eigen value,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 0&1 &0 \\ 0 & 1& 2\\ 0& 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=0 \\ x_2+2x_3&=0 \\ 2x_3 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The solution is [latex]x_2=0, x_3=0, x_1=k[/latex]
So, one eigen vector is [latex]\hat{x_1}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=k:0:0[/latex]
Since, none of the eigen vectors given in choises matches with this, ratio we need to proceed further and find the other eigen vectors corresponding to the other eigen values.
Now, corresponding to [latex]\lambda _2=2,[/latex] we get by substituting [latex]\lambda =2,[/latex], in the eigen value problem, the following set of equations,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -1&1 &0 \\ 0 & 0& 2\\ 0& 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} -x_1+x_2&=0 \\ 2x_3&=0 \\ x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solution is [latex]x_3=0, x_1=k, x_2=k[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_2}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:1:0[/latex]
Since none of the eigen vectors given in the choises is of this ratio, we need to proceed further and find 3rd eigen vector also.
By putting [latex]\lambda =3,[/latex] in the eigen value problem, we get
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -2&1 &0 \\ 0 & -1& 2\\ 0& 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} -2x_1+x_2&=0 \\ -x_2+2x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
putting [latex]x_1=k[/latex], we get, [latex]x_2=2k[/latex] and [latex]x_3=k[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_3}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 2k\\ k \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:2:1[/latex]
Only the eigen vector geven in choise [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is in this ratio.

raw_source.text: For the differential equation [latex]\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+8x=0[/latex] with initial conditions x(0) = 1 and [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}|_{t=0}=0[/latex], the solution is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
\text{Given,  }\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+8x=0\\
x(0)=1\text{  and   }\left.\begin{matrix}
\frac{dx}{dt}
\end{matrix}\right|_{t=0}=0\\
D^2+6D+8=0\\
(D+4)(D+2)=0\\
D=-2, D=-4\\
\therefore \;\;\text{ Solution is }\\
x=C_1e^{-2t}+C_2e^{-4t}\\
\text{Since,   }x(0)=1\\
\text{We have  }C_1+C_2=1\;\;...(i)\\
\frac{dx}{dt}=-2C_1e^{-2t}-4C_2e^{-4t}\\
\text{Since,   }\left [ \frac{dx}{dt} \right ]_{t=0}=0, \text{  we have}\\
-2C_1-4C_2=0\;\;\;...(ii)\\
\text{Solving (i) and (ii) we have } \\ C_1=2 \; and \;C_2=-1\\
\text{So the solution is }\\
x(t)=2e^{-2t}-e^{-4t} 
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The zero-sequence circuit of the three phase transformer shown in the figure
raw_source.solution:
Equivalent circuit for the zero sequence network depends upon the impedances met by the zero sequence currents flowing through the three phases and their sum, [latex]3I_{a0}[/latex], flowing through the neutral impedance and returning through the ground or a neutral conductor.
If there is no complete path for zero sequence currents in a circuit, the zero sequence impedance is infinite.
Thus a Y-connected circuit with ungrounded neutral has infinite impedance to zero sequence currents.
A delta-connected circuit provides no path for zero sequence currents flowing in the line. The zero sequence currents being single phase, circulate within the winding. Hence viewed from its terminals its zero sequence impedance is infinite.

raw_source.text: An eigenvector of [latex]P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1&0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0&0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 &0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0& 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
P is triangular. So eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves. Eigen values are therefore, [latex]\lambda _1=1,\lambda _2=2,\lambda _3=3.[/latex]
Now, the eigen value problem is [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda &1 &0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 2\\ 0& 0 &3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda _1=1[/latex], we get the eigen vector corresponding to this eigen value,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 0&1 &0 \\ 0 & 1& 2\\ 0& 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=0 \\ x_2+2x_3&=0 \\ 2x_3 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The solution is [latex]x_2=0, x_3=0, x_1=k[/latex]
So, one eigen vector is [latex]\hat{x_1}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=k:0:0[/latex]
Since, none of the eigen vectors given in choises matches with this, ratio we need to proceed further and find the other eigen vectors corresponding to the other eigen values.
Now, corresponding to [latex]\lambda _2=2,[/latex] we get by substituting [latex]\lambda =2,[/latex], in the eigen value problem, the following set of equations,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -1&1 &0 \\ 0 & 0& 2\\ 0& 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} -x_1+x_2&=0 \\ 2x_3&=0 \\ x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solution is [latex]x_3=0, x_1=k, x_2=k[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_2}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:1:0[/latex]
Since none of the eigen vectors given in the choises is of this ratio, we need to proceed further and find 3rd eigen vector also.
By putting [latex]\lambda =3,[/latex] in the eigen value problem, we get
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -2&1 &0 \\ 0 & -1& 2\\ 0& 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} -2x_1+x_2&=0 \\ -x_2+2x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
putting [latex]x_1=k[/latex], we get, [latex]x_2=2k[/latex] and [latex]x_3=k[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_3}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 2k\\ k \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:2:1[/latex]
Only the eigen vector geven in choise [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is in this ratio.

raw_source.text: For the differential equation [latex]\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+8x=0[/latex] with initial conditions x(0) = 1 and [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}|_{t=0}=0[/latex], the solution is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
\text{Given,  }\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+8x=0\\
x(0)=1\text{  and   }\left.\begin{matrix}
\frac{dx}{dt}
\end{matrix}\right|_{t=0}=0\\
D^2+6D+8=0\\
(D+4)(D+2)=0\\
D=-2, D=-4\\
\therefore \;\;\text{ Solution is }\\
x=C_1e^{-2t}+C_2e^{-4t}\\
\text{Since,   }x(0)=1\\
\text{We have  }C_1+C_2=1\;\;...(i)\\
\frac{dx}{dt}=-2C_1e^{-2t}-4C_2e^{-4t}\\
\text{Since,   }\left [ \frac{dx}{dt} \right ]_{t=0}=0, \text{  we have}\\
-2C_1-4C_2=0\;\;\;...(ii)\\
\text{Solving (i) and (ii) we have } \\ C_1=2 \; and \;C_2=-1\\
\text{So the solution is }\\
x(t)=2e^{-2t}-e^{-4t} 
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the set of equations, [latex]x_{1}+2x_{2}+x_{3}+4x_{4}=2[/latex] and [latex]3x_{1}+6x_{2}+3x_{3}+12x_{4}=6[/latex]. The following statement is true.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1+2x_2+x_3+4x_4&= 2\\ 3x_1+6x_2+3x_3+12x_4&= 6 \end{aligned} [/latex]
The augmental matrix is [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4\\ 3 & 6 & 3 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 6 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Performing gauss-elimination on this we get
[latex] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4\\ 3 & 6 & 3 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\overset{R_2-3R_1}{\rightarrow}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]rank (A)=rank(A|B)=1 [/latex]
So, system is consistent.
Since, system's rank =1 is less than the number of variables, only infinite (multiple) non-trival solution exists.

raw_source.text: The frequency response of [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex] plotted in the complex [latex]G(j\omega )[/latex] plane (for [latex]0 \lt \omega \lt \infty[/latex]) is
The system [latex]\dot{x}=Ax+Bu[/latex] with [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0&2 \end{bmatrix},B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex] B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex][sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 &-2 \\ 0 & s-2 \end{bmatrix} [sI-A]^{-1}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s-1 &2 \\ 0 & s+1 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+1)(s+2)}\;\;...(i)[/latex]
Transfer function [latex]= C[sI-A]^{-1}B[/latex]
So, denominator of equation (i) gives pole of the system.
[latex](s+1)(s-2)=0 [/latex]
[latex]s=-1 \; and \; 2 [/latex]
One pole lies in RHS of s-plane. Hence, system is unstable.
For controllability, [latex]Q_c[/latex] is defined as
[latex]Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} B\; : & AB \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]AB=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]Q_C=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]|Q_c|\neq 0[/latex]
Hence the system is controllable.

raw_source.text: A 50 Hz synchronous generator is initially connected to a long lossless transmission line which is open circuited at the receiving end. With the field voltage held constant, the generator is disconnected from the transmission line. Which of the following may be said about the steady state terminal voltage and field current of the generator ?
raw_source.solution:
As field voltage is held constant, so field current does not change.
When the generator is connected with open-circuit transmission line, line draws charging current.

Therefore, [latex]V_t[/latex] is higher than [latex]E_g[/latex] i.e. [latex]V_t \gt E_g[/latex]
But when the generator is disconnected from the line, no charging current is delivered by the generator i.e. [latex]I_C=0[/latex]. In this [latex]V_t=E_g[/latex]
So, terminal voltage decreases.
raw_source.tag2: Performance of Transmission Lines, Line Parameters and Corona
options: The magnitude of terminal voltage decreases, and the field current does not change.
The magnitude of terminal voltage increases, and the field current does not change.
The magnitude of terminal voltage increases, and the field current increases

The magnitude of terminal voltage does not change and the field current
decreases.

raw_answer.option_text: The magnitude of terminal voltage decreases, and the field current does not change.

As both the machines are coupled, rotor of both the machines rotate at same speed.
Rotor speed of DC machine = 1600 rpm
Rotor spedd of induction machine =

Speed of stator field in induction machine [latex]=N_s[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_s &= \frac{120f}{P}\\ &= \frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500 \; \text{rpm} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Slip of rotor wrt stator field in induction machine

raw_source.text: A balanced star-connected and purely resistive load is connected at the secondary of a star-delta transformer as shown in figure. The line-to line voltage rating of the transformer is 110 V/200 V. Neglecting the non-idealities of the transformer, the impedance Z of the equivalent star-connected load, referred to the primary side of the transformer, is
raw_source.solution:
Let VA rating of the transformer S.
Rated voltage (line to line) on secondary side = 200V
Rated current [latex]=\frac{S}{\sqrt{3}\;200}[/latex]
Base impedance [latex]=\frac{\text{rated phase to neutral voltage}}{\text{rated current}} [/latex]
[latex]Z_B=\frac{200\sqrt{3}}{S/200\sqrt{3}}=\frac{(200)^2}{S} [/latex]
pu impedance on secondary side [latex]=\frac{4}{Z_B}=\frac{4}{(200)^2 S}=\frac{4S}{(200)^2} [/latex]
pu impedance in primary side and secondary side are equal.
Therefore pu impedance on primary side [latex]Z_{1\; pu}=\frac{4S}{(200)^2} [/latex]
Rated phase to neutral voltage on primary side [latex]V_{p1}=\frac{100}{\sqrt{3}}[/latex]
Rated primary current (phase) [latex]=\frac{S}{\sqrt{3}V_{l-l}}=\frac{S}{\sqrt{3}100} [/latex]
Base impedance [latex]=\frac{\text{rated phase to neutral voltage}}{\text{rated current}} =\frac{100\sqrt{3}}{S/100\sqrt{3}}=\frac{(100)^2}{S} [/latex]
Load impedance reffered to primary side [latex]Z_1=[/latex] base impedance (primary side) [latex]\times[/latex] pu impedance
[latex]=\frac{(100)^2}{S} \times \frac{4S}{(200)^2}=(1+j0)\Omega[/latex]

raw_source.text: The matrix [latex][A]=\begin{bmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is decomposed into a product of a lower triangular matrix [L] and an upper triangular matrix [U]. The properly decomposed [L] and [U] matrices respectively are
raw_source.solution:
Let us try Dolittle's decomposition by putting [latex]l_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]l_{22}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ l_{21}& 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12}\\ 0&u_{22} \end{bmatrix} \\ u_{11}&=2, u_{12}=1 \\ l_{21}u_{11}&=4 \\ l_{21} &=\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ l_{21}u_{12}+u_{22} &= -1\\ \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 1+u_{22} &=-1 \\ u_{22} &=-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So one possible breakdown is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2& 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
But this is not any of the choises given.
So let us do Crout's decomposition, by putting [latex]u_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]u_{22}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0\\ l_{21}& l_{22} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & u_{12}\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\ l_{11} &=2,l_{11}u_{12} =1\\ \Rightarrow \; u_{12}&=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \\ l_{21}&=4,l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \; 4 \times \frac{1}{2}+l_{22} &=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;l_{22} &=-3 \\ So\;\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4 &-1 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 4& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.5\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution: The current coil carries a current of [latex]I +I_P[/latex] and produces a filed corresponding to this current. The compensating coil is connected in series with the pressure coil circuit and is made as nearly as possible identical and coincident with the current coil. It is so connected that it opposes the field of the current coil. The compensating coil carries a current [latex]I_P[/latex] and produces a field corresponding to this current. This field acts as in opposition to the current coil field. Thus the resultant field is due to current [latex]I[/latex] only. Hence the error caused by the pressure coil current flowing in the current coil is neutralized.

raw_source.text:
The open loop transfer function G(s) of a unity feedback control system is given as

[latex]G(s)=\frac{k(s+\frac{2}{3})}{s^{2}(s+2)}[/latex]

From the root locus, at can be inferred that when k tends to positive infinity,
raw_source.solution:
[latex]G(s)=\frac{k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )}{s^2(s+2)}[/latex]
and [latex] H(s)=1 [/latex]
Characteristic equation, [latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; 1+\frac{k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )}{s^2(s+2)}=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; s^3+2s^2+k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; s^3+2s^2+ks+\frac{2k}{3}=0[/latex]
Routh array:

As [latex]k \gt 0[/latex], there is no sign change in the 1st column of routh array. So the system is stable and all the three roots lie on LHS of s-plane.
For [latex]k \gt 0(k\neq 0)[/latex], none of the row of Routh array becomes zero. So root loci does not cross the [latex]j\omega[/latex]-axis.
Number of Zero = Z = 1
Number of poles= P =3
Number of branches terminating at infinity = P-Z = 3-1 =2
Angle of asymptotes [latex]=\frac{(2k+1) \times 180^{\circ}}{P-Z} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\frac{(2k+1) \times 180^{\circ}}{2} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=(2k+1) \times 90^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=90^{\circ} \; and \; 270^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex] Centroid=\frac{\Sigma poles-\Sigma zero}{P-Z} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{0+0-2-\left ( -\frac{2}{3} \right )}{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[/latex]

Since, all the three branches terminates at [latex]R_e(s)=-\frac{2}{3}[/latex]. So, all the three roots have nearly equal real parts.
options: Three roots with nearly equal real parts exist on the left half of the s-plane
One real root is found on the right half of the s-plane
The root loci cross the [latex]j\omega[/latex] axis for a finite value of k;  k[latex]\neq[/latex]0
Three real roots are found on the right half of the s-plane

raw_answer.option_text: Three roots with nearly equal real parts exist on the left half of the s-plane

raw_source.text: The matrix [latex][A]=\begin{bmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is decomposed into a product of a lower triangular matrix [L] and an upper triangular matrix [U]. The properly decomposed [L] and [U] matrices respectively are
raw_source.solution:
Let us try Dolittle's decomposition by putting [latex]l_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]l_{22}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ l_{21}& 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12}\\ 0&u_{22} \end{bmatrix} \\ u_{11}&=2, u_{12}=1 \\ l_{21}u_{11}&=4 \\ l_{21} &=\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ l_{21}u_{12}+u_{22} &= -1\\ \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 1+u_{22} &=-1 \\ u_{22} &=-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So one possible breakdown is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2& 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
But this is not any of the choises given.
So let us do Crout's decomposition, by putting [latex]u_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]u_{22}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0\\ l_{21}& l_{22} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & u_{12}\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\ l_{11} &=2,l_{11}u_{12} =1\\ \Rightarrow \; u_{12}&=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \\ l_{21}&=4,l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \; 4 \times \frac{1}{2}+l_{22} &=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;l_{22} &=-3 \\ So\;\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4 &-1 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 4& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.5\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The two vectors [1, 1, 1] and [latex][1,a,a^{2}][/latex] where  [latex]a=(-\frac{1}{2}+j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})[/latex], are

[latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s} [/latex] (step input)

[latex]C(s)=\frac{1.5}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{0.5}{s+2} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Given [latex]f(z)=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3}[/latex]. If C is a counter clockwise path in the z-plane such that |z+1|=1, the value of [latex]\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint_{C}f(z)dz[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(z)&=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3}\\ &=\frac{(Z+3)-2(Z+1)}{(Z+1)(Z+3)}\\ &=\frac{-Z+1}{(Z+1)(Z+3)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Poles are at -1 and -3 i.e. (-1,0) and (-3,0).
From figure below of |Z+1|=1,
we see that (-1,0) is inside the circle and (-3,0) is outside the circle.

Residue theorem says,
[latex]\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint _Cf(z)dz=[/latex]Residue of those poles which are inside C.
So the required integral [latex]\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint _Cf(z)dz[/latex] is given by the residue of function at poles (-1,0) ( which is inside the circle).
This residue is [latex]=\frac{-(-1)+1}{(-1+3)}=\frac{2}{2}=1[/latex]

raw_source.text: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
raw_source.solution:
The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex]
Which is a linear differential equation
[latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Characteristic equation of A is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0[/latex]
[latex] (-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0 [/latex]
[latex]\text{So, } A^2+5A+6I=0 [/latex]
(by Cayley Hamilton theorem)
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I [/latex]
Multiplying by A on both sides, we have,
[latex]A^3=-5A^2-6A[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I[/latex]

raw_source.text: The maximum value of [latex]f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5[/latex] in the interval [1,6] is
raw_source.solution:
We need absolute maximum of
[latex]f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x+5[/latex] in the interval of [1,6]
First find local maximum if any by putting f'(x)=0.
[latex]\begin{aligned} f'(x) &=3x^2-18x+24=0 \\ x^2-6x+8&=0 \\ x&=2,4 \\ \text{Now } f''(x) &=6x-18 \\ f''(2)&=12-18=-6 \lt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=2 \text{ is a point of local maximum)} \\ f''(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=4 \text{ is a point of local minimum)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now tabulate the value of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below
[latex]\begin{matrix} x& f(x)\\ 1& 21\\ 2 & 25\\ 6& 41 \end{matrix}[/latex]
Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.

raw_source.text: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
raw_source.solution:
The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex]
Which is a linear differential equation
[latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The unilateral Laplace transform of [latex]f(t)[/latex] is [latex]\frac{1}{s^{2}+s+1}[/latex]. The unilateral Laplace transform of [latex]tf(t)[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{If }L[f(t)]&=\bar{f}(s)\\ \text{then, }L[t^nf(t)]&=(-1)^n\frac{d^n}{ds^n}\bar{f}(s)\\ &\text{In this problem,}\\ \text{Given, }L[f(t)]&=\frac{1}{s^2+s+1}=\bar{f}(s)\\ &\text{We need,}\\ L[tf(t)]&=(-1)^n\frac{d^1}{ds^1}\bar{f}(s)\\ &=-\frac{d}{ds}\bar{f}(s)\\ &=-\frac{d}{ds}\left [ \frac{1}{s^2+s+1} \right ]\\ &=-\left [ \frac{-1}{(s^2+s+1)^2} \right ] \times (2s+1)\\ &=\frac{2s+1}{(s^2+s+1)^2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

We need absolute maximum of

First find local maximum if any by putting f'(x)=0.
[latex]\begin{aligned} f'(x) &=3x^2-18x+24=0 \\ x^2-6x+8&=0 \\ x&=2,4 \\ \text{Now } f''(x) &=6x-18 \\ f''(2)&=12-18=-6 \lt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=2 \text{ is a point of local maximum)} \\ f''(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=4 \text{ is a point of local minimum)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now tabulate the value of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below
[latex]\begin{matrix} x& f(x)\\ 1& 21\\ 2 & 25\\ 6& 41 \end{matrix}[/latex]
Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.

[latex]\begin{aligned} y[n]&=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }g[k]h[n-k]\\ h[n]&=\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^n u[n]\\ h[n]&=\left\{\begin{matrix} \left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )^n \; ;& n\geq 0\\ 0& n \lt 0 \end{matrix}\right.\\ h[0]&=0, h[1]=\frac{1}{2}, h[2]=\frac{1}{4}\\ y[0]&=g[0] h[0]+g[1]h[-1]+...\\ 1&=g[0] \times 1+0+0+...\\ g[0]&=1\\ y[1]&=g[0]h[1]+g[1]h[0]+g[2]h[-1]+...\\ \frac{1}{2}&=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}+g[1]\cdot 1+0\\ \Rightarrow \;g[1]&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The Fourier transform of a signal h(t) is [latex]H(j \omega)=(2\cos\omega)(\sin 2 \omega)/\omega[/latex]. The value of h(0) is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} H(j\omega )&=\cos \omega \cdot \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega }\\ &=\frac{e^{j\omega}+e^{-j\omega}}{2}\cdot \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega }\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left [ e^{j\omega}\left ( \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \right )+e^{-j\omega}\left ( \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \right ) \right ]\\ \text{Let, }X(\omega )&=\frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \\ \text{Then, }x(t)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 1 & -2 \lt t \lt 2\\ 0 & \text{ otherwise} \end{matrix}\right. \\ &\text{By time shifting property}\\ h(t)&=\frac{1}{2}(x(t+1)+x(t-1))\\ \therefore \; h(0)&=\frac{1}{2}[x(1)+x(-1)]=\frac{1}{2}[1+1]=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The input x(t) and output y(t) of a system are related as [latex]y(t)=\int^{t}_{-\infty }x(\tau ) cos (3\tau )d\tau[/latex]. The system is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y&=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x{\tau } \cos (3\tau )d\tau \\ y(t-t_0)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t-t_0}x{\tau } \cos (3\tau )d\tau\\ y(t) & \text{ for input }x(t-t_0) \text{ is}\\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x{\tau -t_0} \cos (3\tau )d\tau\\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t-t_0}x{\tau} \cos 3(\tau +t_0 )d\tau\\ y'(t) &\neq y(t-t_0) \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, system is not time invariant for input [latex]x{\tau } =\cos (3\tau )[/latex] bounded input
[latex]y(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{t} \cos ^2 (3\tau )d\tau \rightarrow \infty \; as \; t \rightarrow \infty[/latex]
So, for bounded input, output is not bounded therefore system is not stable.

raw_source.text: Three capacitors [latex]C_1, C_2 \; and \; C_3[/latex] whose values are 10 [latex]\mu[/latex]F, 5 [latex]\mu[/latex]F, and 2 [latex]\mu[/latex]F respectively, have breakdown voltages of 10 V, 5 V and 2 V respectively. For the interconnection shown below, the maximum safe voltage in Volts that can be applied across the combination, and the corresponding total charge in [latex]\mu[/latex]C stored in the effective capacitance across the terminals are respectively,
raw_source.solution:
[latex]Q=CV [/latex]
[latex]Q_1=C_1V_1 =10 \times 10^{-6} \times 10=100\mu C [/latex]

[latex]Q_3=C_3V_3 =2 \times 10^{-6} \times 2=4\mu C [/latex]
Capacitor [latex]C_2 \; and \; C_3[/latex] are in series.
In series charge is same.
So, maximum charge on [latex]C_2 \; and \; C_3[/latex] will be minimum of
[latex](Q_2,Q_3)=min(25\mu C,4\mu C)=4\mu C=Q_{23}[/latex].
In series the equivalent capacitance of [latex]C_2 \; and \; C_3[/latex] is
[latex]C_{23}=\frac{C_2C_3}{C_2+C_3}=\frac{5 \times 2}{5+2}=\frac{10}{7}\mu F [/latex]
So, equivalent voltage,
[latex]V_{23}=\frac{Q_{23}}{C_{23}}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{\frac{10}{7} \times 10^{-6}}=\frac{28}{10}2.8V [/latex]
In parallel, the voltage is same.
[latex]V_1=V_{23}=2.8V [/latex]
Change in capacitor [latex]C_1 [/latex]
[latex]Q_1=C_1V_1 =10 \times 10^{-6}\times 2.8=28\mu C [/latex]
In parallel, the total charge
[latex]Q=Q_1+Q_{23} [/latex]
[latex]Q=4+28=32\mu C[/latex]

The function [latex]f(x)=e^{x}-1[/latex] is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of [latex]x_0[/latex] is taken as 1.0, then the absolute error observed at [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] iteration is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]f(x)=e^x-1[/latex]
or, [latex]f(x_K)=e^{x_K}-1[/latex] and [latex]x_0=1[/latex]
In Newton-Raphson method, we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{K+1}&=\left [ x_K-\frac{f(x_K)}{f'(x_K)} \right ] \\ x_1&= \left [ x_0- \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\right ]\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, } f(x_0)&=e^{x_0}-1=e^1-1=(e-1) \\ \text{and, } f'(x)&=e6x \\ \therefore \;\; f'(x_0) &=e^1=e \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the values, we get:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1&=\left [ 1-\frac{e-1}{e} \right ]=\left [ \frac{e-e+1}{e} \right ]=e^{-1}\\ \text{Also, }x_2&=\left [ x_1-\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)} \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now, }x_1&=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1} \text{ and } f(x_1)=(e^{e^{-1}}-1)\\ f'(x_1)&=e^{e^{-1}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the value, we get:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{e^{-1}}-1)}{e^{e^{-1}}} \right ]\\ &=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{0.37}-1)}{e^{0.37}} \right ]=0.06 \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=xe^{-x}\\ f'(x)&=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}=0\\ e^{-x}(1-x)&=0\\ x&=1\\ f''(x)&=-e^{-x}-e^{-x}+xe^{-x}\\ &=e^{-x}(x-2)\\ f''(1)&=e^{-1}(-1)=-e^{-1} \lt 0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence f(x) has maximum value at x=1
[latex]f(1)=1\cdot e^{-1}=e^{-1}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The solution for the differential equation
[latex]\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}=-9x[/latex]
with initial conditions x(0)=1 and [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}|_{t=0}=1[/latex], is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}&=-9x\\ \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+9x&=0\\ (D^2+9)x &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Auxiliary equation is [latex]m^2+9=0 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} m&= \pm 3i\\ x&= C_1 \cos 3t+C_2 \sin 3t\;\;...(i)\\ x(0) &=1\;\;i.e.\;x\rightarrow 1\; when t\rightarrow 0 \\ 1&=C_1 \\ \frac{dx}{dt}&=-3C_1 \sin 3t+3C_2 \cos 3t\;\;...(ii) \\ x'(0)&=1\;\; i.e.\;x'\rightarrow 1\; when \; t\rightarrow 0 \\ 1&=3C_2 \\ C_2&=\frac{1}{3}\\ \therefore \;x&=\cos 3t+\frac{1}{3}\sin 3t \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} x(0^+) &= \lim_{s \to \infty }[sX(s)]\\ x(0^+) &= \lim_{s \to \infty } \left [ \frac{s(3s+5)}{s^2+10+21} \right ] \\ &= \lim_{s \to \infty }\left [ \frac{3+\frac{5}{s}}{1+\frac{10}{s}+\frac{21}{s^2}} \right ]=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
