raw_source.text: [latex]C_0[/latex] is the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with air as dielectric (as in figure (a)). If, half of the entire gap as shown in figure (b) is filled with a dielectric of permittivity [latex]\epsilon _r[/latex] , the expression for the modified capacitance is
raw_source.solution:
Let A be the area of the parallel plate capacitor and d be the distance between the plates.

Let [latex]C_1[/latex] be the capacitance of half portion with air as dielectic medium and [latex]C_2[/latex] be capacitance with a dielectic of permitivity, [latex]\varepsilon _r[/latex].
Then, [latex]C_1=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area become half)
and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area becomes half)
Now, these two capacitance will be in parallel if a voltage is applied between the plates as same potential difference will be there between both the capacitance.

Equivalent capacitance is
[latex]\begin{aligned} C_{eqv} &= C_1+C_2\\ &=\frac{\varepsilon _0 A}{2d}+ \frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r A}{2d}\\ &= \frac{\varepsilon _0 A}{2d}(1+ \varepsilon _r)=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, modified capacitance,
[latex]C_{eqv}=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r)[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A star connected 400 V, 50 Hz, 4 pole synchronous machine gave the following open circuit and short circuit test results :
Open circuit test : [latex]V_{oc}[/latex] = 400 V (rms, line-to-line) at field current, [latex]I_{f}[/latex] = 2.3 A
Short circuit test : [latex]I_{sc}[/latex]= 10 A (rms, phase) at field current, [latex]I_{f}[/latex] = 1.5 A

The value of per phase synchronous impedance in [latex]\Omega[/latex] at rated voltage is_____.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given, for}\;\;V_{OC} &= 400V(rms)\\ &= \frac{400}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &= 230.94 \;\text{(Phase value),}\\ I_f&= 2.3A\\ \text{for}\;\; I_{sc}&=10A \;\text{(rms, phase)} \\ I_f&= 1.5A\\ & \therefore \;\;\text{Base impedance}\\ Z_{base}&=\frac{V_{OC}}{I_{sc}}\\ &=\frac{230.94}{10}=23.094\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
For finding the synchronous impedance at rated voltage, saturation effect of the machine has to be considered (i.e. the adjusted value of [latex]Z_s[/latex])
short circuit ratio,
[latex]\begin{aligned} SCR &=\frac{I_f \;for \; V_{OC}}{I_f \;for \; I_{sc}} \\ &=\frac{1}{Z_{s_{(sat)pu}}} =\frac{2.3}{1.5}\\ Z_{s_{(sat)pu}} &= 0.65 pu \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, actual value of [latex]Z_s[/latex] at rated voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=Z_{s_{(sat)pu}} \times Z_{base} \\ &=0.65 \times 23.094=15.06\Omega \\ \therefore \;\;Z_s&= 15.06\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The line integral of function F=yzi, in the counterclockwise direction, along the circle [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}=1[/latex] at z=1 is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \bar{F} &=yz\hat{i} \\ \bigtriangledown \times \bar{F} &=\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x} & \frac{\partial }{\partial y} &\frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ yz& 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\ &= \hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(0-y)+\hat{k}(0-z)\\ &=0\hat{i}+y\hat{j}-z\hat{k} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By strokes theoram,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \int _C\bar{F}\cdot d\bar{r}&=\int _S (\bigtriangledown \times \bar{F})\cdot \hat{n}ds\\ &=\int _S (y\hat{j}-z\hat{k})\cdot \hat{k}ds\\ &=\int _S -z \; ds \;\;\;\text{ Since }\; z=1\\ &=\int _S -1 \; ds=(-1)S=(-1)\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}[/latex]
where S is surface area of [latex]x^2+y^2=1[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;S=\pi(1)^2=\pi[/latex]

raw_source.text: In an unbalanced three phase system, phase current [latex]I_a = 1\angle -90^{\circ}[/latex] pu, negative sequence current [latex]I_{b2}=4 \angle( -150^{\circ})[/latex], zero sequence current [latex]I_{c0}=3 \angle -90^{\circ}[/latex] pu. raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_a&= 1\angle (-90^{\circ})pu\\ I_b&= 4\angle (-150^{\circ})pu\\ I_c&= 3\angle (90^{\circ})pu \end{aligned}[/latex]
As zero sequence current in all the three phases of unbalanced [latex]3-\phi[/latex] system are equal, therefore,
[latex]I_{a_0}=I_{b_0}=I_{c_0}=3\angle 90^{\circ}pu[/latex]

Also, [latex]I_{b_2}=4\angle -150^{\circ}[/latex]
=Negative phase sequence current of phase b.
Therefore, referring to the negative phase sequence phasor,
[latex]I_{b_2}=4\angle (-150^{\circ}-120^{\circ})=4\angle-270^{\circ}pu[/latex]
We know that, phase current vectors in matrix form are given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} I_a\\ I_b\\ I_c \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &1 &1 \\ 1& a^2 &a \\ 1 & a &a^2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} I_{a_0}\\ I_{a_1}\\ I_{a_2} \end{bmatrix} \\ \text{Here, } I_a&=I_{a_0}+I_{a_1}+I_{a_2} \\ \text{Given, } I_a&=1\angle -90^{\circ} \\ I_{a_0}&=3\angle 90^{\circ} \\ I_{a_2}&=4\angle -270^{\circ} \\ \text{Therefore,}& \\ I_{a_1}&=I_a-(I_{a_0}+I_{a_2}) \\ &=(1\angle -90^{\circ})-(3\angle 90^{\circ}+4\angle 270^{\circ}) \\ I_{a_1}&=8\angle -90^{\circ}pu \\ \text{Therefore,}& \\ I_b&=I_{a_0}+a^2I_{a_1}+aI_{a_2}\\ &=(3\angle 90^{\circ})+(1\angle 120^{\circ})^2 (8\angle -90^{\circ}) \\ &+(1\angle 120^{\circ})(4\angle -270^{\circ})\\ &=3\angle 90^{\circ}+8\angle 150^{\circ}+4\angle -150^{\circ}\\ I_b&=11.53\angle 154.3^{\circ}pu\\ &\text{Magnitude of phase current,}\\ I_b&=11.53\;pu \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]X(z)=\frac{1}{1-z^{-3}}[/latex]  be the Z -transform of a causal signal x [n]. Then, the values of x[2] and x[3] are
raw_source.solution:
[latex]X(z)=\frac{1}{1-z^{-3}}[/latex]
From z-transform defination,
[latex]\begin{aligned} X(z)&=\sum_{n=-\infty }^{\infty }x[n]z^{-n} \\ &=x(0)+x(1)z^{-1}+x(2)z^{-2}+... \\ X(z)&=\frac{1}{1-z^{-3}} \\ &=1+0\cdot z^{-1}+0\cdot z^{-2}+... \end{aligned}[/latex]
By comparision x(2)=0 and x(3)=1.

raw_source.text:
Let f(t) be a continuous time signal and let F([latex]\omega[/latex]) be its Fourier Transform defined by

[latex]F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t)e^{-j \omega t}dt[/latex]

Define g(t) by
[latex]g(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{-jut}du[/latex]

What is the relationship between f(t) and g(t) ?
raw_source.solution:
Given that,
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(t)&\rightleftharpoons F(\omega )\\ g(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{-jut}du\\ \text{Now, }f(t)&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(\omega)e^{j \omega t}d\omega \\ \Rightarrow \; 2 \pi f(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(\omega)e^{j \omega t}d\omega \\ \omega &\rightarrow u,\\ 2 \pi f(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{j u t}du \\ t &\rightarrow -t,\\ 2 \pi f(-t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{-j u t}du \\ &=g(t)\\ \Rightarrow \; g(t)&=2 \pi f(-t)\\ &= 2\pi f(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[If [latex]f(t)[/latex] is even then [latex]f(t)=f(-t)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; g(t) \propto f(t) \text{ if }f(t) \text{ is even.}[/latex]
options: g(t) would always be proportional to f (t)
g(t) would be proportional to f(t) if f(t) is an even function
g(t) would be proportional to f(t) only if f(t) is a sinusoidal function
g(t) would never be proportional to f(t)

raw_answer.option_text: g(t) would be proportional to f(t) if f(t) is an even function

raw_source.text: The core loss of a single phase, 230/115 V, 50 Hz power transformer is measured from 230 V side by feeding the primary (230 V side) from a variable voltage variable frequency source while keeping the secondary open circuited. The core loss is measured to be 1050 W for 230 V, 50 Hz input. The core loss is again measured to be 500 W for 138 V, 30 Hz input. The hysteresis and eddy current losses of the transformer for 230 V, 50 Hz input are respectively,
raw_source.solution:
Given, at 230V, 50 Hz, core loss =1050 W
and at 138 V, 30 Hz, core loss =500 W
Let, [latex]V_1=230 V, \;f_1=50Hz[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e1} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h1} \\ V_2=138V &, f_230Hz \\ \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e2} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h2} \\ \text{we know that, } & \\ \text{Eddy current loss,}\;& P_e \propto B_m^2f^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto B_m^xf\propto B_m^1.6 f \\ &(\text{Typical value of x=1.6}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
The transformer induced emf equation is:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2} \pi \phi _m N \\ V_1&= \sqrt{2} \pi f B_m A N\\ \text{where,}\;\; \frac{V}{t} &=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex]
i.e. flux = constant ( to avoid over fluxing)
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss,} &P_e \propto V^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto\frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^2=0.36 \\ \text{or,} \;\; P_{e2} &= 0.36P_{e1}\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,} \;\;\frac{P_{h2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{50}{30} \right )^{0.6} \\ &= (0.6)^{1.6} \times \frac{1}{(0.6)^{0.6}}=0.6\\ \therefore \;\; P_{h2} &=0.6P_{h1} \;\;...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given at 230V, 50Hz
[latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e1}+P_{h1}=1050W\;\;...(iii) [/latex]
At 138V, 30Hz,
[latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e2}+P_{h2}=500W [/latex]
or, [latex]0.36P_{e1}+0.6P_{h1}=500W\;\;...(iv)[/latex]
solving equation (iii) and (iv), we get
[latex]P_{h1}=508W [/latex] and [latex] P_{e1}=542W[/latex]
Therefore, hysteresis and eddy current losses at 230V, 50Hz are 508W and 542W respectively.

raw_source.text: A 15 kW, 230 V dc shunt motor has armature circuit resistance of 0.4 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and field circuit resistance of 230 [latex]\Omega[/latex] . At no load and rated voltage, the motor runs at 1400 rpm and the line current drawn by the motor is 5 A. At full load, the motor draws a line current of 70 A. Neglect armature reaction. The full load speed of the motor in rpm is_____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]R_a=0.4\Omega , [/latex] [latex]R_f=230\Omega , [/latex] [latex]V=230 \;\text{volt} [/latex]
At no load, speed, [latex]N_0=1400 \;\text{rpm}, [/latex] [latex]I_{L_0}=5A [/latex]
Field current, [latex]I_f=\frac{V}{R_f}=\frac{230}{230}=1A[/latex]

No load armature current, [latex]I_{a_0}=5-1=4A[/latex]
Induced emf at no-load,
[latex]E_{a_0}=V-I_{a_0}R_a[/latex]
[latex]\;\; \;\;=230-4 \times 0.4=228.4 V [/latex]
Also, at full load,
[latex]I_{L_{fl}}=70A [/latex]
[latex]I_{a_{fl}}=I_{L_{fl}}-I_f=70-1=69A [/latex]
Induced emf at full load,
[latex]E_{a_{fl}}=V-I_{a{fl}}R_a [/latex]
[latex]E_{a_{fl}}=230 -69 \times 0.4=202.4V [/latex]
we know that,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_a&\propto \phi \omega _m \alpha \propto N \\ E_a &\propto N \\ (\text{as flux} \; \phi \; &\text{is constant in shunt motor}) \\ \therefore \; \frac{E_{a_{fl}}}{E_{a_{0}}} &=\frac{N_{fl}}{N_0} \\ N_{fl}&= \frac{E_{a_{fl}}}{E_{a_{0}}} \times N_0 \\ &=\left ( \frac{202.4}{228.4} \right ) \times 1400 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, full-load speed of motor = 1240.63 rpm

raw_source.text: A 3 phase, 50 Hz, six pole induction motor has a rotor resistance of 0.1[latex]\Omega[/latex] and reactance of 0.92[latex]\Omega[/latex] . Neglect the voltage drop in stator and assume that the rotor resistance is constant. Given that the full load slip is 3%, the ratio of maximum torque to full load torque is
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned} R'_2 &=0.1\Omega \\ X'_2&= 0.92\Omega \\ S_{fl}&=3\%=0.03 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Slip at maximum torque,
[latex] S_m=\frac{R'_2}{X'_2}=\frac{0.1}{0.92}=0.1087 [/latex]
We know that,
[latex]\begin{aligned}\frac{T_{fl}}{T_{em}}&=\frac{2}{\left ( \frac{S_m}{S_{fl}}+\frac{S_{fl}}{S_m} \right )}\\ \therefore \;\; \frac{T_{fl}}{T_{em}}&=\frac{2}{\left ( \frac{0.1087}{0.03}+\frac{0.03}{0.1087} \right )}\\ &=\frac{2}{3.623+0.275}=\frac{2}{3.898}\\ \frac{T_{em}}{T_{fl}}&= 1.949 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, ratio of maximum torque to full-load torque [latex]=\frac{T_{em}}{T_{fl}}= 1.949[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A three phase synchronous generator is to be connected to the infinite bus. The lamps are connected as shown in the figure for the synchronization. The phase sequence of bus voltage is R-Y-B and that of incoming generator voltage is R' - Y' - B'.

It was found that the lamps are becoming dark in the sequence [latex]L_a-L_b-L_c[/latex]. It means that the phase sequence of incoming generator is
raw_source.solution:
As,
[latex]\begin{aligned} L_a \; \text{is connected between R-R'} & \\ L_b \; \text{is connected between Y-Y'} & \\ L_c \; \text{is connected between B-B'} & \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
therefore, the given method of synchronization is called "synchronization by dark lmap method".
In this method of synchronization, correct phase sequence of the incoming generator is obtain when all the three lamps become dark together and bright together. Since lamps are becoming dark in the sequence [latex]L_a-L_b-L_c[/latex] therefore, the phase sequence of incoming generator is opposite to the infinite bus.
options: opposite to infinite bus and its frequency is more than infinite bus
opposite to infinite bus but its frequency is less than infinite bus
same as infinite bus and its frequency is more than infinite bus
same as infinite bus and its frequency is less than infinite bus

raw_answer.option_text: opposite to infinite bus and its frequency is more than infinite bus

raw_source.text:
A distribution feeder of 1 km length having resistance, but negligible reactance, is fed from both the ends by 400 V, 50 Hz balanced sources. Both voltage sources [latex]S_1 \; and \; S_2[/latex] are in phase. The feeder supplies concentrated loads of unity power factor as shown in the figure.
The contributions of [latex]S_1 \; and \; S_2[/latex] in 100 A current supplied at location P respectively, are
raw_source.solution:
Let the resistance of whole length of feeder be [latex]R\;\Omega[/latex], length of feeder =1000m.
[latex]\therefore \;[/latex] Resistance per unit length [latex]=\frac{R}{1000}\Omega /meter[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;[/latex] Resistance of 400 m length [latex]=\frac{R}{1000} \times 400 =\frac{2R}{5} \Omega [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;[/latex] Resistance of 200 m length [latex] =\frac{R}{5} \Omega [/latex]
Let the current supplied by the sources be [latex]I_1 \text{ and } I_2[/latex].

Applying KVL from source [latex]S_1 \text{ and } S_2[/latex], we have:
[latex]\begin{aligned} 400 &= \frac{2R}{5}I_1+\frac{R}{5}(I_1-200)\\ & -\frac{R}{5}(I_2-200)-\frac{R}{5}I_2+400\\ 0&= \frac{2}{5}I_1 +\frac{I_1-200}{5}+\frac{200-I_2}{5}-\frac{I_2}{5}\\ 0&=2I_1+I_1-200+200-I_2-I_2 \\ 0&=3I_1-2I_2\\ I_1&=\frac{2}{3}I_2\;\;\;...(i)\\ \text{also, }& I_1 +I_2-400=100\\ \text{or, }&I_1+I_2=500 \;\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{Solvinf eq. (i) and (ii), we have}\\ I_1&=200A \text{ and }I_2=300A\\ &\text{Contribution of }S_1 \text{in 100 A at location}\\ P&=I_1-200=0A \\ &\text{Contribution of }S_2 \text{in 100 A at location}\\ P&=I_2-200=300-200=100A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, [latex]S_2[/latex] alone supplies the total load at location P.

raw_source.text:
A two bus power system shown in the figure supplies load of 1.0+j0.5 p.u.

The values of [latex]V_1[/latex] in p.u. and [latex]\delta _2[/latex] respectively are
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} P_2+jQ_2&=(1.0+j0.5)p.u.\\ P_2&=1=\frac{|V_1||V_2|}{|X|} \sin (\delta _1-\delta _2)\\ 1&=\frac{V_1}{0.1}\sin (-\delta _2)\\ -\frac{0.1}{\sin (-\delta _2)}&=V_1\;\;...(i)\\ Q_2&=0.5=\frac{|V_2|}{|X|}(|V_1| \cos \delta _2 -|V_2|)\\ 0.5&=\frac{1}{0.1}(V_1 \cos \delta _2-1)\\ \frac{1.05}{\cos \delta _2}&=V_1\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{From equation (i) and (ii),}\\ \tan \delta _2&=\frac{-0.1}{1.05}\\ \delta _2&=-5.44^{\circ}\\ \text{substituting } & \delta _2 \text{ value in equation (ii) gives,}\\ V_1&=1.05\;p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The fuel cost functions of two power plants are

Plant [latex]P_1:C_1\equiv 0.05Pg^2_1+APg_1+B[/latex]
Plant [latex]P_2:C_2\equiv 0.10Pg^2_2+3APg_2+2B[/latex]

where, [latex]Pg_1 \; and \; Pg_2[/latex] are the generated powers of two plants, and A and B are the constants. If the two plants optimally share 1000 MW load at incremental fuel cost of 100 Rs/MWh, the ratio of load shared by plants [latex]P_1 \; and \; P_2[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]P_{g1}+P_{g2}=1000 \;\;...(i)[/latex]
Also, incremental cost of production of
[latex]g_1=\frac{dC_1}{dP_{g1}}=0.1P_{g1}+A \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
and incremental cost of production of
[latex]g_2=\frac{dC_2}{dP_{g2}}=0.2P_{g2}+3A\;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
For optimum load sharing
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dC_1}{dP_{g1}}&=\frac{dC_2}{dP_{g2}} \\ 0.1P_{g1}+A&=0.2P_{g2}+3A \\ 0.1P_{g1}-0.2P_{g2}&=2A \\ P_{g1}-2P_{g2}&=20A \;\;\;...(iv) \\ \text{Given, } \frac{dC_1}{dP_{g1}}&=\frac{dC_2}{dP_{g2}}=100\; Rs/MWh \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting this value in equation (ii), we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} 100&=0.1P_{g1}+A\\ A&=(100-0.1P_{g1})\;\;...(v) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using equation (iv) and (v), we have:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{g1}-2P_{g2}&=20(100-0.1P_{g1})\\ 3P_{g1}-2P_{g2}&=20004\;\;...(vi) \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} P_{g1}&=800MW \text{ and } P_{g2}=200MW\\ \therefore \;P_{g1}:P_{g2}&=800:200=4:1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The over current relays for the line protection and loads connected at the buses are shown in the figure.

The relays are IDMT in nature having the characteristic

[latex]t_{op}=\frac{0.14\times Time \; Multipller \; Setting}{(Plug \; Setting \; Multiplier)^{0.02}-1}[/latex]

The maximum and minimum fault currents at bus B are 2000 A and 500 A respectively. Assuming the time multiplier setting and plug setting for relay [latex]R_B[/latex] to be 0.1 and 5 A respectively, the operating time of [latex]R_B[/latex] (in seconds) is_____.
raw_source.solution:
Minimum and maximum fault currents are
[latex]I_{fmin}=500A, I_{fmax}=2000A[/latex]
For relay [latex]R_B,\;TMS=0.1[/latex], plug setting =5A
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{PSM}&=\frac{I_f}{I_{pk} \times \text{C.T. ratio}} \\ \text{C.T. ratio} &=\frac{\text{Full load current}}{I_{pk}} \\ &= \frac{100}{5}\\ \text{At realy, }&R_B\\ \text{with }I_{fmin}\Rightarrow & \text{PSM}_1=\frac{500}{\frac{100}{5}\times 5}=5\\ \text{with }I_{fmax}\Rightarrow & \text{PSM}_2=\frac{2000}{\frac{100}{5}\times 5}=20 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Operating time with TMS=0.1,
and from IDMT characterisrics
[latex]t_{op_2}=\frac{0.14 \times 0.1}{(20)^{0.02}-1}=0.226sec[/latex]

raw_source.text: For the given system, it is desired that the system be stable. The minimum value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] for this condition is ______.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{(s+\alpha )}{s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )} [/latex]
and [latex] H(s)=1[/latex]
Characteristic equation of given control system is given by
[latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0 [/latex]
or, [latex] 1+\left [ \frac{s+\alpha }{s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )} \right ]=0[/latex]
or, [latex] s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )+s+\alpha =0 [/latex]
or, [latex] s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+\alpha s+1=0[/latex]
Routh's array is

For the given system to be stable, there should not be any sign change in the first column of Routh's array.
Therefore, [latex]1+\alpha \gt 0 \;or, \; \alpha \gt -1\;\; ...(i)[/latex]
Also, [latex] \frac{\alpha ^2 +\alpha -1}{1+\alpha } \gt 0 [/latex]
or, [latex] \alpha ^2 +\alpha -1 \gt 0 [/latex]
or, [latex] (\alpha +1.618)(\alpha -0.618) \gt 0 [/latex]
or, [latex] \alpha \lt -1.618[/latex]
or, [latex] \alpha \gt 0.618[/latex]
As [latex] \alpha \gt -1[/latex] (using equation (i))
therefore, [latex]\alpha \gt 0.618 \;\;...(ii) [/latex]
Combining condition (i) and (ii),
[latex] -1 \lt \alpha \lt 0.618 [/latex]
Thus, for the system to be stable minimum value of [latex]\alpha =0.618.[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The Bode magnitude plot of the transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{K(1+0.5s)(1+as)}{s(1+\frac{s}{8})(1+bs)(1+\frac{s}{36})}[/latex] is shown below:
Note that -6 dB/octave =- 20 dB/decade. The value of [latex]\frac{a}{bK}[/latex] is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{K(1+0.5s)(1+as)}{s(1+\frac{s}{8})(1+bs)(1+\frac{s}{36})}[/latex]
(1+as) is addition of zero to the transfer function whose contribution in slope=+20 dB/decade or -6 dB/octave.
(1+bs) is addition of pole to the transfer function whose contribution in slope=-20 dB/decade or -6 dB/octave.
Observing the change in the slope at different corner frequencies, we conclude that,
[latex] a=\frac{1}{4}[/latex] rad/s and [latex]b=\frac{1}{24}[/latex] rad/s
From[latex] \omega =0.01[/latex] rad/s to [latex]\omega =8[/latex] rad/s,
slope=-20dB/decade
Let the vertical length in dB by y
[latex]\therefore \;\; -20=\left ( \frac{0-y}{log8-log0.01} \right )[/latex]
[latex] \;\;\;\; -20=\frac{y}{log 8+2}[/latex]
[latex] \;\;\;\; y=58 dB[/latex]
Applying, [latex]y-mx+C[/latex] at [latex]\omega =0.01[/latex] rad/s,
We have, [latex]58=-20log 0.01 +C[/latex]
[latex]C=58-40=18[/latex]
Now, [latex]C=20logK[/latex]
[latex] LogK=\frac{18}{20}=0.9[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\; K= log^{-1}(0.9)=(10)^{0.9}=7.94[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\; \frac{a}{bK}=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4} \right )}{\left ( \frac{1}{24} \right )\times 7.94}=\frac{24}{4 \times 7.94}=0.755[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system matrix is given as follows
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & -1\\ -6& -11&6 \\ -6 & -11 & 5 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The absolute value of the ratio of the maximum eigenvalue to the minimum eigenvalue is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation [latex]|A-\lambda I|=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 & -1\\ -6 & -11-\lambda & 6\\ -6&-11 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda [-55+11\lambda -5\lambda +\lambda ^2+66] \\ -1[-30+6\lambda +36]-1[66-66-6\lambda ]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda (\lambda ^2+6\lambda +11)-1(6\lambda +6)+6\lambda =0 \\ \Rightarrow \;-\lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2-11\lambda -6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda ^3+6\lambda ^2+11\lambda +6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +3)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda =-1,-2,-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The absolute values of [latex]\lambda[/latex] are [latex]|\lambda |=1,2,3[/latex]
Ratio of maximum and minimum eigen value is [latex]=3:1=\frac{3}{1}=3[/latex]

raw_source.text: The reading of the voltmeter (rms) in volts, for the circuit shown in the figure is _________
raw_source.solution:
Given bridge is shown in figure

From the given bridge circuit, we see that product of opposite arm impedance are equal
[latex]\begin{aligned} i.e. \;\;& (-j) \times (-j)=(j)(j)\\ or\;\;\; & -1= -1 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence, the bridge is balanced, i.e. no current flows through the voltage source V.
Now, [latex]\begin{aligned} v_i(t)&= 100 \sin \omega t\\ &= \frac{100}{\sqrt{2}} \text{Volt(rms value)}\\ \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Net current supplied by the source is
[latex]I=\frac{100\sqrt{2}}{(0.5+Z_{eq})}A [/latex]
[latex]Z_{eq}=0 [/latex](i.e. net impedance of whole bridge=0)
[latex]\therefore \;\; I=\frac{100\sqrt{2}}{0.5}=141.42A [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\frac{I_2}{2}=70.71A [/latex]
Current flow through each parallel path of the bridge circuit, therefore [latex]V=V_a-V_b [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\left ( \frac{I}{2} \times -j \right )-\left ( \frac{I}{2} \times j \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=-jI=-j141.42[/latex] volt (rms value)
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Reading of the voltmeter in volt (rms)
[latex]=V=V_{ab}=141.42[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The dc current flowing in a circuit is measured by two ammeters, one PMMC
and another electrodynamometer type, connected in series. The PMMC meter
contains 100 turns in the coil, the flux density in the air gap is 0.2Wb/[latex]m^2[/latex], and
the area of the coil is 80 [latex]mm^2[/latex]. The electrodynamometer ammeter has a change in
mutual inductance with respect to deflection of 0.5 mH/deg. The spring constants
of both the meters are equal. The value of current, at which the deflections of the
two meters are same, is ______
raw_source.solution:
For a PMMC ammeter, at equilibrim, we have :
controlling torque ([latex]T_c[/latex])=Deflecting torque([latex]T_d[/latex])
[latex]\begin{aligned} K\theta _1 &=GI \; \text{or}\; \theta _1=\frac{GI}{K}\\ where, \;\; G &= nBA\\ \therefore \; \theta _1 &= \frac{nBAI}{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For an electrodynometer ammeter, at equilibrium,
Controlling torque=Deflecting torque
[latex]\begin{aligned} i.e. \;\; T_c &=T_d \; \text{or}\; K \theta _2=I^2 \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; \theta _2 &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\;\;...(ii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

For the deflection in the two meter to be same,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \theta _1 &=\theta _2\\ or, \;\; \frac{nBAI}{K} &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; nBA&=I\frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; I &=\frac{nBA}{\left ( \frac{dM}{d\theta } \right )} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Given, \;\; n&= \text{number of turns}=100\\ B&= 0.2 Wb/m^2\\ A&=80mm^2=80 \times 10^{-6}m^2\\ \text{and}\;\; \frac{dM}{d\theta }&=0.5 mH/rad\\ &=0.5 \times 10^{-3}H/rad \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the values in I, we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} I &=\left ( \frac{100 \times 0.2 \times 80 \times 10^{-6}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} \right ) A\\ &= \frac{1.6}{0.5}=3.2A \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Required value of current,
[latex]I=3.2Amp.[/latex]

raw_source.text: Given that the op-amps in the figure are ideal, the output voltage [latex]V_o[/latex] is

raw_source.text: The figure shows one period of the output voltage of an inverter. [latex]\alpha[/latex] should be chosen such that [latex]60^{\circ} \lt \alpha \lt 90^{\circ}[/latex]. If rms value of the fundamental component is 50V, then [latex]\alpha[/latex] in degree is _____.
raw_source.solution:
The output voltage [latex]V_0[/latex] can be reprresnted by fourier series as under:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0&=\sum_{n=1,3,5,...}^{\infty }a_n \cos n\omega t+b_n \sin n\omega t\\ \text{where, } a_n&=\frac{2}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f(t)\cos n\omega t \;d(\omega t) \\ b_n&=\frac{2}{T}\int_{0}^{T}f(t)\sin n\omega t \;d(\omega t) \\ a_n&=\frac{1}{\pi} [\int_{0}^{\alpha }100 \cos \omega t \;d(\omega t) +\int_{\alpha }^{180^{\circ}-\alpha }(-100) \cos \omega t \;d(\omega t) \\ &+ \int_{180^{\circ}-\alpha}^{180^{\circ} }100 \cos \omega t \;d(\omega t) +\int_{180^{\circ} }^{180^{\circ}+\alpha }(-100) \cos \omega t \;d(\omega t)\\ &+ \int_{180^{\circ}+\alpha}^{360^{\circ} -\alpha }100 \cos \omega t \;d(\omega t) +\int_{360^{\circ}-\alpha }^{360^{\circ} }(-100) \cos \omega t \;d(\omega t)]\\ a_n &=\frac{100}{\pi}[\sin \alpha - \sin (180^{\circ} -\alpha ) + \sin \alpha \\ &+\sin (180^{\circ}) -\sin (180^{\circ} -\alpha )\\ &- \sin (180^{\circ} +\alpha ) + \sin 180^{\circ}\\ &+ \sin (360^{\circ} -\alpha )- \sin (180^{\circ} +\alpha ) \\ &- \sin (360^{\circ} ) + \sin (360^{\circ} -\alpha )]\\ a_n &=0 \\ b_n&=\frac{1}{\pi} [\int_{0}^{\alpha }100 \sin \omega t \;d(\omega t) +\int_{\alpha }^{180^{\circ}-\alpha }(-100) \sin \omega t \;d(\omega t) \\ &+ \int_{180^{\circ}-\alpha}^{180^{\circ} }100 \sin \omega t \;d(\omega t) +\int_{180^{\circ} }^{180^{\circ}+\alpha }(-100) \sin \omega t \;d(\omega t)\\ &+ \int_{180^{\circ}+\alpha}^{360^{\circ} -\alpha }100 \sin \omega t \;d(\omega t) +\int_{360^{\circ}-\alpha }^{360^{\circ} }(-100) \sin \omega t \;d(\omega t)]\\ b_n &=\frac{100}{\pi}[-\cos \alpha +1+ \cos (180^{\circ} -\alpha ) - \cos \alpha \\ &-\cos (180^{\circ}) +\cos (180^{\circ} -\alpha )\\ &+ \cos (180^{\circ} +\alpha ) - \cos 180^{\circ}\\ &- \cos (360^{\circ} -\alpha )+ \cos (180^{\circ} +\alpha ) \\ &+ \cos (360^{\circ} ) - \cos (360^{\circ} -\alpha )]\\ b_n&=\frac{100}{\pi}[4-8 \cos \alpha ] =50\sqrt{2}\\ \cos \alpha &=0.22231=77.15^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the differential equation [latex]x^{2}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=0[/latex]. Which of the following is a solution to this differential equation for [latex]x \gt 0[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x^2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+x\frac{dy}{dx}-y&=0\\ \text{Let, }x=e^z\leftrightarrow z&=\log x\\ s\frac{d}{dx}=xD=\theta &=\frac{d}{dz}\\ x^2D^2&=\theta (\theta -1)\\ (x^2D^2+xD-1)y&=0\\ [\theta (\theta -1)+\theta -1]y&=0\\ (\theta ^2-\theta +\theta -1)&=0\\ (\theta ^2-1)y&=0\\ \text{Auxiliary equation is }m^2-1&=0\\ m&=\pm 1\\ \text{CF is }C_1e^{-z}+C_2e^z&\\ \text{Solution is }y&=C_1e^{-z}+C_2e^z\\ y&=C_1x^{-1}+C_2x\\ y&=C_1\frac{1}{x}+C_2x \end{aligned}[/latex]
One independent solution is [latex]\frac{1}{x}[/latex]
Another independent solution is x.

A parallel plate capacitor consisting two dielectric materials is shown in the figure. The middle dielectric slab is placed symmetrically with respect to the plates.

If the potential difference between one of the plates and the nearest surface of dielectric interface is 2 Volts, then the ratio [latex]\varepsilon _1:\varepsilon _2[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Let, A = Area of plates
Let [latex]C_1= C_3[/latex] be the capacitance formed with dielectric having dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _1[/latex].
[latex]C_{eqv}[/latex] be the equivalent capacitance.
[latex]C_2[/latex] be the capacitance formed with dielectic having dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _{r_2}[/latex].
Then, [latex]C_1=C_3=\frac{\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}{\frac{d}{4}}=\frac{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}{d}[/latex]
and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2A}{\frac{d}{2}}=\frac{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2A}{d}[/latex]
Also, equivalent capacitance [latex]= C_{eqv}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\;\frac{1}{C_{eqv}}&=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}+\frac{1}{C_3}=\frac{2}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2} \\ &(\because \;\;C_1=C_3)(C_1,C_2,C_3 \;\text{all in series}) \\ \frac{1}{C_{eqv}} &= \frac{2d}{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1d}+\frac{d}{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2d}\\ C_{eqv}&=\frac{2\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2\varepsilon _0A}{d(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} &\therefore \; \frac{C_{eqv}}{C_1}=\frac{V_1}{V_{eqv}}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &\frac{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2 A}{d(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)}\times \frac{d}{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &\frac{\varepsilon _2}{2(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &5\varepsilon _2=2\varepsilon _1+2\varepsilon _2 \\ &2\varepsilon _1 =3\varepsilon _2\\ &\varepsilon _1:\varepsilon _2=3:2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider an LTI system with transfer function
[latex]H(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+4)}[/latex]
If the input to the system is cos(3t) and the steady state output is Asin(3t+[latex]\alpha[/latex]) , then the value of A is
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned} H(s)&=\frac{1}{s(s+4)}\\ r(t)&=\text{input}= \cos (3t)=\cos \omega t\\ \therefore \; \omega &=3 \text{ rad/s}\\ H(j\omega)&=\frac{1}{(j\omega)(j\omega+4)}\\ \text{Now, }|H(j\omega)|&=\frac{1}{\omega \sqrt{\omega^4+4^2}}\\ &=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{25}}=\frac{1}{15} \;\;\;(at\; \omega=3)\\ \angle H(j\omega)&=-90^{\circ}-\tan ^{-1}\frac{\omega}{4}\\ &=-90^{\circ}-\tan ^{-1}\frac{3}{4}=-126.86^{\circ}\\ \therefore \; c(t)&=\frac{1}{15} \cos (3t-126.86^{\circ})\\ &=\frac{1}{15} \sin (3t-36.86^{\circ})\;\;...(i)\\ c(t)&=A \sin (3t+\alpha )\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Comparing }&\text{ eq. (i) and (ii), we have,}\\ A&=\frac{1}{15} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider an LTI system with impulse response [latex]h(t)=e^{-5t}u(t)[/latex]. If the output of the system is [latex]y(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)-e^{-5t}u(t)[/latex] then the input, x(t), is given by
raw_source.solution:
Impulse response of an LTI system = transfer function [latex]=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}=H(s)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{where, } y(t)&=e^{-3t}u(t)-e^{-5t}u(t) \\ \therefore \; Y(s) &=\frac{1}{(s+3)}-\frac{1}{(s+5)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+3)(s+5)} \\ \text{Also, } h(t)&=e^{-5t}u(t) \\ \therefore \; H(s) &=\frac{1}{(s+5)} \\ \text{Therefore, } X(s)&=\frac{Y(s)}{H(s)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+3)(s+5)} \times (s+5) \\ &= \frac{2}{(s+3)}\\ \therefore \; \text{Input}&=x(t)=2e^{-3t}u(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single phase induction motor draws 12 MW power at 0.6 lagging power.  Acapacitor is connected in parallel to the motor to improve the power factor of the combination of motor and capacitor to 0.8 lagging. Assuming that the real and reactive power drawn by the motor remains same as before, the reactive power delivered by the capacitor in MVAR is ______.
raw_source.solution:
Given , motor draws 12 MW at 0.6 pf lag
i.e. [latex]\cos \phi =0.6 \;\;\therefore \;\; \sin \phi =0.8 [/latex]
[latex]P=12MW Q=\frac{P}{\cos \phi }\times \sin \phi [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\frac{12}{0.6} \times 0.8 =16MVAR[/latex]

For improving the power factor to 0.8 lag, Q should be reduced i.e. [latex]\phi[/latex] reduces
[latex]\phi '=(16-Q)MVAR[/latex]
Where, Q is the reactive power delivered by the capacitor.
Now, power factor,
[latex]\cos \phi '=0.8[/latex]
or [latex] \phi '=\cos ^{-1}(0.8)=36.86^{\circ} [/latex]
from power traingle,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tan\phi &=\frac{Q'}{P}\\ Q'&=P \tan \phi ' \\ &=12 \tan 36.86^{\circ} \\ Q'&=8.99 MVAR \\ 16-Q&=8.99 \\ Q&= 16-8.99\\ &= 7.01 MVAR \end{aligned} [/latex]
Reactive power delivered by the capacitor, Q=7.07 MVAR

raw_source.text:
The closed-loop transfer function of a system is [latex]T(s)=\frac{4}{(s^{2}+0.4s+4)}[/latex]. The steady
state error due to unit step input is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Closed loop transfer function,
[latex]T(s)=\frac{4}{(s^2+0.4s+4)} [/latex]
or, [latex]\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}[/latex]
[latex]=\left ( \frac{4}{s^2+0.4s+4} \right )\;\;\;\;[H(s)=1] [/latex]
or, [latex](s^2+0.4s+4)=4+4G(s) [/latex]
or, [latex]G(s)=\frac{4}{s(s+0.4)} [/latex]
=Open llop transfer function ( for unity feedback system)
Given, input =u(t)=r(t)
[latex]\therefore \;\;\; R(s)=1/s [/latex]
Steady state error
[latex]e_{ss}=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{sR(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)} \right ] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{sR(s)}{1+G(s)} \right ]\;\;\; [For H(s)=1] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{s \times \frac{1}{s}}{1+\frac{4}{s(s+0.4)}} \right ][/latex]
[latex] \;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{s(s+0.4)}{s^2+0.4s+4} \right ]=0 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Steady state error for step input, [latex]e_{ss}=0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The state transition matrix for the system
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_{1}}\\ \dot{x_{2}} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u[/latex]
is
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1\\ \dot{x}_2 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u [/latex]
or, [latex]\;\; \dot{x}(t)=Ax(t)+Bu [/latex]
Here, [latex] [A]=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}, \;\; B=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
State transition matric is given by,
[latex]e^{At}=L^{-1}[sI-A]^{-1}[/latex]
Now, [latex] [sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 0 -1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]Adj[sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
and [latex] |sI-A|=(s-1)^2 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; [sI-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}Adj[sI-A] [/latex]
[latex][sI-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s-1)^2}\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s-1} & \\ \frac{1}{(s-1)^2} & \frac{1}{s-1} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; L^{-1}[sI-A]^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix} e^t & 0\\ te^t& e^t \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] State transition matrix[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} e^t & 0\\ te^t& e^t \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The saw-tooth voltage waveform shown in the figure is fed to a moving iron voltmeter. Its reading would be close to __________
raw_source.solution:
Moving iron voltmeter reads rms value of voltage and current. From the given waveform of voltage,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V(t) &= \left\{\begin{matrix} 50000t, & 0 \lt t \lt 0.02s\\ 50000(t-0.02). & 0.02 \lt t \lt 0.04s \end{matrix}\right.\\ \therefore \; V_{rms} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}(V(T)^2 \; dt}\\ &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{0.04} \int_{0}^{0.02} (50000t)^2 \; dt +\int_{0.02}^{0.04}(50000(t-0.02))^2 \; dt}\\ &= 25000\sqrt{\left [ \frac{t^3}{3} \right ]_0^{0.02}+\left [ \frac{(t-0.02)^3}{3} \right ]_{0.02}^{0.04}}\\ &= 25000\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}\left [ (0.02)^3+(0.02)^3 \right ]}\\ &= 57.73 \text{Volt} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] Voltage reading by moving iron voltmeter =57.73 Volts

raw_source.text: While measuring power of a three-phase balanced load by the two-wattmeter method, the readings are 100 W and 250 W. The power factor of the load is ______.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]W_1=250W[/latex], [latex]W_2=100W[/latex]
Power factor angle is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} \phi &= \tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{\sqrt{3}(W_1-W_2)}{W_1+W_2} \right ]\\ &=\tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{\sqrt{3}(250-100)}{250+100} \right ] \\ &= \tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{\sqrt{3}\times 150}{350} \right ]\\ &= \tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{7} \right ]=36.58^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, power factor of load [latex]= \cos \phi =\cos 36.58^{\circ} =0.802=0.80[/latex]

raw_source.text: A step-up chopper is used to feed a load at 400 V dc from a 250 V dc source. The inductor current is continuous. If the 'off' time of the switch is 20 [latex]\mu[/latex]s, the switching frequency of the chopper in kHz is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Given step up chopper,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0&=400V\\ V_s&=250V\\ T_{OFF}&=2 \times 10^{-6} sec\\ V_0&=V_s \times \frac{T}{T_{OFF}}\\ 400&=250 \times \frac{T}{20 \times 10^{-6}}\\ T&=\frac{400 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}}{250}\\ &=3.2 \times 10^{-5}\; sec\\ f&=\frac{1}{T}=\frac{1}{3.2 \times 10^{-5}}\\ f&=31.2jHz \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a constant V/f control of induction motor, the ratio V/f is maintained
constant from 0 to base frequency, where V is the voltage applied to the motor
at fundamental frequency f . Which of the following statements relating to low
frequency operation of the motor is TRUE ?
raw_source.solution:
In a [latex]3-\phi[/latex] induction motor, induced emf equation per phase is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{{ph}_{1}} &=k_w \sqrt{2} \pi f \phi N_{ph}\approx V_1 \\ \text{where}\;\; \phi &=\text{flux per pole}=1.5\phi _m \\ \phi &\propto \frac{V}{f} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Since V/f ratio is constant (to avoid over sluxing), therefore,
[latex]\left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )_{\text{rated frequency}} \gt \left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )_{\text{reduced frequency}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\phi _{\text{rated}} \gt\phi _{\text{reduced}}[/latex]
options: At low frequency, the stator flux increases from its rated value.
At low frequency, the stator flux decreases from its rated value.
At low frequency, the motor saturates.
At low frequency, the stator flux remains unchanged at its rated value.

raw_answer.option_text: At low frequency, the stator flux decreases from its rated value.

The magnitude of magnetic flux density [latex]\vec{B}[/latex] at a point having normal distance d meters from an infinitely extended wire carrying current of [latex]I[/latex] A is [latex]\frac{\mu _{0}I}{2\pi d}[/latex] (in SI units). An infinitely extended wire is laid along the x -axis and is carrying current of 4 A in the +ve x direction. Another infinitely extended wire is laid along the y axis and is carrying 2 A current in the +ve y direction. [latex]\mu _0[/latex] is permeability of free space. Assume [latex]\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}[/latex] to be unit vectors along x,y and z axes respectively.

Assuming right handed coordinate system, magnetic field intensity, [latex]\hat{H}[/latex] at coordinate (2,1,0) will be

A discrete system is represented by the difference equation
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} X_{1}(k+1)\\ X_{2}(k+1) \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} a & a-1\\ a+1& a \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} X_{1}(k)\\ X_{2}(k) \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
It has initial conditions [latex]X_1(0)=1;X_2(0)=0[/latex]. The pole locations of the system for a = 1, are
raw_source.solution:
Given that,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K+1)\\X_2(K+1) \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} a & a-1\\ a+1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K)\\X_2(K) \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
With initial conditions,
[latex]X_1(0)=1,\;\;X_2(0)=0[/latex]
For a=1, we can write,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K+1)\\X_2(K+1) \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K)\\X_2(K+) \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; X_1(K+1)=X_1(K) \;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; X_2(K+1)=2X_1(K)+X_2(k) \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Applying z-transform on equation (i),
[latex]\begin{aligned} zX_1(z)-zX_1(0)&=X_1(z) \\ X_1(z)[z-1]&=zX_1(0) \\ X_1(z) =\frac{z}{z-1}\;\;&[Given, \; X_1(0)=1]...(iii) \\ \text{from equation (ii),}\\ zX_2(z)-zX_2(0)&=2X_1(z)+X_2(z)\\ X_2(z)[z-1]&=2X_1(z)+zX_2(0)\\ [Given,\;\; X_2(0)&=0]\\ \frac{X_2(z)}{X_1(z)}&=\frac{2}{z-1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus, transfer function, [latex]H(z)=\frac{2}{z-1}[/latex]
Therefore, pole location is z=1.

raw_source.text:
An input signal x(t)=2+5sin(100[latex]\pi[/latex]t) is sampled with a sampling frequency of 400 Hz and applied to the system whose transfer function is represented by
[latex]\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}=\frac{1}{N}(\frac{1-z^{-N}}{1-z^{-1}})[/latex]
where, N represents the number of samples per cycle. The output y(n) of the system under steady state is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f_s&= 400Hz\\ x(t)&=2+5 \sin (100 \pi t) \\ t\rightarrow xT_s &=\frac{n}{f_s}=\frac{n}{400} \\ x(n)&=2+5 \sin \left ( 100 \pi\frac{n}{400} \right ) \\ &= 2+5 \sin \frac{\pi}{4}n\\ \text{Here, }\omega _0 &=\frac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, N= time-period of [latex]x(n)=\frac{2 \pi }{\omega _0}=\frac{2 \pi}{\pi/4}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, }H(z)&=\frac{1}{N}\left [ \frac{1-z^{-N}}{1-z^{-1}} \right ] \\ \text{Applying, }z &=e^{j\omega } \\ H(e^{j\omega }) &= \frac{1}{N}\left [ \frac{1-e^{-j\omega N}}{1-e^{-j\omega }} \right ] \\ \text{For, } &\text{sinusoidal part of }x(n): \\ H(e^{j\omega _0 }) &= \frac{1}{N}\left [ \frac{1-e^{-j\omega _0 N}}{1-e^{-j\omega _0 }} \right ] \\ [\text{Note: }] \omega _0 N&=\frac{\pi}{4} \times 8 =2 \pi] \\ &= \frac{1}{N}\left [ \frac{1-e^{-j2 \pi N}}{1-e^{-j \pi/4}} \right ]=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, for sinusoidal part of input, system output is zero. For dc part of input,
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(n)&=\text{output}\\ &=H(e^{j0}) \times \text{input dc value}\\ [\because \; &H(e^{j\omega })_{\omega =0}=1]\\ &=1 \times 2=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus, steady state output = 2

raw_source.text: A 250 V dc shunt machine has armature circuit resistance of 0.6 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and field circuit resistance of 125 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. The machine is connected to 250 V supply mains. The motor is operated as a generator and then as a motor separately. The line current of the machine in both the cases is 50 A. The ratio of the speed as a generator to the speed as a motor is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]V=250V, [/latex] [latex]R_a=0.6\Omega , [/latex] [latex]R_f=125\Omega , [/latex] [latex]I_L=50A[/latex] both for motor as well as generator action.
Field current,
[latex]I_f=\frac{V}{R_f}=\frac{250}{125}=2A [/latex]
[latex]\text{For motor action:} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_m}&= V-I_aR_a\\ I_a&=I_l-I_f=50-2=48A \\ \therefore \; E_{a_m}&=250-48 \times 0.6 \\ &=221.2 V \\ \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\text{For generator action:} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_g} &=V+I_aR_a \\ I_a &= I_L+I_f=50+2=52A\\ \therefore \; E_{a_g} &=250+52 \times 0.6=281.2V \end{aligned} [/latex]
For a DC shunt machine, [latex]E_a\propto \phi \omega _n [/latex]
or [latex] \;\; E_a\propto N \;\text{(speed)}[/latex] [latex] (\because \;\phi =constant)[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\;\frac{E_{a_g}}{E_{a_m}}=\frac{N_g}{N_m} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{N_g}{N_m}=\frac{281.2}{221.2}=1.271 [/latex]
Therefore, ratio of the speed as a generator to the speed of motor=1.271

If the rotor winding is open circuited and the system is made to run at rotational speed [latex]f_r[/latex] with the help of prime-mover in anti-clockwise direction, then the frequency of voltage across slip rings is [latex]f_1[/latex] and frequency of voltage across commutator brushes is [latex]f_2[/latex]. The values of [latex]f_1 \; and \; f_2[/latex] respectively are

Frequency of voltage across slip ring = Frequency of voltage induced in the rotor winding. Let speed corresponding to stator frequency, [latex]f=N_s[/latex].
and speed corresponding to [latex]f_r=N_r[/latex]
Then, frequency of rotor induced emf [latex]=f+f_r[/latex]
[latex]=f_1\left ( \text{corresponding to} \; f_1 =\frac{(N_s+N_r)P}{120}\right )[/latex]
Also, frequency of induced voltage across commutator = stator frequency [latex]=f. [/latex]

raw_source.text: A 20-pole alternators is having 180 identical stator slots with 6 conductors in each slot. All the coils of a phase are in series. If the coils are connected to realize single-phase winding, the generated voltage is [latex]V_1[/latex]. If the coils are reconnected to realize three phase star connected winding, the generated phase voltage is [latex]V_2[/latex]. Assuming full pitch, single-layer winding, the ratio [latex]V_1/V_2[/latex] is
For a single phase, two winding transformer, the supply frequency and voltage are both increased by 10%. The percentage changes in the hysteresis loss and eddy current loss, respectively, are
raw_source.solution:
Eddy current loss, [latex]P_a\propto B_m^2 f^2[/latex] and Hysteresis loss,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_h &\propto B_m^x f\propto B_m^{1.6}f \\ \text{when}\;\; \frac{V}{f} &= \text{constant}, \\ P_e&\propto V^2 \\ \text{and}\;\; P_h &\propto \frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \\ \text{Given} \;\; V_2&=1.1V_1 \\ \text{and}\;\; f_2&= 1.1f_1 \\ \frac{P_{e_2}}{P_{e_1}}=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2\\ &=(1.1)^2=1.21\\ \frac{P_{e_2}-P_{e_1}}{P_{e_1}}&=0.21 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Therefore, % increase in eddy current loss
[latex]\begin{aligned} &= \left [ \frac{P_{e_2}-P_{e_1}}{P_{e_1}}\right ] \times 100\%=21\%\\ \text{also}\;\; \frac{P_{h_2}}{P_{h_1}}&= \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=(1.1)^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{1}{1.1} \right )^{0.6}=1.1\\ \text{or}\;\; \frac{P_{h_2}-P_{h_1}}{P_{h_1}}&= 0.1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, % increase in hysteresis loss [latex]=\left ( \frac{P_{h_2}-P_{h_1}}{P_{h_1}} \right ) \times 100\%=10\%[/latex]
Thus, hysteresis loss increased by 10% and eddy current loss by 21%.

raw_source.text: A synchronous generator is connected to an infinite bus with excitation voltage [latex]E_f= 1.3[/latex] pu. The generator has a synchronous reactance of 1.1 pu and is delivering real power (P) of 0.6 pu to the bus. Assume the infinite bus voltage to be 1.0 pu. Neglect stator resistance. The reactive power (Q) in pu supplied by the generator to the bus under this condition is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]E_f=1.3pu, X_s=1.1pu, V=1 pu, P=0.6pu[/latex]
Neglecting stator resistance i.e. [latex]\theta _s=90^{\circ}[/latex]
Output power delivered,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P &=\frac{VE_f}{X_s}\sin \delta \\ \sin \delta &=\frac{PX_s}{VE_f} \\ &= \frac{0.6 \times 1.1}{1 \times 1.3}\approx 0.5\\ \therefore \;\; \delta &=30^{\circ}=\text{Power angle} \\ \therefore \;\; \cos \delta &= \cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Reactive power is given by,
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q&=\left [ \frac{VE_f}{X_s} \cos \delta -\frac{V^2}{X_s} \right ]\\ &=\left [ \frac{1 \times 1.3}{1.1} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1^2}{1.1} \right ]\\ Q&=(1.023-0.909)=0.114pu\\ &\approx 0.11pu \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: There are two generators in a power system. No-load frequencies of the generators are 51.5 Hz and 51 Hz, respectively, and both are having droop constant of 1Hz/MW. Total load in the system is 2.5 MW. Assuming that the generators are operating under their respective droop characteristics, the frequency of the power system in Hz in the steady state is ______.
raw_source.solution:
Let no-load frequency of generator-1 be 51.5 Hz and no-load frequency of generator-2 be 51 Hz.
Given total load = 2.5 Mwand drop of both machines =1 Hz/MW

Let machine-1 shares a load of [latex]P_1[/latex] MW them machine-2 will share a load of [latex](2.5-P_1)[/latex] MW
Le the steady state frequency of the system be f.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, }\frac{51.5-f}{P_1}&=1=droop \\ P_1&= (51.5-f)\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also, } \left ( \frac{51-f}{2.5-P_1} \right )&=1=droop \\ 51-f &=2.5-P_1 \\ P_1 &=f-48.5 \;\;...(ii) \\ \text{equating eq. }&\text{(i) and (ii), we get,} \\ 51.5-f &=f-48.5 \\ 2f&=100 \\ f&=50Hz \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The horizontally placed conductors of a single phase line operating at 50 Hz are having outside diameter of 1.6 cm, and the spacing between centers of the conductors is 6 m. The permittivity of free space is [latex]8.854 \times 10^{-12}[/latex] F/m. The capacitance to ground per kilometer of each line is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} C &=\frac{2 \pi \in _0}{\ln \left ( \frac{d}{r} \right )} \\ &=\frac{2 \pi \in _0}{\ln \left ( \frac{2 \times 6}{1.6 \times 10^{-2}} \right )} \\ &= 8.4 \times 10^{-12} F/m\\ &= 8.4 \times 10^{-9} F/km \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A three phase, 100 MVA, 25 kV generator has solidly grounded neutral. The positive, negative, and the zero sequence reactances of the generator are 0.2 pu, 0.2 pu and 0.05 pu, respectively, at the machine base quantities. If a bolted single phase to ground fault occurs at the terminal of the unloaded generator, the fault current in amperes immediately after the fault is_____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]X_1=0.2pu, X_2=0.2pu, X_3=0.05pu[/latex]
For a line-to-ground fault on generator, fault current is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{f_{LG}}&=3I_{R_0} =3I_{R_1}=3I_{R_2}\\ &= \frac{3E}{Z_1+Z_2+Z_3}\\ &=\frac{3 \times 1}{0.2+0.2+0.05} \\ &= \frac{3}{0.45}=\frac{20}{3}pu \end{aligned}[/latex]
Also, base MVA =100
Base KVA =25
Theerefore, Base current,
[latex]I_b=\frac{100 \times 10^6}{\sqrt{3} \times 25 \times 10^3}=2.309kA[/latex]
Actual fault current in ampere
[latex]=(I_{f_{LG}})_{pu} \times I_b=\frac{20}{30} \times 2.309 \times 10^3[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;I_f=15393 \text{ Ampere}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system with the open loop transfer function
[latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s^{2}+2s+2)}[/latex]
is connected in a negative feedback configuration with a feedback gain of unity. For the closed loop system to be marginally stable, the value of K is ______
raw_source.solution:

raw_source.text:
The second order dynamic system
[latex]\frac{dX}{dt}=PX+Qu [/latex]
[latex] y=RX[/latex]
has the matrices P, Q and R as follows :
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}\; Q=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \; R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The system has the following controllability and observability properties:
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex]\dot{x}(t)=Px+Qu [/latex]
[latex]y=Rx [/latex]
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex], [latex]Q=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex] R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
For controllability,
[latex] Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} Q &PQ \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex] [PQ]=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 1& -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;|Q_c|=-1\neq 0\Rightarrow \;\; controllable [/latex]
Also, for observability,
[latex] Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} R^T & P^TR^T \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} P^T & R^T \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; |Q_0|=(0 \times -3 -0 \times 1)=0\Rightarrow \;\; non-observable[/latex]
Since, [latex] Q_c\neq 0[/latex] and [latex]Q_0=0[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] System is controllable but not observable.

raw_source.text:
Suppose that resistors [latex]R_1 \; and \; R_2[/latex] are connected in parallel to give an equivalent resistor R. If resistors [latex]R_1 \; and \; R_2[/latex] have tolerance of 1% each, the equivalent resistor R for resistors [latex]R_1 = 300 \Omega[/latex]
 and [latex]R_2 = 200 \Omega[/latex] will have tolerance of
raw_source.solution:
Given,[latex]R_1=300\Omega ,[/latex] [latex] R_2=200\Omega [/latex]
Equivalent resistance of parallel combination of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} =\frac{300 \times 200}{500}\\ &= 120\Omega =R_T\\ \text{Given tolerance of} \; R_1&=1\% \\ \therefore \; R_1 &= 300 \pm 3\\ R_1 &= 303 \Omega \; \text{or} 297\Omega \\ \text{Tolerance of} \; R_2&=1\% \\ \therefore \; R_2 &= 200 \pm 2\\ R_2 &= 202 \Omega \; \text{or} 198\Omega \end{aligned} [/latex]
Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] in high range is:
[latex] R_H=\frac{303 \times 202}{303+202}=121.2\Omega [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Tolerance for equivalent resistance R in high range of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] is
[latex]\begin{aligned} \varepsilon _R &=\left ( \frac{R_H-R}{R} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \left ( \frac{121.2-120}{120} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \frac{1.2}{120} \times 100\%=1\% \end{aligned} [/latex]
Note: In low range of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex],
[latex]R_L=\left ( \frac{297 \times 198}{495} \right )=118.8\Omega [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Tolerance of equivalent resistance, R in low range is,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \varepsilon _L &=\left ( \frac{R_L-R}{R} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \left ( \frac{118.8-120}{120} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= -1\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two ammeters X and Y have resistances of 1.2 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and 1.5 [latex]\Omega[/latex] respectively and they give full-scale deflection with 150 mA and 250 mA respectively. The ranges have been extended by connecting shunts so as to give full scale deflection with 15 A. The ammeters along with shunts are connected in parallel and then placed
in a circuit in which the total current flowing is 15 A. The current in amperes indicated in ammeter X is_____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]R_{m_X}=1.2\Omega , [/latex]
[latex]R_{m_Y}=1.5\Omega[/latex]
[latex] I_{m_X}=0.15A, [/latex]
[latex]I_{m_Y}=0.25A [/latex]
and [latex] I= [/latex] full scale deflection current=15A
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Shunt multiplying factor for ammeter X is
[latex]m_X=\frac{I}{I_{m_X}}=\frac{15}{0.15}=100[/latex]
and shunt multiplier resistance,
[latex]R_{{sh}_X}=\frac{R_{m_X}}{(m_X-1)}=\frac{12}{99}=0.012\Omega[/latex]

Also, shunt multiplying factor for ammeteer Y is
[latex]m_Y=\frac{I}{I_{m_Y}}=\frac{15}{0.25}=60 [/latex]
and shunt multiplier resistance,
[latex]R_{{sh}_Y}=\frac{R_{m_Y}}{(m_Y-1)}=\frac{1.5}{59}=0.025\Omega[/latex]
when these ammeters are connected in parrelel as shown in the figure below,

Let current in ammeter X be [latex]I_X[/latex] then,
[latex]\begin{aligned} R_X&=\left ( \frac{ R_{{sh}_X} \cdot R_{m_X}} { R_{{sh}_X}+R_{m_X}} \right )\\ &= \left ( \frac{0.012 \times 1.2}{1.212} \right )\\ &= 0.011 \Omega \\ R_Y &=\left ( \frac{R_{{sh}_Y}\cdot R_{m_Y}}{R_{{sh}_Y}+R_{m_Y}} \right )\\ &= \left ( \frac{0.025 \times 1.5}{1.525} \right )\\ &=0.024\Omega \\ \therefore \; I_X &=\left (\frac{R_Y}{R_X+R_Y} \right )\times 15 \\ &=\left ( \frac{0.024}{0.035} \right ) \times 15 \\ &= 10.28A \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Current in ammeter X=10.28A

raw_source.text:
An oscillator circuit using ideal op-amp and diodes is shown in the figure.

The time duration for +ve part of the cycle is [latex]\Delta t_{1}[/latex] and for -ve part is [latex]\Delta t_{2}[/latex]. The value of [latex]e^{\frac{\Delta t_{1}-\Delta t_{2}}{RC}}[/latex] will be ______.
raw_source.solution:
This circuit is a stable multivibrator (or) free running oscillator.
When [latex]V_0=+V_{sat} [/latex]
[latex]V_{UPT}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +3k\Omega } = \frac{V_{sat}}{4} [/latex]
When, [latex] V_0=-V_{sat} [/latex]
[latex]V_{LTP}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +1k\Omega }=\frac{-V_{sat}}{2}[/latex]

[latex]V_c=V_{final}+(V_{inital}-V_{final})e^{-t/RC}[/latex]
In time [latex] t=\Delta t_1[/latex]
[latex] V_c=V_{UTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{initial}=V_{LTP};[/latex] [latex]V_{final}=+V_{sat}[/latex]
[latex]V_{UTP}=V_{sat}+(V_{LTP}-V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{V_{sat}}{4}=V_{sat}+\left ( -\frac{V_{sat}}{2}-V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]V_{sat}\left ( -1+\frac{1}{4} \right )=-V_{sat}\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\left (1-\frac{1}{4} \right )=\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{2}e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}[/latex]
[latex] e^{\Delta t_1/RC}=2\;\;....(i) [/latex]

In time [latex] t=\Delta t_2 [/latex]
[latex]V_c=V_{LTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{initial}=V_{UTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{final}=-V_{sat} [/latex]
[latex]V_{LTP}=-V_{sat}+(V_{UTP}+V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]-\frac{V_{sat}}{2}=-V_{sat}+\left ( \frac{V_{sat}}{4}+V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\left (1-\frac{1}{2} \right )V_{sat}=V_{sat}\left (1+ \frac{1}{4} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{1}{2}= \frac{5}{4}e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]e^{\Delta t_2/RC}=\frac{5}{2}\;\;....(ii)[/latex]
From equation (i) and (ii),
[latex]\frac{e^{\Delta t_1/RC}}{e^{\Delta t_2/RC}}[/latex]
[latex]=e^{(\Delta t_1-\Delta t_2)/RC}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{2}{5/2}=\frac{4}{5}=0.8[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a synchronous machine, hunting is predominantly damped by
raw_source.solution: Hunting is a phenomenon occuring in case of synchronous generator and motor where the machine oscillates about the equilibrium point. The signal flow graph of a system is shown below. U(s) is the input and C(s) is the output

Assuming [latex]h_{1}=b_{1} \; and \; h_{0}=b_{0}-b_{1}a_{1}[/latex], the input-output transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}[/latex] of the system is given by
raw_source.solution:
Using Mason's gain fomlula,
Transfer function,
[latex]G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{\Sigma P_k\Delta _k}{\Delta } [/latex]
Forward paths are:
[latex]P_1=\frac{h_0}{s^2} ,\; P_2=\frac{h_1}{s} [/latex]
Individual loops are:
[latex] L_1=\frac{-a_1}{s} , \; L_2=\frac{-a_0}{s^2} [/latex]
Non-touching loops=zero
[latex] \therefore \;\;\Delta _1=1, [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\; \Delta _2=1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( 1+\frac{a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;\Delta =1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s}-\frac{a_0}{s^2} \right )=\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta } [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;=\frac{\left ( \frac{h_0}{s^2} \right )\times 1+\left ( \frac{h_1}{s} \right )\times \left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right )}{\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2}} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\left [ \frac{h_0+h_1(s+a_1)}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right ] [/latex]
Given: [latex] h_1=b_1 [/latex] and [latex]h_0=b_0-b_1a_1[/latex]
Thus, [latex] G(s)=\frac{(b_0-b_1a_1)+b_1(s+a_1)}{(s^2+a_1s+a_0)} [/latex]
[latex]G(s)=\left ( \frac{b_1s+b_0}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right )[/latex]

The function [latex]f(x)=e^{x}-1[/latex] is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of [latex]x_0[/latex] is taken as 1.0, then the absolute error observed at [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] iteration is _____.
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]f(x)=e^x-1[/latex]
or, [latex]f(x_K)=e^{x_K}-1[/latex] and [latex]x_0=1[/latex]
In Newton-Raphson method, we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{K+1}&=\left [ x_K-\frac{f(x_K)}{f'(x_K)} \right ] \\ x_1&= \left [ x_0- \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\right ]\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, } f(x_0)&=e^{x_0}-1=e^1-1=(e-1) \\ \text{and, } f'(x)&=e6x \\ \therefore \;\; f'(x_0) &=e^1=e \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the values, we get:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1&=\left [ 1-\frac{e-1}{e} \right ]=\left [ \frac{e-e+1}{e} \right ]=e^{-1}\\ \text{Also, }x_2&=\left [ x_1-\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)} \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now, }x_1&=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1} \text{ and } f(x_1)=(e^{e^{-1}}-1)\\ f'(x_1)&=e^{e^{-1}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the value, we get:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{e^{-1}}-1)}{e^{e^{-1}}} \right ]\\ &=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{0.37}-1)}{e^{0.37}} \right ]=0.06 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex]\omega _1=1 k [/latex] rad/s,
[latex]V_1=100\angle 0^{\circ}V, [/latex]
[latex]I_1=0.03\angle 31^{\circ}A [/latex]
At, [latex]\omega _2=2 k[/latex] rad/s,
[latex]V_2=100\angle 0^{\circ}V, [/latex]
[latex]I_2=2\angle 0^{\circ}A [/latex]

At [latex]\omega _2=2 k[/latex] rad/s, voltage and current are in phase. Thus, it is a case of series resonance,
[latex]X_{L_{\omega 2}}=X_{C_{\omega 2}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;Z=R=\frac{V_2}{I_2}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{100\angle 0^{\circ}}{2\angle 0^{\circ}}=50\Omega [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Resistance of circuit,
[latex]R=50\Omega [/latex]
Now at [latex]\omega _1=1 k[/latex] rad/s,
[latex] Z=\frac{V_1}{I_1}=\frac{100\angle 0^{\circ}}{0.03\angle 31^{\circ}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\; =\frac{100}{0.03}\angle 31^{\circ}\Omega\;\;...(i) [/latex]
Also, [latex] Z=|Z|\angle \tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{X_L-X_C}{R} \right ] \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Comparing equation (i) and (ii), we have:
[latex] -31^{\circ}=\tan ^{-1}\left [ \frac{X_L-X_C}{R} \right ][/latex]
[latex] \tan(-31^{\circ})=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R} [/latex]
[latex]X_L-X_C=R \tan(-31^{\circ}) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=50X-0.6=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; X_{L_{\omega 1}}-X_{C_{\omega 2}}=-30\;\;...(iii) [/latex]
[latex]X_{L_{\omega 2}}=X_{C_{\omega 2}} [/latex] or [latex] \omega _2 L=\frac{1}{\omega _2C} [/latex]
[latex]L=\frac{1}{\omega _2^2C}\;\;...(iv) [/latex]
From equation (iii),
[latex] \omega _1L-\frac{1}{\omega _1C}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\omega _1\left ( \frac{1}{\omega _2^2C}\right )-\frac{1}{\omega _1C}=-30[/latex]
[latex] \frac{\omega _1}{\omega _2^2C}-\frac{1}{\omega _1C}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{1 \times 10^3}{4 \times 10^6 C}-\frac{1}{10^3C}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{10^{-3}}{4C}-\frac{10^{-3}}{C}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{-3}{4C} \times 10^{-3}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]C=\frac{3 \times 10^{-3}}{4 \times 30} [/latex]
Substituting the value of C in equation (iv), we get,
[latex]L=\frac{1}{\omega _2^2C}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{(2 \times 10^3)^2 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\; =\frac{1}{100}=10mH[/latex]
Therefore, values are:
[latex]R=50\Omega , [/latex]
[latex]L=10mH, [/latex]
[latex]C=25\mu F[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An open circuit test is performed on 50 Hz transformer, using variable frequency source and keeping V/f ratio constant, to separate its eddy current and hysteresis losses. The variation of core loss/frequency as function of frequency is shown in the figure

The hysteresis and eddy current losses of the transformer at 25 Hz respectively are
raw_source.solution:
Let core loss at 25 Hz be [latex]P_0[/latex] per Hz:
Then equating the two slopoes of figure, we have: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_0-10}{25}&=\frac{5}{50} \\ P_0&= 2.5+10=12.5W/Hz \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\; \text{Core loss at} \;\; 25 Hz [/latex] [latex]= 12.5 \times 25=312.5 watt[/latex]
Also, core loss at 50 Hz [latex]= 15 \times 50 =750 watt[/latex]
Let at [latex](f_1)[/latex] 25 Hz, eddy current loss [latex]=P_{e1}[/latex] and hysteresis loss [latex]=P_{h1}[/latex] we know that,[latex] P_{e}\propto f^2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \;\; \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{50}{25} \right )^2=4 \\ \therefore \;\; P_{e2} &=4P_{e1} \;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,}\;\; P_h\propto f & \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{P_{h2}}{P_{h1}}&=\frac{f_2}{f_1}=\frac{50}{25}=2 \\ P_{h2}&=2P_{h1}\;\;...(ii) \\ \text{Now, at} \;\; f_1&=25Hz, \\ P_{e1}+P_{h1}&= 312.5\\ \;\;...(iii) \text{and at} \;\; f_2&=50Hz, \\ P_{e2}+P_{h2}&= 750\\ 4P_{e1}+2P_{h1}&=750W \\ 2P_{e1}+P_{h1}&=375 W\;\;...(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving equation (iii) and (iv), we get,
[latex] P_{e1}=62.5 W [/latex] and [latex] P_{h1}=250W[/latex]
Thus, at 25 Hz, hysteresis loss = 250W and eddy current loss =62.5W

The figure shows the single line diagram of a single machine infinite bus system.

The inertia constant of the synchronous generator H = 5 MW-s/MVA. Frequency is 50 Hz. Mechanical power is 1 pu. The system is operating at the stable equilibrium point with rotor angle [latex]\delta[/latex] equal to 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. A three phase short circuit fault occurs at a certain location on one of the circuits of the double circuit transmission line. During fault, electrical power in pu is [latex]P_{max} \sin \delta[/latex] . If the values of [latex] \delta \; and \; d\delta/dt [/latex] at the instant of fault clearing are 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] and 3.762 radian/s respectively, then [latex]P_{max}[/latex] (in pu) is ______.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d^2\delta }{dt^2}&=(P_m-P_e) \\ \text{Let, } \omega _r&=\frac{d\delta }{dt} \\ \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d\omega _r }{dt} &=(P_m-P_e) \\ \text{Multiplying with } &\omega _r \text{ in both side}\\ \frac{H}{\omega _s}\left ( 2\omega _r \frac{d\omega _r }{dt}\right )&= (P_m-P_e)\frac{d\delta }{dt}\\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{H}{\omega _s} 2d(\omega _r)^2&=(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{H}{\omega _s}\int_{\omega _{r_1}}^{\omega _{r_2}}d(\omega _r^2) &= \int_{\delta _1}^{\delta _2}(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \text{where, } & \\ \omega _{r_1}&=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{\delta =\delta _1} =\omega (\delta =\delta _1)-\omega _s\\ \omega _{r_2}&=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{\delta =\delta _2} =\omega (\delta =\delta _2)-\omega _s\\ \frac{H}{\omega _s}(\omega _{r_2}^2 -\omega _{r_1}^2)&=\int_{\delta _1}^{\delta _2}(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \text{In problem, }&\\ \frac{d\delta }{dt}=0, &\frac{d\delta }{dt}=3.762\\ \frac{5}{314}(3.762^2-0^2)&=\int_{30^{\circ}}^{45^{\circ}}(1-P_{max} \sin \delta )d\delta \\ \Rightarrow \;\; P_{max}&=0.23p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider the system described by following state space equations
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_{1}}\\ \dot{x_{2}} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1& -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u; [/latex] [latex] y=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
If u is unit step input, then the steady state error of the system is
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix}, [/latex] [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, [/latex][latex]C=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
Transfer function of the given system is given by
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=C(sI-A)^{-1}B [/latex]
Now, [latex] (sI-A)=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} s & -1\\ 1&s+1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex](sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}(Adj[A]) [/latex]
[latex]|sI-A|=s(s+1)+1=(s^2+s+1) [/latex]
and [latex] Adj[A]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;(sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Transfer function,
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right \} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} (s+1) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right \}[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \times 1 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} [/latex]
Given, input=unit step
[latex] \therefore \;\; U(s)=\frac{1}{s} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; Y(s)=\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}=\frac{1}{s(s^2+s+1)} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Final Value
[latex]\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}[sY(s)][/latex]
[latex]=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \right ]=1 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;[/latex] Error=Final value -Initial value
[latex]e_{ss}=0[/latex]

The maximum phase angle [latex]\phi _{m}[/latex] and the corresponding gain [latex]G _{m}[/latex] respectively, are
raw_source.solution:
From the given Bode plot, it is clear that corner frequencies,
[latex]\omega _{c1}=\frac{1}{3}[/latex] and [latex]\omega _{c2}=1[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Transfer function of given system is given by
[latex]T(s)=\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\left [ \frac{1+3s}{1+s} \right ]=\left [ \frac{1+Ts}{1+\alpha Ts} \right ] [/latex]
Here, [latex]T=3[/latex] and [latex]\alpha T=1,[/latex]
[latex] \alpha =\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
As [latex] \alpha \lt 1[/latex], therefore the transfer function T(s) represents a lead compensator having [latex]\alpha =\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Maximum phase shift,
[latex]\phi _{m}=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1-\alpha }{2\sqrt{\alpha }} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1-\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{2}{3}\times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right ]=30^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; \phi _m=30^{\circ}[/latex]
Also,
[latex]T(j\omega )=\frac{1+j3\omega }{1+j\omega } [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; |T(j\omega )|=\frac{\sqrt{1+9\omega ^2}}{\sqrt{1+\omega ^2}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; Gain G_m[/latex] in dB [latex]=20log |T(j\omega )| [/latex]
[latex]=20 log_{10}\left [ \frac{\sqrt{1+9\omega ^2_m}}{1+\omega ^2_m} \right ][/latex]
Now, [latex] \omega _m=\frac{1}{T\sqrt{\alpha }}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; G_m=20 log_{10}\left [ \sqrt{\frac{1+9\times \left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2}} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=20 log_{10}\left [ \sqrt{\frac{1+3}{1+\frac{1}{3}}} \right ]=20 log_{10}\sqrt{3} [/latex]
[latex]G_m=4.77dB[/latex]

A random variable X has probability density function f(x) as given below:

[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & for \; 0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

If the expected value E[X]=2/3, then [latex]Pr[X \lt 0.5][/latex] is _____________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & \text{for }0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix}\right.&\\ \text{Now given }E(X)&=2/3\\ \int_{0}^{1}xf(x)dx&=\frac{2}{3}\\ \int_{0}^{1}x(a+bx)dx&=\frac{2}{3}\\ a\left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right )_0^1+b\left ( \frac{x^3}{3} \right )_0^1&=\frac{2}{3}\\ a\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )+b\left ( \frac{1}{3} \right )&=\frac{2}{3}\\ 3a+2b&=4\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, }\int_{0}^{1}f(x)dx &=1\\ (\text{total probability} & \text{ is always equal to 1})\\ \int_{0}^{1}(a+bx)dx&=\left ( ax+\frac{bx^2}{2} \right )_0^1=1\\ a+\frac{b}{2}&=1\\ 2a+b&=2\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now solving } & \text{ (i) and (ii), we get}\\ a&=0,b=2\\ So,\; \;f(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 2x & \text{for }0 \lt x lt 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix}\right.&\\ \text{Now we need}&\\ P(x \lt 0.5)&=\int_{0}^{0.5}2xdx=2\left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right )_0^{0.5}\\ &=0.5^2-0^2=0.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If a continuous function f(x) does not have a root in the interval [a,b], then which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Intermediate value theorem states that if a function is continious and [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \lt 0[/latex], then surely there is a root in (a,b). The contrapositive of this theorem is that if a function is continious and has no root in (a,b) then surely [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \geq 0[/latex]. But since it is given that there is no root in the closed interval [a,b] it means [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \neq 0[/latex].
So surely [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \gt 0[/latex] which is choise(C).

raw_source.text: If the sum of the diagonal elements of a 2x2 matrix is -6, then the maximum possible value of determinant of the matrix is ________.
raw_source.solution:
Consider a symmetric matrix [latex]A =\begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ b & d \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Given [latex]a+d=-6[/latex]
[latex]|A|=ad-b^2[/latex]
Now since [latex]b^2[/latex] is always non-negative, maximum determinant will come when [latex]b^2=0[/latex].
So we need to maximize
[latex]\begin{aligned} |A|&=ad-0=ad=a \times -(6+a) \\ &= -a^2-6a\\ \frac{d|A|}{da} &=-2a-6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a &=-3 \text{ is the only stationary point} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, [latex]\left [\frac{d^2|A|}{da} \right ]_{a=-3}=-2 \lt 0[/latex], we have a maximum at [latex]a=-3[/latex].
Since [latex]a+d=-6[/latex], corresponding value of [latex]d=-3[/latex].
[latex]|A|=ad=-3 \times -3=9[/latex]

raw_source.text: A differential equation [latex]\frac{di}{dt}-0.2i=0[/latex] is applicable over [latex]-10\lt t \lt 10[/latex]. If i(4)=10, then i(-5) is _____.

A random variable X has probability density function f(x) as given below:

[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & for \; 0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

If the expected value E[X]=2/3, then [latex]Pr[X \lt 0.5][/latex] is _____________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & \text{for }0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix}\right.&\\ \text{Now given }E(X)&=2/3\\ \int_{0}^{1}xf(x)dx&=\frac{2}{3}\\ \int_{0}^{1}x(a+bx)dx&=\frac{2}{3}\\ a\left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right )_0^1+b\left ( \frac{x^3}{3} \right )_0^1&=\frac{2}{3}\\ a\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )+b\left ( \frac{1}{3} \right )&=\frac{2}{3}\\ 3a+2b&=4\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, }\int_{0}^{1}f(x)dx &=1\\ (\text{total probability} & \text{ is always equal to 1})\\ \int_{0}^{1}(a+bx)dx&=\left ( ax+\frac{bx^2}{2} \right )_0^1=1\\ a+\frac{b}{2}&=1\\ 2a+b&=2\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now solving } & \text{ (i) and (ii), we get}\\ a&=0,b=2\\ So,\; \;f(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 2x & \text{for }0 \lt x lt 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix}\right.&\\ \text{Now we need}&\\ P(x \lt 0.5)&=\int_{0}^{0.5}2xdx=2\left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right )_0^{0.5}\\ &=0.5^2-0^2=0.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If a continuous function f(x) does not have a root in the interval [a,b], then which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Intermediate value theorem states that if a function is continious and [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \lt 0[/latex], then surely there is a root in (a,b). The contrapositive of this theorem is that if a function is continious and has no root in (a,b) then surely [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \geq 0[/latex]. But since it is given that there is no root in the closed interval [a,b] it means [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \neq 0[/latex].
So surely [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \gt 0[/latex] which is choise(C).

raw_source.text: If the sum of the diagonal elements of a 2x2 matrix is -6, then the maximum possible value of determinant of the matrix is ________.
raw_source.solution:
Consider a symmetric matrix [latex]A =\begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ b & d \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Given [latex]a+d=-6[/latex]
[latex]|A|=ad-b^2[/latex]
Now since [latex]b^2[/latex] is always non-negative, maximum determinant will come when [latex]b^2=0[/latex].
So we need to maximize
[latex]\begin{aligned} |A|&=ad-0=ad=a \times -(6+a) \\ &= -a^2-6a\\ \frac{d|A|}{da} &=-2a-6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a &=-3 \text{ is the only stationary point} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, [latex]\left [\frac{d^2|A|}{da} \right ]_{a=-3}=-2 \lt 0[/latex], we have a maximum at [latex]a=-3[/latex].
Since [latex]a+d=-6[/latex], corresponding value of [latex]d=-3[/latex].
[latex]|A|=ad=-3 \times -3=9[/latex]

raw_source.text: A moving average function is given by [latex]y(t)=\frac{1}{T}\int_{t-T}^{t}u(\tau )d\tau[/latex]. If the input u is a sinusoidal signal of frequency [latex]\frac{1}{2\tau }[/latex] Hz, then in steady state, the output y will lag u (in degree) by ______ .
raw_source.solution:
System input: [latex]\sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} f_0&=\frac{1}{2T}Hz\\ \text{Therefore,}\\ \omega _0&=2 \pi f_0=\frac{2 \pi}{2T}=\frac{\pi}{T}\; rad/sec\\ y(t)&=\frac{1}{T}\int_{t-T}^{t}\sin \omega _0\tau \; d\tau\\ &=\frac{1}{T}[-\cos\omega _0 t ]_{t-T}^t\\ &=-\frac{1}{T}[\cos\omega _0 t -\cos\omega _0 (t-T) ]\\ &\left [ \because \; \omega _0=\frac{t}{T} \right ]\\ &=-\frac{1}{T}[\cos\omega _0 t -\cos\left ( \frac{\pi t}{T}- \pi \right ) ]\\ \\ &=-\frac{1}{T}[\cos\omega _0 t +\cos\omega _0 t ]\\ &=-\frac{2}{T} \cos\omega _0 t \\ &=\frac{2}{T}\sin (\omega _0 t -90^{\circ}) \\ &=\text{Output is lagging by }90^{\circ} \text{ w.r.t. input.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A separately excited DC generator has an armature resistance of 0.1[latex]\Omega[/latex] and negligible armature inductance. Assume that the speed remains unchanged during the transient. At what time (in microsecond) after the capacitor is connected will the voltage across it reach 25 V?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} R_a &= 0.1\Omega \\ V_{OC}&= 200V\\ I'_{f}&= \frac{I_f}{2}\\ \omega '&= \frac{\omega _{rated}}{2}\\ E_g&= k\phi \omega \\ E'_g&= k\frac{\phi }{2} \times \frac{\omega }{2}\\ &= \frac{200}{4}=50V\\ V&=V(\infty )-[V(\infty )-V(0)]e^{-t/T} \\ &= 50-[50-0]e^{-t/T} \\ 25&= 50[1-e^{-t/RC} ]\\ \frac{1}{2}&= 1-e^{-t/100 \times 10^{-6}}\\ e^{-t/10^{-4}}&= \frac{1}{2}\\ t&=0.693 \times 10^{-4}\\ &=69.3\mu s \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The self inductance of the primary winding of a single phase, 50 Hz, transformer is 800 mH, and that of the secondary winding is 600 mH. Mutual inductance is 480 mH.

The voltage source [latex]V_1[/latex] is sinusoidal with frequency 50 Hz.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{So,} \;\; V_2&=L_2 \frac{dI_2}{dt}+\frac{MdI_1}{dt} \\ V_2&=0 \\ \text{So,} \;\; j\omega L_2I_2 &=-j\omega MI_1 \\ \text{So,} \;\; I_2&=-I_1 \frac{M}{L_2}=-\frac{4}{5}I_1 \\ \text{Now,} \;\; V_1&= L_1 \frac{dI_1}{dt}+\frac{MdI_2}{dt} \\ V_1 &=j\omega L_1I_1+j\omega MI_2 \\ V_1&=j\omega [L_1I_1+MI_2] \\ V_1&=j\omega [800mH-384mH]I_1 \\ \frac{V_1}{I_1}&=j\omega [416mH] \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, equivalent inductance is [latex]416 mH.[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the economic dispatch problem for a power plant having two generating units. The fuel costs in Rs/MWh along with the generation limits for the two units are given below:

[latex]C_{1}(P_{1})=0.01{P_{1}}^2+30P_{1}+10[/latex]; [latex]100MW\leq P_{1} \leq 150MW[/latex]
[latex] C_{2}(P_{2})=0.05{P_{2}}^2+10P_{2}+10[/latex]; [latex]100MW\leq P_{2} \leq 180MW[/latex]

The incremental cost (in Rs/MWh) of the power plant when it supplies 200 MW is ______ .
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} C_1&=0.01P_1^2+30P_1+10\\ \frac{dC_1}{dP_1}&=2 \times 0.01P_1+30\\ &=0.02P_1+30\\ C_2&=0.05P_2^2+10P_2+10\\ \frac{dC-2}{dP_2}&=0.1P_2+10\\ \text{For optimum } &\text{incremental cost,}\\ \frac{dC_1}{dP_1}&=\frac{dC_2}{dP_2}\\ 0.02P_1+30&=0.1P_2+10\\ 0.02P_1-0.1P_2&=-20 \;\;...(i)\\ \text{Given, }P_1+P_2&=200 \;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Solving } & \text{equation (i) and (ii),}\\ P_2&=200, P_1=0\\ \text{But the }& \text{range of }P_1 \text{ and }P_2 \text{ are specified as}\\ 100MW \leq & P_1 \leq 150MW\\ 100MW \leq & P_2 \leq 180MW\\ \text{hence, }& P_2=200 MW \text{ is not valid}\\ \text{so, both }& P_1 \text{ and } P_2 \text{ are operating at}\\ P_1=100,P_2=100\;& \Rightarrow \; P_1+P_2=200\\ IC_1=\frac{dC_1}{dP_1}&=0.02 \times P_1+30=32 Rs/MW\\ IC_2=\frac{dC_2}{dP_2}&=0.1 \times P_2+10=20 Rs/MW \end{aligned}[/latex]
