raw_source.text: A 50 Hz generating unit has H-constant of 2 MJ/MVA. The machine is initially operating in steady state at synchronous speed, and producing 1 pu of real power. The initial value of the rotor angle [latex]\delta[/latex] is 5[latex]^{\circ}[/latex], when a bolted three phase to ground short circuit fault occurs at the terminal of the generator. Assuming the input mechanical power to remain at 1 pu, the value of [latex]\delta[/latex] in degrees, 0.02 second after the fault is _________.
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]3-\phi[/latex] fault occurs at t=0
[latex]\Rightarrow \; P_e=0\text{ for }t\geq 0^+[/latex]
Now, swing equation for [latex]t\geq 0^+[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d^2\delta }{dt^2} &=P_m \\ \frac{d^2\delta }{dt^2}&= \frac{P_m \omega _s }{2H}\\ \frac{d\delta }{dt}&= \frac{P_m \omega _s }{2H}t+C\\ C=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right| _{t=0^+}&=\omega (t=0^+)-\omega _s\\ C=\omega _s-\omega _s&=0\;(\omega (t-0^+)=\omega _s) \\ \frac{d\delta }{dt}&=\frac{P_m \omega _s }{2H}t \\ \Rightarrow \; \delta &= \frac{P_m \omega _s }{4H}t^2+C'\\ C'&= \delta |_{t=0^+}=\delta _0\\ \delta &= \frac{P_m \omega _s }{4H}t^2+\delta _0\\ \text{Now in problem,}\\ \delta (t=0.02)&\\ &=\frac{1 \times 2 \times 180 \times 50 \times 0.02^2 +5^{\circ}}{4 \times 2}\\ &=5.9^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

In the signal flow diagram given in the figure, [latex]u_{1} \; and \; u_{2}[/latex] are possible inputs whereas [latex]y_{1} \; and \; y_{2}[/latex] are possible outputs. When would the SISO system derived from this diagram be controllable and observable?
raw_source.solution:
Equations from the flow diagram,[latex]\dot{x}_1=5x_1-2x_2+u_1 [/latex]
[latex]y_1=x_1 [/latex]
[latex]\dot{x}_2=5x_1+x_2+u_1+u_2 [/latex]
[latex]y_2=x_1-x_2 [/latex]
[latex]\dot{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2\\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}x+\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \\ 1& 1 \end{bmatrix}u [/latex]
[latex]y=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}x [/latex]
Considering the SISO cases:[/latex]

[latex] 1. \;\;u_1(input)[/latex] and [latex] y_1(output):[/latex]
[latex] A\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2\\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]B\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex] C=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]O\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} C\\ CA \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; Rank (O)=2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; Observable [/latex]
[latex]C\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} B & AB \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &3 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \; Rank(C)\neq 2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; non-controllable [/latex]

[latex]2.\;\;u_2(input) [/latex] and [latex] y_1(output): [/latex]
[latex]A\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2\\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]B\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex] C\triangleq \begin{bmatrix} 1 &-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]O\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; Rank (O)=2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; Observable [/latex]
[latex]C\triangleq\begin{bmatrix} 0 &-2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; Rank(C)=2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; controllable [/latex]

[latex]3. \;\;u_2(input) [/latex] and [latex] y_2(output) : [/latex]
[latex]Rank(O)\neq 2\Rightarrow[/latex] non-observable
[latex]Rank(C) =2 \Rightarrow [/latex] controllable

[latex]4. \; \; u_1 (input) [/latex] and [latex] y_2(output)[/latex]:
non-observale and non-controllable.
options: When [latex]u_{1}[/latex] is the only input and [latex]y_{1}[/latex] is the only output

raw_source.text: Two semi-infinite dielectric regions are separated by a plane boundary at y = 0. The electric field in region 2 is

Given that,
at the interface (y=0) there is no surface charge.
Region 1 ([latex]y \lt 0[/latex]) has [latex]\varepsilon _r=2[/latex]
Region 2 ([latex]y \gt 0[/latex]) has [latex]\varepsilon _r=5[/latex]
Electric field in region 1 is [latex]3a_x+4a_y+2a_z[/latex]
Normal component of electric field is [latex]4a_y[/latex] tangential component of electric field is [latex]3a_x+2a_y[/latex]
Now, [latex]E_1=E_{1t}+E_{1n}[/latex]
The tangentail component of [latex]E_1=[/latex] tangentail component of [latex]E_2[/latex]

raw_source.text: A circular turn of radius 1 m revolves at 60 rpm about its diameter aligned with the x-axis as shown in the figure. If a uniform magnetic field intensity [latex]\vec{H}=10^{7}\hat{z} A/m[/latex] is applied, then the peak value of the induced voltage, [latex]V_{turn}[/latex] ( in Volts), is _________.
raw_source.solution:
The circular turn rotate with 60 rpm, let the angle made by ring w.r.t. x-axis [latex]\theta[/latex]
and [latex]\;\;\; \theta =\omega _0 t[/latex]
the turn rotate at 60 rpm,
so, [latex]\;\;\; \omega _0=2 \pi [/latex]
So, the flux flowing through the circular turn wil be
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Psi &=(\mu _0 H_z \times \text{Area of turn} \times \cos \omega _0 t) \\ \Psi &= 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^7\; A/m \times \pi \times 1^2 \times \cos \omega _0 t\\ &\text{Maximum voltage induced is } \\ \\ \left. \begin{matrix} \frac{d\Psi}{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{max}&=(\omega _0 \times 4 \pi \times \pi \sin \omega _0 t)_{max}\\ V_{max}&=(4 \pi^2 \times 2 \pi)=248.05 volts \end{aligned}[/latex]

A 3-bus power system network consists of 3 transmission lines. The bus admittance matrix of the uncompensated system is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -j6 & j3&j4 \\ j3& -j7 & j5\\ j4 & j5 & -j8 \end{bmatrix}pu.[/latex]
If the shunt capacitance of all transmission lines is 50% compensated, the imaginary part of the [latex]3_{rd}[/latex] row [latex]3_{rd}[/latex] column element (in pu) of the bus admittance matrix after compensation is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Y_{BUS}&=\begin{bmatrix} y_{11}+y_{12}+y_{13} &-y_{12} &-y_{13} \\ -y_{21} & y_{21}+y_{22}+y_{23} & -y_{23}\\ -y_{31}& -y_{32} & y_{31}+y_{32}+y_{33} \end{bmatrix} \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} -j6 & j3 & j4\\ j3& -j7 & j5\\ j4 & j5 & -j8 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A series RL circuit is excited at t = 0 by closing a switch as shown in the figure. Assuming zero initial conditions, the value of [latex]\frac{d^{2}i}{dt^{2}}\; at \; t=0^{+}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Initially [latex](t=0^-)[/latex] the inductor would be uncharged.
So, [latex]I(0^+)=0[/latex]
The KVL in th loop will be
[latex]V=RI+L\frac{dI}{dt}[/latex]
At [latex]t=0^+ [/latex]
[latex]V=RI(0^+)+L\frac{dI}{dt}(0^+) [/latex]
Since, [latex] I(0^+)=0 [/latex]
So, [latex]\frac{dI}{dt}(0^+)=\frac{V}{L} [/latex]
Now, lets differentiate the above equation
So,[latex] \frac{dV}{dt}=R\frac{dI}{dt}+L\frac{d^2I}{dt^2} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;0=R\frac{dI}{dt}+L\frac{d^2I}{dt^2} [/latex]
At [latex]t=0^+[/latex]
[latex] 0=R\frac{dI}{dt}(0^+)+L\frac{d^2I}{dt^2}(0^+) [/latex]
So, [latex] \frac{d^2I}{dt^2}(0^+)=-\frac{R}{L^2}\cdot V[/latex]

[latex](2eq)_A={\left [ \frac{2.5}{a^2}+j\omega (1 \times 10^{-3})\right ]}/b^2 [/latex]
[latex]Z_{in}=\frac{2.5}{a^2b^2}+\frac{ j\omega 10^{-3}}{b^2}+\frac{1}{j\omega (10 \times 10^{-5})} [/latex]

From problem,
[latex]Z_{in}=2.5 \;\;...(ii) [/latex]
From equation (i) and (ii),
[latex]a^2b^2=1 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{5}{b^2}-\frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-2}}=0 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Suppose [latex]x_{1}(t) \; and \; x_{2}(t)[/latex] have the Fourier transforms as shown below.

Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
By observing [latex]X_1(j \omega )[/latex] and [latex]X_2(j \omega )[/latex], we can say that they are not conjugate symmetric. Since, the fourier transform is not conjugate symmetric the signal will not be real. So, [latex]x_1(t), x_2(t)[/latex] are not real. Now the fourier transform of [latex]x_1(t) \cdot x_2(t)[/latex] will be [latex]\frac{1}{2\pi}X_1(j \omega )*X_2(j \omega )[/latex] and by looking at [latex]X_1(j \omega )[/latex] and [latex]X_2(j \omega )[/latex], we can say that [latex]X_1(j \omega ) *X_2(j \omega )[/latex] will be conjugate symmetric and thus [latex]x_1(t) \cdot x_2(t)[/latex] will be real.
By observing [latex]X_1(j \omega )[/latex] and [latex]X_2(j \omega )[/latex], we can say,
[latex]X_2( \omega )=X_1(- \omega )\overset{IFT}{\rightarrow}x_2(t)=x_1(-t)\;\;...(i)[/latex]
Now, [latex]X_1(j \omega )[/latex] is real. Therefore, [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] will be conjugate symmetric.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{i.e., } x_1(t)&=x_1^*(-t) \\ \downarrow t&= -t\\ x_1(-t)&= x_1^*(t)\\ \text{Now, }x_1(t)\cdot x_2(t) &= x_1(t)\cdot x_1(-t) \;\;(from \;(i))\\ &= x_1(t)\cdot x_1^*(t)\\ &= |x_1(t)|^2=\text{real function} \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: [latex]x_{1}(t) \; and \; x_{2}(t)[/latex] are complex and [latex]x_{1}(t) x_{2}(t)[/latex] is also complex with nonzero imaginary part
[latex]x_{1}(t) \; and \; x_{2}(t)[/latex] are real and [latex]x_{1}(t) x_{2}(t)[/latex] is also real
[latex]x_{1}(t) \; and \; x_{2}(t)[/latex] are complex but [latex]x_{1}(t) x_{2}(t)[/latex] is real
[latex]x_{1}(t) \; and \; x_{2}(t)[/latex] are imaginary but [latex]x_{1}(t) x_{2}(t)[/latex] is real

raw_answer.option_text: [latex]x_{1}(t) \; and \; x_{2}(t)[/latex] are complex but [latex]x_{1}(t) x_{2}(t)[/latex] is real

raw_source.text:
The output of a continuous-time, linear time-invariant system is denoted by T{x(t)} where x(t) is the input signal. A signal z(t) is called eigen-signal of the system T, when [latex]T\{z(t)\} =  \gamma z(t)[/latex],
where [latex]\gamma[/latex] is a complex number, in general, and is called an eigenvalue of T. Suppose the impulse response of the system T is real and even. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
Given that impulse response is real and even, Thus [latex]H(j\omega )[/latex] will also be real and even.

Since, [latex]H(j\omega )[/latex] is real and even thus,
[latex]H(j\omega )=H(-j\omega )[/latex]
Now, [latex]\cos (t)[/latex] is input i.e. [latex]\frac{e^{jt}+e^{-jt}}{2}[/latex] is input
Output will be
[latex]\frac{H(j1)e^{jt}+H(-j1)e^{-jt}}{2}=H(j1)\left ( \frac{e^{jt}+e^{-jt}}{2} \right )= H(j1) \cos (t)[/latex]
If, [latex]\sin (t)[/latex] is input i.e. [latex]\frac{e^{jt}+e^{-jt}}{2}[/latex] is input
Output will be
[latex]\frac{H(j1)e^{jt}+H(-j1)e^{-jt}}{2}=H(j1)\left ( \frac{e^{jt}-e^{-jt}}{2j} \right )= H(j1) \sin (t)[/latex]
So, [latex]\sin (t)[/latex] and [latex]\cos (t)[/latex] are eigen signal with same eigen values.
options: cos(t) is an eigen-signal but sin(t) is not
cos(t) and sin(t) are both eigen-signals but with different eigenvalues
sin(t) is an eigen-signal but cos(t) is not
cos(t) and sin(t) are both eigen-signals with identical eigenvalues

raw_answer.option_text: cos(t) and sin(t) are both eigen-signals with identical eigenvalues

raw_source.text: A single-phase 400 V, 50 Hz transformer has an iron loss of 5000 W at the rated condition. When operated at 200 V, 25 Hz, the iron loss is 2000 W. When operated at 416 V, 52 Hz, the value of the hysteresis loss divided by the eddy current loss is ______.
raw_source.solution:
400V, 50Hz transformer, [latex]P_i=5000Watt[/latex]
When,
200V, 25Hz,
[latex]P_i=2000 Watt[/latex]
416V, 52Hz, [latex]\frac{P_h}{P_e}=? [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_i &=P_h+P_e \\ P_h & \propto f B_m^x \\ P_e& \propto f^2B_m^2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
as in the problem
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{V}{f}&=\frac{400}{50}=\frac{416}{52}=8 \\ P_h&=Af \\ P_e&=Bf^2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
From given data,
[latex]\begin{aligned} 2000 &=(P_{25hZ})){i} \\ &= A(25)+B(25)^2\;\;...(i)\\ 5000 &=(P_{50Hz})_i \\ &= A(50)+B(50)^2\;\;...(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving equation (i) and (ii),
[latex]\begin{aligned} A &=60,\;\; B=0.8 \\ (P_h)_{52Hz}&=Af=60 \times 52 \\ &= 3120 Watt\\ (P_e)_{52Hz}&=Bf^2=0.8 \times (52)^2 \\ &= 2163.2 Watt\\ \frac{(P_h)_{52Hz}}{(P_e)_{52Hz}}&=\frac{3120}{2163.2}=1.4423 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A three-phase, 50 Hz salient-pole synchronous motor has a per-phase direct-axis reactance ([latex]X_{d}[/latex]) of 0.8 pu and a per-phase quadrature-axis reactance ([latex]X_{q}[/latex]) of 0.6 pu. Synchronous motor at leading p.f.

raw_source.text: Consider a causal LTI system characterized by differential equation [latex]\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+\frac{1}{6}y(t)=3x(t)[/latex]. The response of the system to the input [latex]x(t)=3e^{-\frac{t}{3}}u(t)[/latex]. where u(t) denotes the unit step function, is
raw_source.solution:
The differential equation
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dy(t)}{dt} &+\frac{1}{6}y(t)=3x(t) \\ \text{So, }sY(s)&+\frac{1}{6}Y(s) =3X(s) \\ Y(s) &=\frac{3X(s)}{\left ( s+\frac{1}{6} \right )} \\ X(s) &=\frac{9}{\left ( s+\frac{1}{3} \right )} \\ \text{So, } Y(s)&=\frac{9}{\left ( s+\frac{1}{3} \right )\left ( s+\frac{1}{6} \right )} \\ &=\frac{54}{\left ( s+\frac{1}{6} \right )} -\frac{54}{\left ( s+\frac{1}{3} \right )}\\ \text{So, }y(t) &= (54e^{-1/6t}-54e^{-1/3t})u(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider a linear time-invariant system with transfer function

If the input is cos(t) and the steady state output is [latex]A \cos (t+\alpha )[/latex], then the value of A is _________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} H(s)&=\frac{1}{(s+1)}\\ \text{Put, }s&=j\omega \\ H(j\omega)&=\frac{1}{j\omega+1}\\ |H(j\omega)|&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega ^2 +1}}\\ \because \; \text{ input }x(t)&=\cos (t)\\ \text{Here, } \omega &=1 \text{rad/sec}\\ \text{and }|x(t)|&=1\\ \text{hence, }&\text{steady state output}\\ y(t)&=|H(j\omega)|_{\omega=1} \cos (t+\angle H(j\omega)|_{\omega =1})\\ A&=|H(j\omega)|_{\omega =1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=0.707 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Let the probability density function of a random variable, X, be given as:

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f_x(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} ax^{4x} &x \lt 0 \\ \frac{3}{2}e^{-3x}& x\geq 0 \end{matrix}\right.\\ \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f_x(x)&=1\\ \int_{-\infty }^{0}ax^{4x}dx+\int_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{2}e^{-3x}dx&=1\\ \left [ \frac{ax^{4x}}{4} \right ]_{-\infty }^0+\left [ \frac{\frac{3}{2}e^{-3x}}{-3} \right ]_0^\infty &=1\\ \frac{a}{3}+\frac{3}{6}&=1\\ a&=2\\ P(x\leq 0)&=\int_{-\infty }^{0}2e^{4x}dx \\ &=\left [ \frac{e^{4x}}{2} \right ]_{-\infty }^0=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The open loop transfer function of a unity feedback control system is given by
[latex]G(s)=\frac{K(s+1)}{s(1+Ts)(1+2s)}, K\gt 0,T \gt 0[/latex]
The closed loop system will be stable if,
raw_source.solution:
Open loop transfer function:
[latex]G(s)=\frac{K(s+1)}{s(1+Ts)(1+2s)};[/latex] [latex] \; K \gt 0 \; [/latex] and [latex]\; t \gt 0[/latex]
For closed loop system stability, characteristic equation is,
[latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0[/latex]
[latex] 1+\frac{K(s+1)}{s(1+Ts)(1+2s)}\cdot 1=0[/latex]
[latex] s(1+Ts)(1+2s)+K(s+1)=0 [/latex]
[latex]2Ts^3+(2+T)s^2+(1+K)s+K=0 [/latex]
Using Routh's criteria,

For stability, [latex]K \gt 0[/latex]
and [latex] (2+T)(1+K)-2TK \gt 0 [/latex]
[latex]K(2+T-2T)+(2+T) \gt 0 [/latex]
or
[latex] -(T-2)K+2(2+T) \gt 0 [/latex]
[latex]-K \gt -\frac{(2+T)}{(T-2)}[/latex] or [latex] K \lt \frac{T+2}{(T-2)} [/latex]
Hence for stability,
[latex]0 \lt K \lt \frac{T+2}{T-2}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_s&=AV_R\\ 400 &=A420\\ A&=\frac{400}{420}=0.9524\\ A&=1+\frac{YZ}{2}\\ &=1+\frac{(r+j\omega L)()g+j\omega C)}{2}\\ &\text{For lossless line,}\\ r&=0,g=0\\ \text{then,}\\ A&=1-\frac{(\omega C)(\omega L)}{2}\\ \beta l&=\sqrt{\omega L\omega C}\\ A&=0.9524=1-\frac{\beta ^2l^2}{2}\\ \beta l&=0.3085\\ \beta &=\frac{0.3085}{l}\\ \frac{V}{f}&=\frac{2\pi}{\beta }\\ \frac{3 \times 10^5}{50}&=\frac{2 \pi}{\left ( \frac{0.3085}{l} \right )}\\ l&=294.52km \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The power consumption of an industry is 500 kVA, at 0.8 p.f. lagging. A synchronous motor is added to raise the power factor of the industry to unity. If the power intake of the motor is 100 kW, the p.f. of the motor is _____________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_1 &= 500 \times 0.8=400kW\\ Q_1&= 500 \times 0.6=300kVAR \end{aligned}[/latex]
The power factor is to be raised to unity
The motor has to supply 300kVAR
The motor rating is 100 kW, 300kVAR
[latex] \begin{aligned} \phi _m &=\tan ^{-1}\left ( \frac{Q}{P} \right ) \\ \phi _m&= \tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{300}{100} \right ) =71.56 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Power factor of motor [latex]= \cos \phi _m=\cos 71.56=0.316[/latex]

raw_source.text: The flux linkage ([latex]\lambda[/latex]) and current (i) relation for an electromagnetic system is [latex]\lambda = (\sqrt{i})/g[/latex]. When i=2A and g (air-gap length)=10cm, the magnitude of mechanical force on the moving part, in N, is ________.
raw_source.solution:
Energy in magnetic system,
[latex]\begin{aligned} W_f &= \int_{0}^{\lambda } i(\lambda )\; d\lambda \\ \because \;\; i &=\lambda ^2g^2 \\ W_f &= \int_{0}^{\lambda } \lambda ^2g^2 \; d\lambda \\ &=g^2\frac{\lambda ^3}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Now, mechanical force,
[latex]\begin{aligned} F_F &=-\frac{\partial W_f (\lambda ,g)}{\partial g} \\ &=-\frac{\partial }{\partial g} \left ( \frac{g^2\lambda ^3}{3} \right )\\ &= -\frac{2}{3}\lambda ^3 g\\ \because \;\; i=2, \;g&=10cm ,\; \lambda =10\sqrt{2} \\ \text{Hence,}\;\;|F_F|&=\frac{2}{3} \times (10\sqrt{2})^3 \times 0.1\\ &=188.56N \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Single Phase Induction Motors, Special Purpose Machines and Electromechanical Energy Conversion System

raw_source.text:
The starting line current of a 415 V, 3-phase, delta connected induction motor is 120 A, when the rated voltage is applied to its stator winding. The starting line current at a reduced voltage of 110 V,
in ampere, is _________.
raw_source.solution:
415V, 3-phase, [latex]\Delta[/latex] connected induction motor

at, V=110V, i.e. reduced voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{st} &=x(I_{st})_{rated} \\ \text{where}\;\; x&= \frac{V_{reduced}}{V_{rated}}\\ &=\frac{110}{415} \\ (I_{st})_{at \; 110V} &= \left ( \frac{110}{415} \right )\times 120\\ &=31.807A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single-phase, 2 kVA, 100/200 V transformer is reconnected as an auto-transformer such that its kVA rating is maximum. The new rating, in kVA, is ______.
raw_source.solution:
2 kVA, 100/200 V transformer,
[latex]\begin{aligned} A_{2 winding} &=\frac{200}{100}=2 \\ [(kVA)_{auto}]_{max} &= (a_{2winding}+1)(kVA)_{2winding} \\ &=(2+1) \times 2 =6 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A full-bridge converter supplying an RLE load is shown in figure. The firing angle of the bridge converter is 120[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. The supply voltage [latex]v_{m}(t) = 200\pi sin (100 \pi t) V [/latex], [latex]R=20 \Omega[/latex], E=800 V. The inductor L is large enough to make the output current [latex]I_L[/latex] a smooth dc current. Switches are lossless. The real power fed back to the source, in kW, is __________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_0&=2\frac{V_m}{\pi}\cos \alpha \\ &=2\frac{200 \pi}{\pi} \cos 120^{\circ}\\ V_0&=-200V\\ |V_0|&=200V\\ &\text{Power balance equation}\\ EI_0&=I_0^2 R+V_0I_0\\ 800I_0&=I_0^2(20)+200I_0\\ I+0&=30A\\ &\text{Power fed to source}\\ &=V_0I_0\\ &=200 \times 30\\ &=6kW \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A three-phase Voltage Source Inverter (VSI) as shown in the figure is feeding a delta connected resistive load of 30 [latex]\Omega[/latex]/phase. If it is fed from a 600 V battery, with 180[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] conduction of solid-state devices, the power consumed by the load, in kW, is __________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_L&=V_{ph}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}V_s\\ V_{ph}&=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \times 600\\ P&=3\frac{V_{ph}^2}{R}=\frac{3 \times \frac{2}{3} \times 600^2}{30}\\ &=24kW \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A DC-DC boost converter, as shown in the figure below, is used to boost 360V to 400 V, at a power of 4 kW. All devices are ideal. Considering continuous inductor current, the rms current in the solid state switch (S), in ampere, is _________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{V_0}{V_s}&=\frac{1}{1-\alpha } \\ \frac{400}{360}&= \frac{1}{1-\alpha }\\ \alpha &= 0.1\\ V_sI_s&= \text{Power}\\ 360I_s &=4000\\ I_s&=11.1A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Neglecting ripple in [latex]i_s[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{\text{switch (rms)}}&=I_s\left ( \frac{T_{on}}{T} \right )^{1/2}\\ &=I_s\sqrt{\alpha }\\ &=11.1\sqrt{0.1}=3.5A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single-phase bi-directional voltage source converter (VSC) is shown in the figure below. All devices are ideal. It is used to charge a battery at 400 V with power of 5 kW from a source [latex]V_s[/latex]=220 V (rms), 50 Hz sinusoidal AC mains at unity p.f. If its AC side interfacing inductor is 5 mH and the switches are operated at 20 kHz, then the phase shift ([latex]\delta[/latex]) between AC mains voltage ([latex]V_s[/latex]) and fundamental AC rms VSC voltage ([latex]V_{c1}[/latex]), in degree, is _________.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} P&=V_sI_s \;p.f.\\ 5 \times 10^3 &= 220 \times I_s \times 1\\ I_s&=22.72A\\ \tan \delta &=\frac{I_s X_s}{V_s}\\ \delta &=\tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{I_sX_s}{V_s} \right )\\ \delta &=\tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{22.72 \times 2 \pi \times 50 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}}{220} \right )\\ \delta &=9.21^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a linear time invariant system [latex]\dot{x}=Ax[/latex], with initial condition [latex]x(0)[/latex] at t=0. Suppose [latex]\alpha \; and \; \beta[/latex] are eigenvectors of (2 x 2) matrix A corresponding to distinct eigenvalues [latex]\lambda_{1} \; and \;  \lambda _{2}[/latex] respectively. Then the response [latex]x(t)[/latex] of the system due to initial condition [latex]x(0)=\alpha[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\dot{x}=Ax[/latex]
Eigen values are [latex]\lambda _1[/latex] and [latex]\lambda _2[/latex]
we can write,
[latex]\phi (t)=\begin{bmatrix} e^{\lambda _1 t} & 0\\ 0& e^{\lambda _2 t} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
Response due to initial conditions,
[latex]x(t)=\phi (t)x(0) [/latex]
[latex]x(t)=\begin{bmatrix} e^{\lambda _1 t} & 0\\ 0& e^{\lambda _2 t} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]=\alpha e^{\lambda _1 t}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A second-order real system has the following properties:
a) the damping ratio [latex]\xi[/latex] = 0.5 and undamped natural frequency [latex]\omega _{n}[/latex]=10 rad/s,
b) the steady state value of the output, to a unit step input, is 1.02.
The transfer function of the system is
raw_source.solution:
Damping ratio [latex]\xi=0.5[/latex]
Undamped natural frequency [latex]\omega _n=10[/latex] rad/sec
Steady state output toa unit step input [latex]C_{ss}=1.02[/latex]
Hence steady state error [latex]e_{ss}=1.02-1.00=0.02[/latex]
[latex] \because[/latex] Characteristic equation is,
[latex]s^2+2 \xi \omega _ns+\omega _n^2=0 [/latex]
[latex]s^2+2 \times 0.5\times 10 s+100=0 [/latex]
[latex]s^2+10s+100=0[/latex]
From options, if we take option (B) then
[latex] C_{ss}=\lim_{s \to 0}s\cdot C(s) [/latex]
[latex]\;\; \; \; \;=\lim_{s \to 0 }s \times \frac{1}{s} \times \frac{102}{s^2+10s+100} [/latex]
[latex]C_{ss}=1.02[/latex]
Hence, Option (B) is correct answer.

raw_source.text: Three single-phase transformers are connected to form a delta-star three-phase transformer of 110 kV/ 11 kV. The transformer supplies at 11 kV a load of 8 MW at 0.8 p.f. lagging to a nearby plant. Neglect the transformer losses. The ratio of phase currents in delta side to star side is
raw_source.solution:
At, 100 kV, load is 8 MW, 0.8 p.f. lagging
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{(V_{ph})_{\Delta }}{(V_{ph})_{Y}} &= \frac{(I_{ph})_{Y}}{(I_{ph})_{\Delta }}\\ \Rightarrow \;\; (I_{ph})_{\Delta } &= (I_{ph})_Y \times \frac{(V_{ph})_{Y}}{(V_{ph})_{\Delta }} \\ \frac{(I_{ph})_{\Delta }}{(V_{ph})_{Y}}&=\frac{11\sqrt{3}}{110}=1:10\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The gain at the breakaway point of the root locus of a unity feedback system with open loop transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{Ks}{(s-1)(s-4)}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]OLTS\Rightarrow G(s)=\frac{Ks}{(s-1)(s-4)}[/latex]
Now, characteristic equation,
[latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0[/latex]
[latex] \frac{Ks}{(s-1)(s-4)}+1=0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \;\; Ks+(s^2-5s+4)=0 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;K=-\frac{(s^2-5s+4)}{s}=\left [ s-5+\frac{4}{s} \right ][/latex]
For break away point [latex]: \frac{dK}{ds}=0[/latex]
[latex] \frac{dK}{ds}=-\left [ 1-0-\frac{4}{s^2} \right ]=0 [/latex]
We get, [latex]s=\pm 2[/latex]
Therefore valid break away point is s=2
Now gain at s=2 is
K=(Product of distances from all the poles to break away point)/(Product of distances from all the zero to break away point)
Gain, [latex]K=\frac{1 \times 2}{2}=1[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rotating conductor of 1 m length is placed in a radially outward (about the z-axis) magnetic flux density (B) of 1 Tesla as shown in figure below. Conductor is parallel to and at 1 m distance from the z-axis. The speed of the conductor in r.p.m. required to induce a voltage of 1 V across it, should be __________.
raw_source.solution:
Voltage insuced [latex]=\int_{0}^{1}E_m \cdot dt[/latex]
(where [latex]E_m[/latex] is induced electric field)
Since,
Volatage induced =1 V
So, [latex]E_m[/latex] = 1 V/m
As we know, [latex]E_m=\bar{V} \times \bar{B}[/latex]
where, V= (radius of path) x (angular velocity)
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{1V}{m} &=(V \times 1 \; \text{Tesla}) \\ V&=1 \; m/sec \\ V&= r \times \omega =1 \; m/sec\\ \text{Since, } r&=1m, \; \text{So }\omega =1 \; \text{rad/sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now from this we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} \omega &=2 \times \pi \times \frac{N}{60}=1 \; \text{rad/sec}\\ N&=\frac{30}{\pi}=9.55 \; \text{revolutions per minute} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For a complex number z, [latex]\lim_{z\rightarrow i}\frac{z^{2}+1}{z^{3}+2z-i(z^{2}+2)}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \lim_{z \to i}&=\frac{z^2+1}{z^3+2z-i(z^2+2)}\\ \lim_{z \to i}&=\frac{2z}{3z^2+2-i(2z)}\\ &=\frac{2i}{3i^2+2-i(2i)}\\ &=\frac{2i}{-3+2+2}\\ &=\frac{2i}{-3+4}=2i \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The matrix [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{3}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\\ 0 & -1 & 0\\ \frac{1}{2}& 0 & \frac{3}{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex] has three distinct eigenvalues and one of its eigenvectors is [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which one of the following can be another eigenvector of A?
raw_source.solution:
The given matrix is symmetric and all its eigen values are distinct. Hence all its eigen vectors are orthogonal one of the eigen vector is
[latex]x_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The corresponding orthogonal vector in the given option is C i.e. [latex]x_2=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0\\ -1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]{x_1}^T\cdot x_2=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0\\ -1 \end{bmatrix}=1+0-1=0[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]I=c\int \int_{R}xy^{2}dxdy[/latex], where R is the region shown in the figure and [latex]c=6 \times 10^{-4}[/latex]. The value of I equals________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
I&=C\int \int xy^2\; dx \; dy\\
&=C\int_{x=1}^{5}\int_{y=0}^{2x}xy^2\; dx \; dy\\
&=C\int_{1}^{5}x\left.\begin{matrix}
\left ( \frac{y^3}{3} \right )
\end{matrix}\right|_{0}^{2x}\; dx\\
&=C\int_{1}^{5}x\frac{8x^3}{3}dx\\
&=C\int_{1}^{5}8\frac{x^4}{3}dx\\
&=C\frac{8}{3}\left.\begin{matrix}
\left ( \frac{x^5}{5} \right )
\end{matrix}\right|_{1}^5\\
&=\frac{8C}{3}\left ( 5^4-\frac{1}{5} \right )\\
&=\frac{8C}{3}(625-0.2)\\
&=\frac{8}{3}(6 \times 10^{-4})(625-0.2)\\
&=0.99968
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the differential equation [latex](t^{2}-81)\frac{dy}{dt}+5ty=sin(t)[/latex] with [latex] y(1)=2\pi[/latex]. There exists a unique solution for this differential equation when t belongs to the interval
raw_source.solution:
The differentail equation,
[latex]\begin{aligned} (t^2-81)\frac{dy}{dt}+5+y&= \sin t\\ \frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{5t}{t^2-81}y&=\frac{\sin t }{t^2-81}\\ P&=\frac{5t}{t^2-81}\\ Q&=\frac{\sin t}{t^2-81}\\ I.F&=e^{\int \rho dt}=e^{\int \frac{5t}{t^2-81}dt}\\ &=e^{\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{2t}{t^2-81}dt}=e^{\frac{5}{2}\ln ({t^2-81})}\\ &=e^{\ln {(t^2-81)^{5/2}}}=(t^2-81)^{5/2}\\ \text{Solution is }&\\ y(t^2-81)^{5/2}&=\int \frac{\sin t}{t^2-81}(t^2-81)^{5/2}dt\\ y&=\frac{\int (\sin t)(t^2-81)^{3/2}dt}{(t^2-81)^{5/2}}+\frac{C}{(t^2-81)^{5/2}}\\ &\text{The solution exist for } t\neq -9, t\neq +9 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Only option (A) not cover 9 and -9. Hence it is correct.

raw_source.text:
A function f(x) is defined as
[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} e^{x}, & x \lt 1\\ lnx+ax^{2}+bx & x\geq 1 \end{matrix}\right. \; where\; x\in \mathbb{R}[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} e^x & x \lt 1\\ \ln x+ax^2+bx & x \gt 1 \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
At x=1,
L.H.S=R.H.S
e=a+b ...(i)
At x=1, f'(x) exists
[latex]f'(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} e^x & x \lt 1\\ \frac{1}{x}+20x+b & x \gt 1 \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
At x=1,
L.H.S=R.H.S
e=1+2a+b
2a+b=e-1 ...(ii)
From equation (i) and (ii),
a=-1
b=e+1
f(x) is differentiable at x=1 for unique value of a and b.
options: f(x) is NOT differentiable at x=1 for any values of a and b.
f(x) is differentiable at x = 1 for the unique values of a and b
f(x) is differentiable at x = 1 for all values of a and b such that a + b = e
f(x) is differentiable at x = 1 for all values of a and b.

raw_source.text: Only one of the real roots of [latex]f(x)=x^{6}-x-1[/latex] lies in the interval [latex]1\leq x\leq 2[/latex] and bisection method is used to find its value. For achieving an accuracy of 0.001, the required minimum number of iterations is ________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^6-x-1\\ a&=1, b=2, \in =0.01=10^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The minimum number of iterations by Bisection method is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{|b-a|}{2^n} &\lt \in\\ \frac{2-1}{2^n} &\lt 10^{-3}\\ \frac{1}{2^n} &\lt \frac{1}{10^{-3}}\\ 2^n &\gt 10^3\\ n &\gt \frac{\ln 1000}{\ln 2}\\ n &\gt 9.96\\ n&=10 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the line integral [latex]I=\int_{c}(x^{2}+iy^{2})dz[/latex] where [latex]z = x + iy[/latex]. The line C is shown in the figure below.

The value of I is
raw_source.solution:
From the diagram C is [latex]y=x[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Assume that in a traffic junction, the cycle of the traffic signal lights is 2 minutes of green
(vehicle does not stop) and 3 minutes of red (vehicle stops). Consider that the arrival time of
vehicles at the junction is uniformly distributed over 5 minute cycle. The expected waiting time
(in minutes) for the vehicle at the junction is ________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]t[/latex] be arrival time of vehicles of the junction is uniformaly distributed in [0,5].
Let y be the waiting time of the junction.

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Then }y&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 0 & t \lt 2 \\ 5-t & 2\leq t \lt 5 \end{matrix}\right.\\ y\rightarrow &[0,5]\\ f(y)&=\frac{1}{5-0}=\frac{1}{5}\\ E(y)&=\int_{-\infty }^{0}y(y)dy=\int_{0}^{5}yf(y)dy\\ &=\int_{2}^{5}y\left ( \frac{1}{5} \right )dy=\frac{1}{5}\int_{2}^{5}(5-t)dt\\ &=\frac{1}{5}\left ( 5t-\frac{t^2}{2} \right )|_2^5\\ &=\frac{1}{5}\left [ \left ( 25-\frac{25}{2} \right )-\left ( 10-\frac{4}{2} \right ) \right ]\\ &=\frac{1}{5}\left ( \frac{25}{2}-8 \right )=\frac{1}{5}\frac{9}{2}=0.9 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let x and y be integers satisfying the following equations
[latex]2x^{2}+y^{2}=34[/latex]
[latex]x+2y=11[/latex]
The value of (x+y) is ________.

Consider a function f (x, y,z) given by
[latex]f(x,y,z)=(x^{2}+y^{2}-2z^{2})(y^{2}+z^{2})[/latex]
The partial derivative of this function with respect to x at the point, x = 2, y = 1 and z = 3 is ________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x,y,z)&=(x^2+y^2-2z^2)(y^2+z^2)\\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=(x^2+y^2-2z^2)(0)+(y^2+z^2)(2x)\\ &=0+(y^2+z^2)(2x)\\ \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \end{matrix}\right|_{x=2,y=1,z=3}&=(1+9)(2)(2)=40 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]y^{2}-2y+1=x[/latex] and [latex]\sqrt{x}+y=5[/latex]. The value of [latex]x+\sqrt{y}[/latex] equals _________. (Give the answer up to three decimal places)
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x}+y&=5\\ \sqrt{x}+1+5x&=5\\ 2\sqrt{x}&=4\\ x&=4\\ y^2-2y+1&=x\\ (y-1)^2&=x\\ y-1&=\sqrt{x}\\ y&=1+\sqrt{x}\\ y&=1+\sqrt{4}=3\\ \therefore \;\;x+\sqrt{y}&=4+\sqrt{3}=5.732 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A person decides to toss a fair coin repeatedly until he gets a head. He will make at most 3

&=C\int_{1}^{5}x\left.\begin{matrix}

&=C\int_{1}^{5}x\frac{8x^3}{3}dx\\

&=\frac{8}{3}(6 \times 10^{-4})(625-0.2)\\
&=0.99968
\end{aligned}[/latex]

A 220 V DC series motor runs drawing a current of 30 A from the supply. Armature and field

[latex]\begin{aligned}
T &\propto N^2 \\ 
 \phi &\propto I_a \\ 
T &\propto I_a^2\\ 
\therefore \; N^2 &\propto I_a^2 \\ 
 \therefore \; \frac{N_2}{N_1}&= \frac{I_{a2}}{I_{a1}}\\ 
 \therefore \; 0.5&= \frac{I_{a2}}{30}\\ 
 \Rightarrow \; I_{a2}&=15A \\ 
&\text{For series motor,}\\

 \therefore \; \frac{E_{b2}}{E_{b1}}&= 0.25\\ 
E_{b1} &=220-30(0.4+0.1) \\ 
E_{b1} &=205V \\ 
\therefore \; E_{b2}&=51.25V \\ 
\therefore \; E_{b2} &= V-I_{a2}(R_a+R_{se}+R_{ext})\\ 
51.25 &= 220-15(0.4+0.1+R_{ext})\\
\therefore \;R_{ext}&=10.75\Omega 
\end{aligned}
[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the differential equation [latex](t^{2}-81)\frac{dy}{dt}+5ty=sin(t)[/latex] with [latex] y(1)=2\pi[/latex]. There exists a unique solution for this differential equation when t belongs to the interval
raw_source.solution:
The differentail equation,
[latex]\begin{aligned} (t^2-81)\frac{dy}{dt}+5+y&= \sin t\\ \frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{5t}{t^2-81}y&=\frac{\sin t }{t^2-81}\\ P&=\frac{5t}{t^2-81}\\ Q&=\frac{\sin t}{t^2-81}\\ I.F&=e^{\int \rho dt}=e^{\int \frac{5t}{t^2-81}dt}\\ &=e^{\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{2t}{t^2-81}dt}=e^{\frac{5}{2}\ln ({t^2-81})}\\ &=e^{\ln {(t^2-81)^{5/2}}}=(t^2-81)^{5/2}\\ \text{Solution is }&\\ y(t^2-81)^{5/2}&=\int \frac{\sin t}{t^2-81}(t^2-81)^{5/2}dt\\ y&=\frac{\int (\sin t)(t^2-81)^{3/2}dt}{(t^2-81)^{5/2}}+\frac{C}{(t^2-81)^{5/2}}\\ &\text{The solution exist for } t\neq -9, t\neq +9 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Only option (A) not cover 9 and -9. Hence it is correct.

raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]R_a=0.1\Omega[/latex]
As, DC generator is connected with DC grid, the output voltage will be constant.
When generator is running at 800 rpm,
Generator emf,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a1} &=V+I_{a1}R-a \\ &= 145+150 \times 0.1\\ &= 160V \end{aligned}[/latex]
When generator is running at 1000 rpm,
Generator emf,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a2} &=E_{a1} \times \frac{N_2}{N_1}\\ &= 160 \times \frac{1000}{800}\\ &= 200V \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, new armature currrent will be,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a2} &=\frac{E_{a2}-V}{R_a}\\ &= \frac{200-145}{0.1}\\ &= 550A \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The magnitude of magnetic flux density (B) in micro Teslas ([latex]\mu[/latex]T) at the center of a loop of wire wound as a regular hexagon of side length 1m carrying a current (I=1A), and placed in vacuum as shown in the figure is __________.
raw_source.solution:
i= 1 A

Here, B at point P is
[latex]B=\frac{\mu _0I}{4 \pi d}(\sin \theta _1 +\sin \theta _2)[/latex]
We know for each segment of hexagon

magnetic field intensity due to element length dx,
[latex]dH=\frac{Idx}{4 \pi r^2}i \times u_r[/latex]
where,
[latex]i \times u_r=(\sin \theta)\hat{k}[/latex]....perpendicular to plane of paper
[latex]\begin{aligned} H &=\int dH=\int \frac{I \sin \theta}{4 \pi r^2}(dx)\hat{k} \\ B&=\mu _0 H \\ B_p&=\frac{\mu _0I}{4 \pi d}(\cos \alpha _1+\cos \alpha _2)\hat{k} \\ d&=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} l\;\;\;...\text{where}\; l=1m\\ \alpha _1&=\alpha _2 =60^{\circ}\\ |B_p| &=\frac{\mu _0 I}{4 \pi \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} }(\cos 60^{\circ} +\cos 60^{\circ}) \\ &\text{for all six segment} \\ 6 \times |B_p| &=\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 6 \times 1}{4 \pi \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} }(1) \\ &=\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}\times 10^{-7}=\frac{1.20}{\sqrt{3}}\times 10^{-6}T \\ B&=0.69 \mu T \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The figure shows the single line diagram of a power system with a double circuit transmission line. The expression for electrical power is [latex]1.5 sin\delta[/latex], where [latex]\delta[/latex] is the rotor angle. The system is operating at the stable equilibrium point with mechanical power equal to 1 pu. If one of the transmission line circuits is removed, the maximum value of [latex]\delta[/latex] as the rotor swings, is 1.221 radian. If the expression for electrical power with one transmission line circuit removed is [latex] P_{max} sin\delta[/latex], the valueof [latex] P_{max} [/latex], in pu is _________.
raw_source.solution:
Using equal area criteria:
[latex]A_1=A_2[/latex]
[latex]\int_{\delta _0}^{\delta _c}(P_{m0}-P_{max1} \sin \delta )d\delta =\int_{\delta _c}^{\delta _2}(P_{max1} \sin \delta -P_{m0})d\delta[/latex]
By solving above integration,
[latex]P_{max1}=\frac{P_{m0}(\delta _2-\delta _0)}{\cos \delta _0- \cos \delta _2}[/latex]
Given data:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{m0} &=1pu \\ P_e&= 1.5 \sin (\delta _0)=P_{m0}=1pu\\ \delta _0&41.8^{\circ}=0.7295\; rad \\ \delta _2 &=1.221\; rad =96.95^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substitute above values in above equation,
[latex]P_{max1}=\frac{1(1.221-0.7295)}{\cos 41.8- \cos 69.95}=1.220 p.u.[/latex]

A 375W, 230 V, 50 Hz capacitor start single-phase induction motor has the following constants
for the main and auxiliary windings (at starting): [latex]Z_{m}=(24.50+j12.75)\Omega[/latex] (main winding), [latex]Z_{n}=(24.50+j12.75)\Omega[/latex] (auxiliary winding).  Neglecting the magnetizing branch the value of the capacitance (in [latex]\mu[/latex]F ) to be added in series with the auxiliary winding to obtain maximum torque at starting is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Auxiliary winding impedance [latex]=(24.5+j12.75)\Omega[/latex]
Let [latex]X_c[/latex] be the reactance of the capacitor connected in auxiliary winding
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_a &= (24.5+j12.75-jX_c)\Omega \\ X_a &=(X_c-12.75),\; R_a=24.5\Omega \\ \therefore \;\; \phi _a &=\tan^{-1}\frac{X_c-12.75}{24.5}\;...(i) \\ Z_m&= 12.5+j15.75\\ &= 20.10\angle 51.56^{\circ}\Omega \\ \phi _m&= 51.56^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For maximum torque at starting, condition on [latex] \phi _a[/latex] and [latex]\phi _m[/latex] is given by [latex]\left [ \phi _a=\frac{90^{\circ}-\phi _m}{2} \right ][/latex]
[latex] \phi _a=\frac{90-51.56}{2}=19.22^{\circ}}\;...(ii) [/latex]
Comparing equation (i) and (ii),
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tan(19.22^{\circ}) &=\frac{X_c-12.75}{24.5} \\ 0.3486 &= \frac{X_c-12.75}{24.5}\\ X_c &=8.541+12.75 \\ \text{Capacitive reactance,}& \\ X_c &= 21.291\Omega \\ \frac{1}{2 \pi fc}&= 21.291\\ \Rightarrow \;C&= \frac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 21.291}\\ &= 149.51\mu F \end{aligned}[/latex]

L.H.S=R.H.S
e=a+b ...(i)

raw_source.text:
Consider a causal and stable LTI system with rational transfer function H(z). Whose
corresponding impulse response begins at n = 0. Furthermore, [latex]H(1)=\frac{5}{4}[/latex]. The poles of H(z) are [latex]P_{k}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}exp(j\frac{(2k-1)\pi }{4})[/latex] for k = 1,2,3,4. The zeros of H(z) are all at z = 0. Let [latex]g[n]=j^nh[n][/latex]. The value of g[8] equals ___________.
raw_source.solution:
Pole locationof H(z) are given as,
[latex]\begin{aligned} z&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{j(2K-1)\frac{\pi}{4}};\;\;K=1,2,3,4\\ z_1&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{j\frac{\pi}{4}} =\frac{1}{2}(1+j)\\ z_2&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{j\frac{3\pi}{4}} =\frac{1}{2}(-1+j)\\ z_3&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{j\frac{5\pi}{4}} =\frac{1}{2}(-1-j)\\ z_4&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{j\frac{7\pi}{4}} =\frac{1}{2}(1-j)\\ \text{Now,}\\ H(z)&=\frac{K\cdot z^4}{(z-z_1)(z-z_2)(z-z_3)(z-z_4)}...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[As h(n) is causal and it starts from n=0, so numerator will have same order as denominator is having]. by solving equation (i)
[latex]\begin{aligned} H(z)&=\frac{K\cdot z^4}{z^4+\frac{1}{4}}\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{Given that,}\\ H(1)&=\frac{5}{4}\\ &\text{From equation (ii),}\\ H(1)&=\frac{K}{1+\frac{1}{4}}\Rightarrow \frac{5}{4}=\frac{K}{\frac{5}{4}}\\ \Rightarrow \; K&=\frac{25}{16}\\ H(z)&=\frac{\frac{25}{16}z^4}{z^4+\frac{1}{4}}\\ &\text{By using division rule,}\\ H(z)&=\frac{25}{16}\left [ 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-4}+\frac{1}{16}z^{-8}+... \right ]\\ \text{Thus, }h(8)&=\frac{1}{16} \times \frac{25}{16}=0.097\\ &\text{it is given that,}\\ g(n)&=j^nh(n)\\ g(8)&=j^8h(8)=h(8)\\ \Rightarrow \; g(8)&=h(8)=0.097 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Only one of the real roots of [latex]f(x)=x^{6}-x-1[/latex] lies in the interval [latex]1\leq x\leq 2[/latex] and bisection method is used to find its value. For achieving an accuracy of 0.001, the required minimum number of iterations is ________.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^6-x-1\\ a&=1, b=2, \in =0.01=10^{-3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The minimum number of iterations by Bisection method is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{|b-a|}{2^n} &\lt \in\\ \frac{2-1}{2^n} &\lt 10^{-3}\\ \frac{1}{2^n} &\lt \frac{1}{10^{-3}}\\ 2^n &\gt 10^3\\ n &\gt \frac{\ln 1000}{\ln 2}\\ n &\gt 9.96\\ n&=10 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two parallel connected, three-phase, 50Hz, 11kV, star-connected synchronous machines A and B, are operating as synchronous condensers. They together supply 50 MVAR to a 11 kV grid. Current supplied by both the machines are equal. Synchronous reactances of machine A and machine B are 1[latex]\Omega[/latex] and 3[latex]\Omega[/latex] respectively. Assuming the magnetic circuit to be linear, the ratio of excitation current of machine A to that of machine B is ________.
raw_source.solution:
Synchronous machine A:
11 kV, 50 Hz, Y connected, [latex]X_s=1\Omega[/latex]

Synchronous machine B:
11 kV, 50 Hz, Y connected, [latex]X_s=3\Omega[/latex]
Given both supplying only reactive power 50MVAR tp 11 kV grid equally
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \; Q_A &=\sqrt{3}VI_A \sin \phi =25mVAR \\ Q_B &= \sqrt{3}VI_B \sin \phi =25mVAR\\ \therefore \;\;I_A &=\frac{25 \times 10^6}{\sqrt{3} \times 11 \times 10^3}=1312.2A \\ \therefore \;\; I_B&= 1312.2A\\ E_A &= V-jI_AX_s\\ &=\frac{11 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3}}-j1312.2\angle 90 \times 1 \\ E_B &=V_jI_BX_s \\ &= =\frac{11 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3}}-j1312.2\angle 90 \times 3 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given magnetic circuit to be linear,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\; E &\propto I_f \\ \therefore \;\; \frac{I_{f_A}}{I_{f_B}}&=\frac{E_A}{E_B} \\ E_A&=7663.05V \\ E_B &= 10287.45V \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, ratio of excitation current of machine A to machine B
[latex] \frac{E_A}{E_B}=0.745[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The positive, negative and zero sequence reactances of a wye-connected synchronous generator
are 0.2 pu, 0.2 pu, and 0.1 pu, respectively. The generator is on open circuit with a terminal
voltage of 1 pu. The minimum value of the inductive reactance, in pu, required to be connected
between neutral and ground so that the fault current does not exceed 3.75 pu if a single line to
ground fault occurs at the terminals is _______ (assume fault impedance to be zero).

Let the signal [latex]x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{+\infty }(-1)^{k}\delta (t-\frac{k}{2000})[/latex] be passed through an LTI system with frequency response [latex]H(\omega)[/latex] , as given in the figure below

The Fourier series representation of the output is given as
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(t)&=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty } (-1)^K \delta \left ( t-\frac{K}{2000} \right )\\ &= \sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty } (-1)^K \delta (t-KT)\\ \text{where, } &=T=\frac{1}{2000} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Time period:
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_0&=2T=\frac{1}{1000}\\ \omega _0&=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=2000 \pi \; rad \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, x(t) is even-halt wave symmetric. So, its expansion will contain only odd harmonics of cos. Therefore, coefficient of fundamental harmonic is
[latex]\begin{aligned} a_1&=\frac{2}{T}\int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2}x(t) \cos \omega _0 t \; dt\\ &=\frac{4}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0/2}\delta (t) \cos \omega _0 t \; dt\\ &=\frac{4}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0/2}\delta (t) \cos 0 \; dt\\ &=\frac{4}{T_0}\left [\int_{0}^{T_0/2}\delta (t) \; dt \right ]\\ &=\frac{4}{T_0}=4000 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, frequency components available in expansion are
[latex]\begin{aligned} \omega _0,3\omega _0,...\\ 2000\pi, 6000 \pi,... \end{aligned}[/latex]
As, LTI system given in the question will pass upto [latex]5000\pi[/latex] rad/sec frequency component of input.So, output will have only one component of sfrequency [latex]2000\pi[/latex] rad/sec
Thus, y(t)= expansion of output [latex]=a_1 \cos \omega _0 t=4000 \cos 2000 \pi t[/latex]

A load is supplied by a 230 V, 50 Hz source. The active power P and the reactive power Q
consumed by the load are such that  [latex]1 kW \leq P \leq 2kW [/latex] and [latex]1{kVAR}  \leq Q \leq {kVAR}[/latex]. A capacitor connected across the load for power factor correction generates 1 kVAR reactive power. The worst case power factor after power factor correction is

Load p.f.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \cos \phi &=\cos \left [ \tan ^{-1}\frac{Q}{P} \right ]\\ &=\cos \left [ \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{1} \right ]\\ &=0.707 \text{ lag}\\ Q_c&=P[\tan \phi _1 -\tan \phi _2]\\ 1&=(\tan \cos ^{-1} 0.707- \tan \phi _2)\\ \phi _2&=45^{\circ}\\ \Rightarrow \; \cos \phi _2&=0.707 \text{ lag} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A three-phase, three winding [latex]\Delta / \Delta / Y[/latex]  (1.1kV/6.6kV/400 V) transformer is energized from AC mains at the 1.1 kV side. It supplies 900 kVA load at 0.8 power factor lag from the 6.6 kV winding and 300 kVA load at 0.6 power factor lag from the 400 V winding. The RMS line current in ampere drawn by the 1.1 kV winding from the mains is _______.
raw_source.solution:
Load on 6.6 kV winding = 900 kVA @0.8 pf lag
[latex]\therefore \;\; I_2=\frac{900 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \times 6.6 \times 10^3}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;=78.73\angle -36.86^{\circ} A [/latex]
Transforamtion Ratio
[latex]\begin{aligned} k &=\frac{1.1}{6.6}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \therefore \;\; I'_2&=\frac{I_2}{k}=472.4\angle -36.86^{\circ} A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Load on 400 V winding = 300 kVA at 0.6 p.f.
[latex]\therefore \;\; I_3=\frac{300 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \times 400}[/latex] [latex]=433.025\angle -53.13^{\circ}A [/latex]
Transformation ratio [latex]= \frac{1.1 \times 1000}{\frac{400}{\sqrt{3}}}=4.76 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} I'_3 &=\frac{I_3}{k}=\frac{4333.025}{4.76} \\ &= 90.97\angle -53.13^{\circ}A \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, line value of current
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\sqrt{3} \times 90.97\angle -53.13^{\circ} \\ &= 157.56 \angle -53.13^{\circ} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Current drawn by 1.1 kV winding will be
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_1&=I'_2+I'_3 \\ &=472.4\angle -36.86 +157.56\angle -53.13^{\circ} \\ &=377.96 -j283.37 +94.53 -126.04 \\ &= 472.49 -j409.41\\ &= 625.19\angle -40.9^{\circ}A \end{aligned}[/latex]

(in minutes) for the vehicle at the junction is ________.

[latex]t[/latex] be arrival time of vehicles of the junction is uniformaly distributed in [0,5].

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Then }y&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 0 & t \lt 2 \\ 5-t & 2\leq t \lt 5 \end{matrix}\right.\\ y\rightarrow &[0,5]\\ f(y)&=\frac{1}{5-0}=\frac{1}{5}\\ E(y)&=\int_{-\infty }^{0}y(y)dy=\int_{0}^{5}yf(y)dy\\ &=\int_{2}^{5}y\left ( \frac{1}{5} \right )dy=\frac{1}{5}\int_{2}^{5}(5-t)dt\\ &=\frac{1}{5}\left ( 5t-\frac{t^2}{2} \right )|_2^5\\ &=\frac{1}{5}\left [ \left ( 25-\frac{25}{2} \right )-\left ( 10-\frac{4}{2} \right ) \right ]\\ &=\frac{1}{5}\left ( \frac{25}{2}-8 \right )=\frac{1}{5}\frac{9}{2}=0.9 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two generating units rated 300 MW and 400 MW have governor speed regulation of 6% and
4% respectively from no load to full load. Both the generating units are operating in parallel to
share a load of 600 MW. Assuming free governor action, the load shared by the larger unit is
_______ MW.
raw_source.solution:
Given: speed regulation of generating unit is from no load to full load.
Hence, the rated frequency (50 Hz) will be common for both units at no load nad will drop to lower value as loaded to full load.
Let, [latex]P_1=[/latex] Load shared by 400 MW machine
[latex]P_2=[/latex] Load shred by 300 MW machine
For 400 MW machine drop in frequency from no load to full load [latex]=\frac{50 \times 4}{100}=2 Hz[/latex]
New frequecy of operation of 400 MW machine, [latex]f_1=50-\frac{2}{400}P_1[/latex]
For 300 MW machine drop in frequency from no load to full load [latex]=\frac{50 \times 6}{100}=3 Hz[/latex]
New frequecy of operation of 300 MW machine, [latex]f_2=50-\frac{3}{300}P_2[/latex]
we also know,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_1+P_2&=600 \\\ (\text{Load shared }& \text{between shared units})\\ P_2&=600-P_1 \\ f_1&=f_2=f \\ (\text{Units operatio }& \text{ is in parallel}) \\ 50-\frac{2}{400}P_1 &=50-\frac{3}{300}(600-P_1) \\ \frac{P_1}{200}&=\frac{600-P_1}{100} \\ 100P_1 &=200(600-P_1) \\ P_1&=1200-2P_1\\ 3P_1&=1200\\ P_1&=400 MW \end{aligned}[/latex]

A 220 V, 10 kW, 900 rpm separately excited DC motor has an armature resistance [latex]R_a=0.02\Omega[/latex].

torque developed by the motor is 70 Nm. Neglecting the rotational losses of the machine, the

raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Neglecting rotor loss,}&\\ E_bI_a &= 10kW\\ (V-I_aR_a)I_a &= 10kW\\ (220-I_a(0.02))I_a &= 10000\\ 220I_a-0.02I_a^2-10000 &=0 \\ 0.02I_a^2-220I_a+10000&=0\\ \text{By sloving,}\;\; & I_a=45.75A\\ \text{Torque corrosponding,}&\\ T&=\frac{60}{2\pi N}E_bI_a\\ \therefore \; T&=\frac{60}{2 \pi (900)}10000\\ &=106.15N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]
Separately excited motor,
[latex]\therefore \;\;T \propto I_a[/latex]
For a torque 106.15 N-m
[latex]I_a=45.75A[/latex]
For a torque 70 N-m,
New [latex]I_a=\frac{70 \times 45.75}{106.15}=30.16A[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 3-phase, 2-pole, 50 Hz, synchronous generator has a rating of 250 MVA, 0.8 pf lagging. The
kinetic energy of the machine at synchronous speed is 1000 MJ. The machine is running
steadily at synchronous speed and delivering 60 MW power at a power angle of 10 electrical
degrees. If the load is suddenly removed, assuming the acceleration is constant for 10 cycles,
the value of the power angle after 5 cycles is ________ electrical degrees.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
 S&=250 MVA \\ 
 \cos \phi &=0.8 \\ 
K.E. &=1000MJ \\ 
 P_e&= 60MW\\ 
 \delta _0&=10^{\circ} \\ 
 t&=10\; cycles\\
&=\frac{10}{50}=0.2\; sec \\ 
 t&=5\; cycle =0.1sec \\ 
 \text{Load}&\text{ is removed,} \\ 
 P_e&=0 \\ 
 P_a&=P_m-P_e \\ 
P_m &=60MW \\ 
 M&=\frac{HS}{180f}=\frac{K.E.}{180f} \\ 
 &= \frac{1000}{180 \times 50}=0.111\\ 
 \frac{d^2 \delta }{dt^2}&=\frac{P_a}{M}=545.45 \text{ ele.degree}/s^2 \\ 
 \text{Integrating}&\text{ the above eq.} \\
\int \left ( \frac{d^2 \delta }{dt^2} \right )dt&=\int \frac{P_a}{M}dt=545.45 \times t\\
\text{Integrating}&\text{ tit once again with dt} \\
&=545.45 \times t(dt)\\
\delta &=\frac{545.45 \times t^2}{2}=2.7^{\circ}\\

raw_source.text: In the circuit shown all elements are ideal and the switch S is operated at 10 kHz and 60% duty ratio. The capacitor is large enough so that the ripple across it is negligible and at steady state acquires a voltage as shown. The peak current in amperes drawn from the 50 V DC source is ________. (Give the answer up to one decimal place.)
raw_source.solution:
Buckboost converter,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0&=\frac{\alpha V_s}{1-\alpha }\\ V_s&=50V\\ \alpha &=0.6\\ V_0&=75V\\ \frac{V_0}{V_s}&=\frac{I_s}{I_0}=\frac{\alpha }{1-\alpha }\\ &=\frac{0.6}{1-0.6}=\frac{3}{2}\\ I_0&=\frac{V_0}{R}=\frac{75}{5}=15A\\ I_s&=\frac{\alpha }{1-\alpha }I_0=\frac{3}{2} \times 15=22.5A \end{aligned}[/latex]


Since capacitor is very large [latex]i_c=0[/latex] at steady state
[latex]\begin{aligned} (i_L)_{avg}&=(I_s)_{avg}+(i_0)_{avg}\\ I_L&=I_s+I_0\\ I_L&=22.5+15=37.5A\\ \Delta I_L&=\frac{\alpha V_s}{fL}\\ &=\frac{0.6\times 50}{10 \times 10^3 \times (0.6 \times 10^{-3})}\\ &=5A\\ (i_L)_{peak}&=I_L+\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}\\ &=37.5+\frac{5}{2}=40A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Peak value of current drawn from source [latex]=(i_L)_{peak}=40A[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let f be a real-valued function of a real variable defined as [latex]f(x)=x^{2}[/latex] for [latex]x \gt 0[/latex], and[latex] f(x)=-x^{2}[/latex] for [latex]x \lt 0[/latex]. Which one of the following statements is true?

f(x) is differentiable but its first derivative is not differentiable at x=0

The value of the directional derivative of the function [latex]\phi (x,y,z)=xy^{2}+yz^{2}+zx^{2}[/latex] at the

raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \phi &= xy^2+yz^2+zx^2\\ \bigtriangledown \phi &=\bar{i}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x}+\bar{j}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y} +\bar{k}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z} \\ &=\bar{i}(y^2+2xz)+\bar{j}(2xy+z^2)\\&+\bar{k}(2yz+x^2) \\ \bigtriangledown \phi _{(2,-1,1)} &= \bar{i}(1+4)+\bar{j}(-4+1)+\bar{k}(-2+4)\\ &= 5\bar{i}-3\bar{j}+2\bar{k}\\ \bar{P} &= \bar{i}+2\bar{j}+2\bar{k}\\ |\bar{P}|&=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
THe directional derivative of f(x,y,z) at (2,-1,1) in the direction of [latex]\bar{P}[/latex] is [latex]\bigtriangledown \phi _{at \; P} \cdot \frac{\bar{P}}{|\bar{P}|}= (5\bar{i}-3\bar{j}+2\bar{k})\left ( \frac{\bar{i}+2\bar{j}+2\bar{k}}{3} \right )=\frac{5-6+4}{3}=1[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a non-singular 2x2 square matrix A. If trace(A)=4 and trace([latex]A^{2}[/latex])=5, the determinant of the matrix A is _________(up to 1 decimal place).

[latex]\begin{aligned} &\int \frac{z^2}{(z^2-3z+2)^2}dz\\ &\int \frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2}dz\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=1}&=\lim_{z \to 1}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-1)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)^2-2z^2(z-2)}{((z-2)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)-2z^2}{((z-2)^3} \right )=\frac{-4}{-1}=4\\ \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=2}&=\lim_{z \to 2}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-2)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{(z-1)^2\cdot 2z-z^22(z-1)}{((z-1)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{2z(z-1)-2z^2}{((z-1)^3} \right )=\frac{4-8}{1}=-4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
By residue theorem, [latex]I=2 \pi i (4-4)=0[/latex]

Let [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0&-1 \\ -1&2 & 0\\ 0& 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]B=A^{3}-A^{2}-4A+5I[/latex], where I is the 3x3 identity matrix. The
determinant of B is ________ (up to 1 decimal place).
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1\\ -1 &2 &0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\\ |A-\lambda I|=0\\ \begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda & 0& -1\\ -1& 2-\lambda & 0\\ 0 & 0 &-2-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0\\ (1-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ))-1(0-0)=0\\ \lambda =1,2,-2\\ \text{Eigen value of A are 1,2,-2}\\ \text{Eigen value of } A^3 \text{ are 1,8,-8}\\ \text{Eigen value of } A^2 \text{ are 1,4,4}\\ \text{Eigen value of } 4A \text{ are 4,8,-8}\\ \text{Eigen value of } 5I \text{ are 5,5,5}\\ A^3-A^2-4A+5I \text{ are 1,1,1}\\ \therefore \;\; |B|=(1)(1)(1)=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The value of the directional derivative of the function [latex]\phi (x,y,z)=xy^{2}+yz^{2}+zx^{2}[/latex] at the
point (2,-1,1) in the direction of the vector [latex]p=i+ 2j + 2k[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \phi &= xy^2+yz^2+zx^2\\ \bigtriangledown \phi &=\bar{i}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x}+\bar{j}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y} +\bar{k}\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z} \\ &=\bar{i}(y^2+2xz)+\bar{j}(2xy+z^2)\\&+\bar{k}(2yz+x^2) \\ \bigtriangledown \phi _{(2,-1,1)} &= \bar{i}(1+4)+\bar{j}(-4+1)+\bar{k}(-2+4)\\ &= 5\bar{i}-3\bar{j}+2\bar{k}\\ \bar{P} &= \bar{i}+2\bar{j}+2\bar{k}\\ |\bar{P}|&=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
THe directional derivative of f(x,y,z) at (2,-1,1) in the direction of [latex]\bar{P}[/latex] is [latex]\bigtriangledown \phi _{at \; P} \cdot \frac{\bar{P}}{|\bar{P}|}= (5\bar{i}-3\bar{j}+2\bar{k})\left ( \frac{\bar{i}+2\bar{j}+2\bar{k}}{3} \right )=\frac{5-6+4}{3}=1[/latex]

raw_source.text: A separately excited dc motor has an armature resistance [latex]R_{a}= 0.05\Omega[/latex]. The field excitation is kept constant. At an armature voltage of 100 V, the motor produces a torque of 500 Nm at zero speed. Neglecting all mechanical losses, the no-load speed of the motor (in radian/s) for an armature voltage of 150 V is _____ (up to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given separately initiated DC motor,
Field excitaion is constant,

Producing a torque of 500 N-m
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{At zero speed,}\\ \because \; N&= 0,\; E_b=0\\ E_b &= V-I_aR_a\\ 0&= 100-I_a(0.05)\\ \therefore \; I_{a1} &=\frac{100}{0.05} =2000A\\ T &= \frac{60}{2 \pi N}E_bI_a\\ &= \frac{60}{2 \pi N}\frac{\phi ZNP}{60A}\cdot I_a\\ \text{Let,}\;\; T_1&=\frac{1}{2 \pi}\frac{ZP}{A}\phi I_{a1}\;\text{N-m} \\ \text{Let,}\;\; T_1 &=kI_{a1} \\ \text{where,}\;\; k &= \frac{1}{2 \pi}\frac{ZP \phi}{A}\\ T_1 &= 500 \text{N-m}, \\ I_{a1}&=2000A\\ k&=\frac{500}{2000}=0.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]
When motor runs on no-load given all mechanical losses neglected. No-load current is negligible and the voltage drop at no-load can be negligible.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\;E_b &\simeq V=150V \\ E_b&= \frac{\phi ZNP}{60A}\\ \text{Already solved,}\\ k&=\frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{ZP \phi }{A}\\ \therefore \;\;\frac{ZP \phi }{A} &=2 \pi (k) \\ \therefore \;\; E_b &= 2 \pi (k) \cdot \frac{N}{60}\\ \therefore \;\; E_b&= k \times \omega \\ (\omega : & \text{No-load speed in rad/sec})\\ \therefore \;\;\omega &= \frac{E_b}{k}\\ \therefore \;\;\omega &= \frac{150}{0.25}\\ \omega &= 600 \text{rad/sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A transformer with toroidal core of permeability [latex]\mu[/latex] is shown in the figure. Assuming uniform flux density across the circular core cross-section of radius [latex]r\lt \lt R[/latex], and neglecting any leakage flux, the best estimate for the mean radius R is
raw_source.solution:
Since we know reluctance of core:
[latex]\Re =\frac{l_c}{\mu a}[/latex]
Here, [latex] l_c= [/latex] mean core length, a= area of core reluctance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Re &=\frac{2 \pi R}{\mu \times \pi r^2}\\ &=\frac{2R}{\mu r^2}\\ [\text{where} R &= \text{mean radius of core}] \\ \text{or}\;\; R&=\frac{\Re \mu r^2}{2} \\ \text{and}\;\; \Re &= \frac{mmf}{flux}=\frac{N_pI_p}{\phi }\\ \text{Here,}\;\; \phi &=-\frac{1}{N_p}\int_{0}^{t}e\;dt \\ [\text{where}\; e &\text{is primary generated voltage}] \\ \text{or}\;\; \phi &=-\frac{1}{N_p}\int_{0}^{t}-(V_p)\;dt \\ \phi &= \frac{1}{N_p}\int_{0}^{t}V \cos \omega t \;dt\\ &= \frac{V}{\omega N_p}\sin \omega t\\ &\text{Now reluctance} \\ \Re &= \frac{N_p I \sin \omega t}{\frac{V}{\omega N_p} \sin \omega t}\\ &= \frac{N_p^2\omega I}{V}\\ & \text{So mean radius,}\\ R&=\frac{N_p^2 \times \omega I \times \mu r^2}{2V} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Single Phase Induction Motors, Special Purpose Machines and Electromechanical Energy Conversion System

[latex]m=\frac{I}{I_m}=\frac{10}{1}=10 [/latex]

30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex], then its value (in degree) at the end of the first iteration is

[latex]\begin{aligned} P(\delta )&=1.4 \sin \delta +0.15 \sin 2\delta =0.8\\ &=1.4 \sin \delta +0.15 \sin 2\delta -0.8=0\\ P'(\delta )&=\frac{d}{d\delta }(P(\delta ))\\ &=1.4 \cos \delta +0.30 \cos 2\delta \text{Given, } \delta _0&=30^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If C is a circle |z|=4 and  [latex]f(z)=\frac{z^{2}}{(z^{2}-3z+2)^{2}}[/latex], then [latex]\oint_{C}f(z)dz[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\int \frac{z^2}{(z^2-3z+2)^2}dz\\ &\int \frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2}dz\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=1}&=\lim_{z \to 1}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-1)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)^2-2z^2(z-2)}{((z-2)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)-2z^2}{((z-2)^3} \right )=\frac{-4}{-1}=4\\ \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=2}&=\lim_{z \to 2}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-2)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{(z-1)^2\cdot 2z-z^22(z-1)}{((z-1)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{2z(z-1)-2z^2}{((z-1)^3} \right )=\frac{4-8}{1}=-4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
By residue theorem, [latex]I=2 \pi i (4-4)=0[/latex]

Capacitance,

[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \; \frac{T_2}{T_1} &=\left ( \frac{I_{a2}}{I_{a1}} \right )^2 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{1.44T_1}{T_1} &=\left ( \frac{I_{a2}}{10} \right )^2 \\ \therefore \;\; I_{a2}^2&= 144\\ I_{a2}&= 12A\\ &\text{At same voltage,}\\ E_{b2}&=V-I_{a2}(R_a+R_{se}) \\ \therefore \;\; E_{b2} &= 200-12(1)=188V\\ &\text{For series motor,}\\ N&\propto \frac{E_b}{\phi }\;\;(\phi \propto I_a) \\ \frac{N_2}{N_1}&=\frac{E_{b2}}{E_{b1}} \times \frac{I_{a1}}{I_{a2}}\\ \frac{N_2}{1000} &=\frac{188}{190}\times \frac{10}{12} \\ N_2&=824.56\; \text{rpm}\\ &\simeq 825\; \text{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A dc to dc converter shown in the figure is charging a battery bank, B2 whose voltage is constant at 150 V. B1 is another battery bank whose voltage is constant at 50 V. The value of the inductor, L is 5 mH and the ideal switch, S is operated with a switching frequency of 5 kHz with a duty ratio of 0.4. Once the circuit has attained steady state and assuming the diode D to be ideal, the power transferred from B1 to B2 (in Watt) is ___________ (up to 2 decimal places). .
raw_source.solution:
During [latex]T_{on}[/latex] the circuit behaves as,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_s&=L\frac{di}{dt} \\ di&=\frac{V_s}{L}dt \end{aligned}[/latex]
Integrating on both sides,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_P&=\frac{V_s}{L}T_{on}\\ T_{on}&=\alpha T=\frac{\alpha }{f}=80 \times 10^{-6}s\\ I_P&=\frac{50}{5 \times 10^{-3}}\times (80 \times 10^{-6})\\ &=0.8A \end{aligned}[/latex]

During [latex]T_{off}[/latex], it is [latex]T_{on}\leq t\leq \beta T[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{KVL, } V_L&=V_s-V_0 \\ (V_L)_{avg}&=0 \\ V_sT_{on}+&(V_s-V_0)(\beta T-T_{on}) =0 \\ V_s\beta T &=V_0(\beta T-T_{on}) \\ \frac{V_0}{V_s}&=\frac{\beta }{\beta -\alpha } \\ \beta &=0.6\\ &\text{Fromt the graph of } i_L, \\ I_{L(avg)}&=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times b \times h}{T}\\ &=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times \beta T \times I_P}{T}\\ &=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.6 \times 0.8=0.24A\\ &\text{Power transferred to } B_2 \text{ is,}\\ P&=V_s \times (I_L)_{avg}\\ \text{ where } I_s&=I_L\\ P&=50 \times 0.24\\ &=12W \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]f=2x^3+3y^2+4z[/latex], the value of line integral [latex]\int _c grad \; f\cdot dr[/latex] evaluated over  contour C formed by the segments (-3,-3,2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (2,-3,2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (2,6,2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (2,6,-1) is_______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f&=2x^3+3y^2+4z\\ \Delta f&=6x^2\hat{i}+6y\hat{j}+4\hat{k}\\ \text{curl} (\Delta f)&=\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}&\frac{\partial }{\partial y} &\frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ 6x^2& 6y & 4\end{vmatrix}\\ \therefore \;\;\int _c\Delta f\cdot dr&=\int _c d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)=0\\ &=\int_{(-3,-3,2)}^{2,-3,2}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &+\int_{(2,-3,2)}^{(2,6,2)}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &+\int_{(2,6,2)}^{(2,6,-1)}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &=70+81+(-12)=139 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If A=2xi+3yj+4zk and [latex]u=x^2+y^2+z^2[/latex], then div(uA) at (1,1,1) is____
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \bigtriangledown \cdot (uA)&=u(\bigtriangledown \cdot A)+(\bigtriangledown A)F\\ &=(x^2+y^2+z^2)[2+3+4]\\ &+(2x\hat{i}+2y\hat{j}+2z\hat{k})(2x\hat{i}+3y\hat{j}+4z\hat{k})\\ &=9(x^2+y^2+z^2)+(4x^2+6y^2+8z^2)\\ At\; (1,1,1)&=9(3)+[4+6+8]\\ &=27+18=45 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The probability of a resistor being defective is 0.02. There are 50 such resistors in a circuit. The probability of two or more defective resistors in the circuit (round off to two decimal places)is ________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} p&=0.02\\ n&=50\\ \lambda &=np=50(0.02)=1\\ p(x\geq 2)&=1-p(x \lt 2)\\ &=1-(p(x=0)+p(x=1))\\ &=1-\left ( \frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^0}{0!}+\frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^1}{1!} \right )\\ &=1-e^{-\lambda }(1+\lambda )\\ &=1-e^{-1}(1+1)=0.26 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A periodic function [latex]f(t)[/latex], with a period of [latex]2\pi[/latex], is represented as its Fourier series,
[latex]f(t)=a_0+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }a_n\cos nt+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }a_n\sin nt[/latex].
If
[latex]f(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} A \sin t, & 0\leq t\leq \pi\\ 0,& \pi\lt t\lt 2\pi \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
the Fourier series coefficients [latex]a_1 \; and \; b_1[/latex] of [latex]f(t)[/latex] are
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
T_0 &=2\pi \Rightarrow \;\omega _0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=1 \\ 
\text{Now, }b_1 &=\frac{2}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0}f(t) \sin \omega _0 t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{2}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(t) \sin t \; dt\;\;[\because \omega _0=1]\\ 
 &= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} A \sin t \cdot \sin t\; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}2 \sin ^2 t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}[1-\cos 2t] \; dt \\ 
 &=\frac{A}{2 \pi} \left [ t-\frac{\sin 2t}{2} \right ]_0^{\pi} \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi} [(\pi-0)-(0-0)]=\frac{A}{2}\\ 
 a_1&=\frac{2}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0}f(t) \cos \omega _0 t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{2}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(t) \cos t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} A \sin t \cdot \cos t\; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin 2t \; dt=0
\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If A=2xi+3yj+4zk and [latex]u=x^2+y^2+z^2[/latex], then div(uA) at (1,1,1) is____

raw_source.text: The probability of a resistor being defective is 0.02. There are 50 such resistors in a circuit. The probability of two or more defective resistors in the circuit (round off to two decimal places)is ________

raw_source.text: The magnetic circuit shown below has uniform cross-sectional area and air gap of 0.2 cm. The mean path length of the core is 40 cm. Assume that leakage and fringing fluxes are negligible. When the core relative permeability is assumed to be infinite, the magnetic flux density computed in the air gap is 1 tesla. With same Ampere-turns, if the core relative permeability is assumed to be 1000 (linear), the flux density in tesla(round off to three decimal places) calculated in the air gap is __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} l_{ag} &=0.2 cm \\ l_m&= 40cm\\ B_0 &= 1 \text{Tesla}\\ \phi &= \frac{mmf}{\Re }\\ &\text{For the same mmf,} \\ \phi &\propto \frac{1}{\Re } \\ \text{In case-1:} &\\ \Re _1&=\frac{l_m}{\mu _0A} \\ &= \frac{l_{ag}}{\mu _0 A}+\frac{l_m}{\mu _0 \mu _r A}\\ \text{as} \;\;\mu _0=0& \\ \therefore \;\;\Re _1&= \frac{0.2 \times 10^{-2}}{\mu _0 A}\\ \text{In case-2:} &\\ \Re _2&= \frac{l_{ag}}{\mu _0 A}+\frac{l_m}{\mu _0 \mu _r A}\\ &=\frac{0.2 \times 10^{-2}}{\mu _0 A}+\frac{40 \times 10^{-2}}{1000\mu _0 A}\\ &=\frac{0.24\times 10^{-2}}{\mu _0 A} \end{aligned} [/latex]
As flux [latex]\phi \propto B[/latex] for uniform cross section area.
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \; B_2&=\frac{B_1 \times \Re _1}{\Re _2} \\ B_2&= \frac{1 \times 0.2 \times 10^{-2}/\mu _0 A}{0.24 \times 10^{-2}/\mu _0A}\\ &= 0.833T \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single-phase transformer of rating 25 kVA, supplies a 12 kW load at power factor of 0.6 lagging. The additional load at unity power factor in kW (round off to two decimal places) that may be added before this transformer exceeds its rated kVA is __________.

[latex]\begin{aligned} S^2 &=(P+P_L)^2+Q_L^2 \\ 25^2&= (P+12)^2+16^2\\ P &= 7.21kW \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 220 V DC shunt motor takes 3 A at no-load. It draws 25 A when running at full-load at 1500 rpm. The armature and shunt resistances are 0.5 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and 220 [latex]\Omega[/latex],respectively. The no-load speed in rpm (round off to two decimal places) is ________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{At full load condition,}\\ N_1&=1500 \; \text{rpm} \\ I_1 &=25A \\ I_f&= \frac{220V}{200\Omega }=1A\\ I_{a1}&=I_1-I_f=24A \\ E_{g1}&=V-I_{a1}R_a \\ &=220-24 \times 0.5=208V \\ &\text{At no-load condition,}\\ I_2&= 3A\\ I_f&= 1A\\ I_{a2}&=I_2-I_f=2A \\ E_{g2}&=220-2 \times 0.5=219V \\ E_g&\propto \phi N \\ & \text{Flux id constant,}\\ E_g&\propto N \\ \frac{E_{g2}}{E_{g1}}&=\frac{N_2}{N_1} \\ \frac{219}{208}&=\frac{N_2}{1500} \\ N_2&= 1579.33 \;\text{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A  three-phase  50  Hz,  400  kV  transmission  line  is  300  km  long.  The  line  inductance  is 1 mH/km per phase, and the capacitance is 0.01 [latex]\mu F/km[/latex] per phase. [latex]\, \, \, =\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}(4.5\epsilon _{o}r^{2})+0+0[/latex]

An 8085 microprocessor accesses two memory locations (2001 H) and (2002H), that contain 8-bit numbers 98H and B1H respectively. The following program is executed:

LXI H, 2001 H
MVIA, 21H
INX H
ADD M
INX H
MOV M, A
HLT

At the end of this program, the memory location 2003H contains the number in decimal (base 10) form ________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} LXI H, 2001 H & \rightarrow  [HL]  \rightarrow 2001 H \\MVI A, 21 H & \rightarrow [A]  \leftarrow 21 H \\INX H & \rightarrow [HL]  \rightarrow 2002 H \\ ADD M & \rightarrow [A] + [2002]  \rightarrow [A] \\ &= (21H + B1 H)  \rightarrow [A] \\ &= D2 H  \rightarrow [A] \\ INX H & \rightarrow [HL]  \rightarrow 2003 H \\  MOV M, A & \rightarrow [2003] \leftarrow [A] \\ [2003] &= D2 H = (1101\; 0010)_2 \\ &= 1 \times 2^7+1\times 2^6+1\times 2^4 +1\times 2^1 \\&= 128 + 64 + 16 + 2 \\&= 210 \end{aligned}[/latex]

If the input x(t) and output y(t) of a system are related as [latex]y\left ( t \right )=\text{max}\left ( 0,x\left ( t \right ) \right )[/latex], then the system is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t) &=\max (0, x(t)) \\ &=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} 0, & x(t) \lt 0 \\ x(t), & x(t)\gt 0 \end{array}\right. \end{aligned}[/latex]


Linearity check:
at input [latex]x_{1}(t)=-2[/latex], output [latex]y_{1}(t)=0 [/latex]
at input [latex]x_{2}(t)=1[/latex], output [latex]y_{2}(t)=1 [/latex]


[latex] \therefore [/latex] system is non-linear because it violates law of additivity.
Check for time-invariance :
Delayed [latex]\mathrm{O} / \mathrm{P}:[/latex]
[latex] y\left(t-t_{0}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} x\left(t-t_{0}\right), & x\left(t-t_{0}\right) \gt 0 \\ 0 & x\left(t-t_{0}\right)\lt 0 \end{array}\right.[/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{O} / \mathrm{P}[/latex] of system when input is [latex]x\left(t-t_{0}\right)=f(t)[/latex]
[latex] y_{1}(t)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} f(t), & f(t) \gt 0 \\ 0, & f(t)\lt 0 \end{array}=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} x\left(t-t_{0}\right), & x\left(t-t_{0}\right)\gt 0 \\ 0, & x\left(t-t_{0}\right)\lt 0 \end{array}\right.\right.[/latex]

By applying inverse ZT,

[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \Delta P\\ \Delta Q \end{bmatrix}=J\begin{bmatrix} \Delta \delta \\ \Delta V \end{bmatrix}, \text{where}\: J=\begin{bmatrix} H & S\\ M &R \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The dimension of the sub-matrix M is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\left[\begin{array}{l} \Delta P \\ \Delta Q \end{array}\right]=J\left[\begin{array}{l} \Delta \delta \\ \Delta V \end{array}\right] \text { where } J=\left[\begin{array}{ll} H & S \\ M & R \end{array}\right][/latex]
For size of M
Row = No. of unknown variables of [latex]Q=N_{L}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Suppose the circles [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}=1[/latex] and [latex]\left ( x-1\right )^{2}+\left ( y-1 \right )^{2}=r^{2}[/latex] intersect each other orthogonally at the point [latex]\left ( u,v \right )[/latex]. Then  [latex]u+v=[/latex] _______________.
raw_source.solution:
If two curves cut orthogonally then product of slopes [latex]= -1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} x^{2}+y^{2} &=1 \\ 2 x+2 y \frac{d y}{d x} &=0 \\ \left(M_{1}\right)_{u, v} &=\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-x}{y}=\frac{-u}{v} \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} &=r^{2} \\ \left(M_{2}\right)_{u, v} &=\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=\left(\frac{-2(x-1)}{2(y-1)}\right)_{(u . v)}=\frac{1-u}{v-1} \\ \because \qquad \qquad M_{1} M_{2} &=-1\\ \frac{-u}{v} \times \frac{1-u}{v-1}&=-1\\ -u+u^{2} &=-v^{2}+v \\ u^{2}+v^{2} &=v+u \\ \because \qquad \qquad x^{2}+y^{2} &=1 \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad u+v &=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the given circuit, the value of capacitor C that makes current [latex]I=0[/latex] is _________ [latex]\mu F[/latex].
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{L} &=(j 5) \|\left(j 5-j X_{c}\right) \\ \frac{(j 5)\left(j 5-j X_{c}\right)}{j 5+j 5-j X_{c}} &=\infty \\ j 5+j-j X_{c} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \qquad j X_{c} &=j 10 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \qquad X_{c} &=10 \Omega \\ X_{c} &=\frac{1}{\omega C}=10 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad \qquad C&=\frac{1}{10 \times 5 \times 10^{3}} \\ C &=\frac{1}{5 \times 10^{4}} \times \frac{10^{2}}{10^{2}}=\frac{10^{2}}{5 \times 10^{6}}=20 \mu \mathrm{F} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two single-core power cables have total conductor resistances of [latex]0.7\;\Omega[/latex] and [latex]0.5\;\Omega[/latex], respectively, and their insulation resistances (between core and sheath) are [latex]600\;M\Omega[/latex] and [latex]900\;M\Omega[/latex], respectively. When the two cables are joined in series, the ratio of insulation resistance to conductor resistance is ___________[latex]\times 10^{6}[/latex].
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \left(R_{\text {eq }}\right)_{\text {conductor }} &=0.7+0.5=1.2 \Omega \\ \left(R_{\text {eq }}\right)_{\text {in }} &=\frac{1}{\left(R_{e q}\right)_{\text {in }}}=\frac{1}{\left(R_{\text {in }}\right)_{1}}+\frac{1}{\left(R_{\text {in }}\right)_{2}}=\frac{1}{900 \times 10^{6}}+\frac{1}{600 \times 10^{6}} \\ \left(R_{\mathrm{eq}}\right)_{\text {in }} &=360 \times 10^{6} \Omega\\ \frac{\left(R_{\text {eq }}\right)_{\text {in }}}{\left(R_{\text {eq }}\right)_{\text {conductor }}}&=\frac{360 \times 10^{6}}{1.2}=300 \times 10^{6} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the given circuit, for voltage [latex]V_y[/latex] to be zero, the value of [latex]\beta[/latex] should be _________. (Round off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{V_{x}-6}{1}+\frac{V_{x}}{4}+\frac{V_{x}-V_{y}}{2} & =0 \\ 4 V_{x}-24+V_{x}+2 V_{x}-2 V_{y} & =0 \\ 7 V_{x}-2 V_{y} & =24 \\ \text { If } V_{y}=0 \qquad\qquad 7 V_{x} & =24 \\ \Rightarrow\qquad\qquad V_{x} & =\frac{24}{7} \\ \Rightarrow\qquad\qquad \frac{V_{y}-V_{x}}{2}+\frac{V_{y}-\beta V_{x}}{3} & =2 \\ 3 V_{y}-3 V_{x}+2 V_{y}-2 \beta V_{x} & =12 \\ 5 V_{y}-(3+2 \beta) V_{x} & =12 \\ V_{y} & =0\\ -(3+2 \beta) \frac{24}{7} &=12 \\ (3+2 \beta) &=\frac{-7}{2} \\ 2 \beta &=\frac{-7}{2}-3=\frac{-7-6}{2}=\frac{-13}{2} \\ \beta &=\frac{-13}{4}=-3.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A [latex]1\;\mu C[/latex] point charge is held at the origin of a cartesian coordinate system. If a second point charge of [latex]10\;\mu C[/latex] is moved from [latex]\left ( 0,10,0 \right )[/latex] to [latex]\left ( 5,5,5\right )[/latex] and subsequently to [latex]\left ( 5,0,0\right )[/latex], then the total work done is ___________[latex]\text{mJ}[/latex]. (Round off to 2 decimal places).
Take [latex]\dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon _{0}}=9\times 10^{9}[/latex] in SI units. All coordinates are in meters.
raw_source.solution:
In this case work done is independent of type of path but depends an intial and final point.
[latex] \begin{array}{ccccccccc} x & y & z & & r & \theta & \phi \\ (0, & 10, & 0) & \rightarrow & (10, & 90^{\circ}, & \left.90^{\circ}\right) & \text { Initial point }\\ x & y & z & & r & \theta & \phi & \\ (5, & 5, & 5) & \rightarrow & (5 \sqrt{3}, & 54.73^{\circ}, & \left.45^{\circ}\right) & \text { Intermediate point } \\ x & y & z & & r & \theta & \phi & \\ (5, & 0, & 0) & \rightarrow & (5, & 90^{\circ}, & \left.0^{\circ}\right) & \text { Final point } \end{array}[/latex]
Work done (by external source) in moving Q-charge ([latex]10 \mu C[/latex]) in the presence of electric field [latex]\vec{E}[/latex] is
[latex]\begin{aligned} W&=-Q \int_{\text {initial point }}^{\text {final point }} \vec{E} \cdot d \vec{l}=-\left(10 \times 10^{-6}\right) \int_{r=10}^{r=5} \frac{9 \times 10^{3}}{r^{2}} \hat{a}_{r} \cdot d r \hat{a}_{r} \\ W&=-10 \times 10^{-6}\left(9 \times 10^{3}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{r}\right)_{r=10}^{5} \\ &=9 \times 10^{-2}\left[\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{10}\right]=9 \times 10^{-2}\left[\frac{10-5}{50}\right]=9 \times 10^{-2}\left(10^{-1}\right) \\ W&=9 \mathrm{~mJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

 is [latex]40 \text{ kW}[/latex] . The total stator losses are [latex]1 \text{ kW}[/latex]. If the total friction and windage losses are [latex]2.025\text{~ kW}[/latex], then the efficiency is _____________%.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} P_{i / p} &=40 \mathrm{~kW}, \quad \text { stator loss }=1 \mathrm{~kW}, \quad \mathrm{~F} \text { and } W=2.025 \mathrm{~kW} \\ \text { Stator } \mathrm{o} / \mathrm{p} &=40-1=39 \mathrm{~kW} \\ \qquad \text { Slip } &=\frac{1000-975}{1000}=0.025 \\ \text { Rotor } \mathrm{o} / \mathrm{p} &=\text { Rotor } \mathrm{i} / \mathrm{p} \times(1-\mathrm{s}) \\ &=39(1-0.025)=38.025 \mathrm{~kW} \\ \text { Motor } \mathrm{o} / \mathrm{p} &=38.025-2.025=36 \mathrm{~kW}\\ \eta&=\frac{\text { Motor output }}{\text { Motor input }}=\frac{36}{40} \times 100=90 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

To calculate [latex]R_{0}[/latex] min' we must find [latex]I_{L}[/latex] max
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{s \min } &=I_{z} \min +I_{L \max } \\ \frac{V_{i \min }-V_{z}}{R_{s}} &=I_{z} \min +I_{L \max } \end{aligned}[/latex]
For ideal zener diode, [latex]I_{z \min }=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{i \min }-V_{z}}{R_{s}} &=I_{L \max } \\ \frac{6-5}{6} &=I_{L \max } \\ I_{L} \max &=\frac{1}{6} \mathrm{~A} \\ R_{0} \min &=\frac{V_{z}}{I_{L \max }}=\frac{5}{1 / 6}=30 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

Suppose the probability that a coin toss shows "head" is p, where [latex]0\lt 
 p\lt 1[/latex]. The coin is tossed repeatedly until the first "head" appears. The expected number of tosses required is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]F(H) = p[/latex], let x = Number of tosses
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \ldots \\ \hline P(x) & p & (1-p) p & (1-p)^{2} p & & \\ \hline \end{array}\\ &\begin{aligned} E(x) &=\sum x_{i} P(x)=p+2(1-p) p+3(p)(1-p)^{2}+\ldots \\ &=p\left[1+2(1-p)+3(1-p)^{2}+\ldots\right] \\ &=p[1-(1-p)]^{-2}=\frac{1}{p} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]
