raw_source.text:
The casual signal with z-transformer [latex]Z^{2}\left ( Z-a \right )^{-2}[/latex] is
([latex]u[n][/latex] is the unit step signal)
raw_source.solution:
As we know,
[latex] \begin{aligned} n \cdot a^{n} u(n) & \rightleftharpoons \frac{a z}{(z-a)^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{a} \cdot n \cdot a^{n} u(n) & \rightleftharpoons \frac{z}{(z-a)^{2}} \\ f(n) &=n \cdot a^{n-1} u(n) \rightleftharpoons \frac{z}{(z-a)^{2}}=F(z) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Time-shifting property,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(n) &\rightleftharpoons F(z) \\ f(n+1) &\rightleftharpoons z \cdot F(z) & \\ x(n)&=(n+1) a^{n} u(n+1) \rightleftharpoons \frac{z^{2}}{(z-a)^{2}}=X(z) & \\ \text{Thus},\qquad \qquad x(n)&=(n+1) a^{n} u(n+1)=(n+1) a^{n} \cdot u(n) \\ &[\because(n+1) u(n+1)=(n+1) u(n) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]f(t)[/latex] be an even function, i.e. [latex]f(-t)=f(t)[/latex] for all t. Let the Fourier transform of [latex]f(t)[/latex] be defined as [latex]F\left ( \omega \right )=\int\limits_{-\infty }^{\infty }\:f\left ( t \right )e^{-j\omega t}dt[/latex]. Suppose [latex]\dfrac{dF\left ( \omega \right )}{d\omega }=-\omega F\left ( \omega \right )[/latex] for all [latex]\omega[/latex], and [latex]F(0)=1[/latex]. Then
raw_source.solution:
[latex]f(t) \rightleftharpoons F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-j \omega t} d t[/latex]
The following informations are given about [latex]f(t) \rightleftharpoons F(\omega).[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} (i) f(t)=f(-t)\\ (ii) \left.F(\omega)\right|_{\omega=0}=1\\ (iii) \frac{d F(\omega)}{d \omega}=-\omega F(\omega)\\ \text{From }(iii), \frac{d F(\omega)}{d \omega}+\omega F(\omega)=0 \end{array}[/latex]
By solving the above linear differential equations, (by mathematics)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \ln F(\omega) &=-\frac{\omega^{2}}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad F(\omega) &=K \cdot e^{-\omega^{2} / 2} \\ \text { Put } \omega=0, \qquad\qquad F(0) &=K \\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad 1 &=K \text { (from info. } \\ \text { From (iv), } \qquad\qquad F(\omega) &=e^{-\omega^{2} / 2} \\ \text{As we know}, e^{-a t^{2}}, a \gt 0 &\rightleftharpoons \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a}} e^{-\omega^{2} / 4 a}\\ \text{At }a=\frac{1}{2}, \qquad\qquad\quad e^{-t^{2} / 2} &\rightleftharpoons \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{1 / 2}} \cdot e^{-\omega^{2} / 2}\\ f(t)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-t^{2} / 2} \rightleftharpoons e^{-\omega^{2} / 2}=F(\omega)\\ \text { Thus, }\qquad\qquad f(t)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-t^{2} / 2} \\ \text { At } t=0, \qquad\qquad f(0)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \lt 1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a single-phase transformer, the total iron loss is [latex]2500\:W[/latex]
 at nominal voltage of [latex]440\:V[/latex] and frequency [latex]50\:Hz[/latex]. The total iron loss is [latex]850\:W[/latex] at [latex]220\:V[/latex] and [latex]25\:Hz[/latex]. Then, at nominal voltage and frequency, the hysteresis loss and eddy current loss respectively are
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} W_{i 1} &=2500 \mathrm{~W} \text { at } 440 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ W_{i 2} &=850 \mathrm{~W} \text { at } 220 \mathrm{~V}, 25 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ W_{i 3} &=R_{e_{3}}+P_{H_{3}} \text { at } 440 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ R_{\theta_{3}} &=?, \quad P_{h_{3}}=?, \quad \frac{v}{f}=\mathrm{constant} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad\quad 2500 &=A f+B f^{2} &\left\{\frac{400}{50}=\frac{220}{25}=\text { Constant }\right\} \\ \text { or, }\qquad \qquad \quad \frac{2500}{f} &=A+B f \\ \text{or},\qquad \qquad \frac{2500}{50}&=A+B(50) &\ldots(i)\\ \text{and}\qquad \qquad \frac{850}{25}&=\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}(25)&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving (i) and (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 25 B &=\frac{2500}{50}-\frac{850}{25}=\frac{2500-1700}{50} \\ &=\frac{800}{50}=16 \\ B &=\frac{16}{25} \\ \text{and from (i)},\qquad A &=50-\frac{16}{25} \times 50=50-32=18\\ \text{So, at} 50 \mathrm{~Hz}\\ P_{h}&=A f=18 \times 50=900 \mathrm{~W} \\ P_{e}&=B f=\left(\frac{16}{25}\right) \times(50)^{2}=1600 \mathrm{~W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 3-Bus network is shown. Consider generators as ideal voltage sources. If rows [latex]1,\:2[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] of the [latex]Y_{Bus}[/latex] matrix correspond to Bus [latex]1,\:2[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex], respectively, then [latex]Y_{Bus}[/latex] of the network is

raw_source.text: Let A be a [latex]10\times10[/latex] matrix such that [latex]A^{5}[/latex] is a null matrix, and let I be the [latex]10\times10[/latex] identity matrix. The determinant of [latex]\text{A+I}[/latex] is ___________________.

One coulomb of point charge moving with a uniform velocity [latex]10\:\hat{X} \text{m/s}[/latex] enters the region [latex]x\geq 0[/latex] having a magnetic flux density [latex]\overrightarrow{B}=\left ( 10y\:\hat{X} + 10x\:\hat{Y}+10\:\hat{Z}\right )T[/latex]. The magnitude of force on the charge at [latex]x=0^{+}[/latex] is _____________ N.
([latex]\hat{X}[/latex], [latex]\hat{Y}[/latex], and [latex]\hat{Z}[/latex] are unit vectors along x-axis, y-axis and z-axis, respectively.)
raw_source.solution:
Force on a charge moving with [latex]\vec{v}[/latex] velocity due to magnetic field is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \vec{F} &=Q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \\ &=1[10 \hat{x} \times(10 y \hat{x}+10 x \hat{y}+10 \hat{z}]\\ &=10(10 x) \hat{z}+10(10)(-\hat{y}) \\ &=100 x \hat{z}-100 \hat{y} \\ \left.\vec{F}\right|_{x=0^{+}} &=-100 \hat{y} \\ |\vec{F}| &=\sqrt{(-100)^{2}}=100 \text { Newton } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a large parallel plate capacitor. The gap 'd' between the two plates is filled entirely with a dielectric slab of relative permittivity 5. The plates are initially charged to a potential difference of V volts and then disconnected from the source. If the dielectric slab is pulled out completely, then the ratio of the new electric field [latex]E_{2}[/latex] in the gap to the original electric field [latex]E_{1}[/latex] is ________.
raw_source.solution:
If voltage source is removed then in both cases charge O is constant.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Case-1: }\left(Q_{1},=Q ; V_{1}=\right.&V) \\ Q_{1} &=C_{1} V_{1} \\ Q &=\frac{\epsilon_{0}(5) A}{d} V_{1} \\ Q &=5\left(\frac{\epsilon_{0} A}{d}\right) V_{1} \\ \text { Case-2: }\left(Q_{2}=Q ; V_{2}\right) & \\ Q_{2} &=C_{2} V_{2} \\ Q &=\frac{\epsilon_{0}(1) A}{d} V_{2} \\ Q &=\left(\frac{\epsilon_{0} A}{d}\right) V_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equation (i) is equal to equation (ii)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow 5\left(\frac{\epsilon_{0} A}{d}\right) V_{1} &=\left(\frac{\epsilon_{0} A}{d}\right) V_{2} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad 5 V_{1} &=V_{2} \\ \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} &=5 \\ E_{1} &=\frac{V_{1}}{d} ; E_{2}=\frac{V_{2}}{d} \\ \frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}} &=\frac{V_{2} / d}{V_{1} / d} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}} &=\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Put equation (iii) in equation (iv),
[latex] \Rightarrow \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}}=5[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a continuous-time signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] defined by [latex]x(t)=0[/latex] for [latex]\left | t \right |> 1[/latex], and [latex]x\left ( t \right )=1-\left | t \right | for \left | t \right |\leq 1[/latex]. Let the Fourier transform of [latex]x(t)[/latex] be defined as [latex]X\left ( \omega \right )=\int\limits_{-\infty }^{\infty }\:x\left ( t \right )e^{-j\omega t}\:dt[/latex]. The maximum magnitude of [latex]X\left ( \omega \right )[/latex] is ___________.
raw_source.solution:
Fourier transform, [latex]F(\omega)=A \tau S a^{2}\left(\frac{\omega \tau}{2}\right) [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { As } A=1, \tau=1 \\ H \omega) &=S a^{2}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right) \\ \left.F(\omega)\right|_{\text {peak }} &=F(0)=S a^{2}(0)=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \because [/latex] Peak value of sampling function occurs at [latex]\omega=0 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A belt-driven [latex]\text{DC}[/latex]
 shunt generator running at [latex]300\: \text{RPM}[/latex]
 delivers [latex]100 \:\text{kW}[/latex]
 to a [latex]200 \:V\: \text{DC}[/latex]
 grid. It continues to run as a motor when the belt breaks, taking [latex]10 \:\text{kW}[/latex]
 from the [latex]\text{DC}[/latex]
 grid. The armature resistance is [latex]0.025 \Omega[/latex], field resistance is [latex]50\:\Omega[/latex], and brush drop is [latex]2 \:V[/latex]. Ignoring armature reaction, the speed of the motor is _____  [latex]\text{RPM}[/latex]. (Round off to 2 decimal places.)
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{L} &=\frac{100 \times 10^{3}}{200}=500 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{S h} &=\frac{200}{50}=4 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{a} &=504 \mathrm{~A} \\ E_{q} &=V+I_{a} R_{a}+\text { Brush drop } \\ &=200+504(0.025)+2 \mathrm{~V} \\ &=214.6 \mathrm{~V}\\ \text{In motoring case:} V I&=10 \mathrm{~kW}, V=200 \mathrm{~V}\\ \therefore \qquad \qquad I &=\frac{10000}{200}=50 A \\ I_{f} &=4 \mathrm{~A}, I_{a}=I_{L}-I_{f} \\ &=46 \mathrm{~A} \\ E_{b} &=V-I_{a} R_{a}-\text { Brush Drop } \\ &=200-46(0.025)-2=196.85 \mathrm{~V} \\ \frac{N_{m}}{N_{g}} &=\frac{E_{b}}{E_{g}} \\ N_{m} &=\frac{E_{b}}{E_{g}} \times N_{g} \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad N_{m} &=\frac{196.85}{214.6} \times 300=275.18 \mathrm{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An 8-pole, [latex]50 \:Hz[/latex], three-phase, slip-ring induction motor has an effective rotor resistance of [latex]0.08\:\Omega[/latex] per phase. Its speed at maximum torque is [latex]650 \text{ RPM}[/latex]. The additional resistance per phase that must be inserted in the rotor to achieve maximum torque at start is _____________ [latex]\Omega[/latex]. (Round off to 2 decimal places.) Condition for maximum [latex]T_{\mathrm{s}}[/latex]

For a unit-step input, the output response has damped oscillations. The damped natural frequency is ___________________ [latex]\text{rad/s}[/latex]. (Round off to 2 decimal places.)

The external disturbance input is D(s). It is desired that when the disturbance is a unit step, the steady-state error should not exceed 0.1 unit. The minimum value of K is _____________.

raw_source.text: The waveform shown in solid line is obtained by clipping a full-wave rectified sinusoid (shown dashed). The ratio of the [latex]\text{RMS}[/latex] value of the full-wave rectified waveform to the [latex]\text{RMS}[/latex] value of the clipped waveform is _______________. (Round off to 2 decimal places.)
raw_source.solution:
We know,
RMS value of full wave rectified sine [latex]=\frac{V_{m}}{\sqrt{2}}=0.707 V_{m}[/latex]
For clipped wave form
As [latex]0 \rightarrow \frac{\pi}{4}[/latex] and [latex]\frac{3 \pi}{4} \rightarrow \pi[/latex] wave form are identical
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\text { rms value of clipped wave } \\ &\left.=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\left[2 \int_{0}^{\pi / 4} V_{m}^{2} \sin ^{2} \omega t+\int_{\pi / 4}^{3 \pi / 4}\left(0.707 V_{m}\right)^{2} d \omega t\right.}\right] \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\int_{0}^{\pi / 4} \frac{2 V_{m}^{2}}{2}[1-\cos 2 \omega t] d \omega t+\frac{1}{2} V_{m}^{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1 / 2}}\\ &=\left[\frac{1}{\pi}\left[V_{m}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2} \sin \frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{4} \pi\right]\right]^{1 / 2} \\ &=\left[\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{\pi}\left[\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\right]+\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{4}\right]^{1 / 2}=0.5838 V_{m} \\ \text { Ratio } &=\frac{0.707}{0.5838}=1.21 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A [latex]\text{100 Hz}[/latex] square wave, switching between [latex]\text{0 V}[/latex] and [latex]\text{5 V}[/latex], is applied to a [latex]\text{CR}[/latex] high-pass filter circuit as shown. The output voltage waveform across the resistor is [latex]\text{6.2 V}[/latex] peak-to-peak. If the resistance R is [latex]\text{820 $\Omega$}[/latex], then the value C is ______________[latex]\mu F[/latex]. (Round off to 2 decimal places.)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} v_{0}&=v_{i}-v_{c}\\ \text{For }1^{\text {st }}\text{ half cycle}, \quad v_{0}&=5-v_{c} \\ \text{For }2^{\text {nd }}\text{ half cycle}, \quad v_{0}&=-v_{c}\\ v_{p-p} &=\left(5-V_{c \;\min}\right)-\left(-V_{c}\; \max \right) \\ 6.2 &=5+V_{c \;\max }-V_{c \;\min} \\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{c \max }-V_{c \;\min } &=1.2 \ldots(\alpha) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For first half cycle i.e. [latex]0 \lt t \lt \frac{T}{2}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} v_{c}\left(0^{+}\right) &=v_{c}(0)=v_{c}\left(0^{-}\right)=v_{c} \min \\ v_{c}(\infty) &=5 \mathrm{~V} \\ \therefore \qquad\qquad v_{c}(t) &=v_{c}(\infty)+\left[v_{c}\left(0^{+}\right)-v_{c}(\infty)\right] e^{-t / \tau} \\ v_{c}(t) &=5+\left[V_{c m i n}-5\right] e^{-t / 2 \tau}=V_{c m a x} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad V_{c} \max &=5\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]+V_{c m i n} e^{-T / 2 \tau} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] For \frac{T}{2} \lt t \lt T[/latex]


[latex]\begin{aligned} v_{c}(t) &=v_{c}\left(\frac{T}{2}\right) e^{-t(t-T / 2) \tau} \\ \therefore\qquad v_{c}(t) &=V_{c m a x} e^{-(t-T / 2) \tau} \\ \text{at } t =T,\qquad \qquad v_{c} &=V_{c} \mathrm{~min} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad V_{C \mathrm{~min}} &=V_{C \max } e^{-T / 2 \tau}\\ \text { As } \quad V_{c \text { max }}-V_{c \text { min }}&=1.2 \qquad \qquad [\text { From }(\alpha)]\\ \therefore \quad V_{\text {cmax }}-V_{c \max } e^{-T / 2 t} &=1.2 \\ V_{c} \max &=\frac{1.2}{1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad\qquad V_{c} \max &=\frac{1.2}{1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}}=5\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]+V_{c \min } e^{-2 \tau} \end{aligned}[/latex]
From (ii),
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{c \max } &=5\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]+\left(V_{c m a x} e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right) e^{-T / 2 \tau} \\ V_{c \max } &=5\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]+V_{c \max } e^{-T / \tau} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad V_{c \max }\left[1-e^{-T / \tau}\right] &=5\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right] \\ V_{c} \max &=\frac{5\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]}{\left[1+e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]\left[1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}\right]} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using equation (iii)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{1.2}{1-e^{-T / 2 \tau}} &=\frac{5}{1+e^{-T / 2 \tau}} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad 1.2+1.2 e^{-T / 2 \tau} &=5-5 e^{-\pi / 2 t} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad 6.2 e^{-T / 2 \tau} &=3.8 \\ e^{-T / 2 \tau} &=\frac{3.8}{6.2}=0.6129 \\ \frac{T}{2 \tau} &=0.4895\\ \text { as }\qquad \qquad T&=\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{100} \mathrm{sec}\\ \text { and }\qquad \qquad \tau & =R C=820 \mathrm{C} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \frac{1}{(100)(2)(820) C} & =0.4895 \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad C & =12.46 \mu \mathrm{F} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A [latex]\text{CMOS}[/latex] Schmitt-trigger inverter has a low output level of [latex]\text{0 V}[/latex] and a high output level of [latex]\text{5 V}[/latex]. It has input thresholds of [latex]\text{1.6 V}[/latex] and [latex]\text{2.4 V}[/latex]. The input capacitance and output resistance of the Schmitt-trigger are negligible. The frequency of the oscillator shown is ____________[latex]\text{Hz}[/latex].(Round off to 2 decimal places.)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} v_{c}(t)&=v_{c \text { final }}+\left[v_{\text {initial }}-v_{c^{\prime}} \text { final }\right] e^{- t / R C} \\ \text { Charging, } \qquad \qquad v_{c}(t)&=5+(1.6-5) e^{-t / R C}\\ &=5-3.4 e^{-t / R C}\\ t=t_{1}, \qquad \qquad v_{c}(t) &= 2.4 \mathrm{~V} \\ 2.4 &=5-3.4 e^{-t / \mathrm{RC}} \\ 3.4 e^{-11 / \mathrm{RC}} &= 2.6 \\ t_{1} &= \ln \left(\frac{3.4}{2.6}\right) R C=0.268 \times R C \end{aligned}[/latex]
Discharging,
[latex] \begin{aligned} v_{c}(t) &=0+(2.4-0) e^{-t / \mathrm{RC}} \\ &=2.4 e^{-t / \mathrm{RC}} \\ t=t_{2}, \qquad v_{c}\left(t_{a}\right) &=1.6 \mathrm{~V} \\ 1.6 &=2.4 e^{-12 / \mathrm{AC}} \\ t_{2} &=\ln \left(\frac{2.4}{1.6}\right) R C=0.405 \times R C \\ T &=t_{1}+t_{2}=(0.268+0.405) \mathrm{RC} \\ T &=0.673 \mathrm{RC} \\ f &=\frac{1}{0.673 R C}=\frac{1}{0.673 \times 10^{4} \times 47 \times 10^{-9}} \\ f &=3157.46 \mathrm{~Hz} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the boost converter shown. Switch Q is operating at [latex]\text{25 kHz}[/latex] with a duty cycle of 0.6. Assume the diode and switch to be ideal. Under steady-state condition, the average resistance [latex]R_{\text{in}}[/latex] as seen by the source is __________ [latex]\Omega[/latex].
(Round off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Checking for continuous conduction mode
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta I_{L} &=\frac{\alpha V_{S}}{f L}=\frac{0.6 \times 15}{25 \times 10^{3} \times 1 \times 10^{-3}}=0.36 \mathrm{~A} \\ \frac{\Delta I_{L}}{2} &=0.18 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{L, \min } &=I_{L}-\frac{\Delta I_{L}}{2}=I_{S}-\frac{\Delta I_{L}}{2} \\ &=(9.375-0.18)=9.195>0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
As it is continuous conduction
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{0}&=\frac{V_{S}}{1-\alpha}=\frac{15}{1-0.6}=37.5 \mathrm{~V} \\ I_{0}&=\frac{V_{0}}{R}=\frac{37.5}{10}=3.75 \mathrm{~V} \\ \frac{V_{0}}{V_{S}}&=\frac{I_{S}}{I_{0}}=\frac{1}{1-\alpha} \\ I_{S}&=\frac{I_{0}}{1-\alpha}=\frac{3.75}{1-0.6}=9.375 \mathrm{~A} \\ R_{\text {in }}&=\frac{V_{S}}{I_{S}}=\frac{15}{9.375}=1.6 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the buck-boost converter shown. Switch Q is operating at [latex]\text{25 kHz}[/latex] and 0.75 duty-cycle. Assume diode and switch to be ideal. Under steady-state condition, the average current flowing through the indicator is ____________A.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\alpha=0.75, \quad f=25 \mathrm{kHz}[/latex]
Assume continous conduction:
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{0}&=\frac{\alpha V_{s}}{1-\alpha}=\frac{0.75 \times 20}{1-0.75} \\ V_{0}&=60 \mathrm{~V}\\ I_{0} &=\frac{V_{0}}{R}=\frac{60}{10}=6 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{L} &=\frac{I_{0}}{1-\alpha}=\frac{6}{1-0.75}=24 \mathrm{~A} \\ \Delta I_{L} &=\frac{\alpha V_{s}}{f_{L}}=\frac{0.75 \times 60}{25 \times 10^{3} \times\left(1 \times 10^{-3}\right)}=1.8 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{L \min } &=I_{L}-\frac{\Delta I_{L}}{2}=24-\frac{1.8}{2}=24-0.9 \\ \left(I_{L \min }=23.1 \mathrm{~A}\right) &>0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Continous conduction assumption is correct.
[latex] I_{L}=24 \mathrm{~A}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A single-phase full-bridge inverter fed by a [latex]\text{325 V DC}[/latex] produces a symmetric quasi-square waveform across 'ab' as shown. To achieve a modulation index of 0.8, the angle [latex]\theta[/latex] expressed in degrees should be _______________. (Round off to 2 decimal places.)
(Modulation index is defined as the ratio of the peak of the fundamental component of [latex]V_{ab}[/latex] to the applied [latex]\text{DC}[/latex] value.)
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \widehat{V_{01}} &=m_{a} V_{S}=0.8 \times 325=260 \mathrm{~V} \\ \widehat{V_{01}} &=\frac{4 V_{S}}{\pi} \sin d=260 \\ \frac{4(325)}{\pi} \sin d &=260 \\ \sin d &=\frac{260 \times \pi}{4 \times 325}=0.628 \\ d &=38.9 \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad \theta &=\frac{\pi}{2}-d=90^{\circ}-38.9=51.1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Which one of the following numbers is exactly divisible by [latex]\left(11^{13}+1\right)[/latex]?

[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\left(11^{13}\right)^{4}-(1)^{4}}{11^{3}+1} &=\frac{\left.\left((11)^{13}\right)^{2}-(1)^{2}\right)\left(\left(11^{13}\right)^{2}+(1)^{2}\right)}{11^{3}+1} \\ &=\left[\left(11^{13}-1\right)\right]\left[\left(11^{13}\right)^{2}+(1)^{2}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

Let X be a continuous random variable denoting the temperature measured. The range of temperature is [latex][0,100][/latex] degree Celsius and let the probability density function of X be [latexf(x)=0.01[/latex] for [latex]0 \leq X \leq 100[/latex].

n is a continuous random variable for continuous random variable

Students who fail the exam in the first attempt must appear for the exam in the following year. Students always pass the exam in their second attempt.
The number of students who took the exam for the first time in the year 2 and the year 3 respectively, are ________.
raw_source.solution:
Total number of student in the year-2
[latex]= 60 + 5 = 65[/latex]
Students who failed in the year and appeared in year-2 = 10
So the students who appeared first time in year-2 [latex]= 65 - 10 = 55[/latex]
Similarly, Total number of students in year-3 = 53
Students who failed in the year-2 and appeared in year-3 = 5
So, the students who appeared first time in year-3
[latex] = 53 - 5 = 48[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a matrix [latex] A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 4 & -2\\ 0&1 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The matrix [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the equation [latex] 6A^{-1}=A^2+cA+dI[/latex] where [latex] c[/latex] and [latex] d[/latex] are scalars and [latex] I[/latex] is the identity matrix.
Then [latex] (c+d)[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation:
[latex]\begin{aligned} |A-\lambda I|&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & 0 &0 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda & 2\\ 0 & -1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ (1-\lambda )[(4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+2] &=0\\ \lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2+11\lambda -6&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
By cayley hamilton theorem
[latex]\begin{aligned} A^3-6A^2+11A-6 &=0 \\ A^2-6A+11I&=6A^{-1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
On comparison : c= -6 and d = 11
Therefore, c + d = -6 + 11 = 5

raw_source.text:
Consider a matrix [latex] A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 4 & -2\\ 0&1 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The matrix [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the equation [latex] 6A^{-1}=A^2+cA+dI[/latex] where [latex] c[/latex] and [latex] d[/latex] are scalars and [latex] I[/latex] is the identity matrix.
Then [latex] (c+d)[/latex] is equal to
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation:
[latex]\begin{aligned} |A-\lambda I|&=0 \\ \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & 0 &0 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda & 2\\ 0 & -1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix}&=0 \\ (1-\lambda )[(4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+2] &=0\\ \lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2+11\lambda -6&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
By cayley hamilton theorem
[latex]\begin{aligned} A^3-6A^2+11A-6 &=0 \\ A^2-6A+11I&=6A^{-1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
On comparison : c= -6 and d = 11
Therefore, c + d = -6 + 11 = 5

raw_source.text: As shown in the figure below, two concentric conducting spherical shells, centered at [latex]r=0 [/latex] and having radii [latex]r=c [/latex]and [latex]r=d [/latex] are maintained at potentials such that the potential [latex]V(r) [/latex] at [latex]r=c [/latex] is [latex]V_1[/latex] and [latex]V(r) [/latex] at [latex]r=d [/latex] is [latex]V_2[/latex]. The expression for [latex]V(r) [/latex] in the region between [latex]r=c [/latex]and [latex]r=d [/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
We have, Laplace equation
[latex] \triangledown ^2V=0[/latex] ...(1)
where, [latex] \triangledown ^2V=\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( r^2\frac{\partial V}{\partial r} \right )+\frac{1}{r^2 \sin \theta }\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\left ( \sin \theta \frac{\partial V}{\partial \theta } \right )+ \frac{1}{r^2 \sin ^2\theta } \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial \phi ^2}[/latex]
V will have only radial component.
From equation (1)
[latex]\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( r^2\frac{\partial V}{\partial r} \right )=0 [/latex]
Integrate both side [latex] r^2\frac{\partial V}{\partial r} =P[/latex]
Again integrate, [latex]V=-\frac{P}{r}+Q [/latex]
Here, P and Q are constant.
Given: at [latex] r=c, V=V_1[/latex]
[latex]V_1=-\frac{P}{r}+Q [/latex] ...(2)
at [latex] r=d, V=V_2[/latex]
[latex]V_2=-\frac{P}{d}+Q [/latex] ...(3)
From eq. (2) & (3)
[latex]P=\frac{(V_2-V_1)cd}{d-c} [/latex]
[latex] Q=V_1+\frac{d(V_2-V_1)}{d-c}[/latex]
From eq. (1),
[latex]V=-\frac{(V_2-V_1)cd}{r(d-c)}+V_1+\frac{(V_2-V_1)cd}{(d-c)} [/latex]
[latex] V=\frac{(V_1-V_2)cd}{r(d-c)}+\frac{(V_2d-V_1c)}{(d-c)}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A 280 V, separately excited DC motor with armature resistance of [latex]1\Omega  [/latex] and constant
field excitation drives a load. The load torque is proportional to the speed. The
motor draws a current of 30 A when running at a speed of 1000 rpm. Neglect
frictional losses in the motor. The speed, in rpm, at which the motor will run, if an
additional resistance of value [latex]10\Omega  [/latex] is connected in series with the armature, is
_______. (round off to nearest integer)
raw_source.solution:
Back emf,
[latex]E_{b1}=280-30 \times 1 =250V [/latex]
When additional [latex] 10\Omega[/latex] resistance connected in series with armature.
[latex]E_{b2}=280-(10+1) I_{a_2} =280-11I_{a_2} [/latex]
Given: [latex] \tau \propto N[/latex]
We know, [latex] \tau \propto \phi I_a \text{ (Here, }\phi \rightarrow constant)[/latex]
So,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \tau &\propto I_a \\ \therefore \; N &\propto I_a \\ or \; \frac{N_2}{N_1}&=\frac{I_{a_2}}{I_{a_1}}\\ I_{a_2}&=N_2 \times \frac{30}{1000}\\ \therefore \; E_{b_2}&=280-\left ( 11 \times \frac{30}{1000} \right )N_2\\ &\text{We also have,}\\ E_b &\propto\phi \omega \\ \therefore \frac{E_{b_2}}{E_{b_1}}&=\frac{N_2}{N_1}\\ &\frac{280-\left ( 11 \times \frac{30}{1000} \right )N_2}{250}=\frac{N_2}{1000}\\ \Rightarrow N_2&=482.758rpm \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 4-pole induction motor with inertia of 0.1 [latex]kg-m^2[/latex] drives a constant load torque of 2 Nm. The speed of the motor is increased linearly from 1000 rpm to 1500 rpm in 4 seconds as shown in the figure below. Neglect losses in the motor. The energy, in joules, consumed by the motor during the speed change is ____________. (round off to nearest integer)
raw_source.solution:
We have
[latex]\begin{aligned} J\frac{d\omega }{dt}&=\tau _e-\tau _L\\ J\omega \frac{d\omega }{dt}&=P_e-P_L \;\;(\because P=\tau \omega )\\ \therefore P_e&=J\omega \frac{d\omega }{dt}+P_L\\ E&=\int P_edt\\ R&=J\int_{1000}^{1500}\omega d\omega +\int_{1000}^{1500}P_Ldt\\ &=\frac{J}{2}\left ( \frac{2 \pi}{60} \right )^2[1500^2-1000^2]+\frac{2 \pi \tau }{60}\int_{1000}^{1500}Ndt\\ &=\frac{0.1}{2}\left ( \frac{2 \pi}{60} \right )^2\times 125 \times 10^4+\frac{2 \pi}{60} \times 2\times [1000 \times 4+\frac{1}{2} \times 500 \times 4]\\ &=1732.586J \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the following differential equation, the numerically obtained value of [latex]y(t)[/latex], at [latex]t=1[/latex], is ___ (Round off to 2 decimal places).

[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{t}}, \alpha=0.01 \text { and } y(0)=0 [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given :
[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha t} [/latex]
[latex]\alpha=0.01[/latex] and [latex]y(0)=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d t^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} & =y^{\prime \prime}(0) \\ & =-\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{T}}-\left.\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{(2+\alpha \mathrm{t})^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} \\ & =-\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{4}=-\frac{3 \alpha}{4} \end{aligned} [/latex]

We know,
Taylor's series
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(t) & =y(0)+y^{\prime}(0)+\frac{t^{2} y^{\prime \prime}(0)}{2 !}+\ldots \\ & =0+t\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(-\frac{3 \alpha}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{t}{2}-\frac{3}{8} \alpha t^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At [latex]\mathrm{t}=1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(1) & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}(0.01) \times 1^{2} \\ & =0.5-\frac{3}{8} \times 0.01 \\ & =0.496 \approx 0.5 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is  ___ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Let probability of head [latex]=\mathrm{P}[/latex]
Let probability of Tail [latex]=q=P-1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline Trial & 1 & 2 & 3 & ... \\ \hline Probability & [\mathrm{P} & \mathrm{qP} & [latex]\mathrm{q}^{2} \mathrm{P} & .... \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Expected No. of trail
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p+2 P q+3 q^{2} P+\ldots \\ & =P\left(1+2 q+3 q^{2}+\ldots\right) \\ & =P(1-q)^{-2} \\ & =\frac{P}{P^{2}}=\frac{1}{P} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Given : Trial [latex]=4[/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{P}=4 \Rightarrow P=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{q}=\frac{3}{4}[/latex]

Now, probability of head for second trail. [latex] \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{qP} \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{16}=0.1875 \end{aligned} [/latex]

The closed curve shown in the figure is described by

[latex] \begin{aligned} I & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi} \vec{F} \cdot \overrightarrow{d l} \\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}(-y \hat{i}+x)(d x \hat{i}+d y) \\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}(-y d x+x d y) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given : [latex]\quad x=r \cos \theta[/latex] and [latex]y=r \sin \theta[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore I&=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}[(-r \sin \theta)(-r \sin \theta) d \theta+(r \cos \theta)(r \cos \theta) d \theta] \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi} r^{2} d \theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}(1+\cos \theta)^{2} d \theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(1+\cos ^{2} \theta+2 \cos \theta\right) d \theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(1+\frac{1+\cos 2 \theta}{2}+2 \cos \theta\right) \mathrm{d} \theta \\ &=3 \pi=9.425 \end{aligned} [/latex]

So, [latex]\quad[/latex] OLTF [latex]=\frac{(3 s+1)}{s(s-1)}[/latex]

Closed loop transfer function,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{Y(s)}{R(s)} & =\frac{3 s+1}{s^{2}+2 s+1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3 s+1}{s\left(s^{2}+2 s+1\right)} \quad\left[\because R(s)=\frac{1}{s}\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]

In the following differential equation, the numerically obtained value of [latex]y(t)[/latex], at [latex]t=1[/latex], is ___ (Round off to 2 decimal places).

[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{t}}, \alpha=0.01 \text { and } y(0)=0 [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given :
[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha t} [/latex]
[latex]\alpha=0.01[/latex] and [latex]y(0)=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d t^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} & =y^{\prime \prime}(0) \\ & =-\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{T}}-\left.\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{(2+\alpha \mathrm{t})^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} \\ & =-\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{4}=-\frac{3 \alpha}{4} \end{aligned} [/latex]

We know,
Taylor's series
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(t) & =y(0)+y^{\prime}(0)+\frac{t^{2} y^{\prime \prime}(0)}{2 !}+\ldots \\ & =0+t\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(-\frac{3 \alpha}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{t}{2}-\frac{3}{8} \alpha t^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At [latex]\mathrm{t}=1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(1) & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}(0.01) \times 1^{2} \\ & =0.5-\frac{3}{8} \times 0.01 \\ & =0.496 \approx 0.5 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is  ___ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Let probability of head [latex]=\mathrm{P}[/latex]
Let probability of Tail [latex]=q=P-1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline Trial & 1 & 2 & 3 & ... \\ \hline Probability & [\mathrm{P} & \mathrm{qP} & [latex]\mathrm{q}^{2} \mathrm{P} & .... \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Expected No. of trail
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p+2 P q+3 q^{2} P+\ldots \\ & =P\left(1+2 q+3 q^{2}+\ldots\right) \\ & =P(1-q)^{-2} \\ & =\frac{P}{P^{2}}=\frac{1}{P} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Given : Trial [latex]=4[/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{P}=4 \Rightarrow P=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{q}=\frac{3}{4}[/latex]

Now, probability of head for second trail. [latex] \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{qP} \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{16}=0.1875 \end{aligned} [/latex]

A three-phase synchronous motor with synchronous impedance of [latex]0.1+j0.3 [/latex]  per unit per phase has a static stability limit of 2.5 per unit. The corresponding excitation voltage in per unit is ____ (Round off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Developed power for motor,
[latex] P_{d e v}=\frac{V_{f}}{Z_{s}} \cos \left(\theta_{s}-\delta\right)-\frac{E_{F}^{2}}{2} \cos \theta_{s} [/latex]

At max. power developed,
[latex] \delta=\theta_{\mathrm{S}} [/latex]

and this is decide steady state stability of motor.
[latex]\therefore \mathrm{SSSL}, \mathrm{P}_{\text {dev }(max)}=\frac{V E_{F}}{\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{S}}}-\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}}{\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{S}}} \cos \theta_{\mathrm{s}}[/latex]
where, [latex]V=1.0 \mathrm{pu}[/latex]

[latex] \mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{S}}=0.1+\mathrm{j} 0.3=0.316 \angle 71.6^{\circ} \mathrm{pu} [/latex]
and [latex]\mathrm{SSSL}=2.5[/latex]

[latex]\therefore \quad 2.5=\frac{1 \times E_{F}}{0.316}-\frac{E_{F}^{2}}{0.316} \cos 71.56^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex]1.001 \mathrm{E}_{F}^{2}-3.16 \mathrm{E}_{F}+2.5=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{F}}=1.595 \mathrm{pu}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A three phase [latex]415 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz}, 6-pole, 960 RPM, 4 HP[/latex] squirrel cage induction motor drives a constant torque load at rated speed operating from rated supply and delivering rated output. If the supply voltage and frequency are reduced by [latex]20 \%[/latex] the resultant speed of the motor in RPM (neglecting the stator leakage impednace and rotational losses) is ____ (Round off to the nearest integer)
raw_source.solution:
Given : Torque is constant.
We have, [latex]\quad \tau \propto \frac{s V^{2}}{f} \quad ...(1)[/latex]
Synchronous speed, [latex]N_{S}=\frac{120 f}{P}[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{120 \times 50}{6}=1000 \mathrm{rpm} [/latex]

[latex] \text { Slip, } S=\frac{1000-960}{1000}=0.04 [/latex]

Now, from eqn. (1), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{0.04 \times \mathrm{V}^{2}}{\mathrm{~F}} & =\frac{\mathrm{S}_{\text {new }} \times(0.8)^{2} \mathrm{~V}}{0.8 \mathrm{~F}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{S}_{\text {new }} & =0.05 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Synchronous speed at reduced frequency i.e. [latex]50 \times 0.8=40 \mathrm{~Hz}[/latex].
[latex] \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{new})}=\frac{120 \times 40}{6}=800 \mathrm{rpm} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Motor speed,

[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{N}&=\left(1-\mathrm{S}_{\text {new }}\right) \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{s} \text { (new) }} & =(1-0.05) \times 800 \\ & =760 \mathrm{rpm} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The discrete-time Fourier transform of a signal [latex]x[n][/latex] is [latex]X(\Omega)=1(1+\cos \Omega) e^{-j \Omega}[/latex]. Consider that [latex]x_{p}[n][/latex] is a periodic signal of period [latex]N=5[/latex] such that

[latex] \begin{aligned} x_{p}[n] & =x[n], \text { for } n=0,1,2 \\ & =0, \text { for } n=3,4 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Note that [latex]x_{p}[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} a_{k} e^{j \frac{2 \pi}{N} k m}[/latex]. The magnitude of the Fourier series coefficient [latex]a_{3}[/latex] is ____ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
Given : [latex]x_{p}(n)[/latex] is a period signal of period [latex]N=5[/latex].
[latex] x_{p}(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc} x(n), & \text { for } n=0,1,2 \\ 0, & \text { for } n=3,4 \end{array}\right. [/latex]

and [latex]\mathrm{x}(\mathrm{n}) \stackrel{\text { DTFT }}{\longrightarrow} \mathrm{X}(\Omega)=(1+\cos \Omega) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j} \Omega}[/latex]

We have,
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{K} & =\frac{X\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N} K\right)}{N} \\ & =\frac{\left[1+\cos \left(\frac{2 \pi}{N} K\right)\right] \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j} \frac{2 \pi}{N} R}}{N} \end{aligned} [/latex]

For, [latex]\mathrm{N}=5[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{K}=3[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{3} & =\frac{\left[1+\cos \left(\frac{2 \pi \times 3}{5}\right)\right] \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{j} \frac{2 \pi}{5} \times 3}}{5} \\ \left|a_{3}\right| & =\frac{1}{5}\left[1+\cos \frac{6 \pi}{5}\right] \\ & =0.0382 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: When the winding [latex]c-d[/latex] of the singlephase, 50 [latex]\mathrm{Hz}[/latex], two winding transformer is supplied from an AC current source of frequency [latex]50 \mathrm{~Hz}[/latex], the rated voltage of [latex]200 \mathrm{~V}[/latex] (rms), [latex]50 \mathrm{~Hz}[/latex]. is obtained at the open-circuited terminals a-b. Considering the magnetizing characteristics to be linear and neglecting core loss, the self-inductance of the winding [latex]a-b[/latex] in millihenry is ____ (Round off to 1 decimal place).

[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{A} & =5000 \mathrm{~mm}^{2} \\ \mathrm{I} & =500 \mathrm{~mm} \\ \mathrm{~B}_{\max } & =1 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{ab}} & =200 \mathrm{~V} \\ \sqrt{2} \pi \mathrm{fN}_{1} \phi_{\max } & =200 \\ \sqrt{2 \pi} \times 50 \times \mathrm{N}_{1} \times 1 & \times 5000 \times 10^{-6}=200 \quad[\because \phi=\beta \mathrm{A}] \\ \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{N}_{1} & =181 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Now, mutual inductance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} M&=\frac{N^{2}}{I / \mu A} \\ & =\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5000 \times 5000 \times 10^{-6} \times(181)^{2}}{0.5} \\ & =2.05843 \mathrm{H} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Therefore, self inductance of winding.
[latex] \begin{aligned} L & =\text { Mutual + leakage } \\ & =2.05843+0.16 \\ & =2.21843 \mathrm{H} \text { or } 2218.43 \mathrm{mH} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.solution:
We know that: directional derivative of '[latex] f [/latex]' at [latex] P(1,1,1) [/latex] in the direction of [latex] \vec{a} [/latex] is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Directional derivative } & =\nabla f \cdot \frac{\hat{a}}{|\bar{a}|} \\ \nabla f & =\hat{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+\hat{j} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}+\hat{k} \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \\ \nabla f & =i \frac{5}{x}+j \frac{3}{y}+k \frac{4}{z} \\ (\nabla f)_{(1,1,1)} & =5 i+3 j+4 k \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Directional derivative [latex] =\overline{\nabla f} \cdot \frac{\bar{a}}{|\bar{a}|}=(5 i+3 j+4 k) \cdot \frac{(2 i+j+2 k)}{\sqrt{2^{2}+1^{2}+2^{2}}}=\frac{21}{3}=7 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The input [latex] x(t) [/latex] and the output [latex] y(t) [/latex] of a system are related as

[latex] y(t)=e^{-t} \int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{\tau} x(\tau) d \tau, \quad-\infty \lt t \lt \infty [/latex]

The system is
raw_source.solution:
System will follow law of superposition. Therefore, system will be linear.
Time-invariance check:
[latex] y\left(t-t_{0}\right)=e^{-\left(t-t_{0}\right)} \int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} e^{\tau} \cdot x(\tau) d \tau [/latex]
For input [latex] x\left(t-t_{0}\right) [/latex], output will be
[latex] y(t)=e^{-t} \int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{\tau} \cdot x\left(\tau-t_{0}\right) d \tau [/latex]
Put [latex] \tau-t_{o}=k [/latex], then [latex] d \tau=d k [/latex] and for [latex] \tau=t, k=t-t_{0} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =e^{-t} \int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} e^{k+t_{0}} \cdot x(k) d k \\ & =e^{-t} \times e^{t o} \times \int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} e^{k} \cdot x(k) d k=e^{-\left(t-t_{0}\right)} \times \int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} e^{k} \cdot x(k) d k \\ & =e^{-\left(t-t_{0}\right)} \times \int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} e^{\tau} \cdot x(\tau) d \tau \end{aligned} [/latex]
Since,
[latex] y(t)=y\left(t-t_{0}\right) [/latex]
So, the system is time-invariant.

raw_source.text:
Consider the discrete-time system [latex] T_{1} [/latex] and [latex] T_{2} [/latex] defined as follows:

[latex] \begin{aligned} & \left\{T_{1} x\right\}[n]=x[0]+x[1]+\ldots+x[n] \\ & \left\{T_{2} x\right\}[n]=x[0]+\frac{1}{2} x[1]+\cdots+\frac{1}{2^{n}} x[n] \end{aligned} [/latex]

Which one of the following statement is true?
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left\{T_{1} x\right\}[n] & =x[0]+x[1]+\ldots+x[n] \\ \left\{T_{1} x\right\}[n]^{-} & =\sum_{K=0}^{n} x[K] \end{aligned} [/latex]
Let,
[latex] \begin{aligned} x[K] & =u[K] \\ \mid x[K] & =|u[K]| \\ \left|\left\{T_{1} x\right\}[n]\right| & =\left|\sum_{K=0}^{n} u[K]\right|=\sum_{K=0}^{n} 1=n \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \mid\left[\left.T_{1} x(n)\right|_{n=\infty}=\infty\right. [/latex] system is not BIBO stable
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left\{T_{2} x\right\}[n] & =x[0]+\frac{1}{2} x[1]+\cdots+\frac{1}{2^{n}} x[n] \\ & =\sum_{K=0}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{K} x(K) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Let,
[latex] \begin{aligned} x(K) & =u[K] \\ |x[K]| & =\mid u[K] \\ \left\{T_{2} x\right\}[n] & =\sum_{K=0}^{n}\left|\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{K} u(K)\right| \\ \left\{T_{2} x\right\}[n] & =\sum_{K=0}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{K} \\ \mid\left[\left.T_{2} x(n)\right|_{n=\infty}\right. & =\sum_{K=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{K}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=2 \text { stable } \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] T_{1} [/latex] is not BIBO stable but [latex] T_{2} [/latex] is [latex] \mathrm{BIBO} [/latex] stable.

From the figure,

Consider the set [latex]S[/latex] of points [latex](x, y) \in \mathfrak{R}^2[/latex] which minimize the real-valued function

[latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex]

Which of the following statements is true about the set [latex]S[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
We are given:
[latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex]

Step 1: Substitute a single variable
Let [latex]u = x + y[/latex]
Then, the function becomes:
[latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]

Step 2: Minimize [latex]f(u) = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]
This is a quadratic function in [latex]u[/latex] with a positive coefficient, so it has a unique minimum.
The minimum occurs at:
[latex]u = \frac{-(-2)}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]

So, the function is minimized when [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]

Step 3: Analyze the set [latex]S[/latex]
All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex].
There are infinitely many such points in [latex]\mathbb{R}^2[/latex].

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\text{The number of elements in the set } S \text{ is infinite}}[/latex]
Correct Option: (B)
options: The number of elements in the set S is finite and more than one.
The number of elements in the set S is infinite.
The number of elements in the set S is exactly one.

raw_answer.option_text: The number of elements in the set S is infinite.

Consider discrete random variables X and Y with probabilities as follows:

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=0)=\frac{1}{4}[/latex],

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=0)=\frac{1}{8}[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=1)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=1)=\frac{1}{8}[/latex]

Given [latex]\mathrm{X}=1[/latex], the expected value of [latex]\mathrm{Y}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Identify the conditional probabilities of [latex] Y [/latex] given [latex] X = 1 [/latex].
From the given:
[latex] P(X=1, Y=0) = \frac{1}{8}, \quad P(X=1, Y=1) = \frac{1}{8} [/latex]
So, total probability [latex] P(X=1) = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the conditional probabilities:
[latex] P(Y=0 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=0)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]
[latex] P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=1)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Step 3: Compute the expected value:
[latex] \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=1] = 0 \cdot P(Y=0 \mid X=1) + 1 \cdot P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Final Answer: (B) [latex] \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Consider a continuous-time signal

Where [latex]u(t)[/latex] is the continuous-time unit step function. Let [latex]\delta(\mathrm{t})[/latex] be the continuous-time unit impulse function. The value of

[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) \mathrm{dt}[/latex]

is
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex]\mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) = -\mathrm{t}^2 {\mathrm{u}(\mathrm{t}+4) - \mathrm{u}(\mathrm{t}-4)}[/latex]
This represents a time-limited signal that exists only between [latex]t = -4[/latex] and [latex]t = 4[/latex]. Outside this interval, [latex]x(t) = 0[/latex].

Also given:
We are to compute the value of the integral:
[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) , \mathrm{dt}[/latex]

Step 1: Use the sifting property of the delta function:
[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t - t_0) , dt = f(t_0)[/latex]
Similarly,
[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t + 3) , dt = f(-3)[/latex]

Step 2: Evaluate [latex]x(-3)[/latex]
[latex]x(t) = -t^2 {u(t+4) - u(t-4)}[/latex]
At [latex]t = -3[/latex],
[latex]u(-3 + 4) = u(1) = 1[/latex] and [latex]u(-3 - 4) = u(-7) = 0[/latex]
So,
[latex]x(-3) = -(-3)^2 (1 - 0) = -9[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) , \mathrm{dt} = x(-3) = -9[/latex]

Selected data points of the step response of a stable first-order linear time-invariant (LTI) system are given below. The closest value of the time-constant, in sec, of the system is

[latex]\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline Time(sec) & 0.6 & 1.6 & 2.6 & 10 & \infty \\ \hline Output & 0.78 & 1.65 & 2.18 & 2.98 & 3 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Analyze the step response of a first-order LTI system
For a first-order LTI system, the step response is given by:
[latex]y(t) = K \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)[/latex]
Where [latex]K[/latex] is the steady-state value (final output), and [latex]\tau[/latex] is the time constant.

Step 2: Use the steady-state value
The output approaches the steady-state value as [latex]t \to \infty[/latex].
At [latex]t = \infty[/latex], the output is 3, which is the steady-state value (K).
Thus, [latex]K = 3[/latex].

Step 3: Relating time and output
For a first-order system, the time at which the output reaches [latex]63%[/latex] of the final value is equal to the time constant [latex]\tau[/latex].
So, [latex]y(\tau) = K \left(1 - e^{-1}\right) = 3 \times (1 - e^{-1}) \approx 3 \times 0.632 = 1.896[/latex].

Step 4: Find the closest data point to 1.896
Looking at the given data points, at [latex]t = 1.6 \text{ sec}, y(t) = 1.65[/latex], which is the closest to 1.896.
Thus, the time constant [latex]\tau \approx 2 \text{ sec}[/latex].

Final Answer:
The closest value of the time constant is [latex]2 \text{ sec}[/latex].

The phase angle difference should be nearly zero at the instant of synchronization.

Instruments used to verify these conditions are:
(A) Voltmeter: Used to ensure the voltage of the alternator matches the grid voltage.

(B) Wattmeter: Measures power; not used for synchronization.

(C) Synchroscope: Used to indicate the phase angle and frequency difference between the alternator and the grid. It shows whether the alternator is running fast or slow and when to close the circuit breaker.

(D) Stroboscope: Used to measure rotational speed visually; not used in electrical synchronization.

raw_source.text:
A continuous time periodic signal [latex]{x}({t})[/latex] is

[latex]x(t)=1+2 \cos 2 \pi t+2 \cos 4 \pi t+2 \cos 6 \pi t[/latex].

If [latex]T[/latex] is the period of [latex]x(t)[/latex], then [latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T}| x(t)| ^{2} dt=[/latex] _________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Find the period [latex]T[/latex]
The signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] consists of cosine terms with frequencies [latex]2\pi, 4\pi, 6\pi[/latex], which correspond to fundamental frequencies [latex]1 , \text{Hz}, 2 , \text{Hz}, 3 , \text{Hz}[/latex]. The period of the signal [latex]T[/latex] is the least common multiple (LCM) of the periods of these individual cosine terms.

The period of [latex]2\pi t[/latex] (1 Hz) is [latex]T_1 = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex].
The period of [latex]4\pi t[/latex] (2 Hz) is [latex]T_2 = 0.5 , \text{sec}[/latex].
The period of [latex]6\pi t[/latex] (3 Hz) is [latex]T_3 = \frac{1}{3} , \text{sec}[/latex].
The LCM of [latex]T_1, T_2, T_3[/latex] is [latex]T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex].

Step 2: Calculate [latex] |x(t)|^2 [/latex]
The signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] is real, so we can calculate [latex]|x(t)|^2[/latex] directly:
[latex]|x(t)|^2 = (1 + 2 \cos(2\pi t) + 2 \cos(4\pi t) + 2 \cos(6\pi t))^2[/latex]
Expanding the square:
[latex]|x(t)|^2 = 1 + 4 \cos(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(4\pi t) + 4 \cos(6\pi t) + 4 \cos^2(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) + \ldots[/latex]
Step 3: Integrate over one period
We now need to compute the integral of [latex]|x(t)|^2[/latex] over one period [latex]T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]. Many of the cross-term integrals, like [latex]\int_0^T \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) dt[/latex], will be zero due to the orthogonality property of the cosine functions.
For the terms that do not vanish:
[latex] \int_0^T 1 , dt = T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]

[latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(2\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2} T = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] (using the identity [latex]\cos^2(x) = \frac{1 + \cos(2x)}{2}[/latex])

Similarly, [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(4\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] and [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(6\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}[/latex].

Step 4: Sum up the integrals
After evaluating the integrals and summing them up, the result of the integral is:
[latex] \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = 1 + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7[/latex].

Step 5: Compute the final result
Now, we divide by the period [latex]T = 1] sec:
[latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = \frac{7}{1} = 7[/latex].

Final Answer:
The value of [latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt[/latex] is closest to 7.

Let [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex] be continuous random variables with probability density functions [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{X}}(x)[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{Y}}(y)[/latex], respectively. Further, let [latex]\mathrm{Y}=\mathrm{X}^{2}[/latex] and

[latex] \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{X}}(x)= \begin{cases}1, & x \in (0,1] \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} [/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Given: [latex] Y = X^2 [/latex], and [latex] X \in (0, 1] [/latex] with uniform distribution:
[latex] P_X(x) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] x \in (0, 1] [/latex]

Step 2: Use the change of variable technique for continuous random variables.
If [latex] Y = g(X) = X^2 [/latex], then [latex] X = \sqrt{Y} [/latex] (since [latex] X > 0 [/latex]), and the PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is:
[latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(x) \cdot \left| \frac{dx}{dy} \right| [/latex]
We know [latex] x = \sqrt{y} [/latex], so:
[latex] \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex]
Therefore:
[latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \left| \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \right| = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex]

Step 3: So the correct PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is:
[latex] P_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, & y \in (0, 1] \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex]

Final Answer: (A) [latex] \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]\mathrm{G}(\mathrm{s})=\frac{1}{(\mathrm{s}+1)(\mathrm{s}+2)}[/latex]. Then the closed-loop system shown in the figure below, is
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Open-loop transfer function:
[latex] G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex],
So the forward path becomes:
[latex] K(s-1)G(s) = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex]

Step 2: Closed-loop transfer function (unity feedback):
[latex] T(s) = \frac{K(s-1)G(s)}{1 + K(s-1)G(s)} = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1)} [/latex]

Step 3: Characteristic equation:
[latex] (s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1) = 0 [/latex]
Compute:
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + K(s - 1) = 0 [/latex]
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + Ks - K = 0 [/latex]
[latex] s^2 + (3 + K)s + (2 - K) = 0 [/latex]

Step 4: Apply Routh-Hurwitz criterion:
For a second-order system [latex] s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 [/latex] to be stable, both coefficients must be positive:
[latex] a_1 = 3 + K > 0 \Rightarrow \text{always true for } K > -3 [/latex]
[latex] a_0 = 2 - K > 0 \Rightarrow K < 2 [/latex]

So the system is stable for [latex] K < 2 [/latex], and unstable for [latex] K \geq 2 [/latex].

Final Answer: (B) unstable for all [latex] K \geq 2 [/latex]

raw_source.text: The continuous-time unit impulse signal is applied as an input to a continuous-time linear timeinvariant system [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex]. The output is observed to be the continuous-time unit step signal [latex]u(t)[/latex]. Which one of the following statements is true?
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Given that the output of system [latex] \mathcal{S} [/latex] for an input [latex] \delta(t) [/latex] (unit impulse) is [latex] u(t) [/latex] (unit step),
So, the impulse response of the system is:
[latex] h(t) = u(t) [/latex]

Step 2: A system is Bounded Input Bounded Output (BIBO) stable if its impulse response is absolutely integrable:
[latex] \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |h(t)| dt < \infty [/latex]
Here, [latex] h(t) = u(t) [/latex], so:
[latex] \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |u(t)| dt = \int_{0}^{\infty} 1 , dt = \infty [/latex]
Hence, the system is not BIBO stable.

Step 3: If a system is not BIBO stable, then there exists at least one bounded input that will produce an unbounded output.

Final Answer: (B) It is possible to find a bounded input signal which when applied to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] results in an unbounded output signal.
options: very bounded input signal applied to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] results in a bounded output signal.
It is possible to find a bounded input signal which when applied to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] results in an unbounded output signal.
On applying any input signal to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex], the output signal is always bounded.
On applying any input signal to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] the output signal is always unbounded.

raw_answer.option_text: It is possible to find a bounded input signal which when applied to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] results in an unbounded output signal.

raw_source.text:
The 3-phase modulating waveforms [latex]({v}_{{a}}({t}), {v}_{{b}}({t}) [/latex] and [latex]{v}_{{c}}({t}) )[/latex], used in sinusoidal PWM in a Voltage Source Inverter (VSI) are

Where [latex]\omega=2 \pi \times 40 {rad} / {s}[/latex] is the fundamental frequency. The modulating waveforms are compared with a 10 kHz triangular carrier whose magnitude varies between +1 and -1 . The VSI has a DC link voltage of 600 V and feeds a star connected motor. The per phase fundamental RMS motor voltage, in volts, is closest to

Step 1: The modulation index [latex] m_a [/latex] is defined as:
[latex] m_a = \frac{V_m}{V_{\text{tri}}} [/latex], where [latex] V_m = 0.8 [/latex] (peak of sine) and [latex] V_{\text{tri}} = 1 [/latex] (peak of carrier)
So:
[latex] m_a = 0.8 [/latex]

Step 2: In sinusoidal PWM for a 3-phase VSI, the peak value of fundamental line-to-neutral voltage is:
[latex] V_{an}^{\text{peak}} = m_a \cdot \frac{V_{dc}}{2} = 0.8 \cdot \frac{600}{2} = 240, \text{V} [/latex]

Step 3: Convert peak to RMS for a sine wave:
[latex] V_{an}^{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{an}^{\text{peak}}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{240}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 169.71, \text{V} [/latex]

raw_source.text: An ideal sinusoidal voltage source [latex]\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{t})=230 \sqrt{2} \sin (2 \pi \times 50 \mathrm{t}) \mathrm{V}[/latex] feeds an ideal inductor L through an ideal SCR with firing angle [latex]\alpha=0^{\circ}[/latex]. If [latex]L=100 \mathrm{mH}[/latex], then the peak of the inductor current, in ampere, is closest to
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Given:
[latex] v(t) = 230\sqrt{2} \sin(2\pi \cdot 50 t) [/latex]
[latex] \omega = 2\pi \cdot 50 = 100\pi [/latex]
[latex] L = 100, \text{mH} = 0.1, \text{H} [/latex]
Firing angle [latex] \alpha = 0^\circ [/latex], i.e., conduction starts at [latex] t = 0 [/latex]

Step 2: The current through an inductor is given by:
[latex] i(t) = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^t v(\tau), d\tau = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^t 230\sqrt{2} \sin(100\pi \tau), d\tau [/latex]

Step 3: Integrating:
[latex] i(t) = \frac{230\sqrt{2}}{L \cdot 100\pi} (1 - \cos(100\pi t)) [/latex]
Step 4: The peak of this expression occurs when [latex] \cos(100\pi t) = -1 [/latex]
Then:
[latex] i_{\text{peak}} = \frac{230\sqrt{2}}{0.1 \cdot 100\pi} \cdot (1 - (-1)) = \frac{230\sqrt{2}}{10\pi} \cdot 2 [/latex]
Calculate it:
[latex] i_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2 \cdot 230\sqrt{2}}{10\pi} = \frac{460 \cdot 1.4142}{10\pi} \approx \frac{651}{31.4159} \approx 20.72, \text{A} [/latex]

The circuit breakers open to isolate the line. The fault self-clears. The circuit breakers reclose and restore the line. Which one of the following diagrams best indicates the rotor accelerating and decelerating areas?

raw_source.text: An air filled cylindrical capacitor (capacitance [latex]\mathrm{C}_{0}[/latex] ) of length [latex]L[/latex], with [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] as its inner and outer radii, respectively, consists of two coaxial conducting surfaces. Its cross-sectional view is shown in Fig. (i). In order to increase the capacitance, a dielectric material of relative permittivity [latex]\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}[/latex] is inserted inside [latex]50 \%[/latex] of the annular region as shown in Fig. (ii). The value of [latex]\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}[/latex] for which the capacitance of the capacitor in Fig. (ii), becomes [latex]5 \mathrm{C}_{0}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Capacitance of a cylindrical capacitor
The capacitance of a coaxial cylindrical capacitor filled with dielectric of permittivity [latex] \varepsilon [/latex] is given by:
[latex] C = \frac{2\pi \varepsilon L}{\ln(b/a)} [/latex]
So, for Fig. (i) with air throughout (i.e., permittivity [latex] \varepsilon_0 [/latex]):
[latex] C_0 = \frac{2\pi \varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)} [/latex]

Step 2: For Fig. (ii)
The cross-section is split into two equal parts (in parallel):
One half is filled with air [latex] \varepsilon_0 [/latex]
The other half is filled with dielectric [latex] \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0 [/latex]

Since they are in parallel, total capacitance is:
[latex] C = \frac{1}{2} C_0 + \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_r C_0 = \frac{C_0}{2}(1 + \varepsilon_r) [/latex]

We are given that [latex] C = 5C_0 [/latex]. So:
[latex] \frac{C_0}{2}(1 + \varepsilon_r) = 5C_0 [/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex] C_0 [/latex]:
[latex] \frac{1 + \varepsilon_r}{2} = 5 [/latex]
[latex] 1 + \varepsilon_r = 10 \Rightarrow \varepsilon_r = 9 [/latex]

Final Answer: (C) 9

raw_source.text: Let [latex]{a}_{{R}}[/latex] be the unit radial vector in the spherical co-ordinate system. For which of the following value(s) of [latex]n[/latex], the divergence of the radial vector field [latex]f(R)=a_{R} \frac{1}{R^{n}}[/latex] is independent of [latex]R[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
We use the divergence formula for a purely radial vector field in spherical coordinates:

[latex] \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^n} \mathbf{a}_R \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^n} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^{2-n} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \cdot (2 - n) R^{1 - n} = (2 - n) R^{-1 - n} [/latex]

We want this expression to be independent of [latex] R [/latex], so the power of [latex] R [/latex] must be zero:
[latex] -1 - n = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = -1 [/latex]

So clearly [latex] n = -1 [/latex] is one valid value. Now check another special case:

Case: [latex] n = 2 [/latex]
Try plugging [latex] n = 2 [/latex] directly into the divergence expression:
[latex] \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^2} \mathbf{a}_R \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^2} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} (1) = 0 [/latex]

So the divergence is zero, which is also independent of [latex] R [/latex].

raw_source.text: Consider two coupled circuits, having selfinductances [latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex], that carry non-zero currents [latex]\mathrm{I}_{1}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{I}_{2}[/latex], respectively. The mutual inductance between the circuits is M with unity coupling coefficient. The stored magnetic energy of the coupled circuits is minimum at which of the following value(s) of [latex]\frac{\mathrm{I}_{1}}{\mathrm{I}_{2}}[/latex] ?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{2}^{2}+\mathrm{MI}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{2}[/latex]
[Based on given options it has to be mutally adding only]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial \mathrm{I}_{1}}=0 & \Rightarrow \mathrm{~L}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{1}+\mathrm{MI}_{2}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{I}_{1}}{\mathrm{I}_{2}}=-\frac{\mathrm{M}}{\mathrm{~L}_{1}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{~L}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{1}=-\mathrm{MI}_{2} \\ \frac{\partial \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial \mathrm{I}_{2}}= & \Rightarrow \mathrm{L}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{2}+\mathrm{MI}_{1}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{I}_{1}}{\mathrm{I}_{2}}=-\frac{\mathrm{L}_{2}}{\mathrm{M}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{~L}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{2}=-M I_{1} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Now put both condition's together only [latex]\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}[/latex] is minimum,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}} & =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{2}^{2}+\mathrm{MI}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left[-\mathrm{MI}_{2}\right]_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left[-\mathrm{MI}_{1}\right] \mathrm{I}_{2}+\mathrm{MI}_{1} \mathrm{I}_{2} \\ & =0 \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let [latex](\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}) \in \mathfrak{R}^{2}[/latex]. The rate of change of the real valued function,

[latex]\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})=\mathrm{x}^{2}+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}^{2}+1[/latex]

at the origin in the direction of the point [latex](1,2)[/latex] is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Direction vector and its unit vector
The direction vector from origin to point (1, 2) is:
[latex] \vec{u} = \langle 1, 2 \rangle [/latex]
Magnitude of this vector is:
[latex] |\vec{u}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} [/latex]
Unit vector in the given direction is:
[latex] \hat{u} = \left\langle \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right\rangle [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the gradient of V(x, y)
[latex] \nabla V = \left\langle \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \right\rangle = \left\langle 2x + 1, 2y \right\rangle [/latex]
At the origin (0, 0), the gradient becomes:
[latex] \nabla V(0, 0) = \langle 1, 0 \rangle [/latex]

Step 3: Compute the directional derivative
Directional derivative of V in the direction of unit vector [latex] \hat{u} [/latex] is:
[latex] D_{\hat{u}} V = \nabla V \cdot \hat{u} = \langle 1, 0 \rangle \cdot \left\langle \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} [/latex]
Numerical value:
[latex] \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \approx \frac{1}{2.236} \approx 0.447 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider ordinary differential equations given by

[latex]\dot{x}_{1}({t})=2 {x}_{2}({t}) [/latex]
[latex] \dot{{x}}_{2}({t})={r}({t})[/latex]

with initial conditions [latex]{x}_{1}(0)=1[/latex] and [latex]{x}_{2}(0)=0[/latex].

If [latex]r(t)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}1, & t \geq 0 \\ 0, & t < 0\end{array}\right.[/latex], then at [latex]t=1, x_{1}(t)=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]\frac{{dx}_{1}}{{dt}}=2 {x}_{2} \quad ...(1)[/latex]
[latex]\frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}={r}({t}), \quad {r}({t})=\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: {t} \geq 0 \\ 0: {t} < 0 \end{array}\right.[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}=1[/latex] for [latex]{t} \geq 0 \quad ...(2)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow {x}_{2}={t}+{c} \quad ...(3)[/latex]
Given [latex]x_{2}(0)=0[/latex]
(3) [latex]\Rightarrow 0=0+c \Rightarrow c=0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore {x}_{2}={t}[/latex]
From (1) [latex]\frac{d x_{1}}{d t}=2 t[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow {x}_{1}=\frac{2 {t}^{2}}{2}+{K} \quad ...(4) [/latex]
Given [latex]{x}_{1}(0)=1:(4) \Rightarrow 1=0+{K}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow {K}=1[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] From (4) [latex]{x}_{1}={t}^{2}+1[/latex]
Now [latex]{X}_{1}(1)=1+1=2[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]C[/latex] be a clockwise oriented closed curve in the complex plane defined by [latex]|z|=1[/latex]. Further, let [latex]f(z)=j z[/latex] be a complex function, where [latex]j=\sqrt{-1}[/latex].
Then, [latex]\oint_{{C}} {f}({z}) {dz}=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Express the function
We are given [latex] f(z) = jz [/latex], and we want to compute:
[latex] \oint_C jz , dz [/latex]

Step 2: Use properties of contour integrals
[latex] j = \sqrt{-1} [/latex] is a constant, so it can be pulled out of the integral:
[latex] \oint_C jz , dz = j \oint_C z , dz [/latex]

Step 3: Recall the standard result
For a closed contour [latex] C [/latex] enclosing the origin (like [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]),
[latex] \oint_C z , dz = 0 [/latex] because [latex] z [/latex] is an analytic function inside and on [latex] C [/latex].

Step 4: Apply the result
[latex] \oint_C f(z) , dz = j \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

raw_source.text: The op-amps in the following circuit are ideal. The voltage gain of the circuit is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Recognize the configuration
The circuit consists of two inverting amplifier stages connected in cascade.
Step 2: Analyze the first op-amp
For an inverting amplifier, the gain is:
[latex] A_{v1} = -\frac{R_f}{R_{in}} [/latex]
From the diagram:
Input resistor: [latex] R_{in1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex]
Feedback resistor: [latex] R_{f1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex]
So,
[latex] A_{v1} = -\frac{10}{10} = -1 [/latex]
Step 3: Analyze the second op-amp
This stage is also an inverting amplifier:
Input resistor: [latex] R_{in2} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex]
Feedback resistor: [latex] R_{f2} = 20\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex] (notice the input is tapped from the junction between two 10 kΩ resistors in series, so it's effectively 10 kΩ from input and 10 kΩ in feedback, making total feedback resistance = 10k + 10k = 20k)
So,
[latex] A_{v2} = -\frac{20}{10} = -2 [/latex]
Step 4: Total Gain
Overall voltage gain is:
[latex] A_v = A_{v1} \cdot A_{v2} = (-1) \cdot (-2) = 2 [/latex]
Final Answer: 2

raw_source.text: In an experiment to measure the active power drawn by a single-phase RL Load connected to an AC source through a [latex]2 \Omega[/latex] resistor, three voltmeters are connected as shown in the figure below. The voltmeter readings are as follows: [latex]\mathrm{V}_{\text {source }}=200 \mathrm{~V}, \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{R}}=9 \mathrm{~V}, \mathrm{~V}_{\text {Load }}=199 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]. Assuming perfect resistors and ideal voltmeters, the Loadactive power measured in this experiment, in W, is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Here [latex]|\mathrm{I}|=\frac{\left|\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}\right|}{2}=\frac{9}{2}=4.5 \mathrm{~A}[\mathrm{RMS}][/latex]


From resultant of vectors's formulae [latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{V}_{\text {source }} & =\sqrt{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}+\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{Load}}^{2}+2 \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{R}} \cdot \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{Load}} \cos \phi_{\mathrm{L}}} \\ 200 & =\sqrt{9^{2}+199^{2}+2(9)(199) \cos \phi_{\mathrm{L}}} \\ \cos \phi_{\mathrm{L}} & =\frac{(200)^{2}-9^{2}-199^{2}}{2(9)(199)}=\frac{318}{3582}=0.08877(\mathrm{lag}) \\ \mathrm{P} & =\left|\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{Load}}\right| \mathrm{I} \mid \cos \phi_{\mathrm{L}} \\ & =|199|\left|\frac{9}{2}\right|(0.08877) \\ \mathrm{P} & =79.5 \mathrm{~W} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The steady state capacitor current of a conventional DC-DC buck converter, working in CCM, is shown in one switching cycle. If the input voltage is 30 V , the value of the inductor used, in mH, is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{S}}=30 \mathrm{~V}, \mathrm{~L}=?[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{D}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{ON}}}{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{30 \times 10^{-6}}{\left(\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{ON}}+\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{OFF}}\right)}=\frac{30 \times 10^{-6}}{50 \times 10^{-6}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An ideal low pass filter has frequency response given by

[latex] H(j \omega)= \begin{cases}1, & |\omega| \leq 200 \pi \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} [/latex]

Let [latex]h(t)[/latex] be its time domain representation. Then [latex]h(0)=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Frequency response
[latex] H(j\omega) = \begin{cases} 1, & |\omega| \leq 200\pi \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex]
Step 2: Find impulse response [latex] h(t) [/latex] by inverse Fourier transform
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} H(j\omega) e^{j\omega t} d\omega [/latex]
But since [latex] H(j\omega) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] |\omega| \leq 200\pi [/latex], and 0 otherwise:
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-200\pi}^{200\pi} e^{j\omega t} d\omega [/latex]
Step 3: Evaluate the integral
This is a standard Fourier inverse transform result:
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{2 \sin(200\pi t)}{t} = \frac{200 \sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} [/latex]
This is the sinc function scaled:
[latex] h(t) = 200 \cdot \text{sinc}(200 t) [/latex] where [latex] \text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x} [/latex]
Step 4: Find [latex] h(0) [/latex]
Use the standard limit:
[latex] \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} = 200 [/latex]
So:
[latex] h(0) = \frac{200 \sin(0)}{\pi \cdot 0} = 200 [/latex]
Final Answer: 200

raw_source.text:
Consider the state-space model

[latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{x}({t}) & ={Ax}({t})+{Br}({t}) \\ {y}({t}) & ={Cx}({t}) \end{aligned} [/latex]

Where [latex]{x}({t}), {r}({t}), {y}({t})[/latex] are the state, input and output, respectively. The matrices [latex]{A}, {B}, {C}[/latex] are given below

[latex] A=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{array}\right], {B}=\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], {C}=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \end{array}\right] [/latex]

The sum of the magnitudes of the poles is ________ (round off to nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Write the state matrix
[latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Step 2: Find the characteristic equation
We compute the determinant of [latex] sI - A [/latex]:
[latex] \det(sI - A) = \left| \begin{array}{cc} s & -1 \ 2 & s + 3 \end{array} \right| = s(s + 3) - (-2)(1) = s^2 + 3s + 2 [/latex]

Step 3: Find the roots of the characteristic equation
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 = 0 [/latex]
Factorizing:
[latex] (s + 1)(s + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow s = -1, -2 [/latex]

Step 4: Compute the sum of the magnitudes of the poles
[latex] |{-1}| + |{-2}| = 1 + 2 = 3 [/latex]

raw_source.text: Using shunt capacitors, the power factor of a 3-phase, 4 kV induction motor (drawing 390 kVA at 0.77 pf lag ) is to be corrected to 0.85 pf lag. The line current of the capacitor bank, in A, is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Line voltage of motor: [latex] V_L = 4000\ \text{V} [/latex]
Apparent power: [latex] S = 390\ \text{kVA} [/latex]
Initial power factor: [latex] \cos\phi_1 = 0.77\ (\text{lagging}) [/latex]
Target power factor: [latex] \cos\phi_2 = 0.85\ (\text{lagging}) [/latex]

Step 1: Compute the active power (real power)
[latex] P = S \cdot \cos\phi_1 = 390 \cdot 0.77 = 300.3\ \text{kW} [/latex]

Step 2: Compute reactive power before correction
[latex] Q_1 = \sqrt{S^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{390^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{152100 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{61919.91} \approx 248.8\ \text{kVAR} [/latex]

Step 3: Compute reactive power after correction
New apparent power [latex] S_2 = \frac{P}{\cos\phi_2} = \frac{300.3}{0.85} \approx 353.3\ \text{kVA} [/latex]
[latex] Q_2 = \sqrt{S_2^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{353.3^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{124821.89 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{34641.8} \approx 186.0\ \text{kVAR} [/latex]

Step 4: Required reactive power by capacitor bank
[latex] Q_c = Q_1 - Q_2 = 248.8 - 186.0 = 62.8\ \text{kVAR} [/latex]

Step 5: Convert to line current
In a 3-phase system, reactive power is:
[latex] Q = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \Rightarrow I_L = \frac{Q}{\sqrt{3} V_L} [/latex]
[latex] I_L = \frac{62.8 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \cdot 4000} = \frac{62800}{6928.2} \approx 9.1\ \text{A} [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{9.1\ \text{A}} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Two units, rated at 100 MW and 150 MW , are enabled for economic load dispatch. When the overall incremental cost is 10,000 Rs./MWh, the units are dispatched to 50 MW and 80 MW respectively. At an overall incremental cost of [latex]10,600 \mathrm{Rs} . / \mathrm{MWh}[/latex], the power output of the units are 80 MW and 92 MW , respectively. The total plant MW-output (without overloading any unit) at an overall incremental cost of 11,800 Rs./MWh is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Let’s define:
Unit 1 outputs: At 10,000 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_1 = 50\ \text{MW} [/latex] At 10,600 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_1 = 80\ \text{MW} [/latex]

Unit 2 outputs: At 10,000 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_2 = 80\ \text{MW} [/latex] At 10,600 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_2 = 92\ \text{MW} [/latex]

We are to find outputs at 11,800 Rs./MWh using extrapolation for both units (assuming linearity of power vs incremental cost curve).

Step 1: Find slope of output with respect to cost for each unit
Unit 1 slope: [latex] \frac{80 - 50}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{30}{600} = 0.05\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh} [/latex]
Unit 2 slope: [latex] \frac{92 - 80}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{12}{600} = 0.02\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh} [/latex]

Step 2: Extrapolate to 11,800 Rs./MWh
Cost increase: [latex] 11,800 - 10,600 = 1,200\ \text{Rs./MWh} [/latex]

Unit 1 output: [latex] P_1 = 80 + (0.05)(1200) = 80 + 60 = 140\ \text{MW} [/latex] (but Unit 1 is rated for 100 MW max ⇒ limit to 100 MW)
Unit 2 output: [latex] P_2 = 92 + (0.02)(1200) = 92 + 24 = 116\ \text{MW} [/latex] (but Unit 2 is rated for 150 MW ⇒ no limit hit)

Step 3: Total Output
[latex] P_{\text{total}} = 100 + 116 = \boxed{216\ \text{MW}} [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{216} [/latex]

raw_source.text: A controller [latex]D(s)[/latex] of the form [latex]\left(1+K_{D} s\right)[/latex] is to be designed for the plant [latex]G(s)=\frac{1000 \sqrt{2}}{s(s+10)^{2}}[/latex] as shown in the figure. The value of [latex]\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}}[/latex] that yields a phase margin of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] at the gain cross-over frequency of [latex]10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex] is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Given phase margin [P.M] [latex]=45^{\circ}[/latex] at gain cross over frequency [latex]\left[\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}\right]=10[/latex]
O.L.T.F with controller [latex]=\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{s})=\mathrm{D}(\mathrm{s}) . \mathrm{G}(\mathrm{s})[/latex]
[latex] \begin{gathered} \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{~s})=\frac{\left[1+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} \mathrm{~S}\right] \times 1000 \sqrt{2}}{\mathrm{~s}[\mathrm{~s}+10]^{2}} \\ \text { P.M }=180^{\circ}+\left.\angle \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{~s})\right|_{\omega=\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}} \\ \text { Given P.M }=45^{\circ} \text { at } \omega_{\mathrm{gc}}=10 \\ 45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle \frac{1000 \sqrt{2}\left[1+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} \mathrm{~s}\right.}{} \mathrm{s}[\mathrm{~s}+10]^{2} \\ 45^{\circ}=\left[180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{gc}} \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}}{1}\right]-2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}=10}{10}\right)\right]_{\mathrm{\omega gc}}=10 \\ 45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]-2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{10}{10}\right) \\ 45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]-2 \times 45^{\circ} \\ \tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]=45^{\circ} \\ 10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}={\tan 45^{\circ}=1}\\{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.1} \end{gathered} [/latex]

The relationship between two variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is given by [latex]x + py + q = 0[/latex] and is shown in the figure. Find the values of [latex]p[/latex] and [latex]q[/latex].
Note: The figure shown is representative. ]
raw_source.solution:
The equation is of the form: [latex]x + py + q = 0[/latex]
Rewriting it in slope-intercept form:
[latex]py = -x - q[/latex]
[latex]y = -\frac{1}{p}x - \frac{q}{p}[/latex]
This is of the form [latex]y = mx + c[/latex] where slope [latex]m = -\frac{1}{p}[/latex] and intercept [latex]c = -\frac{q}{p}[/latex]

From the figure:
The y-intercept is [latex]c = 4[/latex] (line passes through point (0, 4))
The line passes through another point (2, 8), so slope is:
[latex]m = \frac{8 - 4}{2 - 0} = \frac{4}{2} = 2[/latex]

Equating this with [latex]-\frac{1}{p}[/latex],
[latex]-\frac{1}{p} = 2 \Rightarrow p = -\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

Now use y-intercept formula: [latex]-\frac{q}{p} = 4[/latex]
Substitute [latex]p = -\frac{1}{2}[/latex]:
[latex]-\frac{q}{-\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \Rightarrow \frac{q}{\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \Rightarrow q = 2[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]p = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad q = 2[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Spheres of unit diameter are centered at ( [latex]l, {m}, {n}[/latex] ) where [latex]l, {m}[/latex], and [latex]n [/latex] take every possible integer values.
The distance between two spheres is computed from the center of one sphere to the center of the other sphere. For a given sphere, [latex]x [/latex] is the distance to its nearest sphere and [latex]y [/latex] is the distance to its next nearest sphere. The value of [latex]\frac{y}{x}[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution:
Spheres are centered at all points [latex](l, m, n)[/latex] where [latex]l, m, n \in \mathbb{Z}[/latex] (i.e., all integer coordinates).
That means the spheres are placed in a cubic lattice with unit spacing between centers.

Step 1: Nearest sphere distance [latex]x[/latex]
Each sphere has 6 immediate neighbors at a distance of 1 unit along the directions [latex]\pm x[/latex], [latex]\pm y[/latex], and [latex]\pm z[/latex].
So, [latex]x = 1[/latex]

Step 2: Next nearest sphere distance [latex]y[/latex]
The next nearest neighbors are along the diagonals of the faces (e.g., from (0,0,0) to (1,1,0)).
Their distance is:
[latex]y = \sqrt{(1)^2 + (1)^2} = \sqrt{2}[/latex]

Step 3: Compute [latex]\frac{y}{x}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{y}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} = \sqrt{2}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\sqrt{2}}[/latex]

In the triangle PQR, the lengths of PT and TR are in the ratio of [latex]3: 2[/latex].
ST is parallel to QR. Two semicircles are drawn with PS and PQ as diameters, as shown in the figure.
Which one of the following statements is true about the shaded area PQS?
Note: The figure shown is representative.
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Let us assume PQ = 5 units
Given the ratio [latex]PT : TR = 3 : 2[/latex], then [latex]PT = 3[/latex] units and [latex]TR = 2[/latex] units, so total [latex]PR = PT + TR = 5[/latex] units.
Since [latex]ST \parallel QR[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex] lies on [latex]PR[/latex], by Basic Proportionality Theorem:
[latex]\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{PT}{PR} = \frac{3}{5}[/latex]
So, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} \cdot PQ[/latex]

Step 2: Area of semicircle is proportional to square of diameter
Let the diameter [latex]PQ = d[/latex].
Then the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PQ[/latex] is:
[latex]A_{PQ} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8}[/latex]

Now, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} d[/latex], so area of semicircle on PS:
[latex]A_{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi (3d/5)^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8} \cdot \frac{9}{25} = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}[/latex]

Step 3: Shaded Area = Area of semicircle on PQ − Area of semicircle on PS
[latex]A_{\text{shaded}} = A_{PQ} - A_{PS} = A_{PQ} \left(1 - \frac{9}{25}\right) = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}[/latex]

Now convert the shaded area as a multiple of the semicircle on PS:
[latex]\frac{A_{\text{shaded}}}{A_{PS}} = \frac{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}}{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{16}{9}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\frac{16}{9}}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PS[/latex]
options: The shaded area is [latex]\frac{16}{9}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is equal to the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is [latex]\frac{14}{9}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is [latex]\frac{14}{25}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PQ.

raw_answer.option_text: The shaded area is [latex]\frac{16}{9}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
