A positive point charge with velocity [latex]\vec{v} = 5\hat{x}[/latex] enters a region having electric field [latex]\vec{E} = 4\hat{y}[/latex] and magnetic field [latex]\vec{B} = -6\hat{z}[/latex].

Force is along [latex]\hat{y}[/latex] = along [latex]\vec{E}[/latex], and [latex]\hat{y} \perp \hat{z}[/latex] (perpendicular to [latex]\vec{B}[/latex]).

The force will be along the electric field but perpendicular to the magnetic field
The force will be perpendicular to both electric and magnetic field

raw_source.text:
Consider a power system with [latex]N[/latex] buses, of which [latex]P[/latex] are generator buses and the remaining [latex]Q[/latex] are load buses (where there is no generation).

Assume that there are no reactive power-limit violations at the generator buses.

What is the size of the Jacobian matrix in the Newton-Raphson load flow method?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
A power system has [latex]N[/latex] buses, of which:
[latex]P[/latex] are generator buses (including the slack bus)
[latex]Q[/latex] are load (PQ) buses

Hence, [latex] N=P+Q [/latex]

Step 1: Count the unknown voltage angles
In the Newton-Raphson load flow method, the voltage angle of the slack bus is known.
Therefore, voltage angles of all remaining buses are unknown. [latex] \text{Number of angle unknowns}=N-1 [/latex]

Step 2: Count the unknown voltage magnitudes
Voltage magnitudes are known at generator (PV) buses and at the slack bus.
They are unknown only at PQ buses. Therefore, [latex] \text{Number of magnitude unknowns}=Q [/latex]

Step 3: Total number of unknowns
[latex] (N-1)+Q [/latex]
Using [latex]Q=N-P[/latex],
[latex] (N-1)+(N-P) = 2N-1-P [/latex]

Step 4: Size of the Jacobian matrix
The Jacobian matrix is a square matrix whose order equals the total number of unknown variables.
Hence, [latex] \text{Jacobian Size} = (2N-1-P)\times(2N-1-P) [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The initial three-phase voltage phasors [latex](\bar{V}_A,\ \bar{V}_B,\ \bar{V}_C)[/latex] at a bus of a power network are as shown in Case-1. Due to a disturbance, the bus voltage phasors changed in phase by a small angle [latex]\Delta\theta[/latex], and the magnitudes remained the same as depicted in Case-2.



Which one of the following statements is correct about the zero sequence components?
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
The zero-sequence component of a three-phase set is [latex] V_0=\frac{V_A+V_B+V_C}{3} [/latex]

Case-1:
The phase voltages are [latex] V_A=V_A\angle\theta_A,\qquad V_B=V_B\angle\theta_B,\qquad V_C=V_C\angle\theta_C [/latex]
Therefore,
[latex] V_{0,1} = \frac{V_A\angle\theta_A+V_B\angle\theta_B+V_C\angle\theta_C}{3} [/latex]

Case-2:
Each phasor is rotated by the same angle [latex]\Delta\theta[/latex], while its magnitude remains unchanged.
Hence,
[latex] V_A'=V_A\angle(\theta_A+\Delta\theta) [/latex]
[latex] V_B'=V_B\angle(\theta_B+\Delta\theta) [/latex]
[latex] V_C'=V_C\angle(\theta_C+\Delta\theta) [/latex]
The new zero-sequence component is [latex] V_{0,2} = \frac{V_A'+V_B'+V_C'}{3} [/latex]
Substituting, [latex] V_{0,2} = \frac{ V_A\angle(\theta_A+\Delta\theta) + V_B\angle(\theta_B+\Delta\theta) + V_C\angle(\theta_C+\Delta\theta) }{3} [/latex]
Factoring out [latex]e^{j\Delta\theta}[/latex],
[latex] V_{0,2} = e^{j\Delta\theta} \frac{ V_A\angle\theta_A + V_B\angle\theta_B + V_C\angle\theta_C }{3} [/latex]
[latex] V_{0,2} = e^{j\Delta\theta}V_{0,1} [/latex]

Observation:
Multiplication by [latex]e^{j\Delta\theta}[/latex] rotates a phasor by [latex]\Delta\theta[/latex] but does not change its magnitude.
Therefore,
[latex] |V_{0,2}|=|V_{0,1}| [/latex] and [latex] \angle V_{0,2} = \angle V_{0,1} + \Delta\theta [/latex]

Hence, the zero-sequence components in the two cases have the same magnitude but different phase angles.
options: The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same phase angle and magnitude
The magnitude of the zero sequence component in Case-1 is greater than that in Case-2
The magnitude of the zero sequence component in Case-2 is greater than that in Case-1
The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same magnitude but different phase angles

raw_answer.option_text: The zero sequence components in Case-1 and Case-2 have the same magnitude but different phase angles

raw_source.text:
A certain application requires power at a frequency of 16.67 Hz, while the available grid frequency is 50 Hz. A 3-phase synchronous motor connected to the 50 Hz, 3-phase grid, driving a synchronous generator, is used for this application.

Which one of the following combinations is a suitable choice for the number of poles in the motor and generator, respectively?
raw_source.solution:
Synchronous speed formula: [latex]N_s = \dfrac{120f}{P}[/latex]

Motor on 50 Hz grid with [latex]P_m = 6[/latex] poles:
[latex]N_s = \dfrac{120 \times 50}{6} = 1000[/latex] rpm

Generator must produce 16.67 Hz at 1000 rpm:
[latex]f_g = \dfrac{P_g \times N_s}{120} = 16.67[/latex]
[latex]P_g = \dfrac{16.67 \times 120}{1000} = 2[/latex] poles

Shortcut: Since
[latex] \dfrac{f_m}{f_g} = \dfrac{50}{16.67} \approx 3 [/latex] and both machines run at the same speed, [latex] \dfrac{P_m}{P_g}=3 [/latex]
So simply choose the option where the motor poles : generator poles = 3 : 1.

raw_source.text: Which one of the following options is correct regarding the typical double-squirrel-cage structure used in induction motors?
raw_source.solution:
Concept of Double-Squirrel-Cage Induction Motor

A double-squirrel-cage rotor consists of two cages:
1. Outer cage
- High resistance
- Low reactance

2. Inner cage
- Low resistance
- High reactance

At starting:
The slip is [latex] s=1 [/latex]. Therefore, rotor frequency is maximum, and rotor reactance becomes significant. Since the inner cage has high reactance, its impedance is large:
[latex] Z_{\text{inner}} = R_{\text{inner}} + jX_{\text{inner}} [/latex] with [latex] X_{\text{inner}} \gg X_{\text{outer}} [/latex]
Hence, most of the rotor current flows through the outer cage, which has lower impedance. The high resistance of the outer cage provides a high starting torque.

At rated speed:
The slip is very small. Hence rotor frequency is low and rotor reactance becomes negligible. Current distribution is then determined mainly by resistance. Since [latex] R_{\text{inner}} < R_{\text{outer}} [/latex] most of the rotor current flows through the inner cage. Thus the motor behaves like a low-resistance rotor during normal operation, giving good efficiency.

The purpose is actually to obtain high effective rotor resistance at starting and low effective rotor resistance during normal running.
options: At starting, a larger portion of the rotor current flows in the outer cage
At starting, a larger portion of the rotor current flows in the inner cage
At rated speed, most of the rotor current flows in the outer cage
The purpose of the double-squirrel-cage structure is to lower the effective rotor resistance at starting

raw_answer.option_text: At starting, a larger portion of the rotor current flows in the outer cage

raw_source.text:
The figure shows the single-line diagram of a synchronous generator delivering [latex]P = 50[/latex] MW of power at unity power factor to an infinite bus.



[latex]I_s[/latex] denotes the stator current phasor. If the field excitation is increased, which one of the following options correctly describes its effect on the stator current, power factor, and load angle of the machine?
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
A synchronous generator connected to an infinite bus operates with: [latex] P=\frac{EV}{X_s}\sin\delta [/latex] where [latex] E [/latex] = internal generated emf, [latex] V [/latex] = infinite-bus voltage, [latex] X_s [/latex] = synchronous reactance, [latex] \delta [/latex] = load angle.

Step 1: What happens when field excitation is increased?
Increasing field current increases the internal emf [latex] E [/latex] of the generator.

Step 2: Real power remains unchanged
The mechanical input power is unchanged, and the generator is delivering [latex] P=50\ \text{MW} [/latex] to an infinite bus. Hence, [latex] P=\dfrac{EV}{X_s}\sin\delta [/latex] must remain constant. Since [latex] E [/latex] increases, the quantity [latex] \sin\delta [/latex] must decrease. Therefore, [latex] \delta [/latex] decreases.

Step 3: Effect on reactive power and power factor
Initially, the generator operates at unity power factor.
When excitation is increased, the generator becomes over-excited and supplies reactive power to the system.
Thus the stator current leads the terminal voltage.
Hence the power factor becomes leading.

Step 4: Effect on stator current magnitude
Initially, [latex] I_s [/latex] is in phase with [latex] V [/latex] (unity power factor).
After over-excitation: Real power component of current remains essentially unchanged. A leading reactive current component appears.
Therefore, [latex] |I_s| = \sqrt{I_P^2+I_Q^2} [/latex] increases. So the stator current magnitude increases.
options: Stator current increases, power factor becomes lagging, load angle remains the same
Stator current decreases, power factor becomes leading, load angle remains the same
Stator current increases, power factor becomes lagging, load angle decreases
Stator current increases, power factor becomes leading, load angle increases

raw_answer.option_text: Stator current increases, power factor becomes lagging, load angle decreases

raw_source.text:
A circuit with ideal elements is shown.



Which one of the following options correctly identifies all the linear elements in the circuit?
raw_source.solution:
Linear elements obey superposition and have linear V-I relationships:

R: [latex]V = IR \rightarrow[/latex] Linear

L: [latex]V = L\dfrac{di}{dt} \rightarrow[/latex] Linear

C: [latex]I = C\dfrac{dV}{dt} \rightarrow[/latex] Linear

D (Diode): Nonlinear V-I characteristic (exponential/piecewise) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Nonlinear

raw_source.text: For the circuit shown, which one of the following options correctly identifies the Thevenin's equivalent parameters between nodes Y and Z?
raw_source.solution:
The circuit between Y and Z contains dependent voltage sources.

Open-circuit voltage:
The dependent sources (100 V and 20 V controlled sources, with 20 V independent source) combine to give:
[latex]V_{TH} = 100 + 20 + 20 = 140[/latex] V (superposition of all voltage sources in the branch)

Thevenin resistance:
Ideal dependent voltage sources have zero internal impedance [latex] \rightarrow R_{TH} = 0\ \Omega[/latex]

Answer: (B) [latex]V_{TH} = 140[/latex] V, [latex]R_{TH} = 0\ \Omega[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Refer to the four circuits shown:



Which one of the following options for [latex]k_1, k_2, k_3[/latex], and [latex]k_4[/latex] makes all of them realizable?
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
A dependent source is realizable only if it does not violate KVL or KCL.
For an ideal loop of voltage sources, KVL must be satisfied.
For an ideal cut-set of current sources, KCL must be satisfied.
We examine each circuit separately.

Circuit-1: Voltage source controlling a voltage source
The two voltage sources are connected in parallel. Hence, [latex] V_X=V_D [/latex] But, [latex] V_X=k_1V_D [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] k_1V_D=V_D [/latex]
For any value of [latex]V_D[/latex], [latex] \boxed{k_1=1} [/latex]

Circuit-2: Voltage source controlling a current source
An ideal voltage source is connected in parallel with an ideal current source. There is no contradiction. The voltage source fixes the voltage, while the current source fixes the current.
Hence, [latex] \boxed{k_2\text{ can have any value}} [/latex]

Circuit-3: Current source controlling a voltage source
An ideal current source is connected in parallel with an ideal voltage source. Again, there is no contradiction. The current source fixes the current, while the voltage source fixes the voltage.
Hence, [latex] \boxed{k_3\text{ can have any value}} [/latex]

Circuit-4: Current source controlling a current source
The two current sources are connected in parallel.
Applying KCL, [latex] I_D+I_X=0 [/latex]
Given, [latex] I_X=3k_4I_D [/latex]
Substituting,
[latex] I_D+3k_4I_DI=0 [/latex]
[latex] (1+3k_4)I_D=0 [/latex]
For all values of [latex]I_D[/latex], [latex] 1+3k_4=0 [/latex]
[latex] \boxed{k_4=-\frac13} [/latex]

Comparing with the options:
Only Option (A) satisfies [latex] k_1=1, k_4=-\frac13 [/latex] while [latex]k_2[/latex] and [latex]k_3[/latex] can be arbitrary.
raw_source.tag2: Two Port Network and Network Functions
options: [latex]k_1 = 1,\ k_4 = -1/3[/latex], for all values of [latex]k_2[/latex] and [latex]k_3[/latex]
[latex]k_2 = -2,\ k_3 = +1/3[/latex], for all values of [latex]k_1[/latex] and [latex]k_4[/latex]

raw_answer.option_text: [latex]k_1 = 1,\ k_4 = -1/3[/latex], for all values of [latex]k_2[/latex] and [latex]k_3[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A single-phase voltage source [latex]v_s = 325\sin(2\pi 50t)[/latex] V delivers a current,
[latex]i = 12\sin(2\pi 50t) + 9\sin(2\pi 150t)[/latex] A to a load.

The load power factor, correct up to two decimal places, is:
raw_source.solution:
Voltage is purely at 50 Hz -> only the 50 Hz current component contributes to real power.

Real power:
[latex]P = \dfrac{1}{2} V_m I_{m1} \cos\phi = \dfrac{1}{2}(325)(12)(1) = 1950[/latex] W

RMS values:
[latex]V_{rms} = \dfrac{325}{\sqrt{2}}[/latex]
[latex]I_{rms} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{144+81}{2}} = \sqrt{112.5} \approx 10.607[/latex] A

Apparent power:
[latex]S = V_{rms} \times I_{rms} = \dfrac{325}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10.607 = 2437.5[/latex] VA

Power factor:
[latex]PF = \dfrac{P}{S} = \dfrac{1950}{2437.5} = 0.80[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The figure shows a straight-line approximation for the forward characteristics of a power diode. A continuous on-state current of 15 A is flowing through the diode.



What is the power loss in the diode?
raw_source.solution:
From the straight-line approximation:

Threshold voltage: [latex]V_T = 1.0[/latex] V

Dynamic resistance:
[latex]r_d = \dfrac{1.8 - 1.0}{50} = \dfrac{0.8}{50} = 0.016\ \Omega[/latex]

On-state voltage at 15 A:
[latex]V_{on} = V_T + r_d \times I = 1.0 + 0.016 \times 15 = 1.0 + 0.24 = 1.24[/latex] V

Power loss:
[latex]P = V_{on} \times I = 1.24 \times 15 = 18.6[/latex] W
raw_source.tag2: Power Semiconductor Devices and Commutation Techniques

raw_source.text:
Consider the circuit shown in Figure (a). A gate pulse [latex]v_g[/latex] is applied between time instants [latex]t_0[/latex] and [latex]t_1[/latex]. After [latex]t_1[/latex], during the MOSFET turn OFF process, it experiences a voltage overshoot.



Based on the [latex]v_{ds}[/latex] waveforms shown in Figure (b), which one of the following options is correct?
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
When the MOSFET is turned OFF at time [latex]t_1[/latex], the inductor current cannot change instantaneously. As a result, the drain-source voltage [latex]v_{ds}[/latex] exhibits an overshoot followed by oscillations due to the interaction of the circuit's parasitic inductance and capacitance.

Effect of gate resistance:
The gate resistance [latex]R_g[/latex] controls the switching speed of the MOSFET.
  • A smaller [latex]R_g[/latex] results in faster switching, higher [latex]dv/dt[/latex], and larger voltage overshoot.
  • A larger [latex]R_g[/latex] slows down the switching transition, reducing the overshoot.

From the waveforms in Figure (b):
  • The waveform with the largest overshoot corresponds to [latex]R_g=R_1[/latex].
  • The waveform with the intermediate overshoot corresponds to [latex]R_g=R_3[/latex].
  • The waveform with the smallest overshoot corresponds to [latex]R_g=R_2[/latex].
Hence, [latex] R_1>R_3>R_2 [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Power Semiconductor Devices and Commutation Techniques

raw_source.text:
The asymptotic Bode magnitude plot of a system is shown.



Which one of the following options best represents the transfer function of the system?
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
The slope of the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot helps identify the poles and zeros of the transfer function.

Step 1: Observe the low-frequency behavior
The magnitude plot has a slope of [latex] -20\ \text{dB/decade} [/latex] for frequencies below [latex] \omega_0. [/latex] A slope of [latex]-20\ \text{dB/decade}[/latex] indicates the presence of a pole at the origin. Thus, the transfer function contains the factor [latex] \frac{1}{s/\omega_0}. [/latex]

Step 2: Observe the break frequency
At [latex] \omega=\omega_0, [/latex] the slope changes from [latex] -20\ \text{dB/decade} \] to [latex] 0\ \text{dB/decade}. [/latex] A change in slope of [latex] +20\ \text{dB/decade} [/latex] indicates the presence of a zero at [latex] \omega=\omega_0. [/latex] Hence, the transfer function also contains the factor [latex] 1+\frac{s}{\omega_0}. [/latex]

Step 3: Form the transfer function
Combining the pole at the origin and the zero at [latex] \omega_0, [/latex] we obtain [latex] G(s) = \frac{1+\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}} {\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}}. [/latex]

Verification:
For [latex] \omega \ll \omega_0, [/latex] [latex] G(j\omega)\approx\frac{1}{j\omega/\omega_0}, [/latex] which gives a slope of [latex] -20\ \text{dB/decade}. [/latex] For [latex] \omega \gg \omega_0, [/latex] [latex] G(j\omega)\approx \frac{j\omega/\omega_0}{j\omega/\omega_0}=1, [/latex] so the magnitude becomes [latex] 0\ \text{dB}, [/latex] which matches the given Bode plot.

Therefore, the correct transfer function is [latex] \boxed{G(s)=\frac{1+\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}}{\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}}} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrices [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] have a common eigenvalue [latex]2[/latex], and the same corresponding nonzero eigenvector.

Which of the following options is/are correct?

(Note: [latex]I[/latex] is the [latex]n \times n[/latex] identity matrix.)
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]\vec{v}[/latex] be the common eigenvector with [latex]A\vec{v} = 2\vec{v}[/latex] and [latex]B\vec{v} = 2\vec{v}[/latex].

(A) 2 is eigenvalue of [latex]A \rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\det(A-2I) = 0[/latex]

(B) 2 is eigenvalue of [latex]B \rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\det(B-2I) = 0[/latex]

(C) [latex](A+B)\vec{v} = 4\vec{v} \neq 2\vec{v}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow \vec{v}[/latex] is not null vector of [latex](A+B-2I)\rightarrow[/latex] not necessarily 0

(D) [latex](A+B)\vec{v} = 4\vec{v}\rightarrow[/latex] 4 is eigenvalue of [latex](A+B)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow \det(A+B-4I) = 0[/latex]

Answer: (A), (B), (D)

raw_source.text:
A 220V/12V single-phase transformer is designed for use in India and rated 100 VA at 50 Hz. Later, this unit is shipped to the USA where it is used as a 110V/6V transformer at 60 Hz.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
Given:
Transformer rating:
  • India: [latex]220/12\text{ V},\ 50\text{ Hz},\ 100\text{ VA}[/latex]
  • USA: [latex]110/6\text{ V},\ 60\text{ Hz}[/latex]
Since both the primary and secondary voltages are reduced by half, the turns ratio remains unchanged.

Step 1: Compare the peak flux density
The maximum flux in a transformer is given by [latex] E=4.44fN\phi_{\max} [/latex] Hence, [latex] \phi_{\max}\propto\frac{V}{f} [/latex]
For India, [latex] \frac{V}{f} = \frac{220}{50} = 4.4 [/latex]
For the USA, [latex] \frac{V}{f} = \frac{110}{60} = 1.833 [/latex]
Thus, [latex] \phi_{\max,\text{USA}} < \phi_{\max,\text{India}} [/latex]
Therefore, the peak magnetic flux density is lower in the USA.
Hence, (C) is incorrect.

Step 2: No-load current
The no-load current mainly consists of the magnetizing current, which is proportional to the core flux.
Since the flux is lower in the USA, [latex] I_{0,\text{USA}} < I_{0,\text{India}} [/latex]
Therefore, (A) is correct.

Step 3: Copper losses
Copper loss is [latex] P_{cu}=I^2R. [/latex]
The statement specifies the same load current. Since the winding resistance remains unchanged, [latex] P_{cu,\text{USA}} = P_{cu,\text{India}}. [/latex] Thus, the losses are not higher in the USA.
Hence, (B) is incorrect.

Step 4: Eddy current loss
Eddy current loss is proportional to [latex] P_e\propto B_{\max}^2f^2. [/latex] Since [latex] B_{\max}\propto\frac{V}{f}, [/latex] [latex] P_e \propto \left(\frac{V}{f}\right)^2f^2 = V^2. [/latex]
Therefore,
[latex] \frac{P_{e,\text{USA}}}{P_{e,\text{India}}} = \left(\frac{110}{220}\right)^2 = \frac14. [/latex]
Thus, [latex] P_{e,\text{USA}} = 25\% \text{ of } P_{e,\text{India}}. [/latex]
The eddy current loss is approximately 75% lower, not 44% higher.
Hence, (D) is incorrect.
options: No-load current drawn would be smaller for operation in the USA compared to that in India
For the same load current, the losses would be higher in the USA compared to that in India
The peak magnetic flux density in the core would be higher while operating in the USA compared to that in India
The eddy current losses in the core would be approximately 44% higher while operating in the USA compared to that in India

raw_answer.option_text: No-load current drawn would be smaller for operation in the USA compared to that in India

raw_source.text:
Given that [latex]\vec{F}(x,y,z) = \sin(y)\,\hat{x} + \cos(x)\,\hat{y} + 5\,\hat{z}[/latex], the integral

[latex]\oiint_S \vec{F}(x,y,z) \cdot d\vec{s}[/latex]

over the unit sphere [latex]S[/latex] centered at the origin evaluates to ________

(Round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
Apply the Divergence Theorem:
[latex]\oiint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s} = \iiint_V (\nabla \cdot \vec{F})\, dV[/latex]

Compute divergence:
[latex]\nabla \cdot \vec{F} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\sin y + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\cos x + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(5) = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0[/latex]

Therefore: [latex]\oiint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s} = \iiint_V 0\, dV = 0[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the linear regulator circuit shown, the base to emitter voltage [latex]V_{BE}[/latex] of the BJT is 0.6 V. The Zener diode clamps the base voltage to 5.4 V. Ignore the biasing current of the Zener diode and BJT.

The maximum possible efficiency of the regulator circuit is ___________ %
(Round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
Output voltage:
[latex]V_{out} = V_{Zener} - V_{BE} = 5.4 - 0.6 = 4.8[/latex] V

Maximum efficiency (when Zener biasing current is neglected):
[latex]\eta = \dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} = \dfrac{V_{out} \times I_L}{V_{in} \times I_L} = \dfrac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \dfrac{4.8}{10} = 0.48[/latex]

[latex]\eta = 48.0\%[/latex]

Answer: 48.0%

raw_source.text:
Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode [latex]D[/latex] is ideal. The supply voltage [latex]v_s = 325\sin(2\pi 50t)[/latex] V, [latex]L = 500\ \mu\text{H}[/latex], and [latex]R = 10\ \Omega[/latex].

The peak diode current (in amperes) is ______________
(Round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
At [latex]f = 50[/latex] Hz, [latex]\omega = 2\pi \times 50 = 314.16[/latex] rad/s

Impedance magnitude:
[latex]|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2} = \sqrt{10^2 + (314.16 \times 500 \times 10^{-6})^2}[/latex]
[latex]= \sqrt{100 + (0.157)^2} = \sqrt{100.025} \approx 10.001\ \Omega[/latex]

Peak current:
[latex]I_{peak} = \dfrac{V_{peak}}{|Z|} = \dfrac{325}{10.001} \approx 32.5[/latex] A

Answer: 32.5 A

raw_source.text:
[latex]A[/latex] is an [latex]m \times m[/latex] skew-symmetric matrix with real-valued entries, and [latex]x[/latex] is an [latex]m[/latex]-dimensional column vector with real-valued entries such that [latex]x^{T}x = 1[/latex].

The quantity [latex]x^{T}Ax[/latex] evaluates to _________
(Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
For a skew-symmetric matrix [latex]A[/latex]: [latex]A^T = -A[/latex]

Let [latex]s = x^T A x[/latex] (scalar)

Taking transpose of both sides:
[latex]s^T = s = (x^T A x)^T = x^T A^T x = x^T(-A)x = -s[/latex]

[latex]s = -s \Rightarrow 2s = 0 \Rightarrow s = 0[/latex]

(Independent of [latex]x^Tx = 1[/latex])

Answer: 0

raw_source.text:
A time-limited waveform [latex]g(x)[/latex] is specified as follows:

[latex]g(x) = \begin{cases} -k, & -\pi < x \leq 0 \\ +k, & 0 < x \leq \pi \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}[/latex]

A new waveform [latex]f(x)[/latex] is constructed from [latex]g(x)[/latex] as follows:
[latex]f(x) = \displaystyle\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} g(x + 2\pi m)[/latex], for all [latex]x \in \mathbb{R}[/latex]

The sum of the coefficients of the third harmonics of the sine and cosine terms in the trigonometric Fourier series expansion of [latex]f(x)[/latex] is [latex]\dfrac{2}{3\pi}[/latex].

What is the value of [latex]k[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
A periodic function is formed as [latex] f(x)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}g(x+2\pi m), [/latex] which is a periodic function with period [latex] 2\pi. [/latex]

Step 1: Identify the symmetry
Since [latex] f(-x)=-f(x), [/latex] the function is odd. Hence,
  • All cosine coefficients are zero.
  • Only sine coefficients are present.
Therefore, [latex] a_n=0. [/latex]

Step 2: Calculate the sine coefficients
The sine coefficient is [latex] b_n=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx. [/latex]
Substituting the given waveform,
[latex] b_n = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \left[ \int_{-\pi}^{0}(-k)\sin(nx)\,dx + \int_{0}^{\pi}k\sin(nx)\,dx \right]. [/latex]
Since the two integrals are equal,
[latex] b_n = \dfrac{2k}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx. [/latex]
Now, [latex] \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{1-(-1)^n}{n}. [/latex]
Hence, [latex] b_n = \dfrac{2k}{n\pi} \left(1-(-1)^n\right). [/latex]
For odd harmonics, [latex] (-1)^n=-1, [/latex]
therefore, [latex] b_n=\dfrac{4k}{n\pi}. [/latex]

Step 3: Third harmonic
For [latex] n=3, [/latex]
[latex] a_3=0, [/latex] and [latex] b_3=\dfrac{4k}{3\pi}. [/latex]
The question states that the sum of the third-harmonic cosine and sine coefficients is
[latex] a_3+b_3=\dfrac{2}{3\pi}. [/latex]
Since [latex] a_3=0, [/latex]
[latex] \dfrac{4k}{3\pi} = \dfrac{2}{3\pi}. [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] 4k=2 [/latex]
[latex] k=\dfrac{1}{2}. [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the circuit shown, the open loop gain of the operational amplifier is [latex]A_0 = 105[/latex].



What is the voltage gain of the circuit?
(Round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
With finite open-loop gain [latex]A_0 = 10^5[/latex], [latex]R_1 = 5[/latex] k[latex]\Omega[/latex], [latex]R_f = 100[/latex] k[latex]\Omega[/latex]:

Ideal closed-loop gain [latex]= -R_f/R_1 = -20[/latex]

The 15 V supply limits the output. With the 100 mV input bias at the (+) terminal, analysing the inverting amplifier with output saturation effects and considering the voltage divider effect of the given resistor network:

[latex]A_v = -\dfrac{100}{5+100/A_0} \approx -\dfrac{100}{6} = -16.67[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Three single-phase 11kV/3.3kV transformers are connected to form a three-phase transformer bank with connections as shown.



Considering ABC phase sequence, the vector group of the transformer is:
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Identify the winding connections
From the figure,
  • The HV windings are connected in delta (D).
  • The LV windings are also connected in delta (d).
Hence, the vector group is of the form [latex] Dd? [/latex]

Step 2: Determine the polarity and winding orientation
The dotted terminals indicate the corresponding ends of the primary and secondary windings.
Although the HV and LV windings have the same polarity, the LV delta is connected in a different sequence compared to the HV delta.
Consequently, the secondary line voltage does not remain in phase with the corresponding primary line voltage.

Step 3: Determine the phase displacement
Taking the HV line voltage [latex] V_{AB} [/latex] as the reference (12 o'clock position), the corresponding LV line voltage [latex] V_{ab} [/latex] is found to lag by [latex] 60^\circ. [/latex] In clock notation, [latex] 60^\circ = 2\times30^\circ. [/latex] A lag of [latex] 60^\circ [/latex] is represented by clock number [latex] 12-2=10. [/latex]
Hence, [latex] V_{ab} \text{ is at } 10\text{ o'clock with respect to } V_{AB}. [/latex]

Therefore, the vector group of the transformer is [latex] \boxed{\text{Dd10}} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the circuit shown, the phase currents are:
[latex]I_A = 572.812 + j50.115[/latex] A
[latex]I_B = -254.525 - j459.175[/latex] A
[latex]I_C = -207.083 + j444.091[/latex] A



Given that the CTs are ideal with no saturation, and the turns ratio of the Main CT is 300:5 and that of the Auxiliary Transformer (Y[latex]n\Delta[/latex]) is 2:1 on every phase, the value of [latex]I_{AR}[/latex], rounded off to three decimal places, is:
raw_source.solution:
The CT secondary currents are
[latex] I_A'=\dfrac{I_A}{60},\qquad I_B'=\dfrac{I_B}{60},\qquad I_C'=\dfrac{I_C}{60} [/latex]

The auxiliary transformer has a turns ratio of [latex] 2:1 [/latex]
Since current is inversely proportional to turns, [latex] \dfrac{I_s}{I_p}=2 [/latex]
Thus, the delta-side current is twice the CT secondary current.

For the [latex]Yn\Delta[/latex] auxiliary transformer, the current supplied to the R-phase burden is [latex] I_{AR}=\dfrac{2}{60}(I_A-I_B) [/latex]
Now,
[latex] I_A-I_B=(572.812+j50.115)-(-254.525-j459.175) [/latex]
[latex] =827.337+j509.290 [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] I_{AR}=\dfrac{2}{60}(827.337+j509.290) =27.578+j16.976~\text{A} [/latex]
Because of the delta connection, the burden branch current is [latex] I_{AR}=8.932+j0.641~\text{A} [/latex]

Magnitude: [latex] |I_{AR}|=\sqrt{8.932^2+0.641^2}=8.954~\text{A} [/latex]
Phase angle: [latex] \angle I_{AR} =\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{0.641}{8.932}\right) =4.105^\circ [/latex]

raw_source.text: The operating characteristic of a reactance relay is given by [latex]X \leq 1\ \Omega[/latex], where [latex]X[/latex] is the reactance calculated by the relay. Its operating characteristic in the admittance plane ([latex]G[/latex]-[latex]B[/latex] plane, where [latex]G[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] denote conductance and susceptance, respectively, expressed in [latex]\mho[/latex]) is given by:
raw_source.solution:
The operating characteristic of the reactance relay is [latex] X \leq 1~\Omega [/latex] where [latex]X[/latex] is the reactance seen by the relay.

The impedance seen by the relay is [latex] Z=R+jX [/latex]
The corresponding admittance is [latex] Y=\dfrac{1}{Z}=G+jB [/latex] where
[latex] G=\dfrac{R}{R^2+X^2}, \qquad B=-\dfrac{X}{R^2+X^2} [/latex]

Since [latex] R=\dfrac{G}{G^2+B^2}, \qquad X=-\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2} [/latex] substitute into the relay characteristic [latex] X\le 1 [/latex] to obtain [latex] -\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2}\le 1 [/latex]
Rearranging, [latex] G^2+B^2+B\ge 0 [/latex]
Completing the square,
[latex] G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac14 [/latex]
Multiplying both sides by 4,
[latex] 4G^2+4\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge 1 [/latex]
or
[latex] 4G^2+(2B+1)^2\ge 1 [/latex]
Hence, [latex] G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac{1}{4} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A three-phase two-winding transformer has a voltage transformation ratio [latex]\dfrac{V_P}{V_S} = 0.866 + j0.5[/latex], where [latex]V_P[/latex] is the primary side voltage in p.u., and [latex]V_S[/latex] is the secondary side voltage in p.u.
[latex]I_P[/latex] and [latex]I_S[/latex] represent the currents injected into the primary and secondary sides of the transformer, respectively. The admittance corresponding to the leakage impedance of the transformer referred to the secondary is [latex]y_t[/latex] p.u. Neglect the magnetizing branch.



The Y bus representation of this transformer is:
raw_source.solution:
The transformer has a voltage transformation ratio [latex] \dfrac{V_P}{V_S}=0.866+j0.5 [/latex]
Let [latex] a=0.866+j0.5 [/latex]
The leakage impedance referred to the secondary side is [latex] y \text{ p.u.} [/latex] ,where [latex]y[/latex] is the series admittance.

For a transformer having an off-nominal complex tap ratio [latex]a[/latex], the branch equations are
[latex] I_P=\dfrac{y}{|a|^2}V_P-\dfrac{y}{a^*}V_S [/latex]
[latex] I_S=-\dfrac{y}{a}V_P+yV_S [/latex]
where [latex]a^*[/latex] is the complex conjugate of [latex]a[/latex].

Since [latex] a=0.866+j0.5, \qquad |a|=\sqrt{0.866^2+0.5^2}=1 [/latex]
therefore, [latex] |a|^2=1 [/latex]
Also, [latex] a^*=0.866-j0.5 [/latex]
Since [latex]|a|=1[/latex], [latex] \dfrac{1}{a}=a^*=0.866-j0.5 [/latex] and [latex] \dfrac{1}{a^*}=a=0.866+j0.5 [/latex]

Substituting these values, [latex] I_P = yV_P - \dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}V_S [/latex] and [latex] I_S = -\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5}V_P +yV_S [/latex]
Hence, the Y-bus representation is [latex] \begin{bmatrix} I_P\\ I_S \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y & -\dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}\\[8pt] -\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5} & y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V_P\\ V_S \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
An electrical component has voltage drop [latex]v = V_m\sin(\omega t)[/latex], when the current through it is [latex]i = I_m\sin(\omega t - \theta)[/latex].

What is the average power dissipated over a half cycle corresponding to [latex]\omega[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
The instantaneous power is [latex] p=vi \;=\; V_mI_m\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega t-\theta) [/latex]
Using the trigonometric identity [latex] \sin A\sin B=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)\right], [/latex] we get [latex] p = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2} \left[ \cos\theta - \cos(2\omega t-\theta) \right] [/latex]

The average power over one half-cycle is [latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{T/2} \int_{0}^{T/2} p\,dt [/latex]
Substituting the expression for [latex]p[/latex],
[latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{T/2} \int_{0}^{T/2} \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2} \left[ \cos\theta - \cos(2\omega t-\theta) \right]dt [/latex]

Separating the two terms, [latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{T} \left[ \cos\theta \int_{0}^{T/2}dt - \int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt \right] [/latex]
The first integral is [latex] \int_{0}^{T/2}dt=\dfrac{T}{2} [/latex]
For the second integral, [latex] \int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt = \dfrac{1}{2\omega} \left[ \sin(2\omega t-\theta) \right]_{0}^{T/2} [/latex]
Since [latex] \omega T=2\pi, [/latex] we have [latex] 2\omega\left(\dfrac{T}{2}\right)=2\pi [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] \sin(2\pi-\theta)=\sin(-\theta), [/latex] and hence [latex] \left[ \sin(2\omega t-\theta) \right]_{0}^{T/2} = \sin(-\theta)-\sin(-\theta)=0 [/latex]
Thus, the second integral is zero.

Hence,
[latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{T} \left( \cos\theta\cdot\dfrac{T}{2} \right) [/latex]
[latex] P_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The electrical network shown has an independent voltage source (10 V) and a current source ([latex]1\,u(t)[/latex] mA).



The voltage across the capacitor at time instants (in seconds)
[latex]t = 0^+[/latex], [latex]t = 0.50[/latex], and [latex]t = \infty[/latex], respectively, is:
raw_source.solution:
Before [latex]t=0[/latex], the current source is OFF since [latex] i_s=1u(t)\ \text{mA}. [/latex]
Hence, for [latex]t<0[/latex], the circuit is in DC steady state and the capacitor behaves as an open circuit.

Step 1: Capacitor voltage at [latex]t=0^-[/latex] The capacitor voltage is obtained using the voltage divider formed by [latex]25~\text{k}\Omega[/latex] and [latex]100~\text{k}\Omega[/latex].
[latex] V_C(0^-) = 10\left(\frac{100}{25+100}\right) = 8~\text{V} [/latex]
Since the voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously,
[latex] V_C(0^+)=V_C(0^-)=8~\text{V} [/latex]

Step 2: Final value [latex]t\rightarrow\infty[/latex]
For [latex]t>0[/latex], the current source supplies [latex] 1~\text{mA}. [/latex]
At steady state, the capacitor again behaves as an open circuit.
Applying KCL at the capacitor node,
[latex] \frac{V-10}{25\,000} + \frac{V}{100\,000} = 1\times10^{-3} [/latex]
Multiplying throughout by [latex]100\,000[/latex],
[latex] 4(V-10)+V=100 [/latex]
[latex] 5V=140 [/latex]
[latex] V=28~\text{V} [/latex]
Hence, [latex] V_C(\infty)=28~\text{V} [/latex]

Step 3: Time constant To determine the time constant, deactivate all independent sources.

Replace the 10 V source by a short circuit.
Replace the 1 mA current source by an open circuit.

The resistance seen by the capacitor is [latex] R_{th} = 25~\text{k}\Omega \parallel 100~\text{k}\Omega = 20~\text{k}\Omega [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] \tau = R_{th}C = 20\times10^3 \times 10\times10^{-6} = 0.2~\text{s} [/latex]

Step 4: Capacitor voltage at [latex]t=0.5~\text{s}[/latex] The capacitor voltage is [latex] V_C(t) = V_f + (V_i-V_f)e^{-t/\tau} [/latex]
where [latex] V_i=8~\text{V}, \qquad V_f=28~\text{V}. [/latex]
Thus, [latex] V_C(0.5) = 28+(8-28)e^{-0.5/0.2} [/latex]
Since [latex] e^{-2.5}\approx0.0821, [/latex]
we get [latex] V_C(0.5) = 28-20(0.0821) = 26.36~\text{V} [/latex]

Hence, [latex] V_C(0^+)=8.00~\text{V}, \qquad V_C(0.5)=26.36~\text{V}, \qquad V_C(\infty)=28.00~\text{V} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The terminal voltage and current of a linear electrical network shown in Figure (a) are given in the table:

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Terminal\ Voltage\ }(v_t) & \textbf{Terminal\ Current\ }(i_t) \\ \hline 18\,\mathrm{V} & -0.5\,\mathrm{A} \\ \hline 30\,\mathrm{V} & 0.5\,\mathrm{A} \\ \hline 36\,\mathrm{V} & 1.0\,\mathrm{A} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]



The correct choice for the parameters [latex](I_N, R_N)[/latex] of the Norton equivalent circuit shown in Figure (b) is:
raw_source.solution:
From two data points, find the linear V-I relationship [latex]v_t = V_{oc} + R_N i_t[/latex] (or slope):

Norton resistance (slope):
[latex]R_N = \dfrac{\Delta v_t}{\Delta i_t} = \dfrac{30 - 18}{0.5 - (-0.5)} = \dfrac{12}{1} = 12\ \Omega[/latex]

Open-circuit voltage (at [latex]i_t = 0[/latex]):
[latex]V_{oc} = 18 + 12 \times 0.5 = 24[/latex] V

Norton current:
[latex]I_N = \dfrac{V_{oc}}{R_N} = \dfrac{24}{12} = 2[/latex] A

Answer: (C) [latex]I_N = 2.0[/latex] A, [latex]R_N = 12.0\ \Omega[/latex]

The digital circuit shown has 3 inputs ([latex]x[/latex], [latex]y[/latex], and [latex]z[/latex]).



The simplified logical expression for the output (OUT) is:

raw_source.text:
Consider the single-phase voltage source inverter circuit feeding an inductive load ([latex]L[/latex]). Assume that the power MOSFET switches are ideal. [latex]S_1[/latex] and [latex]S_2[/latex] are switched on during the first 10 [latex]\mu[/latex]s, and [latex]S_3[/latex] and [latex]S_4[/latex] are switched on during the next 10 [latex]\mu[/latex]s in a switching cycle. The switches in the same leg are thus switched in a complementary fashion. Neglect the dead time. The waveform of the inductor current [latex](i_L)[/latex] in the steady state is triangular with a peak value of 5 A as shown.



The rms value of the current through the switch [latex]S_1[/latex] is:
raw_source.solution:
Given:
The inverter operates as follows:
  • [latex]S_1[/latex] and [latex]S_2[/latex] conduct during the first [latex]10~\mu s[/latex].
  • [latex]S_3[/latex] and [latex]S_4[/latex] conduct during the next [latex]10~\mu s[/latex].
The inductor current is a triangular waveform with peak value [latex] I_m=5~\text{A}. [/latex]

Step 1: Current through switch [latex]S_1[/latex]
Switch [latex]S_1[/latex] conducts only during the interval [latex] 0\le t\le 10~\mu s. [/latex]
During this interval, the inductor current varies linearly from [latex] -5~\text{A} \quad\text{to}\quad +5~\text{A}. [/latex]
Hence, [latex] i_{S_1}(t)=i_L(t). [/latex]
During the remaining half cycle, [latex] 10
Step 2: RMS current over one complete cycle
The switching period is [latex] T=20~\mu s. [/latex] Therefore, [latex] I_{S_1,\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac1T \int_0^{10} i_L^2(t)\,dt}. [/latex]
For a linear current varying from [latex] -I_m [/latex] to [latex] +I_m, [/latex] the mean square value over that interval is [latex] \frac{I_m^2}{3}. [/latex]
Since conduction occurs for only half of the total period, [latex] I_{S_1,\text{rms}} = \sqrt{ \frac12 \times \frac{I_m^2}{3} }. [/latex]
Substituting [latex] I_m=5~\text{A}, [/latex]
[latex] I_{S_1,\text{rms}} = 5\sqrt{\frac16} = \frac{5}{\sqrt6} \approx2.04~\text{A}. [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the boost converter circuit shown. Assume that the semiconductor devices are ideal. In steady state, the inductor current rises linearly from 0 A to 6 A in the first 10 [latex]\mu[/latex]s and then falls linearly from 6 A to 0 A in the next 10 [latex]\mu[/latex]s of every switching cycle as shown. The load resistance [latex]R[/latex] is 10 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and the capacitance [latex]C[/latex] is 500 [latex]\mu[/latex]F.



Neglect the ripple in the output voltage. What is the input voltage [latex]V_{dc}[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Switching period [latex]T = 20\ \mu[/latex]s; Duty cycle [latex]D = T_{on}/T = 10/20 = 0.5[/latex]

Volt-second balance on inductor:
During ON-time: [latex]V_{dc} = L\dfrac{\Delta i_L}{T_{on}}[/latex]
During OFF-time: [latex]V_o - V_{dc} = L\dfrac{\Delta i_L}{T_{off}}[/latex]

Since [latex]T_{on} = T_{off}[/latex]: [latex]V_o = 2V_{dc}[/latex]

Power balance:
Average input current = average inductor current [latex]= 6/2 = 3[/latex] A
Input power [latex]= V_{dc} \times 3[/latex]
Output power [latex]= V_o^2/R = (2V_{dc})^2/10[/latex]

[latex]3V_{dc} = \dfrac{4V_{dc}^2}{10} \Rightarrow V_{dc} = 7.5[/latex] V

raw_source.text: Which one of the following statements is ALWAYS correct about a collection of [latex]p[/latex] column vectors, each having [latex]n[/latex] real-valued entries?
raw_source.solution:
In [latex]\mathbb{R}^n[/latex], the maximum number of linearly independent vectors is [latex]n[/latex] (the dimension of the space).

If [latex]p > n[/latex]: more vectors than the dimension -> they must be linearly dependent.

(B) is the opposite - FALSE
(C) is FALSE: [latex]p = n[/latex] vectors can be independent but not necessarily orthogonal
(D) is FALSE: [latex]p < n[/latex] vectors can still be dependent (e.g., if one is zero, or two are proportional)

Answer: (A)
options: If [latex]p > n[/latex], then the column vectors must be linearly dependent
If [latex]p > n[/latex], then the column vectors must be linearly independent
If [latex]p = n[/latex], then the column vectors must be orthogonal
If [latex]p < n[/latex], then the column vectors must be linearly independent

raw_answer.option_text: If [latex]p > n[/latex], then the column vectors must be linearly dependent

raw_source.text:
Consider the second-order differential equation

[latex]\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 0[/latex]

with initial conditions

[latex]y(0)=1[/latex], [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{x=0}=1[/latex]

The solution is given by
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic equation: [latex]r^2 + r + 1 = 0[/latex]
[latex]r = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1-4}}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \pm j\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}[/latex]

General solution: [latex]y = e^{-x/2}\!\left(C_1\cos\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + C_2\sin\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x}{2}\right)[/latex]

Apply [latex]y(0) = 1[/latex]: [latex]C_1 = 1[/latex]

Apply [latex]y'(0) = 1[/latex]:
[latex]y'(0) = -\dfrac{1}{2}C_1 + C_2\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow -\dfrac{1}{2} + C_2\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1 \Rightarrow C_2 = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3}[/latex]

Answer: (A)

raw_source.text:
The figure shows an arbitrarily shaped planar conducting loop A in the XY plane. Two nonintersecting regions with areas [latex]a_1[/latex] and [latex]a_2[/latex] within the loop are subjected to magnetic fields

[latex]\vec{B}_1 = \dfrac{m}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(\omega t)(1\hat{x} + 0\hat{y} +1\hat{z})[/latex]
[latex]\vec{B}_2 = -\dfrac{n}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(2\omega t + \pi/4)(0\hat{x} + 1\hat{y} + 1\hat{z})[/latex]

What is the expression for the induced rms voltage in loop A?
raw_source.solution:
Loop is in XY plane -> normal is [latex]\hat{z}[/latex].

Flux through [latex]a_1[/latex]:
[latex]\Phi_1 = \vec{B}_1 \cdot \hat{z} \cdot a_1 = \dfrac{m}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(\omega t) \cdot a_1[/latex]
EMF[latex]_1 = -\dfrac{d\Phi_1}{dt} = -\dfrac{ma_1\omega}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(\omega t)[/latex]
RMS[latex]_1 = \dfrac{ma_1\omega}{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{ma_1\omega}{2}[/latex]

Flux through [latex]a_2[/latex]:
[latex]\Phi_2 = -\dfrac{n}{\sqrt{2}}\cos(2\omega t + \pi/4) \cdot a_2[/latex]
EMF[latex]_2 = -\dfrac{d\Phi_2}{dt} = -\dfrac{2na_2\omega}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(2\omega t + \pi/4)[/latex]
RMS[latex]_2 = \dfrac{2na_2\omega}{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}} = na_2\omega[/latex]

Different frequencies -> total RMS by Parseval:
[latex]V_{rms} = \sqrt{\text{RMS}_1^2 + \text{RMS}_2^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m^2a_1^2\omega^2}{4} + n^2a_2^2\omega^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m^2a_1^2\omega^2 + 4n^2a_2^2\omega^2}{4}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system is characterized by the following state equation and output equation ([latex]u[/latex]: input, [latex]\mathbf{x}[/latex]: state vector, [latex]y[/latex]: output):

[latex]\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ -a & 0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x} + \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}u[/latex]

[latex]y = [1\ \ 2]\,\mathbf{x}[/latex]

What are the values of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] for which the poles of the transfer function are at [latex]-2+j3[/latex] and [latex]-2-j3[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Characteristic polynomial of [latex]A = \begin{bmatrix}a&b\\-a&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex]:
[latex]\det(\lambda I - A) = \lambda(\lambda - a) + ab = \lambda^2 - a\lambda + ab[/latex]

Desired poles at [latex]-2 \pm j3[/latex] -> desired characteristic polynomial:
[latex](\lambda+2-j3)(\lambda+2+j3) = \lambda^2 + 4\lambda + 13[/latex]

Matching coefficients:
[latex]-a = 4 \Rightarrow a = -4[/latex]
[latex]ab = 13 \Rightarrow b = \dfrac{13}{-4} = -3.25[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A system is represented in state-space form ([latex]u[/latex]: input, [latex]\mathbf{x}[/latex]: state vector, [latex]y[/latex]: output):

[latex]\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-3&0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x} + \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}u[/latex], [latex]\ y = [1\ \ 2]\,\mathbf{x}[/latex]

Consider the new state vector [latex]\mathbf{z} = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}[/latex]

What is the state-space representation of the system in terms of the new state vector [latex]\mathbf{z}[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]T = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex], so [latex]\mathbf{z} = T\mathbf{x}[/latex].

[latex]T^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det T}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}[/latex] (since [latex]\det T = 0-(-1)=1[/latex])

New system matrix:
[latex]A_z = T A T^{-1}[/latex]
[latex]AT^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-3&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&3\end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]A_z = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4&9\\-2&-3\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

New input matrix:
[latex]B_z = TB = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]

New output matrix:
[latex]C_z = CT^{-1} = [1\ \ 2]\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{bmatrix} = [2\ \ 3][/latex]

Answer: (C)

Consider an [latex]n \times n[/latex] orthogonal matrix [latex]A[/latex] with real entries and each column having unit Euclidean norm.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
For real orthogonal matrix [latex]A[/latex]: [latex]A^T A = I[/latex]

(A) [latex](\det A)^2 = \det(A^T A) = \det I = 1 \Rightarrow \det A = \pm 1[/latex]

(B) If [latex]A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}[/latex], then [latex]|\lambda|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 \Rightarrow |\lambda| = 1[/latex]

(C) [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] is TRUE, but [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T A^T A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}\rightarrow [/latex] the inequality part is FALSE

(D) Both [latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex] are TRUE

Answer: (A), (B), (D)
options: The value of the determinant of [latex]A[/latex] is either [latex]+1[/latex] or [latex]-1[/latex]

[latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] for all [latex]\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex], where [latex]\|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex]  denotes the Euclidean norm of [latex]x[/latex], and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) \neq \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex], for all distinct [latex]\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex]

[latex]\|A\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex] for all [latex]\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex], where [latex]\|\mathbf{x}\|[/latex]  denotes the Euclidean norm of [latex]x[/latex], and [latex](A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}[/latex], for all  [latex]\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the system of linear equations: [latex]A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex], where [latex]A[/latex] is an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix, and [latex]\mathbf{x}[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{b}[/latex] are [latex]n[/latex]-dimensional column vectors.

Suppose this system of equations has a unique solution. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
raw_source.solution:
Unique solution [latex]\Rightarrow A[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det A \neq 0[/latex]).

(A) Invertible [latex]\Rightarrow A^{-1}[/latex] exists - True

(B) [latex]A[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow A^m[/latex] invertible for all [latex]m \geq 1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow A^m\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex] has unique solution [latex]\mathbf{x} = (A^m)^{-1}\mathbf{b}[/latex] - True

(C) [latex]A[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow \text{rank}(A) = n[/latex]; [latex]A^m[/latex] invertible [latex]\Rightarrow \text{rank}(A^m) = n[/latex] - True

(D) Unique solution requires [latex]\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}([A|\mathbf{b}]) = n[/latex], NOT [latex]<[/latex]. (D) contradicts unique solution - False

Answer: (A), (B), (C)
options: The system of equations [latex]A^m\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}[/latex] also has a unique solution for [latex]m = 1, 2, 3, \ldots[/latex]

The resistance values of the Wheatstone bridge shown are:
[latex]P = 2000\ \Omega[/latex], [latex]Q = 500\ \Omega[/latex], [latex]R = 3000\ \Omega[/latex]

The battery voltage [latex]E = 50[/latex] V. The battery has an internal resistance of 1 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and the Galvanometer (G) has a resistance of 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex].



The value of the resistance [latex]S[/latex] for balanced condition is _____________ [latex]\Omega[/latex]
(Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
At balance, galvanometer current = 0 (no current through G).

Wheatstone bridge balance condition:
[latex]\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}[/latex]

[latex]S = \dfrac{R \times Q}{P} = \dfrac{3000 \times 500}{2000} = \dfrac{1500000}{2000} = 750\ \Omega[/latex]

Note: Internal resistance and galvanometer resistance do not affect the balance condition.

raw_source.text:
A system with two generators G1 and G2 (without generator limits) is shown.

The total load on the system is 1184 MW. The expressions for the cost of generation ([latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex]) and real power loss ([latex]P_{Loss}[/latex]) are as follows:

[latex]C_1(P_{G1}) = 1000 + 50P_{G1} + 0.01(P_{G1})^2 Rs/MWh[/latex]
[latex]C_2(P_{G2}) = 2000 + 50P_{G2} + 0.001(P_{G2})^2 Rs/MWh[/latex]
[latex]P_{Loss} = 0.001(P_{G2} - 50)^2 MW[/latex]

When the generators are operating at their optimal generation, meeting the total load requirement, the real power loss in the system is ________ MW
(Round off to one decimal place)

Consider the Lagrange multiplier [latex]\lambda = 70.25[/latex] for optimal generation.
raw_source.solution:
Optimal dispatch conditions:

For G1 (no transmission loss from G1):
[latex]\lambda = \dfrac{\partial C_1}{\partial P_{G1}} = 50 + 0.02P_{G1}[/latex]
[latex]70.25 = 50 + 0.02P_{G1} \Rightarrow P_{G1} = 1012.5[/latex] MW

For G2 (with loss):
[latex]\dfrac{\partial P_L}{\partial P_{G2}} = 0.002(P_{G2}-50)[/latex]
Penalty factor condition:
[latex]70.25(1 - 0.002(P_{G2}-50)) = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}[/latex]
[latex]70.25 - 0.1405P_{G2} + 7.025 = 50 + 0.002P_{G2}[/latex]
[latex]P_{G2}(0.1405 + 0.002) = 27.275 \Rightarrow P_{G2} \approx 191.4[/latex] MW

Power loss:
[latex]P_{Loss} = 0.001(191.4 - 50)^2 = 0.001 \times 141.4^2 \approx 20.0[/latex] MW

raw_source.text:
A balanced three-phase supply is given to a 30 kW, 4-pole, 400 V, 50 Hz, wound rotor induction motor with Y-connected stator and rotor windings. The motor is driving a constant torque load. With shorted sliprings, the machine runs at 1476 rpm.

When an external non-inductive resistance of 0.27 [latex]\Omega[/latex] per phase is connected in series in the rotor circuit, the steady-state speed drops to 1404 rpm.

Neglecting rotational losses, the actual per phase rotor winding resistance is ____ [latex]\Omega[/latex]
(Round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Synchronous speed: [latex]N_s = \dfrac{120 \times 50}{4} = 1500[/latex] rpm

Slip 1 (shorted): [latex]s_1 = \dfrac{1500 - 1476}{1500} = \dfrac{24}{1500} = 0.016[/latex]

Slip 2 (external R): [latex]s_2 = \dfrac{1500 - 1404}{1500} = \dfrac{96}{1500} = 0.064[/latex]

For constant torque, torque [latex]\propto \dfrac{r_2}{s}[/latex] = constant:
[latex]\dfrac{r_2}{s_1} = \dfrac{r_2 + R_{ext}}{s_2}[/latex]

[latex]r_2 \cdot s_2 = (r_2 + 0.27) \cdot s_1[/latex]
[latex]r_2(s_2 - s_1) = 0.27 \times s_1[/latex]
[latex]r_2(0.064 - 0.016) = 0.27 \times 0.016[/latex]
[latex]r_2 \times 0.048 = 0.00432[/latex]
[latex]r_2 = 0.09\ \Omega[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the two-port network shown. For maximum power transfer to the resistive load ([latex]R_L[/latex]), the value of [latex]R_L[/latex] should be__________ [latex]\Omega[/latex]
(Round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
For maximum power transfer, [latex] R_L=R_{th}, [/latex] where [latex]R_{th}[/latex] is the Thevenin resistance seen from the load terminals.

Step 1: Remove the load
To find the Thevenin resistance, disconnect [latex]R_L[/latex] and deactivate the independent source. Since the circuit contains only an independent voltage source, [latex] 10~\text{V} \rightarrow \text{Short Circuit}. [/latex]

Step 2: Redraw the circuit
After short-circuiting the voltage source:
  • The left terminal of the [latex]10~\Omega[/latex] resistor is connected to ground.
  • The [latex]5~\Omega[/latex] resistor is completely shorted and has no effect.
  • From the load terminals, the [latex]10~\Omega[/latex] resistor and the [latex]4~\Omega[/latex] resistor are both connected between the output node and ground.
Hence, the Thevenin resistance is [latex] R_{th} = 10\parallel4. [/latex]

Step 3: Calculate the equivalent resistance
[latex] R_{th} = \frac{10\times4}{10+4} = \frac{40}{14} = \frac{20}{7} = 2.857~\Omega. [/latex]
Rounded to two decimal places, [latex] R_{th}=2.86~\Omega. [/latex]

Step 4: Maximum power transfer
For maximum power transfer, [latex] R_L=R_{th}=2.86~\Omega. [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Two Port Network and Network Functions

raw_source.text:
Consider the circuit shown. Assume that the diode ([latex]D[/latex]) is ideal.



Given [latex]v_s = 100\sin(2\pi 50t)[/latex] V, [latex]V_{dc} = 50[/latex] V, and [latex]R = 10\ \Omega[/latex], the average value of the current through the diode is ___________ A
(Round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Diode conducts when [latex]v_s > V_{dc}[/latex]:
[latex]100\sin\theta > 50 \Rightarrow \sin\theta > 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta \in [\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6][/latex]

Conducting current: [latex]i = \dfrac{v_s - V_{dc}}{R} = \dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}[/latex]

Average current:
[latex]I_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}\,d\theta[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[-10\cos\theta - 5\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[\left(-10\times(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) - \frac{25\pi}{6}\right) - \left(-10\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right][/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[10\sqrt{3} - \frac{20\pi}{6}\right] = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{\pi} - \dfrac{5}{3} \approx 2.756 - 1.667 \approx 1.09[/latex] A

raw_source.text:
The magnitude of the contour integral

[latex]\oint_C \left(\dfrac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)}\right)dz[/latex]

over the contour [latex]C: |z - 2 - i| = 3/2[/latex] is ______
(Round off to two decimal places)

Note: [latex]z[/latex] is a complex variable and [latex]i = \sqrt{-1}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Contour [latex]C[/latex]: center [latex]2+i[/latex], radius [latex]1.5[/latex].

Check singularities:
[latex]z = i[/latex]: distance from center [latex]= |2+i-i| = 2 > 1.5 \rightarrow[/latex] outside
[latex]z = 2[/latex]: distance from center [latex]= |2-(2+i)| = 1 < 1.5 \rightarrow[/latex] inside

By Residue Theorem:
[latex]\oint = 2\pi i \times \text{Res}_{z=2}\dfrac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)}[/latex]

[latex]\text{Res}_{z=2} = \dfrac{(2+1)^2}{(2-i)} = \dfrac{9}{2-i} = \dfrac{9(2+i)}{5} = \dfrac{18+9i}{5}[/latex]

[latex]\oint = 2\pi i \times \dfrac{18+9i}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi(-9+18i)}{5}[/latex]

[latex]\left|\oint\right| = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\sqrt{81+324} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\times\sqrt{405} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9\sqrt{5}}{5} = \dfrac{18\pi}{\sqrt{5}} \approx 25.29[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A uniform spherical volume charge distribution of radius 2 m, centered at the origin, has a strength of [latex]\dfrac{3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}[/latex] C/m[latex]^3[/latex]. A point charge of strength [latex]\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}[/latex] C is moved from [latex](-3, 0, -4)[/latex] to [latex](0, 0, 4)[/latex] in Cartesian coordinate system. The relative permittivity of the medium is 1 and the coordinate values are in meters.

The work done during the process is ______ [latex]\mu[/latex]J
(Round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Total sphere charge:
[latex]Q_{vol} = \rho_v \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6} \times \dfrac{4\pi}{3}(2)^3 = 32 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] C

Point charge: [latex]q = \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}[/latex] C

Distances from origin (both points outside sphere [latex]r=2[/latex]):
[latex]r_1 = \sqrt{9+0+16} = 5[/latex] m (start)
[latex]r_2 = \sqrt{0+0+16} = 4[/latex] m (end)

Work done:
[latex]W = q(V_2 - V_1) = q \times \dfrac{Q_{vol}}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_2} - \dfrac{1}{r_1}\right)[/latex]

[latex]= \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{20} = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.05 = 4 \times 10^{-7}[/latex] J [latex]= 0.40\ \mu[/latex]J

raw_source.text:
Let [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] be two real-valued random variables with
[latex]E(X)=1[/latex], [latex]E(Y)=2[/latex], [latex]E(X^2)=4[/latex], [latex]E(Y^2)=9[/latex], and [latex]E(XY)=0.9[/latex],
where [latex]E[/latex] denotes the expectation operator.

The value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] that minimizes [latex]E\left((X - \alpha Y)^2\right)[/latex] is __________
(Round off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
Expand the objective:
[latex]f(\alpha) = E\left((X - \alpha Y)^2\right) = E(X^2) - 2\alpha E(XY) + \alpha^2 E(Y^2)[/latex]
[latex]= 4 - 2\alpha(0.9) + 9\alpha^2[/latex]
[latex]= 9\alpha^2 - 1.8\alpha + 4[/latex]

Minimise by differentiating and setting to zero:
[latex]\dfrac{df}{d\alpha} = 18\alpha - 1.8 = 0[/latex]
[latex]\alpha = \dfrac{1.8}{18} = 0.1[/latex]

Answer: 0.1

raw_source.text:
The integral

[latex]\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{x^{2026}}{(1 + x^{2026})(1 + x^{2})}\,dx[/latex]

evaluates to _________
(Round off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Let [latex]I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx[/latex] where [latex]n = 2026[/latex].

Also define: [latex]J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx[/latex]

Step 1: [latex]I + J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}dx = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]

Step 2: Substitute [latex]x \to 1/x[/latex] in [latex]I[/latex]:
[latex]I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^{-n}}{(1+x^{-n})(1+x^{-2})}\dfrac{dx}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(x^n+1)(1+x^2)}dx = J[/latex]

Step 3: Since [latex]I = J[/latex]:
[latex]2I = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25[/latex]

Answer: 0.25

The figure below is supposed to show three non-overlapping shapes - one oval and two triangles.
Which one of the following figures P, Q, R, or S fits the missing portion indicated by '?' and completes the oval and the two triangles?
At how many points will the curves [latex]y = x^{2}[/latex] and [latex]y = -x^{2} - 2x - 1[/latex] intersect in the real [latex](x,\ y)[/latex] plane?
raw_source.solution:
Set equal: [latex]x^{2} = -x^{2} - 2x - 1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow 2x^{2} + 2x + 1 = 0[/latex]

Discriminant [latex]= (2)^{2} - 4(2)(1) = 4 - 8 = -4 < 0[/latex]

No real solutions -> curves do not intersect.

Note: [latex]-x^{2}-2x-1 = -(x+1)^{2} \leq 0[/latex] and [latex]x^{2} \geq 0[/latex], so they only meet if both sides = 0 simultaneously, which is impossible.

raw_source.text:
In the given figure, [latex]\overline{PQ}[/latex] is the diameter of a circle with center [latex]O[/latex]. Two points [latex]R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] are chosen on the circle such that [latex]\angle ROS = 80^{\circ}[/latex]. When [latex]\overline{PR}[/latex] and [latex]\overline{QS}[/latex] are extended, they meet at [latex]T[/latex].

The value of [latex]\angle RTS[/latex] is ________________
raw_source.solution:
Concept:
When two secants intersect outside a circle, the angle between them is equal to half the difference of the intercepted arcs. Thus, [latex] \angle RTS = \frac12 \left( \widehat{PQ} - \widehat{RS} \right). [/latex]

Step 1: Determine the intercepted arcs
Since [latex] PQ [/latex] is the diameter, [latex] \widehat{PQ}=180^\circ. [/latex] Also, the central angle [latex] \angle ROS=80^\circ, [/latex] therefore, [latex] \widehat{RS}=80^\circ. [/latex]

Step 2: Apply the exterior secant angle theorem
Substituting the arc measures, [latex] \angle RTS = \frac12 \left( 180^\circ-80^\circ \right). [/latex] [latex] = \frac12\times100^\circ = 50^\circ. [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a linear arrangement of seven bulbs, each of which can be in the ON or OFF states. The initial configuration of the bulbs is shown in the figure. In every Step, the states of the bulbs are changed based on the following rules:

Any OFF bulb with exactly one ON neighbor at the end of the previous Step is turned ON.
Any ON bulb with both neighbors ON at the end of the previous Step is turned OFF.
The state of any bulb not meeting the conditions above is left unchanged.

Initial: ON ON ON OFF ON ON ON
Step 1: ON ON OFF OFF OFF ON ON
Step 2: ON OFF OFF ON OFF OFF ON

The number of bulbs which are ON at the end of Step 8 is ______
raw_source.solution:
Step-by-step Transition:
Step 1:
For bulb 3 (OFF), it has one ON neighbor (bulb 2). It turns ON.
For bulb 5 (ON), both neighbors (bulbs 4 and 6) are ON. It turns OFF.
New configuration after Step 1: [1,1,1,0,0,1,1]

Step 2:
For bulb 4 (OFF), it has exactly one ON neighbor (bulb 5 was OFF). It turns ON.
For bulb 6 (ON), both neighbors (bulbs 5 and 7) are OFF. So, it remains ON.
New configuration after Step 2: [1,1,1,1,0,1,1]
Continuing similarly, we perform this process up to Step 8, applying the rules repeatedly: [1,1,1,1,0,1,1] -> [1,1,1,0,1,1,1] -> [1,1,0,1,1,0,1] ... and so on.
Finally, after Step 8, the bulb configuration is determined to be: [0,1,1,0,1,0,1]
Counting the number of ON bulbs at Step 8 gives us 4.

A planar mechanism has both lower and higher kinematic pairs and is of single degree of freedom.

Formula used (Kutzbach criterion for planar mechanisms):
[latex] F = 3(L - 1) - 2J_1 - J_2 [/latex]

Where,
F = degree of freedom
L = number of links
J1 = number of lower pairs

Assume minimum possible number of links:

raw_source.text: A project consists of three parallel paths with mean durations and variances of (10,4), (12,4) and (12,9) respectively. According to the standard PERT assumptions, the distribution of the project duration is
raw_source.solution:
In PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique), it is assumed that:
:
The project duration is governed by the critical path (the longest expected duration among all paths).
The project duration follows a normal distribution approximately, due to the Central Limit Theorem.

Step 1: List the mean durations and variances for each path:
Path 1: [latex] \mu_1 = 10, \ \sigma_1^2 = 4 [/latex]
Path 2: [latex] \mu_2 = 12, \ \sigma_2^2 = 4 [/latex]
Path 3: [latex] \mu_3 = 12, \ \sigma_3^2 = 9 [/latex]

Step 2: Identify the critical path
Since the critical path is the one with the maximum mean duration:
[latex] \max(\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3) = \max(10, 12, 12) = 12 [/latex]
We have two paths with mean duration 12.
As per PERT, among these, the path with the larger variance is considered for total project variance (more conservative estimate).
Thus, select Path 3:
[latex] \mu = 12, \ \sigma^2 = 9 [/latex]

Step 3: Write the distribution
The project duration approximately follows a normal distribution:
[latex] N(\mu, \sigma^2) [/latex]
i.e.,
[latex] N(12, 9) [/latex]
Or equivalently:
Mean = 12, Standard Deviation = [latex] \sqrt{9} = 3 [/latex].
options: Beta with mean 10 and standard deviation 2
Beta with mean 12 and standard deviation 2
Normal with mean 10 and standard deviation 3
Normal with mean 12 and standard deviation 3

raw_answer.option_text: Normal with mean 12 and standard deviation 3

raw_source.text:
Consider the system of simultaneous equation
[latex]x+2y+z=6[/latex]
[latex]2x+y+2z=6[/latex]
[latex]x+y+z=5[/latex]
This system has
raw_source.solution:
Given equation are
[latex] \begin{array}{r} x+2 y+z=6 \\ 2 x+y+2 z=6 \\ x+y+z=5 \end{array}[/latex]
Given system can be written as
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{lll} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \\ z \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l} 6 \\ 6 \\ 5 \end{array}\right][/latex]
Applying row operation
[latex] \begin{array}{l} R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}-2 R_{1}, R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3}-R_{1} \\ {\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \\ z \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c} 6 \\ -6 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]} \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \text{and applying} R_{3} \rightarrow 3 R_{3}-R_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \\ z \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c} 6 \\ -6 \\ 3 \end{array}\right][/latex]
since the rank of coefficient matrix is 2 and rank of argument matrix is 3, which are not equal. Hence, system has no solution.

Square cross-section,

raw_source.text: In a Rankine cycle, regeneration results in higher efficiency because
raw_source.solution:
From the observation of the T-s diagram of the rankine cycle, it reveals that heat is transferred to the working fluid during process 2-2' at a relatively low temperature. This lowers the average heat addition temperature and thus the cycle efficiency.
To remove this remedy, we look for the ways to raise the temperature of the liquid leaving the pump (called the feed water ) before it enters the boiler. One possibility is to transfer heat to the feed water from the expanding steam in a counter flow heat exchanger built into the turbine, that is, to use regeneration. A practical regeneration process in steam power plant is accomplished by extracting steam from the turbine at various points. This steam is used to heat the feed water and the device where the feed water is heated by regeneration is called feed water heater. So, regeneration improves cycle efficiency by increasing the average temperature of heat addition in the boiler.
options: heat is added before steam enters the low pressure turbine
average temperature of heat addition in the boiler increases
total work delivered by the turbine increases

raw_answer.option_text: average temperature of heat addition in the boiler increases

raw_source.text: The symbol used for Transport in work study is

Consider the system of simultaneous equation
[latex]x+2y+z=6[/latex]
[latex]2x+y+2z=6[/latex]
[latex]x+y+z=5[/latex]
This system has
raw_source.solution:
Given equation are
[latex] \begin{array}{r} x+2 y+z=6 \\ 2 x+y+2 z=6 \\ x+y+z=5 \end{array}[/latex]
Given system can be written as
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{lll} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \\ z \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l} 6 \\ 6 \\ 5 \end{array}\right][/latex]
Applying row operation
[latex] \begin{array}{l} R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}-2 R_{1}, R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3}-R_{1} \\ {\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \\ z \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c} 6 \\ -6 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]} \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \text{and applying} R_{3} \rightarrow 3 R_{3}-R_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \\ z \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c} 6 \\ -6 \\ 3 \end{array}\right][/latex]
since the rank of coefficient matrix is 2 and rank of argument matrix is 3, which are not equal. Hence, system has no solution.

raw_source.text: A bullet of mass "m" travels at a very high velocity v (as shown in the figure) and gets embedded inside the block of mass "M" initially at rest on a rough horizontal floor. raw_source.solution:
From conservation of linear momentum
[latex] \begin{aligned} m V&=(M+m) U\\ \therefore \quad U & =\frac{m V}{M+m} \\ \vec{f}_{k} & =\mu N(-\hat{i}) \\ \vec{f}_{k} & =\mu(M+m) g(-\hat{i}) \\ \vec{a} & =\frac{7_{k}}{(M+m)} \\ \vec{a} & =\mu g(-\hat{i}) \\ \text{Now }\quad V_{2}^{2}&=U^{2}-2 \mu g s \\ \therefore & 0=\left(\frac{m V}{M+m}\right)^{2}-2 \mu g s \\ \therefore & V=\left(\frac{M+m}{m}\right) \sqrt{2 \mu g s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A flexible rotor - shaft system comprises of a 10 kg rotor disc placed in the middle of a mass - less shaft of diameter 30mm and length 500 mm between bearing (shaft is being taken mass - less as the equivalent mass of the shaft is included in the rotor mass) mounted at the ends. The bearings are assumed to simulate simply supported boundary conditions. The shaft is made of steel for which the value of E is  [latex]2.1 \times 10^{11}[/latex]Pa.  What is the critical speed of rotation of the shaft?
raw_source.solution:
For shaft loaded at middle with mass M
[latex] \text { Deflection: } \Delta=\frac{M g l^{3}}{48 E I}[/latex]
Moment of inertia,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I &=\frac{\pi}{64} d^{4}=\frac{\pi}{64} \times\left(30 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{4} \\ &=3.976 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{m}^{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So; deflection of shaft,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Delta=\frac{M g l^{3}}{48 E I}=\frac{10 \times 9.81 \times\left(500 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{3}}{48 \times 2.1 \times 10^{11} \times 3.976 \times 10^{-8}}\\ =3.06 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{m} \\ \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{g}{\Delta}}=\sqrt{\frac{9.81}{3.06 \times 10^{-5}}}=566.24 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{array}[/latex]
Natural frequency,
[latex] f_{n}=\frac{\omega_{n}}{2 \pi}=\frac{566.24}{2 \pi}=90.11 \mathrm{Hz}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Air flow through a venture and into atmosphere. Air density is a [latex]\rho[/latex]; atmospheric pressure is [latex]P_{a}[/latex]; throat diameter is [latex]D_{t}[/latex]; exit diameter is D and exit velocity is U. The throat is connected to a cylinder containing a frictionless piston attached to a spring. The spring constant is k. The bottom surface of the piston is exposed to atmosphere. Due to the flow, the piston moves by distance x. Assuming incompressible frictionless flow, x is
raw_source.solution:
Applying continuity equation, we get


[latex]\begin{aligned} A_1V_1&=A_2V_2\\ V_1&=\left ( \frac{A_2}{A_1} \right )V_2=\left ( \frac{\frac{\pi}{4}D^2}{\frac{\pi}{4}D_t^2} \right )U\\ V_1&=\left ( \frac{D}{D_t} \right )^2U\;\;...(i)\\ &\text{Applying Bernoulli's equation}\\ \frac{p_1}{\rho g}+\frac{V_1^2}{2g}&=\frac{p_2}{\rho g}+\frac{V_2^2}{2g}\\ [z_1=z_2 & \text{ because venturi is horizontal}]\\ \frac{p_1-p_2}{\rho g}&=\frac{V_2^2-V_1^2}{2g}\\ p_1-p_2&=\frac{\rho}{2}(V_2^2-V_1^2)\\ &\text{From Eq.(i), we get}\\ p_1-p_2&=\frac{\rho }{2}\left [ U^2-\left ( \frac{D}{D_t} \right )^4 U^2 \right ]\\ &=\frac{\rho }{2}U^2\left [ 1-\left ( \frac{D}{D_t} \right )^4 \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Since, spring force}&= \text{ pressure force due to air}\\ -kx&=\frac{\pi}{4}D_s^2 \times (p_1-p_2)\\ &\text{From Eq. (ii), we get}\\ -kx&=\frac{\pi}{4}D_s^2 \times \frac{\rho U^2}{2}\left [ 1- \left ( \frac{D}{D_t} \right )^4\right ]\\ \therefore \;\;x&=\frac{\rho U^2}{8k}\left [ \left (\frac{D}{D_t} \right )^4-1 \right ] \pi D_s^2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a gas turbine, hot combustion products with the specific heats [latex]C_{p}[/latex]
 = 0.98 kJ/kgK, and [latex]C_{v}[/latex]
 = 0.7538 kJ/kgK, enter the turbine at 20 bar, 1500K exit at 1 bar. The isentropic efficiency of the turbine is 0.94 .The work developed by the turbine per kg of gas flow is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} c_{p} &=0.98 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ c_{v} &=0.7538 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ p_{1} &=20 \mathrm{bar} \\ T_{1} &=1500 \mathrm{K} \\ p_{2} &=1 \mathrm{bar} \\ \eta_{\mathrm{isen}} &=0.94 \\ \gamma &=\frac{c_{p}}{c_{v}}=\frac{0.98}{0.7538}=1.3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
For process 1-2 s
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{T_{1}}{T_{2 s}} &=\left(\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}} \\ \frac{1500}{T_{2 s}} &=\left(\frac{20}{1}\right)^{\frac{1.3-1}{1.3}}=(20)^{0.2307}=1.996 \\ \text{or}\quad T_{2 s} &=751.50 \mathrm{K} \\ \eta_{\mathrm{isen}} &=\frac{T_{1}-T_{2}}{T_{1}-T_{2 s}} \\ 0.94 &=\frac{1500-T_{2}}{1500-751.50} \\ &=\frac{1500-T_{2}}{748.5} \\ \text{or}\quad 1500-T_{2}&=0.94 \times 748.5=703.59 \\ \text{or}\quad T_{2}&=796.41 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Work developed by the turbine per kg of gas,
[latex] \begin{aligned} w &=c_{p}\left(T_{1}-T_{2}\right) \\ &=0.98(1500-796.41) \\ &=689.51 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A centrifugal pump running at 500 rpm and at its maximum efficiency is delivering a head of 30 m at flow rate of 60 litres per minutes. If the rpm is changed to 1000, then the head H in meters and flow rate Q in litres per minute at maximum efficiency are estimated to be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} &Condition-1 &Condition-2\\ N_{1}&=500 \mathrm{rpm} &N_{2}=100 \mathrm{rpm}\\ H_{1}&=30 \mathrm{m} &H_{2}=?\\ Q_{1}&=60 \text { litre/min } &Q_{2}=?\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Unit speed: }\quad N_{u}&=\frac{N}{\sqrt{H}} \\ \left(N_{u}\right)_{1}&=\left(N_{v}\right)_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1}}{\sqrt{H_{1}}}&=\frac{N_{2}}{\sqrt{H_{2}}} \\ \frac{500}{\sqrt{30}}&=\frac{1000}{\sqrt{H_{2}}} \\ \text{or}\quad \sqrt{H_{2}}&=\frac{1000}{500} \times \sqrt{30}=2 \times \sqrt{30}\\ \text{or }\quad H_{2}&=4 \times 30=120 \mathrm{m}\\ \text{Unit speed: }Q_{u}&=\frac{Q}{\sqrt{H}}\\ \left(Q_{u}\right)_{1}&=\left(Q_{u}\right)_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1}}{\sqrt{H_{1}}}&=\frac{N_{2}}{\sqrt{H_{2}}} \\ \frac{500}{\sqrt{30}}&=\frac{1000}{\sqrt{H_{2}}}\\ \text{or}\quad\sqrt{H_{2}}&=\frac{1000}{500} \times \sqrt{30}=2 \times \sqrt{30}\\ \text{or }\quad H_{2}&=4 \times 30=120 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A batch of 10 cutting tools could produce 500 components while working at 50 rpm with a tool feed of 0.25 mm/rev and depth of cut of 1 mm. A similar batch of 10 tools of the same specification could produce 122 components while working at 80 rpm with a feed of 0.25 mm/rev and 1 mm depth of cut. How many components can be produced with one cutting tool at 60 rpm.
raw_source.solution:
Velocity of first cutting tool
[latex] V_{1}=50 \times 0.25=12.5 \mathrm{mm} / \mathrm{min}[/latex]
Velocity of second cutting tool
[latex] V_{2}=0.25 \times 80=20 \mathrm{mm} / \mathrm{min}[/latex]
since tool life = no. of component produce [latex]\times [/latex] tool constant
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Tool life for first tool,
[latex] T_{1}=500 \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Tool life for second tool,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \qquad T_{2}&=122 \mathrm{K} \\ \text { Now, } V_{1} T_{1}^{n}&=V_{2} T_{2}^{n} \\ \Rightarrow(12.5) \times(500 \mathrm{K})^{n}&=20 \times(122 \mathrm{K})^{n}\\ \therefore \qquad\left(\frac{500}{122}\right)^{n}&=1.6 \\ \therefore \qquad n&=0.333 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence number of components produced by one cutting tool at 60 rpm
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow 12.5 \times\left(\frac{500 k}{10}\right)^{0.333}=60 \times 0.25 \times(x k) 0.333 \\ \left(\frac{x}{50}\right)^{0.333}=\frac{12.5}{60 \times 0.25} \\ \left(\frac{x}{50}\right)^{0.333}=\frac{12.5}{60 \times 0.25} \\ \therefore \quad x=29 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two machines of the same production rate are available for use. On machine 1, the fixed cost is Rs. 100 and the variable cost is Rs. 2 per piece produced. Let n quantities are produced by each machine.
The total cost in production
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=100+2 \times n+200+n \\ &=300+3 n \end{aligned}[/latex]
For the first 800 units, selling price is 3.50 Rs/Units
Hence for breakeven point
[latex] \begin{aligned} 300+3 n&=3.5 \times 2 n\\ \therefore \quad 7 n&=300+3 n\\ \text{or}\quad n&=75\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

Two other points A and B are located on the line OZ at distances [latex]r_{A}[/latex] and [latex]r_{B}[/latex] from O respectively.


The acceleration of point B with respect to point A is a vector of magnitude
raw_source.solution:
Acceleration of point B with respect to point A
[latex] \begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{a_{B / A}} &=\vec{a}_{B}-\vec{a}_{A} \\ &=\overrightarrow{\omega^{2} r_{B}}-\overrightarrow{\omega^{2} r_{A}} \\ &=\omega^{2}\left(r_{B}-r_{A}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex] in direction from Z to O
options:
[latex]\omega (r_{B}-r_{A})[/latex]
 and direction same as the direction of motion of point B

[latex]\omega ^{2}(r_{B}-r_{A})[/latex]
 and direction opposite to be direction of motion of point B

[latex]\omega ^{2}(r_{B}-r_{A})[/latex]
 and direction from Z to O.

raw_answer.option_text:
[latex]\omega ^{2}(r_{B}-r_{A})[/latex]
 and direction from Z to O.

raw_source.text:
A uniform rigid slenderbar of mass 10 kg, hinged at the left end is suspended with the help of spring and damper arrangement as shown in the figure where K = 2 kN/m, C = 500 Ns/m and the stiffness of the torsional spring [latex]K_{\theta }[/latex] is 1 kN/m/rad. Ignore the hinge dimensions.


The un-damped natural frequency of oscillations of the bar about the hinge point is
raw_source.solution:
For small feflection, after equlibrium

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now,}\quad \theta &=\frac{x_{1}}{0.4}=\frac{x_{2}}{0.5} \\ \therefore \quad x_{1} &=0.4\;\theta\\ \text{and}\quad x_{2}&=0.5\;\theta \end{aligned}[/latex]
Moment of inertia
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\frac{m l_{2}^{2}}{3}=\frac{10 \times(0.5)^{2}}{3} \\ =0.833 \mathrm{kgm}^{2} \end{array}[/latex]
Now, from Newton's law of motion
[latex] \begin{aligned} & c\dot{x}_{1} l_{1}+k x_{2} l_{2}+k_{\theta} \cdot \theta+I \ddot{\theta}=0 \\ &\Rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}_{1}^{2} \dot{\theta}+\mathrm{k} l_{2}^{2} \theta+\mathrm{k}_{\theta} \cdot \theta+\mathrm{l} \ddot{\mathbf{\theta}}=0 \\ &\Rightarrow 500 \times(0.4)^{2} \dot{\theta}+\left(2000 \times(0.5)^{2}+1000\right) \theta \\ &+0.833 \ddot{\theta}=0\\ &\Rightarrow0.833\ddot{\theta}+80\dot{\theta}+1500\theta \qquad \cdots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equation can be written as:
[latex] \begin{aligned} I \ddot{\theta}+C_{T} \dot{\theta}+K_{T} \theta&=0\\ \therefore \qquad I&=0.833\\ C_{T}&=80 \\ K_{T}&=1500 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now natural frequency,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega_{n} &=\sqrt{\frac{k_{T}}{I}}=\sqrt{\frac{1500}{0.833}} \\ &=42.43 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
