raw_source.text:
The overall gear ratio in a 2 stage speed reduction gear box (with all spur gears) is 12. The input and output shafts of the gear box are collinear. The countershaft which is parallel to the input and output shafts has a gear ([latex]Z_{2}[/latex] teeth) and pinion([latex]Z_{3}[/latex] =15 teeth) to mesh with pinion ([latex]Z_{1}[/latex] =16 teeth) on the input shaft and gear ([latex]Z_{4}[/latex] teeth) on the output shaft respectively. It was decided to use a gear ratio of 4 with 3 module in the first stage and 4 module in the second stage.

[latex]Z_{2}[/latex] and [latex]Z_{4}[/latex] are
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{N_{1}}{N_{4}}&=12 \\ \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}&=4=\frac{D_{2}}{D_{1}} \\ m_{1} & =3, m_{2}=4 \\ \text { since, }\qquad & \frac{D_{1}}{Z_{1}}=\frac{D_{2}}{Z_{2}} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{Z_{1}}{Z_{2}}=\frac{D_{1}}{D_{2}}=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ Z_{2} & =Z_{1} \times 4=64\\ \text{and }\quad \frac{N_{1}}{N_{4}}&=\frac{D_{2} \times D_{4}}{D_{1} \times D_{3}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 12&=\frac{D_{4}}{D_{3}} \times 4 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{D_{4}}{D_{3}}&=3 \\ since, \quad \frac{Z_{3}}{Z_{4}}&=\frac{D_{3}}{D_{4}} \\ Z_{4}&=Z_{3} \frac{D_{4}}{D_{3}}=15 \times 3=45 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The overall gear ratio in a 2 stage speed reduction gear box (with all spur gears) is 12. The input and output shafts of the gear box are collinear. The countershaft which is parallel to the input and output shafts has a gear ([latex]Z_{2}[/latex] teeth) and pinion([latex]Z_{3}[/latex] =15 teeth) to mesh with pinion ([latex]Z_{1}[/latex] =16 teeth) on the input shaft and gear ([latex]Z_{4}[/latex] teeth) on the output shaft respectively. It was decided to use a gear ratio of 4 with 3 module in the first stage and 4 module in the second stage.

The centre distance in the second stage is
raw_source.solution:
Centre distance in second stage
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{D_{3}+D_{4}}{2} \\ m &=\frac{D_{3}}{Z_{3}}=\frac{D_{4}}{Z_{4}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 4&=\frac{D_{4}}{45} \\ \Rightarrow \quad D_{4}&=180 \mathrm{mm}\\ D_{3}&=\frac{180}{3}=60 \mathrm{mm} \\ \text{Centre distance }&=\frac{180+60}{2}=120 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A syringe with a frictionless plunger contacts water and has its end a 100mm longer needle of 1mm diameter .The internal diameter of the syringe is 10mm. Water density is [latex]1000kg/m^{3}[/latex]. The plunger is pushed in at 10 mm/s and the water comes out as a jet


Assuming ideal flow, the force F in Newton required on the plunger to push out the water is
raw_source.solution:
Applying continuity equation at sections 1 and 2 we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{1} v_{1} &=A_{2} V_{2} \\ v_{2} &=\left(\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}\right) v_{1} \\ v_{2} &=\frac{\frac{\pi}{4} \times(0.01)^{2}}{\frac{\pi}{4} \times(0.001)^{2}} \times 0.01 \\ &=1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying Bernoulli's equation at sections 1 and 2 we get
[latex] \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}+\frac{v_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{v_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{2} [/latex]
since [latex]\quad z_{1}=z_{2} [/latex]
and taking gauge pressure
[latex]\begin{aligned} p_{2} &=0 \quad (atmospheric)\\ \therefore \quad \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g} &=\frac{V_{2}^{2}-V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}\\ p_{1} &=\frac{\rho}{2}\left(V_{2}^{2}-V_{1}^{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{1000}{2}\left[(1)^{2}-(0.01)^{2}\right] \\ &=499.95 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\\ &\text{Force required on plunger},\\ &=p_{1} \times A_{1}=499.95 \times \frac{\pi}{4} \times(0.01)^{2} \\ &=0.039 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text:
A syringe with a frictionless plunger contacts water and has its end a 100mm longer needle of 1mm diameter .The internal diameter of the syringe is 10mm. Water density is [latex]1000kg/m^{3}[/latex]. The plunger is pushed in at 10 mm/s and the water comes out as a jet


Neglect losses in the cylinder and assume fully developed laminar viscous flow throughout the needle; the Darcy friction factor is 64/Re. Where Re is the Reynolds number. Give that the viscosity of water is [latex]1.0\times 10^{-3}[/latex] kg/s m , the force F in Newton required on the plunger is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Re} &=\frac{\rho V_{2} d_{2}}{\mu}=\frac{1000 \times 1 \times 0.001}{1 \times 10^{-3}} \\ &=1000 \end{aligned}\\ \text{Now Darcy's friction factor},\\ f=\frac{64}{\operatorname{Re}}=\frac{64}{1000}=0.064\\ \text{Head loss in needle,} \\ \begin{aligned} h_{f} &=\frac{f L V^{2}}{2 g d}=\frac{0.064 \times 0.1 \times(1)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.001} \\ &=0.3262 \mathrm{m} \text { of water } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying Bernoulli's equation at points and we get
[latex] \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{2}+h_{f} [/latex]
[latex]\text{since }\quad z_{1}=z_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \text{and }\quad p_{2}=0 \qquad (atmospheric)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g} &=\left(\frac{V_{2}^{2}-V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}\right)+h_{f} \\ p_{1} &=\frac{\rho}{2}\left(V_{2}^{2}-V_{1}^{2}\right)+\rho g h_{f} \\ &=\frac{1000}{2}\left[(1)^{2}-(0.01)^{2}\right] \\ &+1000 \times 9.81 \times 0.3262 \\ &=3699.97 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Force required on plunger,
[latex] =p_{1} \times A_{1}=3699.97 \times \frac{\pi}{4} \times(0.01)^{2}\\ =0.29 \mathrm{N}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text:
Heat is being transferred by convection from water at [latex]48^{\circ}C[/latex] to a glass plate whose surface that is exposed to the water is at [latex]40^{\circ}C[/latex]. The thermal conductivity of water is 0.6 W/mK and the thermal conductivity of glass is 1.2 W/mK. The spatial gradient of temperature in the water at the water - glass interface is [latex]dT/dy =1\times 10^{4}[/latex] K/m


The value of the temperature gradient in the glass at the water-glass interface in K/m is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]T_{w} = 48^{o}C; T_{g}=40^{o}C[/latex]
[latex] k_{w} = 0.6 W/mk; k_{g}= 1.2W/mk[/latex]
[latex] \left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{w}=1 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{m} [/latex]
At water-glass interface,
[latex] \begin{aligned} -k_{w} A\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{w}&=-k_{g} A\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{g} \\ \text { or } k_{w}\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{w} &=k_{g}\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{g} \\ 0.6 \times 1 \times 10^{4} &=1.2 \times\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{g} \\\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{g} &=0.5 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Heat is being transferred by convection from water at [latex]48^{\circ}C[/latex] to a glass plate whose surface that is exposed to the water is at [latex]40^{\circ}C[/latex]. The thermal conductivity of water is 0.6 W/mK and the thermal conductivity of glass is 1.2 W/mK. The spatial gradient of temperature in the water at the water - glass interface is [latex]dT/dy =1\times 10^{4}[/latex] K/m


The heat transfer coefficient h in [latex]W/m^{2}[/latex] K is
raw_source.solution:
For water
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left(Q_{\text {conv }}\right)_{\text {water }} &=\left(Q_{\text {cond }}\right)_{\text {vater }} \\ n_{w} A\left(T_{w}-T_{g}\right) &=k_{w} A\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{w}\\ \text{or} \quad A\left(T_{w}-T_{g}\right) &=k_{w}\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{w} \\ h_{w} \times(48-40) &=0.6 \times 1 \times 10^{4}\\ \text{or }\quad h_{w}&=750 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Nitrogen gas (molecular weight 28) is enclosed in a cylinder by a piston, at the initial condition of 2 bar, 298 K and 1 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]. In a particular process, the gas slowly expands under isothermal condition, until the volume becomes [latex]2m^{3}[/latex]. Heat exchange occurs with the atmosphere at 298 K during this process.

The work interaction for the Nitrogen gas is
raw_source.solution:
For isothermal process
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Work } &=p_{1} V_{1} \ln \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} \\ &=\left(2 \times 10^{5}\right) \times(1) \times \ln \frac{2}{1} \\ &=138629.4 \mathrm{J}=138.63 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Nitrogen gas (molecular weight 28) is enclosed in a cylinder by a piston, at the initial condition of 2 bar, 298 K and [latex]m^{3}[/latex]. In a particular process, the gas slowly expands under isothermal condition, until the volume becomes [latex]2m^{3}[/latex]. Heat exchange occurs with the atmosphere at 298 K during this process.

The entropy change for universe during the process in kJ/K is
raw_source.solution:
Given process is isothermal, so change in entropy of universe

[latex](dS)_{universe}=(dS)_{system}+(dS)_{surrounding}[/latex]
Work done in isothermal process
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=P_1V_1 lm(V_2/V_1) \\ &=200 \times 1 ln(2/1) \\ &= 138.62 kJ\\ \delta Q&=dU+\delta W\\ \delta Q&=138.62 kJ\;\;(\because \; dU=0) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat taken by sirrounding to the system =138.62 KJ
Change in entropy of surrounding
[latex] (dS)_{surr}=\frac{-138.62}{298}=-0.465 kJ/K[/latex]
Mass of nitrogen gas [latex]=\frac{PV}{RT}=\frac{200 \times 1 }{\frac{8.314}{28} \times 298}[/latex]
[latex] m=2.26kg[/latex]
Change in entropy of system
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=mc_v ln\left ( \frac{T_2}{T_1} \right )+mR ln\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right ) \\ &=mR ln \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right ) \;\;\because \; T_1=T_2\\ &= 2.26 \times \frac{8.314}{28} ln\left ( \frac{2}{1} \right )\\ &= 0.456kJ/K\\ (dS)_{universe}&=0.465-0.465 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Therefore, option (C) is correct.

raw_source.text:
A refrigerator based on ideal vapour compression cycle operates between the temperature limits of [latex]-20^{\circ}C[/latex] and [latex]40^{\circ}C[/latex]. The refrigerant enters the condenser as saturated vapour and leaves as saturated liquid. The enthalpy and entropy values for saturated liquid and vapour at these temperatures are given in the table below.


If refrigerant circulation rate is 0.025 kg/s, the refrigeration effect is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]m=0.025 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
[latex] At \quad T_{C}=40^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex]
From given table, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{2}=h_{g}=200 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ s_{2}=s_{g}=0.67 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ h_{3}=h_{f}= 80 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}=h_{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \text{At }\quad T_{e}=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
From given table, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} s_{f} &=0.07 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K} \\ \mathrm{s}_{g} &=0.7366 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ h_{f} &=20 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}, h_{g}=180 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ s_{1} &=s_{2}=s_{f}+x_{1}\left(s_{g}-s_{f}\right) \\ 0.67 &=0.07+x_{1}(0.7366-0.07)\\ \text{or}\quad x_{1} &= 0.9 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Specific enthalpy at point 1
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{1} &=h_{f}+x_{1}\left(h_{g}-h_{f}\right) \\ &=20+0.9(180-20) \\ &=164 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Refrigeation effect
[latex] \mathrm{Re}=m\left(h_{1}-h_{4}\right) =0.025(164-80)=2.1kW[/latex]

A refrigerator based on ideal vapour compression cycle operates between the temperature limits of [latex]-20^{\circ}C[/latex] and [latex]40^{\circ}C[/latex]. The refrigerant enters the condenser as saturated vapour and leaves as saturated liquid. The enthalpy and entropy values for saturated liquid and vapour at these temperatures are given in the table below.


The COP of the refrigerator is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{COP} &=\frac{\text { Refrigeration effect }}{\text { Work input }} \\ &=\frac{\mathrm{Re}}{W}=\frac{2.1}{m\left(h_{2}-h_{1}\right)} \\ &=\frac{2.1}{0.025(200-164)} \\ &=2.33 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylinder is turned on a lathe with orthogonal machining principle. Spindle rotates at 200 rpm. The axial feed rate is 0.25 mm per revolution. Depth of cut is 0.4 mm. The rake angle is [latex]10^{\circ}[/latex] . In the analysis it is found that the shear angle is [latex]27.75^{\circ}[/latex] .

The thickness of the produced chip is
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} N &=200 \mathrm{rpm} \\ \text { Feed }\left(t_{1}\right) &=\text { uncut chip thickness }=0.25 \\ \text { Depth } &=0.4 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Rake angle,
[latex] \alpha=10^{\circ}[/latex]
Shear angle,
[latex] \phi=27.75^{\circ}[/latex]
We Know
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tan \phi &=\frac{\cos \alpha}{\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}-\sin \alpha} \\ \Rightarrow \quad t_{2} &=t_{1}\left[\frac{\cos \alpha}{\tan \phi}+\sin \alpha\right] \\ &=0.25\left[\frac{\cos 10^{\circ}}{\tan 27.75^{\circ}}+\sin 10^{\circ}\right] \\ &=0.511 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylinder is turned on a lathe with orthogonal machining principle. Spindle rotates at 200 rpm. The axial feed rate is 0.25 mm per revolution. Depth of cut is 0.4 mm. The rake angle is [latex]10^{\circ}[/latex] . In the analysis it is found that the shear angle is [latex]27.75^{\circ}[/latex] .

In the above problem, the coefficient of friction at the chip tool interface obtained using Earnest and Merchant theory is
raw_source.solution:
From earnest and merchant theory
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 \phi+\lambda-\alpha &=90^{\circ} \\ \lambda &=90^{\circ}+10-2 \times 27.75^{\circ} \\ \therefore \qquad \lambda &=44.5^{\circ} \\ \mu &=\tan \left(44.5^{\circ}\right)=0.98 \end{aligned}[/latex]

If [latex]x=a(\theta +\sin \theta )[/latex]
 and [latex]y=a(1-\cos \theta )[/latex],  then [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}[/latex]
 will be equal to

A delayed unit step function is defined as [latex]u(t-a)=\int_{1 \;for \; t\geq a}^{0 \; for t \; \lt a}[/latex].
 Its Laplace transform is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} L(u(t-a)) &=\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-s t} u(t-s) d t \\ &=\int_{0}^{a} e^{-s t} u(t-s) d t\\ &+\int_{a}^{\infty} e^{-s t} u(t-a) d t \\ &=\frac{\left[e^{-s t}\right]_{a}^{\infty}}{-s}\\&=e^{-\infty \times t}-\frac{e^{-s a}}{-s}=\frac{e^{-s a}}{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: One dimensional unsteady state heat transfer equation for a sphere with heat generation at the rate of 'q' can be written as
raw_source.solution:
The one dimensional time dependent heat conduction equation can be written more compactly as a simple equation,
[latex]\frac{1}{r^{n}}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( r^{n} \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \right )+\frac{q}{k}=\frac{\rho c}{k }\frac{\partial }{\partial t}[/latex]

where,
n = 0, For rectangular coordinates
n = 1, For cylindrical coordinates
n = 2, For spherical coordinates
Further, while using rectangular coordinates it is customary to replace the r-variable by the x-variable.
For sphere, substitute r = 2 in above equation

[latex]\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( r^{2} \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \right )+\frac{q}{k}=\frac{\rho c}{k }\frac{\partial }{\partial t}[/latex]

[latex]\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( r^{2} \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \right )+\frac{q}{k}=\frac{1}{\alpha }\frac{\partial }{\partial t}[/latex]

as [latex]\alpha =\frac{k}{\rho c}=\text{thermal diffusivity}[/latex]
options: [latex]\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left ( r \frac{\partial T}{\partial r} \right )+\frac{q}{k}=\frac{1}{\alpha }\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} v&=7.4 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ S&=0.88\\ \therefore \qquad \rho&=1000 \times 0.88=880 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ U&=0.5 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ h&=0.5 \mathrm{mm}=0.0005 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]


Dynamic viscosity,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mu &=\rho v=880 \times 7.4 \times 10^{-7} \\ &=6.512 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Ns} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Shear stress: } \tau &=u \frac{d u}{d y} \\ \text { where } d u&=u-0=0.5 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ d y &=h=0.0005 \mathrm{m}\\ \therefore \quad \tau &=\frac{6.512 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.5}{0.0005} \\ &=0.651 \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The compression ratio of a gas power plant cycle corresponding to maximum work output for the given temperature limits of [latex]T_{min}[/latex]
 and [latex]T_{max}[/latex]
 will be
raw_source.solution:
Work output during the cycle
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=m c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right)-m c_{p}\left(T_{4}-T_{1}\right) \\ &=m c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{4}\right)-m c_{p}\left(T_{2}-T_{1}\right) \\ &=m c_{p}\left[T_{3}\left(1-\frac{T_{4}}{T_{3}}\right)-T_{1}\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}-1\right)\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
since
[latex] \frac{T_{3}}{T_{4}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}=\left(r_{p}\right) \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma} \quad\left(\text { Let } \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}=x, m c_{p}=K\right)[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Work/cycle
[latex] =K\left[T_{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{r_{p}^{x}}\right)-T_{1}\left(r_{p}^{x}-1\right)\right][/latex]
For maximum power, differentiate with respect to [latex]r_{p}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d W}{d r_{p}}&=K\left[T_{3} \times \frac{x}{r_{p}(x+1)}-T_{1} \times r_{p}^{(x-1)}\right]=0 \\ &\qquad (For max.)\\ \Rightarrow \frac{x T_{3}}{r_{p}(x+1)}&=T_{1} \times\left(r_{p}\right)^{x-1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad r_{p}^{2 x}&=\frac{T_{3}}{T_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad r_{p}&=\left(\frac{T_{3}}{T_{1}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2 x}} \\ \text{or }\quad r_{p}&=\left(\frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{2(\gamma-1)}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{C} &=2 \mathrm{m} \omega_{n}=2 \times 20 \times 31.32 \\ & \approx 1250 \mathrm{Ns} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Tightening force } &=2200 \mathrm{N} \\ \text { Pitch } &=0.004 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad \text { Torque } &=\text { Tightening force } \times \frac{\text { Pitch }}{2 \pi} \\ &=2200 \times \frac{0.004}{2 \pi}=1.4 \mathrm{Nm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The figure below shows a steel rod of [latex]25 mm^{2}[/latex] cross sectional area. It is loaded at four points, K, L, M and N. Assume [latex]E_{steel}=200 GPa[/latex]. The total change in length of the rod due to loading is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given: } & & \text { Area } &=25 \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ & & E_{\text {steel }} &=200 \mathrm{GPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]


At face [latex] L 250 \mathrm{N} [/latex] axial load is acting towards right hence ([latex]x \gt y[/latex])
[latex] \therefore x-y=250 N[/latex]
At face [latex] M 200 \mathrm{N} [/latex] axial load is acting towards left hence ([latex]z \gt y[/latex])
[latex] \therefore z-y=200 N[/latex]
x=100N [on compairing load on K face of steel rod and K face of I]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { If } \quad & x=100 \mathrm{N} \\ \text { and } \quad x-y &=250 \\ y &=-150 \mathrm{N}\\ \text{If }\quad y&=-150 \mathrm{N}\\ \text { and } \quad z-y &=200 \\ z &=50 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta l_{\mathrm{total}} &=\Delta l_{\mathrm{I}}+\Delta l_{\mathrm{II}}+\Delta l_{\mathrm{II}} \\ \Delta l_{\mathrm{I}} &=\frac{x L}{A E}=\frac{+100 \times 500}{25 \times\left\{200 \times 10^{3}\right\}}=0.01 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex] \Delta l_{\mathrm{Il}}=\frac{y L}{A E}=\frac{-150 \times[1700-\{500+400]]}{25 \times\left\{200 \times 10^{3}\right\}}[/latex]


[latex]\Delta l_{\mathrm{III}}=\frac{z L}{A E}=\frac{50 \times 400}{25 \times\left\{200 \times 10^{3}\right\}}=4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{mm}[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta l_{\mathrm{Total}} &=\Delta l_{1}+\Delta l_{2}+\Delta l_{3} \\ &=0.01-0.024+4 \times 10^{-3} \\ &=-0.01 \mathrm{mm}=0.01 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m}\\ &=-1 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{m} \\ &= \frac{-1 \times 10^{-5} \times 10}{10} \mathrm{m}\\& =-10 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}=-10\mathrm{\mu m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An ejector mechanism consists of a helical compression spring having a spring constant of K = [latex]981\times 10^{3}[/latex] N/m. it is pre-compressed by 100 mm from its free state. If it is used to eject a mass of 100 kg held on it, the mass will move up through a distance of
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\frac{1}{2} K x^{2} [/latex] will be converted into G.P.E. (taking
reference as compressd condition)
[latex] \frac{1}{2} K x^{2}=m g h[/latex]
or [latex] \quad \frac{1}{2} \times 981 \times 10^{3} \times .1^{2}=100 \times 9.81 \mathrm{h} [/latex]
[latex] h=5 \mathrm{m}=5000 \mathrm{mm}[/latex]
OR
When spring will reach its natural length, K.E of the block of mass 100 kg held on it. (taking reference at natural length of spring)
[latex] \frac{1}{2} k x^{2}-m g x=\frac{1}{2} m V^{2} \quad[x=0.1 \mathrm{m}][/latex]
and this K.E will be converted into mgh
Total lift of block
[latex] =h+x [/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{2} \times 981 \times 10^{3} \times .1^{2}-100 \times 9.81 \times 1= m g h=100 \times 9.81 \times h [/latex]
[latex] h =4.9 \mathrm{m} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad h+x =4.9+0.1=5 \mathrm{m}=5000 \mathrm{mm}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rigid body shown in the Fig.(a) has a mass of 10 kg. It rotates with a uniform angular velocity '[latex]\omega[/latex]'. A balancing mass of 20 kg is attached as shown in Fig. (b). The percentage increase in mass moment of inertia as a result of this addition is
raw_source.solution:
Moment of intertia of first [latex] =m k^{2} [/latex]
[latex] =10 \times(0.2)^{2} [/latex]
[latex] =0.4 \mathrm{kgm}^{2}[/latex]
Moment of intertia of second
[latex] =m_{1} k_{1}^{2}+m_{2} k_{2}^{2}[/latex]
[latex] =10 \times(0.2)^{2}+20 \times(0.1)^{2}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Increases in mass moment of intertia
[latex] =\frac{0.6-0.4}{0.4} \times 100=50 \%[/latex]

raw_source.text: The figure shows a pair of pinjointed gripper tongs holding an object weighing 2000 N. The coefficient of friction ([latex]\mu[/latex]) at the gripping surface is 0.1XX is the line of action of the input force and YY is the line of application of gripping force. If the pinjoint is assumed to be frictionless, the magnitude of force F required to hold the weight is
raw_source.solution:
FBD of object

[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 f &=2000 \\ f &=1000=\mu N=0.1 \times N \\ N &=10000 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Considering one tong of gripper.
Taking net moment about hinge point of gripper tong zero (because it is in equilibrium).
As we are taking moment about hinge so no need to consider hinge reaction.

[latex] \begin{aligned} F \times 300 &=N \times 150 \\ F &=\frac{N}{2}=\frac{10000}{2} \\ &=5000 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A solid circular shaft of 60 mm diameter transmits a torque of 1600 N.m. The value of maximum shear stress develop is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\tau_{\max }=\frac{16 T}{\pi d^{3}}=\frac{16 \times 1600 \times 10^{3}}{\pi \times(60)^{3}}=37.72 \mathrm{MPa}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a fluid flow through a divergent pipe of length L having inlet and outlet radii and [latex]R_{1}[/latex]
 and [latex]R_{2}[/latex]
 respectively and a constant flow rate of Q, assuming the velocity to be axial and uniform at any cross section, the acceleration at the exit is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} &a_{x}=u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+w \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\\ &\therefore \quad a_{x}=u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\\ &Q=A u \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{or }\quad u&=\frac{Q}{A} \\ u&=\frac{Q}{\pi \mathrm{R}^{2}} \\ R &= R_{1}+\frac{R_{2}-R_{1}}{L} \cdot x \\ let,\\ R_{1}&=a\text{ and } \frac{R_{2}-R_{1}}{L}=b \\ \therefore \quad R&=a+b x \\ u &=\frac{Q}{\pi(a+b x)^{2}} \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} &=\frac{-2 b Q}{\pi(a+b x)^{3}} \\ a_{x} &=u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \\ a_{x=L} &=\left.u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right|_{x=L} \end{aligned} [/latex]
and also replacing a and b
[latex] a_{x=L}=\frac{-2 Q^{2}\left(R_{1}-R_{2}\right)}{\pi^{2} L R_{2}^{5}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A closed cylinder having a radius R and height H is filled with oil density [latex]\rho[/latex]. If the cylinder is rotated about its axis at an angular velocity of  [latex]\omega[/latex], the thrust at the bottom of the cylinder is
raw_source.solution:
We know that
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial p}{\partial r}&=\frac{\rho v^{2}}{r}=\rho \omega^{2} r \\ \Rightarrow \quad \int_{0}^{p} \partial p&=\int_{0}^{f} \rho \omega^{2} r d r\\ \therefore \quad p&=\frac{\rho \omega^{2} r^{2}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Area of circular ring[latex] =2 \pi r d r [/latex]
Force on elementary ring
= Intensity of pressure x Area of ring
[latex] =\frac{\rho}{2} \omega^{2} r^{2} 2 \pi r d r[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Total force on the bottom of the cylinder due to rotation
[latex] \begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{R} \frac{\rho \omega^{2} r^{2}}{2} \cdot 2 \pi r d r &=\frac{\rho}{2} \omega^{2} \cdot 2 \pi \int_{0}^{R} r^{3} d r \\ &=\pi \omega^{2} \rho\left[\frac{r^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{R} \\ &=\rho \omega^{2} \cdot \frac{\pi R^{4}}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thrust at the bottom of the cylinder = weight of water in cylinder or force due to hydrostatic pressure + total force on the top of cylinder due to rotation
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\rho g \times \pi R^{2} \times H+\rho \omega^{2} \times \frac{\pi R^{4}}{4} \\ &=\pi R^{2}\left[\frac{\rho \omega^{2} R^{2}}{4}+\rho g H\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For air flow over a flat plate, velocity (U) and boundary layer thickness ([latex]\delta[/latex]) can be expressed respectively, as
[latex]\frac{U}{U_{a}}=\frac{3}{2}\frac{y}{\delta }-\frac{1}{2}\left ( \frac{y}{\delta } \right )^{3}; \delta =\frac{4.64x}{\sqrt{Re_{x}}}[/latex]
If the free stream velocity is 2m/s, and air has kinematic viscosity of [latex]1.5\times 10^{-5}m^{2}/s[/latex] and density of [latex]1.23 kg/m^{3}[/latex], the wall shear stress at x = 1m, is
raw_source.solution:
Reynold number
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Re}_{x}=\frac{u_{\infty} x}{u}=\frac{2 \times 1}{1.5 \times 10^{-5}}=1.33 \times 10^{5} \\ \delta=\frac{4.64 x}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Re}_{x}}}=\frac{4.64 \times 1}{\sqrt{1.33 \times 10^{5}}}=0.0127 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \text{Now, }\frac{d u}{d y}=u_{\infty}\left[\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\delta}-\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{y^{2}}{\delta^{3}}\right)\right][/latex]
[latex] \left.\frac{d u}{d y}\right|_{y=0}=\frac{3 u_{\infty}}{2 \delta}[/latex]
Now, shear stress,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tau_{0} &=\mu\left(\frac{d u}{d y}\right)_{y=0}=\mu \times \frac{3 u_{\infty}}{2 \delta} \\ &=\frac{3 u_{\infty} \times v \times \rho}{2 \delta} \quad \because \mu=v \rho \\ &=\frac{3 \times 2 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-5} \times 1.23}{2 \times 0.0127} \\ &=4.36 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: A centrifugal pump is required to pump water to an open water tank situated 4 km away from the location of the pump through a pipe of diameter 0.2 m having Darcy's friction factor of 0.01. The average speed of water in the pipe is 2 m/s. If it is maintain a constant head of 5 m in the tank, neglecting other minor losses, the absolute discharge pressure at the pump exit is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} l &=4 \mathrm{km}=4000 \mathrm{m} \\ d &=0.2 \mathrm{m} \\ f &=0.01 \\ V &=2 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ h &=5 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{f} &=\frac{f l V^{2}}{2 g d}=\frac{0.01 \times 4000 \times(2)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.2} \\ &=40.77 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Head produced by the pump,
[latex] \begin{aligned} H &=h+h_{f} \\ &=5+40.77=45.77 \mathrm{m} \text { of water } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Absolute discharge pressure at the pump exit
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{\text {abs }}&=\rho g H+p_{\text {atm }} \\ &=1000 \times 9.81 \times 45.77 \mathrm{Pa} \\ &=5.503 \mathrm{bar} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A heat engine having an efficiency of 70% is used to drive a refrigerator having a co-efficient of performance of 5. The energy absorbed from low temperature reservoir by the refrigerator for each kJ of energy absorbed from high temperature source by the engine is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta &=70 \%=0.70 \\ (\mathrm{COP})_{R} &=5 \\ Q_{3} &=? \\ Q_{1} &=1 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

For heat engine,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta &=1-\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}} \\ 0.70 &=1-\frac{Q_{2}}{1}\\ \text{or } \quad Q_{2}&=0.3 \mathrm{kJ} \\ W &=Q_{1}-Q_{2}=1-0.3 \\ &=0.7 \mathrm{kJ}\\ \text{For refrigerator,}\\ (\mathrm{COP})_{\mathrm{R}} &=\frac{Q_{3}}{W} \\ 5 &=\frac{Q_{3}}{0.7} \\ \text{or}\quad Q_{3} &=0.7 \times 5=3.5 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A solar collector receiving solar radiation at the rate of 0.6 [latex]kW/m^{2}[/latex]
transforms it to the internal energy of a fluid at an overall efficiency of 50%. The fluid heated to 350 K is used to run a heat engine which rejects heat at 313 K. If the heat engine is to deliver 2.5 kW power, the minimum area of the solar collector required would be
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] Q=0.6 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2}[/latex]
Overall efficiency of the fluid system,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_{\text {fluid }} &=50 \%=0.50 \\ T_{1} &=350 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{2} &=313 \mathrm{K} \\ W &=2.5 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Overall efficiency of the fluid system,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_{\text {fluid }} &=\frac{Q_{1}}{Q} \\ 0.50 &=\frac{Q_{1}}{0.6} \\ \text{or}\qquad Q_{1}&=0.05\times 0.6=0.3 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Let A= Minimum area of the solar collector
[latex] \therefore Q_{1}=0.3 \mathrm{A} \mathrm{kW}[/latex]
For minimum area of the solar collector, the heat engine is reversible
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Thermal efficiency,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta &=1-\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} \\ &=1-\frac{313}{350}=1-0.895=0.105 \\ \text { also } \quad \eta &=\frac{W}{Q_{1}} \\ \therefore \qquad 0.105 &=\frac{2.5}{0.3 A} \\ A &=79.36 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ & \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Second Law, Carnot Cycle and Entropy

raw_source.text: The pressure gauges [latex]G_{1}[/latex] and [latex]G_{2}[/latex] installed on the system show pressures of [latex]P_{G1}[/latex] = 5.00 bar and [latex]P_{G2}[/latex] =1.00 bar. The value of unknown pressure P is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{G_{1}}&=5 \text { bar } \\ P_{G_{2}}&=1 \text { bar } \\ P_{\text {atm }}&=1.01 \text { bar } \end{aligned}[/latex]
For pressure gauge [latex]G_{2}[/latex]
Absolute pressure
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\text { Atmospheric pr. }+\text { Gauge pr. } \\ p_{\text {abs }} &=p_{\text {atn }}+p_{G 2}=1.01+1=1.01 \text { bar }\\ &= \text{ Local atmospheric pr. for pr. gauge }G_{1} \\ &=\left(p_{\text {atm }}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For pressure gauge [latex]G_{1} [/latex]
Absolute pressure = Local atm. pr. + Gauge pr.
[latex] \begin{aligned} P &=\left(P_{\mathrm{atm}}\right)_{1}+P G_{1} \\ &=2.01+5=7.01 \mathrm{bar} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A steel billet of 2000 kg mass is to be cooled from 1250 K to 450 K. The heat released during this process is to be used as a source of energy. The ambient temperature is 303 K and specific heat of steel is 0.5 kJ/kg K. the available energy of this billet is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=m c_{p} \Delta T \\ &=2000 \times(0.5 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK}) \times(1250-450) \\ &=800000 \mathrm{kJ}\\ \Delta S&=m c_{p} \ln \frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=2000 \times 0.5 \times \ln \frac{1250}{450}\\ &=1021.165 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K} \\ \text { A.E. } &=Q-T_{0} \Delta S \\ &=490439.67 \mathrm{kJ}=490.44 \mathrm{MJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A stainless steel tub ([latex]k_{8}[/latex]
 = 19 W/mK) of 2 cm ID and 5 cm OD is insulated with 3 cm thick asbestos ([latex]k_{a}[/latex]
 = 0.2 W/mK). If the temperature difference between the innermost and outermost surfaces is 600[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C, the heat transfer rate per unit length is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} k_{s} &=19 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ d_{1} &=2 \mathrm{cm}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad r_{1} &=\frac{d_{1}}{2}=\frac{0.02}{2}=0.01 \mathrm{m}\\ d_{2}&=5 \mathrm{cm}=0.05 \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \quad r_{2}&=\frac{d_{2}}{2}=\frac{0.05}{2}=0.025 \mathrm{m}\\ t&=3 \mathrm{cm}=0.03 \mathrm{m}\\ \therefore \quad r_{3} &=r_{2}+t=0.025+0.03=0.055 \mathrm{m} \\ k_{a} &=0.2 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ T_{i}-T_{0} &=600^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Heat transfer,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=\frac{T_{i}-T_{o}}{\frac{1}{2 \pi k_{s} l} \log _{e} \frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{2 \pi k_{a} l} \log _{e} \frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}}} \\ \frac{Q}{l} &=\frac{T_{i}-T_{o}}{\frac{1}{2 \pi k_{s}} \log _{e} \frac{\Gamma_{2}}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{2 \pi k_{a}} \log _{e} \frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}}} \\ q &=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2 \times 3.14 \times 19} \log _{e} \frac{0.025}{0.01}+\frac{1}{2 \times 3.14 \times 0.2} \log _{e} \frac{0.055}{0.025}} \\ &=\frac{600}{0.007679+0.627752} \\ &=944.24 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A spherical thermocouple junction of diameter 0.706 mm is to be used for the measurement of temperature of a gas stream. The convective heat transfer co-efficient on the bead surface is 400 [latex]W/m^{2}[/latex]. Thermophysical properties of thermocouple material are k = 20 W/mK, C = 400 J/kg K and [latex]\rho =8500 kg/m^{3}[/latex]. If the thermocouple initially at [latex]30^{\circ}C[/latex]
 is placed in a hot stream of [latex]300^{\circ}C[/latex], the time taken by the bead to reach [latex]298^{\circ}C[/latex], is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] h=400 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} ; \quad k=20 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} ; \quad c=400 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K} [/latex]
[latex] \rho=8500 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} ; \quad T(t)=298^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex]
Now, [latex] L=\frac{V}{A}=\frac{1 / 6 \pi D^{3}}{\pi D^{2}}=\frac{D}{6}=\frac{0.706 \times 10^{-3}}{6}[/latex]
[latex] =1.76 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Biot number,
[latex] \begin{aligned} B i &=\frac{h L}{k}=\frac{400 \times 1.76 \times 10^{-4}}{20} \\ &=0.0023 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since [latex]\mathrm{Bi} \lt 0.1 [/latex]
Lumped system analysis can be used
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}} &=e^{-\left(\frac{h A t}{p c V}\right)} \\ \frac{298-300}{30-300} &=e^{-\left(\frac{400 \times 6 \times t}{8500 \times 0.706 \times 10^{-3} \times 400}\right)} \\ 7.407 \times 10^{-3} &=e^{-t} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex]\log _{\mathrm{e}}[/latex] both sides, we get
[latex] \log _{e} 7.407 \times 1=-t [/latex]
[latex] \text{or }\quad t=4.90 [/latex] seconds

raw_source.text:
In a condenser, water enters a [latex]30^{\circ}C[/latex]
 and flows at the rate 1500 kg/hr. The condensing steam is at a temperature of [latex]120^{\circ}C[/latex]
 and cooling water leaves the condenser at [latex]80^{\circ}C[/latex]. Specific heat of water is 4.187 kJ/kg K. If the overall heat transfer coefficient is [latex]2000 W/m^{2}[/latex], the heat transfer area is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \theta_{1}=120^{\circ}-30^{\circ}&=90^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ \theta_{2}=120^{\circ}-80^{\circ}&=40^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Mass flow rate,
[latex] m=\frac{1500}{3600}=0.4167 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
Log mean temperature difference,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \theta_{m} &=\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{\ln \left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}}\right)}=\frac{90-40}{\ln \left(\frac{90}{40}\right)}=61.65^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ Q &=m c_{\rho w} \Delta T=U A \theta_{\mathrm{m}} \\ 0.4167 \times 4.128 &\times 1000 \times 50\\ &=2000 \times A \times 61.65\\ \text{or }\quad A&=0.707 \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
During a Morse test on a 4 cylinder engine, the following measurements of brake power were taken at constant speed.

The mechanical efficiency of the engine is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} \text { (B.P.) }_{1,2,3,4}=3037 \mathrm{kW} \\ \left(1 . P_{1}\right)_{1,2,3,4}=(\mathrm{B.P.})_{1,2,3,4}+(\mathrm{F.P.})_{1,2,3,4} \ldots \text { (i) } \end{array}[/latex]
Number 1 cylinder not firing,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \left(B . P_{2,3,4}=2102 \mathrm{kW}\right. \\ (1.P) _{2,3,4}=(\mathrm{B.P.})_{2,3,4}+(\mathrm{F.P.})_{1,2,3,4}\quad \cdots(ii)\\ \end{array}[/latex]
Eq. (ii) - Eq. (i), we get
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \left(I.P)_{1,2,3,4}-\left(1 . P_{1}\right)_{2,3,4}=\left(B . P\right)_{1,2,3,4}+\left(B . P\right)_{1,2,3,4}\right. \\ (1 . P .)_{1}=3037-2102=935 \mathrm{kW} \\ \end{array}[/latex]
similarly, number 2 cylinder not firing,
[latex] \begin{aligned} (B . P .)_{1,3,4}&=2102 \mathrm{kW}\\ \therefore \quad (\mathrm{l} . \mathrm{P.})_{2} &=(\mathrm{B.P.})_{1,2,3,4}-(\mathrm{B} . \mathrm{P.})_{1,3,4} \\ &=3037-2102=935 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Number 3 cylinder not firing,
[latex] \begin{aligned} (\mathrm{B.P})_{1,2,4} &=2100 \mathrm{kW} \\ \therefore \quad (\mathrm{l.P.})_{3} &=(\mathrm{B.P.})_{1,2,3,4}-(\mathrm{B.P.})_{1,2,4} \\ &=3037-2100=937 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Number 4 cylinder not firing,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { (B.P.) }_{1,2,3}&=2098 \mathrm{kW}\\ \therefore \quad (I.P.)_{4}&=(\mathrm{B} . \mathrm{P.})_{1,2,3,4}-(\mathrm{B.P.})_{1,2,3}\\ &=3037-2098=939 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Total I.P.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left(I.P.\right)_{1,2,3,4} &=(1 . P .)_{1}+(1 . P .)_{2}+(1 . P .)_{3}+(1 . P .)_{1} \\ &=935+935+937+939 \\ &=3746 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}\\ Mechanical efficiency,\\ \begin{aligned} \eta_{m}&=\frac{(\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{P} \cdot)_{1,2,3,4}}{(\mathrm{I} \cdot \mathrm{P} \cdot)_{1,2,3,4}}=\frac{3037}{3746} \\ &=0.8107=81.07 \%\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An engine working on air standard Otto cycle has a cylinder diameter of 10 cm and stroke length of 15 cm. The ratio of specific heats for air is 1.4. If the clearance volume is 196.3 cc and the heat supplied per kg of air per cycle is 1800 kJ/kg, the work output per cycle per kg of air is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:

 is 2500 kJ/kg. The specific humidity (kg/kg of dry air) and enthalpy (kJ/kg of dry air) of this moist air respectively, are

[latex]\text{Given, } \quad p=1.013\text{bar}[/latex]
[latex] p_{v}=0.02062 \text{ bar }\quad(\text { at dew point })[/latex]
We know that,
Specific humidity,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega &=\frac{0.622 p_{v}}{p-p_{v}} \\ &=\frac{0.622 \times 0.02062}{1.013-0.02062}\\ &=0.01291\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \;\text{of dry air}\\ \text{Enthalpy:}h&=1.005t_{d}+\omega(h_{fg,dp}+2.3t_{dp})\\ &=1.005\times 30 + 0.01291(2500+2.3+3.)\\ &=1.005\times 30+32.809\\ &=63.47\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \;\text{of dry air}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A R-12 refrigerant reciprocating compressor operates between the condensing temperature of [latex]30^{\circ}C[/latex] and evaporator temperature of [latex]-20^{\circ}C[/latex] . The clearance volume ratio of the compressor is 0.03. Specific heat ratio of the vapour is 1.15 and the specific volume at the suction is 0.1089 [latex]m^{3}/kg[/latex] . Other properties at various states are given in the figure. To realize 2 Tons of refrigeration, the actual volume displacement rate considering the effect of clearance is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} C &=0.03 \\ \gamma &=1.15 \\ v_{1} &=0.1089 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Capacity: } Q &=2 \text { tons }=2 \times 3.5 \mathrm{kW}=7 \mathrm{kW} \\ P_{1} &=1.50 \mathrm{bar} ; \quad P_{2}=7.45 \mathrm{bar} \\ h_{1} &=176 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} ; \quad h_{2}=207 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{3} &=h_{4}=65 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Refrigerating effect,
[latex] \mathrm{Re}=h_{1}-h_{4}=176-65=111 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}[/latex]
Mass flow rate,
[latex] \begin{aligned} m &=\frac{\text { Refrigerating capacity: } Q}{\text { Refrigerating effect : Re }} \\ &=\frac{7}{111}=0.063 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that volumetric efficiency of the
compressor
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_{v} &=1+C-C r_{p}^{1 / \gamma} \\ &=1+C-C\left(\frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}\right)^{1 / \gamma} \\ &=1+0.03-0.03\left(\frac{7.45}{1.50}\right)^{1 / 1.15} \\ &=0.9091 \\ \mathrm{also}\quad \eta_{v}&=\frac{\text { Actual suction volume }}{\text { Displacement Volume }} \\ \eta_{v} &=\frac{m v_{1}}{V_{s}} \\ 0.9091 &=\frac{0.063 \times 0.1089}{V_{s}}=\frac{0.00686}{V_{s}} \\ \text{or}\quad V_{s} &=0.00754 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}\\ &=7.54\times10^{-3} \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A soldering operation was work-sampled over two days (16 hours) during which an employee soldered 108 joints. Actual working time was 90% of the total time and the performance rating was estimated to be 120 percent. If the contract provides allowance of 20 percent of the total time available, the standard time for the operation would be
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Total time } &=16 \text { hours }=16 \times 60 \text { min } \\ \text { Actual time } &=\frac{90}{100} \times 16 \times 60=864 \text { min } \\ \text { Normal time } &=\text { Actual time } \times \text { Rating factor } \\ \text { Normal time } &=\text { Actual time } \times \frac{120}{100} \\ &=864 \times 1.2=1036.8 \mathrm{min} \\ \text { Standard time } &=\text { Normal time + Allowances } \\ &=1244.16 \mathrm{min} \\ &\text{Standard time per joint}\\ &=\frac{1244.16}{108}=12 \mathrm{min} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A maintenance service facility has Poisson arrival rates, negative exponential service time and operates on a 'first come first served' queue discipline. Breakdowns occur on an average of 3 per day with a range of zero to eight. The maintenance crew can service an average of 6 machines per day with a range of zero to seven.

The mean waiting time for an item to be serviced would be
raw_source.solution:
Given,
Arrival rate: [latex] \lambda=3 [/latex] per day
Service rate: [latex] \lambda=6 [/latex] per day
Mean waiting time for an item to be serviced

raw_source.text: A company has an annual demand of 1000 units, ordering cost of Rs.100/order and carrying cost of Rs.100/unit -year. If the stock-out costs are estimated to be nearly Rs.400 each time the company runs out-of-stock, the safety stock justified by the carrying cost will be
raw_source.solution:
We need to find stock justified by carrying cost
i.e.,[latex]M^{*} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} M^{\star} &=Q^{*}-S^{*} \\ Q^{*} &=50 \\ S^{*} &=\frac{C_{h}}{C_{b}+C_{h}} \times Q^{\star} \\ &=\frac{100}{100+400} \times 50 \\ S^{*} &=10\\ \text{and }M^{\star}&=50-10=40 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider a steam power plant using a reheat cycle as shown. Steam leaves the boiler and enters the turbine at 4 MPa, [latex]350^{\circ}C[/latex] ([latex]h_{3}[/latex] = 3095 kJ/kg). After expansion in the turbine to 400 kPa ([latex]h_{4}[/latex] = 2609 kJ/kg), the steam is reheated to [latex]350^{\circ}C[/latex] ([latex]h_{5}[/latex] = 3170 kJ/kg), and then expanded in a low pressure turbine to 10 kPa ([latex]h_{6}[/latex] = 2165 kJ/kg). The specific volume of liquid handled by the pump can be assumed to be


The thermal efficiency of the plant neglecting pump work is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{array}{l} h_{3}=3095 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} ; \quad h_{4}=2604 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{5}=3170 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} ; \quad h_{6}=2165 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{g} \\ h_{1}=29.3 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{array}[/latex]


Network output per kg
[latex] \begin{aligned} w_{\text {net }} &=\left(h_{3}-h_{4}\right)+\left(h_{5}-h_{6}\right) \\ &=(3095-2609)+(3170-2165) \\ &=1491 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net heat supplied,
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{s} &=\left(h_{3}-h_{2}\right)+\left(h_{5}-h_{4}\right) \\ &=h_{3}-h_{1}+h_{5}-h_{4} \quad \because h_{2} \approx h \\ &=3095-29.3+3170-2609 \\ &=3626.7 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thermal efficiency,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta &=\frac{w_{\mathrm{net}}}{q_{\mathrm{s}}}=\frac{1491}{3626.7} \\ &=0.4111=41.11 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

If [latex]x^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2xy=\frac{2ln x}{x}[/latex], and [latex]y(1)=0[/latex],

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given}\; x^2\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy&=\frac{2lnx}{x}\;\;...(1) \\ \text{or,} \;\; \frac{dy}{dx} +\frac{2}{x}y&=\frac{2lnx}{x^3}\;\;...(2) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Integrating factor [latex]= e^{\int_{x}^{2}dx} [/latex]
[latex]I.F.=e^{2lnx}=x^2 [/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} yx^2&= \int \frac{2 \ln x}{x^3}x^2\\ x^2y&=\int \frac{2 \ln x}{x} \\ x^2y&= (\ln x)^2+c\\ \text{when}\;\; x&=1;\;\; y=0 \\ \text{then}\;\; c&=0 \\ \therefore \;\; x^2y&=(\ln x)^2 \\ \text{Now at}\;\; x&=e \\ y&=\frac{(\ln e)^2}{e^2}=\frac{1}{e^2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The complete solution for the ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2} y}{\mathrm{d} x_{2}}+ p\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+qy = 0[/latex] is [latex]y= c_{1}e^{-x}+c_{2}e^{-3x}[/latex]

Then, p and q are
raw_source.solution:
Given equation is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+p \frac{d y}{d x}+q y &=0 \\ \left(D^{2}+p D+q\right) y &=0\\ \therefore \quad D^{2}+p D+q&=0 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Its solution is
[latex] \begin{aligned} y&=C_{1} e^{-x}+C_{2} e^{-3 x}\\ \text{Sum of roots } -p&=-1-3 \\ &=p=4\\ \text{Product of roots} q&=(-1)(-3) \\ \therefore q&=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+p \frac{d y}{d x}+(q+1)&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left[D^{2}+P D+(q+1)\right] y &=0 \\ Put \qquad \qquad p&=4\\ and \qquad \qquad q&=3\\ \therefore \quad\left(D^{2}+4 D+4\right) y&=0 \\ \therefore D^{2}+4 D+4 &=0 \\ (D+2)^{2} &=0 \\ D &=-2,-2\\ y=x e^{-2 x} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{5} &=f_{4}+\alpha\left(d_{4}-f_{4}\right) \\ 880 &=876+\alpha(890-876) \\ 14 \alpha &=4\\ \text{or }\qquad \alpha&=\frac{4}{14}=\frac{2}{7} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a single server queuing model with Poisson arrivals [latex](\lambda =4/hour)[/latex]
 and exponential service [latex](\mu =4/hour)[/latex]. The number in the system is restricted to a maximum of 10. The probability that a person who comes in leaves without joining the queue is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned}\text{Given }\quad \lambda&=4\text{ per hour} \\ \mu&=4\text{ per hour} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Traffic intensity,
[latex] \rho=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}=\frac{4}{4}=1[/latex]
We know that
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \sum_{n=0}^{10} P_{n}=1 \\ \therefore P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{3}+\ldots+P_{10}=1 \\ P_{0}+\rho P_{0}+\rho^{2} P_{0}+\rho^{3} P_{0}+\ldots+\rho^{10} P_{0}=1 \\ P_{0}\left(1+\rho+\rho^{2}+\ldots+\rho^{10}\right)=1 \\ P_{0}(1+1+\ldots+1)=1 \\ \therefore \quad P_{0}=\frac{1}{11} \end{array}[/latex]
Probability that a person who comes in leaves without joining the queue i.e.
[latex] P_{11}=\rho^{11} P_{0}=(1)^{11} \times \frac{1}{11}=\frac{1}{11}[/latex]

raw_source.text: With a 1 unit change in b, what is the change in x in the solution of the system of equations [latex]x+y=2,  \; \; 1.01x+0.99y=b ?[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex] \quad x+y=2 \qquad ...(i) [/latex]
[latex] 1.01 x+0.99 y=b\qquad ...(ii) [/latex]
Multiply 0.99 is equation (i), and substract from equation (ii); we get
[latex] \begin{aligned}(1.01-0.99) x &=b-2 \times 0.99 \\ 0.02 x &=b-1.98 \\ \therefore \quad 0.02 \Delta x&=\Delta b \\ \therefore \quad \Delta x&=\frac{1}{0.02}=50 unit \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
By a change of variables x(u,v)=uv, [latex]y(u,v)=\frac{v}{u}[/latex]
  in a double integral, the integrand  f(x,y) changes to [latex] f( uv,\frac{v}{u})\phi (u,v)[/latex]. Then [latex]\phi (u,v)[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}=v\\ &\frac{\partial \bar{x}}{\partial v}=u \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\text { and } \quad \quad \quad \begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}=-\frac{v}{u^{2}}\\ &\frac{\partial y}{\partial v} =\frac{1}{u} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { and } \quad \phi(u, v) &=\left|\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{cc}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{u^{2}} & \frac{1}{u}\end{array}\right| \\ &=\frac{v}{u}+\frac{v}{u}=\frac{2 v}{u} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The right circular cone of largest volume that can be enclosed by a sphere of 1 m radius has a height of
raw_source.solution:
Given R=1 radius of sphere. Let height of cone is H=h+R
Volume of cone [latex] V=\frac{1}{3} \pi \times(\sqrt{R^{2}-h^{2}})^{2}(R+h)[/latex]
for max or largest volume,
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d V}{d h}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \frac{d}{d h}\left[\frac{1}{3}\left(R^{2}-h^{2}\right)(R+h)\right][/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad-2 h(R+h)+\left(R^{2}-h^{2}\right)=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad-2 h R-2 h^{2}+R^{2}-1 h^{2} \Rightarrow 0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow R^{2}-3 h^{2}-2 h R=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad(R+h)(R-3 h)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \quad h =-R, R / 3 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned}\text { Height of cone }= R+\frac{R}{3}=\frac{4 R}{3} \\ =\frac{h \times 1}{3} \mathrm{m}=\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
If [latex]x^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+2xy=\frac{2ln x}{x}[/latex], and [latex]y(1)=0[/latex], 
 and  then what is y(e)?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given}\; x^2\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy&=\frac{2lnx}{x}\;\;...(1) \\ \text{or,} \;\; \frac{dy}{dx} +\frac{2}{x}y&=\frac{2lnx}{x^3}\;\;...(2) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Integrating factor [latex]= e^{\int_{x}^{2}dx} [/latex]
[latex]I.F.=e^{2lnx}=x^2 [/latex]
Multiply by I.F. then integrate the equation we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} yx^2&= \int \frac{2 \ln x}{x^3}x^2\\ x^2y&=\int \frac{2 \ln x}{x} \\ x^2y&= (\ln x)^2+c\\ \text{when}\;\; x&=1;\;\; y=0 \\ \text{then}\;\; c&=0 \\ \therefore \;\; x^2y&=(\ln x)^2 \\ \text{Now at}\;\; x&=e \\ y&=\frac{(\ln e)^2}{e^2}=\frac{1}{e^2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The line integral [latex]\int \bar{V} d\bar{r}[/latex]
 of the vector function [latex] \bar{V} (\bar{r})=2xyz\hat{i}+x^{2}z\hat{j}+x^{2}y\hat{k}[/latex]
 from the 
origin to the point P(1,1,1)
raw_source.solution:
Potential function of [latex] \vec{V}=x^{2} y z[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] line integral of the vector function from origin to the point (1,1,1) is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \;\;\;&=\left(x^{2} y z\right)_{1,1,1}-\left(x^{2} y z\right)_{(0,0,0)} \\ &=1-0=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
options: cannot be determined without specifying the path

raw_source.solution:
From Newton-Raphson method
[latex] x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f(x)}{f^{\prime}(x)} x_{0}[/latex]
Given function is
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^{3}+3 x-7 \\ \text{and} \qquad f^{\prime}(x)&=3 x^{2}+3\\ \text{Putting} \qquad \quad x&=1 \\ \therefore \qquad f(1) &=(1)^{3}+3 \times(1)-7=-3 \\ f^{\prime}(1) &=3 \times(1)^{2}+3=6 \\ \therefore \qquad x_{1} &=1-\left(\frac{-3}{6}\right) \times 1=1.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single die is thrown twice. What is the probability that the sum is neither 8 or 9?
raw_source.solution:
Sample space [latex]=(6)^{2}=36 [/latex]
Total ways in which sum is either 8 or 9 is
[latex] (2,6),(3,5),(3,6),(4,4),(4,5),(5,3),[/latex]
[latex] (5,4),(6,2),(6,3) [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Probability of coming sum 8 or 9
[latex]=\frac{9}{36}=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]
So probability of not coming sum 8 or 9
[latex] =1-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two books of mass 1 kg each are kept on a table, one over the other. The coefficient of friction on every pair of contacting surfaces is 0.3. The lower book is pulled with a horizontal force F. The minimum value of F for which slip occurs between the two books is
raw_source.solution:
Taking, [latex]g= 9.81 m/s^{2}[/latex]


Now as we apply force on lower book B. Firstly book A and B will start moving together with same acceleration slipping from C, so [latex]F_{\text {min }}[/latex] need to overcome [latex] \left[\left(f_{s}\right)_{\max }\right]_{\mathrm{BC}} [/latex]
As there no acceleration in vertical direction, so in vertical direction net force will be zero on A and B both.
[latex] \left[\left(f_{s}\right)_{\max }\right]_{\mathrm{BC}}=\mu_{s}\left[N_{\mathrm{BC}}\right] [/latex]
FBD of A

[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad N_{A B} &=m g=1 \times 9.81 \\ &=9.81 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned} [/latex]
FBD of B

[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{8 C} &=m g+N_{B A} \\ &=9.81+9.81=19.62 \mathrm{N} \\ \left[\left(f_{\mathrm{s}}\right)_{\max }\right]_{\mathrm{BC}} &=0.3 \times 19.62=5.886 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now when we will apply force more than 5.886 N, they will start moving together with same acceleration
Now as we keep on increasing F , acceleration of book B will go on increasing and thus increasing acceleration of book A . But acceleration of book A is increasing because of static friction and it has a maximum value. So after that acceleration of book B will be more than acceleration of A . So there will be relative slipping between B and A
[latex] \left[a_{\max }\right]_{A}=?[/latex]
[latex] \left[a_{\max }\right]_{A} \text{will be corresponding to}\; \left[(f s)_{\max }\right]_{A B} [/latex]


[latex]\begin{aligned} \left[(f s)_{\max }\right]_{A B} &=\mu_{s} N_{A B} \\ &=0.3 \times 9.81=2.943 \mathrm{N} \\ \left(a_{A}\right)_{\max } &=\left[(f s)_{\max }\right]_{A B} / m_{A}=2.943 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At that condition

[latex] \begin{aligned} F_{\min }-8.829 &=m_{B} a_{B} \\ F_{\min } &=8.829+1 \times 2.943 \\ F_{\text {rin }}&=11.772 \mathrm{N}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
At this point both will be moving with same acceleration but beyond this if we will increase F, acceleration of B will be more than A and there will be slipping between the books.

raw_source.text: An elevator (lift) consists of the elevator cage and a counter weight, of mass m each. The cage and the counterweight are connected by a chain that passes over a pulley. The pulley is coupled to a motor. It is desired that the elevator should have a maximum stopping time of t seconds from a peak speed v. If the inertia of the pulley and the chain are neglected, the minimum power that the motor must have is
raw_source.solution:
Power = rate of energy supplied 'or' obtained.
If counter weight is moving with velocity V then cage will also be moving with velocity V
So total [latex] \mathrm{K.E}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}[/latex]
[latex] =m v^{2} [/latex]
and to absorb (or to stop) this energy time available is t second.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Power } &=\frac{\text { Total energy absored }}{\text { time taken for this absorption }} \\ &=\frac{m v^{2}}{t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 1 kg mass of clay, moving with a velocity of 10 m/s, strikes a stationary wheel and sticks to it. The solid wheel has a mass of 20 kg and a radius of 1 m. assuming that the wheel and the ground are both rigid and that the wheel is set into pure rolling motion, the angular velocity of the wheel immediately after the impact is approximately
raw_source.solution:
In this question, we need to neglect mass of clay w.r.t. mass of wheel.
We can't conserve linear momentum as friction is there so we will conserve angular momentum about the point of wheel which is in contact with the surface. (because torque about A of all forces is zero)
Taking both clay and wheel as system.
[latex]L_i=L_f[/latex] (about A)

[latex]\begin{aligned} L_i&= mvr=1 \times 10 \times 1=10\\ L_f&= mv_{cm}r + IW\\ &=20 \times r\omega \times r+\frac{mr^2}{2}\omega \\ &= 20 \times 1 \times \omega \times 1+\frac{20}{2} \times 1^2 \times \omega \\ L_i &=L_f \\ 10 &= 20\omega +10\omega \\ 10 &=30\omega \\ \omega &=\frac{1}{3} \; \text{rad/s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a cam-follower mechanism, the follower needs to rise through 20 mm during 60[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] of cam rotation, the first 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] with a constant acceleration and then with a deceleration of the same magnitude. The initial and final speeds of the follower are zero. The cam rotates at a uniform speed of 300 rpm. The maximum speed of the follower is
raw_source.solution:
Angular velocity,
[latex] \omega=\frac{2 \pi N}{60}=\frac{2 \pi 300}{60}=10 \pi[/latex]
Time taken to move [latex]30^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{\frac{\pi}{180} \times 30}{\omega}=\frac{\frac{\pi}{6}}{10 \pi}=\frac{1}{60} \mathrm{s}[/latex]
During this time, follower moves by distance of 10mm with initial velocity
[latex] \begin{aligned} u&=0\\ \text{Now;} \quad S &=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\ 0.01 &=0+\frac{1}{2} \times a \times\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)^{2} \\ \therefore \quad a &=0.01 \times 2 \times(60)^{2}\\ &=72 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \\ V_{\max } &=U+a t\\ &=0+72 \times \frac{1}{60}=1.20 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rotating disc of 1 m diameter has two eccentric masses of 0.5 kg each at radii of 50 mm and 60 mm at angular positions of 0[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] and 150[latex]^{\circ}[/latex], respectively. A balancing mass of 0.1 kg is to be used to balance the rotor. What is the radial position of the balancing mass?
raw_source.solution:
Let x and y is position of balancing mass along x and y directions. Resolving forces along x-axis
[latex] \begin{array}{l} 0.5\left(-60 \times 10^{-3} \cos 30^{\circ}+50 \times \cos 0 \times 10^{-3}\right) \omega^{2} \\ =0.1 \times x \times 10^{-3}\\ \therefore \quad x=-9.8 \mathrm{mm} \\ 0.5 \times\left(60 \times 10^{-3} \times \sin 30\right) \omega^{2}+0.5(50 \times 10^{-3}\\ \qquad \qquad \times \sin0) \omega^{2}=0.1\omega^{2}y\\ \therefore \quad y=150 \mathrm{mm} \end{array}[/latex]
Position of balancing mass,
[latex] \begin{aligned} r &=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \\ &=150.3 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}=\sqrt{(-9.8)^{2}+(150)^{2}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a spring-mass system, the mass is 0.1 kg and the stiffness of the spring is 1 kN/m. By introducing a damper, the frequency of oscillation is found to be 90% of the original value. What is the damping coefficient of the damper?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given }\quad \omega_{d}&=0.9 \omega_{n} \\ &\text{we know that}\\ \omega_{d} &=\omega_{n} \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.9 \omega_{n} &=\omega_{n} \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}} \\ \therefore \quad \xi &=0.436 \\ \text { Now } \quad \xi &=\frac{c}{2 \sqrt{k m}} \\ \therefore \quad c &=2 \times 0.436 \times \sqrt{1000 \times 0.1} \\ &=8.71 \mathrm{Ns} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A venturimeter of 20 mm throat diameter is used to measure the velocity of water in a horizontal pipe of 40 mm diameter. If the pressure difference between the pipe and throat sections is found to be 30 kPa then, neglecting frictional losses, the flow velocity is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} d_{2}&=20 \mathrm{mm}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ d_{1}&=40 \mathrm{mm}=0.04 \mathrm{m} \\ \Delta p&=p_{1}-p_{2}=30 \mathrm{kPa}=30 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For continuity equation, we get

[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{1} V_{1} &=A_{2} V_{2} \\ V_{2} &=\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} V_{1}=\frac{\frac{\pi}{4} d_{1}^{2}}{\frac{\pi}{4} d_{2}^{2}} \times V_{1} \\ &=\left(\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}\right)^{2} V_{1}=\left(\frac{0.04}{0.02}\right)^{2} V_{1} \\ V_{2} &=4 V_{1} \qquad\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying Bernoulli's equation, we get
[latex] \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{2}[/latex]
For horizontal pipe,
[latex] \begin{aligned} z_{1} &=z_{2} \\ \frac{p_{1}-p_{2}}{\rho g} &=\frac{v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2}}{2 g} \\ \frac{\Delta p}{\rho} &=\frac{1}{2}\left(v_{2}^{2}-v_{1}^{2}\right) \\ \frac{30 \times 10^{3}}{1000} &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(4 v_{1}\right)^{2}-v_{1}^{2}\right] \\ \frac{15 V_{1}^{2}}{2} &=30 \\ v_{1}^{2} &=4 \\ \text{or }\qquad v_{1} &=2 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} \left ( p+\frac{a}{v^2} \right )v &=RT=\text{Constant} \\ p_1v_1+\frac{a}{v_1} &=p_2v_2+\frac{a}{v_2} \\ p_2v_2&=p_1v_1+\frac{a}{v_1}-\frac{a}{v_2} \\ p_2 &=p_1\left ( \frac{v_1}{v_2} \right )+a\left ( \frac{1}{v_1v_2}-\frac{1}{v_2^2} \right ) \\ &= 10\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )+a\left ( \frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \right )=5+\frac{a}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Here, [latex]a\gt 0[/latex], so above equation shows that [latex]p_2[/latex] is greater than 5 and +ve.

raw_source.text: Heat flows through a composite slab, as shown below. The depth of the slab is 1 m. the k values are in W/m K. the overall thermal resistance in K/W is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} k_{1}&=0.02 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ k_{2}&=0.10 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ k_{3}&=0.04 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ \delta_{1}&=0.5 \mathrm{m} \\ \delta_{2}&=\delta_{3}=0.25 \mathrm{m} \\ \text{Depth}\quad w&=1 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Total thermal resistance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{t} &=R_{1}+\frac{R_{2} R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}} \\ \text { where } R_{1} &=\frac{\delta_{1}}{A_{1} k_{1}}=\frac{0.5}{1 \times 1 \times 0.02}=25 \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{W} \\ R_{2} &=\frac{\delta_{2}}{A_{2} k_{2}}=\frac{0.25}{0.5 \times 1 \times 0.10}=5 \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{W} \\ \text { and } \quad R_{3} &=\frac{\delta_{3}}{A_{3} k_{3}}=\frac{0.25}{0.5 \times 0.004}=12.5 \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{W} \\ \therefore \quad \quad R_{t} &=25+\frac{5 \times 12.5}{5+12.5}=25+3.57 \\ &=28.57 \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{W} \simeq 28.6 \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A small copper ball of 5 mm diameter at 500 K is dropped into an  oil bath whose temperature is 300 K. The thermal conductivity of copper is 400 W/m.K, its density 9000 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex]
 and its specific heat 385 J/kg.K. If the heat transfer coefficient is 250 [latex]W/m^{2}[/latex]. K and lumped analysis is assumed to be valid, the rate of fall of the temperature of the ball at the beginning of cooling will be, in K/s,

Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} k=400 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} ; & T_{i}=500 \mathrm{K} ; \quad \rho=9000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ T_{\infty}=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad c_{p}&=385 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} ; h=250 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{k} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} L_{c}=& \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{D}{6}=\frac{0.005}{6} \\ &= 8.33 \times 10^{-4} \\ T &=T_{\infty}+\left(T_{i}-T_{\infty}\right) e^{\frac{-h A t}{\rho c V}} \\ \frac{d T}{d t}&= \frac{-h A}{\rho c V}\left(T_{i}-T_{\infty}\right) e^{\frac{-h A t}{\rho c V}} \\ \left.\frac{d T}{d t}\right|_{t=0} &=\frac{h A}{\rho c V}\left(T_{i}-T_{\infty}\right)[\text { magnitude }] \\ &= \frac{250 \times 200}{9000 \times 385 \times 8.33 \times 10^{-4}} \\ \left.\frac{d T}{d t}\right|_{t=0}&=17.31 \mathrm{K} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A solid cylinder (surface 2) is located at the center of a hollow sphere (surface 1). The diameter of the sphere is 1m, while the cylinder has a diameter and length of 0.5m each. The radiation configuration factor F11 is

raw_source.text:
A leaf is caught in a whirlpool. At a given instant, the leaf is at a distance of 120 m from the center of the whirlpool. The whirlpool can be described by the following velocity distribution: [latex]V_{r}= - \left ( \frac{60 \times 10^{3}}{2\pi r} \right )m/s[/latex]
and [latex]V_{0}= \frac{300 \times 10^{3}}{2\pi r} m/s[/latex],
 where r (in meters) is the distance from the center of the whirlpool. What will be the distance of the leaf from the center when it has moved through half a revolution?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text{Radial distance }=120 \mathrm{m} [/latex]
[latex] V_{r}=-\frac{60 \times 10^{3}}{2 \pi r} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]
[latex] \text{and }\quad V_{\theta}=\frac{300 \times 10^{3}}{2 \pi r} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Let }\quad \theta= \text{ Angle turned by a leaf }[/latex]
[latex] \text{For }\quad \theta=\frac{1}{2} \text{ revolution }[/latex]
[latex] \text{i.e., }\quad \theta=\frac{2 \pi}{2} [/latex]
[latex] \theta=\pi \text{ radian}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{V_{r}}{V_{\theta}}=-\frac{60 \times 10^{3}}{2 \pi r} \times \frac{2 \pi r}{300 \times 10^{3}}=-\frac{1}{5} [/latex]
or [latex] V_{\theta}=-V_{r} [/latex]
We know that
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{r}&=\frac{d r}{d t} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ \text{and }\quad V_{\theta}&=r \omega=r \frac{d \theta}{d t} \\ -5 V_{r}&=r \frac{d \theta}{d t} \\ \text{or }\quad V_{r}&=-\frac{r}{5} \frac{d \theta}{d t} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equating Eq. (i) and Eq. (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d r}{d t}&=-\frac{r}{5} \frac{d \theta}{d t} \\ \text{or }\quad \frac{d r}{r}&=-\frac{d \theta}{5} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Intgegrating both sides, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \int_{120}^{1} \frac{d r}{r}&=-\frac{1}{5} \int_{0}^{\pi} d \theta \\ \left[\log _{\theta} r\right]_{120}^{r}&=-\frac{1}{5}[\theta]_{0}^{\pi} \\ \log _{e} r-\log _{e} 120&=-\frac{\pi}{5} \\ \log _{e}\frac{r}{120}&=-\frac{\pi}{5} \\ \text{or }\quad \frac{r}{120}&=e^{-\frac{\pi}{5}} \\ \text{or }\quad r=120 \times e^{-\frac{\pi}{5}}&=\frac{120}{e^{3.14 / 5}}=64 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

For Otto cycle
[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{3}=600 \mathrm{K} \end{array}[/latex]
For process 1-2,

raw_source.text:
In two air standard cycles - one operating on the Otto and the other on the Brayton cycle - air is isentropically compressed from 300 to 450 K. heat is added to raise the temperature to 600 K in the Otto cycle and to 550 K in the Brayton cycle.

If [latex]W_{O}[/latex] and [latex]W_{B}[/latex] are work outputs per unit mass, then
raw_source.solution:
For Otto cycle
[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{3}=600 \mathrm{K} \end{array}[/latex]
For process 1-2,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}&=\left(\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}\right)^{\gamma-1}\\ \text{or}\quad \frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}} &=\left(\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}=\left(\frac{450}{300}\right)^{\frac{1}{1.4-1}} \\ &=(1.25)^{2.5}=2.75 \end{aligned}[/latex]
i.e., Compression ratio
[latex]\begin{aligned} r&=\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}=2.75\\ \therefore \quad \eta_{\text {Otto }} &=1-\frac{1}{r^{\gamma-1}}=1-\frac{1}{(2.75)^{1.4-1}} \\ &=1-0.667=0.33=33 \% \end{aligned}\\ \text{For Brayton cycle}\\ \begin{aligned} T_{1}&=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K}\\ T_{3}&=550 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For Brayton cycle
[latex] T_{1}=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K}\\ T_{3}=550 \mathrm{K}[/latex]
For process 1-2 Pressure ratio
[latex] \begin{aligned} r_{p} &=\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}} \\ \eta_{\text {Brayton }} &=1-\frac{1}{\left(r_{p}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}} \\ &=1-\frac{1}{\left[\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}} \\ &=1-\frac{1}{T_{1} / T_{2}}=1-\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=1-\frac{300}{450} \\ &=0.33=33 \% \\ \text { Thus, } \eta_{\text {Otto }} &=\eta_{\text {Brajton }}=0.33 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Calculating work output in Otto and Brayton cycle
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { also } \eta_{\text {otto }}&=\frac{\text { Work output : } W_{\text {Otto }}}{\text { Heat supplied : } Q_{1}} \\ 0.33&=\frac{W_{\text {Otto }}}{Q_{1}} \\ \text{or}\quad W_{\text {Otto }}&=0.33 Q_{1}\\ &=0.33 \times c_{v}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right) \\ &=35.54 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \eta_{\mathrm{Braton}} &=\frac{\text { Work output }: \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\text { Heat supplied }} \\ 0.33 &=\frac{W_{\mathrm{B}}}{Q_{1}} \\ \text{or}\quad W_{B} &=0.33 Q_{1}\\ &=0.33 \times c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right)\\ &=0.33 \times 1.005(530-450) \\ &=31.165 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence work output per unit mass of the Otto cycle is more than the work output per unit mass of the Brayton cycle.
options: it is not possible to calculate the work outputs unless the temperature after the expansion is given.

Then, p and q are

The laminar flow Nusselt number is 3.4 for constant wall temperature conditions and, for turbulent flow, Nu=0.023 [latex]Re^{0.8}Pr^{0.33}[/latex]

The Reynolds number for the flow is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Width: } & a=1 \mathrm{m} \\ \text { Depth: } & b=0.5 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Velocity: [latex] \quad V=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]
Air temperature
[latex] T=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
Ambient temperature
[latex] T_{0}=30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
Properties of air
[latex] \begin{aligned} k &=0.025 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ \mu &=1.8 \mathrm{m} \text { Pa.s }=18 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{Pa} . \\ \mathrm{Pr} &=0.73 \\ \rho &=1.2 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equivalent length of duct
[latex] \begin{aligned} L &=\frac{4 \times \text{Cross sectional area }}{\text { Perimeter }} \\ &=\frac{4 A}{P}=\frac{4 \times a b}{2(a+b)} \\ &=\frac{4 \times 1 \times 0.5}{2(1+0.5)}=0.667 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Re} &=\frac{\rho \mathrm{VL}}{\mu}=\frac{1.2 \times 10 \times 0.667}{18 \times 10^{-6}} \\ &=4.44 \times 10^{5} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Neglect the effect of duct construction material. For air in the range of 20-30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C, data are as follows: thermal conductivity =0.025 W/m.K; viscosity = 18[latex]\mu[/latex]Pa.s; Prandtl number =0.73; density = 1.2 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex] . The laminar flow Nusselt number is 3.4 for constant wall temperature conditions and, for turbulent flow, Nu=0.023 [latex]Re^{0.8}Pr^{0.33}[/latex]

The heat transfer per metre length of the duct, in watts, is:
raw_source.solution:
As [latex] \mathrm{Re}>4000 [/latex], the flow is turbulent
Relation for turbulent flow,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Nu} &=0.023 \mathrm{Re}^{0.8} \mathrm{Pr}^{0.33} \\ \frac{h L}{k}&= 0.023 \times\left(4.44 \times 10^{5}\right) 0.8 \\ & \times(0.73)^{0.33} \\ \frac{\mathrm{h} \times 0.667}{0.025}&= 683.173 \\ \text{or} \quad h &=25.60 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Surface area of duct,
[latex] \begin{aligned} A&=2 \times a l+2 \times b l\\ \text{where }\quad l&= length of duct \\ \therefore \quad A &=2 \times 1 \times l+2 \times 0.5 \times l \\ &=(2+1) l=3 l \end{aligned}[/latex]
Rate of heat transfer,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=h A\left(T_{0}-T\right) \\ Q&=25.60 \times 3 l \times(30-20)\\ \text{or }\quad \frac{Q}{l}&=768 \mathrm{W} \simeq 769 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a continuous random variable with probability density function
[latex]f(t)= 1+t[/latex] for [latex] -1\leq t \leq 0[/latex]
[latex]f(t)= 1-t[/latex] for [latex] 0\leq t \leq 1[/latex]
The standard deviation of the random variable is:
raw_source.solution:
Mean [latex] (\bar{t})=\int_{-1}^{\infty} t \cdot f(t) \cdot d t [/latex]
[latex] \quad=\int_{-1}^{0} t(1+t) d t+\int_{0}^{1} t(1-t) d t [/latex]
[latex] \quad=\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}+\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}-\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} [/latex]
[latex] \quad=-\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right]+\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right] [/latex]
[latex] =-\left[\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}\right]=0 [/latex]
Variance [latex]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(t-\bar{t})^{2} f(t) d t [/latex]
[latex] =\int_{-1}^{0} t^{2}(1+t) \cdot d t+\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}(1-t) d t [/latex]
[latex] =\int_{-1}^{0}\left(t^{2}+t^{3}\right) \cdot d t+\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}(1-t) d t [/latex]
[latex] =\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}-\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6} [/latex]
Standard deviation
[latex] =\sqrt{\text { variance }}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Multiplication of matrices E and F is G. Matrices E and G are
[latex]E=\begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta & 0\\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]G=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
What is the matrix F?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]E=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta & 0 \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right][/latex]
[latex] \text{and} G=\left[\begin{array}{lll} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right][/latex]
The according to problem
[latex] E \times F=G[/latex]
[latex] \text{or} \left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta & 0 \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right] \times F=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right][/latex]
Hence we see that product of [latex](E \times F)[/latex] is unit matrix
so F will be the inverse of E
[latex] F=E^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta & 0 \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right][/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a continuous random variable with probability density function
[latex]f(t)= 1+t[/latex] for [latex] -1\leq t \leq 0[/latex]
[latex]f(t)= 1-t[/latex] for [latex] 0\leq t \leq 1[/latex]
The standard deviation of the random variable is:
raw_source.solution:
Mean [latex] (\bar{t})=\int_{-1}^{\infty} t \cdot f(t) \cdot d t [/latex]
[latex] \quad=\int_{-1}^{0} t(1+t) d t+\int_{0}^{1} t(1-t) d t [/latex]
[latex] \quad=\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}+\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}-\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} [/latex]
[latex] \quad=-\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right]+\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right] [/latex]
[latex] =-\left[\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}\right]=0 [/latex]
Variance [latex]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(t-\bar{t})^{2} f(t) d t [/latex]
[latex] =\int_{-1}^{0} t^{2}(1+t) \cdot d t+\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}(1-t) d t [/latex]
[latex] =\int_{-1}^{0}\left(t^{2}+t^{3}\right) \cdot d t+\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}(1-t) d t [/latex]
[latex] =\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}-\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6} [/latex]
Standard deviation
[latex] =\sqrt{\text { variance }}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: According to Von-Mises' distortion energy theory, the distortion energy under three dimensional stress state is repreented by
raw_source.solution:

Shear strain energy due to the principle stresses [latex]\sigma _1,\sigma _2 \text{ and }\sigma _3[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta E&=\frac{1+v}{6E}\left [ (\sigma _1 -\sigma _2)^2 +(\sigma _2 -\sigma _3)^2 + (\sigma _3 -\sigma _1)^2\right ] \\ &=\frac{1+v}{6E}\left [ 2(\sigma _1^2 + \sigma _2 ^2 + \sigma _3^2) - 2 (\sigma _1 \sigma _2 + \sigma _2\sigma _3 +\sigma _3\sigma _1)\right ] \\ &= \frac{1+v}{3E}\left [ \sigma _1^2 + \sigma _2 ^2 + \sigma _3^2 - (\sigma _1 \sigma _2 + \sigma _2\sigma _3 +\sigma _3\sigma _1)\right ] \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega_{n} &=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{100 \times 1000}{250}}=20 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ \text { Now, } \quad r &=\frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}=\frac{377}{20}=18.85 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Transmissibility ratio,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{TR} &=\frac{\sqrt{1+(2 \xi r)^{2}}}{\sqrt{\left(1-r^{2}\right)^{2}+(2 \xi r)^{2}}} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{1+(2 \times 0.15 \times 18.85)^{2}}}{\sqrt{\left.1-(18.85)^{2}\right)+(2 \times 0.15 \times 18.85)^{2}}} \\ &=0.0162 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A two-dimensional flow field has velocities along the x and y directions given by [latex]u=x^{2}t[/latex]
 and [latex]v= -2xyt[/latex]
 respectively, where t is time. The equation of streamlines is:
raw_source.solution:
Equation of streamline,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d x}{u} &=\frac{d y}{v} \\ \frac{d x}{x y} &=\frac{d y}{-2 x y} \\ \frac{d x}{x} &=\frac{d y}{-2 y} \\ 2 \frac{d x}{x}+\frac{d y}{y} &=0 \\ 2 \log _{e} x+\log _{e} y &=\log _{e} c \\ \log _{e} y x^{2} &=\log _{e} c \\ x^{2} y &=c \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The velocity profile in fully developed laminar flow in a pipe of diameter D is given by [latex]u=u_{0}(1-4r^{2}/D^{2})[/latex]
 where r is the radial distance from the center. If the viscosity of the fluid is [latex]\mu[/latex], the pressure drop across a length L of the pipe is:
raw_source.solution:
Given velocity profile,
[latex] \begin{aligned} u=u_{0}\left(1-\frac{u r^{2}}{D^{2}}\right) \\ \text { At } r=0, u=u_{\max } \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore u_{\max }=u_{0}[/latex]


We know that the pressure drop across a length of the pipe,
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{1}-p_{2} &=\frac{32 \mu \bar{u} L}{D^{2}} \\ \text{where}\quad \bar{u} &=\text { Average velocity } \\ \bar{u} &=\frac{u_{\max }}{2} \\ \bar{u} &=\frac{u_{0}}{2}\\ \therefore \quad p_{1}-p_{2}&=\frac{32 \mu u_{0} L}{2 \times D^{2}}=\frac{16 \mu u_{0} L}{D^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: A siphon draws water from a reservoir and discharges it out at atmospheric pressure. Assuming ideal fluid and the reservoir is large, the velocity at point P in the siphon tube is:
raw_source.solution:
Appling Bernoulli's equation at points(1) and (2),
we get


[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}&=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1} \\ \text { where } \quad \frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}&=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}=\frac{p_{\text {atm }}}{\rho g} \\ \quad z_{1}&=h_{2}-h_{1} \\ \quad z_{2}&=0 \\ \quad V_{1}&=0 \\ \therefore \frac{p_{\text {atm }}}{\rho g}+0&+h_{2}-h_{1}=\frac{p_{\text {am }}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g} \\ \text { or } \quad \frac{v_{2}^{2}}{2 g}&=h_{2}-h_{1}\\ or V_{2}&=\sqrt{2 g\left(h_{2}-h_{1}\right)}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
As constant diameter the siphon tube, the velocity of water inside the siphon tube is same.

raw_source.text: A large hydraulic turbine is to generate 300 kW at 1000 rpm under a head of 40 m. For initial testing, a 1:4 scale model of the turbine operates under a head of 10 m. The power generated by the model (in kW) will be
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
For Prototype
Power generated,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & P_{p}=300 \mathrm{kW} \\ \text { Speed: } & N_{p}=1000 \mathrm{rpm} \\ \text { Head: } & H_{p}=40 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For Model
Power generated,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & P_{m}=? \\ \text { Head: } & H_{m}=10 \mathrm{m} \\ \text { Scale ratio: } & \frac{D_{p}}{D_{m}}=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that the head coefficient,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{H} &=\frac{g H}{N^{2} D^{2}} \\\left(C_{H}\right)_{m} &=\left(C_{H}\right)_{p} \\\left(\frac{g H}{N^{2} D^{2}}\right)_{m} &=\left(\frac{g H}{N^{2} D^{2}}\right)_{p} \\ \frac{H_{m}}{N_{m}^{2} D_{m}^{2}} &=\frac{H_{p}}{N_{p}^{2} D_{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{H_{m}}{H_{p}}\left(\frac{D_{p}}{D_{m}}\right)^{2} &=\frac{\left(N_{m}\right)^{2}}{N_{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{10}{40}(4)^{2} &=\frac{N_{m}^{2}}{(100)^{2}}\\ \text{or }\quad N_{m}^{2}=4000000\\ \text{or} \quad N_{m}=2000 \mathrm{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Power roefficient
[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{p} &=\frac{P}{\rho N^{3} D^{5}} \\\left(C_{P}\right)_{m} &=\left(C_{P}\right)_{p} \\\left(\frac{p}{p N^{3} D^{5}}\right)_{m}&=\left(\frac{P}{\rho N^{3} D^{5}}\right)_{p} \\ \frac{P_{m}}{M_{m}^{3} D_{m}^{5}} &=\frac{P_{P}}{N_{P}^{3} D_{P}^{5}} \because \rho=\text { constant } \\ P_{m} &=P_{P}\left(\frac{N_{m}}{N_{p}}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{D_{m}}{D_{p}}\right)^{5} \\ &=300\left(\frac{2000}{1000}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{5} \\ &=2.34 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
