raw_source.text: A horizontal shaft centrifugal pump lifts ware at 65[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. The suction nozzle is one meter below pump centerline. The pressure at this point equal 200 kPa gauge and velocity is 3 m/s. Steam tables show saturation pressure at 65[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C is 25 kPa, and specific volume of the saturated liquid is 0.001020 [latex]m^{3}/kg[/latex]. The pump Net Positive suction Head (NPSH) in meters is:
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Temperature of water
[latex] T=65^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
Section head,
[latex] h_{s}=1 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Gange pressure at section nozzle inlet,[/latex]
[latex] p_{1, g}=200 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex]Absolute pressure
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{1, \mathrm{abs}} &=p_{1, g}+p_{a t m} \\ &=200+101.325 \\ &=301.325 \mathrm{kPa} \\ &=301.325 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Velocity at section nozzle inlet,
[latex] V_{1}=3 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
Saturated pressure at [latex]65^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{v, a b s} &=25 \mathrm{kPa}, \text { vapure pressure } \\ &=25 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Specific volume,
[latex] v=0.001020 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{kg}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \text{Density: }\rho=\frac{1}{0.001020}=980.39 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]


Net positive section head,
[latex] \mathrm{NPSH}=\frac{p_{s, a b s}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{s}^{2}}{2 g}-\frac{p_{v, a b s}}{\rho g}[/latex]
Applying Bernoullis equation at section nozzle inlet
and section of the pump
[latex] \frac{p_{1, a b s}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}=\frac{p_{s, a b s}}{p g}+\frac{v_{s}^{2}}{2 g}+h_{s}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{\mathrm{p}_{1, \mathrm{abs}}}{\mathrm{pg}}+\frac{\mathrm{V}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{g}}+0=\frac{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{abs}}}{\mathrm{pg}}+\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{g}}+\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{s}} [/latex]
[latex] or \frac{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{abs}}}{\mathrm{pg}}+\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{g}}=\frac{\mathrm{p}_{1 \mathrm{abs}}}{\mathrm{pg}}+\frac{\mathrm{V}_{1}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{g}}-\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{s}} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \mathrm{NPSH}=\frac{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{abs}}}{\mathrm{pg}}+\frac{\mathrm{V}_{1}^{2}}{2 \mathrm{g}}-h_{\mathrm{s}}-\frac{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{v}, \mathrm{abs}}}{\mathrm{pg}} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{301 \cdot 325 \times 10^{3}}{980.39 \times 9.81}+\frac{(3)^{2}}{2 \times 9.81}-1-\frac{25 \times 10^{3}}{980.39 \times 9.81} [/latex]
[latex] =31.33+0.45-1-2.56 [/latex]
[latex] =28.22 \mathrm{m} \approx 28 \mathrm{m}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The ultimate tensile strength of a material is 400 MPa and the elongation up to maximum load is 35%. If the material obeys power law of hardening, then the true stress-true strain relation (stress in MPa) in the plastic deformation range is:
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \epsilon &=\ln \left(1+\epsilon_{0}\right) \\ &=\ln (1+0.35)=0.3\\ \text{But at UTS }n&=\epsilon\\ \text { Hence } n&=\epsilon=0.3 \\ \text { Also } \sigma_{f}&=\sigma_{0}\left(1+\epsilon_{0}\right)=400(1+0.35) \\ &=540 \mathrm{MPa}\\ \text{Now,}\quad \sigma_{f}&=K \epsilon^{n}\\ 540 &=K(0.3)^{0.3} \\ \text{or} \quad K &=774.97\\ \text { Hence } \sigma_{f}&=775 \epsilon^{0.3} \\ \text { Where, } \sigma_{f}&=\text { true stress } \\ \epsilon&=\text { true strain } \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a sand casting operation, the total liquid head is maintained constant such that it is equal to the mould height. The time taken to fill the mould with a top gate is [latex]t_{A}[/latex]. If the same mould is filed with a bottom gate, then the time taken is [latex]t_{B}[/latex]. Ignore the time required to fill the runner and frictional effects. Assume atmospheric pressure at the top molten metal surfaces. The relation between [latex]t_{A}[/latex]
and [latex]t_{B}[/latex]
is:
raw_source.solution:
Time taken to fill the mould with top gate
[latex] \begin{aligned} t_{A}&=\frac{A H}{A_{g} \sqrt{2 g h_{m}}} \qquad \cdots(i)\\ \text{where }\quad A&= \text{Area of mould} \\ H&= \text{Height of mould}\\ A_{g}&=\text { Area of Gate } \\ n_{m}&=\text { Gate height } \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that, [latex]h_{m}=H,[/latex] so Eq. (i) become:
[latex] t_{A}=\frac{A \sqrt{h_{m}}}{A_{g} \sqrt{2 g}} \qquad \cdots(ii)[/latex]
Time taken to fill the mould with bottom gate,
[latex] \begin{aligned} t_{B}&=\frac{2 A}{A_{g} \sqrt{2 g}}(\sqrt{h_{m}}-\sqrt{h_{m}-H}) \\ t_{B}&=\frac{2 A}{A_{g} \sqrt{2 g}} \sqrt{h_{m}} \qquad \cdots(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get
[latex] \frac{t_{B}}{t_{A}}=2[/latex]
[latex] \text { or } \quad t_{B}=2 t_{A}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 4 mm thick sheet is rolled with 300 mm diameter rolls to reduce thickness without any change in its width. The friction coefficient at the work-roll interface is 0.1. The minimum possible thickness of the sheet that can be produced in a single pass is:

Frictional coefficient at work-roll interface,
[latex] \mu=0.1[/latex]
Let [latex]t_{f}=[/latex] Final thickness of sheet after rolling
For single pass without slipping minimum possible thickness,
[latex] \begin{aligned} t_{i}-t_{f} &=\mu^{2} R \\ \mu &=\sqrt{\frac{t_{1}-t_{f}}{R}} \\ 0.1 &=\sqrt{\frac{4 \times 10^{-3}-t_{f}}{0.15}} \\ \text{or}\quad t_{f} &=2.5 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a wire drawing operation, diameter of a steel wire is reduced from 10 mm to 8 mm. the mean flow stress of the material is 400 MPa. The ideal force requied for drawing (ignoring friction and redundant work) is:
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\; D_{i}&=10 \mathrm{mm} \\ D_{f}&=8 \mathrm{mm} \\ \sigma_{0}&=400 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Ignoring friction and redundant work means
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mu &=0, \beta=0 \\ \text { Hence } \;\;\sigma_{d} &=2 \sigma_{0} \ln \left(\frac{r_{i}}{r_{f}}\right) \\ &=2 \times 400 \ln \left(\frac{5}{4}\right) \\ &=178.51 \mathrm{MPa} \\ &=178.51 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \times \pi r_{f}^{2} \\ &=178.51 \times 10^{6} \times 3.14 \times(0.004)^{2} \\ &=8968 \mathrm{N}=8.97 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A football was inflated to a gauge pressure of 1 bar when the ambient temperature was 15[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. When the game started next day, the air temperature at the stadium was 5[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Assume that the volume of the football remains constant at 2500 [latex]cm^{3}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Gauge pressure,
[latex] p_{G 1}=1 \text { bar }=100 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
Ambient temperature,
[latex] T_{1}=15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(15+273) \mathrm{K}=288 \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Absolute pressure,
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{1} &=p_{G 1}+p_{\text {atm }} \\ &=100+101.325 \\ &=201.325 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \text{Volume}\;V &=2500 \mathrm{cm}^{3}=2500 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Temperature,
[latex] T_{2}=5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(5+273) \mathrm{K}=278 \mathrm{K}[/latex]
From equation equation of state,
[latex] p_{1} V_{1}=m R T_{1} [/latex]
[latex] 201.325\times 2500 \times 10^{-6}=m \times 0.287 \times 288[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{or}\quad m &=6.089 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Heat loss: }Q&=\mathrm{mc}_{\mathrm{v}}\left(T_{1}-T_{2}\right) \\ &=6.089 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.718 \times(288-278) \\ &=0.0437 \mathrm{kJ}=43.7 \mathrm{J} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At V=C
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{1}}{T_{1}} &=\frac{p_{2}}{T_{2}} \\ \frac{201.325}{288} &=\frac{p_{2}}{278}\\ \text{or }\quad p_{2}&=194.33 \mathrm{kPa} \quad (absolute)\\ \text { also } \quad p_{2}&=p_{G 2}+p_{\text {atm }}\\ \therefore 194.33&=p_{G 2}+101.325\\ \text{or}\quad p_{G z}&=93 \mathrm{kPa}=0.93 \mathrm{bar}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{2} V&=m R T_{2} \\ p_{2} &\times 2500 \times 10^{-6}=6.089 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.287 \times 278\\ \text{or}\quad p_{2}&=194.32 \mathrm{kPa} \quad (absolute)\\ \text { also } \quad p_{2} &=p_{G 2}+p_{\text {atm }} \\ \therefore \quad 194.32 &=p_{G 2}+101.325 \\ \text{or}\quad p_{G 2} &=92.99 \mathrm{kPa} \\ & \approx 93 \mathrm{kPa}=0.93 \mathrm{bar} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A smooth flat plate with a sharp leading edge is placed along a gas stream flowing at U = 10 m/s. The thickness of the boundary layer at section r-s is 10 mm, the breadth of the plate is 1 m (into the paper) and the density of the gas [latex]\rho = 1.0 kg/m^{3}[/latex]. Assume that the boundary layer is thin, two-dimensional, and follows a linear velocity distribution, [latex]u= U(y/\delta )[/latex], the section r-s, where y is the height from plate.

The mass flow rate (in kg/s) across the section q-r is:
raw_source.solution:
Velocity of free stream,
[latex] U=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
Boundary layer thickness at section r-s,
[latex] \delta=10 \mathrm{mm}=0.01 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Width of the plate: b=1m
Density of the gas: [latex] p=1 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Linear velocity distribution,
[latex] u=U \frac{y}{\delta}[/latex]
Mass flow rate entering through section p q
[latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{m} &=\rho A U=\rho b \delta U \\ &=1 \times 1 \times 0.01 \times 10=0.1 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Mass flow rate entering through section s-r
[latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{m}&=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho a u=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b d y u \\ &=\rho b\int_{0}^{\delta}u d y=\rho b \int_{0}^{\delta} \frac{u y}{\delta} d y\\ &\left(\because u=\frac{U y}{\delta}\right) \\=& \frac{\rho b U^{\delta}}{\delta} \int_{0}^{\delta} y d y=\frac{\rho b U}{\delta}\left[\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{\delta} \\=& \frac{\rho b U}{\delta} \times \frac{\delta^{2}}{2}=\frac{\rho b U \delta}{2} \\=& \frac{1 \times 1 \times 10 \times 0.01}{2}=0.05 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text:
A smooth flat plate with a sharp leading edge is placed along a gas stream flowing at U = 10 m/s. The thickness of the boundary layer at section r-s is 10 mm, the breadth of the plate is 1 m (into the paper) and the density of the gas [latex]\rho = 1.0 kg/m^{3}[/latex]. Assume that the boundary layer is thin, two-dimensional, and follows a linear velocity distribution, [latex]u= U(y/\delta )[/latex], the section r-s, where y is the height from plate.

The integrated drag force (in N) on the plate, between p-s, is:
raw_source.solution:
Drag force on plate = rate of change of momentum of the flowing fluid.
Momentum thickness: [latex] \theta=\int_{0}^{\delta} \frac{u}{U}\left(\frac{1-u}{U}\right) d y [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \theta &=\int_{0}^{\delta} \frac{U}{\delta}\left(1-\frac{u}{\delta}\right) d y=\int_{0}^{\delta}\left(\frac{y}{\delta}-\frac{y^{2}}{\delta^{2}}\right) d y \\ &=\frac{y^{2}}{2 \delta}-\left.\frac{y^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right|_{0} ^{\delta}=\frac{\delta}{2}-\frac{\delta}{3}=\frac{\delta}{6} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex]Force on plate per unit width [latex]=\delta U^{2} \times(\theta \times 1) [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Here, } \quad U &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ &=1 \times(10)^{2} \times\left(\frac{10 \times 10^{-3}}{6} \times 1\right) \\ &=0.1666 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: Consider an incompressible laminar boundary layer flow over a flat plate of length L, aligned with the direction of an oncoming uniform free stream. If F is the ratio of the drag force on the front half of the plate to the drag force on the rear half, then
raw_source.solution:
Drag force,
[latex] \begin{aligned} F_{D} &=C_{f} \times \frac{1}{2} \rho A V^{2}=\frac{1.328}{\sqrt{\text{Re}_{L}}} \times \frac{1}{2} \rho A V^{2} \\ &=\frac{1.328}{\sqrt{\frac{\rho L V}{\mu}}} \times \frac{1}{2} \rho \times A \times L \times V^{2}\\ \text{i.e. }F_{D} &\propto \sqrt{L} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now Drag force on front half,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \quad F_{D R} &\propto \sqrt{\frac{L}{2}} \\ \therefore F_{D / 2}&=\frac{F_{D}}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Drag force on rear half,
[latex] \begin{aligned} F_{D / 2}^{\prime}&=F_{D}-F_{D / 2}=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) F_{D}\\ \text{Now} F&=\frac{F_{D / 2}}{F_{D / 2}^{\prime}}=\frac{\frac{F_{D}}{\sqrt{2}}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) F_{D}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}-1}>1\\ \therefore \quad F&>1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: In a steady flow through a nozzle, the flow velocity on the nozzle axis is given by [latex]v = u_{0}\left ( 1+\frac{3x}{L} \right )i[/latex], where x  is the distance along the axis of the nozzle from its inlet plane and L is the length of the nozzle. The time required for a fluid particle on the axis to travel from the inlet to the exit lane of the nozzle is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]v=u_{o}\left(1+\frac{3 x}{L}\right) [/latex]
We know that
Velocity: [latex]\quad v=\frac{d x}{d t} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \frac{d x}{d t}=u_{0}\left(1+\frac{3 x}{L}\right) [/latex]
[latex] \text{or }\quad u_{0}. d t=\frac{d x}{\left(1+\frac{3 x}{L}\right)} [/latex]
Integrating both sides, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} u_{0} \int_{0}^{t} d t &=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{d x}{\left(1+\frac{3 x}{L}\right)} \\ u_{0} t &=\frac{L}{3}\left[\ln \left(1+\frac{3 x}{L}\right)\right]_{0}^{L}=\frac{L}{3} \ln 4 \\ \therefore \quad t &=\frac{L}{3 u_{0}} \ln 4 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The X and Y be two independent random variables.

raw_source.text: The inlet angle of runner blades of a Francis turbine is 90[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. The blades are so shaped that the tangential component of velocity at blade outlet is zero. The flow velocity remains constant throughout the blade passage and is equal to half of the blade velocity at runner inlet. The blade efficiency of the runner is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \beta_{i} &=90^{\circ} \\ V_{w 0} &=0 \\ V_{t_{i}} &=V_{t_{0}}=\frac{u_{i}}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Blade efficiency of the runner,
[latex] \eta_{H}=\frac{V_{w i} u_{i}}{g H}=\frac{u_{i}^{2}}{g H} \quad \because V_{w i}=u_{i}[/latex]
By energy balance equation,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \rho Q g H &=\rho Q V_{w i} u_{i}+\frac{\rho Q V_{0}^{2}}{2} \\ g H &=u_{i}^{2}+\frac{V_{f 0}^{2}}{2}=u_{i}^{2}+\frac{u_{i}^{2}}{8} \\ g H &=\frac{9}{8} u_{i}^{2}\\ \therefore \quad \eta_{H} &=\frac{u_{i}^{2}}{\frac{9}{8} u_{i}^{2}}=\frac{8}{9}=0.8888 \\ &=88.88 \% \approx 89 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

The temperature distribution within the thermal boundary layer over a heated isothermal flat plate is given by [latex]\frac{T-T_{w}}{T_{\infty }-T_{w}}=\frac{3}{2}\left ( \frac{y}{\delta _{t}} \right )-\frac{1}{2}\left ( \frac{y}{\delta _{t}} \right )^{3},[/latex]
 where [latex]T_{w}[/latex]
 and [latex]T_{\infty }[/latex]
  are the temperatures of plate and free stream respectively, and y is the normal distance measured from the plate. The local Nusselt number based on the thermal boundary layer thickness [latex]\delta _{t}[/latex]
 is given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \qquad N u&=\frac{h L}{k_{f}}=\left.\frac{\partial T^{*}}{\partial y^{*}}\right|_{y^{*}=0} \\ \text { where } \quad T^{*}&=\frac{T-T_{w}}{T_{\infty}-T_{w}}\\ \text{and }\quad y^{*}&=\frac{y}{\delta}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
where [latex]T_{w}[/latex] is surface temperature and [latex]T_{\infty} [/latex] is freestream temperature.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow\quad N u &=\frac{3}{2}-\left.\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{y}{\delta_{t}}\right)\right|_{y_{y}^{*}=0} \\ &=\frac{3}{2}-\left.\frac{3}{2} y^{*}\right|_{y^{*}=0}=1.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a counter flow heat exchanger, hot fluid enters at 60[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and cold fluid leaves at 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Mass flow rate of the hot fluid is  1 kg/s and that of the cold fluid is 2 kg/s.  Specific heat of the hot fluid is 10kJ/kgK and that of the cold fluid is 5 kJ /kgK. The Log Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD) for the heat exchanger in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{h1}=60^{\circ}C, T_{c2}=30^{\circ}C, m_h=1\; kg/s\\ m_c=5\; kg/s, c_h=10\; kJ/kgK, c-C=5\; kJ/kgK \end{aligned}[/latex]

Heat lost by hot fluid = Heat gained by cold fluid
[latex]\begin{aligned} m_hc_h(T_{h1}-T_{h2})&=m_cc_c(T_{c2}-T_{c1})\\ 1 \times 10(60-T_{h2})&=2 \times 5(30-T_{c1})\\ 60-T_{h2}&=30-T_{c1}\\ T_{h2}-T_{c2}&=60-30=30^{\circ}C\\ \text{If }\theta _1&=\theta _2\\ \text{Then LMTD}&=\theta _1=\theta _2=30^{\circ}C \end{aligned}[/latex]

The average heat transfer co-efficient on a thin hot vertical plate suspended in still air can be determined from observations of the change in plate temperature with time as it cools. Assume the plate temperature to be uniform at any instant of time and radiation heat exchange with the surroundings is negligible. The ambient temperature is [latex]25^{\circ}C[/latex]
 the plate has a total surface area of [latex]0.1 m^{2}[/latex]
 and a mass of 4 kg. The specific heat of the plate material is 2.5 kJ/kgK.  The convective heat transfer co-efficient in [latex]W/m^{2}K[/latex], at the instant when the plate temperature is [latex]225^{\circ}C[/latex]
 and the change in plate temperature with time  dT/dt = -0.02 K/s, is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} A&=0.1 \mathrm{m}^{2} ; \quad m=4 \mathrm{kg} \\ \mathrm{c}_{p}&=2.5 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net rate of heat transfer
= Rate of change of internal energy
[latex] \begin{aligned} h A\left(T-T_{f}\right) &=-m c_{p} \frac{d T}{d t} \\ h \times 0.1(225-25) &=-4 \times 2.5 \times 1000 \times(-0.02) \\ h &=\frac{4 \times 2.5 \times 1000 \times 0.02}{0.1 \times 200} \\ &=10 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} C_{H} &=\frac{H}{(N D)^{2}} \\ \left(C_{H}\right)_{\text{model}} &=\left(C_{H}\right)_{\text {prootipe }} \\ \frac{H_{m}}{N_{m}^{2} D_{m}^{2}} &=\frac{H_{p}}{N_{p}^{2} D_{p}^{2}} \\ \frac{H_{p} / 4}{N_{m}^{2} \times \frac{D_{p}^{2}}{4}} &=\frac{H_{p}}{N^{2} \times D_{p}^{2}} \\ \text{or}\quad N_{m}^{2} &=N^{2}\\ \text{or }\quad N_{m}&=N \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The stroke and bore of a four stroke spark ignition engine are 250 mm and 200 mm respectively. The clearance volume is 0.001 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]. If the specific heat ratio [latex]\gamma = 1.4[/latex],
 the air-standard cycle efficiency of the engine is
raw_source.solution:
Stroke length,
[latex] \begin{aligned} l &=250 \mathrm{mm} \\ \text{Bore dia:}\quad d &=200 \mathrm{mm}=0.2 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Clearance volume,
[latex] \begin{array}{c} V_{c}=0.001 \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \gamma=1.4 \end{array}[/latex]
Displacement volume,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{s} &=\frac{\pi}{4} d^{2} \times l=\frac{3.14}{4} \times(2)^{2} \times 0.25 \\ &=7.85 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Total volume in the cylinder,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{1} &=V_{c}+V_{s} \\ &=0.001+7.83 \times 10^{-3} \\ &=8.85 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Compression ratio,
[latex] r=\frac{V_{1}}{V_{c}}=\frac{8.85 \times 10^{-3}}{0.001}=8.85[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex]Air-standard cycle efficiency,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta &=1-\frac{1}{r^{\gamma-1}}=1-\frac{1}{(8.85)^{1.4-1}} \\ &=1-\frac{1}{8.85^{0.4}} \\ &=0.5819 \approx 58.2 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A building has to be maintained at [latex]21^{\circ}C[/latex]
 (dry bulb) and [latex]14.5^{\circ}C[/latex]
. (wet bulb). The dew point temperature under these conditions is [latex]10.17^{\circ}C[/latex]
. The outside temperature is [latex]-23^{\circ}C[/latex]
 (dry bulb) and an internal and external heat transfer coefficients are 8 W/ [latex]m^{2}K[/latex]
 and 23 W/[latex]m^{2}K[/latex]
 respectively. If the building wall has the thermal conductivity of 1.2 W/mK. The minimum thickness(in m) of wall required to prevent condensation is
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{i} &=21^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{d p} &=10.17^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{o} &=-23^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ h_{i} &=8 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}, h_{o}=23 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \\ k &=1.2 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The heat transfer rate per unit area in the slab can be calculated by considering convection at inner side.


[latex] \begin{aligned} q &=h_{i}\left(T_{i}-T_{d p}\right) \\ &=8(21-10.17)=86.64 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Further this heat is conducted through wall
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore q&=\frac{T_{d p}-T_{0}}{\frac{x}{k}+\frac{1}{h_{0}}}\\ 86.64 &=\frac{10.17-(-23)}{\frac{x}{1.2}+\frac{1}{23}}=\frac{33.17}{\frac{x}{1.2}+\frac{1}{23}} \\ \text { or } \frac{x}{1.2}+\frac{1}{23} &=\frac{33.17}{86.64}=0.3828 \\ \text { or }\quad \frac{x}{1.2} &=0.3393 \\ x &=1.2 \times 0.3393=0.4072 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Atmospheric air at a flow rate of 3 kg/s (on dry basis) enters a cooling and dehumidifying coil with an enthalpy of   85 kJ/kg of dry air and a humidity ratio of 19 grams/kg of dry air. The air leaves the coil with an enthalpy of 43 kJ/kg of dry air and a humidity ratio of 8 grams/kg of dry air. If the condensate water leaves the coil with an enthalpy of 67 kJ/kg, the required cooling capacity of the coil in kW is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Mass flow rate of dry air
[latex] \begin{aligned} m_{a}&=3 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ h_{1}&=85 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ \omega_{1}&=19 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ &=0.019 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ h_{2}&=43 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ \omega_{2}&=8 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ &=0.008 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \end{aligned}[/latex]

Enthalpy of condenrate water leaves the cooling
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { coil: } h_{f g}&=67 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \omega_{1}&=\frac{m_{v 1}}{m_{a}}\\ \text{or }\quad m_{v 1}&=\omega_{1} m_{a}=0.019 \times 3 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ & =0.057 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}, \text{mass of water vapour at inlet} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly,
[latex] m_{v 2}=\omega_{2} m_{a}=0.008 \times 3[/latex]
[latex] =0.024 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}, [/latex] mass of water vapour at outlet
Mass flow rate of condensate,
[latex] \begin{aligned} m_{w} &=m_{v 1}+m_{v 2} \\ &=0.057+0.024=0.033 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Cooling capacity of the coil,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=m\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)-m_{w} h_{f g}\\ \text{where }m\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)&= \text{sensible heat removed}\\ \therefore m_{w} h_{f g}&= \text{ Latent heat removed}\\ Q &=3(85-43)-0.033 \times 67 \\ &=123.79 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively


Mass flow rate of condensate,
[latex] \begin{aligned} m_{w} &=m_{a}\left(\omega_{1}-\omega_{2}\right) \\ &=3 \times(0.019-0.008) \\ &=0.033 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying energy balance equation, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} m_{a} h_{1} &=m_{a} h_{2}+m_{w} h_{f g}+Q \\ 3 \times 85 &=3 \times 43+0.033 \times 67+Q \\ Q &=123.8 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A heat transformer is a device that transfers a part of the heat, supplied to it at an intermediate temperature, to a high temperature reservoir while rejecting the remaining part to a low temperature heat sink.  In such a heat transformer, 100 kJ of heat is supplied at 350 K. The maximum amount of heat in kJ that can be transferred to 400 K, when the rest is rejected to a heat sink at 300 K is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q_{1}+Q_{2} &=100 \mathrm{kJ} \\ T &=350 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{1} &=400 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{2} &=300 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Entropy change of the heat temperature device:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta S &=-\frac{\left(Q_{1}+Q_{2}\right)}{350}=-\frac{100}{350} \\ &=-\frac{2}{7} \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Entropy change of reservoir- 1
[latex] \Delta S_{1}=\frac{Q_{2}}{T_{2}}=\frac{100-Q_{1}}{300} \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Entropy change of reservoir- 2
[latex] \Delta S_{2}=\frac{Q_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{Q_{1}}{400} \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Total entropy
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta S_{\text {total }} &=0 \\ \Delta S+\Delta S_{1}+\Delta S_{2} &=0 \\ -\frac{2}{7}+\frac{100-Q_{1}}{300}+\frac{Q_{1}}{400} &=0 \\ -\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{Q_{1}}{300}+\frac{Q_{1}}{400} &=0 \\ -\frac{400 Q_{1}+300 Q_{1}}{120000}=\frac{2}{7}-\frac{1}{3} &=\frac{6-7}{21}=-\frac{1}{21} \\ -\frac{100 Q_{1}}{120000} &=-\frac{1}{21} \\ \text{or } \qquad Q_{1} &=57.14 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Second Law, Carnot Cycle and Entropy

Q. For a system undergoing a process, its entropy remains constant only when the process is reversible.
R. The work done by a closed system in an adiabatic process is a point function.

raw_source.solution:
For steady, incompressible forced, vortex flow;
P. Shear stress in zero at all points in the flow. --Incorrect
Shear stress is always exit dut to external torque acting on mass of fluid.
Q.Vorticity is zero at all points in the flow.-- Incorrect
Velocity exists at all points in forced vortex flow field.
R. Velocity is directly proportional to the radius from the centre of the vortex. - Correct.
For forced vortex flow,
[latex] \frac{V}{r}=\text { Constant }[/latex]
[latex] \text{or }\quad V \propto r [/latex]
S. Total mechanical energy per unit mass is constant in the entire flow field. - Correct
[latex] \frac{\rho \omega^{2}}{2}\left(r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}^{2}\right)-\rho g\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or }\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}\left(r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}^{2}\right)-g\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Delta \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E} .-\Delta \mathrm{P.E.}=0 [/latex]
where,
[latex] \Delta K . E .=\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}\left(r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}^{2}\right)-\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right) [/latex]
change in K.E. per unit mass
[latex] \Delta P . E=g\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right) \quad [/latex]
change in P.E. per unit mass
[latex] \therefore \Delta K \cdot E .=\Delta P . E [/latex]
Hence, total mechanical energy per unit mass in constant.

raw_source.text:
Which combination of the following statements about steady incompressible forced vortex flow is correct?
P: Shear stress is zero at all points in the flow.
Q: Vorticity is zero at all points in the flow.
R: Velocity is directly proportional to the radius from the centre of the vortex.
S: Total mechanical energy per unit mass is constant in the entire flow field.
raw_source.solution:
Given:
The flow is a steady incompressible forced vortex flow.

Key property of forced vortex:
[latex] v = \omega r [/latex]

Evaluation of statements:

P: Shear stress is zero at all points in the flow.
In a forced vortex, the fluid rotates like a rigid body. There is no relative motion between adjacent fluid layers, hence no velocity gradient in the radial direction.
[latex] \therefore \text{Shear stress} = 0 [/latex]
Statement P is TRUE.

Q: Vorticity is zero at all points in the flow.
For a forced vortex, vorticity is given by
[latex] \text{Vorticity} = 2\omega [/latex] which is constant and non-zero.
Statement Q is FALSE.

R: Velocity is directly proportional to the radius from the centre of the vortex.
From the forced vortex relation,
[latex] v = \omega r [/latex] Velocity increases linearly with radius.
Statement R is TRUE.

S: Total mechanical energy per unit mass is constant in the entire flow field.
In a forced vortex, pressure and kinetic energy vary with radius, so total mechanical energy is not constant throughout the flow field (it is constant only along a streamline).
Statement S is FALSE.

raw_source.text: A thin spherical pressure vessel of 200 mm diameter and 1 mm thickness is subjected to an internal pressure varying from 4 to 8 MPa. Assume that the yield, ultimate, and endurance strength of material are 600, 800 and 400 MPa respectively. The factor of safety as per Goodman's relation is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \sigma_{1} &=\sigma_{2}=\frac{p r}{2 t} \\ \sigma_{\operatorname{lmax}} &=\frac{8 \times 100}{2 \times 1}=400 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{\operatorname{lmin}} &=\frac{4 \times 100}{2 \times 1}=200 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{\ln 2 x} &=400 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{\operatorname{Trin}} &=200 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{1 \mathrm{m}} &=300 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{la}} &=100 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{Zn}} &=300 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{aa}} &=100 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Equivalent Stresses
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{me}} &=\sqrt{\sigma_{1 m}^{2}+\sigma_{2 m}^{2}-\sigma_{1 m} \sigma_{2 m}} \\ &=\sqrt{300^{2}+300^{2}-300 \times 300} \\ &=300 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \text{Similarly,}& \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{a} e} &=100 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Goodman equation,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\sigma_{a \theta}}{S_{e}}+\frac{\sigma_{m e}}{S_{u t}} &=\frac{1}{n} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{100}{400}+\frac{300}{800} &=\frac{1}{n} \\ n &=1.6 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The equation of motion of a harmonic oscillator is given by
[latex]\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2} x}{\mathrm{d} t^{2}}+2\zeta \omega _{n}\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}+\omega _{n}^{2}x=0[/latex]
and the initial conditions at t = 0 are x (0)= X, [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}(0)=0[/latex]. The amplitude of x(t) after n complete cycle is
raw_source.solution:
We have,
[latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} ^2x}{\mathrm{d} t^2}+2\zeta \omega_n\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}+\omega_n^2 x=0[/latex]
[latex]\ddot x+2\zeta \omega_n\dot x+\omega_n^2 x=0[/latex]
Logarithmic decrement is given by
[latex]\delta=\ln\left ( \frac{x_1}{x_2} \right )=\frac{2\pi \zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}[/latex]
Logarithmic decrement for n cycle is given by
[latex]\delta=\frac{1}{n}\ln\left ( \frac{x_1}{x_{n+1}} \right )[/latex]
Given that, Initially amplitude is [latex]x_1=X[/latex] and we need to find amplitude after n cycle, so we have
[latex]\frac{1}{n}\ln\left ( \frac{X}{x_{n+1}} \right )=\frac{2\pi \zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{X}{x_{n+1}} =e^{\frac{2\pi n\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}}[/latex]
[latex]x_{n+1} =Xe^{-\frac{2\pi n\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{c r} &=\frac{2 \pi^{2} E I}{L^{2}} \\ I &=\frac{\pi}{64}(20)^{4}=7853.9 \mathrm{mm}^{4} \\ E &=200 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=200 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ &=\frac{2 \pi^{2} \times 200 \times 10^{3} \times 7853.9}{(700)^{2}}=63.27 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Factor of safety
[latex] =\frac{\text { Crippling load }}{\text { Working load }}=\frac{63.27}{10}=6.32[/latex]

raw_source.text: A direct current welding machine with a linear power source characteristic provides open circuit voltage of 80 V and short circuit current of 800 A. During welding with the machine, the measured arc current is 500 A corresponding to an arc length of 5.0 mm and the measured arc current is 460 A corresponding to an arc length of 7.0 mm.  The linear voltage (E) - arc length (L) characteristic of the welding arc can be given as (where E is in Volt and L is in mm)
raw_source.solution:
The power source characteristic can be witten analytically as
[latex] E=80-\frac{80}{800}I \qquad(a)[/latex]
The arc characteristic is given as
[latex] I=a L+b [/latex]
where a and b are constant
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{when }I&=500 \mathrm{A}\\ \text{then }L&=5.00 \mathrm{mm}\\ \therefore 500&=5 a+b \qquad(i)\\ \text{when }I&=460 \mathrm{A}\\ \text{then }L&=7.00 \mathrm{mm}\\ \therefore 460&=7 a+b \qquad(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} a&=-20 \\ \text{and }b&=600 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Then arc characteristic equation
[latex] I=-20 L+600 \qquad(a)[/latex]
from equation (a) and (b)
[latex] \begin{aligned} E &=80-\frac{80}{800}(-20 L+600) \\ &=80-0.1(-20 L+600) \\ &=80+2 L-60 \\ &=20+2 L \end{aligned}[/latex]

Two metallic sheets, each of 2.0 mm thickness, are welded in a lap joint configuration by resistance spot welding at a welding current of 10 kA and welding time of 10 milli second. A spherical fusion zone extending up to the full thickness of each sheet is formed. The properties of the metallic sheets are given as:

ambient temperature = 293 K
melting temperature = 1793 K
density = 7000 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex]
latent heat of fusion = 300 kJ/kg
specific heat = 800 J/kg K

Assume: 1) Contact resistance along sheet - sheet interface is 500 micro-ohm and along electrode - sheet interface is zero;
2) No conductive heat loss through the bulk sheet materials; and
3) The complete weld fusion zone is at the melting temperature.

The melting efficiency (in %) of the process is
raw_source.solution:
Given
Current: [latex]I=10^{4} \mathrm{A}[/latex]
Time: [latex]t=10^{-2} \mathrm{s}[/latex]
[latex] \text { Resistance: } \quad R=500 \times 10^{-6} \Omega[/latex]
Ambient temperature
[latex] T_{\infty}=293 \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Melting temperature,
[latex] T_{m}=1793 \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Latent heat of fusion,
[latex] \begin{aligned} L&=300 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Density:}\quad\rho&=7000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Specific heat,
[latex] c_{p}=800 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK}[/latex]
Radius of sphere,
[latex] r=2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Total heat supplied,
[latex] \begin{aligned} H_{S} &=I^{2} R t \\ &=\left(10^{4}\right)^{2} \times 500 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{-2} \\ &=500 \mathrm{J} \\ \text { Mass } &=\frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} \times \rho \\ &=\frac{4}{3} \pi\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{3} \times 7000 \\ &=2.346 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Total heat for melting,
[latex] \begin{aligned} H_{\mathrm{i}} &=m L+m c_{p}\left(T_{m}-T_{0}\right) \\ &=2.346 \times 10^{-4}[300 \times 1000+\\ &800(1793-293)] \\ H_{i} &=351.9 \mathrm{J} \\ \text{Efficiency }\quad&= \frac{H_{i}}{H_{s}}\times100\\ &=\frac{351.9}{500} \times 100 \\ &=70.38 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Capacities of production of an item over 3 consecutive months in regular time are 100, 100 and 80 and in overtime are      20, 20 and 40. The demands over those 3 months are 90, 130 and 110. The cost of production in regular time and overtime are respectively Rs. 20 per item and       Rs. 24 per item. Inventory carrying cost is Rs. 2 per item per month. The levels of starting and final inventory are nil. Backorder is not permitted. For minimum cost of plan, the level of planned production in overtime in the third month is
raw_source.solution:
For 1st month there is no need to overtime, because demand is 90 units and regular time production is 100 units, therefore 10 units are excess in amount. For 2nd month the demand is 130 unit and production capacity with overtime is 100 + 20 = 120 units, therefore 10 units (130 – 120 =10) are short in amount, which is fulfilled by 10 units excess of 1st month. So at the end of 2nd month there is no inventory.

Now for the 3rd month demand is 110 units and regular time production is 80 units. So remaining 110 – 80 = 30 units are produced in overtime (which has 40 units) to fulfill the demand for minimum cost of plan.

raw_source.text:
A thermodynamic cycle with an ideal gas as working fluid is shown below.


If the specific heats of the working fluid are constant and the value of specific heat ratio [latex]\gamma[/latex] is 1.4, the thermal efficiency (%) of the cycle is
raw_source.solution:
the The given cycle is Lenoir cycle for which
efficiency is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta&=1-\frac{\gamma\left(r_{p}^{1 / \gamma}-1\right)}{r_{p}-1}\\ \text{where }\quad \gamma&=1.4 \\ r_{p} &=\frac{p_{3}}{p_{2}}=\frac{400}{100}=4 \\ \therefore \quad \eta &=1-\frac{1.4\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{1.4}}{4-1}\right)}{4-1} \\ &=21.05 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively

Process 2-3
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{23} &=\left(U_{3}-U_{2}\right)+W_{2-3} \\ Q_{23} &=\left(U_{3}-U_{2}\right)+0 \\ &=m_{v}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right) \\ &=m_{v}\left(\frac{p_{3} V_{3}}{m R}-\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{m R}\right) \\ &=\frac{c_{v}}{R}\left(p_{3} v_{3}-p_{2} V_{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{c_{v}}{c_{p}-c_{v}}(400 \times 1-100 \times 1) \\ Q_{23} &=\frac{1}{\gamma-1}(400-100) \\ &=\frac{300}{1.4-1}=\frac{300}{0.4}=750 \mathrm{kJ} \\ Q_{1-2} = & \left(U_{2}-U_{1}\right)+W_{1-2} \\ & =m_{0}\left(T_{2}-T_{1}\right)+p\left(V_{2}-V_{1}\right) \\ & =m_{0}\left[\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{m R}-\frac{p_{1} V_{1}}{m R}\right]+p\left(V_{2}-V_{1}\right)\\ &=\frac{c_{v}}{R}\left[p\left(V_{2}-V_{1}\right)\right]+p\left(V_{2}-V_{1}\right) \\ &=p\left(V_{2}-v_{1}\right)\left\{\frac{c_{v}}{R}+1\right\} \\ &\qquad \because V_{2}=1 \mathrm{m}^{3}\\ &=p\left(1-v_{1}\right)\left\{\frac{c_{v}}{c_{p}-c_{v}}+1\right\} \\ &=100\left(1-V_{1}\right)\left\{\frac{1}{\gamma-1}+1\right\} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Calculating [latex]V_{1}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{3} V_{3}^{\gamma} &=P_{1} V_{1}^{\gamma} \\ \therefore \quad V_{1} &=\left[\frac{P_{3} \cdot V_{3}^{\gamma}}{P_{1}}\right]^{\frac{1}{\gamma}} \\ &=\left[\frac{400}{100} \times 1\right]^{\frac{1}{1.4}}=2.692 \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ Q_{1-2} &\left.=100[1-2.692] \times\left\{\frac{1}{0.4}+1\right\}\right\} \\ &=-592.2 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
(minus sign represent heat is rejected)
There is no heat transfer in process 3-1 as it is reversible adiabatic process.
Efficiency of cycle,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta &=1-\frac{Q_{\text {reject }}}{Q_{\text {added }}}=1-\frac{592.2}{750} \\ &=0.2104=21.04 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider steady one-dimensional heat flow in a plate of 20 mm thickness with a uniform heat generation of 80 MW/[latex]m^3[/latex]. The left and right faces are kept at constant temperatures of 160[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and 120[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C respectively. The plate has a constant thermal conductivity of 200 W/mK.

The location of maximum temperature within the plate from its left face is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \delta &= 20mm=0.02m\\ q_G&= 80 MW/m^3\\ &= 80 \times 10^6 W/m^3\\ &= 80 \times 10^3 kW/m^3\\ T_{s=0} &= 160^{\circ}C\\ T_{s=\delta }&= 120^{\circ}C\\ k&=200 W/mK=0.20 kW/mK \end{aligned}[/latex]

Equation of one dimensional steady state heat transfer with heat generation
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d^2T}{dx^2}+\frac{q_G}{k}&=0\\ \frac{d^2T}{dx^2}+\frac{80 \times 10^3}{0.20}&=0\\ \frac{d^2T}{dx^2}+400 \times 10^3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
On integrating, we get
[latex] \frac{dT}{dx}+400 \times 10^3x=C_1[/latex]
Again integrating, we get
[latex] T+400 \times 10^3 \frac{x^2}{2}=C_1x+C_2[/latex]
[latex] T+200 \times 10^3 x^2=C_1x_2+C_2\;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
where [latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex] are constant of integration that can be determined from the boundary conditions
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{At}\;\; x&=0,\; T=160^{\circ}C \\ \therefore \;\; 160&=C_2 \\ C_2&=160 \\ \text{At}\;\; x &=\delta =0.02m, \; T=120^{\circ}C \\ \therefore \; &120+200 \times 10^3 \times (0.02)2& \\ &=C_1 \times 0.02+160 \\ 200&= 0.02C_1+160\\ 0.02C_1&= 40\\ C_1&=2000 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting the value of [latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex] in equation (i), we get
[latex] T+200 \times 10^3x^2=2000x+160[/latex]
[latex] T=2000x+160-200 \times 10^2x^2[/latex]
The consition for the maximum temperature,
[latex] \frac{sT}{dx}=0[/latex]
[latex] 200-400 \times 10^3x=0[/latex]
[latex] x=0.005m=5mm[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A low carbon steel bar of 147 mm diameter with a length of 630 mm is being turned with uncoated carbide insert. The observed tool lives are 24 min and 12 min for cutting velocities of 90 m/min and 120 m/min respectively. The feed and depth of cut are 0.2 mm/rev and 2 mm respectively. Use the unmachined diameter to calculate the cutting velocity.

When tool life is 20 min, the cutting velocity in m/min is
raw_source.solution:
Given, [latex]T_1=24 min, T_2 =12 min, V_1=90m/min, V_2=120m/min[/latex]
We have to calculate velocity, when tool life is 20 minute.
First of all we calculate the values of n, From the Taylor's tool life equation,
[latex]VT^n=C[/latex]
For case 1st and 2nd, we can write,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_1T_1^n &= V_2T_2^n\\ \left ( \frac{T_1}{T_2} \right )^n &= \frac{V_2}{V_1} \\ \left ( \frac{24}{12} \right )^n &=\frac{120}{90} \\ 2^n&= 1.33\\ n \log 2&=\log 1.33 \\ n \times 0.301 &=0.124 \\ n&= 0.412 \end{aligned}[/latex]
For [latex]V_3[/latex], we can write from tool life equation,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_1T_1^n &= V_3T_3^n\\ 90 \times (24)^{0.412}&=V_3(20)^{0.412}\\ 333.34 &=V_3 \times 3.435\\ V_3 &=97\; m/min \end{aligned}[/latex]

Auxiliary equation is

raw_source.text: A coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting heads exactly 3 times?

raw_source.text: The Eigenvectors of the matrix [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 &2 \\ 0& 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] are written in the form [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ a \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ b \end{bmatrix}[/latex]. What is a + b?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\left|\begin{array}{cc}(1-\lambda) & 2 \\ 0 & (2-\lambda)\end{array}\right|=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \qquad(1-\lambda)(2-\lambda)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \lambda=1,2 [/latex]
Putting the value of [latex] \lambda=1 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \qquad\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ a\end{array}\right]=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \qquad a=0 [/latex]
putting the value of [latex] \lambda=2 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned}\left[\begin{array}{cc}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ b\end{array}\right] &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad b &=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \qquad a+b=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]f=y^x[/latex]. What is [latex]\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}[/latex] at x=2, y=1?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f &=y^{x} \\ \ln f &=x \ln y \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{f} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=\frac{x}{y} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=y^{x}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=y^{x-1} x \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x \partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(y^{x-1} x\right)\\ &=y^{x-1}+x y^{x-1} \ln y \\ &=1^{(2-1)}(1+2 \cdot \ln 1)=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: It is given that y'' + 2y' + y = 0,  y (0) = 0, y(1) = 0. What is y(0.5)?
raw_source.solution:

[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad D&=-1,-1 \\ \therefore \qquad y&=\left(C_{1}+C_{2} x\right) e^{-x} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad 0&=\left(C_{1}+C_{2}(0)\right) e^{-0} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{1}&=0\\ 0 &=\left(C_{1}+C_{2}\right) e^{-1} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{1}+C_{2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{2}&=0 \\ \therefore \qquad y(0.5)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The transverse shear stress acting in a beam of rectangular cross-section, subjected to a transverse shear load, is
raw_source.solution:
For a rectangle cross-section:
[latex]\tau _v=\frac{FA\bar{Y}}{Ib}=\frac{6F}{bd^3}\left ( \frac{d^2}{4}-y^2 \right )F=\text{Transverse shear load}[/latex]
Maximum values of [latex]\tau _v[/latex] occurs at the neutral axis where, [latex]y=0[/latex]
[latex]\text{Maximum }\tau _v=\frac{6F}{bd^3}\times \frac{d^2}{4}=\frac{3F}{2bd}=\frac{3}{2}T_{mean}[/latex]
[latex]T_{mean}=\frac{F}{bd}[/latex]

So, transverse shear stress is variable with maximum on the neutral axis.
options: Variable with maximum at the bottom of the beam
Variable with maximum at the top of the beam
Variable with maximum at the neutral axis

raw_answer.option_text: Variable with maximum at the neutral axis

raw_source.text: A rod of Length L and diameter D is subjected to a tensile load P. Which of the following is sufficient to calculate the resulting change in diameter?
raw_source.solution:
From the application of load P, the length of the rod increases by an amount of [latex]\Delta L[/latex]

[latex]\Delta L=\frac{PL}{AE}=\frac{PL}{\frac{\pi}{4}D^2E}=\frac{4PL}{\pi D^2E}[/latex]

And increase in length due to applied load P in axial or longitudinal direction, the shear modulus is comes in action.

[latex]G=\frac{\text{Shearing stress}}{\text{Shearing strain}}=\frac{\tau _s}{\Delta L/L}=\frac{\tau _sL}{\Delta L}[/latex]

So, for calculating the resulting change in diameter both young's modulus and shear modulus are used.
options: Both Young's modulus and shear modulus

raw_answer.option_text: Both Young's modulus and shear modulus

raw_source.text:
In an M/M/1 queuing system, the number of arrivals in an interval of length T is a Poisson random
variable (i.e. the probability of there being n arrivals in an interval of length T is [latex]\frac{e^{(-\lambda T)}(\lambda T)^{n}}{n!}[/latex]. The
probability density function f(t) of the inter-arrival time is given by
raw_source.solution:
The most common distribution found in queuing problems is poisson distribution. This is used in single-channel queuing problems for random arrivals where the service time is exponentially distributed.
Probability of n arrivals in time t

[latex]P=\frac{(\lambda T)^n\cdot e^{-\lambda T}}{n!}[/latex]
where, n=1,2,3,...

So, Probability density function of inter arrival time (time interval between two consecutive arrivals)
[latex]f(t)=\lambda \cdot e^{-\lambda t}[/latex]

[latex]\left|\begin{array}{cc}(1-\lambda) & 2 \\ 0 & (2-\lambda)\end{array}\right|=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \qquad(1-\lambda)(2-\lambda)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \lambda=1,2 [/latex]
Putting the value of [latex] \lambda=1 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \qquad\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ a\end{array}\right]=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \qquad a=0 [/latex]
putting the value of [latex] \lambda=2 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned}\left[\begin{array}{cc}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ b\end{array}\right] &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad b &=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \qquad a+b=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]f=y^x[/latex]. What is [latex]\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y}[/latex] at x=2, y=1?
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} f &=y^{x} \\ \ln f &=x \ln y \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{f} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=\frac{x}{y} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=y^{x}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=y^{x-1} x \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x \partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(y^{x-1} x\right)\\ &=y^{x-1}+x y^{x-1} \ln y \\ &=1^{(2-1)}(1+2 \cdot \ln 1)=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: It is given that y'' + 2y' + y = 0,  y (0) = 0, y(1) = 0. What is y(0.5)?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y^{\prime \prime}+2 y^{\prime}+y &=0 \\ \left(D^{2}+2 D+1\right) y &=0 \\ \Rightarrow D^{2}+2 D+1 &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(D+1)^{2} &=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad D&=-1,-1 \\ \therefore \qquad y&=\left(C_{1}+C_{2} x\right) e^{-x} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad 0&=\left(C_{1}+C_{2}(0)\right) e^{-0} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{1}&=0\\ 0 &=\left(C_{1}+C_{2}\right) e^{-1} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{1}+C_{2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{2}&=0 \\ \therefore \qquad y(0.5)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

A solid circular shaft of diameter 100 mm is subjected to an axial stress of 50 Mpa. It is further
subjected to a torque of 10 kNm. The maximum principal stress experienced on the shaft is
closest to

[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{T}{I_{P}} &=\frac{\tau}{r} \\ \frac{10 \times 10^{6}}{\frac{\pi}{32}(100)^{4}} &=\frac{\tau}{\frac{100}{2}} \\ \text { or } &=50.95 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The rod PQ of length L with flexural rigidity EI is hinged at both ends. For what minimum force F is it expected to buckle?
raw_source.solution:
Let the axial comp-load acting on the rod is R
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{H} &=R \cos 45^{\circ} \\ R_{V} &=R \sin 45^{\circ} \\ \text{Hence,}\quad R &=\frac{F}{\cos 45^{\circ}}=\sqrt{2} F \end{aligned}[/latex]
Condition for buckling, [latex]R>P_{\theta} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sqrt{2} F &>\frac{\pi^{2} E I_{\min }}{L_{e}^{2}} \quad \text { where } L_{e}=\alpha L \\ F &>\frac{\pi^{2} E I_{\min }}{\sqrt{2} \alpha^{2} L^{2}}\\ \alpha &=1 \quad(\because \text{both ends hinged})\\ \text{Hence }\;F_{\min } &=\frac{\pi^{2} E I_{\min }}{\sqrt{2} L^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a cam design, the rise motion is given by a simple harmonic motion (SHM) [latex]s=\frac{h}{2}(1-cos\frac{\pi \theta }{\beta })[/latex] where h is total rise,
[latex]\theta[/latex] is camshaft angle, [latex]\beta[/latex] is the total angle of the rise interval. The jerk is given by
raw_source.solution:
The jerk is given by [latex]\frac{d^{3} s}{d t^{3}} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \text { if } S=\frac{h}{2}\left(1-\cos \frac{\pi \theta}{\beta}\right) \\ \therefore \quad \frac{d^{3} s}{d t^{3}}=-\frac{\pi^{3}}{\beta^{3}} \frac{h}{2} \sin \left(\frac{\pi \theta}{\beta}\right)\\ \text{where } \theta=\omega t \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A uniform rigid rod of mass m = 1kg and length L = 1m is hinged at its centre and laterally
supported at one end by a spring of spring constant k = 300 N/m. The natural frequency [latex]\omega _n[/latex] in
rad/s is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} \frac{1}{2} I \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} k x^{2}=\text { constant } \\ \frac{1}{2} I \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} k\left(\frac{L}{2} \theta\right)^{2}=\text { constant } \end{array}[/latex]
Differentiating the whole expression w.rt.
[latex] \frac{1}{2} I 2 \ddot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{k}{2} \times \frac{L^{2}}{4} \times 2 \theta \dot{\theta}=0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow I \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K L^{2}}{4} \theta=0[/latex]
Putting the value of [latex]I=\frac{m L^{2}}{12} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{m L^{2}}{12} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{k L^{2}}{4} \theta=0 \\ \Rightarrow \ddot{\theta}+\frac{3 k}{m} \theta=0 \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Natural frequency: [latex]\omega_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}} [/latex]
[latex] =\sqrt{\frac{3 \times 300}{1}}=30 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]

A compression spring is made of music wire of 2mm diameter having a shear strength and shear
modulus of 800 MPa and 80 GPa respectively. The mean coil diameter is 20mm, free length is
40mm and the number of active coils is 10. If the mean coil diameter is reduced to 10mm, the
stiffness of the spring is approximately

[latex]\begin{aligned} k &=\frac{G d^{4}}{8 D^{3} N} \\ \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} &=\left(\frac{D_{1}}{D_{2}}\right)^{3}=\left(\frac{20}{10}\right)^{3}=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A journal bearing has a shaft diameter of 40mm and a length of 40 mm. the shaft is rotating at 20
rad/s and the viscosity of the lubricant is 20mPa-s. the clearance is 0.020 mm. the loss of torque
due to the viscosity of the lubricant is approximately:
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \tau &=\frac{\mu v}{c}=\frac{20 \times 10^{-3} \times 20 \times 20 \times 10^{-3}}{0.02 \times 10^{-3}} \\ &=400 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\\ \text { Force }&=\tau A=400 \times 3.14 \times 0.04 \times 0.04 \mathrm{N} \\ &\qquad(\because F=\tau \cdot \pi d l) \\ \text { Torque }&=400 \times 3.14 \times 0.04 \times 0.04 \times 0.02 & \\ &\qquad(\because\text { Torque }=F \times r)\\ &=0.040 \mathrm{Nm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A clutch has outer and inner diameters 100 mm and 40 mm respectively. Assuming a uniform
pressure of 2 MPa and coefficient of friction of liner material 0.4, the torque carrying capacity of
the clutch is
raw_source.solution:
Using uniform pressure theory torque carrying
capacity of clutch is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} T&=\frac{2}{3} \mu W\left(\frac{R^{3}-r^{3}}{R^{2}-r^{2}}\right) \\ T&=\frac{2}{3} \pi \mu\left(R^{3}-r^{3}\right)\left(\frac{W}{\pi\left(R^{2}-r^{2}\right)}\right) \\ T&=\frac{2}{3} \pi \mu \mathrm{p}\left(R^{3}-r^{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \times 3.14 \times 0.4 \times 2\left(\left(\frac{100}{2}\right)^{3}-\left(\frac{40}{2}\right)^{3}\right)^{3} \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \times 3.14 \times 0.4 \times 2\left(50^{3}-20^{3}\right) \\ &=195936 \mathrm{Nmm}=195.936 \mathrm{Nm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A spur gear has a module of 3 mm, number of teeth 16, a face width of 36 mm and a pressure angle
of 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. It is transmitting a power of 3 kW at 20 rev/s. Taking a velocity factor of 1.5, and a form
factor of 0.3, the stress in the gear tooth is about
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} P&=3 \mathrm{kW}=3000 \mathrm{W} \\ N&=20 \mathrm{rps} \\ y&= \text{Form factor } =0.3 \\ b&= \text{ Face width } =36 \mathrm{mm} \\ C_{v}&= \text{ Velocity factor } =1.5 \\ m&= \text{ Module } =3 \mathrm{mm} \\ Z&= \text{ teeth } =16 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} F_{t} &=\frac{2 T}{D_{1}} \\ D &=m z \\ &=3 \times 16=48 \mathrm{mm} \\ P&=2 \pi N T where N is in rps\\ T&=\frac{P}{2 \pi N}=\frac{3000}{2 \pi \times 20} \\ &=23.8732 \mathrm{Nm} \\ &=23.8732 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{Nmm} \end{aligned} [/latex]
We know
[latex] \begin{array}{c} \left(F_{d}\right)_{\text {Lews }} \leq F_{s} \\ F_{t} \times C_{v} \leq\left(\sigma_{b} \cdot y b m\right) \\ \frac{2 T}{D} \times C_{v}=\left(\sigma_{b}\right) y b m \\ \frac{2 \times 23.8732 \times 10^{3} \times 1.5}{48}=\left(\sigma_{b}\right) 0.3 \times 36 \times 3 \\ \sigma_{b}=46 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ =46 \mathrm{MPa} \end{array}[/latex]

A gas expands in a frictionless piston-cylinder arrangement. The expansion process is very slow,
and is resisted by an ambient pressure of 100kPa. During the expansion process, the pressure of
the system (gas) remains constant at 300kPa. The change in volume of the gas is 0.01[latex]m^3[/latex]. The
maximum amount of work that could be utilized from the above process is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Pressure of gas in a cylinder
[latex] p=300 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
Ambient pressure,
[latex] p_{\mathrm{atm}}=100 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
Change in volume,
[latex] d V=0.01 \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]


Maximum amount of work,
[latex] \begin{aligned} W_{\max } &=\left(p-p_{\mathrm{atm}}\right) d V \\ &=(300-100) \times 0.01 \\ &=2 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The logarithmic mean temperature difference (LMTD) of a counterflow heat exchanger is 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C.
The cold fluid enters at 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and the hot fluid enters at 100[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Mass flow rate of the cold fluid is
twice that of the hot fluid. Specific heat at constant pressure of the hot fluid is twice that of the cold
fluid. The exit temperature of the cold fluid
raw_source.solution:
[latex]m_{c}=2 m_{n} [/latex]
[latex] c_{n}=2 c_{c} [/latex]
By energy balance
[latex] \begin{aligned} m_{h} c_{h}\left(T_{h_{1}}-T_{h_{2}}\right)&=m_{c} c_{c}\left(T_{c_{2}}-T_{c_{1}}\right) \\ T_{h_{1}}-T_{h_{2}}&=T_{c_{2}}-T_{c_{1}} \\ T_{h_{1}}-T_{c_{2}}&=T_{h_{2}}-T_{c_{1}}\\ Let,\quad \theta_{1}&=\theta_{2}\\ L M T D &=\frac{\left(T_{h_{1}}-T_{c_{2}}\right)-\left(T_{h_{2}}-T_{c_{1}}\right)}{\ln \left(\frac{T_{h_{1}}-T_{c_{2}}}{T_{h_{2}}-T_{c_{1}}}\right)} \\ L M T D &=\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{\ln \left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}}\right)}=\theta_{m} \\ \frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{2}} &=x \\ \theta_{m} &=\frac{\theta_{2}(x-1)}{\ln x} \\ \theta_{m} &=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{\theta_{2}(x-1)}{\ln x} \quad \ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
since [latex] \frac{0}{0} [/latex]
Now applying L'Hospital rule
[latex] \begin{aligned} \theta_{\mathrm{m}} &=\theta_{2}=\theta_{1} \\ \text { Given } \quad \theta_{\mathrm{m}} &=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{n_{1}}-T_{c_{2}} &=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ 100-T_{c_{2}} &=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\\ \text{or }\quad T_{c_{2}}&=80^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cyclic device operates between three thermal reservoirs, as shown in the figure. Heat is transferred to/from the cyclic device. It is assumed that heat transfer between each thermal reservoir and the cyclic device takes place across negligible temperature difference. Interactions between the cyclic device and the respective thermal reservoirs that are shown in the figure are all in the form of heat transfer.

The cyclic device can be
raw_source.solution:
According to Clausius's inequality,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \oint \frac{\delta Q}{T} & \leq 0 \\ \frac{100}{1000}+\frac{50}{500}-\frac{60}{300} & \leq 0 \\ 0.1+0.1-0.2 &=0 \\ 0 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence, the cyclic device can be a reversible heat engine.

options: a reversible heat pump or a reversible refrigerator
an irreversible heat pump or an irreversible refrigerator

raw_source.text:
A balloon containing an ideal gas is initially kept in an evacuated and insulated room. The balloon
ruptures and the gas fills up the entire room. Which one of the following statements is TRUE at the
end of above process?
raw_source.solution:
The balloon ruptures in an evacuated and insulated room, the gas fills up the entire room. This case related to free expansion.
[latex] i.e.,\delta Q=0, \quad \delta W=0[/latex]
According to first law of thermodynamics,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta Q &=d U+\delta W \\ 0 &=d U+0 \\ d U &=0 \\ U_{2}-U_{1} &=0 \\ U_{2} &=U_{1} \\ m c_{v} T_{2} &=m c_{v} T_{1}\\ \text{or }\quad m c_{p} T_{2} &=m c_{p} T_{1} \\ H_{2} &=H_{1}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
For free expansion of an ideal gas, both internal energy and enthalpy of the gas remain constant.
options: The internal energy of the gas decreases from its initial value, but the enthalpy remains constant
The internal energy of the gas increases from its initial value, but the enthalpy remains constant
Both internal energy and enthalpy of the gas remain constant
Both internal energy and enthalpy of the gas increase

raw_answer.option_text: Both internal energy and enthalpy of the gas remain constant

raw_source.text: A rigid, insulated tank is initially evacuated. The tank is connected with a supply line through which air (assumed to be ideal gas with constant specific heats) passes at 1 MPa, 350[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C . A valve connected with the supply line is opened and the tank is charged with air until the final pressure inside the tank reaches 1 MPa. The final temperature inside the tank
raw_source.solution:
Applying unsteady flow energy equation,
[latex] \begin{array}{c} Q=m_{2} u_{2}-m_{1} u_{1}+m_{e}\left(h_{e}+\frac{v_{e}^{2}}{2}+g z_{e}\right) \\ m_{i}\left(h_{i}+\frac{V_{i}^{2}}{2}+g z_{i}\right)+W \end{array}[/latex]
For given problem,
[latex] m_{1}=0 \quad \text{evacuated tank}[/latex]
[latex] m_{e}=0 \quad \text{no exit}[/latex]
[latex] V_{i} [/latex] is neglected
[latex] z_{i}=0 ; \quad Q=0 ; \quad W=0[/latex]
Above Eq. (i) becomes
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0 &=m_{2} u_{2}-m_{i} h_{i} \\ \text{or}\quad m_{i} h_{i} &=m_{2} u_{2}\\ h_{i} &=u_{2} \qquad \because m_{i}=m_{2}\\ c_{p} T_{i} &=c_{v} T_{2} \\ \frac{c_{p}}{c_{v}} T_{i} &=T_{2} \\ \gamma T_{i} &=T_{2} \\ \text{or}\quad T_{2}&=\gamma T_{i} \qquad \text{where}\;\gamma=\frac{c_{p}}{c_{v}}\\ &=1.4 \times 623 \mathrm{K} \\ &=872.3 \mathrm{K}=599.2^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The final temperature, [latex]T_{2}=599.2^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex]
inside to tank is greater than [latex]350^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
options: may be greater than, less than, or equal to 350[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C, depending on the volume of the tank

raw_source.text: For the three-dimensional object shown in the figure below, five faces are insulated. The sixth face (PQRS), which is not insulated, interacts thermally with the ambient, with a convective heat transfer coefficient of 10 W/[latex]m^2[/latex].K. The ambient temperature is 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Heat is uniformly generated inside the object at the rate of 100 W/[latex]m^3[/latex]. Assuming the face PQRS to be at uniform temperature, its steady state temperature is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{0}&=W / m^{2} K \\ T_{0}&=30^{\circ} C \end{aligned}[/latex]


[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{G}&=100 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \text { Volume: } V&=2 \times 1 \times 2=4 \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat generated,
[latex] Q=q_{G} \times V=100 \times 4=400 \mathrm{W}[/latex]
Convection heat transfer from face P Q R S
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=h_{0} A\left(T_{s}-T_{0}\right) \\ 400&=10 \times 2 \times 2\left(T_{s}-30\right)\\ \text{or }\qquad T_{s}-30&=10 \\ \text{or }\qquad T_{s}&=10+30=40^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Water, having a density of 1000 kg/[latex]m^3[/latex], issues from a nozzle with a velocity of 10 m/s and the jet strikes a bucket mounted on a Pelton wheel. The wheel rotates at 10 rad/s. The mean diameter of the wheel is 1 m. The jet is split into two equal streams by the bucket, such that each stream is deflected by 120[latex]^{\circ}[/latex], as shown in the figure. Friction in the bucket may be neglected. Magnitude of the torque exerted by the water on the wheel, per unit mass flow rate of the incoming jet, is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \rho&=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ V_{i}&=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \omega&=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ D&=1 \mathrm{m} \\ u&=\omega R=\frac{\omega D}{2}=10 \times \frac{1}{2}=5 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Angle of deflection [latex]=120^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \beta_{0}=180^{\circ}-120^{\circ}=60^{\circ}[/latex]
Force exerted by the water of the wheel per
mass flow rate,
[latex] \begin{aligned} F &=\left(V_{i}-u\right)\left(1+\cos \beta_{0}\right) N /(\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}) \\ &=(10-5)\left(1+\cos 60^{\circ}\right) \\ &=7.5 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Torque exerted by the water on the wheel per unit mass flow rate,
[latex] \begin{aligned} T &=F \frac{D}{2}=7.5 \times \frac{1}{2} \\ &=3.75 \mathrm{Nm} /(\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}) \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A thermal power plant operates on a regenerative cycle with a single open feed water heater, as shown in the figure. For the state points shown, the specific enthalpies are: [latex]h_1[/latex]=2800 kJ/kg and [latex]h_2[/latex] = 200 kJ/kg. The bleed to the feed water heater is 20% of the boiler steam generation rate. The specific enthalpy at state 3 is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{1}&=2800 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{2}&=200 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]


Using energy balance equation for open feedwater heater
[latex] \begin{aligned} m h_{3} &=0.2 m h_{1}+0.8 m h_{2} \\ \text{or}\quad h_{3} &=0.2 h_{1}+0.8 h_{2} \\ &=0.2 \times 2800+0.8 \times 200 \\ &=560+160 \\ &=720 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:

cooler. The air at the entry to the after cooler is unsaturated and becomes just saturated at the exit

A cylindrical container of radius R = 1 m, wall thickness 1 mm is filled with water up to a depth of 2 m and suspended along its upper rim. The density of water is 1000kg/[latex]m^3[/latex] and acceleration due to gravity is 10 m/[latex]s^2[/latex]. The self-weight of the cylinder is negligible. The formula for hoop stress in a thin - walled cylinder can be used at all points along the height of the cylindrical container.


The axial and circumferential stress [latex](\sigma_a ,\sigma_c )[/latex] experienced by the cylinder wall at mid-depth (1 m as shown) are
raw_source.solution:
Axial stress on side face will be due to force on
the bottom face.
Hence [latex]p_{\text {bottom }}[/latex] will be used for calculating axial
stress on section X-X,
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{\text {bottom }} &=\rho g h=\rho g \times 2 \\ \sigma_{\text {axial }} &=\frac{p d}{4 t}=\frac{(\rho g h) d}{4 t}=\frac{(1000 \times 10 \times 2)(2 \times 1)}{4 \times 1 \times 10^{-3}} \\ &=10 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{Pa}=10 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Circumferential stress at section X -X will be due
to pressure of fluid at section X-X
Hence [latex]p=\rho g h=\rho g \times 1 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \sigma_{\text {circumferential }}=\frac{p d}{2 t}=\frac{(\rho g \times 1) \times 2 R}{2 t} \\ =\frac{1000 \times 10 \times 1 \times 2 \times 1}{2 \times 1 \times 10^{-3}}=10 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{Pa}=10 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \text { (10, 10) MPa. } \end{array}[/latex]

The gap between a moving circular plate and a stationary surface is being continuously reduced, as the circular plate comes down at a uniform speed V towards the stationary bottom surface, as shown in the figure. The radial component of the fluid acceleration at r = R is
raw_source.solution:
Radial acceleration,
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{r}=V_{r} \times \frac{\partial V_{r}}{\partial r}+\frac{\partial V_{r}}{\partial t} \\ a_{r}=\frac{V r}{2 h} \times \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{V r}{2 h}\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{V r}{\partial t}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For convective part r is variable and for local acceleration h is variable
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad a_{r}&=\frac{V r}{2 h} \times \frac{V}{2 h} \times \frac{V}{2 h}+\frac{V r}{2} \times\left(\frac{-1}{h^{2}} \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}\right) \\ \frac{-\partial h}{\partial t}&=V\\ \therefore \quad a_{r}&=\frac{V^{2} r}{4 h^{2}}+\frac{V r}{2} \times\left(\frac{V}{h^{2}}\right)\\ a_{1}&=\frac{3 V^{2} r}{4 h^{2}}\\ \text{at }\quad r&=R \\ a_{R}&=\frac{3 V^{2} R}{4 h^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Orthogonal turning is performed on a cylindrical workpiece with shear strength of 250 MPa. The following conditions are used: cutting velocity is 180 m/min, feed is 0.20 mm/rev, depth of cut is 3 mm, chip thickness ratio = 0.5. The orthogonal rake angle is [latex]7^{\circ}[/latex]. Apply Merchant's theory foranalysis.

The shear plane angle (in degrees) and the shear force respectively are
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 \dot{\phi}+\beta-\alpha &=90^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \tan \phi &=\frac{\cos \alpha}{\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}-\sin \alpha} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \tan \phi &=\frac{\cos 7^{\circ}}{2-\sin 7^{\circ}} \\ \phi &=28^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
From Merchant first analysis we know that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 \phi+\beta-\alpha &=90^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow\left(2 \times 28^{\circ}\right)+\beta-7^{\circ} &=90^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \beta &=41^{\circ} \\ F_{s} &=\frac{\tau W t_{1}}{\sin \phi} \\ &=\frac{250 \times 3 \times 0.2}{\sin 28^{\circ}} \\&=319.5 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The cutting and frictional forces, respectively, are
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{F_{c}}{F_{s}} &=\frac{\cos (\beta-\alpha)}{\cos (\phi+\beta-\alpha)} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad F_{c} &=320 \times \frac{\cos \left(41^{\circ}-7^{\circ}\right)}{\cos \left(28^{\circ}+41^{\circ}-7^{\circ}\right)} \\ &=565.08 \mathrm{N} \\ \tan(\beta-\alpha)&=\frac{F_{T}}{F_{C}}\\ \Rightarrow \qquad F_{T} &=F_{c} \tan (\beta-\alpha) \\ &=565 \tan \left(41^{\circ}-7^{\circ}\right) \\ &=565 \tan 34^{\circ}=381.55 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

In the feed drive of a Point - to - point open loop CNC drive, a stepper motor rotating at 200 steps/rev drives a table through a gear box and lead screw - nut mechanism (pitch = 4mm, number of starts =1).
The [latex]gear \; ratio=(\frac{Output \; Rotational \; Speed}{Input\; Rotational\; Speed})[/latex] is given by U = 1/4. The stepper motor (driven by voltage pulses from a pulse generator) executes 1 step/ pulse of the pulse generator. The frequency of the pulse train from the pulse generator is f = 10,000 pulses per minute.


The Basic Length Unit (BLU), i.e., the table movement corresponding to 1 pulse of the pulse generator, is
raw_source.solution:
BLU represents the smallest distance traveled
Given that stepper motor rotate at 200 steps/rev
So, revolution of motor in 1 step [latex]=\frac{1}{200}\;rev/step[/latex]
Output rotational speed or movement of lead screw is given by
[latex]=\frac{1}{200}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{800}\;rev[/latex]
Movement of table after transfer from lead screw is given by
[latex]=\frac{1}{800}\times p=\frac{1}{800}\times 4 =0.005mm=5 \; micron[/latex]
where , p=pitch of screw

The divergence of the vector field [latex]3xz\hat{i}+2xy\hat{j}-yz^{2}\hat{k}[/latex]
 at a point (1,1,1 ) is equal to
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\text{Vector field,}[/latex]
[latex] \vec{f}=3 x z \hat{i}+2 x y \hat{j}-y z^{2} \hat{k} [/latex]
[latex] \vec{f}=\left[f_{1} \hat{i}+f_{2} \hat{j}+f_{3} \hat{k}\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned}&\text{Divergence of vector field} \vec{f}=\nabla \cdot \vec{f} \\ &\text{Div}(f)=\left(i \frac{\partial}{\partial x}+\hat{j} \frac{\partial}{\partial y}+\hat{k} \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\right) \cdot\left(t_{1} \hat{i}+f_{2} \hat{j}+f_{3} \hat{k}\right) \\ &\text{Div}(f)=\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial f_{3}}{\partial z} \\ &\text{Div}(f)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}[3 x z]+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}[2 x y]+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left[-2 y z^{2}\right] \\ &\text{Div}(f)=3 z+2 x-2 z y \\ &\text{Div}(f)|_{(1,1,1)}=3(1)+2(1)-2(1)(1)=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The inverse Laplace transform of [latex]\frac{1}{(s^{2}+s)}[/latex]
 is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s^{2}+s}\right) &=? \\ \frac{1}{s^{2}+s} &=\frac{1}{s(s+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1} \\ L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s^{2}+s}\right) &=L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s}\right)--L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s+1}\right) \\ &=1-e^{-t} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[Using standard formulae]
Standard formula:
[latex] \begin{aligned} L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s}\right) &=1 \\ L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s+a}\right) &=e^{-a t} \\ L^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{s-a}\right) &=e^{a t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If three coins are tossed simultaneously, the probability of getting at least one head
raw_source.solution:
Three coins are tossed simultaneously, the total
number of ways [latex] =2^{3}=8 [/latex]
Number of ways to get all tails = 1
[latex] Probability to get all tails [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{\text { Number of ways for tails }}{\text { Total number of ways }}=\frac{1}{8} [/latex]
Therefore probability to get at least one head is
[latex] =1-\frac{1}{8}=\frac{7}{8}[/latex]
or, Total number of ways with at least one head is
[latex] \left.\begin{matrix} & &\left.\begin{array}{lll} H & T & T \\ T & H & T \\ T & T & H \end{array} \right] \\ &&\left.\begin{array}{lll} H & T & T \\ T & H & T \\ T & T & H \end{array} \right] \\ &&\left.\begin{array}{lll} H & H & H \end{array} \right] \end{matrix}\right\}[/latex]
Therefore probability to get at least one head [latex] =\frac{7}{8} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
An analytic function of a Complex Variables z = x + iy is expressed as [latex]f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)[/latex]
 where [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex]. If u = xy, the expression for v should be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} u &=x y \\ u_{x} &=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=y \\ u_{y} &=\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x \\ f(z) &=u(x, y)+i v(x, y) \\ f^{\prime}(z) &=u_{x}+i v_{x}=v_{y}-i u_{y} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Cauchy Riemann Equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} u_{x} &=v_{y} \\ v_{x} &=-u_{y} \\ f^{\prime}(z) &=u_{x}-i u_{y} \\ f^{\prime}(z) &=y-i x \\ \text{Put x=z and y}&=0\\ f^{\prime}(z) &=0-i z \\ f(z) &=\int(-i z) d z \\ f(z) &=-i \frac{z^{2}}{2}+c_{1}+i c_{2} \\ c_{1} &=0(\text { constant in real part }) \\ f(z) &=\frac{-i z^{2}}{2}+i c_{2} \\ &=\frac{-i(x+i y)^{2}}{2}+i c_{2} \\ f(z) &=x y+\frac{i\left(y^{2}-x^{2}\right)}{2}+i c_{2} \\ f(z) &=u(x, y)+i v(x, y) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing imaginary part
[latex] \begin{aligned} v &=\frac{y^{2}-x^{2}}{2}+c_{2} \\ &=\frac{y^{2}-x^{2}}{2}+k \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The solution of [latex]x\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+y=x^{4}[/latex]
  with the condition [latex]y(1)=\frac{6}{5}[/latex]
 is
raw_source.solution:
Given differential equation is
[latex] \begin{aligned} x \frac{d y}{d x}+y &=x^{4} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}+\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) y &=x^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Standard form
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d x}+P y=Q[/latex]
where P and Q function of x only and solution is given by
[latex] y(\text { I.F. })=\int Q \cdot(I F .) d x+C[/latex]
where, integrating factor (I.F.)[latex] =e^{\int P d x} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Here} \quad P =\frac{1}{x} \text { and } Q=x^{3} [/latex]
[latex] \text { I.F. } =e^{\int \frac{1}{x} d x}=e^{\ln x}=x[/latex]
Solution [latex] \quad y(x)=\int x^{3} \cdot x d x+c [/latex]
[latex] y x=\frac{x^{5}}{5}+c [/latex]
given condition
[latex] y(1)=\frac{6}{5} [/latex]
means at [latex]x=1 ; y=\frac{6}{5} [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \frac{6}{5} \times 1=\frac{1}{5}+c [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad c=\frac{6}{5}-\frac{1}{5}=1 [/latex]
Therefore [latex] y x=\frac{x^{5}}{5}+1 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{x^{4}}{5}+\frac{1}{x}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A path AB in the form of one quarter of a circle of unit radius is shown in the figure. Integration of [latex](x+y)^{2}[/latex] on path AB traversed in a counter-clockwise sense is
raw_source.solution:
Path AB:
[latex] \begin{aligned} x^{2}+y^{2} &=1 \\ x &=\cos \theta \\ y &=\sin \theta \end{aligned}[/latex]
Along path AB [latex] \theta [/latex] varies from [latex]0^{\circ} \; \text { to } \; 90^{\circ}[0 \text { to } \pi / 2] [/latex]
[latex] \int_{\text {Path } A B}(x+y)^{2}(r d \theta)[/latex]
[latex] =\int_{0}^{\pi / 2}(\cos \theta+\sin \theta)^{2} 1 \cdot d \theta [/latex]
[latex] =\int_{0}^{\pi / 2}\left(\sin ^{2} \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta+2 \sin \theta \cos \theta\right) d \theta [/latex]
[latex] =\int_{0}^{\pi / 2}(1+\sin 2 \theta) d \theta [/latex]
[latex] =\theta+\left.\frac{(-\cos 2 \theta)}{2}\right|_{0} ^{\pi / 2} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left[\cos 2 \frac{\pi}{2}-\cos 0\right] [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{1}{2}[-1-1]=\frac{\pi}{2}+1[/latex]

The distance between the origin and the point nearest to it on the surface [latex]z^{2}=1+xy[/latex]
 is

Let the point be the(x,y,z)

The distance between two given coordinates is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} D^{2} &=\sqrt{(x-0)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}-(z-0)^{2}} \\ D^{2} &=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} \\ \text { given } z^{2} &=1+x y \\ D^{2} &=x^{2}+y^{2}+1+x y \end{aligned}[/latex]
Let [latex]D^{2}=U [/latex]
[latex] U=x^{2}+y^{2}+1+x y[/latex]
For minimum or nearest distance
[latex] \begin{aligned} p &=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0 \\ \Rightarrow 2x+y &=0 &... i \\ \Rightarrow \quad q &=\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 \\ &=2y+x=0&... ii \end{aligned}[/latex]
By solving equation (i) and (ii)
[latex] \begin{aligned} &x=0\\ &y=0\\ &z=1\\ &\begin{aligned} r &=\frac{\partial^{2} v}{\partial x^{2}}=2 \\ t &=\frac{\partial^{2} v}{\partial y^{2}}=2 \\ s &=\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x \partial y}=1 \\ r t-s^{2} &=2 \times 2-1^{2}=3 \\ r t-s^{2} &>0 \\r &>0 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] distance is minimum.

raw_source.text: The standard deviation of a uniformly distributed random variable between 0 and 1 is
raw_source.solution:
For uniformly distributed random variable [latex] P(x)=P [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{c} \int_{E\left(x^{2}\right) \text{mean }=}^{1} x P(x) d x \quad \int_{0}^{1} x p d x \\ =\frac{P\left[x^{2} / 2\right]_{0}^{1}}{P[x]_{0}^{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \qquad \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow E\left(x^{2}\right)&=\frac{\int x^{2} P(x) d x}{\int P(x) d x}\\&=\frac{\int_{0}^{1} x^{2} p d x}{\int_{0}^{1} p d x}\\ &=\frac{p\left[x^{3} / 3\right]_{0}^{1}}{p[x]_{0}^{1}} \\ &=\frac{p(1 / 3-0)}{p(1-0)} \end{aligned} \\ \qquad \begin{aligned} \text { variance } \sigma^{2} &=E\left(x^{2}\right)-(E(x))^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\\ &=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{12} \end{aligned} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If three coins are tossed simultaneously, the probability of getting at least one head
raw_source.solution:
Three coins are tossed simultaneously, the total
number of ways [latex] =2^{3}=8 [/latex]
Number of ways to get all tails = 1
[latex] Probability to get all tails [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{\text { Number of ways for tails }}{\text { Total number of ways }}=\frac{1}{8} [/latex]
Therefore probability to get at least one head is
[latex] =1-\frac{1}{8}=\frac{7}{8}[/latex]
or, Total number of ways with at least one head is
[latex] \left.\begin{matrix} & &\left.\begin{array}{lll} H & T & T \\ T & H & T \\ T & T & H \end{array} \right] \\ &&\left.\begin{array}{lll} H & T & T \\ T & H & T \\ T & T & H \end{array} \right] \\ &&\left.\begin{array}{lll} H & H & H \end{array} \right] \end{matrix}\right\}[/latex]
Therefore probability to get at least one head [latex] =\frac{7}{8} [/latex]

A coolant fluid at 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C flows over a heated flat plate maintained at a constant temperature of 100[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. The boundary layer temperature distribution at a given location on the plate may be approximated as  [latex]T=30+70 exp(-y)[/latex]
 where y (in m) is the distance normal to the plate and T is in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. If thermal conductivity of the fluid is 1.0W/mK, the local convective heat transfer coefficient (in [latex]W/m^{2}K[/latex]) at that location will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{s}=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ \text{At}\; \mathrm{y}=0 ; q_{\mathrm{cond}}=q_{\mathrm{conv}} \\ -\left.k_{f} \frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0}=h \Delta T=h\left(T_{s}-T_{\infty}\right) \\ -\left.(1) \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[30+70 e^{-y}\right]\right|_{y=0}=h(100-30) \\ -\left.\left[0+70(-1) e^{-y}\right]\right|_{y=0}=h(70) \\ 70 e^{-0}=h(70) \\ ^{0} \mathrm{h}=1 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \end{array}[/latex]
Alternatively
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{\infty}&=30^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{s}&=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ k_{f}&=1 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ T&=30+70 \exp (-y) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Differentiating w.r.t y, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{At }\quad y &=0\\ \frac{d T}{d y}&=-70 e^{-y}\\ \left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)^{y=0}&=-70 \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that local convective heat transfer coefficient:
[latex] h_{x}=\frac{-k_{1}\left(\frac{d T}{d y}\right)_{y=0}}{T_{s}-T_{\infty}}=\frac{-1 \times(-70)}{100-30}=1 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A frictionless piston-cylinder device contains a gas initially at 0.8MPa and 0.015 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]. It expands quasi-statically at constant temperature to a final volume of 0.030 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]. The work output (in kJ) during this process will be
raw_source.solution:
Given data for constant temperature process
[latex] \begin{array}{l} p_{1}=0.8 \mathrm{MPa}=800 \mathrm{kPa} \\ V_{1}=0.015 \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ V_{2}=0.030 \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{array}[/latex]
We know that work done for constant temperature process,
[latex] \begin{aligned} W &=p_{1} V_{1} \log _{e} \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} \\ &=800 \times 0.015 \log _{e} \frac{0.030}{0.015} \\ &=8.317 \mathrm{kJ} \approx 8.32 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

In an ideal vapour compression refrigeration cycle, the specific enthalpy of refrigerant (in kJ/kg) at the following states is given as:
Inlet of condenser: 283
Exit of condenser: 116
Exit of evaporator: 232
The COP of this cycle is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{2} &=283 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{3} &=116 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ &=h_{4} \\ h_{1} &=232 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Coefficient of performance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{COP} &=\frac{\text { Refrigerating effect: Re }}{\text { Work input: } w} \\ \text { where } \mathrm{Re} &=h_{1}-h_{4}=232-116 \\ &=116 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text { and } \quad w &=h_{2}-h_{1}=283-232 \\ &=51 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{COP} &=\frac{116}{51}=2.27 \end{aligned}[/latex]
