raw_source.text: The velocity triangles at the inlet and exit of the rotor of a turbomachine are shown. V denotes the absolute velocity of the fluid. W denotes the relative velocity of the fluid and U denotes the blade velocity. Subscripts 1 and 2 refer to inlet and outlet respectively. If [latex]V_{2}=W_{1}[/latex] and [latex]V_{1}=W_{2}[/latex], then the degree of reaction is
raw_source.solution:
Degree of reaction
[latex] R=1-\frac{(V_1^2-V_2^2)}{(V_1^2-V_2^2)+(U_1^2-U_2^2)+(W_2^2-W_1^2)}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Where,}[/latex]
[latex]V_1 \text{ and }V_2 \text{ are absolute velocities} [/latex]
[latex]W_1 \text{ and }W_2 \text{ are relative velocities}[/latex]
[latex]U_1 \text{ and }U_2=U \text{ for given figure} [/latex]
[latex]\text{Given } W_2=V_1, W_1=V_2[/latex]
[latex]\text{Hence,} [/latex]
[latex]R=1-\frac{(V_1^2-V_2^2)}{(V_1^2-V_2^2)+(U^2-U^2)+(V_1^2-V_2^2)}[/latex]
[latex]R =1-\frac{(V_1^2-V_2^2)}{2(V_1^2-V_2^2)} [/latex]
[latex]R= 1-\frac{1}{2}[/latex]
[latex] R = 0.5 [/latex]

raw_source.text: Which one of the following configurations has highest effectiveness?
raw_source.solution:
Fin effectiveness,
[latex] \varepsilon=\frac{\text { Heat transfer with fin: } Q_{\text {Fin }}}{\text { Heat transfer without fin: } Q}=\frac{Q_{F_{\text {Fin }}}}{Q} [/latex]
where [latex]\quad Q_{\text {Fin }}=\sqrt{k P h P} \theta_{0} [/latex] for long fin
[latex] Q=h A \theta_{0}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \qquad \varepsilon=\frac{\sqrt{k A h P} \theta_{0}}{h A \theta_{0}}=\frac{\sqrt{k A h P}}{h A}=\sqrt{\frac{k P}{h A}} [/latex]
[latex] \varepsilon \propto \sqrt{P} ; \quad \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{A}}[/latex]
For highest fin effectiveness, perimeter of fin should be large and cross-sectional area should be low. It means, for large value of perimeter, fins should be closely spaced (to increase the total number of fins) and for lower value of crosssectional area, it should be thin

raw_source.text:
An ideal gas of mass m and temperature [latex]T_{1}[/latex]
 undergoes a reversible isothermal process from an initial pressure [latex]P_{1}[/latex]
 to final pressure [latex]P_{2}[/latex]
 . The heat loss using the process is Q. the entropy change [latex]\Delta[/latex]S of the gas is
raw_source.solution:
We know that
[latex] \Delta S=\frac{\delta Q}{T}[/latex]
Integrating between states 1 and 2 gives
[latex] \begin{aligned} \int_{1}^{2} \Delta S &=\int_{1}^{2} \frac{\delta Q}{T} \\ S_{2}-S_{1} &=\frac{1}{T} \int_{1}^{2} \delta Q \quad \because T=C\\ &=\frac{1}{T} \times Q_{1-2}=\frac{m R T \ln \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}}{T} \\ &=m R \ln \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=m R \ln \frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
where [latex]\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}=\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}[/latex] for isothermal process
Alternatively
We know that the entropy change in terms of temperature and pressure ratios,
[latex] S_{2}-S_{1}=m c_{P} \ln \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}-m R \ln \frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}[/latex]
where [latex] T_{1}=T_{2} [/latex] for isothermal process
[latex] \therefore \quad S_{2}-S_{1}=-m R \ln \frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}=m R \ln \frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Second Law, Carnot Cycle and Entropy

raw_source.text:
In the mechanism given below, if the angular velocity of the eccentric circular disc is 1 rad/s, the angular velocity (rad/s) of the follower link for the instant shown in the figure is
Note: All dimensions are in mm
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta P Q O &\sim \Delta S R O \\ \therefore \quad \frac{P Q}{S R}&=\frac{P O}{S O} \qquad\cdots(1) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying Pythagoras theorem in [latex]\Delta PQO[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} (P O)^{2}&=(P Q)^{2}+(O Q)^{2}\\ \therefore \quad (P Q)&=\sqrt{(P O)^{2}-(O Q)^{2}} \\ &=\sqrt{(50)^{2}-(25)^{2}}=43.3 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting value of P Q in Eq. (1), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{43.3}{S R} &=\frac{45+5}{5} \\ S R &=\frac{43.3 \times 5}{50}=4.33 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Velocity of Q is equal to velocity of R
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{Q} &=V_{R} \\ &=SR \times \omega \\ &=4.33 \times 1=4.33 \mathrm{mm} / \mathrm{s} \\ \omega_{P Q} &=\frac{V_{P Q}}{P Q}=\frac{4.33}{43.3}=0.1 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
At x = 0, the function [latex]f(x)=x^{3}+1[/latex]
 has
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Put } \quad f(x)&=x^{3}+1 \\ \quad f^{\prime}(x)&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 3 x^{2}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x&=0 \; \text{is the only critical point at this critical point}\\ f^{\prime}(x) &=6 x \\ f^{\prime}(0) &=6 \times 0=0 \\ \text { Now } \quad f^{\prime \prime}(x) &=6 \text { and }\\ \text{so} \quad f^{\prime \prime \prime}(\)&=6 \;\; \text{which is non zero.} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since the first non zero derivative value occurs at the third derivative which is an odd derivative, this function has a point of inflection at x=0

raw_source.text:
For the spherical surface [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1[/latex]
, the unit outward normal vector at the point [latex]\left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},0 \right )[/latex]
is given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1 [/latex]
[latex] f(x, y, z)=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-1=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text { grad } f=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \hat{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \hat{k} [/latex]
[latex] =2 x \hat{i}+2 y j+2 z \hat{k} [/latex]
[latex] \text { at }\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0\right)[/latex]
[latex] grad f=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{i}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{j}+2 \times 0 \times \hat{k} [/latex]
[latex] \quad=\sqrt{2} i+\sqrt{2} j+0 \hat{k} [/latex]
[latex] |grad\; f|=\sqrt{2+2}=\sqrt{4}=2 [/latex]
The unit outward normal vector at point P is
[latex] n=\frac{1}{|grad\;f|}(grad\;f)_{at\;p}[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2} i+\sqrt{2} j)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} j[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The homogeneous state of stress for a metal part undergoing plastic deformation is
[latex]T=\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 5 & 0\\ 5 & 20 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -10 \end{pmatrix}[/latex]
Where the stress component values are in MPa. Using von Mises yield criterion, the value of estimated shear yield stress, in MPa is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{c} \sigma_{x}=10, \sigma_{y}=20, \tau_{x y}=5, \sigma_{z}=-10 \\ \sigma_{1,2}=\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-\sigma_{y}}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{x y}^{2}} \\ \begin{aligned} \sigma_{1}&=15+\sqrt{25+25} \\ \sigma_{1}&=22.07 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{2}&=7.07 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{3}&=\sigma_{z}=-10 \quad\left[\text { as } \tau_{x z}=\tau_{y z}=0\right] \\ \sigma_{y t}&=\text { yield stress in tension } \\ \sigma_{y s}&=\text { yield stress in shear } \end{aligned} \end{array}[/latex]
According to Von Mises theory
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left(\sigma_{y t}\right)^{2} \geq & \frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\sigma_{2}-\sigma_{3}\right)^{2}+\left(\sigma_{3}-\sigma_{1}\right)^{2}\right] \\ \left(\sigma_{y t}\right)^{2} & \geq 772.435 \\ \sigma_{y t} & \geq 27.79 \\ \text { Now } & \sigma_{y s}=\frac{\sigma_{y t}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \therefore \quad & \sigma_{y s}=16.046 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider two infinitely long thin concentric tubes of circular cross section as shown in figure. If [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{1}[/latex] are the diameters of inner and outer tubes respectively, then the view factor [latex]F_{22}[/latex] is given by
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} F_{11}+F_{12} &=1 \\ F_{11} &=0 \qquad \text{(Convex surface)}\\ \therefore \quad F_{12} &=1 \\ F_{21}+F_{22} &=1 \\ \text{and }\quad A_{1} F_{12} &=A_{2} F_{21} \\ \text{or}\quad F_{21} &=\frac{A_{1} F_{12}}{A_{2}} \\ F_{21} &=\frac{\pi D_{1} L F_{12}}{\pi D_{2} L}=\frac{D_{1}}{D_{2}} \\ F_{22} &=1-F_{21}=1-\frac{D_{1}}{D_{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An incompressible fluid flows over a flat plate with zero pressure gradient. The boundary layer thickness is 1mm at a location where the Reynolds number is 1000. If the velocity of the fluid alone is increased by a factor of 4, then boundary layer thickness at the same location, in mm will be
raw_source.solution:
Boundary layer thickness,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta &\propto \frac{1}{\text{Re}_{x}^{1 / 2}} \text{ for laminar flow}\\ \text{and }\quad \operatorname{Re}_{x}&=\frac{V x}{v} \\ \text{i.e., }\quad \operatorname{Re}_{x} &\propto V \\ \therefore \quad \delta &\propto \frac{1}{V^{1 / 2}} \\ \delta_{1} V_{1}^{1 / 2} &=\delta_{2} V_{2}^{1 / 2} \\ 1 V^{1 / 2} &=\delta_{2}(4 V)^{1 / 2} \\ V^{1 / 2} &=\delta_{2} \times 2 V^{12} \\ \text{or }\quad \delta_{2}&=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \mathrm{mm} \\ \end{aligned} [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text:
A room contains 35kg of dry air & 0.5 kg water vapor. The total pressure and temperature of air in the room are 100kPa and [latex]25^{\circ}C[/latex]
 respectively. Given that the saturation pressure for water at [latex]25^{\circ}[/latex]C is 3.17kPa, the relative humidity of the air in the room is

[latex]\begin{aligned} m_{a} &=35 \mathrm{kg} ; \quad m_{v}=0.5 \mathrm{kg} \\ \omega &=\frac{m_{v}}{m_{a}}=\frac{0.5}{35}=0.01428 \\ a \mathrm{so} & \omega=0.622 \frac{p_{v}}{p_{a}} \\ p_{t} &=100 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \therefore \quad \omega &=0.622 \frac{p_{v}}{p_{t}-p_{v}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now,
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0.01428 &=0.622 \frac{p_{v}}{100-p_{v}} \\ p_{v} &=2.238 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Relative humidity
[latex] \begin{aligned} \phi &=\frac{p_{v}}{p_{v s}}=\frac{2.238}{3.17} \times 100 \\ &=70.6 \% \approx 71 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The inverse Laplace transform of the function [latex]F(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)}[/latex]
 is given by
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} F(s) &=\frac{1}{s(s+1)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1} \\ &=\frac{A(s+1)+B(s)}{s(s+1)} \end{aligned}\\ &\Rightarrow A(s+1)+B(s)=0\\ &\text { Put } \quad s=0\\ &\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & A=1 \\ \text { and } & s=-1 \end{array}\\ &\Rightarrow \quad B=-1\\ &\text { So } \quad F(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}\\ &\begin{aligned} \text { Now } & f(t)=L^{-1}(F(s))=e^{0 t}-e^{-t} \\ & f(t)=1-e^{-t} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For the matrix [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3\\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
one of the normalized Eigenvectors is given as
raw_source.solution:
[latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}5 & 3 \\1 & 3\end{array}\right][/latex]
Characteristic equation is
[latex] \begin{aligned}\left|\begin{array}{cc}5-\lambda & 3 \\1 & 3-\lambda\end{array}\right| &= (5-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-3 &=0 \\\lambda^{2}-8 \lambda+12 &=0 \\\lambda &=2,6\end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, to find eigen vectors:
[latex] [A-\lambda] \hat{x}=0[/latex]
Which is
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{cc}5-\lambda & 3 \\ 1 & 3-\lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Put [latex] \lambda=2 [/latex] in above equation and we get
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{ll}3 & 3 \\1 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\0\end{array}\right][/latex]
Which gives us the equation,
[latex] 3 x_{1}+3 x_{2}=0 [/latex]
and [latex] \quad x_{1}+x_{2}=0 [/latex]
Which is only one equation,
[latex] x_{1}+x_{2}=0[/latex]
Whose solution is
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{r}-k \\k\end{array}\right][/latex]
So one eigen vector is [latex] \hat{x}_{1}=\left[\begin{array}{r}-k \\ k\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Which after normalization is [latex] =\frac{\hat{x}_{1}}{\left|\hat{x}_{1}\right|} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-k)^{2}+\left(k^{2}\right)}}\left[\begin{array}{c}-k \\k\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{array}\right][/latex]
The other eigen vector is obtained by putting the
other eigen value
[latex] \lambda=6 [/latex] in eigen value problem
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{cc}5-\lambda & 3 \\ 1 & 3-\lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Which gives.
[latex] \left[\begin{array}{rr}-1 & 3 \\1 & -3\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\0\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Which gives the equation
[latex] -x_{1}+3 x_{2}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{and }\quad x_{1}-3 x_{2}=0[/latex]
Which is only one equation
[latex] -x_{1}+3 x_{2}=0 [/latex]
Whose solution is
[latex] \hat{x}_{2}=\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}3 k \\k\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Which after normalization is
[latex] \frac{\hat{x}_{2}}{\left|\hat{x}_{2}\right|}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left((3 )^{2}+k^{2}\right.})}\left[\begin{array}{c}3 k \\k\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}3 / 2 \\1 / 2\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Choice (B) [latex] \left[\begin{array}{c}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{array}\right] [/latex] is the only correct choice
since it is a constant multiple of one the normalized vectors which is [latex] \hat{x}_{1}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A large tank with a nozzle attached contains three immiscible, inviscid fluids as shown. Assuming that the changes in h1, h2 and h3 are negligible, the instantaneous discharge velocity is
raw_source.solution:
Total pressure at state 1 ,
[latex] P_{1}=\rho_{1} g h_{1}+\rho_{2} g h_{2}+\rho_{3} g h_{3} [/latex]
Total pressure at state 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{2} &=\frac{\rho_{3} V^{2}}{2} \\ \text { Thus, } P_{2} &=P_{1} \\ \frac{\rho^{3} V^{2}}{2} &=\rho_{1} g h_{1}+\rho_{2} g h_{2}+\rho_{3} g h_{3} \\ V^{2} &=2 g\left(\frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{3}} h_{1}+\frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{3}} h_{2}+\frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{3}} h_{1}\right) \\ V &=\sqrt{2 g\left(h_{3}+\frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{3}} h_{2}+\frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{3}} h_{1}\right)} \\ &=\sqrt{2 g h_{3}\left(1+\frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{3}} \frac{h_{2}}{h_{3}}+\frac{\rho_{1}}{P_{3}} \frac{h_{1}}{h_{3}}\right)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively
Applying the Bernoulli's equation between state 1 and 2, we get
[latex] \frac{P_{1}}{\rho_{3} g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}=\frac{P_{2}}{\rho_{3} g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{2}[/latex]
where,

[latex]h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2}+g z_{1}+q=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2}+g z_{2}+w[/latex]


Assumptions:
[latex]\begin{aligned} z_1 &= z_2\\ q&=0\;\; \text{adiabatic flow} \\ w &=0\;\; \text{always for nozzle} \\ h_1 +\frac{V_1^2}{2}&= h_2 +\frac{V_2^2}{2}\\ c_pT_1+\frac{V_1^2}{2}&= c_pT_2+\frac{V_2^2}{2}\\ 1008 \times 500+\frac{(10)^2}{2}&=1008 \times T_2 +\frac{(180)^2}{2} \\ 504050&=1008T_2+16200 \\ T_2&=483.97K \approx 484K \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The probability that a student knows the correct answer to a multiple choice question is [latex]\frac{2}{3}[/latex]
If the student does not know the answer, then the student guesses the answer. The probability of the guessed answer being correct is [latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex]
Given that the student has answered the question correctly, the 
conditional probability that the student knows the correct answer is
raw_source.solution:
Let A be the event when student knows the answer and B be the event when student guesses the answer. Therefore
[latex]P(A)=P(A\cap B)=\frac{2}{3} [/latex]
[latex]P(B)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{12}[/latex]
where [latex]\frac{2}{3}[/latex] is the probability of correct answer and [latex]\frac{1}{3}[/latex] is the probability that student does not know the answer. So guesses the answer and probability of correct guess is [latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex]. Therefore total probability of correct answer
[latex]=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{12}[/latex]
Conditional probability that student knows the correct answer
[latex]P(A/B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{9}{12}}=\frac{8}{9}[/latex]

The solution to the differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}u} }{\mathrm{d} x^{2}}-k\frac{\mathrm{du} }{\mathrm{d} x}=0[/latex]
 where k is a constant, subjected to the boundary conditions  u(0) = 0  and  u(L) = U,  is
raw_source.solution:
We have [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}u} }{\mathrm{d} x^{2}}-k\frac{\mathrm{du} }{\mathrm{d} x}=0[/latex]
[latex](D^2-kD)u=0 [/latex]
The auxiliary equation is
[latex]\begin{aligned} m^2-km&=0\\ m(m-k)&=0\\ m&=0,k \end{aligned} [/latex]
Thus the complete solution is
[latex]\begin{aligned} u&=C_1e^{0x}+C_2e^{kx}\\ u&=C_1+C_2e^{kx} \end{aligned} [/latex]
From given condition
[latex] u(0)=0:\;\; C_1+C_2=0 \;\;\;...(i) [/latex]
[latex]u(L)=U:\;\; U=C_1+C_2e^{kL}\;\;\;...(ii) [/latex]
Subtracting equation (i) from (ii), we get
[latex]U=C_2(e^{kL}-1) [/latex]
[latex]C_2=\frac{U}{e^{kL}-1} [/latex]
From equation (i), we have
[latex] C_1=-C_2=\frac{-U}{e^{kL}-1} [/latex]
Substitute these values in the expression for u, we get
[latex] u=\frac{-U}{e^{kL}-1}+\frac{U}{e^{kL}-1}e^{kx}=U\left ( \frac{1-e^{kx}}{1-e^{kL}} \right )[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two threaded bolts A and B of same material and length are subjected to identical tensile load. If the elastic strain  energy stored in bolt A is 4 times that of bolt B and the mean diameter of bolt A is 12 mm, the mean diameter of bolt B in mm is
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{1}&=P_{2}=P\\ &\text{(identical tensile load on bolt A \& B )} \\ &\qquad \text{(same length)}\\ L_{1} &=L_{2}=L \\ d_{A} &=12 \mathrm{mm} \\ U_{A} &=\text { strain energy in bolt } A \\ U_{B} &=\text { Strain energy in bolt } B \\ U_{A} &=4 U_{B}(\text { Given }) \qquad \cdots(i)\\ \therefore \quad d_{B} &=? \end{aligned}[/latex]
Strain energy is given by
[latex] U_{A}=\frac{1}{2} P \times \delta=\frac{1}{2} \frac{P^{2} L}{A E}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Eq. (i)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{1 P_{1}^{2} L_{1}}{2} &=4 \times \frac{1}{2} \frac{P_{2}^{2} L_{2}}{A_{2} E} \\ \frac{1}{A_{1}} &=4 \times \frac{1}{A_{2}} \\ \frac{4}{\pi(12)^{2}} &=4 \times \frac{4}{\pi\left(d_{B}\right)^{2}} \\ d_{B}^{2} &=576 \\ d_{B} &=24 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A link OB is rotating with a constant angular velocity of 2 rad/s in counter clockwise direction and a block is sliding radially outward on it with an uniform velocity of 0.75 m/s with respect to the rod, as shown in the figure below. If OA = 1 m, the magnitude of the absolute acceleration of the block at location A in [latex]m/s^{2}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Acceleration of the block at [latex]A=\vec{a}_{c r}+\vec{a}_{r}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\overrightarrow{2 \omega V}+\overrightarrow{\omega^{2} r} \\ \Rightarrow \quad r&=O A\\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 \omega V&=2 \times 2 \times 0.75=3 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \omega^{2} r&=2^{2} \times 1=4 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
As coriolis component and radial component are perpendicular to each other.
So, [latex]\left|\vec{a}_{a b s}\right|=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Customers arrive at a ticket counter at a rate of 50 per hr and tickets are issued in the order of their arrival. The average time taken for issuing a ticket is 1 min. Assuming that customer arrivals form a Poisson process and service times are exponentially distributed, the average waiting time in queue in min is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\lambda=50 \mathrm{cust} / \mathrm{hr}=\frac{50}{60} \mathrm{cust} / \mathrm{min} \\ =0.833 \mathrm{cust} / \mathrm{min} [/latex]
[latex] \mu=1 \mathrm{min} \quad \therefore \rho=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}=0.833 [/latex]
As we know,
[latex] L_{q}=\lambda \cdot \omega_{q} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{\rho^{2}}{1-\rho}&=\lambda \omega_{q} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{(0.833)^{2}}{1-0.833}&=0.833 \omega_{q} \\ \Rightarrow \omega_{q}&=5 \mathrm{min} \end{aligned}[/latex]

(1), we get}\\ t_{2}&=5(2)^{2}=5 \times 4=20 \mathrm{min} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The following surface integral is to be evaluated over a sphere for the given steady velocity vector field F=xi+yj+zk defined with respect to a Cartesian coordinate system having i, j and k as unit base vectors.
[latex]\int \int _{s}\frac{1}{4}(F n)dA[/latex]
where S is the sphere, [latex]x^2+y^2+z^2=1[/latex] and n is the outward unit normal vector to the sphere. The value of the surface integral is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\iint \frac{1}{4}(F \cdot n) d A [/latex]
[latex] \iint \frac{1}{4}(F \times d A)[/latex]
By using Gauss divergence theorem
[latex] \Rightarrow \iiint_{}\frac{1}{4}(\underset{\nabla}{\rightarrow} \cdot F) d V [/latex]

[latex] \Rightarrow \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{4}{3} \times \pi(1)^{3}[/latex]
[latex] =\pi[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The function f(t) satisfies the differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}f} }{\mathrm{d} t^{2}}+f=0[/latex]
 and the auxiliary 
conditions,[latex]f(0)=0, \; \frac{\mathrm{d} f}{\mathrm{d} t}(0)=4[/latex]. The Laplace transform of  f(t) is given by
raw_source.solution:
Apply Laplace on both sides
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \angle\left\{\frac{d^{2} f}{d t^{2}}\right\}+\mathcal{L}\{f\}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & s^{2} \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}-s f(0)-f^{\prime}(0)+\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=0 \\ & \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}\left[s^{2}+1\right]=4 \\ & \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=\frac{4}{s^{2}+1} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Water is coming out from a tap and falls vertically downwards. At the tap opening, the stream diameter is 20 mm with uniform velocity of 2 m/s. Acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/[latex]s^2[/latex]. Assuming steady, inviscid flow, constant atmospheric pressure everywhere and neglecting curvature and surface tension effects, the diameter in mm of the stream 0.5 m below the tap is approximately
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
At section 1-1
Diameter: [latex]\quad d_{1}=20 \mathrm{mm}=0.02 \mathrm{m} [/latex]
Velocity: [latex] \quad V_{1}=2 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} [/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity,
[latex] g=9.81 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}[/latex]
Applying Bernoulli's equation between sections 1 and 2 , we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{1}}{p g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1} &=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{2} \\ 0+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{\rho g}+0.5 &=0+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{\rho g}+0 \\ \frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+0.5 &=\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}\\ \text{ or }\qquad V_{2}^{2}&=V_{1}^{2}+0.5 \times 2 g\\ \text{or }\qquad V_{2} &=\sqrt{V_{1}^{2}+0.5 \times 2 \times g} \\ &=\sqrt{(2)^{2}+0.5 \times 2 \times 9.81} \\ &=\sqrt{13.81}=3.716 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Applying continuity equation between sections and 2, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{1} V_{1} &=A_{2} V_{2} \\ \frac{\pi}{4} d_{1}^{2} V_{1} &=\frac{\pi}{4} d_{2}^{2} V_{2}\\ \text{or }\quad d_{1}^{2} V_{1}&=d_{2}^{2} V_{2} \\ (0.02)^{2} \times 2&=d_{2}^{2} \times 3.716\\ \text{or }\quad d_{2}^{2}&=2.1528 \times 10^{-4}\\ \text{or }\quad d_{2} &=0.01467 \mathrm{m} \\ &=14.67 \mathrm{mm} \approx 15 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A steel ball of diameter 60 mm is initially in thermal equilibrium at 1030[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C in a furnace. It is suddenly removed from the furnace and cooled in ambient air at 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C, with convective heat transfer coefficient [latex]h=20W/m^{2}K[/latex]. The thermo-physical properties of steel are: density  [latex]\rho =7800 kg/m^{3}[/latex], conductivity k = 40 W/mK and specific heat c = 600 J/kgK. The time required in seconds  to cool the steel ball in air from 1030[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C to 430[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C  is
raw_source.solution:
Diameter of ball,
[latex] d=60 \mathrm{mm}=0.06 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
Initial temperature,
[latex] T_{i}=1030^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
Ambient temperature,
[latex] T_{0}=30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
Convective heat transfer coefficient
[latex] h=20 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}[/latex]
Density: [latex] \quad \rho=7800 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Conductivity: [latex] k=40 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} [/latex] Specific heat: [latex] c=600 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} [/latex]
Final temperature of steel ball,
[latex] T=430^{\circ} \mathrm{C}[/latex]
[latex] \text{Time:}\qquad t=?[/latex]
The temperature distribution relation is given by
[latex] \frac{T-T_{0}}{T_{i}-T_{0}}=e^{\frac{h t}{\rho c l}} \cdots(i) [/latex]
where [latex]\quad l=\frac{V}{A} [/latex] characteristic length of balls
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\pi}{6} \frac{d^{3}}{\pi d^{2}}\\ \because \qquad V&=\frac{\pi}{6} d^{3}, A=\pi d^{2} \\ \therefore \qquad l&=\frac{d}{6}=\frac{0.06}{6}=0.01 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting the value of [latex] T, T_{0}, T_{i}, h, \rho, c [/latex] and l in Eq. (i), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{430-30}{1030-30} &=e^{\frac{-20 x t}{7800 \times 600 \times 0.01}} \\ 0.4 &=e^{-4.273 \times 10^{-4} t} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex] \log _{\mathrm{e}} [/latex] both sides, we get
[latex] \log _{e} 0.4=-4.273 \times 10^{-4} \times t \times 1[/latex]
[latex] \text{or }\quad t=\frac{0.9162}{4.273 \times 10^{-4}}=2144.16 \mathrm{s}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A flywheel connected to a punching machine has to supply energy of 400 Nm while running at a mean angular speed of 20 rad/s. If the total fluctuation of speed is not to exceed  [latex]\pm 2[/latex]%, the mass moment of inertia of the flywheel in [latex]kg-m^{2}[/latex]

Two cutting tools are being compared for a machining operation. The tool life equations are:

Carbide tool: [latex]VT^{1.6}=3000[/latex]
HSS tool: [latex]VT^{0.6}=200[/latex]

where V is the cutting speed in m/min and T is the tool life in min. The carbide tool will provide higher tool life if the cutting speed in m/min exceeds

raw_source.text: During the electrochemical machining (ECM) of iron (atomic weight = 56, valency = 2) at current of 1000 A with 90% current efficiency, the material removal rate was observed to be 0.26 gm/s. If Titanium (atomic weight = 48, valency = 3) is machined by the ECM process at the current of  2000 A with 90% current efficiency, the expected material removal rate in gm/s will be
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \mathrm{MRR} &=\frac{\rho I}{\rho f}=\frac{A I}{\rho z F} \\ \Rightarrow \quad 0.26 &=\frac{28 \times 1000 \times 0.9}{\rho \times 96500} \\ \rho &=0.9956 \\ \text { New MRR } &=\frac{\frac{48}{3} \times 2000 \times 0.9}{0.9956 \times 96500} \\ &=0.30 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A single degree of freedom system having mass 1 kg and stiffness 10 kN/m initially at rest is subjected to an impulse force of magnitude 5 kN for [latex]10^{-4}[/latex]
seconds. The amplitude in mm of the resulting free vibration is
raw_source.solution:
At t=0 mass is at rest [latex] F=5 \mathrm{kN} for 10^{-4} [/latex] seconds
Amplitude = x
[latex] \begin{aligned} F &=m \times d v | d t \\ F \cdot \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} d t &=m \cdot \int_{v_{1}}^{v_{2}} d V \\ F\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right) &=m \times\left(v_{2}-v_{1}\right) \\ 5 \times 10^{3} \times & 10^{-4}=1 \times\left(v_{2}-0\right) \\ 0.5 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} &=v_{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} m v_{2}^{2}=& \frac{1}{2} k x^{2} \\ x &=\sqrt{\frac{m v_{2}^{2}}{k}}=\sqrt{\frac{1 \times 0.5 \times 0.5}{10 \times 1000}} \\ &=\frac{0.5}{100}=0.005 \mathrm{m}=5 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

A bar is subjected to fluctuating tensile load from 20 kN to 100 kN. The material has yield strength of 240 MPa and endurance limit in reversed bending is 160 MPa. According to the Soderberg principle, the area of cross-section in [latex]mm^{2}[/latex]
 of the bar for a factor of safety of 2 is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{c} P_{1}=20 \mathrm{kN} ; P_{2}=100 \mathrm{kN} \\ \sigma_{y t}=240 \mathrm{MPa} ; \sigma_{e}=160 \mathrm{MPa} \\ P_{m}=\frac{20+100}{2}=60 \mathrm{kN} \end{array}[/latex]
Let A is are in [latex]\text{mm}^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{v}&=\frac{100-20}{2}=40 \mathrm{kN} \\ \sigma_{v}&=\frac{40}{A} \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By Soderberg principle
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\mathrm{FOS}} &=\frac{\sigma_{m}}{\sigma_{y t}}+\frac{\sigma_{v}}{\sigma_{e}} \\ \frac{1}{2} &=\frac{60 \times 10^{3}}{A \sigma_{y t}}+\frac{40 \times 10^{3}}{A \sigma_{v}} \\ A &=\left[\frac{60}{240}+\frac{40}{160}\right] 2 \times 10^{3} \\ A &=\left[\frac{2}{4}\right] \times 2 \times 10^{3}=1000 \mathrm{mm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Two large diffuse gray parallel plates, separated by a small distance, have surface temperatures of 400 K and 300 K. If  the emissivities of the surfaces are 0.8 and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant is [latex]5.67\times 10^{-8}W/m^{2}K^{4}[/latex], the net radiation heat exchange rate in [latex]kW/m^{2}[/latex]
  between the two plates is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \sigma &=5.67 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}^{4} \\ \frac{Q}{A} &=\frac{\sigma\left(T_{1}^{4}-T_{2}^{4}\right)}{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{1}}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{2}}-1} \\ &=\frac{5.67 \times 10^{-8}\left(400^{4}-300^{4}\right)}{\frac{1}{0.8}+\frac{1}{0.8}-1} \\ &=661.5 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=0.66 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A hinged gate of length 5 m, inclined at 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] with the horizontal and with water mass on its left, is shown in the figure below. Density of water is 1000 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex]. The minimum mass of the gate in kg per unit width (perpendicular to the plane of paper), required to keep it closed is

Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} l &=5 \mathrm{m} \\ \theta &=30^{\circ} \\ \rho &=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \hbar &=2.5 \sin 30^{\circ}=1.25 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} A &=b l=1 \times 5=5 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ I_{G} &=\frac{b l^{3}}{12}=\frac{1 \times(5)^{3}}{12}=10.41 \mathrm{m}^{4} \\ F &=\rho g A \bar{h}=1000 \times 9.81 \times 5 \times 1.25 \\ &=61312.5 \mathrm{N} \\ h^{*} &=\bar{h}+\frac{I_{\mathrm{G}}}{A \bar{h}} \sin ^{2} \theta \\ &=1.25+\frac{10.41}{5 \times 1.25} \sin ^{2} 30^{\circ} \\ &=1.666 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Taking moment about hinge, Moment due F

raw_source.text: The pressure, temperature and velocity of air flowing in a pipe are 5 bar, 500 K and 50 m/s, respectively. The specific heats of air at constant pressure and at constant volume are 1.005 kJ/kgK and 0.718 kJ/kgK, respectively. Neglect potential energy. If the pressure and temperature of the surroundings are 1 bar and 300 K, respectively, the available energy in kJ/kg of the air stream is
raw_source.solution:
Available energy
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\left(h_{1}-h_{0}\right)-T_{0}\left(s_{1}-s_{0}\right)+\left(\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{V_{0}^{2}}{2}\right) \\ \text { where } s_{1}-s_{0}=c_{p} \ln \frac{T_{1}}{T_{0}}-R \ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}\\ =1.005 \ln \left(\frac{500}{300}\right)-0.287 \ln \left(\frac{5}{1}\right) \\ =0.05147 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex]Available energy
[latex] =1.005(500-300)-300(0.5147)+\frac{(50)^{2}}{2} \times 10^{-3}\\ =186.8 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \approx 187 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The probability that a student knows the correct answer to a multiple choice question is [latex]\frac{2}{3}[/latex]
If the student does not know the answer, then the student guesses the answer. The probability of the guessed answer being correct is [latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex]
Given that the student has answered the question correctly, the 
conditional probability that the student knows the correct answer is
raw_source.solution:
Let A be the event when student knows the answer and B be the event when student guesses the answer. Therefore
[latex]P(A)=P(A\cap B)=\frac{2}{3} [/latex]
[latex]P(B)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{12}[/latex]
where [latex]\frac{2}{3}[/latex] is the probability of correct answer and [latex]\frac{1}{3}[/latex] is the probability that student does not know the answer. So guesses the answer and probability of correct guess is [latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex]. Therefore total probability of correct answer
[latex]=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{12}[/latex]
Conditional probability that student knows the correct answer
[latex]P(A/B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{9}{12}}=\frac{8}{9}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The solution to the differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}u} }{\mathrm{d} x^{2}}-k\frac{\mathrm{du} }{\mathrm{d} x}=0[/latex]
 where k is a constant, subjected to the boundary conditions  u(0) = 0  and  u(L) = U,  is
raw_source.solution:
We have [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}u} }{\mathrm{d} x^{2}}-k\frac{\mathrm{du} }{\mathrm{d} x}=0[/latex]
[latex](D^2-kD)u=0 [/latex]
The auxiliary equation is
[latex]\begin{aligned} m^2-km&=0\\ m(m-k)&=0\\ m&=0,k \end{aligned} [/latex]
Thus the complete solution is
[latex]\begin{aligned} u&=C_1e^{0x}+C_2e^{kx}\\ u&=C_1+C_2e^{kx} \end{aligned} [/latex]
From given condition
[latex] u(0)=0:\;\; C_1+C_2=0 \;\;\;...(i) [/latex]
[latex]u(L)=U:\;\; U=C_1+C_2e^{kL}\;\;\;...(ii) [/latex]
Subtracting equation (i) from (ii), we get
[latex]U=C_2(e^{kL}-1) [/latex]
[latex]C_2=\frac{U}{e^{kL}-1} [/latex]
From equation (i), we have
[latex] C_1=-C_2=\frac{-U}{e^{kL}-1} [/latex]
Substitute these values in the expression for u, we get
[latex] u=\frac{-U}{e^{kL}-1}+\frac{U}{e^{kL}-1}e^{kx}=U\left ( \frac{1-e^{kx}}{1-e^{kL}} \right )[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Water (specific heat, [latex]c_{p}[/latex] = 4.18 kJ/kgK) enters a pipe at a rate of 0.01 [latex]kg/s[/latex] and a temperature of 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. The pipe, of diameter 50 mm and length 3 m, is subjected to a wall heat flux [latex]{q_{w}}^{''}[/latex] in [latex]W/m^{2}:[/latex]

If [latex]{q_{w}}^{''}=2500x[/latex] where x is in m and in the direction of flow (x = 0 at the inlet), the bulk mean temperature of the water leaving the pipe in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} c_{p} &=4.18 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K}=4180 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K} \\ m &=0.01 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ T_{i} &=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ d &=50 \mathrm{mm}=0.05 \mathrm{m} \\ l &=3 \mathrm{m} \\ q_{w}^{\prime \prime} &=2500 \mathrm{x} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]


Heat transfer through small length dx
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta Q &=q_{w}^{\prime \prime} \times \pi d \times d x \\ &=\pi d q_{w}^{\prime \prime} d x \\ &=3.14 \times 0.05 \times 2500 x d x \\ &=392.5 x d x\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net heat transfer through whole length l ,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=\int_{0}^{l} 392.5 x d x=392.5 \int_{0}^{3} x d x \\ &=392.5\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{3} \\ &=392.5 \times \frac{3 \times 3}{2}=1766.25 \mathrm{W}\\ \text{also } \quad Q&=m c_{p}\left(T_{0}-T_{i}\right), \text{heat gained by the water}\\ \therefore \quad 1766.25&=0.01 \times 4180\left(T_{0}-20\right) \\ \text{or }\quad T_{o}-20&=42.25 \\ \text{or }\quad T_{0} &=42.25+20 \\ &=62.25^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \simeq 62.25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{At pipe inlet},\\ x&=0\\ \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{w}_{\mathrm{i}}}^{\prime \prime}&=2500 \times 0=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Art pipe exit,
[latex] \begin{aligned} x&=1\\ \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{w}^{\prime}}=& 2500 \times l \times 3=7500 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Average heat transfer
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\prime \prime} &=\frac{q_{w i}^{\prime \prime}+q_{w 0}^{\prime \prime}}{2} \\ &=\frac{0+7500}{2}=3750 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net heat transfer
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=q_{\text {avg }}^{\prime \prime} \times \text { surface area } \\ &=3750 \times \pi d l \\ &=3750 \times 3.14 \times 0.05 \times 3 \\ &=1766.25 \mathrm{W}\\ \text{also }\quad Q&=m c_{p}\left(T_{0}-T_{i}\right),\\ &\text{ heat gained by the water}\\ \therefore \quad 1766.25&=0.01 \times 4180\left(T_{0}-20\right) \\ \text { or } \quad T_{0}-20&=42.25 \\ \text { or } \quad T_{0}&=42.25+20\\ &=62.25^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \simeq 62.25^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Water (specific heat, [latex]c_{p}[/latex] = 4.18 kJ/kgK) enters a pipe at a rate of 0.01 [latex]kg/s[/latex] and a temperature of 20[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. The pipe, of diameter 50 mm and length 3 m, is subjected to a wall heat flux [latex]{q_{w}}^{''}[/latex] in [latex]W/m^{2}:[/latex]

If [latex]{q_{w}}^{''}=5000[/latex] and the convection heat transfer coefficient at the pipe outlet is 1000 [latex]W/m^{2}K[/latex] , the temperature in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C at the inner surface of the pipe at the outlet is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} q_{w}^{\prime \prime} &=5000 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ h &=1000 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat transfer through pipe wall,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=q_{w}^{\prime} \times \text { surface area }\\ &=5000 \times \pi d l \\ &=5000 \times 3.14 \times 0.05 \times 3 \\ &=2355 \mathrm{W}\\ \text{also }\quad Q&=m c_{p}\left(T_{0}-T_{i}\right), \\ & \text { heat gained by the water}\\ 2355 &=0.01 \times 4180\left(T_{0}-20\right) \\ 56.33 &=T_{0}-20 \\ T_{0} &=76.33^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Heat flux [latex] q_{w}^{\prime \prime} [/latex] is same at any two sections,
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{w}^{\prime \prime}&=h\left(T_{s^{\prime} 0}-T_{0}\right) \\ 5000 &=1000\left(T_{s^{\prime} 0}-76.33\right) \\ \text{or }\quad 5 &=T_{s^{\prime} 0}-76.33\\ \text{or }\quad T_{s^{\prime} \circ}&=76.33+5\\ &=81.33^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \simeq 81^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a simple Brayton cycle, the pressure ratio is 8 and temperatures at the entrance of compressor and turbine are 300 K and 1400 K, respectively. Both compressor and gas turbine have isentropic efficiencies equal to 0.8. For the gas, assume a constant value of [latex]c_{p}[/latex] (specific heat at constant pressure) equal to 1 [latex]kJ/kgK[/latex] and ratio of specific heats as 1.4. Neglect changes in kinetic and potential energies.

The power required by the compressor in kW/kg of gas flow rate is
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Pressure ratio,
[latex] \begin{aligned} r_{p}&=8\\ T_{1} &=300 \mathrm{K} ; T_{3}=1400 \mathrm{K} \\ \eta_{c} &=\eta_{T}=0.8 \\ c_{p} &=1 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ \gamma &=1.4 \end{aligned}[/latex]


For adiabatic isentropic process 1-2s,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T_{2 s}}{T_{1}}&=\left(\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}} \\ \frac{T_{2 s}}{300}&=\left(r_{p}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}=(8)^{\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}}=(8)^{0.2857} \\ \frac{T_{2 s}}{300}&=1.811\\ \text{or }\qquad T_{2 s} &=300 \times 1.811=543.3 \mathrm{K} \\ n_{c} &=\frac{\text { Isentropic rise in temperature }}{\text { Actual rise in temperature }} \\ &=\frac{T_{2 s}-T_{1}}{T_{2}-T_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad 0.8 &=\frac{543.3-300}{T_{2}-300}\\ \text{or }\qquad T_{2}-300&=\frac{243.3}{0.8}=304.12\\ \text{or }\qquad T_{2}&=604.12 \mathrm{K}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Power required by compressure,
[latex] \begin{aligned} w_{C} &=c_{p}\left(T_{2}-T_{1}\right) \\ &=1(604.12-300) \\ &=304.12 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In a simple Brayton cycle, the pressure ratio is 8 and temperatures at the entrance of compressor and turbine are 300 K and 1400 K, respectively. Both compressor and gas turbine have isentropic efficiencies equal to 0.8. For the gas, assume a constant value of [latex]c_{p}[/latex] (specific heat at constant pressure) equal to 1 [latex]kJ/kgK[/latex] and ratio of specific heats as 1.4. Neglect changes in kinetic and potential energies.

The thermal efficiency of the cycle in percentage (%) is
raw_source.solution:
For adiabatic process 3-4 s
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T_{3}}{T_{4 s}} &=\left(\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}=(8)^{\frac{1.4-1}{1.4}} \\ &=(8)^{0.2857}=1.811 \\ \text{or}\quad T_{4 s} &=\frac{T_{3}}{1.811}=\frac{1400}{1.811} \\ &=773.05 \mathrm{K} \\ \eta_{T} &=\frac{\text { Actual fall in temperature }}{\text { Isentropic fall in temperature }}\\ \eta_{T} &=\frac{T_{3}-T_{4}}{T_{3}-T_{4 s}} \\ 0.8 &=\frac{1400-T_{4}}{1400-773.05} \\ 0.8 &=\frac{1400-T_{4}}{626.95}\\ \text{or }\quad 1400-T_{4}&=0.8 \times 626.95 \\ 1400-T_{4} &=501.56 \\ T_{4} &=898.44 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Power developed by the turbine,
[latex] \begin{aligned} w_{T} &=c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{4}\right) \\ &=1(1400-898.44) \\ &=501.56 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net power output,
[latex] \begin{aligned} w_{\text {net }} &=w_{T}-w_{C}=501.56-304.12 \\ &=197.44 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat supplied,
[latex] \begin{aligned} q_{2-3} &=c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right) \\ &=1(1400-604.12) \\ &=795.88 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thermal efficiency of the cycle,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_{\mathrm{th}} &=\frac{\text { Net power output : } w_{\text {net }}}{\text { Heat supplied : } q_{2-3}} \\ &=\frac{197.44}{795.88}=0.2480 \\ &=24.80 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

Given that the determinant of the matrix
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 0\\ 2 & 6 & 4\\ -1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
is -12, the determinant of the matrix
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 & 0\\ 4 & 12 & 8\\ -2 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Let D=-12 for the given matrix
[latex] |A|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & 6 & 0 \\4 & 12 & 8 \\-2 & 0 & 4\end{array}\right|=(2)^{3}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 3 & 0 \\2 & 6 & 4 \\-1 & 0 & 2\end{array}\right| [/latex]
(Taking 2 common from each row)
[latex] \begin{aligned}\therefore \text{Det}(A) &=(2)^{3} \times D \\=& 8 x-12=-96\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: [latex]\lim_{x\rightarrow 0} \frac{x-\sin x}{1-\cos x}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x-\sin x}{1-\cos x}[/latex]
Applying L ' Hospital's rule
[latex] \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{d}{dx}(x-sinx)}{\frac{d}{dx}(1-cosx)}=\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{(1-\cos x)}{\sin x}[/latex]
(It is still of [latex] \frac{0}{0}[/latex] form)
Again applying L' Hospital's rule
[latex] \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{d}{d x}(1-\cos x)}{\frac{d}{d x}(\sin x)}=\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\frac{0}{1}=0[/latex]

raw_source.text: The argument of the complex number [latex]\frac{1+i}{1-i}[/latex],where [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex], is
raw_source.solution:

[latex] \begin{aligned} Arg(z) &=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \\ &=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{0}\right)=\tan ^{-1} \infty=\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: One of the eigenvectors of the matrix  [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2\\ -9 & 6 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]  is
raw_source.solution:
The characteristic equation [latex] | A-\lambda D=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{i.e.} \left|\begin{array}{cc}-5-\lambda & 2 \\ -9 & 6-\lambda\end{array}\right|=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or } (\lambda-6)(\lambda+5)+18=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or } \quad \lambda^{2}-6 \lambda+5 \lambda-30+18=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or } \quad \lambda^{2}-\lambda-12=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or } \lambda=\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+48}}{2}=\frac{1 \pm 7}{2}=4,-3 [/latex]
Corresponding to [latex] \lambda=4,[/latex] we have
[latex] \; [A-\lambda I] x=\left[\begin{array}{cc}-5-\lambda & 2 \\-9 & 6-\lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\y\end{array}\right] [/latex]
[latex] =0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{Or, } \left[\begin{array}{ll}-9 & 2 \\ -9 & 2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y\end{array}\right]=0[/latex]which gives only one independent equation,
[latex] -9 x+2 y=0 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \frac{x}{2}=\frac{y}{9}[/latex] gives eigen vector (2,9)
Corresponding to [latex] \lambda=-3, [/latex]
[latex] =\left[\begin{array}{ll}-2 & 2 \\-9 & 9\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\y \end{array}\right]=0[/latex]
which gives -x+y=0 (only one independent equation)
[latex] \therefore \quad \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y}{1} \quad [/latex] which gives (1,1)
So, the eigen vectors are [latex]\left\{\begin{array}{l}2 \\ 9\end{array}\right\} and \left\{\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1\end{array}\right\}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An analytic function of a complex variable [latex]z=x+iy[/latex] is expressed as  [latex]f(z)=u(x,y)+i v(x,y)[/latex] , where [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex]. If [latex]u(x,y)=2xy[/latex], then [latex]v(x,y)[/latex] must be
raw_source.solution:
As per Cauchy-Riemann equation
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}[/latex]
[latex] \text { and } \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} =-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=2 y [/latex]
[latex] \text { and } \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=2 x [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=2 y [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad v=y^{2}+f(x) [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0+P(x)=-2 x [/latex]
[latex] \therefore f(x)=-x^{2}+ \text{constant} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad v=y^{2}-x^{2}+ \text{constant}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider an unbiased cubic dice with opposite faces coloured identically and each face coloured red, blue or green such that each colour appears only two times on the dice. If the dice is thrown thrice, the probability of obtaining red colour on top face of the dice at least twice is _______
raw_source.solution:
n=3 x: red colour
[latex] \begin{aligned} P&=P(\text{Red})=\frac{2}{6} \\ q&=1-P=1-\frac{2}{6}=\frac{4}{6} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Prob. of getting red colour on top face atleast twice is
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=P(x=2)+P(x=3) \\ &=^{n} C_{2} P^{2} q^{n-2}+^{n} C_{3} P^{3} q^{n-3} \\ &=^{n} C_{2}\left(\frac{8}{6}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1}+\frac{3}{3}\left(\frac{2}{6}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{4}{6}\right)^{0}\\ &=3 \cdot \frac{4}{36} \cdot \frac{4}{6}+1 \cdot \frac{8}{216} \\ &=\frac{48+8}{216}=\frac{56}{216}=0.259 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An analytic function of a complex variable [latex]z=x+iy[/latex]  is expressed as [latex]f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)[/latex]  , where [latex]i=\sqrt{-1}[/latex]. If [latex]u(x,y)=x^{2}-y^{2}[/latex], then expression for [latex]v(x,y)[/latex]  in terms of x, y and a general constant c would be
raw_source.solution:
As per Cauchy-Riemann equations:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} and \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} [/latex]
[latex] u=x^{2}-y^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=2 x, \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-2 y [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=2 x [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad v=2 x y+f(x) [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=2 y+f(x) [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=2 y+f^{\prime}(x) [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(x)=0 \quad \text { i.e. } f(x)=c [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad v=2 x y+c [/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider two solutions [latex]x(t)=x_{1}(t)[/latex] and  [latex]x(t)=x_{2}(t)[/latex]  of the differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x(t)}{\mathrm{d} t^{2}}+x(t)=0,\; t\gt 0[/latex]  , such that [latex]x_{1}(0)=1,\; \frac{\mathrm{d}x_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}|_{t=0} =0,x_{2}(0)=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}x_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}|_{t=0} =1[/latex]  . The wronskian [latex]W(t)=\begin{vmatrix} x_{1}(t) & x_{2}(t)\\ \frac{\mathrm{d} x_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} & \frac{\mathrm{d} x_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} \end{vmatrix}[/latex]  at [latex]t=\pi /2[/latex]  is.
raw_source.solution:
Given differential equation in symbolic form is
[latex] \left(D^{2}+1\right) x(t)=0 [/latex]
Its A.E. is [latex] D^{2}+1=0 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad D=\pm i [/latex]
So, C.F. is
[latex] x_{1}(t)=C_{1} \cos t [/latex]
[latex] x_{2}(t)=C_{2} \sin t[/latex]
[latex] \therefore x_{1}(0)=C_{1}=1 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad x_{1}(t) &=\operatorname{cost} \\ \text { it satisfies }\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{\mathrm{d} x_{1}(t)}{d t}\end{matrix} \right|_{t=0} &=0 \end{aligned} \\ \qquad \begin{aligned} x_{2}(0) &=0=C_{2} \sin (0)\left(\because C_{2} \neq 0\right) \\ \frac{d x_{2}(t)}{d t} &=C_{2} \cos t \end{aligned} \\ \left.\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d x_{2}(t)}{d t}\right|_{t=0}=C_{2}=1 \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \therefore \;\; x_{2}(t)=\sin t \\ W(t)= \begin{vmatrix} x_{1}(t) & x_{2}(t) \\ \frac{d x_{1}(t)}{d t} & \frac{d x_{2}(t)}{d t}\end{vmatrix}= \begin{vmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \\ -\sin t & \cos t \end{vmatrix} \\ M(t)=\cos ^{2} t+\sin ^{2} t=1 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A machine produces 0, 1 or 2 defective pieces in a day with associated probability of 1/6, 2/3 and 1/6, respectively. The mean value and the variance of the number of defective pieces produced by the machine in a day,  respectively, are
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} \operatorname{mean} &=\Sigma x \cdot p(x)=0\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)+1\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+2\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{6}=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{3}{3}=1 \\ E\left(x^{2}\right) &=0\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)+1\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+4\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ &=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3} \\ \text { Variance } &=E\left(x^{2}\right)-\left(E(x)^{2}\right)=\frac{4}{3}-1=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)} [/latex]

Again,

[latex] =0.5425 [/latex]

raw_source.text: The number of accidents occurring in a plant in a month follows Poisson distribution with mean as 5.2. The probability of occurrence of less than 2 accidents in the plant during a randomly selected month is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(x) &=\frac{\mu^{x} \mathrm{e}^{-\mu}}{x !} \\ P(x \lt 2) &=P(0)+P(1) \\ &=\frac{\mu^{0} e^{-\mu}}{0 !}+\frac{\mu^{1} e^{-\mu}}{1 !} \\ &=\frac{1}{e^{\mu}}+\frac{\mu}{e^{\mu}}=\frac{1+\mu}{e^{\mu}} \\ \operatorname{As} \mu(\operatorname{mean})=5 & \cdot 2 \\ \therefore \quad P(x \lt 2) &=\frac{6.2}{e^{5.2}}=0.0342 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider an ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}=4t+4[/latex]. If [latex]x=x_{0}[/latex] at [latex]t=0[/latex]  the increment in x calculated using Runge-Kutta fourth order multi-step method with a step size of [latex]\Delta t=0.2[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d x}{d t} &=4 t+4 \\ &=f\left(t_{0}, x_{0}\right) \\ \text { At } t=0, & x=x_{0} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Irrespective of values of [latex] x, f\left(t_{0}, x_{0}\right)[/latex] depends on t only.
[latex] \begin{aligned} k_{1} &=h f\left(t_{0}, x_{0}\right)=0.2 x \times 4=0.8 \\ \mathrm{k}_{2} &=h f\left(t_{0}+\frac{1}{2} h, x_{0}+\frac{k_{1}}{2}\right) \\ &=h f\left(0.1, x_{0}+0.4\right) \\ &=0.2(4 \times 0.1+4)=0.88 \\ k_{3} &=h f\left(t_{0}+\frac{1}{2} h, x_{0}+\frac{k_{2}}{2}\right) \\ &=0.2 f\left(0.1, x_{0}+0.44\right) \\ &=0.2(4 \times 0.1+4)=0.88 \\ k_{4} &=h f\left(t_{0}+h, x_{0}+k_{3}\right) \\ &=0.2 f\left(0.2, x_{0}+0.88\right) \\ &=0.2(4 \times 0.2+4)=0.96 \\ k &=\frac{1}{6}\left(k_{1}+2 k_{2}+2 k_{3}+k_{4}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{6}(0.8+2 \times 0.88+2 \times 0.88+0.96) \\ &=0.88 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.solution:
[latex]\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x-\sin x}{1-\cos x}[/latex]
Applying L ' Hospital's rule
[latex] \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{d}{dx}(x-sinx)}{\frac{d}{dx}(1-cosx)}=\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{(1-\cos x)}{\sin x}[/latex]

[latex] \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{d}{d x}(1-\cos x)}{\frac{d}{d x}(\sin x)}=\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\frac{0}{1}=0[/latex]

raw_source.text: The integral [latex]\oint_c (ydx-xdy)[/latex]  is evalulated along the circle [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{1}{4}[/latex] traversed in counter clockwise direction. The integral is equal to
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{C}(\phi d x+\psi d y) &=\iint_{E}\left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}\right) d x d y \\ \phi &=y \\ \psi &=-x \\ \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} &=-1 \\ \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y} &=1 \\ I &=\iint_{E}\left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}\right) d x d y \\ &=\int_{0}^{1 / 2} \int_{0}^{2 \pi}(-2) r d \theta d r \\ &=-2\left(\int_{0}^{1 / 2} r d r\right)\left(\int_{0}^{2 \pi} r d \theta\right) \\ &=-2\left(\frac{r^{2}}{2}\right)_{0}^{1 / 2} 2 \pi=-\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: If [latex]y=f(x)[/latex]  is the solution of [latex]\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0[/latex] with the boundary conditions y=5 at x=0, and  [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=2[/latex] at x=10, f(15)=_____
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=0 \\ \frac{d y}{d x} &=C_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad C_{1} &=2 \\ y &=C_{1} x+C_{2} \\ at \qquad x &=0 ; \quad y=5=C_{2} \\ \therefore \qquad y &=2 x+5 \\ at \qquad y(15) &=2 \times 15+5=35 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: in the folowing table, x is a discrete random variable and p(x) is the pobability destiny. The standard deviation of x is
raw_source.solution:
Mean,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{x} &=\frac{\Sigma_{i} x_{i}}{\Sigma f_{i}} \\ &=\frac{1 \times 0.3+2 \times 0.8+3 \times 0.1}{1}=1.8 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Standard deviation,
[latex] \sigma=\left(\frac{\Sigma f_{x_{i}}^{2}}{\Sigma f_{i}}-\bar{x}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \sigma=\left(\frac{0.3 \times 1^{2}+0.6 \times 2^{2}+0.1 \times 3^{2}}{1}-1.8^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} [/latex]
[latex] =\left(3.6-1.8^{2}\right)^{1 / 2}=(0.36)^{1 / 2}=0.6[/latex]

raw_source.text: Using the trapezoidal rule, and dividing the interval of integration into three equal subintervals, the definite integral [latex]\int_{-1}^{+1}\left | x \right |dx[/latex]  is ___________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]I=\int_{-1}^{1}|x| \mathrm{d} x [/latex]
[latex] n=3, h=\frac{1-(-1)}{3}=\frac{2}{3}[/latex]


By Trapezoidal rule
[latex] \int_{-1}^{1}|x| d x=\frac{h}{2}\left[\left(y_{0}+y_{3}\right)+2\left(y_{1}+y_{2}\right)\right] [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{2}{3 \times 2}\left[(1+1)+2\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\right] [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1}{3}\left[2+\frac{4}{3}\right]=1.11[/latex]

raw_source.text: The state of stress at a point is given by  [latex]\sigma_{x}[/latex]= -6Mpa, [latex]\sigma_{y}[/latex]=4 MPa  and [latex]\tau_{xy}[/latex]=-8 MPa . The maximum tensile stress (in MPa) at the point is _________
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \sigma_{1} &=\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}}{2}+\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-\sigma_{y}}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{x y}^{2}} \\ &=\frac{+6-4}{2}+\sqrt{\left(\frac{+6-4}{2}\right)^{2}+(-8)^{2}} \\ &=-1+\sqrt{25+64} \\ &=-1+\sqrt{89}=8.4339 \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A block R of mass 100kg is placed on a block S of mass 150kg as shown in the figure. Block R is tied to the wall by a massless and intextensible string PQ. If the coefficient of static friction for all surfaces is 0.4, the minimum force F(in kN) needed to move the block S is
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} F &=\mu\left(W_{S}+W_{R}\right)+\mu W_{R} \\ F &=\mu\left(W_{S}+2 W_{R}\right) \\ &=0.4(150+2 \times 100) \times 9.81 \\ &=1373.4 \mathrm{N}=1.37 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A pair of spur gears with module 5 mm and a center distance of 450 mm is used for a speed reduction of 5:1. The number of teeth on pinion is  _______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{N_{P}}{N_{G}} &=5=\frac{T_{G}}{T_{P}} \\ T_{G} &=5 T_{P} \\ C &=\frac{m}{2}\left(T_{P}+T_{G}\right) \\ T_{P}+T_{G} &=\frac{2 C}{m}=\frac{2 \times 450}{5} \\ &=180 \\ \text{or }\quad 6 T_{P}&=180 \\ \text{or }\quad T_{P}&=30 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a cantilever beam, having negligible mass and uniform flexural rigidity, with length  0.01 m. The frequency of vibration of the beam, with a 0.5 kg mass attached at the free tip, is  100 Hz. The flexural rigidity (in N.[latex]m^{2}[/latex] ) of the beam is _______
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} P &=m g=0.5 \times 9.81=4.905 N \\ L &=0.01 \mathrm{m} \\ f_{n} &=100 \mathrm{Hz} \\ \omega_{n} &=2 \pi f_{n}=628 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ \omega_{n} &=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\\ \text { or } \quad k&=m \omega_{n}^{2}=0.5 \times(628)^{2}\\ &=197192 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}\\ \delta &=\frac{P L^{3}}{3 E I} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{P}{\delta} &=\frac{3 E I}{L^{3}} \\ \text{or}\quad EI&=\frac{P}{\delta }\times\frac{L^{3}}{3}\\ &=197192 \times \frac{(0.01)^{3}}{3} \\ &=0.06573 \mathrm{Nm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An ideal water jet with volume flow rate of 0.05 [latex]m^{3}/s[/latex]  strikes a flat plate placed normal to its path and exerts a force of 1000 N. Considering the density of water as 1000 [latex]kg/m^{3}[/latex], the diameter (in mm) of the water jet is  _______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=0.05 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s} \\ F &=1000 \mathrm{N} \\ \rho &=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] F=\rho a V^{2} [/latex]
where a= cross-section area fo the jet
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q&=a V \\ \therefore \quad F&=\rho Q V \\ 1000 &=1000 \times 0.05 \times V \\ \text{or}\quad V &=20 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ Q &=a V \\ Q &=\frac{\pi}{4} d^{2} V \\ \text{or}\quad 0.05&=\frac{3.14}{4} \times d^{2} \times 20 \\ \text{or}\quad d^{2}&=0.00318 \\ d&=0.05643 \mathrm{m} \\&=56.43mm \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A block weighing 200 N is in contact with a level plane whose coefficients of static and kinetic friction are 0.4 and 0.2, respectively. The block is acted upon by a horizontal force (in newton) P=10t, where t denotes the time in seconds. The velocity (in m/s) of the block attained after  10 seconds is _______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} N &=m g=200 \mathrm{N} \\(f_{s})_{max} &=\mu_{s} N \\ &=0.4 \times 200=80 \end{aligned}[/latex]
upto [latex] 8 \sec [P=10 t] \rightarrow [/latex] no motion
[latex] \Rightarrow [/latex] from 8 sec to 10 sec
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{k} &=\mu_{k} N \\ &=0.2 \times 200=40 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Average applied force
[latex] =\frac{P_{\max }+P_{\min }}{2} [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{100+80}{2}=90 \mathrm{N}[/latex]
Average resultant force = Avg. applied force kinetic friction
[latex] =90-40=50 N[/latex]
Average acceration
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{50 \times 9.8}{200} \\ \Rightarrow \quad V &=u+a t\\ u&=0\\ a&=\frac{50 \times 9.8}{200} \\ t&=2 \text{second}\\ \therefore V&=\frac{50 \times 9.8}{200} \times 2=4.9 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A slider crank mechanism has slider mass of 10 kg, stroke of 0.2 m and rotates with a uniform angular velocity of 10 rad/s. The primary inertia forces of the slider are partially balanced by a revolving mass of 6 kg at the crank, placed at a distance equal to crank radius. Neglect the mass of connecting rod and crank. When the crank angle (with respect to slider axis) is [latex]30^{\circ}[/latex] , the unbalanced force (in newton) normal to the slider axis is _______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \omega &=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ \theta &=30^{\circ} \\ r &=\frac{s}{2}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \\ \text { Unbalanced force }&=m \omega^{2} r \sin 30^{\circ} & \\ &=6 \times 100 \times 0.1 \times \frac{1}{2} \\ &=30 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An offset slider-crank mechanism is shown in the figure at an instant. Conventionally, the Quick Return Ratio (QRR) is considered to be greater than one. The value of QRR is _______
raw_source.solution:
Length of connecting rod: [latex]l_{r}=40 \mathrm{mm} [/latex]
Crank radius: [latex]r=20 \mathrm{mm} [/latex]
Eccentricity: [latex]e=10 \mathrm{mm} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\phi=\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{e}{l+r}\right)-\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{e}{l-r}\right) \\ &=\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)-\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=20.4^{\circ} \\ &\mathrm{QRR}=\frac{\text { Time of advance stroke }}{\text { Time of return stroke }} \\ &=\left(\frac{\theta_{C}}{2 \pi N}\right)\left(\frac{2 \pi N}{\theta_{R}}\right) \\ &\mathrm{QRR} =\frac{\theta_{C}}{\theta_{R}}=\frac{180^{\circ}+\phi}{180^{\circ}-\phi} \\ &=\frac{180^{\circ}+20.4^{\circ}}{180^{\circ}-20.4^{\circ}}=1.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A rigid uniform rod AB of length L and mass m is hinged at C such that AC = L/3, CB = 2L/3. Ends A and B are supported by springs of spring constant k. The natural frequency of the system is given by
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \theta &=\frac{y_{A}}{\left(\frac{L}{3}\right)}=\frac{y_{B}}{\left(\frac{2 L}{3}\right)} \\ I_{0} &=I_{C}+m\left(\frac{2 L}{3}-\frac{L}{2}\right)^{2} \\ I_{C} &=\frac{m L^{2}}{12} \\ \therefore \quad I_{0} &=\frac{m L^{2}}{12}+\frac{m L^{2}}{36}=\frac{m L^{2}}{9} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking, [latex]\Sigma M_{0}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow\left(k y_{A} \times \frac{L}{3}\right)+\left(k y_{B} \times \frac{2 L}{3}\right)+I_{0} \ddot{\theta}=0 \\ \Rightarrow k \theta\left(\frac{L}{3}\right)^{2}+k \theta\left(\frac{2 L}{3}\right)^{2}+\frac{m L^{2}}{9} \ddot{\theta}=0 \\ \Rightarrow\left(\frac{m L^{2}}{9}\right) \ddot{\theta}+\left(\frac{5 k L^{2}}{9}\right) \theta=0 \\ \Rightarrow \ddot{\theta}+\left(\frac{5 k}{m}\right) \theta=0 \\ \omega_{n}^{2}=\frac{5 k}{m} \\ \quad \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{5 k}{m}} \\ \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A hydrodynamic journal bearing is subject to 2000 N load at a rotational speed of 2000 rpm. Both bearing bore diameter and length are 40 mm. If radial clearance is 20 [latex]\mu[/latex]m and bearing is lubricated with an oil having viscosity 0.03 Pa.s, the Sommerfeld number of the bearing is  _______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} r &=20 \mathrm{mm}, \quad N=2000 \mathrm{rpm} \\ c &=20 \times 10^{-3}, \quad \mu=0.03 \mathrm{Ns} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ p &=\frac{2000}{1600} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \qquad \left(p=\frac{W}{A}\right)\\ &=1.25 \mathrm{MPa}, S=? \\ S &=\frac{Z N}{60 p}\left(\frac{r}{c}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{0.03 \times 2000}{60 \times 1.25 \times 10^{6}}\left(\frac{20}{20 \times 10^{-3}}\right)^{2} \\ &=0.8 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A 200 mm long, stress free rod at room temperature is held between two immovable rigid walls. The temperature of the rod is uniformly raised by 250[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. If the Young's modulus and coefficient of thermal expansion are 200 GPa and [latex]1 \times 10^{-5}/C^{\circ}[/latex] , respectively, the magnitude of the longitudinal stress (in MPa) developed in the rod is _______
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] \begin{array}{c} l=200 \mathrm{mm} ; \quad \Delta T=250^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ; \quad \alpha=1 \times 10^{-5} /^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ E=200 \mathrm{GPa} ; \quad \sigma=? \\ \sigma=\alpha \Delta T E=10^{-5} \times 250 \times 200 \times 10^{3} \\ =500 \mathrm{MPa} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: 1.5 kg of water is in saturated liquid state at 2 bar ([latex]v_{f}= 0.001061 m^3/kg[/latex], [latex]u_{f}[/latex]=504.0 kJ/kg,  [latex]h_{f}[/latex]=505 kJ/kg). Heat is added in a constant pressure process till the temperature of water reaches 400[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C  (v=1.5493 [latex]m^3[/latex]/kg, u = 2967.0 kJ/kg, h = 3277.0 kJ/kg). The heat added (in kJ) in the process is  _______
raw_source.solution:
From the first law of thermodynamics
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta q &=d u+p d v \\ \delta q &=\left(u_{2}-u_{1}\right)+p\left(v_{2}-v_{1}\right) \\ \delta q &=(2967-504)+2 \times 10^{2} \\ &(1.5493-0.001061) \\ \delta q &=2463+309.6478 \\ &=2772.6478 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For 1.5kg of water
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=2772.6478 \times 1.5 \\ &=4158.97 \mathrm{kj} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively:
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=m\left(h_{2}-h_{1}\right) \\ &=1.5(3277-505) \\ &=4158 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider one dimensional steady state heat conduction across a wall (as shown in figure below) of thickness 30 mm and thermal conductivity 15 W/m.K. At x = 0, a constant heat flux, [latex]q''= 1\times 10^5 W/m^2[/latex] is applied. On the other side of the wall, heat is removed from the wall by convection with a fluid at 25[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and heat transfer coefficient of 250 [latex]W/m^2[/latex] K. The temperature (in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C), at x = 0 is _______
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta&=30 \mathrm{mm}=0.03 \mathrm{m} ; \quad k=15 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ q^{\prime \prime}&=1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} ; \quad T_{\infty}=25^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ h&=250 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Heat transfer due to convection from outside
surface per unit area:
[latex] \begin{aligned} q^{\prime \prime} &=\frac{Q}{A}=h\left(T_{2}-T_{\infty}\right) \\ 1 \times 10^{5} &=250\left(T_{2}-25\right) \\ \text{or}\qquad T_{2} &=425^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat transfer through wall per unit area,
[latex] \begin{aligned} q^{\prime \prime} &=\frac{k\left(T_{1}-T_{2}\right)}{\delta} \\ 1 \times 10^{5} &=\frac{15\left(T_{1}-425\right)}{0.03}\\ \text{or }\qquad T_{1}&=625^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Water flows through a pipe having an inner radius of 10 mm at the rate of 36 kg/hr at 25[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C.  The viscosity of water at 25[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C is 0.001 kg/m.s.  The Reynolds number of the flow is _______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Radius: }\quad r&=10 \mathrm{mm} \\ \therefore \text{Diameter: }d&=2 r=2 \times 10=20 \mathrm{mm}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ m &=36 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{hr}=\frac{36}{3600}=0.01 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ \mu &=0.001 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{ms} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Reynolds number: [latex]\text{Re}=\frac{\rho V d}{\mu}[/latex]
From continuity equation, [latex]m=\rho A V [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{or }\quad V&=\frac{m}{\rho A}=\frac{m}{\frac{\rho \pi d^{2}}{4}}=\frac{4 m}{\rho \pi d^{2}} \\ \therefore \quad \mathrm{Re}&=\frac{\rho d}{\mu} \times \frac{4 \mathrm{m}}{\rho \pi d^{2}}=\frac{4 \mathrm{m}}{\pi \mu \mathrm{d}}\\ &=\frac{4 \times 0.01}{3.14 \times 0.001 \times 0.02}=636.94 \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: For a fully developed flow of water in a pipe having diameter 10 cm, velocity 0.1 m/s and kinematic viscosity [latex]10^{-5}m^{2}/s[/latex] , the value of Darcy friction factor is _______
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} d&=10 \mathrm{cm} \\ V&=0.1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \mathrm{v}&=10^{-5} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Reynold's number,
[latex] \mathrm{Re}=\frac{V d}{v}=\frac{0.1 \times 0.1}{10^{-5}}=1000[/latex]
Friction factor
[latex] f=\frac{64}{\mathrm{Re}}=\frac{64}{1000}=0.064[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: In a simple concentric shaft-bearing arrangement, the lubricant flows in the 2 mm gap between the shaft and the bearing. The flow may be assumed to be a plane Couette flow with zero pressure gradient. The diameter of the shaft is 100 mm and its tangential speed is 10 m/s. The dynamic viscosity of the lubricant is 0.1 kg/m.s. The frictional resisting force (in newton) per 100 mm length of the bearing is  _______
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} d &=100 \mathrm{mm}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \\ L &=100 \mathrm{mm}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \\ u &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \mu &=0.1 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{ms} \\ d y &=2 \mathrm{mm}=2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \tau &=\mu \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{u}}{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{y}} \\ &=0.1 \times \frac{10}{2 \times 10^{-3}}=500 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text{Frictional area }&= \pi dL=3.14 \times0.1 \times 0.1\\ &=0.0314 \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Frictional resistance force,
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\tau \times \pi \mathrm{d} L \\ &=500 \times 0.0314=15.7 \mathrm{N} \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: The non-dimensional fluid temperature profile near the surface of a convectively cooled flat plate is given by [latex]\frac{T_W-T}{T_W-T_\infty }=a+b\frac{y}{L}+c\left ( \frac{y}{L} \right )^2[/latex], where y is measured perpendicular to the plate, [latex]L[/latex]  is the plate length, and a, b and c are arbitrary constants. [latex]T_{W}[/latex]  and [latex]T_{\infty}[/latex]  are wall and ambient temperatures, respectively. If the thermal conductivity of the fluid is [latex]k[/latex]   and the wall heat flux is [latex]q''[/latex], the Nusselt number [latex]N_u=\frac{q''}{T_W-T_\infty }\frac{L}{k}[/latex]  is  equal to
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} q^{\prime \prime} &=-\left.k \frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0} \\ &=h\left(T_{w}-T_{\infty}\right) \\ T_{w}-T &=\left(T_{w}-T_{\infty}\right)\left[a+\frac{b y}{L}+c\left(\frac{y}{L}\right)^{2}\right] \\ \frac{\partial T}{\partial y} & =\left(T_{w}-T_{\infty}\right)\left[\frac{b}{L}+\frac{2 c}{L^{2}} y\right] \\ -\left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0} &=\left(T_{w}-T_{\infty}\right) \frac{b}{L} \\ \text{or} \quad q^{\prime \prime}&=k\left(T_{w}-T_{\infty}\right) \frac{b}{L} \\ \therefore \quad N u &=\frac{q^{\prime \prime}}{T_{w}-T_{\infty}} \frac{L}{k}=b \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Heat Transfer in Flow Over Plates and Pipes

raw_source.text: In an air-standard Otto cycle, air is supplied at 0.1 MPa and 308 K. The ratio of the specific heats ([latex]\gamma[/latex] ) and the specific gas constant (R) of air are 1.4 and 288.8 J/kg.K, respectively. If the compression ratio is 8 and the maximum temperature in the cycle is 2660 K, the heat (in kJ/kg) supplied to the engine is _______
raw_source.solution:
Given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{1}&=0.1 \mathrm{MPa} ; \quad T_{1}=308 \mathrm{K} ; \quad \gamma=1.4 \\ R&=288.8 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} ; \quad r=8 \\ T_{s}&=2660 \mathrm{K} \\ &\begin{aligned} Q_{s}&=m c_{v}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right) \\ c_{v}&=\frac{R}{\gamma-1}=\frac{288.8}{0.4}=722 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}&=\left(\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}\right)^{\gamma-1}=(8)^{0.4}\\ T_{2} &=308 \times 8^{0.4}=707.6 \mathrm{K} \\ Q_{s} &=m c_{v} \Delta T \\ &=1 \times 722(2660-707.6) \\ &=1409.6 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A reversible heat engine receives 2 kJ of heat from a reservoir at 1000 K and a certain amount of heat from a reservoir at 800 K. It rejects 1 kJ of heat to a reservoir at 400 K. The network output (in kJ) of the cycle is
raw_source.solution:
For reversible heat engine,
[latex]\begin{aligned} (\Delta S)_{\text{ Reversible cycle }}&=0\\ \frac{Q_1}{T_1}+\frac{Q_2}{T_2}-\frac{Q_3}{T_3}&=0\\ \frac{2}{1000}+\frac{Q_2}{800}-\frac{1}{400}&=0\\ Q_2&=0.4 kJ\\ \text{From heat balance, }\\ Q_1+Q_2&=W+Q_3\\ 2+0.4&=W+1\\ W&=1.4 kJ \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Second Law, Carnot Cycle and Entropy

raw_source.text:
An ideal reheat Rankine cycle operates between the pressure limits of 10 kPa and 8 MPa, with reheat being done at 4 MPa. The temperature of steam at the inlets of both turbines is 500[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and the enthalpy of steam is 3185 kJ/kg at the exit of the high pressure turbine and 2247 kJ/kg at the exit of low pressure turbine. The enthalpy of water at the exit from the pump is 191 kJ/kg. Use the following table for relevant data.

Disregarding the pump work, the cycle efficiency (in percentage) is __________
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{2} &=10 \mathrm{kPa} ; \quad p_{1}=8 \mathrm{MPa} \\ p_{3} &=4 \mathrm{MPa} ; \quad h_{2}=3185 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{4} &=2247 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} ; \quad h_{1}=3399 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{3} &=3446 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} ; \quad h_{6}=191 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ w_{\mathrm{T}} &=\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)+\left(h_{3}-h_{4}\right) \\ q_{s} &=\left(h_{1}-h_{6}\right)+\left(h_{3}-h_{2}\right) \\ \therefore \quad w_{T} &=(3399-3185)+(3446-2247) \\ &=1413 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ q_{\mathrm{s}} &=(3399-191)+(3446-3185) \\ &=3469 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \eta &=\frac{w_{\mathrm{T}}}{q_{\mathrm{s}}}=\frac{1413}{3469}=0.4073 \\ &=40.73 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Jobs arrive at a facility at an average rate of 5 in an 8 hour shift. The arrival of the jobs follows Poisson distribution. The average service time of a job on the facility is 40 minutes. The service time follows exponential distribution. Idle time (in hours) at the facility per shift will be
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\lambda=\frac{5}{8} [/latex]
[latex] \mu=\frac{60}{40} \cdot \frac{3}{2} [/latex]
Probability of idleness [latex]=1-\frac{\lambda}{\mu} [/latex]
[latex] =1-\frac{5}{8} \times \frac{2}{3}=\frac{7}{12} [/latex]
Idle time (in hrs) per shift [latex]=\frac{7}{12} \times 8 [/latex]

[latex] \text{or } \quad \lambda^{2}-6 \lambda+5 \lambda-30+18=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or } \quad \lambda^{2}-\lambda-12=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{or } \lambda=\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+48}}{2}=\frac{1 \pm 7}{2}=4,-3 [/latex]
Corresponding to [latex] \lambda=4,[/latex] we have
[latex] \; [A-\lambda I] x=\left[\begin{array}{cc}-5-\lambda & 2 \\-9 & 6-\lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\y\end{array}\right] [/latex]
[latex] =0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{Or, } \left[\begin{array}{ll}-9 & 2 \\ -9 & 2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y\end{array}\right]=0[/latex]which gives only one independent equation,
[latex] -9 x+2 y=0 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \frac{x}{2}=\frac{y}{9}[/latex] gives eigen vector (2,9)
Corresponding to [latex] \lambda=-3, [/latex]
[latex] =\left[\begin{array}{ll}-2 & 2 \\-9 & 9\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\y \end{array}\right]=0[/latex]
which gives -x+y=0 (only one independent equation)
[latex] \therefore \quad \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y}{1} \quad [/latex] which gives (1,1)
So, the eigen vectors are [latex]\left\{\begin{array}{l}2 \\ 9\end{array}\right\} and \left\{\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1\end{array}\right\}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a flywheel whose mass M is distributed almost equally between a heavy, ring-like rim of radius R and a concentric disk-like feature of radius R/2. Other parts of the flywheel, such as spokes, etc, have negligible mass. The best approximation for [latex]\alpha[/latex], if the moment of inertia of the flywheel about its axis of rotation is expressed as [latex]\alpha MR^2[/latex], is _______
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} I &=\frac{M}{2}(R)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{M}{2}\right)\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{M R^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M}{2} \times \frac{R^{2}}{4} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{M R^{2}}{2}+\frac{M R^{2}}{16} \\ I&=\frac{9}{16} M R^{2}=\alpha M R^{2} \\ \alpha&=\frac{9}{16}=0.5625 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: What is the natural frequency of the spring mass system shown below? The contact between the block and the inclined plane is frictionless. The mass of the block is denoted by m and the spring constants are denoted by [latex]k_1 \; and \; k_2[/latex] as shown below.

raw_source.text: Maximum fluctuation of kinetic energy in an engine has been calculated to be 2600 J. Assuming that the engine runs at an average speed of 200 rpm, the polar mass moment of inertia (in kg.[latex]m^2[/latex]) of a flywheel to keep the speed fluctuation within [latex]\pm 0.5[/latex]% of the average speed is _______
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} \Delta E &=2600 \mathrm{J} \\ N_{\text {average }} &=200 \mathrm{rpm} \\ I &=? \\ C_{s} &=\pm 0.5 \% \\ &=2 \times \frac{0.5}{100}=0.01 \\ \Delta E &=I \omega^{2} C_{s} \\ 2600 &=I \times\left\{\frac{2 \pi}{60} \times 200\right\}^{2} \times 0.01 \\ 2600 &=I \times 438.6491 \times 0.01 \\ I &=\frac{2600}{4.3865}=592.73 \mathrm{kgm}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the two states of stress as shown in configurations I and II in the figure below. From the standpoint of distortion energy (von-Mises) criterion, which one of the following statements is true?

Simplified Von mises equation for general load
scenario is given by

Case-I[

[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{11} &=0 \\ \sigma_{22} &=\sigma \\ \sigma_{33} &=0 \\ \sigma_{12} &=0 \\ \sigma_{23} &=0 \\ \sigma_{31} &=\tau \\ \therefore \quad \sigma_{v} &=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \sigma^{2}+6 \tau^{2}\right)}=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+3 \tau^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A spherical balloon with a diameter of 10 m, shown in the figure below is used for advertisements. The balloon is filled with helium ([latex]R_{He}=2.08 kJ/kg.K[/latex] ) at ambient conditions of 15[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and 100 kPa. Step-I: Mass of balloon

raw_source.text: a hemispherical furnace of 1m radius has the inner surface (emissivity, [latex]\varepsilon =1[/latex]  ) of its roof maintained at 800K, while its floor ([latex]\varepsilon =0.5[/latex] ) is kept at 600K. Stefan-Boltzmann constant is [latex]5.668\times 10^{-8}W/m^{2}.K^{4}[/latex]. The net radiative heat transfer (in kW ) from the roof to the floor is _______
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} r&=1 \mathrm{m} \\ \epsilon_{1} &=1 \\ T_{1} &=800 \mathrm{K} \\ \epsilon_{2} &=0.5 \\ T_{2} &=600 \mathrm{K} \\ \sigma &=5.668 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}^{4} \\ \left(F_{9}\right)_{1-2} &=\frac{1}{\frac{1-\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon_{1}}+\frac{1}{F_{12}}+\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}\left(\frac{1-\epsilon_{1}}{\epsilon_{2}}\right)} \\ F_{21} &=1 \\ A_{1} F_{12} &=A_{2} F_{21}\\ \Rightarrow \quad F_{12}&=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}}=\frac{\pi r^{2}}{2 \pi r^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \therefore \quad F&=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1-1}{1}\right)+2+2\left(\frac{1-0.5}{0.5}\right)} \\ \quad=\frac{1}{4}&=0.25 \\ \therefore \quad Q_{1-2} &=\sigma A\left(F_{9}\right)_{1-2}\left[T_{1}^{4}-T_{2}^{4}\right] \\ Q_{12} &=5.668 \times 2 \times \pi \times(1)^{2} \\ & \times 0.25\left(800^{4}-600^{4}\right) \times 10^{-8} \\ Q_{12} &=24916.528 \mathrm{W}=24.916 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Water flows through a 10 mm diameter and 250 m long smooth pipe at an average velocity of  0.1 m/s. Pressure drop in the pipe,
