raw_source.text: The value of [latex]\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}(\frac{-\sin x}{2\sin x+ x \cos x})[/latex]  is ________
raw_source.solution:
Step 1: Identify the form
[latex] -\lim_{x \to 0} \left( \frac{-\sin x}{2\sin x + x\cos x} \right) [/latex]
Substituting [latex]x = 0[/latex]:
[latex] \frac{0}{0} [/latex]
Hence, the limit is an indeterminate form.

Step 2: Apply L'Hôpital's Rule
Differentiate numerator and denominator with respect to [latex]x[/latex]
[latex] \frac{d}{dx}(-\sin x) = -\cos x [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d}{dx}(2\sin x + x\cos x) = 2\cos x + \cos x - x\sin x = 3\cos x - x\sin x [/latex]

Step 3: Substitute and evaluate the limit
[latex] \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{-\cos x}{3\cos x - x\sin x} [/latex]
Substituting [latex]x = 0[/latex]:
[latex] = \frac{-\cos(0)}{3\cos(0) - 0\cdot\sin(0)} [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{-1}{3} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The value of [latex] \int_{c} [(3x-8y^{2})dx + (4y-6xy)dy],[/latex]  (where C is the boundary of the region bounded by x = 0,  y = 0 and x+y = 1) is ________

boundary of region bounded by x=0, y=1 , and
z+y=1
Using Green's theorem
[latex] I=\oint_{c}(P d x+Q d y)=\oint_{R} \oint\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) d x d y [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Here,} P &=3 x-8 y^{2} \\ Q &=4 y-6 x y \\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} &=-6 y \\ \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} &=-16 y \\ I &=\iint(-6 y-(-16 y)) d x d y \\ I &=\iint 10 y d x d y \\ I &=10 \int_{0}^{1} d x \int_{0}^{1-x} \frac{y^{2}}{2} \\ I &=5 \int_{0}^{1} d x(1-x)^{2} \\ I &=5 \int_{0}^{1}(1-x)^{2} \cdot d x \\ I &=1.6666 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: One side of a wall is maintained at 400 K and the other at 300 K. The rate of heat transfer through the wall is 1000 W and the surrounding temperature is 25[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. Assuming no generation of heat within the wall, the irreversibility (in W) due to heat transfer through the wall is ________
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{1}=400 \mathrm{K} ; & T_{2}=300 \mathrm{K} ; Q=1000 \mathrm{W} \\ T_{0} &=25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(25+273) \mathrm{K} \\ &=298 \mathrm{K} \\ \Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}} &=-\frac{Q}{T_{1}}+\frac{Q}{T_{2}} \\ &=-\frac{1000}{400}+\frac{1000}{300} \\ &=-2.5+3.333=0.833 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{K}\\ & Irreversibility,\\ I &=T_{0} \Delta S_{\text {uni }} \\ &=T_{0}\left(\Delta S_{\text {sys }}+\Delta S_{\text {surr }}\right) \\ &=298(0.833+0) \qquad \because \Delta S_{\text {surf }}=0 \\ &=248.23 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A brick wall [latex](k= 0.9\frac{W}{m.K})[/latex] of thickness 0.18m separate the warm air in a room from the cold ambient air. On a particular winter day, the outside air temperature is -5[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C and the room needs to be maintained at 27[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C. raw_source.solution:

[latex] \begin{aligned} k&=0.9 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ \delta&=0.18 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Heat loss: }Q&=\frac{T_{1}-T_{0}}{\frac{\delta}{\mathrm{k} A}+\frac{1}{h_{0} A}} \\ \frac{Q}{A} &=\frac{T_{1}-T_{0}}{\frac{\delta}{k}+\frac{1}{h_{0}}} \\ q&=\frac{27-(-5)}{0.18+\frac{1}{20}} \quad \because q=\frac{Q}{A} \\ &=\frac{32}{0.2+0.05} = \frac{32}{0.25}\\ &=128 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A mixture of ideal gases has the following composition by mass:

If the universal gas constant is 8314 J/kmol-K, the characteristic gas constant of the mixture (in J/kg-K) is ________
raw_source.solution:
Equation state for [latex]N_{2}, [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} p_{N_{2}} V&=m_{N_{2}} R_{N_{2}} T\\ \text{or}\quad \frac{p_{N_{2}} V}{T}&=m_{N_{2}} R_{N_{2}} \\ \text { where }\quad R_{N_{2}}&=\frac{\bar{R}}{M_{N_{2}}}\\ \therefore \quad \frac{p_{N_{2}} V}{T}&=\frac{m_{N_{2}} \bar{R}}{M_{N_{2}}} \qquad\cdots(i)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly for [latex]\mathrm{O}_{2}[/latex] and [latex] \mathrm{CO}_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{O_{2}} V}{T} &=\frac{m_{O_{2}} \bar{R}}{M_{O_{2}}} \qquad\cdots(ii)\\ \text { and } \frac{p_{C O_{2}} V}{T} &=\frac{m_{C O_{2}} \bar{R}}{M_{C O_{2}}}\qquad\cdots(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Adding Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \frac{V}{T}\left(p_{N_{2}}+p_{O_{2}}+p_{C O_{2}}\right)=\frac{m_{N_{2}} \bar{R}}{M_{N_{2}}}+\frac{m_{O_{2}} \bar{R}}{M_{O_{2}}}+\frac{m_{C O_{2}} \bar{R}}{M_{C O_{2}}} \\ \frac{V}{T} p=\left(\frac{m_{N_{2}}}{M_{N_{2}}}+\frac{m_{O_{2}}}{M_{O_{2}}}+\frac{m_{C O_{2}}}{M_{C O_{2}}}\right) \bar{R} \cdots(iv) \end{array}[/latex]
where [latex]p=p_{N_{2}}+p_{O_{2}}+p_{C O_{2}}[/latex]
pressure of mixture
Equation of state for mixture of ideal gas
[latex] p V=m R T[/latex]
[latex] \text{or}\frac{p V}{T}=m R[/latex]
Equating Eqs. (iv) and (v), we get

Gauss-Seidel method is used to solve the following equations (as per the given order):
[latex]x_{1}+2x_{2}+3x_{3}=5[/latex]
[latex]2x_{1}+3x_{2}+x_{3}=1[/latex]
[latex]3x_{1}+2x_{2}+x_{3}=3[/latex]
Assuming initial guess as [latex]x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=0[/latex] , the value of [latex]x_{3}[/latex] after the first iteration is __________
raw_source.solution:
The equations are
[latex] x_{1}+2 x_{2}+3 x_{3}=5 \quad \ldots(3)[/latex]
[latex] 2 x_{1}+3 x_{2}+x_{3}=1 \quad \ldots(2)[/latex]
[latex] 3 x_{1}+2 x_{2}+x_{3}=3 \quad \ldots(1)[/latex]
By poveting we can write
[latex] \begin{aligned} 3 x_{1}+2 x_{2}+x_{3} &=3 \\ 2 x_{1}+3 x_{2}+x_{3} &=1 \\ x_{1} &=\frac{3-2 x_{2}-x_{3}}{3} \quad \ldots(1)\\ x_{2} &=\frac{1-2 x_{1}-x_{3}}{3} \quad \ldots(2)\\ x_{1}+2 x_{2}+3 x_{3} &=5 \\ x_{3} &=\frac{5-x_{1}-2 x_{2}}{3} \quad \ldots(3) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Put [latex] x_{2}=0 \quad x_{3}=0 [/latex] in equation (1)
[latex] x_{1}=1[/latex]
Put [latex]x_{1}=1 \quad x_{3}=0 [/latex] in equation (3)
[latex] x_{2}=-0.333 [/latex]
Put [latex]x_{1}=1 \quad x_{2}=-0.333 [/latex] in equation [latex] (3) [/latex]
[latex] x_{3}=1.555[/latex]

raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} R&=100\;m \\ v&=20\;m/sec \\ \omega _p &=\frac{v}{R} \\ &= 0.2\; rad/sec\\ \omega _s &=100\; rad/sec \\ I&= 10\; Kg-m^2\\ &\text{Gyroscopic moment,}\\ I\omega _s\omega _p &=10 \times 0.2 \times 100\; N-m\\ &=200\; N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single degree of freedom spring mass system with viscous damping has a spring constant of 10 kN/m. The system is excited by a sinusoidal force of amplitude 100 N. If the damping factor(ratio) is 0.25, the amplitude of steady state oscillation at resonance is ________mm.
raw_source.solution:
Forcing function [latex]=F_{0} \sin \omega t [/latex]
Given, [latex]F_{0}=100 \mathrm{N} [/latex]
Damping factor,
[latex] \xi=0.25[/latex]
Spring constant
[latex] \begin{aligned} k&=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}=10 \times 1000=10000 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m} \\ A&=\frac{F_{0} / \mathrm{k}}{\sqrt{\left\{1-\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}\right\}^{2}+\left(2 \xi \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At resonance
[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega &=\omega_{n} \\ \therefore \quad A &=\frac{100}{10000}=\frac{0.01}{2 \xi}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ &=20 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The instantaneous stream-wise velocity of a turbulent flow is given as follows:
[latex]u( x,y,z,t )=\bar{u}(x,y,z)+{u}'(x,y,z,t)[/latex]
The time-average of the fluctuating velocity [latex]{u}'(x,y,z,t)[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Instantaneous velocity : [latex] u=\bar{u}+u^{\prime} [/latex]
The time-average of the fluctuating velocity
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{u}^{\prime} &=\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} u^{\prime} d t \\ &=\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T}(u-\bar{u}) d t \\ &=\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} u d T-\frac{1}{T} \bar{u} \int_{0}^{T} d t=\bar{u}-\frac{\bar{U}}{T} T \\ &=\bar{u}-\bar{u}=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Heat and work are boundary phenomenon and depend upon the path followed between initial and final states. Both heat and work are inexact differential since

raw_source.text: Propane (C3H8) is burned in an oxygen atmosphere with 10% deficit oxygen with respect to the stoichiometric requirement. Assuming no hydrocarbons in the products, the volume percentage of CO in the products is __________
raw_source.solution:
For stoichiometric burning (i.e., chemically correct),
number of moles of [latex]\mathrm{O}_{2}[/latex] required =5.
As it si burnt with 10 % deficient \mathrm{O}_{2} , it will generate CO.
That is, the new equation is
[latex] \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+0.9 \times 5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \alpha \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\beta \mathrm{CO}+\gamma \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}[/latex]
Balancing carbon atoms, we get
[latex] 3=\alpha+\beta \quad \cdots(i)[/latex]
Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 8&=2 \gamma\\ \text{or }\quad \gamma&=4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Balancing oxygen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0.9 \times 10 &=2 \alpha+\beta+\gamma \\ 9 &=2 \alpha+\beta+4 \\ 5 &=2 \alpha+\beta\quad \cdots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Eq. (ii) - Eq. (i), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2&=\alpha\\ \text{or }\quad \alpha&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+\mathrm{aO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{bCO}_{2}+\mathrm{cH}_{2} \mathrm{O}[/latex]
Balancing carbon atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 3&=b\\ \text{or } \quad b&=3\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 8&=2 c\\ \text{or}\quad c&=4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Balancing oxygen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 a &=2 b+c \\ 2 a &=2 \times 3+4=10 \\ a &=5 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting [latex]\alpha=2[/latex] in Eq. (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \quad 5=2 \times 2 \times \beta \\ \text { or } \quad \beta=1 \\ \therefore \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+4.5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{CO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \end{array}[/latex]
The volume percentage of CO in the product
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}\right) \times 100 \\ =\left(\frac{1}{2+1+4}\right) \times 100 \\ =14.28 \% \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider two hydraulic turbines having identical specific speed and effective head at the inlet. If the speed ratio (N1/N2) of the two turbines is 2, then the respective power ratio (P1/P2) is _____________
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{s 1} &=N_{s 2} \\ H_{1} &=H_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}} &=2 \end{aligned}\\ \text{We know that specific speed of the turbine,}\\ \begin{aligned} N_{s}&=\frac{N \sqrt{P}}{H^{5 / 4}}\\ \left(N_{s}\right)_{1} &=\left(N_{s}\right)_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1} \sqrt{P_{1}}}{H_{1}^{5 / 4}} &=\frac{N_{2} \sqrt{P_{2}}}{H_{2}^{5 / 4}} \\ N_{1} \sqrt{P_{1}} &=N_{2} \sqrt{P_{2}} \qquad\therefore H_{1}= h_{2} \\ \text{or}\quad\sqrt{\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}} &=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\\ \text{or}\quad\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} &=\left(\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\right)^{2} \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Under optimal conditions of the process the temperatures experienced by a copper work piece in fusion welding, brazing and soldering are such that
raw_source.solution:
In welding, the two metals (or thermoplastic) must be similar. For example, copper cannot be welded to steel. Welding uses high temperatures to melt and join two metal parts. A filler metal is often used as well. When properly done, the finished weld is as strong as the surrounding metal.

Brazing joins two metals by heating and melting a filler (alloy) that bonds to the two pieces of metal and joins them. The filler obviously must have a melting temperature below that of the metal pieces. Brazing can join dissimilar metals such as aluminum, silver, copper, gold, and nickel.

Soldering is a low-temperature analog to brazing. By the American Welding Society’s definition, soldering takes place with fillers (also known as solders) that melt at below [latex]840^{\circ}F (450^{\circ}C)[/latex]. Metals that can be soldered include gold, silver, copper, brass, and iron. The filler, called solder, melts. When it solidifies, it is bonded to the metal parts and joins them. The bond is not as strong as brazed joint or welded one. Solder was once made mainly of lead, but environmental concerns are pushing industry to lead-free alternatives.

raw_source.text:
Gauss-Seidel method is used to solve the following equations (as per the given order):
[latex]x_{1}+2x_{2}+3x_{3}=5[/latex]
[latex]2x_{1}+3x_{2}+x_{3}=1[/latex]
[latex]3x_{1}+2x_{2}+x_{3}=3[/latex]
Assuming initial guess as [latex]x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=0[/latex] , the value of [latex]x_{3}[/latex] after the first iteration is __________
raw_source.solution:
We are given:
Initial guess: [latex] x_1^{(0)} = 0, , x_2^{(0)} = 0, , x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex].

We rewrite the equations for Gauss-Seidel iteration:
From [latex] x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 5 [/latex]:
[latex] x_1 = 5 - 2x_2 - 3x_3 [/latex]


From [latex] 2x_1 + 3x_2 + x_3 = 1 [/latex]:
[latex] x_2 = \frac{1 - 2x_1 - x_3}{3} [/latex]

From [latex] 3x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 3 [/latex]:
[latex] x_3 = 3 - 3x_1 - 2x_2 [/latex]

First Iteration:
Step 1:
Compute [latex] x_1^{(1)} [/latex]
Using [latex] x_2^{(0)} = 0 [/latex], [latex] x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]:
[latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 - 2(0) - 3(0) = 5 [/latex]

Step 2: Compute [latex] x_2^{(1)} [/latex]
Using [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 [/latex], [latex] x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]:
[latex] x_2^{(1)} = \frac{1 - 2(5) - 0}{3} = \frac{1 - 10}{3} = \frac{-9}{3} = -3 [/latex]

Step 3: Compute [latex] x_3^{(1)} [/latex]
Using [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 [/latex], [latex] x_2^{(1)} = -3 [/latex]:
[latex] x_3^{(1)} = 3 - 3(5) - 2(-3) = 3 - 15 + 6 = -6 [/latex]

Final Answer: After the first iteration, [latex] x_3 = -6 [/latex].

A block of mass m rests on an inclined plane and is attached by a string to the wall as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction between the plane and the block is 0.25. The string can withstand a maximum force of 20 N. The maximum value of the mass (m) for which the string will not break and the block will be in static equilibrium is ____________ kg.
Take [latex]\cos\theta =0.8[/latex] and [latex]\sin\theta =0.6[/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity [latex]g=10m/s^{2}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]M_{\text {static }} =0.25 [/latex]
[latex] F_{max} =20 \mathrm{N}[/latex]


Balancing force along the inclined plane
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad T+f&=m g \sin \theta \\ f &=\mu \mathrm{N} \\ N &=m g \cos \theta \end{aligned} [/latex]
(balancing forces perpendicular to the inclined plane)
[latex] 20+0.25 \times m g \cos \theta=m g \sin \theta [/latex]
[latex] 20+0.25 \times m \times 10 \times 0.8=m \times 10 \times 0.6 [/latex]
[latex] 20=4 m [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad m=5 \mathrm{kg}[/latex]

A simply-supported beam of length 3L is subjected to the loading shown in the figure.

It is given that P = 1 N, L = 1 m and Young's modulus E = 200 GPa. The cross-section is a square with dimension 10 mm x 10 mm. The bending stress (in Pa) at the point A located at the top surface of the beam at a distance of 1.5L from the left end is _____________
(Indicate compressive stress by a negative sign and tensile stress by a positive sign.)

raw_source.text: A slider crank mechanism with crank radius 200 mm and connecting rod length 800 mm is shown. The crank is rotating at 600 rpm in the counterclockwise direction. In the configuration shown, the crank makes an angle of [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex] with the sliding direction of the slider, and a force of 5 kN is acting on the slider. Neglecting the inertia forces, the turning moment on the crank (in kN-m) is __________
raw_source.solution:
Turning moment on crankshaft,
[latex] \begin{aligned} T &=F_{T} \times r=\frac{F}{\cos \beta} \times \cos \beta \times r \\ &=F \times r=5 \times 0.2=1 \mathrm{kNm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively


[latex] \begin{aligned} \sin \beta &=\frac{\text { Perpendicular }}{\text { Hypotenuse }} \\ \sin \beta &=\frac{200}{800}=\frac{1}{4}=0.25 \\ \beta &=\sin ^{-1} 0.25=14.478^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Turning moment on crankshaft,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} T=F_{t} r=\frac{F}{\cos \beta} \sin (\theta+\beta) \times r \\ =\frac{5}{\cos 14.478} \sin \left[90^{\circ}+14.478^{\circ}\right] \times 0.2 \\ =1 \mathrm{kNm} \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In the gear train shown, gear 3 is carried on arm 5. Gear 3 meshes with gear 2 and gear 4. The number of teeth on gear 2, 3, and 4 are 60, 20, and 100, respectively. If gear 2 is fixed and gear 4 rotates with an angular velocity of 100 rpm in the counterclockwise direction, the angular speed of arm 5 (in rpm) is

Given : Gear 2 is fixed
[latex] \therefore \quad N+y=0 \qquad [\therefore N=-y][/latex]
Gear 4 rotates 100 rpm is counter clockwise.
[latex] \begin{aligned} -\frac{N \times 60}{100}+y &=-100 \\ +y \times 0.6+y &=-100 \\ y &=\frac{-100}{1.6}=-62.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence angular speed of arm is 62.5
(counterclockwise).

raw_source.text:
A solid disc with radius a is connected to a spring at a point d above the center of the disc. The other end of the spring is fixed to the vertical wall. The disc is free to roll without slipping on the ground. The mass of the disc is M and the spring constant is K. The polar moment of inertia for the disc about its centre is [latex]J=Ma^{2}/2[/latex]

The natural frequency of this system in rad/s is given by
raw_source.solution:
Total energy of system
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M \times\left(a \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times \\ \qquad \{(a+d) \theta\}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M a^{2}}{2} \times\left(\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let}\qquad \frac{d \theta}{d t}=\dot{\theta} \\ E=\frac{1}{2} M a^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \dot{\theta}^{2} \end{array}[/latex]
since energy of system remains concerned with
respect to time.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t}&=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t}&=\frac{M a^{2}}{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \\ & \qquad \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \cdot 2 \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]0=M a^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{\lt a^{2}}{2} \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex]\dot{\theta} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0&=M a^{2} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta \\ 0&=\left(M a^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \\ 0&=\frac{3}{2} M a^{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \end{aligned}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex] \frac{3}{2} m a^{2} [/latex]
[latex] 0=\ddot{\theta}+\frac{K(a+d)^{2}}{\frac{3 M a^{2}}{2}} \theta[/latex]
[latex] \ddot{\theta}+\omega_{n}^{2} \theta=0[/latex]
Compairing above two equation
[latex] \omega_{n}^{2}=\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}} ; \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}}}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The principal stresses at a point inside a solid object are [latex]\sigma _{1}=100[/latex]  Mpa, [latex]\sigma _{2}=100[/latex] MPa and [latex]\sigma _{3}=0[/latex] Mpa.  The yield strength of the material is 200 MPa. The factor of safety calculated using Tresca (maximum shear stress) theory is [latex]n_{T}[/latex] and the factor of safety calculated using von Mises (maximum distortional energy) theory is [latex]n_{V}[/latex]. Which one of the following relations is TRUE?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}=100 \mathrm{MPa}, \sigma_{2}=100 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{3}=0 \\ \sigma_{y}=200 \mathrm{MPa} \end{array}[/latex]
According to Tresca theory
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tau_{\max } & \leq \frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 F O S} \\ \tau_{\max } &=\frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 n_{T}} \\ \text{now}\quad \tau_{\max _{\mathrm{abs}}} &=\frac{\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}}{2}=50 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \therefore \quad 50 &=\frac{200}{2 n_{T}}\\ \therefore \quad n_{T}&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
According to Von-Mises theory
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}-\sigma_{1} \sigma_{2} \leq\left(\frac{\sigma_{y}}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ 100^{2}+100^{2}-100 \times 100 \leq\left(\frac{200}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ \therefore \quad 100=\frac{200}{n_{v}}\\ \text{or}\quad n_{v}=2 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An inverted U-tube manometer is used to measure the pressure difference between two pipes A and B, as shown in the figure. Pipe A is carrying oil (specific gravity = 0.8) and pipe B is carrying water. The densities of air and water are 1.16kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex] and 1000kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex], respectively. The pressure difference between pipes A and B is __________kPa.
Acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/[latex]s^{2}[/latex] .
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Specific gravity of oil,
[latex] s^{oil} = 0.8[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \rho_{\mathrm{oil}}=0.8 \times 1000=800 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
Density of air: [latex]\rho_{\text {air }}=1.16 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Density of water,
[latex] \rho_{\text {water }}=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity,
[latex] \begin{aligned} g &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \\ h_{1} &=80 \mathrm{mm}=0.08 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{2} &=200 \mathrm{mm}=0.2 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{3} &=100 \mathrm{mm}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Pressure at section 1 on left limb = Pressure at
section 1 on right limb
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{A}-\rho_{\text {oil }} g h_{2}-\rho_{\text {air }} g h_{1}&=p_{B}-\rho_{\text {water }} g\left(h_{1}+h_{2}+h_{3})\right. \\ p_{A}-800 \times 10 \times 0.2&-1.16 \times 10 \times 0.08 =p_{B}-\\ &1000 \times 10(0.08+0.2+0.1) \\ p_{A}-1600-0.928&=p_{B}-3800\\ p_{A}-p_{B} &=-2199.07 \mathrm{Pa} \\ &=-2.199 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Oil (kinematic viscosity, [latex]v_{oil}=1.0\times 10^{-5}m^{2}/s[/latex] ) flows through a pipe of 0.5 m diameter with a velocity of 10 m/s. Water (kinematic viscosity,[latex]v_{w}=0.89\times 10^{-6}m^{2}/s[/latex] ) is flowing through a model
pipe of diameter 20 mm. For satisfying the dynamic similarity, the velocity of water (in m/s)
is __________
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
For prototype
[latex] \begin{aligned} v_{p}&=1.0 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ d_{p}&=0.5 \mathrm{m} \\ V_{p}&=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\\ \text{For model}\\ v_{m}&=0.89 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ d_{m}&=20 \mathrm{mm}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ V_{m}&=? \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that
Reynolds number,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Re &=\frac{V d}{v} \\ (R e)_{m} &=(R e)_{p} \\ \frac{V_{m} d_{m}}{v_{m}} &=\frac{V_{p} d_{p}}{v_{p}} \\ \frac{V_{m} \times 0.02}{0.89 \times 10^{-6}} &=\frac{10 \times 0.5}{1.0 \times 10^{-5}} \\ \text{or }\quad V_{m} &=22.25 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
or The velocity of water is [latex]22.25 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text:
A steady laminar boundary layer is formed over a flat plate as shown in the figure. The free stream velocity of the fluid is [latex]U_{0}[/latex]. The velocity profile at the inlet a-b is uniform, while that at a downstream location c-d is given by [latex]u=U_{0}\left [ 2( \frac{y}{\delta }) -(\frac{y}\delta {})^{2}\right ][/latex] .

The ratio of the mass flow rate, [latex]\dot{m}_{bd}[/latex] leaving through the horizontal section b-d to that entering through the vertical section a-b is ___________
raw_source.solution:
[latex] U_{0}= [/latex] Velocity of free stream
d= Boundary layer thickness at section c-d
b= Width of the plate
Velocity profile,
[latex] u=U_{0}\left[2\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right][/latex]
Mass flow rate through section a-b,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{m}_{\mathrm{ab}} &=\rho A U_{0} \\ &=\rho b \delta U_{0} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Mass flow rate through section c-d
[latex] \dot{m}_{c d}=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b d y U[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b U_{0}\left[2 \frac{y}{\delta}-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right] d y \\ m_{c d} &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{2 y^{2}}{2 \delta}-\frac{y^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]_{0}^{\delta}\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta}-\frac{\delta^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\delta-\frac{\delta}{3}\right] \\ &=\rho b U_{0} \times \frac{2}{3} \delta \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \rho b \delta U_{0}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Mass flow rate through section b-d,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{m_{bd}} &=\dot{m_{ad}}- \dot{m_{cd}} \\ &= \rho b\delta U_0-\frac{2}{3}\rho b\delta U_0\\ &= \frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3}\\ \frac{\dot{m_{bd}}}{\dot{m_{ab}}}&=\frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3 \times \rho b\delta U_0}=\frac{1}{3}=0.333 \end{aligned}[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: A steel ball of 10 mm diameter at 1000 K is required to be cooled to 350 K by immersing it in a water environment at 300 K. The convective heat transfer coefficient is 1000 [latex]W/m^{2}-K[/latex]  Thermal conductivity of steel is 40 W/m-K. The time constant for the cooling process [latex]\tau[/latex]  is 16 s. The time required (in s) to reach the final temperature is __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Diameter of ball } &=10 \mathrm{mm} \\ T_{\text {initial }} &=1000 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{\text {final }} &=350 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{\infty} &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ h &=1000 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \\ k &=40 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ \text { Time constant } &=16 \mathrm{s} \\ \text { Time required } &=t \mathrm{s} \\ \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}} &=e^{-\frac{h A t}{\rho v c}} \\ &=16 \mathrm{second} \\ \text { But } \quad \frac{\rho v c}{h A} &=\text { Time constant } \\ \frac{350-300}{1000-300} &=e^{-\frac{1}{16}} \times t \\ 0.07143 &=e^{-t/ 16} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex] \log _{e} [/latex] both sides, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \log _{e} 0.07143 &=\frac{-t}{16} \log _{e} e & &\left(\because \log _{e} e=1\right) \\ -2.639 &= \frac{-t}{16} \\ \text{or}\quad t &=42.23 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
An infinitely long furnace of 0.5 m x 0. 4 m cross-section is shown in the figure below. Consider all surfaces of the furnace to be black. The top and bottom walls are maintained at temperature [latex]T_{1}=T_{3}=927^{\circ}C[/latex] while the side walls are at temperature [latex]T_{2}=T_{4}=527^{\circ}C[/latex] . The view factor, [latex]F_{1-2}[/latex] is 0.26. The net radiation heat loss or gain on side 1 is_________ W/m.
Stefan-Boltzmann constant = [latex]5.67\times10 ^{-8}W/m^{2}-k^{4}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given: } F_{12}&=0.26 \\ F_{12}=F_{14}&=0.26 \qquad [symmetry]\\ \text{Given}\quad \sigma&=5.67 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}^{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
side (1) and (3) will not exchange and heat being at same temp.
side (2) and (4) will not exchange any heat being at same temp.
Hence side (1) and side (2) and side (1) and side
(4) will exchange heat
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{1-2} &=A_{1} F_{12} \sigma\left[T_{1}^{4}-T_{2}^{4}\right] \\ &=0.5 \times 0.26 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} x \\ &=12265.34 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m} \\ Q_{1-4} &=0.5 \times 0.26 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{x} \\ &=12265.34 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m} \\ Q_{\text {net }} &=Q_{1-2}+Q_{1-4}=12265.34+\\ &=24530.68 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A fluid (Prandtl number, Pr = 1) at 500 K flows over a flat plate of 1.5 m length, maintained at 300 K. The velocity of the fluid is 10 m/s. Assuming kinematic viscosity, v=30 [latex]\times 10^{-6}m^{2}/s[/latex],  the thermal boundary layer thickness (in mm) at 0.5 m from the leading edge is __________
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} P r &=1 \\ T_{\infty} &=500 \mathrm{K} \\ \text { Length } &=1.5 \mathrm{m} \\ T_{\text {plate }} &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ U_{\infty} &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ v &=30 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thermal boundary layer at [latex]0.5 \mathrm{m}[/latex] from leadra edge [latex] =\delta_{t} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Re}_{x=0.5}=\frac{U x}{v}=\frac{10 \times 0.5}{30 \times 10^{-6}}=166,666.67 [/latex]
since [latex] \text{Re}_{x=0.5} \lt 5 \times 10^{5}[/latex]. Hence flow is laminar
[latex] \begin{aligned}\therefore \quad \delta &=\frac{5 x}{\sqrt{\text{Re}_{x}}} \\ &=\frac{5 \times 0.5}{\sqrt{166,666.67}} \\ &=6.1237 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \frac{\delta_{t}}{\delta} &=\left(P_{f}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ \delta_{t} &=(1)^{1 / 3} \times \delta \\ &=1 \times 6.1237 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ &=6.1237 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For water at [latex]25^{\circ}C[/latex] , [latex]dp_{s}/dT_{s}=0.189 KPa/K[/latex]  ([latex]p_{s}[/latex]   is the saturation pressure in kPa and [latex]T_{s}[/latex]  is the saturation temperature in K) and the specific volume of dry saturated vapour is 43.38  [latex]m^{3}[/latex] /kg. Assume that the specific volume of liquid is negligible in comparison with that of vapour. Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, an estimate of the enthalpy of evaporation of water at [latex]25^{\circ}C[/latex]  (in kJ/kg) is __________
raw_source.solution:
At [latex]25^{\circ}C, \frac{dp_s}{dT_s}=0.189kPa/K[/latex]
Specific volume of saturated vapour,
[latex]v_s=43.38 m^3/kg[/latex]
From clausis-clapeyron equation neglecting specific volume of liquid
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dp_s}{dT_s}&=\frac{h_{fg}}{T_s \times v_s}\\ h_{fg}&=\text{Enthalpy of vapourisation}\\ 0.189&=\frac{h_{fg}}{(25+273) \times 43.38}\\ \therefore \;\; h_{fg}&=2443.248\; kJ/kg \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: An ideal gas undergoes a reversible process in which the pressure varies linearly with volume. The conditions at the start (subscript 1) and at the end (subscript 2) of the process with usual notation are: [latex]p_{1}[/latex]  = 100 kPa, [latex]V_{1}[/latex]  =0.2 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]  and [latex]p_{2}[/latex]  =200 kPa , [latex]v_{2}[/latex] = 0.1 [latex]m^{3}[/latex]  and the gas constant, R = 0.275 kJ/kg-K. The magnitude of the work required for the process (in kJ) is ________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} p_{1}=100 \mathrm{kPa}, v_{1}=0.2 \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ p_{2}=200 \mathrm{kPa}, v_{2}=0.1 \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ R=0.275 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ p \propto V \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] p-V diagram will be a straight line

Work done is equal to area under p-V diagram,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \text { Work } &=\frac{1}{2}(100+200) \times(0.2-0.1) \\ &=15 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The work is done on the gas, since the process is compression.
since only magnitude is asked hence final answer is without -ve sign.

raw_source.text:
In a steam power plant operating on an ideal Rankine cycle, superheated steam enters the turbine at 3 MPa and [latex]350^{\circ}C[/latex] .The condenser pressure is 75 kPa. The thermal efficiency of the cycle is ________ percent.
Given data:
For saturated liquid, at P = 75 kPa. [latex]h_{f}=384.39[/latex] kJ/kg, [latex]v_{f}=0.001037 m^{3}/kg[/latex] , [latex]s_{f}=1.213[/latex] kJ/kg-K
At 75 kPa, [latex]h_{fg}[/latex] =2278.6 kJ/kg,[latex]s_{fg}[/latex] =6.2434 kJ/kg-K
At P = 3 MPa and T = [latex]350^{\circ}C[/latex] (superheated steam), h = 3115.3kJ/kg, s = 6.7428 kJ/kg-K
raw_source.solution:
Calculating dryness fraction at point 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{1} &=S_{2} \\ 6.7248 &=s_{f}+x_{2} s_{f g} \\ &=1.213+x_{2} \times 6.2434 \\ x_{2} &=\frac{6.7428-1.213}{6.2434}\\ &=0.8857 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Calculating enthalpy at point 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{2} &=h_{f}+x_{2} h_{f g} \\ &=384.39+0.8857 \times 2278.6 \\ &=2402.546 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text { Given: } \quad h_{1} &=3115.3 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{4} &=h_{3}+v d P \\ &=384.39+0.001037 \times[3000-75] \\ &=387.423 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text { Pump work } &=v d P \\ &=0.001037 \times[3000-75] \\ &=3.033 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ w_{\text {net }} &=w_{T}-w_{P}=\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)-3.033 \\ &=(3115.3-2402.546)-3.033 \\ &=709.721 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text{Heat input }&=h_{1}-h_{4}\\ &=3115.3-387.423 \\ &=2727.877 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text{Efficiency of cycle }&=\frac{\text { Work delivered }}{\text { Heat input }} \\ & \frac{709.721}{2727877} \\ &=0.2601=26.01 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

A hypothetical engineering stress-strain curve shown in the figure has three straight lines PQ, QR, RS with coordinates P(0,0), Q(0.2,100), R(0.6,140) and S(0.8,130). 'Q' is the yield point, 'R' is the UTS point and 'S' the fracture point.

raw_source.text:
Heat is removed from a molten metal of mass 2 kg at a constant rate of 10 kW till it is completely solidified. The cooling curve is shown in the figure.

Assuming uniform temperature throughout the volume of the metal during solidification, the latent heat of fusion of the metal (in kJ/kg) is __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=m \times \mathrm{L} . \mathrm{H} \\ Q &=\text { total heat removed } \\ m &=\text { mass } \\ \text { L.H. } &=\text { Latent heat of fusion } \\ Q &=\dot{Q} \times t \\ \dot{Q} &=\text { Heat removal rate, } \\ t &=\text { time } \\ \therefore 10 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{s} \times(20-10) \mathrm{s}&=2 \times \mathrm{L} . \mathrm{H} \\ \text { or }\text { L.H. }&= 50 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Alternatively
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=m \times \mathrm{L} . \mathrm{H} \\ Q &=\text { total heat removed } \\ m &=\text { mass } \\ \mathrm{L} . \mathrm{H} &=\text { Latent heat of fusion } \\ Q &=\dot{Q} \times t \\ \dot{Q} &=\text { Heat removal rate, } \\ t &=\text { time } \\ \therefore 10 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{s} \times(20-10) \mathrm{s}&=2 \times \mathrm{L} . \mathrm{H} \\ \text{or}\quad\text{ L.H. }&=50 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The tool life equation for HSS tool is [latex]VT^{0.14}f^{0.7}d^{0.4}= Constant[/latex]. The tool life (T) of 30 min is obtained using the following cutting conditions:
V = 45 m/min, f = 0.35 mm, d = 2.0 mm
If speed (V), feed (f) and depth of cut (d) are increased individually by 25%, the tool life (in min) is

45000 \times 30^{0.14} \times 0.35^{0.7} \times 2^{0.4}=K \\
K=45,842.58 \\
\Rightarrow T^{0.14}=\frac{K}{(1.25 V)(1.25 f)^{0.7}(1.25 \times d)^{0.4}} \\

raw_source.text: A cylindrical job with diameter of 200 mm and height of 100 mm is to be cast using modulus method of riser design. Assume that the bottom surface of cylindrical riser does not contribute as cooling surface. If the diameter of the riser is equal to its height, then the height of the riser (in mm) is
raw_source.solution:
According to modulus method
[latex] \begin{aligned} M_{R} &=1.2 M_{C} \\ \left(\frac{V}{A_{s}}\right)_{R} &=1.2\left(\frac{V}{A_{s}}\right)_{C}\\ \text{Since, for riser } D&=H \text{, we have}\\ \left (\frac{V}{A_s} \right )_R&=\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}D^2H}{\pi DH+\frac{\pi}{4}D^2}=\frac{D}{5} \\ \text{Also, } & \\ \left (\frac{V}{A_s} \right )_C&=\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}D^2H}{\pi DH+2\times\frac{\pi}{4}D^2} \\ \left (\frac{V}{A_s} \right )_C&=\frac{200^2(100)}{4 (200)(100)+2\times200^2}=25\\ \text{Hence, }&\text{from (i) we have} \\ \frac{D}{5} &=1.2\times 25 \\ D&=H=150\;mm\end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider the radiation heat exchange inside an annulus between two very long concentric cylinders. The radius of the outer cylinder is [latex]R_{0}[/latex]  and that of the inner cylinder is [latex]R_{i}[/latex] . The radiation view factor of the outer cylinder onto itself is
raw_source.solution:
To find: Radiation view factor of the outer cylinder onto itself.
Hence [latex] F_{11} [/latex] is required.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow A_{1} F_{12}&=A_{2} F_{21} \qquad[\text { Reciprosity }]\\ F_{11}+F_{12}&=1 \qquad \text { [Summation] }\\ F_{21}+F_{22}&=1\\ \therefore \quad F_{11}&=1-F_{12} \\ F_{22}&=0 \text { [No radiation leaving }\\ &\text{surface 2 reaches back to 2]}\\ \therefore \quad F_{21} &=1 \\ F_{12} &=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}} \times F_{21}=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}} \times 1 \\ &=\frac{2 \pi R_{i} L}{2 \pi R_{0} L} \times 1=\frac{R_{i}}{R_{0}} \\ F_{11} &=1-F_{12}=1-\frac{R_{i}}{R_{0}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Consider a simple gas turbine (Brayton) cycle and a gas turbine cycle with perfect regeneration. In both the cycles, the pressure ratio is 6 and the ratio of the specific heats of the working medium is 1.4. The ratio of minimum to maximum temperatures is 0.3 (with temperatures expressed in K) in the regenerative cycle. The ratio of the thermal efficiency of the simple cycle to that of the regenerative cycle is _________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given: }r_{p}&=6\\ y&=1.4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }}=0.3 \quad[/latex] [for regenerative cycle ]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_\text { Tregenerative cycle } &=1-\frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }} \times\left(r_{p}\right)^{(\gamma-1) / \gamma} \\ &=1-0.3\times(6)^{\frac{0.4}{1.4}}\\ &=0.49945 \times(6)^{\frac{0.4}{1.4}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \eta_{\text {simplecycle }} &=1-\frac{1}{\left(r_{p}\right)^{(\gamma-1) / \gamma}} \\ &=1-\left(r_{p}\right)^{(1-\gamma) / \gamma} \\ &=1-(6)^{-\frac{0.4}{1.4}}=0.4066 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Required ratio } &=\frac{\eta_{\text {simple cycle }}}{\eta_{\text {regenerative cycle }}} \\ &=\frac{0.40666}{0.49945}=0.8141 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The error in numerically computing the integral [latex]\int_{0}^{\pi }(\sin x+\cos x )dx[/latex] using the trapezoidal rule with three intervals of equal length between 0 and [latex]\pi[/latex]  is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{2 \pi}{3} & \pi \\ \hline f(x) & 1 & 1.366 & 0.366 & -1 \\ & y_{0} & y_{1} & y_{2} & y_{3} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
By Trapezoidal
[latex] \int_{0}^{\pi}(\sin x+\cos x) d x=\frac{\pi / 3}{2}(1+(-1)+ [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A simply supported beam of length 2L is subjected to a moment M at the mid-point x = 0 as shown in the figure. The deflection in the domain [latex]o\leq x\leq L[/latex] is given by
[latex]w=\frac{-Mx}{12EIL}(L-x)(x+c)[/latex]
where E is the Young's modulus, I is the area moment of inertia and c is a constant (to be determined)

The slope at the center x = 0 is
raw_source.solution:
Equation of deflection
[latex] \begin{aligned} W &=\frac{-M}{12 E I L}\left[L x^{2}-x^{3}+L c x-C x^{2}\right] \\ \frac{d W}{d x} &=\frac{-M}{12 E I L}\left[2 L x-3 x^{2}+L C-2 C x\right] \\ \frac{d^{2} W}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-M}{12 E I L}[2 L-6 x-2 C] \\ \therefore \quad E I \frac{d^{2} W}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-M}{12 L}[2 L-6 x-2 C] \\ \text { now } \quad E I \frac{d^{2} W}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-M}{12 L}[2 L-6 x-2 C]\\ \text{at }\quad x&=L, M_{x}=0 \\ \therefore \quad C&=2 L\\ Slope\\ \frac{d W}{d x} &=\frac{-M}{12 E I L}\left[2 L x-3 x^{2}+2 L^{2}-4 L x\right] \\ \therefore \quad \left|\frac{d W}{d x}\right|_{x=0} &=\frac{-M L}{6 E I} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The system shown in the figure consists of block A of mass 5 kg connected to a spring through a massless rope passing over pulley B of radius r and mass 20 kg. The spring constant k is 1500 N/m. If there is no slipping of the rope over the pulley, the natural frequency of the system is_____________ rad/s.
raw_source.solution:
Total energy of system
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} k x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} m\left(r \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times(r \theta)^{2} \\&+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M r^{2}}{2} \times\left[\frac{d \theta}{d T}\right]^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} M r^{2} \cdot(\dot{\theta})^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times r^{2} \theta^{2}+\frac{M r^{2}}{4}(\dot{\theta})^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since total energy remains constant with respect to time.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t} &=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t} &=\frac{1}{2} m r^{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K r^{2}}{2} \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M r^{2}}{4} 2 \dot{\theta} \dot{\theta} \\ 0 &=m r^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K r^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M r^{2}}{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex]\dot{\theta} [/latex]
[latex] 0=m r^{2} \ddot{\theta}+K r^{2} \theta+\frac{M r^{2}}{2}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex]r^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0 &=m \ddot{\theta}+K \theta+\frac{M \ddot{\theta}}{2} \\ 0 &=\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K \theta \\ 0 &=\ddot{\theta}+\left[\frac{K}{m+\frac{M}{2}}\right] \theta \\ \omega_{n}^{2} &=\frac{K}{m+\frac{M}{2}} \\ \omega_{n} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 k}{M+2 m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1500}{20+(2 \times 5)}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{3000}{20+10}}=\sqrt{100} \\ &=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a structural member under fatigue loading, the minimum and maximum stresses developed at the critical point are 50 MPaand 150 MParespectively. The endurance, yield, and the ultimate strengths of the material are 200 MPa,300 MPa and 400 MPa, respectively. The factor of safety using modified Goodman criterion is
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned}  \sigma _{max}&=150MPa\\ \sigma _{min}&=50MPa\\ S_e&=200MPa\\ S_{yt}&=300MPa\\ S_{ut}&=400MPa\\ \sigma _a&=\frac{\sigma _{max}-\sigma _{min}}{2}\\ &=\frac{150-50}{2}\\ &=50 MPa\\ \sigma _m&=\frac{\sigma _{max}+\sigma _{min}}{2}\\ &=\frac{150+50}{2}\\ &=100 MPa\\ &\text{Goodman sequation}\\ \frac{\sigma _a}{S_e}+\frac{\sigma _m}{S_{ut}}&=\frac{1}{FS}\\ \frac{50}{200}+\frac{100}{400}&=\frac{1}{FS}\\ FS&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The force F required to hold the plug in its position

raw_source.text:
Consider a parallel-flow heat exchanger with area [latex]A_{p}[/latex]  and a counter-flow heat exchanger with area [latex]A_{c}[/latex]. In both the heat exchangers, the hot stream flowing at 1 kg/s cools from [latex]80^{\circ}[/latex]C to [latex]50^{\circ}[/latex]C .  For the
cold stream in both the heat exchangers, the flow rate and the inlet temperature are 2 kg/s and [latex]10^{\circ}[/latex]C , respectively. The hot and cold streams in both the heat exchangers are of the same fluid.
Also, both the heat exchangers have the same overall heat transfer coefficient. The ratio  [latex]A_{c}[/latex]/ [latex]A_{p}[/latex] is _________
raw_source.solution:
Parallel flow

[latex]A_{p} =[/latex] Area of parallel flow heat exchanger
Counter flow

[latex]A_{c}= [/latex] Area of counter flow heat exchanger
Heat lost by hot stream in both heat exchanger
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=m c\left[T_{h i}-T_{h o}\right] \\ &=1 \times c \times\left[T_{h i}-T_{h o}\right] \\ &=1 \times c \times[80-50]=30 \mathrm{ckW} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat gained by cold stream in both exchange
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=m c\left[T_{co}-T_{c i}\right] \\ &=2 \times c\left[T_{c o}-10\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Heat lost by hot stream = Heat gain by cool stream
[latex]\begin{aligned} 30c &=2c(T_\infty -10) \\ T_\infty &= \frac{30}{2}+10\\ &=15+10=25^{\circ} C\\ A_P, LMTD&= \frac{\Delta T_i-\Delta T_e}{ln(\Delta T_i/\Delta T_e)}\\ &= \frac{70-25}{ln(70/25)}=43.705^{\circ} C\\ Q_H&=UA_P 43.705 \\ A_C, LMTD&= \frac{\Delta T_i-\Delta T_e}{ln(\Delta T_i/\Delta T_e)}\\ &= \frac{55-40}{ln(55/40)}=47.103^{\circ} C\\ Q_H&=UA_C 47.103 \\ \therefore \; UA_P 43.705 &=UA_C 47.103\\ \frac{43.705}{47.103}&=\frac{A_C}{A_P}=0.927 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Two cylindrical shafts A and B at the same initial temperature are simultaneously placed in a furnace. The surfaces of the shafts remain at the furnace gas temperature at all times after they are introduced into the furnace. The temperature variation in the axial direction of the shafts can be assumed to be negligible. The data related to shafts A and B is given in the following Table.

The temperature at the centerline of the shaft A reaches [latex]400^{\circ}[/latex] C after two hours. The time required (in hours) for the centerline of the shaft B to attain the temperature of [latex]400^{\circ}[/latex] C is _______
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{(r, t)} &=T_{0}+\left(T_{\infty}-T_{0}\right) \operatorname{erf}(z) \\ \frac{T_{(r, t)}-T_{0}}{T_{\infty}-T_{0}} &=\operatorname{erf}(z) \\ \frac{T_{(r, t)}-T_{0}}{T_{\infty}-T_{0}} &=\operatorname{erf}(z) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For shaft A [latex]\quad \frac{T_{0.2, t}-T_{i}}{400-T_{i}} [/latex]
For shaft B [latex]\quad \frac{T_{0.05, t}-T_{i}}{400-T_{i}} [/latex]
Hence error function of both shafts will be same.
[latex] \therefore \qquad z_{A}=z_{B}[/latex][latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\Gamma_{A}}{2 \sqrt{\alpha_{A} t_{A}}} &=\frac{T_{B}}{2 \sqrt{\alpha_{B} t_{B}}} \\ \frac{\Gamma_{A}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{A} t_{A}}} &=\frac{\Gamma_{B}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{B} t_{B}}} \\ \frac{\Gamma_{A}^{2}}{\alpha_{A} t_{A}} &=\frac{r_{B}^{2}}{\alpha_{B} t_{B}} \\ t_{B} &=\left(\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}\right)^{2} \times \frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_{B}} \times t_{A} \\ \alpha_{A} &=\frac{k}{\rho c_{p}}=\frac{40}{2 \times 10^{6}}=\frac{20}{10^{6}} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ \alpha_{B} &=\frac{k}{\rho c_{p}}=\frac{20}{2 \times 10^{7}}=\frac{1}{10^{6}} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ t_{B} &=\left(\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}\right)^{2} \times \frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_{B}} \times t_{A} \\ &=\left(\frac{0.1}{0.4}\right)^{2} \times \frac{20}{10^{6} \times \frac{1}{10^{6}}} \times 2 \\ &=\frac{1}{16} \times 20 \times 2=2.5 \mathrm{hrs} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A piston-cylinder device initially contains 0.4 [latex]m^{3}[/latex] of air (to be treated as an ideal gas) at 100 kPa and [latex]80^{\circ}[/latex]C. The air is now isothermally compressed to 0.1 [latex]m^{3}[/latex] .The work done during this process is ________ kJ.
(Take the sign convention such that work done on the system is negative)
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{c} V_{1}=0.4 \mathrm{m}^{3} ; \quad p_{1}=100 \mathrm{kPa} \\ T_{1}=80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(80+273) \mathrm{K}=353 \mathrm{K} \\ V_{2}=0.1 \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{array}[/latex]
For isothermal process
[latex] \begin{aligned} W &=p_{1} V_{1} \log _{e} \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} \\ &=100 \times 0.4 \log _{e} \frac{0.1}{0.4} \\ &=-55.45 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A reversible cycle receives 40 kJ of heat from one heat source at a temperature of [latex]127^{\circ}[/latex]C and 37 kJ from another heat source at [latex]97^{\circ}[/latex]C. The heat rejected (in kJ) to the heat sink at  [latex]47^{\circ}[/latex]C is __________
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{1} &=127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(127+273) \mathrm{K} \\ &=400 \mathrm{K}\\ T_{2} &=97^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(97+273) \mathrm{K} \\ &=370 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{3} &=47^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(47+273) \mathrm{K} \\ &=320 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For reversible cycle
Clausius inequality, [latex] \oint \frac{S Q}{T}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \qquad \frac{40}{400}+\frac{37}{370}-\frac{Q_{3}}{320}&=0 \\ 0.1+0.1&=\frac{Q_{3}}{320}\\ \text{or}\qquad Q_{3}&=64 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A refrigerator uses R-134a as its refrigerant and operates on an ideal vapour-compression refrigeration cycle between 0.14 MPa and 0.8 MPa. If the mass flow rate of the refrigerant is 0.05 kg/s, the rate of heat rejection to the environment is _________ kW.
Given data:
At P = 0.14 MPa, h =236.04 kJ/kg, s =0.9322 kJ/kg-K
At P = 0.8 MPa, h = 272.05kJ/kg (superheated vapour)
At P = 0.8 MPa, h = 93.42 kJ/kg (saturated liquid)
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} m&=0.05 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}\\ \text{At }\quad p_{e}&=0.14 \mathrm{MPa} \\ h_{1}&=236.04 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ s_{1}&=0.9322 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K}\\ \text{At }\quad p_{c}&=0.8 \mathrm{MPa} \\ h_{3}&=h_{4}=h_{f}=93.42 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] h_{2}=272.02 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}[/latex]
Rate of heat rejection to the environment,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{2-3} &=m\left[h_{2}-h_{3}\right]=0.05 \times[275.02-93.42] \\ &=8.93 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The partial pressure of water vapour in a moist air sample of relative humidity 70% is 1.6 kPa, the
total pressure being 101.325 kPa. Moist air may be treated as an ideal gas mixture of water vapour
and dry air. The relation between saturation temperature ([latex]T_{s}[/latex]  in K) and saturation pressure ([latex]p_{s}[/latex]  in KPa) for water is given by [latex]ln(p_{s}/p_{o})[/latex]=14.317-5304/[latex]T_{s}[/latex] , where [latex]p_{o}[/latex] = 101.325 kPa. The dry
bulb temperature of the moist air sample (in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex] C) is __________
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
Relative humidity,
[latex] \phi=70 \%=0.70[/latex]
Partial pressure,
[latex] p_{v}=1.6 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
Total pressure,
[latex] p_{0}=101.325 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex]
We know that,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \phi&=\frac{p_{v}}{p_{s}}\\ 0.70 &=\frac{1.6}{p_{s}} \\ \text{or}\quad p_{s} &=\frac{1.6}{0.70}=2.2857 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Temperature corresponding to saturation pressure
is dry bulb temperature,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \ln \left\{\frac{p_{s}}{p_{o}}\right\} &=14.317-\frac{5304}{T_{s}} \\ \ln \left\{\frac{2.2857}{101.325}\right\} &=14.317-\frac{5304}{T_{s}} \\ -3.79166 &=14.317-\frac{5304}{T_{s}} \\ \frac{5304}{T_{s}} &=14.317+3.79166 \\ \frac{5304}{T_{s}} &=18.10866 \\ \text{or}\quad T_{s} &= 292.89 \mathrm{K}\\ &=(292.89-273)^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ &=19.89^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

In a binary system of A and B, a liquid of 20% A (80% B) is coexisting with a solid of 70% A
(30% B). For an overall composition having 40% A, the fraction of solid is

raw_source.text: Gray cast iron blocks of size 100 mm x 50 mm x 10 mm with a central spherical cavity of diameter 4 mm are sand cast. The shrinkage allowance for the pattern is 3%. The ratio of the volume of the pattern to volume of the casting is _________
raw_source.solution:
Ratio of volume of pattern to volume of casting is given by

[latex]=\frac{(1.03\times100)\times(1.03\times50)\times(1.03\times10)}{100\times50\times10}=1.093[/latex]

Volume of cavity is assumed to be small and negligible as it will complicate the question to a higher level.
If your answer was less than 1, read below.

There are three things to be understood here :-

1. Liquid Shrinkage
It refers to the reduction in volume when the metal changes from liquid state to solid state at the solidus temperature. The liquid shrinkage is rarely a problem, because the molten metal is continuously flowing in mold cavity and also riser to compensate the shrinkage of liquid in the cavity.

2. Solidification i.e Liquid to solid phase transformation (GCI expands in this process unlike other metals)
So now during phase transformation gray cast iron expands (unlike other metals which contract) and there is no need of riser (used to take care of phase transformation shrinkage + liquid shrinkage).

3. Solid state Cooling (GCI contracts in this process just like other metals)
It refers to the reduction in volume caused when metal loses temperature in solid state. To account for this, shrinkage allowance is provided on the patterns. The Shrinkage allowance depends primarily upon Coefficient of thermal expansion. For Grey CI in particular it is positive, it means solid grey cast iron expands on increasing temp and contracts on decreasing temperature just like any other metal.

Adding all above factors

Neglecting the Liquid shrinkage we see that GCI expands in during solidification and contracts when cooled in solid form. So the net result would be sum of them. According to NPTL in the table for GCI they have given the net value of shrinkage’s which is positive and hence the pattern size would be more than the casting.

Note: The expansion of GCI during phase change (solidification) is a fact but at the same time we need to consider the contraction of GCI when cooling in solid state. So net result according to IISC and NPTEL is contraction so the size of pattern will be more than that of casting.

raw_source.text: The voltage-length characteristic of a direct current arc in an arc welding process is v=(100+40[latex]l[/latex]) , where [latex]l[/latex]  is the length of the arc in mm and V is arc voltage in volts. During a welding operation, the arc length varies between 1 and 2 mm and the welding current is in the range 200-250 A. Assuming a linear power source, the short circuit current is_________ A.
raw_source.solution: [latex]\begin{aligned} V &=100+40 \mathrm{L} \\ \text{When}\quad L &=1 \quad I=250 \\ V &=(100+40 \times 1)=140 \\ &=V_{0}-\frac{V_{0}}{I_{0}} \times 250 \\ L &=2 \quad I=200 \\ V &=(100+40 \times 2) \\ 180 &=V_{0}-\frac{V_{0}}{I_{0}} \times 200 \\ V_{0} &=140+\frac{4}{5} \times 250=340 \\ I &=\frac{V_{0} \times 5}{4}=\frac{340 \times 5}{4} \\ &=425 \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: For a certain job, the cost of metal cutting is Rs. 18C/V and the cost of tooling is Rs. 270C/(TV),where C is a constant,  V is the cutting speed in m/min and T  is the tool life in minutes. The Taylor's tool life equation is [latex]VT^{0.25}[/latex] =150. The cutting speed (in m/min) for the minimum total cost is _______
raw_source.solution:
Total cost = metal cutting cost + tooling cost
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{180 C}{V}+\frac{270 C}{V T}\\ \text { Here, } T&=\left(\frac{150}{V}\right)^{\frac{1}{0.25}}=\left(\frac{15}{V}\right)^{4} \\ C_{t} &=\frac{18 C}{V}+\frac{270 C}{V \cdot\left(\frac{150}{V}\right)^{4}}\\ \frac{d C_{t}}{d V} &=0 \\ -\frac{18 C}{V^{2}}+\frac{270 C}{(150)^{4}} \times 3 v^{2}&=0\\ \text { or } \quad V^{4}&=\frac{150^{4} \times 18}{270 \times 3} \\ V&=57.91 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{min} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The surface irregularities of electrodes used in an electrochemical machining (ECM) process are 3 [latex]\mu m[/latex] and 6 [latex]\mu m[/latex] as shown in the figure. If the work-piece is of pure iron and 12V DC is applied between the electrodes, the largest feed rate is ___________mm/min.

raw_source.solution: In a wire-cut EDM process, a thin metallic wire is fed on to the conducting workpiece, which is submerged in a tank of dielectric fluid such as de-ionized water. Wire is fed in the programmed path & material is cut from the workpiece accordingly. Material removal takes place by a series of discrete discharges between the wire electrode & workpiece in the presence of a dielectric fluid. The di-electric fluid gets ionized in between the tool electrode gap thereby creating a  path for each discharge. The area wherein discharge takes place gets heated to very high temperature such that the surface get melted & removed. The cut particles (debris) get flushed away by continuous flowing dielectric fluid. Generally, wire-cut EDM is used for cutting Aluminium, brass, etc. & wire material used for quicker cutting action is zinc coated brass wires.

raw_source.text:
The value of the line integral [latex]\oint_{c}\bar{F}\cdot \bar{r'} \; ds[/latex] ,where C is a circle of radius [latex]4/\sqrt{\pi}[/latex] unit is ___
Here, [latex]\bar{F}(x,y)= y\hat{i}+2x\hat{j} \; and \; \bar{r}'[/latex] is the UNIT tangent vector on the curve C at an arc length s from a reference point on the curve. [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] are the basis vectors in the x-y Cartesian reference. In evaluating the line integral, the curve has to be traversed in the counter-clockwise direction.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{c} \bar{F} \cdot \vec{r}\acute{} d x=\int_{c} \bar{F} \cdot & d \bar{r}=\int_{c} F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y \\ &=\iint_{R}\left(\frac{\partial F_{2}}{d x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{d y}\right) d x d y \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{rl} F_{1}=y & F_{2}=2 x \\ & =\iint_{R}(2-1) d x d y \end{array} \\ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}=1 \quad \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x} &=2 \\ &=\iint d x d y \end{aligned} \end{array}\\ &=\text { Area of the circle with radius } \frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}=\pi\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}\\ &=\pi \frac{16}{\pi}=16 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A single degree of freedom spring-mass system is subjected to a harmonic force of constant amplitude. For an excitation frequency of [latex]\sqrt{3k/m}[/latex] the ratio of the amplitude of steady state response to the static deflection of the spring is __________

raw_source.text: Consider a fully developed steady laminar flow of an incompressible fluid with viscosity [latex]\mu[/latex] through a circular pipe of radius R. Given that the velocity at a radial location of R/2 from the centerline of the pipe is [latex]U_{1}[/latex], the shear stress at the wall is [latex]K\mu U_{1}/R[/latex], where K is __________
raw_source.solution:
Shear stress at the wall,
[latex] \tau_{0}=\tau_{\max }=\frac{k \mu U_{1}}{R}[/latex]
We know that the velocity at any point for laminar
flow through pipe,
[latex] \begin{aligned} u&=-\frac{1}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right)\left(R^{2}-r^{2}\right)\\ \mathrm{At} \quad r&=\frac{R}{2}, u=U_{1}\\ \therefore \quad U_{1} &=-\frac{1}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right)\left(R^{2}-\frac{R^{2}}{4}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) \frac{3}{4} R^{2} \\ &=-\frac{3}{16 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R^{2}\\ \therefore \tau_{0}&=-\frac{K \mu}{R} \times \frac{3}{16 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R^{2}\\ \tau_{0}&=-\frac{3}{16} K\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that maximum shear stress at wall.
[latex] \tau_{0}=-\frac{R \partial p}{\partial} \frac{\partial p}{\partial x}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore-\frac{3}{16} K\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R=-\frac{R}{2} \frac{\partial p}{\partial x} [/latex]
[latex] \text{or}K=\frac{8}{3}=2.66[/latex]

The water jet exiting from a stationary tank through a circular opening of diameter 300 mm impinges on a rigid wall as shown in the figure. Neglect all minor losses and assume the water level in the tank to remain constant. The net horizontal force experienced by the wall is ___________ kN.
Density of water is 1000 kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex].
Acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/[latex]s^{2}[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Diameter of jet,
[latex] d = 300\mathrm{mm} = 0.30 \mathrm{m}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad [/latex]Cross-section area,
[latex] \begin{aligned} a &=\frac{\pi}{4} d^{2}=\frac{3.14}{4} \times(0.30)^{2} \\ &=0.07065 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text{Jet Velocity: }V \;&=\sqrt{2 g h}\\ &=\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 6.2} = 11.135\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Net horizontal force
[latex] \begin{aligned} F &=m[V-0] \\ &=\rho a V \times V \\ &=\rho a V^{2} \\ &=1000 \times 0.07065 \times(11.135)^{2} \\ &=8759.76 \mathrm{N} \\ &=8.76 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
For a two-dimensional flow, the velocity field is [latex]\vec{u}=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\hat{j}[/latex], where [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] are the basis vectors in the x-y Cartesian coordinate system. Identify the CORRECT statements from below.
(1)The flow is incompressible
(2)The flow is unsteady.
(3) y-component of acceleration, [latex]a_{y}=\frac{-y}{(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}}[/latex]
(4) x-component of acceleration,[latex]a_{x}=\frac{-(x+y)}{(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
For [latex]2 \mathrm{D}[/latex] -flow velocity field is:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \vec{V}&=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \hat{i}+\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \hat{j}\\ so \quad u&=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} and v=\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \\ a_{x} &=u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \\ &=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right] \\ &+\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right] \\ &= \frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\left[\frac{x(-2 x)}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right]\\ &+\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \left[\frac{x(2 y)}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}}\right]\\ &=\frac{-2 x^{3}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}}+\frac{x}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}}\\ &+ \frac{2xy^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}}\\ &=\frac{-2 x^{3}+x\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)-2 x y^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}} \\ &=\frac{-2 x^{3}+x^{3}+x y^{2}-2 x y^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}}\\ &=\frac{-x^{3}-x y^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}} \\ &=\frac{-x\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} a_{x} &=\frac{x}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}} \\ a_{y} &=u \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+u \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\ &=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right] \\& +\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right] \\ &=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \frac{(-2 x y)}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}}\\& +\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}} \times\left[\frac{-2 y^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right]\\ &=\frac{-2 x^{2} y}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}}+\frac{2 y^{3}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}}\\&+\frac{y}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}} \\ &=\frac{-2 x^{2} y-2 y^{3}+y\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}} \\ &=\frac{-x^{2} y-y^{3}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}}=\frac{y\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{3}} \\ a_{y}&=\frac{-y}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Two large parallel plates having a gap of 10 mm in between them are maintained at temperatures  T1 = 1000 K and T2 = 400 K. Given emissivity values, [latex]\varepsilon{1}=0.5[/latex] ,  [latex]\varepsilon_{2}=0.25[/latex]  and Stefan-Boltzmann constant [latex]\sigma= 5.67 \times 10^{-8} W/m^{2}-K^{4}[/latex], the heat transfer between the plates (in kW/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]) is __________ _________
raw_source.solution: [latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=\frac{\sigma\left[T_{1}^{4}-T_{2}^{4}\right]}{\frac{1}{\epsilon_{1}}+\frac{1}{\epsilon_{2}}-1}=\frac{5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times\left(1000^{4}-400^{4}\right)}{\frac{1}{0.5}+\frac{1}{0.25}-1} \\ &=11049.7 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=11.05 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A cylindrical steel rod, 0.01 m in diameter and 0.2 m in length is first heated to [latex]750^{\circ}C[/latex]  and then immersed in a water bath at [latex]100^{\circ}C[/latex] .  The heat transfer coefficient is 250 W/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]-K. The density, specific heat and thermal conductivity of steel are [latex]\rho = 7801 kg/m^{3}[/latex], c = 473 J/kg-K, and  k = 43 W/m-K, respectively.  The time required for the rod to reach [latex]300^{\circ}C[/latex]  is ________  seconds.
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \mathrm{D}=0.01 \mathrm{m} ; \quad L=0.2 \mathrm{m} ; \quad T_{i}=750^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex]
[latex] T_{\infty}=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ; \quad h=250 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} ; \quad \rho=7801 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{c}=473 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}}&=\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{h A t}{\rho V c}}\\\text{ Where }\quad \frac{V}{A}&=\frac{\pi D^{2} L}{4 \times \pi D L}=\frac{D}{4}=\frac{0.01}{4} \\ &=2.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \frac{300-100}{750-100}&=e^{\frac{-250 \times t}{7801 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 473}} \\ \frac{200}{650}&=e^{-0.0271 t} \\ 0.30769&=e^{-0.0271 t}\end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex] \log _{e} [/latex] both sides, we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} \log _{e} 0.30769&=-0.0271 t \log _{e} e \\ &\qquad\left(\because \log _{\theta} e=1\right) \\ t&=\frac{1.1786}{0.027}=43.65 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Steam at an initial enthalpy of 100 kJ/kg and inlet velocity of 100 m/s, enters an insulated horizontal nozzle. It leaves the nozzle at 200 m/s. The exit enthalpy (in kJ/kg) is __________
raw_source.solution:
Applying steady flow energy equation between
section 1 and 2.
[latex] h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2}+g z_{1}+q=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2}+g_{2}+w [/latex]
where q=0 insulated nozzle
[latex] z_{1}=z_{2} \quad[/latex] horizontal nozzle
w=0 always for nozzle
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2} &=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2} \\ h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2000} &=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2000} \end{aligned}[/latex]
where [latex] h_{1}[/latex] and [latex]h_{2}[/latex] are in kJ/kg and [latex]V_{1}[/latex] and [latex]V_{2}[/latex] are in m/s
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore 100+\frac{(100)^{2}}{2000} &=h_{2}+\frac{(200)^{2}}{2000} \\ 100+5 &=h_{2}+20 \\ \text{or}\quad h_{2} &=85 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a mixture of dry air and water vapor at a total pressure of 750 mm of Hg, the partial pressure of water vapor is 20 mm of Hg. The humidity ratio of the air in grams of water vapor per kg of dry air  ([latex]g_{w}/kg_{da}[/latex]) is __________

Given data:
Total pressure,
[latex] p=750 \mathrm{mm} \text { of } \mathrm{Hg}[/latex]
Partial pressure,
[latex] p_{v}=20 \mathrm{mm} \text { of } \mathrm{Hg}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega &=\frac{0.622 p_{v}}{p-p_{v}} \mathrm{kg} w.v./ \mathrm{kg} d.a. \\ &=\frac{0.622 \times 20}{750-20} \\ &=0.01704 \;\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{w} . \mathrm{v} . \mathrm{kg} \text { of } \mathrm{d.a} \\ &=17.04 \;\mathrm{g} \text { of } \mathrm{w} . \mathrm{v} . / \mathrm{kg} \text { of } \mathrm{d.a} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: In a 3-stage air compressor, the inlet pressure is [latex]p_{1}[/latex], discharge pressure is [latex]p_{4}[/latex] and the intermediate pressures are [latex]p_{2}[/latex] and [latex]p_{3}[/latex] ( [latex]p_{2}\lt p_{3}[/latex]). The total pressure ratio of the compressor is 10 and the pressure ratios of the stages are equal. If [latex]p_{1}[/latex] = 100 kPa, the value of the pressure [latex]p_{3}[/latex] (in kPa) is __________
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{p_{4}}{p_{1}}&=10 \\ \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}&=\frac{p_{3}}{p_{2}}=\frac{p_{4}}{p_{3}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
To calculate [latex]p_{3}=? [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{4}}{p_{3}} \times \frac{p_{3}}{p_{2}} \times \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}&=10 \\ r_{p} \times r_{p} \times r_{p}&=10 \\ r_{p}^{3} &=10 \\ r_{p} &=(10)^{1 / 3}\\ p_{2}&=r_{p} p_{1} \\ p_{3}&=r_{p} p_{2}=r_{p}^{2} p_{1}=(10)^{2 / 3} \times 100\\ &=464.16 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
In the vapour compression cycle shown in the figure, the evaporating and condensing temperatures are 260 K and 310 K, respectively. The compressor takes in liquid-vapour mixture (state 1) and isentropically compresses it to a dry saturated vapour condition (state 2). The specific heat of the liquid refrigerant is 4.8 kJ/kg-K and may be treated as constant. The enthalpy of evaporation for the refrigerant at 310 K is 1054 kJ/kg.

The difference between the enthalpies at state points 1 and 0 (in kJ/kg) is ____________
raw_source.solution:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{e} &=260 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{c} &=310 \mathrm{K} \\ c_{p l} &=4.8 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ h_{fg} &=1054 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { at } T_{c}=310 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Taking reference temperature T , at which entropy is [latex] s_{T} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad s_{3}-s_{T} &=c \ln \frac{T_{3}}{T} \\ s_{3} &=s_{T}+c \ln \frac{T_{3}}{T}=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T} \\ \text { Similarly, } s_{0} &=s_{T}+c \ln \frac{260}{T}=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{260}{T} \\ \therefore \quad s_{2}-s_{3} &=\frac{h_{f g}}{T}=\frac{1054}{310} \\ s_{2} &=s_{3}+\frac{1054}{310} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substitute the value of [latex]s_{3}[/latex] in above equation, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} s_{2} &=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310} \\ s_{2} &=s_{1} \\ s_{1} &=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310} \\ h_{1}-h_{0} &=T_{e}\left[s_{1}-s_{0}\right] \\ =& 260 \times\left[s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310}\right.\\ &\left.-s_{T}-4.8 \ln \frac{260}{T}\right] \\ &=260\left[4.8 \ln \left(\frac{310}{T} \times \frac{T}{260}\right)+\frac{1054}{310}\right] \\ &1103.51\mathrm{kJ}/\mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider [latex] A-\lambda I=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2-\lambda & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3-\lambda\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Ch. equation is [latex] |A-\lambda I|=0 [/latex]
[latex] (2-\lambda)(2-\lambda)(3-\lambda)=0 [/latex]
[latex] \lambda=2,2,3 [/latex]
[latex] \lambda=3 [/latex] there is one L.I. Eigen vector
[latex] \lambda=2 \quad [/latex]Consider [latex] (A-2 I) x=0 [/latex]
[latex] \text{rank} =2 \quad [/latex] The equation are [latex] x_{2}=0 [/latex]
No. of variables [latex] =3 x_{3}=0 [/latex]

[latex] \therefore \text{Eigen vector is}\; \left[\begin{array}{l}k \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right]=k\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Only one independent Eigen vector in the case of
[latex] \lambda=2 [/latex]
Hence finally no. of L.I. Eigen vectors =2

raw_source.text:
The value of the line integral [latex]\oint_{c}\bar{F}\cdot \bar{r'} \; ds[/latex] ,where C is a circle of radius [latex]4/\sqrt{\pi}[/latex] unit is ___
Here, [latex]\bar{F}(x,y)= y\hat{i}+2x\hat{j} \; and \; \bar{r}'[/latex] is the UNIT tangent vector on the curve C at an arc length s from a reference point on the curve. [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] are the basis vectors in the x-y Cartesian reference. In evaluating the line integral, the curve has to be traversed in the counter-clockwise direction.
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{c} \bar{F} \cdot \vec{r}\acute{} d x=\int_{c} \bar{F} \cdot & d \bar{r}=\int_{c} F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y \\ &=\iint_{R}\left(\frac{\partial F_{2}}{d x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{d y}\right) d x d y \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{rl} F_{1}=y & F_{2}=2 x \\ & =\iint_{R}(2-1) d x d y \end{array} \\ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}=1 \quad \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x} &=2 \\ &=\iint d x d y \end{aligned} \end{array}\\ &=\text { Area of the circle with radius } \frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}=\pi\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}\\ &=\pi \frac{16}{\pi}=16 \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Saturated steam at [latex]100^{\circ}[/latex]C condenses  on the outside of a tube.cold fluid enters the tube at  [latex]20^{\circ}[/latex]C and exits at [latex]50^{\circ}[/latex]C the value of the log mean Temperature Difference (LMTD) is _________[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C.

raw_source.text: The molar Specific heat at constant volume of an ideal gas in equal to 2.5 times the universal gas constant(8.314 J/mol K). When the temperature increases by 100 K, the change in molar specific enthalpy is__________ J/mol.
raw_source.solution:
Given that:[latex] \bar{C}_{v}=2.5 \bar{R} [/latex]
[latex] \bar{C}_{v} \rightarrow [/latex] Molar specific heat at constant volume
[latex] \begin{aligned} \bar{C}_{p}-\bar{C}_{v}&=\bar{R}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \bar{C}_{p}&=\bar{R}+\bar{C}_{v}=\bar{R}+2.5 \bar{R} \\ \bar{C}_{p}&=3.5 \bar{R} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Molar specific enthalpy change of ideal gas (A H)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Delta H &=n \bar{C}_{p} \Delta T \\ \overline{\Delta H} &=\frac{\Delta H}{n}=\overline{\Delta H}=\bar{C}_{p} \Delta T \\ &=3.5 \times 8.314 \times 100 \\ \overline{\Delta H} &=2909.9 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{mole} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A heat pump absorbs 10kW of heat from outside environment at 250 K while absorbing 15 kW of work. It delivers the heat to a room that must be kept warm at 300K. The coefficient of Performance (COP) of the heat pump is _________.

Given that: [latex] \dot{Q}_{L}=10 \mathrm{kW} [/latex]

[latex]\dot{W}=15 \mathrm{kW}[/latex]
Applying first law on heat pump
[latex] \begin{array}{c} \dot{Q}_{L}+\dot{W}=\dot{Q}_{H} \\ 10 \mathrm{kW}+15 \mathrm{kW}=\dot{Q}_{H} \\ \dot{Q}_{H}=25 \mathrm{kW} \\ (\mathrm{COP})_{\mathrm{H.P.}}=\frac{\dot{Q}_{H}}{\dot{W}}=\frac{25 \mathrm{kW}}{15 \mathrm{kW}}=1.67 \end{array}[/latex]

raw_source.text: P(0,3), Q(0.5, 4), and R (1,5) are three points on the curve defined by f(x). Numerical integration is carried out using both Trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule within limits x = 0 and x =1 for the curve. The difference between the two results will be.
