raw_source.text:
In a direct current arc welding process, the power
source has an open circuit voltage of 100 V and
short circuit current of 1000 A. Assume a linear
relationship between voltage and current. The
arc voltage ([latex]V[/latex]) varies with the arc length ([latex]l[/latex]) as
[latex]V = 10 + 5l[/latex], where [latex]V[/latex] is in volts and [latex]l[/latex] is in mm. The
maximum available arc power during the process is
_________ kVA (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Given, OCV = 100 V and SCC = 1000 A
Voltage Arc length characteristic [latex] V_{arc}=10+5l[/latex]
We have,
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_P&=OCV-\frac{OCV}{SCC}I\\ V_P&=100-\frac{100}{1000}I\\ _P&=100-\frac{I}{10} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For stable arc
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{arc}&=V_P\\ 10+5l&=100-\frac{I}{10}\\ I&=900-50l\\ \text{Arc Power} (P)&=V \times I\\ P&=(10+5l)(900-50l)\\ P&=9000+4000l-250l^2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
For Maximum Arc Power
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{dP}{dl}&=0\\ \frac{d}{dl}(9000+400l-250l^2)&=0\\ l=4000/500&=8mm \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, for Maximum arc power, arc length is 8 mm
Voltage at [latex]l=8mm [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} V&=10+5l\\ V&=10+( 5 \times 8)\\ V&=50 \;Volt \end{aligned} [/latex]
Current at [latex]l=8mm [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} I&=900-50l\\ I&=900-( 50 \times 8)\\ I&=500 \;A \end{aligned} [/latex]
Maximum Arc Power
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{max}&= V \times I\\ P_{max}&=50 \times 500\\ &=25000VA\\ &=25 kVA \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylindrical billet of 100 mm diameter and 100 mm length is extruded by a direct extrusion process to produce a bar of [latex]L[/latex]-section. The cross sectional dimensions of this [latex]L[/latex]-section bar are shown in the figure. The total extrusion pressure ([latex]p[/latex]) in MPa for the above process is related to extrusion ratio (r) as
[latex] p=K_s\sigma _m\left [ 0.8+1.5 \ln (r)+\frac{2l}{d_0} \right ] [/latex]
where [latex] \sigma _m [/latex] is the mean flow strength of the billet material in MPa, [latex] l [/latex] is the portion of the billet length remaining to be extruded in mm, [latex] d_0 [/latex] is the initial diameter of the billet in mm, and [latex] K[/latex] is the die shape factor.
If the mean flow strength of the billet material is 50 MPa and the die shape factor is 1.05, then the maximum force required at the start of extrusion is ________ kN (round off to one decimal place).
raw_source.solution:
Original length of the billet [latex](L_0)=100mm [/latex]
Original diameter of billet [latex] (d_0)=100mm[/latex]
Mean flow stress of billet material [latex](\sigma _m)=50MPa [/latex]
Die Shape factor[latex] K_S=1.05[/latex]
Original Cross Sectional Area of Billet
[latex]A_0=\frac{\pi}{4}d_0^2=\frac{\pi}{4}100^2=7853.981 [/latex]
Cross sectional area of extruded product
[latex]A_f=(10 \times 50)+ (10 \times 50)=1000 mm^2 [/latex]
Extrusion ratio [latex]r=\frac{A_0}{A_f}=\frac{7853.9816}{1000}=7.854 [/latex]
Extrusion pressure will be maximum at the start of extrusion process where [latex] L_0=100mm[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_{max}&= K_S\sigma _m\left [ 0.8+1.5 \ln (r)+\frac{2L_0}{d_0} \right ]\\ &=1.05 \times 50 \left [ 0.8+1.5 \ln (7.854)+\frac{2 \times 100}{100} \right ]\\ &=309.305 MPa \end{aligned} [/latex]
Maximum Extrusion force
[latex]\begin{aligned} F_{max}&= P_{max} \times A_0\\ &=309.305 \times \frac{\pi}{4}(100)^2\\ &=2429265.97N\\ &=2429.3kN \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A project consists of five activities (A, B, C, D and E). The duration of each activity follows beta distribution. The three time estimates (in weeks) of each activity and immediate predecessor(s) are listed in the table. The expected time of the project completion is __________ weeks (in integer).
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Activity} & \text{Optimistic time (week)} & \text{Most likely time (week)} &\text{Pessimistic time (week)} &\text{Immediatepredecessor(s)} \\ \hline A& 4 & 5 &6 & None\\ \hline B& 1& 3 & 5 & A\\ \hline C& 1& 2 & 3 & A\\ \hline D& 2& 4 & 6 & C\\ \hline E& 3& 4 & 5 &B,D \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Activity}& t_e=\frac{t_0+4t_m+t_p}{6}\\ \hline A&5\\ \hline B&3\\ \hline C&2\\ \hline D&4\\ \hline E&4 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Path}& \text{Duration}\\ \hline 1-2-4-5(A-B-E)&12\\ \hline 1-2-3-4-5 (A-C-D-E)&15\\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
Expected completion time of the project = critical path duration = 15 weeks

raw_source.text:
A rigid tank of volume of 8 [latex]m^3[/latex] is being filled up with air from a pipeline connected through a valve. Initially the valve is closed and the tank is assumed to be completely evacuated. The air pressure and temperature inside the pipeline are maintained at 600 kPa and 306 K, respectively. The filling of the tank begins by opening the valve and the process ends when the tank pressure is equal to the pipeline pressure. During the filling process, heat loss to the surrounding is 1000 kJ. The specific heats of air at constant pressure and at constant volume are 1.005 kJ/kg.K and 0.718 kJ/kg.K, respectively. Neglect changes in kinetic energy and potential energy.
The final temperature of the tank after the completion of the filling process is _________ K (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
Initially the tank is completely evacuated ([latex]m_1 = 0[/latex])
After the gas is filled with tank, the gas pressure in the tank is 600 kPa.
Heat lost to surroundings (Q) = 1000 kJ
[latex]c_p=1.005 KJ/kgK [/latex]
[latex] c_v=0.718KJ/kgK[/latex]
[latex]R=c_p-c_v=0.287 kJ/kgK [/latex]
(Changes in KE and PE are negligible)
Final temperature of gas [latex] T_f=?[/latex]
m = mass of gas entering to tank
The energy balance equation is energy carried by gas in the pipe = energy of gas in the rigid tank + Heat lost to surrounding
[latex]\begin{aligned} mh_i&=mu_f+Q\\ h_i&=u_f+\frac{Q}{m}\\ C+pT_i&=C_vT_f+\frac{1000}{\frac{16724.73868}{T_f}} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Mass of gas in the tank
[latex]\begin{aligned} m=\frac{P_fV_f}{RT_f}\\ &=\frac{600(8)}{0.287(T_f)}\\ &=\frac{16724.73868}{T_f}\\ 1.005(306)&=0.718T_f+\frac{1000T_f}{16724.73868}\\ &=0.718T_f+0.05979T_f\\ &=0.77779T_f\\ \therefore \; T_f&=\frac{1.005 \times 306}{0.77779}\\ &=395.389K\approx 395K \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
At steady state, [latex]500 kg/s[/latex] of steam enters a
turbine with specific enthalpy equal to [latex]3500 kJ/
kg[/latex] and specific entropy equal to  [latex]6.5 kJ \dot kg^{-1}\dot K^{-1}[/latex]. It
expands reversibly in the turbine to the condenser
pressure. Heat loss occurs reversibly in the turbine
at a temperature of [latex]500 K[/latex]. If the exit specific
enthalpy and specific entropy are [latex]2500 kJ/kg[/latex] and
 [latex]6.3 kJ\dot kg^{-1} \dot K^{-1}[/latex], respectively, the work output from
the turbine is ________ MW (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
Mass flow rate of stem [latex] \dot{m}=500kg/s [/latex]
[latex]h_1=300 kJ/kg [/latex]
[latex] S_1=6.5 kJ/kgL[/latex]
[latex] h_2=2500kJ/kg[/latex]
[latex] S_2=6.3 kJ/kgK[/latex]


Surrounding temperature [latex]T_o=500 K [/latex]
Work output from turbine
[latex] \begin{aligned} W_T&=(h_1-h_2)-T_o(S_1-S_2)\\ &=(3500-2500)-500(6.5-6.3)\\ &=1000-100\\ &=900 kJ/kg \end{aligned}[/latex]
Power output of turbine
[latex] \begin{aligned} P&=\frac{W_T}{kg} \times \dot{m}\\ &=900 \times 500\\ &=450000 kW\\ &=450 MW \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A uniform wooden rod (specific gravity = 0.6, diameter = 4 cm and length = 8 m) is immersed in the water and is hinged without friction at point A on the waterline as shown in the figure. A solid spherical ball made of lead (specific gravity = 11.4) is attached to the free end of the rod to keep the assembly in static equilibrium inside the water. For simplicity, assume that the radius of the ball is much smaller than the length of the rod.
Assume density of water [latex]= 10^3 kg/m^3[/latex] and [latex] \pi = 3.14[/latex].
Radius of the ball is _______ cm (round off to 2 decimal places).
raw_source.solution:
As the system is in equilibrium,
[latex]\Sigma M_o=0 [/latex]
[latex](F_{B1}-W_1) \times \frac{L}{2} \cos \theta +F_{B2}-W_2) \times L \times \cos \theta =0 [/latex]
[latex] (\rho gV_1-\rho _1gV_1) \times \frac{1}{2}+(\rho gV_2-\rho _2gV_2) =0[/latex]
[latex] (\rho -\rho _1) \times g \times \frac{\pi d^2L}{4} \times \frac{1}{2}+(\rho -\rho _2) \times \frac{4}{3} \times \\pi R^3 \times g=0 [/latex]
[latex] (100-600) \times \frac{0.04^2 \times 8}{8} +(1000-11400) \times \frac{4}{3} \times R^3=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow R=0.03587m=3.59cm [/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text: Consider steady state, one-dimensional heat conduction in an infinite slab of thickness [latex]2L (L = 1 m)[/latex] as shown in the figure. The conductivity [latex](k)[/latex] of the material varies with temperature as [latex]k = CT[/latex], where [latex]T[/latex] is the temperature in [latex]K[/latex], and [latex]C[/latex] is a constant equal to [latex]2 W\dot m^{-1} \dot K^{-2}[/latex]. There is a uniform heat generation of [latex]1280 kW/m^3[/latex] in the slab. If both faces of the slab are maintained at 600 K, then the temperature at [latex]x = 0 [/latex] is ________ K (in integer).
raw_source.solution:
General Heat conduction equation in Cartesian coordinates is
[latex]\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( K_x\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left ( K_y\frac{\partial T}{\partial y} \right )\frac{\partial }{\partial z}\left ( K_z\frac{\partial T}{\partial z} \right )+q_g=\rho c\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} [/latex]
For one dimensional steady state heat generation with variable thermal conductivity, the above equation can be written as
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( CT\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+q_g&=0\\ C\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+q_g&=0\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+\frac{q_g}{C}&=0\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )&=-\frac{q_g}{C}\\ \int \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )&=-\int \frac{q_g}{C}\\ \text{For 1-D heat flow}\\ \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}&=\frac{dT }{\partial x}\\ T\frac{dT}{dx}&=-\frac{q_gx}{C}+C_1\\ x=0\;\;\frac{dT}{dx}&=0\;\;C_1=0 \text{ (At centerline)}\\ T\frac{dT}{dx}&=-\frac{q_gx}{C}\\ \int TdT&=\int -\frac{q_gx}{C}dx\\ \frac{T^2}{2}&=\frac{-q_gx^2}{2C}+C_2 . . . (1)\\ T=T_s&=\text{Outside surface temperature}\\ \frac{T_S^2}{2}&=\frac{-q_gL^2}{2C}+C_2\\ C_2&=\frac{T-s^2}{2}+\frac{q_gL^2}{2C}\\ \text{Put }&c_2 \text{ in equation (1)}\\ \frac{T^2}{2}&=\frac{-q_ax^2}{2C}+\frac{T_s^2}{2}+\frac{q_gL^2}{2C}\\ \text{At }&x=0,T=T_{max}\\ \frac{T_{max}^2}{2}&=\frac{T_s^2}{2}+\frac{q_gL^2}{2C}\\ \frac{T_{max}^2}{2}&=\frac{600^2}{2}+\frac{128010^3 \times 1^2}{2 \times 2}\\ T_{max}&=1000K \end{aligned} [/latex]

 = 4 kJ\dot kg^{-1} \dot K^{-1}[/latex]
enters at [latex] 100^{\circ}C[/latex] on the tube side. If the effectiveness
of the heat exchanger is 0.9, then the mass flow rate
of the fluid in the tube side is ____ kg/s (in integer).

Hot fluid
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{h1} &=T_{h2}=200^{\circ} C\\ \dot{m}_h &=150kg/s \\ &= h_{fg}&=2400kj/kg \end{aligned}[/latex]
Cold fluid
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{c1} &=100^{\circ} C\\ \in &=0.9\\ \dot{m}_c &= ? kg/sec \end{aligned}[/latex]
If fluid is under phase change then that fluid have in finite heat capacity rate.
In this case hot fluid is under phase change so [latex]C_{max}=\infty [/latex]
It means cold fluid have minimum heat capacity rate
[latex]\begin{aligned} c_{min}&=\dot{m}_c c_c\\ \in &=\frac{Q_{act}}{Q_{max}}\\ 0.9&=\frac{\dot{m}_c c_c(T_{c2}-T_{c1})}{c_{min}(T_{h1}-T_{c1})}\\ 0.9&=\frac{T_{c2}-100}{200-100}\\ T_{c2}&=190^{\circ}C\\ Q&=\dot{m}_hh_{fg}=\dot{m}_cc_c(T_{c2}-T_{c1})\\ 150 \times 2400&=\dot{m}_c \times 4 \times (190-100)\\ \dot{m}_c&=1000kg/sec \end{aligned}[/latex]

Consider a hydrodynamically and thermally fully-developed, steady fluid flow of 1 kg/s in a uniformly heated pipe with diameter of 0.1 m and length of 40 m. A constant heat flux of magnitude 15000 [latex]W/m^2[/latex] is imposed on the outer surface of the pipe. The bulk-mean temperature of the fluid at the entrance to the pipe is [latex] 200^{\circ}C[/latex].
The Reynolds number [latex](R_e)[/latex] of the flow is 85000, and the Prandtl number [latex](P_r)[/latex] of the fluid is 5. The thermal conductivity and the specific heat of the fluid are 0.08 [latex]W\dot m^{-1} \dot K^{-1}[/latex] and 2600 [latex]J \dot kg^{-1} \dot K^{-1}[/latex], respectively. The correlation [latex]N_u = 0.023 Re^{0.8} Pr^{0.4}[/latex] is applicable, where the Nusselt Number [latex](N_u)[/latex] is defined on the basis of the pipe diameter. The pipe surface temperature at the exit is ________ [latex] ^{\circ}C[/latex] (round off to the nearest integer).
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{m}&=1kg/sec\\ Re&=85000\\ Pr&=5\\ K&=0.08 W/mK\\ C&=2600J/kgK\\ Nu&=0.023R_e^{0.8}Pr^{0.4}\\ Nu&=\frac{hD}{k}\\ T_s&=?\\ Nu&=\frac{hD}{k}=0.023R_e^{0.8}Pr^{0.4}\\ \frac{h \times 0.1}{0.08}&=0.023(85000)^{0.8}(5)^{0.4}\\ h&=307.56 W/m^2K\\ Q&=qA_s=\dot{m}c_p(T_o-T_i)\\ q \pi DL&=\dot{m}c_p(T_o-T_i)\\ 15000 \times \pi \times0.1 \times 40&=1 \times 2600 \times (T_o-200)\\ T_o&=272.5^{\circ}C\\ &\text{Newtons law of cooling}\\ q&=h(T_s-T_m)\\ T_s-T-m=\frac{q}{h}=constant \end{aligned}[/latex]


At outlet, [latex] x=LT_m=T_o. T=T_s[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} q&=h(T_s-T_o)\\ T_s-T_o&=\frac{q}{h}\\ T_s&=T_o+\frac{q}{h}\\ T_s&=272.5+\frac{15000}{307.56}\\ T_s&=321.27^{\circ}C\\ T_s&=321^{\circ}C \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The initial value problem

[latex]\frac{dy}{dt} +2y=0,\;\;y(0)=1[/latex]

is solved numerically using the forward Euler's method with a constant and positive time step of [latex]\Delta t[/latex].
Let [latex]y_n[/latex] represent the numerical solution obtained after [latex]n[/latex] steps. The condition [latex]|y_{n+1}| \leq |y_n|[/latex] is satisfied if and only if [latex]\Delta t[/latex] does not exceed _____. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Solution of differential equation given by forward Euler's method is
[latex] y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h f\left(x_{n}, y_{n}\right) [/latex]
Given: [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}+2 y=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y[/latex]
and step size, [latex]\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad y_{n+1}=y_{n}+\Delta t\left(-2 y_{n}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}=\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}(1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t})[/latex]
[latex]\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}=1-2 \Delta t \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]

Given:
[latex] \left|y_{n+1}\right| \leq\left|y_{n}\right| [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad\left|\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}\right| \leq 1[/latex]

From equation (i)
[latex]\therefore \quad|1-2 \Delta t| \leq 1[/latex]

Case (i) when [latex](1-2 \Delta t) \gt 0[/latex] :
Then, [latex]\quad 1-2 \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]
[latex] \Delta t \geq 0 [/latex]

Case (ii) when [latex](1-2 \Delta t) \lt 0[/latex] :
then [latex]-(1-2 \Delta t) \leq 1[/latex]
[latex] 1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t} \geq-1 [/latex]
[latex] \Delta \mathrm{t} \leq 1 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Value of [latex]\Delta t: 0 \leq \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]

Consider a steady incompressible flow through a channel as shown below.

The velocity profile is uniform with a value of [latex]u_0[/latex] at the inlet section A. The velocity profile at section B downstream is
[latex]u=\left\{\begin{matrix} V_m\frac{y}{\delta }, & 0\leq y\leq \delta \\ V_m,& \delta \leq y\leq H-\delta \\ V_m\frac{H-y}{\delta }, & H-\delta \leq y\leq H \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

The ratio [latex]V_{m}/u_{0}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Applying continuiting equation at sections A and B, mass flow rate at inlet section A = Mass rate at section B.


[latex]m_A=m_B[/latex]
Hence, per unit width of the channel, we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} \rho u_0 H \times 1 &=\rho V_m(H-2\delta )\times 1+2\rho \int_{0}^{\delta }udy \times 1 \\ u_0 H &=V_m(H-2\delta )+2 \int_{0}^{\delta }\frac{V_my}{\delta }dy \\ u_0 H &=V_m(H-2\delta )+2 \frac{V_m}{\delta } \left [ \frac{y^2}{2} \right ]_0 ^\delta \\ u_0 H &= V_m(H-2\delta )+2 \frac{V_m}{\delta } \times \frac{\delta ^2}{2}\\ u_0 H &= V_m(H-2\delta )+ V_m\delta \\ u_0 H&= V_mH-2V_m\delta +V_m\delta \\ u_0 H&= V_mH-V_m\delta \\ u_0 H &=V_m(H-\delta ) \\ \frac{V_m}{u_0}&=\frac{H}{H-\delta }=\frac{1}{1-(\delta /H)} \end{aligned}[/latex]

raw_source.text: The S-N curve from a fatigue test for steel is shown. Which one of the options gives the endurance limit?
raw_source.solution: For some ferrous (iron base) and titanium alloys, the S-N curve becomes horizontal at higher N values; or there is a limiting stress level, called the fatigue limit (also sometimes the endurance limit), below which fatigue will not occur. This fatigue limit represents the largest value of fluctuating stress that will not cause failure for essentially an infinite number of cycles. For many steels, fatigue limits range between 35% and 60% of the tensile strength.

raw_source.text:
Air (density = [latex] =1.2kg/m^3[/latex], kinematic viscosity [latex] =1.5 \times 10^{-5} m^2/s[/latex]) flows over a flat
plate with a free-stream velocity of [latex]2 m/s[/latex]. The wall shear stress at a location
[latex]15 mm[/latex] from the leading edge is [latex] \tau _w[/latex]. What is the wall shear stress at a location
[latex]30 mm[/latex] from the leading edge?
raw_source.solution:
Step-1: First check type of flow by Reynold No
[latex]\begin{aligned} Re&\propto \frac{u_\infty L}{v} \\ Re &= \frac{2 \times 0.0.3}{1.5 \times 10^{-5}}=4000 \end{aligned}[/latex]
As Reynold no. is less than [latex]5 \times 10^5[/latex] , it is laminar flow

Step-2: Wall shear stress in laminar flow -
[latex] \tau _w\propto \left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \right ) [/latex]

[latex] \frac{\tau _ {w_2}}{\tau _{w_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{x_1}{x_2}}=\sqrt{\frac{15}{30}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\tau _ {w_2}}{\tau _{w_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} [/latex]
So, [latex] \tau _ {w_2}=\frac{tau _{w_1}}{\sqrt{2}} [/latex]

raw_source.solution:
Step -1: First identify type of flow - Subsonic or Supersonic by finding out Mach number

Mach no at start of flow

[latex] u_1 [/latex] is velocity of gas

raw_source.text:
Two surfaces P and Q are to be joined together. In which of the given joining
operation(s), there is no melting of the two surfaces P and Q for creating the joint?
raw_source.solution:
Soldering is define as a metal joining process wherein coalescence is produced by heating the surface to be joint to a suitable temperature and melting the filler metal which is a fusible alloy called solder (melting point usually less than [latex] 427^{\circ}C[/latex] ).
Principle underlying soldering is that when the surface to be jointed are cleaned off well from oxides they can be joined together using molten solder that may adhere easily with the workpiece.
Brazing is also one of the type of welding process which is used for joining the two similar or dissimilar metal piece together by heating the surface and by using a non-ferrous filler metal having its melting point above [latex] 427^{\circ}C[/latex] but below the melting point of metal to be brazed. The molten filler metal is distributed between the joint surface by the capillary action which on cooling results in a sound joint.

[latex]\mathrm{m}=20 \mathrm{~kg}[/latex]
So, [latex]\quad \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{K_{\text {eq }}}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2000}{20}}=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
So, [latex]\quad T_{n}=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega_{n}}=\frac{2 \pi}{10}[/latex]
Time taken for 10 oscillations [latex]=10 \times T_{n}=10 \times \frac{2 \pi}{\omega_{n}}=10 \times \frac{2 \pi}{10}=6.28 \mathrm{sec} [/latex]

A vector field
[latex] B(x,y,z)=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}-2z\hat{k}[/latex]
is defined over a conical region having height [latex] h=2[/latex], base radius [latex] r=3[/latex] and axis along [latex] z[/latex], as shown in the figure. The base of the cone lies in the [latex] x-y[/latex]plane and is centered at the origin.

Put in (i)

raw_source.text:
The value of [latex]k[/latex] that makes the complex-valued function

[latex] f(z)=e^{-kx}(\cos 2y -i \sin 2y)[/latex]

analytic, where [latex]z=x+iy[/latex], is _________. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned} & f(z)=e^{-k x} \cos 2 y-i e^{-k x} \sin 2 y \\ & \text { Suppose }=e^{-k x} \cos 2 y=4(x, y) \\ & =-i e^{-k x} \sin 2 y=v(x, y) \end{aligned} [/latex]
If function is analytical then it satisfy the equation
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=-k e^{-k x} \cos 2 y &...(i)\\ & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-2 e^{-k x} \sin 2 y &...(ii)\\ & \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=-k e^{-k x} \sin 2 y &...(iii)\\ & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=-2 e^{-k x} \cos 2 y &...(iv) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Cauchy-Riemann equation [latex]\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}[/latex]
by putting equation (i), (iv) and solve then [latex]k=2[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Which one of the options given is the inverse Laplace transform of [latex] \frac{1}{s^3-s}[/latex]
[latex] u(t)[/latex]denotes the unit-step function.

Inverse Laplace of [latex]\frac{1}{s^{3}-s} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A spherical ball weighing 2 kg is dropped from a height of 4.9 m onto an immovable rigid block as shown in the figure. If the collision is perfectly elastic, what is the momentum vector of the ball (in kg m/s) just after impact?
Take the acceleration due to gravity to be [latex]g=9.8 m/s^2[/latex]. Options have been rounded off to one decimal place.
raw_source.solution:
Let '[latex]\theta[/latex]' be the angle about line of impact through which ball will move often the impact.
Let '[latex]u[/latex]' be the vertical downward velocity of the ball before striking and '[latex]v[/latex]' be the velocity of ball after the impact which make an angle '[latex]\theta[/latex]' with the line of impact. As ball fall freely under the gravity from height [latex]\mathrm{h}=4.9 \mathrm{m}[/latex], hence downward velocity '[latex]\mathrm{u}[/latex]' at the instance of striking the rigid body
[latex]u=\sqrt{2 g h}=\sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 4.9}[/latex]
or, [latex]u=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
for perfectly elastic collision, [latex]e=1[/latex]
As [latex]e=\frac{\text { relative velocity of seperation }}{\text { relative velocity of approach }}=1\;\;...(i)[/latex]
As block is rigid, so block velocity [latex]=0[/latex].
So, along the line of impact,
relative velocity of approach [latex]=u \cos 30^{\circ}-0 =u \cos 30^{\circ}[/latex]
relative velocity of separation along the line of impact [latex]=v \cos \theta-0=v \cos \theta[/latex]
so, by equation (i)
[latex]u \cos 30^{\circ}=v \cos \theta \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
In the direction normal to the impact, the component velocity is not affected so,
[latex]u \sin 30^{\circ}=v \sin \theta \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
So, by equation (ii) and (iii)
[latex]V=\sqrt{u^{2} \cos ^{2} 30^{\circ}+u^{2} \sin ^{2} 30^{\circ}}[/latex]
or, [latex]V=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
by equation (ii) and (iii)
[latex]\tan \theta=\tan 30^{\circ}, \theta=30^{\circ}[/latex]
So, inclination to the plane for of the section
[latex]=90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}[/latex]
So, momentum equation is given by during seperation:

[latex] \vec{P}_{s}=m v \cos 30^{\circ} \hat{i}+m v \cos 30^{\circ} \hat{j} =17 \hat{i}+9.8 \hat{j} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The figure shows a wheel rolling without slipping on a horizontal plane with angular velocity [latex]\omega _1[/latex]. A rigid bar PQ is pinned to the wheel at P while the end Q slides on the floor.
What is the angular velocity [latex]\omega _1[/latex] of the bar PQ?
raw_source.solution:
As Disc (Link 2) roll without slipping on Link 1 (surface) so their I-centre of rotation lies on point of contact to avoid relative motion in between them. So [latex]\mathrm{I}_{12}[/latex] lies on point of contact.
Link 2 and 3 have instantaneous center of rotation at [latex]\mathrm{I}_{13}[/latex] due to fixed surface of Link 1.

As per point Plies on link 2 and 3 both so, point [latex]P[/latex] has same velocity for Link 2 and 3 both.
As per Kennedy's theorem, if three plane bodies have relative motion among themselves, their I-centre must lie on a straight line. So, [latex]\mathrm{I}_{23}[/latex] must be on line joining [latex]\mathrm{I}_{13}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{I}_{12}[/latex] at point P.
By similar [latex]\triangle \mathrm{PI}_{12} \mathrm{~B}[/latex] and [latex]\Delta \mathrm{Pl}_{13} \mathrm{~A}[/latex], we have
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{l}_{12} \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{l}_{12} \mathrm{~B}}=\frac{\mathrm{Pl_{13 }}}{\mathrm{PA}} [/latex]
or, [latex]\quad \frac{\mathrm{I}_{12} \mathrm{I}_{23}}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{23} \mathrm{l}_{13}}{8}[/latex]
or, [latex] \mathrm{I}_{12} \mathrm{l}_{13}=0.25 \mathrm{I}_{23} \mathrm{l}_{13} \;\;\;...(i) [/latex]
Velocity of point [latex]P[/latex] is same w.r.t. all instantaneous rotation so,
[latex] \omega_{1} \times I_{12} I_{23}=\omega_{2} \times I_{23} l_{13} [/latex]
By equation (i), we get
[latex] \omega_{2}=0.25 \omega_{1} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The figure shows a thin-walled open-top cylindrical vessel of radius [latex]r[/latex] and wall thickness [latex]t[/latex]. The vessel is held along the brim and contains a constant-density liquid to height [latex]h[/latex] from the base. Neglect atmospheric pressure, the weight of the vessel and bending stresses in the vessel walls.
Which one of the plots depicts qualitatively CORRECT dependence of the magnitudes of axial wall stress [latex](\sigma _1)[/latex] and circumferential wall stress [latex](\sigma _2)[/latex] on [latex]y[/latex]?
raw_source.solution:
Unit weight of liquid [latex]=\gamma[/latex]
[latex] \text { Weight of liquid }=\gamma \times \text { volume } [/latex]
[latex] W=\gamma \times\left(\pi r^{2}\right)(h) [/latex]
[latex] \sigma_{1}=\frac{W_{T}}{(2 \pi r \times t)}=\frac{\gamma \times \pi r^{2}(h)}{2 \pi r t}=\frac{\gamma r h}{2 t} [/latex]
[latex] \text { Pressure at } y^{\prime}=\gamma \times y [/latex]
[latex] \sigma_{2}(\text { circumterential stress })=\frac{P d}{2 t}=\frac{\gamma \times y \times 2 r}{2 t}=\frac{\gamma r y}{t} [/latex]

raw_source.text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
raw_source.solution:
Ideal gas follow the adiabatic equation [latex]\mathrm{PV}^{\gamma}=\mathrm{C}[/latex] and also follow the gas law [latex]P V=m R T[/latex]
Any real gas at low pressure and high temperature follow gas law, e.g. Air conditioning system.
Real gas follow Van der waal's gas equation for an adiabatic process as
[latex] \left(P+\frac{n^{2} a}{V^{a}}\right)(V-n b)^{\top}=k [/latex]
where
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}}}+1 \\ & \mathrm{k}=\mathrm{nRZ} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Enthalpy of an ideal gas is independent of pressure at constant temperature and the internal energy of an ideal gas is independent of volume at constant temperature.
options: For an ideal gas, the enthalpy is independent of pressure.

For a real gas going through an adiabatic reversible process, the process equation is given by [latex]PV^\gamma =[/latex] constant, where [latex]P[/latex] is the pressure, [latex]V[/latex] is the volume and [latex]\gamma [/latex] is the ratio of the specific heats
of the gas at constant pressure and constant volume.

For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible polytropic process [latex]PV^{1.5} =[/latex] constant, the equation
connecting the pressure, volume and temperature of the gas at any point along the process is [latex]\frac{P}{R}=\frac{mT}{V}[/latex]  where [latex]R[/latex] is the gas constant and  [latex]m[/latex] is the mass of the gas.

Any real gas behaves as an ideal gas at sufficiently low pressure or sufficiently high
temperature.

raw_source.text:
Consider a fully adiabatic piston-cylinder arrangement as shown in the figure. The piston is massless and cross-sectional area of the cylinder is [latex]A[/latex]. The fluid inside the cylinder is air (considered as a perfect gas), with [latex]\gamma [/latex] being the ratio of the specific heat at constant pressure to the specific heat at constant volume for air. The piston is initially located at a position [latex]L_1 [/latex]. The initial pressure of the air inside the cylinder is [latex]P_1 \gt \gt P_0 [/latex], where [latex]P_0 [/latex] is the atmospheric pressure. The stop [latex]S_1 [/latex] is instantaneously removed and the piston moves to the position [latex]L_2 [/latex], where the equilibrium pressure of air inside the cylinder is [latex]P_2 \gt \gt P_0 [/latex].
What is the work done by the piston on the atmosphere during this process?
raw_source.solution:
Initial volume [latex]\mathrm{V}_{1}=\mathrm{L}_{1} \times \mathrm{A}[/latex]
Final volume [latex]V_{2}=L_{2} \times A[/latex]
Work done by atmospheric air [latex]=\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}} P d v[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =P_{0} \int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}} d V \\ & =P_{0}\left(L_{2} A-L_{1} A\right) \\ & =P_{0} A\left(L_{2}-L_{1}\right) \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylindrical rod of length [latex]h [/latex] and diameter [latex]d [/latex] is placed inside a cubic enclosure of
side length [latex]L [/latex].  [latex]S [/latex]denotes the inner surface of the cube. The view-factor [latex]F_{S-S} [/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Surface area of centrifugal rod [latex]=\pi d h+\frac{2 \pi d^{2}}{4}[/latex]
Or [latex] A_{1}=\pi\left(d h+\frac{d^{2}}{2}\right) [/latex]
Surface area of cube [latex]A_{2}=6 \times \mathrm{L}^{2}[/latex]

For surface 1 (cylinder), [latex]\mathrm{F}_{11}=0[/latex]
So [latex] \mathrm{F}_{12}=1 \quad \text {...(i) } [/latex]

For surface 2(cube)
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{F}_{21}+\mathrm{F}_{22} & =1 \\ \mathrm{F}_{22} & =1-\mathrm{F}_{21} \\ \mathrm{F}_{21} & =1-\mathrm{F}_{22}\;\;...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
By reciprocity theorem for surface 1 and 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} A_{1} F_{12} & =A_{2} F_{21} \\ F_{21} & =\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\left[F_{12}=1\right.[/latex] from equation (i)]
So, By equation (ii)
[latex] F_{22}=F_{s S}=1-\left(\frac{\pi \mathrm{dh}+\frac{\pi d^{2}}{2}}{6 L^{2}}\right) [/latex]

raw_source.text:
In an ideal orthogonal cutting experiment (see figure), the cutting speed [latex]V[/latex] is 1 m/s, the rake angle of the tool [latex]\alpha =5^{\circ} [/latex], and the shear angle, [latex] \phi [/latex], is known to be [latex]45^{\circ} [/latex].
Applying the ideal orthogonal cutting model, consider two shear planes [latex]PQ[/latex] and [latex]RS[/latex] close to each other. As they approach the thin shear zone (shown as a thick line in the figure), plane [latex]RS[/latex] gets sheared with respect to [latex]PQ[/latex] (point [latex]R1[/latex] shears to [latex]R2[/latex], and [latex]S1[/latex] shears to [latex]S2[/latex]).
Assuming that the perpendicular distance between [latex]PQ[/latex] and [latex]RS[/latex] is [latex]\delta =25\mu m [/latex], what is the value of shear strain rate (in [latex]s^{-1} [/latex]) that the material undergoes at the shear zone?
raw_source.solution:
Data given [latex] \alpha=5^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \phi & =45^{\circ} \\ \Delta H & =25 \mu \mathrm{m} \\ \mathrm{V} & =1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}} & =\frac{\mathrm{V} \cos \alpha}{\cos (\phi-\alpha)}=\frac{1 \times \cos 5^{\circ}}{\cos (45-5)} \\ & =\frac{\cos 5}{\cos 40}=1.3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Shear strain rate [latex]=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\delta \mathrm{H}}=\frac{1.3}{25 \times 10^{-6}}=5.20 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{s}^{-1}[/latex]

raw_source.text: A CNC machine has one of its linear positioning axes as shown in the figure, consisting of a motor rotating a lead screw, which in turn moves a nut horizontally on which a table is mounted. The motor moves in discrete rotational steps of 50 steps per revolution. The pitch of the screw is 5 mm and the total horizontal traverse length of the table is 100 mm. What is the total number of controllable locations at which the table can be positioned on this axis?
raw_source.solution:
Revolution of motor is one step [latex]=\frac{1}{50} \mathrm{rev} / \mathrm{step}[/latex]
Pitch of lead screw [latex]=5 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
movement of table
[latex] \Rightarrow 100 \mathrm{~mm}=\frac{1}{50} \times 5 \times \text { no. of steps } [/latex]
or, no. of steps [latex]=1000[/latex]

raw_source.text:
Cylindrical bars P and Q have identical lengths and radii, but are composed of different linear elastic materials. The Young's modulus and coefficient of thermal expansion of Q are twice the corresponding values of P. Assume the bars to be perfectly bonded at the interface, and their weights to be negligible.
The bars are held between rigid supports as shown in the figure and the temperature is raised by [latex]\Delta T[/latex]. Assume that the stress in each bar is homogeneous and uniaxial. Denote the magnitudes of stress in P and Q by [latex]\sigma _1[/latex] and [latex]\sigma _2[/latex], respectively.
Which of the statement(s) given is/are CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Given: [latex] \alpha_{Q}=2 \alpha_{P} [/latex]

Given [latex]\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=\beta \ell [/latex]
[latex]E=[/latex] young's modulus
Change in temperature [latex]=\Delta \mathrm{T}[/latex]

where [latex]A=[/latex] cross sectional area of bar and is same for both due to same radii.
So, [latex]\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}[/latex]
Deformation in [latex]\mathrm{P}=\ell \alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}-\frac{\mathrm{P} \ell}{\mathrm{AE}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{P}}[/latex]
Deformation in [latex]\mathrm{Q}=2 \alpha \ell \Delta \mathrm{T}-\frac{\mathrm{P} \ell}{2 \mathrm{AE}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{Q}}[/latex]
[latex]\Delta_{\mathrm{Q}} \gt \Delta_{\mathrm{P}}[/latex]
options: The interface between P and Q moves to the left after heating
The interface between P and Q moves to the right after heating

option_texts: The interface between P and Q moves to the left after heating

raw_source.text: A very large metal plate of thickness [latex]d[/latex] and thermal conductivity [latex]k[/latex] is cooled by a stream of air at temperature [latex]T_{\infty }=300K[/latex] with a heat transfer coefficient [latex]h[/latex], as shown in the figure. The centerline temperature of the plate is [latex]T_P[/latex]. In which of the following case(s) can the lumped parameter model be used to study the heat transfer in the metal plate?
raw_source.solution:
For lumped heat analysis
[latex] \mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{i}} \leq 0.1 [/latex]
[latex] L_{c} =\frac{\text { volume }}{\text { surface area }} =\frac{d \times L \times L}{L \times L+L \times L}=\frac{d}{2} [/latex]

(a) [latex]B_{i}=\frac{100 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-3}}{100}=0.5 \times 10^{-4} \leq 0.5[/latex]

(c) [latex]B_{i}=\frac{h L_{c}}{\mathrm{~K}}=\frac{100 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-3}}{1000}=0.5 \times 10^{-4} \leq 0.1[/latex]

(b) [latex]\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{\mathrm{hL}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{K}}=\frac{100 \times 0.5}{100}=0.5 \gt 0.1[/latex]

(d) [latex]B_{i}=\frac{1000 \times 0.5}{1}=500 \gt 0.1[/latex]
Hence, answer is [latex](A, C)[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Heat Transfer in Flow Over Plates and Pipes

raw_source.text:
The smallest perimeter that a rectangle with area of 4 square units can have is
______ units.
(Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Given [latex]\quad B \times L=4[/latex]
Perimeter [latex](P)=2 B+2 L[/latex]
perimeter to be smallest possible
[latex] \frac{d P}{d B}=0=\frac{d}{d B}\left(2 B+2 \times \frac{4}{B}\right)=0 [/latex]
[latex]2-\frac{8}{B^{2}}=0 [/latex]
[latex]B=\pm 2 \Rightarrow B=2 \quad L=2[/latex]
Smallest perimeter [latex]=2(B+L)=2(2+2)=8 [/latex]

[latex] \frac{x d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+\frac{x d y}{d x}-y=0, x \geq 1 [/latex]
This is an Euler-cauchy equation and has solutions of the form
[latex] \begin{aligned} & y=x^{n} \\ & y^{\prime}=n x^{n-1} \\ & y^{\prime \prime}=n(n-1) x^{n-2} \\ & x^{2}(n)(n-1) x^{n-2}+x\left(n x^{n-1}\right)-x^{n}=0 \\ & x^{n}[x(n-1)+n-1)=0 \\ & n^{2}-1=0 \\ & n=\pm 1 \\ & y_{1}=x \\ & y_{2}=\frac{1}{x} \\ & y=C_{1} x+\frac{C_{2}}{x} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given [latex]y(x=1)=6[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 6 & =C_{1}(1)+\frac{C_{2}}{(1)} \\ C_{1}+C_{2} & =6 \;\;\;...(i)\\ \frac{d y}{d x} & =C_{1}-\frac{C_{2}}{x^{2}}=2 \\ x & =1 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] C_{1}=C_{2}=2 [/latex]
[latex]C_{1}=4, C_{2}=2 [/latex]
[latex]y(x=2)=4(2)+\frac{2}{(2)}=9 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The initial value problem

[latex]\frac{dy}{dt} +2y=0,\;\;y(0)=1[/latex]

is solved numerically using the forward Euler's method with a constant and positive time step of [latex]\Delta t[/latex].
Let [latex]y_n[/latex] represent the numerical solution obtained after [latex]n[/latex] steps. The condition [latex]|y_{n+1}| \leq |y_n|[/latex] is satisfied if and only if [latex]\Delta t[/latex] does not exceed _____. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Solution of differential equation given by forward Euler's method is
[latex] y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h f\left(x_{n}, y_{n}\right) [/latex]
Given: [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}+2 y=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y[/latex]
and step size, [latex]\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad y_{n+1}=y_{n}+\Delta t\left(-2 y_{n}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}=\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}(1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t})[/latex]
[latex]\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}=1-2 \Delta t \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]

Given:
[latex] \left|y_{n+1}\right| \leq\left|y_{n}\right| [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad\left|\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}\right| \leq 1[/latex]

From equation (i)
[latex]\therefore \quad|1-2 \Delta t| \leq 1[/latex]

Case (i) when [latex](1-2 \Delta t) \gt 0[/latex] :
Then, [latex]\quad 1-2 \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]
[latex] \Delta t \geq 0 [/latex]

Case (ii) when [latex](1-2 \Delta t) \lt 0[/latex] :
then [latex]-(1-2 \Delta t) \leq 1[/latex]
[latex] 1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t} \geq-1 [/latex]
[latex] \Delta \mathrm{t} \leq 1 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Value of [latex]\Delta t: 0 \leq \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]

raw_source.text:
The atomic radius of a hypothetical face-centered cubic (FCC) metal is [latex](\sqrt{2}/10)[/latex] nm. The atomic weight of the metal is 24.092 g/mol. Taking
Avogadros number to be [latex]6.023 \times 10^{23}[/latex]  atoms/mol, the density of the metal is
_______ [latex]kg/m^3[/latex]. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Data given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} r & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{10} \mathrm{~nm} \\ M & =24.092 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{mol} \\ \mathrm{A} & =6.023 \times 10^{13} \end{aligned} [/latex]
For FCC structure [latex]a=2 \sqrt{2} r=2 \sqrt{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{10}=\frac{4}{10}[/latex]
So,volume of unit cell [latex]=a^{3}=\left(\frac{4}{10}\right)^{3}=0.064 \mathrm{~nm}^{3}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{Ne}=4[/latex] for [latex]\mathrm{FCC}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \rho & =\frac{N_{e} \times M}{A \times \text { Volume of unit cell }} \\ & =\frac{4 \times \frac{24.092}{1000}}{6.023 \times 10^{3} \times \frac{0.064}{\left(10^{-9}\right)^{3}}} \\ & =2500 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A steel sample with 1.5 wt. % carbon (no other alloying elements present) is slowly cooled from [latex]1100^{\circ}C[/latex] to just below the eutectoid temperature ([latex]723^{\circ}C[/latex]). A part of the iron-cementite phase diagram is shown in the figure. The ratio of the pro-eutectoid cementite content to the total cementite content in the microstructure that develops just below the eutectoid temperature is ________.
(Rounded off to two decimal places)
raw_source.solution:
Mass friction of proeutectoid cementite [latex] \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{Fe}_{3}} C^{\prime}=\frac{1.5-0.8}{6.7-0.8}=0.1186 [/latex]

Mass fraction of total cementite
[latex] \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{Fe}_{3}} \mathrm{C}=\frac{1.5-0.035}{6.7-0.035}=0.2197 [/latex]

So, [latex]\quad \frac{W_{F_{3}} C^{\prime}}{W_{F_{e 3}} C}=\frac{0.1186}{0.2197}=0.54[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A part, produced in high volumes, is dimensioned as shown. The machining process making this part is known to be statistically in control based on sampling data. The sampling data shows that D1 follows a normal distribution with a mean of 20 mm and a standard deviation of 0.3 mm, while D2 follows a normal distribution with a mean of 35 mm and a standard deviation of 0.4 mm. An inspection of dimension C is carried out in a sufficiently large number of parts.
To be considered under six-sigma process control, the upper limit of dimension C should be ______ mm.
(Rounded off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
D1 and D2 follow normal distribution.
So,
Upper limit [latex]=\mu +3\sigma [/latex]
Lower limit [latex]=\mu -3\sigma [/latex]
[latex]\bar{D1}=20mm, \bar{D2}=35mm, \sigma _{D2}=0.4mm,\sigma _{D1}=0.3mm[/latex]
Mean value of [latex] (\bar{C}) =\bar{D2}-\bar{D1}=35-20-15[/latex]
Standard Devialtion of C
[latex]\sigma _C^2=\sigma _{D2}^2 -\sigma _{D1}^2 [/latex]
[latex]\sigma _C=\sqrt{0.4^2-0.3^2}=0.2645 [/latex]
Upper Limit of C [latex] \bar{C}+6 \times \sigma _C=15+6 \times 0.2645=16.587 [/latex]

raw_source.text: A coordinate measuring machine (CMM) is used to determine the distance between Surface SP and Surface SQ of an approximately cuboidal shaped part. Surface SP is declared as the datum as per the engineering drawing used for manufacturing this part. The CMM is used to measure four points P1, P2, P3, P4 on Surface SP, and four points Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 on Surface SQ as shown. A regression procedure is used to fit the necessary planes. The distance between the two fitted planes is _______ mm. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Since [latex]y[/latex]-coordinate of all four points [latex]P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{P}_{4}[/latex] is zero. Hence the regression plane fitted by points [latex]P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}[/latex] and [latex]P_{4}[/latex] is [latex]x-z[/latex] plane.
The distance of any point (i.e. [latex]\mathrm{Q}_{1}, \mathrm{Q}_{2}, \mathrm{Q}_{3}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Q}_{4}[/latex] ) from [latex]x-z[/latex] plane is equal to [latex]y[/latex] co-ordinate

Therefore,
The distance of [latex]Q_{1}[/latex] from [latex]x-z[/latex] plan [latex]=6 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
The distance of [latex]Q_{2}[/latex] from [latex]x-z[/latex] plan [latex]=6 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
The distance of [latex]Q_{3}[/latex] from [latex]x-z[/latex] plan [latex]=4 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
The distance of [latex]Q_{4}[/latex] from [latex]x-z[/latex] plan [latex]=4 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
The distance of best fitted plane by [latex]Q_{1}, Q_{2}, Q_{3}[/latex] and [latex]Q_{4}[/latex] from [latex]x-z[/latex] plane is equal to average of 6,6,4 and 4 , which is equal to [latex]5 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex].
Hence, the distance between two fitted planes is [latex]5 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex].

raw_source.text:
A solid part (see figure) of polymer material is to be fabricated by additive manufacturing (AM) in square-shaped layers starting from the bottom of the part working upwards. The nozzle diameter of the AM machine is [latex]a/10[/latex] mm and the nozzle follows a linear serpentine path parallel to the sides of the square layers with a feed rate of [latex]a/5[/latex] mm/min.
Ignore any tool path motions other than those involved in adding material, and any other delays between layers or the serpentine scan lines.
The time taken to fabricate this part is _______ minutes. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \begin{aligned}
 V&=(3a)^2 \times 1.5a+ (2a)^2 \times a+(a)^2 \times 0.5a\\ 
 &= 18a^3\\ 
 T&=\frac{V}{\left ( \frac{a}{10} \right )^2 \times \left ( \frac{a}{5} \right )} \\
&=\frac{18a^3}{a^3} \times 100 \times 5=9000 min
\end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text: An optical flat is used to measure the height difference between a reference slip gauge A and a slip gauge B. Upon viewing via the optical flat using a monochromatic light of wavelength 0.5 [latex]\mu m [/latex], 12 fringes were observed over a length of 15 mm of gauge B. If the gauges are placed 45 mm apart, the height difference of the gauges is ______ [latex]\mu m [/latex]. (Answer in integer)

Ignoring the small elastic region, the true stress  [latex](\sigma) -  [/latex] true strain [latex]( \varepsilon)  [/latex] variation of a
material beyond yielding follows the equation [latex]\sigma =400 \varepsilon ^{0.3}  [/latex] MPa. The engineering
ultimate tensile strength value of this material is ________ MPa.
(Rounded off to one decimal place)
raw_source.solution:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{T}} & =400 \varepsilon^{0.3}=400 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{T}}^{0.3} \;\;\;...(i)\\ \varepsilon & =\text { true strain }=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{T}} \\ \mathrm{n} & =0.3=\text { strain hardening exponent } \end{aligned} [/latex]
The true strain [latex]\left(\varepsilon_{T}\right)[/latex] at the onset of necking equal to the strain hardening exponent i.e. at ultimate tensile point.
So, [latex]\quad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{n}=0.3[/latex] at ultimate point
So, from equation (i)
[latex] \sigma_{\mathrm{T}} =400 \times(0.3)^{0.3} =278.74 \mathrm{MPa} \text { at ultimate point } [/latex]
As [latex] \varepsilon_{\mathrm{T}}=\ln (1+\varepsilon) [/latex]
So, [latex] \varepsilon=\mathrm{e}^{\varepsilon} \mathrm{T}-1=\mathrm{e}^{0.3}-1=0.35 [/latex]
and [latex] \sigma_{\mathrm{T}}=\sigma(1+\varepsilon) [/latex]
So [latex] \sigma_{\text {ultimate }}=\frac{\sigma_{T}}{1+\varepsilon}+\frac{278.74}{1+0.35}=206.55 \mathrm{MPa} [/latex]

raw_source.text: The area moment of inertia about the y-axis of a linearly tapered section shown in the figure is ______ [latex]m^4[/latex]. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
Above figure is symmetrical about [latex]{x}[/latex] axis so, moment of inertia of whole section will be two times of the one section above [latex]x[/latex]-axis.

Moment of inertia of rectangular section OABC about [latex]y[/latex]-axis i.e. OC.
[latex]=\frac{1}{3} \times \mathrm{OC} \times(\mathrm{AB})^{3}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{1}{3} \times d \times b^{3}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{OC}}=\frac{1}{3} \times 3 \times(12)^{3}=1728[/latex]

Moment of inertia of triangular section BCD about [latex]y[/latex]-axis i.e. about DC
[latex] \mathrm{I}_{D C}=\frac{1}{12} \times(D C) \times(B C)^{3} =\frac{1}{12} \times 1.5 \times(12)^{3}=216 [/latex]

So, moment of inertia of tapered section OABD about y-axis:
[latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{y}^{\prime} \mathrm{y}^{\prime}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{OC}}-\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{DC}}[/latex]
[latex]=1728-216=1512[/latex]
So, moment of inertia of whole tapered section
[latex]I_{y y}=2 l_{y^{\prime} y^{\prime}}=2 \times 1512=3024 \mathrm{~m}^{4}[/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylindrical bar has a length [latex]L=5m [/latex] and cross section area [latex]S=10m^2 [/latex]. The bar is made of a linear elastic material with a density [latex]\rho =2700kg/m^3 [/latex] and Young's modulus [latex]E=70GPa [/latex]. The bar is suspended as shown in the figure and is in a state of uniaxial tension due to its self-weight.
The elastic strain energy stored in the bar equals ____ J. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
Take the acceleration due to gravity as [latex]g=9.8 m/s^2 [/latex]
raw_source.solution:
Given data length [latex]L=5 \mathrm{~m}[/latex]
cross-sectional area [latex]A=10 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex]
Density of bar, [latex]\rho=2700 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
Young's modulus [latex]\mathrm{E}=70 \mathrm{GPa}[/latex]
Bar is in a state of uniaxial tension due to its self weight so the elastic energy stored in the bar.

[latex] \begin{aligned} U & =\int_{0}^{L} \frac{P_{e}^{2} d x}{2 A E}=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{\left(\frac{w}{L} x\right)^{2} d x}{2 A E} \\ & =\frac{w^{2} L^{3}}{L^{2} 6 A E}=\frac{\gamma^{2} L^{3} A}{6 E} \end{aligned} [/latex]
where, [latex]\gamma=[/latex] weight/volume [latex]=\frac{\mathrm{W}}{\mathrm{AL}}[/latex]
weight of the bar [latex]W=\rho g V[/latex]
So,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \gamma & =\frac{\rho g V}{A L} \quad \because V=A \cdot L \\ \gamma & =\rho g \\ V & =\rho g \frac{(\rho g)^{2} L^{3} \mathrm{~A}}{6 \mathrm{E}} \\ & =\frac{(2700 \times 9.8)^{2} \times(5)^{3} \times 10}{6 \times 70 \times 10^{9}} \\ & V=2.08 \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
A cylindrical transmission shaft of length 1.5 m and diameter 100 mm is made of a linear elastic material with a shear modulus of 80 GPa. While operating at 500 rpm, the angle of twist across its length is found to be 0.5 degrees.
The power transmitted by the shaft at this speed is _______kW. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
Take [latex]\pi= 3.14[/latex].
raw_source.solution:
Given: Length, [latex]L=1.5 \mathrm{~m}[/latex], Dia, [latex]d=100 \mathrm{~mm}=0.1 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex]
Shear modulus, [latex]\mathrm{G}=80 \mathrm{GPa}[/latex]
[latex] N=500 \mathrm{rpm} \text {, } [/latex]
angle of twist,
[latex]\theta=0.5^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex] \theta=0.5 \times \frac{\pi}{180^{\circ}} \mathrm{rad} [/latex]

[latex]\because [/latex] As, We know,
[latex] \frac{\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{J}}=\frac{\mathrm{G} \theta}{\mathrm{L}} [/latex]
where [latex]\mathrm{J}[/latex] for cylinder solid shaft [latex]=\frac{\pi \mathrm{d}^{4}}{32}[/latex]

Torque,
[latex] T=\frac{G \theta \cdot J}{L}=\frac{\left(80 \times 10^{9}\right) \times\left(0.5 \times \frac{\pi}{180}\right)}{1.5} \times \frac{\pi}{32} \times(0.1)^{4} =4.56 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{m} [/latex]

Now, power,
[latex]\quad P=T \times \omega=T \times \frac{2 \pi N}{60} =4.56 \times 10^{3} \times \frac{2 \pi \times 500}{60}[/latex]
[latex] P =238.64 \mathrm{~kW} [/latex]

Consider a mixture of two ideal gases, X and Y, with molar masses [latex]\bar{M}_X=10kg/kmol [/latex] and [latex]\bar{M}_Y=20kg/kmol [/latex], respectively, in a container. The total pressure in the container is 100 kPa, the total volume of the container is [latex]10m^3 [/latex] and the temperature of the contents of the container is 300 K. If the mass of gas-X in the container is 2 kg, then the mass of gas-Y in the container is ____ kg. (Rounded off to one decimal place)
Assume that the universal gas constant is 8314 [latex]J \;kmol^{-1}K^{-1}[/latex]
raw_source.solution:
By gas law
[latex] \mathrm{Pv}=\mathrm{nRT} [/latex]
where [latex]\mathrm{n}=[/latex] total value of gas in container
[latex] \begin{aligned} 100 \times 10 & =n \times 8.314 \times 300 \\ n & =0.4 \end{aligned} [/latex]
and [latex] \mathrm{n}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{y}} [/latex]
Or, [latex]0.4=\frac{m_{x}}{M_{x}}+\frac{m_{y}}{M_{y}}=\frac{2}{10}+\frac{m_{y}}{20}[/latex] or, [latex] m_{y}=4 \mathrm{~kg} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The velocity field of a certain two-dimensional flow is given by
[latex]V(x,y)=k(x\hat{i}-y\hat{j}) [/latex]
where [latex]k=2s^{-1}[/latex]. The coordinates [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] are in meters. Assume gravitational effects to be negligible.
If the density of the fluid is [latex]1000kg/m^3[/latex] and the pressure at the origin is 100 kPa, the pressure at the location (2 m, 2 m) is _____________ kPa. (Answer in integer)
raw_source.solution:
To find the pressure at location [latex](2 m, 2 m)[/latex] we apply Bernouli's equation

[latex] P_{1}+\frac{1}{2} \rho V_{1}^{2}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} P V_{2}^{2} [/latex]

We will apply this equation between two points Origin [latex](0,0)[/latex] and location [latex](2 \mathrm{~m}, 2 \mathrm{~m})[/latex]

At Origin [latex](0,0)[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & V=k(x \hat{i}-y \hat{j}) \\ & V_{1}=2(0-0)=0 \\ & P_{1}=100 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At Iocation [latex](2,2)[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & V=2(2 \hat{i}-2 \hat{j}) \\ & \vec{V}=4 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j} \end{aligned} [/latex]

magnitude of velocity
[latex] \begin{aligned} & V_{2}=\sqrt{4^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{32} \\ & V_{2}=\sqrt{16 \times 2}=4 \sqrt{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Applying Bernouli's theorem
[latex]100,000+\frac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times 0=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times 32[/latex]
So [latex]P_{2}+16,000=100,000[/latex]
[latex] P_{2}=100,000-16,000 [/latex]
[latex] P_{2}=84,000 \mathrm{~Pa}=84 \mathrm{kPa} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider a unidirectional fluid flow with the velocity field given by
[latex]V(x,y,z,t)=u(x,t)\hat{i}[/latex]
where [latex]u(0,t)=1[/latex]. If the spatially homogeneous density field varies with time [latex]t[/latex] as
[latex]\rho (t)=1+0.2e^{-t}[/latex]
the value of [latex]u(2,1)[/latex] is _______. (Rounded off to two decimal places)

Assume all quantities to be dimensionless.
raw_source.solution:
Continuity equation for unsteady flow
[latex]\rho \frac{\partial \mathrm{u}}{\partial \mathrm{x}}+\rho \frac{\partial \mathrm{v}}{\partial \mathrm{y}}+\rho \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \mathrm{z}}+\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \mathrm{t}}=0[/latex]
Here [latex]V(x, y, z, t)=u(x, t) \hat{i}[/latex]
So [latex] v=0 [/latex]
[latex] \omega=0 [/latex]
[latex] \rho \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}=0 [/latex]

Given [latex]\rho(t)=1+0.2 e^{-t}[/latex]
So, [latex]\left[1+0.2 e^{-t}\right] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left[1+0.2 e^{-t}\right]=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\left(1+0.2 e^{-t}\right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}-0.2 e^{-t}=0 \\ &\left(1+0.2 e^{-t}\right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0.2 e^{-t} \\ & \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\left[\frac{0.2 e^{-t}}{1+0.2 e^{-t}}\right] \\ & u=\left[\frac{0.2 e^{-t}}{1+0.2 e^{-t}}\right] x+C \end{aligned} [/latex]

Since
[latex] \begin{aligned} u(0, t) & =1 \text { so } C=1 \\ u & =\left[\frac{0.2 e^{-t}}{1+0.2 e^{-t}}\right] x+1 \\ u(2,1)(x, t) & =\left[\frac{0.2 e^{-1}}{1+0.2 e^{-1}}\right] \times 2+1 \\ u(2,1) & =1.137 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \approx 1.14 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{F}_{2}=[/latex] Area of rectangle [latex]\mathrm{DEBF} \times[/latex] width

Location of forces from top

Pressure at depth [latex]1 \mathrm{~m}=\rho_{1} \mathrm{gh}_{1}[/latex]

[latex] BF=9810 \frac{N}{m^{2}} [/latex]

Pressure at depth [latex]3 m[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \rho_{1} g h_{1}+\rho_{2} g h_{2} \\ & 9810+2000 \times 9.81 \times 2 \\ & 9810+39240=49050 \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] (B F)+(F C)=B C [/latex]

Location of forces from bottom hinge
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{F}_{1} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{~m}-\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{~m}=\frac{7}{3} \mathrm{~m} \\ & \mathrm{~F}_{2} \rightarrow 3 m-2 m=1 \mathrm{~m} \\ & \mathrm{~F}_{3} \rightarrow 3 m-\frac{7}{3} \mathrm{~m}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Moment about hinge [latex] \mathrm{F}_{1} \times \frac{7}{3}+\mathrm{F}_{2} \times 1+\mathrm{F}_{3} \times \frac{2}{3} [/latex]
[latex]4905 \times \frac{7}{3}+19620+39240 \times \frac{2}{3}[/latex]

An explosion at time [latex]t=0[/latex] releases energy [latex]E[/latex] at the origin in a space filled with a gas of density [latex]\rho [/latex]. Subsequently, a hemispherical blast wave propagates radially outwards as shown in the figure.

raw_source.solution:
Radius, [latex]R=f(t, E, \rho)[/latex]
Where, [latex]\mathrm{t}=[/latex] time, [latex]\mathrm{E}=[/latex] Release energy [latex]\& \rho=[/latex] density
Dimension, [latex]\mathrm{R}=[\mathrm{L}][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & t=[\mathrm{T}] \\ & E=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{2} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right] \\ & \rho=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-3}\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]
Fundamental dimensions are [latex]\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{T}[/latex] (basic)
Total no. of variables [latex]=4[/latex]
No. of [latex]\pi[/latex]. terms [latex]=4-3=1[/latex]
So, [latex]R=t^{a} E^{b} \rho^{c}[/latex]
[latex] [\mathrm{L}]=[\mathrm{T}]^{\mathrm{a}}\left[\mathrm{ML}^{2} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]^{\mathrm{b}}\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-3}\right]^{\mathrm{c}} [/latex]
Comparing both side indices of [latex]M, L, T[/latex]
[latex]a-2b = 0, 2b-3c = 1, b+c = 0 \Rightarrow b-c[/latex]
[latex]a = 2 b, 2(-c) - 3c = 1 [/latex]
[latex]-5c = 1, c =(-1)/5 \Rightarrow b=1/5[/latex]
So, [latex]a=2 \times \frac{1}{5} = \frac{2}{5} [/latex]
Relation, [latex] R=kt^{2/5}E^{1/5}\rho ^{-1/5}=\frac{kt^{2/5}E^{1/5}}{\rho ^{1/5}} [/latex]
[latex] [/latex]
Where, [latex]a=\frac{2}{5}=0.40 [/latex]

Consider the following inequalities

[latex] p^2-4q \lt 4[/latex]
[latex]3p+2q \lt 6[/latex]

where [latex] p[/latex] and [latex] q[/latex] are positive integers.

[latex] \begin{aligned} p^2-4q &\lt 4 \\ p^2-4&\ lt 4q \;\;...(i)\\ 3p+2Q& \lt 6 \\ 6p-12 &\lt -4q\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{by equation (i) + (ii)} \\ p^2+6p-16 &\lt 0 \\ (p+8)(p-2)& \lt 0 \\ \therefore \; p&\in (-8,2) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given p is positive integer
[latex]\therefore \;p=1[/latex]
Now, from equation (i), [latex]1-4 \lt 4q [/latex]
[latex] q \gt \frac{-3}{4} [/latex]
from equation (ii),
[latex]q \lt 3/2 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \frac{-3}{4} \lt q \lt \frac{3}{2} [/latex]
Given q is positive integer
[latex]\therefore \;\; q=1 [/latex]
Thus [latex] p + q = 1+1 = 2 [/latex]

Consider a steady incompressible flow through a channel as shown below.

The velocity profile is uniform with a value of [latex]u_0[/latex] at the inlet section A. The velocity profile at section B downstream is
[latex]u=\left\{\begin{matrix} V_m\frac{y}{\delta }, & 0\leq y\leq \delta \\ V_m,& \delta \leq y\leq H-\delta \\ V_m\frac{H-y}{\delta }, & H-\delta \leq y\leq H \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

The ratio [latex]\frac{P_{A}-P_{B}}{\frac{1}{2}\rho u_{0}^{2}}[/latex] (where and [latex]P_{A}[/latex] are [latex]P_{B}[/latex] the pressures at section A and B, respectively, and [latex]\rho[/latex] is the density of the fluid) is
raw_source.solution:
Applying Bernoulli's equation at sections A and B,we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{A}}{p_{g}}+\frac{u_{0}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{A}&=\frac{p_{A}}{p g}+\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{B} \\ \frac{p_{A}}{\rho g}+\frac{u_{0}^{2}}{2 g}&=\frac{p_{B}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{2 g} \quad \because z_{A}=z_{B}\\ \text{or }\quad \frac{p_{A}}{\rho g}-\frac{p_{B}}{\rho g}&=\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{2 g}-\frac{u_{0}^{2}}{2 g} \\ \text{or }\quad p_{A}-p_{B}&=\frac{\rho V_{m}^{2}}{2}-\frac{\rho u_{0}^{2}}{2} \\ \text{Now, the ratio}\\ \frac{p_{A}-p_{B}}{\frac{1}{2} \rho u_{0}^{2}} &=\frac{\frac{\rho V_{m}^{2}}{2}-\frac{\rho u_{0}^{2}}{2}}{\frac{1}{2} \rho u_{0}^{2}} \\ &=\frac{V_{m}^{2}-u_{0}^{2}}{u_{0}^{2}}=\left(\frac{V_{m}}{u_{0}}\right)^{2}-1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting the value of [latex]\frac{V_{m}}{u_{0}}=\frac{1}{1-(\delta / H)} [/latex]

[latex] \frac{p_{A}-p_{B}}{\frac{1}{2} \rho u_{0}^{2}}=\frac{1}{[1-(\delta / H)]^{2}}-1[/latex]
raw_source.tag2: Viscous, Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer Theory

raw_source.text:
In order to numerically solve the ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}=-y[/latex] for [latex]t > 0[/latex], with an initial condition [latex]y(0)=1[/latex], the following scheme is employed

[latex]\frac{\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}-\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}-1}+\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}\right)[/latex]

Here, [latex]\Delta t[/latex] is the time step and [latex]y_{n}=y(n \Delta t)[/latex] for [latex]n[/latex] [latex]=0,1,2, \ldots[/latex] Thus numerical scheme will yield a solution with non-physical oscillations for [latex]\Delta \mathrm{t} > \mathrm{h}[/latex]. The value of [latex]\mathrm{h}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{y_{n+1}-y_n}{\Delta t} & =\frac{1}{2}\left(y_{n+1}+y_n\right) \\ y_{n+1}-y_n & =\frac{\Delta t}{2}\left(y_{n+1}+y_n\right) \\ y_{n+1}-\frac{\Delta t}{2} y_{n+1} & =y_n+\frac{\Delta t}{2} y_n \\ y_{n+1} & =\frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t} y_n \end{aligned} [/latex]
For stability or non physical oscillations,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left|\frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t}\right| & \leq 1 \\ -1 & \leq \frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t} \leq 1 \\ -1 & \leq-1+\frac{4}{2-\Delta t} \leq 1 \\ 0 & \leq \frac{4}{2-\Delta t} \leq 2 \\ \frac{1}{2} & \leq \frac{2-\Delta t}{4} \leq 0 \\ 2 & \leq 2-\Delta t \leq 0 \\ 0 & \leq-\Delta t \leq-2 \\ \Delta t & \geq 2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \Delta t \geq 2 [/latex]
Thus from given options, option (D) is correct.

raw_source.text:
The value of the surface integral

[latex] \oiint_{S} z d x d y [/latex]

where [latex]S[/latex] is the external surface of the sphere [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=R^{2}[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
Surface Integration is defined as
[latex]\int_{\mathrm{S}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{n} d s}=\oiint_{\mathrm{R}} \mathrm{F}_{1} \mathrm{dydz}+\mathrm{F}_{2} \mathrm{~d} x \mathrm{dz}+\mathrm{F}_{3} \mathrm{dx} \mathrm{dy}[/latex]
[latex]=\oiint_{\mathrm{R}} z \mathrm{dxdy}[/latex]

This means [latex]F_{1}=0, F_{2}=0, F_{3}=Z[/latex]
[latex]\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=Z \hat{\mathrm{K}}[/latex]
[latex]\nabla \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=1[/latex]

Using Gauss Divergence Theorem [latex]\int_{S} \vec{F} \cdot \hat{n} d s=\int_{V} \nabla \cdot \vec{F} d V=\int_{V} d V[/latex]
[latex]=[/latex] Volume of surface [latex]=\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^{3}[/latex]

raw_source.text: Let [latex]f(z)[/latex] be an analytic function, where [latex]z=x+i y[/latex]. If the real part of [latex]f(z)[/latex] is [latex]\cosh x \cos y[/latex], and the imaginary part of [latex]f(z)[/latex] is zero for [latex]y=0[/latex], then [latex]f(z)[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
The necessary and sufficient condition for a function [latex]f(z)=u(x, y)+i v(x, y)[/latex] to be analytic is it should satisfy the cauchy Riemann equation.

C.R. equation:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \quad \text { or, } \quad u_{x}=v_{y} [/latex]
[latex]\&, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}[/latex] or, [latex]u_{y}=-v_{x}[/latex]
Given: [latex]\quad \mathrm{u}=\cosh \mathrm{x} \cos y[/latex]
Now, [latex]\quad u_{x}=\sinh x \cos y[/latex]
and, [latex]\quad u_{y}=-\cosh x \sin y[/latex]

To find [latex]f(z)[/latex], put [latex]x=z \& y=0[/latex];
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(z)&=\int\left(u_{x}-i u_{y}\right) d z \\ &=\int[\sinh z \cdot \cos 0-(-\cosh z \cdot \sin 0)] d z \\ &=\int \sinh z d z=\cosh z+C \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Consider the system of linear equations.

[latex]x+2 y+z=5[/latex]
[latex]2 x+a y+4 z=12[/latex]
[latex]2 x+4 y+6 z=b[/latex]

The values of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] such that there exists a non-trivial null space and the system admits infinite solutions are
raw_source.solution:
If [latex]\rho(A B)=\rho(A) \lt [/latex] No. of unknowns, then the system having infinite number of solutions.
Given:
[latex] \begin{aligned} x+2 y+z & =5 \\ 2 x+a y+4 z & =12 \\ 2 x+4 y+6 z & =b \end{aligned} [/latex]
Augmented matrix, [latex]\rho(A B)=\left[\begin{array}{ccc:c}1 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & a & 4 & 12 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 & b\end{array}\right][/latex]
[latex] R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}-2 R_{1} \quad \& \quad R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3}-2 R_{1} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \rho(A B)=\left[\begin{array}{ccc:c} 1 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & a-4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & b-10 \end{array}\right] [/latex]

Now, for infinite solution
[latex] \begin{array}{ll} & \rho(A)=\rho(A B) \lt 3 \\ \text { i.e. } & \rho(A)=\rho(A B)=2 \end{array} [/latex]
Since, for [latex]\rho(A)=2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & a-4=0 \\ \Rightarrow & a=4 \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex]\&[/latex], for [latex]\rho(A B)=2[/latex],
[latex] b-10=4 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad b=14 [/latex]

raw_source.text:
The velocity field of a two-dimensional, incompressible flow is given by

[latex] \vec{V}=2 \sinh x \hat{i}+v(x, y) \hat{j} [/latex]

where [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] denote the unit vectors in [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] directions, respectively. If [latex]v(x, 0)=\cosh x[/latex], then [latex]v(0,-1)[/latex] is
raw_source.solution:
For an incompressible flow, [latex]\nabla \cdot \vec{V}=0[/latex]
Given; the velocity field of a two-dimensional, incompressible flow,
[latex]\vec{V}=2 \sinh x \hat{i}+v(x, y) \hat{j} \& \quad v(x, 0)=\cosh x[/latex]
Now, [latex]\nabla \cdot \vec{V}=0[/latex] (for an incompressible flow)
i.e. [latex]\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0[/latex]
[latex] 2 \cosh x+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \partial \mathbf{v}=-2 \cosh \mathrm{x} \cdot \partial \mathrm{y}[/latex]

Integrate both sides,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \int \partial v=-\int 2 \cosh x \cdot \partial y \\ & v=-2 y \cosh x+C \;\;\;...(1) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given; [latex]\mathrm{v}(\mathrm{x}, 0)=\cosh \mathrm{x}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \cosh x=-2(0) \cosh x+C[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{C}=\cosh \mathrm{x}[/latex]

Now, from equation (1)
[latex] \begin{aligned} v(x, y) & =-2 y \cosh x+\cosh x \\ & =(1-2 y) \cosh x \end{aligned} [/latex]
At [latex](0,-1)[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{v}(0,-1) & =[1-2(-1)] \cosh (0) \\ & =3 \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] \dot{\mathrm{q}}_{\mathrm{g}} \rightarrow 0 [/latex]
As [latex]\quad \dot{\mathrm{q}}=-\mathrm{kA} \frac{\mathrm{dT}}{\mathrm{dx}}[/latex]
or, [latex]\quad \frac{\dot{q}}{\mathrm{~A}}=\mathrm{C}[/latex]
[latex] =-k\left(\frac{d T}{d x}\right) \text { for steady state } [/latex]
So, [latex]\quad-k\left(\frac{d T}{d x}\right)=[/latex] constant

Assume the center-of-mass of the body is at its geometric center and [latex]g=[/latex] [latex]9.81 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}[/latex]. For striking the object [latex]P[/latex] with a horizontal velocity of [latex]5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]. [latex]\mathrm{h}=7-7 \cos \theta=7(1-\cos \theta)[/latex]

Principle of Conservation of Energy

raw_source.text: A linear spring-mass-dash pot system with a mass of [latex]2 \mathrm{~kg}[/latex] is set in motion with viscous damping. If the natural frequency is [latex]15 \mathrm{~Hz}[/latex], and the amplitudes of two successive cycles measured are [latex]7.75 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex] and [latex]7.20 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex], the coefficient of viscous damping (in N.s/m) is
raw_source.solution:
[latex] \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{n}}=7.75 \mathrm{~mm} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{n}+1} & =7.20 \mathrm{~mm} \\ \omega_{\mathrm{n}} & =\frac{2 \pi}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{n}}}=2 \pi(\mathrm{fn}) \\ & =2 \pi \times 15=30 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \frac{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{n}+1}} & =\frac{7.75}{7.20}=1.07638 \\ \delta & =\ln \left(\frac{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{n}+1}}\right) \\ & =\ln (1.07638)=0.0736 \\ \delta & =\frac{2 \pi \varepsilon}{\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}} \end{aligned} [/latex]
or [latex]\quad 0.0736=\frac{2 \pi \varepsilon}{\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}}[/latex]
or [latex] \varepsilon=0.0117 [/latex]

Critical damping co-efficient
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{C} & =\varepsilon \times 2 \mathrm{~m} \times \omega_{\mathrm{n}} \\ & =0.0117 \times 2 \times 2 \times 30 \pi \\ & =4.41 \mathrm{~N} . \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

raw_source.text:
Which one of the following failure theories is the most conservative design
approach against fatigue failure?
raw_source.solution:
Gerber Line. A parabolic curve joining [latex]S_{e}[/latex] on the ordinate to [latex]S_{u t}[/latex] on the abscissa is called the Gerber line.
Soderberg Line A straight line joining [latex]S_{e}[/latex] on the ordinate to [latex]\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{yt}}[/latex] on the abscissas called the Soderberg line.
Goodman Line. A straight line joining [latex]S_{e}[/latex] on the ordinate to [latex]S_{u t}[/latex] on the abscissa is called the Goodman line.

The Gerber parabola fits the failure points of test data in the best possible way. The goodman line fits beneath the scatter of this data. Both Gerber parabola and Goodman line intersect at [latex]\left(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{e}}\right)[/latex] on the ordinate to [latex]\left(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{ut}}\right)[/latex] on the abscissa. However, the Goodman line is more safe from design considerations because it is completely inside the Gerber parabola and inside the failure points. The Soderberg line is a more conservative failure criterion and there is no need to consider even yielding in this case.
raw_source.tag2: Static Dynamic Loading and Failure Theories

raw_source.text: The "Earing" phenomenon in metal forming is associated with
raw_source.solution:
Fig. Earning in a drawn steel cup, caused by the planar anisotropy of the sheet metal

In deep drawing, the edges of cups may become wavy, called earing. Ears are objectionable on deep-drawn cups because they have to be trimmed off, as they serve no useful purpose, and interfere with further processing of the cup, resulting in scarp. Earing is caused by the planar anisotropy of the sheet metal, and the number of ears produced may be two, four or eight, depending on the processing history and microstructure of the material. If the sheet is stronger in the rolling direction than transverse to the rolling direction, and the strength varies uniformly with respect to orientation, then two ears will form. If the sheet has high strength at different orientations, then more ears will form.

raw_source.text: The allowance provided to a pattern for easy withdrawal from a sand mold is
raw_source.solution:
Types of allowances:
Draft/taper allowances.
Machining allowance/finishing allowance.
Distortion allowances/camber allowance
Shrinkage allowance/contraction allowances.
Shake allowance/rapping allowance.

Shake allowance
Before withdrawal from the sand mould, the pattern is wrapped all around the vertical faces to enlarge the mould cavity slightly, which facilitates its removal. Since it enlarge the final casting made, it is desirable that the original pattern dimensions should be reduced to account for this increase. There is no sure way of quantifying this allowance, since it is highly dependent on the foundry personnel and practices involved.
It is negative allowance and is to be applied only to those dimensions, which are parallel to the parting plane. One way of reducing this allowance is to increase the draft, which can be removed during the subsequent matching.

Draft/taper allowances
Once pattern is embedded in the moulding sand now it is required to withdrawing the pattern from moulding sand, for this propose a vertical force is required to lift the pattern. For easy removal of pattern from mould cavity there should be some degree or [latex]\mathrm{mm}[/latex] taper in the pattern.
If there is no taper in the pattern then more chance to break the mould cavity wall during withdrawing the pattern. Draft allowance varies with the complexity of job.

Machining or Finishing allowance
In sand casting operation machining/finishing allowances is given in the pattern as on solidification every metal get shrinked up to some extend and the outer surface of object (casting) is rough, therefore, to smoothing the outer surface of casting machining allowance is must.

Distortion allowance/Camber allowance
On just solidification of metal casting is weak, therefore, more chances to distorted casting. Chance of distortion are basically in [latex]U, V[/latex], then long section or complicated casting. Distortion can be minimized or eliminated by providing an allowance and constructed the pattern initially distorted, i.e. opposite in outer side direction. Among of distortion allowance varies from 1.5[latex]20 \mathrm{~mm}[/latex].
It is the tendency of all metals that they shrink after cooling except bismuth, Shrinkage is only due to inter atomic vibration which are implified by increasing in temperature. Metal shrink or contract in three ways :

Liquid Contraction
Solidification Contraction
Solid Contraction

In the pipe network shown in the figure, all pipes have the same cross-section and can be assumed to have the same friction factor. Consider the following statements:

I. The flow rate in pipe connecting [latex]J[/latex] and [latex]E[/latex] is Q/21.
II. The pressure difference between [latex]\mathrm{J}[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{N}[/latex] is equal to the pressure difference between J and [latex]\mathrm{E}[/latex].

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
raw_source.solution:
Due to symmetry [latex]\left(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{N}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{S}}\right)[/latex] and equal length and friction factor flow distributed in JN and JS will be same. Let it be [latex]\mathrm{Q}_1[/latex].
From continuity, flow in [latex]J E=\left(Q-2 \mathrm{O}_1\right)[/latex].
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_N & =P_E=P_S[\text { Given }] \\ P_J-P_N & =\frac{f Q_1^2}{12.1 d^5} \\ P_J-P_E & =\frac{f(10 /)\left(Q-2 Q_1\right)^2}{12.1 d^5} \end{aligned} [/latex]
From (A) and (B),
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{O}_1^2=10\left(\mathrm{Q}-2 \mathrm{Q}_1\right)^2 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{Q}-2 \mathrm{Q}_1}{\mathrm{Q}_1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{Q}_1}=2+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_1=\mathrm{Q}\left[\frac{\sqrt{10 \mathrm{O}}}{1+2 \sqrt{10}}\right] \\ & \mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{Q}_1=\mathrm{Q}\left[1-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{1+2 \sqrt{10}}\right] \\ & \mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{Q}_1=\mathrm{Q}\left[\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}{1+2 \sqrt{10}}\right]=\text { Flow in JE } \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, correct option is I is False and II is true.
options: I is True and II is False
I is False and II is True
Both I and II are True
Both I and II are False

raw_answer.option_text: I is False and II is True

raw_source.text: A company orders gears in conditions identical to those considered in the economic order quantity (EOQ) model in inventory control. The annual demand is 8000 gears, the cost per order is 300 rupees, and the holding cost is 12 rupees per month per gear. The company uses an order size that is [latex]25 \%[/latex] more than the optimal order quantity determined by the EOQ model. The percentage change in the total cost of ordering and holding inventory from that associated with the optimal order quantity is
raw_source.solution:
[latex]D=8000[/latex] gear/year
[latex]\mathrm{C}_{0}=300[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{h}}=12 /[/latex] month [latex]=144 /[/latex] year
[latex]\mathrm{Q}_{\text {actual }}=\left(1+\frac{25}{100}\right) \mathrm{EOQ}=1.25 \mathrm{EOQ}[/latex]
[latex]E O Q=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{DC}_{0}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{h}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 8000 \times 300}{144}}=182.5[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{Q}_{\text {actual }}=1.25 \times \mathrm{EOQ}=1.25 \times 182.5[/latex]
[latex]=1.25 \times 182.5=228.125[/latex]

Total cost at EOQ
[latex]\mathrm{TIC}_{1}=\sqrt{2 \times \mathrm{C}_{0} \times \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{h}} \times \mathrm{D}}[/latex]
[latex]=\sqrt{2 \times 300 \times 144 \times 8000}=26920.4[/latex]

Total cost at actual order [latex]\left(\mathrm{Q}_{\text {actual }}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{TIC}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{Q}_{\text {actual }}}{2} \times \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{h}}+\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{Q}_{\text {actual }}} \times \mathrm{C}_{0}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{228.125}{2} \times 144+\frac{8000}{228.125} \times 300[/latex] [latex]=26945.54[/latex]

[latex]\% \uparrow=\frac{26945.54-26290.68}{26290.68} \times 100=2.5 \%[/latex]

raw_source.text:
At the current basic feasible solution (bfs) [latex]v_{0}\left(v_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{5}\right)[/latex], the simplex method yields the following form of a linear programming problem in standard form.

[latex] \begin{aligned} minimize \;\;\;& z=-x_{1}-2 x_{2} \\ s.t. \;\;\;& x_{3}=2+2 x_{1}-x_{2} \\ & x_{4}=7+x_{1}-2 x_{2} \\ & x_{5}=3-x_{1} \\ & x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, x_{5} \geq 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Here the objective function is written as a function of the non-basic variables. If the simplex method moves to the adjacent bfs [latex]v_{1}\left(v_{1} \in \mathbb{R} ^{5}\right)[/latex] that best improves the objective function, which of the following represents the objective function at [latex]v_{1}[/latex], assuming that the objective function is written in the same matter as above?
raw_source.solution:
[latex]\mathrm{z}=-\mathrm{x}_{1}-2 \mathrm{x}_{2}\;\;\; ...(A)[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{x}_{3}=2+2 \mathrm{x}_{1}-\mathrm{x}_{2} \;\;\; ...(i)[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{x}_{4}=7+\mathrm{x}_{1}-2 \mathrm{x}_{2} \;\;\; ...(ii)[/latex]
[latex]x_{5}=3-x \;\;\; ...(iii)[/latex]
and [latex]x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, x_{5} \geq 0[/latex]

From eq. (i)
[latex]x_{2}=2+2 x_{1}-x_{3}[/latex]

Putting this value in the objective function eq. (A)
[latex]z=-x_{1}-2\left(2+2 x_{1}-x_{3}\right)[/latex]
[latex]=-4-5 \mathrm{x}_{1}+2 \mathrm{x}_{3}[/latex]

From eq. (ii)
[latex]\mathrm{x}_{1}=\mathrm{x}_{4}+2 \mathrm{x}_{2}-7[/latex]
Put these value in eq. (A)
[latex]z=-\left(x_{4}+2 x_{2}-7\right)-2 x_{2}[/latex]
[latex]=7-4 \mathrm{x}_{2}-\mathrm{x}_{4}[/latex]

From eq. (iii)
[latex]\mathrm{x}_{1}=3-\mathrm{x}_{5}[/latex]
Put these value in eq. (A)
[latex]z=-\left(3-x_{5}\right)-2 x_{2}[/latex]
[latex]=\mathrm{x}_{5}-3-2 \mathrm{x}_{2}[/latex]
(A) and (B) both are correct but question type is mcq so go for option (A).
